9691	An astonishing shift of power A crucial speech by Sir Peter Imbert underlines the extent of the differences between him and his predecessors .
9692	THE EXTENT of the philosophical shift taking place at the top of the Metropolitan Police was illustrated in a speech delivered by Sir Peter Imbert to the International Police Exhibition and Conference in London at the end of September .
9693	The brief reports which have appeared of this remarkable address dealt with Sir Peter 's appeal for glasnost within the force .
9694	‘ Openness must be central to the policing of a democratic and pluralist society , ’ he said : all too often , the police had retreated behind ‘ one of many walls of silence , ’ giving one of a series of stock excuses to the press and public for refusing to disclose information .
9695	But the depth of the speech 's radicalism has not reached a wider public .
9696	Sir Peter justified his call for openness in terms which would have been unthinkable from his immediate predecessor , Sir Kenneth Newman , and indeed from any predecessor : ‘ Professions , including police , tend by definition to be monopolists of knowledge and through that knowledge , power .
9697	Yet to set ourselves up in such a manner contradicts our cherished notion of being part of the community . ’
9698	Key parts of the speech signalled a conscious , almost revolutionary departure from some of Sir Kenneth 's most cherished notions .
9699	Its full title was Preparing Police to Deal with a Multicultured Society , and it was on the subject of policing black communities — still the most vexatious and controversial for both police and their critics — that Sir Peter made his thoughts most plain .
9700	The doctrines and policy of Sir Kenneth Newman were set out candidly in an unpublished , private lecture to the European Atlantic Group in 1983 , entitled Public Order in Free Societies .
9701	The text has achieved great influence , disseminated widely among senior officers , and taught formally at the Bramshill Police College .
9702	Its terms and implications are unmistakably authoritarian .
9703	All democratic societies , Sir Kenneth said , must strike a balance between order and freedom , and in ‘ multi-ethnic societies , ’ this posed an acute dilemma .
9704	In Britain , as in Germany , the first generation of immigrants had been ‘ relatively law-abiding , ’ but discussion on ethnic minorities now centred on ‘ crime and crime control ’ .
9705	As Lord Scarman , reporting after the 1981 riots , had pointed out , the underlying crisis was social and economic .
9706	But this was outside the police remit , and meanwhile , they had to be careful not to jeopardise public tranquillity .
9707	A permanent state of war with the community was untenable , but the law must be enforced .
9708	In multi-ethnic areas , with their ‘ symbolic locations ’ like All Saints Road and Broadwater Farm , used for the sale of drugs and stolen goods , police could not act alone .
9709	Sir Kenneth said : ‘ It is not sufficient to think only in terms of crime control .
9710	We need to lift the problem to a higher level of generality , encompassed by the expression ‘ social control , ’ in a benign sense , in order to provide a unifying concept within which the activities of police and other agencies can be co-ordinated . ’
9711	Sir Kenneth 's agent in this project was ‘ multi-agency ’ cooperation , a buzzword throughout the 1980s in police and Home Office circles .
9712	But in his vision , the police would be giving the lead , laying down a ‘ clear social policy ’ .
9713	It was crucial that the police maintain ‘ operational independence ’ .
9714	Party political interference , he said , rejecting the possibility of a London police authority , was especially to be abhorred .
9715	He was trying , he said , to avoid a shift in the balance between freedom and order .
9716	But nevertheless : ‘ We should not forget that an over-regard for individual liberties can put at risk that sense of order and security without which no community can be truly free . ’
9717	Sir Kenneth concluded with a sideswipe at his critics .
9718	It was in these very multi-ethnic areas with their myriad problems that ‘ political agitators exploit civil liberties issues , and play down the issue of communal security … individual liberties are important , but we must not become so obsessed with them that we overlook the importance of communal freedom . ’
9719	Like Sir Kenneth , Sir Peter Imbert recalled the riots of 1981 and 1985 , and the conflict between police and ethnic minorities .
9720	But the intellectual foundation of his proposed solution was diametrically opposed to that of his predecessor .
9721	There were some ‘ basic principles ’ to be adopted in police/community relations , Sir Peter said .
9722	But in seeking to broaden this perspective , there were ‘ a number of propositions which police officers need to understand . ’
9723	First , he said , ‘ the community itself should be the primary focus , not the police . ’
9724	The community was not homogenous , but made up of a multitude of different groups with different attitudes and beliefs , while ‘ relations within the community , between different groups , are significantly outside the control of the police ’ .
9725	Sir Peter then tackled the Newman concept of an interventionist , social controlling police force directly .
9726	‘ Members of the community are themselves in the course of events engaged in a great deal of informal social control , ’ he said .
9727	‘ It is the community who should , in the main , determine whether police are to be involved in resolving community conflicts . ’
9728	As police , he went on , ‘ we sometimes quite wrongly assume the monopoly of good ideas on good community relations and good policing … the public have a right to be actively involved in determining how policing is developed ’ .
9729	Sir Kenneth Newman 's retreat behind ‘ operational independence ’ was cast out .
9730	The major precepts of his philosophy Sir Peter declared to be : ‘ Openness , access , power sharing and the sharing of responsibility . ’
9731	Such precepts , according to one senior officer , were in the context of the previous 150 years of the Metropolitan Police , ‘ simply astonishing ’ .
9732	Again , developing the idea of power sharing , Sir Peter implicitly criticised his predecessor and his vision of the multi-agency approach .
9733	‘ If openness and access are problematic , power sharing is likely to be even more problematic .
9734	Early efforts to become involved in multi-agency approaches to crime and associated topics were painful experiences … we wanted to maintain the lead in every forum , to be the gatekeepers of power and have the right of veto if decisons were made which did not suit us . ’
9735	Those attitudes , Sir Peter said , still lingered .
9736	Power sharing was not an easy path to tread .
9737	But it ‘ does not mean a surrender of power ; rather it involves sharing of the knowledge which allows different interpretations and constructions to be placed on that information and which in turn can lead to a different conclusion and different solutions ’ .
9738	Police must ‘ find out from our consumers what it is they require from us , how sensitive we are being to their needs and how satisfied they are with the service ’ .
9739	Polls of Asians , for example , had shown that they felt particularly vulnerable and dissatisfied : it was essential to ‘ have the will to act ’ on this information when allocating scarce resources .
9740	The police , he concluded , must possess ‘ an unswerving commitment to communication and consultation within which police and the community are equal partners . ’
9741	Well-founded criticism could only be met with ‘ a willingness to change ’ .

9743	An opening at the Met Despite resistance by its more conservative elements , the Metropolitan Police has begun a process of reform that should lead to improvements in the way it operates and encourage better relations with the public .
9744	THROUGH the corridors of Scotland Yard , a wind of change is blowing .
9745	The small faction of senior officers who believe that the police must undertake radical reform in order to remain viable has gained an increasingly confidentially in the shape of the Metropolitan Commissioner , Sir Peter Imbert .
9746	Implicitly , they have accepted many of the criticisms made for more than a decade by Labour councils and civil libertarians : that a force which has dug itself in behind ramparts of elitist isolationism must begin to respond to demands of the public it serves and their political representatives .
9747	Sir Peter speaks frequently of ‘ power sharing , ’ a notion which goes well beyond mere participation in the local consultative groups established by the Police and Criminal Evidence Act .
9748	It is no coincidence that since Sir Peter became Commissioner in 1987 , the relationship between Scotland Yard and London 's 13 Labour authorities has seen a new detente .
9749	With the new Home Secretary , David Waddington , displaying a marked lack of enthusiasm for Sir Peter 's other pet project , the creation of a national detection agency , senior officers are beginning to consider the prospect of a Labour Home Office with equanimity .
9750	They find themselves , for the first time , able to contemplate the two main features of Labour policy , greater independence in the investigation of complaints and a London police authority , with something less than total horror .
9751	The signs of reform were stirring before the advent of Sir Peter .
9752	The anonymous authors of the 1986 annual Met internal appraisal , for example , wrote in deeply critical terms of the effects of government economic policy on the inner city , and the consequences for policing .
9753	But the seminal event was Sir Peter 's decison to publish A Force for Change , the survey carried out last year by the Wolff Olins consultancy .
9754	The report said that the Met was scruffy , rude , and operating from shabby police stations .
9755	These important barriers in the fostering of a good realtionship with the public were bad enough : but the force was also undertrained , riven with internal struggle , and isolated from society — in a ‘ state of siege ’ .
9756	Most policemen felt beleaguered and misunderstood , their isolation further deepened by criticism from politicians and the media .
9757	Reforming and reactionary police officers are not unaware that public confidence in the police has meanwhile ebbed away .
9758	Causes celebres like the Guildford Four are bad enough : ‘ Frankly , we all know the criminal justice system is in tatters , ’ one superintendent said last week .
9759	But as demonstrated by a variety of research — including both internal police studies and external work like the 1985 Islington Crime Survey — more damaging still is the accumulation of the public 's direct and disappointing contacts with police .
9760	The publication of A Force for Change was crucial because it represented an important internal victory for the reformers , and established glasnost as the principle by which the Met was to be put right .
9761	The conservatives at the Yard , who include the considerable figure of the Deputy Commissioner , John Dellow , believe that the Met has been reorganised quite enough recently and has been unsettled by a succession of commissioners , all with strong and mutually conflicting ideas .
9762	In their opinion , the calling in of Wolff Olins was more of a symptom of this malaise than any kind of cure .
9763	The Wolff Olins authors commented that the publication of their work represented a ‘ profound cultural change ’ .
9764	This , they said , should accompany the ‘ profound managerial change ’ which must be next on the agenda , somehow to tackle Londoners ' personal and local dissatisfaction with the police .
9765	THE main public response to A Force for Change is the Plus Programme , a continuing series of measures drawn up by Deputy Assistant Commissioner Charles Pollard and Commander Alec Marnoch .
9766	Reports of the programme have concentrated on its cosmetic aspects .
9767	But its greater underlying significance is demonstrated by the fact that it , too , has been strongly opposed by Yard conservatives .
9768	According to members of the reforming faction , some officers have attempted to use Sir Peter Imbert 's apparent discomfiture over his role in the Guildford Four case to discredit the Plus Programme , with which he is closely identified .
9769	At the heart of the strategy is a change of balance in the police 's own perception of their role .
9770	For 150 years , police have regarded their job as the control of crime and criminals , of coping with social deviancy .
9771	Under the programme , what internal documents describe as the ‘ public service tradition ’ of the Met is to be emphasised as never before .
9772	Aggressive behaviour is to be not only discouraged but monitored and disciplined : the public regarded as consumers , customers and paymasters of policing , not potential villains or troublemakers .
9773	Accompanying the programme is To Serve and Protect , 10 commandments for everyday policing issued to every officer , after consultation over its text with MPs and community organisations .
9774	The first ‘ value of every member of the organisation ’ is ‘ to uphold the law fairly and firmly ’ .
9775	But some of the others are less familiar .
9776	Stressing the need ‘ to behave in a manner which is neither racist nor sexist , ’ ‘ to uphold individual rights , ’ and ‘ to cooperate and consult with the community and other agencies in pursuing our purpose ’ has not gone down well with conservative officers .
9777	It would be possible to dismiss the Plus Programme as merely an expression of a different style , without substance or commitment to institutional change .
9778	Evidence that it is not is provided by a confidential , internal report on CID work circulated to senior officers earlier this year , the Crime Investigation Priority Project ( CIPP ) .
9779	Its authors , significantly , were not an outside firm but police officers .
9780	Identifying many of the same failings as Wolff Olins , CIPP 's first core recommendation was ‘ that crime investigation should be made victim-focussed , ’ and that CID departments give ‘ higher priority to the victims of crime and witnesses ’ .
9781	The needs of victims , it continued , ‘ can be clearly stated , are feasible and are not being met .
9782	An orientation towards customers ’ needs and rights is becoming a prevailing ethos in society which the police can not ignore . ’
9783	But , CIPP said , ‘ a number of officers we interviewed do not understand these needs . ’
9784	The report went on : ‘ Victim satisfaction is not directly linked to the outcome of individual investigations .
9785	It is much more closely concerned with how closely the police adhere to the kind of standards the public expects from any large organisation , including promptness , a sympathetic attitude which indicates individual attention , some conspicuous activity and clear information about what will happen next . ’
9786	It was CIPP which first recommended the abolition — announced earlier this week — of the controversial system of crime screening , by which many offences were not investigated because of a lack of evidence .
9787	It was ‘ discouraging officers from investigating crimes fully ’ , even those which could be cleared up .
9788	The report made a series of recommendations on increasing CID strength , which has fallen sharply from 10 per cent of the force in 1973 to 7.4 per cent , despite an overall large increase in numbers and a recommendation by Her Majesty 's Inspectorate that provincial CIDs should make up 12.4 per cent of police .
9789	These are now being implemented .
9790	But the most significant part of CIPP dealt with institutional change : the perestroika to follow Sir Peter Imbert 's glasnost which , if implemented , would represent exactly the ‘ profound managerial change ’ recommended by Wolff Olins .
9791	The height and extent of the inbuilt hurdles in the way of reforming a police force are not commonly appreciated .
9792	The incoming chairman of a public company can swiftly dispose of dead wood , to arrange a board in sympathy with new policies .
9793	But police officers can be dismissed only if severe disciplinary charges are proven against them .
9794	It is possible to arrange retirements on spurious ‘ medical ’ grounds , but this practice was heavily criticised by the Commons Home Affairs select committee earlier this year .
9795	The ensuing problems for a reforming commissioner begin at the top , with the Scotland Yard policy committee — the deputy , assistant and deputy assistant commissioners , by whom all major changes have , effectively , to be ratified .
9796	The reformer , like a US president with a recalcitrant supreme court , can secure a majority in his favour only as they retire , die or move on to better things .
9797	BROUGHT about by lifetime tenure The lack of accountability is analagous at divisional level .
9798	Conservative CIDs , for example , have all sorts of tricks to frustrate an incoming radical chief superintendent , by which they can legally send clear-up rates into a tailspin — so leading to the rapid transfer of the reforming senior officer .
9799	Incredibly , it is almost impossible even to return a detective to uniform simply on the grounds that he is n't very good .
9800	CIPP grasped this nettle .
9801	Supervision of subordinates ‘ is focussed on bureaucratic procedures and not on the quality of service at the point of delivery to the public . ’
9802	All supervising officers , including senior divisional managers — chief superintendents — ‘ should not only hold themselves accountable , but be actively held accountable for the overall level of their subordinates ’ .
9803	To achieve these goals , senior police officers needed a weapon : what the CIPP report delicately called ‘ deselection ’ .
9804	This might , it said , mean the removal of CID officers to uniform .
9805	However , ‘ many officers interviewed were in favour of administrative dismissal , not currently available under police regulations . ’
9806	An overwhelming majority of those who still baulked at actual sacking favoured return to uniform , with the view that ‘ CID officers who are lazy and incompetent were so primarily because of the absence of the eventual sanction of removal from specialist duty . ’
9807	Sir Peter Imbert and the Yard reformers have important allies in the regional forces : Geoffrey Dear , the West Midlands chief constable , whose boldness at disbanding his serious crimes squad can not be discounted , whatever his eventual career ambitions ; and Paul Condon , the new Kent chief , formerly in charge of Met training and personnel .
9808	But circumstances , and the perceived depth of public alienation , are driving even natural conservatives into their camp .
9809	Presently underway is a huge opinion survey of police and their customers , covering policing priorities , the quality of service provided , screening and the image of the force .
9810	Its co-sponsor is none other than the Police Federation , the junior officers ' staff association , traditionally the organisation most wary of reform .

10028	Rugby Union : All black over Ireland Charles Edwards explains how the game has acquired a dim profile with the public .
10029	PSYCHOLOGICALLY the Aztecs were probably better prepared for the invasion of Cortes than Irish rugby is for the arrival of the All Blacks .
10030	Two undistinguished international seasons , only token involvement with the Lions in Australia and bitter controversy about South Africa have combined to give the game in Ireland possibly the worst public profile it has had .
10031	The visit to South Africa of several eminent Irish Rugby Football Union officers and their wives — among them the president , Ronnie Dawson — triggered off an acrimonious debate which looks likely to run on in spite of an IRFU statement regretting the safari .
10032	The union 's promise that no Irish team will be allowed to go to South Africa ‘ whilst the remainder of the apartheid laws exist ’ has not convinced many people , while drawing the wrath of their recent hosts down about the heads of Dawson and his fellow-travellers .
10033	The IRFU 's South African links have been criticised in the past , notably when Ireland toured there in 1981 amid a storm of public and governmental condemnation .
10034	Now those critics have been joined by what entrenched IRFU committeemen may regard as the Enemy Within .
10035	For the Irish rugby schools and clubs have loudly condemned the IRFU which , they say , purports to represent them yet made no efforts towards consultation before participating in the South African Rugby Board 's centenary celebrations .
10036	The absence of Dawson — or any deputy — from Ireland 's recent tour to North America has also been deplored .
10037	This courtesy might not be necessary , strictly speaking , but the fact that All the President 's Men were in South Africa as guests of the SARB at the same time was not a help .
10038	And the IRFU did nothing for its cause by not awarding caps for the matches against Canada and the United States and by refusing to pay the players the regulation daily allowance because the tour was one day short of the stipulated duration .
10039	So the union — and the game — are held in low esteem at present .
10040	And , in the battle for sporting hearts and minds , Irish rugby simply can not afford that unhappy situation .
10041	In terms of mass appeal rugby comes fourth after Gaelic football , hurling and soccer .
10042	Many believe that playing standards will improve only when more young players are attracted to rugby , which means getting them into the clubs at youth level .
10043	But , if and when Jack Charlton brings the national team to the World Cup , every boy in the country will be kicking a soccer ball about .
10044	But that is in the future .
10045	At present the advent of the All Blacks is concentrating the national rugby mind wonderfully and all four provinces have been in early-season action .
10046	Munster , the only Irish team ever to defeat the New Zealanders , drew with Glasgow and District and overwhelmed Pontypool .
10047	Leinster did a similar demolition job on Llanelli and lost narrowly to the South-west Division .
10048	Ulster , the reigning inter-provincial champions and the most consistent province over the past five seasons , enjoyed an easy win over the Scottish Saltires .
10049	But Connacht , traditionally the weakest of the provinces , had a disastrous start , losing heavily to Glasgow and District and also to the humble Scottish North-Midlands , whose victory was their first for seven years .
10050	The inter-provincial championship went to Ulster for the sixth consecutive year , and Munster have shown good form .
10051	But realistically it is hard to predict anything other than a 100 per cent success rate for the All Blacks in Ireland .
10052	The international at Lansdowne Road in 10 days could be traumatic for Ireland , whose only successes since January 1988 have been achieved against weak opposition which , oddly enough , includes Wales at the Arms Park last February .
10053	Ireland have decided not to introduce a string of new players against New Zealand .

10055	And the captain ?

10057	Anderson captained Ireland on their short tour of France , led them to an unexpected victory over a French XV and keeps the job now but age and waning powers put a question-mark over his selection for the team at all .

10064	Hong Kong form is all Chinese to the average punter .

10066	SIS will also be covering Kelso , Newbury and greyhound racing from Bristol so the need to give punters the opportunity to additionally sample delights from the orient hardly seems necessary .
10067	There has been some sharp criticism in some areas of the sporting press — principally on three counts : That the turnover generated does not contribute to the levy ; that it is a snub to the all-weather experiment ; that it is pure exploitation of the punter .
10068	Terry Ellis , racing director at SIS , answered these points for me yesterday , commenting : ‘ First of all it is factually incorrect to say that the turnover is not subject to levy .
10069	All horse racing is .
10070	I can not understand how that misconception arose .
10071	Secondly , the decision to screen 16 Hong Kong meetings between now and the end of March was taken last year before firm plans about all-weather racing had been drawn up .
10072	Our yearly schedules are finalised in October by our users committee .
10073	‘ We covered Lingfield 's inaugural all-weather meeting because that simply replaced a flat fixture scheduled for that day .
10074	Southwell 's all-weather meeting last Wednesday was not on the original fixture list and neither is today 's , but we will be covering meetings there on November 14 and 21 because there were ordinary jump meetings already scheduled .
10075	‘ At the turn of the year we shall cover every all-weather fixture at Lingfield and Southwell in addition to the usual turf fixtures .
10076	‘ The third point that we are merely exploiting the punter is unfair .
10077	Although the major bookmaking firms are represented on the users committee , they were originally not keen on Hong Kong because it meant bringing in extra staff in the mornings .
10078	‘ By arrangement with the sporting press we are providing full racecards and form for Hong Kong so punters are hardly betting blind .
10079	And in any case , the punter has the final veto — no one forces him to bet . ’
10080	This is true but Hong Kong form means nothing to the average punter .
10081	It is like looking at the menu in a French restaurant .
10082	Ellis declined to say how much the Royal Hong Kong Jockey Club is being paid for the service , but this is not money which British racing is missing out on , as a contract , subject to review after three years , was drawn up with the Racecourse Association at the beginning of SIS transmission .

10331	By PETER STANFORD is right in maintaining ( Weekend Guardian , November 4 ) that Graham Greene is not alone in calling himself a ‘ Catholic agnostic ’ .
10332	An earlier thinker who declined to see any mutual contradiction between similar terms was Leslie Weatherhead , psychologist and cleric , who published his Creed of a Christian Agnostic .
10333	Weatherhead was honest enough to realise that there are many aspects of religion about which one has to remain uncertain , that is , agnostic .
10334	These ‘ difficult ’ areas will vary from one individual to another .
10335	As a self-confessed Christian agnostic he himself , however , was sure of a number of the major tenets of Christianity .
10336	His ‘ creed ’ claimed ( in part ) : ‘ I believe that God exists …
10337	I believe there is mind behind the universe …
10338	Such a mind must be love rather than hate …
10339	I believe in the divinity of Christ …
10340	I believe that sin is a grisly fact in the world …
10341	I believe that God 's forgiveness is one of the most blessed and therapeutic experiences and that it is offered to all who seek it …
10342	I believe that our relationship with God is the most important thing in the world …
10343	I believe that each individual is precious to God . ’
10344	Within this creed appear supportive rational arguments but also agnostic admissions , such as ‘ I can understand little about that mind ’ and ‘ I do not know what ‘ divine ’ means ’ .
10345	I imagine that many honest people would sympathise with Weatherhead and happily echo his final paragraph : ‘ All this gives me as much as I need , and seems to me the essential credo of Christianity .
10346	About the rest I am content to be agnostic . ’

10359	A Country Diary : CROOK , Co .
10360	DURHAM
10361	These are the quiet days before winter .
10362	For most of this week the landscape has been draped on shifting fog patches .
10363	On some days the top of Pea Hill has been bathed in brilliant sunshine , while the valley of the River Wear ahead has been awash in a sea of grey , with tentacles of fog creeping outwards along hedges and gulleys into fields .
10364	We have yet to experience any hard frosts , so autumn leaves still cling to branches and there are still a few flowers of white dead nettle , red campion and yarrow to attract the last of the drone flies .
10365	Hedgerows take on an additional dimension on foggy days ; when the distant landscape is blotted out immediate surroundings assume a new prominence .
10366	Hundreds of spiders ' webs , suspended between twigs bearing yellowing leaves and clusters of scarlet rose hips are decorated with water droplets that sparkle in the weak sun that occasionally penetrates the murk .
10367	Amongst the dead hogweed umbels and seed heads of willow herb there are clusters of ladybirds , packed into tight groups in every available crevice .
10368	Ladybirds have done well out of the exceptional summer , as have sweet chestnut trees ; this is the first year that I can recall collecting chestnuts locally that are large enough to eat .
10369	The warmth and mildness has brought a fine crop of toadstools .
10370	The most spectacular of these have been some magnificent specimens of Verdigris agaric , Stroparia aeruginosa , shown to me by Maureen Defty , a local farmer .
10371	They had sprouted from buried wood in the vegetable garden and sported livid blue-green , slimy caps .
10372	We had our first moderate snow fall in mid-November last year , but so far it looks as though this winter will be milder than ever .
10373	One sign of approaching winter comes from the parties of siskins feeding on catkins of birch seeds , moving from tree to tree in noisy flocks .

10440	GOSSIP .
10441	I love it .
10442	Unashamedly , unrepentingly .
10443	Most people do , though few will admit it these days .
10444	To gossip : to natter , to prattle , to chatter , to tittle-tattle , to jabber , to jaw .
10445	As far back as 700 BC Hesiod was wary of it : ‘ Gossip is mischievous , light and easy to raise , but grievous to bear and hard to get rid of . ’
10446	In other words , mud sticks .
10447	But gossip has n't always had such bad press .
10448	Even Oscar Wilde called it charming — granted he was one of history 's great gossipers , but he was an even greater gossipee .
10449	It has often been noted that while barbarians fight with hatchets , civilised men fight with gossip .
10450	Well , frankly , I 'd rather have a little mud than a hatchet thrown at my back .
10451	And gossip need n't be malevolent ; my Little Oxford Dictionary defines it simply as ‘ informal talk , esp about persons . ’
10452	In any case , when someone gossips well they are called a wit or a conversationalist ; only those who gossip badly are tarred with the appellation ‘ Gossip ’ .
10453	Good gossip must have an esential core of truth to it , and a dose of compassion , concern or at least good humour attached ; it is bad gossip that has no basis in fact , that is driven obviously and primarily by maliciousness .
10454	That sort of gossip certainly should be condemned ; that is the sort Hesiod warned against .
10455	But even he went on to say that gossip has ‘ a kind of divinity ’ .
10456	And Seneca seven hundred years later spoke of ‘ that most knowing of persons — ( the ) gossip ’ .
10457	The word gossip itself actually means ‘ God 's kin ’ .
10458	Originally it was a term of respect denoting a godparent — as Queen Elizabeth I was the gossip at the baptism of her godson James VI , or indicating friends with a common spiritual bond .
10459	Following the peasant habit of referring to any elder as ‘ Mother/Father ’ or ‘ Grandmother/Grandfather ’ , the word was also applied to any gathering of older folk .
10460	It was only when it began to be associated exclusively with women that gossip began its slippery slide into the gutter .
10461	From denoting women friends or gossips , the word came to denote the speech of gossips .
10462	And so it acquired its contemporary , pejorative connotation of idle chatter .
10463	There is a theory that gossip is a form of speech particular to women — to women , old people , servants and slaves .
10464	In other words , to the powerless .
10465	But while Daisy and Rose were gossiping in the downstairs pantry , does anybody really doubt what Lord Bellamy was doing upstairs in the drawing room ?
10466	Discussing affairs of state — no doubt .
10467	The sort of affairs that lose elections and topple governments .
10468	Not philosophy , not theology , but — you guessed it — gossip .
10469	A psychiatrist friend of mine recently returned from an international conference in Athens .
10470	When I asked him what those eminent shrinks did with themselves in the evenings he explained that they gathered in the hotel bar .
10471	‘ And what did you all talk about ? ’
10472	‘ Shop-talk : who 's getting ahead , and how , and why ; who 's feuding with whom ; who 's working with whom ; who 's screwing with whom . ’
10473	‘ Oh , you mean gossip . ’
10474	‘ No ! ’ he protested , indignantly .
10475	‘ We were talking shop ; it was shop-talk , not gossip . ’
10476	When Lawson resigned the pundits gathered , and mused , and offered up their conjectures and reflections , and it was called Political Speculation .
10477	When women gather to do the same , it is called gossip .
10478	When academics delve into someone 's life it is called Biography ; when therapists posit theories on human behaviour it is called Psychology ; when sociologists ruminate on society it is called Sociology .
10479	When women ponder on an individual , emotion or social phenomenon , it is called Gossip .
10480	So what exactly is gossip — this thing that is so reviled and condemned ?
10481	Gossip is Speculation .
10482	About human affairs , about human motives , actions and desires .
10483	As women are largely responsible for the emotional wellbeing of society , it is hardly surprising that the shop-talk of women is gossip .
10484	Gossip is Old Wives ' Tales .
10485	Women 's wisdom has long been feared : Old Women , Witches , Sibyls , Seers .
10486	Those who scorn or censure women 's talk diminish women .
10487	Or seek to .
10488	Gossip is Stories .
10489	Stories provide entertainment , but also instruction .
10490	The best , most satisfying gossip is like the best , most satisfying art ; it is cathartic .
10491	Through gossip we learn from other people 's lives without undergoing the pain or danger of their experiences .
10492	In short , gossip is a chronicle of humanity .
10493	As Ogden Nash put it , ‘ Another good thing about gossip is that it is within everybody 's reach/And it is much more interesting than any other form of speech … ’
10494	Imagine if Colette or Jane Austen or Dorothy Parker or Chaucer or Shakespeare or Marcel Proust had lived in a world without gossip !
10495	Their works would be skeletal ; their insights would be meagre and mean .
10496	You can keep your philosophers speculating on language or your theologians speculating on God , I 'll speculate on the human heart — gossip 's good enough for me .

10538	Lesley Nelson London NW3
10539	Liliane Landor reports on an issue that has shaken the foundations of French politics and put the question of immigration firmly back on the agenda A country divided .
10540	LEILA and Fatima Achaboun and Samira Saidani are the most talked-about schoolgirls in France .
10541	For two months they have been relegated to their school 's library , forbidden to attend classes or take part in any school activity .
10542	Since they turned up on the first day of term wearing headscarves , their teachers , supported by the headmaster , have refused to teach them unless the girls remove the offending headgear .
10543	The Gabriel-Havez school in Creil where they live stands in the heart of the town 's industrial estate .
10544	It 's a sad grey prefab , put up some 20 years ago as a temporary measure and still servicing the needs of this economically depressed small town some 62km north of Paris .
10545	The 825 youngsters who attend the school are mainly children of immigrants of over 25 different nationalities .
10546	Today the school finds itself in the midst of a public debate which is shaking the foundations of French politics — some say ethics — has split Mitterand 's Socialist Party down the middle and has put the questions of immigration and integration back on the agenda with a vengeance .
10547	Mr Cheniere , the school 's headmaster , is a practising Catholic of Martinican origin , a freemason whose authoritarian methods do not endear him to his students .
10548	He is adamant that any open manifestation of religious or cultural identity at school goes against the principles of secular state education .
10549	To his credit , Cheniere did attempt a conciliatory gesture when he suggested that the three adolescents could wear their scarves at school outside class hours .
10550	The girls insist that it is their fundamental right to wear their scarves at all times , just as some of their fellow students wear skullcaps or the cross .
10551	They say they do not understand why their headmaster is so intent on persecuting them when 20 Jewish students do not attend school on Saturdays , a normal part of the school week in France .
10552	Confronted with this , Cheniere retorts that there are some differences that are more salient than others .
10553	Let them wear their scarves at home , he adds ; this school is French and secular .
10554	The ‘ Affair of the Scarf ’ , as it has become known , has taken the French media by storm .
10555	In the past month , not a day has gone by without national newspapers devoting reams of print to the issue , asking in big headlines , as Le Point put it , ‘ Should we let Islam colonise our schools ? ’
10556	The left-leaning weekly Le Nouvel Observateur has invited anthropologists , philosophers of many persuasions , feminists ( mostly French ) and Muslim intellectuals ( men ) to pronounce their verdicts .
10557	Opinion polls have been taken by Le Figaro and L'Evenement du Jeudi , with wildly differing results , readers have been encouraged to write and religious leaders of all shades have been called upon to give the benefit of their wisdom .
10558	Today in France , the Koran is the flavour of the day as ‘ specialists ’ dissect its verses and explain the mysteries of Islam to the lay masses .
10559	Yet it remains that , for the first time in 15 years and since the controversy over abortion , opinions are divided so haphazardly that traditional political alliances have ceased to operate .
10560	No sooner had the Minister of Education , Lionel Jospin , stated that the scarves could not be a motive for excluding the girls from school than the teachers ' union , traditionally close to the Socialist Party , called him a traitor and 50 of his deputies signed a petition publicly disaffiliating themselves from his line and asking for his resignation .
10561	They found themselves rubbing shoulders with right-wing MPs , the same who in 1984 organised a million-strong demonstration in support of private schools and for the right of the parents to choose , and who today declare themselves staunch supporters of the state secular education system .
10562	Mme Mitterrand 's support of the girls , in the name of respect of religious cultures within the bounds of secularity , brought an angry reaction from French feminists .
10563	Along with four other intellectuals , including Regis Debray , feminist writer Elisabeth Badinter signed an open letter to Mr Jospin , saying that the scarf is a symbol of Muslim women 's oppression and warning him not to capitulate .
10564	A compromise on this issue , they wrote , would damage all that the French Republic has stood for since the Revolution .
10565	Remarkably , the voice of those primarily concerned by the issue , namely Arab women , has been totally missing .
10566	Les Nanas Beurs , an organisation of women of North African descent , believe that the scarf battle has to be fought .
10567	‘ As Arab feminists of Muslim culture , we believe that fundamentalism in all its forms is dangerous and that the scarf is oppressive , ’ said spokeswoman Souad Benani .
10568	‘ But it should not be used as a pretext to exclude 12- or 13-year-old girls from school when it is precisely these secular schools that should offer them the opportunity to learn , grow and make their own choices . ’
10569	For her organisation , as well as for SOS Racisme , the mass movement of young French of immigrant descent , this debate hides another agenda .
10570	What is really being debated , according to Hayat Boudjema , vice-president of SOS Racisme , is immigration and the integration of migrants and their children in French society .
10571	Already the opposition has united to set up a working group on immigration , with a view to formulating a new bill .
10572	Boudjema believes that the opposition parties are settling a score with the Socialist government and using the schoolgirls as a scapegoat .
10573	There 's more and more talk about the inability or unwillingness of the North Africans to adapt and conform .
10574	‘ This controversy has been tainted by racism parading as a concern for the adolescents ’ welfare , ’ says Boudjema .
10575	‘ The scarves are being used to fan the age-old fear of the Arab which has been dormant — simmering — since the Algerian war . ’
10576	For her the real issue is the second generation 's right to education , but not any old education .
10577	‘ We are still being taught about ‘ our ancestors , the Gauls ’ .
10578	The history of our countries of origin in Africa , Asia or the Arab world has remained totally obliterated . ’
10579	Boudjema , who is of Algerian descent , says she was totally shocked when she first heard of the Affair of the Scarf .
10580	‘ When women in North Africa and the Arab world are struggling so hard for equality and respect , it is ironic that here in France a fundamentalist minority is pushing them to conform to tradition .
10581	But we ca n't sacrifice these girls on the altar of a sacrosanct secularity which , in my view , needs to be urgently redefined and adapted to a multiracial society . ’
10582	As the debate goes on and the political parties bid for votes and support , Leila , Fatima and Samira are still confined to the library .
10583	In the meantime , in the Paris suburb of Montfermeil , the mayor refused to register children of immigrant descent in his town 's primary school , declaring that he 'd filled his quota of foreign children .
10584	Similarly , in the small town of Beaucaire in the South , a like-minded mayor refused to admit 40 new children of North African origin .
10585	When forced by the Inspectorate of Education to retract his decision , the good mayor refused them access to the school canteen , controlled by the municipal services .
10586	‘ As far as I 'm concerned , ’ he said , ‘ they do n't exist . ’

10588	Quentin Falk on how five minutes of TV documentary grew into a feature film Love among the bigots .
10589	THE source material of A Private Life , one of the first theatrical projects funded by the BBC , derives to all intents and purposes from a five-minute segment in an award-winning BBC series from 1978 called The White Tribe Of Africa .
10590	This disturbing profile of Afrikaners in their own backyard was drawn by David Dimbleby and directed by London-born but South Africa-educated Francis Gerard who , more than a decade later , makes his feature debut with A Private Life .
10591	During his extended research for the TV series , he met a close couple , Ray and Diana de Proft , living in the Cape Town suburb of Maitland .
10592	Recalls Gerrard : ‘ Ray and Diana were n't married then , although they would dearly like to have been , because they were citizens of the Republic .
10593	They had been living together across the colour bar for the best part of 30 years .
10594	‘ They had met when he was a young and not tremendously enthusiastic policeman and she was a waitress in a seafront cafe .
10595	He took her out , they fell in love and started to live together .
10596	Then in 1950 the Population Registeration Act became law .
10597	‘ And something they had never considered suddenly became very important .
10598	Ray was white .
10599	When Diana 's classification came through , she had been designated Coloured .
10600	At about the same time came the Immorality Act , which made sexual relations between different races a crime against the state . ’
10601	So Ray then found himself in the position of spending a good many of his working hours enforcing a law which he was breaking himself and increasingly afraid of being arrested by one of his mates .
10602	Their relationship became more and more covert ; he left the police and they moved to a suburb where they ‘ passed for white ’ and began the long struggle called ‘ trying for white ’ .
10603	When children arrived , matters became even more complicated and ultimatley more tragic .
10604	‘ Ray and Diana were n't revolutionaries , nor were they political dissidents .
10605	All they had done was to try to live an ordinary private life in South Africa with the dignity that we all take for granted , ’ says Gerrard .
10606	This extraordinary story was ruthlessly edited down to its allotted span and eventually tucked away in the last of four hour-long programmes .
10607	But its impact far outweighted its tiny ration .
10608	It made Gerard determined to try to tackle the material ‘ at the length and depth — and with the budget — it deserved . ’
10609	With the backing of the BBC , the guarded co-operation of the couple and the collaboration of a fine screenwriter , Andrew Davies , a full-length film drama was prepared and Gerard even secured permission to film in Cape Town .
10610	Then a money crisis hit the BBC and A Private Life was one of the casualties .
10611	The project went into cold storage , periodically resurfacing over the next six years only to sink once more .
10612	Gerard confined himself to documentaries and it was while making a 90-minute update on South Africa , Back On The Frontier , for ITV in 1986 , that he became fired up to press ahead again single-mindedly with the feature .
10613	‘ With the Government slowly clamping down on all media coverage , unless I moved fast any chance of filming within South Africa would be gone and I did want the accuracy and flavour of the country itself to come through in the film . ’
10614	The BBC still , happily , seemed keen to see the film produced and so Gerard budgeted it to be made as simply as possible in 16mm for television , with the hope that cinema distributors would find it irresistible and give it a release on the big screen .
10615	On the eve of shooting , the co-production partner — an offshore bank — withdrew from the project .
10616	The BBC itself , via its Enterprises section , rescued the day by coming up with the other half of a total £450,000 budget .
10617	With the same actors in tow anda thumbs-up from the African National Congress , Gerard cranked up again .
10618	This time , and just four days before shooting , his cameraman , Ernie Vincze , was refused entry to the republic on the grounds he was an ‘ undesirable alien ’ .
10619	After labyrinthine inquiries , it was discovered he once photographed a series of ducumentaries of which the Government disapproved .
10620	A replacement was approved and shooting finally went ahead .

11141	Tennis : Germans reject Grand Slam .
11142	By Alan Page in Essen
11143	THE projected £4 million Grand Slam Cup has brought the international tennis community to a state of deadlock .
11144	At a meeting in Frankfurt the West German Federation refused steadfastly to bow to mounting pressure from the Grand Slam committee to sanction the cup .
11145	‘ We believe it is bad for German tennis , ’ the West German Federation 's chairman , Claus Stauder , said in Essen yesterday .
11146	‘ They tried everything to convince us but we did n't buy it .
11147	They clearly did n't expect we would stand firm . ’
11148	The Grand Slam committee , including the chairman of the Wimbledon committee Buzzer Hadingham , and the International Federation are now in the embarrassing situation of having their event outlawed by the most powerful federation in the game .
11149	Stauder referred to ‘ this exorbitantly rewarded and grotesque event which gives the winner more prize money than Boris Becker has made this year ’ .
11150	He admitted the federation could not stop the tournament .
11151	‘ But we can not and will not sanction it , ’ he said .
11152	German fears are fourfold : uncontrollably escalating prize money ; a form of financial saturation-bombing of the wealthiest tennis market in the world ; downgrading of the German Open , which has a tradition stretching back 80 years ; and a clash with the ATP finals scheduled for Frankfurt three weeks earlier .
11153	For Stauder , the solution may lie in a merger of the ATP finals and the Grand Slam Cup .

11242	Obituary Rene Muawad .
11243	Controversial conciliator : .
11244	LEBANESE President Rene Muawad , killed in a car bomb assassination on Wednesday , was a conciliator who tried to restore Lebanese peace and unity after 14 years of civil war .
11245	He was 64 .
11246	He was murdered one day after he told Lebanese , on the eve of their 46th independence anniversary , that their divided country was close to peace .
11247	In the short period since his election by Parliament on November 5 , Muawad tried in vain to spread his government 's hold beyond Syrian-controlled regions and a part of the Christian enclave north of Beirut .
11248	Muawad was elected during a Parliament session held at an air base in northern Lebanon .
11249	The election was part of an Arab League-sponsored peace plan .
11250	But he immediately faced opposition from a fellow Maronite , the Christian army commander Gen Michel Aoun , who denounced Muawad as a Syrian puppet and claimed his election was unconstitutional .
11251	Muawad had been a member of the 99-seat Parliament since he was elected to represent his home region in 1957 at age 32 .
11252	An early advocate of national reconciliation , Muawad had taken part in the 20-member ‘ national dialogue committee ’ formed in September 1975 to find a settlement to the civil war , then five months old .
11253	The Muawad family , and the Issa Khoury clan to which his wife Naila belongs , are allied with the powerful Franjiehs in the northeastern region .
11254	The Franjiehs , who have their own Marada , or Giants , militia , are headed by former president Suleiman Franjieh , one of the last of the old-style Maronite warlords .
11255	Muawad graduated from the French-affilated St. Joseph University in Christian east Beirut with a law degree in 1947 .
11256	He started his own practice in the northern provincial capital of Tripoli two years later , but gave it up when he entered Parliament .
11257	But Muawad spent his first year in Parliament as an exile in the Syrian port city of Lattakia , after a member of a rival family accused him of taking part in an inter-clan clash in June 1957 near Zghotra in which 16 people were killed .
11258	The House refused demands it stripped Muawad of his parliamentary immunity .
11259	He returned to Lebanon in 1958 , shortly after newly elected President Fuad Chahab dropped charges against him for ‘ lack of undisputed evidence . ’
11260	Later , the witness who had testified against Muawad withdrew his allegation , saying it was ‘ politically motivated . ’
11261	Muawad was Minister of Telegraphs and Telecommunications from 1961 .
11262	He was named Minister of Public Works in 1969 and Minister of Education in 1980 .
11263	While he held the Education Portfolio , Muawad sliced through sectarian hatreds to organise school examinations for Christian and Moslem youngsters whose studies had been interrupted by the war .
11264	Muawad married Nayla Khoury on Feb. 11 , 1965 .
11265	They have a daughter , Rima , 22 , and a son , Michel , 17 .
11266	Muawad ( right ) meeting the Soviet Ambassador this month
11267	The Russians are coming Faced with social turbulence and resurgent anti-Semitism , many thousands of Soviet Jews are emigrating to their spiritual home .
11268	Ian Black in Tel Aviv asks whether Israel , willing but hardly prepared for the influx , can cope .
11269	VALERY and Ina and their children were visibly tired as they traipsed into the Ministry of Immigrant Absorption reception hall at Ben Gurion Airport .
11270	It had been a long , slow journey from Odessa and although it was already 1am there were still many more official forms to fill out before their new life in Israel could begin .
11271	Victoria , aged 12 , made a beeline for the reconstituted orange juice and sandwiches prepared by a pair of stout volunteer ladies who arrived from Russia themselves a few years back , and two-year-old Oleg was soon roaring about wildly on a plastic fire-engine in the playroom .
11272	There were about 100 of them on Sunday 's evening flight from Bucharest to Tel Aviv , unmistakably Soviet with their fur hats , cheap wintry clothes and suitcases and quiet , mechanical submission to the first taste of Israeli bureaucracy .
11273	Fair-haired Jews from Moscow and Leningrad mingled with olive-skinned Georgians to read the Cyrillic slogans welcoming them and then sank down in rows of plastic chairs or gazed at the panoramic photograph of Jerusalem covering an entire wall .
11274	A toothless old man from Baku , his double-breasted jacket beribboned with the medals of two world wars , looked dazed .
11275	At 93 , little remained of the liturgical Hebrew he had studied before the October Revolution , but he was pleased to be leaving his quarrelsome Armenian and Azerbaijani neighbours behind .
11276	Dimitri Bogakovsky , a 36-year-old doctor from Kiev , was radiantly happy .
11277	‘ I feel I have come home , ’ he said .
11278	‘ I 'm only sorry I did n't come to Israel 20 years ago . ’
11279	Ina , a teacher , was more cautious .
11280	‘ At the moment I can say I wanted to come here and not to America , ’ she smiled .
11281	‘ What I 'll be saying in a year 's time I do n't know . ’
11282	Several flights like these , some from Budapest and Vienna , are now arriving at Ben Gurion every week , their human cargoes eloquent testimony to the swelling numbers of Soviet Jewish emigrants and the vast changes that Mikhail Gorbachev 's policies have wrought in their homeland .
11283	Economic and political uncertainty and the rise of truculent local nationalisms from the Baltic to the Caspian have raised the ancient spectre of anti-Semitism , never far below the surface of Soviet life .
11284	Under glasnost and perestroika , the last great untapped pool of world Jewry is on the move .
11285	Exact numbers are unavailable : 2.5 to three million is the accepted figure , though 70 years of cultural and religious suppression , intermarriage and assimilation means that the real number — in Zionist terms those who qualify for automatic Israeli citizenship under the Law of Return — may be far higher .
11286	Turbulence at home , combined with an American decision to restrict Jewish immigrants from the Soviet Union , mean that the stream of emigration is now directed almost exclusively at Israel .
11287	The challenge is immense , and no one is sure whether it can be met .
11288	According to the latest projections , 100,000 Soviet Jews will arrive in Israel over the next three years , and the numbers may be even higher if and when direct flights start from Moscow to Tel Aviv , the most important tangible sign of the rapid thaw in Soviet-Israeli relations .
11289	In comparative terms , such an influx is the equivalent of the movement of three million East Germans to West Germany , a country ( unlike Israel ) with a healthy economy where difficulties of acclimatization for the newcomers will be at a minimum and language problems non-existent .
11290	If the Russians do arrive on this scale it will be the largest single wave of what Israelis call aliya ( literally ‘ ascent ’ ) since the immediate post independence years in the early 1950s , a heady return to the heart of the Zionist idea at a time when the country — still fighting the Palestinian uprising , on a permanent war footing and its economy slipping into recession — is far from ready .
11291	THE FIRST big wave of Russians came after the 1967 war , when Zionist feelings were awakened by Israel 's six day victory and Soviet support for the Arabs .
11292	Moscow underestimated the phenomenon , believing that if the hard core of ‘ provocateurs ’ were allowed to emigrate the vast majority would stay .
11293	The emigration movement reached a peak in 1973 with 33,000 Jews leaving .
11294	It dipped after the Yom Kippur war , rising again to 51,000 in 1979 .
11295	Until 1982 figures dropped steadily again , reaching a low point in 1986 .
11296	Even in the good years Israel had only a share .
11297	Between 1968 and 1988 280,000 Jews emigrated , but only 165,000 came to Israel .
11298	In 1988 the drop-out rate reached a staggering 92 per cent .
11299	But in the first 10 months of 1989 alone over 7,000 have arrived , and there are expected to be 10,000 by the end of the year .
11300	The new wave is not in the heroic mould of famous ‘ refuseniks ’ like Anatoly Scharansky , Ida Nudel and Josef Begun , who finally arrived in Israel after years of persecution , exile and imprisonment .
11301	Few of the newcomers know any Hebrew and few have more than the vaguest idea about Israel .
11302	Many would have preferred America .
11303	With the Berlin Wall , the most famous barrier of all , falling , the more media-conscious activists among the Soviet Jews already here are warning that Israel is just not prepared for the influx .
11304	‘ Israel 's lack of preparedness for mass Soviet Jewish immigration is psychologically understandable but not politically forgivable , ’ says Yuri Stern , a Muscovite who came in 1981 .
11305	‘ Its very difficult to appreciate a revolution , to see today as really qualitatively , dramatically different from the day before .
11306	Its difficult to go beyond normal scepticism and see this huge number not just as a potential but as a reality . ’
11307	Israelis are pleased with the change in the US regulations , which effectively signal an end to the drop-out phenomenon .
11308	‘ Israel , ’ says one senior official , ‘ has never been interested in emigration as such , but in aliya — in having as many Jews as possible come to Israel . ’
11309	In this perspective , places like the Ladispoli transit camp near Rome , where thousands of Soviet Jews are still awaiting visas to the US , are a disgrace .
11310	A thriving Jewish life in New York 's Brighton Beach will not reinforce Israel .
11311	Freedom of choice is no longer on the agenda , especially now that American Jews have discovered that it is easier to raise money for absorbing Soviet Jews in Israel than it is for resettling them in the US .
11312	The Israeli government has been agonisingly slow to take up the challenge , although it has calculated that US$3 billion will be needed over three years for housing , job creation and other aspects of large-scale immigrant absorption .
11313	The bureaucracy certainly needs streamlining : the immigrants are met initially by the Absorption Ministry , but once in the country many of their needs are looked after by the Jewish Agency , the semi-private organisation that dates back to the early years of Jewish settlement in Palestine .
11314	The two bodies are often at loggerheads , and there are constant disputes over methods : are the newcomers best served by direct absorption — being given money and subsidies for their first year and then left to cope on their own , or by being placed in one of the 38 Jewish Agency absorption centres .
11315	LEARNING Hebrew is a priority for all , and places in the famous ulpan system are available at once .
11316	But even after six months of intensive study many other problems remain .
11317	A Soviet engineer who lost his job a decade ago after applying to emigrate needs to catch up .
11318	Doctors need to retrain for eight months .
11319	At the big Mevasseret absorption centre near Jerusalem , where there are 77 Russian families in different stages of acclimatization , only half the breadwinners are working .
11320	Unskilled workers tend to do better than the professionals , enjoying the advantages of a free market for the first time in their lives .
11321	On the positive side , the changes inside the Soviet Union will help : with the unprecedented flowering of Jewish cultural freedom , Hebrew classes are now a possibility ; potential immigrants can now learn more about Israel before they come .
11322	Another innovation is the stream of Jewish tourists visiting Israel from Russia : 25,000 have been since 1988 , and the Jewish Agency sees this is a uniquely helpful way to win hearts and minds .
11323	Forty thousand are expected next year .
11324	The new arrivals , like their predecessors , tend towards the right of the political spectrum .
11325	‘ Of course we thought about political problems , but everyone in Israel suffers from the same ones , ’ says Igor , a railway engineer studying at the Mevasseret ulpan .
11326	‘ I 'm content to go into the army , and I 'm definitely against giving up territory to the Arabs . ’
11327	The veterans are pleased , but accept that the newcomers are coming here less out of choice than of necessity .
11328	Haim Scheider , an economist who left Lithuania 10 years ago , has been unemployed for 18 months , but still has no regrets .
11329	He visited his former homeland last summer and could n't bear it .
11330	‘ You make comparisons all the time and the comparison is in Israel 's favour , there 's no doubt about it .
11331	People have achieved things here that they coud n't do in Russia , not even in their wildest dreams . ’
11332	Haim , who speaks halting Hebrew with a heavy accent , still leads an intensely Russian life in the new West Bank settlement north of Jerusalem where he lives with his wife and two children .
11333	‘ My son is already an Israeli , ’ he laughs , ‘ he prefers humus and felafel to gefilte fish . ’
11334	Difficulties abound , but it seems that the Russians are coming anyway .
11335	‘ In times of emergency we behave differently from normal times , ’ says Meir Edlestein , the director of the Mevasseret absorption centre .
11336	‘ This is a very Zionist answer . ’
11337	More practical answers will have to be provided as the Jews pour in , huddled on the platform of rapidly changing history , anxious to change their lives in an imperfect world .
11338	‘ The marriage between Soviet Jews and Israel is a marriage that is probably going to happen , ’ argues Yuri Stern , ‘ whether or not the bride and groom feel they are really ready for it . ’

11359	OVERNIGHT FILE
11360	Prototyping is crucial to systems development , argues Ian Richards Tailored to fit .
11361	IN SYSTEMS development nothing is more fundamental than assessing user requirements .
11362	If you do n't know what the system is required to do ; you do n't know anything .
11363	But many system developers are unable to assess requirements properly .
11364	They seem to think that you can ask a businessman what his requirements are and get an answer that amounts to a draft system specification .
11365	A doctor does n't ask his patient what treatment to prescribe .
11366	The patient can explain only what the problem is .
11367	It is the doctor that provides the remedy .
11368	If you ask a user what sort of system he wants you will be met with a blank look .
11369	A user may have a deep knowledge of business problems , but knowing little about computers , has no idea how they should be tackled .
11370	Yet , analysts are heard asking time and again , ‘ Tell me what you want .
11371	We 've gone away from the days of systems imposed by the data processing department , this is going to be a system for the users . ’
11372	But of course the users do n't know what they want , so they end up getting another duff system .
11373	An effective analyst provides the same service to the business as the doctor provides to the patient .
11374	He finds out what the needs of the business are , and prescribes the cure .
11375	The user tells the analyst what the problems are , and the analyst decides , at least in broad terms , what the user requires .
11376	But the analyst has one great advantage over the doctor .
11377	Once the user becomes familiar with the proposed system , helpful comments come thick and fast .
11378	‘ Oh , this will be of great help in ordering raw materials , but sometimes we get part deliveries , could we have an extra facility to deal with those ?
11379	And sometimes non-standard discount is given , a pig to deal with on the old system , but if you could add one extra input box on that screen there …
11380	And what about orders not delivered on time ?
11381	If we could list those we 'd have advance warning of shortage problems on the assembly lines two months before they occur .
11382	Now that would be a great leap forward . ’
11383	Unfortunately you can not reach this stage until you have developed a prototype system .
11384	And you ca n't develop a prototype system because the users have n't got a clue what they want .
11385	Most of them are probably muttering , ‘ I 'm too busy to get involved in this sort of thing .
11386	What 's wrong with the old system anyway ? ’
11387	The only way to develop a prototype is for the analyst to get inside the head of the user and , thinking like a user , decide what sort of system is required .
11388	Of course , the initial system will not be perfect .
11389	The analyst can not hope to understand the business as well in a few weeks as the user does after many years .
11390	But once the user sees the system , channels of communication will open .
11391	Instead of persuading the user to specify requirements , the analyst will be driven by the user to meet key needs .
11392	Good system development goes through two distinct phases .
11393	Initially the analyst does all the work , leading the user towards a system he thinks is right for the business .
11394	But once the user sees the potential of the system , a change in attitude takes place .
11395	The process becomes demand driven by the user .
11396	The analyst is then forced on the defensive , explaining why new features can not be included because they are technically difficult or prohibitively expensive .
11397	Traditionally , systems were validated by users agreeing functional specifications .
11398	In theory , validation meant that the user had read the specification , imagined how the system would work in practice , and agreed the design .
11399	It was only when using a ‘ test ’ version of the system ( available just before the planned implementation date ) that difficulties would come to light , and a host of change requests be issued .
11400	The advent of fourth generation languages ( 4GLs ) has made system development much easier .
11401	With a 4GL an initial prototype can be put together quickly .
11402	This means feedback is obtained early in the development process , and the system can grow around the user 's requirements .
11403	Crucial to the development process is the relationship built up between the analyst and the user .
11404	The best systems arise when both have a deep understanding of each other 's jobs .
11405	Many developers use business analysts to ensure that the development team maintain a proper focus on business requirements .
11406	But this can be counter-productive , as it cuts off communication between the systems analyst and the user .
11407	Too much specialisation is bad for systems development ; it feeds the temptation to get engrossed in technical difficulties and forget about the underlying business needs .
11408	If you should stroll into a pub and meet an analyst and a user talking about work , and you can not tell one from the other , they have probably developed a successful system together .
11409	Ian Richards ' book , How to Use a Computer to Improve Your Business , has just been published by Graham &amp; Trotman ( £8.95 paperback ; £16 hardback ) .
11410	Tel : 01-821 1123 .

11412	Microfile .
11413	By Jack Schofield Computer editor
11414	ALPHA is a new master operating system designed to interconnect disparate and widely distributed systems to act as a single cohesive whole .
11415	It is being financed largely by the US Department of Defense , and made available free .
11416	Alpha is being developed for systems like the US Advanced Tactical Fighter , which has about 20 real-time computer systems on board , the NASA space station , and possibly the Strategic Defense Initiative .
11417	The project is being led by Doug Jensen at the Concurrent Computer Corp. , Massachusetts .
11418	He originally developed Alpha as a research project at Carnegie-Mellon University .
11419	Then General Dynamics used it to demonstrate a ground-based air defense application .
11420	Alpha is written in C++ and will run initially on Concurrent 's Mips-based multi-processor mini-supercomputers , which will be launched next month .
11421	It co-exists with Concurrent 's RTU ( Real-Time Unix ) , and has an object-orientated user interface designed for the production of large , complex , real-time applications .
11422	Alpha assumes the computing system is distributed , and it includes replication mechanisms to provide distributed programming and ‘ survivability ’ .
11423	It manages tasks by setting deadlines for their completion , instead of using interrupts simply to start them going .
11424	When deadlines ca n't be met , Alpha ‘ gracefully degrades ’ by meeting as many as possible of the most important ones .
11425	Although the defence applications are obvious , Alpha could become important in ‘ mission critical ’ commercial systems .
11426	Examples include factory automation and large on-line financial networks .
11427	A ‘ Baby Alpha ’ will be developed , using VRTX , for smaller integrated systems .
11428	The beta-test version of Alpha is due for release at the end of 1990 , with the first commercial release in 1993 .
11429	Concurrent says the ultimate aim is to produce a supplier-independent , open operating system that will rank alongside Unix , and be complementary to it .
11430	Concurrent is seeking European partners for the Alpha project via its UK office in Maidenhead ( tel : 0753 77777 ) .
11431	More Mips .
11432	NIXDORF and Tandem are developing a fault-tolerant mini based on Risc ( Reduced instruction set computer ) chips from Mips Computer Systems and the Unix operating system .
11433	The new machine will be marketed by both firms next year .
11434	Nixdorf is also co-operating with Pyramid Technology , whose technology is used in Nixdorf 's Targon/35 .
11435	( Pyramid is yet another Mips reseller . )
11436	Meanwhile , Control Data has signed an agreement to sell Mips ' cheap Unix-based RC6280 mini/mainframe .
11437	With a Risc processor rated at 55 mips ( million instructions per second ) , this is the industry 's fastest general-purpose computer .
11438	Wizard .
11439	IBM has announced the Wizard adaptor , which puts a 33MHz Intel i860 Risc 64-bit processor on an expansion card for 386-based PCs with MCA ( Micro Channel Architecture ) buses and the OS/2 operating system .
11440	It will be used for oil industry and financial modelling and similar supercomputing tasks .
11441	The card delivers about 27 mips and costs £5,568 plus VAT , with the memory expansion at £2,915 .

11472	Jack Schofield provides a user-friendly guide to the home computers on offer this Christmas and picks the best-value buys Avoiding turkeys .
11473	CHRISTMAS is coming , and the home computer companies are hoping to get fat .
11474	Lots of machines have been nicely packaged for the market , but there are no bargains to be had .
11475	Anyone who just wants to play arcade-type games might as well buy a games console .
11476	These are relatively cheap , the games come on easy-to-load cartridges and are , on average , better than the home computer versions .
11477	Atari invented the console , and its old 2600 is the cheapest on the market at £40 or less .
11478	But in the US and Japan , Nintendo has become the standard , with NEC and Sega being the main challengers .
11479	However , with NEC 's PC Engine not officially available in the UK , and the Nintendo system overpriced at around £100 , the Sega Master ( £80 or less ) is the best choice .
11480	It has good colours and , although it uses a Zilog Z-80 processor , like the Spectrum , the games are fast .
11481	There are three points to bear in mind about 8-bit consoles .
11482	First , all the suppliers are preparing superior but incompatible 16-bit versions , including the Nintendo Super Famicom and the Sega Megadrive ( the latter having already arrived as an unofficial import , at £200 ) .
11483	Second , games cost much more than those for 8-bit home micros .
11484	Third , you can get a real computer for less .
11485	Indeed , the cheapest ‘ real computer ’ has a dual nature .
11486	The Atari XE is an £80 games console which comes with dedicated cassette recorder and an add-on keyboard which can be used for word processing or , say , adventure games .
11487	It is also available as the Atari 65XE home micro for about £10 more .
11488	The XE is a good machine , barely changed from the Atari 800 from 1979 .
11489	It has 64K of memory , an 8-bit 6502 processor and a poor Basic .
11490	It is rather faster than a Commodore 64 , and has similar graphics and sound , which makes the hardware good value .
11491	You can add disc drives and printers for serious use .
11492	However , the XE is not well supported by software houses , and although it still has a lot of games , most of these are very old .
11493	Top 20 games are now almost never converted to run on it , which purchasers would find very frustrating .
11494	Today 's 8-bit standards are the Commodore 64 , Spectrum +2 and +3 , and Amstrad CPC-464 and 6128 .
11495	Of these , only the Commodore 64C is now worth buying , and only then if you never plan to add a disc drive .
11496	The Commodore 64 also has a 6502-type processor , 64K , very good graphics and sound , and the worst Basic still fitted to a home micro .
11497	But it is very well supported for games , since it is a standard in both the US and in Europe , whereas the Amstrad and Sinclair Z-80-based machines failed in the US .
11498	The drawback with the C64 is that it is expensive at about £150 .
11499	The price includes a dedicated cassette recorder , the C2N , which does n't work particularly well , if at all , with today 's fast-loading games .
11500	It is much better to buy a naked C64 and one of the superior independent cassette players such as Mills Associates ' Load-It .
11501	Further , the price means it is n't worth upgrading a C64 by adding Commodore 's slow disc drive .
11502	You might as well buy an Atari ST , with its better built-in disc drive , to start with .
11503	Nevertheless , the C64 is far superior to the Amstrad-made Spectrum , which is on sale at the same price .
11504	The Spectrum +2 , with its built-in cassette recorder , simply is n't worth £150 .
11505	The +3 is better value at £200 , since this includes a built-in disc drive .
11506	However , this is the 3-inch drive peculiar to Amstrad products , and you would be better off paying the extra £35 for a discount Atari ST .
11507	The Amstrad CPC , although quite a good micro , is also poor value now .
11508	The CPC-464 comes with cassette recorder and mono monitor for £200 , which makes the C64 a better buy .
11509	The CPC-6128 comes with a built-in 3-inch disc drive and colour monitor for £400 , which again makes an Atari ST a better buy , and the Commodore Amiga a tempting alternative .
11510	Amstrad has held its CPC prices constant for over five years now , apart from throwing a few extra baubles ( joystick , games ) into the mix .
11511	They used to be extremely good value ; now they are eminently ignorable .
11512	Is Alan Sugar happy to watch this range decline ?
11513	Of course , Atari has not cut the price of its ST micro for two years , but at least the raw 520ST-FM has a powerful 16/32-bit Motorola 68000 processor , 512K of memory , upgraded 720K disc drive and a mouse .
11514	Also this £300 machine is often sold for much less , and old models ( which have a single-sided 360K drive ) are available for as little as £175 .
11515	The Atari ST has dominated the 16-bit market over the last couple of years as a ‘ dual purpose ’ machine .
11516	It can be used for serious computing , as a ‘ poor man 's Apple Macintosh ’ , with Atari 's high-quality monochrome screen , and plugged into a TV set for games .
11517	Recently , the Atari ST has been selling bundled with £400-£500 worth of games for £399 .
11518	At this price it has come under increasing pressure from the Commodore Amiga , which starts at the same price and attracts similar discounts .
11519	The Amiga also has a Motorola 68000 , 512K , a built-in 3.5 inch disc drive and a mouse , but it has much better colour graphics and sound .
11520	The Amiga 's technical superiority counted for little when there were hardly any games for it , and hardly any of them used its facilities .
11521	But after Commodore cut the price by £100 , and threw in the £25 add-on TV adaptor , the Amiga took off as a games machine .
11522	Now it is at least as well supported as the ST , and its advantages are finally starting to count .
11523	Atari has announced an enhanced STE range with graphics and sound facilities more like the Amiga 's , but at no extra cost .
11524	However , the new facilities have yet to win any support from software houses , and you would be surprised to find an STE actually on sale .
11525	The Amiga does not have as much serious software as the ST , nor does it have the equivalent of the ST 's mono monitor .
11526	However , it now has a reasonable range of productivity software ( word processors , databases , etc ) , and in specialised areas — colour graphics , desktop video — it is well ahead .
11527	At the lowest level , the 520ST still looks slightly better value than an Amiga , which has an operating system not everyone likes .
11528	But for those willing to upgrade the A500 to one megabyte , and add an A590 hard disc and a colour monitor , it becomes a very attractive system .
11529	Finally , there 's the Acorn Archimedes A3000 , which is by far the most powerful home micro available .
11530	Instead of being made in Taiwan ( Atari ) or Hong Kong ( Commodore ) this is even made in the UK .
11531	Unfortunately , it does not have a lot of software support , and the price — about £750 — puts it beyond most people 's reach .
11532	In value-for-money terms , the Sega looks the best buy among the games machines , the Commodore 64 for a tape-based home micro , and then either the Atari ST or Amiga A500 — both disc-based systems — depending on specific needs and disposable income .
