11542	Why the M-word is baloney American columnist John C.Dvorak argues that multimedia is a sham — the old , failed teaching machine dressed up in new clothes .
11543	ITHINK if we are ever to see grand hokum in the Mac marketplace we 'll see it in the months ahead , as the M-word — multimedia — becomes the in thing to discuss in the 1990s .
11544	Multimedia used to be defined as a fancy slide show that you sat and watched .
11545	They were the ones with the bank of 40 computer-controlled projectors — popular at expositions and amusement parks .
11546	I remember a multimedia show in the Iran pavilion at the world 's fair in Spokane , Washington , in the early 1970s .
11547	It was about the Shah and the glories of the country .
11548	It seems that while the definition of the word multimedia has changed , the baloney factor has n't .
11549	Nowadays , multimedia means a computer using different media , such as a laser disc , a CD-ROM , cable TV and who knows what else .
11550	The most-talked-about end use is as a grandiose teaching machine .
11551	You remember teaching machines , do n't you ?
11552	They were one of the biggest flops in educational history .
11553	Not that they did n't work ; it just seems that teaching machines have no charisma or charm .
11554	I remember back when I was a college student .
11555	One summer I went to California State University at Hayward and discovered that the school had a basement laboratory with about a dozen expensive teaching machines .
11556	You could sign up for a series of courses , which you could take at your own pace .
11557	The machine tested , paced and graduated you .
11558	For the life of me I ca n't remember what courses I took — it was so boring .
11559	Soon afterwards the famed Plato computerised teaching system was marketed by Control Data .
11560	It included special terminals and was the be-all , end-all teaching machine .
11561	I have n't heard about it for years .
11562	The hot , hot multimedia system out there right now was developed by Robert Abel , the noted Hollywood middleman and go-getter extraordinaire .
11563	Abel has put together a demonstration system called Guernica , which is a multimedia approach to learning about the famed Picasso painting that depicts the Nazi destruction of a peaceful Basque village by air attack during the Spanish Civil War .
11564	Based mostly on using a laser-disc player controlled by a Mac II , the system allows a user to explore — as the developers like to say — the painting and its history .
11565	Fronted by a HyperCard-like interface — SuperCard , actually — the system lets users click and move from point to point on the painting and get lectures and comments from old bores , ex-mistresses , ‘ people who were there ’ , dopey ex-Nazi pilots , Picasso mavens and all sorts of experts .
11566	You can jump from the history of the town to a backgrounder on Spanish dance .
11567	You can jump from that to something else .
11568	The system is supposed to exemplify the potential of multimedia .
11569	Bob Abel and his pals , when they show this system , make the mistake of using the word empower when describing the value of this approach to learning .
11570	With me that rings a warning bell , since it 's one of those suspicious New Age buzzwords that always portend a scam or screwball notion such as crystal therapy or out-of-body travel .
11571	This system , he says , ‘ empowers the individual . ’
11572	This is presumably because it allows you to explore the knowledge contained therein .
11573	The promoters tell us that it 's not like a book in which someone is telling you something .
11574	This new multimedia thingamajig allows you to discover things on your own through the wondrous use of the hypermedia approach to education .
11575	Linearity is dead .
11576	By the time the demo was over I was nearly nauseous at the presumptuousness of these notions and despondent over the lack of scepticism in the room .
11577	In fact , nobody anywhere — as far as I can tell — has questioned any aspect of this nonsense .
11578	Let's make some quick points that need to be made .
11579	Multimedia education is nothing more than a new version of a teaching machine , albeit with real-time video , and teaching machines do n't work .
11580	Just try to learn French on your computer .
11581	This multi- media concept is to education what a demo program is to software .
11582	Teachers teach .
11583	Computers compute .
11584	With multimedia , people do not really explore and are not empowered .
11585	The information provided on such a system is predistilled by the producers .
11586	It 's not a base of knowledge but a subset that can be easily manipulated .
11587	Abel , for example , is obviously a Democrat , as he slipped more than a few anti-Reagan barbs into his presentation .
11588	Video media , with its powerful images used interactively for teaching , will find its niche as a propaganda tool .
11589	I get a bad feeling when I see this thing in action .
11590	Especially when I look around at the bug-eyed gawkers staring , almost hypnotised , at the images .
11591	Multimedia is , simply put , a sham .
11592	A fancy sham , but a sham nonetheless .
11593	It 's promoted by the natural-born hucksters within Apple because it has all the earmarks of something trendy and fashionable .
11594	It keeps people talking .
11595	It keeps the excitement level high .
11596	It generates interest in Apple and it sells hardware .
11597	I 'm not going to say that some of these projects , such as Guernica , wo n't be fun to play around with , assuming that you can afford to buy all the necessary - and expensive — hardware to add to your already expensive system .
11598	Institutions , of course , will be the suckers conned into spending the big money for all this equipment .
11599	It will all end up in those grim audio-visual departments where it will eventually be auctioned off for peanuts during a cost-saving period .
11600	And for those of you who want to learn about Picasso , try the library or go to a museum .

11604	Tata for now India could become to software in the 1990s what Taiwan and South Korea are to electronics today .
11605	Radhakrishna Rao reports .
11606	IN THE popular Western imagination , India continues to be a country steeped in backwardness and poverty with very little to show by way of scientific innovation or technological achievement .
11607	It has hardly been recognised that India is among the few countries in the world that has a proven capability to undertake orbital missions or detonate a nuclear device .
11608	Indeed , with some 2.5 million fully qualified scientific and technical personnel , and several million more high school science graduates , India possesses the world 's third largest pool of scientific and technical skill , after the US and the Soviet Union .
11609	Its influence is felt as far away as the London Underground , which is having its new , networked , interactive time-tabling system , Cart , programmed by a Delhi firm , CMC .
11610	The fluency of Indians in English , a legacy of British rule , has made India a lucrative hunting ground for US computer firms on the lookout for qualified computer manpower .
11611	Areas in which Indian software professionals are particularly strong are systems software , CAD/CAM , expert systems , microcomputer software , telecommunications and applications software development .
11612	This year at Cebit 1989 , the huge electronics fair held in Hanover , the head of the government 's electronics commision , P.S. Deodhar , ‘ launched India into the European Information market . ’
11613	The West German software industry , handicapped by an acute manpower shortage , responded by switching labour-intensive software engineering work to India .
11614	West Germany needs about 4,000 electronic data processing specialists , and can fill this gap by using India 's skilled and relatively inexpensive manpower .
11615	The Indian software industry is growing at an average rate of 35 per cent a year .
11616	Of the total 2,550 million rupees ( £100 million ) earned by Indian software firms in 1988-89 , exports accounted for almost a third .
11617	More than 60 per cent of Indian exports are accounted for by the two Tata outfits , Tata Consultancy Services ( TCS ) and Tata Unisys Ltd , which employ around 1,500 professionals in Bombay and Bangalore .
11618	Tata Unisys has a collaborative arrangement with MicroSoft .
11619	Both the government and the industry are committed to boost its software exports , specialising in systems that overcome the problem of early obsolescence .
11620	Thus India could become for the software scene in 90s what Taiwan and South Korea are to electronics today .
11621	In July 1988 , a new organisation , the National Association of Software and Services Company ( Nasscom ) was set up to serve the interests of software sector .
11622	According to Nasscom Chief Executive , Prem Shivdasani , there are about 300 Indian firms devoted to computer software engineering .
11623	The government has already set up technology parks in Bangalore and Pune , with two more expected in Chandigarh and Bubaneshwar , to boost software exports .
11624	One feature of these parks is the facility for real-time transmission of software code through dedicated satellite channels to clients in the US and elsewhere .
11625	Under a policy announced in 1986 , a 50 per cent rebate is provided on customs duty payable for import of hardware used for software development .
11626	Another feature of the new approach is that the software industry has been exempted from the licensing provision of the Industries Act : there are no constraints on the setting up of software houses , and programming is not treated as an industrial activity .
11627	About 90 per cent of exports are to the US , where Indian software systems cost half as much as American ones .
11628	Two American companies with an eye on available and inexpensive manpower have set up software export units in the southern hill city of Bangalore , India 's own Silicon Valley .
11629	The $5 million Texas Instruments facility has a staff of 35 US-trained Indian engineers and exports software through a dedicated satellite link to its clients in the US .
11630	DEC , in association with Hinitroan of India , exports its software via a Bangalore-Madras-Hong Kong satellite link .
11631	At Bombay 's Santacruz Free Trade Zone , Citicorp Overseas Software is generating software for the bank 's worldwide use .
11632	Hewlett-Packard is also planning to set up a software export unit in India .
11633	Recently , TCS entered into an agreement with Lotus Development Corporation that gave them exclusive distribution rights for the whole range of Recently there was uproar in India following ‘ body shopping ’ by American software firms .
11634	Recruitment of 40 top staff was the last straw .
11635	Lotus PC software , while Thapar is planning a tie-up with Hitachi of Japan for setting up software units with 100 per cent buy-back arrangements .
11636	Nearly 50 Indian software producers belong to the Engineering Export Promotion Council which is making vigorous efforts to find new markets , particularly in East Asia and Europe .
11637	The Bombay-based Larsen and Toubro ( L&amp;T ) , which has already exported software services to a number of countries , is negotiating with European countries for the supply of software engineering .
11638	It is also contemplating tie-ups with software houses or large user organisations abroad .
11639	However , only a few large companies — 25 of them — have been registered as software exporters with branch offices abroad .
11640	Small local software firms , which can ill afford overheads like publicity and advertising , are worried that the increasing preference for tie-ups will stunt their growth .
11641	Also , industry observers say Indian companies must put more money into research and development to ensure that quality remains uncompromised .
11642	Indian companies tend to allocate at most two per cent of turnover to R&amp;D as against 15 per cent by US firms .
11643	The Indian Department of Electronics says overseas computer firms can take advantage of the trained manpower available in India due to liberal economic policies and incentives provided by the government .
11644	But India is itself likely to face an acute manpower shortage in the immediate future .
11645	Courses aimed at training computer professionals have been started at nearly 250 institutions in the country .
11646	But right now , about 3,000 professionals are available against the projected need for over 10,000 by the end of the decade .
11647	Recently there was uproar in India following ‘ body shopping ’ by American software firms .
11648	The recruitment of 40 top staff from Indian companies , including some from Bangalore-based Wipro Information Systems , proved to be the last straw .
11649	The Indian government put severe restrictions on the flight of ‘ talented brains ’ to the US .
11650	In a leader , the Economic Times , Bangalore , noted that at best , body-shopping by foreign firms ‘ may be substituted by sub-contracting , and that too , to their own subsidiaries rather than Indian companies . ’
11651	Thus Indian software houses , ‘ will have to develop their own products based on indigenous R&amp;D .
11652	But for this to happen … the government should come down heavily on piracy , which militates against domestic development .
11653	A rapid growth of the home market must also be ensured .
11654	In software particularly , exports will have to be led by the domestic market . ’

11707	A dragon without fire Michael Billington misses the menace in the RSC 's revival of Shakespeare 's best political play .
11708	IT is twelve years since the last Stratford Coriolanus : an absurd neglect of Shakespeare 's best political play .
11709	But the new production at the Royal Shakespeare Theatre , directed by Terry Hands and John Barton , has a lot going for it .
11710	Pace .
11711	Clarity .
11712	The best Volumnia in years from Barbara Jefford .
11713	But , in an ideal world , one would look for more dangerous animalism than one gets from Charles Dance 's Coriolanus in order to sharpen the edge of political debate .
11714	What makes this such a great play is Shakespeare 's analytical power : as John Barton once pointed out , Shakespeare is neither right-wing nor left-wing but wing-less .
11715	Coriolanus is seen as a magnificent warrior , a psychologically damaged mother-worshipper and a potential threat to an evolving republic .
11716	The people , on the other hand , are suffering from famine at a time when the patricians are hoarding the grain-harvest but are themselves easily manipulated by the Tribunes .
11717	Shakespeare does not so much take sides as show how the state is threatened by the tragic collision of opposing forces : for antique Rome read Jacobean England .
11718	What is good about the current production is that it does not seek to tilt the play either way : it allows us to decide where we stand .
11719	It also implies , rather than re-creates , the past : Christopher Morley 's set consists of three mobile siege-towers with the Romans , in costume terms , veering to black leather , the Volscians to scarlet greatcoats .
11720	And along the way the production makes a number of intelligent points .
11721	The Tribunes are strongly contrasted , with Geoffrey Freshwater 's bullish rabble-rouser of a Sicinius Velutus offset by the ineffectual moderation of Joe Melia 's Junius Brutus .
11722	The continuity of martial values is also brilliantly suggested at the end when Coriolanus 's son ritually receives his father 's sword from Volumnia while his mother looks grievingly on .
11723	What I miss , however , in Charles Dance 's Coriolanus is a sense of implacable danger .
11724	Mr Dance gives us many of the man 's essential qualities : his psychological dependence on his mother , his solitariness ( he is constantly placed down front gazing over the audience 's heads ) , his antique , tribal valour .
11725	But there is a dragonish aspect to Coriolanus which Mr Dance has yet to catch .
11726	He also throws away too many key phrases : ‘ This Triton of the minnows ’ is a magnificent epithet for Sicinius but it here gets lost and although in the great banishment-speech Mr Dance 's body-language is good ( as he hurls his coat to the ground in fine disdain ) it is significant that the directors resort to an echo-chamber effect on ‘ There is a world elsewhere . ’
11727	Olivier , one wanly recalls , had his own built-in reverberations .
11728	Without a dictatorial Coriolanus , Shakespeare 's point about the implied threat to the republic is stated rather than felt .
11729	But there is rich compensation in Barbara Jefford 's magnificent Volumnia : why has this superb actress been given only two roles by the RSC in 30 years ?
11730	She is , essentially , a voluptuous Volumnia whose hold over her son is dangerously sexual .
11731	Greeting him on his return from battle , she hands him over to his wife with palpable reluctance ; seeking to calm him before his confrontation with the people , she shackles him in an iron grip ; and , in the great plea with him not to sack Rome , she pinpoints the lines about him treading on his mother 's womb ‘ that brought thee to this world ’ .
11732	Volumnia can easily be played as a sexless harridan : Ms Jefford interprets her as a passionate woman who dominates her son physically as well as spiritually , even to the extent of giving his face a resounding slap when he is recalcitrant .
11733	But the other key roles are also strongly cast .
11734	Malcolm Storry 's bullet-headed Aufidius is not simply a rude barbarian but an acute analyst of Coriolanus 's character : Mr Storry has the priceless gift of making the language tangible so that when he says ‘ I think he 'll be to Rome as is the osprey to the fish ’ the image comes resonantly alive .
11735	Joseph O'Conor also makes Menenius infinitely more than a wily patrician : he seems the only one capable of communicating sanely with the several , warring factions .
11736	In what is normally seen as a male-dominated play , it is also worth noting that Hands and Barton give the women unusual prominence .
11737	Amanda Harris 's Virgilia is no simpering wet but a loyal wife who vehemently thumps the tribunes for their banishment of her husband .
11738	And Jane Maud 's Valeria is characterised in the programme as ‘ priestess of Diana ’ and , in the final peace-mission , is given unusual symbolic weight .
11739	That is a sign of how the play has been intelligently re-thought .
11740	The production also takes on board the point Anne Barton makes in the programme that Shakespeare , following Livy , sees Coriolanus as a threat to the balance of the state .
11741	But for the idea to be made manifest one needs a Coriolanus who is not only a truculent fighter but also a thrillingly horrific force of nature .
11742	Charles Dance as Coriolanus … a threat to the republic ?

11907	Official figures are hard to credit as families fail to claim benefit .
11908	By Mike George
11909	ASTAGGERING number of the hard-up are failing to claim benefit under the Family Credit Scheme — despite a recent change in government calculations .
11910	Families struggling on low incomes can get help from the scheme provided at least one adult is working at least 24 hours a week .
11911	When it was introduced in place of the old family income supplement scheme last year , just 38 per cent of those entitled claimed family credit .
11912	The government subsequently altered its estimate of those able to claim and came up with a 50 per cent take-up rate .
11913	And now Tony Newton 's social security department is hoping a recent £7 million advertising campaign will boost that to 60 per cent .
11914	Family credit is a means tested benefit paid on top of wages , or earnings from self employment .
11915	It is almost always paid to a woman .
11916	To qualify you must be responsible for one or more children aged under 16 , or under 19 if they are still in full-time non-advanced education .
11917	Your savings must total less than £6,000 though £1 of ‘ notional income ’ is added in when working out your income level for every £250 ( or part thereof ) of savings over £3,000 .
11918	Any children 's savings are ignored , unless one of them has over £3,000 , in which case you ca n't get family credit for that child .
11919	The scheme is based on a so-called ‘ applicable amount ’ , currently £54.80 a week .
11920	Anybody whose income is less than this will get full family credit .
11921	The payments are based on set amounts : £33.60 for a lone parent or a couple : £23.30 for each child aged 18 : £16.35 for each child aged 16 or 17 : £12.90 for each child aged 11 to 15 , and £7.30 for each one up to 10 years of age .
11922	If your income is above £54.80 a week , 70 per cent of the additional amount is cut from the set payments .
11923	Sheila is a lone parent with two children , aged 13 and 15 .
11924	She works part-time , averaging 28 hours a week .
11925	After paying tax and national insurance she gets £75 a week take home pay .
11926	This is £20.20 above the £54.80 applicable amount , and 70 per cent of this is £14.14 .
11927	Her set amounts are £33.60 as a lone parent , plus £25.80 for the children .
11928	That totals £59.40 , but £14.14 is deducted , leaving her total family credit at £45.26 a week .
11929	Child benefit payments , one parent benefit , housing benefit , income support and mobility and attendance allowances are all ignored as incomes for the purposes of family credit .
11930	So Sheila 's actual income is £75 from earnings , plus £14.50 child benefit ( £7.25 each ) , £5.20 one parent benefit and £45.26 from Family Credit .
11931	Earnings are always taken net of tax and national insurance .
11932	For those who are weekly paid , normal earnings are estimated by looking at the last five weeks pay , or the last two months for the monthly paid .
11933	For the self-employed it is either the last 26 weeks or the last year 's set of accounts which are used .
11934	Self-employed child minders only have one third of their net earnings taken into account as income , the rest is ignored .
11935	Family credit is also available on unemployment benefit , although this is counted as income .
11936	Pam and Errol have two children , aged 13 and 16 .
11937	Errol is on unemployment benefit of £34.70 a week , while Pam is bringing home £75 a week .
11938	This adds up to £109.70 , some £54.90 above the applicable amount , and 70 per cent of that is £38.43 .
11939	Their set amount for family credit is £62.85 , from which £38.43 is deducted , leaving a final payment of £24.42 .
11940	With child benefit included their income has been increased from £124.20 to £148.62 a week .
11941	If one partner has been getting statutory sick or maternity pay for a continuous period of 13 weeks or more , this is counted as income .
11942	Otherwise these payments are ignored .
11943	Family credit lasts for 26 weeks at a time , then you will have to reapply .
11944	However , it will end sooner if someone else claims income support or family credit in respect of a child who was included in your family credit award .
11945	If you feel that your award is wrong in some way you can ask for the decision to be reviewed or make an appeal — details of how to do this are available from social security benefit offices .
11946	If you 're getting housing benefit this will be affected if you claim a family credit award , as your income will increase .
11947	In some cases this may make the prospect of an award less attractive .
11948	Some local authorities also assume you 're getting family credit , even if you have n't claimed it , and so reduce your housing benefit .

11966	Spending on information technology has also declined , demonstrating that the computer industry is no longer recession-proof .

11973	‘ Downsizing ’ simply means that firms are tending to buy smaller computers to do jobs which used to require big ones , and big computers are where IBM makes most of its money .
11974	Downsizing has been made possible by the growing power of the microprocessor and the new ‘ economies of small ’ .
11975	Given that microcomputer power costs a tenth of the price of minicomputer power , while minicomputer power costs a tenth of the price of mainframe power , a small shift in this direction can make a dramatic difference to revenues .
11976	Portable operating systems , such as Unix , are also a threat to IBM and other companies which once prospered on proprietary ones , such as Wang and Data General .
11977	Traditionally , computer manufacturers have used proprietary software to ‘ lock in ’ users , who would then find it impossible or prohibitively expensive , to move their applications to other manufacturers ' machines — or even , in IBM 's case , different machines from the same manufacturer .
11978	This strategy is being made obsolete by Unix , an ‘ open ’ operating system that runs on hundreds of different computers from hundreds of different manufacturers , from micros and minis through mainframes to supercomputers .
11979	Moving applications becomes relatively simple , and turns hardware into a commodity .
11980	Manufacturers can no longer charge according to some idea of ‘ value ’ but must compete on price and performance .
11981	This can have a dramatic effect on margins .
11982	Open networking provides the means for computers from different vendors to be connected together using OSI ( open systems interconnection ) standards .
11983	OSI enables all the different manufacturers to work to a common set of standards .
11984	Again this works against IBM , which is irrevocably committed to its own proprietary networking system , SNA .
11985	These changes are not just a matter of following technological devlopments , but reflect the way businesses are changing .
11986	Major firms like General Motors and Heinz no longer see themselves as machines needing only periodic maintenance to run forever .
11987	They are no longer isolated and no longer see computers as providing mainly internal services such as payroll and stock control .
11988	Instead , large corporations are becoming more like living organisms , continually changing and adapting .
11989	They must interact with the outside world , and networks of computers are the way to do it .
11990	Examples include electronic data interchange ( EDI ) — ordering stocks and materials and paying bills electronically , instead of using paper — factory automation and JIT ( just-in-time ) production systems .
11991	IBM wants to compete in all these markets and is apparently enthusiastic about AIX ( its version of Unix ) and OSI .
11992	But open systems are backed by governments and controlled by committees , which means IBM can not dominate or control them .
11993	Also by competing it risks cannibalising its own best profit sources : IBM selling an AS/400 mini is a triumph if the buyer would otherwise have chosen a DEC VAX , but a financial disaster for IBM if it replaces an IBM mainframe .
11994	Although one IBM manager recently got widespread publicity for pointing out that PCs were overtaking mainframes as IBM 's largest source of revenues , this is misleading .
11995	IBM 's revenues from mainframe processors in calendar 1988 may have been only about $12billion , but sales of peripherals ( $11billion ) , software ( $8billion ) and maintenance ( $7billion ) should be added to this .
11996	Perhaps two-thirds of IBM 's income and an estimated 75 per cent of profits are still tied up in this threatened area .
11997	There 's no way round that .
11998	As one IBMer said : ‘ You ca n't build a $60billion corporation out of selling $400 networking cards . ’

12214	New rules mean a set-back for army of casual workers .
12215	By Linda Lennard
12216	Unemployment benefit .
12217	NEW rules to be introduced from tomorrow will hit many part-time workers receiving unemployment benefit .
12218	Those who earn £43 a week or more will lose benefit for the whole of that week — even if they work only part of it and are unemployed for the remaining days .
12219	Only people who earn £12 or less in any week will escape having their entitlement affected at all .
12220	Anybody who earns between £12 and £43 in a given week may still be able to qualify for unemployment benefit on the days they are not working .
12221	However , they will have to satisfy unemployment benefit officers that part-time work is not their usual pattern , and they are just doing it while looking for full-time employment .
12222	In general , it has been accepted that people can take on part-time work in this way if it has not been their usual employment pattern .
12223	But adjudication officers may eventually claim that part-time employment is your normal pattern , and that you should not be entitled to benefit on the days you do n't work because you would not normally expect to be working anyway .
12224	This so-called ‘ full extent normal rule ’ has come under considerable criticism from the Court of Appeal downwards .
12225	The new rules coming in tomorrow effectively mean the end of the full extent normal rule for people earning £12 or less in a week .
12226	The government says the changes are interim measures and it intends to reconsider the whole question of the treatment of earnings received by people on unemployment benefit .
12227	If you do any part-time work while on unemployment benefit and your earnings do not affect your benefit entitlement , you will still have to meet the rest of the conditions for this benefit on the remaining days .
12228	These include a new stringent ‘ actively seeking work ’ test which was introduced this October , as well as showing that you are available for work the rest of the week .
12229	As well as earnings from part-time work , other income can affect your entitlement to unemployment benefit .
12230	If you are aged 55 or over and have a personal or occupational pension which is more than £35 per week , the rest will be deducted from your benefit .
12231	Money from a redundancy payment should not affect your right to this benefit .
12232	Also note that if your partner earns more than £21.40 the adult dependants increase will not be payable for her or him .

12244	Throughout the year we have all had to pay huge amounts for advertising and for fees to PR firms and City advisers .
12245	This has added insult to injury of a privatisation carried out against the wishes of the public .
12246	‘ The industry has been massively undersold .
12247	The price the Government has put on the water industry is a small fraction of the values of the assets shown in the prospectus . ’
12248	The 500,000 acres of land held by the water companies would be prey to ‘ massive exploitation . ’
12249	PAGE
12250	Next Thursday Chileans will go to the polls to elect a successor to General Pinochet , who has ruled with an iron fist since the overthrow of Allende in 1973 .
12251	Whoever wins will face a dilemma — whether to prosecute military personnel for human rights abuses .
12252	During the 1970s Andres Valenzuela , right , served in a death squad which hunted and killed Chilean Communists .
12253	Most were tortured before they died .
12254	Valenzuela now lives among other exiles in France .
12255	Iain Guest talked to him there Portrait of a torturer .
12256	NEXT Thursday 's elections will mark a red letter day for tens of thousands of Chileans who have been exiled by Pinochet 's harsh rule .
12257	Many are already eagerly making plans to return home .
12258	But for one Chilean exile , Andres Valenzuela , Thursday will be much like any other day — long , boring and lonely .
12259	It will pass in a succession of aimless walks and endless glasses of beer in the picturesque little French town where he has sought refuge .
12260	It 's only when you 've heard his extraordinary story that you realise this is no ordinary man .
12261	I found myself surreptitiously studying him .
12262	Does he face show courage and conviction — or does it betray guilt ?
12263	Are those eyes shifty , or merely tired ?
12264	Certainly , he seems too slight of stature to have handcuffed heavier men and hauled them up by their wrists to hang , agonisingly , from hooks .
12265	Too unsettled to have been a torturer .
12266	During the past 16 years , by conservative estimates , 782 Chileans have disappeared , another 2,000 have been killed , and several thousands have been tortured .
12267	Valenzuela took an active part in this dirty war .
12268	He served in a shadowy military death squad that kidnapped and murdered scores of Chileans .
12269	But he has also confessed , and this makes him special .
12270	Valenzuela could be a star witness for the prosecution in the event of any inquiry into human rights abuses by the next Chilean government .
12271	Torturer .
12272	The word is bald , impersonal .
12273	But what of the person behind the label ?
12274	How did Andres Valenzuela get sucked in , and what prompted his change of heart ?
12275	These were the questions I wanted to put when I sought him out in France .
12276	I 'm not sure I have all the answers .
12277	He was direct and helpful , but he also steered me away from his personal life .
12278	He knows that words , too , can wound .
12279	His disclosures have already caused several deaths , and every time he talks it reminds the world of his unsavoury past .
12280	Other Chilean exiles in France still find it hard to accept him .
12281	As he says , ‘ I have very few friends . ’
12282	How does a torturer get started ?
12283	Valenzuela 's experience suggest — disturbingly — that it could happen to anyone .
12284	He was born into a lower-class family in the small seaside village of Papudo where his father caught conger eels for the tourist restaurants .
12285	It was , remembers , Andres , a happy , uncomplicated upbringing .
12286	In April 1974 , seven months after the coup which brought Pinochet to power , he arrived at the Air Force base of Colina on the outskirts of Santiago to begin his two years of military service .
12287	He was just 18 .
12288	After three months at Colina the young recruit was posted to the Academy of Aerial War in an affluent Santiago suburb .
12289	Valenzuela 's dirty war was about to begin .
12290	He was assigned to what was vaguely described as ‘ guard duty , ’ warned not to talk about his work and taken down to the basement to start .
12291	‘ I was very , very frightened ’ he recalls .
12292	Blindfolded , handcuffed prisoners were crammed into dormitories and passages , many wearing Air Force uniforms .
12293	These officers had been loyal to Allende .
12294	The young conscript was broken in slowly .
12295	He did not attend torture personally , but he found his natural aversion to mistreating a defenceless person gradually being eroded .
12296	The prisoners in the basement were dehumanised , blindfolded , anonymous ‘ subversives ’ .
12297	It was in the War Academy that Valenzuela learned how to detain , interrogate , and exploit the fears of prisoners — while psychologists looked for weakness in the young draftees and weeded out those who seemed sentimental .
12298	Valenzuela himself was promoted from guard duty to acting as a back-up in kidnapping operations .
12299	These early months gave him a brutally clear idea of what lay ahead .
12300	He knew that kidnap and torture were a blatant violation of the Chilean military code and that under the same code he was entitled to register any reservations with a superior officer .
12301	But he never protested .
12302	Why ?
12303	‘ What could I have said ?
12304	That I was not in agreement ?
12305	I would have been killed . ’
12306	In Mid 1975 , the counter-intelligence services of the Navy , Air Force and Police linked up to form the ‘ Joint Command against Subversion ’ , and began working out of two suburban safe-houses , or ‘ nests ’ .
12307	The Command 's strength rarely exceeded 25 men , but they were carefully selected for their ferocity and reliability .
12308	The man who commanded the Air Force unit , Roberto Fuentes Morrison , was a fanatical anti-Communist known as ‘ Wally ’ .
12309	He was ruthless with anything short of total obedience .
12310	The Joint Command began to hunt down prominent Communists , and on August 28 , 1975 , they seized a Young Communist leader named Miguel Rodriguez Gallardo .
12311	Gallardo had pulled himself up from poverty by sheer force of personality , tapping the electricity lines that ran above the shanty town and reading Marx by the light .
12312	He was mercilessly tortured , blindfolded and trussed up in a cupboard for four months , but he refused to break .
12313	Valenzuela was fascinated by Gallardo 's willpower , and as their relationship changed Gallardo established a subtle ascendancy over his young captor .
12314	On one occasion , Valenzuela arrived in a torture room to find Gallardo hanging by handcuffs from a hook and whimpering .
12315	Valenzuela touched his arm : ‘ I 'll let you down . ’
12316	‘ Do n't , ’ replied Gallardo .
12317	‘ Wally might come in , and you 'd be in trouble .
12318	I 'll stick it out . ’
12319	One important Communist still eluding capture was Jose Weibel , Secretary General of the Young Communists , and the Joint Command decided to try and locate him through his brother Ricardo , a bus driver .
12320	Ricardo Weibel was seized and brought to the base for 12 days of rough treatment , before being released and sent home .
12321	Then an order came to pick up Weibel again ‘ I had to hide my dismay when Weibel was bought back without a blindfold — a sure sign that he was to be killed . ’
12322	Sure enough , soon afterwards Weibel and Gallardo were pushed into a van .
12323	VALENZUELA was told to burn their ID cards , wallets and spectacles .
12324	Before they left , Gallardo shook Valenzuela 's hand and thanked him for the cigarettes he had given him in captivity .
12325	It was a wrenching moment .
12326	‘ I admired Gallardo the most ’ , says Valenzuela .
12327	‘ He was brave until the very last moment . ’
12328	Valenzuela 's only real friend was another recruit named Bratti Cornejo who had been drafted at the same time .
12329	Within weeks of Gallardo 's murder , Valenzuela found himself taking part in Bratti 's execution .
12330	Bratti had been discovered spying for a rival security service .
12331	He was drugged , bundled into the boot of a car and driven to a canyon on the outskirts of Santiago .
12332	As Valenzuela took off Bratti 's handcuffs his friend murmured , ‘ It 's cold tonight ’ .
12333	Valenzuela choked out a reply and watched while Bratti was shot by ‘ Fifa ’ Palma Ramirez , one of the most savage officers .
12334	They pushed the body off the cliff , but it caught in bushes .
12335	Valenzuela , holding on to the killer 's hand , dislodged his friend 's corpse .
12336	‘ I looked down and thought he 'd let me fall too . ’
12337	The Joint Command began taking risks .
12338	Jose Weibel , Ricardo 's brother , was snatched off a bus in broad daylight while travelling with his family .
12339	The man who succeeded him as Secretary General of the Young Communists , Carlos Contreras Maluje , was picked up after putting up a struggle in the street .
12340	As people crowded round , Valenzuela and the others bundled Maluje , kicking and screaming , into a car .
12341	The injured man was taken back and beaten up before being taken off and killed .
12342	With this , the freewheeling murder came to an end .
12343	Maluje 's spirited resistance had provoked such an uproar that the muzzled Supreme Court issued a habeas corpus order to locate him — the first against the Air Force since 1973 .
12344	But did Valenzuela himself participate directly in torture ?
12345	He was certainly present on many occasions .
12346	Every detainee was tortured , irrespective of age , sex or background .
12347	Valenzuela admits to beating prisoners at the moment of their detention , hauling them to the torture rooms , watching them writhe and holding them down .
12348	He also handcuffed prisoners , swung them up on hooks and watched them dangle .
12349	All this constitutes torture under international law .
12350	But he also insists that his main task was to deliver the prisoner to the torturers , who were specialists in interrogation with long experience in the service .
12351	Not all the interrogators were veterans .
12352	The ferocious ‘ Wally ’ Fuentes Morrison only joined up after the 1973 coup .
12353	Bratti tortured .
12354	Even a prisoner named Carol Flores , who turned informant , tortured .
12355	Valenzuela himself was instructed in interrogation techniques .
12356	Whatever his personal misgivings , Valenzuela hid them well and when his compulsory military service ended he signed on for a permanent career in the Air Force .
12357	In 1978 , in an attempt to wipe the slate clean , Pinochet declared an amnesty to cover all human rights abuses since the coup .
12358	Valenzuela felt reassured .
12359	Between 1976 and 1983 , he rose steadily through a series of promotions and posts in Air Force security .
12360	Then in September 1983 , ‘ Wally ’ Fuentes Morrison let him know that his skills were once again required for a special operation .
12361	Several members of the left wing Revolutionary Movement , MIR , were hiding out in a residential safe-house .
12362	On the evening of September 7 a small army of security agents , including Wally and Valenzuela , began converging on the house .
12363	Around 9 pm they opened fire with a heavy machine gun .
12364	At the same time , Andres Valenzuela shot out the street lights .
12365	The attackers then called by loudhailer on those in the house to surrender .
12366	A young man came out with his hands in the air .
12367	Two agents ran up and shot him dead .
12368	As soon as the shooting stopped , Valenzuela was told to pull the body away from the house .
12369	He then went in and found the body of a young woman .
12370	By the time he had pulled the corpse out into the street , Valenzuela 's clothes were stained with blood .
12371	IT WAS a full year before he made the break — but eventually , on August 21 , 1984 , he went over to one of the more independent local magazines , Cauce , and asked for its leading journalist Monica Gonzalez .
12372	The resulting interview was heavy going for both of them .
12373	Monica had been a close friend of Ricardo and Jose Weibel .
12374	Now she was listening to their kidnapper .
12375	What she remembers most was his self-disgust and terror .
12376	Monica rang lawyers at the Vicariate of Solidarity , which had been set up by the Catholic Church in 1975 and was by now Chile 's leading human rights organization .
12377	The lawyers took Valenzuela off to record his testimony .
12378	A few days later , Valenzuela went underground .
12379	After several months in hiding he crossed into Argentina and left for France .
12380	Monica 's interview was published in December 1984 and its impact was swift and savage .
12381	First to suffer were the relatives of those who had been kidnapped by the Joint Command .
12382	They now knew the terrible truth , even though without a body they still could not mourn .
12383	They gave Valenzuela little credit for speaking out .
12384	The impact on the Vicariate of Solidarity was even more violent .
12385	The Valenzuela file had passed to Jose Manuel Parada , a senior Vicariate official .
12386	On March 29 1985 , Jose Manuel 's inquiry came to a brutal end .
12387	He was picked up with two other Communists .
12388	The following morning , the three bodies were found near Santiago airport , with the throats cut .
12389	Chilean justice was not totally intimidated .
12390	Judge Carlos Cerda from the Santiago Appeals Court was investigating the disappearance of several leading Communists and Valenzuela 's testimony was the first solid proof that the security forces had been involved in kidnapping .
12391	Cerda interviewed those named in his testimony , including Wally Fuentes Morrison , and then threw down the gauntlet to Pinochet .
12392	Ignoring Pinochet 's 1978 amnesty , he described the Joint Command as an ‘ illegal association ’ and charged 40 of those implicated with ‘ illegal deprivation of liberty . ’
12393	They included Andres Valenzuela .
12394	The judge 's colleagues in the Judiciary , however , had no wish to confront Pinochet .
12395	The Supreme Court charged Cerda himself with ‘ lack of discipline ’ , suspended him on half pay for two months , and replaced him by another judge who dutifully closed his case .
12396	Judge Cerda points out that the case remains technically open until he personally closes it .
12397	He strongly implies that this loophole could allow him to resume the case after elections , in which case Andres Valenzuela could be a key witness .
12398	If , that is , Valenzuela can ever return to Chile .
12399	This has been open to doubt since June 8 , 1989 when an extreme left-wing group pumped 20 bullets into Valenzuela 's former chief , ‘ Wally ’ Fuentes Morrison .
12400	Valenzuela 's testimony had confirmed Wally 's involvement in several brutal killings , and Valenzuela 's first reaction was that he had unwittingly taken yet another life .
12401	His second reaction was gut terror that his former comrades would come looking for him .
12402	Valenzuela insists he 's willing to return to Chile .
12403	‘ There is ’ , he says , ‘ a lot more to tell . ’
12404	By a strange twist of fate , the first Chilean to welcome Valenzuela to his new home in France was Castro , a ‘ Mirista ’ who was captured in broad daylight and stripped to his underwear back in December 1974 , while Valenzuela stood guard at the corner .
12405	Castro has swallowed his doubts and hired Valenzuela as a cook in his small restaurant .
12406	It is one of the few gestures of real friendship encountered by this lonely man in his long and tormented odyssey .
12407	Iain Guest is the reporter in next Sunday 's BBC-1 Everyman programme , Called To Account ( 10.20pm ) , which examines justice in Chile .
12408	Gallardo , the Young Communist leader who was tortured then killed - ‘ I admired him most ’ , says Valenzuela
12409	A Country Diary .
12410	NORTHUMBERLAND : Roe deer are among the most difficult wild creatures for humans to succour and rehabilitate .
12411	Abandoned fawns have been reared on a bottle , only to die within a few months .
12412	So it was interesting to hear this week from Mrs Bolton of Wildlife In Need in the north of our country that she has recently saved the life of a six-month old roe doe fawn .
12413	The little deer was seen staggering in a distressed and bloated condition , captured with difficulty and taken to a vet who pumped fermented corn from the stomach — presumably the fawn had gorged herself on pheasant feed .
12414	Mrs Bolton kept her in a pen where , despite remaining in a very frightened state , the little beast recovered and started eating small amounts of hay .
12415	After three days , when scouring had stopped , she was tagged , put in a sack and taken to a field which a neighbour was certain her siblings frequented .
12416	‘ It was wonderful to see her reaction , ’ said Mr Bolton .
12417	‘ She shot up the field and then paused , stood her ground although we were still quite close and suddenly began to eat grass . ’
12418	She knew that she had come home .
12419	A few days later the doe was seen in the company of her mother and twin sister .
12420	At present an agoraphobic shag is languishing at the wildlife centre and , despite every inducement , Mrs Bolton can not persuade him even to get his feet wet .
12421	She has five hedgehogs hibernating in mounds of leaves and a kestrel which was left on her doorstep with a damaged foot .
12422	It has been a bad autumn for birds of prey and five kestrels have been brought into the sanctuary in an emaciated condition .
12423	Worms are a staple diet and these have been in short supply due to the summer drought .
12424	VERONICA HEATH
12425	Divers dangers The dramatic rise in diving 's popularity has led to fears for the safety of people new to the sport .
12426	John Illman reports .
12427	THE spectacular beauty of coral is attracting an ever increasing number of people to scuba diving .
12428	Many Britons undergo training in the UK after trying the sport abroad and then continue diving in our colder UK waters .
12429	The British Sub Aqua Club ( BSAC ) has just reported a record-breaking year , with the number of dives off the UK coast estimated at about two million — 100 per cent up on the previous year .
12430	But medical diving experts are concerned that many newcomers to the sport are diving too deep , especially in the UK , exposing themselves to life-threatening injury from ‘ the bends ’ or decompression sickness .
12431	Writing in Diver Magazine , BSAC 's ‘ incidents adviser ’ , Chris Allen , warns : ‘ The statistics show that too many divers are still diving deeper than indicated by their abilities , ignoring commonsense recommendations or simply failing to plan their dives properly . ’
12432	The longer a diver remains under water and the greater the depth , the more nitrogen is absorbed .
12433	When pressure is reduced during ascent , this nitrogen must be slowly eliminated through breathing , or bubbles will form in the bloodstream , giving rise to the bends .
12434	A diver absorbing excessive nitrogen must ascend to a designated depth to reduce the pressure and remain there for a specified time for what is known as a ‘ decompression stop . ’
12435	But Allen warns : ‘ A number of cases of decompression sickness have resulted after required decompression stops have been missed due to divers running out of air towards the end of their dives . ’
12436	Some are diving to 50 metres or more .
12437	Surgeon Commander James Francis , senior medical officer ( diving medicine ) at the Institute of Naval Medicine , says : ‘ I would have thought that 30 metres was a reasonable depth for most sports divers .
12438	Below that your ‘ bottom time ’ — the time between leaving the surface and commencing your ascent — is so limited that it 's hardly worthwhile . ’
12439	Despite the dangers , BSAC , whose training is among the most rigorous in the world , insists that diving compares favourably with other sports .
12440	This year there were 12 fatalities linked to diving .
12441	BSAC spokesman Kendal McDonald claims that this compares with the 35 fatalities a year associated with angling , 39 with boating , and 44 with swimming .
12442	The club is pressing for recognition of decompression sickness as an NHS liability .
12443	Many health authorities have been refusing to pay for treatment , arguing that divers should take out decompression insurance .
12444	Treatment can cost anything from a few hundred pounds to up to £15,000 in exceptional circumstances .
12445	BSAC medical officer Dr Peter Wilmhurst , of St Thomas ' Hospital , London , says : ‘ Divers are entitled to treatment under the NHS Act in the same way as a skater who breaks a leg on the ice or a rider who breaks his back falling off a horse .
12446	It would be a false economy not to treat divers .
12447	If you have a diver with spinal bend , and you do n't recompress them , you have someone paralysed from the waist down .
12448	The cost to society of treating them is immense . ’

12450	Good sense and justice sought in immigration issue : .
12451	Queen 's Bench Division Regina v Immigration Appeal Tribunal , ex parte Rafique Before Mr Justice Simon Brown December 7 1989
12452	WHEN a man applies to come to the United Kingdom to marry a woman settled here , it is not necessary for him to be able to state specifically whether he intends to settle in this country forever or whether he wishes to marry and return to his own country .
12453	If an applicant is uncertain as to his plans after marriage , the entry clearance officer should treat it as an application for settlement , and consider whether all the requirements for settlement are satisfied .
12454	The facts .
12455	Abid Hussain , a Pakistani , is engaged to be married to Miss Rafique , a British citizen , and they want to be married in England .
12456	Mr Hussain was refused entry clearance to come to England , mainly because he could not say what were his long term intentions .
12457	When interviewed Mr Hussain said he had not decided whether , following marriage , he , or his fiancee , would wish to remain in England or return to Pakistan .
12458	The entry clearance officer ( ECO ) said he was not satisfied that the primary purpose of Mr Hussain 's intended marriage was not to obtain admittance to the UK .
12459	Mr Hussain appealed .
12460	The adjudicator concluded that Mr Hussain 's application was for a short-term stay and dismissed the appeal after hearing evidence from Miss Rafique that she had no intention of living in Pakistan .
12461	The immigration appeal tribunal said the onus was on an applicant to bring himself within the specific immigration rule , and if he was unable or unwilling to do so he could not expect to succeed .
12462	Mr Hussain appealed .
12463	The Rules .
12464	Rule 41 of the Statement of Changes in Immigration Rules ( HC 169 ) provides : ‘ A man seeking to enter the UK for marriage to a woman settled here and who intends to settle here thereafter ’ will be refused entry clearance unless the ECO is satisfied that it is not the primary purpose of the marriage to obtain admission to the UK .
12465	Under rule 17 a man may apply for entry clearance to the UK for marriage where he and his wife will leave the UK after the marriage .
12466	The decision .
12467	Mr Justice Simon Brown said that shortly before the tribunal came to its decision in this case a tribunal chaired by Professor Jackson took a different approach in a similar case , Syed Jabar Hussain Shah .
12468	That tribunal said that to force an applicant to state whether he intends to live here forever , or for a period of not less than six months , invites deceit and was somewhat removed from reality .
12469	That tribunal said that where there was uncertainty as to the duration of the stay it was proper to consider the application as if ordinary residence was contemplated .
12470	Mr Justice Simon Brown said he greatly preferred the approach adopted by Professor Jackson 's tribunal .
12471	It accorded with good sense and justice , and also properly reflected the important impact of the House of Lords ' decision in Shah v Barnet Borough Council [ 1983 ] 2 AC 309 upon the statutory definition of settlement for Immigration Act purposes .
12472	In Shah 's case Lord Scarman said , ‘ All that is necessary is that the purpose of living where one does [ eg , for education , employment , health , family or merely love of the place ] has a sufficient degree of continuity to be properly described as settled ’ .
12473	Why should an applicant , who must in any event be prepared to satisfy the primary purpose test , be worse off because he contemplates the possibility of a relatively short stay in the UK than one who had the fixed intention of permanent UK residence ?
12474	It was logical to construe the phrase ‘ intending to settle ’ in rule 41 differently from the contrasting phrase ‘ admitted for settlement ’ which appears elsewhere .
12475	There was no possible good reason why rule 41 should not encompass those genuinely undecided as to their long term ambitions .
12476	Accordingly the tribunal in Mr Hussain 's case fell into error .
12477	They categorised all applicants , genuine or otherwise , who were unable or unwilling to specify their long term intentions , as necessarily falling outside the ambit of the rules and thus doomed to inevitable failure when applying for entry clearance .
12478	The essence of what Mr Hussain said was that following the marriage he would remain in England on a settled basis as a married man for just so long as his wife dictated .
12479	And for good measure , it should be noted that the ECO long ago expressed his own conclusion that settlement in the UK was the intention in this case .
12480	The tribunal 's decision was quashed and the appeal restored for hearing as an appeal against a refusal of entry clearance under rule 41 .
12481	The crucial issue still to be determined was whether the primary purpose of the marriage was to obtain admission to the UK .
12482	If the immigration authorities concluded that Mr Hussain 's assertion that he was undecided as to his long term intentions was pretended rather than genuine , clearly that would weigh against him in the primary purpose issue .
12483	That was a general possibility and there was no reason to suppose that that would be the conclusion .
12484	Appearances : Ramby De Mello instructed by Bean McDonald , Birmingham for Mr Hussain and Miss Rafique ; John Laws instructed by the Treasury Solicitor for the Home Secretary .
12485	Shiranikha Herbert barrister
12486	Warren Tute : .
12487	A MAN of many parts , Warren Tute was thought by those who knew him only slightly to be a good raconteur and a popular member of the Garrick .
12488	However , he was a writer with a number of plays to his credit , none of them great successes but all worthy of note .
12489	After leaving the Navy he also wrote much fiction , and as a novelist in the early post-war years his first published work , The Felthams ( 1950 ) , was thought highly of and his bestseller , The Rock ( 1957 ) , served to establish him as a writer of more than a little promise .
12490	With such biographical works as Admiral Cochrane , Earl of Dundonald ( 1965 ) , and his absorbing record of those 1940 operations involving the French fleet , The Deadly Stroke ( 1973 ) , he broke into non-fiction too .
12491	Tute was educated at Wrekin College , joined the Navy as a paymaster-cadet and served his apprenticeship throughout the thirties , becoming secretary to the Captain of the Fleet , Mediterranean .
12492	He took part inthe naval landings in North Africa , helped plan further landings in Sicily , and towards the war 's end he became deputy secretary to the chief of combined operations .
12493	After the war , Tute worked in a variety of jobs where his skills as both sailor and writer were much in demand — broadcasting , film-making , and as script editor for London Weekend Television .
12494	He also had a finger in theatrical production and I first knew him when he was associated with Elspeth Cochrane 's literary management during the 1960s .
12495	One of his most enterprising productions was Little Mary Sunshine in 1962 .
12496	Happy and novel and thoroughly charming , it gave several talented artists their first big chance , going on to bigger , if hardly better things .
12497	None was so sweet ( without being cloying ) as that burst of theatrical sunshine at the Comedy Theatre in the West End during a fatal summer heatwave which put paid to the show 's box office takings as well as Warren 's plucky managerial debut .
12498	His tenacious belief in the venture by keeping it running cost him heavy personal financial loss and his ‘ nursing ’ of this satire on operetta that has rarely been equalledis largely forgotten ( but not by me ) .
12499	Peter Cotes Warren Tute born February 22 , 1914 ; died November 26 , 1989 .
12500	Edoardo Amaldi .
12501	Ragazzi of distinction : .
12502	IN December , 1943 , the men working feverishly to create the first American atomic bomb sent a team of ‘ spooks ’ to Naples .
12503	One of their main assignments was to contact Edoardo Amaldi , a physicist thought to be in hiding near Rome .
12504	Six months later , the day before Rome 's liberation by the Allies , Amaldi was found .
12505	He was interviewed by Moe Berg , then one of the most famous baseball players in America .
12506	Berg was also an agent of the Office of Strategic Services , which was later to give birth to the CIA .
12507	His job was to convince Amaldi to pack his bags because there was a ship waiting at Naples to take him to the United States .
12508	Amaldi 's presence there had been sought by two other Italian colleagues , also physicists .
12509	His mentor , Enrico Fermi , later to be called ‘ the father of the bomb ’ , and Emilio Segre ( who died in California earlier this year ) .
12510	Amaldi dodged the American invitation , perhaps because ( with Rome liberated ) Fermi 's mantle in physics had fallen on his young shoulders and there were younger minds to teach .
12511	He wore that mantle well at Rome University until his retirement in 1978 .
12512	But Amaldi never really retired nor grew old .
12513	He kept regular hours in the university 's physics building , spoke at scientific meetings this year in Moscow and Washington .
12514	As President of the Accademia Nazionale dei Lincei he had delivered the welcoming address on Tuesday to a symposium of scientists .
12515	He then ordered a car to call for him the next morning for a similar occasion and was felled by a stroke while waiting for the lift .
12516	Amaldi grew up in a small town in Lombardy , and took his doctorate in physics from Rome at the remarkably early age of 21 .
12517	In 1929 , he became one of the ragazzi di Via Panisperna — the street where Fermi 's ‘ kids ’ carried out their own experiments under the master in their own under-financed lab .
12518	Emilio Segre was one kid , and Bruno Pontecorvo , later to defect from Britain to the Soviet Union , another .
12519	It is interesting to note that the ‘ pope ’ — as the kids called Fermi — ‘ because he 's always right ’ , was only seven years older than Amaldi .
12520	Amaldi astounded his group in October 1934 with his discovery that by slowing down , rather than accelerating , neutrons , he could provoke intense nuclear reactions .
12521	He held a chair in physics from 1937 until his retirement publishing more than 150 papers on atomic and nuclear physics .
12522	He was awarded honorary degrees by Algiers , Glasgow and Oxford .
12523	He became a founder , and active executive , of the European Centre for Nuclear Research in Geneva .
12524	I had the pleasure of two long talks last year with Professor Amaldi about his knowledge of what the German physicists were doing with their atoms during the war years .
12525	Apart for his incongruously white hair , Amaldi seemed to have the mental lucidity and expected energy of a man half his age .
12526	His modesty , considering his world-wide fame in his field , was endearing .
12527	I knew almost nothing about physics but we shared some jokes about the Rome telephone system .
12528	In 1949 , Amaldi wrote to the Italian prime minister asking for permission to produce and sell sealing wax for letters , ‘ so that we may raise needed funds for our physics lab ’ .
12529	The reply came from an under-secretary who said that the present funding was considered adequate and the commercial undertaking would be ill-advised .
12530	It was signed by Giulio Andreotti , the present prime minister .
12531	George Armstrong Edoardo Amaldi , born Carpaneto Piacentino September 5 , 1908 ; died Rome , December 5 , 1989 .
12532	In the US , workers can now lose their jobs through drug tests .
12533	Will the same procedure be introduced here ?
12534	Richie Denenberg reports Putting jobs on the line .
12535	BUILDING work on a new county jail in Florida was falling woefully behind schedule , despite the critical need for additional space to house the many arrested as suspected drug offenders .
12536	Pressed to account for the delay , an embarrassed local official explained that the project was lagging because too few construction workers could pass the drug test required of all job seekers .
12537	The Florida county 's ironic predicament illustrates the extent to which drug testing is relied upon by some US employers to screen the workforce .
12538	The growing propensity to sample bodily fluids for contraband chemicals has engendered a bitter legal struggle over an employee 's right of privacy , a conflict which could spread to Europe along with fear of ‘ crack . ’
12539	For many workers , the ability to survive a drug test , most commonly a urinalysis for illicit chemicals such as cannabis and cocaine , is becoming a prerequisite to getting and holding a job .
12540	On orders from the White House , perhaps as many as a million federal government emloyees are now subject to testing .
12541	Wielding its regulatory stick , Washington is compelling the aviation , rail and trucking industries to test thousands of pilots , train crews and lorry drivers .
12542	A survey by the US Department of Labor revealed that about a fifth of private-sector workers , mainly employees of large corporations , are already subject to testing .
12543	Job applicants are spurned if they register ‘ positive ’ on a test , often without learning the reason for their rejection .
12544	Successful applicants may be subjected to surprise random testing once they are hired -names of those who must provide a urine specimen are picked in a computerised lottery .
12545	Others are tested when an industrial accident occurs , on the theory that it creates a ‘ reasonable suspicion ’ of drug impairment , even though faulty equipment or poor weather conditions may more plausibly account for the mishap .
12546	Still others are tested if they apply for promotion to positions which are deemed ‘ sensitive . ’
12547	Refusing to be tested or coming up positive usually results in immediate sacking .
12548	Many unfair dismissal hearings centre on the arcane testimony of forensic chemists , toxicologists and psychopharmacologists ( specialists in mood-altering substances ) .
12549	The testing boom has been resisted vigorously by civil liberties groups and trade unions , who view this aspect of the ‘ war on drugs ’ as a frontal assault on a worker 's dignity and entitlement to due process .
12550	The obligation to urinate on demand offends many employees , particularly when an offical monitor — given the Orwellian title of ‘ Collection Site Person ’ in government regulations — stands by to guard against deceptive practices .
12551	Urine advertised as free of detectable drugs is on offer by mail-order to anxious test takers , who could try to substitute it for their own .
12552	Last spring , the US Supreme Court dealt the unions a blow by ruling , in a suit brought by treasury employees and rail workers , that for critical occupations ( such as a customs agent ) testing does not curtail constitutional rights .
12553	Applying a balancing test , the court held that the danger posed by drug abuse outweighed the individual 's expectation of privacy .
12554	Despite that setback , opponents strive to contain the spread of testing through further litigation .
12555	An argument often made in their briefs , against random testing in particular , is that it reverses the normal presumption of innocence : an employee is deemed guilty unless he can prove himself innocent by producing ‘ clean ’ urine .
12556	Unlike the familiar blood alcohol tests in motoring cases , urinalysis does not demonstrate that the employee is impaired by drugs .
12557	It merely detects residues of drugs ingested as much as weeks in the past , when the worker may well have been off-duty or on holiday .
12558	An official of the American Civil Liberties Union has protested : ‘ Firing people who come to work sober because of their condition on Saturday night is of debatable value . ’
12559	The civil libertarians argue that testing permits the employer to delve deeply into an employee 's personal life ; a specimen can be analysed , without the subject 's knowledge , to reveal confidential medical conditions , such as epilepsy or pregnancy .
12560	Drug testing also may disproportionally victimise members of racial minority groups whose subcultures sanction casual marijuana smoking , reversing much of the progress that has been made in eliminating employment discrimination .
12561	AKEY ISSUE in the litigation is the accuracy of the analytical technology .
12562	Testing has created a gold rush for the ‘ diagnostics industry ’ , the largely unregulated private laboratories in which boxes of specimen jars , resembling crates of milk bottles , are processed in assembly-line fashion .
12563	Errors sometimes occur , in part because an innocuous substance may trigger a positive .
12564	Poppy seeds sprinkled on bread as a flavouring have a disconcerting tendency to react chemically in the same way as the extract of the opium poppy , so that a worker could be mistaken for a heroin user because of what he ate for breakfast .
12565	The government 's own Center for Disease Control discovered serious reporting errors when quality verification samples were posted to a number of laboratories as an experiment .
12566	Although the government has since promulgated guidelines to standardise analytical methods , doubts remain about whether laboratories can be relied upon not to make technical and clerical mistakes which could result in someone 's discharge .
12567	When mistakes are made , they can prompt complex law suits .
12568	An electricity generating company in California sued a laboratory which failed to properly document its analysis ; the company was trying to recover from the laboratory the costs of settling a suit for unfair dismissal brought by an employee who lost her job because of the test .
12569	Appearing as witnesses in court , some physicians have suggested that it is foolhardy to jeopardise a person 's livelihood because of a laboratory report when the worker appears to be performing his job normally .
12570	No doctor would order surgery or other treatment on the basis of a single test result , they point out , without corroborating clinical evidence .
12571	Job-related performance testing , such as use of flight simulators to check the condition of pilots , has been suggested as a preferable substitute for the drug hunt .
12572	There is a theory that even if drug testing is flawed , it at least deters drug use .
12573	Yet addiction specialists scoff at the notion that someone who already faces death through overdose or through contracting Aids from hypodermic needles is likely to change his behavour because of a drug test .
12574	And , although the Supreme Court upheld testing of customs agents , a few members of the bench doubted that a drug-imbibing agent would be deterred by a test if he was not already fearful , as one put it , that he ‘ may be shot dead in unequal combat with unimpaired smugglers . ’
12575	TESTING for a short list of illicit drugs has been labelled as myopic , since the working population as a whole tends to abuse a vast pharmacopoeia of legal but impairing substances , many of them heavily promoted by distilleries and pharmaceutical firms .
12576	A consumer group recently forced the withdrawal of a medical advertisement which invited doctors to prescribe tranquilizers for air traffic controllers suffering from job stress as they pore over their radar scopes .
12577	The addiction specialists urge that the emphasis be shifted to eliminating underlying conditions , such as job stress and tedium , against which workers often seek to medicate themselves .
12578	Rather than focusing on a few substances which are painted in lurid colours , the specialists say , the goal should be a workplace free of compulsive chemical use of all kinds .
12579	Since testing is typically used not to facilitate treatment of addicted workers but to sack them — a process sardonically referred to as ‘ dismissal therapy ’ — the upshot could be a ‘ recriminalisation ’ of addiction .
12580	That would undo decades of effort to have chemical dependency recognised as a treatable disorder rather than as a moral lapse deserving of punishment .
12581	Even though drug testing has attracted the most controversy , it is merely part of a broad movement in America toward a Darwinian worker-selection policy , which has been dubbed ‘ employment of the fittest . ’
12582	Employees are routinely subjected to psychological screening and polygraph tests to evaluate their honesty .
12583	Character is probed by handwriting analysts .
12584	Genetic screening , to determine if the worker 's chromosomes render him vulnerable to occupational illness , looms on the horizon .
12585	Multiple layers of screening , much of it of dubious scientific validity , may become a routine feature of working life unless restraints are imposed by law , as some states have begun to do .
12586	While it approved some types of drug testing , the Supreme Court did leave the anti-testing forces a glimmer of hope for ultimate legal containment .
12587	It held that in principle a drug test is a ‘ search ’ within the meaning of the Fourth Amendment in the Bill of Rights .
12588	Since the amendment bans ‘ unreasonable searches and seizures , ’ the possibility remains that a test may be found unreasonable if the job is so non-critical that public needs fail to outweigh individual privacy interests .
12589	Drug testing opponents may also take comfort from the surprising dissent by arch-conservative Justice Antonin Scalia .
12590	He disparaged the customs service testing programme as mere display , a gesture of solidarity with the President 's anti-drug campaign .
12591	Sacrificing civil liberties , Justice Scalia sneered , ‘ can not be the means of making a point . ’
12592	R. V. Denenberg , a former editor at the New York Times , is the author of Understanding American Politics ( Fontana Press ) .
