20130	Although the eugenic risk ( that the child of an incestuous relationship between father — daughter or brother — sister will have congenital defects ) was known at the time and was probably a factor , most of the arguments of the reformers were based on the protection of children from sexual exploitation .
20131	Those arguments have great force today , as increasing evidence of child sexual abuse within the family comes to that power to lead a daughter into sexual activity from a relatively early age .
20132	All kinds of pressure may be exerted on the child to keep quiet about the behaviour , with sometimes disastrous effects on his or her emotional development .
20133	Indeed , the primacy of this anti-exploitation rationale over eugenic reasons makes it desirable to extend the offence to cover adopted children as well as blood-relationships .
20134	The offence of incest is committed by a man who has sexual intercourse with a person whom he knows to be his granddaughter , daughter , sister or mother , and by a woman aged 16 or over who permits her grandfather , father , brother , or son to have sexual intercourse with her .
20135	The first thing to notice about this definition is that , like the offence of rape , it is restricted to ‘ sexual intercourse ’ .
20136	In the context of incest this is even less defensible — first , because eugenic reasons no longer provide the main grounds for criminalization ; and second because the primary rationale of punishing the sexual exploitation of children within the family applies no less to other serious sexual behaviour , such as oral and anal sex .
20137	Surely the offence of incest should cover all cases of vaginal or anal penetration or penetration involving the penis .
20138	Another feature of the offence is that it applies irrespective of the ages of the parties ( save that a woman can not commit the offence of ‘ permitting ’ intercourse unless she is aged 16 or over ) .
20139	Thus the crime of incest covers sexual relations by mature adults , in situations where the rationale of punishing exploitation of the young should no longer apply .
20140	One question , therefore , is whether the age should be reduced to 16 , which is the general age of consent for sexual activity .
20141	There might appear to be an argument in favour of consistency here , but it is surely eclipsed by the need to recognize that many children remain dependent on their parents until they are at least 18 .
20142	Indeed , the CLRC recommended that the age should be no lower than 21 .
20143	Another issue is whether brother — sister incest should remain criminal where both parties are aged 18 or over : when sentencing , the courts treat this as a much less serious form of the offence than father — daughter incest , and a majority of the CLRC accepted that brother — sister incest should cease to be an offence when both parties are aged 21 or over .
20144	The reasoning behind this proposal seems to be that the two parties are adult , and any exploitation deriving from the family tie seems no more likely than in other adult relationships .
20145	However , adulthood begins at 18 rather than 21 , and once again we have an example of a desire to shield those aged under 21 which may actually lead to the penalization of some brothers and sisters of that age .
20146	8.8 PARAMETERS OF THE LAW ON SEXUAL ASSAULT
20147	It is evident from this survey of English law on sexual assault that the parameters are open to considerable argument .
20148	Rules of antiquity ( such as the definition of rape , and the marital exemption ) , of modernity ( such as the definition of incest ) , and of recent creation ( such as the doctrine of mistake in rape ) are being called into question .
20149	There can be little doubt that the administration of criminal justice has paid insufficient attention to problems of sexual abuse over the years , and recent improvements in police procedures and in services for victims are to be welcomed .
20150	The difficult issue is how far this movement should be taken : changes which make it easier to convict men of sexual assault on women , or parents of the sexual abuse of children , can not be welcomed unless one has a clear conception of the rights of defendants as well as the rights of victims .
20151	It is one thing to maintain that victims of sexual assault have in the past suffered oppressive questioning by the police and oppressive cross-examination in court .
20152	It is quite another thing to suggest that it is therefore proper to place higher burdens of proof on defendants , and to restrict the presentation of the defence .
20153	Each of these proposals deserves careful examination from both points of view .
20154	The starting-point must be the empirical evidence of the effects of sexual assaults .
20155	These are variable , of course , but in many cases there are severe psychological after-effects — trauma , fear , and mistrust — which deeply affect the victim 's ability to lead a normal life for some time to come .
20156	It is not suggested that each offence should be ranked according to the seriousness of its after-effects on the particular victim — although there is an argument for assuming that young victims will be particularly damaged by unwanted sexual experiences , and therefore for regarding such offences as more serious .
20157	To transfer this judgment of seriousness into desirable legal responses is no easy matter , however , for two powerful reasons .
20158	First , children might refrain from reporting or at least giving evidence if they know that a substantial prison sentence for a member of their family is the probable outcome .
20159	Second , defendants might defend cases more vigorously , causing greater trauma to child witnesses , if substantial imprisonment is probable .
20160	It can therefore be argued that , serious as the offence usually is , a policy of non-custodial treatment might be preferable in view of the effects on child victims .
20161	So far as ranking the relative seriousness of sexual assaults is concerned , however , full account should be taken of the psychological effects of such offences .
20162	Above all , one must avoid any tendency to equate the degree of harm with the degree of physical injury in a particular case , since the psychological harm may be far more severe .
20163	This chapter has dealt chiefly with the non-consensual offences , and this is important , because it is the absence of consent which is the crucial factor in many cases of sexual assault .
20164	Such offences attack the principle of freedom of choice in sexual matters , and this , together with the punishment of those who exploit the young , the mentally handicapped , and those for whom they have responsibility , should form the bedrock of the scheme of offences .
20165	This is not the place to embark upon detailed discussion of possible schemes for grading sexual assaults , but questions have been raised about the exclusion from the English offence of rape of oral and anal intercourse and penetration of the vagina by other objects .
20166	There is evidence to suggest that victims of these other forms of serious sexual assault regard them as no less serious than rape ( narrowly defined ) .
20167	There is a strong argument for extending the offence of rape to cover these other sexual indignities , or for restructuring the law so that there are degrees of sexual assault .
20168	The sentencing decision in Billam ( 1986 ) marks out some of the more serious varieties of sexual assault , and this could be used as a basis for introducing a new scheme of three or four graded offences : there are precedents for this in other countries .
20169	One approach would be to have first-degree sexual assault defined so as to include penetration involving the penis , vagina , or anus , together with the threat or infliction of grievous bodily harm ; then a second-degree offence of the same nature involving a threat or infliction of actual bodily harm ; and then a third-degree offence covering all other sexual assaults involving penetration , and a fourth offence to cover indecent assaults not involving penetration .
20170	The CLRC did give serious consideration to dividing indecent assault into two grades , so the idea of grading is not entirely alien to England .
20171	One argument sometimes raised against it is that it would lead to plea-bargaining , and thus to offenders escaping with lesser convictions and lesser sentences .
20172	The fact is that this is a prominent feature of the existing law , in which there are only two major offences ( rape and indecent assault ) and in which some 42 per cent of those charged with rape have a plea of guilty to indecent assault accepted by the court .
20173	A more refined gradation of offences could not be worse in this respect , and might improve the fairness of the labels and sentences imposed on sexual offenders .
20174	One other consequence of a fresh gradation of sexual offences might be that they would cease to be gender-specific : there are some strange inconsistencies in the law at present , and it is not at all difficult to draft offences which might be committed by males or females against males or females .
20175	One feature of the discussion in this chapter has been to challenge the use of the concepts of consistency and ‘ inexorable logic ’ as unanswerable standards of appraisal of the law .
20176	This is not to suggest that consistency is an unworthy value : the argument is rather that there is a need to decide upon the categories to which the argument of consistency is being applied , and above all to recognize that simple resort to the allegation of inconsistency might serve to conceal the conflict between a number of social interests or principles .
20177	One example is the doctrine of mistake in rape : it might appear to be ‘ inexorable logic ’ that if the offence of rape is only committed where D knew that the woman was not consenting or was reckless as to her non-consent , a mistaken belief that she was consenting would lead to an acquittal .
20178	The inexorable logic does not , however , establish that the result is morally or socially desirable .
20179	There is a powerful argument that as far as sexual behaviour is concerned , an area in which consent makes the difference between gross violation and shared pleasure , and in which physical proximity makes it relatively easy to ask about consent , the law should in effect impose a duty to enquire .
20180	This would be done by limiting exculpatory mistakes to those based on reasonable grounds .
20181	It would partly alter the definition of rape or serious sexual assault ; it would introduce an element of negligence liability ; and it would also make D liable for an omission .
20182	But all those changes could be justified out of respect for the principle of freedom of choice in sexual matters , particularly where the enquiry is so straightforward .
20183	A similar argument could be mounted in relation to mistakes about age in the offences against girls and boys under 16 : the basic principle of fairness to defendants underpins the subjective requirement of fault , but there is also the social policy against exploitation of the young and vulnerable .
20184	This social policy might support a duty to enquire about age wherever there might be room for doubt , and the ease of compliance ( because of the inevitable physical proximity of the parties ) again favours the requirement .
20185	In practice , there might be situations of doubt ; a man might claim that there was nothing to alert him to the girl 's age ( e.g. a 15-year-old girl , who looks much older , soliciting in a street with other prostitutes ) .
20186	Moreover , if the criminal law is to impose duties of these kinds , it should publicize them widely , so as to ensure compliance with the principle of legality .
20187	The point of this argument is not to maintain that there would be no practical problems , but to demonstrate that there are weighty issues of principle on both sides .
20188	Appeal to ‘ inexorable logic ’ or consistency can not conclude the argument : it over-simplifies the issues .
20189	One policy , already mentioned , which should continue to shape the law of sexual offences is the criminalization of those who exploit the young and vulnerable .
20190	This is achieved through special offences and through rules invalidating apparent consent given by those under 16 , and it is supported by the Tyrrell rule against convicting a participant who falls within the class protected by the offence concerned .
20191	The relevant ages of consent in English law vary : 16 seems to be the general age , but the offence of gross indecency with or towards children only applies where the child is under 14 , and the age of consent for homosexual offences is 21 and the recommendation is to lower it only to 18 .
20192	Once again , consistency is a proper starting-point for critical appraisal , but it is important to examine any special circumstances attendant on particular offences .
20193	For example , is there any substance in the claim that young men of 16 and 17 are more vulnerable , socially and psychologically , than young women of a similar age ?
20194	Certainly there appears to be some sense in restricting any changes in the law of incest so that it continues to be an offence for a parent or grandparent to have sexual relations with a child aged 16 or 17 , because children of that age are often dependent and living at home , and so the conditions for exploitation are still present at that age .
20195	Once again , the policy of using the law against those who indulge in sexual exploitation of the vulnerable may conflict with the ‘ logic ’ of overall consistency in age-limits , and this conflict must be acknowledged and confronted .

20392	City Comment : John Smith prepares for leap in the dark
20393	JOHN SMITH is preparing to launch the biggest tax assault ever on middle income families while claiming that he does not know what the effect of his tax hike will be on incentives , confidence or on the economy .
20394	Asked a few pertinent questions on Thursday 's Question Time television programme , he was reduced to mumbling about an academic study by a ‘ distinguished ’ Stirling University economist .
20395	Sadly , this guru died before passing on any decisive conclusion .
20396	The man who hopes to be Chancellor next week can not surely be preparing a leap in the dark .
20397	If his taxes did deter hard work , the economy would wilt , jobs would be lost and he and his colleagues would run short of the tax revenue for financing their favourite causes .
20398	Nobody would win and his tax victims would suffer in vain .
20399	Mr Smith implicitly recognises the disincentive effect .
20400	He has been careful to confine his biggest tax penalties to those ‘ trapped ’ salaried employees who can not substitute leisure for work , while giving the self-employed special dispensation from higher National Insurance contributions .
20401	This suggests he is worried that those who can might rather walk the dog or paint the house than work for miminal benefit .
20402	Yet Mr Smith is not only proposing to raise tax in one go by more than anyone has ever dared to before but also concentrating the effect on a relatively small group .
20403	This will cause economic disruption comparable with a hike in oil prices or interest rates .
20404	The Keynesian economists on whom Mr Smith relies claim that the impact of his redistributive taxes will be negligible , since the money taken from the better off will be redistributed to lower earners .
20405	Since total income is unchanged , these apologists see little reason to worry about the sectoral and regional effects , claiming that consumption will hardly change .
20406	This is the conclusion reached by the National Institute of Economic &amp; Social Research and London Business School .
20407	But Mr Smith should not put too much trust in their findings .
20408	He will probably find his Treasury advisers are far less sanguine : the Treasury believes that the same factors which produced the late 1980s ' consumer boom are now working in reverse , with falling confidence and asset values undermining consumption though incomes are relatively buoyant .
20409	Mr Smith should listen .
20410	City Comment : Homeowner will be one who suffers
20411	THERE is no need for Mr Smith to impose taxes on capital or on financial institutions though : his policies look set to do their damage by knocking the most valuable asset owned by most voters — their homes .
20412	House prices , already up to one-fifth below their peak , look more likely to fall far further under a Labour government than to revive .
20413	Good news for first-time buyers ?
20414	Not if a month later their house is worth less than they paid .
20415	Nor is it good news for the majority of people who already own-especially those who became first-time buyers over the past four years and whose complete capital has been wiped out : more than a million such people are probably technically bankrupt but need not admit it so long as they keep paying their mortgage .
20416	Such people are effectively under house arrest .
20417	They can not move until values again exceed the size of their loan .
20418	Those one step up the housing ladder may have had more equity in their home to absorb falling values , but they can not move either , unless those former first-time buyers can trade up .
20419	True , it is the people at the bottom of the ladder and below it who benefit from Mr Smith 's thin tax cuts but £100 a year helps little — and the saving would be more than eliminated by an upward move in mortgage rates .
20420	The majority of owners are above average earners , however , and if higher taxes reduce take-home pay , they will find it harder to take on larger loans .
20421	Prices and values can not be higher than what people can pay — which means , how much people can borrow — and lenders , belatedly learning prudence , are no longer willing to give the high multiples of gross income they did in the 1980s or the high proportion of price .
20422	All this will combine to keep the lid on prices .
20423	But on top of this mathematical restraint on prices there is the confidence factor .
20424	Who wants to buy a home if the mortgage costs may rise , pay is set to fall and values look like following ?
20425	As neither political party can cut unemployment overnight , that fear will continue to discourage potential purchasers and add to the tally of repossessions which is flooding the market with unwanted homes .
20426	Indeed , the financial institutions would be hit by a continued slip in house prices .
20427	Potential purchasers can willingly stay out of the market and owners can stay put , but lenders — and the insurance companies which share the losses — will face yet further provisions as more repossessed homes are sold at a loss .
20428	Mr Smith must learn that hitting the pay packet hits the housing market , and that hits the institutions .
20429	There are enough problems for the occupier of 11 Downing Street without adding a crisis at the banks or building societies .
20430	City Comment : Time to come down hard on ‘ softing ’
20431	‘ BEST-EXECUTION' — an adviser or broker dealing on the best available terms — was one of the pillars on which the Financial Services Act was built six years ago .
20432	Yesterday the Securities &amp; Investments Board , the champion of that Act , came perilously close to removing the pillar by allowing stockbrokers ' soft-commissions practices to continue .
20433	It would be easy to dismiss ‘ softing ’ as an esoteric corner of the stock market which could be ignored , if it did not account for one deal in every six .
20434	Softing involves a broker supplying technical equipment such as information screens or research to an institutional investor who in return guarantees business for the broker .
20435	Some regard it as so close to bribery it should be banned .
20436	Independent soft-commission brokers regard it as an acceptable method of payment so long as they deal at the best price .
20437	But even they complain at brokers who buy shares from market-makers in the same ownership group , irrespective of whether the sister company offers the best price .
20438	Last year the Securities &amp; Investment Board , in the latest of several consultation papers , suggested that brokers should tie officially to market-makers .
20439	Yesterday the board announced that , after protests , there will be no rule change-because unofficial ties work so well without any change .
20440	It is a compromise solution which leaves the best-execution pillar swaying precariously .

20552	Family Money-Go-Round : Plastic path to cheaper travelling
20553	By IAN COWIE
20554	AS THE political parties ' election campaigns grind into their final week , many peoples ' thoughts are turning to Easter holidays and plans to get away from it all-assuming they can still afford it , that is .
20555	Whether you intend a five-star sojourn in the Bahamas or a fortnight under canvas in Calvados you can trim costs by choosing the form of travel money which best suits your needs .
20556	Most holidaymakers still opt for travellers ' cheques which are no longer the cheapest means of funding trips abroad .
20557	Automatic Teller Machine ( ATM ) cards , or other forms of plastic which may already be in your pocket , cost less and serve just as well , provided you do not stray too far from the beaten track .
20558	There are now 71,000 ATM machines worldwide , providing local currency to those with Link or Plus ATM cards issued by a wide range of British banks and building societies .
20559	This method of funding travel has the great advantage of allowing your money to earn interest until the moment you need the cash and it is free of charge .
20560	A spokesman for the Link network , which trades as Plus abroad , said : ‘ Cardholders from every other part of the world have to pay a transaction charge to cover the cost of the service but , interestingly enough , United Kingdom-based corporate members have decided not to charge their customers .
20561	A growing number of people are coming to realise this is a cheap and efficient way to access money abroad , just as they already do on the high street at home . ’
20562	Some banks ' machines , particularly in Spain , may levy a small charge but a warning should always appear on screen before this is deducted .
20563	The system funds itself by operating on the Royal Bank of Canada 's over-the-counter exchange rates which are not as fine as those obtained by the institution itself .
20564	And , while there are Link/Plus ATMs from Guam to Canada and from Japan to America , there are none in Italy or France .
20565	Another drawback is that Link cards issued by some British institutions — including the Halifax and Woolwich building societies — can not be used to access Plus machines .
20566	Credit cards also allow you to convert only just as much as you need into local currencies .
20567	Visa and Access , the latter known as Mastercard abroad , can be used in more than 7m places worldwide .
20568	Again , there is no charge for purchases other than paying an exchange rate 2 p.c. or 3 p.c. worse than the wholesale money market rate .
20569	Even so , it is likely to be much better than that obtainable in hotels or bureau de change .
20570	A 1.5 p.c. fee is levied for foreign currency withdrawals .
20571	By contrast , travellers ' cheques look like yesterday 's technology .
20572	First there is the problem of having to convert your sterling cash into the cheques in advance .
20573	This costs up to 2 p.c. of the sum converted with the possibility of a £3 handling charge if you opt for non-sterling or American dollar denominated cheques .
20574	Then you may have to pay commission to convert them into local currency on your travels and could have to pay to reconvert those left over back into sterling on your return to Britain .

20588	Haven against inflation — P26
20589	Money-Go-Round : Putting off the day when tax falls due
20590	By IAN COWIE AND MALCOLM CRAIG
20591	SAVERS anxious to avoid the risk of 60 p.c. deductions from their ‘ unearned income ’ should take a deep breath and consider the possibilities of split capital investment trusts .
20592	Daunting though the terminology may seem , these offer the chance to defer tax for years , in some cases until the millenium .
20593	So , by the time tax is calculated and paid , rates could be considerably lower than they might be next week .
20594	Zero dividend preference shares , one type of capital issued by split investment trusts , pay no income at all but instead accumulate earnings to provide a capital gain on maturity .
20595	Those who prefer to see earnings credited to their account on a regular basis may use personal equity plans to shelter dividends from tax ; here , the high-yielding income shares of splits including River &amp; Mercantile , General Consolidated and River Plate may prove best .
20596	For example , income shares in River &amp; Mercantile — largely invested British blue chips — yield 12 p.c. , adjusted for last year 's rights issue .
20597	Priced at 102p , they are to be redeemed in April , 2000 , at 100p — implying a capital loss of rather less than 0.25 p.c. per annum .
20598	Thus the yield is 11.75 p.c. before Pep charges which should not reduce the income received below 10.25 p.c. per annum — while retaining the possibility of higher returns if dividends paid by the underlying stocks rise .
20599	Financial adviser Kean Seager of Whitechurch Securities said : ‘ That is better than you can get in the building society — but how much extra risk is being taken ?
20600	‘ The answer is ‘ not much ’ because , in the case of River &amp; Mercantile , only 0.6 p.c. per annum growth is needed over the remaining eight years to pay the income shares 100p .
20601	And dividends do tend to grow .
20602	While share prices are little changed on their 1987 peak , dividends have grown by 70 p.c . ’
20603	But investors do need to be wary of new-style income shares — such as those issued by Olim Convertible , Kleinwort High Income and Edinburgh Income — which rely more heavily on growth in the underlying assets to prevent substantial capital loss .
20604	This is an area where professional advice may be needed , although the Association of Investment Trust Companies produces an excellent range of free guides .
20605	The same caveat applies to the 21 zero coupons on offer , currently rolling up notional interest of between 9 p.c. and 13 p.c. into projected , but not guaranteed , capital gains .
20606	For tax purposes , zeros are treated like any other share with capital gains after the annual exemption and indexation relief for inflation are taken into account .
20607	Alternatively , zeros can be included in a Pep .
20608	And zero shareholders have preferential rights to trusts ' assets when they are wound up .
20609	However , the price of the zeros on redemption is not guaranteed — hence the high yields on offer .
20610	They can be bought direct via a stockbroker , or via a managed fund set up for the purpose .
20611	The broker Financial Services has a Zero Dividend Portfolio Fund with £10m to £12m invested in zeros .
20612	The fee is between 0.5 p.c. and 1 p.c .
20613	Exeter Fund Managers also offers a Zero Preference Unit Trust with a 5 p.c. initial charge , 0.8 p.c. annual .
20614	To illustrate how zeros work in practice , TR Technology Trust 's zeros have a market price of 166p and mature on April 30 , 1998 at a projected price of 313p — equivalent to a yearly gross redemption yield of just over 10.5 p.c .
20615	Looking further ahead , Exmoor Dual 's zeros are 185p and have a projected redemption price of 489p at 31 August 2001 — equivalent to a yearly gross redemption yield of nearly 10.5 p.c .
20616	However , Lewis Aaron , a director of stockbroker Barclays de Zoete Wedd , warned : ‘ It is essential that the investor pays attention to what is available to cover the notional interest being rolled up .
20617	Only River Plate &amp; General has its projected price on redemption doubly covered .
20618	‘ High inflation could erode the capital gain attractions of zeros , ’ added Mr Aaron .
20619	‘ For example , in 1979 the equity market rose in nominal terms by 9.7 p.c. but fell by 6.5 p.c. in real terms as a result of inflation . ’
20620	Money-Go-Round : Making the most of allowances
20621	UNLIKE those rich enough to set aside assets for a period of years in order to avoid tax , those dependent on income — particularly those subject to Pay As You Earn — have limited scope to fend off the taxman .
20622	Broadly speaking , their best strategies to cope with a Labour win would be to ensure they make the most of allowances created through the independent taxation of husbands and wives , and — where possible — to take income on a self-employed basis rather than as employees .
20623	Married couples , where one of the spouses has little or no income , should transfer income from deposits and investments into the account of the non-working spouse to use up his or her allowance — that is , a slice of tax free income .
20624	For this tax year , the individual personal allowance is £3,295 and the married couples allowance is £1,720 .

20627	Alternatively , they could seek to arrange their affairs so that part of their income is received on a self-employed basis , rather than being treated as overtime .
20628	The reason is that Labour said it will retain the present National Insurance contributions ceiling for the self employed at £21,060 whereas employees will suffer an additional 9 p.c. deduction on earnings above that threshold .
20629	But the Inland Revenue has already warned that it will investigate any changes of status to ensure that they are genuine .

20686	INVESTORS who fear that membership of the European Monetary System will not prevent a resurgence of inflation in coming years should examine the virtues of index-linked gilts .

20688	They guarantee that for every £100 nominal worth of gilts bought by an investor , £100 will be paid on maturity , plus the increase in the Retail Prices Index over the years to that maturity .

20690	Is this the right time to consider adding such gilts to your portfolio ?
20691	David Newton , head of gilts trading at Barclays de Zoete Wedd , said : ‘ The longer-dated gilts in this sector have suffered as a result of the government 's higher-than-expected borrowing requirement .
20692	‘ The most attractive gilts are in the middle maturity section of the spectrum .
20693	The 2½ p.c .
20694	Treasury 2001 and the 2 p.c. 2006 are particularly attractive to the high rate tax payer .
20695	‘ At a 40 p.c. marginal rate of tax the real yield over and above inflation is 3¼ p.c .
20696	At a 59 p.c. tax rate the real yield would be 2¾ p.c .
20697	This outperforms the return on conventional gilts of the same maturity so long as inflation is above 1 p.c. to 2 p.c . ’
20698	Given that the index-linked gilt is a difficult investment to evaluate , is it worth the private investor buying via a specialist gilt fund or direct ?
20699	Derek McLean , fund manager of Abbey Life Investment Services which provides two gilt and fixed interest unit trusts , said : ‘ We have included short dated index-linked gilts in our Capital and Reserve Trust .
20700	One drawback is the higher dealing costs for index-linked gilts .
20701	‘ The market is less liquid and market-makers quote wider prices .
20702	There is a tax difference as between private investors buying such gilts direct and buying via a fund , such as ours , in that the former strategy is exempt from capital gains tax .
20703	‘ However , the tax difference is small and affects relatively few people .
20704	Index-linked gilts are complex investments to assess and the investor does obtain professional management by buying via a specialist fund .
20705	‘ For example , when working out the redemption yield , the investor must make assumptions as to the future level of inflation .
20706	In addition , there is continual switching between the conventional gilt market and the index-linked .
20707	‘ This can mean that the latter does not move in response to levels of inflation in the way that the private investor thinks it should .
20708	A rise in the inflation rate can be bad for both conventional and index-linked gilts .
20709	There is also the question of supply and demand .
20710	There is little doubt that under any future administration we will get a larger supply of index-linked gilts . ’
20711	For the investor who decides to buy direct rather than invest via a gilt unit trust , which may have a front end charge of 6 p.c. plus an annual management fee , the cheapest buying route is via the Post Office .
20712	The National Savings Stock Register can be used to hold more than 80 p.c. of the different types of gilts .

20714	Interest paid on gilts bought via the register is gross of tax .
20715	Buying such gilts via a stockbroker normally incurs a higher cost .
20716	The index-linked gilts on the market have maturities of up to 2024 and most of them stand at a substantial premium to their par value .
20717	This is proof of the erosive effects of past inflation rate which climbed to banana republic levels in the 1970s .
20718	Surprisingly there is only one index-linked gilt unit trust ; it is run by Guinness Flight .

20828	Like all United Kingdom unit trust providers — with the exception of Lazards Merchant Bank which offers investors free entry into all eight of its unit trusts ( minimum investment £5,000 ) — Murray Johnstone has traditionally relied on commission hungry financial advisers to introduce its business .
20829	Since it can only pay advisers a standard 3 p.c. commission by loading its funds with an equivalent charge , it runs the substantial risk of losing business now that the charge has been cut .
20830	Richard Eliott Lockhart , managing director , said this week that ideally he would have liked to have compromised .
20831	Rather than dropping his company 's commission bearing charge completely , he would have preferred to have reduced it and moved it from the front to the back end of his unit trusts — that is , charging investors as they leave the fund rather than as they enter .
20832	He said : ‘ Originally we went for an American-style back-end load or exit charge which was tapered to reduce by a percentage point for each year an investment was held .
20833	This was blocked ; the current rules do not allow it .
20834	‘ The prime advantage of an exit charge would have been to the investor because he would have got into our funds at a nil cost and out again at a very low cost if he held his investment for , say , three years . ’
20835	New rules forcing all unit trust companies to disclose clearly their charges would also increase competition on prices and — with the introduction of exit charges — encourage longer term saving rather than speculation .
20836	In America , and to a lesser extent Europe , such choice is already evident .
20837	Of the 222 new American funds launched last year , 99 were of the Lazards variety and carry no initial or exit charges .
20838	Just 87 had charges ranging from 4 to 8 p.c. , while the remainder had either very low charges or long term investment — encouraging exit charge arrangements .
20839	On all of these funds , charges are clearly visible to investors and are made in addition to the single price at which units are purchased .
20840	In Britain , with our complex bid to offer system , investors often think that the standard 5 p.c. or 6 p.c. initial charge is all they must pay , when in fact the spread between a unit trust 's offer and bid prices can be much greater .
20841	Mary Blair , a director of Fidelity , whose parent company runs ‘ no-load ’ funds in America , said : ‘ Greater flexibility on charges would certainly be welcome and exit charges are something we would be quite interested to look at .
20842	Flexibility would increase competition between providers which will benefit investors .
20843	‘ It will open the doors much wider to product innovation .
20844	Under the Financial Services Act such innovation has been sadly stifled . ’
20845	Mrs Blair added that any move away from the bid and offer system to single pricing would not be accepted if it threatened to reduce or ‘ dilute ’ the value of existing unit holders investments .
20846	‘ I think that any down-side would more than be offset by the increased simplicity which single pricing would bring the client , allowing him or her to see exactly what they are getting . ’

20849	By QUENTIN COWDRY
20850	COMPLACENCY is almost a sacking offence at Hunslet Transportation Projects , the Birmingham-based firm which in June 1990 startled railway experts by winning a contract to supply 37 electric passenger trains to Regional Railways .
20851	It was a remarkable achievement for a company created just over a year earlier and which had had to pitch against some of the world 's largest train-builders , including GEC Alsthom , Siemens , and BREL , the dominant British manufacturer .

20853	In both contract races Hunslet benefited greatly from its low overheads .
20854	But running between the feet of elephants , as the company colourfully describes its market position , is a dangerous business , particularly when the trend in the train-building industry is towards the creation of larger international suppliers .
20855	Management at Hunslet is acutely aware of the risks of operating in a sector acutely vulnerable to too much or too little government interference .
20856	Its order book is now approaching £150 million .
20857	‘ Our aim is to provide excellence in the design , project management and assembly of smaller railway rolling stock contracts , ’ says Peter Johnson , one of the firm 's directors .
20858	Essentially the company is a project management operation .
20859	A core team of technicans and engineers , all with backgrounds in the rail industry , design rolling stock to the most exacting specifications and then oversees construction using components from various countries .
20860	The original intention was to hive off assembly operations to sub-contractors .

20862	The Regional Railways order made waves not only because it went to a newcomer in train-building .
20863	The design chosen was the most innovative of those submitted — a train made from an aluminium bodyshell and driven by a novel A.C. motor which saves some of the energy created when trains brake and feeds its back to the overhead power supply .
20864	Hunslet claims its trains , based on three cars with a driver 's cab at either end , will use 30 per cent less energy than similar electric models .
20865	The capital cost of Hunslet 's traction equipment , supplied by a Netherlands firm , is higher than that of many D.C. varieties , but Regional Railways accepted the argument that it would work out cheaper long-term because of its economic use of energy and low maintenance .
20866	Designed to run on heavily-used urban networks , the trains , designated Class 323 , can seat 289 passengers .
20867	They are to be used in West Yorkshire and the Birmingham and Manchester areas to replace ageing diesel and electric rolling stock .
20868	Regional Railways has been assured that they will knock 16 minutes off the journey between Redditch and Lichfield in the West Midlands .
20869	The first results of the order — said to be worth about £81 million — are due on the network this summer .
20870	Peter Johnson says : ‘ We 're hoping that our pollution-free and energy-efficient units will mark the start of a new generation of sophisticated electric trains which will eventually run all over the Regional Railways network . ’
20871	Hunslet is also breaking new ground with its Malaysian contract .
20872	The trains it has designed will be the first electric rolling stock to run on Malaysia 's rail system .
20873	Ganz Hunslet , Hungary 's largest train-builder ( Telfos Holdings was one of the first British firms to take a majority stake in a major East European company following the collapse of Communism ) , is building the bodyshells and bogies , but final assembly will take place in Malaysia .

20901	Property : Do n't let yourself in for trouble Choosing the right agent is essential if you want to rent your property .
20902	Francesca Simon describes some of the pitfalls — and how to avoid them
20903	By FRANCESCA SIMON
20904	DEBBIE ADAMS had to let her East End terrace house in London in a hurry when her husband was re-located to Ireland with two months ' notice .
20905	She went to a local letting agency , Landlords of 41 Roman Road , Bethnal Green , London E2 , who found a tenant that day .
20906	She also employed Landlords to manage the let .
20907	As is common practice , Landlords kept the tenant 's deposit of £650 and told Debbie they would take their entire fee of £881 up front , so she expected no rent for the first month .
20908	But July also passed without Debbie receiving any money .
20909	‘ I phoned and said , ‘ Where 's the money ? ’ and was told there were problems with the book-keeper , who would be coming in to sort it out , ’ says Debbie .
20910	‘ But nothing happened and I never heard from them . ’
20911	She repeatedly phoned Landlords , but was either unable to get an answer or told that manager Howard Keizner was unavailable .
20912	Finally , after the third month passed with no rent received , Debbie phoned the tenants , asked them to pay her directly , and sent Landlords a recorded-delivery letter , which was returned , and finally one by ordinary post stating that Landlords were no longer employed as the managing agents .
20913	Because they had n't done any management , Debbie felt Landlords were entitled only to the 10 per cent tenant-finding fee and therefore owed her £2,400 ( 3 months ' rent plus the deposit ) .
20914	In December 1991 she sued .
20915	Landlords did n't acknowledge the writ , so in January Debbie 's solicitor requested a judgment in default for the full amount plus interest and court fees , a total of £2,453.24 .
20916	Just before the court was due to hear the request her solicitor received a cheque for £2,400 .
20917	‘ They had n't paid the interest and court fees , but we got back every single penny they owed .
20918	We were lucky , ’ says Debbie Adams .
20919	Howard Keizner , of Landlords , said : ‘ There were a lot of complications with this particular letting and management . ’
20920	But he declined further comment .
20921	Last week he promised to supply us with a written explanation of the way his company had treated Debbie , but it never arrived .
20922	Yusuf and Shabira Gulamali were less fortunate .
20923	They lost over £4,000 dealing with two letting agencies which closed down without paying them the rent and tenants ' deposit owed on their Wembley flat .
20924	They hired the first agent , ‘ Digs ’ , of Oxford Street , to manage as well as to let their flat .
20925	The Gulamalis received their rent for the first three months , then nothing for four months , and were told the computer was broken , the accounts were being moved , the cheque was in the post , and so on .
20926	‘ After four months they closed down owing us £3,500 , ’ says Shabira .
20927	‘ Together with some other clients we took the owner to court but he escaped to Spain . ’
20928	The second time round they dealt with R. and B. Lettings in London NW10 , who they instructed just to find a tenant .
20929	The Gulamalis never received the agreement form , the tenants ' deposit or the first month 's rent .
20930	‘ Finally , we went to the office and they gave us a cheque , which bounced . ’
20931	The offices of R and B. Lettings are now up for sale .
20932	‘ Anyone can set up a letting agency , ’ says David Galsworthy , Vice President of the National Association of Estate Agents .
20933	‘ They come and go , so it pays to deal with a member of a professional body , such as the NAEA , the Royal Institute of Chartered Surveyors or the Incorporated Society of Valuers and Auctioneers .
20934	In case of a dispute you can complain to the professional body , and members are bonded , which means that deposits and rent are covered in case of fraud or dishonesty . ’
20935	If you are thinking of letting your property , the following points will help to safeguard your interests :
20936	Ask any agency you are considering using if they are a member of one of the above professional associations .
20937	If in doubt , ask to see proof of their membership .
20938	If , in addition to finding a tenant , the agency is managing the let , you should be paid every month , less a tenant-finding fee of between two and four weeks ' rent .
20939	The agency will keep the tenant 's deposit until the tenant leaves .
20940	If the letting agent is not managing the flat , the tenant 's deposit should be given to the owner immediately .
20941	Expect to pay a management fee of up to 15 per cent .
20942	Some agencies deduct it every month , others want it all up front , so shop around .
20943	If the owner is abroad , the agent will also collect tax at the standard rate of 25 per cent , which will be deducted from your monthly rent cheque .
20944	Letting agencies should never charge tenants a finder 's fee , although according to Galsworthy , many agencies do .
20945	‘ It 's not ethical as they are acting for the landlord , ’ he says .
20946	The self-regulating NAEA has 10,000 members , of which 2,000 also do letting and management .
20947	But Galsworthy believes there is a clear need for the licensing of all letting agents .
20948	‘ We want everyone to be licensed , but the Government did n't think it necessary .
20949	Section 22 of the 1979 Estate Agents Act dealing with bonding , licensing and standards of competency has not been brought in .
20950	But we must have a common code and we must have licensing , ’ he said .
20951	Until then , owners and tenants beware .
20952	Property : The Irish blessings worth counting Simon Courtauld looks for gold in the Emerald Isle
20953	By SIMON COURTAULD
20954	THE ADVANTAGES of living in Ireland may become more apparent next week .
20955	The increase in tax rates for higher earners , which would follow a Labour victory on Thursday , would then be comparable to the top tax rate across the Irish Sea , which this month is to be reduced below 50 per cent .
20956	There are several other attractions of buying a house in Ireland : prices are much lower than in Britain , and the annual property tax can be avoided by opening the house to the public , if it is architecturally interesting enough , for no more than four weeks in the year .
20957	In addition — and this is a concession which the British Government refuses to grant — tax relief is available against the costs of repairing and maintaining historic houses .
20958	There are one or two magnificent examples coming on to the market .
20959	Few of Ireland 's great Ascendancy houses , perhaps no more than 50 , remain in private family occupation : one of the most significant , Stackallan , in County Meath , is a rare early-18th-century , pre-Palladian pile in the Boyne valley between Navan and Slane , which will be offered for sale later this month .
20960	Most neo-Classical houses in Ireland date from 1730 onwards ; Stackallan , however , was built around 1714 for Gustavus Hamilton , one of William III 's generals , who raised six regiments for the King , including the Inniskillings , and was made Viscount Boyne by George I.
20961	At some time in the 19th century it became a school , then reverted to being a private house , but was in a sadly neglected state when bought by Major and Mrs Anthony Burke in 1953 .
20962	Their daughter recalls that the family drove up from Waterford to see Stackallan , looked over the wall and fell in love with it .
20963	The house was re-roofed and the interior gradually restored ; lots of roses were planted in the formal gardens ; and from 1960 Mrs Burke began , with two cheap mares , to establish a highly successful stud farm .
20964	The 275 acres of pasture are of the best and surround the house on all sides , undulating towards distant hills — and to Dublin airport only half-an-hour away .
20965	Though unarguably a large property — with 11 bedrooms , three staff cottages and a gate lodge — Stackallan retains the atmosphere of a family house .
20966	The three principal reception rooms are well-proportioned and linked by double doors ; and the colonnaded entrance hall leads to a magnificent central double staircase .
20967	Above it the Boyne coat of arms , surrounded by a cannon , flags and spears , forms the centre-piece of the ceiling .
20968	Mrs Burke leaves a remarkable house which deserves to be looked after with the same care that she has lavished on it for almost 20 years .
20969	While the agents ( Savills with Hamilton Osborne King ) have yet to declare an asking price for Stackallan , an offer of around £1.5 million would , I understand , not be rejected out of hand .
20970	Almost as fine — and described by the agents , Sotheby 's International Realty , as ‘ one of Ireland 's great Georgian houses ’ — is Coollattin , near Shillelagh , south of the Wicklow Mountains , which is on the market at IR £750,000 .
20971	The house was built for Earl Fitzwilliam in the first years of the 19th century by John Carr of York , then in his 80s .
20972	The entrance front is simple enough , with two storeys , a wide pediment and a central curved bow on each of the side elevations .
20973	But when the house was enlarged in 1880 , it became rather ungainly and would probably benefit now from some judicious pruning .
20974	Handpainted wallpapers , a round room and a galleried landing with cupola are the main features of the Georgian part of the house .
20975	There is a handsome stable block , a huge walled garden and 63 acres with glorious views .
20976	Both Coollattin and Stackallan are in good hunting country , which is hardly unusual in Ireland , but may become more significant after next week .
20977	With a Labour Government in Britain committed to abolishing foxhunting , there should be no lack of demand for these enduring legacies of ‘ old England ’ .

21077	He won two novice hurdles by wide margins in his first campaign , and then two novice chases the following winter before running away with the County Hurdle at Cheltenham from a field which included the smart mare Travel Mystery .
21078	Apart from his Midlands Grand National triumph in 1990 he also gained a verdict over Norton 's Coin at Cheltenham — two months before that horse 's Gold Cup success — and would have been an easy winner of the Greenall Whitley Chase but for falling when clear at the last fence .
21079	That remains his only fall , and it was more a case of a slip one stride after landing than a regulation fall .
21080	The Pitman yard , which has done so well in this race — one winner , a second and two thirds since 1983 — believe he will adapt to the unique Aintree fences , and as long as he copes with the first few , they feel he must go close .
21081	My opinion is that , as long as Willsford is among the leaders coming to the last two fences and six furlongs , his speed will be a potent weapon , especially as he carries the minimum weight .
21082	Victory for Willsford would give Michael Bowlby , Mrs Pitman 's brother-in-law , his biggest win .
21083	Bowlby has been under pressure ever since the Cheltenham Gold Cup , over his riding tactics on Golden Freeze , coincidentally brought down at The Chair in Thursday 's John Hughes Memorial Chase here .
21084	The Gold Cup has had a greater than usual bearing in the Grand National build-up this year , with Cool Ground , the winner , and Docklands Express , the close third , renewing rivalry .
21085	Adrian Maguire 's injury robs the young Irishman of the chance of a rare double , and the prospects of Cool Ground , now to be ridden by Martin Lynch , may not be quite as obvious as the ground dries .
21086	But Cool Ground is a dour stayer with a wealth of experience , who should adapt to Aintree .
21087	The change in conditions has added to the confidence behind Docklands Express and Brown Windsor .
21088	Both have run in a previous Grand National , Brown Windsor finishing a remote fourth when favourite two years ago , and Docklands Express a first-fence faller 12 months ago .
21089	Since that lapse , Docklands Express has won the Whitbread Gold Cup ( controversially , on the disqualification of Cahervillahow ) and the Racing Post Chase , and finished second in the King George VI Chase in addition to his fine Gold Cup display .
21090	The booking of Peter Scudamore in place of the luckless Anthony Tory means his chance is not impaired , but his price is likely to be significantly cramped .
21091	Brown Windsor , also a Whitbread Gold Cup winner , in 1989 , is trained by Lambourn-based Nicky Henderson , who has gone close in the Grand National on several occasions .
21092	Victory for Brown Windsor would be universally popular .
21093	Like Henderson , Arthur Stephenson , has been agonisingly close at Aintree , particularly with the evergreen Durham Edition .
21094	He relies on Stay On Tracks , a consistent stayer who has the benefit of the fearless Chris Grant 's assistance from the saddle .
21095	Twin Oaks , who heads the weights , was the fancy of many for Aintree glory as he continued a brilliant sequence of handicap wins at Haydock Park .
21096	But his latest third there behind Cool Ground in the Greenalls Gold Cup suggests he will find the Gold Cup winner too strong again on these terms .
21097	Seagram , last year 's winner , has been a long way behind that excellence this season , as has Bonanza Boy , the 1991 favourite , whose desertion by Peter Scudamore was clearly influenced by the drying conditions .
21098	Bonanza Boy 's trainer Martin Pipe fancies Huntworth ahead of Bonanza Boy and Omerta , the Irish National winner who makes a belated seasonal reappearance .
21099	The 11th-hour acquisition by Mrs David Thompson , wife of the owner of Cheveley Park Stud , of Roc de Prince and Party Politics , may be in vain , again on the expectation of near-perfect going .
21100	Auntie Dot , third 12 months ago , Rawhide and New Halen , are others to consider , as is the consistent Romany King , second-string for the Toby Balding stable behind Cool Ground , and a good fourth in the Ritz Club Chase at Cheltenham last time .
21101	Those looking for a rank outsider at rewarding odds may do worse than invest a little each-way on New Halen , who was still in contention when unseating his rider a mile from home last year .
21102	He won the Mildmay of Flete at Cheltenham two years ago at 66–1 and could give Robert Bellamy a memorable ride .
21103	Irish horses have found Aintree unpromising territory , but Laura 's Beau and the talented Rawhide could make an impact .
21104	In the hope that Willsford adapts to the place , I take him to come home first , ahead of Cool Ground , Brown Windsor and Stay On Tracks .

21139	The Grand National : My best chance yet
21140	By Peter Scudamore
21141	AN OUNCE of luck is always welcome in racing and I have to admit that I feel the most fortunate man around this morning having been asked to ride Docklands Express in the Grand National — a race I have never won .
21142	The fact is that if I had n't taken part in the BBC television previews of the big event I would probably be riding my old friend Bonanza Boy .
21143	The whole story is that I was asked to ride Docklands Express , Cool Ground , Auntie Dot and Bonanza Boy in home gallops for the television cameras and then to compare the quartet .
21144	Not many other jockeys are so lucky .
21145	Even leading up to the filming , there were doubts about Adrian Maguire riding Cool Ground as he had a previous tie to Omerta .
21146	Also , Anthony Tory , regular jockey for Docklands Express , had been having trouble with his shoulder for a while , and Mark Perrett , another of the horse 's regular riders , had been claimed for Rubika .
21147	I can remember vividly the whole episode with Docklands Express .
21148	It was our first morning of filming and when I rode the horse I really liked him .
21149	He felt great , he worked with class and he had the right attitude .
21150	I thought : ‘ This is the one . ’
21151	When we had finished filming I said to Kim Bailey , the trainer : ‘ If you ever need somebody to ride this little horse , I would love to be considered . ’
21152	How quickly things change in racing and change they certainly have this week .
21153	When I rode Docklands Express in his work , I was thinking I would probably be having my fourth Grand National ride on Bonanza Boy — then there were reports of rain across the country , which made me feel quite satisfied to be on Martin Pipe 's runner .
21154	He knows his way around the course and , with any luck , I felt the ground would come up soft .
21155	However , when I got to Liverpool on Thursday and saw the state of the ground , instead of thinking about such horses as Laura 's Beau , Rubika and Cool Ground as the major chances , suddenly it was the good-ground types such as Docklands Express who re-entered calculations .
21156	When I sat on Cool Ground I was impressed with him too .
21157	He had not been prepared for Cheltenham the same as some horses are , because there had been a last-minute change of plan for him and he would not have been really galloped hard .
21158	Racing against other horses is an entirely different thing from riding horses in their work and it is not always the ones who work the best that are necessarily the winners .
21159	In fact , Cool Ground worked with Romany King and Sirrah Jay , and they actually worked better than he did .
21160	Although , when we came back from one of our canters , Cool Ground was very bright .
21161	He really marched in and he pulled 20 lengths ahead of the other two just walking .
21162	He is in great form .
21163	The other interesting runner I rode was Auntie Dot , particularly as she has the advantage of being schooled over a National-type fence on her trainer John Webber 's gallops .
21164	With the TV cameras there , Julian Wilson asked Mr Webber if I could pop her over the fence .
21165	I joked about a jockey needing a large port and brandy to do that sort of thing cold in the morning — and besides we might be risking the horse suffering a mishap .
21166	‘ You let me worry about any injuries my horse might suffer , ’ said Mr Webber .
21167	I thought to myself : ‘ Oh no ’ but Auntie Dot went into the fence and was brilliant at it .
21168	Originally I thought the ground might be too soft for her , making it a real test of stamina , and we know that she only just gets the trip .
21169	But as the ground is a lot quicker now , she must have a bright chance .
21170	Bonanza Boy , one of my old favourites , has been a remarkable horse over the years and I am a touch sad in having to desert him for a horse I consider to have a better chance .
21171	But Martin Pipe is a realist , and never for a moment did he stand in my way when the Docklands Express ride came up .
21172	Bonanza Boy will have blinkers back on and this may assist him .
21173	He knows the place so well and is a real hardy customer .
21174	I suppose I am in a good position to weigh up the prospects of the major contenders in today 's race , at least , and I have no hesitation in declaring my delight at being on Docklands Express .
21175	On the Form Book and after riding him , I consider Docklands Express to be a first-class prospect .
21176	Twin Oaks looks a great type for the fences and may be the hardest to beat but I also have a healthy respect for Cool Ground and Brown Windsor .
21177	This racing game can be funny , ca n't it ?
21178	I set off as a television test pilot and have ended up with my best-ever chance of winning the race .

21295	SATURDAY PROFILE Man for all seasons sees out winter of discontent DAVE STRINGER
21296	By Colin Gibson
21297	WHEN Dave Stringer glances across to the Sunderland bench at Hillsborough tomorrow he will have some sympathy for Sunderland 's Malcolm Crosby .
21298	Mr Stringer , 48 , began his managerial apprenticeship at Carrow Road five years ago in similar circumstances to those Mr Crosby is facing at Roker Park .
21299	Though he survived and prospered , there have been times this season when the chances of Mr Stringer lasting as Norwich manager until FA Cup semi-final day seemed remote .
21300	In mid-February Norwich appeared on the verge of crisis .
21301	They had slipped down the First Division , losing five consecutive League matches .
21302	The fans became restless and the soccer grapevine was alive with names of likely successors to Mr Stringer .
21303	So intense did the criticism become that Mr Stringer , who has been connected as player , coach and now manager with Norwich for almost 30 years , took the unprecedented step of going on national radio to defend himself and his players .
21304	Had Norwich not defeated Notts County in the fifth round that afternoon , it could well have been Mr Stringer 's first and last address to the nation 's footballing public .
21305	But win Norwich did and they have since gone on to preserve their First Division lives and reach the FA Cup semi-finals .
21306	Mr Stringer now appears relatively safe , but he could have been the victim of his own success .
21307	After taking over from Ken Brown in the winter of 1987 he guided the club to unexpected heights .
21308	The day he walked into the manager 's office Norwich were bottom of the First Division and relegation was more a probability than possibility .
21309	Within 18 months he had taken the club to the FA Cup semi-final and their highest League position in the club 's 87-year history .
21310	Suddenly a soccer backwater had tasted success but , as Mr Stringer readily admits : ‘ We have always had the problem of being sidetracked . ’
21311	This season threatened to be another one of disruptive distractions .

21313	It was then that the club 's management co-operative gave Mr Stringer so much support , and the relationship is now reciprocated with Mr Stringer only too happy for the role of coaches Dave Williams and Mike Walker to be appreciated .
21314	‘ We all contribute , ’ he said without the slightest hint of a bruised ego .
21315	‘ We all have our roles to play and I am delighted that people like Dave Williams should receive the credit for their work . ’
21316	But he also recognises that part of his role is to accept the criticism .
21317	‘ I know that comes with the job , ’ he said .
21318	‘ If I am the target , though , I can be the shield so that others can carry on with their jobs .
21319	‘ I might understand it but I do n't know anyone who enjoys the criticism .
21320	You would have to be a masochist to do that . ’
21321	Despite the disquiet at the club this year , Mr Stringer still appears more relaxed and more in control than he did when he first took charge in that winter of 1987 .
21322	‘ It was not really the normal way of getting a manager 's job .
21323	The circumstances were very similar to those the lad at Sunderland finds himself in now , ’ he said .
21324	‘ The position almost evolved . ’
21325	Unlike Mr Crosby , the Norwich manager did not have the groundswell of support when he was appointed .

21525	By CHARLES RANDALL
21526	ADRIAN DAVIES , the Welsh international rugby union outside-half , runs out with the Cambridge University soccer side to take on Oxford at Fulham this morning with the roar of Twickenham fresh in his memory .
21527	Davies the rugby player captained Cambridge to a 17–11 victory over Oxford in his fourth Varsity match last December and is almost certainly creating history by becoming the first to earn a rugby-soccer double Blue in the same season .
21528	Dr John Little , president of the Cambridge club , said : ‘ I ca n't say unequivocally but I have gone through a history of the club and there is no mention of it there . ’
21529	Oxford 's past reveals that , in 1894 , C B Fry , a future England cricketer and then the world long jump record-holder , was prevented by injury from gaining a rugby Blue in the same season as winning the third of his four soccer Blues .
21530	Davies , though a useful club cricketer , could hardly be compared with Fry , but he can boast an achievement that eluded arguably the greatest of all-round English sportsmen .
21531	Davies , 23 , a nimble midfield player , might one day be able to tell his grandchildren of a winning double Blue .
21532	Perhaps his only regret is missing the chance of adding Wembley , no longer the soccer venue , to Twickenham .
21533	Giving time to both sports is now easier than it was .
21534	The matches used to be held little more than a week or so apart but soccer has since switched to the Lent term .
21535	The talented Davies played soccer for Wales Schools Under-15s while at Pencoed Comprehensive , a rugby school , before switching codes in the sixth form to captain Wales Schools at rugby .
21536	He was good enough to be invited for trials by Leeds and Sheffield Wednesday .
21537	He declined , and was sucked into rugby with Neath and Wales .

21539	It 's been a bit of a pity , really , that rugby has taken over so much that I have n't been able to continue playing football .
21540	‘ I decided not to play rugby this term .
21541	My neck is still not quite right and I have injured a shoulder .
21542	I could still run , so I turned up for football training and things have gone on from there .
21543	‘ The training is a lot different .
21544	Although I 'm reasonably fit , the difference in sharpness is immense .
21545	Everything in football is 100 miles an hour .
21546	‘ You do n't have a rest when the ball goes into touch and the line-out forms and so on .
21547	There is far more running to do playing midfield . ’
21548	If the softly spoken Welshman is making history as the first rugby man to conquer soccer , he will not be the last .

21682	At Home : Not quite creased up by the new , improved wonder iron
21683	By MARK EDMONDS
21684	WITH the average freelance ironer charging Gentlemen Who Do n't 50 pence a shirt , the ‘ professional ’ steam iron to be launched next month by Philips sounds excellent value at £170 .
21685	Slobs like me who iron only when they are forced to , and then only the bits that show , stand to recoup their investment after less than a year 's worth of shirts .
21686	The huge price tag attached to the iron certainly promises a great deal .
21687	Since you can pick up a no-frills steam iron for £40 or £50 I assumed it would take all the angst out of what is arguably the last of the genuinely ghastly domestic chores .
21688	I had every hope that the industrial-strength whoosh of steam the manufacturers trumpet so loudly would present me with crease-free shirts and service my morning cappuccino .
21689	Philips says this is the first example of a ‘ professional ’ steam iron to hit the British shops .
21690	In Italy and France , however , these super-irons are commonplace and account for 50 per cent of annual sales .
21691	This probably indicates one of two things : Continental Europeans are more particular about the state of their shirts , or they are less particular about the claims of the manufacturers .
21692	It comes in two parts .
21693	The first seems conventional enough — standard iron shape , flex attachment to power source from handle — although its separate ‘ vapour tank ’ was a new one on me .
21694	The whole caboodle , heavy and cumbersome , looked as though it might be more at home in a grand hotel than a north London flat : precisely the image the manufacturer is trying to get across .
21695	It is the vapour tank that is the key to the machine 's alleged superiority over other steam irons .
21696	This takes a full litre of water — enough for one-and-a-half hours of constant steam ironing without going back to the tap .
21697	The tank produces 50 grams of steam per minute — about three times that of a conventional steam iron — and feeds it directly into the iron via a cord in its side .
21698	A separate sole plate heats up the steam even more , producing a much more powerful jet .
21699	Once I 'd mastered a none-too-straightforward control panel , which looks rather like those muticoloured ever-flickering computers you find on the dashboard of executive cars , my test run got under way .
21700	Briefed comprehensively by my fastidious fiancee on ironing strategy — ‘ Never start from the front/make sure you give the cuffs a decent jet of steam … not like that , you chump ! ’ — I set about a pile of shirts , mainly cotton but one silk , and a range of trousers .
21701	First you must fill the tank — a relatively idiot-proof exercise , though you must remember to unscrew it carefully and slowly when replenishing it , since the steam is kept under considerable pressure .
21702	A pilot light on the tank 's control panel conveniently lets you know when the iron is running out of steam .
21703	There is no doubting the iron 's power .
21704	Even the shirts which had been left for many weeks in my laundry out-tray responded to the punishment it dished out .
21705	The iron 's ‘ trigger ’ , concealed in its handle , was jolly good fun to operate .
21706	One squeeze and you 've strafed even the most determined of creases out of existence : a separate jet of steam , which is activated by a button on top of the handle , is useful for sniper attacks on hard-to-defeat cuff wrinkles .
21707	Irons I 've used before have also offered this facility , but I 've always found I 've ended up toing and froing between the tap once too often .
21708	The capacity of the Philips iron keeps this to a minimum .
21709	Also useful , I 'm sure , is the facility for ironing curtains , upholstery , and even jackets and shirts vertically .
21710	The jet of steam can be aimed at particularly stubborn creases , and there is also a spray attachment which you can use to cover larger areas .
21711	Its bulk , however , was a problem , which might make vertical ironing a little impractical .
21712	A broad-beamed fellow like myself should have no difficulty careering it across the ironing board , although a woman or even a bachelor-wimp might sooner resort to an old-fashioned metal iron than attempt to put this monster through its paces .
21713	Another design fault rests with the flex : since it protrudes from the heel , you ca n't stand it up when you 're not using it .
21714	You also need plenty of room , since the iron does not operate independently of the vapour tank .
21715	But I could n't argue with the machine 's efficiency .
21716	My shirts and trousers emerged from the exercise crease-free , with only the minimum of effort on my part .
21717	It coped admirably with a range of different materials .
21718	While I ca n't say I actually enjoyed the experience — as usual , two shirts flaked me out and put me in a bad mood for the rest of the day — I did find the whole process a whole lot easier on the nerves than throwing a glass of water across a shirt in the hope that somehow the creases , along with the water , would eventually evaporate .
21719	At Home : PRIZED POSSESSIONS
21720	By JOHN BLY
21721	SENT BY a reader in Redhill , this picture shows a good example of an early 17th-century oak ‘ gate-leg ’ table , circa 1685 , and the photograph clearly shows the reason for its name .
21722	Drop-leaf tables which could be placed against the wall when not in use developed during the pre-Commonwealth period , but the method of framed ‘ joined ’ construction necessitated the use of a securing pivot at the top and the bottom of the swing-out supporting leg .
21723	Hence gate-leg .
21724	By the 1730s this construction had been superseded by a knuckle joint at the top and the gate-leg had become virtually obsolete .
21725	Thus , unless the table shown is a reproduction , which it is not , it would have been made within a comparatively short period .
21726	Guides to authenticity visible in the photograph are type and colour of timber , construction of the underframe and the drawer side .
21727	The turning to the legs is particularly attractive here .
21728	Given that it is a comfortable six-seater , this table should be insured for £2,500 .

21764	At Home : Pots of gold from under the ocean Leslie Geddes-Brown looks behind the mania for shipwreck china
21765	By LESLIE GEDDES-BROWN
21766	SHIPWRECK CARGOES have everything the antique collector could desire : romance , history , provenance , beauty — and buoyant prices .
21767	So , next Tuesday and Wednesday , Christie 's in Amsterdam expects a full turnout of buyers when it sells 28,000 pieces of Chinese porcelain from a burnt-out junk shipwrecked around 1690 off Con Dao Island , Vietnam .
21768	The Vung Tau Cargo , snagged in a Vietnamese fisherman 's nets , looks like being a repeat of the astonishing success of the Nanking Cargo — 150,000 pieces of mid-18th-century porcelain plus 126 gold bars — salvaged by an ex-Barnardo 's boy , Michael Hatcher , and auctioned in 1986 .
21769	The auction house had expected £3 million from the sale — it got £10 million .
21770	It was not always thus : in 1983 , when Christie 's sold the first batch of 25,000 pieces of Ming porcelain , found ( also by Hatcher ) in a junk on a reef on the South China Sea , prices were low , because neither auction house nor collectors could see beyond the porcelain 's dull glaze to its historic possibilities .
21771	A year later , with a second sale , the British Museum and other astute buyers started to collect shipwrecked porcelain , which was beginning to tell historians a lot about the 18th-century European buyers and their influence on the East .
21772	By 1986 , 20,000 people queued to view the Nanking ware in Amsterdam .
21773	When large quantities of Chinese blue and white porcelain first arrived in Europe in the 17th century the demand was so high it was nicknamed ‘ Chinamania ’ ; the phrase is just as apt today .
21774	Michael Cohen , a specialist dealer in oriental porcelain who expects to be a big bidder at next week 's sale , spent more than £1 million buying Nanking pieces .
21775	‘ I bought a lot at the sale .
21776	We sold over 22,000 objects in two or three days .
21777	Then I started buying from other dealers to satisfy demand .
21778	‘ At the start , a tea cup and saucer was selling for around £30 in my shop ; by the third day they were nearer £200 and still selling . ’
21779	Though Christie 's says that the Vung Tau sale is lotted to encourage private buyers , with sets of between five and nine matching vases offered per lot ( and designed to be shown , as they were in the 17th century , massed together on a chimneypiece or high shelf ) , Cohen believes buying is more easily done through a dealer .
21780	‘ Only 30 per cent of Vung Tau is perfect ; the rest is damaged , from a small chip to half the piece missing .
21781	Then it 's necessary to re-view the lots to make sure they have n't been further damaged during the view . ’
21782	He 's had 10 times the number of commission bids for Vung Tau as he had for Nanking — ‘ and this is a much smaller cargo ’ .
21783	Colin Sheaf , who will auction Vung Tau , rang me from Hong Kong to say there was a great deal of interest there and in Singapore in the cargo , and catalogues were selling fast .
21784	The first print run of 6,000 sold out and a second of 4,000 is moving quickly .
21785	Anyone worrying — as dealers and Christie 's once did — that these thousands of 300-year-old pots will flood the market need only look at Harrods , where Nanking Cargo plates have been selling regularly and at increasing prices since the auction ( £195 for a good teabowl , £7,000 for an ‘ encrusted ’ tureen ) and where , after the Vung Tau auction , the new pieces will also be for sale from , they expect , £50 to £10,000 .
21786	Michael Cohen also plans a major exhibition — 15 or 20 Nanking pieces , silver bars from the Dutch bullion ship Bredenhof , auctioned in 1986 , anything he can get from Vung Tau and , he hopes , a few pieces from the first Hatcher junk , which are the earliest of them all .
21787	These will be at his shop , 84 Portobello Road , from April 13 .
21788	Christie 's seems to be becoming the shipwreck specialist : next week 's sale is its 13th since 1982 .
21789	In 1983 it sold the contents of a Spanish galleon which went down off Cartagena carrying uncut emeralds and gold , and in 1988 homely spades , belaying pins and scrubbing brushes from HMS Invincible , a Royal Navy warship which foundered on a sandbank .
21790	But , for my money , the most heart-wrenching of all was the discovery of the wreck of Nuestra Senora de Atocha , which sank in 1622 , dragged to the bottom in a gale by the weight of silver and gold aboard — no less than 17 tons of silver and 500 pounds of gold .
21791	None of the 268 people on her escaped — they were trapped beneath the storm-battened hatches .
21792	The rosaries and crucifixes of four drowned priests , the contraband smuggled aboard , perhaps by a doomed explorer and his soldiers , and a crested silver dish , belonging to a Spanish grandee who perished with his wife and teenage daughter , were all salvaged .
21793	It took Mel Fisher , an American obsessed with finding gold , 17 years to track down the wreck of the Atocha ; in the process , his son and daughter-in-law drowned .
21794	So , if you ask how many more shipwrecks there are out there , ready for the eager auctioneers , the answer is plenty — but very few have any undamaged treasure on board .
21795	Shipwrecks , says Colin Sheaf , are usually violent affairs in which valuable cargoes are scattered or smashed .
21796	‘ If ships go down in shallow water , ’ adds Michael Cohen , ‘ cargoes are damaged by the tides .
21797	So the ones we are looking for are all in deep water .
21798	‘ No-one knew the true routes of the ships and virtually all the best wrecks have been found by accident .
21799	Just think of the Titanic — everyone knew where she went down , but it still took years to find her . ’

21891	For centuries past , our attitude towards the young was characterised by British Reserve .
21892	‘ The want of affection in the English is strongly manifested towards their children , ’ wrote one Venetian envoy , in 1497 .
21893	With the domestic revolution of the past three decades , our family emotions have certainly thawed , but there is still something to be said for resisting the tendency to involve children in every aspect of the parental life .
21894	It is a commonplace that children now seem to grow up alarmingly fast , education and the media combining to erode the apparent gap between the generations .

21896	One of the most difficult things for modern parents is to remind ourselves that we must maintain a life of our own .

21942	With sound , the garden can begin to work its magic on even the youngest ears .

21944	Most fruit trees will encourage the presence of birds .
21945	Cherry , apple and plum are much loved by bullfinches , tits and blackbirds .
21946	The rowan ( Sorbus aucuparia ) is a great favourite of starlings , which provide an amusing display of gluttony as they devour the bright red autumn berries .
21947	It is a robust tree , tolerant of atmospheric pollution , making it ideal for urban areas , easily grown in all but shallow , chalky soils .
21948	Ladybirds and other insects should be equally welcome .
21949	Bright attractions such as the damselfly are only encouraged with a pond or running stream .
