21957	Yellows are abundant , silver-greys equally so .

21960	Ophiopogon planiscapus nigrescens is worthy of note , forming spidery clumps or near-black , grass-like leaves .
21961	Making patterns with plants is possible even in the smallest of gardens .
21962	There are many delightful alpines with a height and spread of just a few inches .
21963	For larger and less subtle shapes or patterns , topiary may be an amusing experiment ; even a small maze could be created .
21964	The shapes of the flowers are just as intriguing .
21965	Stars , spikes , trumpet , bells , hearts , and feathers can all be represented , along with the plants that have their own curious designs and forms .
21966	Fritillaria meleagris deserves close inspection of its pendant blooms and chequerboard pattern of purple and white squares .
21967	The amusing pom-poms of the giant onion , Allium giganteum , are a must for any child 's garden .
21968	Decorative vegetables are an excellent source of oddities .
21969	The tree onion , Allium cepa Prolifera , produces its bulbs at both ends of the plant , and is fine for culinary use .

21975	Miscanthus sacchariflorus and the evergreen Arundinaria nitida are equally effective for the purpose .

21992	But this means that the soil for seed-sowing can be done simply by covering a patch for a few days with a sheet of polythene anchored by bricks or stones — in the absence , of course , of cloches .
21993	The plastic ones now on sale in every garden centre are much more manageable than the old glass type , which were always getting broken .
21994	The arrival of fibre fleece , a lightweight fabric , also sold in garden stores , has transformed vegetable growing in several ways .
21995	Once you have sown the seed , you cover the whole area with this .
21996	It traps the warmth of the odd sunny spell , and wards off the critical few degrees of cold .
21997	It admits both light and rain , though impedes the force of those heavy showers that can cake the soil , and sometimes wash out the seeds .
21998	You can leave the fabric in place almost until you are ready to gather your crops as it is so light the plants just push it up as they grow .
21999	Of course , this lightness means the wind can take it unless you anchor it down .
22000	Regular users of it wrap the edges round wooden batons , secured with a few tacks , leaving these to rest on the ground , and rolling it up on the batons when the season is over .
22001	All this applies to open-ground sowings , and of course it is the crops from these that move fastest as they suffer no transplanting adjustments .
22002	They include beet , lettuce , broad beans , carrots , peas and spinach , all of which need to be sown as soon as possible now .
22003	What must seem stupid to non-gardeners , or those who take a rational view of the whole business , is that when you prepare the ground for sowing you first dig it over and make it loose , only to tread it firm again .
22004	But in the process you are refining the soil to the liking of the roots that in a little while will ramify in it .
22005	You are letting in the air they like .
22006	You are incorporating humus on which the beneficial bacteria thrive and which both drains the soil of surplus moisture , yet holds it in the right degree .
22007	You are also turning up the relics of perennial weeds that can be difficult to eliminate later .
22008	While vegetables generally have the capacity to germinate soon after spring sowing , however low the temperature drops , flower seeds , also due for sowing soon on adjacent land to provide cut flowers during the summer , do need more warmth to get going .
22009	The same techniques and ground preparation suits them , though of course the fleece has to be removed when the seedlings are up .

22011	It is also quite possible to grow several exotic-looking annuals from direct ground sowings ; the trumpet-like salpiglossis , so ornately marked , the schizanthus usually seen as an early summer pot plant and zinnias , the closest thing you can get to those expensive gerberas .
22012	When you tip the seed from the packet it is hard to believe that from almost every one a plant will arise , so do not let them fall too thickly into the soil .
22013	The impulse to ‘ make sure ’ must be curbed .
22014	Again , when the seedlings are up you have to be harsh and thin , thin , thin .

22019	By MARK EDMONDS
22020	THE depressed state of our own economy recently presented holidaymakers bound for Asia and Africa with an unexpected opportunity to practise shopping techniques common in some parts of the globe before they set off .
22021	With retail sales in decline , haggling — usually more appropriate to the souks of Tangier than our domestic department stores — is becoming more common here .
22022	In Morocco and many other Arab countries , haggling is a deeply ritualised affair .
22023	And while holidaymakers are whipped up to almost frenzied levels of opportunistic greed by guidebooks which insist that real travellers never pay the first price they are quoted , few have any prospect of coming out of a deal better than the merchant who initiated it .
22024	‘ Sometimes a merchant in a souk will settle for perhaps a profit of only five per cent , ’ says Mr Latif of the Moroccan Tourist Board .
22025	‘ That will be enough for him , because he knows that next time he will make more money , perhaps 10 , perhaps even 50 per cent .
22026	That is the way he conducts his business and that is the way it has been for centuries . ’
22027	‘ If you do n't want or do n't have time to haggle , ’ says Mr Latif , ‘ you should make sure you buy your carpet , your jewellery , or your woodwork from a fixed-price store .
22028	These shops sell items which are produced and sold by co-operatives , and both price and quality is guaranteed .
22029	If you do decide to buy from a private bazaar you will be expected to haggle .
22030	No merchant will imagine that you will agree to pay the first price he suggests .
22031	Your first offer should be about half what the merchant asks and you should beat him down from there . ’
22032	Guidebooks and holiday brochures make a point of explaining ploys which can be adopted to bring a price down .
22033	The Rough Guide for Morocco , for instance , suggests that it may help to take along an apparently disinterested friend to the shop or bazaar : in an effort to hurry the deal along , your friend is supposed to express the desire to leave .

22036	Although haggling is common in countries such as India , it is a mistake to assume that it is standard practice throughout the world .
22037	To their shame , many tourists fired up by the prospect of making a fast rupee , dirham or peso are prepared to haggle for everything , ranging from the price of a cup of tea to an airline ticket .
22038	Such is their determination that the actual value of the item they want to buy — in comparison with what it would cost at home — becomes irrelevant .
22039	All that matters is getting one over the trader .

22041	Middlemen , as Trisha Barnett of the pressure group Tourism Concern points out , are much less vulnerable .
22042	‘ We came across some people from Papua New Guinea who were selling handicrafts and were confronted with a boatload of western tourists — all convinced they could buy for a knock-down rate .
22043	The people selling the stuff had never come across haggling before and they were left thinking that it is the norm in western society .
22044	‘ The saddest thing is that we 've been persuaded that true travellers know how to haggle .

22066	BUREAUX de change are at last being forced to offer travellers detailed information about the rates they offer and the commission they charge .

22095	‘ When you consider that Austrian lifts handled 480 million passengers last year and that 2.5 million native Austrians are skiers — excluding tourists — the accident figures are very small .

22097	Travel : A Wright little gem Hugh Massingberd visits an intimate manor house , newly opened to the public , in the Derbyshire plague village of Eyam
22098	By HUGH MASSINGBERD
22099	TO ARRIVE from London at Chesterfield station in Derbyshire — avoiding the gents ' toilet , where I have slipped up before — and then , after admiring the celebrated crooked spire , to find myself , within a few minutes , in the rugged landscape of the Peak , is an exhilarating experience .
22100	My townie taxi-driver also found it a bewildering one , for the village of Eyam , tucked away behind the hills that form Middleton Dale , is still a pretty remote and isolated spot .
22101	‘ Say , duck , ’ he accosted a woman petrol pump attendant , ‘ is this the right road for Eyam ? ’
22102	‘ Ay , luv , ’ she replied , ‘ it is . ’
22103	Ah !
22104	These warm-hearted Northerners , I reflected , so gloriously ‘ incorrect ’ in their dealings — a sentiment amplified by the sighting of an advertisement for local keep-fit classes headed ‘ Tums and Bums ’ .
22105	The driver assumed that I had come to see the church at Eyam , with its special exhibition featuring the events of 1665 and 1666 , when the bubonic plague visited the village .
22106	In my ignorance , I had never heard of this extraordinary saga , and I did indeed spend some absorbing time in the church learning something about it .
22107	The story goes that in September 1665 a parcel of cloth arrived in Eyam from London , where the plague was then rife , and infected the villagers .
22108	As the plague spread , some residents fled , including , I was sorry to see , the local squirearchical family , the Bradshaws — ancestors , incidentally , of that doughty opponent of Fascism , Christopher Isherwood , who decamped to California in 1939 .
22109	But the Rector , the Rev William Mompesson , stood firm and declared a kind of quarantine , setting bounds round the parish beyond which no-one was supposed to pass .
22110	The big landowner of the region , the Earl of Devonshire , arranged for food and other necessities to be left at dropping zones .
22111	This way the infection was kept within the parish boundaries .
22112	It was an act of heroic self-sacrifice .
22113	Out of some 350 who remained in Eyam , only 83 survived .
22114	Mompesson , whose wife was among those to succumb , wrote that Eyam had become ‘ a Golgotha — a place of skulls ; and had there no been a small remnant of us left , we had been as Sodom and Gomorrah .
22115	‘ My ears never heard such doleful lamentations .
22116	My nose never smelt such noisome smells , and my eyes never beheld such ghastly spectacles ’ .
22117	Moving and inspiring though all this was , in fact I had come to Eyam to attend the opening of Eyam Hall , in the village , by the present Duchess of Devonshire .
22118	It was , as the Duchess said in her speech , an exciting event because Derbyshire had so few smaller manor houses of this type open to the public — and what made it all the more special was the fact that Eyam Hall is still the family home of the Wrights , who built ( or rather rebuilt ) it , a few years after the plague , in 1671 .
22119	Eyam is , in short , a little gem .
22120	Set above a handsome forecourt , the stone house has four well-spaced bays , mullioned windows , parapets and gables .
22121	Inside is a cosy familial atmosphere , enhanced by portraits of such worthies as Maj John Wright ( ADC to ‘ Gentleman Johnny ’ Burgoyne in the American War of Independence ) , and by fine English furniture .
22122	The robust staircase would seem to be in an earlier style than the architecture of the house .
22123	Upstairs , the tapestry room is full of pastoral patchwork incorporating pieces from 15th-century Flemish work , as well as 16th-century Brussels tapestries .
22124	In the library there is a hair-raisingly gory book on display entitled A Survey of the Microcosm or The Anatomie of the Bodies of Man and Woman ( 1675 ) by Michael Spaher .
22125	More reassuringly , there is an evocative collection of old toys in the nursery , including a rocking horse made by Ayres in the 1890s .
22126	The present Wright squire , Robert , a 43-year-old solicitor , inherited the property from the widow of his cousin Charles ( a schoolmaster known as ‘ Daddy Wright ’ to his pupils at King Edward VI Grammar School in Sheffield ) , in 1990 .
22127	Since then , Robert and his wife Nicola have carried out a thorough and sympathetic restoration .
22128	Renovations in the old kitchen have revealed an impressive array of stone arches and flagstones .
22129	‘ The most nerve-wracking moment , ’ recalls Nicola Wright , ‘ was when we discovered the live First World War German mortar bomb , which cousin Charles had brought home as a souvenir . ’
22130	The bomb , which has been safely disposed of , is not on display , but there is much else to admire in the way of embroidery , china , glass , silver and costume .
22131	Eyam is a small , intimate house , so do n't all rush to see it at once , for the guides can accommodate only limited numbers on their tours .
22132	But while you are waiting , there is plenty to see in the historic ‘ plague village ’ , such as the village stocks , the original ‘ Plague Cottage ’ and , of course , the church of St Lawrence .
22133	Apart from the plague exhibition , there is a modern stained-glass window by Alfred Fisher depicting the plague story ; a Saxon cross combining pagan and Christian symbolism ; a rare 18th-century sundial ; and the tomb of Mrs Mompesson .
22134	Oh yes , and do n't miss the gravestone in the churchyard of the Derbyshire cricketer Harry Bagshaw .
22135	The ending of old Harry 's innings is represented by a ball shattering his stumps and an umpire 's finger raised unequivocably upwards to that great pavilion in the sky .
22136	Eyam Hall in Derbyshire is off the A623 , 12 miles west of Chesterfield , 15 miles south-west of Sheffield .
22137	Open until Oct 25 on Wednesdays , Thursdays and Sundays , plus Bank Holiday Mondays , from 11am — 4.30pm .

22187	Travel : Copse and robbers Christopher Somerville sees how woodland has usurped the ancient cattle thieves of the Cheviot Hills
22188	By CHRISTOPHER SOMERVILLE
22189	WHEN a Charlton chief sat down to dinner in times gone by and found a spur on the table where his meal should have been , he knew the cupboard was bare once . His wife was telling him to saddle up and steal a fresh batch of cattle from his neighbour 's herds .
22190	The families of North Tynedale in westernmost Northumberland — Charltons and Robsons , Milburns and Dodds — were never slow to lay hands on each other 's property in the lawless old days .
22191	Here , where the Scottish border ran across the Cheviot Hills , far from civilisation , ‘ reiving ’ , or cattle-thieving , was a way of life .
22192	Remoteness is still the keynote of this region , but a Charlton reiving party would be hard put to it these days to work up a good gallop along the upper reaches of the North Tyne River .
22193	Since 1926 the western fringes of the Cheviots have been planted with 250 square miles of close-packed conifers , while in their depths sprawl the seven miles of the Kielder Water reservoir , Europe 's largest man-made lake .
22194	I found it hard to picture what kind of landscape those statistics might have shaped , until I opened the Ordnance Survey map to find half of it coloured green with a great blue stain in the centre .
22195	Kielder Water is beautiful , and the Kielder trees formidably impressive in their domination of the hills .
22196	But by the time I had turned off the road from Bellingham at Kielder village and driven up the bumpy Forest Drive to East Kielder Farm , I was longing for the sight of something other than water and trees .
22197	Relief was at hand .
22198	The farm stands on a spur of moorland on the northern edge of the forest , and within 10 minutes I had turned my back on the corduroy battalions of trees and was striding under a still , cloudy sky over tussocks of rush and coarse grass , with my face to the long , bare shoulders of open hillside that flank the winding shallows of the East Kielder Burn .
22199	The footpath that runs with the burn is not one of those carefully waymarked and leafleted by the Forestry Commission .
22200	There are few attractions for the Kielder tourist here .
22201	The burn threads a wild and inhospitable crevice of the hills , where the wind blows cold and the sense of isolation grows with each lonely mile .
22202	Walking here , you leave the 20th century behind on the outskirts of the forest and enter the reconstructed emptiness in which the reivers and cross-border raiders of the past could operate unhindered .
22203	I squelched across tiny burns running in black channels of peat , and stood looking down from the hillside on to the grey roofs of Scaup Farm .
22204	The hollow barking of a dog came from one of the stone sheds , but there was no sign of life around the buildings .
22205	Scaup must be just about the loneliest farm in England , tucked down in the shelter of the hills with Kielder Forest 's dark mass blocking its southward view and the narrowing valley of the burn filling half the sky to the north .
22206	The East Kielder Burn divides here into Scaup Burn and White Kielder Burn .
22207	I dropped down the hill to ford White Kielder upstream of the ruined farmstead of Kielder Head , where a line of stunted alders , shaggy with lichen , leaned over their leafless reflections in the peat-brown water .
22208	Spring comes late to this windbitten and rain-soaked valley .
22209	But there were new-born lambs in the sheep pens of Scaup , and a cheery ‘ Hello now ’ from the farmer and his wife tending them .
22210	Those were the last human voices I heard all day .
22211	No-one lives up here in the cleft of the White Kielder Burn .
22212	The rough land is altogether too harsh and unyielding , giving sustenance only to sheep , and to the conifers high on the flanks of East Kielder Moor and Grey Mares Knowe , immense sweeps of hillside to right and left of the valley .
22213	The footpath on the left bank of the burn was little better than a sheep track , but there were clues to its former importance as a droving road over the hills to Byrness in Redesdale .
22214	Large boulders stood out beside the path as grey blobs in the featureless sheets of pale grass , and flat stones had been placed as bridges across the burns , their backs hollowed by the tread of feet through the centuries .
22215	Following these now disregarded signs of past activity along the old path , I traversed the hillside and came down to a crumbling stone sheepfold with the roofless remains of a shepherd 's hut built into one wall .
22216	The tiny single room was jammed with the mossy timbers of disused sheep pens , but the little iron fire grate that once warmed the hardy men who worked here was still set in the foot of the hut 's tottering gable end , and the massive stone lintel had not yet fallen from its place above the doorway .
22217	A dipper flew up from the burn as I emerged from the hut , his white breast flashing as he darted downstream .
22218	Somewhere ahead in the crags of Kielderhead Moor a hawk was whistling , a piercing sound in the lonely valley , overlain for a few heart-stopping moments by the snarl of a jet .
22219	That jarring manifestation of furious technology seemed as remote and ridiculous as a dream , as silence settled down on Kielderhead and the hawk 's whistle came down from the moors .
22220	The valley of the White Kielder Burn steepened again as I trudged north , its curves tightening .
22221	Now the path ran through heather high above the burn , past circular sheepfolds long disused and over the stony beds of side streams where the grass hung smooth and inviting , concealing ankle-breaking drops .
22222	A mile above the shepherd 's hut the hillsides ceased their upward rolling and curved together to form a dead-end valley of broad-breasted slopes five miles from the nearest tarmac road , hidden deep in the folds of the moors .
22223	The old drover 's road turned aside here and climbed under the rock faces of White Crags to continue its lonely course over Girdle Fell and down into Redesdale .
22224	I could have gone with it , giving myself four blissful miles of upland walking followed by as many miserable hours of fruitless searching for return transport to East Kielder Farm .
22225	Instead I lay back in the heather and savoured the trickle of the burn and the crisp smell of peat-laden ground .
22226	Not a sign of spring had yet penetrated this secret valley , but another month would put that right .
22227	There were five miles of return tramping to face , but they , too , could wait awhile .
22228	Travel : A pilgrimage sans progress Elisabeth de Stroumillo potters round Poitou
22229	By ELISABETH DE STROUMILLO
22230	PEOPLE tend to look vague when you mention Poitou .
22231	‘ Umm … not a part of France we know … where exactly is it ? ’
22232	Inland of La Rochelle , you say ; north of Cognac and east of Limoges .
22233	You sort of pass it without realising , going to the Dordogne .
22234	‘ Ah yes — Cognac .
22235	Nice is it ? ’
22236	Well , better than that , and one of the best things about it is the fact that so few people , except the French themselves , bother with it .
22237	Even for France , the variety to be found is enormous .
22238	My passion is for its numerous Romanesque churches , in most cases humbly proportioned but elevated into unique works of art by the richness of their exquisitely-sculpted decoration ; to go to Poitou/Saintonge and not look at any of its churches would be like going to an African game reserve and ignoring the animals .
22239	For serious drinkers there is the production of cognac to investigate around Cognac , plus the chance to sample pineau , the powerful local aperitif made from young wine laced with cognac .
22240	To the north , where Poitou borders on the Vendee , shapely clumps of trees are almost the only punctuation marks on widespreading marshy landscapes ; to the south it bubbles with little rolling hills .
22241	Water is everywhere : canals , streams , small busy rivers with charming names like the Boutonne , the Mignon and the Belle , and big lazy rivers like the Sevre Niortaise and the Charente .
22242	The lower reaches of the Sevre Niortaise are swollen with the waters that once covered the whole area , until medieval monks started to dig a spider-web of ditches to drain it .
22243	Now the Marais Poitevin is a pleasantly low-profile tourist attraction where you can take canal-boat trips from villages that have hardly changed in the 15-odd years I 've known them : Maillezais , with a huge and rather dull ruined abbey , and Coulon , where I first ate the delicious local version of moules marinieres called mouclade .
22244	Drifting between grassy polders to which farmers have to ferry their cattle in punts , or following leafy twisting lanes marked only by rusty signs proclaiming the ‘ Venise Verte ’ , you 're in an all-green , mysteriously silent world ; only the occasional fisherman , twitching his rod above the algae-smothered waters , disturbs the stillness .
22245	There is more greenery further south in the deep forest of Chize ( with the fine Renaissance chateau of Dampierre-sur-Boutonne at its edge ) ; and more marshes to the west around Rochefort and Marennes , where those mussels and oysters are raised .
22246	One of the region 's strangest townlets sits on those marshes : Brouage .
22247	Somnolent now within its low grey walls and stumpy towers , it was once rich on salt , and powerful to boot .
22248	It had a son to be proud of : Samuel Champlain , founder of Quebec , who was born there around 1569 .
22249	A century later , it had an adoptive daughter to weep for : 20-year-old Marie Mancini , niece of Louis XIV 's minister Mazarin .
22250	She went there when her romance with the young king was quashed for political reasons .
22251	Months later , when Marie had departed , Louis is said to have paused nostalgically at Brouage on his way to Paris after marrying the Spanish Infanta at St Jean-de-Luz .
22252	As you come back from Brouage towards St Jean-d'Angely — on the D18 via the canalside village of Pont-l'Abbe-d'Arnoult , with a lovely Romanesque church faade — a sign at the junction of the D122 points you to the chateau whose improbably perfect lake and gardens stare at you from posters throughout the region : La Roche Courbon .
22253	Its most surprising room , covered from ceiling to floor in 17th-century paintings , should be a salon or library ; instead , a dotty stone bathtub was set into one wall at a later date by a lady called Charlotte .
22254	She never used it , having got some of the plumbing details wrong .
22255	Wriggling across country on the D216 to Port-d'Envaux , you come to two more chateaux : 18th-century Panloy , flaking romantically away on its hillock overlooking a bend in the Charente and , almost next door , the much older , moated Crazannes , half-smothered in amazing flamboyant Gothic carving .
22256	Crossing the autoroute and turning north on the D127 brings you to St Jean-d'Angely by way of the isolated church of Fenioux .
22257	Its conically-roofed tower , hugged about by a brood of smaller roofs shaped like candle snuffers , is visible for miles .
22258	St Jean-d'Angely is a charming little town : there are good shops as well as half-timbered houses along its narrow old streets , one spanned by an ancient bell-tower .
22259	There 's also a Renaissance fountain , and an extremely odd conglomeration of church buildings comprising one ancient ruin , one proper church , and the skeleton faade and nave of a rather pompous and unfinished 18th-century abbey .
22260	It makes a conveniently central hub : the Marais Poitevin village of Coulon is 27 miles to the north by the D120 , which inexplicably changes its number at the top of a hill to D115 .
22261	Niort is about the same distance by the parallel N150 .
22262	Saintes , with Gallo-Roman remains , a beautiful Romanesque abbey and an atmospheric medieval quarter , is 17 miles south of St Jean ; 15-odd miles to the north-west is Surgeres , all of whose public buildings , including an engagingly asymmetrical church , are within the 16th-century castle walls , scattered among beautiful gardens and parkland — perfect for picnicking .
22263	Just under 10 miles south-west of St Jean , on the Brouage road , St-Savinien is at the upper limit of the tidal reaches of the Charente .
22264	The villagers ' main hobby seems to be fishing with peculiar , saucer-shaped nets suspended from precariously-perched bankside huts .
22265	One fisherman waxed lyrical about the variety of fish in the river .
22266	‘ Even salmon , ’ he assured me , ‘ but of course those are protected and must be thrown back .
22267	Which they are … normalement . ’
22268	Like almost every other Poitevin town and village , St-Savinien has a sweet Romanesque church ; Melle , indeed has three .
22269	But Aulnay , just over 10 miles north-east of St Jean , is probably the best , its unassuming architecture a perfect frame for the sheer artistry of the carvings round its doors and windows .
22270	Biblical motifs recur — some art-experts call them sermons in stone , and their messages would certainly have been clear to the often-illiterate medieval pilgrims trudging to Santiago de Compostela in Spain .
22271	But these themes are always interspersed with more fanciful ones : grimacing masks , weird animals , exuberant abstract patterns .
22272	I think those 10th- and 11th-century sculptors were motivated not just by piety but also by a certain competitive spirit : if a church was finer than the one in the next village , more pilgrims would surely pause there .
22273	Today 's attraction-merchants are doing no more to lure 20th-century tourists than their medieval forebears did for pilgrims .

22276	By CLARE KEEN
22277	OUR CAMPING gear included army surplus hammock , mosquito net and waterproof poncho .
22278	The one essential not on our kit-list was a sense of humour , and anyone who forgot this suffered for it .
22279	At least the teasing was entirely indiscriminate .

22282	The expeditions are based on the ethos of ‘ Challenge , Participation and Environment ’ , and strong emphasis is also placed on teamwork and leadership .
22283	Selection for the trip involved an interview for every candidate and , for some , an assessment weekend , though I missed this as I was a late entrant .
22284	The build-up training at Easthampstead Park , in Berkshire , was a chance for the group and the two leaders to get to know each other .
22285	People came from all over Britain — from a quiet Scottish village to the suburbs of Manchester — but everyone appeared to have a relatively comfortable background .
22286	This did not mean their parents had happily shelled out the £2,000 for the trip — many had been sponsored by local firms and one girl had taken out a bank loan .
22287	As guidebooks will tell you , you should not rush your acclimatisation period when you arrive in the Far East .
22288	But we had only a month in Borneo and after just three days — rather than the recommended three weeks — relaxing in Miri , the capital of Sarawak , we were looking forward to getting down to some trekking , the purpose of the trip .
22289	This first ‘ phase ’ of the trip took us to the caves of Mulu National Park and Gunung Mulu mountain .
22290	Once we started trekking we soon discovered that mental attitude and camaraderie were far more important than physical fitness .
22291	There was a lot of teasing and we had soon thought up nicknames for each other .
22292	As we walked some of us played Twenty Questions to keep us going .
22293	‘ Yes , ’ said the Mr Bean lookalike .
22294	‘ Is he an entertainer ? ’
22295	Others preferred Walkmans .
22296	Singing along to them in the middle of the jungle did seem a little odd , but it kept our minds off things , even if it invited torrents of abuse .
22297	Our first trek , up Gunung Mulu , was the hardest of the whole expedition and came as a shock to the system .
22298	It was supposed to take three to five days , but we aimed to do it in two .
22299	Although there were tracks , they were not very clear , and the going was made harder by the tree roots and vines which tripped up anyone who was foolish enough to try to look around .
22300	The climb was so steep that in places it could be made only with the help of ropes .
22301	The group tended to string out , with the fittest boys at the front , and the girls well behind .
22302	The leaders had their work cut out keeping the group together , and one or both had to remain at the back to motivate the slower ones — the most effective method seemed to be carrying their kit , though this tended to be a last resort .
22303	When we got to the halfway camp , two of us were not feeling up to the rest of the climb , and spent the night there .
22304	For those who made the summit , it was , disappointingly , shrouded in cloud .

22310	This was about the only use for insect repellent , as the mosquitoes seemed to have become hardened to the hundreds of tourists who had trekked through before us .
22311	The next trekking phase , in Bario , was a much easier eight-day walk through a series of villages .
22312	Although described by the World Challenge brochure as an area rarely visited by Europeans , it turned out to be popular enough with tourists for each village to have its own visitors ' book !
22313	The villagers lived in a single , communal building known as a longhouse , built on stilts to prevent flooding in the rainy season .
22314	Each family had its own bedrooms in one building , joined by short plank walkways to the main living area , where again each family had its own space with a small cooking area .
22315	There were no solid divisions between neighbours , and the children played up and down the length of the house .

22317	The longhouses were a welcome break after a day 's trek and were a great experience .
22318	Our hosts were most generous , sharing their food with us and insisting on giving us their bedrooms .
22319	This made our Bario trek the easiest in terms of home comforts .
22320	For much of the rest of the time we slept and cooked out , though most people never actually slept in their hammocks as the trees grew inconveniently far apart .
22321	Instead we used our ponchos as makeshift tents .
22322	Between two people one poncho was used as a groundsheet and the other was strung up and pinned down with home-made pegs .
22323	The high point of the whole trip for me came when seven of us trekked into the mountains to spend the night by a waterfall .
22324	The climb was very tough , taking eight hours in all , and in places the guides had to cut away the plants to clear a route .
22325	As we climbed higher the jungle became more marshy and exotic , with the sort of plants you usually only see as plastic decorations .
22326	Now the guides ' training in jungle warfare came into its own .
22327	Their curious calling attracted some gibbons , our first real sighting of wildlife .
22328	Then the guides lured a barking deer , with the sound of a pipe they made out of half-split bamboo .
22329	They promptly shot it for dinner , a welcome break from dehydrated rations .
22330	They spent half an hour skinning it and gutting it , taking almost everything , including the brain and intestines ( which , fortunately , they kept for themselves to eat ! ) .
22331	The waterfall itself was spectacular , a 50 ft torrent falling over a sheer rockface , with moss-covered precipices rising on either side .
22332	We made our camp in a small clearing by the top of the falls .
22333	As it began to get dark , we all settled around the guides ' fire , sharing the barbecued deer for supper .
22334	As one of the leaders commented , this day 's trek was exactly what we had come to the jungle for .
22335	Our month in Borneo certainly did n't feel like an organised holiday .
22336	The fact that we had definite goals on each trek , such as reaching a summit by sunrise , made the whole thing feel like an expedition .
22337	But our two leaders had bitten off more than they could chew when they tried to make leaders out of the rest of us .
22338	Our sense of adventure only went so far and we relied on them to make the decisions .
22339	Team spirit was much in evidence though , with the fitter people helping the strugglers and always giving encouragement .
22340	In this friendly atmosphere , plans for a reunion had already started before we were halfway through , and many people still keep in touch with each other back home .

22351	Travel : When the young cry freedom Mary Keen takes a look at overseas adventure from the parent 's point of view
22352	By MARY KEEN
22353	NEGOTIATING a holiday for teenagers is extremely delicate work .
22354	Tears ( though thankfully no blood ) have been shed in our house trying to reconcile demands for freedom , adventure and excitement with worries over health , safety and expense .
22355	The result for our three daughters has been French and Italian exchanges , Eurorailing , and country holidays in England or Ireland .

22362	I said , playing for time .

22366	World Challenge Expeditions meant nothing to us .

22368	The Borneo trip might have been designed to match Clare 's wildest dreams , but it undoubtedly involved real risk .
22369	A group of teenagers with two team leaders were to survive the rigours of a difficult climate while trekking through remote jungle and mountain areas with their possessions on their back and only their fellow expedition members to rely on .
22370	The organisation 's credentials and experience looked impressive , but our anxieties were genuine as we sent Clare off for her interview .
22371	However , World Challenge has a way with worried parents .

22381	Again , everything was done to reassure us .
22382	We had coffee with the team members and their families and saw a slide-show of last year 's trip .
22383	Passports , travellers ' cheques and malaria pills were all checked .
22384	One of the organisers , Charles Rigby , put the whole thing into proportion as I was anxiously sorting out with Clare a second name for the next-of-kin slot at the back of her passport .
22385	‘ It 's a wonderful thing that they 're all here and all OK , ’ he said .
22386	‘ One of the team members of our Nepal expedition had to drop out yesterday .
22387	He 'd picked up dysentery at a game fair in Hampshire ! ’
22388	A month later we all met again at London Airport .
22389	Clare looked incredibly fit and had had a wonderful time .
22390	She is saving for another trip , probably in an informal group of friends .
22391	The advantage of having trekked with a World Challenge Expedition is that another time she will know how things ought to be planned .
22392	Their treks cost a lot of money , but strike a good balance between looking after people and keeping planning flexible enough to take advantage of unforeseen opportunities : on the Borneo trip some of them camped by a waterfall and , instead of eating dried provisions , cooked a deer shot by one of their guides .
22393	The calibre of the expedition leaders ensures that these young travellers are able to complete trips that would be too complicated to organise for themselves .
22394	My conclusion is that if your teenager has the temperament and enthusiasm for an expedition type of holiday , and if your purse will stretch to it , you should go for it — but choose the organisation carefully .

22471	Motoring : Can R-R keep up with the times ?
22472	John Langley asks whether ‘ the best car in the world ’ has any sort of future
22473	By JOHN LANGLEY
22474	TWENTY-ONE years ago , Rolls-Royce Ltd went bust , and the nation shuddered .
22475	Developing the new RB211 aero engine had proved too much for the world-famous engineering group 's financial resources .
22476	The collapse was not directly linked to the motor car side , but it threatened the cars ' future .
22477	So we all swelled with pride when , a fortnight later , the car company went ahead with the launch of its new Corniche coupe in the South of France .
22478	Since then , Rolls-Royce Motors , the new public company formed two years later from the ashes of the parent group , has successfully re-established itself in its own rarefied niche at the top of the world 's luxury car market .
22479	Even those who did not endorse the company 's claim to produce ‘ The Best Car in the World ’ were prepared to give it the benefit of the doubt .
22480	But now there is a new battle for the body and soul of Rolls-Royce .
22481	Once again , the car company is in trouble and some are questioning its future .
22482	From record profits of about £34 million and near-record sales of 3,333 cars in 1990 , the car business turned in a loss of about £60 million last year as worldwide sales dropped to 1,731 , dragging down the profits of the parent group , Vickers .
22483	The setback has led to new speculation about a take-over or co-operative deal with BMW , Toyota , General Motors and others .
22484	There are suggestions that Rolls-Royce may be unable to fund the cost of the new model , due out in the next few years , and that Vickers will not be able to carry the burden much longer .
22485	More ominously , some are now asking whether the days are numbered for the last of the Edwardian motor cars — Rolls-Royce was founded in Manchester in 1904 — and whether cars of this size , weight and cost can really be justified in an era of increased social awareness and growing environmental concerns .
22486	However , both Sir David Plastow , the Vickers chairman , and Peter Ward , the Rolls-Royce Motors chairman and chief executive , insist that the gloom has been overdone and that structural changes introduced in the last year have made the company leaner and more efficient .
22487	The introduction of Japanese-style working practices at Crewe is said to have brought the break-even point down from sales of about 2,700 cars a year to about 2,000 .
22488	Even so , some analysts question whether the company can finance a new model costing , perhaps , £250 million without outside help .
22489	Sir David , who piloted Rolls-Royce Motors back to success after the ‘ 71 crash and who is due to retire next month , says : ‘ It depends how we do it — there are so many ways of developing a new Rolls-Royce .
22490	We are under no pressure to do anything immediately .
22491	We are not anxious to sell the company , but we are in discussion with a variety of people about co-operation and prospective linkages of various sorts . ’
22492	Peter Ward agrees : ‘ People are not walking away from the car .
22493	We knew we would get a big loss this year partly because of the cost of the changes we have made .
22494	Now , with sales of around 2,600 cars a year , we could actually make the same profits as we did in 1990 with 3,300 sales . ’
22495	But one insider who believes more radical changes will be needed is the erstwhile engineering director , Michael Dunn , who resigned this week to join an engineering consultancy group .
22496	Dunn was brought in from Ford , where he was director of product development in 1983 ; he will be best remembered for the development of the Bentley Turbo R , now the company 's best-selling model .
22497	He did the engineering for the new Rolls , but is believed to have felt that a smaller , lighter and more economical new car should have been developed .
22498	He says that ‘ surgery rather than an aspirin ’ was required , especially at the top of the company .
22499	Is there a future for the Rolls-Royce ?
22500	‘ Is it still ‘ the Best Car in the World ’ ? ’
22501	I asked him .
22502	‘ I never say it 's the best car in the world , ’ he replied , ’ but I believe we are the best at making a car in our class .
22503	There is a future for Rolls-Royce .
22504	The challenge is to produce a car which is more attractive to more people and costs less to make , and to minimise or eliminate any social embarrassment in running one .
22505	There is a change in social awareness .
22506	‘ We have to make better use of material resources , with lighter and more efficient cars .
22507	It has to be seen to be more socially responsible , to make people feel more comfortable about owning a Rolls . ’
22508	Although the fuel economy has improved by around 30 per cent over the past decade , there is evidence that the younger generation , in particular , feels the car is too ostentatious in today 's environment .
22509	Dunn believes the company has failed to put across the significant improvements made in the new car 's fuel economy , reduced emissions and extra safety .
22510	And he says : ‘ I do n't think Rolls-Royce buyers want a small car .
22511	They want space and they would expect it to be one of the bigger cars .
22512	But we could well encounter sales resistance if it is the biggest .
22513	‘ The main need is to minimise weight .
22514	Now , with the demands for fuel economy , carbon dioxide emissions and toxic emissions , people will be taking extreme measures to reduce weight . ’
22515	So does Rolls-Royce still have a credible future — with or without outside help ?
22516	The success of the new Continental R , and before that the Bentley Turbo , shows that if it can make the sort of car that new customers approve of , it should still be able to find 3,000 buyers a year around the world .
22517	But even Rolls-Royce must be seen to be moving with the times .
22518	That will certainly mean a slightly smaller , lighter car with an engine of less than the present 6.75 litres .

22527	A year or so ago I motored for the fun of it through Latvia and Estonia , from Riga to what was then still Leningrad , and never thought to encounter such ramshackle roads again .
22528	But nearly half a century of neglect has left the former DDR 's network in a no less lamentable state of collapse .
22529	They 're working on it , but there are about 50,000 kilometres of roads in all and I was told that fully half of them need to be torn up and rebuilt from scratch .
22530	Unfortunately , it appeared to be the same half that I had picked to explore .
22531	And joining me on the journey was a never-ending line of lumbering construction plant , Brobdingnagian concrete-mixers , and juggernauts laden with rocks and sand .
22532	Coming the other way , between convoys of trucks , was a motley mixture of Soviet or Polish-built old bangers , sleek new Golfs , beaten-up Wartburgs , the occasional Toyota , brand-new Audis , or still spluttering Trabants .
22533	Even among that cosmopolitan crowd I felt awkward in my 1990s rented Renault runabout , but Berlin airport did not have anything for hire with half-tracks at the back , no period Kubelwagen Type 82 staff cars , a Schwimmwagen perhaps , or what I might have really gone for — an old Humber Super Snipe finished in khaki with white mudguards .
22534	The creepy feel of the roaring '40s was more in evidence on the Berlin-to-Leipzig Autobahn , route No 1 .
22535	That was built by Hitler and , by the look of it , long stretches of its concrete had hardly been touched since .
22536	Deserted watchtowers on stilts loom over major intersections .
22537	I passed a military truck in the hedge .
22538	Filling stations , rest rooms , or any other signs of roadside life can be 50 or more bleak kilometres apart .
22539	Then , just as I 'd half a mind to twiddle with the radio in case Marlene Dietrich was still on , there would be another lurch of the Tardis-like mood and I 'd come upon a garishly-lit motel , freshly shipped across from the West , or else be smartly overtaken by a monstrous new Mercedes doing 200 kph or more with effortless abandon , at least until the next plunge into potholes and waterlogged scree .
22540	Central Leipzig presented a similarly surreal mixture of eager aspirations and a down-at-heel recent past .
22541	Shiny new BMWs were lined up for sale on the forecourt of what I took to be a condemned block of woefully austere flats , with a dilapidated factory next door .
22542	I was carved up by a let-me-through Porsche , with a chap at the wheel chatting into his Deutsche Telekom mobile phone , and then caught up with the car again a few kilometres further on , where it had slithered on the wet cobbles and collided with an antique tram .
22543	Later I turned and walloped back towards Berlin , by way of Magdeburg , with just the one tweak of the Tardis en route as I saw the signs for Potsdam .
22544	Next day I was thrashing along the Kingston bypass again .
22545	The traffic queue into London stretched back miles , for a sewer had collapsed in the centre of Wandsworth and gangs of workmen were tearing up the shattered road , apparently rebuilding it from scratch .
22546	I sang Lili Marlene to myself as I inched past the concrete-mixers and lorries full of sand , wondering where the Tardis might be sending me next .

22588	Food and Drink : The relaunch of lunch Restaurants are more fun at midday , says John Whitley
22589	By JOHN WHITLEY
22590	LUNCHTIME in Britain was never an occasion to whet the appetite of the serious private eater : most decent restaurants were cluttered up with expense-account company clodhoppers , making maximum use of their up-market luncheon vouchers .
22591	But nowadays there 's more elbow room and less cigar smoke — and the shrewder restaurateurs have set out to replace their lost business regulars by constructing lunch menus that are brief , light and designed to show off the chef 's talents rather than the customer 's credit rating ; it 's hard to believe that anyone can produce a good meal so cheaply .
22592	Often the set lunches are so cheap , in fact , that they work as a loss leader — a taster to tempt people back in the evening .

22606	Food and Drink : Tales of the unexpected Oz Clarke tries wines that break the rules — and win
22607	By OZ CLARKE
22608	I THOUGHT I 'd write this week about wines from unsung corners of the world , and began to round up the usual suspects — Cyprus , Israel , Canada , Belgium .

22611	This wine is so good , let's deal with it straight away .

22614	The Australians often use this grape combination , but they would be hard put to equal this quality for £4.65 .

22619	Australian Chardonnay has become so popular they have been suffering shortages , but there has always been loads of Semillon available .
22620	So the Aussies blend them together and , when they apply a little oak ageing too , the result is a lovely fat wine , mildly spicy , but with a streak of lime .
22621	Yet no-one else in the world had even considered such a blend , certainly not the Californians .

22626	And on these gravelly soils , the Semillon flourishes just as it does in Bordeaux .
22627	Semchard ( Oddbins , £4.99 ) — I know , I do n't like the name either — is 75 per cent Livermore Semillon and the rest Sonoma Chardonnay ; the flavour is quite unlike anything from California or Australia .
22628	There is a lovely smell of apricot and cinnamon spice , a light but extremely attractive dry texture and the same gentle , approachable apricot and cinnamon taste .

22632	The Baden region is well to the south of Germany 's more famous wine areas , and so receives far more sunshine , giving the growers greater flexibility in what kinds of wine they can make .
22633	Because Germany 's reputation was created by the Riesling wines of the Mosel and Rheingau areas , there has always been a sniffy attitude to the south .
22634	Sniff no more .
22635	Baden is undergoing the same transformation that is revitalising southern France .

22642	Corney &amp; Barrow does this one too , at £4.97 .

22832	Village Voice : The times they are a-changin'

22844	I know there are other irreconcilables out there somewhere .

22846	The towns accepted the new time , but not the country areas .
22847	Farmers argued that as their day already began at sunrise , they would gain nothing and would also lose an hour for their workers insisted on finishing at the same time as town dwellers .
22848	They refused to alter their clocks .
22849	So in the same village , there would be two different sorts of time .
22850	Post offices , railway stations and schools had the new , and the rest the old ; in the cottages there was friction as children and their fathers turned up for meals at different times .
22851	The women , as usual , bore the brunt of it , for everyone stayed up late , children refused to go to bed at night and men would not get up in the morning .
22852	It must have been the most bewildering social change since the Enclosures , and yet I can find no reference to it in the village School Log .
22853	Of course they got used to it , just as they got used to the closing of the railway , the death of the last squire , the demolition of the hall , the theft of the common land .
22854	The story of a village is , contrary to popular belief , one of continual change .

22936	In The Country : Outdoors : It 's mink that gets the blame Michael J. Woods feels that the declining vole faces more than one enemy
22937	By MICHAEL J WOODS
22938	THE PLOP of the fleeing water vole , followed by an underwater smoke-screen of silt , was once a familiar indicator of the presence of these mammals on our waterways .
22939	No longer .
22940	According to Rob Strachan , who has recently completed the field work for a Water Vole Survey of Britain , funded by the Vincent Wildlife Trust , only 30 per cent of the sites where water voles were found before 1939 still have them today .
22941	At the turn of the century , Kenneth Grahame could confidently give the water vole a leading role in The Wind in the Willows : almost everyone knew this small rodent from almost daily acquaintance .
22942	Even 20 years ago , Rob Strachan recalls , the vole was much more common .
22943	There were rivers he visited as a child where he could sit and watch water voles every day .
22944	He can not do that now .
22945	The water vole is about the same size as a brown rat , but with blunter features , smaller ears , a furry tail and a more gingery coat .
22946	Almost entirely herbivorous , it excavates a maze of galleries in the banks of waterways and ponds .
22947	There are entrances at different levels , including some below the normal waterline for use in emergencies .
22948	In times of flood the water vole moves upwards through its various tunnels until , in extreme conditions , it is forced to leave its underground refuge and resort to thick cover on the bank .
22949	The vole prefers slow-moving rivers , pools and marshy areas with some deep water whose level changes little , but there have been great changes to Britain 's wetlands during the past 40 years as a result of agricultural intensification .
22950	Modern farming techniques have diminished the number and quality of the wetlands which remain .
22951	During the same period , the North American mink has escaped or been released from fur farms and has spread almost nationwide .
22952	Gordon Woodroffe , a zoologist who has studied the water voles of the North York Moors , does not consider that the mink is the total rogue it is held out to be in some quarters , but it certainly appears to have caused the vole 's extinction on the Moors .
22953	He actually witnessed the death of the last animal in his study group .
22954	It was wearing a radio collar at the time .
22955	As Woodroffe recounts , he was watching it from the opposite bank of the narrow stream and was so close that he was worried the vole would hear his receiver pulsing loudly .
22956	As he watched , a mink pounced on the vole and , although the vole dived from the bank for safety at the last minute , the mink had grabbed it almost before it hit the water .
22957	Dr Johnny Birks has been studying mink for many years and he admits with some reluctance that this extremely successful marten may have contributed to the vole 's decline .
22958	The North American mink , he says , has fitted into the niche which would otherwise have been occupied by the European mink had it ever reached Britain .
22959	He is convinced , though , that the water vole would have withstood the pressures on it brought about by the mink had the vole 's habitat been less degraded .
22960	He is not surprised by accounts like Gordon Woodroffe 's , for upland streams are certainly not prime areas for the water vole .
22961	But where the habitat remains of high quality — Tregaron Bog in Wales or Stodmarsh in Kent — mink and voles co-exist in good numbers .
22962	Strachan and Birks agree that water vole numbers were in significant decline before the arrival of the mink — which can overcome the water vole 's traditional defences by following it into water and even , in the case of smaller mink , into its tunnels .
22963	Circumstantial evidence suggests that this animal is a significant problem for water voles .
22964	Strachan 's work shows that , when field signs of mink increase , those of voles diminish .
22965	It is always easy to blame an individual species , says Birks .
22966	An alien carnivore is the perfect answer .
22967	But we have to look past the mink to find the underlying reasons for the vole 's disappearance .
22968	Without doing so , we could miss vital factors of detriment both to water voles and other wetland wildlife .
22969	Rob Strachan stresses that the water vole survey is the first of its kind .
22970	It is only the baseline from which a repeat exercise can be carried out , in seven to 10 years ' time .
22971	Meanwhile , Strachan views the water vole as an indicator of wetland habitat quality , and he looks forward with little optimism .
22972	The vole , he says , appears to be coming perilously close to being endangered ; and this means that Britain 's wetlands are going the same way .

23015	In The Country : NATURE NOTE
23016	By Robert Burton
23017	THE STOCK dove must be one of our most overlooked larger birds .
23018	It is easily dismissed as ‘ just another pigeon ’ but it is smaller than its close relative the wood-pigeon .
23019	The two species sometimes associate in the fields , and their behaviour is similar , so a special watch must be kept for the stock dove .
23020	It lacks the wood-pigeon 's white bars on wings and neck .
23021	Look , instead , for black edges to otherwise pale wings when the stock dove is in flight .
23022	Its gruff double coo , with the second note clipped and emphatic , also reveals its identity .
23023	At one time confined to the south and east of the country , the stock dove spread as arable farming expanded in the 19th century ; but the introduction of organo-chlorine seed dressings in the 1960s was a disaster .
23024	The stock dove almost disappeared from some areas , but , like other species that were hard-hit at the same time , it has since made a good recovery .
23025	It is now , however , less abundant in intensively farmed countryside because herbicides have robbed it of weed seeds to eat , and the old farm buildings and ancient hollow trees where it nested have frequently disappeared .
23026	There is some mystery about the origin of the stock dove 's name , but it probably came from the habit of nesting in the stocks or trunks of trees .
23027	Although tree holes are the most common nesting place , stock doves have been found nesting in rabbit holes and they occasionally take over the abandoned nests of wood-pigeons .
23028	In The Country : The boys from the black stuff Sara Jackson sees how charcoal burners are surviving as a symbol of traditional methods of woodland conservation
23029	By SARA JACKSON
23030	IN A WOOD in South Ockendon , Essex , on the very outskirts of London , two brothers spend their days cutting dead timber , loading it into a steel kiln and setting it alight .
23031	The brothers , Ray and Alan Mitchell , are charcoal burners .
23032	Theirs was once a common line of business , but now there are only about two dozen professional burners left in the country .
23033	Ray and Alan , who took it up only two years ago , use a method practised for 150 years .
23034	As ex-plumbers they are unlikely candidates for resurrecting ancient woodland traditions , yet they are part of a growing drive to do just that .
23035	The Mitchells set up Eden Woodland Products in 1990 , after the builder they were contracted to went bust in the 1988 crash .
23036	They wanted a new start and found one in the form of nearby Hangman 's Wood , owned by the Marley Paving company .
23037	‘ After the storm of 1987 it was just devastated , ’ says Alan .
23038	‘ We thought : there 's got to be something we can do with all that wood . ’
23039	Now they produce barbecue charcoal from it .
23040	It 's a growing market .
23041	In 1987 Britain imported 20,000 tons , and by 1990 , 90,000 tons .
23042	Hangman 's Wood suffered so severely from the gales because , like much of our woodlands , it had been neglected for decades .
23043	Yet until the 1950s most had been managed as coppice since Norman times .
23044	It provided grazing land , timber , fruits and fuel , while remaining an undamaged wildlife habitat .
23045	Coppice management involves dividing a woodland into compartments , or coupes , which are cut on a rotation of five to 25 years .
23046	The small ‘ underwood ’ trees ( or coppice ) are chopped back to stumps , producing shoots cut for sticks and brushwood .
23047	A portion of ‘ standards ’ , such as oaks , are cut for timber at the same time , but saplings are left to replace them .
23048	Grazing should be prohibited in the newly-cut coupe for about seven years to allow the establishment of new seedlings .
23049	The wood therefore is constantly regenerated , yet also yields a steady supply of timber and grazing .
23050	The Mitchells were granted permission to burn charcoal from coppiced timber at Hangman 's Wood if they returned it to this state of management .
23051	They have cleared their first coupe and , aided by the Woodland Grant Scheme , will replant next spring , replacing weed species — such as sycamore — with oak , cherry and ash .
23052	‘ Last spring , bluebells grew in this cleared area for the first time in years , ’ Alan said .
23053	‘ They could n't get through the undergrowth before . ’
23054	The Mitchells coppice their woodland to earn a living .
23055	But other organisations supporting traditional woodland management have more far-reaching objectives in mind .
23056	The idea is a simple one ; begin working our dwindling woodland again and we could be providing the best argument for preserving it .
23057	These organisations include the Woodland Trust , and Thames Chase : the Community Forest in whose area Hangman 's Wood lies .
23058	Community Forests , funded by the Forestry and Countryside Commissions , were set up in 1990 on the outskirts of major cities .
23059	They encourage landowners and businesses to plant on their own land .
23060	But the woodland they create will be managed as it was in the past .
23061	The principle behind this effort to resurrect the countryside is ecnomic viability .
23062	Landowners are more likely to plant and maintain woodland if it provides income .
23063	So far , local companies have been the most responsive .
23064	Rhone Poulenc at Dagenham is financing the planting of 2,000 trees at nearby Eastbrook School .
23065	Two thousand trees on a two-acre site is a lot — too many to survive as fully mature trees — but this excessive planting keeps the programme economically viable .
23066	After 20 years or so thinning can begin ; the excess trees are used as timber and the remainder form a naturally spaced woodland .
23067	But it is the farmers who are the hardest to interest ( although all planting is grant-aided ) .
23068	For companies the benefits of co-operation are clear .
23069	It is good public relations .
23070	‘ The mineral companies especially will find future planning permission easier if they put the land back to good use , ’ says Max Hislop , a community forester .
23071	Hislop believes that , as crop subsidies fall , farmers will see woodland creation as a practical alternative .
23072	Meanwhile , recession has n't helped the programme .
23073	‘ We 'd have so much more planted , ’ says Hislop .
23074	‘ But when companies are laying off workers , they ca n't then be seen to donate money to charity .
23075	It 's very difficult . ’
23076	It 's very difficult too for Ray and Alan Mitchell .
23077	The UK imports 95 per cent of its charcoal , mostly from rainforests .
23078	Charcoal consumption from these sources is not environmentally acceptable .
23079	But the price is .
23080	To produce their charcoal , Ray and Alan cut the wood , load the kiln , empty it into sacks after the burn and then re-bag it for retail sale .
23081	They also drive around trying to market it .
23082	Last year their turnover was £6,000 .
23083	None of this was profit .
23084	They subsidise their income by doing odd jobs for Marley Paving .
23085	‘ We ca n't compete on price with Third World countries , ’ says Ray , ‘ because it 's so labour-intensive .
23086	Wholesalers buy imported charcoal at around £1.80 a bag , add 130 per cent and sell it on .
23087	We sell these bags at £2.49 and have added only 15 per cent profit . ’
23088	But the brothers have faith in the product 's future .
23089	They believe it will sell because , if consumers are boycotting tropical hardwoods stocked by DIY stores , there is no reason why they should condone burning them on the barbecue .
23090	As a sign of their optimism they have begun producing artist 's charcoal from willow .
23091	The concept behind planting and working woodland deserves to survive current hardships .
23092	After all , if the Normans had n't thought long-term and picked up their trowels 1,000 years ago , there would be no New Forest today .
23093	It is ironic that it has taken until the dawn of the 21st century to realise that the best methods of utilising — and hence preserving — our woodlands are those employed a millennium ago .

23104	‘ Temple of the law is turning into a casino ’ THE JASON DONOVAN LIBEL CASE : Damages award reinforces the need for reform , say lawyers
23105	By Terence Shaw , Legal Correspondent
23106	THE £200,000 damages awarded to Jason Donovan will be seen by many lawyers as another illustration of the urgent need for libel law reform .
23107	The award was made despite one of the strongest warnings ever by a judge to a libel jury about excessive pay-outs .
23108	It will lead to renewed demands that the judge should fix the amount of damages if a jury has decided that defamation has been proved or at least be given power to lay down minimum and maximum limits for juries .
23109	Since the Court of Appeal judgment in the Sonia Sutcliffe case , when damages of £600,000 awarded to the wife of the Yorkshire Ripper against Private Eye were reduced by consent to £60,000 , judges have been encouraged to give general guidance to juries .
23110	Mr Justice Drake used this power to full in summing up in the Donovan case , warning the jurors that they should not think they had to ‘ fix sums with lots of noughts on the end because it 's fashionable ’ .
23111	He urged them to compare any sum they had in mind with damages that might be awarded for physical injuries that lasted a lifetime .
23112	But he was not able to give any more specific guidance to the jury on how they should seek to compare the harm suffered by Donovan as a result of the libel with that suffered by those claiming damages in personal injury cases .
23113	In his libel action seeking aggravated damages , Donovan claimed he suffered serious injury to his professional and personal reputation , considerable distress and embarrassment and that the article implied he was guilty of gross hypocrisy and deceit by denying that he was homosexual .
23114	Donovan told the jury that he was not and never had been a homosexual .
23115	His counsel , Mr Charles Gray , QC , suggested that the libel had damaged his reputation at a time when he was about to break into serious acting after a string of top 10 hits as a pop star and a stint in the Australian TV soap , Neighbours .
23116	There is an accepted tariff of damages for personal injuries laid down on a case-to-case basis by judges .
23117	But damages awarded by juries in libel cases for injury to reputation are ‘ at large ’ and only subject to the general guidance by judges and limited powers for the Court of Appeal to correct those that are excessive .
23118	One libel expert , Mr Geoffrey Robertson , QC , author of the leading textbook on Media Law , said after yesterday 's verdict that huge awards were turning ‘ the temple of the law into a casino ’ .
23119	Britain did not have free speech because of the libel laws , he said .
23120	‘ It has expensive speech .
23121	Most western democracies have laws which offer a better balance between freedom of expression and the right to reputation . ’
23122	A new media law package was needed to guarantee freedom of expression and information and to liberalise the libel and contempt laws , balanced by a law to protect unjustifiable invasion of privacy .
23123	The key reform would be the introduction of a Bill of Rights with a free speech guarantee of the sort enjoyed by America and most European countries .
23124	The libel laws should be changed to provide a ‘ fast track ’ system allowing victims of media falsehoods to correct them quickly without having to wait a long time for their cases to go to court and gamble on the result .
23125	‘ The only cases where heavy damages should be awarded are where the words have been published out of malice , ’ said Mr Robertson .

23196	Politicians keep their silence on the big questions of the future
23197	By ANTHONY KING
23198	ASK ANY thoughtful person for a list of the problems likely to confront Britain in the next few decades and he or she will have no trouble answering .
23199	What is striking is that the responses bear almost no resemblance to the issues being discussed in the election campaign .
23200	There is an almost total disjunction between the big issues facing the country and the issues the politicians are willing to talk about .
23201	It is worth going through the list to see how great the disjunction is .
23202	Somewhere near the top must come the so-called ‘ demographic time-bomb ’ .
23203	On current projections , in 2001 there will be more than nine million people aged 65 or more , well over four million aged 75 or more and over a million aged 85 or more .
23204	Old-age pensioners will constitute 15 per cent of the population — a figure expected to rise steeply in subsequent years .
23205	The consequences of this will be enormous .
23206	Fewer and fewer people of working age will have to support more and more people no longer earning .
23207	The take-home pay of the young will have to be substantially reduced to provide pensions for the increased numbers of elderly .
23208	More special housing will be needed .
23209	The strains on the NHS and other social services , already great , will grow inexorably .
23210	The demographic time-bomb is ticking away .
23211	The consequences of its exploding will be momentous .
23212	Yet the party leaders are silent .
23213	Another demographic change is altering — and will alter even more in future — the basic pattern of working and family life .
23214	The low birthrate of recent years means that , by the end of the decade , much of the world 's work will be done by women .
23215	Eleven million women are now in full or part-time employment .
23216	Government statisticians estimate that 96 per cent of the growth in the labour force between now and 2001 will be among women .
23217	The consequences will again be momentous .
23218	Will the birthrate continue to fall ?
23219	Who will look after the children ?
23220	By 2001 , mothers looking after their children at home , already a vanishing species , will be virtually extinct .
23221	Governments , whatever their own inclinations , will have no choice but to fashion childcare policies .
23222	Whole generations of children will otherwise be in danger of emotional and physical neglect .
23223	The issues are already clear .
23224	Yet the politicians again have little to say .
23225	The same is broadly true of Aids .
23226	Official projections of the spread of Aids have mercifully been revised downwards , but around 50,000 are believed to be infected in Britain , and the disease is pandemic in parts of Africa .
23227	Some medical experts believe the chances of an explosive spread of the disease to Europe , including Britain , can not be discounted .
23228	The list of 1992 non-issues can be extended .
23229	Apart from the Liberal Democrats , the politicians are saying little about Britain 's future relationship with the EC .
23230	In private , politicians discuss the wisdom of membership of the Exchange Rate Mechanism and widely predict a devaluation within the ERM whichever party is in power next weekend .
23231	Yet apart from a few scattered Tory voices , there is no public debate .
23232	Politicians are also largely silent on how the next government will be able to carry out spending plans in view of the state of the productive economy .
23233	Environmental issues — resource depletion , global warming , England 's drought , the degradation of cities and countryside — likewise produce , for electoral purposes , a shrug of politicians ' shoulders .
23234	The problems associated with nuclear power , and the imminent proliferation of nuclear weapons , have yet to produce a party election broadcast .
23235	The Green voice is hardly audible .
23236	Politicians can not reasonably be blamed for all this .
23237	They are by nature reactive rather than pro-active .
23238	There is nothing in the political system that forces them to consider the future .
23239	They can protest that voters show little interest in the demographic timebomb , or childcare problems .
23240	Yet general elections are supposed to be ‘ the grand inquest of the nation ’ .
23241	On present form , future generations are likely to look back on the 1992 election — with its emphasis on marginal tax rates — as at best rather quaint , or at worst a tragic irrelevance .
23242	Anthony King is Professor of Government at Essex University .

23288	The ‘ startling ’ facts about increased education spending under the Tories would ‘ leave many parents , teachers and administrators gasping in disbelief as they pick their way through pot-holed playgrounds to book-starved classrooms , ’ he added .
23289	‘ As in the National Health Service , perceptions of real life in public institutions do not fit well with the statistics . ’
