23676	By MARTYN HARRIS
23677	AT THE drop-in centre on South Meadowell , Labour candidate Paddy Cosgrove has dropped in to meet the people — mostly fat ladies in shellsuits with laps full of chips .
23678	‘ You all know me , ’ says Paddy , and a fat lady with good timing says , ‘ I do n't know you .
23679	Never seen you in me life . ’
23680	On the floor a toddler peels more chips from a congealed , bluish mass and feeds them to a baby .
23681	Another digs the cream from the centre of a pink fancy and smears it in his hair .
23682	Paddy Cosgrove , councillor and barrister , in candidates ' pinstripes , sits tensely on the edge of his plastic chair .
23683	‘ I 'm a regular visitor to this estate … ’
23684	‘ Who does he say he is ? ’ says a second fat lady .
23685	‘ That Liberal , Paddy Ashgrove … ’
23686	‘ He 's better looking on TV … ’
23687	‘ He 's only come because the press are here , ’ says the first fat lady .
23688	And Paddy Cosgrove blushes .
23689	Political consciousness is low on the Meadowell Estate .
23690	Turnout at the last election was around 50 per cent , and with the thinning of the electoral roll brought by the poll tax , will be even lower this time .
23691	They are mostly Labour voters but several confuse their Labour candidate with the leader of the Liberal Democrats .
23692	Very few know their MP is a Conservative , and hardly anyone that his name is Neville Trotter , defender of a slender 2,500 majority .
23693	By most measures Meadowell is the worst council estate in Britain , and probably the most notorious since the riots last September , which followed the deaths of joyriders Colin Atkins and Dale Robson in a police chase .
23694	In fact Meadowell is an Elastoplast name like Sizewell , invented in the 1970s to disguise what was already a running sore .
23695	When built in 1938 it was The Ridges , which is still what they call it locally — a slum clearance project on the north bank of the Tyne , 10 miles east of Newcastle .
23696	Its first inhabitants were shipyard and fishquay workers from the riverside towns of North Shields and Wallsend , who moved happily from their tumbledown terraces to these fine new houses with inside toilets and gardens .
23697	Many , like Ronnie Collyer , a retired shipyard worker , still live here and are still proud of the place .
23698	All the trouble , says Ronnie , is down to ‘ a few families who doa n't keep their young ’ uns in order .
23699	And then the media coom down and blow everything up . ’
23700	He has polished shoes , a close shave , and too much pride for a free drink .
23701	‘ It 's a canny place The Ridges , with plenty of good folk . ’
23702	But something was wrong from the start .
23703	Some say it was the importing of whole streets of fighting families from the fishquays , with their dockland diversions of prostitution , drug-dealing and handling .
23704	Others say it was the shortage of pubs , shops , churches , transport and police stations .
23705	By the 1950s , The Ridges was the criminal ghetto of Newcastle , and by the 1970s a costly council manicure job had turned it into a free-fire zone .
23706	Paths and boundaries vanished , allowing the tides of street life to wash right up to the doorsteps .
23707	Joyriders used front lawns to practise their handbrake turns .
23708	Car theft became so common that private cars virtually disappeared from the area .
23709	Shops like greengrocers and chippies , with pitiful cash takings , were routinely subjected to armed robberies with shotguns , balaclavas — the whole bit .
23710	When I ask the fat ladies at the drop-in centre what is the one thing that would do most to improve the estate they say ‘ get rid of the kids ’ and they are only half joking .
23711	The age structure of Meadowell means it is awash with teenagers , whose only pastimes are having babies and body-building .
23712	Do your husbands come here ?
23713	I ask , and they all laugh .
23714	‘ The men are all useless — sitting indoors if there 's trouble in the street .
23715	It 's women have to go out and deal with it . ’
23716	By the time of the riots a quarter of all houses on the estate were boarded up and burned out by infant petrol bombers .
23717	Unemployment was 80 per cent on some streets .
23718	In Meadowell Primary , which has 232 children , every one was receiving a clothing grant .
23719	The area had effectively been abandoned by the authorities , a fact which became clear during the riot itself , when police waited five hours to enter the estate and put down the disturbances .
23720	‘ And there were never more than a few dozen ringleaders , ’ Bob Mather , a local butcher , tells me .
23721	‘ I was stood outside me shop all night , and most were no more than kids . ’
23722	Eight months on and little has changed — if anything it is rather worse .
23723	Unemployment is up another 17 per cent ; more houses and shops are boarded up ; burglaries and joyriding continue — and if there is less ram-raiding it is only because 50 or so of the hardest cases are still behind bars .
23724	A food co-op which tried to replace the burned-out shops has been closed after several break-ins , and even the drop-in centre is burgled weekly , according to project worker Sheila Auld .
23725	There is a new phone box , ripped from the wall and lying on the floor of her office to prove it .
23726	Meadowell has even discovered a new martyr in the shape of one Willy Hunter , a local hard nut awaiting trial for murder , and allegedly the victim of a police frame-up .
23727	‘ Free Willy Hunter ’ say the graffiti , next to the old , fading graffiti for Dale Robson and Colin Atkins .
23728	My friend Kevin , muscleman and minicab driver , says the lads would be out rioting for Willy now if it was n't tipping down with rain the whole time .
23729	A few things have been achieved , I suppose .
23730	There are some posh flats going up at neighbouring Royal Quays which will provide building jobs : ‘ It 's Sun City in the middle of Bantustan , ’ a Labour councillor said to me .
23731	The Cheviot housing association is slowly taking over property in South Meadowell .
23732	A new police station is to be built .
23733	The government sponsored Meadowell Initiative makes noises in the north of the estate — but does pitifully little , painfully slowly .
23734	North Tyneside council says it is too starved of funds by central government to do much .
23735	Tory ministers , like Michael Heseltine who visited Meadowell last November , say the cash shortages are due to council profligacy and bad management .
23736	MP Neville Trotter is a pear-shaped Tory with pear-shaped vowels who has little appeal to the people of Meadowell , and a dwindling appeal in the middle-class suburbs where unemployment is also climbing .
23737	Paddy Cosgrove , his likely replacement , is a council hack of 21 years standing and ideal backbench fodder , though it is hard to imagine him leading a crusade for Meadowell .
23738	When I ask the people of the estate what they want from this election some say they want Cheviot to rebuild it and others that it would be better grassed over .
23739	Some say they should bring back hanging ; others say it is the politicians they should hang ; but most say there is nothing anybody can do at all .
23740	General Election : N Trotter ( C ) 25,113 , P Cosgrove ( Lab ) 22,530 , D Mayhew ( L/All ) 10,446 .
23741	Con Maj : 2,583 .
23742	Election 1992 : Labour anger after Tory phone ‘ prank ’
23743	By George Jones , Political Editor
23744	LABOUR launched a strong protest last night over the latest Conservative election broadcast , which invited Tory supporters to telephone Labour 's London headquarters to complain over the way it gave prominence to ‘ bad news ’ about Britain .
23745	The broadcast sought to contrast the record of the past 13 years of Tory rule with Labour 's Winter of Discontent in 1978–79 .
23746	It also launched a fierce personal attack on Mr Kinnock 's fitness for high office , highlighting his changes of view on nationalisation , Scottish devolution , nuclear disarmament and European Community membership .
23747	Describing the Labour leader as a former leader of the ‘ hard left ’ , it said people ‘ ca n't trust a man who will change any principle , abandon any policy , say anything to get elected ’ .
23748	But the most controversial feature of the broadcast was the inclusion of the telephone number of Labour 's headquarters .
23749	The broadcast began with an upbeat picture of life in Britain — asking the viewers if they recognised which country it was .
23750	There were clips of interviews with people in France , Germany , Italy and Holland saying it was not their country .
23751	‘ The country we are describing is Britain , and Labour do n't seem to recognise it .
23752	Labour have been talking Britain down so hard , relishing every piece of bad news , rubbing their hands at any failure in public services , that they have chosen to forget what a great country Britain really is , ’ said the broadcast .
23753	It then invited people to ring Labour 's headquarters .
23754	Labour launched an immediate protest over what they described as a ‘ pathetic prank ’ , and voiced concern that their legitimate work as a political party in the election campaign could be affected if their switchboard was jammed .
23755	But the Tories were unrepentant , declaring that the broadcast was ‘ making a point ’ and the telephone number was already publicly available in the telephone book .
23756	The broadcast , which featured Mr Hurd , Foreign Secretary , and Mr Heseltine , Environment Secretary , acknowledged there had been a recession which had caused pain for some people .
23757	It added : ‘ It would be a tragedy if the frustrations and the hardships that the recession has caused , and for some it is still causing , if it meant that Britain threw away all the achievements of the last decade .
23758	Remember British living standards have never been so high . ’
23759	Harking back to the ‘ terrible Winter of Discontent ’ under the last Labour government , the 10-minute film recalled patients being turned away from hospitals , rubbish going uncollected and the dead being left unburied .
23760	With images of picket-line strife , the broadcast warned : ‘ The last thing we need now is for Labour to come in and wreck Britain 's recovery . ’
23761	The Prime Minister appeared at the end of the broadcast to warn of further turmoil if the Government 's health and trade union reforms were undone .
23762	Mr Major said : ‘ There is only one real choice at this election .
23763	Going forward with me or backwards with Mr Kinnock . ’
23764	He said a Conservative victory would bring confidence that would get the economy ‘ really humming ’ .
23765	Labour would put the economy into reverse .

23864	By Ben Fenton
23865	FALLING electoral rolls may threaten Labour 's chances in several marginals and even in some ‘ safe ’ seats .
23866	Poll tax evasion is thought to be the main reason for the falling numbers .
23867	Figures from the Office of Population Censuses and Surveys show that the number of voters is significantly less than at the time of the 1987 election , even though the adult population has grown .
23868	The independent Electoral Reform Society said the drop was largely due to efforts to evade the poll tax .
23869	The biggest drop is in Hackney , east London , which has two safe Labour seats .
23870	The electorate has fallen by 24,985 — more than 18 per cent — since 1987 .
23871	The number of voters missing in the Labour seats held by Ms Diane Abbott and Mr Brian Sedgemore is in each case about twice the size of their majority .
23872	More worryingly for Labour , in six key target seats the number disappearing from the electoral rolls is higher than the majority it is trying to overturn .
23873	In Hampstead and Highgate , north London , where Miss Glenda Jackson is trying to overturn a Tory majority of 2,221 , the register has dropped by 5,156 , and in Hornsey and Wood Green , north London , the chances of Labour reversing a 1,779 Conservative lead may be hit by the disappearance of 6,673 names from the list .
23874	The majorities in Labour target seats are also smaller than the reduction in the rolls in Dulwich , Streatham , Greenwich and Wallasey .
23875	The Electoral Reform Society believes most of those who have gone off the rolls are potential Labour supporters , if only because of their assumed strong opposition to the poll tax .
23876	Labour argues that it will not be significantly affected because most of those who evade the register would have been among the large proportion — between 20.1 per cent and 31.2 per cent in their top 10 target constituencies — who did not vote in 1987 .

23900	Some people said that their incomes were so low that they could not obtain mortgages and 18 were squatted in by former occupants who refused to pay the money .
23901	An attempt to have them evicted failed because the county court judge ruled that the law only applied to people who had no interest in the property .
23902	The trust has failed to sell some of the other houses because of local concern about the squatters .
23903	The trust , which has lost £153,000 on the project , has restored about 200 properties and was prominent in preserving Pell Well Hall in Shropshire and the 12th century Siddington Barn near Cirencester , Glos .

24206	Letter to the Editor : Scandinavia poor guide for Labour
24207	SIR — Neil Kinnock tends to use Scandinavian countries , and Sweden in particular , as models of socialist ideals in practice .
24208	But these countries are rather different below the veneer of social justice which is apparent to the casual observer .
24209	Sweden has recorded an 8.4 per cent fall in industrial production in 1991 , a figure which compares rather badly with the United Kingdom 's latest year-on-year figure of 1.1 per cent .
24210	Denmark and Sweden are deep in a trough of domestic and foreign debt .
24211	The former owes 63 per cent of its Gross National Product as accumulated public sector borrowing compared to the British figure of 43 per cent .
24212	Every Dane owes ca £5,000 to foreign creditors when the foreign debt is divided equally , dwarfing the problem encountered in ‘ debtor ’ countries such as Poland and Brazil .
24213	Paddy Ashdown 's solution to the poll tax is a local tax a la Scandinavia .
24214	But he fails to mention that Denmark has a local income tax of 13.5–22 per cent , as well as a property tax .
24215	Marginal rates of income tax reach 68 per cent for many ordinary families , VAT is 25 per cent on all goods , and a wealth tax of 2.2 per cent per annum on assets over £125,000 causes successful people to emigrate .
24216	In Denmark , there are just as many unemployed people as there are workers in manufacturing industry .
24217	More than half the adult population receive unemployment benefit grants or pensions from the government , which in addition employs around 40 per cent of the workforce .
24218	We do need to learn some more fiscal discipline in the United Kingdom .
24219	We should learn to pay ourselves wage rises lower than inflation when necessary , and not to press for devaluation within the EMS .
24220	What we do not need is another socialist experiment starting next Thursday .

24236	Leading Article : The road to chaos
24237	THE Conservative Party and the Liberal Democrats are quite clear about proportional representation .
24238	The Tories regard it as an aberration that would be catastrophic for Britain 's system of government .
24239	The Liberal Democrats support it as their one chance of grasping real political power .
24240	Meanwhile , Neil Kinnock , leader of the one party that could actually bring PR about , is refusing to say where Labour stands on the issue .
24241	Pressed to do so in a television interview on Thursday night with Sir Robin Day , Mr Kinnock allowed that he had formed a view , but he was not prepared to disclose it .
24242	On an issue of such constitutional significance , this is a disgraceful evasion .
24243	Labour simply can not fudge its views on PR .
24244	As Roy Hattersley , himself an opponent of the scheme , reminded journalists yesterday , proportional representation would involve a radical change from one form of democracy to another ; it is n't something which can be taken lightly .
24245	Yet Mr Kinnock , repeating the offer he has made to the Liberal Democrats of a committee of inquiry into electoral reform , has upped the stakes by speaking of a commitment to reform Britain 's constitution by consensus .
24246	What needs to be spelt out very clearly before polling day is that PR would bring about the opposite effect to what many voters comfortably believe .
24247	A vote for PR , as represented by the Liberal Democrats , is not a vote for fairness , but for injustice ; not a vote for stability , but for political chaos .
24248	Take the example of Belgium where , as the Prime Minister pointed out on Thursday , PR has created a political culture of backstairs deals and perpetual campaigning .
24249	Take the example of Italy , where proportional representation has created permanent instability , with a series of coalition governments that have had to depend on several minor parties whose influence has been out of all proportion to their success in the polls .
24250	If anybody wishes to see just how pernicious that influence can be , they can look at the Likud government in Israel , which has had to impose repressive legislation at the behest of religious extremists who hold the balance of power .
24251	PR ( much diluted ) has been an indisputable success only in Germany , which has enjoyed , until recently , a natural consensus between its political parties , founded on the need for regeneration .
24252	In Britain , under PR , no government since the Second World War would have won an overall majority .
24253	We should have had , at best , a continuous middle-of-the-road government which could never have taken radical reforming measures .
24254	Under PR , the trade unions would still have a stranglehold over industrial policy , education would still be in the grip of local authorities and any proposals for effective tax cuts would have been quietly shelved .
24255	Worse still , our elected representatives , far from strengthening their links with voters , actually become less accountable to them .
24256	Under some forms of PR , their names are put on a list and seats are awarded to them by party managers .
24257	PR creates that grim parasite upon democracy , a ‘ political class ’ of career politicians who are less vulnerable to electoral swings , and whose convictions are compromised in the constant brokering of deals and searching for consensus .
24258	PR is all about horse-trading .
24259	It may be argued that there is nothing too morally reprehensible about this in many areas of our public life : but when it affects life-and-death issues , such as Northern Ireland , the idea of making legislation on internment , for example , subject to back-room bargains struck at Westminster , is one which would stick in the throats of many voters .
24260	Mr Kinnock 's soft shoe shuffle , as he prepares to court the Liberal Democrats in the event of a hung Parliament , is an earnest of what could lie ahead .
24261	He has refused to rush legislative changes through , but he has not ruled out proposals on electoral reform which could be put before the electorate either in a referendum or at the next general election .
24262	This is his inducement to Paddy Ashdown .
24263	The voters have the right to know whether his heart is in it , or whether it 's a con .

24295	Sit , they said , but he would n't This week John Major began to appear on a different kind of box .
24296	In the last of his series on the leaders , Frank Johnson reports
24297	By FRANK JOHNSON
24298	WE WERE in the West Country .
24299	The Prime Minister was on his soapbox .
24300	Just up the road , at Langport in Somerset , was the birthplace of Walter Bagehot ( 1826–1877 ) , although as he directed his microphone at Liberal Democrat hecklers John Major had other things on his mind .
24301	The relevance is that Bagehot was the first political commentator .
24302	The travelling chaos of a modern party leader 's election entourage had carried Major within a few miles of the home of the founder of the profession , a few of whose more troublesome contemporary practitioners are said to have caused him much irritation over the 16 months of his premiership .
24303	‘ A Liberal ?
24304	He 's admitted to being a Liberal ! ’
24305	Major cried , jabbing a finger in the direction of one heckler .
24306	The man had a Liberal Democrat rosette pinned to his cap .
24307	He was also carrying an orange poster on a pole , urging a vote for the local Liberal Democrat candidate .
24308	Therefore the admission which the Prime Minister wrung from him could hardly be said to have been grudging .
24309	But , like all the best soapbox orators , Major had prepared his repartee in advance .
24310	‘ I knew there was one here , ’ he continued , meaning Liberal Democrats .
24311	There were , in fact , about a score .
24312	Then came the passage , which appeared on the television news that evening and in the papers the next day , about the Liberal Democrats being the Trojan horse that would let Labour in .
24313	There were also some lines intended for local consumption : ‘ Higher petrol prices from the Liberal Democrats … that 's not gon na help a rural area …
24314	’ What would Bagehot have made of him ?
24315	Like the heckler , he was a Liberal .
24316	There the similarity ends , since judging from his writings Bagehot was a roaring snob , whereas judging from his heckles the heckler was not .
24317	More to the point , it was Bagehot who said : ‘ A constitutional statesman is in general a man of common opinions and uncommon abilities . ’
24318	The statesman to whom he was referring was Peel .
24319	A political commentator of our own day , Paul Johnson , quoted it not long after Major became Prime Minister to suggest that it was also true of him .
24320	But is it still ?
24321	B AGEHOT 'S phrase comes in a passage in which he appears to propound the dispiriting theory that a politician , if he wants to get anywhere , must appeal to ‘ the average man ’ .
24322	The average man is ‘ a cool , common person , with a considerate air , with figures in his mind , with his own business to attend to , with a set of ordinary opinions arising from and suited to ordinary life .
24323	He ca n't bear novelty or originalities …
24324	Original theories give trouble ’ .
24325	Bagehot goes on to say of Peel : ‘ From a certain peculiarity of intellect and fortune , he was never in advance of his time .
24326	Of almost all the great measures with which his name is associated , he attained great eminence as an opponent before he attained even greater eminence as their advocate . ’
24327	That last sentence has more to do with Kinnock than with Major .
24328	It is also a warning to all hack Tories who think that it is a telling blow against Kinnock to keep on pointing out that he has reversed his opinions about unilateral nuclear disarmament , British membership of the EC , or anything else .
24329	But the most striking thing about Bagehot 's essay on Peel , in the light of the last full week of this election campaign , is that it simply does not apply to Major at all .
24330	Common opinions were what got Major into difficulties in the first place .
24331	Between his becoming Prime Minister and his party 's fall in the polls about 10 days ago , Major did nearly everthing that common opinion wanted him to do .
24332	This was true of what he did about both high policy and low politics .
24333	For example , on high policy common opinion said that there was nothing for it but to stay in the ERM .
24334	He stayed in , and the recession worsened .
24335	In low politics , common opinion — no less common for being expensively hired by Conservative Central Office — encouraged him in the belief that he should fight much of the election sitting down .
24336	He did so , and he looked like the questioner in the studio audience rather than the answerer .
24337	The result was Wobbly Week , the second week of the campaign .
24338	But last Saturday Major climbed on to that soapbox in Luton .
24339	Until then , he had been that most inhuman of creatures — the public figure described by others as ‘ very human ’ .
24340	Now he really was human — unscripted , jokey , even a bit passionate .
24341	The jubilant word from Kinnock 's camp was that Major was behaving more like an opposition leader than a prime minister .
24342	But there seemed nothing wrong with the head of government appearing to be the challenger on the hustings .
24343	President Truman did so in a campaign which no-one expected him to win , and he won .
24344	It is justified if the head of government is challenging something powerful .
24345	Kinnock complains of the alleged power of the Tory tabloid press , but he has powers on his side too .
24346	Ninety per cent of his party 's cash comes from the unions , which will expect a return .
24347	The British people have in the past found them rather more powerful than the corporations which are popularly supposed to finance the Conservative party .
24348	Then there are all those schoolteachers , dons , television producers , writers on arts pages and members of the agitating classes who want a Labour win in order to impose Political Correctness .
24349	That is to say , they will have what the Jesuits once attached such importance to : power over young or impressionable minds .
24350	As the week went by , Major rejected common opinion about two other large subjects : proportional representation and Scottish devolution .
24351	He hardened his opposition to both , despite the fact that his own party chairman had once favoured the first , and vocal forces within his Scottish party were in support of the second .
24352	E VEN at this late hour , psephology , demographics and luck suggest that the Tories could still emerge as the biggest single party in a hung Parliament .
24353	Is it possible that Major would rather go into opposition — with the dangers that would mean for his continued leadership of the Conservative party — than offer PR and Scottish devolution to the Liberal Democrats ?
24354	If so , we are dealing with a more Quixotic , romantic or principled figure than some of us used to think .
24355	Once that soapbox came out , Major campaigned as if he would now do and say what he really thought .
24356	Was it too late ?
24357	From Central Office , and from around his entourage , came the unmistakable signs of fair-weather friends preparing to detach themselves from blame for defeat .
24358	And then , on Thursday morning , when Major 's election tour reached the Daily Mail Ideal Home Exhibition , Sir David English , the paper 's editor , was not there to greet him .
24359	A junior spin doctor is reported to have muttered , though admittedly out of my earshot : ‘ We 've been snubbed . ’
24360	Not Sir David !
24361	Some in the profession of political commentating would opt for Bagehot as their formative influence , but mine has long been Sir David — a founder of biased Tory journalism .
24362	His lack of humbug about political balance has always made him more honest than all the employees of BBC Current Affairs awaiting with glee the Kinnock years .
24363	Eventually , Sir David 's office issued a statement about the Prime Minister .
24364	Normally , a prime minister 's office would issue a statement about an editor .
24365	But Major makes a point of not being grand , and with Sir David it is the other way about .
24366	‘ Sir David English was not informed of the visit and in consequence had no plans to attend the Ideal Home Exhibition that day , ’ the official statement announced .
24367	Faith in Sir David 's leadership was restored .

24389	Scrap trendy changes , urges police chief
24390	By Neil Darbyshire , Crime Correspondent
24391	POLICE should abandon ‘ fashionable management theories ’ which blur traditional relationships between ranks and return to the hierarchical principles of leadership , a senior officer said yesterday .
24392	Recent pressure to end the obligation of junior officers to salute or stand in the presence of their seniors and recommendations to scrap the existing discipline code for a new ‘ code of ethics ’ applicable equally to all had dangerous implications , said Deputy Assistant Commissioner Lawrence Roach .
24393	‘ Many of our recent troubles in retaining and maintaining public confidence might have been less severe and more easily solved if we had not begun to depart from the traditional relationships between ranks , ’ he added .
24394	Writing in the influential Police Review magazine , Mr Roach , head of policing for north-west London and a member of the Association of Chief Police Officers , said that , since the time of Sir Robert Peel , the police had always had to reassure the public that their powers and privileges would not be misused .
24395	‘ Peel 's response was to construct a service with a severe code of discipline and a structure of supervisory ranks designed to ensure strict control of policing and police officers .
24396	‘ It is for the protection of the public that police officers are subject to [ this ] code , which reaches into every aspect of their professional duties and into much of their private lives . ’
24397	When junior officers saluted , they were recognising the authority vested in them by Parliament , he argued .
24398	It was not a simply a courtly ritual or a question of deference but an acceptance of the office and powers their superiors held .
24399	If a senior officer were to be viewed as no more than a member of an amorphous managerial team , said Mr Roach , the public would be led to believe that any complaint against a policemen was merely being investigated by ‘ one of the boys .
24400	‘ Far from departing from the traditional view of the relationship between ranks , the moment has come for a return to it , ’ said Mr Roach .
24401	‘ The time is ripe to abandon not the rank structure but the tendency to impart fashionable management theories which are not necessarily appropriate to policing and which only confuse supervisors throughout the service .
24402	‘ The benefits of such a development would be a renewal of public confidence and a reawakening of the morale of police officers of all ranks . ’
24403	Mr Roach stressed yesterday that his views were personal and were an attempt to defend the status quo in the police service .
24404	Obituary of Harry Neubauer
24405	HARRY NEUBAUER , who has died aged 59 , was a psychiatrist of multifarious qualities — not least an exuberant personality which lent his earnest profession a splash of much-needed colour .
24406	Neubauer launched his career in the relatively new field of neurochemistry , and carried out research in America into neuro-transmission in schizophrenia .
24407	This included work on LSD ( later known as ‘ acid ’ , the hippy drug ) , which Neubauer found surprisingly efficacious in certain treatments .
24408	A paediatrician 's son , Harry Neubauer was born in 1932 at Karlsbad , Germany , but during the Second World War the family found refuge in Newcastle upon Tyne .
24409	In later life he was fond of Tom Stoppard 's remark about being a bounced Czech .
24410	As a medical student at Newcastle University in the 1950s Neubauer was inspired to take up psychiatry by Prof Martin Roth .
24411	After qualifying , he settled at Bath , where he set up one of the first acute psychiatric units in a general hospital in the country .
24412	A dedicated polymath , with a passion for the arts , Neubauer was an expert on the English visionary artists , particularly the engravings of Turner .
24413	He was a champion of 19th century book illustration , which he regarded as the last relatively unexplored corner of the English artistic tradition .
24414	He is survived by his second wife , Jenny , and by a son and daughter from his first marriage .
24415	Obituary of Christian K Nelson
24416	CHRISTIAN K NELSON , the confectioner and inventor , who has died at Laguna Hills , California , aged 99 , created the ‘ choc ice ’ — known in America as ‘ Eskimo Pie ’ — and later revolutionised the manufacture and storage of ice cream products .
24417	Christian Kent Nelson was born on March 12 1893 at Gunstrup in Denmark .
24418	He emigrated to the United States as a child and received a teacher 's certificate from Nebraska University in 1916 .
24419	He served in the US Army Signals Corps during the latter stages of the First World War before settling in Onawa , Iowa , where he worked as a teacher and ran a sweetshop in his spare time .
24420	One day in 1921 an eight-year-old boy walked into the shop .
24421	The child could not decide whever he wanted a chocolate bar or a scoop of ice cream : it occurred to Nelson to combine the two .
24422	After months of experimentation he came up with a vanilla ice cream bar on a stick , bonded with cocoa butter to a coating of chocolate .
24423	Initially , Nelson called this the ‘ I-Scream ’ bar .
24424	This was because a slogan — which he himself coined — had been set to music and became a hit tune of the period : ‘ I-Scream , you scream .
24425	WE all scream .
24426	FOR ICE CREAM ! ’
24427	Nelson , however , feared that once the song was no longer in vogue , his product would become similarly unfashionable .
24428	He accordingly renamed it the ‘ Eskimo Pie ’ and chose the distinctive Eskimo symbol that still appears on the wrapping .
24429	The bar was patented and Nelson duly became president of the Eskimo Pie Corporation .
24430	The popularity of these treats was enormous , and Nelson had to redirect his inventiveness towards devising new production methods to meet the burgeoning demand .
24431	He invented a precursor of the high-speed continuous extrusion freezer which could cut novelties out of slabs of vanilla ice cream .
24432	The original version of this machine — which Nelson eventually patented in 1955 — could cut about a dozen bars a minute : the version now in use can cut up to 400 a minute .
24433	At the same time Nelson invented a freezer for ready-made products , now known to the frozen food industry as the ‘ Nelson Box ’ .
24434	This device froze mini-slabs of ice cream at -40 degrees Farenheit , which made them hard enough to be sealed with warm chocolate .
24435	Nelson sold the Eskimo Pie Corporation to the US Foil Company ( now the Reynolds Metal Company ) in 1924 , but retained his affiliation : he stayed as vice-president , moving with the company to New York and to Richmond , Virginia , in the 1940s .
24436	Even after his retirement to Orange County , California , in 1961 , Nelson continued to travel across America , promoting Eskimo Pies and inventing new ways to store and deliver frozen novelties .
24437	Today the frozen sweets industry is worth $1.3 billion per annum .
24438	Among 400 different brand names Eskimo Pie has held its own , selling half a billion bars each year .
24439	Even in an era of ‘ Political Correctness ’ and hyper-sensitivity over racial slights , Eskimo Pie has retained its name and its logo .
24440	Its television advertisements still portray a genuine Eskimo fisherman , who proudly declares : ‘ You know what I like about Eskimo Pie ?
24441	It 's refreshing , even when it gets way into the twenties ! ’
24442	‘ Chris ’ Nelson can justly be described as the Henry Ford of ice cream novelty production .
24443	He seems to have enjoyed greater success with the public than he did at home , however .
24444	‘ I do n't think that his wife cared much for ice cream , ’ said a relative .
24445	Nelson married , in 1926 , Myrtle Rhoda Skidmore , who predeceased him .

24485	Scientists click over a way to save dolphins
24486	by Greg Neale Environment Correspondent
24487	HUNDREDS of thousands of dolphins could be saved from death thanks to pioneering work by British scientists .
24488	They believe they have found a cheap , practical means of preventing dolphins entangling themselves in monofilament drift fishing nets — the ‘ walls of death ’ believed to be responsible for killing large numbers of dolphins off Cornwall this year .
24489	But their work is hampered by lack of money .
24490	So far they have received nothing from the Government , little EC assistance and are running out of funds donated by individuals and industry .
24491	The researchers , headed by Dr Margaret Klinowska , a Cambridge biologist , and David Goodson , an expert on acoustic engineering at Loughborough University , say new data shows that plastic sound reflectors attached to fishing nets can warn dolphins of hazards .
24492	Data to be published shortly draws on experiments including observations of Freddy , the dolphin that has been living off the Northumbrian coast for four years .
24493	Using equipment donated by Racal , the scientists have analysed recordings of the ‘ clicking ’ dolphins make while hunting .
24494	Observations of Freddy led them to conclude that dolphins use sonar while hunting .
24495	They emit an intense , broad-band ‘ click ’ or pulse of sound .
24496	Echoes of the signal alert them to possible prey , at ranges up to 80–90 metres in shallow waters .
24497	Mr Goodson , who became interested in the sonar capacity of dolphins after hearing one while swimming off the Welsh coast , has experimented with various shapes of sound reflectors .
24498	The most promising is eliptical , about 3½in long .
24499	The theory is that its internal air pocket will ‘ bounce ’ back the dolphin 's sonar signal , regardless of the direction of approach .
24500	Last autumn , Dr Klinowska , Mr Goodson and their team put the theories into practice .
24501	In the Moray Firth , they placed a ‘ headline barrier ’ , from which they had suspended reflectors at two-metre intervals .
24502	The movement of dolphins around the barrier was observed , using electronic equipment to monitor sonar activity .
24503	‘ The results exceeded our expectations , ’ said Mr Goodson .
24504	Dolphins swimming near the barrier altered their behaviour to avoid it , the result , the scientists believe , of them detecting sonar echoes from the reflectors .
24505	Dr Klinowska said that , although it was necessary to be cautious about the findings , a combination of reflector devices and some modification of fishing gear might reduce deaths .
24506	But the Moray Firth experiments were only possible after the naturalist Dr David Bellamy helped secure a donation from the Co-operative Wholesale Society .
24507	‘ Our work is being delayed simply through the lack of funding , ’ said Dr Klinowska .
24508	The scientists hope to raise £100,000 through an appeal by Windsor Safari Park .
24509	Donations can be made to the Dolphin Research Project c/o Windsor Safari Park , Windsor , Berkshire SL4 4AY .
24510	Eureka !
24511	Cracking Creation 's code Mankind 's emergence from primordial slime was no miracle , believes Robert Matthews
24512	By ROBERT MATTHEWS
24513	A LOT OF PEOPLE are very sceptical about Darwin 's theory of evolution .
24514	I know this after answering questions for two mind-boggling hours on a phone-in about the mysteries of science for Piccadilly Radio in Manchester last week .
24515	There were the inevitable late-night nutters ringing in after a beer too many , but many of the questions revolved around the evolution of humans .
24516	The sheer implausibility of the emergence of humans from primordial slime in just three billion years is clearly too much for many .
24517	The stock response to such qualms is that it is difficult for humans to grasp a time scale of such length .
24518	This , combined with the process of survival of the fittest — which promotes the emergence of ever better creatures — is what enables the ‘ miracle ’ of human life to develop .
24519	But , over the past few months , I have been investigating something that makes such abstractions far more impressive .
24520	Back in the mid-1970s , an American computer scientist called John Holland hit on the idea of using the theory of evolution to solve notoriously difficult problems in science .
24521	A classic example is the so-called Travelling Salesman Problem .
24522	Imagine a carpet salesman whose ‘ patch ’ covers , say , 10 different towns .
24523	He wants to visit them all , while minimising his time on the road .
24524	How does he find the quickest route ?
24525	Trying out all the different permutations of routes is clearly impractical : there are 3,628,800 different ways of making a journey between 10 towns .
24526	Dr Holland realised that the basic idea behind evolution could help .
24527	This would mean starting with a random set of , say , 20 possible routes between the towns , and calculating how long the journeys would be .
24528	One would then throw out all but the best — that is , the shortest — routes , and keep these for a kind of ‘ survival of the fittest ’ .
24529	One then ‘ breeds ’ a new generation of routes by combining features of the best ones , and randomly altering a few details as a form of mutation .
24530	This next generation of routes is then assessed , and the whole fitness-rating , breeding and mutation process repeated .
24531	This Darwinian recipe for solving the Travelling Salesman Problem has proved incredibly effective , rapidly finding the shortest routes between scores of towns , where the number of possible routes is so large it could never be written down .
24532	In recent months , I 've been having a lot of fun using a similar ‘ biological ’ approach to crack a certain type of code .
24533	I started off with a random set of guesses as to how to break the code , and then checked each guess to see how good it was at turning the garbled message into English .
24534	What has amazed me and the friends I 've press-ganged into watching the process is the speed with which the ‘ genetic algorithm ’ sniffs out the way to decode the message .
24535	In just a few minutes , the encoded gibberish on the computer screen starts to turn into plain English .
24536	Frankly , it 's rather spooky .
24537	Building this genetic algorithm for code-breaking has certainly left me in no doubt that evolution is quite capable of performing miracles in no time at all .
24538	Indeed , I now find it puzzling why , after all this time , evolution only produced something as dismal as a human .
24539	IN THIS week of the election , we can expect to see Peter Snow doing his impersonation of John Cleese , with lots of statistics produced by computers accompanied by the timeless phrase — ‘ it 's just a bit of fun ’ .
24540	I hope he does n't suffer the same fate as those who first used a computer to predict an election 's outcome .
24541	In 1952 , CBS Television used Univac , the first commercial computer system in America , to do a Peter Snow for the Stevenson-Eisenhower election battle .
24542	At about 9pm on election night , with just seven per cent of the votes in , Univac predicted 438 electoral votes and 43 states going to Eisenhower , and just 93 electoral votes and five states to Stevenson .
24543	Univac 's masters decided the machine had a screw loose : most human pollsters were predicting a close race .
24544	The programmers were called in and told to fiddle with Univac 's brain to make the prediction more realistic .
24545	Univac 's watered-down prediction went out at 10pm .
24546	But as the night wore on , it became clear that Univac had been right all along .
24547	By midnight , its masters had thrown in the towel , and put out the computer 's original forecast .
24548	The final result was 442 votes and 39 states to Eisenhower , and 89 votes and nine states to Stevenson .
24549	As the legendary CBS reporter Ed Murrow drily observed : ‘ The trouble with machines is people . ’
24550	Review : By gum , mother knew best all along There are times when a doctor 's diagnosis is no match for widely held beliefs about illness .
24551	Dr James Le Fanu tells two cautionary tales
24552	By DR JAMES LE FANU
24553	THERE have been two instances recently where populist concepts of health and illness — much derided by doctors — have been partially vindicated .
24554	The first concerns teething .
24555	For as long as I can remember , it has been standard medical teaching that teething of babies causes no symptoms .
24556	Nelson 's classic Textbook of Paediatrics says that ‘ teething can lead to intermittent localised discomfort ’ , and little else .
24557	However , mothers bringing their babies to surgery attribute a bewildering variety of symptoms to teething , including poor sleeping , refusal to feed , earache , diarrhoea and fever .
24558	The situation calls for considerable tact on the doctor 's part .
24559	There seems little point in saying that teething is a non-existent condition which has never reliably been shown to cause any distress .
24560	So a sensible compromise is to examine the baby to see if there is any obviously treatable cause for its symptoms , and if there is not to advise a treatment for the temperature or diarrhoea , or whatever the baby is suffering from .
24561	It now transpires that mothers have been right all along .
24562	Researchers at the Tel Aviv School of Medicine asked 46 of them to take their babies ' temperatures and monitor their symptoms in the two weeks before the eruption of their first tooth .
24563	Sure enough , its appearance was associated with a distinct fever , which in some babies rose as high as 38C ( 100.4F ) .
24564	There are complex reasons why doctors deny what can so easily be demonstrated , but in the case of teething I am sure there is a strong historical element of guilt .
24565	From the 16th century , doctors widely accepted that teething was responsible for a multiplicity of childhood illnesses , including convulsions and death , and recommended a protective measure that babies ' gums should be lacerated ‘ to liberate the death ’ .
24566	Besides being extremely painful , this often resulted in a nasty infection leading to many problems that they attributed to teething itself .
24567	The custom fell out of favour at the turn of this century and I suspect that , as a reaction to the damage the treatment caused , the contrary view that teething is harmless has been passed down through generations of doctors .
24568	They have been equally disparaging about low blood pressure as a cause , among other things , of tiredness , fainting and dizziness , although their colleagues in Germany , France and several Mediterranean countries not only recognise the condition but actually treat it .
24569	The British view is uncompromising : except where low blood pressure is secondary to some underlying condition , such as shock or septicaemia , it is a non-illness .
24570	Indeed , the lower the blood pressure the better , because statistically it reduces the subsequent risks of stroke and heart attacks .
24571	The symptoms attributed to low blood pressure are , it is argued , essentially neurotic , with a high prevalence among young women .
24572	There is , it must be said , a lot to be said for this robust view .
24573	The unhappy and depressed frequently complain of tiredness and lack of energy and , if they are young women , they invariably have a blood pressure in the lower range of normal .
24574	Yet , the European doctors are also right .
24575	Dr Simon Wessely at the Institute of Psychiatry has recently shown quite convincingly that , independent of underlying psychological problems , tiredness is associated with low blood pressure .
24576	Perhaps , he suggests , British doctors should be less condescending towards their Continental colleagues and refuse the evidence of the efficacy of their treatment for this condition .
24577	THE New England Journal of Medicine tells a grim story in which seven people were infected with the Aids virus by a man after his death .
24578	Surgeons operated on a 22-year-old American male who had died from gunshot wounds .
24579	Tissues and organs were transplanted into 50 recipients .
24580	Unfortunately , the donor must have been infected with the Aids virus just before his death , and over the next few years seven of his beneficiaries have become HIV positive .
24581	It is a contemporary tale of medical misfortune which paradoxically illustrates quite dramatically the remarkable achievements of modern medicine .
24582	Had Aldous Huxley introduced a sub-plot into Brave New World , where the remains of a dead man were cannibalised to save the lives of 50 strangers , only for them to succumb to a lethal virus hidden in his tissues , his readers would have been impressed by the fertility of his futuristic imagination .
24583	They would certainly have thought that such events were unlikely to happen for millennia to come — if at all .
24584	Huxley was , after all , writing at a time when medical horizons were limited to digoxin for heart failure , morphine for pain and a handful of other remedies .
24585	In 50 years , such fantastic imaginings can become reality .
24586	If only the politicians seeking our vote on Thursday had achieved a fraction as much .
24587	Out And About : NATURE NOTES
24588	By Austin Hatton
24589	ALTHOUGH treetops are thick with big , about-to-burst buds , hardly a tinge of summer verdure shows yet against the sky .
24590	Russet and grey still prevail in the recently gale-thrashed boughs .
24591	Shafts of sunlight probe down into secret nooks and woodland hollows , just as they did in the wintry days to frustrate the birds in their efforts to conceal nests .
24592	Vexatious , persistent winds have rarely seemed so unnecessary .

24599	So , gratitude it has to be for the glimpse of a hornbeam 's golden rain of catkin pollen in a sheltered copse where , among primroses and the first bluebells , sorrel shows its delicate pink flowers and ( useful in salads ) triple leaflets , which Saint Patrick used to demonstrate the nature of the Trinity .
24600	There , too , are the ramsons , the wild garlic whose white petals are delicious , the smell less so .
24601	Indeed , every day brings possibilities of new flowers , some new kind of insect : a fat , steel-blue oil beetle thrusting her way out of the earth to blunder over hedge-bottom debris in search of a slimmer but scarcely less clumsy male .
24602	Flick over a crisp , curled leaf and out prances a black hunting spider , or a green tiger beetle scuttling for the obscurity of darkness , or a wolf spider abroad with her cubs .
24603	All 's well , if only the very large and very sticky buds in the tree-tops would burst into leaf .

24663	The Arts : Never more in Neverland Hugo Davenport on Hook , Steven Spielberg 's sad betrayal of J. M. Barrie 's classic ; a kiss of death in Amazonia ; and k. d. lang in Alaska
24664	By HUGO DAVENPORT
24665	THE word ‘ hook ’ is Hollywood slang for the distinctive twist in the plot set-up of an otherwise familiar generic story .
24666	It is designed , like a fishing lure , to catch the audience 's eye and yield a rich haul at the box-office .
24667	And , just as an effective fishing lure may be fabricated from cheap , shiny metal , it is generally possible to summarise a commercial movie 's hook in one sentence .
24668	What , then , is Hook 's hook ?
24669	The fearsome implement ( fashioned in this case from expensive , shiny metal ) that sparkles so on the poster ?
24670	No , the true Hollywood hook of Steven Spielberg 's film is just the sort of bold , fatuous one-liner that gladdens the hearts of Hollywood producers .
24671	To wit : Peter Pan grows up .
24672	Never mind that this idea destroys the fundamental premise of J. M. Barrie 's story , which ends with a vision of Wendy 's descendants continuing to visit the Neverland with an eternally youthful Peter ‘ so long as children are gay and innocent and heartless ’ ; nor yet that Captain James Hook has somehow escaped from the jaws of the ticking crocodile to dream of a return engagement with the leader of the Lost Boys .
24673	There is also the small point that the original Peter had paid the price of rejecting his family when he returned to find his window barred and another little boy in his bed .
24674	Strange , then , that Spielberg 's grown-up Peter must recover his original , youthful Hook ( U , Barbican , MGMs Baker Street , Chelsea , Odeons Kensington , Leicester Square , Marble Arch , UCI Whiteleys , 141 mins ) self in order to reclaim his estranged family .
24675	In Hollywood , we must remember , anything is possible .
24676	In this sense , it is unlike Barrie 's Neverland — a place which , however fantastical and fey , is governed by the alternative rules that must underpin any convincing alternative universe .
24677	If anyone should object , the film-makers can always retort that the idea of Peter Pan growing up came originally from the six-year-old son of one of the scriptwriters .
24678	QED , huh ?
24679	With a budget of $70 million , Spielberg has splashed out on elaborate sets and fancy effects , while the bigger stars deferred their salaries in favour of a share of profits .
24680	At 44 , the director can say , seemingly without blushing : ‘ I 'm also Peter Pan .
24681	I 've always been Peter Pan .
24682	That 's why I wanted to do this movie . ’
24683	Perhaps he hoped thus to outmanoeuvre those critics who have accused him of infantilism .
24684	What he has done on screen , however , is to reduce the Neverland to the lowest common denominator of American junk culture .
24685	The film is brash , forced , overblown and soulless .
24686	It has none of the spontaneity of Barrie , nor any of the wistful melancholy that lies submerged beneath the bright surface of the tale .
24687	Alternately manic and twee , it has , instead , only the ugliness of wilfully arrested adolescence .
24688	Through the wonders of adoption , Peter Pan has become Peter Banning ( Robin Williams ) , a 40-year old wheeler-dealer American lawyer too busy with his mobile phone to turn up at his son 's baseball games or take much heed of his daughter .
24689	And he has quite forgotten his past until , during a London visit to his erstwhile playmate , the 92-year-old ‘ Grandma Wendy ’ ( Maggie Smith ) , Hook ( Dustin Hoffman ) spirits Banning 's children away to Neverland in an attempt to lure his old adversary back .
24690	So Banning ( note , if you please , the repressive implications of the name change ) must learn to fly again , put on his tights , and lead the Lost Boys once more into battle .
24691	He is coaxed along by Tinkerbell ( Julia Roberts ) , still sufficiently enamoured of Peter to grow woman-sized at one point in order to obtain from him ‘ a real kiss ’ .
24692	In an American film , we must expect characters derived from our native tradition to acquire a pervasive transatlantic twang .
24693	Here it grates more than usually , despite British voices in the mix : the unmistakable tones of Maggie Smith ; Bob Hoskins taking a break from a long run of phoney American accents to play a cockney Smee .
24694	Dustin Hoffman , essaying Old Etonian , comes out like a poor take-off of Terry-Thomas .
24695	The cultural onslaught is not just a matter of intonation .
24696	Spielberg 's film swamps the Neverland with baseball and basketball , with burgers and skateboards and rap music .
24697	John Williams 's score is a triumph of meaningless assertion .
24698	Amber Scott , playing Banning 's daughter , entertains the sighing pirates with a ballad of such sick-making sentiment that it makes Shirley Temple look like Billie Holiday .
24699	The Lost Boys romp in what Banning knowingly describes as ‘ a Lord of the Flies free-school ’ , hurling multi-coloured food and gross insults .
24700	When their interim leader , Rufio ( Dante Basco ) , a leather-clad street punk , kneels before a 40-year-old man with a shaven chest to whisper in awe , ‘ It 's The Pan ’ , one is tempted to shout ‘ No , it 's The Close-Up ! ’ .
24701	For Hollywood seems to understand the word ‘ pan ’ only as a horizontal camera movement .
24702	Knowingness , in fact , is everywhere .
24703	Spielberg 's last attempt at an adult theme was the nave , saccharine spirituality of Always ; and yet , paradoxically , his children 's Neverland lacks innocence .
24704	All directors , including Spielberg , grow up , and in this film the result is not a pretty sight .

24709	It 's called News .
24710	Should anyone remain unconvinced , I rest my case on the Leaning Tower of Pisa syndrome .
24711	When the tower was being constructed at the end of the 12th century , it started keeling over .
24712	As a result , it has become one of the great monuments of the world and a national symbol , like the Eiffel Tower , the Statue of Liberty and the Great Wall of China .
24713	If anyone points out that these artefacts have achieved international renown while remaining perfectly upright , I shall sulk and not reveal the most significant point in last night 's QED ( BBC1 ) documentary , Propping Up Pisa .
24714	Namely , that the last people who want the tower restored to the vertical are the Pisans .
24715	At a stroke , they would lose a flourishing tourist trade and their place on the world map .
24716	QED indeed .
24717	On the other hand , as Cynthia Page 's fascinating and delightful documentary revealed , if something is n't done PDQ , all they will have is a pile of marble rubble .
24718	Good for tourism in the short term , maybe .
24719	Hardly a long-term investment .
24720	Most people who have visited Pisa know that the Torre Pendente began toppling while it was still being built .
24721	Few will previously have been aware that it started out leaning the other way , then righted itself , and — after a 100-year gap when the money ran out — went into reverse .
24722	Or that it describes a daily shudder of one whole millimetre in all directions as the marble expands and contracts under the Italian sun .
24723	The guru behind these startling revelations was John Burland , Professor of Soil Science at London 's Imperial College of Science and Technology , and a member of the latest commission to examine the problem .
24724	He thinks the Pisans are lucky to have a tower at all .
24725	‘ If it had been built in one go , ’ he claimed , demonstrating with a model and bucket of clay , ‘ it would have fallen over . ’
24726	The spectacular aerial shots , Prof Burland 's lightly worn erudition , the delicious dollops of Verdi and Rossini and the ever-so-slightly tongue-in-cheek commentary added up to a ‘ Carry on Leaning ’ that I felt obliged to watch all over again .
24727	Not out of obsession with the abnormal ; just for the pleasure .
24728	I 'm beginning to worry about Inspector Morse ( ITV ) .
24729	He has always majored , like Pisa 's tower , in eccentricity , but now the complexity of the stories and some of the directorial quirks are becoming self-defeating .
24730	Last night 's mystery was set in an open prison so relaxed that you wondered if the female governor went round tucking up the inmates at night .
24731	Chief Supt Strange , once a likeable fusspot , seems to be going round the bend , and Morse got the answer wrong a whole reel before the end .
24732	Only Lewis , unshakeable symbol of dependability , stays his old self .
24733	The Arts : Suitable subjects to sing about ?
24734	Charles Manson , terrorists and Steve Biko feature in new operas .
24735	Geoffrey Wheatcroft wonders if murder strikes quite the right note
24736	By GEOFFREY WHEATCROFT
24737	IN DR JOHNSON 's all too familiar phrase , opera is an exotic and irrational entertainment .
24738	Is it becoming more irrational and exotic than it can handle ?
24739	Several recent or forthcoming operas sound as if they were designed for — or perhaps by — what in Soho are known as people of strange and unusual tastes .
24740	These works raise a serious question as to whether their subjects are suitable cases for treatment — that is , by librettists and composers .
24741	The Death of Klinghoffer , with music ( if that 's the word ) by John Adams , had its European premiere in Brussels last year .
24742	It is based on a real-life episode of seven years ago : the murder of an elderly Jewish-American tourist on a Mediterranean cruise ship by Palestinian terrorists .
24743	Next month sees the world premiere in Birmingham of Biko , by Priti Paintal and Richard Fawkes .
24744	And now comes John Moran 's opera , The Manson Family .
24745	This work was commissioned by the Lincoln Center in New York for its Serious Fun ! festival and performed recently with the composer himself playing the mass murderer , whose victims included the actress Sharon Tate .
24746	Now opera has rarely been a naturalistic medium , and never an understated one .
24747	For more than its first hundred years , in the 17th and 18th centuries , its stories were all set in classical antiquity .
24748	Some were based on historical fact — L'Incoronazione di Poppea , Giulio Cesare — but most were mythological .
24749	And the most outre modern librettist makes no advance in terms of weirdness or bloodthirstiness on these tales : have a look at the story of Orfeo or Idomeneo , human sacrifice and all .
24750	The great advance in Mozart 's time was operas set in the here and now .
24751	Some of these were again off-beat or disturbing : the stories of Cos fan tutte and Fidelio are both shocking in their way , though both are supposedly based on real life .
24752	In the early 19th century , the historical opera was reborn in Italy under the impact of the Romantic movement , Schiller 's plays and Scott 's poems and novels .
24753	Despite the way these are sometimes now staged , these ottocento operas were meant to be taken seriously .
24754	And they dealt with gruesome subjects .
24755	One of the very first of them was Rossini 's Elisabetta Regina d'Inghilterra , which revolves around a real enough subject : the execution of what might now be called political prisoners .
24756	Verdi 's Don Carlos — just opened at the ENO in a fine new production — contains an auto-da-fe scene .
24757	And Wagner 's operas are in a class of their own : blood , thunder , and a sex scene in which a chap gets off with his sister .
24758	And yet we are shocked — we are certainly meant to be — by ‘ daring ’ contemporary operas .
24759	The ENO 's stagings of Henze 's The Bassarids ( still more classical mythology with Bacchic orgies and killings ) and Greek by Mark Anthony Turnage ( with a foul-mouthed , violent libretto after Steven Berkoff ) would fall into this category .
24760	ENO is distressed that ‘ opera has not generally been the property of the youngest type of creative talent ’ .
24761	And so it has now set its ‘ education and outreach ’ department ‘ to encourage young people from across Britain to use their music and song to tell their stories ’ .
24762	The New Visions , New Voices initiative is restricted to ‘ anyone under 30 ’ .
24763	But among the oldies who have given the project their support are Malcolm McLaren and Elvis Costello , which suggests that the ENO is looking for something a little off the beaten operatic track , not to say strange and unusual .
24764	These strange and unusual subjects may be relevant — but will they be ‘ suitable ’ ?
24765	As I wrote on this page recently , opera is barely a living art form any longer .
24766	The living ‘ opera ’ of today is arguably the musical .
24767	Until not long ago that form , too , had its conventions , and on the whole steered clear of ‘ unsuitable ’ or even grown-up subjects .
24768	There were exceptions , again , like Carousel , which is being revived at the National Theatre later this year , and which has a plot bizarre by Verdi 's standards .
24769	Then came Sondheim .
24770	His shows are serious and grown-up , by his lights , and they certainly have storylines so odd as to make The Ring look like a sit-com .
24771	Sondheim 's latest New York musical , due here in the autumn , is The Assassins .
24772	One of its characters from real life is Squeaky Fromme , she who tried to assassinate President Gerald Ford , who sings a duet with John Warnock Hinckley , the would-be assassin of President Ronald Reagan .
24773	And Squeaky , it may be remembered , was a member of the Manson ‘ family ’ …
24774	It might say something about the Americans that they remain so obsessed with this repellent , perverted killer and his pathetic entourage .
24775	But it may say something also about the condition of the musical theatre that this subject has caught the attention of two composers .
24776	In the end , no subject is too serious for opera to treat , or necessarily too unpleasant , or too poignant .
24777	What matters is how it is handled .
24778	Perhaps the most unbearably poignant opera of the last half-century is The Emperor of Atlantis , which was written in Theresianstadt concentration camp , while composer and librettist waited to be sent to Auschwitz .
24779	The poignancy of that piece is the circumstance of its composition , not its subject matter .
24780	An opera set in the camps would be a very different thing .
24781	There are , after all , considerations of taste or , if that 's too namby-pamby , of simple decency .
24782	Of course , the subject can be dramatic and terrible .
24783	Steve Biko , a brave and remarkable man who met a tragic death in the course of a patriotic struggle : this is the very stuff of opera .
24784	Any number of romantic operas likewise deal with patriotic heroes , from Rossini 's William Tell , just revived at the Royal Opera , to Smetana 's Dalibor ( which is due for a revival ) .
24785	But it all depends on the treatment .
24786	This is what is wrong with Klinghoffer .
24787	The murdered tourist left a widow whose permission was not asked before the work was written .
24788	Adams was the composer of the ‘ minimalist ’ score ( which means that its musical content is minimal ) , and his librettist was Alice Goodman , but its begetter was the ubiquitous director Peter Sellars , whose work is clever , gifted , silly and camp .
24789	There was indeed something rebarbative — as there may prove to be about The Manson Family when and if we see it on stage here — about the use of a serious story for a work which struck many as frivolous and even posturing .
24790	Opera can take almost , if not quite , any subject and make something worthwhile of it .
24791	What matters is the making .
24792	The Arts : Gay 's dark laughter
24793	By CHARLES SPENCER
24794	AFTER a dismal start to the new Stratford season with Bill Alexander 's glum staging of The Taming of the Shrew , it is good to report that the RSC has quickly recovered its form with a splendidly enjoyable production of The Beggar 's Opera .
24795	Despite the fame of John Gay 's ballad opera , which broke all box-office records when it opened in 1728 , it is performed surprisingly rarely these days .
24796	I still shudder at the memory of the only previous production I 've seen , which attempted to drag this 18th-century masterpiece kicking and screaming into the 20th century with the help of rap and reggae music and rewritten dialogue that sounded like a rejected Minder script .
24797	John Caird makes no such mistake at the Swan Theatre .
24798	This is an ensemble show in the RSC 's great tradition of Nicholas Nickleby and Les Miserables ( Caird was co-director of both with Trevor Nunn ) and it could well repeat their success at the box office .
24799	Right from the start the production creates a seething sense of life , as the underworld characters swarm over Kendra Ullyart 's ramshackle wooden set of tilted balconies and ladders .
24800	The effect is of an animated Hogarth painting and , like Hogarth 's work , The Beggar 's Opera combines a surface vitality with a bleak and bitter vision of fallen humanity .
24801	Caird 's achievement is to capture the sheer energy of the piece while also doing justice to its underlying darkness .
24802	Fears that the staging might be a little too picturesque are quickly dispelled as realistic dummies drop from the ceiling on ropes and dangle above the actors ' heads .
24803	The shadow of the gibbet is a constant presence in The Beggar 's Opera .
24804	Gay conjures up a nightmarish world , in which ‘ thief-takers ’ inform on fellow criminals for the £40 reward , marriage for love is regarded as a family disgrace , and man is presented as an animal of prey .
24805	‘ Every one of us preys upon his neighbour , and yet we herd together , ’ says Lockit , the Newgate jailer , and Caird 's production memorably suggests the huddled , vicious humanity of London low-life .
24806	It 's also a real pleasure to encounter a show with so many fine tunes .
24807	Gay added his own elegant and often ironic lyrics to traditional airs and ballads which have been atmospherically arranged by Ilona Sekacz for an excellent band .
24808	Without the radio mikes which have become de rigueur in most musicals , some of the solo singing sounds a little thin , and it 's a shame that Gay 's excellent words are n't always audible .
24809	But a few rough edges are welcome in these days of vacuous , glossy musicals , and numbers like Over the Hills and Far Away and Macheath 's bitter hymn about Tyburn Tree to the tune of Greensleeves are beautifully performed .
24810	There are some great set pieces — a brilliantly evoked highway robbery , with Macheath 's gang riding invisible horses and commandeering a stage coach suggested by just a table and a few boxes ; and a grotesque parade of whores , some of them played by men in drag , in which the ladies of the night emerge through a trap-door like beauty contestants from hell .
24811	Some of the individual performances could do with more definition and detail , but there 's terrific work from David Burt , who has exactly the right mixture of romantic swagger and ruthless cynicism as Macheath , as well as a first-rate singing voice .
24812	Paul Jesson has some memorable moments of pitch-black comedy as the fence and thief-taker Peachum , as well as sudden outbursts of vicious violence that wipe the smile right off your face .
24813	As Polly Peachum and Lucy Lockit , Elizabeth Renihan and Jenna Russell battle entertainingly for Macheath 's dark heart , and there 's strong support from Susan Jane-Tanner as an entertainingly sour Mrs Peachum , Anthony O'Donnell as a rotund Lockit , Nick Holder as a hilarious Brummie highwayman and from Alan Cox as the beggar who has supposedly written the opera .
24814	It is he who draws the moral , declaring that the low-life characters are no worse than the corrupt ruling class , the only difference being that the poor are punished for their vices .
24815	His reluctant agreement to append an entirely unconvincing ( but uproariousy staged ) happy ending to the show is a coup de theatre that still seems strikingly modern more than 250 years after the premiere of this bracing comedy .

24864	Letter to the Editor : Wainwright beyond revision
24865	Sir — How unfortunate that you used the headline ‘ Wainwright on the wrong path ’ ( article , April 4 ) .
24866	It implies that in some way Wainwright himself was to blame for the outdatedness of some of his copious details .
24867	We might just as well grumble about Constable 's omission of tractors from his landscapes .
24868	As a user and devotee of Wainwright 's books , I am convinced that he wrote them primarily as works of creative art , for sharing with those of like mind .
24869	He had no expectations or intentions that they would ever become constantly updated guidebooks for the use of millions .
24870	So what is to be done ?
24871	Ban his books , because they are a bit out of date ?
24872	To do so would be to deprive English art and literature of a unique 20th-century contribution .
24873	Update them ?
24874	If so , how often ?
24875	From my personal experience of writing a Wainwright-inspired , though only palely comparable , book about York 's alleyways , I have learnt that updating is a never-ending task , with a new edition necessitated every two years .
24876	Who could update Wainwright , with the impossible task of retaining the inimitable stamp of his personality ?
24877	Wainwright 's books must continue to be available to all who are prepared to accept his own work , as he wrote it , and as the product of his own generation ( and preferably bearing the cherished stamp of the Westmorland Gazette ) .
24878	His books should always be to hand , to enlighten and inspire us .
24879	But for practical walking purposes , we will need in our other hand an up-to-date 1:25,000 Ordnance Survey map , with a compass in our pocket , and knowledge of how to use it .
24880	We will also need an ever greater sensitivity to our own responsibilities when we set forth to enjoy the countryside .
24881	That , dare one suggest , is what Wainwright would have expected of us .
24882	MARK JONES Bulmer , York

24918	Obituary of Brian Shaw
24919	BRIAN SHAW , the former leading male virtuoso dancer in the Royal Ballet , who has died aged 63 , was a meticulous and suave performer , never more so than as the male partner in the Bluebird pas de deux in Sleeping Beauty .
24920	Although the Bluebird appeared only in the last act , Shaw 's performance was widely considered the highlight of the evening 's entertainment ; and his brisees volees — little beats of the feet as he appeared to fly through the air — amazed even the Russians , on the company 's original visit to the Maryinsky .
24921	Shaw joined the company in 1944 and was still only 17 when Ashton used him as one of the three male dancers in Symphonic Variations .
24922	Ashton continued creating roles for him in Birthday Offering , Monotones and Ondine Act III , and he excelled as the Blue Boy in Les Patineurs .
24923	All that Shaw lacked to become a danseur noble were the necessary inches .
24924	His medium stature condemned him to character parts — unless a choreographer created something especially for him , as John Cranko did in Prince of the Pagodas and Bonne-Bouche and Kenneth MacMillan in Noctambules .
24925	A Yorkshireman , he was born Brian Earnshaw on June 28 , 1928 , and was taught by Mary Shaw and Ruth French before joining the Sadlers Wells ( later Royal ) Ballet School .
24926	Shaw was one of the star pupils of Vera Volkova , who taught both the company and school from 1943 to 1950 , before going off to Copenhagen where for 25 years she revolutionised , and Russianised , the style of the Royal Danes .
24927	With his precision of line , careful musicality and swift little steps close to the ground , Shaw , in ballets like Les Rendezvous , embodied everything that was best about Ashton 's choreography and which made the Royal Ballet unique .
24928	His career as a virtuoso dancer came to an end in the 1960s , when he suffered an injury , but he continued to take on character parts , notably as the widow Simone in Ashton 's Fille , and remained with the company until 1989 .
24929	From 1972 he was also a dancing master and served as principal teacher until his final illness in 1991 .
24930	The Royal Ballet remained very much the centre of Shaw 's world , and his pithy comments revolved around its artistic and social manoeuvres , but the mainspring of his life — the glory and challenge of being a supreme athlete and artist on stage — could not be replaced .
24931	Intelligent and witty , Shaw became somewhat embittered , and at times his company teaching could seem perfunctory .
24932	He seldom corrected , and could not bring himself , as company teachers should , regularly to attend company performances to watch his pupils in action .
24933	But he would give generously of his time to such organisations as the British Council , helping to audition young people with ambitions to dance .
24934	A discriminating host , he was cherished by a wide circle of friends , and in conversation was humble and diffident about his own success .
24935	The Royal Academy of Dancing awarded him its Queen Elizabeth II Coronation Award in 1975 .
24936	Shaw never married .

24942	Sex education for priests urged by Pope
24943	By Bruce Johnston in Rome
24944	THE POPE has told Roman Catholic priests they should receive sex education to understand their own sexual urges and the confessions of their flocks .
24945	His advice is contained in a 220-page apostolic exhortation on the proper formation of the clergy .
24946	The document says priests should be given ‘ a properly-informed sexual education ’ to prevent the ‘ love of chastity ’ being displaced by the temptations of the flesh .
24947	The Pope gives a warning that , even when the ‘ charisma ’ of celibacy is ‘ authentic and proven ’ , it still leaves intact ‘ inclinations towards affection and the pulsations of the instincts ’ .
24948	The best way to cope with such an enemy , he says , is to understand it .
24949	After referring to ‘ feminine charisma ’ , the document says there are many other pitfalls awaiting unsuspecting and unprepared priests .
24950	The clergy have to be humble and ‘ men of chastity ’ who refuse to submit ‘ to the tyranny of this contemporary world , which puts all its faith in money and material security ’ .
24951	Hence , the priesthood , says the Pope , must exhibit ‘ a preferential love for the poor ’ , and a compassionate love for sinners , in other words those who are poor in spirit .
24952	The document contains many guidelines .
24953	For example , priests must not be ‘ arrogant or quarrelsome ’ , but rather ‘ friendly , sincere in word and in heart , prudent and discreet , and generous and available for service ’ .
24954	The priest must offer his help in a personal way , must be genuine and brotherly , and always ready to understand , to pardon and to console .
24955	But he also must be celibate and chaste , ‘ a man of God who belongs to God and who makes one think of God ’ , and one whose heart knows ‘ no divisions ’ .
24956	The document says it is impossible not to notice how society , for the most part , makes human sexuality banal , since it interprets it in a reduced and impoverished way , ‘ connecting it only with the body and egoistic pleasure ’ .
24957	The Pope urges that students in seminaries should be taught about sex in seminaries .
24958	Ordained priests should also be specially educated to arm themselves with ‘ more than supernatural means ’ against possible temptation .
