25070	The Arts : The curse of having good taste
25071	Joe Boyd has a fatal flaw : he has taste .
25072	Robert Chalmers meets the man who helped Pink Floyd to fame but has never scaled music 's financial heights
25073	By ROBERT CHALMERS
25074	AFTER a few minutes in the company of Joe Boyd , I was wondering whether there was anybody in world music he had not heard of .
25075	In a misguided attempt to impress the veteran American producer , I brought up the name of Jaume Sisa : a songwriter I once met by chance in a bar in Barcelona , and a man whose work is considered obscure even in Catalonia .
25076	Boyd has all his albums .
25077	Wild eclecticism has been the hallmark of Boyd 's 30-year career as record producer , failed film mogul and quixotic entrepreneur .
25078	As stage manager at the 1965 Newport Folk Festival , he was at Bob Dylan 's elbow after the singer was first barracked for using electric instruments .
25079	The discoverer and producer of the English folk-rock group Fairport Convention , Boyd also collaborated with Stanley Kubrick on the soundtrack for A Clockwork Orange .
25080	Since 1980 , when he founded his own label , Hannibal Records , he has been an enthusiastic supporter of music from Africa and Eastern Europe , but has still found time to produce albums by mainstream American groups such as REM and 10,000 Maniacs .
25081	‘ The great thing about Joe Boyd , ’ says Andy Kershaw , whose Radio 1 show provides one of the rare outlets for the African percussionists and Bulgarian tractor mechanics ' choral ensembles currently recording for Hannibal , ‘ is that he has consistently put his artistic principles before his commercial instincts .
25082	He is , in the nicest sense , one of life 's brilliant failures . ’
25083	Boyd , who will be 50 next year , has changed little in appearance since he graduated from Harvard in the early Sixties .
25084	His manner is the epitome of Ivy League rectitude : one of Boyd 's friends told me that the producer once ticked him off for breaching etiquette on opening a car door for a lady .
25085	Yet this is the same man who , in the mid-Sixties , ran the UFO club in Tottenham Court Road .
25086	Here Boyd promoted ‘ free-form art groups ’ with names like David Medella and the Exploding Galaxy .
25087	It was indicative of the UFO 's distinctive ambiance that the lighting was provided by a 50-year-old naturist .
25088	‘ He was from Watford , ’ Boyd explains .
25089	‘ He was very interested in lighting , but basically he was a nudist .
25090	There were a lot of people like that . ’
25091	Joe Boyd 's career began in Princeton , New Jersey , when , as an 18-year-old , he discovered that Lonnie Johnson , the legendary blues guitarist , had been reduced to washing dishes in a Philadelphia hotel kitchen .
25092	Boyd borrowed his parents ' car , brought Johnson up to the family home in New Jersey , and charged his friends a dollar each to attend the impromptu concert .
25093	The journey from Philadelphia was a fraught one , Boyd says , principally because Johnson — an uncompromisingly direct ladies ' man whose prolonged career as a plongeur had left him unused to the excitements of the open road — offered robust salutations to every woman pedestrian they passed en route .
25094	Boyd first came to Britain in the early Sixties as the organiser of one of the first package tours of blues and gospel musicians , featuring artists such as Muddy Waters and the Reverend Gary Davis .
25095	In the mid-Sixties , as a prominent if unlikely member of London 's ‘ underground ’ , he produced the first single by the Pink Floyd .
25096	Boyd 's other proteges from this time included Fairport Convention , whose singer , Sandy Denny , died tragically at the end of the Seventies , and a gifted young songwriter called Nick Drake .
25097	Drake , who served an unusual rock ‘ n ’ roll apprenticeship at Marlborough and Cambridge University , released three LPs of inspired , if doom-laden , songs before taking his own life in 1974 .
25098	You can not help noticing that the incidence of fatalities among Boyd 's artistes seems remarkably high , even by the alarming standards of the pop business .
25099	Of Denny and Drake , Boyd says that , while he feels their deaths keenly , he does not hold himself personally culpable .
25100	‘ I think there is a major difference between Nick Drake and Sandy Denny and a ‘ rock casualty ’ like Sid Vicious , ’ Boyd says , ‘ in that there was a direct correlation between their level of fame and their musical talent .
25101	I was not manipulating them or elevating them artificially , so much as attempting to support talent to reach its natural level . ’
25102	Boyd 's activities in the late Sixties set the pattern for his subsequent enterprises .
25103	Typically , his discoveries receive substantial , sometimes posthumous , critical acclaim , but fail to make him , or themselves , any money .
25104	He had no better luck when he went to Hollywood in the Seventies and attempted ( unsuccessfully ) to produce a number of intriguing projects , including a cinema version of Ian Gibson 's book on the death of Garca Lorca , to have been directed by Francesco Rosi , director of Christ Stopped at Eboli .
25105	‘ Good ideas , ’ Boyd says , ‘ none of which ever got made . ’
25106	Boyd says that Scandal , the film about the Profumo affair ( one of his few ideas which did materialise ) has ‘ not yet shown any profits ’ .
25107	On the verge of bankruptcy a couple of years ago , Hannibal was rescued by an American company in a deal which left Boyd in charge as manager of the label .
25108	These days , he is attempting to persuade record-buyers to share his enthusiasm for music from Eastern Europe : the Trio Bulgarka , from Sofia , and the hauntingly beautiful songs of the Hungarian Marta Sebestyen .
25109	If these projects seem likely to enhance Boyd 's musical reputation , they are showing no immediate signs of improving his bank balance .
25110	‘ The trouble with Joe , ’ one of his more affluent colleagues in the pop business told me , ‘ is that he suffers from the fatal curse of taste . ’
25111	The Arts : Beating the colour barrier
25112	One rarely sees a black swan in classical ballet .
25113	Why ?
25114	Nadine Meisner visits a Royal Ballet project that is encouraging a different sort of child to put on pointed shoes
25115	By NADINE MEISNER
25116	TWENTY more or less innocent little faces looked at the pianist and the two teachers and chanted : ‘ Thank you Mary , thank you Brenda , thank you Michael . ’
25117	Wonderfully neat in their red and black practice clothes , they had gone through the rigours of a simplified ballet barre ( with varying degrees of stoicism ) , a mime sequence ( much enthusiasm ) and foot-stretching exercises ( giggles and pretend moans ) .
25118	Now they were in the end-of-class ritual of thanks , part of ballet 's insistence on grace not only of body but also of spirit .
25119	Hundreds of ballet classes exist up and down the country , but this one , in Shepherd 's Bush , west London , is special : many of the children are black .
25120	It is part of a Royal Ballet project called A Chance to Dance , designed to stimulate an interest in ballet , principally but not exclusively among black children , in deprived areas .
25121	Over two years the children get free weekly training and dancewear .
25122	The scheme was launched last autumn by the company 's education officer , Darryl Jaffray , for absolute beginners aged between seven and nine .
25123	With the help of two London boroughs , Hammersmith and Fulham and Lambeth , 2,000 children from 16 schools auditioned for approximately 25 places in each borough .
25124	But why the scheme ?
25125	‘ I had been aware , ’ Jaffray says , ‘ that there were more people with potential for ballet than ever considered entering a ballet class . ’
25126	Ballet is essentially a middle-class interest , the domain of white little girls whose parents can afford the fees .
25127	A Chance to Dance aims to encourage children of all ethnic groups and social backgrounds .
25128	Jaffray started by targeting boroughs with a high black population ( although the children were subsequently selected purely on merit ) .
25129	The classes certainly do not mirror what you see on the British ballet stage , especially at the Royal Ballet .
25130	In the total absence of black dancers , Covent Garden lags behind other ballet companies in the West .
25131	It admits that remarkably few black students have passed through its school .
25132	Yet the modern-dance stage presents a different picture .
25133	Look at a troupe like London Contemporary Dance Theatre : its numbers are tiny by ballet standards , but they have always included black dancers .
25134	None too soon , the Royal Ballet has decided to take notice .
25135	A Chance to Dance is a step towards producing students trained to the company 's standards and style .
25136	Children usually have a strong ballet grounding long before they apply to enter the Royal Ballet School from the age of 11 .
25137	So the group at Shepherd 's Bush has a way to go before some of them might be deemed fit to audition there or at other vocational schools .
25138	But they have made startling progress since they started last November .
25139	Tummies have flattened , shoulders have straightened .
25140	‘ To point your right foot to the side , transfer your weight to the left , ’ their teacher Brenda Garratt-Glassman tells them .
25141	‘ And do n't look at your feet , it distorts your posture . ’
25142	Their other teacher , Michael Moore , walks round adjusting bodies , whispering reminders .
25143	Both teachers are black , former members of Dance Theatre of Harlem , the American black ballet company .
25144	They are also English .
25145	They are living evidence of the past lack of opportunity for black classical dancers in this country .
25146	The barrier has held back both sides .
25147	Not only have ballet companies tended to overlook black dancers , but black dancers , observing the prevailing whiteness , have discarded ballet ambitions .
25148	The Royal Opera House elicits the greatest suspicion .
25149	‘ It does scare people off , ’ admits the Royal Ballet 's director , Anthony Dowell .
25150	‘ Even a lot of white people sometimes feel it is a no-go area .
25151	But I hope that we will widen the net with this project so that people wo n't be scared to come forward . ’
25152	But there has been a gradual shift in attitudes within this bastion of British ballet .
25153	The dancer Evan Williams joined the Royal Ballet 's sister company , the Birmingham Royal Ballet , two years ago , the third in a succession of black recruits to that troupe .
25154	Having started dancing on the advice of a PE teacher , he was accepted at 16 into the Royal Ballet Upper School , the only black student there .
25155	He had auditioned on his own stubborn initiative , although people had warned him that because of his colour he was wasting his time .
25156	So why did he succeed ?
25157	‘ I think the timing has a lot to do with it .
25158	Probably doors were closed in the past .
25159	People said black dancers do n't have the right body , the right feet .
25160	And black dancers had gone in for contemporary or modern dance because they had felt ballet to be a white art form to be watched by white people . ’
25161	It goes even deeper than that .
25162	Ballet simply does not figure in black or working-class lives ; such children tend to go into dance through rock music , reggae , discos — and that means modern dance .
25163	For that reason Jaffray considered it important to provide concrete images of ballet performances .
25164	‘ It struck us that these children had n't really had a chance to see what ballet was . ’
25165	Parents have been invited to an open day at the Royal Opera House which includes a back-stage tour , as well as dance and make-up sessions .
25166	In July , the children will be taken to watch a performance of La Fille mal gardee , judiciously chosen for its humour .
25167	‘ We want their first performance to be a real knock-out , ’ Jaffray says .
25168	She is equally keen that they should have black role-models .
25169	So it is no accident that the teachers are black ; or that she enlisted the active help of Dance Theatre of Harlem .
25170	Two of their members , alongside Jaffray and the Covent Garden ballerina Fiona Chadwick , presented lecture-demonstrations to children and families before the auditions last October .
25171	And over recent months , Dance Theatre of Harlem principals have been guesting at Covent Garden ; one of these , Virginia Johnson , took part in a Shepherd 's Bush class .
25172	Prejudices take time to crumble .
25173	( None is more rock-like than the attitude to men in ballet ; several of the boys in the Shepherd 's Bush class have left because of teasing . )
25174	But when Covent Garden does put black dancers on its payroll , what then ?
25175	Will they feature as the attendants and train-bearers of the classics or in ‘ special ’ roles , such as the Moor in Petrushka ?
25176	Or shall we see black faces among a row of white swans ?
25177	Dowell is adamant it will be the second option : ‘ As young dancers they would start and be used in the corps like everybody else . ’
25178	The old uniformity is no more and we will be all the richer for it .

25229	The Arts : Comic study of gold fever
25230	By ROBERT GORE-LANGTON
25231	TWO new RSC shows that have just transferred from Stratford to the Barbican could not be more different .
25232	In the main house there is The Alchemist in a fast , hilarious production .
25233	The play comes over as both an astute social comedy and a door-slamming farce .
25234	Ben Jonson 's plot milks the greedy Jacobean obsession with the transmutation of base metal into gold , the deluded quest for cure-alls , and the lure of easy money .
25235	Though set vaguely in period it is surprising just how contemporary it all seems .
25236	The playwright 's scornful eyebrow seems equally arched over today 's bunch of New Agers , TV evangelists , pyramid-selling reps and complimentary quacks .
25237	Jonson 's notorious prolixity seems absent from this crisply funny production by Sam Mendes , which is performed in a bare brick room beneath a panorama of a metropolis mad with gold fever .
25238	Duping everyone who comes to their absent master 's door , Jonathan Hyde and David Bradley ( as Face and Subtle ) act wonderfully as partners in crime abetted by Joanne Pearce as Doll Common , their tarty sidekick .
25239	Meanwhile , upstairs , above the sulphurous glow of the conmen 's laboratory , Philip Voss 's splendid Sir Epicure Mammon fantasises about the luxuries , fabulous meals , wealth and women that his alchemist 's gold will bring him .
25240	A steady stream of mad priests , gullible clerks and city gadabouts supply the prey for this story of entrapment .
25241	Littered with well-played character parts , the show leaves a lasting comic impression and the dazzling vocabulary of alchemical mumbo-jumbo is in itself a feast .
25242	Down in the Barbican 's Pit , Thomas Heywood 's censorious rural drama , A Woman Killed with Kindness , offers much less in the way of entertainment .
25243	Set somewhere in the puritanical North Country early this century , it is performed on a stage covered in a lorry-load of Fison 's border compost .
25244	The play 's pleasures are largely connoisseurial ( it has n't been seen for 20 years ) , though one suspects its absence from the stage is a case of understandable neglect .
25245	Feuding factions pile on the agony as one shire knight is ruined by another and an honoured guest seduces his host 's new bride .
25246	The evening takes wing in the touching performances of Michael Maloney and Saskia Reeves as her betrayal eventually leads to a fine deathbed reconciliation scene .
25247	Katie Mitchell 's revival sets this strictly moral tale of wrongdoing in a very Christian context in which everyone behaves with an irritating and folksy religiosity .
25248	As an early domestic melodrama it is not without interest , but this sermonising evening is , frankly , a slog with only fitful rewards along the way .

25690	By GEORGE JONES
25691	THE NEW Health Secretary , Mrs Virginia Bottomley , set herself an ambitious target yesterday — to ‘ take the politics ’ out of the National Health Service .
25692	But her desire to provide a period of stability for nearly one million people employed by the NHS is coupled with a fierce determination to maintain the momentum of reform , with the overwhelming majority of hospitals becoming self-governing trusts by the mid-1990s .
25693	Labour sought to turn the general election into a referendum on the NHS , asking voters for a mandate to reverse the changes .
25694	Mrs Bottomley is convinced the Tory victory provides the opportunity to entrench the reforms — and to give doctors , nurses and managers the confidence to make them work .
25695	In her first full interview since being appointed Health Secretary , she said the election result , and Mr Major 's unequivocal commitment to the NHS , had finally ‘ nailed the lie ’ about privatisation of health care .
25696	‘ The NHS is not for profit .
25697	It is not for sale .
25698	It will continue to be true to its founding principles , available to all and free at the point of delivery , ’ she said .
25699	She recalled a promise made by Mr Major when he became Prime Minister : that he would work for a nation at ease with itself .
25700	‘ I want to see a health service at ease with itself — optimistic and confident about its essential work .
25701	Health is something which touches every individual and family in the country , ’ she said .
25702	‘ But there must be changes .
25703	An organisation that does n't change fossilises .
25704	Health needs to develop and alter . ’
25705	By next year , she is confident that two thirds of hospitals will have become self-governing trusts within the NHS .

25711	The next step is to ensure that , from March , no one should have to wait more than 18 months for a hip or knee replacement or a cataract operation .
25712	A national standard will also be set for outpatient waiting times .
25713	Mrs Bottomley 's first big test as Health Secretary will come this summer with the annual public spending round , which will be conducted against a background of concern over high Government borrowing and pressure from the Tory Right for public spending cuts .
25714	The Conservative manifesto contained a commitment to increase , year by year , the level of ‘ real resources ’ committed to the NHS — though it put no figure on the extra money to be allocated .
25715	Mrs Bottomley , representing ‘ caring Conservatism ’ , will face Mr Michael Portillo , the new Treasury Chief Secretary , who is equally keen to establish his Right-wing credentials by demonstrating he can keep keep a tight grip on the public purse strings .
25716	She acknowledged that there could be difficult times ahead .
25717	‘ It will always be the case that the holder of my office will need to fight the corner of the health service and there will always , inevitably , be more than we can do . ’
25718	But she stressed there would be no let-up in the search for greater efficiency .
25719	As well as fighting for more money , her task was to ensure that ‘ every last pound ’ was spent as effectively as it could be .
25720	Her priorities include giving more encouragement to medical research ; emphasis on preventive health to make the NHS a ‘ health as well as a sickness service ’ , with the publication shortly of new national targets for reducing deaths from heart disease and cancers ; and pressing ahead with care in the community .
25721	As a former psychiatric social worker , Mrs Bottomley is determined to improve standards of care for mentally ill and handicapped people .
25722	‘ It is not acceptable to have people who require a home confined to long-stay institutions when they could be in more domestic settings .
25723	That is a real challenge , ’ she said .
25724	Mrs Bottomley 's rise to the top has been swift , with only four years between her first ministerial post and a seat at the Cabinet table .
25725	But she bridles at suggestions that the inclusion of two women — Mrs Gillian Shephard at the Department of Employment and herself — has excluded more able men from the Cabinet .
25726	‘ Prime Ministers always have to consider balance in the Cabinet — and at least we now have the same number of women as old Etonians in John Major 's team , ’ she said .
25727	Friday Matters : Marital strife comes out in the wash
25728	By SUZANNE LOWRY
25729	FRENCH magazines love telling their women readers that while French lovers may be romantic , French husbands are scruffy , barely domesticated louts who do n't clean their teeth , do n't shave at weekends and wo n't use deodorants .
25730	The direst accusations always seem to centre on husbandly refusal to wash or change underwear and a tendency to wear socks in bed .
25731	If there is any truth in this colourful myth , how do the women stand it ?
25732	How about their own standards ?
25733	The French , notoriously obsessed with appearances , are disinclined to wash their dirty linen in public .
25734	But sociologist Jean-Claude Kausmann has found out what they are doing with it in private in a major piece of research that takes the lid off the French marital laundry basket .
25735	He has definitively discovered what happens to socks and underwear once the wearers have been persuaded to shed them , how co-habiting men and women care for their most intimate garments , and how couples come to joint terms with the washing machine — or fail to .
25736	His two-year study of 20 couples reveals that the humble , often smelly male sock is indeed at the centre of a secret linen war being waged up and down the land .
25737	‘ The sock is a highly sensitive conjugal object , ’ he declares in La Trame Conjugale ( a cunning title ; la trame means framework , it can also mean linen ) .
25738	Socks are often at the centre of the mini-wars at which couples engage .
25739	For instance , one of the bitterest reproaches from a wife to an untidy husband is : ‘ You might at least put away your socks . ’
25740	Socks smell and get lost .
25741	They are also slightly ridiculous and can turn anger and tears to laughter very quickly .
25742	But beware , says Kausmann .
25743	This laughter may not be a safety valve reducing tension , but a device to conceal an urge to violence .
25744	Kausmann is not a fetishist and is much more interested in the couple 's relationship than in the efficiency of soap powder .
25745	But he believes that linen is the ideal instrument by which to probe the hidden depths of marital life .
25746	Linen ‘ is everywhere , all the time , stuck to the couple like their skin ’ , he writes .
25747	It is ‘ a reminder of the feminine role modified by ideas of equality ’ .
25748	It symbolises the subjugation of the individual to the joint personality .
25749	At all times , he claims , linen bears the traces of the war between the partners .
25750	Dirty washing makes an equal division of tasks impossible , even for those couples who wish to achieve it .
25751	Kausmann shows how far we have come from the 19th century , when a girl 's linen box , full of beautifully embroidered monogrammed sheets , was part of her dowry .
25752	( Shreds of these hoards can now be picked over in provincial brocante shops , brave remnants of another , more confident age . )
25753	Such brides had cared for their treasure .
25754	These days laundry should be easier thanks to machines .
25755	Even a man can do it .
25756	Ironing is another matter .
25757	Given that Paris shop windows are piled with ever more beautiful bed and table linen , there must be plenty of that to do .
25758	Young bourgeois wives , I am told , solved the problem by heaving the basket home to mother , who is still likely to have a bonne to wash it .
25759	Some of Kausmann 's female subjects did likewise , others actually liked washing ; some even ironed socks .
25760	But most others were desperate to avoid it .
25761	One was even teaching her husband to do it .
25762	Some women in the study were obsessional about cleanliness and tidiness .
25763	One insisted on cleanliness but did n't care about tidiness , while her husband did n't care about cleanliness but was fanatical about tidiness .
25764	Sabine begins the day by making her husband look at a pile of dirty washing by the bed .
25765	Anne-Sophie , on the other hand , lives a life wracked by doubt because she can never decide whether a garment is dirty or not .
25766	Each time she tries to judge she suffers ‘ a feeling of agitation and indeed anguish ’ .
25767	Her chief horror is to have clothes lying around that are neither one thing nor the other .
25768	She inspects the scene , she smells the garment .
25769	Eventually she puts it away , deciding not to wash it because she hates ironing .
25770	But the malaise persists and all day she feels ‘ destabilised ’ .
25771	One of the most vexing problems is when and how to mingle the male and female laundry .
25772	Some couples mix it , some do n't .
25773	One couple , alas , put too much strain on their new relationship by buying a washing machine .
25774	But then they could n't bear the clothes to go in together .
25775	They tried having two machines but never had enough laundry to justify running them both .
25776	They could reach no sane accommodation about sharing and are , Kausmann reports , no longer together .
25777	Other families also experience other territorial difficulties .
25778	Elaine can not bear the thought of her husband using her handkerchief .
25779	While Sabine sees no need to wash table napkins after one party : ‘ That would be stupid .
25780	They are not dirty because people have spat on them once . ’
25781	Leon and Madelaine , meanwhile , have chairs on either side of their bed on which to put their respective clothes .
25782	They pile up .
25783	Madelaine refuses to put Leon 's away .
25784	This bothers him deep down .
25785	He believes it is her job .
25786	Out loud , he complains about the pile on her chair .
25787	She resents this .
25788	When tasks are shared , it can be even worse : Anne and Pat both do the laundry but have waged a nine-year guerrilla war over the temperature of the water in the machine .
25789	Anne wants it at 30 degrees , Pat at 60 degrees .
25790	The dispute now ‘ rules their existence ’ .
25791	Although they rarely speak about it .
25792	Pat puts his work clothes aside , so he can wash them at 60 degrees .
25793	But Anne then does them at 30 degrees .
25794	After she has washed , dried and ironed the clothes , he quietly puts them all back in the machine at 60 degrees .
25795	Jean-Claude Kausmann does n't get involved in laundering in his own home — but he does do all the shopping and cooking .
25796	And far from showing that the couple is going out of fashion in France , he feels his research demonstrates that it is still at the centre of people 's dreams .
25797	It is just more and more complex and difficult to achieve the right water temperature .
25798	Friday Matters : CALLED TO ORDER
25799	SUE BELGROVE had to tackle a wilderness when she married a farmer and moved into his 350-year-old cottage on the borders of Oxfordshire and Buckinghamshire .
25800	Mrs Belgrove , a 32-year-old agricultural graduate , started by hacking down trees and giant weeds , under which were plants such as sedum and aquilegia which had been hidden since before the First World War .
25801	Over the next four years , she also dug a wide herbaceous border down one side for traditional plants such as foxgloves , bleeding heart and Papaver Orientale .
25802	During this time her two-year-old daughter died .
25803	To soothe her grief , Mrs Belgrove , who had just had a little boy , designed an all-white garden beyond the lawn .
25804	‘ About 18 months later , my mother joked that we should open to the public .
25805	The idea stuck in my mind and I contacted the local NGS organiser , who suggested we open the following year .
25806	After that , it was a mad dash to get ready . ’
25807	The hectic preparation , coupled with looking after two small children ( by then the Belgroves had had another daughter , Alice ) , was worth it .
25808	On her first opening day , 300 visitors made their way up the farm 's single-track drive .
25809	Last year , there were 400 in one afternoon .
25810	‘ I do n't plan to open more than twice a year , otherwise you garden with a view to what others will think . ’
25811	The Belgroves ' garden is open on May 3 and July 12 , 2 pm-6 pm .
25812	a Non-punitive Paradigm of Probation Practice : Some Sobering Thoughts L.R. SINGER
25813	Lawrence Singer is an Assistant Chief Probation Officer with Merseyside Probation Service .
25814	Beforehand he worked as a probation officer for Berkshire Probation Service and later as a research officer for Somerset Probation Service where he undertook the research reported here .
25815	The paradigm which is described originates from doctoral research into generic probation practice and has been presented in a book Adult Probation and Juvenile Supervision : Beyond the Care-Control Dilemma ( 1989 , Gower ) .
25816	SUMMARY
25817	The Government White Paper Crime , Justice and Protecting the Public proposes a radical change for probation practice .
25818	Henceforth probation work will no longer be an alternative to punishment but an alternative form of punishment .
25819	This article challenges the conceptual and practical appropriateness of applying the notion of punishment to the probation context .
25820	Probation officers , it is argued , are concerned with establishing rules for probationers and not inflicting pain on them .
25821	An alternative non-punitive paradigm of probation practice is described .
25822	The paradigm is based on the joint supervisory aims of support and surveillance which are implemented through the methods of counselling , assisting , directing , and monitoring .
25823	To illustrate the paradigm , reference is made to an alcohol education course developed for offenders in trouble through drink .
25824	The efficacy of the alcohol project and the non-punitive paradigm is demonstrated by the results reported from a three year evaluation study covering 152 offenders .
25825	The article concludes with an affirmation of the disciplined but non-punitive character of current probation work and argues that , to successfully protect the public and reintegrate offenders into the community , the probation officer 's employment of established social work knowledge , skills , and values is a strength not a weakness .
25826	The aim of this article is to challenge the assertion contained in the White Paper Crime , Justice and Protecting the Public ( Home Office , 1990a ) that probation practice can be conceived of as a form of punishment in the community .
25827	Issue will be taken with the appropriateness of applying the concept of punishment to the probation context through reference to a demanding and successful probation project concerned with offenders in trouble through drink .
25828	In describing the project , a non-punitive model for understanding probation practice will be developed .
25829	This non-punitive paradigm will provide a framework for contrasting the efficacy of current practice with future plans inappropriately to transform probation work into ‘ a new approach to punishment in the community ’ ( p. 18 , para. 4.3 ) .
25830	The punitive approach anticipated for the Probation Service in the White Paper is underpinned by a definition of punishment that resides ‘ in the restrictions on liberty and in the enforcement of the orders ’ .
25831	The White Paper goes on to emphasize : ‘ It is the loss of liberty involved in carrying out the terms of the order rather than the activities carried out during the order which is the punishment ’ ( p. 18 , para. 4.4 ) .
25832	Notwithstanding the popular appeal and political capital to be derived from such a humane-sounding statement , this definition is nevertheless at variance with the traditional understanding of the meaning of punishment .
25833	Discourses on punishment and dictionary definitions of the term clearly specify the central feature of punishment as being the infliction of pain rather than the loss of liberty per se ( Hudson , 1987 ) .
25834	The conceptual and practical implications of this discrepancy will be examined in the third and final section of this article .
25835	Beforehand , however , consideration will be given first to the probation project and second to its evaluation .
25836	In these sections punishment will be understood to mean the infliction of pain and the review of the project will seek to demonstrate that the probation practice described is not only more demanding but also more effective than this traditional understanding of punishment .
25837	At a time when the Home Secretary is inviting the Probation Service to ‘ move centre stage in the Criminal Justice System ’ ( NACRO , 1990 , p. 17 ) it may seem misguided and unnecessarily pedantic to take issue with the White Paper 's notion of punishment .
25838	Punishment is just a word after all : nothing more than convenient political rhetoric meriting only lip-service from probation managers and practitioners poised at the ‘ window of opportunity ’ .
25839	However , this fails to acknowledge a fundamental axiom of social work practice ; namely that language not only reflects but also shapes social reality .
25840	As Davies ( 1981 ) has pointed out , speech is the basic tool of the social worker .
25841	What we say influences what we think and in turn , what we do .
25842	If punishment is assimilated into the probation glossary it will inevitably influence the sort of practice the Service undertakes .
25843	In the sections to follow the stark question is therefore put ‘ Is the Probation Service in the business of inflicting pain ? ’ and the answer which unfolds may be summarized ‘ No , because it neither aspires nor wishes to ! ’
25844	THE PROJECT : MORE DEMANDING THAN PUNISHMENT
25845	Government concern about the problem of drink-related offending is as old as the Probation Service .
25846	Indeed , as Bochel ( 1976 ) has shown , the establishment of a Probation Service in England and Wales was inextricably linked with work undertaken with offenders in trouble through drink .
25847	Almost a century later the new approach to punishment in the community outlined by the White Paper once again presents alcohol misuse as a key problem requiring community-based intervention .
25848	‘ Alcohol ’ , the White Paper states , ‘ is implicated in a wide variety of crimes , drunken driving , offences of public disorder and domestic violence ’ ( p. 21 , para. 4. 14 ) .
25849	In describing its vision of effective supervision the White Paper goes on to note :
25850	offenders take part in alcohol education programmes so that they can learn to drink sensibly .
25851	They learn about the relative strength of different drinks , the amount which is safe to consume , and the pitfalls to avoid ( e.g. competitive drinking and buying ‘ rounds ’ ) ( p. 37 , para. 7.11 ) .
25852	As a summary of alcohol education programmes , this is something of a simplification .
25853	However it does provide a useful introduction to the origins of the Alcohol Education Course reported here .
25854	Furthermore , it highlights the suitability of referring to this type of project for testing out the appropriateness of applying the notion of punishment to probation practice .
25855	In 1985 the management of Somerset Probation Service was faced with the fact that nearly one in three of the offenders supervised in their area were either known to be or suspected of misusing alcohol ( Singer , 1985 ) .
25856	Aware of practitioners ' frustration in not being able to work effectively with these problematic clients , Probation management , in partnership with the voluntary sector , determined to develop an Alcohol Education Course ( AEC ) .
25857	By 1986 , when social inquiry report monitoring information covering 1,257 offenders indicated that the problem of drink-related offending was virtually as great for pre- as for post-sentence clients , that is , alcohol was cited as a pre-offence problem in twenty-nine per cent of cases , a specialist project worker had been appointed .
25858	Towards the end of 1986 an AEC was launched and has been running ever since .
25859	The aim of the course is to educate offenders about alcohol to facilitate a lasting change in their subsequent use of this drug .
25860	This aim is underpinned by three interrelated objectives and it is not without significance how they complement and serve to implement the White Paper 's own trinity of ‘ aims of supervision ’ , that is , protection of the public , prevention of reoffending and successful reintegration of the offender in the community ( p. 35 , para. 7.3 ) .
25861	These were :
25862	1 .
25863	To increase knowledge about alcohol so that future alcohol use can be more informed and therefore more prudent .
25864	2 .
25865	To instil or reinforce responsible drinking attitudes and behaviour .
25866	3 .
25867	To encourage the maintenance of , or , where appropriate , a reduction to a personally and socially safe level of alcohol unit intake .
25868	To meet these objectives the AEC has a structured programme involving group and individual contact , that is , six group sessions sandwiched between one-to-one interviews held immediately before and after the group contact .
25869	The initial one-to-one meeting , held with one of the two group leaders , serves to clarify what participants can expect from the course and what is expected of them .
25870	A standard contract which covers conditions of attendance and an agreement to complete various assignments between group sessions is signed by each participant .
25871	The final interview entails a personalized review of the course , as well as the formulation of a follow-up plan to be undertaken with the offender 's supervising officer .
25872	The course employs a variety of materials and techniques including the use of checklists , magazine and newspaper clippings , quizzes , videos , brainstorm exercises , discussions , drink diaries , and role plays ( Menary , 1986 ) .
25873	The AEC is primarily intended for young adults subject to a probation order with a special condition of attendance ( Schedule 11 4A(II) Criminal Justice Act 1982 ) and reflects the fact that most Somerset offenders in trouble through drink commit serious offences and/or possess a substantial number of previous convictions .
25874	In short , they are seriously at risk of committing further offences and becoming trapped in the revolving door of custody .
25875	The development of the Somerset AEC both accords with and constitutes a practical example of the Home Office 's recent guidance to sentencers :
25876	In recent years the probation service has devoted increasing resources to supervising the more serious and persistent offenders .
25877	Probation orders which are combined with constructive , disciplined and effective programmes of supervision are increasingly being used for offenders who stand to receive custodial sentences ( 1990b , p. 35 ) .
25878	From the description of the AEC already given the demanding and disciplined nature of the course can be appreciated .
25879	However , the course is not punitive ; it is not concerned with the infliction of pain .
25880	Instead , it is concerned with the establishment of rules .
25881	This is plainly evident from the section of the contract signed by each participant where what is expected of them is spelt out :
25882	You will be expected to keep a drink diary throughout the course , and make attempts at reducing the amount you drink if it is greater than accepted healthy drinking levels .
25883	You must be willing to be helped and help others — your experiences will be useful to other group members .
25884	You must attend 8 sessions ( these will consist of : an introductory session , six group sessions and a final assessment interview ) .
25885	You must not drink before the session .
25886	You must be on time — lateness will count as an absence .
25887	Unlike the prison inmate , AEC participants can not sit back and passively do their time .
25888	Probation practice is not , however , solely concerned with the establishment of rules .
25889	As has been demonstrated elsewhere with regard to the generic probation setting ( Singer , 1989 ) , the supervision of offenders involves two overarching aims : namely support and surveillance .
25890	Support refers to anything which is said or done to help the offender solve or mitigate their personal or social problems : surveillance to anything which is said or done to induce the offender to conform to socially acceptable standards of behaviour .
25891	These aims are implemented through the practice of four distinguishable but related methods .
25892	In terms of support , there is counselling and assisting : in terms of surveillance , there is directing and monitoring .
25893	Each of these four methods are employed during the eight sessions .
25894	Although summarized as an alcohol education course , the sessions are not just concerned with giving information but also with enabling participants to make practical use of it .
25895	In the first group session the counselling method is registered in the course tutor 's notes ( Menary , 1986 ) by the explanation : ‘ This session aims to get participants to consider the subject of alcohol in ways they had not thought of in the past ’ ( p. 3 ) .
25896	During this session the importance of monitoring is also emphasized :
25897	Drinks exercises introduce the notion of measurement , concentration of alcohol content ; information which will be necessary to carry out the recording of alcohol consumption throughout the duration of the course ( p. 3 ) .
25898	In the fifth group session entitled ‘ Focus on the Individual ’ , the counselling and the monitoring combine with the directing and assisting methods .
25899	At the start of the session the tutor 's notes make clear that directing extends beyond enforcing the conditions of attendance :
25900	This session allows for an in depth examination of the drinking diaries over the last five weeks — identifying the risky circumstances or situations … .
25901	The aim at the end of the session is to encourage participants to make rules for their future drinking which will lead to a lessening of identified problems ( p. 4 ) .
25902	Similarly , the assisting extends beyond simply providing handouts of useful information :
25903	It is important that participants are provided with the skills to reduce their drinking levels or handle more effectively ‘ pub centred ’ problems .
25904	The use of role play , incorporating previously discussed difficulties ( i.e. homework assignment session 4 ) in ‘ real ’ or set up situations provides an opportunity for testing these skills .
25905	Probably the best illustration of the assisting method in action during the course comes in the fifth session when Somerset practitioners take the logic of working with the problem in the community to its ultimate conclusion .
25906	In the second half of the session , course leaders sponsor participants to an evening at the pub for the purpose of practising drinking skills and purchasing non-alcoholic drinks .
25907	The counselling , assisting , directing , and monitoring on the AEC give substance to the aims of support and surveillance and provide the basis for establishing a model of probation practice .
25908	Punishment has no place in this model .
25909	Instead the AEC can best be understood as an example of a non-punitive paradigm of probation practice .
25910	Twenty years ago the Advisory Council on the Penal System observed that notions of punitiveness do not accord with ‘ the British concept of probation as an alternative to , rather than a suspension of , punishment ’ ( quoted in Bochel , 1976 , p. 238 ) .
25911	Twenty years later the AEC demonstrates that this remains no less true now than it was then .
25912	But does the AEC work ?
25913	THE EVALUATION : MORE EFFECTIVE THAN PUNISHMENT
25914	According to Home Office statistics , probation practice is more efficient and no less effective than imprisonment .
25915	At 1988/89 rates ( Home Office , 1990b , p. 110 ) , it cost on average £288 per week to keep an offender in custody , compared with £19 per week to supervise an offender on probation ; yet the Home Office acknowledge : ‘ It is hard to show any effect that one type of sentence is more likely than any other to reduce the likelihood of reoffending , which is high for all ’ ( p. 7 ) .
25916	If anything can be shown , it would appear that probation is more effective than prison in reducing the risk of further offending .
25917	In a review of reconviction rates , for example , a Home Office report concluded : ‘ Those given probation orders were therefore less likely to be reconvicted within two years of being given probation than those released from custody ’ ( Home Office , 1986 , p. 5 ) .
25918	Methodological objections could be made to comparing the two groups because of the different periods of time monitored , that is , for prisoners the period of time refers to after the sentence has been served whereas for probationers it is after the sentence has been imposed .
25919	Moreover , it could be argued that prisoners are more at risk of further offences than probationers because of , first , their commission of relatively more serious offences , and second , their more extensive and therefore more entrenched criminal careers .
25920	This may be so for the population of probationers generally but does not apply to the AEC sample .
25921	As noted earlier , the AEC was designed for offenders at risk of further offending and/or custody .
25922	Between 1986 and 1988 152 offenders undertook the AEC while simultaneously being monitored to assess the impact of the course upon them .
25923	As a sample of offenders , the course participants have more in common with prisoners than probationers .
25924	In Table 1 below a comparison of the offences committed by the sample and those committed by persons commencing probation or entering custody nationally is given .
25925	Whereas for theft and fraud type offences there were almost twice as many commencing probation nationally as amongst the AEC participants , the reverse was true for violence , burglary and criminal damage type offences .
25926	The similarity between the AEC participants and offenders entering custody — rather than persons commencing probation nationally — is clearly shown by the identical proportions each group recorded for violent offences .
25927	Furthermore , the greater proportion of other indictable offences for the AEC sample , compared with probationers nationally , reflected the large number of drink-driving offenders , that is , 25 .
25928	Given this array of serious offences committed by the AEC sample it is not surprising that the average number of previous convictions was seven , with only 10 per cent having no previous convictions compared with 28 per cent who had ten or more .
25929	In this connection it is relevant to note that 84 per cent of the sample had consumed alcohol prior to the commission of their current offences and three out of four of the convictions for previous offences had been drink-related .
25930	The possibility that the sample 's previous convictions simply reflected persistent petty offending can be discounted because over a third had already received a custodial sentence ( 37 per cent ) ; a further fifth community service ( 20 per cent ) ; and nearly another fifth a probation or supervision order ( 17 per cent ) .
25931	Most of the sample were male ( 94 per cent ) , aged between seventeen and twenty-four ( 61 per cent ) and the risk of further offending and custody is highlighted by the fact that over half of the sample had committed an offence within a year of the current offence .
25932	In Somerset the management of the Probation Service has reached an agreement with the local and neighbouring courts that Schedule 11 probation orders , that is , orders containing day centre or specified activity requirements , are operated as a direct alternative to custody .
25933	In this light the at-risk status of the sample is further indicated by the fact that 91 per cent of the sample were subject to Schedule 11 , with only six per cent being on ordinary probation and three per cent on statutory licence following release from custody , that is , parole and youth custody licence .
25934	The large proportion of schedule 11 cases in the AEC sample contrasts dramatically with the proportion commencing probation nationally in 1988 , that is , 63 per cent of the AEC 's probationers were subject to a day centre requirement compared with only six per cent nationally ; similarly , 31 per cent of the AEC probationers were subject to a specified activity requirement compared with only six per cent nationally ( Home Office , 1990c , p. 46 ) .
25935	The more highly convicted and at-risk profile of the AEC sample was also reflected by the fact that whereas nationally as many as 80 per cent of the persons commencing probation in 1988 had no additional requirements made to their probation orders , only six per cent of the probationers undertaking the AEC received this traditional type of probation order from the courts .
25936	The evaluation of the AEC was based upon a comprehensive assessment of the extent to which the course was able to achieve its stated objectives .
25937	This involved the collection and analysis of five different types of information : an alcohol knowledge test , a drink profile questionnaire , a drink diary , a consumer questionnaire and reconviction rate statistics .
25938	The nature of the method , its relation to course objectives and the results obtained are described below .
25939	As will gradually become evident , the AEC has proven itself to be an unambiguous success .
25940	ALCOHOL KNOWLEDGE TEST
25941	The alcohol knowledge test ( AKT ) is a twenty item multiple choice test of alcohol knowledge .
25942	Each question , like the course overall , is practical in focus and concerned with information about the relative strength of different alcoholic drinks , detoxification times , legal limits and medical effects .
25943	The purpose of the test is to provide an objective basis for assessing the nature and extent of participants ' alcohol knowledge before and after doing the course .
25944	Accordingly , the AKT was administered during the first and last of the group sessions and constituted a straightforward method for evaluating the success of the first course objective : specifically , to increase participants ' alcohol knowledge so that future alcohol use can be more informed and therefore more prudent .
25945	It will probably not surprise the reader to learn that at the outset of the course serious gaps in participants ' knowledge were identified .
25946	For example , over half of the participants ( 56 per cent ) did not know how many beers they could drink before reaching the legal limit for driving and well over two-thirds of them knew neither how long it took for alcohol to be burned up by the body ( 71 per cent ) nor what , if anything , was an effective way of sobering up ( 71 per cent ) .
25947	However , by the conclusion of the course over three-quarters of the sample knew the beer equivalent to the legal limit ( 77 per cent ) ; the correct detoxification time ( 78 per cent ) ; and the fact that there is no effective way to accelerate the detoxification process ( 79 per cent ) — including a cold shower or a cup of strong coffee !
25948	When the sample 's average score out of twenty was calculated , it revealed an increase from 9.5 to 14.3 out of twenty .
25949	This means that there was an overall increase in the participants ' alcohol knowledge between the start and the finish of the course of 50.5 per cent : not abstract knowledge , but knowledge that is relevant to drinking with associates in the pub or elsewhere .
25950	To test whether each of the participants ' before and after scores were simply a fluke occurrence , as distinct from a genuine increase in alcohol knowledge , a Wilcoxon Matched Pairs Test was undertaken using SPSS and the result proved statistically significant , that is , Z= - 10. 1839 , 2-tailed , P=0.0000 .
25951	DRINK PROFILE QUESTIONNAIRE
25952	It does not necessarily follow that knowing more about alcohol will automatically result in more responsible drinking attitudes and behaviour , that is , the second course objective .
25953	Participants could , for example , attempt to make their attitudes consonant with their recently acquired knowledge only to find themselves unable to break from their established pattern of behaviour ( Festinger , 1957 ) .
25954	To measure the extent to which the AEC was able to successfully anticipate and overcome this potential problem a drink profile questionnaire ( DPQ ) was devised and administered before and after the course .
25955	The DPQ is a Likert-style schedule comprising five possible answers attracting a score of between one and five points for twenty-five different questions concerned with key aspects of drinking attitudes and behaviour .
25956	When completing the DPQ participants were told that , unlike the AKT , there were no right answers .
25957	Regarding attitudes , participants were invited to rank from strongly agree ( five points ) to strongly disagree ( one point ) their level of agreement with statements such as ‘ To enjoy yourself , it is necessary to have something to drink ’ and ‘ If you limit the amount you drink , it spoils your enjoyment ’ .
25958	Regarding behaviour , participants were asked to indicate from always ( five points ) to never ( one point ) the frequency of instances occurring where , for example , they got drunk even when they did not intend to ; their drinking left them short of cash ; they drank to help themselves deal with a crisis ; and they missed meals because they wanted to drink instead .
25959	The participants ' answers were scored and their grand totals then checked against where they fell on a continuum of five risk levels ranging from very low to very high .
25960	Whereas in the AKT an upward trend is indicative of success , the reverse is true for the DPQ , that is , the lowering of risk level represents a shift towards having instilled or reinforced responsible drinking attitudes and behaviour .
25961	It was precisely this type of downward shift that was recorded .
25962	Between the first and the second DPQ over three-quarters of the participants either reduced to ( 72 per cent ) or remained at ( six per cent ) a medium or low level of risk .
25963	To assess whether this before — after difference was merely a fluke occurrence the Wilcoxon Test was undertaken and the result proved statistically significant , that is , Z=-7.7565 , 2-tailed , P=0.0000 .
25964	Bearing in mind the course leaders ' concern to instil or reinforce responsible drinking attitudes and behaviour , it is worth noting that before the course 77 per cent of the participants agreed with the statement ‘ To enjoy yourself , it is necessary to have something to drink ’ ; yet by the end of the course 88 per cent disagreed with this attitude .
25965	Similarly , whereas over half of the sample ( 57 per cent ) admitted to always or mostly continuing to drink even when they knew they were intoxicated , at the end of the course 60 per cent said this rarely or never occurred .
25966	DRINK DIARY
25967	The third objective of the AEC is to encourage the maintenance of , or , where appropriate , a reduction to a personally and socially safe level of alcohol unit intake .
25968	Determining how much is too much is debatable but authoritative ( if somewhat tough ) guidelines have been set by Alcohol Concern in consultation with the Health Education Council and the medical professions ( Alcohol Concern , 1986 , p. 5 ) .
25969	Three levels of alcohol consumption are specified : low , moderate , and high .
25970	Males consuming over 36 units of alcohol a week and females consuming more than 22 units have a high level and are advised to cut down immediately .
25971	AEC participants were required to keep a weekly drink diary after each of the group sessions to monitor their drinking levels .
25972	Although it must be acknowledged that there is a danger of deliberate under-recording , the emphasis placed by the course on the value and importance of being honest with oneself appears to have resolved this problem .
25973	The non-punitive approach of the course is reflected in its policy neither to reward low scores nor to punish underscoring .
25974	This is because the aim of the exercise is to provide the participants with a practical tool for monitoring their drinking : if they want to cheat , they will only be cheating themselves .
25975	In this connection the comments from two of the participants were typical .
25976	The first time I went he got us to do a drink diary and I know I did n't tell the truth .
25977	I put down a bit less than I had been drinking .
25978	I do n't know why I did that .
25979	I thought ‘ What 's the other person going to put down , is he going to do the same ?
25980	Well I do n't want to be seen drinking more than he is ! ’
25981	As the group went on I was being truthful , I put down what I was drinking .
25982	The two lads that were with me at the end , they were being truthful .
25983	Theirs went down but mine went up .
25984	These drink diaries are excellent , brilliant way as long as nobody cheats .
25985	You 're only cheating yourself when you cheat .
25986	They were easy to do .
25987	Information from the drink diaries , based on a comparison of the averages for the first and the last three weeks of the course , revealed a shift from high to moderate drinking levels for males , that is , from 40 to 32 units per week .
25988	The nine females who undertook the course remained within the high zone but nevertheless registered a reduction from an average of 39 units to 28 units per week .
25989	Overall , almost three-quarters of the participants either reduced their intake ( 61 per cent ) or remained at the same level ( 11 per cent ) between the first and the last three weeks of the course .
25990	Using the Wilcoxon test this downward trend was again found to be statistically significant , that is , Z= — 4.9595 , 2 — tailed , P= 0–0000 .
25991	CONSUMER FEEDBACK
25992	After completing the AEC , participants were interviewed to provide them with an opportunity to reflect and comment on the course .
25993	Interviews were conducted by the research officer or the alcohol project worker ( instead of the course leaders ) to ensure confidentiality ; and a semi-structured interview guide was used .
25994	The guide covered questions about the participants ' expectations , experience and evaluation of the course .
25995	The interview transcripts run to some 121 pages and can only be superficially summarized here .
25996	However , five points of direct relevance to the success of the course and the applicability of the non-punitive paradigm warrant a brief mention .
25997	First , out of all the responses made , only two participants stated that their attendance on the course had not been worthwhile and none said that the course should be discontinued .
25998	Second , the vast majority of participants were able to indicate the practical , as distinct from abstract , usefulness of the course .
25999	With regard to drinking and driving for example :
26000	I 've learnt a lot , my job depends on me driving and it 's made me realise how much I can drink , how much I ca n't drink , what I can drink and realising about road accidents .
26001	The amount you drink does affect your driving quite considerably
26002	Third , different aspects of the course appeared to cater for different needs .
26003	For some the counselling was particularly appreciated :
26004	A lot more knowledge , it made you think a lot more about what you were doing really .
26005	For others it was the assistance that was especially useful :
26006	When we all went to the pub and some of them went up and got non-alcoholic drinks and that , and they all said they could n't go into a pub and do that and they done it , no problem .
26007	I think it was useful going to the pub .
26008	Fourth , many participants frankly admitted that they had very low expectations at the outset : specifically that the course was simply designed to punish them , in return for which they would give the minimum amount of attention possible .
26009	All agreed that this was not
26010	Their experience as the following comments clearly demonstrate :
26011	I thought they were out to get me to be honest with you .
26012	I thought they were out to get me as a punishment .
26013	But I do n't think so now .
26014	He was just telling us and you learn .
26015	You 've got ta face it have n't you , you 've got ta face it whatever .
26016	If you do n't face anything , you do n't get anywhere .
26017	I was frightened .
26018	I thought it was going to be worse than it was .
26019	It was good once it got going .
26020	I did n't think we would have the opportunity to say things — we all got a chance to speak .
26021	I really thought it was going to be sort of ‘ You must not drink ever again' and ‘ You naughty boy , you must n't do it ever again' sort of thing .
26022	I had the idea that it was going to be ‘ Do this , do that ’ but it was n't like that .
26023	Finally ( and in direct accord with the non-punitive approach of the course ) , the emphasis upon participants by the end of the course making their own rules — as opposed to them being made by others — was greatly appreciated .
26024	My rules are to cut down drinking , control my temper if I am drinking , not to drink in a such a large group and not to waste much money .
26025	It 's a good idea , you should set yourself your own targets so you can know .
26026	RECONVICTION RATE STATISTICS
26027	Positive test results and favourable feedback might be sufficient evaluation criteria outside of the Criminal Justice System but reconviction rates for probation practice must remain the acid test .
26028	Before and after course results are important indices of immediate impact , but did participants manage to keep out of trouble with the law twelve months after completing the course ?
26029	Thanks to the assistance of the statistics department of Avon and Somerset Police , it was possible to answer this question and provide a fifth and final indicator of success .
26030	In spite of the high risk profile of the participants , that is , an average of seven previous and often recent convictions ( see above ) , 95 or 63 per cent of the sample were not recorded as having committed further offences during the twelve month follow-up .
26031	In other words , almost two out of three of the participants had kept away from further trouble through drink .
26032	As one participant observed :
26033	Yea , drinking 's always got me into trouble in the past , I mean now I 've thought about it , I 've thought what a stupid idiot I 'd be , so you know if it was n't for the course , then I probably would have gone and done it again , you know , without a second thought .
26034	Without the benefit of the results from a random allocation study based on experimental and control groups , second thoughts about how much of the two out of three success rate can be directly attributed to the AEC are inevitable .
26035	However , Phillpotts and Lancucki 's ( 1979 ) authoritative study for the Home Office on reconviction rates offers a basis for provisional optimism .
26036	In their six year follow-up study of 5,000 offenders convicted of standard list offences in January 1971 , they reported that :
26037	Offenders who were reconvicted within the follow-up period were likely to have their first reconviction fairly soon after sentence ( or , for those given custodial sentences , after discharge ) .
26038	Offenders with a large number of previous convictions were not only more likely to be reconvicted but were reconvicted sooner than those with few previous convictions ( 1979 , p. 41 ) .
26039	What is of particular relevance to the AEC sample is Phillpott and Lancucki 's finding that 53 per cent of all male offenders with five or more preconvictions were reconvicted within a year ( 1979 , p. 24 ) .
26040	If the AEC had made no difference to the male participants with five or more preconvictions we would expect over half of them to have been reconvicted .
26041	However , as might be anticipated from the progress registered earlier in connection with improvements regarding alcohol knowledge , attitudes and behaviour , instead of 53 per cent only 42 per cent of the ‘ five or more ’ male offenders were reconvicted .
26042	DISCIPLINE : MORE APPROPRIATE THAN PUNISHMENT
26043	The idea espoused in the White Paper that restrictions on liberty will become ‘ the connecting thread in a range of community penalties as well as custody ’ ( p. 19 , para. 4.5 ) is conceptually flawed for two basic reasons .
26044	First , if restriction on liberty is the defining feature of punishment , what are we to make of the experience of children who have to go to school and adults who have to work for a living ?
26045	Is their liberty not being restricted in terms of both intention and effect ?
26046	For example , employers and teachers keep registers of attendance and prescribe as well as supervise the activities of their employees/pupils , that is , restriction by intent .
26047	Moreover , children attending school and adults turning up for work inevitably have their liberty restricted : simply because the engagement in one activity necessarily restricts their opportunity to participate in other activities , that is , restriction by effect .
26048	It is patently absurd to regard attendance at school or work per se as a punishment .
26049	Second , the notion of a continuum of restriction ranging from community penalties to custody — neat as it sounds — fails to acknowledge the unique and painful experience of imprisonment .
26050	As Sykes ( 1971 ) has shown , confinement to and within a prison entails a number of pains .
26051	These involve physical , financial , and psychological hardships including the loss of liberty , goods and services , heterosexual relationships , autonomy , security and life chances post-custody .
26052	Lest anyone doubt the validity of these observations in England and Wales , consider the following admission about a custodial sentence from the Home Office :
26053	It is likely to affect an offender 's personal or financial prospects .
26054	There is the possibility that serious hardship will be inflicted on the offender 's family , particularly those responsible for the care of young children … .
26055	On release from custody , it can be very difficult for the offender to be reintegrated into the community .
26056	Furthermore , tor the young or inexperienced offender , mixing with more sophisticated inmates may deepen his anti-social attitudes and increase his criminal skills ( 1990b , pp. 8–9 ) .
26057	Probation practice can not legitimately be placed on this sort of continuum .
26058	The description and evaluation of the AEC clearly demonstrates that , in their particular sphere of constructive influence , probation officers , like employers and teachers , are concerned in part with the establishment of rules and not the infliction of pain .
26059	Put another way , it is discipline , not punishment , which constitutes the connecting thread running through the diverse range of probation practice .
26060	This point was made by one commentator during the first review of the ‘ Probation System ’ at the beginning of this century : his comments remain pertinent for the Home Office in their current review at the end of the century .
26061	Probation … is a test or trial of the character of a convicted offender under suspension of judgment , in order that the court may determine if the probationer be fit to retain his or her place as a helpful member of society , or being unfit , must be deprived of his or her liberty as a menace to society .
26062	It is established for the purpose of correction and oversight .
26063	It is a conditional freedom .
26064	It recognises that the newer and better way to govern the law-breaker is not through the expiring system of the cell and the lash , but rather through the mind and the heart ( Bridgwater , 1909 , p. 9 ) .
26065	The punitive calculus , with its just deserts gloss , may have political appeal and offer an antidote to the soft image that has beset the Service since its inception .
26066	However , this is to mistake not only the demanding nature of current practice but also the non-punitive knowledge , skills , and values which provide for its success .
26067	The AEC is but one example of a number of fruitful initiatives undertaken by practitioners in and through the medium of counselling , assisting , directing and monitoring .
26068	The non-punitive approach of probation officers is a strength rather than a weakness .
26069	Some years ago the ‘ Nothing Works ’ school of thought dominated the Probation Service .
26070	Now it seems that some things work , especially those like the AEC that are associated with what has come to be described as the problem-focused/task-centred approach ( Roberts , 1990 ) .
26071	These new ways of working are simply a consolidation of the established pattern among officers of personalizing their practice , that is , carefully matching their particular social work knowledge and skills to the unique needs of the individual offender ( Singer , 1989 ) .
26072	This trend reflects a developing and successful specificity of probation practice : the pity is that this specificity of practice has not been complemented by a more appropriate specificity of language from the authors of the White Paper .
26073	The Role of Residential and Nursing Homes in the Last Year of People 's Lives ANN CARTWRIGHT
26074	Ann Cartwright , B.Sc. , Ph.D. , is Director of the Institute for Social Studies in Medical Care
26075	SUMMARY
26076	Almost a quarter of a random sample of adults dying in 1987 had spent at least part of the last year of their lives in a residential or nursing home ; one in eight spent all of that year in one .
26077	The old , the unmarried .
26078	those with difficulty looking after themselves , the confused , the incontinent , the blind , the deaf , and the bad tempered were more likely to be in such homes than others .
26079	With their greater dependency .
26080	people living in residential homes received rather more consultations and home visits — although not night calls — from their general practitioners .
26081	But they did not get more help from community nurses and they were less likely to be admitted to , or to die in , a hospital or hospice .
26082	According to the assessments of relatives , friends , and neighbours who answered the questions , the quality of life of people who had been in a residential home for a year or more before their death was similar to that of others who died but had never been in such a home .
26083	It was those who were admitted in the year before they died who were perceived as having a relatively poor quality of life in that year .
26084	Increasingly , the quality of life during the year before death is going to depend on the attributes of residential homes and their staff .
26085	The marked rise in the number of residential homes , particularly the recent growth in the private sector ( DHSS , 1987 ; Bebbington and Tong 1986 ; Laing , 1985 ) has drawn attention to the somewhat uncertain role of these homes ( Judge and Sinclair , 1986 ) .
26086	Two areas of concern are first , who should have residential care and second , the relationship between residential and community care .
26087	A recent study of people 's lives in the year before their death makes it possible to examine the part residential and nursing homes play in caring for people during the twelve months before their death .
26088	This paper then looks at the characteristics of the people who spent some or all of their time in such homes and at the care they got from general practitioners , community nurses and hospitals .
26089	Care and conditions in the homes and the extent of visiting are described and a final section considers the quality of people 's lives as perceived by their relatives and others .
26090	METHODS
26091	The data come from a study of a random sample of adult ( aged 15 and over ) deaths in ten areas of England in October and November 1987 .
26092	For these deaths we tried to identify and then interview the people who could tell us most about the last twelve months of the lives of the people who died .
26093	Someone was interviewed about 639 of the deaths , 80 per cent of the original sample of 800 .
26094	Husbands or wives were seen about 36 per cent of the 639 , other relatives about 43 per cent , friends or neighbours about 10 per cent , staff of institutions about 10 per cent and other officials about one per cent .
26095	Staff of institutions responded about 18 per cent of those who had been in residential homes for less than a year , 47 per cent of those in one for longer .
26096	In general , the answers from different types of respondent did not differ all that widely and the variations that emerged seemed , for the most part , understandable in terms of the characteristics and circumstances of the people they were telling us about , although there did seem to be a tendency for the staff of homes to put a more rosy interpretation on situations .
26097	For an analysis of these differences , and for further details about the study , see Cartwright and Seale ( 1990 ) .
26098	TYPES OF HOMES AND NUMBERS RECEIVING CARE
26099	The ‘ homes ’ covered in this study include residential homes for older people , nursing homes and other institutions excluding hospitals or hospices .
26100	For convenience they are referred to here as residential homes .
26101	Fourteen per cent of the sample of deaths occurred in such homes ; this compares with a much lower proportion , 5 per cent in 1969 ( Cartwright et al . ,
26102	1973 ) .
26103	A further 9 per cent of the people who died spent at least part of the last twelve months of their lives in such homes ; so almost a quarter , 23 per cent , were in residential homes at some stage in the last year of their lives .
26104	The length of time they spent there and the types of homes involved are shown in Table 1 .
26105	Those classed as ‘ other homes ’ included convalescent homes , a rehabilitation centre , an assessment centre , a holiday home for the disabled and rest homes which may in practice have been homes for older people ( the classification was made on the basis of the information given by the person interviewed ) .
26106	A relatively high proportion of those in other types of home were there for less than a month .
26107	Sixty-two per cent of those in old people 's homes had been there for a year or more compared with 47 per cent of those in nursing homes , but this difference might have occurred by chance .
26108	Of the old people 's homes , 56 per cent were said to be run by the Council , 6 per cent by a charity and 39 per cent were private .
26109	In contrast the great majority of nursing homes , 83 per cent , were privately run .
26110	Nearly a quarter of those in nursing homes had not had to pay towards the cost of living there compared with only 7 per cent of those in old people 's homes .
26111	The reason for the difference seemed to be that the DHSS paid for nursing home treatment in a number of instances : ‘ They took the pension and attendance allowance and the DHSS paid the rest . ’
26112	Nevertheless the proportion for whom payment was thought to have been something of a problem was 7 per cent of all those in old people 's homes ( 15 per cent for private ones , 6 per cent for others ) and 17 per cent of those in nursing homes — further differences which did not reach statistical significance .
26113	WHO SPENDS ALL OR ANY PART OF THE LAST YEAR OF THEIR LIFE IN A RESIDENTIAL HOME ?
26114	AGE , SEX AND FAMILY ?
26115	People who lived longer were more likely to have spent some or all of the last year of their lives in residential homes .
26116	People have been counted as spending all of the last year of their lives in residential homes if they had lived in one for a year or more .
26117	( In fact , as will be seen later , a number of them were admitted to hospital during the last twelve months of their lives and some died in hospital . )
26118	Few under 75 had spent any time in such homes but more than half those dying when they were aged 85 or more had spent at least some of the last year of their lives in one .
26119	The figures are in Table 2 which also shows expected age related differences with sex and marital status .
26120	Further analyses by age and marital status showed that married people less often spent any time in residential homes than single or previously married people of the same age .
26121	The proportions among those aged 75 — 84 were 8 per cent of the married , 34 per cent of the others , and for those aged 85 or more 25 per cent compared with 61 per cent .
26122	Neill et al .
26123	( 1988 ) found that few married people applied for residential care and those who did so were less likely to be admitted than applicants who were single or widowed .
26124	There were no significant differences in the present study between the never and the previously married although it might be expected that people with children might be less likely to go into a home than those without any and the widowed , divorced , or separated are much more likely to have children than the single : 75 per cent compared with 6 per cent .
26125	An analysis by marital status and number of children showed that for the married the main difference was between those with no children , 17 per cent of whom had been in a residential home , and those with one or more , for whom the proportion was 5 per cent .
26126	For the widowed or divorced there was no difference between those with and without children nor any significant trend with the number of children .
26127	So it would seem that children may assist one parent to care for the other who might otherwise go into a home , but apart from this they have to residential homes for some while caring for and thus avoiding the admission of others , and that these two influences cancel each other out in the statistics .
26128	An analysis by the sex of children showed no significant differences between those with a son or sons only and those with only a daughter or daughters .
26129	An earlier study ( Cartwright et al . ,
26130	1973 ) found that those with a daughter or daughters were more likely to die in their own homes than those with just a son or sons .
26131	Data in Table 2 suggest that those with living brothers or sisters may be less likely to be admitted to a home .
26132	Part of this is an age effect : the proportion with such relatives falling from 86 per cent of those aged 45 — 54 to 41 per cent of those aged 85 or more .
