27201	The most famous ( or notorious ) is the giant squid at 15 m or more in length , but some of the extinct ammonites and nautiloids were of similar dimension , and were the largest shelled animals ever to have lived .
27202	Fossil glass sponge , Hydnoceras tuberosum from the Devonian of New York.This exceptionally large beautiful sponge is preserved in full relief in a fine sandstone .
27203	Hydnoceras is a Devonian and Carboniferous genus , but glass sponges of similar general form ( but without knobs have a History going back to the Cambrian , and surviving species today .
27204	A large species with length of 20 cm .
27205	The giant foraminiferan Nummulites gizehensis ( nummulites ) from the Eocene of Egypt .
27206	Numerous species of this species are preserved together , actually forming the rock — an example of fossils as rock builders .
27207	The small , lentil-shaped fossils are a separate form of the same species .
27208	The ‘ coins ’ are up to 4 cm across .

27210	These two specimens are beautifully preserved , extracted from a matrix of white chalk , which gives them their colour .
27211	Species of Coeloptychium can be found in England and elsewhere in Europe .

27274	Peculiar , screw-like bryozoan , archimedes sublaxus , Carboniferous .

27276	Whilst most bryozoa require microscopic examination , a few form colonies large and distinctive enough to be easily recognizable .
27277	This is one such form , with its colonies forming peculiar miniature helter-skelters .
27278	The genus is named after the famous Greek philosopher , and inventor of the ‘ Archimedes screw ’ .
27279	Numerous Archimedes species occur worldwide in rocks of Carboniferous and Permian age .
27280	The colonies grow to a length of 5 cm .
27281	Larger species have been described .
27282	Because the molluscs are such a large and varied group , with such an extensive fossil record , we shall consider them below in their various classes .
27283	Accurate identification of molluscs is a skilled business , and there is a vast literature describing fossil species , but it is easy to recognize the most important types preserved in fossils .
27284	The fossil record , particularly in the Cambrian , is still turning new and fascinating kinds of molluscs , some of them really weird , and a few of these will be touched upon after the most important and familiar groups have been described .
27285	Tellin bivalve , Tellinella rostralis .
27286	Eocene .
27287	The original shell is here preserved in a sandstone .
27288	In life the tellin would have had two valves , but only one is preserved here .
27289	The species has an elongated form , which is extended at one end into a shovel-like tongue ; fine concentric ribs are nearly parallel to its margin .
27290	Species somewhat resembling that shown are numerous in the Tertiary marine formations , and similar species live today in sandy sea bottoms .
27291	This species is from the Eocene of Belgium ; related species are very widespread .
27292	The specimen is about 3 cm long , but may grow larger
27293	THE CLAMS — CLASS BIVALVIA ( Colour plates 14 , 15 )
27294	In clams the body is enclosed in a pair of valves , which in most species are mirror images of one another .
27295	The valves are composed of calcium carbonate , are quite strong in most species , and hence easily fossilized .
27296	Between the valves a springy ligament keeps the valves in a gaping attitudes — the position used for feeding .
27297	If danger threatens powerful muscles can snap the valves tightly shut , and once a bivalve has closed itself in this way it can be very difficult to force it open — it has ‘ clammed ’ up .
27298	the strong muscles leave scars on the interior of the shell at the places to which they were attached ( usually two in each valve ) , and these muscle scars may also be seen on fossil shells .
27299	To make the the hinge strong and efficient there are usually complex arrangements of teeth and sockets there , and the arrangement of these articulating devices is very important in identifying the different kinds of clams .
27300	So it is important to find the internal structures in fossil bivalves , as in the brachiopods .
27301	The clams use their foot for digging and movement generally .
27302	The group has adapted to a range of marine and fresh water habitats where they are often filter-feeders .
27303	Their fossils often occur gregariously as they lived , forming beds largely composed of fossil shells .
27304	Many living species burrow into sand or mud , sometimes to a considerable depth — these species maintain contact with the sea by means of long siphons , tubes that permit the passage in and out of water and bring to the animal both the necessary oxygen and the small organic particles on which it feeds .
27305	Other species are attached to rocks by means of tough threads ( byssus ) that enable them to hang on even in turbulent situations ; mussels can colonize even the most inhospitable rock surfaces in this way .
27306	A few bivalves have become free-swimming — such pectinids can escape predators rapidly by ‘ clapping ’ their valves together .
27307	Still others have taken to burrowing into wood or even into limestone , and fossils of these curious animals can be found lying in their home-made burrows ( see p. 21 ) .
27308	With such a wide range of adaptations it is not surprising to find that the shapes of bivalves are highly varied — some are globular , others flat and plate-like , some like razor shell ( Ensis ) have become greatly elongated to avoid burrowing , and some in forms of the usual ‘ mirror image ’ symmetry has been lost .
27309	The thicker shelled species often carry a distinctive sculpture , which is also important in identifying fossil species .
27310	Fossil gastropod Poleumita discors , Silurian .
27311	The shell is preserved in calcite , with a limestone infilling .
27312	The topmost whorls of the shell are broken off .
27313	this is a very ancient snail with a flat nearly disc like form , with fine growth lines and occasional courser knobs .
27314	The outer perimeter carries a raised ridge .
27315	Gastropods of this kind are typical of Ordovician and Silurian strata , where there are a number of genera and many species of comparable form .
27316	This species is from the Wenlock Limestone of Dudley , England .
27317	Similar species can be found in Silurian limestones all over Europe and North America .
27318	The specimen has a diameter of 6 cm .
27319	Gastropods of this antiquity preserved in limestone can be difficult to clean .
27320	In this case the shell material is a little more resistant than the enclosing limestone , and the specimen has been weathered out of the rock in good condition .
27321	Most bivalve fossils are a few centimetres long ; the ideal size for collecting .
27322	But a few giants are known .
27323	The Cretaceous genus Inoceramus sometimes grew well over a metre in length ; fragments of this particular genus are frequently important components of the soft , white Cretaceous limestone known as chalk .
27324	The giant clam ( Tridacna ) of modern reefs is a familiar living goliath , but reports of it greedily trapping divers are legends of dubious veracity .
27325	The bivalves have long geological history , with a few doubtful species known even in Cambrian strata , but like many other molluscan groups they really become established and diverse during the Ordovician .
27326	By the end of the Ordovician they had already radiated into many of the niches they occupy today .
27327	Their story from then on is one of slow , but steady , increase and diversification .
27328	Bivalves seem generally to have evolved at a slow canter rather than a brisk gallop ( see ammonites pp. 73–6 ) and some living bivalves have a very long ancestry ; the small sized genus ( Nucula ) has relatives in Ordovician rocks not very different from Recent species .
27329	But the ancestors of many of the modern bivalves arose during the Mesozoic , and unlike many of the animals in this book the bivalves were affected in a much lees dramatic way by the Mesozoic-Tertiary extinction events that extirpated so many other major elements in the marine fauna .
27330	In spite of their general conservatism the bivalves did produce some short-lived , bizarre forms with no living survivors .
27331	Most extraordinary of these are the Cretaceous rudists ( p. 47 ) a group in which one valve became modified to a long cone , on which the other valve rested like a lid , the whole effect being most un-clammish .
27332	Some clams have shells composed of the form of calcium carbonate known as aragonite ( like scleractinian corals ) which is easily dissolved away when they are entombed in sediment : this leaves the clam preserved as an impression on the sediment of its internal and external surfaces ( internal and external moulds ) .
27333	It is important to collect both ‘ halves ’ of the fossil to get an accurate representation of the shell — the external mould will preserve the overall shape and sculptural details , while the internal mould shows what the teeth and muscle scars were like .
27334	The reader may be confused to find what we here call bivalves , referred to in other books as pelecypods or lamellibranchs — these are just different names for the same animals .
27335	The name accepted by most scientists today for the two-shelled class of molluscs is also fortunately the simplest — Bivalvia .
27336	THE SNAILS — CLASS GASTROPODA ( Colour plates 16 , 18 )
27337	‘ Slugs and snails and puppy dogs ' tails ’ — there seems to be something in the popular imagination that finds snails slightly repulsive .
27338	But this class of molluscs includes not only the greatest number of living molluscan species , including those that have most successfully colonized land , but also some of their shells have a financial value that may even be out of proportion to their aesthetic qualities .
27339	The gastropods are molluscs with a single , usually helically-coiled shell , with the foot modified into an efficient creeping organ with a head usually with eyes and tentacles , and with a rasp like feeding organ ( radula ) composed of a series of pointed teeth .
27340	The gastropods have become adapted to a very wide range of habitats , from high mountain streams to deep oceans , and each habitat type has its own species confined to it .
27341	Fresh water gastropods are different from marine ones , and within the marine habitat itself the gastropods are strongly zoned ecologically , so that even on the same shore different species will be found in different areas according to their relation to the tide marks , degree of exposure , their diet , and so on .
27342	Usually such fine habitat details are not preserved in the fossil record , and the gastropods we find are a jumble of shells displaced from their original microhabitats .
27343	Many gastropods are grazers : they use their radula to rasp away at algae .
27344	Some feed more or less directly on sediment , from which they extract edible particles .
27345	There are a large number of living species that are predators , some species using the modified radula as a kind of poison dart , others employing it to bore neat , perfectly round holes through the shells of prey ( often bivalves ) in order to get at the nutritious interior .
27346	Some of these predators are specialists concentrating on one particular prey type .
27347	It will now be clear why you can sometimes find so many different fossil gastropod shells together in a single fossil deposit .
27348	Fossil limpet gastropod , Symmetrocapulus tessonii , Jurassic .
27349	The species is preserved with its original shell , its interior being filled with limestone .
27350	The fossil shows well the original concentric growth wrinkles .
27351	Fossil limpets of this kind are generally rare as fossils , and the amateur will be lucky to find one .
27352	This specimen is very rare indeed .
27353	It is from the Jurassic limestone of Les Moutiers en Cinglais , France .
27354	It is 11 cm long — large for a limpet-like mollusc .
27355	Fossil sundial shell , Architectonica millegranosa Pliocene .
27356	The well preserved shells of this gastropod have been washed almost free of their enclosing silty matrix .
27357	The low spire of this species , with a minutely beaded ornament , and the sharp rib around its outside edge , are features that discriminate this species from other gastropods .
27358	This species is one of a fairly large genus that survives today .
27359	They are uncommon in the tropical or subtropical molluscan faunas of the Tertiary .
27360	Species resembling this one in general shape are met with in rocks of Cretaceous and younger age .
27361	This species is from Orciano , Italy .
27362	Diameter about 3cm .
27363	Gastropod , Harpagodes wrightii , Jurassic .
27364	This large gastropod is preserved in an oolitic limestone .
27365	The long , stout spines are an unusual feature which discriminates this species from other gastropods .
27366	Note that the surface of this species bears encrusting oysters of a species that took advantage of the hard surface of the dead gastropod .
27367	This species is a real rarity .
27368	It was discovered in the Great Oolite limestones of Gloucestershire , England .
27369	A few related species occur in the Jurassic .
27370	The longest diameter of the specimen is nearly 15 cm .
27371	Cleaning out gastropods from oolitic limestones can be a lengthy business .
27372	Usually the weathering has done part of the job , but thereafter a combination of small chisels and stout needles ( to prise away individual grains ) is needed .
27373	Always remember to keep clear of the soft calcite shell with these tools .
27374	Typhis pungens , a fossil gastropod , Eocene .
27375	These specimens are well-preserved in a clay matrix , some of which adheres to one of the specimens .
27376	Such spiny little fossils are unlikely to be confused with other gastropods .
27377	Note also the oval aperture surrounded by a narrow rim .
27378	There are a number of Typhis species , with various numbers and arrangements of the spines .
27379	Fossil Typhis are frequent fossils in the Eocene rocks of Europe .
27380	Typhis still lives today — in the seas around Japan , for example .
27381	The series of fossils shown here demonstrate the different sizes gastropods of one species attain .
27382	The largest here is 3 cm long .
27383	The gastropod shell can vary from a millimetre in length to several tens of centimetres ; many are thick and robust , others delicate and fragile .
27384	While the majority are coiled in an upward spiral , some are modified into simple , cap-like forms ( like the limpets ) , and others are coiled in a flat plane , like a ram 's horn .
27385	Some genera have high spires , with many turns of the shell visible externally , others have low , broad spires in which the last whorl overlaps the earlier ones .
27386	Perhaps more than any other group of molluscs the gastropods are remarkable for the variety and beauty of the external sculpture on the shell , which may be covered with a delicate tracery of ribs and lines , or stout spines , or fine prickles .
27387	Many species have the aperture flared , or extended into a long tube ( siphonate forms ) .
27388	Sometimes you can find a lid ( operculum ) preserved as a fossil , that closed the aperture when the mollusc withdrew into its shell .
27389	All these characters are used in the identification of fossil species , but of course the colour patterns that may be characteristic of living species are not available in the great majority of fossils .
27390	Like some of the bivalves , some gastropods had shells composed of the mineral aragonite , and these are usually preserved as moulds : but a cast taken from the external mould will replicate the fine detail of the external sculpture .
27391	Right The Pliocene gastropod Busycon contrarium .
27392	As with most fossils of this comparatively recent date , the shell looks now much as it would have done when the animal first died , except for the loss of pigment .
27393	This gastropod is unusual in that its aperture lies on its left-hand side , not on the right as in most other species .
27394	Its specific name ‘ contrarium ’ indicates this .
27395	Its low spire and long , projecting apertural extension are also characteristic .
27396	Forms related to this species are quite widespread in the Pliocene .
27397	The specimen is from Florida , USA .
27398	The species still lives in the seas off Florida today The specimen is 6 cm long — but like all gastropods , smaller or larger specimens can be found according to growth .
27399	Far right The Eocene gastropod Athleta spinosa .
27400	These exquisitely preserved gastropods are largely free of the enclosing matrix , and look now much as they would have done 60 million years ago .
27401	Gastropods of this type are characterized by strong ribs produced into spines , a long aperture , and relatively low spire looking rather like a Mayan pyramid .
27402	There are many similar species , widespread in Tertiary times .
27403	These specimens are from the Eocene of Grignon , France , but similar species occur on most continents The specimens illustrated range from 2–4 cm long , according to the stage of growth they have reached .
27404	Many species of Athleta occur in clays , and the matrix can usually be removed with only gentle washing to give fine , clean specimens .
27405	The species shown here is in a crumbly limestone , easily removed with gentle brushing .
27406	There are small helically-coiled shells present even in Cambrian rocks , and it seems likely that the gastropods diverged from the other molluscs late in the Precambrian .
27407	By the Ordovician the gastropods were a varied group present in a variety of shallow water habitats .
27408	As might be expected most of the Palaeozoic gastropods belong to primitive groups : a few of these primitive snails survive today as inconspicuous members of the Recent fauna .
27409	By the Carboniferous many of the shapes we see in living gastropods can be matched in the fossils , but despite these similarities the majority of the Palaeozoic forms were not closely related to their living analogues ; this is another example of similar-looking forms evolving independently probably in response to similar life habits .
27410	It was during the Mesozoic that the forms ancestral to many of the living gastropods evolved .
27411	In particular the adoption of predatory habits was a new departure for the gastropods , and was in part responsible for a proliferation of the group unmatched in their Palaeozoic history .
27412	They continued to evolve with undiminished vigour through the Tertiary , and their fossil remains are nowhere more abundant than in the ‘ crags ’ of later Tertiary age .
27413	The gastropods are one of many groups that record the faunal changes connected with the advance and retreat of the Ice Sheets during the Pleistocene .
27414	The invasion of the non-marine habitat probably first happened in the Carboniferous , but relatives of the living land snails are rare before the Cretaceous , at which time the familiar Helix made its first appearance .
27415	The slugs were derived from this group by reduction of the shell , at which stage they become distinctly less qualified to have a fossil record !
27416	Gastropods can leave other evidence of their activities .
27417	Grazing species leave characteristic winding trails , and these have been tentatively identified as fossils , but with the usual caution that the trail makers themselves are never apparently preserved at the end of their tracks .
27418	NAUTILOIDS , AMMONOIDS , BELEMNOIDS , SQUIDS — CLASS CEPHALOPODA ( Colour plates 17 , 19 , 20 , 21 )
27419	The cephalopods include the most complex and ‘ advanced ’ of the molluscs , and are a group of the greatest geological , as well as biological interest .
27420	They have muscular tentacles in a well-developed head region , highly efficient eyes which are similar in construction to those of vertebrates ( although obviously independently derived ) , and they feed with the aid of strong , beak-like jaws .
27421	They are predators , and probably always have been , and it may have been the adoption of hunting habits that favoured the development of high intelligence .
27422	Certainly , living cephalopods have a sophisticated nervous system and a relatively large ‘ brain' : octopuses seem to be capable of very rapid learning .
27423	Perhaps H. G. Wells made the right choice when he cast octopus-like animals in the role of intelligent alien invaders in The War of the Worlds .
27424	The cephalopods evolved from another ( gastropod-like ? ) mollusc at some time during the Cambrian , but their earliest history is little known .
27425	Like most other molluscan groups they rapidly diversified in the Ordovician .
27426	These early nautiloids were probably predators also , and if this were so they may have been the first rapidly moving , efficient hunters in the sea .
27427	Their impact on the marine communities of the Ordovician must have been profound .
27428	The presence of efficient predators would have acted as a stimulus in the evolution of other groups : even algal grazers would be compelled to evolve protective devices or rapid reproductive strategies to outpace predatory depredations .
27429	We have seen how many animal groups diversified during the Ordovician ; the rapid evolution of nautiloid cephalopods at the same time may be more than coincidence .
27430	Rapid movement in cephalopods is achieved by expulsion of water from a muscular funnel beneath the head .
27431	Most of the living cephalopods also have an ink sac which injects a smoky fluid into the water when the animal is threatened , under cover of which they can make their own jet-propelled escape .
27432	Since living Nautilus does not have an ink sac , this must have been a protective device evolved at a later stage in cephalopod evolution .
27433	Many cephalopod species behave gregariously today , travelling in swarms in pursuit of their favourite prey ( often small crustacea ) .
27434	Fossil cephalopods belonging to one species are often found together in large numbers and this may reflect similar gregarious habits , but there are other possible explanations — for example , concentrations of fossil shells may have been sorted by currents .
27435	The living pearly Nautilus ; section showing its internal division into chambers
27436	NAUTILOIDS
27437	The earliest cephalopods found as fossils are nautiloids and they also have the longest history , because the living pearly Nautilus belongs to the same group .
27438	The single Recent genus scarcely reflects the diversity attained by the group in Palaeozoic seas , and more than a hundred different genera have been described from the Lower Palaeozoic alone .
27439	Sections through the living Nautilus ( see p.72 ) are often sold as ornaments , and well illustrate the distinctive features of nautiloid hard parts .
27440	The body of the animal occupied the cavity at the end of the spiral — the living chamber .
27441	Behind the living chamber the rest of the shell is divided into smaller chambers .
27442	As the animal grew it secreted a wall ( septum ) between the body chamber and the chamber immediately behind — walled off part of its home as it were .
27443	Running along the middle part of the shell there is a narrow tube — the siphuncle — which connects the living chamber with the earlier parts of the shell .
27444	The empty chambers are usually supposed to have been filled with gas , which help to give the animal buoyancy , and via the siphuncle the animal can vary its buoyancy to control its position in the water column .
27445	Some of the early nautiloids deposit calcium carbonate in the voided chambers , which may also have been connected with controlling buoyancy .
27446	Where the septum meets the body wall it does so in a smooth curve .
27447	Internal moulds of fossil nautiloids often reveal a series of such lines marking the boundaries of the chambers — these are known as suture lines .
27448	All nautiloids have simple suture lines .
27449	When they first appear in the early Ordovician the majority of nautiloid shells are straight or slightly curved ; they are ‘ unwound ’ forms .
27450	Some of these straight orthocone nautiloids achieve considerable dimensions , several metres long , and they must have been formidable predators on the other marine animals of the time .
27451	Quite early in their history some partly coiled or even tightly coiled species evolved , and the various coiling types seem to have coexisted successfully side by side .
27452	Some of these early nautiloids occurred in such abundance that they are conspicuous enough to form an appreciable part of limestone formations — the ‘ Orthoceras Limestone ’ ( Ordovician ) is one of these , widely distributed through Scandinavia .
27453	The nautiloids achieved their widest range of adaptations and greatest variety of form in the Ordovician and Silurian periods , with various coiled forms , straight , pipe-like forms , and curious dumpy species with restricted apertures that may have adopted a sluggish ( possible filter-feeding ) mode of life .
27454	Thin sections show a great variety of internal structures important in accurate identification .
27455	In the Devonian period the nautiloids were still abundant and varied , but they suffered a slow eclipse coincident with the rise of the ammonoids .
27456	Nonetheless unlike many of their Palaeozoic companions , they survived the late Permian extinction , and the ancestors of the living Nautilus even underwent a minor evolutionary burst in the Mesozoic , where forms quite similar to the pearly Nautilus can be common fossils .
27457	And in the end the nautiloids even survived the ammonites , the molluscan group that evolved more rapidly and more spectacularly than any other .
27458	AMMONOIDS ( ‘ AMMONITES ’ )
27459	The ammonoids were derived from the nautiloids probably during the early Devonian , and from the Carboniferous until the Cretaceous are among the most abundant of fossil groups , in some rock types dominating to the exclusion of most other members of the fauna .
27460	Ammonoids differ from nautiloids in the suture lines being wavy or crimped ; this of course reflects an elaboration of the outer part of the walls ( septa ) separating the chambers in the earlier part of the shell .
27461	The siphuncle in most ammonoids runs not through the middle of the whorl but along the outer edge .
27462	There has been a lot of debate about the reasons for producing complicated patterns on the suture line ; what advantage would this have given the ammonoids over their nautiloid ancestors , that allowed for the explosive bursts of ammonoid evolution ?
27463	It can not be coincidence that the folding of the septal walls occurs at the point where they meet the body shell of the animal ; this is a point of relative weakness , and all good joinery benefits from strengthening the joint .
27464	The earlier ammonoids had gently wavy sutures , and many of the Mesozoic ones had sutures almost incredibly folded and contorted , so it looks as if natural selection were generally favouring increase in the elaboration of the folds .
27465	One simple explanation , which is attractive and plausible , is that the strengthening enabled the ammonoid shell to withstand the hydrostatic pressure at relatively great depths in the ocean — they need not be confined to the surface waters or to relatively shallow depths .
27466	Certainly individual ammonoid species became extremely widespread , and oceans were not a barrier to their distribution .
27467	They became masters of the pelagic realm , possibly swimming in schools like their distant relatives the squids .
27468	Like living pelagic animals they had preferences for particular water temperatures ; different types of ammonoids were found in high or low latitudes .
27469	Since the disposition of continents has changed , these ‘ faunal realms ’ offer a method of deducing the distribution of past climatic belts .
27470	Ceratite ammonoid , Ceratites nodosus , Triassic .
27471	This specimen is an internal mould in limestone , and shows the suture lines well — the boundaries between chambers on the inside of the shell .
27472	This ammonite has only a few strong ribs , with a number of small tubercles in addition .
27473	The looping form of the suture lines is also characteristic Ceratites are typical of Triassic rocks and there are numerous related species differing in details of ribbing and suture lines Such ammonites are plentiful in marine limestones of the right age across the continent of Europe ( though not in England ) .
27474	Related forms occur in America The specimen shown here is from Göttingen .
27475	This specimen has a diameter of 6 cm but some are larger .
27476	Jurassic ammonite , Promicroceras planicosta .
27477	Numerous small specimens are preserved higgledy-piggledy in an impure limestone .
27478	Some retain their shell , others show the dark internal moulds .
27479	Small size , unbranched and strong ribs , giving the shell a ramshorn appearance , are important characters This form has a number of related species , but the situation is complicated by the fact that some large ammonites have inner whorls looking rather like Promicroceras This specimen is from the Lias of Somerset , England .
27480	Individuals do not exceed 2 cm in diameter .
27481	Whatever the reasons for their change from their nautiloid ancestors , the ammonoids were an enormously successful group : thousands of different species have been described , and their variety is so bewildering that many specialists devote their lives to studying only the ammonoids of a particular , short time period .
27482	The changes that they underwent are an infinite set of variations on a relatively limited number of themes .
27483	Most important , perhaps , are the characteristics of the suture lines , which are displayed on internal moulds .
27484	The mature shell size also varies from small species a few centimetres across to giants of a metre or more in diameter .
27485	Some species grew in such a way that the last whorl overlaps the inner ones ; often these species become flat and discus-shaped : it has been suggested that this was a more ‘ streamlined ’ shape for active swimmers .
27486	Other species have squat whorls , the whole ammonoid being so tightly rolled up as to be almost spherical .
27487	The exterior surface of most ammonoids is covered with ribbing — dense on some species , sparse on others — the ribs often split into two or more smaller ribs as they pass over the back of the whorls .
27488	Many ammonoids additionally carry spines , warts , tubercles or lumpy excrescences , so that the large shells can look positively burdened with sculpture .
27489	It is difficult to imagine that such species were rapid swimmers .
27490	Others , particularly the discus-shaped forms , were smooth externally .
27491	All these features are used in the classification of the group .
27492	A particularly puzzling aspect of the ammonoids is a great resemblance between external shell features that can be produced at different times by otherwise unrelated ammonoids .
27493	Such homoeomorphs are presumably produced in response to very similar life habits .
27494	The origins of a particular homoeomorph can usually be deduced by studying the internal features ( in particular the suture lines ) , or by tracing its derivation from geologically older species in underlying beds .
27495	It is only in relatively recent years that two sexes have been recognized in ammonoid species .
27496	They were originally thought to have been two closely related species occurring together in the same rocks , but these ‘ pairs ’ were so consistently found together that it became more and more probable that they were sexual forms of the same species .
27497	The smaller of the two is considered to be the male , which also tends to have rather stronger ribbing , and sometimes a differently shaped aperture from the larger female .
27498	A group of belemnites , Acroceolites subtenuis , Jurassic .
27499	This fine group of belemnites is preserved on a soft shale .
27500	The belemnite guards themselves are composed of calcite There are very many belemnite species in Jurassic and Cretaceous rocks , sometimes occurring in vast numbers .
27501	They require expert determination .
27502	The specimen shown here is from the Jurassic shales of Yorkshire , England , but similar species occur worldwide .
27503	The longest specimen shown here is 9 cm long .
27504	Some belemnites are as much as twice that length .
27505	Anomalous ammonites : the Cretaceous genus Nipponites .
27506	About × 1½ .
27507	The early ammonoids of the Devonian ( Anarcestes and allied genera ) have only gently sinuous suture lines .
27508	In the Carboniferous a great variety of forms with highly zig-zag suture lines are a distinctive group of ammonoids usually known as goniatites .
27509	By the Permian-Triassic the suture lines of many ammonites had begun to assume the highly crimped and complex form that was to characterize much of their later history ; the ceratites of the Triassic combined broad loops and tight folds in a distinctive pattern ( see p.74 ) .
27510	It was in the Jurassic that the ammonoids achieved their greatest flowering , when the clays and shales of the period may be solid with the remains of their shells .
27511	The whole gamut of shell shapes , ornaments , and sutural complexity was present during this time .
27512	Their rise was not , however , one of simple and progressive increase in variety .
27513	At several times , notably at the end of the Palaeozoic , they suffered massive and largely unexplained extinctions , a few survivors giving rise to the variety of forms that followed .
27514	In spite of their success they seemed to be vulnerable to extirpation in a way that some of the less imaginative molluscs , like the bivalves seemed to be immune .
27515	The group persisted , successfully , into the Cretaceous , at the end of which period the whole group , apparently rather suddenly , became extinct .
27516	We shall return to this sudden death of an important group in Chapter 6 .
27517	No description of the ammonoids is complete without mentioning the heteromorphs These are forms which abandoned the usual plane spiral mode of coiling , and instead became partially or even completely uncoiled , or became twisted in some other fashion .
27518	Some forms ( Turrilites ) adopted the helical spire , and were it not for the obligatory suture lines it might be possible to mistake these species for large gastropods .
27519	In others the coils became loose , like a watch spring .
27520	Still others developed a bizarre backward hook in their mature stage .
27521	The extreme heteromorphs are perhaps to be found in the genus Nipponites , which looks like a tangle of whorls where any obvious semblance of symmetrical coiling seems to have been lost ( see left ) , and Baculites which is virtually straight after its earliest whorls .
27522	Most of these heteromorphs were derived from ‘ normal ’ ammonoids , but there is one famous example where an uncoiled form actually gave rise to a conventional-looking ammonoid by coiling up again !
27523	Heteromorphs are particularly common in , but by no means confined to , Cretaceous rocks .
27524	At one time it was supposed that the ammonoids were suffering from ‘ racial senescence ’ at that time and that the uncoiling represented a kind of genetic exhaustion .
27525	This resulted in their reversion to resemble some of their earliest ancestors ( the straight nautiloids ) and squared with the observation that some of the heteromorphs even reverted to simple , wavy sutures again .
27526	However , the heteromorphs were extremely successful and widespread , and they are accompanied by , and even survived by other species with a perfectly usual appearance .
27527	The explanation lies in something less mysterious than ‘ racial senescence ’ .
27528	Far from being an expression of decline the heteromorphs show the ammonoids adopting new ( and successful ) life habits .
27529	Some of them may have become bottom living , crawling hunters for which a gastropod-like shell would have been more appropriate .
27530	Loss of active swimming habits may have rendered the complex suture lines superfluous .
27531	But their displacement from a dominant role in the pelagic habitat may have accompanied the rise of squid , sepioids , and octopods .
27532	Ammonoids , heteromorphs included , are almost without parallel as stratigraphic indicators .
27533	They evolved rapidly and spread widely , and have a range of distinctive characters to help the investigator in his identifications .
27534	Study of evolving populations of ammonoids has produced very fine subdivisions of Jurassic and Cretaceous rocks , and their only disadvantage , curiously enough , is the feature that makes them so attractive to collectors .
27535	They are large , and hence the chances of recovering complete specimens from all boreholes is relatively low .
27536	Microfossils ( Chapter 8 ) are often used in their stead for subsurface work .
27537	BELEMNOIDS
27538	The cigar-shaped belemnoids ( 'belemnites ' ) are common fossils accompanying the ammonoids in Jurassic and Cretaceous rocks .
27539	The fossil is an internal skeleton ( enclosed within the body ) of a squid-like animal , in a way comparable with the cuttle bone of the living cuttle-fish .
27540	The solid calcite of this internal skeleton makes the belemnoid a resistant fossil , and fragments are common survivors of erosion , often picked up on ‘ Recent ’ beaches .
27541	The chambered shell ( phragmocone ) is less conspicuous — it is tucked into the broad end of the fossil guard , where the series of closely-spaced septa reveal the cephalopod nature of these otherwise somewhat featureless fossils .
27542	Belemnites vary from small fossils a centimetre or two long to large specimens tens of centimetres long : of course these are only a fraction of the size of the living animal , with their tentacles extending well beyond the guard .
27543	The belemnoids disappear from the fossil record at the end of the Cretaceous , but some of the group gave rise to living squid-like animals , and so they are not to be regarded as extinct in the same , final way as the ammonoids .
27544	OTHER MOLLUSCAN CLASSES
27545	Some molluscs are found as fossils which belong to groups other than the familiar ones described previously .
27546	Although they are rarer fossils , some of them are of such interest that they are worth mentioning here .
27547	One of the most exciting are the Monoplacophora .
27548	These are a group of extremely primitive molluscs , which are found in any abundance only in Lower Palaeozoic rocks .
27549	They are usually simple cap-shaped shells looking somewhat like limpets , but on their internal surfaces they carry a series of paired muscle impressions .
27550	Many authorities regard the Monoplacophora as lying at the root of the other molluscan groups ; gastropods , cephalopods and even bivalves may have been derived from them .
27551	For many years they were known only from fossil representatives and were believed to be extinct .
27552	It was an amazing discovery to find that monoplacophorans were still alive and well — living ones were dredged from the deep ocean in the early 1950's .
27553	Not only that , the living form had hardly changed from its Silurian predecessor ( see p. 77 ) .
27554	The monoplacophorans really reached their acme in the Cambrian , with curious forms having shapes that have never been paralleled in other molluscs ( Yochelcionella ) .
27555	Another odd group that did not survive the Palaeozoic were the Rostroconchs .
27556	These look rather like bivalves without a hinge .
27557	They really are extinct , but managed to compete successfully with the bivalves for a considerable time .
27558	Finally , the tusk shells ( Scaphopoda ) are a long-lived group with a record stretching from the Ordovician to the present .
27559	They are the only molluscs with a truly tubular shell , usually gently curved , with an opening at both ends .
27560	They live today with the broad end buried in the sediment , where they forage for food using small prehensile filaments .
27561	Their habits have probably always been similar , and if survival is to be taken as a measure of success , their conservative way of life has ensured them of a leading place in the evolutionary marathon .
27562	Other animals described in this book have occupied a specific ecological niche where they can quietly pursue their own speciality without embarking on any spectacular radiation in the manner of the ammonoids .
27563	It is a curious paradox that often the most spectacularly successful and numerous organisms are also those with a finite geological record .
27564	Primitive molluscs : Monoplacophora .
27565	Silurian fossils very like the ‘ living fossil ’ Neopilina ( above ) , and the peculiar Cambrian form Yochelcionella ( below ) .
27566	THE ECHINODERMS — PHYLUM ECHINODERMATA
27567	Sea urchins , starfish , sea lilies and sea cucumbers are living echinoderms — the ‘ spiny skinned ’ animals , according to the Greek name of the phylum .
27568	It is an appropriate name , for most echinoderms do feel prickly to the touch , and the sea urchins are equipped with fearsome spines .
27569	The skeleton of all echinoderms except the sea cucumbers is a relatively strong assembly of calcite plates ; the animals are built from an interlocking mosaic of such plates , and mostly the skeletons are rigid enough to have a high chance of fossilization .
27570	The geological record of the phylum is accordingly excellent .
27571	The echinoderm skeleton is not a truly external one , like that of the molluscs , for it is surrounded on the outside by a thin skin of living tissue .
27572	The mosaic of calcite plates is a particular feature of the phylum , and serves as one of the characters linking together such dissimilar-looking animals as starfish and sea lilies .
27573	Another unique feature is the water vascular system , a system of internal plumbing that drives the tube feet : mobile , club-shaped sacs arranged in serried ranks on the outside of the animal , which operate in harmony to convey food to the mouth , or in locomotion .
27574	They have a well-developed nervous system .
27575	Most echinoderms also have an unique five-rayed radial symmetry in the overall shape of the skeleton .
27576	This five-fold ( pentameral ) symmetry seems a peculiar number to be present over such a wide range of organisms .
27577	Why not four , six or thirteen ?
27578	The answer is still not clear , but what is certain is that the five-rayed plan was established even in the Cambrian in a number of diverse echinoderms ; it is evidently highly functional .
27579	In detail the echinoderms show evidence of bilateral ( mirror image ) symmetry , from which five-fold symmetry was probably derived .
27580	Once acquired it is rarely lost , even in echinoderms like sea urchins that ( perhaps ) could also function on a different symmetry pattern .
27581	Each plate of an echinoderm is composed of a single crystal of calcite , whereas all of the organisms we have discussed above have skeletons composed of felt-like masses of tiny crystals .
27582	Broken echinoderm plates ‘ catch the light ’ — the single crystals break along cleavage planes and so present a uniform reflective surface .
27583	Many rocks are composed of a high proportion of echinoderm debris , which is easily recognized because of this optical property .
27584	Through their long history the echinoderms have never left the sea , but within their preferred medium they have adopted most of the life habits available to marine organisms .
27585	They include grazers , feeding on simple plants , scavengers , mud eaters , filter-feeders extracting microorganisms from currents , and some efficient and versatile hunters .
27586	Like other marine organisms they have a planktonic larval stage that assists their dispersal , but almost all adult echinoderms lead a bottom dwelling existence ; a few sea lilies have successfully cast off their anchorage to the sea floor and become widespread swimmers .
27587	The echinoderms are such a varied and important group that the different kinds have to be considered separately .
27588	I should add that some of the most interesting echinoderms are also some of the rarest — peculiar , plated animals that do not fit comfortably into the array of living forms .
27589	Many of these occur in the Cambrian — it is as if the echinoderms tried out various designs before settling for the successful models that mostly survive today .
27590	The echinoderms are a phylum closely allied to the Chordates — including the vertebrates , and both phyla probably have a common ancestor in the Precambrian .
27591	SEA LILIES — CLASS CRINOIDEA , AND OTHER STEMMED ECHINODERMS ( Colour plates 22 , 23 , 24 )
27592	Crinoids are abundant and important fossils from the Ordovician to the Tertiary .
27593	They are still abundant at present , although a little less common in shallow water sites than they were in the Palaeozoic and Mesozoic , but they are conspicuous and varied components of deep water faunas .
27594	The great majority of the group have long stalks , which are anchored to the bottom .
27595	The main part of the animal consists of a cup ( or calyx ) to which the stalk is attached at its upper end , and from the top of the calyx stretch long arms , which are five in number or more usually a multiple of five .
27596	The arms are often repeatedly branched .
27597	The distal parts of the arms carry fine pinnules , which are instrumental in gathering the fine , water-borne food such as micro-organisms on which the animal feeds .
27598	Since crinoids often occur together in large numbers ( 'gardens ' ) with their arms waving in the currents , it is easy to see how they came to acquire their botanical analogy .
27599	Food grooves in the arms channel the food to the mouth , which lies in the centre of the calyx .
27600	Stem , calyx , and arms are all made of calcite plates .
27601	The stems are often common fossils , even when the calyx can not be found — many of the ‘ crinoidal limestones ’ are composed largely of stem debris .
27602	The individual plates of the stem slot together like a stack of coins ; they are termed ossicles .
27603	These can be round , or five-sided , up to a centimetre or so across , and have a small hole in their centre ; the stems can look like corals to the casual observer , but where they are broken they show the typical echinoderm reflective surfaces .
27604	Detailed classification of the crinoids is based principally on the way the calcite plates are arranged on the calyx with the number and branching patterns of the arms , the external sculpture on the calyx , and important internal features of the cup connected with the nervous and respiratory systems .
27605	In detail they are a very complicated group .
27606	Complete specimens of fossil crinoids are rather rare , and deserve pride of place in anyone 's collection .
27607	Complete cups are more common — many of them were evidently rigid , and they are easily preserved as fossils .
27608	There are famous examples where whole ‘ gardens ’ seem to have been preserved , with the arms frozen , as it were , in motion , and even the roots at the base of the stems in place .
27609	Crinoid , Onychocrinus exsculptus from the Carboniferous ( Mississipian ) .
27610	The species is preserved in relief in limestone , which is very fine grained , and retains many fine details .
27611	The long stem of this crinoid , with a small cup at the top , and stout arms composed of easily visible calcite plates , these first arms themselves dividing , are some of the more important characteristics of this species .
27612	There are numerous Carboniferous crinoids not unlike this one , which require expert knowledge in their discrimination .
27613	This specimen is from Illinois , USA , but forms related to it may be found in Carboniferous limestones in many areas .
27614	The specimen is 15 cm long .
27615	The crinoids have had an eventful geological history .
27616	True crinoids are doubtfully known before the Ordovician , but once established they diversified rapidly in the manner we have seen repeatedly with other groups .
27617	They soon spread to a variety of habitats , but in the Palaeozoic they were conspicuously abundant in relatively shallow environments .
27618	The most mouthwatering specimens tend to be found in limestones — famous sites are in the Silurian rocks of England and Mississipian rocks of the U.S.A. The group as a whole had a major crisis in the Permian , during which most of the Palaeozoic forms died out .
27619	A very few of these survived into the Triassic .
27620	In the Mesozoic there was another great radiation of the crinoids , the typical forms having flexible arms , and it is crinoids of this kind that survive today .
27621	Some of the most famous crinoidal deposits are of Jurassic age , and marvellous specimens have been collected from the Lias rocks of Britain and Germany .
27622	A new and successful innovation was the evolution of stemless crinoids — some of these acquired pelagic habits , and during the Cretaceous the genera Marsupites and Uintacrinus ( see p.79 ) were widespread enough to be useful marker fossils .
27623	Some of these stemless forms developed grappling hooks at the base of the calyx — with these they can attach in a favourable site , and move when conditions become adverse .
27624	Such feather stars are very numerous in some reef habitats today .
27625	The long and varied history of the crinoids demonstrates how well the echinoderms have attacked the problems of filter-feeding .
27626	The stemless crinoid Uintacrinus , widespread during the Cretaceous .
27627	Natural size .

27635	Blastoid , Pentremites spicatus , Carboniferous ( Mississipian ) .
27636	The specimen is preserved in its original calcite ; its lack of distortion may be seen from its perfect five-fold symmetry .
27637	The five finely striated food grooves , which in this view occupy much of the surface of the animal , are typical of the blastoid .
27638	The name ‘ blastoid ’ is derived from the Greek for ‘ bud ’ because of the resemblance of the animal to a flower bud .
27639	Pentremites is a large genus with many species in limestone of Carboniferous age , particularly in the Mississipian limestones of North America .
27640	This specimen is from Grayson co. , Kentucky , USA .
27641	Similar species occur in North and South America , and related genera almost worldwide The specimen has a diameter of 3 cm .
27642	In the Palaeozoic rocks there were other stalked filter-feeding echinoderms , which failed to survive the crisis at the end of the Permian , weathered by the crinoids .
27643	These extinct groups can exceed crinoids in number and variety at certain horizons , and they were evidently competing on equal terms .
27644	The blastoids ( class Blastoidea ) had compact cups up to a few centimetres long , with five broad food grooves running down the sides ( lacking crinoid arms ) .
27645	In life the food grooves were flanked by lines of delicate armlets ( brachioles ) which served to gather the food .
27646	Blastoids are sometimes abundant fossils in rocks ( usually limestone ) of Silurian to early Permian age , and their perfect , compact pentameral symmetry makes their calices among the most attractive of fossils .
27647	Like crinoids they evidently grew in gardens , for their remains ( especially in Carboniferous rocks ) tend to occur packed together in thousands .
27648	Cystoids ( class Cystoidea ) are even odder animals : often rather irregular bags of calcite plates , or if composed of a few plates these may carry powerful ribbing .
27649	The five-fold symmetry is often hard to detect in the calyx as a whole , although five food grooves are usually developed .
27650	They are a primitive , but very interesting , group with Cambrian origins , and reached their greatest variety in the Ordovician .
27651	Some of them evidently lacked a stem , and must have lain loosely on the bottom .
27652	There are several more groups of odd echinoderms in the Lower Palaeozoic rocks — some of them only recently discovered , like the bizarre helicoplacoids , which look like nothing so much as spinning tops ( see p. 84 ) .
27653	All are of the greatest interest , and any plated animal from the Cambrian is likely to be an important specimen .
27654	Sometimes these early forms are found as moulds — the original calcite having dissolved away .
27655	The external moulds then present a characteristic appearance , like the impression of a mosaic pressed into the rock .
27656	It is well worth keeping a special watch for fossils of this kind when hunting in Cambrian localities — it is still perfectly possible to discover a completely new kind of echinoderm !
27657	18 Eocene gastropod , Voluta muricina .

27659	It is distinguished by its tall spire , elongate aperture , prominent spines , but without the spiral ridges seen on many species .
