27693	Total length 18 cm .
27694	25 Cidaroid sea urchin , Plegiocidaris coronata , Jurassic , Ulm , Germany .
27695	Two beautiful examples of this sea urchin are illustrated preserved in a fine-grained limestone in full relief .
27696	Note however , that the stout spines are not preserved on these specimens .
27697	Plegiocidaris is found in Triassic and Jurassic rocks of Europe .
27698	The specimens have 5 cm diameter .
27699	26 Jurassic sea urchin , Hemicidaris intermedia , Wiltshire , England .
27700	This specimen is exceptionally well-preserved , retaining its spines where they fell around the animal as it died .
27701	The matrix is a yellow limestone .
27702	The long spines of this species are characteristic — they resemble lances used in medieval jousting .
27703	Note the prominent articulating tubercles , like those of other cidaroids .
27704	The longest spine on this specimen has a length of 7 cm .
27705	27 Sea urchin , Tylocidaris clavigera , Cretaceous , Gravesend , England .
27706	Magnificently preserved in its original calcite in a matrix of chalk , this specimen is unusual because it has the spines still joined to the rest of the animal .
27707	The ferocious-looking spines , which seem almost too large for the central animal , are mostly attached , but one or two have come adrift .
27708	8 cm across .
27709	28 Spatangoid sea urchin , Micraster coranguinum Cretaceous .
27710	This specimen is preserved in its original calcite .
27711	It is frequently found also as siliceous internal moulds .
27712	Micraster is sometimes called the heart urchin , because of its distinctive shape .
27713	Most specimens have a length of 5–7 cm .
27714	29 Sea urchin , Schizaster canatifera , Pliocene , Perpignan , France .
27715	The specimen is perfectly preserved — retaining even the finest details of its external surface .
27716	But the fine fuzz of tiny spines that covered it in life are not present .
27717	This species looks rather like the heart urchin but the petal-like areas are much more deeply sunken , the forward pair very short .
27718	Related species are worldwide .
27719	It is 8 cm long .
27720	30 Fossil starfish , Archastropecten cotteswoldiae , Jurassic , Gloucestershire , England .
27721	The original calcite of the starfish is stained slightly yellow on the surface .
27722	The specimen occurs in a fine-grained limestone , one which fortunately splits easily around the enclosed fossils .
27723	This species has a small central disc , and long , slender arms .
27724	A related genus , Astropecten , occurs in Tertiary rocks , and survives today .
27725	Maximum diameter 7 cm .
27726	31 Carpoid , Cothurnocystis evae , Ordovician , Ayrshire , Scotland .
27727	This curious species is preserved in a fine-grained sandstone as an external mould — that is , all the original shell material has been dissolved away , but this still allows an accurate view of the original organism , especially if an artificial cast is taken from the natural mould .
27728	The greatest length of this specimen is 4 cm .
27729	Fossil brittle ( serpent ) star , ( Palaeocoma egertoni , Jurassic Lias , England .
27730	A beautiful species preserved in an impure limestone .
27731	The limestone was deposited in very quiet water conditions , which accounts for the preservation of this delicate little fossil .
27732	The long slender arms are flexible , unlike the starfish shown previously .
27733	Other localities for brittle stars include Miocene rocks in Maryland , USA .
27734	Maximum diameter 8 cm .
27735	Permian blastoid , Deltoblastus delta .
27736	These beautifully preserved little blastoids are stained slightly , because of iron compounds .
27737	The slender stems , like those of the crinoids are not preserved here .
27738	Compared with the other blastoids in this book the food grooves are very long , extending almost to the base of the animal , and occupying much of its surface area .
27739	This species may be one of the last of this kind of echinoderm , which did not survive beyond the Permian .
27740	This rare species is unlikely to fall into the hands of the amateur , being from a unique echinoderm fauna in the Permian rocks of Amanoebang Province , Indonesia .
27741	The largest specimen here does not greatly exceed 2 cm in length .
27742	SEA URCHINS — CLASS ECHINOIDEA ( Colour plates 25–29 )
27743	Anyone who has waded into the clear blue waters of the Mediterranean without proper footwear may have encountered the protective covering of the sea urchins .
27744	Many of the living echinoids are protected by spines , some sharp and breaking off easily into the unwary foot , others stout and clublike ; a few groups have taken to burrowing into sediment , and the spines have become small and felt-like .
27745	Under the spines there is a test composed of hundreds of calcite plates .
27746	Of course there is no stem — the sea urchins are self-propelled .
27747	Looking more closely at the arrangement of the calcite plates the fivefold symmetry is still in evidence — in this group there are five areas of finer plates ( ambulacra ) radiating from the centre .
27748	Under a lens these small plates show perforations , and during life the tiny tube feet passed through these to assist the animal in locomotion .
27749	The perfect polygonal joinery of all the plates is a striking feature of the echinoid test .
27750	Some sea urchins are almost spherical , with large strong plates looking rather like shields with a boss in the centre .
27751	These kinds of sea urchins carry the stoutest of spines attached to the bosses .
27752	Many living sea urchins have undergone a modification of the pentameral symmetry typical of the rest of the echinoderms — they have become bilateral again .
27753	Perhaps this is not surprising in animals that are accustomed to moving in a particular direction — they need a front and a back .
27754	In burrowing forms the mouth moves to one ( forward ) side and the anus to the back , which is obviously a sensible arrangement .
27755	Some species have become greatly flattened like the living sand dollar , which has a covering of very fine spines and can bury itself in sand with remarkable speed .
27756	The sea urchins are among the most efficient scavengers in the sea-hence their somewhat unsavoury association with human effluvia .
27757	They also include species that eat their way through enormous quantities of sediment , extracting edible particles from it , and in the process reprocessing all the sediment ; some of the fossil heart urchins probably had this habit ( see p. 128 ) .
27758	These vacuum cleaners of the sea are vital in preventing fouling of the marine environment .
27759	Species with club-shaped spines include active hunters ( although they tend to hunt sluggish animals like other sea urchins ) and they have powerful jaws on the lower side of the animal that can munch their way through a sand dollar as if it were a biscuit .
27760	Some urchins use their jaws to make burrows in solid rock .
27761	Like other major echinoderm groups the geological record of the sea urchins goes back to the Ordovician .
27762	In my experience they are generally rare fossils in the Palaeozoic , but as so often with echinoderms there are localities where large numbers of specimens can be recovered from a bedding plane or two .
27763	They must have been gregarious from the start .
27764	The early sea urchins tend to have rather a large number of plates in a much less regular mosaic than their later relatives .
27765	By the end of the Palaeozoic , echinoids with club-shaped spines and beautifully regular tests had become well-established , and their distant descendants survive today .
27766	It was in the Mesozoic that a really considerable proliferation of urchins occurred , and they acquired the importance in the marine economy that they retain .
27767	They are abundant in Jurassic and Cretaceous rocks , represented both by the spherical spiny forms , and some of those with bilateral symmetry .
27768	Isolated spines are common fossils , and useful ones too , because their patterns vary from species to species .
27769	Some of the burrowing forms have left their burrows behind as well .
27770	In England sea urchins are especially easy to collect from the Cretaceous chalk , where they have been used as one of the fossils for dating the rocks .
27771	STARFISH — CLASS STELLEROIDEA ( Colour plates 30 , 32 )
27772	The starfish are among the most important of invertebrate predators living today .
27773	They make major depredations on oyster beds and the recent activities of the ‘ Crown of Thorns ’ starfish ( Acanthaster ) in chewing up great chunks of the Great Barrier Reef have become a modern ecological object lesson ( and , incidentally , a source of funds for many marine biologists ) .
27774	There are two major kinds of starfish ( which may not be closely related ) — the familiar large , stiff-armed asteroids , and the delicate ophiuroids , brittle stars , with lithe , slender , snake-like arms radiating from a circular central disc .
27775	Ophiuroids are especially abundant in deep sea environments , and it is unusual for a deep sea dredge to miss one of these small animals .
27776	Asteroids often have five arms , but many species have more — up to about forty .
27777	Although they are common today starfish are not generally common fossils , but as so often with echinoderms , they seem to be local in occurrence .
27778	Their remains are commoner from the Mesozoic onwards , and at some levels , as in the Cretaceous chalk , they can be found in considerable numbers .
27779	Their history goes back at least to the Ordovician , although some of the Palaeozoic asteroids are distantly related , if at all , to the living species .
27780	Ophiuroids have fossil representatives as old as Carboniferous .
27781	Cassiduloid sea urchin , Pygurus costatus , Jurassic .
27782	The species is preserved without flattening in a hard limestone , which fills the interior of the specimen .
27783	This species looks rather like a bun , but not highly convex , and with a five-sided outline .
27784	The five ambulacral areas — like the petals of a flower — are clearly visible .
27785	They are not sunken into hollows as on many echinoids This genus and its allies are quite commonly found in Jurassic and Cretaceous rocks .
27786	This species is from the Corallian rocks of England , but its relatives occur in Europe , North America and Africa .
27787	This specimen has a diameter of 8 cm .
27788	Related species often grow to twice the diameter .
27789	Jurassic echinoids in this sort of preservation in hard limestones are often difficult to clean .
27790	Sometimes the natural processes of erosion will etch a perfect specimen .
27791	THE CARPOIDS — ECHINODERMS OR CHORDATES ?
27792	( Colour plate 31 )
27793	One of the oddest groups of animals covered with calcite plates are known as carpoids ( occasionally referred to as calcichordates ) .
27794	Although they have been known for many years their evolutionary position is still hotly debated .
27795	They lack any pretence of five-fold symmetry , some are bilaterally symmetrical , but others have no obvious plane of symmetry at all , a most unusual thing for any animal .
27796	They appear to have a stem : could they be related to the crinoids ?
27797	But the ‘ stem ’ tapers out to a point , and in some cases had a whip-like flexibility ; the same structure has been interpreted as a ‘ tail ’ .
27798	Similar kinds of arguments can be applied to different parts of these extraordinary fossils .
27799	Internally they are really quite complicated , and some possess lobes and channels incised within the plates strikingly similar to the appearance of the brain and nerves in some fishes .
27800	Some authorities have suggested that the carpoids may include ancestors of particular chordates .
27801	They have a record going well back into the Cambrian , when it might be supposed that the chordates were undergoing a major diversification .
27802	Regardless of whether they include direct ancestors or not , the carpoids do serve to demonstrate the likelihood of evolutionary links between chordates — including vertebrates — and the echinoderms .
27803	Carpoids are rare fossils ranging from the Cambrian to the Devonian , when they disappeared completely — unless their descendants live on in one of the chordate groups .
27804	Starfish , Crateraster coombi , Cretaceous .
27805	The starfish is preserved in soft white chalk , which fills in the interior of the animal .
27806	The individual calcite plates can be clearly seen .
27807	This starfish has a broad central disc , and slender arms .
27808	They are stout plates around the perimeter , but tiny-plates in the central part of the animal .
27809	Starfish are uncommon fossils , particularly in this state of completeness , since they easily break into their component plates .
27810	A few species generally resembling this one occur in Jurassic and Cretaceous rocks .
27811	This specimen is from Kent , England , but similar forms occur in the chalk over Europe and in Cretaceous rocks in North America .
27812	Related forms survive today .
27813	The specimen measures 10 cm across its longest diameter .
27814	THE ARTHROPODS — PHYLUM ARTHROPODA
27815	There are more living arthropod species than all other phyla combined ; if diversity is a measure of success then the arthropods are the easy winners .
27816	Arthropods are those animals with an external , usually ‘ chitinous ’ skeleton ( exoskeleton ) and have characteristic legs , feelers , etc. , with joints to give them flexibility ( arthropod is derived from the Greek for ‘ jointed leg ’ ) .
27817	They have bodies divided into segments , and their legs and jaws are arranged in pairs .
27818	They are mostly small and there is a good physiological reason for this : gigantism is mechanically difficult for animals with external skeletons , and above a certain size it is difficult to get enough oxygen into the organism to sustain activity .
27819	Despite this one limitation the arthropods have the most varied habits and habitats of any phylum : they can be found anywhere on land , sea or in the air .
27820	They inhabit the driest parts of the desert and the deepest parts of the ocean with equal facility .
27821	This is partly due to the flexibility of the external skeleton — it can be modified into wings , fortified into claws , sealed against searing heat , or turned into eye lenses .
27822	Segmentation , too , has proved very versatile ; individual pairs of legs , or appendages , can be specialized for particular functions without affecting the routine business of locomotion taken by the others ; appendages are modified for feeding in a host of ways , for grasping , swimming , spinning , copulating , cleaning or camouflaging .
27823	And their small size enables tiny arthropods , some almost too small to see with the naked eye , to live in crannies , within the soil , between sand grains , and the like .
27824	They are truly ubiquitous .
27825	Helicoplacoid — a peculiar and puzzling Cambrian echinoderm
27826	Tube of polychaete worm , Rotularia bognoriensis , Eocene .
27827	Serpulid tubes are preserved here in a siltstone , with parts of the original shell material adhering .
27828	The same piece of rock also includes internal moulds of gastropods and bivalves .
27829	Worm tubes like these may , at first sight , be confused with gastropod molluscs .
27830	The irregularity of the tubes , which become straight near their apertures , distinguishes them from snail shells .
27831	Serpulid worm tubes are found in many different sediment types in rocks of Mesozoic and Tertiary age .
27832	Some species are very tiny , and encrust other shells .
27833	This species is from Bognor , England , but related forms occur the world over .
27834	Overall length of specimens about 3 cm .
27835	Cambrian trilobite , Wanneria walcottana , preserved on a fine sandstone , with a certain amount of crushing .
27836	This is one of the most primitive trilobites known .
27837	The crescent-shaped eyes are attached to the middle part of the head .
27838	There are a number of similar species from early Cambrian rocks distinguished on the size of the eyes and details of the thorax .
27839	The specimen has a length of 10 cm .
27840	They are also an ancient group , since obvious arthropods , of primitive kinds , can be found in the earliest of Cambrian rocks .
27841	At this time , of course , they were wholly marine .
27842	They were probably derived from some sort of segmented worm ( annelid ) — a few scientists adopt the view that different arthropods may have come from different and separate worms , independently , which became ‘ arthropodized ’ by acquiring an external skeleton .
27843	With certain exceptions , the fossil record of the arthropods is not commensurate with their diversity today , and their probable diversity in the past .
27844	Some forms have delicate exterior skeletons that are only preserved under exceptional circumstances ( see p. 16 ) .
27845	Many terrestrial forms simply did not live in environments in which preservation was possible .
27846	So the record of the group as a whole is a bit patchy , with ‘ jumps ’ in time between one fossil find and the next .
27847	Some groups , those with good , solid ( and especially calcified ) hard parts are frequent and important fossils , with an unparalleled record .
27848	A brief summary of the arthropods can not do justice to all the fascinating specialized groups — sea spiders and mites for example — that have an incomplete fossil record .
27849	We shall concentrate on the arthropods with the best fossil record .
27850	Some of these are common enough to dominate fossil assemblages , and they are among the most attractive of the common invertebrate groups .
27851	TRILOBITES — CLASS TRILOBITA ( Colour plates 33 , 34 , 36 , 43 )
27852	The North American Indians had a name for trilobites that meant ‘ little water bug in the rocks ’ , which shows extraordinary zoological acuity .
27853	The trilobites were one of the dominant forms of marine life in the Lower Palaeozoic , known from thousands of different species and found in every continent .
27854	Not surprisingly they were among the first fossils to attract widespread attention .
27855	They have a high degree of organization and a variety of form that shows how quickly the arthropods were able to exploit the advantages of their external skeleton .
27856	All trilobites are divided lengthways into three lobes — hence their name .
27857	They can also be divided crossways into three regions , a well-defined head ( cephalon ) at the front , usually equipped with a pair of eyes , a thorax with a variable number of articulated segments , and at the back end a tail ( or pygidium ) formed by the fusion of several segments .
27858	The parts of the animal we find fossilized are usually only the carapace , the hard parts that formed a protective covering on the back of the animal .
27859	If we could have turned over a living trilobite we would have seen an array of jointed legs on the underside , and flexible antennae .
27860	The traces of these appendages are preserved in exceptional circumstances , so we do know that trilobites had walking legs gills , antennae , and the bases of the legs modified into primitive jaws in some species .
27861	The appendage pairs are generally similar along the length of animal .
27862	Few examples of complete trilobites are known and for the most part we have to be content with the exterior skeleton .
27863	Photograph of ‘ happy buttons ’ taken through the lenses of the eye of the trilobite Phacops ( see p. 87 ) of Devonian age .
27864	Cambrian trilobite , Elrathia kingi .
27865	This trilobite has been preserved in a curious way : the original shell has been thickened by mineral growth , still of calcite , to give the fossil a distinctive , medallion-like appearance This trilobite has a large number of wide thoracic segments , not greatly convex .
27866	The tail is wide , well-segmented .
27867	The inflated middle part of the head tapers forwards This species occurs in great numbers in the Wheeler Shale of Utah , USA .
27868	Related species occur over a much wider area around the margin of North America and in Europe .
27869	Complete specimens are usually ½-3 cm long .
27870	They are sold in rock shops and souvenir centres , often mounted into jewellery .
27871	Moulting in trilobites ; breakup of the exoskeleton into several pieces helped the animal shed its old carapace
27872	The great variety of form of the hard parts surely shows that trilobites were adapted to a wide range of habitats and life styles .
27873	We know that they could live in extremely shallow to very deep-water environments , that most lived on or near the sea bottom , but a few were adapted to open-ocean swimming .
27874	They probably had a variety of different habits , some no doubt were scavengers , others sediment grazers , and it seems probable that some trilobites were also active hunters , pursuing worms and other soft-bodied prey , which they shredded using the spines on the base of their legs .
27875	The eyes of trilobites include some very sophisticated structures that show they were far from primitive visually .
27876	Many species have thousands of lenses — like a fly 's eye — which were very sensitive to detecting any movements in their field of view .
27877	Others had fewer lenses of remarkably efficient construction ; photographs have actually been taken ( p. 86 ) using these ancient lenses in a camera — and they still focus precisely after 400 million years or so .
27878	The lenses , like the rest of the exoskeleton , are made of calcite .
27879	Trinucleid trilobite , Trinucleus fimbriatus , Ordovician .
27880	An extraordinary little trilobite looking like an ancient medallion , preserved in shale , with some of its original exoskeleton retained , coloured by iron compounds .
27881	Trinucleid trilobites are blind , and with a greatly inflated mid-part of the head region .
27882	Around the perimeter of the head there is a pitted fringe , which is unique to this kind of arthropod .
27883	Trinucleid trilobites , with various types of fringe , are characteristic of Ordovician rocks .
27884	There are more than 100 species .
27885	This species is from Builth , Wales .
27886	While perhaps commonest in Europe ( Wales , Scotland , Sweden , Norway , Czechoslovakia ) , trinucleids are also known from North America ( Virginia , Nevada and various localities in Canada ) , North Africa and South America .
27887	Specimens do not usually exceed 2½ cm in length .
27888	Trilobites vary in length from a millimetre or two to fifty centimetres or more — the ‘ average ’ trilobite is 5 cm or so long .
27889	It is actually rather unusual to find a complete trilobite as a fossil — usually they are in pieces .
27890	Trilobites , like most arthropods , grew by moulting ( casting off the old carapace and growing a new , larger one ) and many of the bits we find are probably the ‘ cast offs ’ and not the dead animal .
27891	During moulting the head split into several pieces along special sutures , the thorax often parted into its individual segments and the tail was displaced ( see p. 86 ) .
27892	The early moults , ‘ baby trilobites ’ , have been discovered .
27893	Some trilobites lost their eyes , probably those that burrowed in mud or lived in lightless parts of the ocean .
27894	Many trilobites could enroll when threatened , just like the living woodlouse some of them even evolved locking devices to make their enrollment really secure .
27895	In some places you can find dozens of enrolled trilobites together ; these are the remains of the animals themselves , not the moults , which presumably perished together after a fruitless attempt to protect themselves from a miniature catastrophe such as a sudden influx of sediment .
27896	Typical trilobites of several kinds are present in the earliest Cambrian rocks ; they must have had late Precambrian ancestors , but of these nothing is known .
27897	They swarmed in the Cambrian seas , outnumbering all other invertebrates in most localities .
27898	The trilobites evolved rapidly , and can therefore be used extensively in the dating of rocks at this time .
27899	They continued to proliferate in the Ordovician , although many of the Cambrian kinds had died out ; in terms of the variety of forms present this period was perhaps their heyday .
27900	Several kinds of trilobite failed to survive the end of the Ordovician , but other trilobites were still conspicuous during the Silurian and Devonian .
27901	Only a few major groups survived into the Carboniferous , but they can still be locally abundant .
27902	The last trilobites are found in Permian rocks , and before the Triassic they had disappeared forever .
27903	We might perhaps hope that one species lingered on , like the brachiopod Lingla , in some inaccessible part of the sea , but as even the deep sea faunas become well-known this possibility is fading .
27904	Since many of the extremely ancient rocks in which trilobites can be found are folded or otherwise distorted their remains can often be found twisted or fractured .
27905	But in other sites , particularly in limestones , they can be found with every fine skeletal detail preserved .
27906	The many different kinds are distinguished by the nature of the segmentation , particularly in the head region , the structure of the thorax and pygidium , the size , position and structure of the eyes , the development of the moulting sutures , and the surface patterns on the exterior of the exoskeleton .
27907	New trilobites are being discovered every year , and there is always the possibility of finding one with its legs preserved !
27908	Asaphid trilobite , Isotelus gigas , Ordovician .
27909	This fine , large trilobite is preserved in relief in a limestone — a common mode of preservation for North American Ordovician trilobites .
27910	A ‘ smoothed out ’ trilobite , with the head of similar size and shape to the tail , and only eight thoracic segments ( contrast the Cambrian trilobites in this book ) .
27911	The eyes are small .
27912	Asaphid trilobites of many species are common in rocks of Ordovician age .
27913	Many grew to an impressive size .
27914	Isotelus is typical of the North American continent , where it occurs in many localities .
27915	Other asaphids occur in most countries of Europe , especially Norway and Sweden , and widely in Asia and Australia .
27916	This specimen has a length of 9 cm .
27917	CRABS , LOBSTERS , SHRIMPS AND THEIR ALLIES — CLASS CRUSTACEA ( Colour plates 39 , 41 )
27918	The seas today swarm with crustacean arthropods ranging in size from the tiniest krill in the surface waters to giant bottom-living crabs with a reach like that of a man .
27919	The majority of crustacea have appendages that are specialized to do different jobs along the length of the animal — some for grasping , some for swimming and so on .
27920	Most smaller crustacea have exoskeletons that are rather delicate , and for this reason the fossil record of the shrimps , for example , is somewhat incomplete .
27921	Undoubted crustaceans are found in rocks as old as Cambrian , at which time free-swimming species were living happily alongside the trilobites .
27922	It is not until the Carboniferous that we start to find evidence of a variety of forms including the putative ancestors of some of the living dominant groups .
27923	Crabs and lobsters have the thickest exoskeleton of all the group — one like that of the trilobites reinforced with calcium carbonate — and the fossil record of this important group ( only a small part of the whole class however ) is much better .
27924	Lobster-like animals are found as far back as the Triassic , and both crabs and lobsters are frequent and appealing fossils in Cretaceous and Tertiary rocks .
27925	The group was hardly set back at all by the major extinction at the end of the Cretaceous , and has never been more varied than it is today .
27926	The most highly specialized crustacea are probably the barnacles ( Cirripedia ) and individual barnacle plates are rather commonly encountered in rocks of Cretaceous age and younger .
27927	Finally the diminutive , bivalved ostracods are important and abundant fossils , which we will consider with other microfossils in Chapter 8 .
27928	SPIDERS , SCORPIONS , SEA SCORPIONS , HORSESHOE CRABS — CLASS CHELICERATA ( Colour plates 37 , 38 , 40 )
27929	This large and varied group of arthropods includes the giants of the phylum , as well as tiny spiders hardly visible to the unaided eye .
27930	They are classified together because of basic similarities in the appendages , even though they have diversified into very different-looking creatures living equally happily on land and in the sea .
27931	Predatory habits are typical , and many species have specialized clutching appendages , or stinging organs .
27932	None of the group is especially common as fossils , but they make up for their general rarity by their interest .
27933	Most spectacular are the sea scorpions ( eurypterids ) , which include arthropods as large as any that have lived ( two.metres or more in length ) .
27934	Appendages in the ‘ head ’ region often include powerful claws , and it does not take much imagination to conclude that these eurypterids were among the fiercest predators of their day .
27935	They were prominent in the Silurian and Devonian , where they can be found with the fish-like animals that abounded in the fresh- and brackish water deposits of the time , although some of the Ordovician ones are in marine sediments .
27936	Some of the eurypterids may even have made tentative excursions on to the land .
27937	They are also probably the earliest animals in which two sexes can be certainly identified .
27938	The eurypterids are probably allied to the scorpions , which originated in the Silurian or even earlier , and successfully made the transition from the aqueous environment to land .
27939	They are abundant enough today in warmer climates to be a serious cause of death in some countries .
27940	Perhaps it was the transition to land that enabled the scorpions to survive beyond the Palaeozoic , which saw the end of the sea scorpions .
27941	Spiders are known as far back as the Carboniferous , but their remains are principally known fossilized from the Tertiary ambers , where perfectly preserved specimens retain even the hairs on the legs .
27942	The Horseshoe Crab ( Limulus ) is one of the most celebrated of ‘ living fossils ’ , and it is a genuine survivor having changed little in 150 million years ( see p. 91 ) .
27943	It is the last of the merostomes the group of fossil horseshoe crabs that were varied and numerous in the coal swamps of the Carboniferous and have a history that extends back to the Cambrian .
27944	Why Limulus alone should have survived is something of a mystery .
27945	It appears to have rather generalized habits , feeding on everything from worms to clams , which it can crush with its powerful appendages , using the bases of its legs like nutcrackers .
27946	It can swim , flipped over on to its boat-like carapace , or crawl .
27947	Presumably its ancestors were not so different when they shared the marine habitat with the trilobites .
27948	Below left Fossil spider , Eomysmena moritura , Oligocene .
27949	This is another amber specimen , exquisitely preserved in its entirety .
27950	It is an important and rare specimen .
27951	This species has a short and fat abdomen , which preserves something of its original light colour .
27952	The legs are shorter than those of the other spider in this book , and the four pairs are clearly visible .
27953	This fossil specimen is probably unique .
27954	There are species living today related to this fossil species .
27955	This specimen was obtained from the Baltic bays .
27956	The spider is just over ½cm long
27957	Below Fossil swimming crab , Notopocorystes broderipi , Cretaceous .
27958	This crab is preserved in a rather soft clay , which makes it more fragile than the other crabs in this book .
27959	The crab has a longer body than the other species shown here , and the legs are flattened and held away from the carapace .
27960	There are a number of species generally similar to this one in rocks of Cretaceous and younger age .
27961	This specimen is from Folkestone , England .
27962	Length of the carapace is 2½ cm , but the species grows to more than twice this size .
27963	INSECTS — CLASS INSECTA ( Colour plates 35 , 44 , 45 )
27964	The insects — flies , butterflies , beetles , ants , fleas , bugs , dragonflies , grasshoppers , aphids , wasps , etc. — are the most varied and numerous of the arthropods both in numbers of species and individuals .
27965	They are also the most perfectly adapted of terrestrial organisms , inhibited neither by extremes of climate nor altitude .
27966	If this book were written in proportion to the number of species in the group the rest of it would have to be devoted to the insects .
27967	But the fossil record of the insects is far from perfect — very sporadic and selective .
27968	Where insects are preserved they seem to occur in large numbers and in variety , so that a few famous localities have yielded a disproportionate number of the fossil species .
27969	Insects are fragile and easily damaged , and it is not surprising that they are sometimes destroyed completely .
27970	Many species live , and presumably lived in the past , in inland or upland sites where little sediment accumulates .
27971	Naturally the commonest insect fossils are the most durable parts , like the wing cases ( elytra ) of the beetles .
27972	But their small size also means that insect fossils are easily overlooked and they may be more common than is supposed .
27973	The best sites are in rocks originating from sediments that accumulated in quiet , freshwater sites — lake bottoms , peat bogs and the like and they are generally rarer in marine facies .
27974	Fossil crab , Xanthopsis rugosus , Eocene .
27975	This specimen comes from a clay ; the best specimens often occur in slightly harder , nodular layers within the clay .
27976	Two strong furrows run across the back of the carapace of this crab , which is knobbly , and , on a fine scale , covered with minute pits .
27977	As with Palaeocarpilius powerful claws are held close to the body , like the living shore crab .
27978	A number of Xanthopsis species are one of the characteristic crabs of Eocene deposits .
27979	This specimen was obtained from a tunnel under London !
27980	Similar specimens are to be obtained from elsewhere in southern England , in France , and in the USA .
27981	Diameter of the carapace 6 cm .
27982	Most insects have six legs in three pairs , and are equipped with wings ( a number of primitive forms are wingless ) .
27983	The early evolutionary stages of development of wings are still in question they may have developed from outgrowths of exoskeleton from the body that assisted gliding initially , and then acquired a propulsive function .
27984	In any case winged insects were well established by the Carboniferous , when some of the giant ‘ dragonflies ’ ( not really a close relative of the living species ) had a wingspan of tens of centimetres .
27985	No doubt many of the crucial steps in insect evolution took place during the Devonian , but of this phase of insect history there is very little record .
27986	In the Carboniferous and Permian the insects were highly diverse , and there is still debate over how closely these forms are related to our living fauna : some forms , like the cockroaches , undoubtedly have a long history .
27987	Flight gave the insects the chance to exploit habitats previously vacant , and unrivalled dispersal .
27988	The extraordinary flexibility of the group has meant singular problems in their classification , but certain characteristics , like the structure of the mouthparts or the wing vein patterns serve to define major subdivisions .
27989	During the Mesozoic some of the most important types of insects still living — like the butterflies originated .
27990	Butterflies have an intimate relationship with flowering plants , which they pollinate , and themselves derive nourishment from the nectar .
27991	It is difficult to imagine a butterfly without a plant to feed on , and we have to assume that both the plants and the appropriate pollinators diversified together .
27992	Other kinds of insects besides butterflies have used the nectar of plants for a livelihood , including bees and some flies .
27993	The living horseshoe crab , Limulus ; compare with Fig. 38 .
27994	The fossil record of insects is at its best from Tertiary deposits , where amber , the fossil resin of coniferous trees in which insects became entrapped , yield great numbers of exquisitely preserved specimens .
27995	Even the most delicate are present .
27996	The oldest amber is Cretaceous .
27997	The fossil remains of beetles , including the hard elytra , have been extensively used in the interpretation of the climatic history of the Pleistocene ice advances and retreats , because the species of beetle present in peat deposits change in harmony with the climatic fluctuations .
27998	PHYLUM CHORDATA
27999	The chordates include the dominant living animals , if you measure dominance by size , or the capacity to alter the world .
28000	Man is a chordate .
28001	The phylum at the present is dominated by its more advanced members — the vertebrates .
28002	But in the Cambrian or earlier the chordates no doubt included animals little more highly organized than the contemporary arthropods or brachiopods .
28003	A few of these survive .
28004	The lancelet , Branchiostoma , one of the standard laboratory animals for dissection , is a primitive chordate ( there is a single fossil lancelet from the Middle Cambrian ) .
28005	Hardly anything is known about the fossils from the earliest history of the phylum , possibly because the early chordates lacked hard parts , unless the enigmatic carpoids belong here .
28006	The acquisition of a skeleton of calcium phosphate marked the point at which the fossil record began to contribute to the history of the group which , from our selfish viewpoint , we are conditioned to think of lying at the pinnacle of all evolutionary trees .
28007	Curiously enough the use of phosphatic material to build hard parts is generally primitive — calcium phosphate shells are nowhere more numerous than in the earliest Cambrian .
28008	All chordates have a nerve chord running along the back , and all higher chordates were derived from forms with gill slits .
28009	We are mostly concerned with the history of the vertebrates .
28010	Once the vertebrates were established they quickly acquired hard parts displaying great complexity when compared with most invertebrate phyla ( we should except the arthropods , perhaps ) .
28011	So it is possible to deduce more about the course of evolution from the study of vertebrate skeletal remains than is possible with most invertebrate groups , but even now , many mysteries remain .
28012	As a generality , the fossil record of the vertebrates is not as complete as that of many of the invertebrate groups , and particularly those with a continuous fossil record like the ammonoids .
28013	Vertebrate remains are decidedly patchy , particularly the terrestrial species .
28014	This is not altogether surprising considering the factors militating against their preservation — break-up of skeletons after death , the necessity to have a skeleton incorporated with sediment , and the activities of predatory and scavenging animals to destroy remains .
28015	So land vertebrates in particular tend to come from relatively few sites , which become exhaustively collected compared with most invertebrate localities .
28016	Some of the sites are enormously rich , however , and the history of palaeontology is punctuated by quite unscientific feuds between experts trying to find and hold on to the best sites for the most spectacular vertebrates .
28017	The more impressive the animal the greater the feud ; the fights between Professors Cope and Marsh in the last century over the dinosaur remains of North America include examples of double dealing that would not shame an oil tycoon .
28018	Even fish remains are rather local , and do not adequately reflect the abundance of a group that has occupied the seas for more than 400 million years .
28019	There is room here to give only the briefest account of the different kinds of vertebrates .
28020	The higher vertebrates , fossil mammals and dinosaurs in particular , have been described in so many books that they sometimes seem to have as much flesh and blood as any animal in the zoo .
28021	The dinosaurs alone have commanded as much popular attention as the rest of the fossil animal kingdom combined .
28022	This reflects their spectacular size and the drama of reconstructions of battles to the death between Tyrannosaurus and its armoured contemporaries .
28023	The sad truth is that the average collector is unlikely to recover more than the most fragmentary remains of dinosaurs .
28024	The commonest vertebrate remains are of teeth or other resistant pieces .
28025	Fortunately the teeth of higher vertebrates can tell us a good deal .
28026	JAWLESS FISH ( Colour plate 47 )
28027	The oldest fossil fish , which are the earliest known vertebrates , lack jaws — the mouth is a simple opening — and are covered on the outside with bony skeleton .
28028	The first ones seem to have lived in the sea , but by the Silurian the jawless ( Agnathan ) fish were a prominent component of fresh- and brackish-water sites in many areas of the world , and continued to diversify into the Devonian period .
28029	Some of these freshwater fish are heavily armoured and make robust fossils — particularly the headshields .
28030	The insides of the shield have been known to preserve quite tiny details of the nervous system , for example .
28031	It is probable that the jawless fish lived by grubbing in the sediment , or perhaps by filter feeding , possibly exploiting organic material derived from the plants that were taking to life on land at the same time .
28032	A few living jawless fish are the only remnant of this ancient group , and they are highly specialized forms .
28033	The hagfish feeds on dying fish using its rasp-like tongue in conjunction with a solitary tooth on the roof of its mouth .
28034	The lampreys ( Petromyzon ) are rather nasty external parasites of other fish , to which they attach themselves with a sucker , and proceed to rasp away at the living flesh .
28035	The specialized habits of both these ‘ pseudo-fishes ’ may have contributed to their survival , when none of their bony-plated relatives survived the Palaeozoic .
28036	Modern specialists often divide the jawless fishes into two broad groups , one containing the hagfish and the other the lamprey , with the fossil jawless forms distributed between the two .
28037	Jawless fish are particularly common in red rocks of the Silurian and Devonian periods , which was a time when non-marine rocks were widespread , and have survived subsequent erosion .
28038	They accompany the eurypterid arthropods ( which may have preyed upon them ) , and we can visualize the rivers and lakes of the time thronging with the first invaders from the sea .
28039	The subsequent development of the jaw enabled the vertebrates to exploit a wider range of lifestyles than were available to the jawless fish , and it would not be too gross a generalization to say that much of the evolution of the vertebrates was intimately related to things that happened to jaws .
28040	SHARKS AND ALLIES
28041	The sharks and their relatives ( known by the indigestible class name Elasmobranchiomorphi ) are the most successful of long survivors among the vertebrates .
28042	Their rapacious habits have been the subject of bloody hyperbole in films and bestsellers , so everybody knows that the shark has ranks of fearsome , pointed teeth , an elegant , incessant swishing swimming motion , a tail with a long ‘ point ’ uppermost , and a big appetite .
28043	Their skeleton is made of cartilage — bone has not ‘ grown into ’ the cartilage , as in the higher vertebrates .
28044	Their true jaws are of obvious advantage for grasping prey .
28045	Cartilage does not preserve as fossil as a rule , so most of the evidence of the shark-like fish rests upon teeth .
28046	Sharks of essentially modern type go back to the Jurassic .
28047	In the later Palaeozoic a number of shark-like fish include some related to living forms , others whose zoological position is still a puzzle .
28048	The Devonian placoderms are an especially exciting group of fish ( see p. 4 ) with powerful , armour-plated heads and frequently fang-like teeth , the function of which is obviously predatory .
28049	The lower jaw of these fish is loosely slung to the brain case so that they had a very wide ‘ gape ’ .
28050	The trunk was also protected with a shield .
28051	This group may include the distant ancestors of the sharks , but they must have been somewhat ponderous animals compared with the streamlined hunters of modern seas .
28052	Most of them were dogfish-sized , but Dunkleosteus was twice the length of a man , and was surely the most formidable predator of its day .
28053	Sharks of modern type replace their worn teeth with new ones by a sort of conveyor belt system .
28054	Isolated , bladed shark 's teeth are really rather frequent finds in Mesozoic and Tertiary rocks , often in the absence of any other fish remains .
28055	They have a handsome shiny lustre which makes them conspicuous from a distance .
28056	The rays are related to sharks , and are in essence sharks that have been ‘ squashed ’ flat in response to life as rather sluggish bottom dwellers .
28057	The mollusc-crushing teeth of rays , with the same lustre as shark 's teeth , but formed as low , ridged cushions , can also be found in Mesozoic and younger rocks .
28058	The early jawed fish , Cheiracanthus murchisoni , from the Devonian .
28059	The fish is preserved in a siltstone nodule , which has partially formed around the body of the fish .
28060	The body is of normal ‘ fishy ’ outline covered with minute rhomboidal scales Note prominent spines which supported paired fins .
28061	The species is named after Sir Roderick Murchison , a great pioneer of the study of Palaeozic rocks .
28062	Acanthodian fishes generally resembling this one are known from quite complete specimens from Devonian to Permian rocks .
28063	Some achieved a considerable size In the Devonian rocks , fishes of this kind are known from ( mostly ) freshwater deposits in Scotland , Wales , Norway and arctic Canada .
28064	This specimen is from Banffshire , Scotland .
28065	It is 15 cm long .
28066	BONY FISH — OSTEICHTHYES ( Colour plates 46 , 48 , 49 )
28067	Every experience with an unfilleted kipper demonstrates the aptness of the general name of this group .
28068	The vast majority of living fish belong here ( 18,000 species or so ) , which rival the insects in their multitude of adaptations and variety of external form .
28069	They can live in hot springs , or can be dredged from the deepest abyssal depths of the ocean ; the latter are grotesque gargoyles that seem to belong in the paintings of Heironymus Bosch .
28070	Some are rapid swimmers gathered together in silvery shoals , others sluggish bottom dwellers spending most of their time buried in sediment .
28071	Most have a characteristic arrangement of paired fins , but these can be lost , or fantastically modified to form fans or poisonous barbs .
28072	Most species are a few centimetres to a few tens of centimetres long .
28073	Their rapidity of evolution is well known : dozens of species have evolved in African fresh water lakes within the last million years .
28074	They have as wide a range of life habits as any group , from scavengers , grazers , filter feeders , vegetarians , omnivores , to fierce predators with reputations to rival that of the sharks .
28075	A coating of scales is characteristic , and the gills are covered by a movable flap ( the operculum ) .
28076	It would be difficult to overestimate the importance of the bony fish in the economy of the sea .
28077	Fish of various sizes feed on the plankton ( and on each other ) , and themselves are food for larger predators , such as seals and many whales , and man .
28078	Many of them have bizarre adaptations , as parasites , or as permanent ‘ guests ’ within particular species of coral or sponge , which it would be impossible to infer from fossil remains .
28079	Many have good sight , but there are a few forms which have lost their eyes , some of them living in the lightless world of caves .
28080	Considering their abundance in the oceans and rivers today , bony fish fossils are rather rare , and poorly reflect their true importance .
28081	Where they occur , however , they are found in large numbers , and in variety .
28082	Presumably these sites were protected from the kinds of influence that normally destroy fish remains , such as the activity of scavenging animals that disarticulate the skeletons , or currents .
28083	The classic fish sites produce fossils of quite outstanding beauty ( see Plate 49 ) and ones which have considerable monetary value .
28084	The fish of the Eocene and later are clearly related to today 's fauna , and some relatives of the living groups can be found in Mesozoic rocks .
28085	The classification of bony fish is extremely complicated , particularly fitting in the fossil forms , and there are many bones of contention ( literally ! ) .
28086	The group as a whole goes back to the Devonian ( ?
28087	Silurian ) period , and from rocks of this age predatory fish ( Palaeoniscus and allies ) have been recovered .
28088	Some living survivors of these early forms include the sturgeons and bichirs ( the former have reverted to a cartilage skeleton ) .
28089	The early fossil bony fish have tails with the long blade uppermost , whereas the more advanced living bony fish have a tail that is symmetrical , and more effective in producing a horizontal thrust .
28090	The surface of their body was covered with an interlocking series of shiny scales ( ‘ ganoid ’ ) which are still found in the bichir .
28091	One important division of bony fishes includes the lungfish and the ‘ lobe-finned ’ fishes ( including the coelacanth , the most famous of living fossils ) .
28092	This group of fish was also fully fledged in the Devonian , and this is of particular significance because the origin of all land vertebrates has been considered as lying within a species of this group .
28093	The freshwater lungfish retain their lungs , which help them to survive periods of drying in the rivers in which they live .
28094	Many fish specialists believe that in the Devonian all the bony fishes had lungs ( and that the swim bladder of the recent forms was a modification of the early breathing apparatus ) .
28095	It is not an easy business to identify the actual ancestor of the land-going organisms , and perhaps it has not yet been found .
28096	For many years there have been proponents of the theory that one of the ‘ lobe-finned ’ fishes included the ancestor of the tetrapods , and it is not difficult to imagine their stumpy fins , with a fleshy core , making the uneasy transition into a walking leg .
28097	Other features do not agree with this , and recently there has been a swing to favour the lungfishes as nearer the origin of amphibians and , ultimately , ourselves .
28098	Whatever momentous steps they took in the Devonian , the lungfish and lobe fins have been very conservative since , for the living lungfish are clearly similar to their Palaeozoic relatives and coelacanth lobe fins like the living genus ( Latimeria ) are known from Cretaceous rocks .
28099	Armoured placoderm fish of the Devonian
28100	AMPHIBIANS — CLASS AMPHIBIA ( Colour plate 51 )
28101	Frogs , newts , and salamanders are living amphibians .
28102	The frogs in particular are one of the most diverse of the higher vertebrate groups and peculiarly endearing animals with their lugubrious expressions and vocabulary of squeaks and belches .
28103	Yet the amphibia as a whole represent an early level of terrestrial organization ; they are tied to water for reproduction , because their larvae have to pass through a wholly subaqueous phase , and desiccation of the adult is a constant danger .
28104	The amphibians had their origins in one of the freshwater lung-carrying fishes in the Devonian .
28105	We have to visualize the process of change as a gradual one , with progressive forays from the water , until the first animal with true limbs developed ( the bony elements of the limb are present in the fish fin ) .
28106	From the Devonian of Greenland and other localities comes a true four-legged animal ( tetrapod ) that is not far from the ‘ fish with legs ’ we might have visualized ( which is commemorated in its name — Ichthyostega ) .
28107	But as always it is not quite that simple .
28108	The transition from water to land required not only the perfection of a walking limb , but modifications to the hearing system , palate , eyes and so on , and Ichthyostega had already established most of these terrestrial modifications , so it is in no sense an ‘ ancestor ’ , although it has many ancestral features .
28109	Bony scales were inherited from its ancestors and no doubt this helped the animal against desiccation .
28110	The subsequent history of the amphibians includes a further development of terrestrial forms , but others remained wholly or partly aqueous .
28111	These flourished in the waterlogged swamps of the Carboniferous period .
28112	The earliest amphibians were certainly predators , and there was suitable prey both on land and in the water .
28113	Bony fish , Lycoptera middendorfi , Cretaceous This little fish is preserved in a soft , pale grey shale Like many shale specimens it is flattened , but the still-water conditions under which the rock was deposited have permitted complete preservation of a delicate skeleton .
28114	This fish has a rather expanded , frog-like head behind which there are prominent fins ; a slender body , which is flexible , supported by a host of tiny ribs , which are clearly visible .
28115	A number of related fossil species are known from cretaceous rocks This species is from Cretaceous fish beds in Turga , Nertchinsk , Siberia .
28116	Similar species occur in Mongolia and China .
28117	It is 6 cm long .
28118	The Carboniferous is popularly known as the ‘ Age of Amphibians ’ , and it is true that the amphibians reached a dominance in the vertebrate world at this time which they never again equalled .
28119	All of the walking species had the widely-splayed legs that gave them a slow and lumbering gait , but , in the absence of more streamlined animals , they prospered .
28120	The group informally known as labyrinthodonts ( from their characteristic labyrinth-ridged teeth ) included some impressive animals almost as long as a man : perhaps the alligators of the time .
28121	Most of the fossils recovered are of wholly or partly aquatic amphibians , the sort that were easily preserved in the coal swamps that were characteristic of the Carboniferous non-marine environment .
28122	Other environments , particularly later in the Permian period , which was one of general ‘ drying out ’ , probably included species that were more truly terrestrial in their habits .
28123	But even during the Carboniferous the first true reptiles had evolved , and this was the group that was to make itself wholly independent of the water .
28124	The living amphibians have turned the limitations of the aqueous connection to advantage .
28125	Frogs have their origins in the Triassic ( they are a relatively recent amphibian innovation , and highly specialized ) .
28126	Their tadpoles can exploit bodies of water not excessively populated with competitors , and some are adapted to very restricted niches .
28127	The adult frogs have a different diet ( worms , flies , etc. ) , and the species therefore get ‘ the best of both worlds ’ .
28128	Frogs throng in almost any site with high humidity and standing pools of water .
28129	The large amphibians of the Palaeozoic did not survive beyond the Permian , and so our inferences about their modes of life have to be made entirely from the bony fossils that survive .
28130	Palaeontologists recognize fossil Palaeozoic amphibians from their teeth , their flattened skulls and the arrangements of bones on the skulls .
28131	They are not generally common fossils , but there is always a chance of turning up a skeleton from the coal deposits , or finding a fossil frog ( see Fig. 51 ) in the Mesozoic .
28132	REPTILES — CLASS REPTILIA
28133	The living reptiles are almost all predators , and the vast majority are also small , the only giants remaining being the crocodiles , alligators and caymans ( and one or two big lizards ) .
28134	We tend to think of the reptiles as somehow past their ‘ prime ’ , but it would be more accurate to say that they had been displaced from the top jobs in nature , while more than holding their own in the shop floor .
28135	The warmer the climate the more they are in evidence , because the living reptiles are ‘ cold blooded ’ ( without their own internal heat regulator ) and they can not successfully live in very cold climates .
28136	Living snakes and lizards are highly varied , and manage to live in some environments ( e.g. dry deserts ) where the mammals are pushed to survive .
28137	Most living reptiles and all of the primitive ones lay eggs , and this amniote egg , from which perfectly-formed baby reptiles hatch , marks the complete emancipation from the necessity of returning to water for reproduction .
28138	And a scaly skin solves the problem of drying out even in intense heat .
28139	Add to this the change in orientation of the legs in many reptiles , which can be used in an efficient running action , unlike the ungainly waddling of the amphibians and it will be apparent why the reptiles were better adapted to terrestrial life than the amphibians , and why they largely displaced them .
28140	This was far from instantaneous , and the Permian period saw both advanced amphibians and early reptiles living side by side .
28141	The reptiles were probably derived from an amphibious ancestor , probably early in the Carboniferous .
28142	Once established they underwent a number of evolutionary ‘ bursts ’ in which diverse kinds of reptiles occupied a variety of habitats , the most spectacular of which was the dinosaur radiation in the Mesozoic , to which we shall return later .
28143	by no means all of the large reptiles that are found in the Mesozoic rocks are dinosaurs — the reptile groups that took up life in the sea or the air were only distantly related .
28144	One of the most important steps for the complete colonization of the land was the evolution of herbivorous ( plant-eating ) reptiles , tapping a prolific and nourishing source of food that opened up a new dimension to the ‘ food chain' .
28145	Larger and better herbivores meant larger and more ferocious carnivores to prey upon them , scavengers to clean up the mess , and a whole host of subordinate trades for other animals .
28146	The reptiles underwent tremendous changes in their skeletal structure , their jaws and their teeth during over their history of more than two hundred million years , some of the predators developing razor sharp rows of fangs , other herbivores losing their teeth and acquiring beak-like jaws .
28147	At some time in the Permo-Triassic one group of reptiles ( ‘ mammal-like reptiles ’ ) actually gave rise to the warm-blooded mammals , which were to lead a rather subordinate existence during the heyday of the dinosaurs .
28148	And the birds probably had their origin in a particular group of dinosaurs .
28149	So in a sense the reptile dominance is still with us , transmuted by time and evolution .
28150	The scenes of Jurassic or Cretaceous landscapes in picture books show dinosaurs swarming over the landscape , giving the impression that we know the whole story .
28151	The truth is that there are a few sites ( especially in North America ) where abundant remains of complete animals have been recovered , and from which a passable idea of the fauna of the Mesozoic can be obtained , but there are still great gaps in our knowledge , and many of the dinosaurs are known from a handful of individuals , or even a single specimen .
28152	There are doubtless still new kinds to discover

28225	Living Iridomyrmex are found principally in Australia and South America , with a few species in India .

28230	This specimen is from the Achanarras fish bed , Caithness , Scotland , a famous locality .

28236	48 Eocene bony fish , Pristigenys substriatus , Monte Bolca , Verona , Italy .
28237	This exquisite fish is preserved flattened on the bedding plane of a flaggy limestone .
28238	The original outline of the fish is clearly visible .
