28240	From tail to mouth the fish measures 10 cm .
28241	These other groups of reptiles lived alongside the more spectacular dinosaurs during the Mesozoic : turtles , lizards and crocodiles
28242	The dinosaurs have dominated the popular conception of the fossil reptiles , sometimes to the extent of seeming almost synonymous with the word ‘ fossil ’ !
28243	The group includes by far the largest of terrestrial animals ever to have lived ( Brachiosaurus ) , creatures to dwarf the largest bull elephants .
28244	The predators that preyed on the giants were even more spectacular , and by now the name of Tyrannosaurus is so well-known that it seems to be one of the first tongue-twisters mastered by small children .
28245	Of course there is little chance of an amateur collector acquiring an appreciable part of one of these great animals , but in the right site fragments of dinosaur skeletons may be picked up .
28246	The term ‘ dinosaur ’ includes a number of really rather separate groups of animals , with more or less independent evolutionary history during the Jurassic and Cretaceous .
28247	The real giants were the lumbering sauropods ( Diplodocus , Brachiosaurus , etc. ) , four-legged dinosaurs , with enormously long necks only matched by equally long tails .
28248	The giant predators that walked on their hind legs ( Tyrannosaurus , Allosaurus and other theropods ) share structures of the hip bones with the sauropods that show they are more closely related to them than to the rest of the dinosaurs .
28249	These latter ( Ornithischians ) include some animals that walked on their hind legs like Tyrannosaurus , but with vegetarian habits ( Iguanodon , the first dinosaur to be discovered ) ; the group also includes various types of vegetarian armoured and plated dinosaurs , often shown in pitched battle with their carnivorous contemporaries .
28250	These well-protected dinosaurs each diversified into a number of genera ; the three main groups are : the stegosaurs of the Jurassic , with paired plates along the back and a nastily spiked tail ( Stegosaurus ) ; the ceratopsians , horned , rhinoceros-like dinosaurs of the Cretaceous , including the familiar Triceratops ; the spiky armoured ankylosaurs , tanks on stumpy legs .
28251	Specialized ornithischians in the late Cretaceous were the remarkable duck-billed dinosaurs , animals that lost their front teeth and had arrays of tiny grinding teeth at the back of the jaw that were continually replaced , like those of the shark , and must have been able to cope with tough vegetation .
28252	Some of the duck-billed forms evolved crests and protuberances on top of their heads .
28253	All the dinosaurs , vegetarian and carnivore alike , became extinct at the end of the Cretaceous period ( see p. 135 ) .
28254	A whole range of other reptiles were present in the Jurassic and Cretaceous ; none of them are dinosaurs .
28255	They include the products of the spread of the reptiles back into the aqueous environment from which their distant ancestors emerged , and , for the first time in the history of the vertebrates , the conquest of the air .
28256	The marine plesiosaurs , with their long flexible necks and sharp teeth , were formidable hunters of Mesozoic fish .
28257	The limbs were modified into efficient paddles , perfectly adapted for sculling through the water .
28258	Even more streamlined for marine life were the ichthyosaurs ( 'fish lizards ' ) , which , as their name implies , include species that look remarkably fish-like , although perhaps the better analogy would be with the porpoises , a group of mammals that ‘ returned to the sea ’ , and may fill a similar role in modern seas to that of the ichthyosaurs in the Jurassic .
28259	These marine reptiles have a higher chance of preservation than many of the terrestrial species , and their carcasses often seem to have sunk to the sea floor , so that some localities have yielded numerous complete specimens .
28260	The Liassic ( Lower Jurassic ) rocks of Europe furnished many of the magnificent specimens which are now on display in museums .
28261	Some of the ichthyosaurs include baby individuals within their skeletons which either implies cannabalistic habits , or , more probably , the ability to give birth to their young alive .
28262	Isolated vertebrae of marine reptiles ( see Fig.50 ) are one of the reptilian fossils that are the easiest to collect .
28263	The pterosaurs , flying reptiles , also had their origins in the Triassic and became widespread and varied during the Jurassic and Cretaceous .
28264	Like the bats , the pterosaurs had membranous wings stretched between highly modified arms and ‘ hands ’ and the fore part of the legs ; unlike the bats some of them grew to an enormous size and the front support for the wing was provided by only one finger of the hand , grotesquely extended .
28265	Most of them , and particularly the larger ones , combined slow , flapping flight with gliding , spending a large part of their lives effortlessly aloft .
28266	As in the case of the sauropod dinosaurs they seem to have got bigger and bigger during the Cretaceous — some of these later pterosaurs are supposed to have had wing spans exceeding lo metres , which would make them almost comparable to a man-made glider .
28267	Why this large size evolved is something of a mystery : it may have been that larger gliders cruise at slower speeds without ‘ stalling ’ .
28268	Quite how these amazing animals landed and took off ( if they did ) can only be guessed at .
28269	Like the plesiosaurs and ichthyosaurs , they were successful and varied for a long time , but all three groups failed to survive the Cretaceous .
28270	Examples of the two major kinds of dinosaurs , showing the structure of the hip bones which distinguishes them .
28271	Above saurischian ( Tyrannosaurus ) , below , ornithischian ( Scelidosaurus )
28272	Other groups of reptiles were not exterminated at this time , even though their fossils may be found in rocks as old as those that yield dinosaurs and the other spectacular , extinct groups .
28273	Crocodiles and lizards have a fossil record extending back to the Triassic , snakes to the Cretaceous .
28274	The turtles and tortoises have almost as long a history as the crocodiles .
28275	The fused , bony plates that protect their soft parts make them well-nigh invulnerable .
28276	All the long survivors show every sign of flourishing today : one might suppose that the tortoise will continue its lumbering progress no matter what catastrophes may come to pass in the future .
28277	MAMMALS — CLASS MAMMALIA
28278	Mammals animals with mammary glands that suckle their young — were certainly present during the Triassic , and were a continuous if subordinate component of fossil faunas throughout the acme of the dinosaurs .
28279	It was only after the demise of the ruling reptiles that the class had the opportunity to capitalize on the evolutionary advantages which propelled them to the dominance they have enjoyed ever since .
28280	Many of the early mammals were probably insect eaters , as are many of the primitive representatives of the group today .
28281	Small mammals were present in the Triassic — shrew-like animals with long noses , and probably insatiable appetites for smaller items of the fauna .
28282	We can imagine animals like these darting through the undergrowth in search of food while the colossal reptiles lumbered obliviously around them .
28283	It would be wrong to suppose that there was no evolutionary activity among these early mammals : in fact there were considerable changes , which by the late Cretaceous had established early members of several of the principal groups of mammals which dominate the terrestrial world today .
28284	The marsupial ( pouched ) and placental ( womb-bearing ) mammals had separated , and lived side by side .
28285	Many of the early mammalian remains are fossil teeth .
28286	More than those of any other vertebrate group , the teeth of mammals have changed in distinctive ways , and the different types of mammals can be reliably identified from a study of their dentition alone .
28287	This is particularly fortunate , because teeth have a high fossilization potential , exceeding that of other parts of the skeleton .
28288	The sediments filling caves or fissures in limestone are frequently repositories for fossil teeth .
28289	Sampling for mammal fossils often involves the patient sieving of great quantities of sediment to extract the fossil teeth .
28290	If you are very lucky you might find a whole jaw ( see p. 100 ) .
28291	Mammal jaws often have specialized teeth for particular jobs — nipping , chewing , biting , gnawing teeth and so on — which function in perfect cooperation between the upper and lower jaws .
28292	Mammal teeth often have distinctive patterns of crests or bumps ( cusps ) that serve to identify large groups within the mammals .
28293	Teeth for grinding vegetation are often large and ridged , while the rodents have their fast-growing gnawing teeth at the front of the jaw .
28294	The most specialized dental structures of all are probably the baleen plates of the largest whales , modified for straining plankton from sea water .
28295	The evolution of mammals after the Cretaceous was both extremely rapid and very complex , and we can do no more than give the roughest sketch here .
28296	Compared with what was happening in contemporary marine invertebrates , the visible changes in mammalian skeletons during the early part of the Tertiary were fast and dramatic ; it did not take long before the roles of larger herbivores and carnivores were filled by mammalian animals .
28297	By the end of the Palaeocene , only a few million years from the Cretaceous extinction of the giant reptiles , there were representatives of many of the living mammalian orders , including , for example , the primates ( the order to which man belongs ) , the carnivores ( cats dogs , and most living predators ) and the rodents ( rats , mice ) .
28298	The history of the mammals in the Tertiary involved not only this one major diversification , but several , with major extinctions between , so that the largest mammals of the earlier parts of the Tertiary are not related to the large mammals of the Recent .
28299	The roots of our present European fauna extend back to the Miocene .
28300	The whole story is complicated by the fact that this was also the time of break-up of the supercontinent Pangaea .
28301	Mammalian faunas on isolated continental fragments could evolve , at least for a time , separately from faunas in other parts of the world , producing a whole series of peculiar animals that have no direct relationships to animals with a similar mode of life elsewhere .
28302	The obvious example is Australia , which was separated early , and in which the marsupial mammals had the opportunity to adapt to a whole range of ecological niches , which they managed with remarkable success in spite of a low cranial capacity and a primitive mode of reproduction .
28303	Some of the largest marsupials ( Diprotodon ) seem to have survived to a time tantalisingly close to the present .
28304	Similarly , in South America a whole range of peculiar mammals evolved largely in isolation , including giant sloths , specialized grazing species , and the extraordinary glyptodonts ( see p. 100 ) .
28305	A lot of argument among mammalian palaeontologists seems to centre on how and when links between North America , Europe and Asia existed , resulting in interchange and invasions of animals between the two regions .
28306	It is clear that some groups of animals , like the proboscideans ( elephants and allies ) , are much reduced now compared with the late Tertiary , both in variety and geographic distribution .
28307	A late stimulus for the evolution of distinctive mammals was the Pleistocene Ice Age , although a variety also became extinct at this time .
28308	A number of species , adapted to the widespread cold conditions , roamed widely around the northern hemisphere , including woolly mammoths and rhinoceros , and extinct species of tigers .
28309	On the other hand interglacial periods were very much warmer than conditions in temperate latitudes today , and these climatic fluctuations resulted in periods when hippopotamus and tropical rhinoceros thrived in the areas occupied by Europe 's capital cities today .
28310	With the final retreat of the ice many of the cold climate specialists perished ( possibly with the help of man ) , although some of the species that accompany them , like lemmings or musk ox , survive today in the harsh conditions of the arctic tundra .
28311	BIRDS — CLASS AVES
28312	Fossil birds are distinctly rare , and to find a well-preserved and complete example is a palaeontological event .
28313	The evolution of flight led to generally light and fragile skeletons , and it is perhaps not surprising that avian fossils are so uncommon , and when found , so often fragmentary .
28314	The derivation of the birds from a reptilian ( possibly dinosaur ) ancestor is certain , and because the earliest fossil bird , Archaeopteryx , is Jurassic in age , it is usually assumed that the split from the reptiles occurred in the earlier part of the period .
28315	Unfortunately , there is much that is not understood about the history of the birds between Archaeopteryx ( see p. 101 ) and the good assemblages of fossil birds undoubtedly related to living species in the Eocene and Miocene .
28316	Cretaceous birds are generally scarce , and some of the ‘ toothed ’ birds that are known , like the flightless , aquatic Hesperornis , seem to be difficult to relate to any of the living species .
28317	It is probable that like the mammals the roots of the great variety of living birds are to be found in the Cretaceous , but fossils , which could document this , are only now slowly coming to light .
28318	Right The Berlin skeleton of the early bird , Archaeopteryx
28319	Left Some of the specialized mammals which evolved in isolation in South America : top Glyptodon ; middle , Toxodon ; bottom , Megatherium
28320	Below Lower jaw of Pleistocene bear showing typical mammalian specialization of teeth : sharp canines , chewing teeth at the rear
28321	FOSSIL PLANTS
28322	The fossils of plants are some of the most attractive that the amateur collector is likely to find .
28323	Those plants that concern us here were terrestrial or lived in bogs , rivers or lakes .
28324	Like animals that dwelt on land , the terrestrial flora also arose from ancestors that lived in the seas , a change that is known to have happened before the end of the Silurian .
28325	However , marine algae were very important in the early history of the evolution of the earth , and they are described in some detail in Chapters 7 and 8 .
28326	They are not generally conspicuous fossils in the field .
28327	A few algae , however , produced hard calcareous skeletons , and were abundant enough to produce small gardens beneath the sea .
28328	Such calcareous algae ( see Plate 52 ) have a long history , extending back into the Precambrian , and they are still numerous today .
28329	They were often components of reefs , and in some environments it is the algae that bear the full brunt of the attack by the breakers on the exposed , seaward side of the reef .
28330	They are also important rock builders ; in northerly latitudes today limestones are being formed from the skeletal debris of such calcareous algae as Lithothamnion .
28331	The first land plants must have been derived from a marine alga .
28332	We have to visualize this as a very gradual process , the early transitional plants perhaps creeping across mud flats , or partially submerged .
28333	The change involved the production of a protective ‘ skin ’ to ensure that water loss to the atmosphere was not excessive , and the stems had to acquire sufficient rigidity to stand up without the support of surrounding water , but also the cellular structure had to allow the passage of nutrients to the growing shoots ( ultimately , a vascular system ) .
28334	The evolution of such a plant could not have been achieved at a single stroke .
28335	Reproduction in these early plants was by means of minute spores .
28336	Quite a variety of Silurian plants are now known , and by the end of the Devonian it is apparent that most of the problems of terrestrial living had been solved , to the extent that large tree ‘ ferns ’ of the time would have had dimensions comparable with forest trees today .
28337	The fossil record of plants is not good enough simply to ‘ read out ’ the story of their evolution by collecting from successively younger , non-marine rock formations .
28338	Some of the earliest plants do not appear to be the most primitive , and vice versa .
28339	True , there is a general drift through time towards more complex plants , more perfectly adapted to life away from water , but primitive species have persisted alongside the innovations .
28340	The fossil record is full of curious plants that do not fit comfortably into classifications — this is one of the things that makes the study of fossil plants so fascinating .
28341	Consequently there are arguments among botanists about the relationships of many plants , living and fossil , and some classifications have quite large categories containing only a few plants , which may be rare .
28342	Not all of the major groups will be described here , but only those that are likely to be found by the non-specialist collector .
28343	Some important groups , like the mosses and liverworts , have a sporadic fossil record extending back to the Carboniferous , but they are not likely to be encountered without a special search .
28344	Plant fossils are often to be found in particular beds , reflecting conditions of deposition that were just right for their preservation .
28345	Of course , the rocks that contain abundant plant remains are mostly those which were deposited in freshwater lakes , or on deltas , or the fossilized remains of peat beds .
28346	There were probably plants living in hilly regions from quite early which have left little fossil record , and this may account for some of the gaps in the preserved fossils .
28347	Many fossil plants are now more or less black , carbonized ( ‘ coalified ’ ) compressions .
28348	In some cases , however , the fine structure , even down to individual cells , is splendidly preserved , and these are the most important specimens from a scientific point of view .
28349	The problems of associating the different organs of the same fossil plant species were mentioned earlier in this book ( p. 23 ) . .
28350	Right Seed fern , Trigonocarpus parkinsoni , Carboniferous .
28351	These fossil seeds are preserved in a relatively coarse-grained sandstone .
28352	Although they are uncrushed , only parts of the original seed covering remain — so that they are largely internal moulds .
28353	They are the seeds produced by the fern-like plants such as Mariopteris , but because they are difficult to link with their foliage they have been given separate names .
28354	The three raised ridges on their surface are typical .
28355	Seeds of similar type have been found associated with a number of the Carboniferous seed-fern leaves .
28356	They are from Ayrshire , Scotland ; length , 2 cm
28357	EARLY LAND PLANTS — DIVISION PSILOPHYTA
28358	The earliest land plants , to be found in Silurian and Devonian rocks , had simple shoots that arose from a creeping ‘ axis ’ , which were little different in structure from the shoots themselves .
28359	Leaves , if they were present at all , were humble scales or spine-like projections .
28360	The upright twigs often branched in a simple way , forking into two , and then into two again , and sometimes terminating in little capsules that carried the spores .
28361	The plants are often preserved as dark markings on shales , and were less than half a metre in length .
28362	The best-preserved examples , from which their cellular construction has been described , are from the Devonian Rhynie Chert ( p. 17 ) .
28363	FERNS — DIVISION PTEROPHYTA ( Colour plate 60 )
28364	Right Some of the commoner types of fern-like foliage from the Carboniferous Such foliage often belongs to the seed ferns , rather than the true ferns
28365	The feathery and delicate fronds of the ferns make them among the most beautiful of the foliage plants , and they attract a fanatical group of devotees dedicated to growing exotic species in inhospitable cities .
28366	They are also a very ancient group , with many Carboniferous representatives and a number of preferns in the Devonian as well ( plate 59 ) .
28367	Then as now they are generally preferred humid environments in which to live .
28368	They reproduce by means of minute spores , which form in clusters on the undersides of the fronds , or sometimes on specially modified fronds .
28369	To be really sure that one is dealing with a fossil fern it should be possible to see the spore cases , because other kinds of plants can produce fern-like foliage .
28370	In practice , many of the fossil fronds that one finds are sterile , and for these there a number of form genera , units of classification based on the shape of the fronds alone ( see p. 23 ) .
28371	Although many ferns are low herbaceous plants , they have periodically attained the dimensions of trees ; forests of such tree ferns exist today in humid regions , for example in New Zealand .
28372	Large ferns were present as early as the Upper Devonian and different genera as large or larger were significant components of forests during the Carboniferous to Cenozoic .
28373	In these cases one never finds a whole tree fossilized , and it is necessary to piece together the whole plant by making intelligent guesses about whether a frond of one kind is persistently found with a particular fossil trunk .
28374	SEED FERNS — DIVISION PTERIDOSPERMOPHYTA ( Colour plate 57 )
28375	Many of the fern-like fronds that can be found in Carboniferous rocks belong to an extinct group of plants sharing a common ancestor with the ferns , but distinct enough to be regarded as entirely separate .
28376	These seed ferns had much-enlarged female reproductive bodies — forming true seeds which were fertilized by pollen born on separate organs .
28377	Some of the seeds hung like bells from the ends of the ferny frond , and in some species they were several centimetres long .
28378	The plants were generally bushy shrubs , but some may have been climbers , and others robust enough to form small trees .
28379	A lot of the species belonging to the commonest of the Carboniferous and Permian ‘ leaf genera ’ — like Neuropteris , Alethopteris and Mariopteris were seed ferns of this kind ( rather than true ferns ) , but associations of seeds with foliage are extremely rare .
28380	The seeds themselves ( see p. 103 ) can be locally common .
28381	Although they are commonest in rocks of the Late Palaeozoic , some Mesozoic plants have been regarded as a later branch of the seed ferns .
28382	Fossil fern , Onychiopsis mantelli , Cretaceous .
28383	This delicate fern is preserved in a very fine-grained sandstone , which fractures rather irregularly .
28384	Slender and delicate branching patterns with many fine subdivisions are characteristic of this kind of fern .
28385	There are a few similar species , known rarely from rocks of Cretaceous and Tertiary age , distinguished on the branching patterns of the fronds .
28386	This specimen is from Sussex , England .
28387	Related forms occur in North America .
28388	The total length of the frond is 12 cm , but it was originally part of a much larger plant
28389	LYCOPODS — DIVISION LYCOPHYTA ( Colour plates 53 , 54 , 56 )
28390	Many of the great trees of the Carboniferous were lycopods , the trunks of which contributed largely to the formation of coal .
28391	This large and important group of plants is represented today by a mere four genera of humble herbaceous plants — Lycopodium , Selaginella , Isoetes and Phylloglossum — living fossils which have survived with little change from the Mesozoic or even the Carboniferous .
28392	The lycopods have long , narrow leaves like little straps , each of which leaves a characteristic scar on the stem at its point of attachment .
28393	The plants reproduced by means of spores , which were born in cones ; the spores were often of two kinds — large ( female ) megaspores up to 2 mm in diameter and much smaller ( male ) microspores .
28394	The study of the spores of these plants is important in correlating rocks of late Palaeozoic age .
28395	The large trees had extensive roots , which grew nearly horizontally through the soil , repeatedly forking , and often bearing long rootlets .
28396	Fossil roots ( Fig. 5 6 ) are quite common , and may be preserved even when the trunks are not .
28397	The distinctive patterns formed by leaf scars are visible on fossils of the bark , which is often found in coal and in the deposits overlying ones containing roots .
28398	Lepidodendron has many spiral rows of lozenge-shaped leaf scars , while Sigillaria has long rows of elliptical scars ; both are very common fossils in association with coal measures .
28399	Cones are much rarer ; these are about the size and shape of an asparagus spear , with rows of cavities , which contained spores , so that if they are flattened they can appear almost segmented in the manner of an arthropod fossil .
28400	Some of the best specimens of trunks were preserved cell by cell in silica , and these show even the finest details if they are cut and polished .
28401	The lycopods can be found in Devonian or even Silurian rocks , but they are generally uncommon in rocks younger than Permian , and all the tree species apparently disappeared before the end of the Palaeozoic .
28402	HORSETAILS — DIVISION ARTHROPHYTA ( Colour plate 58 )
28403	On any walk through a bog or fen one can see the delicate shoots of the horsetails , looking almost like miniature fir trees , sometimes clustering into dense masses .
28404	If one plucks a piece from one of these plants it will almost certainly break along one of the numerous joints that divide the whole plant into segments , right to the tips of the branchlets .
28405	These joints give the arthrophytes ( ‘ jointed plants ’ ) their scientific name , and the little whorls of tiny branches produce the bushy appearance which accounts for their popular one .
28406	There is only one living genus of horsetails — Equisetum — although its many species are very widespread .
28407	The group were formerly varied and numerous , and even included trees perhaps 20 metres in height .
28408	The horsetails reproduce by means of spores , which are born in small cone-like structures at the tip of the branches or on modified shoots .
28409	They are among the easiest of fossil plants to recognize , for even flattened stems retain the characteristic jointing , and the feathery distal branches can not be mistaken for anything else .
28410	The flattened whorls are particularly easy to recognize , and are frequently encountered in the soft , dark shales associated with coal seams .
28411	As with so many of the primitive plants the arthrophytes had their heyday in the Carboniferous after a probable origin in the Devonian .
28412	Because they are common in aquatic environments they have a rather good fossil record , and are not uncommon in freshwater sediments of Jurassic and Cretaceous age .
28413	It is a mystery why only one genus of this formerly diverse group should have had the capacity to survive to the present day .
28414	CYCAD-LIKE PLANTS
28415	In the forests of the Mesozoic there were large numbers of trees and shrubby plants that looked at first glance like palm trees , with leafless stems crowned with bouquets of stiff , large leaves , deeply divided into long , unbranched leaflets .
28416	These were cycads and bennettites .
28417	A small number of cycad genera survive in the tropical and subtropical regions today , but they are much less conspicuous today than they were 120 million years ago .
28418	The resemblance to palms is no indication of their true relationships , because the cycad-like plants were not true flowering plants like palms .
28419	They do , however , have a most extraordinary fructification , a large knob arising from the centre of the crown , looking something like a corncob , and bearing numerous , very large seeds .
28420	Nowadays botanists divide the cycad-like plants into two major groups which may not be particularly closely related : the Cycadales , which include the living species , and the Bennettitales , an important Mesozoic group of plants which have smaller fructifications scattered among the bases of the leaves .
28421	Marie Stopes , who later became a famous pioneer of birth control started life as a palaeobotanist interested in the cycads .
28422	Some specimens of the trunks of bennettites ( see p 107 ) are among the most spectacular of fossils , and they even attracted the attention of the Etruscans , who included them among their sacred relics more than four thousand years ago !
28423	The amateur collector is most likely to come across the cycad foliage , with its characteristic narrow central rib and flat leaflets .
28424	Their fossils are commonest in Triassic , Jurassic and Cretaceous rocks .
28425	Reconstruction of a Carboniferous coal swamp , showing large lycopod and cordaite trees , an amphibian , giant dragonfly and millipede
28426	CONIFERS — DIVISION CONIFEROPHYTA
28427	The conifers are as varied and successful a group of plants today as they have ever been .
28428	But again they are an ancient group with ancestors back in the Carboniferous forest , a melting pot for plant evolution .
28429	Botanists are not fully in accord about how many separate groups of plants there are within the conifers , and they are all lumped together here .
28430	The fir cones of modern species will be familiar to the reader , often littering forests in their thousands , and containing seeds , which may be equipped with wings .
28431	The close , needle foliage of most modern conifers , which seems as much immune to desert heat as arctic cold , was probably derived from lusher leaves in the later Palaeozoic .
28432	In the Carboniferous swamps large trees with leaves , of the genus Cordaites grew to 30 or more metres in height , with long slim trunks terminating in branches that bore strap-shaped leaves up to a metre in length .
28433	The cordaite ‘ cone ’ was a longer and more complex structure than that of any living conifer .
28434	The leaves of this tree are rather common fossils , striped with longitudinal veins that give it a superficial resemblance to the leaf of an iris .
28435	Most of the steps leading to the modern conifers seem to have taken place by the end of the Palaeozoic ; no other group of organisms of such antiquity has retained such an unbroken hold over vast areas of the earth as the conifers .
28436	Some primitive conifers , like the monkey-puzzle tree Araucaria , have survived with little change since the Triassic .
28437	Large trunk of a bennettite Cycadeoidea , Cretaceous , USA .
28438	These conspicuous fossils are often over half a metre across .
28439	Left Varied shapes of leaves of fossil ginkgos , typically Mesozoic , with photograph of fossil example , natural size ( below ) .
28440	Right Frond of a cycad , Nilssonia kendalli , Jurassic .
28441	The fossil is preserved on the surface of a fine-grained siltstone .
28442	There are many other fragments of plants in the same block , but the frond is unusually complete .
28443	Cycad leaves have characteristic flattened leaflets arranged in rows on a very slender axis .
28444	There are a number of species of Nilssonia from the Jurassic distinguished on the form of the leaflets .
28445	Related genera include many species with a wide distribution , and there are living representatives occurring in tropical regions today .
28446	This specimen is from the famous plant beds of Yorkshire , England .
28447	Other well-known bennettite localities are the Black Hills of Dakota and from Maryland , USA .
28448	The frond has a length of 15 cm .
28449	The long-leafed plant Glossopteris ( Plate 55 ) is something of a botanical puzzle , but probably belongs within this broad group .
28450	It is common in later Palaeozoic rocks of South Africa , peninsular India , Australia and South America , and is thought to have lived almost exclusively in the cooler areas of the supercontinent Pangaea ( p. 32 ) .
28451	The ginkgos are often placed in a separate group .
28452	They are represented today only by the maidenhair tree Ginkgo biloba , one of the obligatory ‘ living fossils ’ to be found in every botanical garden , and many parks in inner cities .
28453	Ginkgo leaves are particularly beautiful , perfect fans with splayed veins , and specimens of this general type are found in many localities from rocks of Triassic age onwards ( see p. 108 ) .
28454	The Mesozoic ginkgos were a varied and numerous group of plants , but unlike the spruces and pines they slowly declined in variety throughout the Tertiary .
28455	FLOWERING PLANTS — DIVISION ANTHOPHYTA ( Colour plates 61 64 )
28456	The flowering plants dominate the floral world today , except perhaps in the lonely spruce stands of the Arctic .
28457	They are the broad-leaved trees , the grasses , and myriads of tiny creeping plants , as well as the showy flowers which attract man and pollinating insects ( p. 91 ) alike .
28458	Their diversity is truly extraordinary : in tropical forests there are hundreds of species of trees alone .
28459	Yet a good deal of this diversification probably happened in the last 70 million years , during the Tertiary .
28460	However , like the mammals and the birds , the flowering plants certainly originated , and probably did much of their evolutionary groundwork , during the Mesozoic and especially the Cretaceous .
28461	The details of their origins are still not clear .
28462	For one thing , flowers do not readily fossilize — and leaves alone can be misleading .
28463	The flowering plants ( angiosperms ) appear almost ready-made in the Cretaceous , and many of these fossils can even be placed into living genera .
28464	There is still much to discover of their even earlier history , and we hope that the crucial steps did not all take place in some site where fossils have little chance of preservation .
28465	Whatever their early history , fossils of flowering plants — leaves , seeds and wood — are common in rocks of Tertiary age .
28466	They do not even have to be rocks deposited under fresh water conditions , because wood and seeds are perfectly capable of drifting long distances before becoming waterlogged enough to sink to the bottom of the sea .
28467	Leaves , however , tend to be preserved in the deposits laid down in lakes and the like .
28468	Where the sediments are fine-grained the leaves form fossils of exquisite beauty , preserving even the finest veins , which can be directly compared with the leaves of their living relatives .
28469	Another mode of preservation of Tertiary plants is beneath flows of lava ( Oregon and the island of Skye , for example ) where whole floras can be preserved in enough detail to reconstruct the detailed botanical ecology of the time .
28470	Fossil plants are of great use in plotting the many shifts of climate that happened during the Tertiary : a humid-tropical flora may be found in what is now an arid region , or a warm-climate flora may be found in an area that is now decidedly cool .
28471	This makes the assumption , of course , that the plants have not changed their habits since they were fossilized .
28472	During the dramatic climatic fluctuations of the last ice age — warm to cold to warm repeated several times — the flowering plants acted as thermometers for the climate , sensitive recorders of the shifts that affected everything from beetles to man .
28473	Oligocene sumac tree , Rhus stellariaefolia .
28474	These leaves are beautifully preserved in a flat-bedded and very highly fissile shale , laid down at the bottom of a fresh water lake .
28475	Long , graceful leaves are divided into about twelve spindle-shaped leaflets with undivided margins , and a terminal leaflet .
28476	Each leaflet carries a prominent vein in the middle .
28477	A few other fossil species of Rhus are known from the Tertiary rocks .
28478	Living sumacs are familiar in temperate regions , their leaves turning a beautiful dark red late in the year .
28479	The specimen shown here is from the renowned Florissant beds of Colorado , USA .
28480	Other fossil Rhus have been recovered from Eocene rocks in Colorado , Utah and California .
28481	The longest leaf here is 12 cm long .
28482	BRINGING FOSSILS BACK TO LIFE
28483	In this chapter some of the ways in which palaeontologists determine the way fossil animals lived are described , reanimating the dead fragments to build up a living creature .
28484	Since popular ideas of life in the past are often founded on vividly coloured reconstructions of ‘ The World in the Jurassic Period ’ and the like , it is important to remember that these imaginative scenes are all inferences from bones , and similar fragments .
28485	In fact there is nothing fixed about such interpretations , because the way the fossils are understood may change over the years , but it is usually some time before new discoveries percolate into the popular presentations .
28486	Even the most solid-looking dinosaurs may have changed their habits in the last few years !
28487	Many different lines of evidence may be used to flesh out the bare bones of the fossils .
28488	The first of these is the evidence of the rocks from which the remains were recovered .
28489	The sediments themselves reveal much about the environment of deposition , as was shown in Chapter 3 .
28490	It is important to establish whether the fossil animal actually lived in the environment which furnished its sedimentary cover , or whether its remains were swept in from some other place .
28491	Fortunately it is usually easy to spot such intruders .
28492	The type of sediment and the associated fossils will show whether the environment was marine , freshwater or terrestrial , providing the basic information into which the ecology of the animal has to be accommodated .
28493	The sediments themselves may have preserved some of the tracks left by the animal ( p. 20 ) to give direct evidence of its past activities .
28494	From the tracks alone it is possible to be certain of the bipedal stance of certain dinosaurs , and to measure their stride .
28495	The character of the rocks , and their setting in the past geography at the time when they accumulated , diagnoses the climatic setting in which the extinct fauna lived , and climate imposes certain restraints on possible modes of life .
28496	Savannah animals differ from those of tropical rain forests , and these again from inhabitants of the tundra at high latitudes .
28497	Looking at the fossil animal itself , the first necessity is to reconstruct it as accurately as possible from its fragmentary remains .
28498	Sometimes this is a very complex business , particularly for vertebrates with numbers of small bones .
28499	To proceed from the reconstruction to an assessment of probable life habits two different but complementary approaches are used .
28500	One method attempts to compare the structures of teeth or limbs or some other feature of the extinct animal with living analogues .
28501	These do not have to be biologically related organisms .
28502	The basic argument is that structures that are closely similar were probably adapted to a similar function .
28503	Sometimes these similarities are quite obvious : the ferocious teeth of a predatory dinosaur are a sure indication of hunting habits , with hardly a glance at the fangs of living mammalian carnivores .
28504	But the structure and functioning of grinding or chewing teeth in other mammals , in which opposing teeth co-operate in action , and which can be matched in extinct , unrelated mammals , is a much more subtle matter , involving detailed studies on the operation of living dental systems to help elucidate the functioning of fossil ones .
28505	The technique of ‘ hunt the analogue ’ is a favourite one practised by palaeontologists , but it is certainly not a foolproof one , because there are many fossil animals that defy comparison with living organisms , and some analogues do not stand up to detailed scrutiny .
28506	The second method tries to analyse the structure of the fossil almost as if it were a piece of engineering .
28507	If the fossil is constructed in a certain way , then there are only a limited number of ‘ jobs ’ that the structure could perform .
28508	The idea here is to decide which of the possibilities is the most likely one .
28509	This assumes that nature only manufactures efficient designs .
28510	For the most part this is a reasonable assumption to make .
28511	Most animals today do seem to have bodies that accord well with the functions they have to carry out to survive : flyers are aerodynamically efficient , active swimmers have suitable streamlining , herbivorous mammals have teeth appropriate for grinding plant food , and so on .
28512	Ideally one could construct a model of the fossil to test out these various functions in experiments , but the number of examples where the analysis has been pursued this far are limited .
28513	Of course it can never be known whether the right answer has been reached ( unless somebody dredges up a ‘ living fossil ’ from the depths of the ocean ) — there are only varying degrees of probability .
28514	But the best answers are probably obtained where the functional design of the fossil points to the same life habits as a living analogue , and where both are consistent with the geological circumstances in which the fossil remains occur .
28515	SWIMMING TRILOBITES
28516	There are thousands of different kinds of trilobites .
28517	All of them were marine and all of them are extinct .
28518	Since many kinds of trilobites co-existed at any one time they were probably occupying different ecological niches , behaving in different ways , corresponding with the wide variation in shape that they show .
28519	We can use the methods described above to elucidate some of these occupations , and get a glimpse , albeit an imperfect one , of the trilobite as it lived .
28520	I will take an example where all the methods can be used , and where all point in the same direction , so that the answer is probably correct .
28521	Most trilobites were broadly oval-shaped being rather longer than wide , not greatly convex , and with eyes that occupy perhaps a quarter of the length of the head .
28522	There are a few trilobite species , however , with enormous , globular eyes ( see below ) .
28523	By examining the way these animals were put together it is possible to suggest a likely mode of life .
28524	Giant-eyed Ordovician trilobite , seen from the top and side .
28525	Twice its natural size .
28526	Enlargement shows a section through the lenses to show the direction of the field of view .
28527	We can take the eyes first .
28528	The trilobite eye was of a compound type , and each lens was made up of a calcite crystal .
28529	From the optical properties of this mineral we know that the lens was able to interpret light coming from a direction more or less at right-angles to the lens surface .
28530	So we can deduce what the field of vision of our globular-eyed trilobite was , by looking at the directions in which all the lenses face .
28531	It turns out that our animal was able to see in almost every direction — upwards , downwards , sideways and forwards , and even backwards , because the eyes bulged out beyond the line of the rest of the body .
28532	Most other trilobites have a predominantly lateral field of view .
28533	If the animal lived on the sea bottom , it seems unlikely that it would have eye lenses specialized for looking downwards , and we begin to suspect that the animal habitually dwelt above the sea floor .
28534	Other features of its shape are consistent with this .
28535	At the edge of the eyes are a pair of long spines , and these point downwards at a steep angle , at very awkward attitude for resting comfortably on the sea floor .
28536	Most ‘ normal ’ trilobites have a more or less horizontal rim around the forward margin , which may have rested on the sediment surface .
28537	The thorax of the large-eyed trilobite is remarkably long compared with the average trilobite ( compare Fig. 33 ) .
28538	The convex , middle part of the thorax contained the musculature that operated the appendages ( which , as usual , are not preserved ) , and the relatively large volume of this region shows that the musculature was powerful .
28539	The construction of this giant-eyed trilobite suggests that it lived an actively swimming life well above the bottom , and possibly in the surface waters of the sea .
28540	Of course because there are no living trilobites we can not find direct confirmation of this hypothesis , but we can look for other arthropods that have the same modifications of the eyes , for example , in the present day oceans .
28541	The analogy is found in such ocean-going amphipods ( a kind of ‘ shrimp ’ ) as Cystosoma , which also has enormously expanded eyes , looking like headlamps , compared with its bottom-dwelling relatives ( see above ) .
28542	In fact many of the arthropods that inhabit the water column have large , globular eyes of this kind .
28543	49 Fossil bony fish , Lates gracilis , Eocene .
28544	This fish is preserved in a fine-grained limestone which preserved most of the skeletal details of the fish ( but not its colours ) .
28545	This is a stout-bodied fish , something like a perch in general proportions , with long , low fins on upper and lower rear of the body ( fin rays finely divide near their ends ) .
28546	Head to tail the fish measures 17 cm .
28547	50 Vertebra of the Jurassic pliosaur , Liopleurodon species , Kimmeridge , southern England .
28548	This is only one vertebra of an animal much too bulky to appear in a book of this size !
28549	The original porous bone has been consolidated to become much heavier than it would have been in life .
28550	Diameter of the vertebra is about 10 cm .
28551	51 Fossil frog , Rana species , Miocene , Spain .
28552	This species is preserved in a soft shale , but one which allows for the skeletal anatomy to be preserved in its entirety .
28553	The outline of the soft parts are also clearly displayed , so that the animal has been preserved almost in frozen motion .
28554	Frogs are one of the more numerous of amphibian fossils .
28555	Specimen 12 cm long .
28556	52 Fossil calcareous alga , belonging to the genus Coelosphaeridium , Ordovician , Ringsaker , Norway .
28557	These spherical algae are preserved as internal moulds in a mudstone , the original calcite having disappeared .
28558	Canals within the algae stand out as rods in this kind of preservation , which is common in Ordovician rocks .
28559	There is a central sphere visible on one of the specimens .
28560	Related forms are spread over much of the world in Ordovician and Silurian times .
28561	Individual globes have a diameter of 1½–2 cm .
28562	53 Fossil lycopod bark , Lepidodendron rimosum , Carboniferous , Newcastle , England .
28563	This is a typical ‘ coal shale ’ ; shales and silts occurring between productive coal seams often contain impressions of the plants that went to form the coal .
28564	The plant material itself is converted to black carbon .
28565	This fossil bark is typified by its lozenge-shaped leaf scars arranged in spiral rows .
28566	This fragment is 1O cm long .
28567	54 Fossil bark of the lycopod tree , Sigillaria laevigata , Carboniferous .
28568	This specimen lies on a slab of mudstone , the specimen itself having been converted into coal-like material — that is , into carbon .
28569	Sigillaria bark is covered with little horseshoe-shaped scars ( leaf cushions ) .
28570	It is found in North America ( Canada and the US ) , England , Belgium , France , Germany and Russia .
28571	This piece is 9 cm long .
28572	55 Leaves of the enigmatic plant , Glossopteris linearis , Permian .
28573	Many of these long leaves are preserved on the bedding planes of a siltstone .
28574	Glossopteris is characterized by its long strap-shaped leaves , which have a conspicuous midrib , with many fine , smaller veins branching off it to form a network .
28575	Its classification in relation to other plants is still unsolved .
28576	These leaves have a length of 7–8 cm .
28577	56 Fossil root , Stigmaria ficoides , Carboniferous .
28578	This root is preserved as an internal mould , in a tough sandstone .
28579	It has been slightly crushed .
28580	The infilling sandstone is derived from the fossil soil over which the root was growing .
28581	Stigmaria is the name given to roots of the giant lycopod Lepidodendron ( this page ) .
28582	This specimen is 15 cm long , but roots have been found which attain a length of 14 metres !
28583	57 Leaf of a Carboniferous seedfern , Mariopteris muricata , Staffordshire , England .

28585	This is quite a common preservation in coal measures .
28586	Microscopical details are not so well-preserved , and the fossil is , of course , only a fragment of a larger plant .
28587	The leaflets are attached to the axis along their entire base .
28588	6 cm long .

28600	Reproductive structures should really be found to distinguish it from other , superficially fern-like plants .

28603	The leaf is excellently preserved on the flat bedding-plane of a limestone laid down under fresh water .
28604	Poplar leaves have an elegant outline resembling that of an arab minaret .
28605	This species has a finely toothed margin ; a large , wide leaf born on a long stem .
28606	This type of tree has a history extending back to the upper Cretaceous .
28607	Length of leaf is 18 cm .

28609	Seeds of the maple family are typically in pairs , joined at the base , with flat ‘ wings ’ that help the seeds to disperse .
28610	Seeds of Acer are rare compared with the leaves , which can be found in rocks dating back to the Cretaceous period .
28611	This is from the Oeningen , Switzerland .
28612	Seeds are about 3 cm long .
28613	63 Miocene maple leaf , Acer trilobatum .
28614	This leaf is exquisitely preserved in a fine-grained , flat-bedded marly limestone .
28615	Although much of the fine detail can be seen most of the tissue of the leaf is destroyed .
28616	The leaf is divided into three parts with a broad central lobe ( finely toothed ) and two flanking lobes .
28617	Simple , distinct veining can also be seen .
28618	The leaf is 10 cm long .
28619	64 Fossil flower , Porana oeningensis , Miocene .
28620	These beautifully preserved flowers are from the Oeningen deposits like the maple leaf and seeds illustrated here .
28621	Fossil flowers are extremely rare because of their delicacy and because they are shortlived .
28622	These flowers have five oval petals , finely veined .
28623	No details of the stamens are present in the fossil state .
28624	Diameter of the flowers is about 2 cm .
28625	Giant-eyed living crustacean ( Cystosoma )
28626	If it is correct that our trilobite lived above the sea bottom , actively swimming in the water , there are certain predictions we can make about its geological occurrence which can be tested by looking in the rocks .
28627	Most bottom-dwelling trilobites preferred to live at a particular water depth , or on a particular type of sea bottom ( mud , sand or lime ) .
28628	No such restriction should apply to our large-eyed species ; it should be found with all other different kinds of trilobite assemblages without preference .
28629	This has been proved in several places : in some arctic localities it is found with trilobites that lived at great depths in the muds of the Ordovician ocean , while in Canada the same species occurs mixed with the inhabitants of the shallow-water seas , where limestones were accumulating .
28630	By the same token the free-swimming trilobite may be expected to have a very wide geographical distribution , for oceans would be no barrier to it .
28631	And again this proves to be the case : our example is found in Arctic Canada , in the high Arctic island of Spitsbergen , thousands of miles away in what is now the desert country of Nevada and Utah in the United States , in western Ireland , in Russia , and in northwestern Australia .
28632	So in this case the different sources of evidence all point in the same direction , whether derived from a detailed consideration of the way the trilobite is constructed , or by analogy with living animals with similar adaptations , or from the evidence of the rocks or the distribution of the fossils .
28633	These giant-eyed trilobites of the Ordovician were active swimmers in the surface waters , as near certainly as we can ever know .
28634	There are all kinds of different questions we can ask about the life habits of these trilobites , which are not subject to the same kind of careful scrutiny .
28635	What did they eat , for example ?
28636	Because we do not have the legs preserved , it is not possible to see how the mouth appendages functioned in feeding , and neither are the stomach contents preserved .
28637	So here there are only more or less likely speculations .
28638	Active swimmers in the surface waters of the present oceans are likely to feed directly on the plankton , and the trilobites may have had a method of harvesting large quantities of minute food .
28639	Or they may have been hunters after larger prey , in which case when appendages are eventually discovered they may prove to have adaptations for grasping and manipulating larger food .
28640	Puzzles remain , even though we can be certain of the rudiments of the story .
28641	CONTROVERSY AMONG THE GIANT DINOSAURS
28642	The giant sauropod dinosaurs like Brachiosaurus were the largest land animals the world has seen they weighed more than 80 tonnes and present quite different problems in the interpretation of their life habits from the diminutive trilobites .
28643	Such spectacular animals have obviously attracted much attention , and one might suppose that the problem of how they lived would have been satisfactorily solved long ago .
28644	Most of the popular books showing the Mesozoic giants in their natural setting portray them wallowing about in swamps flanked by deep vegetation , their bodies largely under water .
28645	Surely an animal of this bulk , it was argued , must be partly supported by water , and their relatively inconsequential teeth must have been adapted for chewing on the kind of soft , luxuriant vegetation that flourishes in and around swamps .
28646	Because their nasal openings were on the top of their heads they could even continue to breathe if it became necessary ( see p. 115 ) to totally submerge .
28647	Recently the life habits of the giants have been looked at in a way that disproves most of these traditional notions .
28648	Consider the structure of their legs .
28649	The sauropods have relatively long , pillar-like legs , resembling those of the elephant , the largest living land animal , and may have been well adapted for supporting the huge bulk of the animal .
28650	The feet of the sauropod are small ( relatively speaking ! ) , with short , stubby toes , yet animals that walk on soft mud tend to have spreading feet to distribute their weight more evenly .
28651	It is difficult to see how the compact feet of the sauropod could avoid becoming stuck fast in the soft , muddy bottom of a lake .
28652	If the dinosaur did , after all , live on dry land , then the long neck could have usefully functioned to allow the animal to browse the high foliage of trees ( see p. 116 ) .
28653	It has been suggested that an animal of the size of Brachiosaurus could not have breathed under water because of the pressure on the lungs .
28654	Their fossil remains seem to occur with other animals and plants , which are generally accepted as terrestrial .
28655	There is even some evidence from the tracks they have left behind that Diplodocus and its allies moved about in herds .
28656	They may have been the gigantic reptilian analogue of the elephant , and it may be no coincidence that the elephant also has its nasal openings on top of the skull , with the nostrils in this case sited at the end of the trunk it has been suggested that some sauropods may have had a proboscis of some sort .
28657	The balance of evidence seems to be swinging away from the original idea of swamp-dwelling giant dinosaurs to fully terrestrial habits .
28658	But other aspects of the dinosaur living habits are still more strongly debated .
28659	In the last few years a powerful controversy has arisen over whether the dinosaurs as a whole were cold-blooded , like all living reptiles ( and there is no doubt that dinosaurs were reptiles ) , or warm-blooded , resembling mammals in this respect .
28660	Cold-blooded animals have to ‘ warm up ’ before they can be fully active ; that is why lizards and snakes bask in the sun in temperate climates .
28661	For this reason they can not cope with climates having greatly extended winters .
28662	Warm-blooded animals have the same body temperatures at all times , and can be more continuously active , but they use far more energy — and hence need more food — than cold-blooded animals of the same size .
28663	The posture of many dinosaurs , and particularly the carnivorous theropod dinosaurs , was fully erect with the legs beneath the body , and unlike the sprawling legs of living reptiles ( see p. 116 ) .
28664	The long back legs of such hunters look highly suitable for running , and as they did so the long tail may have been held erect as a kind of counter-balance ( see p. 116 ) .
28665	For any kind of prolonged activity , warm-bloodedness would have been a distinct advantage .
28666	Under the microscope even the bone structure of these dinosaurs looks more like that of living mammals than cold-blooded reptiles .
28667	On the other hand it can be argued that the sauropods like Brachiosaurus were so large , and with a relatively small surface area through which to cool compared with their enormous volume , that their cooling rate could have been slow enough to allow them to sustain more continuous activity than smaller , living reptiles .
28668	It has also been argued that the small mouths of the giants simply could not have downed enough food to support a warm-blooded metabolism , particularly plant food that needs a lot of processing before it becomes available as energy .
28669	The armoured or plated dinosaurs include some species that seem too heavily burdened with protective armour to have been very active , but this does not necessarily mean that they had to be cold-blooded .
28670	Protagonists of the warm-blooded theory will show some of the horned dinosaurs charging over the Cretaceous plains like furious reptilian rhinoceroses !
28671	One idea about the life habits of the dinosaur giants , published in Joc and Colette at the Natural History Museum in 1935
28672	The warm-blooded supporters tend to ally themselves with the supporters of a theory about the relationships of the dinosaurs .
28673	This is that the dinosaurs , or a close dinosaur relative , included the ancestors of the living birds .
28674	Some of the smaller , and most certainly highly active dinosaurs were about the size of a chicken , and there is more than a passing similarity between a running ostrich and the kind of reconstruction that shows fleet-footed , running dinosaurs .
28675	The point is that birds themselves are warm-blooded , like mammals , and if birds and dinosaurs are as closely related as now seems likely , then it obviously increases the likelihood that the dinosaurs themselves may have been warm-blooded .
28676	The pros and cons of this theory are the subject of much contentious debate by experts , but it would probably be correct to say that the greater number of specialists believe that at least the more bipedal of the dinosaurs , including small and large carnivores , were warm-blooded , active animals .
28677	A lot of the argument among the authorities on these animals is about the equivalence or otherwise of certain bones in dinosaurs and bird skeletons ( and particularly the Jurassic bird Archaeopteryx ) ; this makes for rather dry reading for the layman .
28678	But the end-product is the accurate reconstruction of the Jurassic and Cretaceous terrestrial world , over which the dinosaurs were indisputably dominant .
28679	GRAPTOLITES — FLOATING COLONIES
28680	In the 1830s and 40s geologists were beginning to unravel the mysteries of the early Palaeozoic rocks .
28681	The past world recorded in the rocks could not have seemed more alien .
28682	Many of the organisms that left fossil remains were of kinds now extinct , although some , like the trilobites , could obviously be placed into a phylum with many living representatives .
28683	The graptolites , however , were initially completely enigmatic ; they were first described as plants !
28684	Their remains were so abundant that they could not be ignored .
28685	Their colonies , looking like so many miniature hacksaw blades , often completely covered bedding planes , and usually they were found in the absence of other kinds of fossils .
28686	It also became apparent that they could be useful in subdividing the intractable stretch of time from Late Cambrian to Silurian ; they changed in obvious ways from one rock formation to the next .
28687	Ones with numerous branches seemed to dominate the earlier rocks , ones with fewer branches were later , while in rocks we would now recognize as Silurian and early Devonian , forms with but a single branch ( or stipe ) were abundant .
28688	With the discovery of better-preserved material it became apparent that the graptolites consisted of rows of tiny cups which were interconnected by a common canal — they were colonial animals .
28689	As noticed ( p. 59 ) it is now known that the graptolites were an extinct branch of the phylum Hemichordata , an insignificant group today , consisting of a few encrusting colonial organisms .
28690	How did these mysterious organisms live ?
28691	In this case it is difficult to apply argument from analogy , because the graptolites are really rather different from any animals now alive .
28692	The modern hemichordates are all encrusters and virtually all colonial organisms ( such as corals or bryozoa ) are bottom dwellers in the sea .
28693	On this argument the graptolites should have been bottom dwelling-colonial organisms , living by filtering small particles of food from the water .
28694	Some of the graptolites ( dendroid graptolites ) were shrubby colonies , looking very much like living hydroids or some bryozoa .
28695	These were equipped with ‘ roots ’ , and an inference of bottom-living habits seems eminently reasonable for them .
28696	But the great majority of the class , including all those with typical saw-blade profiles ( graptoloids ) which were widely used in the dating of rocks , certainly lacked any kind of rooting structure .
28697	When they were looked at in more detail it was found that the colonies grew from one single tube ( sicula ) which is often facing in a different direction from the tubes inhabited by the rest of the colony ( see below ) .
28698	A slender rod ( nema ) usually grows from the top of the sicula .
28699	Since some of the graptoloids are large and robust , this slender rod seemed an inadequate basis for attachment to the sea floor , particularly in any sort of turbulent environment .
28700	Then there were some forms , like Phyllograptus ( see p. 118 ) , in which the colony grew over the slender nema to leave no visible means of attachment at all .
28701	It begins to look as if the graptoloids could have been free-floating animals , of a kind without any living counterpart .
28702	Left A modern reconstruction of the life habits of the giant sauropods , which could scarcely be more different from the 1935 version
28703	Centre left The posture of a dinosaur compared with that of a living reptile
28704	Bottom left The active , running posture of a dinosaur in the modern interpretation
28705	Below Growth and budding of a graptolite colony , enlarged about 20 times
28706	Now the geological circumstances in which the most abundant graptolite faunas are found can be introduced into the argument .
28707	The most typical occurrence of these fossils is in dark , often sooty , black shales .
28708	In many localities graptolites are the only fossils to be found , but they occur in abundance .
28709	Sometimes they occur with cherty rocks that contain the remains of indubitably planktonic radiolaria .
28710	Some , at least , of the graptolitic black shales are what we can recognize , with the hindsight of plate tectonic theory , as the deposits laid down of the edge of the continental shelf , in a truly oceanic environment .
28711	These are frequently associated with volcanic rocks of oceanic type .
28712	So there seems little room for doubt that the graptolites were capable of living in an open-ocean environment .
28713	The fact that they occur in shales without other benthic remains makes it very likely that they were free floating , and this is consistent with the way some of the species were constructed .
28714	Dead graptoloids simply drifted down to the bottom where they were preserved by dark muds at a depth at which there was little oxygen in the water to support bottom-dwelling organisms .
28715	A few examples have been found where a number of graptoloids seem to have been associated together attached ( by the nema ) to a ‘ float ’ .
28716	Other species seem to have the nema extended into a kind of vane .
28717	There may have been some species which were attached to floating seaweed .
28718	Of course , many graptoloids also drifted into shallower water , where they are associated with a more normal kind of fossil assemblage .
28719	Like the pelagic trilobites , individual graptoloid species are very widespread , which is what one would expect of an animal with the wide ocean as its habitat .
28720	It is not surprising to find that the widespread species have been used extensively to correlate rocks between different continents — they form the standard for the Silurian period , where the graptolite faunas are nearly the same all over the world .
28721	Above Phyllograptus , a graptolite colony with no means of attachment .
28722	About twice natural size .
28723	Above right A sample of the different shapes achieved by the brachiopods : different shapes for differing modes of life
28724	In this case a combination of geological evidence and the evidence of the shape of the animal itself has been used to say something about how the animal lived .
28725	Many problems remain .
28726	Which way up did they float ?
28727	Were there species adapted for living at particular depths ?
28728	Why did graptoloids have an evolutionary trend from many branches to few branches ?
28729	There are plenty of different answers available to these questions , but , like the metabolism of dinosaurs , no concensus has been reached as yet .
28730	ANIMALS WITH TWO VALVES
28731	Graptolites , trilobites , and dinosaurs are all extinct , and so in the examples we have considered so far there is no direct recourse to the study of living animals to help us bring our fossils back to life .
28732	Any analogies have to be with living creatures that are distantly related in the zoological sense , although there may be reasons to suspect that they have similar life habits to those that the fossil animals once enjoyed .
28733	Some of the fossils with the simplest construction are those with the soft parts encased within two valves , principally the bivalves and the brachiopods .
28734	These two groups of animals are quite unrelated , but both still have living representatives in the oceans , and so it is possible to look at living animals to help with the interpretation of fossil examples .
28735	Of the two , the bivalve molluscs are much the most significant in the sea today .
28736	The brachiopods are still numerous in some environments , but these tend to be rather inaccessible , such as in the deep sea , which inhibits their direct study in the field .
28737	Most brachiopods lead a rather uneventful life , attached by a stalk to a hard surface , like the underside of a rock , or another shell , filtering food from the surrounding sea water .
28738	There is nothing to suggest that the innumerable fossil brachiopods had any other method of feeding .
28739	Yet it is obvious that there are a great variety of shapes ( see above ) among the fossil forms , many of them unmatched in living species .
28740	There must have been many different ways for brachiopods to exploit their simple mode of life .
28741	For a filter-feeding animal , it is sensible to separate the inhalent current , bringing food , from the exhalent one , which carries away waste products .
28742	Brachiopod feeding is carried out by the lophophore ( p. 61 ) , a ciliated band usually carried on a loop , which also creates the currents used in feeding .
28743	Many brachiopods have developed a broadly wavy margin of the valves ( see below ) , with the middle bent downwards .
28744	This form of the shell reflects the separation of the feeding currents from the exhalent currents .
28745	Currents pass in through the sides of the shell , over the ciliated lophophore where the food is extracted , and then out through the depression in the margin of the valves .
28746	The lophophore is supported in several different ways .
28747	In some species the support is on a spiral made of calcium carbonate ( see p. 120 ) .
28748	This increases the length of the lophophore available to extract food from the feeding current , and so increases the efficiency of the process .
28749	Brachiopods begin to seem rather more complex animals than their simple shape suggests .
28750	Many species have a finely folded margin , crumpled like corrugated cardboard .
28751	Since the shell grows at the margins , a ribbed shell is produced , with fine or coarse ribs according to the species .
28752	A ribbed shell of this kind is often stronger than one without ribs ( for the same reason that corrugated iron is used for roofing ) , and it is probably no coincidence that ribs may be developed on bivalves too .
28753	But the wavy margin may serve another function .
28754	For one thing it increases the length of the margin , allowing the animal to admit more food per unit of length .
28755	The wavy margin also prevents the entry of irritating particles of sand , with which the animal can not cope .
28756	However , there is still a problem at the crests of the corrugations , where the gap between the valves is larger ; many brachiopods solve this particular problem by having fine , hair-like spines which cover the crests of the corrugations , and so prevent the intrusion of unwanted particles .
28757	Wavy valve margins in brachiopod .
28758	Note also the ribbing .
28759	Four times life size .
28760	Although most brachiopods were attached to a firm substrate by a stalk which emerges through a hole in the pointed end of the animal , there are some in the fossil record in which there is no opening for such a stalk .
28761	These must have lain freely on the surface of the sediment .
28762	In some of these species one valve is greatly thickened .
28763	This is likely to have been the lower valve , and fossils are sometimes found in ‘ life position ’ , which confirms this .
28764	The other valve sits in the thick one like a lid , and the whole animal is curved so that the margins of the valves were kept clear of the sediment .
28765	The end result is an animal that looks very much like some kinds of oyster , although a glance at the internal feeding structures shows at once that they are brachiopods , unrelated to the bivalves they superficially resemble .
28766	Some species had long spines ( anchors ? ) attached to the lower , thicker valve .
28767	Unlike the brachiopods , many of the modes of life of living bivalve molluscs can be more or less directly matched in fossil examples .
28768	So by studying how the life habits of living bivalves are reflected in the shapes of the shells we can make deductions about how the fossils lived .
28769	A major difference between brachiopods and bivalves is that the latter are capable of moving freely , using their foot to crawl or dig .
28770	Of course , some bivalves , like mussels and oysters , do remain fixed throughout their adult life , and it is possible that these fill the ecological role today of some of the large brachiopods of the Palaeozoic .
28771	Some of these lived in shallow water sites and were gregarious like mussels .
28772	But since brachiopods were unable to do many of the things that bivalves do very efficiently , it would be unwise to attribute the decline of the brachiopods to diversification of the bivalves .
28773	Above Swimming in bivalves : living Chlamys escaping starfish predators
28774	Right Burrowing bivalve mollusc in life position ; the siphons retain contact with the surface
28775	Left Spiral supports for the brachiopod feeding system , preserved inside one of the valves , and etched out with acid
28776	Burrowing bivalves , which are typically found in the soft bottoms of shallow seas today , dig themselves down into the sediment , where they escape the attention of many predators ( except birds with long bills ! ) .
28777	Many of them retain contact with the surface of the sediment by means of long siphons ( see left ) , which enable them to breathe and feed on small organic particles .
28778	Most bivalves with siphons develop a gape at one end of the valves , so that they do not close entirely in the region from which the siphons protrude .
28779	It is easy to recognize such gaping valves in fossils , and there are accompanying changes on the internal structure of the shell which are associated with species with long siphons .
28780	Hence bivalves as old as Palaeozoic can be identified with some confidence as ancient burrowers .
28781	It can be confirmed by discoveries of fossils preserved in their life position .
28782	Often the process of ‘ digging in ’ is assisted by a characteristic pattern of chevron-shaped ribs on the surface of the shell , which are also obvious features of some fossil shells .
28783	Such V-shaped ribs are not found on brachiopods , which have never developed the capacity for burrowing .
28784	Other kinds of bivalves have used their capacity for free movement to the utmost by becoming efficient swimmers , clapping their valves together like castanets to move through the sea to find new feeding grounds or to escape the threat of predators .
28785	These bivalves have fan-like shells , often strongly ribbed ( Chlamys ) .
28786	While the bottom-dwelling or burrowing bivalves mostly have a pair of strong muscles to pull the valves together , in the swimming forms the muscles have become modified so that there is one particularly powerful muscle , centrally placed , to produce the powerful clapping movement that propels the animal through the water .
28787	This muscle leaves a conspicuous scar on the inside of the shell , an impression which is easily preserved in the fossil state .
28788	So it is possible to deduce swimming habits in fossil bivalves by comparison with the living forms .
28789	These swimming habits go back into the Palaeozoic , to the Carboniferous or earlier .
28790	There are a few bivalves which are found in rocks deposited in the same sort of black shale environment that was mentioned above in the discussion of graptolite life habits .
28791	Some experts maintain that these molluscs were able to swim in the open ocean , or that they were attached to floating seaweed : some such mechanism has to be invoked to explain how these bivalves came into an environment that lacked bottom-living animals .
28792	I have only selected a few examples of deducing modes of life from these fossils with two valves ; the examples could be multiplied many times .
28793	The most important point is that relatively complicated life habits can be inferred from a careful consideration of the anatomy of even the simplest looking animal , particularly when there are related , similarly adapted animals for comparison .
28794	PALAEONTOLOGICAL ENIGMAS
28795	Every now and then the fossil record throws up fossils which are palaeontological puzzles .
28796	They are obviously the remains of some kind of animal , but the problem is to decide what kind .
28797	They tend to be rather rare , preserved in a special way .
28798	And , of course , like so many palaeontological matters , they stir up arguments between specialists who think they have a way of solving the enigmas .
28799	Some of these puzzling fossils are quite small .
28800	A few years ago a minute fossil only about 2 mm long was recovered from limestones of Ordovician age , and christened Janospira .
28801	It looks remarkably like a trumpet .
28802	The ‘ mouthpiece ’ and the ‘ horn ’ of the trumpet are both open , and a coil hangs down from the middle .
28803	The end of the coil is closed , and it seems reasonable to assume that the animal started growing as a coiled shell .
28804	Then it must have changed its mind , and started to grow in two directions , a narrower tube into the ‘ mouthpiece ’ and a broader one into the ‘ horn ’ , and there is some evidence that the ‘ horn ’ end continued to get wider and longer .
28805	The problem is that it is hard to equate this kind of growth with that of any known animal group .
28806	It looks like some kind of mollusc , but no mollusc fits easily into this pattern of growth ; various people have suggested it might be some kind of snail , or perhaps a monoplacophoran ( see p. 76 ) .
28807	It remains a puzzle .
28808	It is found along with fossils of planktonic organisms and it is possible to explain the change in growth between coil and trumpet as a change that happened when the larval shell settled on the bottom .
28809	But since virtually all phyla of animals have planktonic larvae , this is no help in solving the puzzle .
28810	A palaeontological enigma : Janospira , a small Ordovician fossil of unknown relationships
28811	Some larger fossils are even more puzzling .
28812	A number from the famous Middle Cambrian Burgess Shale of western Canada are so strange that they have even been claimed as the representatives of ‘ extinct phyla ’ .
28813	Certainly they are difficult to accommodate comfortably in groups alive today .
28814	One of these , Hallucigenia is shown opposite .
28815	This curious animal has what was probably a gut and a set of tubules arising from it ; below this are curious pointed structures .
28816	What can it be ?
28817	One suggestion is that early on in metazoan evolution there were a number of experimental designs which were not to give rise to direct descendants ; naturally these do not fit into the pigeon holes based on living animals .
28818	Hallucigenia may have been one of these .
28819	There are problems with designating these as new phyla , not least that nobody can define a phylum objectively , and my own view is that , marvellous though these animals are , we should still try to relate them to other organisms ( fossil and living ) .
28820	Hallucigenia would defy all such attempts at the moment .
28821	Action and Inaction in the Cities
28822	Susanne MacGregor and Ben Pimlott
