30277	The theory seems to have a middle class bias in that it assumes that all criminal and rule-breakers accept and cherish middle-class goals , but many delinquent activities do not appear to be aiming for material gains .
30278	This is a general danger or problem with theories that are based on a consensus view of society — a view that society is held together by common values , shared by all .
30279	Merton 's theory does not explain why some individuals faced with a situation of anomie conform while others break the rules .
30280	Nor does it explain why one type of adaptation rather than another occurs ; for example , why innovation occurs rather than retreatism , or vice-versa .
30281	Also , no explanation is offered as to how society defines criminal behaviour , why some acts are made illegal and others not .
30282	Nonetheless , the work of Merton has certain strengths .
30283	It explains criminal behaviour in terms of the structure and culture of society , rather than individual characteristics .
30284	Hence it is a structural theory of crime .
30285	Further , in developing this approach Merton laid the ground for later work on crime based on the notion of subculture , the notion that there are certain groups who will be more liable to break the rules of society .
30286	We will now review some of the major developments from functionalist theory based on notions of culture and subculture .
30287	Albert Cohen and subcultural theories
30288	In his widely cited study Delinquent Boys , Cohen questions whether delinquent behaviour is caused directly by the desire for material goals .
30289	While some forms of delinquent behaviour are clearly centred on acquiring goods or money , a large amount of delinquency is expressive in character .
30290	That is , it is not directly concerned with material gain ; delinquency centring on vandalism or violence is an obvious example .
30291	Cohen looks to the educational system for his explanation of delinquency .
30292	Schools , he argues emphasise and embody middle-class values .
30293	Thus , individuals socialised into the working classes will suffer from status frustration , and will adopt an outlook set on turning the middle-class value system on its head .
30294	Anything which the school sees as wrong , the working-class delinquent will see as good ; delinquency is explained as a direct denial of middle-class values .
30295	In his study , Cohen compares what he terms the ‘ street corner boy ’ with the ‘ college boy ’ .
30296	Because working-class boys suffer disadvantages in the educational system and are not brought up to accept the values of this system , they are likely to reject the school values and form a delinquent subculture ( Cohen 's definition of this subculture is reproduced as Reading 2 in Chapter 5 ) .
30297	Cohen stresses therefore , the collective response as central to delinquency , rather than seeing such behaviour as an individual response to the failure to achieve middle-class goals , as Merton argued .
30298	His theory is , however , open to similar criticisms to those made about Merton 's work .
30299	The claim that status frustration is the motivating factor also suffers from a middle-class bias , in that it is assumed that delinquents cherish middle-class status goals , such as educational success .
30300	Moreover , it is perhaps doubtful whether many delinquents hold openly oppositional views or values as Cohen suggests .
30301	Furthermore , although delinquency is invariably a group activity it does not always take place within organised delinquent gangs , which is the basis of Cohen 's theoretical approach .
30302	Certainly , organised , structured delinquent gangs do not appear to be the norm in Britain today .
30303	Another ‘ subcultural ’ -type theory that stresses deprivation and develops and draws on the work of Merton and Cohen is that of Cloward and Ohlin .
30304	Briefly , Cloward and Ohlin argue that there is greater pressure on members of the working class to behave criminally or delinquently due to the fact that they have less opportunity to succeed by legitimate means .
30305	They agree with Cohen 's argument that working-class boys are likely to form and join delinquent subcultures , but they feel he has not taken account of the different and specialised types of subculture that exist .
30306	They suggest that the potentially delinquent individual may respond to his situation by joining one of three types of subculture : a criminal subculture , where delinquency is linked with adult criminality ; a conflict subculture , which occurs in areas where links between juvenile and adult criminality are not established ; and , thirdly , a retreatist or ‘ escapist ’ subculture .
30307	Recent developments in the sociology of crime : the deviant as normal
30308	The theories looked at thus far have moved away from the view of the criminal as clearly distinguishable from the non-criminal .
30309	The biological and psychological theories stressed this distinctiveness .
30310	The functionalist approaches see crime as a response of people to their social situation .
30311	However , in responding to their situation criminals are seen as becoming distinct from the mainstream , non-criminal population .
30312	We will now turn to theoretical approaches which see the criminal as ‘ normal ’ , and which centre on how society defines certain individuals as criminal or deviant .
30313	In particular , the Interactionist and Marxist approaches .
30314	Interactional theories
30315	To overcome some of the problems associated with the structural and subcultural-orientated theories based on the functionalist perspective , Interactionism has adopted a different theoretical perspective for examining crime and rule-breaking .
30316	One of the major criticisms of these previous theories has been that they have tended to see their subject matter ( that is , rule-breaking ) as straightforward and easily identifiable — crime being behaviour that breaks certain of the rules of society .
30317	This implies that social groups are characterised by consensus .
30318	Interactionists would question that implication , and argue that they are made up of a plurality of values and norms , which may often conflict .
30319	As suggested above , Interactionists would also deny that criminals are essentially different from other , so-called ‘ normal ’ , people .
30320	Various studies have demonstrated that very few people have not broken laws , and many people do so frequently without ever having their ‘ crimes ’ recorded .
30321	Thus , if a majority of people commit criminal actions it becomes somewhat dubious to maintain a distinction between criminal and non-criminal , in terms of personal characteristics .
30322	LABELLING
30323	Interactionist approaches to crime and deviance have centred around the concept of labelling , with the term labelling theory sometimes used to refer to the Interactionist perspective on rule-breaking .
30324	From this viewpoint , the criminal is an individual who has been labelled so by society , and this labelling does not apply to all individuals who break laws .
30325	As mentioned , many people who break laws are never found out and are thus not labelled as criminals .
30326	Interactionism stresses the arbitrariness of this labelling of someone , or of some action , as criminal .
30327	It focusses on the interaction between the criminal or deviant and those who define him/her as such .
30328	The classic statement on the labelling perspective is found in the work of Howard Becker :
30329	Social groups create deviance by making rules whose infraction constitutes deviance and by applying those rules to particular people and labelling them as outsiders .
30330	From this point of view deviance is not a quality of the act a person commits , but rather a consequence of the application by others of rules and sanctions to an offender .
30331	The deviant is the one to whom that label has been successfully applied ; deviant behaviour is behaviour that people so label .
30332	Becker , 1963
30333	Labelling , therefore , refers to the process by which individuals and groups classify and categorise social behaviour and other individuals .
30334	If a criminal is a person labelled as such , an initial question we must ask is ‘ Who does the labelling ? ’
30335	And , when we see terms such as ‘ social problem ’ or ‘ criminal ’ , we need to ask ‘ who defines these terms ? ’ , and to be as concerned with the actions and motives of the labellers as those who are labelled .
30336	The reason for this emphasis on the way in which people are labelled is that laws are essentially political products .
30337	They reflect the fact that some groups in society can create laws , and can determine what behaviour is seen as criminal .
30338	Interactionists stress that definitions of crime reflect the power of groups who have managed to impose their ideas about right and wrong , normality and so on on society .
30339	Of course , there are laws to curb the powerful also .
30340	However , Interactionists suggest that they are less frequently and vigorously applied .
30341	This point leads us on to an examination of the selective nature of law enforcement .
30342	SELECTIVE ENFORCEMENT OF THE LAW
30343	In a study of the administration of juvenile justice in the USA Cicourel ( The Social organization of Juvenile Justice , 1976 ) looked at the actual process of how delinquency and criminality is defined and applied to certain individuals .
30344	Without going into his work in any detail , Cicourel found that white , middle-class youths are less liable to be identified by police and probation officers as having committed or being likely to commit a crime .
30345	The police are more likely to react toward those groups and individuals whom they see as being prone to commit criminal actions ; often labelling such individuals before they actually commit a criminal act .
30346	The police , like most people , have stereotypical views as to the ‘ typical ’ criminal or delinquent .
30347	In the procedures of arresting and charging individuals and in their treatment in court , there are clear differences across the middle/working-class divide ; and these serve to reinforce the public 's ( and the police 's ) perception that certain groups are inclined to criminality .
30348	Cicourel suggests that certain groups are selected , processed and labelled as criminal .
30349	Interactionist approaches to explaining crime imply that for the purpose of studying such behaviour there is a correlation between being regarded as a criminal and in fact becoming one .
30350	Sociological study does not aim to discover who is innocent of the charges against them and who is guilty .
30351	For our purposes , being found guilty is the same as being guilty .
30352	Now , you might feel that there is a significant difference between a murderer or bank robber and someone who has been wrongfully convicted of murder or bank robbery .
30353	However , this difference is not likely to have any effect on the way in which the individuals will be treated .
30354	The wrongfully convicted prisoner will be treated identically to any other prisoner by prison officers .
30355	Furthermore , protesting one 's innocence will be seen as the kind of thing that everyone who is convicted does .
30356	Being convicted involves being identified publicly as a criminal , and it is in this context that we can say that being found guilty is the same as being guilty .
30357	Thus , being known to be a criminal is the same as being one in terms of treatment .
30358	It is for this reason that Interactionists stress that labelling is crucial to understanding criminal behaviour , as the labelling process publicly identifies individuals as guilty of criminal acts .
30359	THE AMPLIFICATION OF CRIMINALITY
30360	Thus far we have examined the process by which individuals become labelled .
30361	One important issue we have not considered is what happens to the individual once he or she is labelled as criminal .
30362	In other words , what is the effect of labelling on the individual ?
30363	Labelling an individual will tend to mark them out , and knowing a person has been labelled is liable to influence others ' behaviour toward that person .
30364	For example , knowing someone has been convicted of theft might influence one 's reactions and attitudes to that person .
30365	Furthermore , the individual who has been labelled is likely to view him/herself in terms of the label and act accordingly .
30366	This leads to a process of amplification or snowballing : individuals who are caught and labelled as criminal see themselves so and act accordingly , thus the label becomes more widely applied and firmly fixed , and the criminal becomes more attached to that label .
30367	Interactionists argue that societal reaction , in terms of labelling , can actually increase or ‘ amplify ’ the criminal behaviour of the labelled individual or group .
30368	This amplification process occurs on the wider , societal level as well as on the individual level .
30369	Jock Young 's work on ‘ Hippies ’ and police in London during the late 1960s illustrates this wider application ( Young , in Cohen , S. ed. , 1971 ) .
30370	Young found that the harder the police tried to stamp out drug use the more it grew , becoming a symbol of defiance for hippies .
30371	He suggested that the police acted as amplifiers of this illegal behaviour .
30372	Attempts to control drug use , through the formation of drug squads , helped to amplify it .
30373	The drug squads discovered more cases of drug use , which led to more police manpower and money being invested , which led to more discovery .
30374	There was thus a ‘ spiral of amplification ’ .
30375	the Interactionist approach — critical comments
30376	Labelling theory implies that criminals are powerless , passive victims who have had the misfortune to be labelled criminal , and have not been able to do anything about it .
30377	By placing such emphasis on social reaction it can be argued that Interactionists have minimised the role of the individual criminal .
30378	Linked with this point , labelling theories tend to disregard the origins of criminal behaviour .
30379	They concentrate on the present situation and the reaction of society and show little interest in the criminal 's background , although labelling theory does not argue that all that is involved in making someone a criminal is to call them one .
30380	Labelling is acknowledged as a complex process involving social norms and values .
30381	So far as the amplification of criminal behaviour is concerned , no explanation is offered as to how and why this process ends .
30382	Logically , the social reaction could be expected to grow , as would the individual 's criminality , with all law-breakers becoming extreme and committed criminals .
30383	While some follow this path , many others conform again , and do not become committed in their ways .
30384	People vary in how they respond to labelling ; being labelled may deter criminal activity as well as amplify it .
30385	Moreover , labels need not be permanent and irreversible .
30386	Finally , Interactionists lay great stress on social reaction without really attempting to explain why some actions are made illegal , without examining who constructs specific laws , and why .
30387	Interactionism raises the issue of the relation between power and crime , but does not really answer it .
30388	It concentrates on the specific interactions , the ‘ drama ’ , without investigating the importance of the social system itself .
30389	Interactionists look at the police , the courts and the criminals without examining the power underlying the system .
30390	To do this would require an analysis of how decision-making and power is distributed in society .
30391	This is an area of investigation central to Marxist-based work on crime .
30392	Marxist theories
30393	Marxist-based studies of crime are sometimes referred to under the titles of radical or critical criminology .
30394	This work centres on a examination of how crime is related to the power structure of society .
30395	We should remember that neither Marx nor Engels , his co-author , proposed a theory of crime ; and it has been later social theorists working within a Marxist framework who have developed a Marxist theory of crime .
30396	From a Marxist perspective crime is largely the product of capitalism , and the relatively high rate of crime in capitalist society is an indicator of the contradictions and problems inherent in such a system .
30397	Thus , many forms of crime are to be expected under a capitalist system .
30398	This is due , in part , to the ability of the powerful to criminalise and stigmatise that which threatens their interests ; and to the fact that basic motivations of capitalist societies , such as materialism and self-enrichment , can be pursued both legally and illegally .
30399	In relation to crime , perhaps the crucial question for Marxists is not ‘ Why does crime occur ? ’ , but ‘ Why does n't it occur more often ? ’
30400	Crime and the wider Marxist analysis
30401	A Marxist analysis of crime is not easily explainable , and has to be understood in relation to wider aspects of Marxist theory .
30402	As Jock Young suggests , ‘ it is not the criminal nor even the administration of crime , but , in the final analysis , the system itself that must be investigated ’ .
30403	Marxists hold that there is a basic distinction between the economic base of society , which determines the organisation and structure of society , and the superstructure , the cultural , legal , religious , political aspects of society .
30404	These aspects of the superstructure reflect the economic base .
30405	Therefore , the law will reflect the interests of the dominant economic class , and as an instrument of the dominant class the state passes laws which support its interests .
30406	The various social control agencies of the state , such as the police and courts , perform in a way that is consistent with the interests of the powerful , and against the interests of other groups , particularly the working classes .
30407	Criminal law is assumed to express and reflect the interests of the ruling class .
30408	As evidence for this , Marxists point out that much of the criminal law is about the protection of property .
30409	Furthermore , there has been a vast increase in the range of behaviour that has come under the control of the law .
30410	In their introduction to Critical Criminology ( 1975 ) , Taylor , Walton and Young point out that old laws have been reactivated and new laws created in order to control and contain an ever widening range of socially problematic behaviour .
30411	New laws have been created in this country to regulate industrial dissent and the rights of workers to organise .
30412	This extension of the law has created new criminals who do not fit the picture of the ‘ typical criminal ’ , the young , working-class male .
30413	In view of this , Taylor and colleagues argue that criminology needs to centre on theories of rule-making and breaking in relation to the distribution of power in society .
30414	However , power in modern capitalist societies is not just the ability to influence the way people think , and includes the control of knowledge and of ideas .
30415	It is from the dominant ideology that standards of acceptable , normal behaviour are defined ; and it is from this ideology that what constitutes social problems and criminal actions are also defined .
30416	A good example of this is the way in which the law , the media and public opinion view supplementary benefit fraud , ‘ fiddling the dole ’ .
30417	It is commonly assumed that this is widespread and costs enormous sums of money , and that it is a more serious offence than tax-evasion , which in fact costs the exchequer billions of pounds , far in excess of the cost of social security fiddling .
30418	Various Marxist-based studies have aimed to demonstrate how the law reflects economic interests , viewing the legal system as an instrument that supports the interests of the dominant class against threatening or disruptive behaviour .
30419	It has also been argued that the legal system enables the powerful to get away with exploiting other people without actually breaking the law .
30420	Frank Pearce has argued that organised crime in the USA is dominated by big business ; and William Chambliss , in a detailed study of crime in Seattle , Washington , has demonstrated the numerous interconnections between organised crime and the ruling groups in society .
30421	Another important example of the way in which the criminal law reflects ruling-class interests is the way in which the ‘ crime problem ’ tends to be equated with working-class crime , often of a very trivial nature , rather than the more important , in terms of money , white-collar crime .
30422	White-collar crime is crime that is centred around systematic fraud and fiddling by white-collar , middle-class employers and employees .
30423	One aspect of this type of criminality , business or corporate crime , will be discussed in some depth in Chapter 3 .
30424	A further aspect of the Marxist approach to crime concerns the way in which the law is enforced .
30425	It is argued that the law is selectively enforced in the interests of the ruling classes — an issue dealt with more fully in Chapter 4 .
30426	Very briefly , the basic Marxist argument is that the selective enforcement of the law , by largely ignoring white-collar/business crime , gives the impression that criminals are mainly from the working classes , which serves to direct attention away from ‘ ruling-class crime ’ .
30427	Marxist approach — critical comments
30428	As we have suggested , Marxist approaches to crime are based on the wider Marxist theory of society .
30429	Criticism of this approach to crime would , therefore , require a criticism of Marxist theory as a whole .
30430	For example , if the predominance of economic interests and power over other areas of society is not accepted , then the Marxist theory of crime would not be accepted .
30431	Nonetheless , some specific issues can be raised .
30432	Firstly , it is difficult to argue that every law defining certain actions as criminal is related to supporting the interests of the dominant classes .
30433	Many criminal actions appear to offer little threat to the capitalist class system .
30434	A more basic and crucial point is that the logical conclusion of the Marxist approach would be that the introduction of socialism will lead to a society without crime , where collective interests and responsibilities are all important .
30435	Can one be convinced of this ?
30436	It is certainly the case that crime rates in socialist countries are far less than in the USA and other capitalist societies .
30437	However , even if all criminality in western societies could be related to the capitalist system , there is plenty of evidence of both criminal and deviant behaviour in communist societies , such as theft , murder and dissent .
30438	It is doubtful that such activities can be interpreted as remnants from pre-communist society , soon to disappear as socialism or communism comes of age .
30439	Studying crime : pictures of contemporary criminality
30440	In the previous chapter we looked at crime and criminality in a very broad and general manner .
30441	This chapter will provide a more detailed examination of specific aspects of criminality .
30442	In Chapter 4 we will examine the statistics on crime .
30443	For the purposes of the present discussion we can say that these statistics display a number of clear patterns .
30444	Firstly , the statistics show an ever increasing rate of crime and imply , therefore , that much crime is a new , peculiarly modern phenomenon .
30445	Secondly , they show that crime is predominately a working-class phenomenon .
30446	Thirdly , that it is a male phenomenon .
30447	We will examine and discuss each of these patterns in this chapter , and in doing so will aim to look behind the picture of crime and criminals provided by criminal statistics .
30448	Extended readings from a number of the studies we look at will be included in Chapter 5 .
30449	Crime as a modern phenomenon
30450	This section will take issue with the notion of crime as somehow unique to contemporary society .
30451	While no one would deny the existence of horrendous acts of violence and criminality in earlier times , it is a widely held belief that western , advanced societies are becoming more and more criminal .
30452	This is reflected in the tendency to look back to a ‘ golden age ’ when these societies were thought to be more peaceful and law abiding .
30453	To examine the truth and relevance of these notions , we will look at juvenile delinquency , in particular hooliganism and vandalism .
30454	It is this sort of criminal behaviour which is commonly seen as characteristic of ( if not central to ) mass , urban society .
30455	We have all heard the prophets of social and moral decay recalling the days when such ‘ senseless and mindless ’ violence did not exist .
30456	Our discussion will be divided into two main parts .
30457	Firstly , we will look at the history of delinquency and will refer in some detail to Geoffrey Pearson 's recent study , Hooligan : A history of respectable fears , and his attempt to locate the supposed ‘ golden age ’ of a traditional way of life based on respect for law and order and all forms of authority .
30458	Secondly , we will look at modern delinquency , and specifically football hooliganism .
30459	A history of delinquency
30460	In a journey back through the history of crime and delinquency , Pearson shows that for generations Britain has been plagued by the same problems and fears as today .
30461	Yet , the myth that Britain has historically been a stable , peaceful and law-abiding nation , and that violence is somehow foreign to the national character , shows little sign of waning .
30462	Pearson searches for the period when such a stable , traditional way of life supposedly held sway .
30463	He found this ‘ golden age ’ was always just over the horizon , one generation further back ( see Reading 3 , Chapter 5 ) .
30464	The most striking aspect of the history of delinquency is the consistency with which each generation characterises the youth of the day and the way of life of twenty years previously .
30465	So let us start with present-day society and compare it with the situation twenty years or so ago , and then compare that generation with its predecessor .
30466	Although there are bound to be difficulties in comparing different ages and periods , such as different definitions of crime , different measuring techniques and a lack of adequate records and poor communications in previous times , an impression of the style and extent of crime — and of the popular concern about it — can nevertheless be formed .
30467	Pearson 's study starts with present-day attacks on our ‘ permissive age ’ by contemporary public figures and ‘ guardians of morality ’ .
30468	In March 1982 the Daily Telegraph suggested that ‘ we need to consider why the peaceful people of England are changing … over the 200 years up to 1945 , Britain became so settled in internal peace ’ .
30469	We have warnings of a massive degeneration among the British people which is destroying the nation .
30470	Kenneth Oxford , the Chief Constable of Merseyside , prophesies that ‘ the freedom and way of life we have been accustomed to for so long will vanish ’ .
30471	There are numerous instances of such statements from prominent politicians and public figures alleging that contemporary society is witnessing an unprecedented increase in violence and decline in moral standards .
30472	There is a consistent view that Britain 's history has been characterised by stability and decency , and that the moderate ‘ British way of life ’ is being undermined by the upsurge in delinquency .
30473	Twenty years previously , however , we can find remarkably similar comments .
30474	At the Tory Party conference in 1958 there was discussion about ‘ this sudden increase in crime and brutality which is so foreign to our nature and our country ’ .
30475	The Teddy Boys were arousing similar apocalyptic warnings of the end of British society .
30476	Rock and roll was the musical focus of this youth subculture , and the reaction which the Teddy Boys engendered was one of outrage and panic .
30477	The press , in particular , printed sensational reports of the happenings at cinemas and concerts featuring rock and roll films and music .
30478	An article in the Evening News of 1954 suggested that ‘ Teddy Boys … are all of unsound mind in the sense that they are all suffering from a form of psychosis .
30479	Apart from the birch or the rope , depending on the gravity of their crimes , what they need is rehabilitation in a psychopathic institution ’ .
30480	This reaction was widespread , off-duty soldiers were banned from wearing Teddy Boy suits and Teddy Boys were viewed by the rest of society as ‘ folk devils ’ .
30481	Nowadays , when we look back at old photographs and films of the 1950s rock and roll craze , and the Teddy Boys , it is easy to wonder what all the fuss was about .
30482	In comparison to groups who have come since then , they look quite straight .
30483	If anything , Teds are remembered with a degree of nostalgia and viewed as something quaint .
30484	Quite a contrast with the reaction in the mid-1950s illustrated above .
30485	Could it be that pre-war Britain was characterised by law-abiding youth and stability ?
30486	The Second World War has been seen by some as a kind of watershed , with the post-war period being morally inferior to the ‘ full rich back street life and culture of pre-war England ’ .
30487	However , when we look more closely at this period familiar declarations and allegations appear .
30488	In the 1930s there was a similar bemoaning of the ‘ passing of parental authority ’ and the ‘ absence of restraint ’ .
30489	The targets of criticism have a common ring — football rowdyism and the increasing crime and disorder .
30490	In the 1920s there were fierce street battles in North London between Spurs and Arsenal fans .
30491	It is sometimes implied that such incidents , and delinquencies in general , have become more ‘ serious ’ or ‘ violent ’ over time .
30492	The evidence would not seem to back up such suggestions .
30493	Crime in Me inter-war years was characterised by razor gangs , feuds between armed gangsters , vice rackets and so on .
30494	Moving back to the turn of the century and the pre-First World War period we seem little nearer to finding the traditional way of life based on a ‘ healthy respect for law and order ’ .
30495	A wide range of popular culture came under severe criticism in the early twentieth century .
30496	The music halls , professional football and the noisy presence of working-class people at seaside resorts on bank holidays were all attacked .
30497	As ever , youth of the period were compared unfavourably with previous generations .
30498	Baden Powell in his Scouting for Boys , published in 1908 , suggests that professional football was betraying the British traditions of ‘ fair play ’ and sportsmanship :
30499	Thousands of boys and young men , pale , narrow-chested , hunched-up , miserable specimens , smoking endless cigarettes , numbers of them betting , all of them learning to be hysterical as they groan and cheer in panic unison with their neighbours — the worst sound of all being the hysterical scream of laughter that greets any little trip or fall of a player .
30500	One wonders whether this can be the same nation which had gained for itself the reputation of being a stolid , pipe-sucking manhood , unmoved by panic or excitement , and reliable in the tightest of places .
30501	Neither does Victorian Britain provide any comparative baseline of a tranquil , law-abiding society .
30502	The first ‘ Hooligans ’ of the 1890s and the ‘ Garotters ’ of the 1860s do little to kindle nostalgia for Victorian city life and culture .
30503	In was in the late 1890s that the words ‘ Hooligan ’ and ‘ Hooliganism ’ were used to describe delinquent youth .
30504	There were regular news reports of Hooligan gangs smashing up coffee-stalls and public houses , robbing and assaulting old ladies , attacking foreigners and setting upon policeman in the streets .
30505	In line with later youth subcultures and gangs , Hooligans had a distinct style of dress , and a recognisable look .
30506	As with so many of the later youth subcultures , there was no doubt an over reaction to Hooligans .
30507	Nevertheless , whether correct or not , there was a widely held feeling that hooliganism was a major problem .
30508	Earlier in the Victorian period , in the winter of 1862 , panic swept through respectable London over a new variety of crime called ‘ garotting ’ , a type of violent robbery that involved choking the victim .
30509	A Victorian parallel with present-day ‘ mugging ’ perhaps .
30510	The press reacted in familiar manner , with The Times observing that it was ‘ becoming unsafe for a man to traverse certain parts of London at night ’ .
30511	The possibility that it was industrialisation that destroyed the stable and peaceful life of pre-industrial Britain does not appear to hold up either .
30512	Certainly , in the mid-nineteenth century it was widely felt that life in the previous century had been greatly superior and that the increase in juvenile crime was a blot on this age .
30513	However , writing in 1751 Henry Fielding paints a very similar picture with his prediction of an imminent slide into anarchy when the streets of the cities ‘ will shortly be impassable without the utmost hazard ’ .
30514	It is difficult to find evidence that there has been massive deterioration in the morality and behaviour of the common people , in comparison to the preindustrial work .
30515	From the late seventeenth century there had been complaints of increasing wickedness , crime and disorder .
30516	The streets of pre-industrial London were very dangerous , and there was no effective system of street-lighting nor a police force .
30517	Pearson also examines the recurrent nature of different explanations of the criminal question .
30518	Time and again a permissive present is contrasted with the not too distant past .
30519	If such accusations are accepted , we would be forced to conclude that with each generation crime and disorder increase dramatically .
30520	Looking back over Pearson 's historical review , it is hard to believe that Britain 's cities are any more perilous today than those of pre-industrial times , or when they were frequented by gangs of Garotters and Hooligans .
30521	This is not to deny , of course , that crime and violence in contemporary society is an important social reality .
30522	However , the preoccupation with violence and lawlessness is part of a long and continuous tradition , rather than a new and unique phenomenon .
30523	It is well nigh impossible to compare the rate of crime over extended periods of time ( as Reading 10 , Chapter 5 , taken from Pearson 's study , indicates ) .
30524	What we can say , though , is that juvenile crime and street violence have been characteristics of British society over hundreds of years , rather than being indicative of a contemporary moral and social disintegration .
30525	This does not make it any the less disturbing and below we will discuss contemporary styles of delinquency in greater detail .
30526	Delinquency in contemporary society
30527	Although violence at seaside resorts on bank holidays appears frightening enough when described by the media , various studies have pointed to the ritualistic character of this and other delinquent activity .
30528	Paul Corrigan suggests that teenagers behave the way they do at the seaside , or at football matches , because they are looking for a memorable experience to balance the boredom of the rest of their lives .
30529	However , teenagers do not go out saying to themselves that they are going to smash a couple of telephone boxes or fight another group of teenagers .
30530	They will not know what they are going to do , and will probably end up doing nothing .
30531	Certainly there is fighting and delinquency at seaside resorts and elsewhere , but if teenagers were seeking real violence then the casualties would be enormous .
30532	As Corrigan puts it : ‘ The kids are not crazy .
30533	They do n't want to get stabbed … or sent away for six months .
30534	What they want out of a gang fight is a nice big bruise … that they can show around during the week . ’
30535	However , whether ritualistic or not , juvenile delinquency is widespread .
30536	The issue we will examine is why delinquency is so attractive to some and unappealing to other youth .
30537	In particular , we will look at why the delinquent response is attractive to working-class male youth .
30538	In his study of working-class boys in the north-east of England , Corrigan looks at how and why many of these boys get into trouble and engage in delinquent activities .
30539	All of the youths studied were in their last year of school , and all were going to leave at the minimum school leaving age ( Corrigan , 1979 ) .
30540	The leisure activities of these youths centred on the ‘ street ’ , the arena where most illegal activity takes place , where most of the fighting and thieving occurs .
30541	They made little use of the youth clubs and other leisure facilities , other than as places to meet their mates .
30542	As previous research into juvenile delinquency has found , spare time activities are carried out in groups .
30543	In virtually every interview in Corrigan 's study the immediate response to the question ‘ What do you do on Saturday night ? ’ was to mention the ‘ mates ’ .
30544	So , with regard to delinquency , the two important factors would seem to be the street and the group .
30545	The major activity of the youths seemed to be ‘ doing nothing , , and when asked what they did on the street that was the standard reply .
30546	Of course , they were doing something , standing around on comers in groups for example , but as far as the boys were concerned nothing memorable seems to happen to them on Saturday night .
30547	When asked a question such as ‘ What do you do ? ’ , it is implied that something more should be going on , that standing around on a comer must be a means to an end .
30548	However , standing on street comers or walking around is not done with any definite end in mind .
30549	Nevertheless , between the general walking around , carrying on and joking things emerged that the youths called ‘ ideas ’ , and these ideas formed the basis of group actions .
30550	The development and carrying out of such ideas is one of the most active parts of the general ‘ hanging around ’ .
30551	It is these ideas that lead to what is seen as juvenile delinquency .
30552	They are born out of boredom , and a good idea must contain the chance of excitement ( Reading 4 , Chapter 5 is taken from Corrigan 's examination of the street based leisure/delinquent activities of these working-class youths ) .
30553	Another common diversion is getting into a fight , and , again within the context of ‘ doing nothing ’ these fights are important and exciting occasions .
30554	They are not particularly violent fights and participants are rarely hurt .
30555	When asked , ‘ What sort of fights ? ’ , one of the lads replied , ‘ Well , not real fights , as some of them might be quite matey … when you put the boot in , you put the boot in , but we are friendly after , like ’ .
30556	The youths studied — and you might like to consider the extent to which their experiences and expectations are commonplace — and are aware that in their leisure time they are doing nothing , are bored with it .
30557	Essentially they want something to happen , and their street activity can best be understood as an attempt to maximize the chances of something interesting happening .
30558	Although the street activity is seen as boring , there is always the chance that something will happen the following night or week .
30559	The delinquency undertaken by these youths is the result of certain actions which they feel are not very remarkable , based around the search for a bit of interest and excitement .
30560	Football hooliganism
30561	Professional football matches offer contemporary youth , particularly working-class youth , an opportunity to identify with one another as a solid group in opposition to other such groups .
30562	It offers an opportunity to engage in group delinquency and , occasionally , in group fights .
30563	And as we saw in our review of the history of delinquency , this has been the case throughout this century .
30564	Football hooliganism is not a particularly new phenomenon , nor is it a peculiarly British problem , it has occurred all over the world .
30565	Research into football hooliganism by Williams , Dunning and Murphy from Leicester University suggests that many of the common explanations for hooliganism , such as alcohol , violence on the pitch , the lack of all-seater stadiums , are too simplistic .
30566	The fact that the problem has persisted throughout this century indicates that its roots are deeper .
30567	Hooligan fans are predominantly from lower working-class backgrounds .
30568	One of the characteristic features of their communities is the street-based group activity .
30569	Such communities emphasise the ties of territory and the ability to ‘ defend ’ it .
30570	Also , due in part to increasing media attention , delinquent-prone youths who are more interested in fighting than football see the terrace ‘ ends ’ as places to maintain and improve tough reputations .
30571	Just as rival groups from different parts of a town or different estates will defend their areas , so they will join together to defend their ‘ end ’ of the football ground from fans from other towns .
30572	In fact , the chants and taunts of supporters are as much about the merits and demerits of the areas or towns as about the particular teams .
30573	Arsenal , for example , sing ‘ Maybe it 's Because I 'm a Londoner , and Leeds United chant ‘ York-shire ’ , with both sets of supporters mimicking the other 's accents .
30574	At international level , such local support is subordinated to the national reputation and hooligan fans from different clubs will join forces .
30575	Certainly , the fans of the English national team have earned an unenviable reputation around the football-playing world .
30576	While football hooliganism is not solely an ‘ English disease ’ , to be an English supporter at a match abroad clearly has a powerful image that attracts many young fans , an image which sees local fans and passers-by retreating in terror , and which has , it must be said , little to do with the achievements of the English football team itself .
30577	As Williams and colleagues indicate , the struggle for national pride can be exciting and intoxicating , especially in comparison to the everyday life of most of the hooligan fans .
30578	To return to football hooliganism in Britain itself , it is clear that the existence of ‘ ends ’ at football grounds all over the country plays a central part in maintaining working-class boys ' street-based culture .
30579	What goes on at these ‘ ends ’ is intelligible only to those involved .
30580	People from a wide range of social backgrounds go to watch football , but their interest and involvement will not be the same as the hooligan fans .
30581	As Corrigan puts it , the young supporter ‘ knows that a crowd of teachers chanting ‘ We hate Nottingham Forest' ’ is just not on' .
30582	Violence at football matches has been explained in terms of the changing nature of the game itself and of the relationship between football clubs , and their players , and the communities in which they exist .
30583	The close identity between fans and their club has weakened as football has become big business and as the players , who were once from the same working-class community as the fans , have become rich superstars .
30584	Thus , it has been suggested that the attempts to re-organise football in a more businesslike manner , to make it more professional , have alienated young working-class fans from their football clubs .
30585	Hooliganism on the terraces can be seen as an organised resistance to such changes .
30586	Chanting , taking territory and violence have extended the contest of the game onto the terraces .
30587	From this viewpoint , football violence has been given a new meaning since the early 1960s .
30588	It is a sign of the young fans commitment to their side 's cause , and also an attempt to resist changes in the organisation of football .
30589	The changing relation of football , and the football club , to working-class culture is seen as an aspect of the wider decomposition of the traditional working-class community .
30590	However , this sort of explanation does not seem to hold up in the face of evidence that football hooliganism is by no means a uniquely modern , post-1960 occurrence .
30591	The history of Glasgow Rangers Football Club , for example , makes it clear that riots , violence and vandalism have been well-established since at least the 1870s .
30592	This suggests that theories linking football hooliganism to changes in working-class community life are based on a somewhat dubious history .
30593	Working-class community life is as strongly established in Glasgow as anywhere , and football violence has occurred there for over a century .
30594	Similarly , in England football hooliganism has a long history .
30595	In the twenty years prior to the First World War there were numerous incidents of football hooliganism .
30596	The Football Association recorded 116 occasions between 1894 and 1914 when English league clubs were disciplined for trouble at their grounds .
30597	These occasions would clearly refer only to the more serious incidents where the Football Association felt it necessary to discipline clubs formally , and many more examples of hooliganism can be found in the newspapers of the period .
30598	Such evidence indicates that a whole range of disorderly behaviour occurred at football grounds during this period — missile throwing , pitch invasions and other supposedly ‘ contemporary ’ phenomena .
30599	Let us look more closely at the football hooligans themselves .
30600	A study of the fans of Oxford United and Millwall found that actual physical violence played only a small part in life on the terraces ( Marsh , Rosser and Harre , 1978 ) .
30601	This study centred on the group nature and aspects of football support and of delinquency at football matches .
30602	As we have seen , the sense of territory is a crucial aspect of this behaviour .
30603	Each football ground has a distinct area or ‘ end ’ for the ( generally young ) home supporters , and these ends acquire distinctive names — the North Bank of Arsenal , The Stretford End of Manchester United , for example .
30604	The distinctive nature of the ends is reinforced by the fact that the occupants are often physically con fined to the particular area for the whole of the football match .
30605	In more and more grounds , fences and grilles have been built around the ‘ ends ’ and the areas set aside for the visiting supporters , further highlighting the sense of territory .
30606	Marsh and colleagues found that there was a clear and established career structure among the youths on the terraces .
30607	To begin with , there were the ‘ Novices ’ , young boys of around 9 , 10 and 11 , who stood at the front of the ‘ end ’ and whose major occupation consisted of watching the activities of the older youths behind them .
30608	Then there were the ‘ Rowdies ’ , boys of 15 and 16 , who were the most identifiable group by virtue of their appearance , the noise they made and their tendency to run around the most .
30609	Lastly , were the ‘ Town Boys ’ , older boys and young men up to the age of 25 or so , who had previously demonstrated their ‘ worth ’ in the Rowdies ; who rested on their reputations but would still participate in acts of violence if called upon .
30610	Eventually , this group would move to other parts of the ground to watch the match with wives and girl-friends .
30611	In this division or career framework it is the Rowdies who are the typical football hooligans .
30612	Within this group there are a series of distinct and specialised roles , such as ‘ chant leader ’ , ‘ aggro leader ’ or ‘ nutter ’ .
30613	The fact that such roles are well established would seem to demonstrate that football fans such as ‘ Rowdies ’ can not be viewed simply as a bunch of disordered maniacs .
30614	The group is ordered and structured , as are its activities .
30615	For example , the members of the Rowdies group were well aware of their positions , and where they stood in relation to one another was clearly defined .
30616	This career framework should not be seen as being wholly rigid or fixed .
30617	It is only used as a pattern for understanding the organisation of terrace life for young supporters .
30618	Many fans drift into and out of groups rather than making a gradual progress .
30619	Furthermore , the fans themselves , although recognising the different types of football supporter , will not think in terms of a career structure .
30620	Nevertheless , the notion of career structures can help to explain behaviour which might otherwise appear irrational and disorganised ; it places the activity of the individual within the wider context of age and class dimensions .
30621	The activities of delinquent fans might be more intelligible if they can be related to particular roles and positions with respect to other fans .
30622	To summarise , the seemingly disordered nature of football hooliganism can be seen as conforming to a distinct and orderly system of roles , rules and shared meanings .
30623	What the football terraces offer young working-class males is a chance to escape the boring world of their everyday life .
30624	They see the terraces as potentially dangerous and exciting .
30625	However , these fans know that the terraces are not really dangerous , thus this sense of adventure and danger has to be constructed and exaggerated .
30626	This exaggerations is well illustrated in a visit by Oxford United fans to the ground of their arch-rivals Swindon Town .
30627	The fans knew that very little had happened at the match , but on the way picture , aided by songs , ‘ We took Swindon and all of them in it , We took Swindon in half a minute … ’
30628	By the time the coach arrived back at Oxford the day had been made remarkable and worthy of being talked about .
30629	Of course , the fact that structure and rules are to be found within the behaviour of football hooligans does not mean that there are no problems at football terraces and that such behaviour is to be condoned .
30630	We are not trying to excuse the behaviour , but to explain it .
30631	Social order can be found in events that are generally seen as dangerous and irrational .
30632	Crime as a working-class phenomenon
30633	This section will question the presumption that crime is overwhelmingly perpetrated by the working classes , or that the ‘ real ’ and serious crimes are those which are typically committed by this group — crimes like burglary , robbery and vandalism .
30634	The official criminal statistics present a picture of crime as being predominantly a working-class phenomenon .
30635	However , these statistics probably underestimate the extend of middle and upper-class criminality to a much greater extent than they underestimate crime in general .
30636	While prosecuted crime may be largely working class , whether crime as a wider category is so is rather debatable , given that a large amount of middle and upper-class criminality goes undetected .
30637	Moreover , even when it is detected , it is often not formally and legally dealt with ( the middle class bias in criminal statistics will be discussed in more detail in Chapter Four ) .
30638	Crimes which are committed by those in higher positions in the social stratification system are commonly referred to as white-collar crimes .
30639	Originally the term referred to ‘ business , crime , but is now generally attributed to any crimes of the middle classes .
30640	Edwin Sutherland 's famous pioneering work in 1940 produced evidence that white-collar crime might be substantially underestimated in official criminal statistics .
30641	He found that petty crimes of stealing from work , and the more major crimes of bribery and corruption , often passed unnoticed or were dealt with informally and unofficially by firms .
30642	White-collar crime appeared to be a normal and accepted part of business practice , being both very costly and highly organised .
30643	Virtually all the largest American corporations broke the law in one way or another ; laws controlling pollution , the adulteration of products , the regulating of prices and so on were ignored and broken at will .
30644	The work of Sutherland , and later writers , clearly makes it difficult to identify crime with lower social status , with poverty , social problems and the like .
30645	Criminality is also linked with power , respectability and wealth .
30646	Below we will concentrate on an examination of corporate , business crime , the law-breaking of businesses and corporations .
30647	Such crimes will be used to illustrate the massive and largely unrealised extent of the ‘ crimes of the powerful ’ .
30648	We will also look briefly at the more trivial , but widespread , crimes of employee theft — ‘ fiddling at work ’ — as an example of another aspect of work-related crime .
30649	Crimes of the powerful : corporate crime
30650	The fact that criminality is linked with respectability and power is central to Marxist-based studies , such as those of Chambliss ( see Chapter 2 ) .
30651	In his book On The Take , Chambliss examines the social character of crime networks in Seattle , USA ( Chambliss , 1978 ) .
30652	His conclusion is that the forces behind organised crime in America are leading members of the ruling group , and the book 's subtitle is ‘ From Petty Crooks to Presidents ’ .
30653	Chambliss 's evidence is based on several years ' participant observation in Seattle .
30654	After ‘ hanging around ’ bars in which gambling , drug and vice connections might be made and being involved with card schools , Chambliss found various contacts with inside knowledge .
30655	It was from these informants that he pieced together a picture of organised crime as being controlled by key personnel in the police force , local government , business and the legal profession .
30656	He goes on to argue that the emergence of organised crime networks is bound to happen in a capitalist system .
30657	Such a system stresses economic self-interest as all-important , rather than community spirit , public duty and so on ; everybody is out for what they can get .
30658	Looking at corporate crime generally , it is noticeable how such crime is greatly under-reported in the media , in comparison with ‘ conventional ’ crime .
30659	The most popular television crime series , such as The Sweeney , Minder , The Professionals , Juliet Bravo , Hill Street Blues , tend not to deal with corporate crime and the business criminal .
30660	As well as being neglected in popular entertainment , this type of crime has also been neglected as an area of study .
30661	It is not difficult to see why corporate crime has not received the same publicity as murder , robbery , theft , rape and so on — both in the mass media and in the study of crime .
30662	Corporate crime is not visible in the way that ‘ conventional ’ crime is , due to the complex nature of such crime and the ineffective laws and minimal punishments associated with it .
30663	Moreover , those who suffer from the effects of corporate crime , the victims , tend to remain unaware that they have been victimised .
30664	Their misfortune is often put down to being ‘ no one 's fault , or an accident .
30665	In his recent study of the links between power and crime , Box states that corporate crime is crime committed for the corporate organisation and not against it ( Box , 1983 ) .
30666	Thus , employee theft , including crimes of fraud against one 's employer and embezzlement , are not included in his discussion of corporate crime .
30667	Corporate crime , then , refers to illegal acts ( including acts of omission ) of an individual or group within a legitimate formal organisation which are in accordance with the goals of that organisation .
30668	They must have some detrimental effect , either physical or economic , on employees , consumers or the general public .
30669	That definition , which is taken from Box 's study , is rather long-winded , but corporate crime is a complex issue .
30670	The easiest way to understand the nature and extent of this type of crime is to look at some examples of the effect of specific corporate crimes .
30671	Firstly , we should make the point that crime does not have to be intentional .
30672	Very serious consequences can and do follow from people or organisations being indifferent to the results of their actions .
30673	Indifference rather than intention may be the cause of greater human suffering , particularly with regard to corporate crime .
30674	It could be argued , in fact , that being indifferent to the consequences of one 's actions indicates a high degree of contempt for ( other ) people .
30675	It is important to realise that the law-breaking of large businesses and corporations can have severe consequences .
30676	It does not just refer to ‘ sharp business practices ’ and people making slightly greater profits than they should .
30677	There are numerous cases of corporate crime causing injury and death .
30678	To cite one example given by Box :
30679	Early in 1979 , fifty people lost their lives as a result of an explosion aboard the tanker Betelgeuse whilst it was anchored at Bantry Bay in County Cork .
30680	An Inquiry headed by an Irish High Court Judge , Mr Justice Declan Costello , firmly placed the responsibility for this on two corporations , Total and Gulf , who deliberately decided not to carry out necessary repair work costing a mere £130,000 because they intended to sell the tanker .
30681	It is very difficult to assess accurately the costs of corporate crime .
30682	The economic costs are almost incomprehensibly large .
30683	It is not easy to grasp the financial significance of organisations diluting their products , for instance , so that many millions of customers are paying a few pence extra for their goods .
30684	While the few pence — or less — extra for the individual customer might seem insignificant , an organisation may be making a massive illegal profit .
30685	All studies of the economic costs of corporate crime agree that individuals are deprived of far more money by such crime than by the more conventional crimes of robbery and theft .
30686	There are also social costs which are , again , immeasurable .
30687	As well as corporate crime undermining the public 's faith in the business world , it is also likely that crimes of bribery and corruption by large corporations affect the poorer , less powerful sections of society more than other sections .
30688	Powerful business institutions operate in a way that ensures their interests are given priority , rather than the interests of the less powerful sectors of the community .
30689	In general terms , then , corporate crime involves robbing the poor to benefit the rich .
30690	It rewards those who put self-interest ahead of the public interest .
30691	Of course , corporate crime is actually carried out by individuals ; organisations can not themselves plan and commit crimes .
30692	Businessmen who commit corporate crime are not forced to do so .
30693	They will be able to weigh up the advantages of breaking a law and not doing so ; and they will tend to choose the former path if it seems likely to secure economic and career advancement .
30694	One corporate lawyer said that he went along with producing false insurance policies without thinking anything of it , ‘ It was something the company needed done , that 's all ’ .
30695	There are instances where individuals are caught between their conscience and the corporate policy , and occasionally between their conscience and their jobs .
30696	In explaining why he had gone along with ‘ doctoring ’ data so as to secure a contract deadline , a supervisor pointed out , ‘ If I refused to take part in the fraud , I would have to either resign or be fired ’ .
30697	With regard to the control of corporate crime , there is little to deter the corporate criminal .
30698	Many such crimes are looked into by special regulatory bodies rather than the police .
30699	In the UK , there are factory inspectorates , railway inspectorates , monopolies and mergers commissions .
30700	Although such bodies have the power to recommend criminal prosecution , they are mainly concerned with the inspection and regulation of organisations .
30701	There is a fraud squad within the police force , but the majority of their work is concerned with employee theft rather than crimes committed by and for business organisations .
30702	Furthermore , the typical penalties for those individuals and organisations who are found guilty of corporate crime do little to deter the would-be criminal .
30703	In addition , the skilful corporate law-breaker or law-bender will often be able to discover new schemes to avoid or get round criminal laws that are introduced to regulate particular corporate activities .
30704	Laws introduced to regulate corporate behaviour differ from most criminal laws in that they do not centre on the results of the breaking of the particular regulation .
30705	To give an example , a company was found responsible for a hoist accident at a power station in Kent in 1978 in which four people died and five were seriously injured .
30706	However , the company was not prosecuted for the fact that four people died , but because the machinery was not properly maintained ; they were fined £5,000 .
30707	In conventional crime one is charged with the results of one 's actions .
30708	As Box puts it , a person accused of stabbing someone is not likely just to be charged with ‘ carrying an offensive weapon ’ .
30709	This is not to say that businessmen should be responsible for all the indirect effects of their policies and actions , or that , for example , the individuals in the company responsible for the hoist accident described above should be charged and sentenced for murder .
30710	The point is that as the laws do not focus on the results of corporate crime , the corporate criminal need only worry about relatively lenient punishment for breaking a particular regulation , and not be concerned with the wider consequences of that action .
30711	In concluding his discussion of corporate crime , Box raises the question of whether it can be justified to send thousands of people to prison each year because they are too poor to pay fines ( in 1981 , 20,000 males were imprisoned for defaulting on fine payments ) when their crime is trivial in the extreme in comparison with corporate crime .
30712	While the powerful seem to get away with serious crimes , the powerless commit less serious offences and get prison .
30713	Concluding our discussion of corporate crime , the existence of criminal corporations should also be mentioned .
30714	As well as crime for corporations and crimes against corporations ( employee theft ) , there are corporations deliberately set up for the sole purpose of committing criminal activity .
30715	A study of long-firm fraud , one form of corporate crime , by Levi illustrates this type of criminal activity ( Levi , 1981 ) .
30716	Long-firm fraud : an example of corporate crime
30717	Over the past fifty years there has been a massive expansion in the extent and importance of fraud .
30718	Frauds comprise almost 5% of all recorded indictable ( serious ) crime in England and Wales , compared to only 0.5% in 1928 .
30719	This expansion has imposed a strain on the control of fraud .
30720	In the metropolitan police there is only one fraud squad officer for every hundred officers .
30721	Moreover , fraud trials generally take longer than other criminal trials , due to the sophisticated and complex nature of many frauds , and they often stretch over many months .
30722	Levi defines long-firm fraud as referring to businesses which order substantial quantities of goods on credit at a time when the owners of the business either intend not to pay for them or suspect that they will not be able to pay for them .
30723	The first record of the term ‘ long-firm fraud ’ which Levi uncovers was in a journal of 1869 , while the obtaining of goods under the false pretence that one had an honest and solvent business is an activity with a much longer history .
30724	Long-firm frauds are to be found in most western countries , and are liable to occur wherever there is extensive use of credit in business transactions .
30725	Levi classifies various sub-types of such fraud , although for our purposes we will look at this type of corporate crime in general terms .
30726	The background of long-firm fraudsters is far more varied than is found with convicted criminals as a whole .
30727	They include businessmen who have never before committed any substantial crime ; people who make their living principally from fraud ; and other professional criminals who engage in a range of crimes of which long-firm fraud is one .
30728	The precise details and mechanics of long-firm fraud vary from case to case , and many are exceedingly complex .
30729	The basic pattern nevertheless remains the same .
30730	Looking at an example of one such fraud will indicate this basic procedure .
30731	The success of the fraudster often hinges on the ability to tell a convincing story .
30732	In the 1960s a man with an American accent arrived at a coastal resort in South Wales and announced that he represented an American corporation which wished to purchase a leisure and amusement arcade in the town .
30733	He offered a generous price which the owners of the arcade accepted .
30734	However , he explained that the money was temporarily tied up .
30735	While waiting for this money to come through , he asked the owners if they would allow him to order goods for the coming summer season .
30736	They agreed to this and even gave him their headed notepaper to use in ordering .
30737	He wrote to various suppliers implying that he owned the arcade and obtained around £350,000 worth of goods on credit .
30738	One night all these goods were secretly taken away and disappeared for good .
30739	The man 's identity has never been discovered .
30740	In order to become a successful fraudster , these skills of being able to present a convincing front and remain calm under pressure have to become almost second nature .
30741	As we suggested above , long-firm frauds can be carried out by people who have no social or business contact with the criminal fraternity .
30742	Like most upper-class criminals , the ‘ businessman-fraudster ’ can make large amounts of money from crime without every becoming a known or convicted criminal .
30743	The initial motivations that lead a previously ‘ honest ’ businessman to commit a long-firm fraud are liable to be financial , perhaps a temporary shortage of money .
30744	However , the more or less honest businessman who decides to commit a fraud ‘ just this once ’ may become excited by the fun and challenge of it , as well as by the material pro fits .
30745	The reasons given by those who take part in commercial crime rather than straight business tend to stress the pleasure involved in ‘ trying to beat the system ’ , and the battle of wits with creditors , as well as the pleasure that the proceeds of crime bring .
30746	Fraud is one of the risks which result from the spread of credit .
30747	However , fraud is only a minor commercial risk for most suppliers of goods and credit .
30748	It does not deter firms from supplying on credit , and there is always insurance cover to fall back on .
30749	Thus , although there has been an extension of fraud as credit facilities have expanded , this has not affected the central principle on which the regulation of fraud is based — that at all costs ‘ free enterprise ’ should not be discouraged by fear of prosecution .
30750	The result of this is that the law relating to fraud and commercial affairs in general is strictly limited in its scope .
30751	Long-firm fraudsters seem to get treated more leniently by the police and the legal system than do ‘ conventional ’ criminals .
30752	Moreover , the complex nature of many frauds makes it difficult for the police to prepare a sound case .
30753	As one officer said to Levi : ‘ If we nicked everybody we thought might have done a long-firm , we 'd never finish our paperwork , the cases might never come to court , and if they did , they 'd never have the room to try them . ’
30754	As far as sentencing is concerned it would seem to be the case that long-firm fraudsters are sentenced on the basis that they are business law-breakers rather than ‘ villains ’ .
30755	Judges might find it easier to sympathise with and understand such law-breakers in comparison to other types of criminal .
30756	Furthermore , there is no shocked outcry from the mass media if such criminals are given relatively minor sentences .
30757	The amount of time that even ‘ professional ’ long-firm fraudsters spend in prison is remarkably small in relation to the generally large amounts of money that are obtained from such frauds ( Reading 5 , Chapter 5 , taken from Levi 's study , looks at the long-firm fraudster and imprisonment ) .
30758	‘ Fiddling at work ’ : employee theft
30759	In this section we have concentrated on one type of white-collar crime , corporate crime .
30760	Before concluding , it would be useful to refer to the more common crime of employee theft , ‘ fiddling at work ’ .
30761	Clearly , the nature oft heft will vary with different types of employment .
30762	To gain an impression of the extent of employee theft , we will look at a study of fiddling and pilferage at a medium-sized factory-production bakery in south-east England , undertaken by Jason Ditton ( 1977 ) .
30763	The idea that everyone ‘ makes a bit on the side ’ and ‘ has their little perks ’ was prevalent throughout the factory .
30764	As the night manager said , ‘ You 've got to allow for losses … you get the odd loaf taken home and not paid for ’ .
30765	But always there is the implication that , ‘ we all make a bit on the side … know what I mean ? ’ .
30766	Ditton worked in the bakery over vacations for a few years and reckoned that each man had an illegal income of about 10 per cent of his bread sales , very little of which appeared as a loss in the firm 's financial records .
30767	Rather than assuming that a few corrupt workers steal large amounts , it would seem more reasonable to contend that many , if not the majority , of employees regularly take small amounts .
30768	An American firm which used lie detectors on 1400 employees found that 62 per cent admitted petty theft before the tests were administered and a further 14 per cent after .
30769	This finding has been supported by various other firms and factories .
30770	To return to Ditton 's study , skill at fiddling customers was a major criteria or unofficial status among the bread salesmen .
30771	This fiddling included overcharging , increasing the price of bread to unknowing customers , and keeping the price the same but reducing the size of the bread delivery .
30772	Also , the salesmen distinguished between those on their rounds who should not be fiddled ( such as disabled people , ex-salesmen ) and those who qualified as ‘ fair game ’ .
30773	This distinction can be seen as allowing the salesmen to defend themselves through providing a justification for fiddling .
30774	Of course , this is common to many criminals who define the victim of their criminality as being rich enough to withstand the loss .
30775	It is almost a Robin Hood notion : ‘ you do n't feel so guilty with big stores … they allow wastage ’ .
30776	Generally , most of the men did feel some guilt and disliked fiddling , but said , ‘ I do n't like it but I have to ’ .
30777	On the other hand , this guilt is reduced by counter accusations of ‘ they deserve it ’ and the like .
30778	Furthermore , maxims such as ‘ look after number one ’ and ‘ it 's a dog eat dog world ’ are taken by fiddlers as principles for action .
30779	If it is discovered , employee theft is one of the least stigmatised of crimes .
30780	In Ditton 's study , the majority of offenders were dealt with quickly and leniently — ‘ Put that bloody loaf down ’ or ‘ Do n't you try and fiddle me ’ being examples of reactions .
30781	The workers who were fiddling at this particular factory were able to keep their self-image and conduct their working lives as good citizens ; like most unconvicted white-collar criminals they were not stigmatised .
30782	Two extracts from Mars ' recent study of workplace crime which illustrate the wide range of fiddling at work are included as readings in Chapter 5 ( Readings 6 and 7 ) .
30783	Crime as a male phenomenon
30784	Here we will examine the supposition — supported by statistics on sex differences in crime — that crime is characteristically a male activity .
30785	We will look at sociological explanations for the under-representation of females in criminal activity .
30786	Table 3.1 below shows the ratio of females to males convicted for certain crimes and makes clear the male domination of criminality .
30787	Only in the crime of shoplifting does the ratio of females convicted even approach that of males .
30788	While the vast majority of offenders are men , a small proportion are women .
30789	It is sometimes claimed that female criminal activity is restricted to limited types of crimes .
30790	However , women do in fact contribute to all kinds of offences .
30791	The most common offences for both sexes are crimes against property , with shoplifting being regarded as the ‘ typical ’ female offence ( although adolescent males also indulge in this particular form of crime in significantly high numbers ) .
30792	Women tend to commit few crimes of violence , and those which do occur are mainly committed within the confines of the family .
30793	We will break down and discuss two basic , possible explanations for these marked differences between the crime figures for men and women : firstly , that women do not indulge in criminality to the same extent as men ; secondly , that female crime is greatly underestimated by the statistics , in other words there is more female crime than the statistics indicate .
30794	Women do not indulge in criminality to the same extent as men
30795	Biological and Psychological arguments
30796	These arguments suggest that the biological and/or psychological make-up of women does not predispose them to criminality to the same extent as men .
30797	Until recently differences in the rate of crime between the sexes was generally explained as being due to biological or psychological differences .
30798	Lombroso , whose somewhat bizarre theories of crime and criminals we looked at in Chapter Two , claimed that ‘ a delinquent woman is more unnatural than a delinquent man ’ .
30799	He argued that criminals were physically distinguishable by , for example , large jaws , high cheek bones , extra toes and so on .
30800	He found fewer of these traits in women , which led him to assert that women are ‘ congenitally less inclined to crime than men ’ .
30801	Furthermore , women who did commit crime were seen as not feminine .
30802	He suggested that women are by nature passive and therefore less inclined to crime than men — although such a suggestion does not take account of the fact that by no means all crimes involve violence .
30803	Lombroso 's work is dated ( The Female Offender by Lombroso and Ferrero was originally published in 1895 ) and largely discredited .
30804	However , the biological argument that women are naturally averse to crime and that female criminals are in some way maladjusted has never been fully abandoned .
30805	A series of studies , usually by men , have argued that the female biology determines their temperament or personality , and makes women more passive and timid .
30806	Female criminals are often seen as suffering from some physical or mental pathology ( disease ) and the courts still accept the arguments , that female offenders have biological problems , with the menopause , pregnancy , pre-menstrual tension and so on regularly used as explanations or excuses for their criminality .
30807	There is little evidence to support such explanations , which are insulting to women in that they are viewed as faulty biological mechanisms which spend some of their time malfunctioning .
30808	There are a number of problems to be found in the attempts to explain the low level of female crime as being due to physical or mental maladjustment .
30809	The female personality is not biologically determined , as researches in different cultures have shown .
30810	The female ( and male ) personality and behaviour is culturally determined , through the socialisation process .
30811	Moreover , these interpretations emphasise too heavily individual rather than social causes of crime and delinquency .
30812	They tend to restrict the causes of criminality to hereditary characteristics and overlook the effects of environmental influences and cultural traditions .
30813	Finally , as we have shown earlier , what is defined as criminal varies across time and place , thus making it difficult to argue that in-built differences between the sexes can explain what is a variable phenomena .
30814	patterns of socialisation and social control
30815	The basic argument with which we are concerned here is that the low level of female crime is a result of the expectations and constraints that are placed on women by society .
30816	Traditionally , women have been viewed as dependent and passive , and males as aggressive and assertive .
30817	The socialisation process tends to emphasise these conventional views .
30818	This is especially the case among the working classes in that working-class females most strongly represent and support traditional sex roles .
30819	A study of working-class girls by Sue Sharpe demonstrated that their main aims and priorities were to marry , have children and settle down ( Sharpe , 1976 ) .
30820	Moves toward emancipation and liberation started , and have largely remained , with middle-class women .
30821	Different role expectations for men and women lead to different patterns and practices of socialisation .
30822	Men , rather than women , learn the skills necessary for certain types of criminal activity .
30823	Boys learn how to fight and handle guns , and have the strength required to break into houses .
30824	Burglary , for example , is an untypical female crime , as it requires the criminal to be out alone on the streets at night , and to possess ‘ masculine ’ skills such as the ability to force an entry .
30825	Linked with socialisation is social control .
