30826	There is often stronger social control evident in the socialisation of girls in comparison to boys .
30827	Girls are expected to conform to a stricter morality , by their parents in particular .
30828	They are likely to be allowed less freedom to go out on the streets and stay out late .
30829	It is argued that this is a significant factor in reducing the likelihood of girls joining delinquent groups .
30830	Thus .
30831	adolescent boys are out on the streets and more likely to join gangs , and this is where they can become involved in minor law-breaking which may lead to more serious criminality .
30832	If it is more heavily impressed on girls that certain types of behaviour are wrong , then they will tend to feel greater apprehension and guilt if they are tempted by delinquent or criminal activities .
30833	The basic argument is that the more adolescents are supervised by their parents and , perhaps , their teachers , the less likely they are to become involved with or influenced by delinquent contemporaries and delinquent values .
30834	Girls are generally more closely controlled and supervised by their parents .
30835	Hoffman-Bustamente has argued that these differing patterns of socialisation and social control for boys and girls have tended to concentrate those women who do break the law into certain categories of offence .
30836	In particular , criminal behaviour in women tends to involve non-violent crimes which do not involve the use of physical strength or agility , since women have not been ‘ trained ’ to develop such skills ( Hoffman-Bustamente D.Y. , ‘ The nature of female criminality ’ , Issues in Criminology 8 , 2 , 1973 ) .
30837	It may be that with greater equality and emancipation the proportion of female criminals will rise .
30838	As women take greater advantage of educational and occupational opportunities so sex differences in the level of criminal activity may diminish .
30839	If this does occur there is a danger that womens ' movements will be blamed for the rise in the female crime rate , and that this may be used to argue against further female emancipation .
30840	Certainly , there is evidence that the number of women convicted of assaults , woundings and violent crime has risen over the last two decades .
30841	Generally , there has been a rise in the female crime rate , especially in the 14–21 age group .
30842	However , such statistics can be misleading .
30843	It could be that teenage girls nowadays act in a more self-confident manner , and that this fuels notions that they are becoming more violent .
30844	This then becomes a self-fulfilling prophecy , police officers , magistrates and social workers will be more likely to be stricter with female offenders ; and thus more females will be convicted of crimes .
30845	Although there is no evidence that liberation has led to greater female criminality , such a view is widely held and has been strongly expressed in the popular press .
30846	The Sun reported a ‘ Crime Wave of the ‘ Lib' ’ Girls ' ( 1 September , 1975 ) , while the Daily Mail claimed that ‘ Women 's Lib ‘ ‘ pushes up crime'' ’ ( 1 February , 1980 ) .
30847	But it is not just the popular press who have argued such a case .
30848	For example The Sunday Times has asserted that , ‘ In recent years we 've experienced a new , aggressive , liberated criminality in women ’ ( 30 March , 1980 ) .
30849	There is not doubt that the behaviour of the police and the courts , as well as the wider public , will be influenced by their image of female crime .
30850	If this image has changed because of the way the media has portrayed female crime , and linked liberation with violent crime , then women are liable to be treated more severely by the police and the courts .
30851	This will , of course , push up the female crime figures .
30852	Opportunities for crime
30853	Differing roles without society limit or increase opportunities to commit crime .
30854	It is still the case that the majority of girls do not see themselves as primarily workers or careerists .
30855	As was suggested above , girls have been socialised into viewing work as secondary to marriage and child-rearing .
30856	If women 's careers and position in society generally con fine them to the home , they will have less opportunity to commit crimes which are associated with work , such as fraud .
30857	Employee theft , after all , is impossible if one is not employed .
30858	Because women are largely con fined to jobs with low status and power , they will be relatively less able to engage in serious forms of white-collar and corporate crime .
30859	In addition , the fact that women are less mobile than men and more confined to the home means that they are less likely to be exposed to situations which lack effective informal social controls .
30860	In areas where women have similar opportunities to men they appear as likely to break laws .
30861	The high incidence of shoplifting among women , for example , reflects the day-to-day activities in which female criminality is liable to be expressed .
30862	In the world of organised , professional crime , sex-segregation is the norm .
30863	Women are likely to be viewed in terms of traditional sex-role stereotypes , as unreliable , emotional , illogical and so on .
30864	Moreover , male criminals tend to see the crimes they commit as too dangerous for women , or too difficult , or their masculine pride may not be willing to accept women as organisers of crime , as ‘ bosses ’ .
30865	Female crime is greatly underestimated by the criminal statistics
30866	The issue here is whether the statistics on female crime provide an accurate picture of the actual extent of such crime .
30867	There are a number of points and arguments worth considering .
30868	The more minor crimes are less liable to be known to the police and recorded in the statistics than are serious crimes .
30869	Thus , if women tend to commit more minor crimes , they will have a much better chance of avoiding detection .
30870	With regard to crimes that are known about , the police and courts may be more lenient with female offenders .
30871	For example , when deciding whether to caution , arrest or charge an individual , the police may be influenced by the sex of the offender .
30872	The stereotypical views held by agents of social control will tend to suggest that women are less delinquent and crime-prone than men , that they are not ‘ real ’ criminals .
30873	Females are less likely than males to be labelled as delinquent and to be processed accordingly .
30874	Also , the fact that police officers will know that female crime rates are lower than male crime rates will further incline them to the view that women are not by nature ‘ criminal types ’ .
30875	If women are convicted of crimes in greater numbers ( and , as mentioned , female convictions have increased in recent years ) , it will be interesting to see how the police and the courts react .
30876	The male prison population vastly outnumbers the female ; in 1979 , 143,000 males spent some time in prison , in comparison to 8,000 females .
30877	Thus , if convicted , women are far less likely to be given a custodial sentence .
30878	One reason for this is that more women are first offenders , who are generally treated more leniently .
30879	However , the reluctance of sentencers to imprison women does not seem to be based on any clear principles , given the supposed principle of equality before the law .
30880	An example of this differential sentencing policy was reported in the Guardian 18 August , 1980 , which quoted a male judge , who told a female defendant , ‘ If you were a man I would send you to prison without hesitation ’ .
30881	The more lenient punishments given to women probably reflect a belief that female crime is a result of sickness , of some physical or emotional problem , rather than being rational action with specific , often financial , motives .
30882	In other words , the old view that women 's crime is physically explainable would still appear to be influential , despite the fact that there is no real evidence for such explanations .
30883	Another point to consider in relation to the statistics on female crime is the view that men may adopt a more chivalrous attitude to women , based on misconceptions of women as passive and gentle .
30884	Therefore , the police , magistrates and judges , who are all predominantly male , will tend to leniency .
30885	If a woman is tearful and apologetic and can claim some biological disturbance , then she is not likely to be treated as severely as a man .
30886	So far we have looked at the view that sex differences affect the way in which the police and the courts act toward offenders , and that this enables women to escape criminalisation to a greater extent than men .
30887	However , it has also been argued that women are discriminated against by the agents of the law , just as they are in other areas of life .
30888	It is maintained that the courts , in particular , view young females as in need of ‘ protection ’ .
30889	Thus , young female offenders are more likely to be placed in protective and custodial institutions than are boys whose delinquent or criminal behaviour is similar .
30890	Boys are left in the community because they are not felt to need such protection .
30891	These arguments , however , refer to the less serious , juvenile criminality .
30892	They do not necessarily contradict the view that for more serious crimes women are less severely treated then men .
30893	As we have mentioned , judges , the police and the public may have more difficulty in understanding serious female crime and tend to believe that the woman offender is not really criminal .
30894	Her action is seen as an irrational or emotional response to a particular situation ; she ‘ only did it for love ’ , for example .
30895	Overall , however , the bulk of evidence on female crime suggests that sex plays a relatively minor role in determining the response of the legal system .
30896	There is no clear evidence that women receive massively more favourable treatment from the police or the courts .
30897	Thus , we would suggest that these second types of explanation for the differences in the rate of crime between men and women — that female crime exists to a much greater extent than is indicated by the statistics but is just less often recorded — can not explain the enormous sex differences in recorded rates of crime .
30898	It would appear that the explanation for the strong link between sex and crime must lie in the wider stratification system in society .
30899	Women are far more restricted than men in their access to the reward structure of society , and women are still largely restricted to the private , family sphere .
30900	In contrast , crime , when it is recorded , is a public occurrence .
30901	The continuing importance of sexual divisions in employment and of traditional stereotypes of the woman 's role are central to explanations for sexual divisions in the sphere of criminality .
30902	In this chapter we have looked at specific aspects and illustrations of crime and the study of it .
30903	In the next chapter we will examine in greater detail the statistics on crime .
30904	In doing so we shall return to some of the issues raised above , including the question of class and sex biases in these statistics .
30905	PART 3 Statistical data and documentary readings
30906	Measuring crime : criminal statistics
30907	In popular debate about crime one issue always comes to the fore : how much crime is there in our society , and is it increasing or decreasing ?
30908	To answer these questions people invariably turn to the official criminal statistics which are collected and published by the Home Office .
30909	In this chapter we will examine what these statistics show and discuss the extent to which they provide an accurate picture of the range and extent of criminal behaviour .
30910	Criminal statistics are usually quoted as ‘ hard facts ’ ; that is , they are accepted unquestioningly , and are often used to support the view that there is a rapidly increasing rate of serious crime in modern society .
30911	It is also important to recognise that it is on the basis of these statistics that important decisions are made by governments in relation to their policies towards crime and its treatment .
30912	Decisions concerning the most effective and efficient way of allocating resources ( of money and manpower ) in the attempt to deal with crime-related social problems will be influenced by criminal statistics .
30913	For example , in 1980 the Home Secretary , William Whitelaw , introduced the ‘ short , sharp , shock ’ punishments for young offenders , involving a few months ' strict discipline and almost para-military training in detention centres .
30914	This widely publicised policy was intended to relieve public concern over the rise in violent crimes against persons and property committed by juveniles .
30915	However , the questions we should keep in mind during our examination of criminal statistics are whether they really justify such public concern , and , most importantly , what do they really tell us ?
30916	The first section of the chapter will provide an overview of patterns and trends in criminal behaviour , as indicated by the official criminal statistics .
30917	In the second section problems associated with the use of these statistics will be examined .
30918	The pattern of crime
30919	Broadly speaking , the official statistics indicate that there is an increasing rate of crime , and that the increase has accelerated rapidly in the post-war period , especially since the mid-1950s .
30920	Figure 4.1 summarises the total number of serious offences per 100,000 of the population for the period 1957 to 1977 , and shows a 290 per cent increase over those two decades .
30921	In 1900 the police in England and Wales recorded less than three crimes for every thousand of the population .
30922	By 1974 , however , they recorded four crimes for every hundred of the population — a thirteen-fold increase in seventy odd years ( Radzinowicz , L. and King , J. , The Growth of Crime , 1977 ) .
30923	While this increase is startling , it is worth noting that a concern over ‘ crime waves ’ , and rising levels of juvenile crime in particular , is not a new phenomenon .
30924	In parts of London during the last century , for example , it was certainly not safe to walk the streets at night , with violence and robbery commonplace , as the stories of Charles Dickens illustrate .
30925	So , while criminal statistics have risen substantially , theft and violence is clearly not a modern problem .
30926	So far as the type of crime committed is concerned throughout this century the great bulk of crime has always involved stealing of one kind or another .
30927	Simple theft is still the commonest variety of stealing .
30928	But there have been significant changes in the nature of stealing since the Second World War .
30929	In particular , there has been a major and disproportionate increase in shoplifting ( 3 per cent of theft in 1945 , compared with 14 per cent in 1978 ) and in thefts from , and of , motor vehicles .
30930	Crimes of violence comprise less than 4 per cent of recorded crime , and while crimes of violence have risen rapidly in numbers in the post-war period there have been changes in the pattern of such offences .
30931	In 1945 , 28 per cent of violent crimes against the person were of the most serious nature — such as serious wounding or homicide — but by 1975 this proportion had dropped to 9 per cent , and by 1979 to 6 per cent .
30932	The main factor causing this redistribution seems to have been a massive increase in non-serious wounding .
30933	Thus , it is indisputable that the volume of recorded crime has risen .
30934	However , the statistics indicate that criminal activity is not randomly distributed throughout the whole population , and we need to examine the social incidence of recorded crime .
30935	According to the figures , the people most likely to commit criminal offences in Britain live in urban areas , are young , male and working class .
30936	We will look briefly at each of these elements in turn .
30937	Urban/rural differences
30938	The crime rate is higher in urban areas than it is in rural areas , and the larger the urban area the greater the crime rate is .
30939	Thus , London and other large cities have higher rates of crime per 100,000 of population than do smaller and medium-sized towns .
30940	However , although the rates of crime in the large cities have always exceeded the rates in rural areas , the increase in crime rates this century has been a universal phenomenon .
30941	In other words , there has been a large proportional increase in recorded crime in all parts of the country , as Table 4.1 illustrates .
30942	The figures shows an increase in crime rates for all areas , yet there are curious differences in the extent and timing of the change in such rates in different police forces .
30943	The crime rate in Liverpool/ Bootle in 1921 and 1931 was several times the rate in Manchester/ Salford , for example , but the massive increases in that area between 1938 and 1971 put it above the Liverpool area by 1971 .
30944	Students might find it useful to examine and discuss the figures in Table 4.1 ; it should be born in mind , however , that definitions of indictable crimes have changed over time , as we mentioned in Chapter 1 .
30945	In spite of the variations , crime rates are significantly higher in urban areas than in rural areas .
30946	This might be the result of a number of factors , assuming , of course , that urban dwellers are not inherently more devious and criminal than rural dwellers :
30947	THE ROLE OF OPPORTUNITY
30948	Large urban areas afford greater opportunities for criminal activity with the presence of large department stores , warehouses , financial institutions , large car parks and so on .
30949	THE CHARACTERISTICS OF THE COMMUNITY
30950	It is likely to be easier to commit crime in urban areas in that it is easier to be unnoticed and to remain anonymous in such areas .
30951	In rural areas there is a tendency for many of the inhabitants to know one another ; strangers are highly visible and liable to cause suspicion .
30952	In urban areas , therefore , the effectiveness of informal social control is reduced .
30953	In rural areas it might be that people will tell the parents of youths whom they see committing some offence ; and although crimes may be committed they will often be dealt with informally and so will not figure in the criminal statistics .
30954	POLICE PROCEDURE
30955	In rural areas the police tend to be more integrated with the community .
30956	They are more likely to know offenders personally , or to know their families , and thus to warn rather than ‘ book ’ offenders .
30957	This is , of course , only a tendency , and the move away from local policemen to larger , centralised policing may reduce this effect .
30958	Reading 9 in Chapter 5 , from Cain 's study of rural and urban police forces , illustrates very distinctly the differing styles of policing in different areas .
30959	Age Differences
30960	In both sexes criminal activity appears to peak in adolescence and early adulthood — between the ages of 14 , and younger , and 21 .
30961	In 1977 , 8 per cent of males aged 14 to under 17 were found guilty of , or cautioned for , offences ; in comparison with 0.7 per cent of the 30+ age group .
30962	Similarly , in 1977 , 1.6 per cent of females aged 14 to under 17 were found guilty of , or cautioned for , offences ; in comparison with 0.2 per cent of females in the 30+ age group .
30963	This does not mean that people become more honest as they grow older .
30964	It is more likely that the types of crime committed by older people will be less noticed and less liable to be recorded in the criminal statistics .
30965	Older people spend less time out of the house , on the street where the bulk of criminal activity occurs .
30966	To take a somewhat simplistic example , stealing low-priced goods from shops is more likely to be reported than stealing goods of equal value from one 's place of work .
30967	Having said that , as the figures given above indicate , the younger age groups , the 14 to under 17 's followed closely by the 17 to under 21's , contain far higher proportions of people who are found guilty of , or cautioned for , criminal offences than do older age groups .
30968	With regard to theft , for example , in 1970 38 per cent of persons convicted of theft were juveniles ( that is , under 17 ) .
30969	However , a couple of points should be made about these statistics .
30970	Firstly , the peak age for conviction is around the school-leaving age and the likelihood of conviction after that age declines ; and , secondly , a very significant proportion of the offences committed by juveniles are very trivial — stealing milk bottles for example .
30971	It is popularly held that juvenile delinquency is on the increase .
30972	Certainly there have been fears in the media over a ‘ new school-age crime wave ’ .
30973	Recent statistics issued by the Metropolitan Police indicated that a quarter of all serious crimes in Greater London are committed by school-children .
30974	One arrest in four is of persons aged 10–16 years and half of all arrests are of persons under 21 years .
30975	As we have already pointed out , the crime rate in general is increasing for all age groups , and there is little evidence that juvenile criminality is increasing at a very much greater rate than crime in general .
30976	Between 1959 and 1977 the number of offences per 100,000 of the population for males aged 14 to under 17 increased by 148 per cent , compared to a rise of 136 per cent for males aged 21 and over — hardly a massive difference .
30977	What seems to have happened over the last twenty years or so is that a higher proportion of juveniles are being dealt with officially by the police rather than being dealt with unofficially or warned .
30978	Thus higher proportions of juveniles are figuring in the criminal statistics .
30979	Sex differences
30980	Criminal statistics in all countries have consistently shown that more males than females appear before the courts and are convicted for criminal activities .
30981	Of all offenders found guilty , in all courts , both magistrate and crown courts , females make up approximately 11 per cent of the total ( magistrate courts deal with relatively minor crimes and civil actions , whereas the more serious indictable offences , which can be tried by jury , are dealt with by crown courts ) .
30982	Females make up an even smaller proportion of the prison population in this country , between 3 and 4 per cent at any one time .
30983	Furthermore , 12 per cent of males compared to 2 per cent of females are found guilty of , or cautioned for , criminal offences by the age of 17 .
30984	Statistics also show that while the crime rate has increased regularly for all groups , the rise in female crime has been far steeper than the rise in male crime .
30985	Between 1959 and 1977 , the number of female offenders per 100,000 of the population aged 14 to under 17 increased by 379 per cent ( compared to a 148 per cent increase for males of the same age group ) .
30986	For females aged over 21 there was a 281 per cent increase ( compared to 136 per cent for males of the same age group ) .
30987	Although male offenders still heavily outnumber female offenders , these changes have led to an alteration in the male-female ratio for crime and delinquency .
30988	Figure 4.2 shows the changed male-female ratio for the 14 to 17 age group .
30989	In 1957 the ratio was 10.79 to 1 , but by 1977 it had fallen to 4.97 to 1 .
30990	In Chapter 3 , we looked at explanations for the differences in male and female criminality .
30991	This section has just presented some statistical data on such differences .
30992	Class differences
30993	The fourth element in the pattern of criminal statistics is that recorded crime is largely a working-class phenomenon .
30994	Although crime occurs across all social classes , and is not just restricted to individuals from working-class backgrounds , official statistics show a clear link between social class and crime .
30995	It has been a long and widely held assumption that crime is very much more frequent among those of low social status .
30996	Furthermore , this presumed strong association between crime and social class has been the basis for most of the leading sociological theories of crime .
30997	In our discussion of theories of crime , in Chapter Two , we examined various theoretical approaches which centred on class differences in crime and , in particular , juvenile delinquency .
30998	For example , the Functionalist-based theories see crime and delinquency as a response to frustrations arising from lower social position and status .
30999	Although a range of sociological theories has suggested that crime is due to deprivation of one sort or another , it is worth stressing that many middle-class children also engage in delinquent behaviour .
31000	A national survey in 1979 found that whereas 22 per cent of boys from ‘ lower-manual ’ families had been convicted for criminal offences , only 4 per cent of boys from ‘ upper-middle ’ families had been .
31001	This does not necessarily mean that working-class boys commit more delinquencies , but that they are more likely to fall foul of the legal system .
31002	While these figures refer to crimes committed by juveniles , they do give a good indication of the extent of class differences in crime statistics generally , given the high proportion of offenders who are juveniles .
31003	It might be that the reason working-class criminals far outnumber middle-class criminals ( proportionately , given that there are more working-class people in this country ) is because middle-class crimes are less regularly recorded and middle-class offenders are less severely punished .
31004	This issue of whether there is differential treatment accorded to working and middle-class crime and criminals will be examined in the next section of this chapter .
31005	The statistical evidence therefore suggests there is some association between crime and social class .
31006	But whilst this association is most noticeable between the extremes of the social class scale , it is far less marked between the middle groups .
31007	The national survey referred to above , for instance , found that both the ‘ lower-middle ’ and ‘ upper-manual ’ groups had the same rates of delinquency — 12 per cent .
31008	One final point on the relationship of social class to crime : it may not be low social class in itself which is associated with crime , but rather that low social class is liable to be linked with other factors , perhaps parental criminality , deprivation or inadequacy of some kind , which might predispose individuals brought up in certain social classes toward criminality .
31009	Having given a brief overview of the social incidence , or the pattern of recorded crime , we will turn now to some of the problems involved in the use of criminal statistics .
31010	A critique of official criminal statistics
31011	Official crime figures provide a classic example of why social scientists should treat statistics on social problems with suspicion .
31012	As a general point , statistics are social products , in that they are produced for organisations and governments .
31013	They are often organised and structured in the interests of influential and powerful bodies in order to make a particular point , perhaps to make a case for more money or resources , or to show a particular body or organisation in a good light .
31014	Although the validity of official crime statistics has been questioned and doubted , they nevertheless provide an important basis for people 's ideas about crime and criminals .
31015	But in fact there are two major and important deficiencies with them .
31016	Firstly , there is the problem of omissions : only a proportion of crimes and offenders are included in the official figures .
31017	Secondly , there is the problem of bias — in that those crimes and offenders included in the statistics might not be a representative picture of all crime and of all offenders .
31018	We will consider , firstly , the question of omission ; then we will examine the issues concerned with bias in the statistics ; and thirdly we will look at attempts to overcome some of the problems with the official criminal statistics .
31019	The ‘ dark figure ’ of unrecorded crime
31020	Criminal acts are defined by the Home Office as ‘ those acts against the law for which the offender is caught , tried and found guilty ’ .
31021	This obviously represents only a proportion of criminal activity in Britain since a number of crimes remain undetected and a number of offenders are not convicted .
31022	In particular , criminal statistics only show what police forces record , and the police clearly can not be expected to record the numerous offences which they do not know about .
31023	Criminal statistics , therefore , only indicate the crimes that are reported to the police and recorded by them as crimes .
31024	On top of this , there also exists what is termed a ‘ dark figure ’ of unrecorded crime .
31025	The bulk of this non-recording is due to crime not being reported to the police .
31026	However , it is also the case that not all events reported to the police as crimes are treated by them , and recorded , as crimes .
31027	A significant proportion of crime reports are subsequently written off as ‘ no crimes ’ .
31028	Furthermore , the role of the police is crucial in determining whether offences that they do know about are proceeded against .
31029	It is the police who have to decide whether the unruly pickets or drug users they pick up are prosecuted ; and if the police took every offender to court the legal system would not be able to cope .
31030	Thus recorded crime can only be seen as an indication of criminal activity .
31031	One Chief Constable has estimated that only about 10 per cent of all crime is reported to the police .
31032	As you might expect , a much higher proportion of serious crime is liable to be reported to the police and thus recorded .
31033	The reporting rate , and the detection rate , for murder is over 90 per cent , and for serious assault over 80 per cent .
31034	Such crimes are , by their very nature , difficult to hide , and they are crimes to which the police will devote great effort and resources to solve and ‘ clear up ’ .
31035	In contrast , petty theft has a very low rate of reporting to the police , and a low detection rate .
31036	Therefore , the degree to which official statistics underestimate the actual level of crime depends on the particular category of crime .
31037	Almost all cars that are stolen are reported for the simple reason that that is the only way owners will get insurance compensation ; and insurance is often a major reason for reporting other thefts and burglary .
31038	So the extension of insurance provision has led to a greater likelihood of the reporting of many crimes .
31039	There are a number of reasons why crimes are not reported to the police and thus not recorded in the official criminal statistics .
31040	Below we will suggest and discuss some of these reasons .
31041	Before reading through these suggestions you might like to jot down some of your own ideas , or to discuss possible explanations with colleagues .
31042	This list is by no means exhaustive and is only intended to illustrate some of the most commonplace reasons for the non-reporting of crime .
31043	Firstly , many crimes do not have victims , and only the offender(s) will know that a crime has been committed — for example , illegal drug use and supply , soliciting by prostitutes or illegal abortion ( here we are talking about victims in the conventional sense of a separate and visible victim , although it could be argued that the user of illegal drugs is a victim him or herself , or that the unborn foetus is a victim in the case of illegal abortion ) .
31044	These ‘ victimless ’ crimes often involve one party or individual providing a service which the other party wants .
31045	In the examples given above neither of the parties involved would inform the police ; consequently the true numbers of such crimes are never known to the police .
31046	The extent to which these crimes are known and recorded will depend almost entirely on police activity and efficiency .
31047	Secondly , embarrassment may be a reason for not reporting a crime ; victims may want to hide an offence rather than report it .
31048	This is particularly the case with victims of sexual offences .
31049	Rape victims , for example , may fear the consequences of reporting the act , and may not wish to be cross-examined by the police or in court and be exposed to possible innuendoes and suggestions that they ‘ encouraged ’ their assailant .
31050	Recent court cases where the victims of rape have been seen by judges as contributing to the crime through their ‘ negligence ’ — for example hitch-hiking alone — are not likely to act as an encouragement for other victims to report such offences .
31051	Thus , very serious crimes might go unrecorded .
31052	Similarly , parents of children who have been victims of sexual offences may not want their child to be interrogated and to go through the trauma of reliving the experience in court .
31053	Thirdly , and linked with the above point , it is sometimes not in the best interest of the victim to report a crime to the police .
31054	Firms may not wish to prosecute an employee who has been fiddling them but may prefer to deal with the matter informally , to avoid bad publicity or appearing inefficient and the Possible loss of the confidence of their clients .
31055	Fourthly , victims may feel that there is no point in informing the police , because there is no chance of getting retribution .
31056	Minor thefts , for example , may not be reported as the victims feel there is little chance of them getting their goods back or of the offender getting caught .
31057	Fifthly , victims or witnesses of crimes may dislike of not trust the police .
31058	Crimes among criminals are not likely to be reported to the police for obvious reasons .
31059	In a similar vein , victims or witnesses may sympathise with the offender , or be unwilling to inform on a member of their family or a friend .
31060	Another reason for the non-reporting of crime is that many victims are unaware that they actually are victims of specific crimes .
31061	Firms may be unaware of theft by their employees , and shops will not be aware of particular instances of shoplifting .
31062	Such actions are commonly built into firms ' and shops ' accounting procedures , as ‘ stock shrinkage ’ perhaps .
31063	Thus , an unknown but potentially vast amount of crime remains unknown to the police , and is therefore not included in official criminal statistics .
31064	Furthermore , even when examining recorded crimes only , changes in the figures may be accounted for by reasons other than the fact that the actual number of offences have changed , and there are a variety of other ways in which an increase in recorded crime can be accounted for .
31065	Below we will suggest and examine a number of possible reasons or explanations .
31066	Again , our list is not intended to be exhaustive and you might try to suggest other potential reasons .
31067	Firstly , improved police efficiency will affect the rate of recorded crime .
31068	Better police equipment might lead to more offences being recorded , as might an increase in police numbers , and over the last few years there has been a recruitment drive by the police .
31069	Secondly , and linked with this point , criminal statistics reflect the intensity of law enforcement itself .
31070	The police may respond to pressure to concentrate their time and resources on certain specific areas of criminal activity , often areas which have received heavy coverage in the mass media , such as football hooliganism or drug use .
31071	In such circumstances the figures for those activities will rise as a result of the police having spent more time and money in dealing with them .
31072	Thirdly , an increased willingness on the part of the public to report offences will influence the statistics .
31073	There may , for example , be changes in public opinion towards the police and the reporting of criminal activity .
31074	It is also relevant to add that it has become increasingly easy to report matters to the police as a result of the spread of private telephones .
31075	A fourth and very important influence on the rate of recorded crime is the effect of changes in the law , which may lead to an alteration in the definition of what is or is not a crime .
31076	In general terms , there are far more laws in operation today than in the past , thus there are more laws to be broken .
31077	So legal changes , not merely changes in behaviour , will be reflected in the statistics .
31078	On this point , a central problem with criminal statistics is that they only cover what is officially defined as crime at any one time .
31079	Thus new definitions of crime and new laws raise problems in the comparison of statistics on a ‘ before and after ’ basis , and thereby lead to problems in talking about rises or falls in crime .
31080	Fifthly , there are greater opportunities for crime in modern society .
31081	For example , the huge increase in the number of motor vehicles has led to a massive increase in auto-crimes .
31082	The growth of self-service stores since the Second World War has been important in encouraging shoplifting .
31083	It is likely that certain crimes have increased not because people have become more dishonest but because it has become easier to commit such crimes .
31084	Similarly , the much greater availability of illegal drugs has led to a phenomenal growth in drug offences .
31085	A final possible reason — which relates to police practice — is that individual police officers may feel under pressure to make arrests in order to appear efficient and to get on .
31086	As a young policewoman interviewed as part of a recent study on Merseyside 's police said , ‘ It 's always at the back of your mind , you just ca n't get rid of it .
31087	Oh hell , I 've got to do somebody .
31088	I 've got my progress ( report ) due ’ .
31089	( McClure , J. , Spike Island , 1981 ) .
31090	So the more closely one looks at the criminal statistics the more complicated and problematic they become .
31091	And the more dubious must we be of sweeping generalisations made on the basis of such statistics .
31092	It may be that we are becoming a more ‘ criminal ’ nation as the increase in crime rates would suggest , but this can not just be assumed and it is important to be aware of other possible reasons for such an increase .
31093	At the same time it is obvious that full enforcement of the law would be totally impractical .
31094	The police have to exert some discretion .
31095	If the police recorded and acted on every offence they knew about , they would be overwhelmed with paperwork and the courts would be flooded with cases .
31096	The police officer on patrol has to ask whether it is worth proceeding with and against every suspect , and will often decide it is not worth it .
31097	One of the arguments we will examine below is the view that the police use this discretion , this freedom to decide when to proceed and when not to , to favour ‘ respectable ’ and middle-class individuals rather than working-class individuals .
31098	The middle-class bias in statistics
31099	As well as questioning the validity and use of official criminal statistics , more fundamental questions as to their meaning and implications have also been raised .
31100	There is no doubt for one thing , that these statistics are incomplete .
31101	In developing theories of crime this would not necessarily be important if the figures gave a representative sample of crime and criminals .
31102	For example , if only 10 per cent of crime is recorded in the statistics , but this nevertheless accurately reflects the full range of crime and criminals , then the statistics would provide a representative sample .
31103	However , it has been demonstrated that the official criminal statistics give an unrepresentative and misleading picture of the social distribution of criminal behaviour .
31104	Recent studies of crime , particularly Marxist-based work , have suggested that there is a systematic bias in favour of the powerful in the way that the law is applied and enforced .
31105	Broadly speaking , the higher an individual is in the social strata the less likely he or she is to be arrested , prosecuted and ( if prosecuted ) found guilty .
31106	Of course , this is not the same as saying that the rich and powerful never get prosecuted : there are many specific cases which illustrate this point , and which are generally well publicised .
31107	Nonetheless , such instances tend to be exceptions to the rule .
31108	The statistics show that recorded crime is predominantly working-class .
31109	To assess whether this is an accurate picture it is necessary to address the question as to whether crime itself is predominantly working-class .
31110	The issue to examine is whether the fact that more working-class offenders are caught means that more working-class people break laws .
31111	A number of factors need to be taken into account here , and we will examine some of them below .
31112	Those crimes which are reported are more likely to be committed by the working class because they are more visible , such as crimes against property .
31113	Middle-class crimes , such as fraud or embezzlement , are far less likely to be discovered and reported .
31114	Furthermore , people are more likely to report suspicious circumstances surrounding an individual who appears to be of lower-class origin .
31115	Whether intentionally or not , police procedures may be biased against those of lower social status .
31116	When a crime is reported to the police they do not work on the assumption that anyone could have done it .
31117	This is not practical or possible .
31118	Therefore , they tend to look for a certain ‘ type ’ .
31119	This is a very important factor because it biases police activity against the poorly spoken , badly dressed and ill-educated individuals who have the least power , and the fewest people of influence to back them up .
31120	There is also an element of bias when the individual comes into contact with the official , whether police officer or magistrate , which has similarities with the relationship between middle-class teachers and working-class pupils .
31121	The police tend to operate with different expectations of individuals from different social backgrounds .
31122	They are far more likely to use their discretion when dealing with the middle-class offender , thus the middle-class offender is far less likely to actually come to court .
31123	It is important to bear in mind that there may be a significant amount of delinquency and crime amongst the middle classes , but we are less likely to be made aware of it .
31124	‘ One law for the rich and another for the poor ’ is an old saying which is certainly true of the way the law is enforced .
31125	To provide an illustration , a child who gets into trouble is much more likely to come before a court if he or she is from a poor home and has parents who do not get on with the welfare authorities or the police , than if his or her family is prosperous , respectable and willing to co-operate with the police and social services .
31126	In the last section of this chapter we will examine the attempts that have been made to find out more about the actual extent of crime , and to provide some sort of indication of the ‘ dark figure ’ of crime and to discover the ‘ real ’ rather than the recorded rate and character of crime .
31127	The two major forms such attempts have taken are victim studies and self-report studies .
31128	Victim studies and self-report studies
31129	While victim studies and self-report studies overlap to some extent and are sometimes used in conjunction , they are distinct approaches which need to be defined separately .
31130	Victim or victimisation studies are designed to investigate the number of individuals who have been victims of crime .
31131	They ‘ took off ’ in the mid-1960s in the USA .
31132	A Washington survey , for example , showed that 38 per cent of those asked revealed that they had been a victim of a serious crime within the last year , compared to the 10 per cent revealed by police statistics .
31133	The purpose of this and of other victim studies was to elicit from respondents whether they had been the victim of a crime , and if so , which types of crime and whether they had reported it to the police .
31134	All victim studies show that police records cover , at the most , about one quarter of the serious crime actually committed .
31135	Such studies do themselves , however , suffer from limitations .
31136	For example , individuals find it difficult to remember how often they have been ‘ victimised ’ , or tend to exaggerate their experiences .
31137	Moreover , while they do show that official statistics tend to underestimate the amount of crime , it is likely that victim studies also under-record the amount — mostly because people can only report having been victims of crime if they know that they have been victimised .
31138	Although such a statement is transparently obvious , as we have demonstrated earlier there are a vast number of crimes where people do not know they are victims , such as minor thefts , and many white-collar crimes .
31139	Nonetheless , it is likely that victim studies provide a fairly reliable guide for measuring ‘ conventional ’ crimes such as assault , robbery and burglary , where the individual will be well aware that he or she was victim .
31140	Even with such ‘ conventional , crimes , however , different people might interpret events differently , and there might be a degree of under-reporting because of this .
31141	Some people may define a vague tampering with a door or window at night as an ‘ attempted burglary ’ while others will not .
31142	Victim 's interpretations and memories indicate that victim studies can not be assumed to accurately reflect the ‘ real ’ extent of crime ; and the search for more reliable and direct indicators has included the development of self-report studies .
31143	Self-report studies usually involve asking people to give information about their past illegal activities , in response to a questionnaire or interview .
31144	As well as being asked how often they commit illegal acts , respondents are generally asked details of their social characteristics , social class , race and so on , in an attempt to get round the biases in official criminal statistics .
31145	A range of self-report studies have indicated that a majority of people admit to some kind of illegal activity , whether trivial or serious , which could result in a court appearance .
31146	For example , studies have shown that 90 per cent of boys in the Inner London area admit to having travelled on public transport without a ticket , or to deliberately under-paying ; 82 per cent admit breaking windows of empty houses ; and only a small percentage claim to have committed no offences .
31147	Again , there are likely to be problems of reliability with such data .
31148	Will people admit to having committed criminal offences , even if they are guaranteed confidentiality ?
31149	It seems to go against common-sense notions that individuals would want to hide any misdemeanours or crimes .
31150	Alternatively , respondents may exaggerate their delinquencies out of bravado , especially likely with juveniles .
31151	Others may under-report due to dishonesty , forgetfulness or paranoia .
31152	Attempts that have been made to check the ‘ honesty ’ of respondents have indicated that about a quarter of respondents are liable to conceal information .
31153	A further difficulty is the impossibility of including all criminal acts in a questionnaire or interview .
31154	Thus , the researcher has to be selective , which raises problems as to which offences should be mentioned and questioned about and which not .
31155	As you will realise , some offences are predominantly working-class and others predominantly middle-class , and it is important that self-report studies do not include too many offences typical of one group or class .
31156	A final problem with self-report studies concerns the representativeness of the sample being studied .
31157	Many self-report studies have been carried out in schools , which will tend to result in school drop-outs and truants being excluded from the sample and lead to an unrepresentative sample .
31158	Also , those most likely not to complete the questionnaire or do the interview are most likely to be delinquent ; and one can not force people to fill in questionnaires correctly .
31159	Notwithstanding these difficulties , self-report studies do indicate that middle-class individuals are as likely to commit crimes as working-class individuals .
31160	The British Crime Survey of 1983 , a research project carried out by the Home Office , is a recent example of how victim and self-report studies can be used to attempt to get round the problems of and deficiencies with the official criminal statistics .
31161	The first report was written by Mike Hough and Pat Mayhew and involved in-depth interviews with 11,000 households in England and Wales .
31162	People were asked what crimes they had been victims of ( victim study ) and about their own law-breaking ( self-report study ) , and they were also asked about their attitudes towards the police and policing .
31163	Thus , this survey combined the two methods we have been looking at above .
31164	While such victim and self-report surveys are not new what was new for this country was the scope of this survey .
31165	The British Crime Survey showed that there were about four times as many crimes committed each year as the police were ever told about .
31166	Although such figures might create public alarm , the main reason given for non-reporting was because the offence was considered too trivial to waste police time ( 38 per cent of reasons given ) , or that the police could do nothing about it ( 16 per cent ) .
31167	Fear or dislike of the police was way down the list , at 6 per cent .
31168	The survey also found that those who most feared violence , the elderly and women , were the least likely to experience it , while those most at risk were young males who went out regularly .
31169	With regard to particular crimes , the survey perhaps offered some reassurance to those accustomed to the image of a massive upsurge in crime which is so regularly portrayed by the media .
31170	The average household can expect to be burgled once every forty years , for example , while violent confrontation between the intruder and victim is very rare — one per cent of ail cases .
31171	The survey tells us that the chances of being burgled are less than the risk of domestic fire and that the chances of robbery are smaller than those of being admitted to a psychiatric hospital — not that such statistics will be a lot of consolation to those who are burgled or robbed .
31172	The British Crime Survey suggests that one in four crimes are officially reported , although sociologists and criminologists suggest that between 10 and 15 per cent is a more probable figure .
31173	However , such a difference can be reconciled , because these type of victim-based surveys can only include crimes where there is a victim who can be interviewed .
31174	Thus , they exclude a range of offences , such as shoplifting and stealing from work , where the non-reporting is particularly high .
31175	Furthermore , some interviewees will not wish to talk about painful experiences just for the benefit of a survey interviewer .
31176	The figure of one in four crimes being reported refers to crime in general , and this ratio of recorded to unrecorded crime varies according to the particular crime .
31177	The survey shows that there were twice as many burglaries as were recorded by the police , nearly five times as much wounding , twelve times as much theft from the person and , most unexpectedly perhaps , thirteen times as much vandalism or criminal damage to personal and household property .
31178	Thus , the ‘ dark figure ’ of unrecorded crime depends on the sort of offences that are considered , and if different groups of offence categories are examined , different ratios will be found .
31179	To conclude our review of criminal statistics , it is clear that official statistics on crime , like most statistics , should not be taken at face value as ‘ facts ’ to be accepted uncritically .
31180	They are the product of social processes and they involve the activities not just of offenders but also of decision-makers and enforcers in the area of law and order .
31181	Attempts to remedy the deficiencies in these statistics suffer from a number of problems and difficulties themselves .
31182	In fact , any crime rate , whether produced by the police , victim study , self-report study or whatever , will depend on a classification of crime that is socially produced .
31183	Documentary readings
31184	The purpose of this chapter is to fill out certain of the areas of the study of crime which have been discussed or referred to in earlier chapters , and to provide readings or extracts from original sociological work in this field .
31185	Some of the extracts are extended illustrations of particular areas and issues in the study of crime ; others illustrate particular theoretical or methodological issues .
31186	Extracts from a number of the studies referred to in the previous chapters are included ; as are extracts from works not specifically cited in these chapters but which are closely related to topics and issues raised in them .
31187	As far as possible , the extracts are ordered so as to follow the structure of the earlier chapters .
31188	Thus , extracts related to Chapter 2 precede those related to Chapter 3 and so on , although certain studies are of course relevant to more than one particular aspect of the sociology of crime .
31189	Each of the extracts is introduced briefly and related and cross-referenced to earlier section(s) of the book .
31190	H. S. Becker : Problems in the study of crime and deviance
31191	In his famous study , Outsiders , Becker outlines the basic interactionist approach to the study of crime and deviance .
31192	It has become one of the basic and seminal texts in the sociological study of this topic .
31193	The first two chapters explain the labelling perspective , with later chapters applying this perspective to specific types of deviant behaviour , such as drug use .
31194	In the final chapter Becker discusses some of the problems involved in the study of crime and deviance .
31195	The following extract is taken from this last chapter , and elaborates on some of the problems we mentioned in our first chapter , ( pp 7–8 ) .
31196	Reading 1
31197	It is in the nature of the phenomenon of deviance that it will be difficult for anyone to study both sides of the process and accurately capture the perspectives of both classes of participants , rule-breakers and rule-enforcers .
31198	Not that it is impossible , but practical considerations of gaining access to situations and the confidence of the people involved in any reasonable length of time mean that one will probably study the situation from one side or the other .
31199	Whichever class of participants we choose to study and whose viewpoint we therefore choose to take , we will probably be accused of ‘ bias ’ .
31200	It will be said that we are not doing justice to the viewpoint of the opposing group .
31201	In presenting the rationalisations and justifications a group offers for doing things as it does , we will seem to be accepting its rationalisations and justifications and accusing other parties to the transaction in the words of their opponents .
31202	If we study drug addicts , they will surely tell us and we will be bound to report that they believe the outsiders who judge them are wrong and inspired by low motives .
31203	If we point to those aspects of the addict 's experience which seem to him to confirm his beliefs , we will seem to be making an apology for the addict .
31204	On the other hand , if we view the phenomenon of addiction from the point of view of the enforcement officials , they will tell us and we will be bound to report that they believe addicts are criminal types , have disturbed personalities , have no morals and can not be trusted .
31205	We will be able to point to those aspects of the enforcer 's experiences which justify their view .
31206	In so doing , we will seem to be agreeing with his view .
31207	In either case , we shall be accused of presenting a one-sided and distorted view .
31208	But this is not really the case .
31209	What we are presenting is not a distorted view of ‘ reality ’ , but the reality which engages the people we have studied , the reality they create by their interpretation of their experience and in terms of which they act .
31210	If we fail to present this reality , we will not have achieved full sociological understanding of the phenomenon we seek to explain .
31211	Becker , H. S. , Outsiders : studies in the sociology of deviance , 1963 , pp. 173–174
31212	Discussion question
31213	1
31214	Sociological research into crime faces particular problems due to the nature of the subject being investigated .
31215	Suggest some of these problems .
31216	A. K. Cohen : The delinquent subculture
31217	In the first chapter of his study , Delinquent Boys , Cohen provides a very clear definition of the term delinquent subculture , with the main portion of the book then showing how this subculture is vital to the occurrence of delinquency .
31218	Below we reproduce Cohen 's definition of a delinquent subculture .
31219	Reading 2
31220	The expression , ‘ the delinquent subculture ’ , may be new to some readers of this volume .
31221	The idea for which it stands , however , is a commonplace of folk — as well as scientific — thinking .
31222	When Mrs Jones says : ‘ My Johnny is really a good boy but got to running around with the wrong bunch and got into trouble ’ , she is making a set of assumptions which , when spelled out more explicitly , constitute the foundations of an important school of thought in the scientific study of juvenile delinquency .
31223	She is affirming that delinquency is neither an inborn disposition nor something the child has contrived by himself ; that children learn to become delinquents by becoming members of groups in which delinquent conduct is already established and the ‘ thing to do ’ ; and that a child need not be ‘ different ’ from other children , that he need not have any twists or defects of personality or intelligence , in order to become a delinquent .
31224	In the language of contemporary sociology , she is saying that juvenile delinquency is a subculture …
31225	When we speak of a delinquent subculture , we speak of a way of life that has somehow become traditional among certain groups in American society .
31226	These groups are the boys ' gangs that flourish most conspicuously in the ‘ delinquent neighbourhoods ’ of our large American cities .
31227	The members of these gangs grow up , some to become law-abiding citizens and others to graduate to more professional and adult forms of criminality , but the delinquent tradition is kept alive be the age-groups that succeed them …
31228	Delinquency , according to this view , is not an expression or contrivance of a particular kind of personality ; it may be imposed upon any kind of personality if circumstances favour intimate association with delinquent models .
31229	The process of becoming a delinquent is the same as the process of becoming , let us say , a Boy Scout .
31230	The difference lies only in the cultural pattern with which the children associates .
31231	Cohen , A. K. , Delinquent Boys ; the culture of the gang , 1955 , pp. 11–14
31232	Discussion questions
31233	1
31234	In what ways does the social environment predispose certain individuals to join delinquent subcultures ?
31235	2
31236	Discuss some of the difficulties with the concept of the delinquent subculture ( refer to the section on subcultural theories in Chapter 2 ) .
31237	G. Pearson : The history of crime and delinquency
31238	In Chapter 3 , we examined in some detail Pearson 's review of the history of street crime in Britain , and his criticism of the widely held belief that such crime is a unique feature of present-day society .
31239	The following extract from this fascinating historical study deals with the problems of locating a ‘ golden age ’ when Britain was relatively free of crime and lawlessness .
31240	Reading 3
31241	Now , what I wish to ask in this book is whether this way of thinking about Britain 's decline is useful and accurate .
31242	And if it is not ( and I will argue that it is not ) then to what extent does this tradition of anguished regret for the past hinder our actions in the present and the future ? …
31243	This view of Britain 's history as one founded on stability and decency is deeply ingrained in the self-understanding of the British people .
31244	The present , we hardly need to be told , is extremely tense .
31245	But the past , say the accumulated traditions of our national culture , was a ‘ golden age ’ of order and security .
31246	Nowadays we need the iron fist of policing in order that we might sleep soundly in our beds .
31247	Whereas formerly we did not , and our love of tolerant freedom was spontaneous , unregimented and natural .
31248	The extremity of these awful judgements against the moral deterioration of the British people , and the enormous vision of chaos and disorder which they conjure up , suggest the need for a cautious organisation of our thought and feeling as we approach these matters .
31249	Clearly , there is an impressive consistency in this line of thinking — both in terms of the belief in a pre-existing era of tranquillity , and in the agreement that the natural moderacy of the ‘ British way of life ’ has been eclipsed in the hooligan deluge .
31250	However , when we come to more details considerations — such as exactly where this ‘ golden age ’ is to be located in real historical time — then we are confronted with such a disorderly jumble of datemarks and vague historical allusions as to allow for wide margins of disagreement even among dedicated ‘ law-and-order ’ enthusiasts .
31251	Indeed , at the centre of the preoccupation with declining standards and mounting disorder , there is an immense historical ‘ black hole ’ .
31252	Pearson , G. , Hooligan : A History of respectable fears , 1983 , pp. 7–8
31253	P. Corrigan : Contemporary delinquency — the problem of leisure
31254	In our discussion of delinquency in contemporary society ( Chapter 3 , pp. 34–35 ) we looked at Paul Corrigan 's study of working-class boys in the north-east of England .
31255	Corrigan points out that the delinquency of these boys can not be explained or understood outside the context of their leisure activities ( or lack of them ) .
31256	In particular , the boys drift into and out of minor delinquencies while hanging around the streets in groups looking for something to do , as the following extract from his study illustrates .
31257	Reading 4
31258	It was between the area of talking , joking and carrying on that things emerged that the boys called ‘ ideas ’ .
31259	These ‘ ideas , formed the basis for group action and it is the way in which these spontaneously evolve and are carried out that constitutes one of the most active elements of ‘ hanging about ’ …
31260	Albert ( one of the boys studied ) : Well , somebody gets a weird idea into their head , and they start to carry it out , and others join in .
31261	Question : Weird idea ?
31262	Albert : Things … like going around smashing milk bottles .
31263	Boys on a Saturday night in Sunderland , in a group , on a street comer , are aware that they are ‘ doing nothing ’ and are bored with it in their own minds , essentially wanting something to happen .
31264	They want to have an interesting or exciting time , a time that would not be boring , where they could create some action …
31265	If we analyse the street-comer activity of doing nothing in groups in the light of always hoping that something will happen , then the creation and the putting into effect of ‘ ideas ’ by the group can be seen as one of the most significant group experiences .
31266	Their significance is not only in terms of the group experience but also in terms of the wider society , for it is these ideas born out of the street-corner groups , doing nothing , that are to a large extent the ‘ juvenile delinquency ’ of the police and criminologists .
31267	Most significantly , these ideas are born out of boredom and the expectation of future and continuing boredom , and this affects the sort of ideas that they are .
31268	A good ‘ idea ’ must contain the seeds of continuing change ( from the boring situation ) as well as excitement and involvement .
31269	Smashing milk bottles is a good example of this since it typifies the way in which they are put into effect .
31270	Methodologically , it is not possible for any researcher to get the kids to talk with much sense of ideas since the question ‘ Why ? ’ to the smashing of milk bottles is one that is not possible for the boy to answer outside the context of the whole Saturday evening …
31271	For the sort of interaction that we are referring to here is not the planned smashing of things .
31272	It is not that boys go out on a Saturday night looking for milk bottles or other things to smash .
31273	Rather they use smashing as something interesting to do …
31274	Question : What sort of things do you do on a Saturday evening ?
31275	Peter : Usually play football down the street , play footy .
31276	Just gang down the court or somewhere then come home .
31277	Question : What other things do you do ?
31278	Peter : On Saturday I knock around with me mates .
31279	Question : What do you do ?
31280	Peter : Well , cause trouble , you know ; play knocking on doors , throw stones at windows and that .
31281	Cause fights mostly .
31282	Is it really necessary to explain the excitement of smashing things , whether they are milk bottles , shop windows , buses , telephone boxes or whatever , if the alternative is to stand there and do nothing .
31283	Corrigan , P. , Schooling the Smash Street Kids , 1979 , pp. 128–130
31284	Discussion questions
31285	1
31286	Which sociological method do you feel would be most appropriate to the sort of research carried out by Corrigan ?
31287	2
31288	Suggest possible difficulties with the use of other sociological methods for studying the leisure activities of these boys .
31289	3
31290	Explain how boredom is crucial to the sort of minor delinquencies Corrigan is examining .
31291	M. Levi : The corporate criminal in prison
31292	In Chapter 3 we looked at Levi 's study of long-firm fraud as an example of corporate crime .
31293	Below we include a brief extract from this study which looks at the problems and consequences of conviction for the business , ‘ respectable ’ criminal in comparison to the regular criminal — bearing in mind , of course , that the business criminal is far less likely to be convicted that most other types of criminal .
31294	Reading 5
31295	Most long-firm fraudsters manage quite successfully in prison , although its entertainments and amenities are hardly to their taste …
31296	They are rarely troublesome prisoners , although they often continue their ‘ operator ’ habits while inside …
31297	Long-firmers are experienced manipulators , and they make entertaining company for both prisoners and staff .
31298	Consequently , unless there are ‘ gangsters ’ around , they usually manage to get the best jobs in prison …
31299	It might be argued that despite their relative success at ‘ making out ’ in prison , long-firm fraudsters suffer far greater ‘ relative deprivation ’ than do other prisoners .
31300	For on the outside , they live far more lavishly than do ‘ ordinary ’ criminals , and experience a correspondingly greater contrast between ‘ normal ’ and prison life …
31301	Although there is some truth in this relative deprivation argument , it is equally important to note that the pains of imprisonment are mitigated by pleasant recollections : to be doing ‘ a lot of bird ’ without having lived well seems far more futile and absurd that to be paying for the rich fruits that crime has already brought .
31302	At least there are benefits to be weighed against the costs !
31303	Levi , M. , The phantom Capitalists : the organisation and control of long-firm fraud , 1981 , pp. 115–116

31307	G. Mars : Cheats at work : employee theft
31308	In Chapter 3 we discussed briefly employee theft , and , in particular , Ditton 's study of fiddling at a factory-production bakery .
31309	In a similar vein , Mars has studied the everyday crimes of normal people in the normal circumstances of their work — what Ditton calls ‘ part-time crime ’ .
31310	Mars is not concerned with the spectacular or the ‘ one-off ’ crime , but with activities that are an accepted part of everyday jobs .
31311	The extent and variety of these activities are astonishing , but while almost everyone is aware of them , and although the majority of us fiddle in one way or another , fiddling is generally considered a trivial activity without serious implications .
31312	Mars ' book challenges this view , and we will include two extracts from it .
31313	The following extract is part of an examination of how management have periodic ‘ purges ’ on their workforce in an attempt to control and crack down on fiddling .
31314	Reading 6
31315	When workers think a periodic purge is imminent , everyone feels equally threatened .
31316	No one knows where lightening may strike , the precise purpose of an investigation , or who specifically will be investigated .
31317	So everyone takes avoiding action .
31318	A waitress told me of such an incident when she heard a rumour that her hotel management had appointed private detectives with the power to search staff homes — a not uncommon fear among hotel workers and one paralleling similar periodic fears in other occupations of this type .
31319	I was at the Embassy then , and it used to be very busy .
31320	Everyone was fiddling like mad when we got a leak through from the office that they were sending private detectives round the houses …
31321	I was petrified because all my sheets and tableclothes and all my cutlery and silver were all stamped with the Embassy crest .
31322	Well , I did n't know that to do .
31323	As I say , I was petrified !
31324	So I made an excuse , I said I was ill , and rushed off home .
31325	I piled everything i could on a sheet in the middle of the floor and tied up the corners …
31326	I dashed into the garden — nut there — and started digging a bloody great hole .
31327	I was n't laughing at the time , though , I can tell you , because the more I dug down , the more I was digging up !
31328	There was a pile of coffee pots , cutlery and rotten linen already in the garden that had been buried there by the waiter who 'd had the house before me !
31329	He must have done exactly the same thing as I did when the panic hit him .
31330	Mars , G. , Cheats at Work : an anthropology of workplace crime , 1982 , pp. 130–131
31331	Later in the book , Mars attempts to put fiddles into context , to point out the conditions that favour them and the places where they are most likely to flourish .
31332	The opportunities and indeed the pressures for people to fiddle vary widely and Mars suggests a number of ‘ fiddle-prone ’ factors attached to particular occupations .
31333	One of these factors he terms ‘ exploiting expertise ’ , and is the subject of our second extract .
31334	Reading 7
31335	A widespread factor is found where real or suggested expertise is involved in a transaction and where at the same time it may be assumed that the customer is ignorant about what it is he is paying for .
31336	This factor therefore depends upon an imbalance in power which is based on an imbalance in knowledge .
31337	These conditions typically exist in garage servicing , though they are by no means con fined to it .
31338	They are indeed well represented among repairmen of all kinds and are also found , to a degree , among the professions .
31339	It is useful , however , if we begin this discussion with garage servicing …
31340	The economic base to garage servicing ( following O'Brien , Motor Magazine , 10th September 1977 ) lacks two conditions that normally operate in pricing : the first is that consumers should have speedy knowledge of defects in what they buy ; the second that they are free to move from an unsatisfactory supplier to a more satisfactory one .
31341	In competitive trading these conditions exist and the price system benefits the consumer …
31342	These two conditions are absent from garage servicing .
31343	O'Brien uses the phrase ‘ perverse incentives ’ to explain how a garage that performs poorly is likely to do better than one that performs well .
31344	He argues that bad garages drive out good ones because the typical customer can not judge whether a service has been done properly , and it is difficult for him to check .
31345	Thus a garage can , with impunity , charge for a full service which has only been half done …
31346	For if a garage habitually does half the service its costs are very much lower than if it has done the full service ; and since it can charge the full price , because of the ignorance of the consumer , its pro fits are maximised when it does as little of the service as it can get away with .
31347	There is probably some lower limit below which the garage will not go in skimping the service , because the risk of detection then becomes too high ( O'Brien ) .
31348	The garage benefits even further since faults from defective service are unlikely to occur immediately after collection of a vehicle .
31349	An ignorant motorist is likely , therefore , to absolve the garage from responsibility and pay it further to rectify these new faults .
31350	Mars , G. , Cheats at Work : an anthropology of workplace crime 1982 , pp. 142–144

31357	A. Campbell : Shoplifting — the ‘ typical ’ female crime

31359	Contrary to popular belief , shoplifting is neither a new word nor a new occurrence .

31371	Reading 8

31380	But as well as this , it is important to consider the extent to which self-representation and appearance are particularly important to girls economically and therefore psychologically …

31382	The function of women is decorative .
31383	Every minute spent in physical self-improvement is an investment , not only materially but in terms of emotional adjustment too .
31384	To be old and unmarried still represents a cloud on a teenage girl 's horizon …
31385	Sharpe ( Just Like Girl , 1976 ) looked at job preferences among a group of London girl school-leavers .
31386	Four girls in every 10 chose office work , and , by including the jobs of teachers , nurses , shop assistants , bank clerks , receptionists , telephonists , hairdressers and nannies , three-quarters of the choices were accounted for …
31387	With the exception of teaching and nursing , these jobs require little specialised training , and for most a good physical appearance is a distinct advantage .
31388	The importance of looks becomes even more pronounced when considering the types of occupations to which girls , often unrealistically , aspire — the glamour jobs .
31389	The role of air hostesses , models , actresses , public relations officers , sales representatives , promotion girls and personal assistants is often one of sexual window-dressing and male ego-boosting .

31398	M. Cain : Different styles of policing and their effects on criminal statistics
31399	Cain 's study on rural and urban police forces illustrates very distinctly the differing styles of policing in different areas .
31400	It shows how these different styles are likely to have a marked effect on the crime statistics collected by particular police forces , an issue we looked at in the previous chapter on criminal statistics .
31401	Reading 9
31402	Certainly country policemen in the present study had a ‘ peace-keeping ’ orientation to their work .
31403	Their aim , explicitly , was to have a ‘ quiet patch ’ …
31404	A beat patrol was usually a leisurely affair , with ample time to stop and chat .
31405	People would address the beat policeman by name or else as ‘ sir ’ , while he in turn would have a ‘ Good morning ’ for everyone encountered …
31406	At the time of the study the city operated a system of foot patrols plus an emergency car service ( distinct from traffic patrol ) .
31407	Two or three vehicles patrolled the division throughout the day , and it was claimed , with slight exaggeration , that any point could be reached within four minutes …
31408	The result was that the man left walking the beat had little of interest to do by way of responding to requests for emergency services …
31409	After postings to the cars and station offices this left 2⅔ men ‘ on the ground ’ per sub-division , or one man for every 26,838 of the population .
31410	Contrast this with the mean population of a rural one-man beat , a constant and stable 1,307 identifiable individuals …
31411	There were three main responses by the men to this situation .
31412	The first , which was the officially approved response , was ‘ to make the work interesting ’ by developing contacts with shopkeepers and others on the beat , and keeping an eye open for unusual activity …
31413	The second response to the endemic boredom , monotony and frequent cold , and to the impossibility of achieving the formally stated goals , was ‘ easing behaviour ’ …
31414	The third means of making a dull and cold eight hours more tolerable was to seek marginally legitimate arrests .
31415	This gave excitement , the opportunity to go off duty early or at least to return to the warmth and relative conviviality of the police station , as well as prestige …
31416	During 1963 , at the central police station on the research division , 76 per cent of the 611 arrests made by uniformed men were for offences against the public order such as vagrancy , loitering , and above all drunkenness …
31417	Impressions gained in this study suggest that ‘ crime work ’ ranks high in the police value system …
31418	Certainly men at the central station boasted proudly of the fact that they took more prisoners per year than any other division in the whole force .
