31427	G. Pearson : Problems with the historical study and comparison of crime
31428	The main focus of our examination of criminal statistics , Chapter 4 , was on the problems and deficiencies with these statistics .
31429	Pearson 's study of the history of street crime in Britain clearly illustrates the problem of using criminal statistics as a means for comparing the rate of crime over extended periods of time .
31430	The following reading , from the final part of Pearson 's book , gives specific examples of how changes in the way in which the law is enforced makes historical comparisons of the rate of criminality virtually impossible .
31431	Reading 10
31432	Criminal statistics are notoriously unreliable as measures of the actual extent of criminal activity , to such a degree that it is not unknown for historians to discount them altogether .
31433	The reason for their notoriety is that they are complicated by a number of factors others than real changes in the levels of crime .
31434	The growing size of the police force and its supporting apparatus is the most obvious and general factor .
31435	Changes in the routines of law enforcement , the increased mobility of the police , changes in what the law counts as crime , fluctuations in the vigour with which the law is applied , and shifts in public attitudes and tolerance — these must all be counted within the hidden dimensions of the manufacture of crime figures …
31436	Between 1900 and the late 1970s … we are asked to strike comparisons between such different styles of law enforcement as to make little sense .
31437	First , in the earlier period there were wide margins of discretion within an extremely informal mode of policing — the proverbial clip around the ear , or the dreaded flick of the Edwardian policemen 's rolled cape — which has been replaced by the more likely possibility of prosecution , or the issue of formal caution .
31438	And a formal caution , unlike a clip around the ear , goes into the record book as a ‘ known crime ’ .
31439	We have also seen how in earlier times people involved in acts of gross disorder would commonly be charged only with simple assault or drunkenness … street violence was too much of an everyday occurrence to count as ‘ real ’ crime .
31440	There was also a tendency not to record incidents which could not be cleared up .
31441	Until the 1930s , for example , it was a routine practice of the London police to record thefts reported to them by the public as ‘ lost property ’ .
31442	When this practice was changed , recorded levels of property crime soared : but , obviously , as a consequence of changes in policing and not as a result of changes in crime .
31443	In overall terms , between 1900 and the present day , the state apparatus for collecting and sorting criminal information has changed so dramatically that we must question whether it can supply us with a valid measuring-stick with which to compare the two periods .
31444	The cluttered informality of the Edwardian local police station with its rudimentary procedures for record-keeping has been replaced by elaborate computer-assisted systems of information retrieval .
31445	And whether or not they enhance the efficiency of the police , they certainly expand the crime statistics …
31446	To ask us to strike meaningful comparisons across such a technological gulf is like trying to compare a theory of the origins of the universe based on observations through Galileo 's lens with one facilitated by radio telescope .
31447	It simply will not do .
31448	Pearson , G. , Hooligan : a history of respectable fears , 1983 , pp. 213–215

31510	Methodology
31511	The areal interpolation problem : estimating population using remote sensing in a GIS framework
31512	Mitchel Langford , David J. Maguire and David J. Unwin
31513	Introduction
31514	Data integration is one of the fundamental GIS operations ( Burrough 1986 ) .
31515	It involves transformation of data so that they are reported at a comparable geographical scale , projection and set of geographical units .
31516	The need for data integration arises because many of the questions which scientists and social scientists investigate require data from a wide range of sources which are only reported on disparate spatial bases .
31517	Data integration is especially a problem for geographers because information synthesis is at the very heart of the discipline .
31518	The difficulties of integrating data are compounded by the fact that there are few standards governing the way in which geographical data are collected and reported .
31519	Hearnshaw et al. ( 1989 ) , for example , highlight the problem in the context of Leicestershire , a county in the Midlands of England , and show the difficulties of linking enumeration district ( ED ) , ward , parish and postcode data .
31520	Similarly , Openshaw et al. ( 1986 ) report that the data in the Domesday System are available for 25 different and incompatible types of areal unit .
31521	Strategies for integrating data reported at different geographical scales and for different map projections have received considerable attention over the past few decades ( Robinson et al. 1984 ; Burrough 1986 ) .
31522	Although there are still a number of problems to be solved , in contrast to the difficulties of comparing data reported for different spatial units , these aspects of data integration are fairly well developed and understood .
31523	In this chapter we concentrate on the problem of integrating geographical data reported for different areal spatial units , one of the most intractable of all data integration problems .
31524	A fuller description of the process of data integration is presented by Flowerdew and Green in Chapter 4 .
31525	Areal interpolation
31526	There have been a number of published attempts to provide solutions to the cross-area aggregation , or ‘ areal interpolation ’ problem ( Goodchild and Lam 1980 ; Lam 1983 ) .
31527	These have been summarized and classified by Flowerdew and Openshaw ( 1987 ) and several examples are given in Hearnshaw et al. ( 1989 ) .
31528	The areal interpolation problem can be defined as the transfer of data from one set ( source units or zones ) to a second set ( target units ) of overlapping , non-hierarchical areal units .
31529	Where the source zones nest hierarchically into the target zones , for example UK administrative EDs nest exactly in wards , transfer of data from the source units to the target units is one of simple aggregation .
31530	However , where the units are overlapping and non-hierarchical the problem is more complex and it is this that we investigate here .
31531	The nature of the problem can be illustrated with an example .
31532	A common problem in geographical information systems ( GIS ) , and one which has been known about for many years in the context of choropleth mapping , is that of producing maps from population data aggregated over selected arbitrary areal units .
31533	In the UK , the decennial Census of Population records the number of individual people and households , but almost all population data are reported as various aggregations which ensure that data about individuals can not be recovered .
31534	Unfortunately , the aggregations are generally chosen for non-statistical reasons and so differ from data set to data set and are often unstable over time .
31535	This makes any comparative analysis of data recorded at different times or using different aggregation units problematical .
31536	The difficulty is particularly important in studies where it is necessary to find the denominator , in order to estimate the incidence of a property as a proportion of some population total .
31537	For example , the numerator might be a count of people in a postcode sector who have , say , a cancer , yet , because the census and health data are reported for different areal units , it is not possible to find the appropriate at-risk population for the denominator and so compute a reliable incidence ratio .
31538	Although this example relates to what have been termed ‘ imposed ’ areal units , that have no landscape reality ( Unwin 1981 ) , it is increasingly necessary to create aggregations of population over ‘ natural ’ areal units such as a soil association or outcrop of a particular rock type .
31539	The solutions to this type of problem utilize either point interpolation or areal interpolation methods ( Lam 1983 ) and these will be examined in turn .
31540	The point interpolation methods essentially use a point , usually the centroid , as a surrogate for the areal units and then apply conventional point interpolation methods .
31541	The crudest of these involves matching the centroids of source and target units by minimum distance nearest neighbour techniques .
31542	A slightly less crude method is to use the centroids to generate a continuous surface by interpolation .
31543	The target zones are then overlain and the interpolated value is transferred into the zones .
31544	However , this technique is particularly unsuitable for population estimation because as Tobler ( 1979 ) points out , there is a danger that people can be created or removed .
31545	Martin ( 1988 , 1989 ) describes a simple algorithm that uses the ED centroids , with a spreading function to allocate people to neighbouring grid squares , which incorporates Tobler 's idea .
31546	An intermediate method between the point and areal methods uses point-in-polygon techniques ( Burrough 1986 ) to locate the centroids of the source units in the boundaries of the target units .
31547	Although relatively unsophisticated , this method is reasonably fast and it seems to work satisfactorily where the target units are much larger than the source units
31548	Also in situations where the target units are much larger than the source units , polygon-in-polygon areal interpolation techniques can be used to obtain reasonable estimates by locating the source units within the target units .
31549	A simple decision rule can be used to decide what to do in the case of source units which cross the target unit boundaries .
31550	The most reliable and accurate estimates can normally be obtained using one of the true cross-areal interpolation methods .
31551	Lam ( 1983 ) suggests that there are two types of true areal interpolation methods : polygon overlay and pycnophylactic interpolation ( Tobler 1979 ) .
31552	These are well known and have been described elsewhere ( Lam 1983 ; Wagner 1989 ) .
31553	The above areal interpolation methods are alike in that , other than the purely spatial information given by the boundaries , areas or centroids of the areal units involved , no extra information is used in interpolation .
31554	In a truly integrated GIS framework ( Jackson and Mason 1986 ) it is almost certain to be the case that other potentially useful information is available .
31555	This additional information can be used for ‘ intelligent ’ interpolation .
31556	Flowerdew ( 1988 ) developed a theoretically sound and very general statistical approach using Poisson regression which incorporated an additional binary variable .
31557	He predicted the population characteristics of parliamentary constituencies in Lancashire ( the target units ) from district level data ( the source units ) using the party affiliation of the constituency 's Member of Parliament as a binary variable .
31558	In this chapter , we develop a method similar to Flowerdew 's in which we use GIS techniques to enable areal interpolation to be informed by the distribution of land-cover types , as inferred from a classified Landsat Thematic Mapper ( TM ) image , in both the source ( 1981 Census wards ) and target ( National Grid kilometre squares ) units .
31559	The basic approach
31560	The basic idea is simple .
31561	A suitable satellite image is classified using image-processing techniques to identify the various types of land cover which exist over the entire study area at very fine spatial resolution .
31562	Thus , for each census ward for which a 1981 population total exists , it is possible to determine the number of pixels classified as a certain land-cover type .
31563	It is then feasible to express the known ward populations as a function of these pixel counts .
31564	Provided the model relating population to these land-cover data is reasonably good , the resulting relationship can then be used to estimate populations for any set of imposed or natural areal units that can also be located on the image .
31565	The use of remotely sensed data to inform population mapping is not new .
31566	Previous attempts to estimate entire populations , especially of Third World cities , include studies by Ogrosky ( 1975 ) , Lo and Welch ( 1977 ) and Han ( 1985 ) .
31567	Similarly , a number of authors have used vertical aerial photography to estimate residential densities across individual cities ( see , for example , Collins and El-Beik 1971 ; Hsu 1971 ; Clayton and Estes 1980 ) while others have experimented with the use of satellite imagery ( Iisaka and Hegedus 1982 ) .
31568	Convenient summaries of this previous work are to be found in Lo ( 1986 ) and Griffiths ( 1988 ) .
31569	The work described here involves four distinct steps .
31570	First , there is the choice of satellite image and the production of a land-cover map .
31571	Second , there is the overlay on to this map of the 1981 Census ward boundaries and summation of pixels falling into each of the recognized land-cover types .
31572	Third , there is the statistical modelling of the relationship between population and land cover and the validation of the resulting model .
31573	Finally , at the end of the process lies the estimation of the population over some target set of areal units , in our case the kilometre squares of the UK National Grid .
31574	Obtaining a land-cover classification
31575	A Landsat TM image of Leicestershire recorded on a cloud-free day in July 1984 constitutes the basic data source .
31576	This area was selected for study because of the authors ' familiarity with it , the adequate rural-urban contrast and the availability of a suitable image .
31577	The ground resolution of a TM image is such that a pixel has about a 30 m side , which seems appropriate for the scale of analysis used .
31578	Indeed , it may be that an image of higher spatial resolution , such as one obtained by a SPOT satellite ( 20/10 m ) , would prove counterproductive , giving too much local variation in pixel reflectance .
31579	The full seven bands of image data were loaded into an ERDAS ( Earth Resources Data Analysis System ) software system and ground control point information entered to rectify the image to National Grid coordinates .
31580	This rectified image was then subsetted to give an area covering the 49 wards that make up the districts of Oadby and Wigston , Leicester , and Charnwood in northern Leicestershire ( Fig. 5.1 ) .
31581	Since a faithful classification of land cover is an essential component in the proposed scheme , several attempts were made in an effort to obtain a consistent and suitably detailed product .
31582	An unsupervised classification provided an acceptable separation between rural and urban cover , but finer detail was concentrated in agricultural subdivisions at the expense of intra-urban differentiation .
31583	Information on agricultural land use is unimportant to this application , whereas urban detail illustrating housing densities or alternative urban land is highly desirable .
31584	A second classification was made using a supervised approach so that we could capitalize on our local knowledge of the study area .
31585	The supervised approach enabled urban subdivision of dense and less dense housing .
31586	The result was an improvement over the unsupervised product , and yet we still felt that further urban differentiation might be possible .
31587	This led us to undertake a principal components transformation of the seven bands of image data , which gave encouraging results similar to those obtained by Forster ( 1985a ) .
31588	As a data compression exercise , the first four components of the transformation reduced the storage requirement by 42 per cent for less than 1 per cent loss in information content .
31589	However , of great significance was the information displayed in the transformed images .
31590	The first principal component , carrying 50 per cent of the original variance , was dominated by land-cover differences in the rural area .
31591	The second component ( 40 per cent of variance ) revealed the urban distribution very clearly with a strong rural/urban differentiation .
31592	The third component , despite carrying only 6 per cent of the original variance , revealed intra-urban differentiation with a clarity unseen in any RGB ( red-green-blue ( colour ) ) , composite taken from the original bands .
31593	The fourth component ( 2 per cent of variance ) was dominated by the thermal infra-red band , recording thermal characteristics of the surface at poor spatial resolution .
31594	Finally , the remaining three components seemed to consist of uninterpretable noise .
31595	As previously stated , rural land cover was not an important consideration , and so the first component image was discarded , together with the last three , leaving components 2 , 3 and 4 .
31596	When these components were displayed as an RGB composite they continued to show good urban differentiation , closely matching both our local knowledge of the area and the ground truth data that were collected .
31597	The final attempt at classification involved a supervised classification of principal components , 2 , 3 and 4 .
31598	This produced the land-cover classification shown for a part of the area in Fig. 5.2 .
31599	Other , similar attempts to produce urban cover classification using satellite data are discussed in Jackson et al. ( 1980 ) , Forster ( 1983 , 1985b ) , Wheeler ( 1985 ) , Lam et al. ( 1987 ) and Griffiths ( 1988 ) .
31600	In an interesting variation of the work described here , Quarmby et al. ( 1988a ) outline the use of census data to derive training sets for classifying urban areas into housing types .
31601	Quarmby et al. ( 1988b ) also discuss the use of SPOT data for monitoring urban land-use change in south-east England .
31602	For analytical purposes , the 12 categories of land cover recognized during the classification stage were compressed into five representing :
31603	1 .
31604	Industry and commerce ( presumably detected by large single buildings and different building materials ) ;
31605	2 .
31606	Dense residential areas ;
31607	3 .
31608	Ordinary residential areas ;
31609	4 .
31610	Areas that logically have no population ( quarries , woods , water bodies ) ;
31611	5 .
31612	All agricultural land uses .
31613	Overlaying census ward boundaries
31614	In the second phase of the work , digitized 1981 Census ward boundaries and population totals were compiled using GIMMS and SASPAC ( at Manchester Computer Centre ) .
31615	These data were transferred into ERDAS and rasterized .
31616	ERDAS GIS functions were used to overlay the ward boundaries on to the classified image and then count the number of pixels of each recognized land-cover type within each ward .
31617	The result was a data matrix giving pixel counts for five land-cover types together with the recorded population for the 49 wards .
31618	These data are summarized in Table 5.1 and Fig. 5.3 is a map of the population density .
31619	Towards a statistical model
31620	Table 5.2 shows the matrix of intercorrelations between these six variables .
31621	The ward population , the response variable , has a relatively high positive correlation with the ‘ industry and commerce ’ , ‘ dense residential ’ and ‘ ordinary residential ’ variables and low negative correlations with ‘ nobody ’ and ‘ agriculture ’ .
31622	There are equally logical intercorrelations between the various land-cover pixel counts which are used as the carrier variables .
31623	Our intention is to express the ward populations as some function of the pixel counts for each land-cover type .
31624	It should be apparent that there is a very large number of possible models that might be used and , indeed , a number of considerations involved in making this choice ( see Dunn 1989 ) .
31625	In particular , three such considerations influenced our analysis and selection of carrier variables .
31626	First , there is a conflict between a desire to maximize the fit obtained , by inclusion of as many statistically significant terms as possible , and simple logic which suggests that the correct form of any fitted model should be a linear weighted sum of only those land-cover types that actually contain mostly housing ( ’ dense ’ and ‘ resid ’ ) without any intercept term .
31627	In such a model the weights themselves will have a direct interpretation as the average population density per Landsat pixel .
31628	Second , although there is no reason to expect any model to be other than linear and additive , there is an argument , presented by Flowerdew ( 1988 ) , which says that since the response variable compromises count data , the appropriate regression model should combine a Poisson error distribution with an identity link function ( see Aitkin et al. 1989 ; 217 ) .
31629	Third , there are a number of criteria for goodness of fit .
31630	Although the usual coefficient of determination or scaled deviance can be used to indicate the global fit of any specified model , it is also important to examine model performance when estimating populations over areal units other than the wards from which the models were derived .
31631	In this study , this was achieved by examining the estimated kilometre square populations together with those which were reported for the same areal units in the 1971 Census of Population .
31632	Three methods were examined in detail using the MINITAB and GLIM packages .
31633	A ‘ Shotgun ’ model
31634	The overall regression equation , calibrated by ordinary least squares , relating population to the carrier variables is Table 5.3 gives further details .
31635	It will be seen that although the overall fit , at 84 per cent is good , only industry , dense residential and ordinary residential have significant regression constants .
31636	The same set of variables used in a model with a Poisson error term gives the model which is remarkably similar .
31637	Figure 5.4 shows the standardized residuals for this model .
31638	Four wards are particularly badly fitted .
31639	In the western central area , two rural wards ( Charnwood 16 and 17 ) actually have almost doubled the fitted value .
31640	In the west of Leicester 's urban area , Newton ward , with population 20 440 , has a fitted value of only 13 495 and is badly fitted by all the models examined .
31641	This is probably due to the large preponderance of low-rise multi-storey council housing .
31642	Finally , there is an over-prediction of the population of central Leicester itself ( The Castle ward ) , which is another feature shown by all the models .
31643	Although this Shotgun model gives the best fit to the observed ward population data , it is logically flawed in at least two respects .
31644	First , it is evident that the correct form of any model linking population to land cover should not have an intercept constant ; if there is no residential cover , then there should be no population .
31645	Second , three of the variables incorporated into it have negative signs , indicating that as the number of pixels of these types increases , so population decreases .
31646	At first sight , this seems reasonable , but when the model is used to estimate populations of any other arbitrary areas there is a possibility that , if there is very little housing , it will predict negative populations .
31647	A further point is that the Shotgun model includes a large number of carrier variables and that it is worth further investigation to see if a more parsimonious model provides a satisfactory relationship .
31648	A ‘ Focused ’ model
31649	It is thus argued that any statistical model linking pixel counts of land cover to population should be simple , linear , additive and without any intercept constant .
31650	In such a model , the individual coefficients have a direct interpretation as the average density of people in each 30 m square pixel of the specified type .
31651	The ordinary least squares focused model is pop 81 = 9.89 dense + 5.03 resid whereas specification of Poisson errors gives pop 81 = 10.93 dense + 4.82 resid Note that the estimated population densities for a 30 m square pixel for the two types of residential housing identified using the Landsat data seem reasonable and that this model can not produce negative population estimates .
31652	In the intercept constant form , this greatly simplified model has an R2 of 81.8 per cent .
31653	The reduction to just the two land-cover categories , concerned with housing , loses only 3 per cent explanation when compared with the Shotgun model .
31654	for these re ; sons , the Focused model is considered to be superior to the Shotgun model .
31655	Figure 5.5 shows the standardized residuals for the least squares Focused model .
31656	The fit is reasonable over most of the area and , as might be expected , is broadly similar to that given by the Shotgun model .
31657	Again it tends to under-predict values for wards surrounding the centre of Leicester ( Humberstone , Aylestone and Newton ) and massively over-predicts for The Castle ward which includes the city centre .
31658	Here an actual ward population of 10 149 is predicted to be 18 373 .
31659	A ‘ Simple ’ model
31660	The final model investigated is the simplest of all .
31661	In this the ‘ dense ’ and ‘ residential ’ variables ( equivalent to ‘ houses ’ ) were summed and regressed against population in a simple linear model .
31662	Figure 5.6 shows that the plot of ‘ houses ’ against ‘ population ’ is remarkably linear , with a correlation coefficient of 0.869 .
31663	The ordinary least squares model , with forced zero intercept term , is pop 81 = 5.41 houses or , with Poisson errors : pop 81 = 5.40 houses This result implies that each pixel classified as having people living in it , and there are 86 178 of these , will on average contain 5.4 people .
31664	Examined in detail ( Fig. 5.7 ) this simple model repeats the problems of fitting the city wards identified by both the Shotgun and the Focused models , but adds to this a tendency towards relative over-prediction in the rural wards to the north and east of the area .
31665	An areal interpolation application
31666	The final step is to use the results of these models to predict the distribution of population over other arbitrary areal units for which pixel land-cover counts can be obtained .
31667	A particularly severe test is to use the results to estimate the population of the area over the kilometre square grid given by the UK Ordnance Survey .
31668	In this , the estimation not only involves a cross-area element , it also embraces a considerable areal disaggregation , from an average ward size of 7.7 km&amp;sup2 ; ( range 0.74–38.7 km&amp;sup2 ; ) down to the individual kilometre square .
31669	Figures 5.8–5.10 have been produced using UNIRAS to show the predicted 1984 population for the Shotgun , Focused and Simple models outlined above .
31670	All three pick out the major features of the population density variation across northern Leicestershire but , of course , as they stand they are impossible to validate in any direct way .
31671	First , the 1981 Census of Population was not made available for grid squares and , second , our estimates were produced using a 1984 satellite image and 1981 Census ward data .
31672	There are two indirect ways of validating these estimates .
31673	First , they can be compared with the actual distribution of population as reported on a grid square basis by the 1971 Census of Population ( Fig. 5.11 ) .
31674	Figures 5.12–5.14 show the differences between the actual population for 1971 and the predicted population for 1984 .
31675	Table 5.4 provides a summary of the overall fit in the form of the root mean squares ( RMS ) of the differences for each map .
31676	All point to precisely the same problems as were identified when evaluating the original model fits .
31677	The average ward population is 9488 ( Table 5.1 ) and so the RMS errors are comparatively small ( the range of RMS errors is from 815.13 for the Shotgun ordinary least squares ( OLS ) to 1035.29 for the Simple Poisson ) .
31678	There is little difference in the values obtained using OLS and Poisson regression and the Simple models produce only slightly higher errors .
31679	Figure 5.12 shows the differences given using the Shotgun model which has the lowest RMS value .
31680	Throughout most of the area , the differences are less than 1000 .
31681	In fact , only 30 ( or 5.3 per cent ) grid squares have absolute differences greater than this .
31682	Unfortunately , some urban squares in Leicester and Loughborough have large individual differences which have a total range from -4466 to +6976 .
31683	Thirteen years , between the 1971 Census and the 1984 image used , is a long time and has encompassed considerable population change in both magnitude and distribution .
31684	The general tendency of this model to overestimate central city population and underestimate around the urban fringe is consistent with the known pattern of change .
31685	Figure 5.13 shows the same data for the Focused model which , although it has much the same proportion of grid squares with differences in excess of 1000 people , now gives a total range from -4799 to +8339 .
31686	Even Fig. 14 , for the Simple model , has only 6.5 per cent of squares with absolute differences greater than 1000 but , as might be expected , the range is now from -3506 to +11 204 .
31687	A second indirect way of validating the regressions is to produce models relating population to 1981 land cover calibrated using the 1971 populations .
31688	If the general approach is fairly robust , it ought to be that the relationship between population and land cover is fairly stable , so that we would expect the model coefficients to be similar to those obtained from the ward data .
31689	Table 5.5 presents these coefficients , estimated using ordinary least squares , for exactly equivalent models to those reported in section 5.6 .
31690	It can be seen that in every case the two sets of coefficients have the same sign and general magnitude .
31691	However , even allowing for the fact that the population and satellite data were collected 13 years apart , the differences are greater than we would have liked .
31692	Conclusions and further work
31693	We regard these results as encouraging .
31694	They suggest that it is possible to use satellite remotely sensed data to help inform population mapping by allowing cross-area estimation and some element of areal disaggregation .
31695	Given that the remotely sensed data add a great deal of information to these processes this is hardly surprising , but this general approach is relatively easy to carry out in a GIS environment .
31696	We are currently extending this work in three ways .
31697	We are applying this technique in another part of the East Midlands , as a further test of the utility of this approach .
31698	We are working on other methods of classifying images , including textural classifiers , in order to improve the statistical modelling .
31699	Finally , we are trying to obtain independent 1 km grid square estimates for the 1981 population .
31700	Error propagation : a Monte Carlo simulation
31701	Stan Openshaw , Martin Charlton and Steve Carver
31702	Introduction
31703	The absence of facilities within GIS software for handling the effects of input data uncertainty and possible error propagation by GIS operations creates a question mark over the safe utilization of many aspects of the technology .
31704	The problem arises because it is thought that the positional errors and attribute uncertainties which are characteristic of all spatial databases , may be propagated and amplified by GIS operations and thus adversely affect some or all applications .
31705	These input data uncertainties are attributable to a number of sources ranging from errors in the original cartographic map documents through to the effects of the GIS operations themselves .
31706	Specific types of error in digital map data include : locational uncertainty , measurement errors in digitization , map-scale-dependent accuracy and resolution , and classification and generalization error in both categorical and remotely sensed map data .
31707	For thematic maps the principle cause of error is the original map document and its conversion to digital form .
31708	For remotely sensed data error depends on the accuracy of the sensing device and the pixel classification technology used in image processing .
31709	There is nothing new about the existence of map-related errors .
31710	Error and uncertainty have always been a feature of cartographic information .
31711	Previously , however , the worst effects were largely avoided by a combination of the expertise of the cartographer , who knew about the inherent generalization implicit in analogue maps , while the difficulty of manipulating maps by manual means precluded most forms of analysis likely to be sensitive to the effects of error .
31712	The advent of GIS has significantly changed all this .
31713	The ease of use and flexibility of GIS allow the user to perform operations on map data that were previously impossible on a large scale .
31714	The typical end-user of GIS output will probably care or know little about the cartographic and uncertainty characteristics of the map data being used , while the GIS itself has no procedures for handling the varying accuracy and reliability of the digital map data being processed .
31715	A GIS gives the user complete freedom to combine , overlay and analyse data from many different sources , regardless of scale , accuracy , resolution and quality of the original map documents and without any regard for the accuracy characteristics of the data themselves .
31716	The mixing of geographical information from different map scales and sources is a key aspect of GIS functionality , but it does raise the question as to what effects the combination of different levels of data uncertainty has on both the output maps and on the data derived from spatial query and analysis .
31717	It must be recognized that there are many good reasons for wishing to combine data in these ways , but a major problem arises because GIS packages fail to offer any means of keeping track of the effects of error propagation and how it affects the results .
31718	Despite research into some aspects of the error propagation issue in spatial data processing ( e.g. Blakemore 1984 ; Chrisman 1984 ; Drummond 1987 ; Goodchild and Dubuc 1987 ; Walsh et al. 1987 ) , Burrough ( 1986:103 ) correctly points out that ‘ It is remarkable that there have been so few studies on the whole problem of residual variation and how errors arise , or are created and propagated in geographical information processing , and what the effects of these errors might be on the results of studies made . ’
31719	This neglect is widely perceived to be a major unresolved problem .
31720	Such is its importance that the National Center for Geographic Information and Analysis ( NCGIA ) in the USA , has placed this issue first in its list of research priorities ( NCGIA 1989 ) .
31721	This chapter is concerned with developing methods able to provide estimates of the confidence regions around GIS map-based outputs by taking into account certain selected sources of uncertainty affecting spatial databases .
31722	A Monte Carlo simulation-based approach is used as a general means of estimating the effects of input data uncertainty on the map outputs after an arbitrary sequence of GIS operations .
31723	The objective is to identify and handle the effects of data uncertainty in a GIS by defining uncertainty envelopes to create ‘ credibility regions ’ around the results .
31724	This is considered to be the minimum needed to allow a GIS to function in a mixed data environment .
31725	Sources of error in GIS
31726	Error and uncertainty are common features of cartographic information , so it is hardly surprising that these aspects are also present in digital versions of analogue maps .
31727	It follows , therefore , that no map-related spatial data exist which are wholly error-free .
31728	There are many different causes of uncertainty and those which are explicitly due to GIS-based manipulations of geographic information are merely a more recent problem .
31729	However , it is also obvious that the power of GIS has the potential dramatically to increase both the magnitude and importance of errors in spatial databases .
31730	Burrough ( 1986 ) identifies three main groups of factors that govern the errors which may be associated with spatial data processing .
31731	These are :
31732	1 .
31733	Obvious sources of error ; ,
31734	2 .
31735	Errors resulting from natural variations or from ordinal measurements ; and
31736	3 .
31737	Errors arising through processing .
31738	Group 1 errors include such sources of age as the data , areal coverage , map scale and density of observations .
31739	Group 2 errors include positional accuracy , attribute uncertainty , and generalization arising from data classification and spatial variations in map quality .
31740	Group 3 errors include those arising through the processing of geographical data , such as numerical computing errors , faulty topological analyses and errors in interpolation .
31741	The three groups represent errors of increasing complexity and difficulty of handling , such that those in groups 2 and 3 require intimate knowledge of the data , their structure and the algorithms used and some means of converting this knowledge into quantitative measures of impact .
31742	It is useful to start by examining some of these sources of error .
31743	Digitizing error
31744	Despite the availability of hardware for the automated conversion of geographic data from paper maps to digital form ( e.g. optical scanners ) much data input to GIS is still done by hand using a digitizing table .
31745	As a result of human and other complicating factors involved , a high level of error is often present in digital map data .
31746	Manual digitizing is consequently recognized as a significant source of map error in GIS ( Otawa 1987 ; Keefer et al. 1988 ) .
31747	However , error introduced into digital map databases through the digitizing process is often ignored because the characteristics of digitizing error have not been fully defined and because no practical means of handling input data uncertainty exist within proprietary GIS software .
31748	Sources of error in the digitizing process can be broken down into two main streams : source map error and operational error .
31749	Source map error includes the accumulated error of the map being digitized , while operational error includes those errors propagated during the digitizing process itself .
31750	In looking at the first of these it must be recognized that no map , however detailed or carefully compiled , can perfectly represent the ‘ ground truth ’ , while in the second instance , the digitizing process merely serves to compound the errors present in the original map ( Poiker 1982 ; Blakemore 1984 ) .
31751	Going back to the source map , the level of detail and accuracy depends very much on the map scale .
31752	Large-scale maps can be topologically very detailed and have complex legends while smaller-scale maps are more generalized .
31753	This scale-related generalization gives rise to both locational errors and attribute uncertainty .
31754	Consider line thickness on paper maps .
31755	All lines on maps , depicting features such as roads , contours and boundaries , are drawn so as to be easily visible to the user .
31756	The thickness of some lines are even emphasized to accentuate their importance ( e.g. major roads ) .
31757	This can be misleading ( e.g. a road shown as a line 1 mm thick on a 1 : 50000 scale map implies a width of 50 m on the ground — an obvious exaggeration ) and as a result leads to difficulties in the digitizing process .
31758	Common sense suggests that the true course of a line on a map is along its mid-point .
31759	However , as the operator traces a line extra errors arise because it is impossible to follow the centre of the line exactly and some displacement of the cursor on either side of the line is inevitable .
31760	Burrough ( 1986 ) suggests that the area of the map covered by lines can be assumed to be an area of uncertainty .
31761	In one example he states that a 1 : 25 000 scale soil map measuring 400 by 600 mm may have as much as 24 000 mm of drawn lines , covering 24 000 mm&amp;sup2 ; or 10 per cent of the total map area .
31762	Blakemore ( 1984 ) attempts to estimate the uncertainty caused by cartographic line thickness and associated digitizer error by adapting an idea forwarded originally by Perkal ( 1966 ) .
31763	Perkal defined a distance ( ’ epsilon ’ ) about a cartographic line as a means of objective generalization .
31764	Blakemore inverted the concept , suggesting that it can be used to indicate an error band about a digitized line .
31765	This can be applied to polygon overlay operations to ascribe descriptive levels of certainty to the resulting map .
31766	A point-in-polygon problem was used as an example which results in five classes of answer depending on the position of the point relative to the digitized boundary and the ‘ epsilon ’ distance ( Fig. 6.1 ) .
31767	Empirical investigation using UK Department of Industry 1 km square data overlaid on polygon boundaries of north-west England employment office areas revealed that only 60 per cent of the points in the industry database could be positively assigned to an employment office area by being within a polygon and away from the boundary by a distance greater than epsilon .
31768	The accuracy of a digital representation of a line depends not only on the ability of the person using the digitizer to follow the centre of the line on the map exactly but also on the number of points they input to describe the shape of the line ( Aldred 1972 ) .
31769	Converting a line on a map into a series of x , y coordinates involves a sampling process .
31770	The number of sample points required accurately to copy a straight line is much less ( 2 ) than that required for a curve or complex line feature ( &gt;&gt;2 ) .
31771	The relative error associated with digitizing straight lines ( e.g. power lines ) is considerably less than that associated with digitizing line features made up of complex curves ( e.g. coastlines ) .
31772	Although a number of methods are available for sampling only those vertices which describe the basic shape of the line ( e.g. Douglas and Peucker 1973 ) , the difference between digitizing straight lines and complex curves suggests that Blakemore 's use of distance ‘ epsilon ’ is an over-simplification of reality .
31773	This could be improved by more detailed consideration of the processes of error propagation inherent in digitizing procedures .
31774	Several empirical studies have examined digitizing error by comparing digital data to their source maps ( Traylor 1979 ; Otawa 1987 ; Keefer et al. 1988 ) .
31775	From such studies appropriate models of digitizer error could be formulated .
31776	Errors in digital overlay analysis
31777	Much of the functionality of GIS lies with their ability to overlay one or more digital maps for the purposes of Boolean or network analyses .
31778	This kind of map analysis used to be done manually ( before the advent of practical GIS ) by overlaying transparent map sheets , establishing the required spatial relationships and drawing the new map on a clean top sheet with felt pens ( McHarg 1969 ) .
31779	Digital cartography promised a more efficient and flexible way of doing this kind of work .
31780	However , making the step between simple paper overlays and digital overlay proved difficult .
31781	Much research and development was carried out into this problem during the 1970s ( e.g. McAlpine and Cook 1971 ; Goodchild 1978 ) .
31782	Results from this work have , however , created more questions about data quality and error propagation .
31783	These questions need to be answered , at least in part , before GIS can realize their full potential .
31784	McAlpine and Cook ( 1971 ) experimented with the polygon overlay problem by overlaying different sized hexagons over a hexagonal grid with random orientation and displacement .
31785	Their results showed a surprisingly large proportion of small , ‘ sliver ’ polygons on the output maps .
31786	When applied to a case study , involving the overlay of three maps of Papua New Guinea containing 7 , 42 and 101 polygons respectively , the output map was comprised of 304 polygons , of which those less than 3.8 km&amp;sup2 ; ; amounted to 38 per cent of the total area .
31787	McAlpine and Cook evaluated these results by classifying the derived polygons by size and boundary complexity .
31788	A 10 per cent random sample of derived polygons was evaluated to determine the measure of agreement between the initial and derived descriptions .
31789	It was found that approximately 30 per cent of the map area was made up of polygons which did not agree with the initial map descriptions .
31790	Goodchild ( 1978 ) suggests that the number of derived polygons is more a function of boundary complexity than the actual number of polygons .
31791	When the boundaries of overlaid polygon networks are highly correlated ( e.g. as for certain types of administrative areas ) serious problems are created through the introduction of large numbers of ‘ spurious ’ sliver polygons .
31792	In the case of administrative boundaries , different units present in different maps often share a common boundary ( e.g. a river or stretch of coastline ) .
31793	These common boundaries will have been digitized separated , and so will not , therefore , coincide exactly .
31794	Furthermore , the more accurately common boundaries are digitized in each map and the more coordinates are used , then the larger the number of spurious sliver polygons produced ( Goodchild 1978 ) .
31795	Elimination procedures are available in GIS software to remove sliver polygons on the basis of minimum area ( e.g. ARC/INFO , ESRI 1987 ) .
31796	It is likely , however , that the resulting common boundary will be moved from its true position by the elimination procedure , thereby introducing further uncertainty into the output map .
31797	An attempt to estimate the cumulative effect of thematic map errors in digital overlay analysis has been made by Newcomer and Szajgin ( 1984 ) .
31798	Using conditional probability theory they suggest that the accuracy of maps resulting from overlay analysis is determined by the number of map layers , their accuracy and the coincidence of errors at the same position in several map layers .
31799	As a result the accuracy of a composite map from overlay analysis is generally less than the accuracy of the least accurate map layer used ( Newcomer and Szajgin 1984 ) .
31800	Newcomer and Szajgin go on to define the lower and upper bounds of accuracy in the output map .
31801	The upper bound is at best equal to the accuracy of the least accurate map layer ( when all errors in other layers are coincident in their location ) , while the lower bound results when the errors in each map layer occur at unique locations .
31802	Other researchers have compared spatial databases with ground truth observations .
31803	for example , Walsh et al. ( 1987 ) made an assessment of the error inherent in Landsat data , digital terrain models ( DTMs ) and digital thematic soil maps by comparing the data from these sources with information collected in the field .
31804	They found that the error ranged from 43 per cent for the soil maps to 83 per cent for the DTMs .
31805	Using the techniques described by Newcomer and Szajgin ( 1984 ) Walsh et al. ( 1987 ) found that the combination of inherent and operational error ranged from 71 per cent ( upper bound ) to 83 per cent ( lower bound ) .
31806	The problem is knowing what these results mean in the context of a particular application .
31807	Errors associated with vector to raster conversion
31808	There are generally recognized to be two major sources of error when converting vector maps ( either paper or digital ) into gridded or raster format .
31809	These are coding errors and topological mismatch errors .
31810	The first , and probably most obvious , source of error is associated with the problem of coding those grid cells which contain parts of several different vector polygons each in similar proportions .
31811	How should the grid cell be coded ?
31812	This problem arises because each grid cell can only have a single attribute value and because the chosen grid dimensions are too large to resolve the spatial detail required .
31813	One answer is to use a finer grid to achieve finer detail ( Walsh et al. 1987 ) , but this causes a corresponding increase in the size of the raster database .
31814	The second source of error is the problem of topological mismatch when a polygon map is represented by a grid .
31815	Again this can be reduced by using a finer grid , but problems with the increased amount of data storage required still occur .
31816	Methodological outline
31817	In conclusion to their paper Walsh et al. ( 1987 ) state that ‘ additional research in inherent and operational error assessment is warranted .
31818	Research in methods for cartographic display of errors , and the setting of statistical confidence limits of databases , are particularly required ’ ( Walsh et al. 1987 ; 1429 ) .
31819	Expanding on this it is possible to identify five major tasks in the study of error propagation within GIS .
31820	These are :
31821	1 .
31822	The development of mathematical models to represent the uncertainty characteristics of digital map databases ;
31823	2 .
31824	The development of procedures for estimating the effects of input data uncertainties and their propagation through GIS ;
31825	3 .
31826	The application of these models and techniques to a representative range of case studies to derive empirical estimations of likely error levels in GIS output ;
31827	4 .
31828	The development of techniques to utilize output data uncertainty estimates ; and
31829	5 .
31830	The incorporation of the technology as standard GIS tools .
31831	Task 1 is of critical importance .
31832	A means of modelling the distribution of errors is needed .
31833	One way of meeting this need is to take some commonly used map data sources ( both analogue and digital ) and perform numerical experiments on them to investigate the effects of scale and map resolution on data accuracy .
31834	In doing so there are a number of important areas to consider : mathematical modelling of the distribution of positional errors in digital maps derived from source maps of different scales ; the level and distribution of error which characterize digital map data ; and the types of probability models which best represent these errors .
31835	The long-term aim of this research should be to obtain a reasonable representation of the various errors that exist , although practical considerations would limit the scope and complexity of the representations used .
31836	It should be possible to obtain reasonable error models relating to positional accuracy , classification errors , attribute uncertainty and normal sampling aspects of spatial data .
31837	Such an approach conforms to Chrisman 's concept of a total error model as a decomposable set of stochastic processes which operate simultaneously .
31838	As more components of the total error model become available as a result of research then they could be adopted .
31839	As a result , any error-handling and estimation procedures should be sufficiently general as to be able to incorporate any new error model that may emerge at a later date .
31840	Task 2 may be solved by using a Monte Carlo approach .
31841	The generality and flexibility of such a procedure are a very attractive feature of the technology .
31842	Here , a Monte Carlo based simulation procedure for estimating the impact of error in GIS is proposed and developed .
31843	The concept is simple and universal in its applicability .
31844	It does , however , present a number of operational difficulties that require basic research before it can be widely used .
31845	The procedure is to simulate the effects of input data uncertainty by a Monte Carlo approach that is often used in statistics to perform exact significance tests .
31846	Each input data source is assumed to be characterized by an error model that represents reasonable estimates of the levels and nature of the data uncertainty thought to be present .
31847	This allows the map data to be replaced by probability distributions of known form and parameters .
31848	A single simulation is made by generating random numbers from these probability distributions and adding them to the observed geographic coordinates ( defining point , line or area features ) with these random values .
31849	This process is repeated for each source of data input .
31850	The randomized input map data are then subject to an arbitrary sequence of GIS operations .
31851	The final output results are saved .
31852	The entire process is repeated M times ( where M may be up to 100 ) .
31853	Research is required to determine the appropriate value of M .
31854	If the GIS output is merely numeric , then the distribution of M results gives some indication of the effects of input data uncertainty .
31855	If the result is a map , then the total set of output maps can be used to draw confidence intervals or ‘ credibility regions ’ which can be overlaid on the deterministic results as a visual indication of the effects of data uncertainty .
31856	For example , suppose a series of map overlays is being used to define suitable locations for a facility .
31857	The certainty of the output map being correct can be estimated using Monte Carlo simulation .
31858	In a vector GIS the set of M different output maps would be rasterized and a count made of the frequency that each cell appears in the final map .
31859	Those cells in locations which are little affected by the sensitivity analyses would accumulate high counts .
31860	They could then be converted back into vector form as polygon data and superimposed on the deterministic results .
31861	There is a useful analogy here with Monte Carlo significance testing which could be used to add a further degree of inferential screening to assessing the descriptive significance of the uncertainty bands in the context of a particular application .
31862	This simulation procedure is totally independent of the error models used and the nature and sequence of the GIS operations employed .
31863	The GIS component can include all manner of map manipulation , evaluation and statistical procedures .
31864	However , there are a number of basic research tasks that need to be resolved before this technique can be widely applied .
31865	These include : defining suitable values for the number of simulations required in a GIS environment rather than a statistical hypothesis-testing one ; assessing the utility of kernel estimators as an approximation that may allow smaller numbers of simulations to be used ; investigating the possibility of predicting the final output regions without performing large numbers of simulations ; and investigating possible hardware solutions to speed up the simulation process .
31866	The Monte Carlo simulation technique offers an effective means of identifying and demonstrating the effects of data uncertainty in a number of case studies drawn from the natural and social sciences .
31867	This is important as a means of drawing end-user attention to the problems of error propagation .
31868	The resulting ‘ error audits ’ would also provide a platform for illustrating to vendors the importance of installing error estimators in GIS software .
31869	A practical means of identifying approximate levels of output uncertainty also requires that some basic recommendations are made about how this variability can be retained , used and passed on to subsequent operations and applications using the data .
31870	Some US research groups appear to be tackling part of this problem by tagging databases with error information .
31871	Attention might be better focused on more technical questions such as how this error information may be used in GIS and spatial analysis .
31872	For example , development of spatial retrieval techniques and nearest neighbour analyses which can operate with fuzzy data .
31873	Other issues relate to investigating how this uncertainty information can best be presented to the user .
31874	Finally , the simulation approach and associated error models should be capable of being incorporated into standard GIS software .
31875	The principal problem area concerns the additional amount of computation that may be necessary successfully to implement Monte Carlo based techniques .
31876	It is possible , however , that quick approximations could be devised that would reduce the work-load by a factor of 5 , while improvements in hardware over the next few years may well absorb the rest .
31877	Monte Carlo simulation methodology
31878	Some preliminaries
31879	Although the methodology is of general applicability , it has been developed here using ARC/INFO running under the VMS operating system on a microVAX 2 .
31880	Some of the terminology , therefore , relates to the ARC/INFO GIS software ( see Table 6.1 ) .
31881	The basic sequence of operations
31882	The nature of the simulation methodology is outlined in Fig. 6.2 .
31883	The simulation of input data uncertainty involves replacing the deterministic input data values by those from a probability distribution that reflects an appropriate error model .
31884	The GIS operations are then performed and the results saved for evaluation .
31885	The GIS software used in this case study is the widely used ARC/INFO package ( ESRI 1987 ) .
31886	The methodology is operationalized in a macro which calls a separate program to perturb the input data without changing the topology .
31887	This is achieved by accessing the binary arc files directly from a FORTRAN program and then replacing the deterministic values by probabilistic ones , checking in the process that the implicit topology is retained .
31888	There are a number of approaches to implementing the methodology in ARC/INFO .
31889	The sequence of events is :
31890	1 .
31891	Perturb the arc data for the coverages , preserving polygon topology ;
31892	2 .
31893	Carry out the GIS operations on the perturbed coverage ;
31894	3 .
31895	Rasterize the results ; Steps 1–3 are repeated 100 times .
31896	4 .
31897	Calculate frequencies for each raster ; and
31898	5 .
31899	Map the results for a given probability level .
31900	Steps 1–3 are contained within the macro , written in the ARC/INFO macro-language , AML .
31901	Step 1 is implemented in a separate macro .
31902	Step 4 is implemented in a VAX DCL command procedure .
31903	The results are then mapped on a micro , using a Postscript driver ( Adobe Systems 1985 ) of the authors ' own devising ( step 5 ) .
31904	The first major problem is to access the arc data .
31905	In ARC/INFO , the binary arc/node topology information is kept in one subdirectory , while the tables which access these attributes are stored in another subdirectory .
31906	Initial attempts used the ARC UNGENERATE command to extract the binary data in ASCII character form for input to the FORTRAN perturbation program , followed by a GENERATE and BUILD to re-create the coverage .
31907	There are two disadvantages to this approach ; first , it is enormously time consuming and second , the polygon topology of the input coverage is not preserved , so one can not work back to the initial coverage attributes .
31908	The easiest solution is to access the binary files directly .
31909	All the information is then contained in only one file .
31910	The ARC/INFO programmer 's guide ( Aronson 1985 ) give some clues as to what to expect , but the actual file structure can only be determined by inspection .
31911	Fortunately , the VAX command DIR/FULL gives enough information to allow a FORTRAN program to be written which can read the data block by block , and then replace the arc coordinates by randomized values drawn from some appropriate probability distribution .
31912	The complexity of the record structure provides extra problems for coding the perturbation program .
31913	Integer and real data representations are mixed together in the logical records in the data .
31914	The trick is to recognize which are which , and deal with them accordingly .
31915	The header/trailer and topology information must also be preserved exactly , and only the coordinate data perturbed .
31916	finally , the node information can be perturbed only once , which involves creating a node table into which the perturbed nodes are stored as they are read in , and from which they can be retrieved in later references to the same node .
31917	The GIS overlay operations follow next .
31918	In this case , the operations are a series of overlays , designed to remove infeasible areas from the base coverage .
31919	Lastly the polygon data in the output coverage are rasterized and the rasterized coverage stored .
31920	Rasterization is used to provide an easy way of visualizing the uncertainty in the output results .
31921	The object of the final analysis is to create a data set which contains , for each raster , the number of times it is simulated to be inside the areas resulting from the sequence of GIS operations .
31922	There are several ways of achieving this .
31923	The methodology used here is a three-stage operation ; first , the binary raster files or single variable files ( SVFs ) are expanded into character form , compressed ( Held 1983 ) , and a row number added ; second , the files area is sorted by the row number so that all records with the same row number are contiguous in the file ; third , a count is made of all the rasters in each row which are simulated to be inside the required areas .
31924	These frequencies can then be mapped to yield credibility regions corresponding to particular significance levels .
31925	A case study
31926	Searching for radwaste sites
31927	Openshaw et al. ( 1989 ) discuss the use of ARC/INFO to identify feasible sites for radwaste dumps .
31928	The GIS operations constitute little more than a sequence of map overlays in the form of a Boolean search .
31929	This process is re-examined here with particular attention to northern England to reduce the computational resources required .
31930	The object of the overlay exercise is to determine potentially feasible sites for the dumping of waste material from the nuclear industry , in particular , low- and intermediate-level radioactive waste .
31931	This chapter is not itself concerned with the mechanics or politics of the matter , the example chosen is merely a convenient one for purposes of illustrating a very common GIS procedure .
31932	For the dumping of such radioactive matter four criteria need to be considered :
31933	1 .
31934	The waste dump must be on a site with a suitable underlying geology ;
31935	2 .
31936	The site must be accessible from the UK rail network ;
31937	3 .
31938	The site must not be within a conservation area ( that is , a national park , area of outstanding natural beauty , etc. … ) ; and
31939	4 .
31940	The site must be away from areas of population concentration .
31941	Four coverages are used in the case study .
31942	The underlying suitable geologies , defined by the British Geological Survey ( Chapman et al. 1986 ) , were digitized from 1 : 625 000 scale maps .
31943	The rail network was digitized from 1 : 250 000 maps , and buffered at 3 km .
31944	The national park data were digitized from 1 : 250 000 maps .
31945	The population counts those grid squares with a population greater than 490 residents , representing a population density of greater than 4.9 persons/ha .
31946	The coverages are shown in Fig. 6.3 and the error estimates for them are contained in Table 6.2 .
31947	The first step involves processing a suitable geology coverage ( GEOLOGY ) .
31948	The ARC/INFO ERASE command ( the Boolean equivalent of NOT ) is used to remove the constrained areas from the coverage to build up a composite coverage .
31949	The elimination sequence is presented in Fig. 6.4 .
31950	Those areas which are outside the rail buffer , RAILBUF , are removed ( to give ERASRG ) , and next the conservation areas , CONSV ( to give ERASRGC ) .
31951	finally , the densely populated areas , POP490 , are deleted to give a set of feasible areas for site investigation ( ERASRGCP ) .
31952	The characteristics of each of the coverages are shown in Tables 6.3–6.6 , and the ARC command sequence to obtain the final overlay is in Table 6.7 .
31953	It is difficult to attempt to determine what are suitable estimates of the error in the map .
31954	ARC/INFO works to a minimum tolerance — the smallest distance between any pair of coordinates — known as the fuzzy tolerance .
31955	As a default , the fuzzy tolerance is 1/50 000 of the width of the base map , in this case , 0.48 mapunit .
31956	As the mapunits are 10 m , the fuzzy tolerance represents 4.8 m on the ground .
31957	The population data arc rather more problematic , since they are generated from the ‘ centroids ’ of census enumeration districts ( EDs ) ; the boundaries of the census EDs do not conveniently follow a grid , it is assumed they have a similar fuzzy tolerance to the other coverages .
31958	Clearly , the quantization noise which is introduced to the data requires a rather more sophisticated error model .
31959	The case study uses the error estimates in Table 6.2 as a guide to likely levels of uncertainty until further research yields more realistic models .
31960	The simulation is run 100 times .
31961	In each simulation :
31962	1 .
31963	Leftovers from any previous run are removed ;
31964	2 .
31965	A copy is taken of each of the unperturbed coverages ;
31966	3 .
31967	All nodes and vertices of each coverage are perturbed ;
31968	4 .
31969	The file structures are reorganized into a form the ARC i/o routines can deal with .
31970	This step is highly VAX/VMS specific and could probably be replaced by some more universal coding in the perturbation software .
31971	5 .
31972	The overlay sequence takes place ; remnants of any previous failures are removed ; and
31973	6 .
31974	The output vector coverage is rastered , prior to plotting .
31975	Step 6 introduces a series of problems .
31976	The rasterization process introduces noise .
31977	For the experiments here , a raster size of 1 km ( 100 mapunits ) is used .
31978	Given that the fuzzy tolerance is 25 mapunits , then the raster size should be that or less , to remove the quantization noise .
31979	However , reducing the raster size from 100 to 25 mapunits increases the disc space required to store the raster files by a factor of 16 as well as increasing processing times .
31980	ARC/INFO is not well tuned to handle this sort of problem .
31981	Simulation results
31982	The error model used here is an obvious over-simplification of reality .
31983	Each vertex in the coverage was perturbed by selecting random numbers from a uniform distribution , with ranges defined in Table 6.2 .
31984	Steps were taken to ensure that the nodes were not perturbed more than once , but no checks were made to determine whether the perturbation process caused sliver polygons to be created .
31985	The fuzzy tolerance of 25 mapunits was chosen to try to eliminate these from the final coverage .
31986	The process required 16 140 s of CPU time and 20 h of elapsed time on a lightly loaded microVAX 2 , under VMS .
31987	The resulting maps are shown in Fig. 6.5 .
31988	There are seven maps , showing 90 , 95 , 96 , 97 , 98 , 99 and 100 per cent , ‘ credibility regions ’ .
31989	The credible region is that which contains the feasible region n or more times out of M ; in this case M is 100 .
31990	As the ‘ credibility level ’ increases , so fewer and fewer areas are included in the map , reflecting the increasing confidence in the map .
31991	More areas are included in the map where the user is willing to be wrong 10 times out of 100 , but far fewer in that which they are willing to run the risk of being wrong once in a hundred times ; a comparison of the 90 and 99 per cent maps will make this clear ( figs 6.5a and f ) .
31992	There is little difference between the 90 , 95 , 96 and 97 per cent maps ( Figs 6.5a-d ) , but between the 97 and-98 per cent maps a considerable region in the north-east corner of the map is lost ( Figs 6.5d-e ) .
31993	Between 99 and l00 per cent , virtually all the map ( figs 6.5f-g ) is lost with the exception of the region in the south-east corner of the map .
31994	The overlay process has been most reliable here .
31995	Comparing this map with the ERASRGCP map from Fig. 6.4 will reveal the effect of trying to take uncertainty in the input data into account explicitly on the resulting map pattern .
31996	There are far fewer areas in the simulated map about which one would risk a definitive statement than in the map from the unsimulated process .
31997	Discussion
31998	The main problem with using a Monte Carlo approach is its slowness .
31999	A lightly loaded microVAX 2 can expect to take over 24 h of elapsed time to carry out 100 simulations on a small problem .
32000	Fortunately the process is explicitly parallel and were it to be run on multiprocessor hardware then there could be substantial speed-up .
32001	The simulation process is parallel , since one simulation does not depend on the outcome of a previous one .
32002	The selection of a suitable error model is problematic .
32003	One approach is to carry out experiments with a digitizing table in order to determine empirically an appropriate distribution for digitizing errors .
32004	Synthetic data which are themselves a GIS-derived product may be the most difficult to deal with .
32005	The grid square population data used here are a case in point .
32006	These data had to be estimated from census ED information .
32007	The aggregation process merely allocates to a grid square the populations of the ED whose ‘ centroid ’ happens to fall in that grid square .
32008	In the case where two or more EDs fall in the same grid square , then the grid square 's population is the sum of those of the individual EDs .
32009	It can also be argued that the error present in this data , given its crudity , would swamp any of the other data .
32010	However , it is only fair to point out that the population distribution is uneven , and any swamping will take place in urban areas .
32011	In the context of radwaste disposal , this is not critical , but for some other operations , it obviously is .
32012	There might be alternatives to using a grid .
32013	Very few ‘ natural ’ data come in grid form .
32014	One might buffer the ED centroids , assign populations to the resulting zones , then determine the population densities .
32015	The choice of buffer distance would need to be the subject of some experiment .
32016	The use of Theissen polygons has been suggested , although the statistical properties of processes giving rise to such areas are poor surrogates for digitized ED boundaries .
32017	The varying size of EDs in urban and rural areas , and the discontinuous nature of the population distribution inside the larger rural EDs is also difficult to parametrize .
32018	The selection of a raster size presents some other problems .
32019	The authors used an IBM 4216–010 PagePrinter as an output device .
32020	This is a device which supports PostScript , and which has a specified resolution of 300 pixels/inch , both the vertical and horizontal direction .
32021	In the case study maps , 1 pixel represents a square of size 118 m .
32022	With a l200 dpi printer ( such as a phototypesetter ) , each pixel would represent a square of size 29.5 m .
32023	These set minimum sizes for output .
32024	It should be noted that all the experiments thus far have used vector representations .
32025	It may be easier to implement it in a raster environment , but much would depend on the size of the rasters chosen to represent the areas .
32026	Clearly this is yet another area for further research .
32027	Conclusions
32028	This chapter has introduced some of the issues surrounding the propagation of error in GIS and described the preliminary application of a Monte Carlo approach to assessing their effects .
32029	The empirical research carried out here is intended to test the feasibility of this approach , as well as providing some general indications of what the effects might be and of one way by which they can be represented on the final output map .
32030	In so doing it is recognized that many of the questions raised are left open for subsequent investigation and that the results are initial and tentative .
32031	Although conceptually clear , the method is not easy to implement with current hardware .
32032	There is likely to be substantial increases in CPU times , although it might be possible to reduce this by a factor of 5 .
32033	However , with faster hardware likely to be on the market in the near future and the possibility of the emergence of parallel GIS machines , there is some justification for believing that extra effort is both worth while and acceptable .
32034	The challenge is to resolve the outstanding questions and perfect the technology as soon as possible .
32035	Perusal of Fig. 6.5 indicates that it does appear to work , and that it offers a pragmatic solution that could probably be developed further into a general-purpose GIS ‘ error button ’ .
32036	User interfaces
32037	Jonathan F. Raper
32038	Introduction
32039	Geographical information systems ( GIS ) make considerable demands on the user : the wide variety of data types recorded in digital maps , the complex data structures used to organize them and the range of operations available , amount to a formidable obstacle for most users with standard requirements .
32040	As such , the quality of interfaces to GIS has taken on a considerable importance in terms of awareness , training and usage , both to the providers of GIS software and users of GIS alike ( Rhind , et al. 1989 ) .
32041	However , there are many aspects to the definition of an interface for systems as complex as GIS , and the solutions to this problem are developing extremely rapidly at the time of writing .
32042	Accordingly , this chapter aims to set out the requirements for a fully configured GIS interface , and profiles the development of a new GIS user interface system called UGIX .
32043	This model is also used to define a research agenda for the next 5 years ; the reader may judge the accuracy of this analysis by the commercial reality of available systems during the early and mid-1990s .
32044	There is a wide recognition that the problems of poor interfaces are of considerable importance to the development of GIS .
32045	The UK Government Committee of Enquiry chaired by Lord Chorley ( DoE 1987 ) on the Handling of Geographic Information suggested in recommendation 59 that GIS technology projects be promoted since the report noted that the existing interfaces to GIS systems were poor .
32046	The shortcomings of GIS user environments can be divided into two groups :
32047	1 .
32048	Task complexity — the system functions implementing spatial operations are often complex and obscure ;
32049	2 .
32050	Poor database view tools — few systems make available database views meaningful to the user .
32051	Accordingly , it is clearly desirable that improved
32052	interfaces be developed so that the range of spatial operations in a system can be organized into standardized functions or tasks , and so that the spatial database can be visualized .
32053	The quality of GIS user interfaces is also an important factor in the acceptance , uptake and efficiency of the integrated GIS which are currently on the market .
32054	In a recent study by Willis and Nutter ( 1990 ) of 136 publicly funded utilities and municipalities in the UK 57 per cent stated that they were inhibited in their GIS developments by ‘ a lack of staff with the right expertise ’ .
32055	At a time when there is a national and international shortage of staff skilled in the computer handling of geographical data ( Rhind and Mounsey 1989 ) , ‘ ease of use ’ is a vital criterion for the selection of an appropriate GIS .
32056	It is generally accepted that a system which is easy to use can help cut recruitment and training costs , and help retain staff .
32057	Organizations which are in the process of implementing GIS strategies also appreciate that the ‘ ease of use ’ factor is a key control over how quickly GIS programmes can be implemented , and therefore the speed with which financial targets for paying off capital costs can be met .
32058	It may also be true that ‘ ease of use ’ can influence the quality of work done and the effectiveness of a GIS as a decision support system .
32059	To illustrate this in the negative , Beard ( 1989 ) for example , showed how ‘ use error ’ in GIS was an important but neglected aspect of quality control in GIS .
32060	In summary , the user interface is a vital element of any GIS .
32061	Long ignored as an esoteric aspect of GIS design while GIS development was driven by the need to extend functionality , the user interface is now beginning to attract its due attention .
32062	However , the implementation of a GIS user interface involves considerably more than the improvement of the human-computer interaction ( HCI ) process .
32063	Since GIS are conceptually complex and involve diverse operations ranging from data modelling to geometric transformations , improving the HCI can not be a complete solution to the improvements of GIS use .
32064	Consideration also needs to be given to the embedding of knowledge , task definitions and database view manipulations into such interfaces .
32065	A key assumption , therefore , which remains to be tested is whether a GIS user interface should condition GIS use .
32066	While there are many who would argue that a measure of technical knowledge is desirable in those who use a GIS and a protection against the misuse of a powerful tool , it must now be established that maximum ‘ achievable ’ use of a software system owes much to the creation of a structured use environment , with logic controls built into the interface .
32067	The user is then free to choose the environment which best matches their use characteristics or which improves their aggregate efficiency measured in time , error or quality terms .
32068	Characteristics of a user interface
32069	A user interface , at its most basic , consists simply of a system for communication with the computer .
32070	Since the demise of the punch-card system for entering commands this has normally been undertaken using a keyboard and a screen driven by a cathode ray tube ( CRT ) or liquid crystal display ( LCD ) , although voice entry of data and touch screens have also been used .
