34215	This particular situation will be discussed later in Section 20.2 .
34216	At this point , we may simply note that the method involved is essentially the same .
34217	Although the method described above does give an explicit integral expression for V , in practice it is extremely difficult to evaluate this integral for arbitrary initial data .
34218	Thus , it does not really provide a viable method for generating analytic solutions for any given analytic description of the approaching waves .
34219	Another problem with the method of Riemann is that it is not practically possible to generalize it to the case for non-colinear collisions .
34220	The method only applies to linear hyperbolic equations and , if the polarization of the approaching waves is not aligned , the field equations describing the resulting interaction are non-linear .
34221	In view of this , Hauser and Ernst ( 1989 a , b , 1990 ) have developed an alternative method which can be generalized to the non-colinear situation .
34222	The method employed by Hauser and Ernst ( 1989 a ) is first to find a one-parameter family of basic solutions by means of a suitable separation of variables and then to express the final solution as a linear super-position of these basic solutions .
34223	In fact their approach is based on the solution ( 10.8 ) , which may be re-expressed in the form ( 14.8 ) for suitable functions and which must depend on the initial data .
34224	An interesting feature of the method is that the functions and are obtained in terms of the prescribed initial data by solving generalized versions of Abel 's integral equation for the tautochrone problem of classical particle mechanics .
34225	Generalized versions of Abel 's integral equation are required because f' ( u ) and g' ( v ) are zero on the boundaries and respectively .
34226	Full details of the method have been described by Hauser and Ernst ( 1989 a ) .
34227	However , the techniques are still difficult to use in practice for arbitrary initial data .
34228	Hauser and Ernst ( 1989 b ) have also reformulated the initial-value problem for the colinear case as a Hilbert problem in a complex plane in two different ways .
34229	They have presented solutions of both forms of the Hilbert problem and shown that each of these agrees with the solution that is obtained by the method referred to above ( Hauser and Ernst , 1989 a ) .
34230	The non-colinear case
34231	Hauser and Ernst ( 1989 a , b , 1990 ) have developed the techniques mentioned at the end of the previous section to deal specifically with the case when the polarization of the approaching waves is not aligned .
34232	The initial data have already been described in Section 14.1 .
34233	It was also pointed out that , for the colinear case , it was convenient to rescale the approaching waves such that at the point of collision .
34234	For the non-colinear case , Hauser and Ernst have found it convenient to work with the complex function Z defined by ( 11.5 ) and to use the transformation ( 12.20 ) which consists of a rotation and rescaling to put at the point of collision when and .
34235	For the colinear case the main field equation ( 14.3 ) is linear .
34236	However , for the non-colinear case this is replaced by two non-linear equations , or by the complex Ernst equation .
34237	The non-linearity of this equation introduces considerable difficulty into any attempt at solving the general problem .
34238	Hauser and Ernst ( 1990 ) have developed a method for considering the initial-value problem for general colliding plane gravitational waves .
34239	They have achieved this by replacing the usual initial-value problem in terms of the Ernst equation by an equivalent 2 × 2 matrix homogeneous Hilbert problem in the complex plane .
34240	In the case when the polarization of the approaching waves is colinear , this approach reduces to the relatively simple one-dimensional Hilbert problem that was previously considered ( Hauser and Ernst , 1989 b ) .
34241	A detailed description of the method developed , however , is beyond the scope of this book and interested readers are directed to the original papers .
34242	In spite of these advances , there is strong evidence that the general solution of the initial-value problem for the non-colinear case is not expressible in a finite closed form .
34243	In addition , practical methods for solving the matrix homogeneous Hilbert problem for particular non-colinear cases still need to be developed .
34244	Clearly this is an area where considerable further work is required .
34245	COLLIDING ELECTROMAGNETIC WAVES : THE BELL-SZEKERES SOLUTION
34246	In an important paper , Bell and Szekeres ( 1974 ) gave an exact solution which describes the collision and subsequent interaction of two electromagnetic plane waves .
34247	This solution , which appears to be remarkably simple , will be described in this chapter .
34248	Other exact solutions describing colliding electromagnetic waves will be described in Chapters 16 and 17 , after more powerful techniques have been developed .

34308	Clarke and Hayward ( 1989 ) have also shown that the Bell-Szekeres solution is extendable to the future through the surface , but the extension is not unique because of the presence of the singularities .
34309	They have further suggested two possible extensions which will be described in the next section .
34310	It is also somewhat remarkable that the global structure of the Bell-Szekeres solution , as described by Clarke and Hayward ( 1989 ) , is very similar to that of the collision of an impulsive gravitational wave with a null shell of matter , as described by Babala ( 1987 ) .
34311	This will be discussed in Section 19.3 .
34312	Chandrasekhar and Xanthopoulos ( 1988 ) have conducted a thorough perturbation analysis of this particular solution .
34313	Throughout the interaction region subsequent to the collision they have obtained a complete set of bounded normal modes that are expressed in terms of spin-weighted spherical harmonics .
34314	These modes exhibit a behaviour of ever-increasing frequency as the Cauchy horizon is approached .
34315	Chandrasekhar and Xanthopoulos ( 1988 ) have also considered perturbations in the initial regions which contain the approaching waves .
34316	For the approaching wave in region II which propagates along the null line , , they have shown that v -independent perturbations are not permitted to all orders , while all the v -dependent perturbations exhibit strong divergences along the ‘ fold ’ singularity .
34317	Unfortunately , these perturbations can not be joined continuously to those of the interaction region .
34318	It is therefore not possible to consider the effects of these perturbations subsequent to the collision .
34319	Extensions of the solution
34320	In the Bell-Szekeres solution , it has been shown that the hypersurface on which the opposing waves mutually focus each other is a Cauchy horizon rather than a curvature singularity .
34321	It is therefore appropriate to consider possible extensions to this solution through the horizon , even though any such extension will not be unique .
34322	Two possible extensions have been given by Clarke and Hayward ( 1989 ) .
34323	One natural extension of region IV is simply the future extension of the region as described by the line element ( 15.14 ) .
34324	This is achieved by extending the coordinate range to ( 15.17 ) where .
34325	In this extension , the waves cross and focus .
34326	The subsequent space-time is unchanging .
34327	Another equally natural extension of region IV is obtained by noting that the line element ( 15.14 ) admits a reflection symmetry about the hyperplane ( or about ) .
34328	Thus , there is an extension in which region IV is extended as far as and is then followed by the time reverse of the entire solution .
34329	In this extension , the waves cross , mutually focus each other , re-expand and then separate leaving Minkowski space between them to the future .
34330	This situation is illustrated in Figure 15.1 in terms of the original null coordinates and the line elements ( 15.3 ) and ( 15.7 ) .
34331	Other apparent extensions of the Bell-Szekeres solution have been suggested by Gürses and Halilsoy ( 1982 ) in which the approaching electromagnetic waves consist of a sequence of steps .
34332	The step lengths , however , have to be double the distance to the fold singularities .
34333	Thus , these solutions necessarily extend the space-time through the covering space singularities and can not , therefore , be considered as appropriate solutions for colliding plane waves .
34334	In all these solutions the space-time can only be extended uniquely up to the fold singularities in regions II and III and the surface in region IV on which .
34335	It must therefore be concluded that the Gürses-Halilsoy extensions are not physically significant .
34336	Figure 15.1 An extension of the Bell-Szekeres space-time .
34337	Regions marked I are flat .
34338	Regions marked II and III contain electromagnetic waves with , and respectively , having metrics given by ( 15.3 ) .
34339	There are impulsive gravitational waves along the boundaries of region IV , which has metric ( 15.7 ) .
34340	A non-colinear collision
34341	In the Bell-Szekeres solution , the polarization of the approaching electromagnetic waves is aligned .
34342	It is appropriate now to consider how this solution may be generalized to include the case when the polarization is not aligned .
34343	In the approaching waves a rotation of the polarization is expressed by a rotation of the components Φ 2 or Φ in the complex plane .
34344	The metrics in both regions are unaltered , since a null electromagnetic field is defined by the metric only up to a constant duality rotation .
34345	Thus , to extend the Bell-Szekeres solution , the same initial conditions are given except that the component becomes complex and , from ( 6.22e ) , W must become non-zero in the interaction region .
34346	A solution presented by Griffiths ( 1985 ) satisfying this condition may be written in the form ( 15.18 ) where ( 15.19 ) The relative polarization angle of the two waves prior to the collision is given by α .
34347	It may be noticed that the expression for U here is equivalent to those of ( 15.4,5 ) and ( 15.6 ) .
34348	The common multiple 2 has been inserted so that this solution can be more directly related to the Bell-Szekeres solution to which it reduces when .
34349	It can be shown that this solution has exactly the same properties as the aligned Bell-Szekeres solution .
34350	It is conformally flat everywhere except at the boundaries of the interaction region where there are impulsive gravitational waves that may be considered to be generated by the collision .
34351	These are given by ( 15.20 )
34352	According to a theorem of Tariq and Tupper ( 1974 ) , this new solution must as be the Bertotti-Robinson space-time in a different coordinate system .
34353	In fact it can be obtained from the Bell-Szekeres line element ( 15.7 ) by the simple rotation ( 15.21 )
34354	Thus , the gravitational field in this case is identical to that of the Bell-Szekeres solution , as may have been expected .
34355	In the collision of plane electromagnetic waves with non-aligned polarization , it must therefore be concluded that the dynamics remains unaltered .
34356	It is only the form of the metric in the interaction region that needs to be modified to that given in this section .
34357	Family burgled yet again
34358	A GANG of professional thieves who staked out a house in Bentworth last week got away with a £20,000 caravan .
34359	Now the angry owner , whose home has been burgled four times this year , is offering a £500 reward for information .
34360	Twenty-three year-old Allen Taylor is ‘ sick and tired ’ of the continuing attacks on his parents ' house and is appealing for help .
34361	The latest raid at Ashley Road happened between 6 p.m. and 7.15 p.m. on Friday evening .
34362	It is believed that the gang had been watching the property from a nearby field .
34363	Two days before they struck , a sensor light set up outside the house was smashed .
34364	The Swift Challenger 490 caravan had been parked in the driveway behind another vehicle , but the thieves were undeterred and made their move under the cover of darkness soon after two members of the family left the home .
34365	They forced their way onto adjoining land and cut through chain-link fencing and large wooden posts cemented into the ground .
34366	Gap in the fence
34367	The gang manhandled the 18-foot caravan through the gap in the fence and began pushing it across the field towards the road .
34368	When the villains were unable to get the caravan up a small incline , they hitched it to a stolen vehicle and wheel-spun their way onto the road .
34369	Once they were outside the grounds , the thieves dumped one vehicle and used another to make their get-away , with the cream coloured caravan in tow .
34370	The daring raid was executed in minutes , according to Mr. Taylor .
34371	‘ My mother had taken my little brother to tennis at Winchester , ’ he said .
34372	‘ My 20-year-old sister was at home alone when they struck .
34373	‘ She heard the three dogs barking , but before she went to see what was up , the phone rang .
34374	She was only on the phone for a minute but that was all it took . ’
34375	A short while later his mother and brother arrived home to discover the caravan gone .
34376	They immediately phoned Allen , who has a car business at Lower Wield , and he set off in pursuit of the gang .
34377	‘ I drove home and then followed the road into Alton , but I could find no sign of them , ’ he said .
34378	‘ I stopped a policeman in the High Street and he radioed in the information I gave him .
34379	‘ In the meantime , my dad had arrived at the house and spotted two men hanging around the ditched vehicle .
34380	When they saw him they just sped off . ’
34381	Allen is certain that somebody must have seen the caravan at some point that evening .
34382	With the narrow lanes around Bentworth , any approaching traffic would have had to give way and cars travelling in the same direction could have been held up .
34383	If no-one saw the caravan being towed along any of the main roads in the area , then Allen believes the gang may have stored it somewhere in the vicinity .
34384	He is appealing for anyone who saw the caravan or knows of its whereabouts to contact him .
34385	‘ Anyone who gives me the information that leads to these people will get the reward money , ’ he said .
34386	However , he is also keen to hear from residents who have also suffered at the hands of thieves .
34387	‘ Being burgled four times since the start of the year is something you 'd associate with the inner-cities — but this is Bentworth . ’
34388	Anyone who has information about the gang or the caravan can contact Mr. Taylor at his work on 0256 389000 .

34419	Company fined after river pollution
34420	A POISONOUS cocktail of chemicals which found its way into the River Wey at Alton killed some 100 fish .
34421	Last week , the company responsible for the pollution , Laleham Healthcare Plc , were fined £2,000 by the town 's magistrates on Friday .
34422	The court heard how the river turned a milky white colour as it was contaminated with toxic residue from shampoo , moisturiser , and hair lightener products .
34423	An investigation was immediately launched by the National Rivers Authority following a tip-off from a member of the public .
34424	An officer visited the Mill Lane Industrial Estate and found the company still carrying out their cleaning operation .
34425	Laleham Healthcare Plc pleaded guilty to the charge of polluting the river on September 19th .
34426	Magistrates heard that employees had been hosing out residue from used drums — using a high pressure jet — in a defined ‘ washing area ’ .
34427	But the surrounding drain designed to carry all the toxic effluent away in the foul sewer system had become blocked .
34428	Instead , the poisonous waste was overflowing into a surface water drain , hidden underneath some pallets , and running out into the River Wey .
34429	Surface water
34430	The NRA officer blocked the outlet to prevent any further pollution leaving the site , and Laleham 's called in a contractor later that day to clean out the surface water system .
34431	Defending solicitor Bob Booker told the court : ‘ If the grating which surrounds the washing area had been clear there should n't have been any problems .
34432	‘ And as soon as they realised it was an emergency , the offending drain was fitted with a plug . ’
34433	Mr. Booker said that the company had since fitted blocks on top of all their surface water drains and that a four foot wall has been built around the washing area .
34434	In addition to the £2,000 fine , magistrates ordered Laleham Healthcare to pay £250 towards the prosecution costs .

34746	Village school prepare for a new history lesson
34747	BENTLEY Primary School are celebrating their 150th anniversary this year and preparations are well under way for a week under way for a week of special events in May .
34748	Highlights will be an exhibition of photographs and artefacts depicting village life , a Victorian Day in school when everyone will be in costume , a drama production and a Victorian fete .
34749	The exhibition will not only show life in Bentley during the past 150 years , but also that of Froyle , concentrating on the development of both village schools , culminating in their merger in 1986 .
34750	Head teacher of Bentley School , Philip Callaway , told the Herald that during the week , the children 's topic work would also be looking at changes in everyday life over the 150 years .
34751	‘ Hopefully we will be able to make history come alive for the children , ’ Mr. Callaway said , adding that the school would still be grateful for as many old photographs and bits and pieces of memorabilia as possible .
34752	‘ We would also like former pupils of the school , both locally and from more distant parts , to visit us during the celebrations , he said .
34753	Bentley School was built 150 years ago on half an acre of land given by Bishop Sumner of Winchester but its history prior to 1882 is almost non-existent since the log books for the early years have long since been lost .
34754	But from the log books of 100 years ago , there is a very vivid picture of school life in Bentley .
34755	Main industry
34756	Hop growing was the main industry in the village and the school 's calendar was very much influenced by the farming calendar : ‘ August 24th , 1883 — broke up for the harvest and hop tying today .
34757	Very few children have been present during this week , many with their parents in the field .
34758	We should have broken up before but there is every prospect of a late and long hopping in which case we should have difficulty in making the necessary attendances . ’
34759	The building itself , today so warm and modern , left a lot to be desired : ‘ March 3rd , 1890 — Temperature at school at 9.30 a.m. is 32F …
34760	December 23rd , 1891 — It has been impossible to do much work this week , for the room has been so cold , we have been obliged to drill to keep ourselves warm .
34761	It was no better in the summer : ‘ July 10th , 1885 — The hot weather makes the work very difficult .
34762	As the ditches smell so badly we are obliged to keep the north windows shut … ‘
34763	In 1892 , the school managers ’ book reveals that the infant classroom was enlarged and in 1893 the ‘ excellent master 's house ’ was built by public subscription at a total cost of £613.7.3d .
34764	Then , in 1914 , major renovation of the building was undertaken to give a new large room , some 5ft. wider and 7ft. higher , as well as a new infants ' classroom and cloakrooms .
34765	During these alterations the school moved into a nearby hop kiln , to the great delight of the children .
34766	Walter Sherfield , who had started school the year before , remembers the time well , particularly during the long hot summer days when lessons were held out in the open , under the old oak trees .
34767	He remembers that work on the new school building had to be completed by the end of August since the hop kilns were needed in September .
34768	With the coming of the first world war , the children of Bentley School were soon busy with their own war efforts — they had a collection for the Blue Cross Fund for horses and a War Loan Savings Association was formed .
34769	A war school garden was started in 1917 with some 20 boys planting potatoes … in October the records show that ‘ Each of the 20 boys received about 56 lbs .
34770	of potatoes . ’
34771	Acorns and horse chestnuts were collected to be used in the making of munitions and several old pupils , on leave from the front , visited the school .
34772	In 1918 it 's disclosed that : ‘ The managers have arranged to supply those children , who remain , to dinner with a hot meal for a penny halfpenny per day per child . ’
34773	Each day , the meal was made up of baked potatoes and either rice pudding , soup , hashed beans and vegetables or oatmeal porridge .
34774	Forefathers
34775	Around the time of the renovations , there was some discussion on handing the school over to the state , but the management committee , headed by the rector , the Rev. Henry Moody , concluded : ‘ The time has not yet come … for the surrender of these schools and the forfeiting thereby of the gifts and labours of our forefathers . ’
34776	Indeed , it was n't until 1958 that the committee 's successors decided that the increase in pupils needed better amenities than the dwindling funds could provide .
34777	State aid was accepted for the school , although the Church still retained some control .
34778	In recent years , the school has seen major changes with the enlargement and modernisation of the building to accommodate the extra children from nearby Froyle , following the closure of the school there in 1986 .
34779	An entry in the school log book after the earlier renovation in 1914 might have been written today .
34780	It states : ‘ I received a letter from the chief inspector , Mr. Wynne Williams , today saying that he wishes to congratulate the managers on the new buildings , ‘ among the best in the county ’ .
34781	He adds : ‘ Educationally , the school seems to have a future ’ … ‘ .
34782	If you can help the school with photos or exhibits or would like to get involved in some way , ‘ phone 0420 23273 .
34783	Bentley School in 1913 before it was enlarged .

34816	A comic hoard to treasure
34817	THE Royal Exchange Theatre Company 's production of a new translation of Moliere 's The Miser is playing at the Yvonne Arnaud Theatre , Guildford until tomorrow ( Saturday ) .
34818	On a set of Heath Robinson ingenuity with suspended buckets , antique plumbing and piles of dusty books and furniture — all part of the Miser 's hoard of battered possessions — Tom Courtenay schemes , struts and raves as he seeks to protect his two million francs .
34819	It is Tom Courtenay , the programme says so , but beneath a straggly white wig , black beret and tattered frock coat with trousers surely cast off by Cyril Smith and insecurely fastened by an army of safety pins , it is difficult to recognise him .
34820	There 's no difficulty , however , in recognising his mastery of the role .
34821	He is wonderfully avaricious , devious and a genius at avoiding parting with even a sou , all to great comic effect .
34822	But to his unfortunate son and daughter ( William Armstrong and Margo Gunn ) he seems to ‘ make Shylock look like Dr. Barnardo ’ as he keeps them in penury with each request for money causing him acute physical pain .
34823	Polly James , as the matchmaker Frosine , is energetic and endlessly scheming as she attempts to marry off the daughter and her lover Valère , who is masquerading as the Miser 's steward , and the son and Mariane , who is also the object of the father 's desire .
34824	The complications are endless and the resolution a hilarious bundle of coincidence and tortuous explanation worthy of the worst soap .
34825	Colin Prockter is excellent as the downtrodden cook- cum -coachman , with a particularly revolting bloodstained apron .
34826	As the daughter , Margo Gunn is somewhat expressionless and William Armstrong as her brother at times inaudible so emotionally choked is his delivery .
34827	As Valère , Alex Hardy exhibits a Basil Fawlty brand of obsequious contempt for his master .
34828	But Tom Courtenay rivets the attention and elicits a certain sympathy as he bemoans the loss of his cash box — despite his paranoid security measures .
34829	‘ Oh my poor dear money …
34830	I have lost my consolation , my joy , I ca n't live without you . ’
34831	No one is safe from suspicion — let alone the audience on whom he turns with an accusatory stare .
34832	‘ You all look highly suspicious to me . ’
34833	Loss of his money is like evisceration .
34834	It is no matter to him that he loses his hold over his children and his erstwhile fiancée .
34835	The morals and ethics are obvious , the comedy more subtle and highly entertaining .
34836	Worth seeing for Courtenay alone .

34849	Wide boy Gary chats up Sue but she does n't want to be called a slut .
34850	Rick fancies Sharon from afar but neither has the confidence to make a move .
34851	The loutish Eddie meanwhile fancies his chances with ‘ Frigid ’ Bridgit and makes a bet with his pals that he can score by the end of the evening .
34852	The moves , counter moves , rejections , romances and broken hearts are spun together effortlessly through the music and will strike a chord with any teenagers and ex-teenagers who have fallen in love on a Saturday night .
34853	It was written four years ago by Neil , Lea , John and Charlie Heather and is based on their teenage experiences .
34854	All four brothers were in a band together and began writing the musical while on the road in Africa and Europe .
34855	‘ We 'd just sit around a table and write it together .
34856	We never had any arguments and we could all contribute some experience that each of us had had , ’ John told the Herald .
34857	All the brothers are attending the opening nights of the show , which is seven weeks into a national tour .
34858	The show ran for nearly two years at the Arts Theatre in the West End to rave reviews .
34859	Despite all the publicity through word of mouth and a high profile national tour last year with Gary Glitter , the show remains relatively unknown .
34860	All that could change , however , as another West End run , a film and possible TV series based on the play are all in the pipeline .
34861	Successful productions are currently running in New Zealand , South Africa , Ireland , Germany — in both German and English — and Japan , in Japanese .
34862	Others are set to open in Australia , Mexico , Israel , Russia , Canada and America .
34863	Its main appeal to audiences everywhere is surely the sense of history .
34864	Although a perfect antidote to those who yearn for a return of those days .
34865	It is just as relevant to today 's youngsters and the emotions are just the same .
34866	The same characters can probably be found in any nightclub across the world .
34867	The production compares well with the West End show and is thoroughly recommended .
34868	A Slice of Saturday Night is at the Festival Theatre , , Chichester , until tomorrow ( Saturday ) .

34900	PETERSFIELD MUSICAL FESTIVAL
34901	The youth concert
34902	I MISSED the first performance of Peter Thompson 's Chinese Lantern Music at last year 's Summer Serenade , was so delighted to hear the complete work — the third in a series of commissions for local composers — played by the Petersfield Area Youth Orchestra on Wednesday .
34903	The twelve cameos , each written to display the talents of individual instrumentalists , made an enchanting effect .
34904	As well as heroic pieces for full orchestra , oboe , flutes , bassoon , euphonium and piano all had their moments , though only in one section , ‘ Distant Hills ’ , did I detect any specific Chinese influence .
34905	The conductor was David Thomas , whose In Nubibus , the second of the series , was a highlight of last year 's festival .
34906	The presence in the orchestra of the composer of the first , showed just what happy family occasions these youth concerts have become .
34907	PAYO , themselves a revelation last year , have progressed well , and it is to the credit of the young string players that they were not outclassed by the wind .
34908	Their thoroughly professional performance of Bizet 's Overture Dr. Miracle , under Anne Claxton , reflected great credit on her training .
34909	The orchestra also accompanied a rousing group of music hall songs , in arrangements by members of Petersfield School 's 6th form , Victoria Scott , Annette Pearce and Laurence Evans .
34910	The singing of the choirs was less assured here than it had been in the group of European folk songs , arranged and conducted by Duncan Hanner at the start of the concert .
34911	The fresh toned singing of such favourites as Alouette , A-roving and the Skye Boat Song must have taken many of the audience back to their own school days .
34912	The Festival Wind Band , emanating mainly from Churcher 's College , gave a highly authentic rendering of Sousa 's Liberty Bell ; minus a piccolo perhaps , but splendid in every respect .
34913	Their Music of the Beatles made an effective contrast .
34914	Youth concerts always have to include a major work written in the current ‘ Cantata ’ fashion .
34915	This year the choice fell on Richard Stilgoe 's The Big Band , an updated version , for bass soloist , narrators , instrumentalists , chorus and audience of the creation story .
34916	No disrespect to Philip Young , the conductor , or to any of the performers , but I have to agree with the member of the audience sitting behind me who commented that it seemed more of a damp squib than a big band !
34917	One has to question if these pieces justify the enormous amount of rehearsal they require .
34918	Mention has to be made of Julia Chapman 's singing of ‘ Joshua ’ , of the trio called Full Swing , who entertained with modern jazz in the foyer as the audience arrived and , inevitably , the Petersfield School Dance Band ( another happy family ) who set out feet a-dancing in the Rose Room after the concert .
34919	Ann Pinhey
34920	Petersfield Orchestra
34921	AS festival chairman I was already very heartened , before a note had been played , to see a 60 strong orchestra assembling before an all-but capacity audience on Thursday .
34922	The orchestra , consisting almost entirely of local musicians , included a satisfying mixture of professional players , teachers , amateurs and students and the audience included many faces familiar from the choirs which perform on the festival 's choral evenings .
34923	It is these cross-relations which put the festival at the heart of local music-making .
34924	In Borodin 's Overture to Prince Igor the orchestra established themselves convincingly with secure intonation and ensemble and some distinguished solo wind playing .
34925	Trumpets and trombones provided bold splashes of colour , but some sections of the orchestra — notably horns and violins — were slow to warm up , and underplayed the romantic and exotic element in the music .
34926	Judith Bailey 's firm , clear beat led perhaps to an unduly deliberate tempo and heaviness of phrasing in the first movement of Beethoven 's Emperor Concerto and narrowly missed coinciding with the soloist at a few important junctions .
34927	In their accompaniments , the strings could have contributed greater warmth and colour — particularly by using more vibrato .
34928	Soloist Annette Servadei played beautifully with an involvement entirely free from any kind of ostentation .
34929	This suited the broad sweep of the first movement and the magical filigree of the second movement splendidly , but the finale perhaps asks for a degree of conscious showmanship .
34930	Towards the end Miss Servadei suffered several stumbles and a memory lapse , which unsettled this listener .
34931	Sibelius ' Fifth Symphony was an ambitious choice but Judith Bailey 's impressive grasp of the music carried both orchestra and audience through the technical difficulties to the final magnificent blaze of Nordic splendour .
34932	Philip Young

34959	Extrovert finale
34960	SATURDAY 'S finale was a thoroughly extrovert affair , dominated by Bernstein 's Chichester Psalms , Copland 's Clarinet Concerto and Constant Lambert 's The Rio Grande .
34961	One had heard the ominous rumblings from the singers regarding the complexity of both choral and works , and the language of one of them ( Hebrew ) , but in performance on Saturday evening they sounded tremendous .
34962	Judged by the highest standards there may have some stiffness in the rhythm , some slack articulation of the words and some raucous tone from certain voices , yet , urged on by the dynamic playing of the Guildford Philharmonic Orchestra , and especially by the cohorts of percussion , the singing was exhilarating .
34963	The conductor William Llewellyn may well have had a few sleepless nights but must have been proud of his singers .
34964	These were much the best performances I have heard from him , and say a lot for the state of Horndean , Petersfield and Rogate Choral Societies , from whom the Festival Chorus were drawn .
34965	The choice of a counter-tenor for the solos in both works was inspired , and , it seems , truly authentic .
34966	The music often lies extremely high , but Nicholas Clapton had no difficulty with the tessitura , and displayed remarkable breath control .
34967	The pianist was Roger Bluff , who seemed able to draw a singing tone from the Festival piano that I have not heard matched for some time .
34968	He also accompanied three American Folk songs by Copland , which were sensitively sung , and joined Keir Rowe in the Clarinet concerto .
34969	Mr. Rowe projected his highly contrasted part with the utmost clarity and assurance , though the violins of the Guildford Philharmonic Orchestra had , understandably , some difficulties at the start of the final section .
34970	Samuel Barber 's Adagio for Strings was well enough played but lacked the last ounce of passion , and suffered badly from the aurally obtrusive air conditioning system , Randall Thompson 's Alleluya showed that the Festival Chorus on this occasion were equally as adept at unaccompanied singing as their counterparts had been last week .
34971	Perhaps it is too much to hope that this concert finally dragged the Petersfield Musical Festival into the 20th century , but with a promised appearance by the acclaimed National Youth Jazz Orchestra next year , as well as The Dream of Gerontius , it remains only for the committee to do something about the slow start to the week for the festival to regain some of its former splendour .
34972	Ann Pinhey

34989	PAUL MERRILL REPORTS
34990	VIDEO : A Rage in Harlem ( 18 ) **
34991	MUCH touted as the definitive account of the black ghetto , A Rage in Harlem has an impressive cast list and an intriguing story but stops well short of expectations .
34992	Robin Givens is the sexy femme fatale who , on the run from her former lover , lures unsuspecting undertaker Forest Whitaker into her deadly web before sucking his bank account dry .
34993	The backdrop of 1950s Harlem is violent and sinister and the direction pulls few punches .
34994	This is warts and all film making which , though done to good effect , is hardly uplifting .
34995	Whitaker and Givens give the proceedings a much needed lift and the latter shows promise and the conniving seductress .
34996	The supporting cast , especially Danny Glover and Gregory Hines , are also superb .
34997	Why is it then that the film fails to deliver ?
34998	It has all the right ingredients but somewhere during preparation something went wrong producing an unsatisfying dish with a bitter aftertaste .
34999	In truth it drags along far to slowly and is never quite interesting or gripping enough in the right places despite the considerable efforts of the players .

35067	News from Alresford
35068	Does the town want a new cemetery ?
35069	COUNCIL ASKS FOR RESIDENTS ' VIEWS
35070	THE limited powers of the parish council , which are in turn further limited by lack of resources cause much frustration , said chairman Roy Downham at Alresford Parish Council 's annual meeting held in the Phair Hall of the Community Centre on Friday evening .
35071	There is always , he said , more than needs doing , than can be afforded .
35072	Mr. Downham asked the public their views on two subjects currently under discussion .
35073	One is the need for a burial ground , as the town cemetery , in St. John 's churchyard , is very nearly full , and there is no possibility of any extension .
35074	A new ground will be costly and a suitable area will need to be found .
35075	He asked if residents wanted a new cemetery in Alresford , rather than use the Winchester cemetery .
35076	Water fears
35077	The second subject was that two dry winters are inevitably leading towards a summer of water shortages .
35078	The council are considering asking the Southern Water Authority to impose restrictions on use of water now rather than wait until matters become really serious .
35079	Mr. Downham also presented the financial account , saying that it had been decided not to increase the parish council 's share from the community charge , by more than five percent .
35080	Reporting for the recreation grounds committee , Barbara Griffiths said that £25,688 had been spent on recreation in Alresford in the past year .
35081	The major project , costing £20,698 , had been the refurbishment of the play area at the Stratton Bates recreation ground , including new equipment and a safety surface .
35082	It has been agreed that the changing rooms at the Stratton Bates playing field needs to be replaced and £10,000 has already be set aside in the current budget towards the cost , which is anticipated to be in the region of £55,000 .
35083	The Sun Hill recreation ground is in need of similar treatment to that of Stratton Bates .
35084	A grant has been requested towards the cost of installing a safety surface and a number of residents have volunteered to form a family fund-raising group to help with providing equipment .
35085	This has been welcomed by the council .
35086	New lights
35087	The shelter and the shed at the War Memorial gardens have been vandalised .
35088	The tennis courts at Arlebury Park are to be resurfaced shortly , and the football pitches at both Arlebury and Stratton Bates continue to be well used and are an ongoing maintenance expense .
35089	Bill Liddiard , chairman of the lighting committee , referred to new lighting in Station Road , additional lighting in The Avenue , and the proposed changes to lighting in Broad Street .
35090	The lights in Broad Street are both corroded and obsolete .
35091	Lighting columns now have to be to regulation safety standards , and it is hoped that the new lights chosen will be complementary to the street .
35092	Two sample lights have been installed , and plans showing the changes are on view in Eddolls shop window in Broad Street .
35093	Members of the public expressed some dismay that the new lighting would be yellow , pointing out that the white light gives a character and atmosphere to this conservation area which should not be altered .
35094	Chris Webb reported a quiet year for the planning committee , with only 78 applications , most of them for extensions , alterations and change of use , although it had included plans for low cost housing .
35095	A new amenities committee had been formed within the parish council during the year , and chairman Ken Yeldham explained that it had been formed to deal with the things that fell outside the scope of the present committees .
35096	Six committees of the new committee had taken place , with a watchful eye being kept on environmental improvements , the need for bus shelters , involvement in finding a place for the youth of the town to meet , and consideration of the difficulties faced by the very elderly and disabled in the town centre .
35097	The committee had also carried out a survey of parking problems in residential areas .
35098	Currently they are seeking suitable permanent parking places for the local St. John Ambulance vehicles , and organising an official Spring Clean Day on April 4th .
35099	Hampshire county councillor Peter Maxwell was at the meeting and he said that the community charge had been set at £237 , which is £33 below the government guideline .
35100	Winchester city councillor Major Dougie Covill requested that more pressure be put upon the county council to improve the footpaths and pavements which are in a very dangerous condition , and a Broad Street businessman wondered if residents were really aware of the changes going on in Broad Street , and the manner in which they were to be undertaken .
35101	The meeting ended with a talk with slides presented by Rod Murchie of the National Rivers Authority .

35109	Manuscript evening reveals ‘ things not generally known ’
35110	FROM memories of a journey through Alresford in the 1920s to a paper on Rasputin , the stories told by members at Alresford Historical and Literary Society 's annual manuscript evening held the large audience 's attention with their detail and variety .
35111	Reg Sanders ' ‘ Things not generally known ’ opened the evening with a mish-mash of information gleaned through some 300 historical reference books .
35112	For instance , he said that the expression ‘ by hook or by crook ’ came from the period of Charles II when there were two judges called Hook and Crook and ‘ a man of straw ’ he discovered , was one who could be brought to bear false witness — recognisable by the straw in his shoes .
35113	Ursula Oxley read from the memoirs of Henry Hunt who was born Wiltshire , was elected to parliament , and worked for the repeal of the corn laws .
35114	On February 15th , 1835 , en route to the west country he stopped at Alresford , was seized by paralysis and died .
35115	His mistress , Mrs. Vince , wanted his body to be placed in her family vault , but the family objected , and the corpse was eventually removed to Parham .
35116	Some years later , another Henry Hunt , Alresford 's famous architect , was born but there is no connection between the two .
35117	Mrs. Oxley concluded her reading with three poignant poems about her son that she wrote herself .
35118	The Russian monk Rasputin , who was influential in Tsar Nicholas II 's court , was the subject of Cyril Flack 's manuscript .
35119	Mr. Flack 's own interest began in 1934 when he was in court for the libel case brought against the MGM film company who had made a film about Rasputin .
35120	The case became the standard for setting the difference between libel and slander .
35121	Early memories of Northern Rhodesia were the inspiration for Robin Grieves-Cook 's manuscript .
35122	He remembered small birds cleaning teeth of 14ft. crocodiles and a close encounter when he accompanied a hunter and ‘ bagged ’ six crocodiles .
35123	Motorcycle ride
35124	One of the highlights of the evening was Roy Robins ' beautifully written ‘ A journey through Alresford ’ .
35125	This recalled a journey from his home in Farnham to Dorset by motorcycle and sidecar in the 1920s .
35126	His lively description had the audience sharing the thoughts of the small boy as he travelled through Alresford , Romsey , Wimborne and Blandford , and almost feeling his stiff limbs and sore bottom .
35127	Elsie Sanders concluded the evening with a visit to West Meon cemetery , to the grave of Tom Lord , cricketer and founder of Lord 's Cricket Ground .
35128	He retired to Hampshire and died in 1832 at the age of 76 .
35129	The MCC continue to care for his grave .
35130	In contrast , on the other side of the same cemetery is the grave of the Burgess family , where the ashes of the spy Guy Burgess , who died in Russia , were placed .
35131	Appropriately , this manuscript was called ‘ The Famous and Infamous ’ .

35189	LETTERS
35190	4,000-year Holy Land link — and that 's alien ?
35191	Sir , — It saddened me to see Mr. Reg Cleaver describe the Jews as ‘ an alien people ’ in relation to the land of Israel .
35192	The Jewish people have had continuous relationship with the Holy Land for nearly 4,000 years .
35193	Sometimes the Jews were independent ( as in the periods of the Judges and the biblical Kings ) , sometimes a beleaguered subject people .
35194	They were often an impoverished and persecuted remnant , victims of wave after wave of invaders and persecutors — Babylonians , Greeks , Romans , Moslem Arabs , Byzantines , Crusaders and Ottomans until the present century brought British troops under General Allenby and the British Mandate in 1917 .
35195	But alien ?
35196	Never that .
35197	There were always Jewish communities in the land .
35198	Augmented by their co-religionists through the centuries , often in response to waves of persecution such as the expulsion from Spain which occurred 500 years ago this month .
35199	Many great poets and spiritual leaders produced work of benefit to all mankind from the homeland of the Jewish people .
35200	There are very few countries and groups of people which have had as devoted and heartfelt connection to a land as have the Jews to the land of Israel .
35201	I share Mr. Cleaver 's sentiment of placing equal value on every human life ‘ whether that be Jew , Christian or Muslem ’ ; the world would be a better place if more people did so .
35202	But I am troubled that he mentions the deaths of British servicemen without any references to the closing of the gates of Mandatory Palestine to the desperate refugees who tried to leave Nazi Germany but found the rest of Europe and the Jewish homeland closed to them .
35203	Perhaps Mr. Cleaver has forgotten that the British authorities turned away from Palestine ships laden with hopeless would-be immigrants who were forcibly , returned to Europe and the death camps .
35204	Some of the ships sank on the way to or from the Promised Land , while millions perished for want of a safe haven .
35205	By virtue of the existence of Israel , the threatened or endangered Russian and Ethiopian Jew can find a home , as did the 800,000 Jews who were expelled from Iraq and other Arab countries when the Jewish State came into being .
35206	Yet Israel occupies less than a quarter of the mandatory territory controlled by Britain after the first world war .
35207	Its area is a tiny fraction of that occupied by the 21 hostile Arab states ; Syria alone is seven times as large .
35208	One may well blame politicians for much Middle East misery , as Mr. Cleaver maintains , but without forgetting that Palestine has been partitioned a number of times .
35209	77 percent of it was cut off in 1922 and called Trans-Jordan ; the remaining section was partitioned by the United Nations in 1947 .
35210	This would have given Israel about 10 percent of the original Mandated territory .
35211	The Jewish community accepted the partition plan .
35212	By contrast , the Arab population and surrounding countries did not accept this United Nations decision and five Arab armies attacked the new State of Israel as soon as it was declared in May 1948 .
35213	Hostility to the Jewish State has been unremitting except in the case of Egypt since 1977 .
35214	In his article , Mr. Cleaver omits any mention of successive attacks by Arab armies on Israel since in 1948 .
35215	In the Yom Kippur war of 1973 , with no declaration of war , the Arab launched a ferocious war , the Arab launched a ferocious war on two fronts on the most sacred day of the Jewish year .
35216	Mr. Cleaver also omits to mention any of the many infiltrations , bombardments and acts of terror towards a country which has not known a single day of peace in 44 years .
35217	( It is curious that Mr. Cleaver is at pains to accuse Israel of war crimes , when his previous correspondence in the press has shown a soft spot for Nazi war criminals who may still be living in Britain ) .
35218	To omit this background is rather like accusing the RAF of bombing innocent women and children in Berlin without mentioning that world war two was going on at the time .
35219	For every act of violence quoted by Mr. Cleaver , one could cite an Arab attack , massacre or atrocity , not least during the Intifada which has seen well over 500 Palestinians murdered by his fellow Palestinians .
35220	But what good would this do ?
35221	Arabs and Israelis inhabit the same part of the world and will continue to do so .
35222	The way forward should be for both sides to try and understand one another , to recognise each others ' rights , feelings and beliefs .
35223	If all sides in the conflict make every effort to co-operate in good faith then new life could come to the area .
35224	Not only would the desert bloom but the commandment ‘ Love Thy Neighbour as Thy Self ’ would come to fruition .
35225	That is why the peace process , for which Israel has been striving for 44 years , has to be seen as the only viable solution .
35226	For Mr. Cleaver to seek to demonise one side while leaving out huge relevant chunks of history is hardly conducive to a proper understanding of the issues , let alone their resolution .
35227	Rona Hart
35228	The Board of Deputies of British Jews ,
35229	Woburn House ,
35230	Tavistock Square ,
35231	London WC1H 0EZ .
35232	The conversion of farm buildings
35233	Sir , — The district council 's countryside manager , Robin Truscott , recently said that easing planning controls on the conversion of redundant farm buildings would counter the decline of rural communities .
35234	The wholesale conversion of farm building to expensive housing could seal the fate of a small community .
35235	Thriving small settlements must have an active and mostly locally based economy .
35236	That economy has traditionally depended on the land .
35237	The main artery of rural life is being cut by intensive agricultural methods including use of pesticides and fertilisers supplied by large businesses , while retailing of produce is done by large companies taking a big slice of the profit .
35238	The investment in equipment required to thrive in a market devoid of ecological and social concern has led to traditional sustainable farming being squeezed out .
35239	Realistic energy pricing and policies that safeguard the long-term well-being of the land are needed , instead of short-term narrow market accounting .
35240	A countryside under intensive farming which depends on leisure and service industries is a cosmetic , lifeless countryside .
35241	It means fewer species , crises in food production , sameness .
35242	The world turns a shade greyer .
35243	Rural industry and agriculture could help to conserve our countryside and its people .
35244	Mr. Truscott is faced by the demands of agribusiness and land speculators .

35315	Canal recreation and ecology
35316	ABOUT STRIKING A BALANCE
35317	Sir , — What a peculiar letter from Mr. Holford of Churt , about the Basingstoke Canal .
35318	From his wording , it would appear he has picked up these rumours secondhand from somewhere .
35319	But would it not have been sensible to go and see for himself , before rushing off a wholly inaccurate letter ?
35320	I live only half a mile from the canal , and visit those parts of it nearby regularly .
35321	Last August I walked the entire towpath from Greywell to New Haw , and can report it is in good condition throughout , is very well used except in the most rural parts , and is maintained regularly by the canal authority .
35322	The canal did have an ‘ official opening ’ last May , but it did not stay open for long .
35323	Shortly after , the Sheerwater section , which has a history of troubles , began leaking , and the canal below St. Johns had to be closed for the rest of the summer .
35324	In August the navigation had to be closed at Ash Lock , in order to conserve water in the Hampshire pound .
35325	It is well known that this canal always had water shortages , even before modern water extraction diverted part of its natural supply at Greywell , and thousands of thirsty trees grew up on its banks on what had been open country in 1790 .
35326	Additional supplies of water are being actively sought , but the simple truth is that the Basingstoke Canal was never designed for the types and levels of boating some people dream of .
35327	Locks have suffered some deterioration , but this seems to have been mainly a result of idealistic notions of when the canal would be fully operational .
35328	Some of the locks were ready long before the canal which serves them , and were literally high and dry for a time .
35329	Lock timber needs to be wet .
35330	On the matter of boat traffic , Mr. Holford seems unaware that the Basingstoke Canal has the dual role of a recreational amenity and a nationally important nature conservation site .
35331	Some of the ‘ weeds ’ , as he calls them , are national rarities .
35332	The unique plant community of this canal ( 94 wetland species recently recorded , higher than any other wetland in Britain ) , means that a balance must be struck between the need to conserve rare plants , and the desire by some people to use motor cruisers on it .
35333	Motor cruisers are the one type of recreational use which is harmful to wetland wildlife .
35334	This is established beyond doubt , as a result of years of scientific study .
35335	Motorised boats harm the ecology of waterways , unless use is kept at a low level , when there are some benefits .
35336	The problem is to seek the correct balance , and to this end monitoring and studies have been in progress since 1989 .
35337	Some realistic guidelines are beginning to emerge , but further work is needed this year .
35338	Boat traffic is low in Surrey because much of the canal there has been closed , and there have been further restrictions due to water conservation .
35339	In Hampshire it is possible that boat traffic is too high at 1991 levels .
35340	Boat traffic needs to be kept at modest levels in order to protect one of Britain 's most outstanding botanical treasures .
35341	Chris Hall
35342	30 Florence Road ,
35343	Fleet .

35369	Two-tier system of general practice clearly unfair
35370	Sir , — I should like to say how much I agree with some of the sentiments expressed by Peter Cowan in your paper last week .
35371	Outpatient appointments have need sorting out for many years .
35372	It would be nice , too , if patients had an obligation to keep their side of the bargain .
35373	In my own practice the equivalent of two complete surgery sessions of people fail to turn up each week without letting us know .
35374	This means that other people have to wait longer than necessary to see a doctor ; if we could charge non-attenders , as dentists do , it would help .
35375	However , improvements such as this could have been introduced without going wholesale into a market economy for health with its inevitable two-tier system for general practice .
35376	The government claim that GP fund-holding has been a success .
35377	Of course it has ; for the seven percent of the population covered by the scheme .
35378	However , it has definitely produced an unequal system , whatever Mr. Waldegrave , and Mrs. Bottomley might say .
35379	It would be very difficult , if not downright negligent , for such a scheme to fail when it has been overloaded with money .
35380	The seven percent of the first wave fund-holders was allocated £14.5 million to set up the administrative side of the scheme , but the remaining 93 percent were given a total of £19 million in the 1991 autumn statement .
35381	Non-fundholders have to wait ten weeks in Guildford for an ultra-sound scan ; fund-holders can have one within two weeks .
35382	Non-fundholders wait ten months for some outpatient appointments , fundholders can bring the consultant to the surgery to see the patient within a couple of weeks ; this of course helps to get a quicker place on the operation waiting list .
35383	Fund-holders can spend any budget savings on things such as new equipment , extra rooms and extra staff .
35384	Non-fundholders have to provide these facilities out of their own pockets .
35385	The NHS was supposed to treat all equally but now it has become similar to the difference between first class and tourist class air travel .
35386	We would all prefer to be in first , and becoming a fund-holder is a bit like a traveller being given the difference in the fare between the two classes .
35387	Who would then opt to stay in ‘ tourist ’ ?
35388	No wonder GPs are queueing up to join , even though a recent BMA survey , shows that a lot are doing so with misgivings .
35389	The scheme has been a success for fund-holders ' own patients , but detrimental to the rest .
35390	The advantages that they are getting are admirable and important but reforms that only give these advantages to a select minority can not be called fair .
35391	We all pay the same towards the NHS ; should we not get equal benefits ?
35392	It will take at least ten years before all general practices can join the fund-holding scheme .
35393	This means ten years of persisting inequality .
35394	In this country , quite rightly , people can not be discriminated against on grounds of race , sex , or religion .
35395	How strange , then , to bring in a scheme that disadvantages people in the basis of the status of their GP .
35396	What a retrograde step !

35479	— CANDIDATES ASKED
35480	Sir , — The following is an open letter to the general election candidates .
35481	A lot of people would welcome statements from each of them :
35482	I have listened in vain to hear anyone , in any political party , who has been courageous enough to face up to the crisis in the social services .
35483	The recession , education , health , taxation , etc. are all being hotly debated , but nobody mentions the problems being experienced by social services , so vital to disadvantaged people , the chronically sick and disabled people , and the mighty army of the elderly .
35484	I therefore challenge candidates of all parties to state clearly and publicly where they stand on the chronic and continuous underfunding of a service which is increasingly being asked to undertake more and more duties .
35485	Pompous people are very quick to lay blame on the social services when things go wrong , but why does it happen ?
35486	It is the Cinderella service because it mainly deals with powerless people .
35487	Please candidates , do not deafen us with meaningless statistics about global sums and ‘ improvements in real terms ’ — they are political jargon for covering up the truth .
35488	Those of us on the receiving end know that there is a real financial crisis .
35489	How are you going to ensure that Care in the Community is not just a pipe dream ?
35490	Some of know that it is not working now , and will never work unless some government really faces up to the reality of the cost involved .
35491	Those of us in the disabled world are weary of words without action .
35492	We have seen the removal of former care facilities .
35493	Our unofficial carers are tired from unrelieved caring .
35494	WE have seen the imposition of charges from so called care groups and the imposition of VAT on private care charges .
35495	We have watched the drying up of provision of aids and equipment .
35496	The abolition of the old 75 percent grant system for adaptations to privately owned homes has been replaced by the bureaucratic nightmare on the new system which has dramatically decimated the number of grants made to enable us to live in our own homes .
35497	We have seen mass employers getting awards for schemes for employing disabled people , when they operate in premises which are completely inaccessible .
35498	The traditional , massive unemployment of employable disabled people is far worse than it has ever been .
35499	We still have to travel in guards vans like parcels , and are denied mobility in most forms of transport .
35500	Every tiny improvement has to be fiercely fought for in the fields of housing , education and social pleasure .
35501	We still have to wait months for payment of vitally important benefits such as the attendance allowance .

35504	Please can we have some honest answers which really address the true situation ?

35514	Tony Chivers reported that a number of villagers had volunteered to be footpath representatives and had been allocated two paths each , which they had agreed to walk at least twice a year .
35515	Concern was again expressed about the proliferation of horses in the countryside .

35518	Mr. Kimber said the parish councils were now recommended to hold a contingency fund within their budget to deal with such problems .
35519	The legal fees involved in removing a caravan , for example , could be crippling , he said .
35520	Nuisance caused by travellers could escalate in Hampshire , according to the chairman , with an overspill from Wiltshire ‘ who seem to have solved the problem of itinerants ’ .
35521	Certainly Medstead appeared to attract ‘ its fair share ’ .

35543	A NEW HQ FOR THE ARCHITECTS
35544	THE president of the Royal Institute of British Architects , Richard MacCormac , officially opened the new headquarters of the southern region of the institute at Upper Farringdon yesterday ( Thursday ) .
35545	The red brick and terracotta building was constructed by the vicar , the Rev. Thomas Massey , over a period of 30 years from 1881 .
35546	In 1925 it became used partly as the school and partly as the village hall .
35547	The school closed in 1987 and it is this part , together with the old playground and grassed area , which the RIBA have purchased and converted into offices .
35548	Architects for the conversion were Cecil Denny Highton and Partners and the work was carried out in two phases , the contractors for the first being Newman and Kerry of Aldershot , and J. Edwards and Sons of Waterlooville for the second .
35549	The second phase included the construction of a mezzanine floor in the old school hall to be used as a conference room , with two offices under , making five altogether .
35550	The west wing of two large offices , toilet and kitchenette , not presently required by the RIBA , is being leased to a local company .
35551	The regional council voted to purchase Massey 's Folly to escape the ‘ rental spiral ’ in Winchester and the problems of traffic and parking .
35552	It is intended to create a centre for the public seeking the services of architects and for members of the RIBA to hold meetings in their own premises and for large events to use the village hall facilities next door .
35553	Regional chairman Andy Pottinger said : ‘ The new headquarters will give a permanent base for the RIBA to market architects ’ services to clients and will provide a meeting place for all interested in the built environment . ’

35714	Verse comes first for laughtermaker Les
35715	IT 'S seeing the funny side that keeps Les Barker buoyant .
35716	His amusing analysis of human frailty has made him one of the folk world 's more unlikely heroes — a bard who takes the knocks but never shows the bruising .
35717	He was at The Wine Garden , Alton , on Tuesday night and quickly tickled the chucklebuds with his sharp and sparkling verse .
35718	Les , whose cultured scruffiness adds pathos to the pzazz , is a shrewd operator .
35719	He 's appeared at folk festivals all over the land and is in constant demand for club work .
35720	He mixes humour with humility and anger with understanding , but never lets indulgence obscure the entertainment .
35721	His homespun philosophy soon found favour at the Wine Garden , one of the newer and most welcome venues on the local folk circuit .
35722	Les clearly liked the look of the place , took an immediate shine to the audience and launched himself into a neatly structured tirade on what makes tradition tick .
35723	His main target was vanity , and how materialism has put a brake on the human race .
35724	But Les , who was preceded in the Alton spotlight by Odiham duo Acoustic Bikini , is more than just a humorist .

35741	CHURCH SERVICES
35742	Friday Focus
35743	Prayers and the election
35744	DURING the furore of the next three weeks of General Election campaigning , for Christians perhaps a few reflections about the institution which is the House of Commons — and especially about the men and women who are sent there — would not come amiss .
35745	A thought first for those who have decided to retire , many after a quarter of a century or more as members .
35746	Whether or not they expected it when they were first elected , nearly all of them will have learned to accept ant to derive fulfilment from the ‘ welfare ’ function .
35747	Relief there will be from the grind of the daily pile of constituency correspondence and the regular weekend surgeries .
35748	For most , the tedium of weekly travel , the long sitting hours and the heartache of separation from normal family life may soon begin to fade from the memory .
35749	But , for certain , the fellowship of the place , the friendships — many of them cross-party — will be things they will long miss and never forget .
35750	We should give thanks for their work and pray for them .
35751	Next a thought for those who will lose their seats .
35752	That they are an essential part of any system of parliamentary democracy will be of limited consolation to them .
35753	Most will hope to return to the House ; and on part form many will do so , but the immediate problems of adjustment will be hard .
35754	They , too , will deserve our prayers .
35755	The greatest number will be those returning for their second , third , fourth or later terms .
35756	For some promotion will engender a proper sense of pride and excitement ; but a sense of humility and service will equally be called for .
35757	For others there may be a lack of preferment and other problems of staleness and complacency .
35758	There are endless variation .
35759	But this group are the bedrock of the institution — and as such should figure prominently in our prayers .
35760	Finally , there will be the new Members .
35761	Most will privately confess to an initial sense of utter bewilderment , but necessity will drive them to adapt to their new way of life .
35762	Almost before they realise it , they may even find themselves defending some of the more absurd parliamentary conventions .
35763	Their families will also find life very different and testing .
35764	In some ways this group may be in most need of our prayers , but the sense of freshness and opportunity pervades .
35765	All these thoughts seem right and proper at this time but , when all is said and done , might not much of the above be applied to any institution ?
35766	The House of Commons may be the cradle of our democracy — a little better understood perhaps now that its proceedings are televised .
35767	But , however special , it is first and foremost a workplace — in just the same way as a factory , a hospital , or school .
35768	In commending it to God , we should couple it with all the workplaces in our land .
35769	A member of the congregation , St. John the Evangelist , Churt .
35770	When a person goes up in smoke
35771	THE DOCTOR
35772	‘ I STARTED smoking 40 cigarettes every day , but I do n't finish 40 .
35773	I find them ‘ dead ’ in the ashtray or unlit between my fingers .
35774	I just forget about them .
35775	What a waste of money ! ’
35776	This was Mr. Spiers speaking in my surgery .
35777	I wondered if this happened to many other smokers .
35778	Does it happen to you ?
35779	As an experienced 40-a-day man for 40 years , he was very interesting to talk to .
35780	He had tried to give up and was going over the problems he 'd come across and continued :
35781	‘ You need something to do with your hands — hold a pencil in one hand and a rubber in the other or grasp the car steering wheel with both and keep them there .
35782	When hands are fully occupied , smoking is more difficult .
35783	‘ Resist the temptation to light up , especially in the mornings , ’ he added .
35784	‘ I reckon that if I did n't have that cigarette first thing in the morning , I could last out and resist the rest of the day .
35785	That 's the crucial one . ’
35786	So , we discussed how to avoid that first one in the morning .
35787	Finish the last packet of cigarettes the night before and not dash out to the off-license or garage before going to bed in order to stock up .
35788	I had n't bargained for the next difficulty : ‘ It wo n't work , ’ he commented , ‘ because my son smokes and he 'll take pity on me and give me one when I run out . ’
35789	‘ Why not try to stop with a friend and add an element of competition to the task .
35790	Perhaps a small bet on who can stop first ?
35791	Better still , stop with your son and you wo n't be able to feed each other fags in a crisis , ’ I suggested .
35792	‘ As soon as you wake up pop a piece of nicotine chewing gum into your mouth and chew it slowly whilst you are getting dressed and shaving .
35793	That will give you a boost of the drug to start the day without the nasties . ’
35794	Nicotine is incredibly addictive — at least as powerful as cocaine or heroin .
35795	However , it wo n't kill you — unless you inject it into yourself and then it is more lethal than those other drugs .
35796	Jean Nicot , the French ambassador to Portugal who sent tobacco seeds back to the French court in 1560 , has a lot to answer for !
35797	Nicotine gums are safer than smoking .
35798	The real damage comes from the nasties — tars , chemicals and the irritant effects of the smoke itself which causes lung and heart disease .
35799	Nicotine chewing gum can now be bought over the counter at the chemists .
35800	Mr. Spiers had n't realised that .
35801	Chewing and sucking are comforting for the human being and the roots of this go right back into babyhood .
35802	Hence the comfort from eating , sucking sweets or a pipe , and drawing on a cigarette .
35803	Nicotine chewing gum helps in more than one way , I explained .
35804	He thought these were helpful plans — something positive to get to grips with the habit and see an end to cash shortages in the housekeeping as money was siphoned off for another packet ; no more sandpaper taste in the mouth ; no clothes reeking of stale tobacco and an end to the shakes .
35805	He did n't like the tremors that went with the addiction — the wavering match as he lit up again and spilling his tea during a work-break was embarrassing .
35806	‘ I 'll start now , ’ he vowed , suddenly making up his mind .
35807	‘ Tonight , ’ I reminded him , ‘ after that last packet .
35808	But no more .
35809	If you 've none in the house you ca n't smoke them .
35810	No time like the present and anyway it is the first day of Lent . ’
35811	He grinned .
35812	I do n't think he thought of that !
35813	I 'll keep you posted on his progress and the best of luck to you as you give up .

36070	Church outline plans to expand
36071	MORE PASTORAL CARE
36072	THE Church of the Good Shepherd at Four Marks have announced far reaching plans to extend pastoral care further into the parish .
36073	At the annual meeting , some 70 people heard of the parish Outreach scheme and of plans to extend the building itself to provide a much larger Christian centre .
36074	Speaking after the meeting , the Rev. Colin Noyce told the Alton Herald that since arriving in the parish some 16 months ago , he has realised the need for an extension of pastoral care , together with extra room at the church .
36075	‘ The two go in tandem , ’ said the vicar , who would like to see ‘ a living building as part of a living church . ’
36076	The need , on one level , is for extra space , particularly for the Children 's Church ‘ which is growing like mad . ’
36077	At present the parochial church council are awaiting the result of a planning application to install a Portakabin , which would provide a temporary home for the youngsters , as well as creche facilities .
36078	What is needed in the long term is a larger worship area which can be adapted for other uses .
36079	The vicar and his team , led by outgoing churchwarden Robert Parker , envisage an extension which would double the width of the existing church , and which would include a parish office and a private room for counselling and other meetings .
36080	A lot of money
36081	But , said Mr. Noyce , ‘ these plans are still very much in embryo form .
36082	We still have to get permission from the deanery synod and the diocese , and plans have to be drawn up .
36083	We are looking two to three years ahead at least .
36084	And it will require a lot of money . ’
36085	Any future extension would dovetail with the present scheme to extend pastoral care into the community .
36086	A lot of work is already being done by the village care group and good neighbours , but Mr. Noyce feels the need to emphasise this work with the help of committed Christians .
36087	An Outreach scheme has been devised which divides the parish into six areas , each manned by teams of church members whose job it is to identify ways in which they can provide help and report back to the church .
36088	Mr. Noyce firmly believes that the work of Outreach is even more important than providing the improved facilities at the church itself .
36089	‘ I believe that the church exists for the community , ’ he said , ‘ and not just for itself . ’

36141	‘ Vandalism ’ charge over the footpath plans
36142	ANCIENT TRACK CHANGES
36143	A LOCAL historian has called plans to change the name of an ancient public footpath at the end of a leafy lane of substantial and secluded homes in Haslemere as ‘ nothing short of environmental and archaeological vandalism ’ .
36144	Proposals to re-classify the ancient track crossing National Trust commonland as a ‘ byway open to all traffic ’ has brought growing fears that Farnham Lane could eventually become a link to the new A3 Hindhead bypass .
36145	Residents have expressed fears about the move by Surrey County Council after a notice appeared on a wooden pole at the top of Farnham Lane with a map showing the changes affecting three rights of way in Haslemere and one in Chiddingfold .
36146	Roman times
36147	A favourite spot for horse-riders , ramblers and walkers , the right of way which runs in a straight line from a point close to the Royal Naval School comes out at the Hindhead gibbet .
36148	The plans have already led to a number of Farnham Lane residents and others interested in protecting the track — which is believed to pre-date Roman times — to object to the reclassification scheme .
36149	An anonymous notice has also been placed beneath the original at the beginning of the right of way urging people to oppose any plans to re-classify the track , and alerting them to possible future proposals .
36150	Secretary of Hindhead preservation Group , Chris Woodward , who is an amateur historian and has been an active campaigner for the area for the past five years , said he was ‘ totally opposed to the change ’ .
36151	Describing the track ‘ as one of the most ancient and well preserved sunken trackways in the south of England that could well pre-date Roman times , ’ he said he was concerned about its ‘ possible destruction ’ .
36152	Traffic plans
36153	Although difficult to date he believes the trackway to have been in existence for at least 2,000 years and may well pre-date Roman times .
36154	There was also , he said , ‘ already enough vehicular access points on to the common without more being introduced ’ he said .
36155	Mr. Woodward said that there was a substantial and clearly defined trackway used by local traffic presently running parallel to the east of the track joining others to the west and north of the parish boundary .
36156	‘ The re-classification of this public path to that of a byway open to all traffic is unnecessary ’ said Mr. Woodward .
36157	A Farnham Lane resident who did not wish to be named said that he was strongly opposed to any footpath being opened up to traffic .
36158	‘ If the Yellow Route is finally adopted for the A3 Hindhead bypass it could be the first step to bringing a lot of traffic and development to Farnham Lane ’ he said .
36159	‘ Once the terminology for the right of way is changed , the authorities may well find it a lot easier to change their minds about the sort of traffic it carries ’ said another resident .
36160	Dispel fears
36161	Surrey County Council 's assistant county director for highways and transport , Paul Higerty , said he was able to ‘ dispel any fears that residents may have over the reclassification scheme ’ .
36162	It was , he said , solely a legal exercise and would n't physically change the rights of way .
36163	‘ It is something required by the highway authority and is purely a legal classification ’ , he said , and ‘ it is extremely unlikely that any roads used as public paths would ever be considered as anything else than they are now ’ said Mr. Higerty .

36178	Alan leads the bike veterans
36179	THE 55th annual pioneer run for veteran motor-cycles was held last Sunday in damp and blustery conditions with 356 motor cycles , all pre-1915 , taking part .
36180	Among those taking up the challenge was Haslemere architect Alan Coombes , who entered for the 15th time with his 1914 three-and-a-half horsepower three-speed , 4,500cc Douglas .
36181	‘ I 've entered every year for the past 15 years and my bike has covered the distance every time — with a few minor running repairs sometimes .
36182	‘ It is quite a rare model and only three or four others exist in this country and one or two in Australia .
36183	This model was only made in 1913 and 1914 .
36184	‘ This year 's run was rather windy , ’ he said ‘ and quite a few people did have problems .
36185	There were also some roadworks along the route and we did not pass our usual stopping place for a cup of tea so we pressed straight on to Brighton . ’
36186	The run has been held every year since 1930 , apart from the war years and is the main event in the veteran calendar .
36187	All machines have to meet stringent dating requirements and the organisers only accept pre-1915 veterans .
36188	Entries come from all over the country to take part in the run — from Epsom Downs to Brighton — and there were also several entries from the continent , the US and Australia .
36189	The oldest competitor on the run was 85-year-old Graeme Brown , from Godalming , and the youngest was Edward Baldock of Goudhurst , aged 17 , riding an 1897 Leon Bollee tricycle .
36190	Haslemere architect Alan Coombes arriving at Brighton on his 1914 500cc Douglas motorcycle last Sunday after his 15th successful entry in the annual veteran motor-cycle pioneer run .
36191	Close behind is his son , Simon , who came along for the ride on his 1916 600cc Douglas , which falls outside the official December 1914 entry date .
