36193	DAN AIR LEAGUE CLASS ELITE CUP : Semi-Final
36194	Town 's ten men reach another cup final
36195	FARNHAM TN. 2 , CRANLEIGH 1
36196	Farnham reached their second cup final of the season — and they did it the hard way when they met Cranleigh in the semi-finals of the Class Elite Cup at the Memorial Ground on Saturday .
36197	Town might have been expected to dispose of a side they have already beaten twice this season , but not necessarily with ten men for 68 minutes of the game .
36198	They seemed well in control after 20 minutes , having taken an early lead and looked a class better than their mid-table opponents .
36199	But Peter Browning 's dismissal after 22 minutes changed all that and Cranleigh , having drawn level by half-time , looked a good bet to record a shock victory over the Dan Air leaders .
36200	However , Farnham showed their true mettle in the second half with a gritty performance allied to Ernie Howe 's shrewd redeployment of his players .
36201	He withdrew striker Steve Flanagan and brought on young Sean Dowling at right-back , Farnham were thus able to rely on a strong midfield presence of Millard , Daly and May , with Deighan and Stairs looking to stretch Cranleigh wide on the flanks .
36202	Dowling , in fact , showed great composure under pressure and Farnham were able to regain the defensive security that Cranleigh — chiefly through the pace of Roger Carpenter — had undermined in the first half .
36203	Earlier , things had looked black for the visitors as Farnham moved into the lead after just 14 minutes .
36204	Shaun May had already brought a diving save from 'keeper Jukes with a hard ground shot and the midfielder was also involved with the goal .
36205	After combining with Gary Millard at a short corner , May lifted a high cross over a crowded goalmouth and Steve Harris stormed in on the far post to hit a great first-time shot into the opposite corner .
36206	The determined Cranleigh side were far from downhearted and they almost got a quick equaliser when Chris Lamboll , having beaten 'keeper Paul Cann , saw his shot booted off the line by Steve Buckingham .
36207	It was quite out of character when Browning , having tangled with Edwards , aimed a kick , apparently in retaliation at the Cranleigh player right in front of the referee John Ford .
36208	After receiving treatment for himself , Browning was sent off .
36209	Millard dropped to left-back , with Buckingham switching to the right , but Farnham 's rhythm was disrupted and Cranleigh were quick to take advantage .
36210	On 30 minutes , Farnham 's defence was all over the place at a free-kick and the ball fell at a perfect height to an unmarked Lamboll who struck an unstoppable volley past Cann .
36211	Carpenter 's speed and control was even causing problems for Harris , himself no slouch , and Farnham 's hearts must have been in their mouths when the Cranleigh number 10 , having broken clear on the right , hit the deck after a late challenge by Cann who had raced out of his area .
36212	However , referee Ford judged it to be a yellow card offence and the free-kick came to nothing .
36213	After a narrow escape straight from the start of the second half , when Carpenter screwed the ball wide from a good position , Farnham 's re-organised side played with growing authority .
36214	The strong cross-wind was now more in Town 's favour and they managed to keep play in Cranleigh 's half for long periods .
36215	It was not pretty to watch , with the ball often being held up and played back to Cann , but it was effective , and Farnham were ready to strike when their own chance came along .
36216	A free-kick some 30 yards out gave them their opportunity with 12 minutes remaining .
36217	Jukes could only parry May 's blockbuster at the foot of the post and the alert Deighan squared the ball back in for Steve Stairs to force it over the line .
36218	Cranleigh manager Roy Kelsey made a double substitution as Cranleigh battled to force extra time and they were almost rewarded in the final minutes , with Cann charging the ball down before the ever-dangerous Carpenter could place his shot .

36723	The move for Haslemere to play the Tauntonians second XI resulted in a hard-fought , tenacious encounter .

36725	Playing the ball through midfield meant no players were left isolated and easy options enabled possession to be kept .
36726	Good pressure produced a string of short corners , and a goal .
36727	In a sweet movement of speed and motion , the ball was left to run long to Patel who deftly feinted with his left shoulder before picking out David Mayson .
36728	With true brotherly love , he provided a cross for Anthony Mayson to finish in style for the lead .
36729	Within five minutes , the ‘ Blues ’ were two up .
36730	Sims threaded a pass to Richardson , who , after two shots against the 'keeper , changed his angle to put a cross ball to the right post .
36731	This was met by a diving A. Mayson who showed agility beyond his height-weight ratio to push the ball in for number two .
36732	The second half was very even and , as the sides tired , the mistakes and gaps in midfield were more common .
36733	The visitors were unlucky to have a goal disallowed and were denied again by 'keeper Law who tipped a shot over the bar .
36734	Mayson was denied his hat-trick by good ‘ keeping and twice Smyth was through , only to go for the unselfish option when perhaps a shot would have been better .
36735	Eventually , the third goal arrived , Bogaers made the initial run and Patel showed mature coolness as he slipped the ball beneath the prostrate 'keeper .

36950	Past reflections for the Camera Club
36951	PRINTS made from 100 year old negatives had the members at Friday 's meeting of Alton Camera Club envious of the quality .
36952	The Lassavette — Glass Negative Prints of 100 Years Ago had been taken along by Peter Macdonald of Godalming Photographic Club .
36953	Until his retirement three years ago , he had spent 38 years working in the photographic studio at the Victoria and Albert Museum .
36954	The negatives had originated in Dublin and then had been stored in Bond Street .
36955	On the verge of being destroyed , they had been rescued and stored in an alcove at Pinewood Studios .
36956	It was here that they were found , over 30,000 of them , stored in boxes and covered in dust , some of them in a poor condition .
36957	Some , mainly those of war time subjects and taken in the 30 's and 40's were given to the National Portrait Gallery , but the best were retained by the V. and A.
36958	Almost all the prints were portraits and Mr. Macdonald spoke of the problems associated with the use of long focal length lenses and the exposures required .
36959	Supports were usually provided for the subject of these were ‘ touched out ’ of the negative .
36960	The backgrounds and items such as papier maché columns used in the settings for the portraits recurred in several prints .
36961	Celebrities
36962	Royalties and celebrities of the time were the subjects .
36963	One large group of negatives had apparently been taken at a fancy dress party organised by the Duke of Devonshire — over 100 guests had been photographed , most of them with different background settings .
36964	Mr. Macdonald spoke of the methods used for making the prints , the shading required , the need for softer grades of paper and the treatment needed for cracked negatives .
36965	A print of H.M.S. Discovery he regarded as ‘ a triumph of the printer 's art ’ .

36997	7 day tv guide
36998	The agony is over for Anthony Hopkins
36999	Sally Lowe 's TELEVIEW
37000	ANTHONY Hopkins ' appearance on The South Bank Show is well timed — the following day he is in the running for an Oscar for his performance as the monstrous Hannibal Lecter , In Silence of the Lambs .
37001	Past interviews have portrayed him as dour , introverted and something of a depressive , but now it 's obvious he has turned that corner and views the world in a thoroughly positive light .
37002	He smiles broadly as he describes his nomination for the Best Actor award alongside Nick Nolte for Princes of Tides , as ‘ wonderful , fabulous and an honour .
37003	I 'm thrilled — you are around for years , and then suddenly you are discovered overnight , ’ he muses .
37004	‘ Everything I ever wanted has happened to me .
37005	It may sound smug , but I 'm very fortunate .
37006	I 've had a very blessed career . ’
37007	The role had already gained him honours , including the Chicago Critics ' Award and Bafta Best Actor Award .
37008	But he is no stranger to monsters , having played Lambert Le Roux in Pravada and Hitler in The Bunker during the last 15 years .
37009	He tells interviewer Melvyn Bragg in Sunday 's South Bank Show that acting was a therapy that saved him from self-destruction .
37010	He says : ‘ I do n't know if I would have been slightly criminal , but would not have been a very nice human being .
37011	In a way , it has helped me to touch parts of my own personality , my own inner darkness . ’
37012	He revisits his birthplace in Port Talbot , where he was the son of a fiery Welsh baker who was himself a frustrated actor .
37013	He admits he is not a professional Welshman , since he does n't speak the language , does n't play rugby and does n't sing too well .
37014	Hopkins , 54 , a reformed alcoholic , was desperately lonely at school and a poor student and he now thinks he may have been slightly dyslexic .
37015	He has a daughter of 23 by his first marriage and is happily married to his second wife Jenny .
37016	The programme reveals that the actor was a notable pianist and once considered becoming a concert pianist .
37017	He refuses to be filmed at the piano , but improvised the show 's incidental music which he can be heard playing off-camera .
37018	A superb mimic , Hopkins has had two years of varied non-stop work , which he loves because ‘ I come alive , I feel it enriches me ’ .
37019	He has recently been on location in Switzerland filming Richard Attenborough 's movie about the life of Charlie Chaplin .
37020	His latest project is the screen version of E. M. Forster 's Howard 's End , in which he plays Henry Wilcox .
37021	Also due for imminent release is the science fiction film Free Jack featuring Mick Jagger , and the Australian comedy Spotswood , starring Hopkins as a time and motion expert .
37022	Later this year he will be seen in Francis Ford Coppola 's version of Bram Stoker 's Dracula , in which fellow British actor Garry Oldman appears dressed as a bat .
37023	‘ I am constantly in a state of surprise that I have survived this long as an actor .
37024	I find it easier now than I have ever done .
37025	I know what I 'm doing now , more or less .
37026	It 's not agony now . ’
37027	His current philosophy is summed up by a note on his fridge door — ‘ Ask nothing , expect nothing and accept everything ’ .
37028	He says : ‘ If you expect too much of people , you are going to be disappointed .
37029	If you do n't expect much , the bonuses are terrific . ’
37030	For years he had an inner voice which was always putting him down .
37031	But now he has got the measure of it .
37032	‘ I say to this little voice — thank you for your opinion , go back to your room . ’
37033	And Hopkins grins like a man who is at last easy in his skin .

37109	Now you TAP into plans for new careers
37110	COMPUTER NETWORK AT LIBRARIES
37111	HAMPSHIRE Training and Enterprise Council have relaunched a counter-wide computer network to help businesses and individuals tap into thousands of training opportunities .
37112	TAP ( Training Access Points ) systems of user-friendly computer terminals located in libraries , shopping centres , careers offices and businesses — has been taken over by the TEC and is the focal point of a marketing campaign to extend career opportunities .
37113	Each one of the 36 terminals provides information on thousands of local work-related training programmes which can be easily accessed .
37114	A print-out is instantly available .
37115	The TEC have taken over responsibility for the service in keeping with their aim to encourage commitment to training .

37287	Alan Mitchell 's NATURE NOTES for March
37288	AFTER a slow , grudging and hesitant start , spring had suddenly sprung on March 16th .
37289	The sparsely flower speckled crowns of Pissard plums became clouds of densely held , bunched white and the later opening rather harsh pink flowers of the form Nigra emerged fully .
37290	The lovely Accolade trees , having waited two weeks with deep rose-red buds and a few open flowers , burst into copious rows of sumptuous semi-double flowers of pure icing-sugar pink .
37291	The related hybrid Pandora opened many of its pink buds into white flowers like a later , superior form of Pissards ' on a neat crown .
37292	The almonds moved into top gear , as did the sallows , the male trees now great bushes of bright gold , and a sycamore by the main road between Birdworld and Forest Lodge at Holt Pound has spread its leaves .
37293	All this has happened in the absence of any balmy warm spell , just a few days without cold nights and with midday temperatures hardly as high as 50F .
37294	It could be imagined that the trees had said : ‘ Blow this for spring .
37295	It never seems to arrive properly .
37296	We have waited too long .
37297	Let's go . ’
37298	It is , on the whole , more likely that they are responding to the cumulative temperature building up slowly until a threshold has been passed , and they are away .
37299	The danger of our treacherous spring unleashing a killing frost , has receded to some extent , and although recent Aprils have done much damage , the early flowers are over by then and the bad spells are , every day , likely to be shorter .
37300	Blackbirds and starlings
37301	Where until two years ago , the scattering of currants near the door was eagerly awaited by a clamouring mix of blackbirds , starling , robins and a songthrush or two , lately there has been almost an indifference to the largesse .
37302	The birds are still around , but remain largely aloof in the bushes .
37303	Perhaps they really prefer more natural food and this has been plentiful , but that it not obviously so .
37304	The crumb-spreading area of the lawn still attracts its full quota and the statutory trio of dunnocks is perennially on view and a pair of jays are often hopping around .
37305	For a week or so in February , a pair of longtailed tits was often to be seen in and beneath the shrubs near the nutbag .
37306	This was odd as it indicated that the winter flock had already scattered as separate pairs at this very early date .
37307	Their feeding , however , was more strange still and out of character .
37308	When the birds were not foraging with greenfinches , chaffinches and robins on the fragments beneath the bags , they were feeding on the nuts in the bag like other tits do , and this is seldom seen .
37309	The great spotted woodpecker began brief but intense bursts of drumming in the second week of January which is a week or so earlier than in most recent years and many weeks earlier than was normal a decade ago .
37310	Today , on March 18th , the lesser spotted woodpecker had a spell of drumming .
37311	It was interesting to note a complete change in the timbre and resonance when the bird moved to another song-perch .
37312	This could have been an argument for the theory of the mechanical origin of the sound in the days when some still insisted that it was vocal .
37313	Not conclusive , of course , but an indication .
37314	Today no such evidence is needed as the matter was settled in favour of the mechanical explanation , although it is hard to envisage any human attempt to produce the resonant sound from a branch with any contraption without a strong amplifier .
37315	March 17th is my traditional early chiffchaff date and although a journey south to Poole and a short time near possible sites on that day , yielded no hearing of the bird , one has been singing in this garden today .
37316	Snow-white flowers
37317	The roadsides yesterday from Farnham to Winchester were spectacular over large stretches by Holybourne , Alton , and towards the Winchester bypass , and in many places between , with great drifts of snow-white flowers of Myrobalan plum .
37318	It will inevitably by called ‘ blackthorn ’ , which should not be in flower for a month , bringing its ‘ winter ’ with it , and growing on short-jointed tangles of stems rather than on the slender longer shoots of these bushy trees .
37319	I do wonder if some of these are in fact the wild plum rather than Myrobalan , and I marvel that in summer we hardly notice any plum-like shrubs where we now see them so dominant over long stretches of banks .
37320	It may also be noted that last year the true blackthorn overlapped the Myrobalan in flowering season .
37321	Our robin with the white flashes in its wings has ceded the prime territory nearest the house to another and is now with its mate , centred on the next bed along and ventures only occasionally into the crumb-patch , from which it is firmly evicted .
37322	Not being voyeurs , we have not observed the intimate occasions from which the sex of this bird can be determined .
37323	Recognising the unsafe young , male driver
37324	A PIONEERING study into why so many young men are unsafe drivers suggest that driver training should focus on attitudes and relationships as well as mechanics .
37325	The study was undertaken for the AA Foundation for Road Safety Research by the department of Psychology and the transportation Research Group at the University of Southampton .
37326	Its findings challenge traditional thinking about road safety education , suggesting that pre-licence training should include social influences on driving : the impact of parent , peer and passenger behaviour , drinking , music and mood .
37327	Over confident
37328	A significant minority of men aged 17–24 take risks when they drive because they feel confident in their ability behind the wheel .
37329	They must be made to realise that driving skills alone will not prevent accidents , says the AA report .
37330	Some young men believe that they are safe drivers even when they are not , the research finds .
37331	As a result , road safety campaigns have little effect on them because they are seen as being directed at ‘ unsafe ’ drivers .
37332	Successful road safety campaigns , says the report , are likely to be those that encourage responsible and considerate driving to be the norm .
37333	Too many young people , particularly young men , seek to earn the respect of their peers through risky driving
37334	The AA Foundation study also suggests that car radio/cassette players should be designed to be as automatic as possible , and sold with an information leaflet highlighting the possible influences of music on driving .
37335	Young men generally find drink-driving unacceptable , according to the research .
37336	If they do drive over the legal limit , it is usually because they are left with no other way to get home and they worry about parental reaction if they are late getting home .
37337	The research
37338	An earlier study undertaken for the AA Foundation by Southampton University compared the driving performance , attitudes and behaviour of 439 drivers between the ages of 17 and 40 .
37339	The report of that research — Accident risk and behavioural patterns of younger drivers , published last year — showed that more than a third of the men aged 17 to 25 were assessed as ‘ unsafe ’ drivers , and suggested that this had more to do with lifestyle than with driving skills .
37340	For the new study , a researcher from the university 's department of psychology conducted interviews with 56 young men who the earlier research had assessed as either safe or unsafe drivers .
37341	Each was questioned on driving behaviour , experience , attitude to other drivers , the influence of others and leisure activities .
37342	The use of in-depth qualitative methods is relatively untried in driver research , but here is shown to be most valuable .
37343	Laughed at
37344	Generally , drink-driving was frowned on by both the ‘ safe ’ and ‘ unsafe ’ drivers ; it often happened only when there was no other way to get home .
37345	Being let down by friends or a lack of public transport not only encouraged drink-driving , it also led young people to accept lifts from friends who had been drinking .
37346	‘ A couple of boys used to make a thing about getting pretty drunk and then going out , ’ said one of the interviewees .
37347	‘ It was laughed at , but secretly we 'd say ‘ Oh God , they 're being stupid ’ . ’
37348	But the same stigma was not associated with accident involvement or dangerous driving .
37349	Unsafe drivers , in particular , accepted that every male driver would at some time do something risky .
37350	A crash or a motoring conviction was viewed as unlucky , rather than something that should have been avoided .
37351	A 19-year-old commented : ‘ People buy a wreck and do n't mind wrecking it .
37352	Funnily enough , none of them would drink and drive or not wear a seatbelt . ’
37353	A small number said that pressure of work made them take risks .
37354	One driver told the interviewer : ‘ I 'm always thinking that they 're sat back in the office thinking ‘ Where has he got to ’ , and it puts you on edge so I always drive faster in a company car because time is against me . ’
37355	The ‘ unsafe ’ driver is more likely than the ‘ safe ’ driver to be a non-manual worker and to have stayed on at school after the age of 16 .
37356	Others said that their driving was risky because friends and , to a lesser extent , the public , police and insurance companies labelled him as ‘ high risk ’ and charged him a high premium , he might as well get his money 's worth .
37357	Passenger 's influence
37358	Ninety percent of the drivers reported that passengers had an influence on their driving .
37359	Parents , adults and girlfriends as passengers encouraged safer or slower driving .
37360	But some drivers who were assessed to be unsafe admitted that their peers encouraged them to drive fast .
37361	Drivers of both groups said that drunken passengers were a problem : they ‘ messed about ’ in the car , grabbed the steering wheel and pulled on the handbrake .
37362	While media seemed to have little influence on driving behaviour , both groups of drivers felt that it showed cars in an unrealistic light — only seven percent thought otherwise .
37363	As one driver put it : ‘ It 's ridiculous .
37364	It makes people think they 're invincible , they can put a seatbelt on and they 'll be all right .
37365	You see a car roll over in a film and people get up and walk away ; people I know have rolled cars and broken arms and legs . ’
37366	A profile of the unsafe driver can be made from the findings .
37367	He is interested in high risk thrill-seeking sports such as hang-gliding or motorcycling .
37368	When he goes out in the evening he is invariably with his mates whose influence may encourage him to take risks .
37369	He may well be a skilled driver with quick reactions , but he will deliberately take risks .
37370	He loves driving , rather than seeing his car as a way of getting him from A to B , and sees his car as a status symbol , and means to power and freedom .
37371	He also enjoys working on his car and talking about cars with his friends .
37372	Affected by moods
37373	His mood can affect his driving — ‘ If I 'm depressed , I drive quite gently .
37374	If I 'm pissed off , I drive like a lunatic . ’
37375	A bad mood can be brought on by what he sees as ‘ stupid ’ behaviour by other motorists .
37376	‘ Clearly , only a minority of young men are dangerous drivers , but of those , too many are influenced by their peers to drive dangerously , ’ said Kenneth Faircloth , the AA 's deputy director general .
37377	‘ This situation must be changed if we are to reduce their involvement in road accidents .
37378	‘ The success of drink drive campaigns hinges on urging society as a whole to reject this behaviour — and they have been particularly successful among younger drivers ; the same tactics should be employed to target unsafe driving . ’
37379	Project boosts history
37380	HAMPSHIRE County Council planners are awaiting the results of a major archaeological research project which should provide valuable new information on sites , dating back to the Stone Age , located in gravel deposits throughout the area .
37381	The Southern Rivers Project , which began last year and is funded by English Heritage , is concerned about the future preservation of nationally important Paleolithic sites .
37382	Although the project is due to run for another year , the county council 's planning department hope information will be made available this summer .

37528	The actresses , of course , were frequently loaned gowns by the house free of charge for the publicity that would be gained when they were pictured wearing them , and there were those among the society women who considered themselves above coming to the couture , ordering instead from the videos that nowadays replaced the weeks of shows of the old days — and staying away all the more determinedly as the great Paris houses vied with one another to tempt them to lend their presence to the occasion .
37529	But there were plenty of beautiful and recognisable faces to be seen amongst the anonymous , but none-the-less powerful , fashion editors , still enough buying power in this room alone to rock empires , even if no house made a profit from the couture but rather used it for a loss-leading advertisement and a mark of prestige .

38230	CHAPTER THREE
38231	In his office high up in the twenty-five storey building that is 550 Fashion Avenue , mecca of the New York fashion industry , Hugo Varna sat at his desk and fiddled with the executive toy Sally had bought for him last Christmas .
38232	It was a stupid thing , he thought , three gold baubles on springs that set up a continual motion , banging one against the other , and he kept it on his desk only to please her .
38233	But today with his mind too preoccupied to work he seemed quite unable to keep his hands off it .
38234	It clicked irritatingly and Hugo pushed it aside , swivelling his chair around to face the window and the panoramic view of Manhattan .
38235	Hugo Varna 's showrooms occupied an entire floor of the 550 building and from the moment a potential client stepped out of the brass elevator she was treated to an ambience of unashamed luxury .
38236	The vast foyer was carpeted in the softest green imaginable , the walls were even paler , so that at first glance they might have been taken for white , and the venetian blinds were a perfectly blended shade of moss .
38237	The minimum of furniture emphasised the impressive size of the foyer — only small modern tables bearing huge smoked glass ash trays , two or three low chairs and a huge arrangement of dried ferns and foliage in shades of brown and gold graced the enormous expanse .
38238	From cunningly concealed speakers piped music wafted , but music played so softly that it was almost inaudible to the human ear , a faint teasing melody that soothed the soul and created a restful atmosphere almost without one being aware of it .
38239	This soft green womb formed an oasis of peace in the chaotic tumble that was Fashion Avenue .
38240	Outside in the street the traffic might roar , here there was hush broken only by that soft subliminal music , outside the air might be heavy with the mingled smells of petrol fumes and donuts , Macdonalds ' burgers , trash cans , and sweat , here there was just the faintest perfume of a pine pot-pourri , subtle as the music .
38241	Even the bustling atmosphere of the 550 building itself seemed not to have invaded the Hugo Varna floor .
38242	Here the sales staff glided about with languid grace more reminiscent of Paris than New York , the house models managed to look like elegant advertisements for Varna even after a long session of standing stock still while a toile was pinned and draped and adjusted around them , and even when a rail of sample clothes had to be wheeled across the hallowed expanse of green , carefully hidden inside grey and black sample bags to make sure they were safe from the photographic eye of a fashion spy , it was managed with what Hugo referred to as ‘ panache ’ .
38243	‘ The simplest of jobs can be done with panache ’ , he would instruct whenever one of his staff fell short of his standards of perfection — the standards that endeared him to his ‘ Shiny Set ’ customers and staff alike .
38244	Hugo himself was lithe , elegant and charming with a slight edge of fascinating middle-European foreignness that came from his Bulgarian father .
38245	But it was his own formidable talent that set him apart .
38246	Mostly nowadays Hugo took for granted all the assets that talent had brought him .
38247	Twenty years at the pinnacle of his profession had paid him handsomely and he accepted the accolades and the financial rewards as no more than his due .
38248	But on occasions he stopped in his tracks to wonder just what he was doing here , amidst all this elegance and opulence , numbering the rich and famous and powerful amongst his clients — and his friends .
38249	Not bad for the son of a penniless illegal immigrant , he thought then , not bad for a boy raised on the wrong side of town .
38250	‘ Where exactly do you hail from , Hugo ? ’
38251	Margie Llewellyn , the chat-show queen , had asked him once when she had interviewed him , and he had mesmerised her millions of viewers with the story he had told .
38252	His father , a seaman , had jumped ship to seek a better life when Bulgaria had been on the brink of civil war in the 1920s .
38253	He had taken the name of Varna from the name of the port from which he had sailed but he had lived his life in terror of deportation , a fear that had haunted him long after it had ceased to be a real threat , so that he had never been able to enjoy his son 's success , seeing it only as something which drew unwelcome attention to the Varna family .
38254	Hugo had been perfectly happy to talk at length on the Margie Llewellyn Show about the days when he had played on the streets of the Bronx , and how in this unlikely setting a talent for sketching had developed into an interest in designing clothes .
38255	Apart from his father , Hugo 's family had consisted entirely of women — his mother , his three sisters , his maternal grandmother and various assorted aunts and cousins all of whom ( his mother excepted ) had striven to dress with what Hugo would later call ‘ panache ’ on a pittance .
38256	He had taken far more interest in their efforts than his father had thought was right and proper for a boy and when Leonie , his eldest sister , had been apprenticed to a dressmaker his fascination had grown .
38257	From sketching the outfits she made to inventing designs of his own was but a short step and by the time he left High School he knew exactly what he wanted to do .
38258	His sisters , all working by this time , supported him through a course at the New York Fashion Institute of Technology .
38259	They were inordinately proud of him , if slightly puzzled by their unusually talented brother .
38260	When he graduated Hugo took a succession of low-paid jobs in 7th Avenue and the optimism with which he had set out began to be dimmed by the sheer sick-making banality of what he had to do — cutting samples in the disgusting fabrics with which the greedy cutthroat manufacturers he worked for made their living .
38261	But all the while he was learning and soon the time had come when he was no longer satisfied to design for others .
38262	He began cutting his own samples on his mother 's kitchen table and getting them made up by his sister and her friends at the dressmaker 's where she worked .

49860	Profit from our 10 resolutions
49861	Liz Dolan
49862	AS 1993 dawns , it 's time to shake up your financial lifestyle .
49863	Here are 10 New Year resolutions to get you in the mood .
49864	1 .
49865	Declare war on debt .
49866	Do n't hoard savings when they could be better used to repay borrowings .
49867	Falling interest rates have made debts cheaper , but they could still be costing you more than you 're earning on investments .
49868	2 .
49869	If you ca n't afford to repay debts on time , do n't bury your head in the sand .
49870	Contact lenders and work out a new repayment schedule , or visit your local Citizens ' Advice Bureau or money advice centre ( ask local councils or libraries , for details ) .
49871	3 .
49872	Take a long , cool look at your shares .
49873	Some privatised stocks are nearing their sell-by date .
49874	British Airways , British Aerospace and Rolls Royce are all under a cloud at the moment , for instance .

49877	4 .
49878	Check out building society savings rates in the weekend press .
49879	If your cash has been in the same account for some time , make sure it has n't been closed to new customers .
49880	These ‘ obsolete accounts ’ usually pay derisory rates , but many people do n't notice .
49881	5 .
49882	Does your current account pay interest ?
49883	Most banks leave customers in non-interest bearing accounts unless they ask to be moved .
49884	6 .
49885	Open a Tax Exempt Special Savings Account ( Tessa ) , or top up the one you 've got .
49886	Early cash withdrawals wipe out the tax-free element , but you still benefit from better-than-average savings rates .
49887	7 .
49888	Switch to a credit card with lower interest charges and an interest free period .
49889	Most cards now charge interest from the date of transaction .
49890	Repay in full each month , otherwise it 's a horrendously expensive way of borrowing .
49891	8 .

49902	Buy regional Factory Shop guides from WH Smith for £3.95 .

50722	Cathy Gunn
50723	CITY people will celebrate Christmas with lighter hearts .

50725	New Lord Mayor of London Francis McWiliams is said to have played a key role in persuading Mr Heseltine to turn again .
50726	The Government 's earlier reluctance to put its hand in its pocket had led property experts to accuse it of unwittingly aiding and abetting the IRA 's efforts to disrupt the City .
50727	They feared that , without proper cover , the City would lose out as an international financial centre as large overseas institutions moved their European offices to less-exposed capitals .
50728	London , City workers , and Britain 's balance of payments , all stood to lose billions if that happened — something the Government , in its desire to cut public spending , seemed remarkably slow to grasp .
50729	The drama blew up , so to speak , when top reinsurance companies refused to offer cover for next year against terrorist attack after counting the £800m cost of last April 's expensive election night bomb in the City .
50730	London is seen as the insurance capital of the world .
50731	But top insurers said terrorism was a political problem not a commercial one , so the Government should pick up at least part of the tab for future claims .
50732	It already pays all claims of more than £220 in Northern Ireland — at a cost of £680m over the past 23 years .
50733	But the Government was not keen to give blanket cover on the mainland .
50734	True to modern Tory principles , it said the insurance market should find a solution on its own — forgetting that even the battered UK insurance market can , and sometimes does , reject unappealing business .
50735	‘ Not a risk we want to cover alone at any price .
50736	Sorry chaps , ’ the insurers said .
50737	Market karma had ( as the old joke goes ) just run over the Tory dogma — and the shock has brought the Government to heel .
50738	With many companies ' insurance arrangements due for renewal from December 31 , financial institutions had faced starting the New Year exposed to ruin should other City buildings become the terrorist targets .
50739	But industries right across the UK faced the same risk .
50740	Most City firms rent their office space from the big institutions that invest in commercial developments .
50741	Leases are long , perhaps 25 years , and tenants agree to be responsible for general insurance and repairs .
50742	Policies usually cover such things as riot and falling objects .
50743	But if the entire building is so damaged that it has to be torn down and rebuilt , the landlord collects from his insurer to rebuild .
50744	With terrorism suddenly specifically excluded , tenants and landlords faced being left with a very expensive hole in the ground , and no cover for the disruption of their business .
50745	Now the Government is set to contribute to a central fund set up by leading insurers that will meet bills for terrorist damage .
50746	Companies will have to pay between 5% and 10% more for their property insurance and the extra money , estimated at £300m-£350m , will go into the pool .
50747	The deal covers the whole UK mainland , and was greeted in the City as an important breakthrough .

53768	By then 100 operations would have been cancelled .
53769	Some of the patients waiting for surgery are young children born with congenital problems .
53770	Musgrave Park is the regional centre for orthopaedic surgery and has a reputation second to none for its geriatric work .
53771	A new geriatric centre is due to open later this month .
53772	The bomb blast fractured the ventilating system and spewed dust particles along the system throughout the hospital .
53773	Piping carrying phone cables were also been fractured and the steel gland which carries the steam for sterilising equipment in the theatres had to be closed down .
53774	The maintenance staff has been working 18-hour shifts to bring the hospital into full operation .

53781	Information technology
53782	ONE of the most fashionable computer applications at the moment is Desk Top Publishing .
53783	Unfortunately , the level of interest is not backed up by the right level of knowledge either from prospective users or from many of the suppliers .
53784	Indeed , there is no agreed definition of what constitutes ‘ desk top publishing ’ .
53785	The narrowest definition would be the use of page layout software on a PC and using a laser printer .
53786	However , others may have a broader view eg. the use of appropriate software on PCs to create formatted printed material for widespread distribution .
53787	Even using the narrow definition it is clear that desk top publishing is a complex and technical area !
53788	It is highly technical not just in the sense that it involves computer technology but also because it is totally based in the area of printing .
53789	The latter abounds with its own specialists eg. designers , editors , pasteup artists , typographers and all using their own jargon .
53790	To gain the most benefit from installing a desk top publishing system you must be prepared to learn something about the general area of printing .
53791	You must also have a clear idea of why you want such a system .
53792	It is not enough to have a wish to improve the quality of your reports , price lists etc .
53793	You need to define the sort of layout you require eg columnar , different type styles , photographs or diagrams .
53794	If you define your requirements in enough detail you could find that a good word processing package used with a laser printer could satisfy your needs .
53795	Even if you do require a full desk top publishing system these can range quality in price depending on exactly what you require .
53796	Generally speaking , a full desk top publishing system requires at least the following .
53797	• appropriate software — the ‘ desk top publishing ’ package .
53798	• a PC with enough memory , processing power and disk space .
53799	• a high quality monitor to display the documents prior to printing .
53800	• a suitable laser printer .
53801	Most people would also consider a scanner so that they can capture images and documents .
53802	Desk Top Publishing can bring benefits to an organisation but only if the requirements are properly defined and there is an appreciation of what such systems can do and the learning curve involved .
53803	However , all too often such systems end up as glorified word processors just producing documents with different sizes of print and maybe a few boxes .

53872	A growing problem for Britons
53873	THE number of fat people is rising and Britons must radically change their diet if they are to meet Government health standards by the end of the century , a nutritionist said yesterday .
53874	Although people cut down fats and sugar in the 1980s following official advice , there were more fat and very fat people in 1987 than in 1980 , Dr David Buss told nutritionists and doctors at a Royal College of Physicians conference in London .
53875	There were also more fat women than fat men .
53876	The proportion of very fat women had risen from 8 per cent to 12 per cent , while the proportion of obese men had risen from 6 per cent to 8 per cent , said Dr Buss , head of nutrition at the Ministry of Agriculture Food and Fisheries .
53877	Women did not eat as many sausages , pies , or fish and chips than men , yet did have more fruit and recommended reduced fat milk .
53878	Consumption of butter today was only half what it was in 1980 and a quarter of the 1970s figures , Dr Buss said .
53879	The increase in numbers of fat and very fat people in the 1980s showed diet was not the only factor .
53880	‘ Lack of exercise and the motor car probably play a part , ’ Dr Buss said .
53881	People needed to return to something nearer the wartime diet — with the fruit it lacked — to meet health targets , ‘ though how , I do not know .
53882	You can not drag people screaming to one . ’

54247	ICL 's Gary Burnett answers questions
54248	I 've heard that by next year 60 per cent of all PCs will be connected to local area networks .
54249	What are the major networks that are being used ?
54250	THe local area network business is growing much more quickly than the PC industry as a whole .
54251	By 1994 , it is likely that there will be more business PCs attached to LANs than there were total business PCs two years ago .
54252	The fuel for this growth has been the demand by users to share applications and data , and to connect disparate information systems and environments , rather than computing in isolation .
54253	‘ Workgroup computing ’ is the new industry buzz word that describes this trend amongst business PC users .
54254	In addition , the proliferation of networks has been assisted by the arrival of effective PC networking standards a couple of years ago .
54255	Now more than 60 per cent of the networked market has standardized on Novell Netware , to the point where the choice of a PC network is termed a ‘ no-brainer ’ decision by US analysts .
54256	The Novell system is supported by virtually all the leading PC software products that run on networks .
54257	The most advanced version of Netware , Netware 3.11 , is a sophisticated network management system , with support for up to 250 users , ‘ fault-tolerant ’ computing features and facilities to link into minicomputers , mainframe systems and Wide-Area Networks .
54258	In addition , it has the ability to link a huge variety of hardware and operating systems platforms — these include , as well as DOS , OS/2 and Windows , Apple Macs , Sun Systems and a number of UNIX workstations .
54259	Novell 's network products are mostly for PCs , but the next few years will see them move into the traditional minicomputer market with support for a number of minicomputer systems , thus re-enforcing their dominance .
54260	Dominant Novell may be , but there are alternatives .
54261	Microsoft is fighting hard to compete in the PC network market with their Lan Manager .
54262	The current version of the product is designed to fit in with Microsoft 's Windows NT ( New Technology ) strategy and allows Microsoft to offer an environment that runs on anything from laptops to 80486 servers and engineering workstations .
54263	It remains to be seen who will end up being the dominant supplier , but it would seem that the sheer volume of Novell and DOS/Windows users will dictate that future PC Lan systems will have to be compatible with them .

54282	The spirit of spring explodes into life
54283	IT is perhaps difficult to understand why The Rite of Spring caused a theatrical scandal when first it was danced in Paris in 1913 .
54284	Everybody keeps their clothes on and in any case the French were not then , or now , a people to blanche at mere nudity .
54285	What they witnessed , and what was recreated for us by the Ulster Youth Dance Company in Stranmillis College Theatre at the weekend was a spectacle far more disturbing and revolutionary .
54286	For The Rite Of Spring celebrates the mythical and timeless regeneration of both the natural and the human world in a spirit far removed from the tranquil and ordinary daffodils immortalised by Wordsworth .
54287	The dance responds to another rhythm — the violent modern dissonances of Stravinsky 's famous musical score and spring releases itself with a boundless , dangerous energy in movements tense , muscular and frankly sensual .
54288	If you were expecting the graceful and chaste fluidity of Swan Lake , you would surely have got the right gunk .
54289	The stage at Stranmillis is too small for the 90-odd cast and a couple of fainting youngsters had to receive kindly ministrations from an American nurse .
54290	( Tip for reviewers : Bring a medic . )
54291	Nonetheless , the great pulsating wheels , the furious criss-cross rushes over the floor , the rapid shift from gentle , undulating movement to angular violence and the sheer weight of numbers on stage gave to the performance an undeniable exhilaration .
54292	But more than that , it gave a sense of tension , amounting at times to menace — which was , perhaps , what shocked those urbane Parisians .
54293	Here is Earth , clad in what looks disconcertingly like a badly crocheted red dress , here is a stage where an eerie pale yellow orange light plays over small details of figures , and here is a child carried off on a pole — one in a series of victims in the sacrificial Rite Of Spring .
54294	Under the rational conventions of the cycle of the seasons there is revealed a subversive world where the sensual and violent creation of new life is enacted .
54295	The lid is lifted , the subconscious reveals itself , God-like and demonic , both challenging to light assumptions .
54296	An established order of seeing , of understanding , of ruling , is simply exploded — the Modernist spirit asserts itself .
54297	Especially spectacular was the veil scene where three spectral figures hang suspended above a billowing orange red cloth , held like a tent over the dancers .
54298	And memorable too was the dance of the Earth in her bloody red dress — rapacious and , equally , hunted .
54299	From a purely technical point of view , this may not have been the standard performance , but in a place almost completely lacking in a tradition of classical dance , it is a delight to watch native talent channelled so joyously and with such a spirit of challenge to the myth that we exist only from the neck upwards .
54300	Letters to the Editor :
54301	Dreams become nightmare
54302	On Saturday , November 2 , the sanctuary of hospital was defiled by the Provisional IRA .
54303	This profane act will long be remembered and its perpetrators too will not be spared for it will live with them until the end of their days .
54304	Conscience , the great intruder , is a formidable companion .
54305	Granted they may point to the assassination of Marie Drumm in hospital .
54306	Granted , too , they may point out that the bombers of Hiroshima , Nagasaki and Dresden blew to oblivion hospitals by the score in fireballs along with everything else .
54307	By comparison the PIRA may view its action as of little consequence — a perverted act of war in a vicious campaign — but they would be wrong for , by this act on top of so many others , they have turned the Ireland of hope and dreams into a nightmare of guilt , shame , resentment , remorse , anger and grief .
54308	The crucifix which used to adorn the portrait of the Protestant patriot Robert Emmet in so many of the simple homes of Ireland symbolised the ennoblement of failure .
54309	What nobility can members of the IRA claim for the future by an act such as this ?
54310	From the mists of antiquity the spirit of the most ancient of Irish healers , Dian Cecht must surely be calling to you to ponder on what you have done .
54311	Finian — physician to the heroic King of Ulster , Connor MacNessa of Emhain Macha , may well be calling too in grief as the chivalrous upholder of the ancient Gaelic comraind legis or ‘ impartial treatment of the wounded ’ .
54312	In those days the warriors fought by day — in the open — and at night they dressed one another 's wounds .
54313	The PIRA choose instead to ignore the plight of the wounded in their sanctuary and to plan instead to destroy it , killing in the process .
54314	The Brehon Laws representing the most ancient code in Europe and existing centuries before the birth of Christ , long , long before any conquest or plantation in Ireland , made special provision for the sick both for their accommodation and for their protection .
54315	In Medieval times the Benedictine monasteries had a rule which called for ‘ the care of the sick to be placed above and before every other thing , as if indeed Christ were being directly served in waiting upon them ’ .
54316	The wartime bombers did n't seem to care what went up ; by contrast the PIRA did and cared so deliberately as to set out selectively to destroy what is now an illusion — the sanctity of hospital in which , regardless of loyalty or background , so many thousands of victims of our vicious little civil war have received care since those nights in August 1969 .
54317	With the vision of Robert Emmet and the crucifix in mind , could the PIRA not stop to ask how they — or any of the rest of us for that matter — may redeem the bitter legacy of centuries by adding to it ?

54463	We docked at midday .

54466	A couple of our bareboat yachts were still at sea , and Wavebreaker had one more paying charter to complete , but otherwise McIllvanney 's yard had the torpor of tropical summer about it .
54467	Even Stella , McIllvanney 's long-suffering secretary , had taken the day off , leaving the office locked , which meant I had to walk into town to find a public telephone from which I called the Bahamian Police and told them about Hirondelle , and added that I had rescued a chart and a handful of cartridges from the stricken boat .
54468	The police sounded surprised that I had bothered to call them , and I walked back to the boatyard feeling strangely foolish .
54469	Ellen laughed at my punctiliousness .
54470	Doubtless the police had responded to my call by sharpening their cutlasses and charging their muskets , she mocked , in readiness for an invasion of Murder Cay ?

54475	In the middle of the afternoon , when it seemed that the work would never be done on time , Bellybutton arrived at the yard .
54476	Bellybutton was McIllvanney 's foreman , and for a few seconds I dared hope that he had come to help us , but instead he told me that one of the bareboat thirty-three-footers was in trouble .
54477	‘ The man radioed that his engine broke , ’ Bellybutton grumbled , ‘ so I have to fetch the idiot in Starkisser . ’
54478	He was pretending that the errand was a nuisance , though at the same time he was grinning with pleasure at the thought of taking McIllvanney 's brand new sportsboat to sea .
54479	Starkisser 's midnight-blue hull had metalflake embedded in its fibreglass so that the sleek boat seemed to scintillate with an internal and infernal dark blue light .
54480	She had to be one of the fastest production boats in the islands ; her twin big-block engines could hurl the three-ton wedge-shaped hull at over eighty miles an hour , and it worried neither McIllvanney nor Bellybutton that at such a speed a man could not hear himself scream and that even the smallest wave shook the bones right out of their flesh .
54481	‘ There ai n't a girl in creation who do n't melt after a ride in Starkisser , ’ Bellybutton liked to boast .
54482	His real name was Benjamin , but no one ever called him Benjamin or even Ben .
54483	To the whole island he was Bellybutton .
54484	It was rumoured he had earned the nickname by biting the navel clean out of a whore who had displeased him , and I found the rumour all too believable for he was not a pleasant man .
54485	In fact he was a black version of McIllvanney himself ; rangy , knowing , tall and sarcastic .

54487	‘ He says you 're to go to his place at sundown . ’
54488	‘ Why is n't he in the yard today ? ’
54489	I asked .

54491	Bellybutton said in an indignant voice , as though my question had impugned McIllvanney 's honour .

54506	He wore the elegantly cut suit over a white shirt and an old Etonian tie .

56777	‘ The worst thing about cocaine is that once it has exhausted all the dopamine from the brain , then what 's left is a black hole of depression so big and so awful that not all the misery in the world can fill it .
56778	People try to beat that misery with barbiturates , but nothing can cure it because you 've taken away from yourself all chance of feeling pleasure .
56779	The doctors have a word for that misery ; they call it anhedonia , which only means an inability to feel enjoyment , and that 's what it is , but it feels like hell , like true hell , and it 's a hell you ca n't even escape from in sleep because overdosing on cocaine gives you chronic insomnia . ’
56780	Hell was being without God , I thought , but I said nothing , just stared instead at the white wash of cabin light on the rushing water , and I wondered why some people could take cocaine and just walk away from it , while others ended up in hell , or in a peep-show which was probably the same thing .
56781	‘ Of course , ’ Robin-Anne went on , ‘ the brain eventually manufactures more dopamine , so after a day or two the cocaine can work again , and you go soaring up from hell into heaven .
56782	It 's a roller-coaster , Mr Breakspear , up and down , up and down ’ — her thin white hand suited the action to her words — ‘ from heaven to hell and back again , and if heaven is euphoria then let me assure you that hell is a terrible place . ’
56783	‘ So remember the hell , ’ I said , as though I really could help her with my tuppence worth of cheerful encouragement , ‘ and perhaps that will stop you ever going back to it ! ’
56784	‘ But there 's another kind of hell , ’ Robin-Anne 's voice was dulled , as though my cheap optimism had depressed her , ‘ which is remembering the euphoria , and having to surrender the means of creating it .
56785	That hell is giving up cocaine .
56786	I 'm in the easy stage , the first few days when you just sleep and eat , but quite soon I 'll be in the hell of denial , Mr Breakspear . ’
56787	I looked past Robin-Anne to where the moon 's path gleamed on the long waves , and then I glanced forward and saw another belt of silver , but this one diffuse and hazy , showing where the first crepuscular light seeped over the world 's grey edge .
56788	‘ Dawn , ’ I said in a hopeful voice .
56789	But Robin-Anne did not react , and I looked down to see that she was not watching for the new day , but was crying .
56790	I did not know what to say or do .
56791	I should have knelt beside her and put my arms around her and promised her that she would be freed from the hell of anhedonia , and that there really was a God and that she did have the strength to tear herself free from cocaine , as others had freed themselves , and I should have assured her that there was true happiness without a drug , but I did not know her well enough to embrace her , so I just let her weep as the sun streaked up in glory from the east .
56792	Thus Wavebreaker sailed towards the light , carrying her passengers to hell .
56793	I rousted Thessy out of his bed with a cup of tea , then went to my own bed as he took over the wheel .
56794	I slept , dreaming of Masquerade sinking through waves of steel into torrents of fire .
56795	I woke just before lunchtime to find Wavebreaker still sailing eastwards .
56796	Ellen was showing Rickie Crowninshield all the elaborate electronic toys that only Ellen wholly understood ; the radios , radars , weatherfaxes and satellite receivers , and Rickie was being surprisingly attentive , but as soon as he saw me he scowled and clamped a pair of headphones over his ears as though to make sure that he did not have to hold any kind of conversation with me .
56797	Ellen shrugged at his rudeness .
56798	‘ How 's the weather ? ’
56799	I asked her .
56800	‘ No change . ’
56801	I squinted through a porthole and saw the sky was scraped blue and bright above an empty sea .
56802	‘ You faxed a chart ? ’
56803	I asked Ellen .
56804	‘ Sure did . ’
56805	She handed me the sheet of grey paper with its synoptic chart which had been transmitted from Florida just a few moments before .
56806	I pretended to despise such modern aids , but that was really a defensive reaction because I knew I could never afford such frills for Masquerade .
56807	I saw that there was not even a ripple of low pressure off to the east , which was the reassurance I wanted , for a depression to the east could swiftly twist itself into a full-blooded storm .
56808	‘ Good morning , Rickie , ’ I said loudly , wanting to demonstrate that I held no grudge for his behaviour in the night .
56809	‘ Yo . ’
56810	His voice was surly , but suddenly he twisted round to face me and took off the headphones , and I thought he was going to apologise for his rudeness of the previous night , but instead he demanded to know if it was true that we were out in the open ocean and were not planning to make a landfall for some days .
56811	‘ That 's true , ’ I said .
56812	‘ But I wanted to do some scuba ! ’ he said in outrage .
56813	‘ There 'll be a chance , I promise . ’
56814	‘ Jesus ! ’ he said in exasperation , then turned abruptly away .
56815	I waited to see if he would say any more , but he evidently did not want my company .
56816	I grimaced at Ellen , then went topsides where I found the ship being steered by its automatic pilot and Thessy and Jackson Chatterton perched halfway up the mainmast with reels of rigging wire from which Thessy was fashioning a parallel set of starboard shrouds .
56817	I wanted to double up all Wavebreaker 's standing rigging , just in case we did try to take her across the ocean .
56818	There was no sign of Robin-Anne who was presumably asleep .
56819	Chatterton climbed down to the deck and told me that Robin-Anne had eaten a huge breakfast .
56820	‘ What about Rickie ? ’
56821	‘ He just played with his food , ’ Chatterton frowned , ‘ and that means he must be over the crash period , which means his behaviour 's going to be difficult . ’
56822	‘ Even more difficult ? ’
56823	I asked with dread .
56824	The big man laughed .
56825	‘ Nick , you ai n't seen nothing yet . ’

56827	When he had joined the ship he had been nothing but eagerness and smiles , romping about like a new puppy , but now he had turned unrelentingly morose .
56828	At lunchtime he scowled at his sister who , wrapped in a dressing gown , fell on the sandwiches as though she had not eaten in weeks .
56829	‘ I 'm famished ! ’
56830	Rickie would not even try a sandwich , but instead pushed his plate away and lit a cigarette .
56831	He sipped at his can of diet soda and grimaced at the taste .
56832	‘ Have we got any beer on this boat ? ’ he suddenly asked .
56833	‘ No , ’ Ellen said placidly .
56834	‘ Doctor 's orders . ’
56835	‘ Fuck the doctors . ’
56836	No one responded , which merely annoyed Rickie .
56837	He stared at his sister whose pale face was made even paler by the sun-block ointment she had liberally smeared on her skin .
56838	‘ You like this shit-for-drink , Robbie ? ’
56839	Robin-Anne nodded , but was too busy eating to take much notice of her brother , though she did manage to mumble that she thought the diet soda was really kind of good .
56840	‘ I think it 's really kind of crap . ’
56841	Rickie turned his truculent gaze on me .
56842	‘ You must have some liquor aboard , Nick ? ’
56843	‘ Not a drop , ’ I lied .
56844	‘ That 's very un-British of you . ’
56845	He attempted an atrocious imitation of my English accent .
56846	‘ I thought all British ships were fuelled by rum , sodomy and the lash .
56847	Is n't that what they say ? ’
56848	‘ That 's what they say . ’
56849	I kept my voice friendly , for I was determined not to be drawn by his provocation .
56850	‘ Are you gay , Nick ? ’
56851	Rickie suddenly asked me in what purported to be a tone of serious enquiry .
56852	I did not answer , while everyone but Robin-Anne , who was too busy eating , seemed embarrassed .
56853	Once again the lack of response infuriated Rickie who , seeking some other means of provocation , hurled his can of soda across the deck .
56854	‘ Shit-juice ! ’ he shouted .
56855	Ellen caught my eye , and we stared at each other for a sympathetic fraction of a second , then I looked away to see that the sticky liquid had sprayed across the teak planks .
56856	‘ Clean it up , ’ I said mildly .
56857	‘ Rum , sodomy and the lash ! ’
56858	Rickie chanted at me with a sudden and extraordinary vindictiveness .
56859	Jackson Chatterton stirred as though he proposed to clean up the mess himself , but I waved him down and kept my eyes on Rickie .
56860	‘ Clean it up , ’ I said again .
56861	‘ You clean it up .
56862	This is our vacation !
56863	I did n't suggest coming on this heap of a boat to work like a house-servant , is n't that right , Robbie ? ’
56864	Robin-Anne just went on eating .
56865	‘ Clean it up , ’ I told Rickie again .
56866	Rickie seized Thessy 's can , pulled open its top , and hurled it messily after the first .
56867	‘ Now what are you going to do ?
56868	Flog me ? ’
56869	He suddenly laughed , then looked at Ellen whom he perceived as a possible ally .
56870	‘ You can never tell with a Brit , can you ?
56871	It 's either a flog or a fuck . ’
56872	Ellen said nothing to encourage him .
56873	Robin-Anne ate stolidly on , while poor Thessy looked terrified .
56874	Only Jackson Chatterton seemed comfortable with Rickie 's display of petulant temper .
56875	‘ The man said clean it up , ’ Chatterton said calmly , ‘ so clean it up ! ’
56876	But Rickie was long beyond sense .
56877	‘ This is a vacation ! ’ he screamed at me , ‘ so why are we out here ?
56878	I want to see a beach !
56879	A beach , you know what a beach is ?
56880	Sand ?
56881	Surf ?
56882	I want to go board-sailing , maybe do a little water skiing .
56883	I want to do some scuba , for Christ 's sake ! ’
56884	I ignored him , fetching instead a mop and bucket from one of the big stern lockers .
56885	The bucket had a rope attached to its handle and I skimmed it over the stern to haul up a gallon or so of sea-water which I slammed down in front of Rickie .

56887	I threw the mop at him .
56888	He ignored the mop , just staring at me , and I saw him take a breath ready to defy me so I spoke before he could .
56889	‘ Either you clean the deck , Rickie , or I 'll scrub it with your hair . ’
56890	He began to weep .
56891	Robin-Anne glanced at him , then smeared mustard on a roast beef sandwich .
56892	‘ It 's real good food , ’ she said enthusiastically .
56893	‘ I 'll help you , ’ Ellen said to Rickie , then she took his hand and placed it on the mop handle .
56894	‘ Come on , ’ she said gently .
56895	Thus , as Rickie feebly dabbed at the deck and as his sister ate , our happy ship sailed on .
56896	Evil was a stupid word .
56897	It had the same sort of sense , largely meaningless , amorphous , diffuse , woolly , as applied to ‘ love ’ .
56898	Everyone had a vague idea of what it meant but none could precisely have defined it .
56899	It seemed , in a way , to imply something supernatural .
56900	These thoughts had been inspired in her husband 's mind by a sentence from a review on the cover of a paperback novel Lili Manjusri had bought at Salzburg airport .
56901	‘ A brooding cloud of evil , ’ the commentator had written , ‘ hovers over this dark and magnificent saga from the first page to the astonishing denouement . ’
56902	Lili had bought it because it was the only work in English she could find at the bookstall .
56903	Whenever Shiva considered the word he saw in his mind 's eye a grinning Mephistopheles with small , curly ram 's horns , capering in frock coat .
56904	Events in his own past he never thought of as evil but rather as mistaken , immensely regrettable , brought about by fear and greed .
56905	Shiva thought most of the folly of the world was brought about by fear and greed and to call this evil , as if it were the result of purposeful calculation and deliberate wrongdoing , was to show ignorance of human psychology .
56906	It was in this way that he was thinking when , with Lili by his side and their suitcases on a trolley he would abandon at the tube-station entrance , he looked up and met the eyes of Adam Verne-Smith .
56907	Shiva had no doubt it was Adam he saw .
56908	To him Europeans did not specially all look alike .
56909	Adam and Rufus Fletcher , for instance , though both white , Caucasian and of more or less Anglo-Saxon-Celtic-Norse-Norman ancestry , were very dissimilar in appearance , Adam being slight and white-skinned with a lot of bushy ( now receding ) dark hair , while Rufus was burly and fair with curiously sharp , pointed features for so fleshy a man .
56910	Shiva had seen Rufus some years before , though he was absolutely certain Rufus had either not seen or not recognized him , while he was equally sure Adam knew perfectly well who he was .
56911	He began to smile from exactly the motive Adam had attributed to him , a desire to ingratiate and to defend himself , to turn away wrath .
56912	He had been born in England , had never seen India , spoke English as his cradle tongue and had forgotten all the Hindi he had ever learned but he had all the immigrant 's protective reactions and all his self-consciousness .
56913	Indeed , he had more , he thought , since the events at Ecalpemos .
56914	Things had got worse since then .
56915	There had been a gradual slow decline in his fortunes , his fate , his happiness and his prosperity , or prospect of prosperity .
56916	Adam glared back at him and looked away .
56917	Of course he would not want to know me , Shiva thought .
56918	Lili asked him what he was looking at .
56919	‘ A chap I used to know years ago . ’
56920	Shiva used words like ‘ chap ’ now , and ‘ kiddy ’ , words used by Indians wanting to sound like true Brits , though he would not have done this once .
56921	‘ Do you want to go and say hallo to him ? ’
56922	‘ Alas and alack , he does n't want to know me .
56923	I am a poor Indian .
56924	He is not the kind of bloke who wishes to know his coloured brethren . ’
56925	‘ Do n't talk like that , ’ said Lili .
56926	Shiva smiled sadly and asked why not but he knew he was being unfair to Adam as well as to himself .
56927	Had they not all agreed when they left Ecalpemos and went their separate ways that it.was to be as if they had never met , known each other , lived together , that in future they must be strangers and more than strangers ?
56928	Adam , no doubt , adhered to this .
56929	So , probably , did Rufus and the girl .
56930	There was something , some quality , more fatalistic , more resigned , in Shiva .
56931	He might deceive others but he was incapable of deceiving himself , of pretending , of denying thoughts .
56932	It would not have occurred to him to attempt forgetfulness by inhibiting memories of Ecalpemos .
56933	He remembered it every day .
56934	‘ It was at that place I told you about that I knew him , ’ he said to Lili .
56935	‘ He was one of the group of us there .
56936	Well , he was the one , it was his place . ’
56937	‘ All the better not to know him then , ’ said Lili .
56938	She bought their tickets .
56939	Adam had been right , and it was in an east London near-ghetto that Shiva lived .
56940	Lili tucked the two slips of green cardboard into a fold of her sari .
56941	She was only half Indian , her mother being a Viennese woman who had come to England as an au pair and married a doctor from Darjeeling , a surgical registrar in a Bradford hospital .
56942	When Lili grew up and the doctor died her mother went home and settled in Salzburg , selling Glockenturm beer mugs in a souvenir shop .
56943	It was there that they went each summer , in Shiva 's holidays , their fares paid by Sabine Schnitzler who , having reverted to her maiden name and largely to her native tongue , sometimes wore a surprised , even bewildered , look at being surrounded , as she put it , by ‘ all those Indians ’ .
56944	For Lili , whose skin was nearly as white as Adam Verne-Smith 's , was more Indian than true Indians , wore the sari , grew her curly brown Austrian hair down to her waist and took language lessons from a Bengali neighbour of theirs .
56945	In her voice were hints of the sing-song tone , Welsh in its rhythms , so characteristic of the Indian speaking English .
56946	Shiva thought he should be grateful for all this , though he was not .
56947	How would he have felt , he sometimes asked himself , if he had married a woman who set herself against his ethnic origins ?
56948	He had told Lili about Ecalpemos before they married .
56949	It would not have been in his nature , nor would he have been inclined , to do otherwise …
56950	But he had not gone into details , giving only the bare outline , the facts , and Lili had asked few questions .
56951	He bore in mind that the time might come when he would have to tell her everything .
56952	‘ It was n't your fault , ’ she had finally said .
56953	‘ It 's true that they never consulted me .
56954	If I had given my advice it would have been ignored . ’
56955	‘ Well , then . ’
56956	He began haltingly to explain , but stopped himself .
56957	He could tell the truth but not all the truth .
56958	Openness did not demand that he tell her he had suggested it .
56959	‘ You should try to forget , ’ she said .
56960	‘ I suppose I feel that would be wrong .
56961	I ought never to forget about the kiddy . ’
56962	And it was perhaps inevitable that he should see the death of his own child , his and Lili 's , as retribution , as a just punishment .
56963	Yet he was not a Christian , to look at things in this light .
56964	He was not really a Hindu either .
56965	His parents had neglected this aspect of his upbringing , having largely abandoned their religion but for a few outer forms before he was born .
56966	Some lingering race memory remained though , some pervading conviction common to all Orientals , that this life was but one of many on the great wheel of existence and that reincarnation as someone better endowed or worse ( in his case surely worse ) awaited him .
56967	He saw himself returning as a beggar with limbs deliberately deformed , whining for alms on the sea-front at Bombay .
56968	The incongruity was that at the same time he was convinced of retribution in this world .
56969	He saw the death of his son , a placenta previa child who died during Lili 's labour , as direct vengeance , though he could not have said who was exacting it .
56970	Crossing the hospital courtyard which divided the maternity wing from the general wards and administration building , hearing over and over in his head the words they had gently but coldly told him , the announcement of his son 's death , leaving Lili asleep , carefully sedated , he had lifted his eyes and seen Rufus Fletcher .
56971	Rufus was wearing a white coat and had a stethoscope hanging round his neck .
56972	He was walking very rapidly , far faster than Shiva was going in the opposite direction , from a building with long windows and white-uniformed men and girls behind them that looked like a lab , towards the main block .
56973	He turned his head to look at Shiva , cast on him an indifferent glance , and turned away .
56974	Rufus had simply not known who he was , Shiva was sure of that , had not recognized him as one of the other two male members of the little community in which they had all lived in such contiguity for something like two months .
56975	Shiva was astonished to find that Rufus had in fact finished his studies and become a doctor .
56976	Of course he had known Rufus had this in mind , was three years through his time at medical school , had already considerable knowledge and nous — who could forget that ? — but somehow he had imagined that the same fate would have overtaken the others as had overtaken him , a deathly stultifying , an inhibition on all that was ambitious and of ascendant character , a remorseful withdrawing into the shade .
56977	Only if they did not show their faces , only if they kept their heads low and lived in obscure corners , could they hope to pass at least in physical safety through life .
56978	So he had thought .
56979	But the others evidently had not , or Rufus had not , walking jauntily and with swinging stride across the tarmac , his stethoscope bobbing up and down , letting himself into the main hospital block , Shiva later saw , by a door marked ‘ Private ’ , which he slammed behind him with a fine disregard for the notices exhorting all to silence .
56980	Lili had had no more babies .
56981	Perhaps they would have another child one day .
56982	Lili was still under thirty and there was no reason , the hospital staff had said , why such an unfortunate thing as a placenta previa should occur again , or if it did , they would be ready for it .
56983	Shiva was not too keen .
56984	The area in which they lived was overcrowded and unsalubrious and if there was rather less unemployment than in the north of England , that was about all that could be said for it .
56985	The name of their street was Fifth Avenue .
56986	It is not the custom in English cities to name streets by numbers but it has happened .
56987	There are , for instance , no less than fourteen First Avenues in the London area , twelve Second Avenues , nine Third Avenues and three Fourth Avenues .
56988	The only other Fifth Avenues are in West Kilburn and Manor Park , both of which also possess a Sixth , while the latter possesses a Seventh .
56989	Shiva 's Fifth Avenue was a long , curving , treeless street that dipped steeply down and switchbacked up again , though the neighbourhood was not in general a particularly hilly place .
56990	At the end nearest the tube station was a block of shops containing a small supermarket run by Pakistanis , a Greek restaurant run by Cypriots , a triple-fronted emporium given over to the sale of motor-cycle spare parts and equipment and a paper shop run by people who when asked where they came from ingenuously replied that they were Cape Coloureds .
56991	In the middle of Fifth Avenue , where Pevsner Road crossed it , was another small grocer 's and a pub called the Boxer , and at the far end , opposite each other , a unisex hairdresser 's and a betting shop .
56992	These were linked by belts of houses in infrequently broken blocks , composed of bricks in a dull purplish red or khaki yellow , and all now between ninety-seven and ninety-nine years old .
56993	A double line of parked cars ran parallel to the pavements from the paper shop to the pub and the grocer 's to the hairdresser 's .
56994	If you half-closed your eyes and looked at it you might have likened it to a string of coloured beads .
56995	Shiva went into the paper shop .
56996	There were two Jamaican boys in there and they made a point of crowding the counter , holding their elbows akimbo , so that Shiva was unable to pick up his paper from the pile in front of them .
56997	Quietly he asked for the Standard and handed across his money between the jutting arms ; he did n't want any trouble .
56998	It was the Indians they hated down here , not the whites .
56999	Well , there were few whites left except for very old people who could n't have moved if they had wanted to .
57000	Lili was waiting outside , standing between their cases .
57001	She was very brave , he thought , to wear the sari and shop in the Indian shops and have her Bengali lessons when all these things drew attention to her .
57002	It would have been easy for her to pass for a white girl .
57003	Only her eyes , distinctive dark bluish-brown , with somewhat protuberant , bluish whites , betrayed her .
57004	But people were not that perceptive and for God 's sake this was London , not Johannesburg in the fifties .
57005	She could have got away with it and he had more than once suggested she should , begged her almost .
57006	But it was her identity , she said , it was all she had , and she went on putting a caste mark which she had no right to on her forehead and wearing all her gold bracelets and cooking sag ghosht and dal instead of the defrosted hamburgers and chips which was what most people ate around there .
57007	He picked up the cases and she took their hand-cases and they walked home , passing three separate black people who looked at them with silent hostility and two elderly white women who did not look at them at all .
57008	Lili would start unpacking at once .
57009	She would put all the light clothes into one bag and all the dark into another and take them to the launderette in Pevsner Road .
57010	He knew it would be useless to try and hinder this , she would be fidgety and fretful if there were dirty clothes about .
