57012	Nothing much could happen to her on a sunny September afternoon between here and the launderette , and Mrs Barakhda who ran it was a friend of hers , or the nearest Lili had to a friend .
57013	He made her a cup of tea while she sorted the washing , closed up the cases and pushed them into the cupboard under the stairs .
57014	At least they had a whole house , with three bedrooms .
57015	Most of the houses down here were divided into.two flats , two front doors squeezed in under the tiny porch .
57016	He offered to carry the bags for her but she would n't hear of it .
57017	In her reactionary way — for Lili had been brought up by an independent , feminist mother — she thought it all right for men to carry suitcases but not bags of washing .
57018	With his second cup of tea in front of him , he sat down to look at the newspaper .
57019	There was a big picture of the Princess of Wales visiting a home for handicapped children .
57020	The main story was about trouble in the Middle East and a subsidiary one about racial trouble in West London , street fighting mainly and breaking shop windows .
57021	Shiva 's eye travelled down the page .
57022	At the foot of one of the left-hand columns he read a headline .
57023	For the amount of text underneath it , a mere paragraph , it was a disproportionately large headline .
57024	It even rather spoiled the symmetry of the page .
57025	The headline said : ‘ Skeleton Found in Woodland Grave ’ , and the story beneath it ran : ‘ While digging a grave for his pet dog a Suffolk landowner , with a home near Hadleigh , unearthed a human skeleton .
57026	The remains appear to be those of a young woman .
57027	Police declined to comment further at this stage and Mr Alec Chipstead , a chartered surveyor , was not available for questioning . ’
57028	Shiva read it twice .
57029	It was rather strangely put , he thought .
57030	He felt this about most accounts and articles in newspapers .
57031	They did n't know much but they told you what they did know in the most cryptic way possible to whet your appetite and make you speculate .
57032	For instance , they did n't tell you if the landowner and Mr Alec Chipstead were one and the same person , though you could tell that was what they meant .
57033	He could feel sweat standing on his face , on his upper lip and forehead .
57034	Wiping it away with his handkerchief , he closed his eyes , opened them and looked round the room , then back at the newsprint in front of him , as if he might have been dreaming or have imagined it .
57035	The paragraph , of course , was still there .
57036	There was no reason , Shiva thought after the first shock had subsided , to suppose any connection between this find and Ecalpemos .
57037	Suffolk was the only link and he could remember quite distinctly , on first going to Nunes , how there had been some dispute as to whether it was in Suffolk or Essex .
57038	The blurring of boundaries , which took place at about that time , had created such anomalies as a householder having an Essex postal address while paying his rates to Suffolk County Council .
57039	This , surely , was what had actually happened to Adam Verne-Smith .
57040	It was not quite true that this was the only connecting link .
57041	The other , of course , was the body , the young woman 's body .
57042	Shiva thought , I must wait for more news , I must bear it and wait .
57043	His patient was getting on for fifty , a handsome , tall woman , very well-dressed .
57044	Her expensive clothes — Jasper Conran , he guessed — she had put on again and , while behind the screen , a little more lipstick .
57045	He had just done a smear test on her .
57046	‘ You have a very nice inside , ’ he told her , smiling .
57047	The nurse smiled too .
57048	She could afford to , being twenty years younger and with her gynaecological problems , if any , taken care of by Dr Fletcher for free .
57049	Mrs Strawson said she was very glad to hear it .
57050	She looked happy and relaxed .
57051	Rufus gave her a cigarette .
57052	One of the many aspects of his personality which endeared him to his patients — the others being good looks , charm , youth , boyishness and treating them like equals — was his inability to give up smoking .
57053	‘ I am that monstrous sinner , ’ he would say to them , ‘ the doctor that smokes .
57054	Each one of us is said to be worth fifty thousand pounds of advertising per year to the tobacco companies . ’
57055	And the patient , especially if she did n't smoke , would feel empathy for him and maternal towards him .
57056	Poor boy , with all that stress , he works so hard , it 's only natural he needs something to keep him going .
57057	Mrs Strawson inhaled gratefully .
57058	This was her first visit to Rufus Fletcher in Wimpole Street and she was already delighted to have taken up her friend 's recommendation .
57059	‘ Now how about contraception ?
57060	Do you mind telling me what method you 're using ? ’

59673	Insurer takes the risk out of Russian empires
59674	By Cathy Gunn in the City
59675	BRITISH companies seeking new markets get a helping hand today for any projects they fancy setting up in Russia .
59676	With our own economy still struggling along , anything that can boost overseas ventures for UK groups is welcome news .
59677	And Russia is , after all , where the first English joint-stock company , of the sort whose shares we would recognise on the market today , got off the ground .
59678	It was the Muscovy Company , formed by enterprising English merchants in the year 1554 to trade with the country then ruled by Tzar Ivan the Terrible .
59679	It marked the beginning of the London Stock Exchange and an international trading boom for Britain .
59680	Let's hope this new move has a similar effect .
59681	American insurers already reckon there is a $40bn ( about £26bn ) market for foreign investors brave enough to risk their capital in the old Soviet Union .
59682	This neatly matches the region 's external debt and , says David Forrest — underwriting director of the London-based political risk insurer EIGA — ‘ we have to encourage investors to give it the ability to earn the foreign exchange to repay that debt . ’
59683	But UK firms will have to be quick off the mark to benefit .
59684	The new scheme offered from today by EIGA is open to any European company or EC subsidiary of a foreign firm aiming to build up a Russian business empire .
59685	The plan will protect EC-based foreign investors in Russia from political upheavals damaging their business .
59686	It will cover anything from sudden nationalisation to just being deprived of the use of their assets , or a block on repatriating dividends .
59687	EIGA reckons its plan will appeal to UK and European businesses ranging from hoteliers trying to set up in Moscow to oil giants eyeing the vast energy resources of Kazakhsthan .
59688	Normally a company buying insurance against political upheavals , nationalisation or blocks on the repatriation of dividends , is required by its insurer to keep this cover a dark secret from the government of the country in question .
59689	Otherwise it might decide to nationalise the foreign firm 's assets on its soil knowing that the company will just be able to claim the compensation anyway .
59690	But , in a ground-breaking move , EIGA has struck a deal that involves the Russian Agency for International Cooperation and Development giving companies buying the cover a letter promising not to pounce .
59691	While this does not rule out the risk of a change of regime there , it does cut down the danger of a simple change of heart by the existing government .
59692	And that means that the insurance premiums should be cheaper — at between 2% and 3% of the capital at risk — than the 3%-plus normally charged by private political risk providers .
59693	EIGA says its plan plugs big gaps in the cover available from EC government agencies for European companies seeking a toe-hold in this potentially attractive and massive new market .
59694	At the moment seven of the 12 EC member countries do not offer their exporters any protection in the old Soviet Union , particularly for short-term projects .

60304	VATman threatens our budding entrepreneurs
60305	Cathy Gunn
60306	VAT rules are threatening a valuable scheme that helps people on unemployment and other benefits to get the first foot on the ladder to running their own businesses .
60307	But in an eleventh-hour move late on Friday afternoon — and just hours after a query about the situation from this column — VAT headquarters agreed to consider a new interpretation of the rules .
60308	VAT staff playing it by the book were close to destroying the Enterprise Rehearsal scheme , run by Barfield Enterprise Training Ltd for Barnet Enterprise Trust and Enfield Enterprise Agency .
60309	Barfield feared it would have to close the ER scheme this week — ironically , just as Hertfordshire was inquiring about joining it .
60310	Set up in agreement with the Board of Trade and the Department of Social Security , the ER scheme allows new entrepreneurs to set up in business for three months without losing any state benefits .
60311	This gives them time to see if their idea works or not .
60312	Nearly 300 people have tried it out over the past four years and ‘ the success rate is significantly higher than with any other start-your-own-business scheme , ’ said Barfield 's joint MD Cliff Maxen .
60313	‘ Currently we have 35 on it . ’
60314	For the first three months Barfield is officially the ER businesses ' proprietor and holds any surplus funds they generate .
60315	Thus the would-be entrepreneur can keep drawing benefits , and , if the business fails , they have n't lost out .
60316	If the business is a goer , the entrepreneur moves on to the full Enterprise Allowance system and gets back any surplus funds .
60317	But suddenly the local VATman said that as the money held by Barfield exceeds the VAT threshold , it must pay 17.5% VAT on it — even though each business involved would be under the VAT threshold .
60318	The local VATman 's refusal to budge clashed directly with the work of Baroness Denton , the government 's small firms minister at the Board of of Trade .
60319	Former rally driver Jean Denton is battling to reduce red tape and bureaucratic burdens on small firms and start-ups .
60320	Maxen wrote to her office seeking help to persuade the VATman to change his mind .
60321	‘ It is wonderful to think that someone in a government ministry may be paying attention and trying to help us , ’ he said last night .
60322	‘ It is in no-one 's interest , nor was it intended , that the holding company should have to register for VAT .
60323	‘ It makes the scheme more complicated and less popular .
60324	‘ We have stopped taking new people on to it , and thought we would have to close it altogether . ’
60325	The scheme is not out of the woods yet ; and rather than break the law Maxen last week filled in the local VATman 's registration form .
60326	But on Friday night news came through that VAT HQ had agreed to study the ER scheme ‘ to see if it can be classified as a training activity , which would be VAT exempt , rather than as a business activity , ’ Maxen reported .
60327	These matters came to a head in the very week that Baroness Denton launched a £300,000 London Growth Fund to help small firms .
60328	The fund offers cheap loans of up to £5,000 , at 2% under base rate , to businesses being started by the unemployed , disabled , ethnic minorities and women ; and loans of up to £10,000 to existing small businesses .
60329	It is backed by Midland Bank and the nine London Training &amp; Enterprise Councils .

60958	A FORMER nurse accused of sexually assaulting residents at a hospital for the mentally handicapped has lost his claim for unfair dismissal .

60963	Both are on final written warnings .
60964	‘ Responsible ’
60965	Rico Gopul , a staff nurse in the villa at the time of the alleged incidents , told the tribunal he had been accused of the same offences as Mr Reid but had received only a written warning .
60966	He too denied the charges .
60967	Director of specialist support for New Possibilities Fay Gerrie said she took the original decision to sack Mr Reid , who has 28 years ' service at the hospital , because he was the charge nurse and therefore responsible for the villa .
60968	Procedures at the NHS trust were criticised during the hearing with tribunal chairman Richard Smith questioning why formal notes were not taken during disciplinary hearings .
60969	Mr Reid maintains he was refused the right to call witnesses on his behalf while Mrs Gerrie said she could not remember a request being made at the original hearing .
60970	After the tribunal , director of personnel for New Possibilities Andrew Arnold said there were lessons to be learned and not only would proper records now be kept of disciplinary hearings but a new ‘ whistle-blowing ’ policy was being introduced to make it easier for staff to expose wrong-doing .
60971	Counsel for Mr Reid , Philip Aliker , said he was very surprised and disappointed at the ruling .
60972	His client , he said , had lost his job because of the statements of two nurses when many others had said the allegations were false .

61136	PM revamps honours list
61137	Prime Minister John Major announces changes to the honours system
61138	THE Prime Minister yesterday matched his words about a classless society with action — sweeping away the class basis of the honours system .
61139	From now on everyone in the country will have the chance to recommend ‘ deserving cases ’ for an award .
61140	And the days of virtually ‘ automatic gongs ’ for civil servants are to end .
61141	In future , honours will have to be earned .
61142	However , Mr Major said he will retain the system of political honours — and that provoked an angry reaction from Labour .
61143	Opposition leader John Smith called it a ‘ shoddy misuse ’ of the system .
61144	But the first shake-up since the First World War does mean a deep-seated reform in the principle behind the choice of names in the Birthday and New Year Honours lists .
61145	In future the accent will be on voluntary service , and unsung , worthy people up and down the country beavering away on charitable work .
61146	It will be up to ordinary people as ‘ shareholders ’ in the system to winkle out these deserving cases who would otherwise pass unnoticed .
61147	Downing Street will supply them with special forms to state the reasons for their recommendations .
61148	No longer even can ambassadors assume that a knighthood will come along automatically .
61149	Senior law officers , like the Attorney General , may have to remain plain ‘ mister ’ .
61150	Mr Major told MPs that the awarding of honours had been a valued part of British life for centuries but the system must from time to time be reviewed .
61151	‘ Honours should be awarded on merit for exceptional achievement or exceptional service , over and above what normally might be expected .
61152	‘ There should be different levels of award to reflect different levels of achievement .
61153	Awards should not be automatic and follow simply as a result of doing a particular job .
61154	Awards should place more emphasis on voluntary service . ’
61155	The overhaul of the system includes abolishing the British Empire Medal , widely regarded as ‘ the gong for the working classes ’ .
61156	In future , those who would have received it will be made Members of the British Empire , seen as a ‘ white-collar award ’
61157	And the distinction between commissioned officers and NCOs and other ranks in military gallantry awards will be abolished .

61470	A year ago he promised his creditors that the pound sterling would never be devalued , and six months ago he had to break his word to them .
61471	A year ago he was promising economic growth in the UK , which should by now have been accelerating to three per cent per year but , of course , it never happened .
61472	This year the Chancellor has been insisting that the pound can not be allowed to go any lower , because of the dangers of inflation ; and he has allowed the Bank of England to give a strong endorsement of his argument .
61473	Nobody is yet convinced that he really would be willing to raise interest rates if there were a prolonged run on the pound sometime this year .
61474	At home , while Ministers are careful not to use such words as ‘ green shoots ’ in public , they use them off the record all the time to political journalists , who dutifully pass the message on to the reading public .
61475	Nevertheless , the opinion polls which test public confidence in the future of the economy are showing a substantial majority on the side of gloom , if not doom .
61476	There are positive signs ; there is more money in circulation and some of it is being spent .
61477	The market for houses and cars is better than it was , and there is an improved turnover in the shops .
61478	Yet there does not seem to be any end to the announcements of redundancies in major companies , which make the headlines and arouse general anxiety elsewhere .
61479	The classic response to this situation is to take from the rich and to give to the poor on the grounds that the poor spend their money much faster than the rich .
61480	The circulation of money is thereby improved , creating more economic activity and more jobs — and all this without printing money which would lead to inflation .
61481	After bullying the Queen into paying income tax ‘ like everybody else ’ the Government has been embarrassingly reminded by the Birt affair of the many high earners who do not by any means pay tax like everybody else .
61482	Mr Lamont will be expected to respond by making a serious attempt to plug tax loopholes before he talks of increases in general taxation .
61483	He will also be expected to end the anomaly whereby high earners are excused national insurance contributions on earnings of over £21,000 a year .
61484	That would give him a chance to reduce tax on lower incomes , which are so discouraging to people caught in the poverty trap .
61485	An adjustment of this kind would serve to promote recovery , and it should also go some way to reassure international opinion .
61486	Bankers like to see governments breaking their election promises because this proves that they are in earnest in their attempts to put the economy to rights .
61487	The budget needs to be a holding operation , so that a recovery can become established before the real attack on the budget deficit is made in December .
61488	Its success will depend upon people believing that Mr Lamont knows what he was doing , and that his forecasts are reliable ; and it is difficult not to reflect that an alternative Chancellor would have had carried more conviction .

62308	Hell on earth for war rape victims
62309	Captive forced by attackers to lick her own blood
62310	EVIDENCE is emerging that thousands of women have been systematically and brutally raped in the conflict in former Yugoslavia .
62311	CHARLOTTE ADCOCK spoke to a woman who has interviewed some of the victims .
62312	( Readers may find parts of this account upsetting ) R ape in warfare has often been overlooked .
62313	Widely considered a routine , if regrettable , fact of war , it has rarely been prosecuted .
62314	Reports on the armed conflict in the former Yugoslavia , however , suggest not only that rape and the sexual abuse of women have been carried out on a massive scale , but that it has been systematic and organised .
62315	Evidence is now emerging that women have been detained in order to be raped and even impregnated , and that political and military leaders knew , but condoned it.One woman who can testify to the existence of rape camps and the suffering of women , is Francoise Hampson , senior lecturer at Essex University and an expert in the law of armed conflict .
62316	She has just returned from interviewing rape victims in Bosnia during a nine-day mission led by the International League of Human Rights.While European Community officials estimate 20,000 women have been raped , Francoise Hampson says quantification is impossible .
62317	‘ The only value in the figures is the indication of the scale and an adjective would be better .
62318	The word I would pick is ‘ widespread ’ . ’
62319	Human rights organisations remain wary of publishing figures because they have been widely used as propaganda .
62320	Amnesty International has , however , released details of individual accounts to ‘ illustrate at least part of what has occurred ’ .
62321	The accounts include those of Moslems from Kljuc .
62322	One mother described how her daughter was locked up and she was raped by three drunk , uniformed men whom she knew .
62323	Another woman in her mid-sixties said she had been one of eight raped by ‘ Serbian irregulars ’ .
62324	‘ Three of them raped her , one first forced his hand into her at knifepoint and then made her lick her own blood .
62325	Two of the women had their throats slit after the rapes , ’ the report states.Victims have been assaulted in different situations , said Ms Hampson .
62326	Women have been randomly raped by individuals , gang-raped by uniformed men , and raped in detention centres either by the guards or people let in by the guards .
62327	There has also been a high incidence of murder following rape.Allegations have to be handled with care , but there is clear evidence that rape camps have been set up .
62328	‘ I interviewed someone from a rape camp in Doboj .
62329	It was unequivocally a place where women were held in order to be raped , ’ she said.Observers have also identified a specific category of women raped in order to be made pregnant .
62330	Rape has happened on all sides and across the sexes , but according to Ms Hampson ‘ the overwhelming majority of the rape victims are non-Serbs ’ .
62331	Several factors have made the abuse particularly cruel and degrading .
62332	‘ The fact that it 's so systematic , going effectively unpunished and often performed by people known to the victims makes it more horrific .
62333	It 's been made even more humiliating by the circumstances in which it 's been done like public rape .
62334	‘ In no case where we interviewed had the woman only been raped by one man .
62335	Plenty of them had only been raped over one period of 24 hours but never less than by six or seven men .
62336	Two women passed out when raped by number three so they do n't know . ’
62337	The effect on women , in a Moslem culture which perhaps considers rape more dishonourable than murder , has been profound .
62338	Victims have been openly accused by their husbands of being ‘ Chetnik whores ’ .
62339	Some have been abandoned by their families and others forced to leave .
62340	‘ There is n't even guaranteed support from other women because it 's seen as so shameful .
62341	Some have n't told their mothers .
62342	They believe they know and look at them differently , and it 's avoided as a topic of conversation . ’
62343	Resources are scarce , medical treatment limited and abortions not always available .
62344	Many victims are also having to come to terms with the trauma while looking after children and the elderly in overcrowded refugee camps.Whether rape has been singled out by military commanders as a weapon of war remains open to question , but victims ' testimony suggests the abuse is part of a wider pattern of warfare and ‘ ethnic cleansing ’ .
62345	Ms Hampson believes the abuse is more than an incidental or sexual act .
62346	It is clearly being used as an instrument to achieve a military purpose .
62347	‘ People are n't raping for rape 's sake .
62348	In some instances where villages are being ‘ cleansed ’ , rape is being used to terrorize and humiliate communities . ’
62349	There is evidence that rape , regarded as good for morale , increased after a military setback and that peer group pressure is strong .
62350	‘ Clearly the authorities know the rape camps are there and what they 're being used for .
62351	A lot of people who have n't previously raped must be going around raping . ’
62352	She admits in the final analysis she finds it difficult to make sense of the ‘ gratuitous savagery ’ .
62353	‘ I 'm left with extremely uncomfortable questions about what makes men tick and I do n't see any reason to believe that men in the former Yugoslavia are different from men elsewhere .
62354	‘ That does n't mean I think all men are rapists but … it means a significant proportion of the men around us in that situation of social breakdown would rape and I ca n't even begin to digest that notion . ’
62355	What she is clear about is that rape is a war crime and ought to be prosecuted .
62356	Rape clearly contravenes international law and she cites the 1907 Hague Conventions , the '49 Geneva Conventions and the '77 Protocols to make her point .
62357	It is not new laws that are required but enforcement of existing ones , she says.The International League is now calling for effective individual accountability for serious violations of the law and the creation of a war crimes tribunal .
62358	‘ Reconciliation requires a coming to terms with the past not its burial or denial , ’ it states .

62463	COULD DO BETTER
62464	LAST YEAR the Conservatives were telling us how clever they were to have been able to cut taxation and to increase public spending at one and the same time .
62465	Yesterday , Norman Lamont presented the bill for that cleverness , with a demand for more than £10,000 million a year in extra taxation from 1995/6 onwards .
62466	It is a large sum , and yet it may not be enough .
62467	It will certainly not allow the Chancellor to meet the target that he set himself last year of a balanced budget in the medium term .
62468	In the coming year , he expects to borrow £50,000 million , and he hopes to reduce that to around £20,000 million over four years .
62469	Apart from raising taxes , the Government hopes to be able to curb its spending programmes , and a review is already under way .
62470	No results , however , are expected for some time ; and in any case , Whitehall expenditure reviews are notorious for failing to deliver anything of significance .
62471	There is , therefore , a strong reliance upon economic growth to yield higher tax revenues and a lower social security budget .
62472	Mr Lamont forecasts that the economy will be growing at the rate of three per cent per year in 12 months ' time ; he would have carried more conviction , if he had not made the same ‘ jam tomorrow ’ forecast a year ago .
62473	Many of his proposals are intended to help British industry and in themselves these are welcome .
62474	In Suffolk , we are particularly glad that Customs and Excise has at last been persuaded that horse-racing is an industry not a hobby , and that it will adjust its VAT demands accordingly .
62475	Yet in racing , in export credit guarantees and elsewhere , the Chancellor was reacting late in the day to complaints that had been clearly audible for some considerable time .
62476	He should have been doing this a year or two ago , in the hope that extra jobs would have been created before now .
62477	As it is , it will be much harder to persuade employers to expand , now that they can see the storm clouds of swingeing tax increases ahead of them .
62478	Even in the short term , they can see a dismally weak market in the rest of Europe , and no obvious sign that the British public has the confidence to start spending again .
62479	This last is the main disappointment of the budget .
62480	The bad news for the average householder is written large , while the good news is in small print .
62481	The net result may be neutral as Mr Lamont claims , but it does not look that way to the casual viewer who may as a result end the day in a gloomier mood than he began .
62482	For example , Mr Lamont referred to the unemployed , expressing his deepest sympathy for them , and promising to do something to help .
62483	Having raised expectations , he went on to limit that help to just 100,000 people ; and of those 100,000 , 60,000 were offered no more than the chance to work on a community scheme for next to nothing .
62484	There are times when Chancellors are right to fuss with mini-measures , and there are times when they need to make an instant impact .
62485	Mr Lamont should have concentrated on doing his own job well , instead of making a series of announcements on behalf of the Departments of Transport , Health , Social Security and Industry , all of which have articulate Ministers of their own .
62486	His impact at home was weak , and it has to be hoped that his impact abroad was rather better .
62487	On the figures he gave , it is an open question whether foreign bankers will want to finance the continuing borrowing requirement at existing interest rates and at the existing parity of sterling .
62488	The financial situation of the country is such that no budgetary proposals could have been guaranteed to rescue it .
62489	While appreciating the extraordinary difficulties facing Mr Lamont , it must still be said that he could have handled them better than this .

64846	Then still holding it , she went to the toilet and , just as she was , she sat down on the edge of the seat and , bending forward , she went through the motion of wringing out the cloth once again .
64847	Presently , her teeth pressed tightly down on her lip , she turned her head and leant her brow against the stone wall .
64848	As Mrs Robson said , people had taken to war like they did to life : they had accepted it and were living with it and with all the things it did to them ; but why did them up top have to go and stop the flower trains coming from Cornwall ?
64849	There was nothing like a flower to cheer you up on a dark day .
64850	It was to save transport , the government said .
64851	That was just a gimmick , like when they stopped the holiday trains .
64852	Yet , when there was any racing on , transport could be found for that , could n't it ?
64853	And who went to the racecourses ? she wanted to know .
64854	Aha !
64855	And income tax eight and sixpence in the pound .
64856	And then the daft things they were up to : ordering booksellers to destroy their maps , and ordinary folk an' all , as if the Germans when they landed would n't know where they were going .
64857	Men , really !
64858	It was women they wanted up there to spread some common sense among them .

64860	Giving them a taste of the Battle of Britain , hitting their churches and cathedrals , just as the Jerries had done here .
64861	Dealing with wireless every day , Joe rarely listened when off duty to accounts of small successes put over in the announcer 's authoritative tone and the defeats intoned as if reporting a death : which it was , though not a single death , such as when Tobruk had fallen in June and Mussolini went into Libya .
64862	Names like Rommel , Auchinleck , El Alamein sounded as common to the ear as Smith , Jones and Robinson ; yet Joe had the feeling that he was being forced to stand on the sidelines and watch a game in which he had not the slightest interest .
64863	Yet he knew , at least in this he was n't alone : the feeling , if it did n't pervade the camp , certainly pervaded his section .
64864	This part of the country did n't seem to be in the war .
64865	The munitions factory in Hereford seemed to be the only concession to it .
64866	The people went about their daily work in an ordinary fashion : there were no air raids , no scurrying to shelters , no fire engines tearing through the countryside .
64867	Naturally , most of the staff in the camp considered themselves lucky to have been posted here and dreaded the idea of a move , which created the feeling of being on the sidelines .
64868	For himself , he would n't have minded a posting ; in fact , he would have welcomed it , because there was another complication entering his life : vague , but nevertheless there .

64871	And then it was dark and their entry into camp had gone unnoticed .

69605	But the world 's most devastating fast bowler played in two other matches when umpires reported Surrey to Lord 's under Law 42.5 which exclusively governs unfair play .
69606	Struggle
69607	He destroyed Yorkshire 's second innings at Guildford with six for 40 last year but struggled to break through against Gloucestershire in a drawn match at Cheltenham in 1990 .
69608	Last night Surrey skipper Alec Stewart , the England vice-captain , who appeared before the tribunal , said : ‘ I have absolutely no comment to make , on the instructions of Surrey . ’
69609	Lord 's secretly warned Surrey in writing at the end of the 1991 season .

72501	FERGIE IS A JOKE
72502	THE TRUTH about United and ME
72503	‘ He made me an outcast at Old Trafford ’
72504	PAUL McGRATH
72505	TED MACAULEY
72506	WHEN Alex Ferguson joined Manchester United as the new boss he wanted me out of Old Trafford so badly he tried to make me redundant .
72507	And it nearly worked .
72508	I was so downhearted and at such a low ebb because he made it painfully clear I did n't figure in that great club 's future , however much I loved the place .
72509	He was so tough , so unbending and uncompromising , and I do n't think he 's changed .
72510	He made doubly sure I realised I was an outcast in a heavy-handed way — and he could n't get rid of me fast enough .
72511	I felt then as if my whole life had collapsed .
72512	And he 's made it even worse just now by raking ashes that are three years old .
72513	Why ?
72514	What 's he trying to do to me ?
72515	He got rid of me and that should have been the end of it .
72516	But in a book he 's written he 's had a real big pop at me in a sour way .
72517	And it 's just not on .
72518	Concerned
72519	Fergie has been saying that he was so concerned about my life-style away from football he called in Sir Matt Busby , the club doctor and even a parish priest to try to get me sorted out .
72520	What absolute rubbish — he 's gone right over the top with a load of old cobblers there and I do n't know why .
72521	He 's making it sound as if I was stretched on a couch , locked in a room with a ‘ Do not disturb ’ sign on the door while Sir Matt , the doc and a priest I have certainly never met , got to work straightening me out , socially , medically and religiously .
72522	What a joke .
72523	I 'm not the least bit religious so the idea of a priest having any influence on my life is ridiculous .
72524	I ca n't ever recall even meeting a priest when I was at United , though there always seemed to be plenty of them around .
72525	As for saying Sir Matt was called in to counsel me — well , that 's sheer nonsense .
72526	I only ever spoke to him socially and not very often at that .
72527	The great man just was not in my orbit .
72528	So I feel I have every right to defend myself .
72529	And I 'm sure I would have left the club readily and earlier if I 'd known what he was going to say later .
72530	Collision
72531	He 's making me out to be some sort of thick , brainless loony on a self-destruct road to ruin .
72532	And that me and my old pal Norman Whiteside were on a collision course with him , that we needed to be split up .
72533	And with him adding that he had to get rid of a notion in football that Manchester United was a drinking club .
72534	I do n't know Norman 's reaction to Fergie 's story but I can say they have left me with a bitter feeling .
72535	All my dreams of playing for United to the end of my career — and I was on a seven- year contract — vanished when Ferguson called me into his office and offered me a cash pay-off to clear out and go and do something else with my life .
72536	Rise
72537	I was staggered .
72538	I 'd only once asked for a transfer and not because of any discontent or fall- out with the club .
72539	I wanted a pay rise because I found out I was way behind most of the first-team lads and barely on much more than the apprentices ' wages .
72540	It was amazing how little the money was at such a famous and unbelievably well-supported club .
72541	And when I found out after a bit of dressing-room chat what the other lads were on I had to make a point .
72542	I figured that if I asked for a transfer I 'd either get a rise or would be able to work out a better deal for myself if I went elsewhere .
72543	In truth , I did n't want to quit United if it could be avoided , I was totally hooked on the place .
72544	But things just went from bad to worse .
72545	Ferguson refers to a pub and club session that Norman Whiteside and I had , and that come Friday I could n't train — even though , he said , I was supposed to be playing against Queens Park Rangers .
72546	He says that after he does n't know how many reprimands , I refused to play on Saturday protesting that I was n't fit enough .
72547	Fergie 's memory has failed him there .
72548	He had already told me on the Friday at the training session , and in front of about 20 of the lads , that I was n't in the team .
72549	And that was that .
72550	But he changed his mind and only wanted me to play against QPR when Lee Sharpe went down poorly .
72551	But I really was n't fit .
72552	Agony
72553	One of the bigger problems was that Fergie believed I was taking the mickey out of him by either cheating or going soft and feigning injury .
72554	And I was missing too many games complaining of a bad knee when there was nothing really wrong with it .
72555	I honestly believe that 's what he thought .
72556	But I knew differently .
72557	I finished some games in absolute agony , but said nothing and kept it to myself .
72558	But it worried me .
72559	I trained as often and as hard as I could , as hard as anybody on the staff — and that includes my old pal Bryan Robson , who was notorious for his unflagging effort — but the pain was excruciating .
72560	Crazy
72561	No professional likes to miss the chance to play — that 's why , really , we 're in the game — and I was no exception .
72562	But Fergie wanted more from me than I was able to give .
72563	What with that and a few crazy reports to him about my off-duty life-style flying about he decided United and me were going nowhere together .
72564	He wanted me out .

72658	HUMAN RESOURCES AND SYSTEM DESIGN
72659	Concepts
72660	The human contribution
72661	The human role as a system controller
72662	The business of designing machines , processes and systems can be pursued more or less independently of the properties of people .
72663	Nevertheless people are always involved , the designer himself is a human being and his product will shape the behaviour of many workers and other users .
72664	More fundamentally , the design activity will be meaningless unless it is directed towards serving some human need .
72665	In spite of all this , the design process itself is often thought about and executed without any formal considerations about people .
72666	Inevitably the engineer , architect or other designer devotes most of his attention and expertise to devising mechanisms , buildings and so on which support some human activity more effectively than those currently available .
72667	The new machine or system must not be very different from the old one for a variety of reasons .
72668	The old one did its job , not perfectly but well enough to justify its existence .
72669	The new one is usually designed on the basis of copying the old one but removing as many as possible of the faults .
72670	There are other reasons such as commonality of components and , of course , shortage of imagination which lead to most design and development being a progressive iterative process .
72671	This happens to suit the human operators because most of their skills will transfer along the line of development of the machines and systems .
72672	From the engineering point of view the hardware technology is central and the operators tag along supporting the activity of machines which are basically doing the work .
72673	In nineteenth century transport for example , the coach and horses was not a serious competitor for the steam-engined train , nor was the man with a spade as productive as the operator with a steam shovel .
72674	This was the earliest technology in which power was derived from sources other than animal muscles and the output was so obviously superior that men did not mind putting up with the inconvenience of machines which were uncomfortable or awkward to use .
72675	They even took pride in developing new skills which enabled them to use difficult machines which inexperienced people could not use .
72676	This attitude was reinforced by the second wave of technology which provided instrumentation , ways of sensing and recording data which gave more accurate and reliable data than that which can be detected directly by the human senses .
72677	At this stage the typical machine operator manipulated machine controls on the basis of data presented on instruments .
72678	The machine controls caused power to be applied and consequences to occur which resulted in changed readings on the instruments .
72679	The man was in the control loop ( Hick and Bates , 1950 ) .
72680	More recently , in the third wave of technology the man has been removed from the responsibility for continuous control ( this is best done by computers working to a moderately flexible range of programs ) but he remains as the monitor of the system performance and a selector of the appropriate program determined by the changing short-term objectives .
72681	He may keep the responsibility for setting-up and shutting-down the system or this also may be partially delegated to computers .
72682	This is the ‘ Supervisory Control ’ role ( Sheridan and Johannsen , 1976 ) .
72683	Information flow in these three phases of development of system control is shown in fig. 1.1
72684	Supervisory control is by no means universal , in fact it remains restricted to high technology systems such as aircraft , computer controlled machine tools , chemical plants and power stations .
72685	( Edwards and Lees , 1974 ) .
72686	There are still many systems where the man is in the control loop , for example in vehicle driving and in most manufacturing production processes .
72687	There are many tasks where the operator is assisted only by hand-tools and simple powered machines , for example in craft-work and surgery .
72688	There are also plenty of tasks , although these are now perhaps more common in leisure than in paid work , where the man supplies the muscle power , for example the manual labourer and the active sportsman .
72689	In general , the working man may function at any level from the senior partner in high technology operations to the provider of muscle power in physically demanding jobs .
72690	In all cases the ergonomic requirement is that the task as designed should make use of his abilities and be adaptive to his limitations .
72691	The human contribution in high technology systems
72692	All working systems , including those incorporating advanced technology of processes and process control , depend on skilled operators .
72693	There are social , economic and technical reasons for this .
72694	Socially the public will not easily accept automatic systems .
72695	When seeking reassurance that a system is safe they study the people who are responsible for it .
72696	They have no means of assessing the reliability of automatic control systems but they can make some assessment of a skilled individual and without knowing very much about his working procedures they will trust his actions if he seems calm , competent and mature .
72697	The most direct example is the nervous airline passenger who is comforted by the belief that the middle-aged pilot he saw sitting on the flight deck is flying the aeroplane .
72698	Less directly but equally importantly , people living in the vicinity of a large plant would not take kindly to the idea that it was not under the control of human beings who are on the spot and are assumed to know exactly what is happening .
72699	Economically it remains true that it is inordinately expensive to construct a system which must continue to be reliable without direct human intervention , for example under the sea or in space .
72700	Equally it is expensive to ensure that equipment will continue to function under rough handling conditions , for example the necessary ‘ ruggedising ’ of military equipment .
72701	A system can be designed much more economically if it can be assumed that skilled personnel are available to control and take care of it .
72702	Technically the state of the art seems to be that systems are most efficient , reliable and safe when control is largely automatic but the human operator remains in a monitoring and supervisory role .
72703	That is , continuous dynamic dealing with minor perturbations is automatic and so also is the application of basic rules about safety ; for example , the system or some part of it might be programmed to go through a step-change function such as a shut-down if certain parameters exceed prescribed limits .
72704	The role of the human operator in these circumstances is largely specified by operating instructions which are mandatory .
72705	Given this and this — he must do that .
72706	Characteristically his intervention in this way is a response to some other human requirement ; for example , a maintenance man may wish to have a particular sub-system shut down for his attention or a user of the system product may wish to receive a different input to meet his purposes .
72707	Many of these interactions could be made automatic were it not for the basic need for a human presence for the social/ economic reasons mentioned above and because the human operator has to act as the ultimate back-stop when things go badly wrong .
72708	Things go badly wrong when there has been some extreme untoward event such as a fire , an earthquake or a bomb , alternatively an unanticipated combination of faults may occur within the plant itself .
72709	In either case the human intervention must be a very high level one based on complex diagnosis and innovative design-type thinking about how best to cope so as to avoid a catastrophe .
72710	A catastrophe can happen when the system energy is no longer channelled as intended by the designers or because there is a release of toxic substances or both .
72711	The demands on the operator stem from two kinds of task which are not compatible because they require very different levels of skill .
72712	On the one hand he must cope with routines where the demand is for precise obedience to established instructions and on the other hand he might suddenly be faced with a need to respond in a creative manner totally outside any instructions .
72713	Superficially the solution would seem to be to have two kinds of operators , those who carry out the routines and others who are on call should unforeseen emergencies arise .
72714	There are two snags about this approach .
72715	Firstly there may not be time or it may not be physically possible to suddenly introduce a high level operator , for example we can not put a different pilot on the flight deck when an aircraft gets into trouble .
72716	Secondly , the high level operator will not maintain his skill and familiarity with the system unless he operates regularly within it .
72717	His ability to intervene effectively must be a function of his ‘ hands on ’ experience supported of course by his conceptual knowledge of how the system functions .
72718	This last proposition is based on experience of systems where the intervention requires complex manipulative activity , for example a surgeon dealing with an emergency during an operation or an aircraft pilot taking over manually .
72719	It is not so obviously true where the intervention takes the form essentially of a decision to initiate a single direct action such as closing a particular valve or starting up a stand-by pump .
72720	In these circumstances it is not clear whether or not the effectiveness of the intervention is quite so dependent on operating experience .
72721	Taking for example the nuclear power plant control room , the question is whether the desk operators should be expected to cope with all emergencies which appear within the total information presentation or whether , for complex and dangerous situations , a more senior person such as the shift-charge engineer should be called upon to make the decisions .
72722	This policy issue must be cleared before the basic personnel decisions about selection and training of staff at the various levels can be made and before the information presentations can be designed .
72723	The human contribution in low technology systems
72724	The extreme case of man as a source of muscle power is dealt with in the previous book in this series — The Body at Work .
72725	Such working situations are now relatively rare in developed countries and the man is more usually employed in tasks where there is a considerable control element requiring extensive information processing .
72726	Such tasks range from the use of simple hand tools to tracking using complex powered machinery .
72727	Human beings are needed for those tasks for a variety of reasons from their highly dexterous manipulative potential through to their ability to accept informal instructions .
72728	These reasons are given in detail in the discussion of man-machine function allocation ( p. 35 ) .
72729	The demands on the human operator are difficult to quantify or even to describe because the process is essentially an interactive one .
72730	The skilled operator is working in harmony with his tools and machines .
72731	The concept of ‘ demand ’ is often not appropriate because it implies confrontation , the process is more aptly considered as one of cooperation and persuasion .
72732	The human operator is pursuing an objective , usually to make something or to go somewhere , and he achieves this with the assistance of the hardware at his disposal .
72733	This hardware , if it is well-designed , aids him in his progress toward his objective .
72734	There may be demands in the sense that there are always obstacles to be overcome but these stem from the nature and the variability of the situation he is in ; that is , the materials he has to deal with or the environment he has to move through .
72735	The skilled operator will aim for efficient performance .
72736	Efficiency incorporates not only quantity and quality of achievement but also preservation of his own safety and health and that of others who might be involved as working partners , passengers or the general public in the neighbourhood .
72737	Of course , if his tasks are badly designed they may well make unnecessary demands .
72738	These begin with bodily aspects of the operating posture required and the forces which must be exerted to operate controls .
72739	for a work-space which is used full-time very slight departures from the optimum may lead to problems in the long term , for example in strained ligaments , tendons and muscles .
72740	Posture is constrained not only by the physical dimensions of the work-space but also by the need to be in a position to see certain events and to feel others through control operations or machine movement .
72741	Other demands will arise if the information presented is inadequate in content , e.g. poor lighting may make it difficult to detect some relevant cues , or in structure , e.g. because of poor coding and presentation of information on dials , charts or screens .
72742	Correspondingly there may be output demands created by control operations which result in things happening too quickly or unexpectedly .
72743	The level of demand is to do not only with the tasks as they are done but also with the duration for which they must continue to be done .
72744	This applies particularly to routines and repetitive work where the main operator limitation is not capacity or skill but stamina .
72745	In principle , repetitive work is best left to automatic machines but the flexibility of human performance is often needed because slight changes are required either to modify the product or to cope with different materials .
72746	Batch production work is often of this kind and in general it is by no means as unchanging or boring as it might appear to the casual visitor to the factory .
72747	In all the clothing trades for example there are continuous changes in sizes , materials , colours , styles and so on which provide the appropriate variety for the customers and incidentally for the producer .
72748	Work design must take account of the needs of the consumer as well as those of the worker .
72749	Ergonomics and other aspects of technology
72750	The technical specialist who represents the people point of view implicit in the approach just described is the ergonomist .
72751	In the previous book in this series the relationship of ergonomics to other aspects or kinds of technology was discussed in detail .
72752	The unique feature of ergonomics is its emphasis on the characteristics of human operators and their relevance to the design of work .
72753	The role of the ergonomist is essentially an advisory one .
72754	In the case of high technology design he must provide a service for the engineers and scientists who carry the technical design responsibility .
72755	This service may simply be as a source of information or the ergonomist can have more power in that the design decisions involving people have to be approved by him .
72756	This is usually restricted to obvious cases of man-machine interaction such as the design of displays , controls and work-spaces .
72757	In the case of low technology design again he has an advisory role but with a general emphasis on awareness of the kinds and ranges of people who are being catered for .
72758	for systems which are already operating the ergonomist is likely to cooperate with occupational health and safety specialists and to play a part in the consideration of accidents and occupational diseases which might arise from unnecessarily stressful work situations ( p. 294 ) .
72759	It will be appreciated that for most kinds of work and most working organisations it is not feasible to employ specialist ergonomists .
72760	In such cases those who have responsibilities for work design need to have some awareness of the principles of ergonomics .
72761	The philosophy of work
72762	Ergonomics is sometimes confused by questions such as , who is the ergonomist servicing — the employer or the worker ? or , to whom is he ultimately responsible — the state , the employer , the producer or the consumer ? fortunately it is possible to dispose of these issues without taking up any particular political position .
72763	Ergonomics seems to flourish equally well in capitalist and socialist/communist systems , ergonomics activity can be sponsored with equal validity by employers organisations and by workers organisations .
72764	This is because , as already mentioned , ergonomics is about efficient use of people .
72765	There can be no good reason to object to this when it is recognised that efficiency incorporates personal factors such as safety , health and quality of working life as well as system factors such as productivity and quality of work .
72766	There is rarely any conflict in that good ergonomics is in line with the objectives of the worker , the employer and the consumer or customer .
72767	There are sometimes larger issues of whether what the system does is acceptable or not , for example in weapon systems , and the ergonomist as a citizen will have his own opinion on these matters but the ergonomist as an ergonomist is confined to questions of efficiency .
72768	There is an underlying necessary ethic which is best summarised as the social contract .
72769	An individual is a member of a community from which he obtains considerable benefits , in return he develops special skills which he applies for the benefit of the community .
72770	The application of special skills in this way is called work .
72771	The ergonomist has to believe that work is a good thing and that to conduct it efficiently is always better than to conduct it inefficiently .
72772	The design of systems .
72773	The system concept
72774	A system is a set of interacting parts which has meaning as a whole because it is possible to define a purpose — a reason why the parts are seen to be related to the whole and a justification for the concept of the whole ( Singleton , 1974 ) .
72775	Thus , systems theory is essentially teleological — explanations are in terms of consequences rather than causes .
72776	The parts may themselves be complex and may be conceived as having their own subsidiary purposes in confluence with the system purpose , these are sub-systems .
72777	The system in turn is part of a larger complex — the parent system .
72778	Thus , systems are hierarchical and at each level the unit is considered as a functional rather than a physical entity .
72779	The systems approach is often a convenient way of looking at human behaviour either internally — this is man as a set of sub-systems or in terms of the man interacting with mechanisms — man-machine systems , or man interacting with organisations — socio-technical systems .
72780	The enormous flexibility of the systems approach has its penalties in potential confusion due to the highly variable relationship between functional and physical entities .
72781	Sometimes this relationship is fairly close ; for example , in the nervous system , the endocrine system , the digestive system and so on , and sometimes it remains almost entirely unknown , for example , the perceptual system and the decision-making system .
72782	These last two are obviously each related to the nervous system and to the brain but not necessarily to a particular part of the brain and taken together they overlap in such obscure ways that they are best regarded as sub-systems in different domains , one can talk in terms of one or the other but not both simultaneously .
72783	Systems theory is a useful way of identifying complex entities , particularly those which have a functional unity and of talking about relationships but it remains at some level of abstraction from reality .
72784	for example , to solve any design problem there has at some stage to be a switch from systems thinking to thinking in terms of physical entities because these are the things that can be created , precisely located and manipulated in the real world .
72785	Nevertheless , there are enormous dividends in being able to discuss functions independently of physical mechanisms and to explain relationships without being restricted to established and readily observable physical connections or separations .
72786	For example , thinking of a power station as a way of translating energy from fuel into electric power enables the designer to consider various options .
72787	Should the fuel be of a fossil type such as coal or oil or should it be the radioactive elements in a nuclear reaction ?
72788	When the heat has appeared how best should it be taken away — by pressurised water , by steam , by liquid sodium or by carbon dioxide ?
72789	This heat has to be turned into mechanical energy , currently always by a steam turbine and the mechanical energy in a rotating shaft is then translated by a generator into electricity .
72790	The losses in this transfer of energy from one form to another can be calculated and the flow through the various sub-systems can be traced .
72791	The initial consideration of the power station as an energy processing system aids design discussions about the relative advantages and limitations of various mechanisms and their performance in practice .
72792	As the system operates it has to be controlled .
72793	The control of the flow of energy is partly through automatic servomechanisms and partly through human operations .
72794	The design problem of which does what is also best thought about initially in system terms .
72795	Distinct from the flow of energy the designer is , at this stage , thinking about the flow of information .
72796	Energy and information are processed by systems and sub-systems .
72797	In these terms , the human operator is a particular sub-system .
72798	Mechanical devices and human operators are not comparable physically beyond the mundane level of size but they are comparable as different sub-systems whose performance can be described and assessed in terms of the common metrics of energy and information .
72799	Hence the importance of systems concepts to ergonomics .
72800	If the human operator is to control functions within other sub-systems he must receive information about the system state through a man-machine interface .
72801	This interface takes its physical form in the control room .
72802	The control room is part of the communications channel between the human operators and the mechanisms and its design , as a man-machine interface , is one of the key ergonomics problems in power stations .
72803	Office organisations also can be considered as systems .
72804	There will be certain physical mechanisms such as telephones , typewriters and computers but the flow of energy is trivial and the interest centres entirely on the flow of information .
72805	Consider , for example , a travel office .
72806	There is a vast amount of information available either in printed form or through computer networks .
72807	The objectives are to help members of the public to find their way through this information store and to transmit their orders for particular journeys or holidays to the providers of those services .
72808	The manager or designer of the office has to consider the various sub-systems he requires ; one for dealing with enquiries , one for handling money , one for receiving new information , one for confirming orders and so on .
72809	The interface between the public and the information store is a counter manned by people .
72810	The counter assistants are parts of the interface .
72811	Information is exchanged verbally and through written documentation .
72812	In this kind of office the variety of requests for service is probably such that it would be necessary to provide a set of categories of the main kinds of activities or functions .
72813	It would then be possible to devise the appropriate system for presenting the required information .
72814	It is a very different situation from a power station control room but nevertheless the same principles of starting by the analysis of the required information apply .
72815	The power station , the travel office and all other man-made systems have in common the employment of people so that sub-systems are required which are associated with personnel functions .
72816	It is necessary to attract and select staff , to train them , to provide them with various services and with potentiality for advancement as their skills increase with experience .
72817	The design of tasks is the common ground between personnel activities such as training and engineering activities such as workplace design .
72818	Consideration of people in system terms provides the possibility of generalisations which apply across great varieties of physical and intellectual activities .
72819	The resulting knowledge is the content of ergonomics .
72820	Fig. 1.2 shows the outline of the systems design process in a way which emphasises the parallel roles of the engineer and the ergonomist concerned respectively with the design of the hardware and the personnel sub-systems and their common design problems of allocation of function and interface design .
72821	The design of high technology systems
72822	The insertion of an adequate Human factors approach into a comprehensive design process is not easy , partly for the reason mentioned already that it has not habitually been regarded as necessary and partly because it cuts across all other decision-making .
72823	The Human Factors specialist can rightly be accused of wanting to have a finger in every pie because , as he sees it , behavioural considerations do affect every design decision .
72824	If ergonomics was confined to , say , the determination of the physical dimensions of the work-space then it would be more readily accepted by traditional designers , but the broad claim that ergonomics has a contribution to make to every design and operational aspect which involves the behaviour of people is a proposition which it is much more difficult for an engineer or other designer to digest ( fig. 1.3 ) .
72825	The questions begin with the formulation of the design objectives .
72826	What are the human requirements which the new product or process is intended to meet and how far are they not met by those already available ?
72827	This would normally be regarded as a matter for economists and market-research specialists but behind the formidable array of evidence which they will generate are more fundamental questions of consumer preference , customer requirements and so on which are matters of human needs and prejudices .
72828	Competent market research should cover these aspects but the ergonomist can remind the policy-makers that such evidence is needed and that it should be acquired by studies of people which are properly conducted .
72829	If the evidence is favourable then the next step will be to set up a design team containing members covering the relevant range of expertise .
72830	How much design effort is needed in the different areas will not be clear at this stage but unless the system is very simple there are bound to be problems of overlap and of how far to arrange sub-teams by discipline , by function or by problem ( Singleton , 1987 ) .
72831	The usual compromise is that there should be problem-orientated sub-teams but with additional support available from discipline-orientated specialists .
72832	If these latter are part of the design team then already we have a matrix organisation but they may well be provided on a service basis from some other part of the parent organisation .
72833	Difficulties will emerge later unless considerable thought is given at this stage to the appropriate range of skills required and the consequent problems of interdisciplinary communication .
72834	The art of good sub-system design is to identify problem areas where work can proceed relatively independently of other areas so that the need for intercommunication is minimised .
72835	There will always be the need for some intercommunication and the appropriate interfaces should be provided .
72836	Nevertheless , if committees , working parties and task forces begin to proliferate within the design team , this is a sure indication that the basic allocation into sub-systems was not optimal .
72837	Communication should be mainly through the central command and control centre which may be no larger than the project leader and his small personal staff as may be a group of heads of sub-systems or both .
72838	These issues are discussed from another viewpoint in Chapter 3 ( p. 140 ) .
72839	The analysis of required skills ought in principle to have an ergonomics input but in practice it is usually done on the basis of experience of similar system designs in the past .
72840	There can be a useful discussion between the project leader and an ergonomist where the former is invited to clarify how he sees these intercommunication problems being dealt with including such criteria as what is reported to him , what to the meeting of sub-heads and what occurs directly between sub-teams .
72841	Organisational rules of this kind can be very helpful in steering between the excessive information flow , e.g. memoranda copied to many people , and excessive unilateralism , e.g. refusing further discussion after the issue of formal documents .
72842	Having allocated the human and other resources needed for the overall design task it is then appropriate to develop a more detailed model of the system functions in terms of materials , energy and information flow .
72843	Most designers have an intuitive but unformalised picture in these terms but it is of great utility to produce these pictures in flow diagram form so that any differences of view are revealed and can be reconciled by discussions during the process of agreeing the diagrams .
72844	When there are a number of individuals or groups from different disciplines and pursuing different objectives within some overall specification it is obviously crucial that all their activities should be in line with the common goal .
72845	To this end , it is necessary that there should be intercommunication not only about particular design decisions but also about underlying philosophies so that the ultimate system is conceptually as well as operationally coherent .
72846	Sometimes this is achieved by a dominant project leader who imposes his own philosophy and then makes many of the decisions leaving only detailing for team members .
72847	In recent times it is more usual to have some element of discussion , partly because of the increasingly democratic style of organisations and partly because the variety of relevant technology requires a correspondingly wide range of expertise .
72848	In any case there is a need for widespread intercommunication which may be mainly informal but requires some formality to ensure that clashes of attitude do not delay or distort decisions and to make sure also that finalised decisions are unambiguously recorded .
72849	If this intercommunication is not properly arranged there will be the familiar symptoms of frustrating reiteration , decisions being misunderstood or being constantly revised , political manoeuvring and even concealment of progress within one or more of the teams .
72850	As the overall design progresses the information storage system becomes increasingly important .
72851	If insufficient attention has been devoted to the design of this and also the related access procedures the symptoms are a plethora of documentation which no individual entirely understands , the temptation to do it again rather than waste time finding out how something has already been done and too much reliance on the human memory .
72852	The behavioural symptoms of inadequate organisation of design teams are summarised in Table 1.1 .
72853	As the system is made more definitive by the selection of particular physical mechanisms there should be parallel activity in the consideration of how these things are to be used and maintained by the human operator .
72854	Note that the philosophy here is that all the hardware is ultimately an extension of and a support for human functions .
72855	This is the concept of all systems as human beings with various kinds of engineering aids ( Singleton , 1967a ) .
72856	functions are delegated from the human operator rather than allocated to him .
72857	This extreme ergonomics stance serves as an antidote to the equally extreme engineering approach in which systems are regarded basically as hardware which for reasons of economic or technological limitations have to depend occasionally on some human performance .
72858	Even if there is no dependence on human performance in the on-line operational mode it is bound to exist in the maintenance mode .
72859	In either case , there will eventually be a need for the consideration of the kinds of human operators required and how they are to be selected and trained .
72860	Traditionally these personnel functions were regarded as quite separate from design functions and indeed they were often left until the hardware design and commissioning was virtually complete .
72861	The essence of the systems approach is that personnel decisions should proceed in parallel with engineering decisions , partly to economise on development time and partly to provide scope for trade-offs .
72862	One factor which has given renewed emphasis to this need for cooperation is the increased use of simulation ( p. 128 ) .
72863	Simulators were originally considered to be training devices but their use is now extending into other fields such as personnel assessment and as aids to the design of the information interfaces .
72864	It used to be considered that simulator specifications could only be proposed when the on-line system design had been completed but there are considerable advantages in developing the simulator before the on-line system so that it becomes a dynamic mock-up of the real situation .
72865	Detailed evaluations can be carried out on this mock-up before the real system is constructed .
72866	All systems are constructed from bought-in components which may themselves be complex enough to warrant a human factors evaluation .
72867	for example , a motor/pump system may well have its own controls , there will be standard maintenance procedures and there will be an operation/maintenance manual .
72868	All of these can be assessed from the point of view of clarity of presentation and ease of use .
72869	The system being constructed will require its own operating instructions , maintenance procedures and perhaps safety regulations .
72870	The design and preparation of this documentation has a Human factors component .
72871	It is a matter of storage , access to and presentation of information .
72872	Even at the design stage it is useful also to recognise that all this material will require procedures for updating in the light of experience
72873	Finally it must be accepted that technological and operational expertise is never complete .
72874	The operators of plant are bound to discover by experience aspects of the design which could be improved .
72875	There should be a mechanism for feeding this information back to the designers so that the succeeding system designs will avoid these problems .
72876	In particular , human performance within systems is impossible to predict with any precision and details of this performance as it occurs in practice or on simulators is the only basis for prediction on matters such as safety and system reliability either for the current system or for future systems .
72877	Potential human factors inputs to the large scale design process are summarised in fig. 1.4 .
72878	In all behavioural matters and indeed in many technical matters also it is important to avoid the impression that when operations in practice contain undesirable features not predicted by designers then the designers have made mistakes .
72879	This may be true in a formal sense but allocation of blame is not usually a productive exercise particularly from a learning view-point .
72880	It is valuable to inculcate the attitude that everyone learns , that is , design and operating staff all improve on the basis of experience with feed-back .
72881	The exposure and remedy of facets of systems performance which are not entirely as predicted is in everyone 's interest .
72882	One example of this is matters to do with safety : it is always useful to collect ‘ critical incident ’ data as well as accident data as one part of the feed-back about system performances .
72883	The setting up of routines for this communication is another aspect of ergonomics .
72884	In summary , although the basic contribution of the ergonomist is to the design of information interfaces these interfaces extend far beyond the man-machine interface found in the control room .
72885	They include the documentation of the design itself , communication within the design team , between designers and suppliers and between designers and operators ( fig. 1.5 ) .
72886	The operations staff include those who set it up , those who control it during operations , those who maintain it , and eventually those who have to dismantle it .
72887	To give one example of the size of the documentation problem it is not unusual for a large process plant to have two or three hundred volumes of instructions .
72888	These include the operating instructions , the maintenance instructions , the suppliers ' instruction manuals , the safety regulations and instructions for particular emergencies .
72889	The design of smaller systems
72890	The design of a machine or device which is assigned as an aid for one person will not usually encounter the problems associated with elaborate design teams just described , but nevertheless some human factors sensitivity will help to provide a better product .
72891	This can be important not only from the point of view of efficiency in design and use but also in improving the sales appeal .
72892	It is increasingly common for advertisements to emphasise features such as ‘ man-machine harmony ’ or ‘ user friendliness ’ .
72893	The implication is that ergonomics has been properly applied .
72894	There is a need for formal ergonomics in any design where the designer himself is not an experienced user .
72895	Some hand tools are beautifully designed to match the user , e.g. the two-handed scythe .
72896	In these cases it is clear that the design developed by constant trial in practice .
72897	There are others , however , where even after centuries of use this matching is not obviously satisfactory , for example violin playing would seem to be posturally a disaster , but there may be some subtle aids to very precise control of the sound generated in having the source of sound very close to the ear and perhaps some vibration transmission by the direct contact of this instrument and the jawbone .
72898	Ergonomics is concerned with the transmission of information .
72899	for modest design enterprises information exchange is needed between the designer and the potential user , between the designer and the producer and between the designer/producer and the customer/actual user ( Fig. 1.6 ) .
72900	The designer needs to know about the tasks which his new device is intended to aid and also about the kind of person who will use it .
72901	Clearly , designing for fit young men in the armed forces has different constraints from designing for middle-aged female workers in manufacturing .
72902	Some of the required information may be susceptible to precise description in numerical terms such as body size and strength , but most of it will be of the ‘ awareness ’ kind when the designer recognises broadly that particular kinds of people have particular advantages and limitations .
72903	Similarly the range of tasks for which the device is required may not be known in the kind of detail which is available from comprehensive task descriptions but the designer will consider the extremes of what it is likely to be used for and the environment in which it will be used , for example designing a machine-tool for use in a factory has different requirements from designing a powered garden tool where the user could be wearing heavy gloves , will not be wearing safety-boots and will not receive any formal training .
72904	Communication between the designer and the producer used to be done almost entirely by traditional engineering drawings but there is now a tendency to use sketches , schematic drawings , photographs and models including computer-based models , for example complicated shapes in three dimensions are difficult to represent as rectangular projections and are not easily interpreted .
72905	Communication with the customer/user takes the form of operating instructions which are contained in an instruction book .
72906	The design of this book , booklet or even leaflet is a much neglected art and is frequently very badly executed — hence the common attitude reflected in the aphorism ‘ when all else fails try reading the instructions ’ .
