74004	Those responsible are interested in an effective total process not just an effective interview and all the stages in the process interact .
74005	For these reasons it is difficult to generate principles of interviewing , there are always alternative viewpoints and exceptions .
74006	for example :
74007	1 .
74008	Always try to put the interviewees at ease .
74009	For senior posts it can be instructive to do the opposite to see how far the candidate can cope with the stress .
74010	2 .
74011	Always ask open-ended questions .
74012	If the interviewee is very nervous it can help to ask some questions which can readily be answered with a yes or no , this provides the opportunity to adjust the tension .
74013	3 .
74014	Do not make jokes .
74015	Sometimes the interviewee exhibits too much respect creating a communication barrier , a demonstration that the interviewer is only human by a weak joke can remove this barrier .
74016	4 .
74017	Always structure the interview to ensure that all essential points are covered .
74018	On the contrary a free-wheeling interview with direction changes as key points emerge can yield unexpected but valuable evidence .
74019	5 .
74020	Assess the interviewee under various headings to obtain a comparable profile score .
74021	Part of the skill of the interviewer is in extracting different salient points from individuals and appropriately weighting totally disparate facets .
74022	On the other hand it must be acknowledged that there are many bad interviews and , as always , improvement is possible by design , consideration of procedures and training .
74023	The design of the situation and the process should adhere to standard practices which have been found to be helpful by experience and commonsense .
74024	1 .
74025	Obtain all the relevant factual data ( biography and testscores ) before the final interview .
74026	2 .
74027	Provide a waiting room which has accessible toilet facilities including mirrors .
74028	3 .
74029	The interviewer should collect the interviewee , not have him sent for from the waiting room .
74030	4 .
74031	Provide the interviewee with a written job aid which indicates the name and function of the interviewer(s) .
74032	5 .
74033	The relative positioning of the two main interactors and the direction of lighting are significant .
74034	The obvious ‘ third-degree ’ lighting should be avoided but not being able to see the interview clearly is equally deleterious .
74035	Face to face is the most formal , side by side the least formal , seating at right angles is often a suitable compromise .
74036	6 .
74037	Provide the interviewee with opportunities to make points which have not been covered in questions and to ask other questions on matters important to him .
74038	This is not mere courtesy , what the interviewee regards as important can be very revealing .
74039	7 .
74040	Provide clear if indirect indications that the interview is ending .
74041	8 .
74042	Tell the interviewee what the next stage in the process will be and when .
74043	9 .
74044	Escort the interviewee at least to the door , again the behaviour at the parting point can be significant .
74045	In view of the above discussion training of interviewers and interviewees must necessarily be based on principles of training ( p. 121 ) rather than principles of interviewing .
74046	Role playing and case studies are often used and they can be effective in reducing self-unease ( self-awareness and self-analysis are necessary attributes of the good interviewer in action ) and highlighting idiosyncratic features such as mannerisms and biases .
74047	The most powerful tool of the interview trainer is the closed circuit television system .
74048	So powerful that it needs to be used circumspectly to avoid reducing self-confidence .
74049	Normally the trainer will go through a reproduced interview and discuss the good and bad points which are usually clearly evident .
74050	This provides salutary knowledge of results of the interview itself if not of its degree of success in terms of a real objective .
74051	Randell ( 1978 ) suggests that an interviewing at work course can reasonably take two days covering ‘ unfreezing ’ , conceptual analysis , technique development and practice with feedback .
74052	Rutter ( 1979 ) devised an interview training programme for medical students involving a history taking scheme and two video-taped 15 minute diagnostic sessions one week apart , with discussion feedback based on a nine-point method of scoring information elicited .
74053	These scores were also used to validate the training by comparing experimental and control groups .
74054	Psychological testing
74055	The design and development of tests is a well established formal procedure involving checking for internal consistency and absence of ambiguity , efficiency of administration and marking procedures and the production of norms for definitive populations .
74056	There is a comprehensive list and description of available tests in the ‘ Mental Measurement Yearbook ’ which is updated at intervals of a few years .
74057	The reliability of a test is measured by correlation between the test scores , obtained at two different times , between different forms of the same test or between samples of questions in different parts of the same test .
74058	The interpretation of this measure of consistency is not as straightforward as it seems at first sight .
74059	For example , it has been pointed out that one person can not be asked the same question twice , the second time he is not the same person because he has already been asked the question once .
74060	The validity of a test is an even more complex concept .
74061	It refers in general to the confidence the tester can attach to decisions based on the test scores .
74062	There are at least three kinds of validity : construct validity which refers to the degree to which the test seems to be based on psychological theory , content validity which describes how well the test measures what it is intended to measure and criterion validity which indicates its value as a predictor using as criteria other measures of relevant performance .
74063	The problems of criterion validity nicely illustrate the difficulty of finding any solid foundation on which to construct a psychometric measure .
74064	Suppose that the purpose of a particular test is to predict success in a particular job .
74065	Even with hindsight this is not easy to determine .
74066	The measure of success in a training course depends on the validity of the training course itself , supervisors ' opinions based on experience of job performance are subject to distortion by various biases and measured performance such as productivity is subject to many vicissitudes independent of the ability of the producer .
74067	Faced with all these uncertainties the strategies adopted in the U.S.A. and Europe are in general different but usefully complementary .
74068	The American approach is to be as formal and rigorous as possible with insistence on systematic sampling , correlating and so on .
74069	The European approach is less tidy and more humanistic with continuous questioning of philosophies and methodologies .
74070	A good example of the latter is Heim ( 1970 ) in which intelligence and personality testing is discussed in the context of the meaning of intelligence , creativity , personality , test taking as a skill and the different but inseparable limitations of speed and accuracy based measures .
74071	For further discussion of these elusive topics see Super and Bohn ( 1971 ) , Drenth ( 1978 ) and Jessup and Jessup ( 1975 ) .
74072	The aim of psychological measurement is optimal discrimination between individuals , for this purpose the difficulty of the test should match the range of abilities of the testees .
74073	For example an intelligence test may be too easy so that all testees have almost perfect scores , or too difficult in that all testees have very low scores , in both cases discrimination will be poor .
74074	One answer to this problem is tailored testing in which questions are computer-based and the test is adaptive in focussing the range of presented questions at about the level of success/failure which is appropriate for each testee .
74075	In this way discrimination is much improved without excessively lengthening the test time ( Killcross and Cassie , 1975 ) .
74076	The value and extent of the use of tests is subject to other changes in the history of the particular community .
74077	Obviously testing can be extensively utilised in war-time when many people are changing jobs both in military and civilian life .
74078	In peace-time the selection ratio , the ratio of applicants to available jobs is a key feature , there tends to be more testing in times of economic depression when jobs are scarce and also in post-war periods when there is extensive experience of using tests .
74079	The use of tests is not , of course , confined to selection procedures .
74080	Indeed there is currently much greater utilisation in guidance and therapy .
74081	Surveys
74082	In common with tests , surveys are required to be as reliable and valid as is feasible in the circumstances .
74083	Surveys are however different from tests in their objective : a test is usually carried out to find out about an individual , a survey is carried out to find out about an issue which is across people .
74084	The issue itself must be specified as precisely as possible usually in terms of both what we want to know and why we want to know .
74085	‘ Why ’ will clarify ‘ what ’ and will also contribute to the practical question of how much to spend on finding out .
74086	For reasons of economy the population of individuals approached is usually a small sample of the total relevant population .
74087	The size of the sample is less important than its structure .
74088	The first rule of sampling is that each member of the relevant population must have some chance of being included .
74089	If the probability of being included is equal for each member of the relevant population then the sample is said to be a random one .
74090	Often the relevant population is stratified to ensure that the sample will be more representative in certain respects .
74091	for example a survey of hospital staff would not usually be carried out by selecting names at random from the total staff list , it might concentrate on doctors , nurses or cleaners only , or might sample medical , paramedical , administrative and support staff in proportions of their total numbers depending on the purpose of the survey .
74092	Sampling might also be carried out progressively involving different stages .
74093	For example a survey concerned with the whole National Health Service staff might begin by separating the hospital and the general practice services , then sample key regions of the country , separate urban , suburban and rural services and then select within organisations as mentioned above .
74094	Sampling might also involve time phasing as in attempting to detect opinion trends leading up to a general election .
74095	It is possible to estimate sample sizes required if the tolerable error is known and vice versa ( Yates 1960 ) .
74096	Data may be obtained purely by observation but usually involve asking questions .
74097	The design of questionnaires is itself an art with certain ground rules .
74098	Clearly the questions must be such that the relevant population can be expected to understand them and to make informed responses .
74099	The questions must avoid ambiguities which is not as easy as it might seem , it is desirable to obtain several opinions about the interpretation of each question from the same kind of people as those who will be in the survey .
74100	The sequence of questions may bias the answers e.g. a likely alternation of Yes/No answers is more ‘ natural ’ than a uniform series of Yes or No answers .
74101	The style of the question can also be unintentionally ‘ loaded ’ towards a particular response .
74102	There is a temptation to put in questions which will check against each other but this can irritate the responder who will easily detect redundancy .
74103	There is also the temptation to make the questionnaire too long in the hope of getting just that little bit more information , this can more than defeat its object by reducing the response rate .
74104	A new questionnaire should always be piloted , that is tried out on a small sample , before it is finalised .
74105	The main factor influencing response rate is whether the survey is postal or personal .
74106	The response rate to a verbal questionnaire can easily be 90% or more but a mailed questionnaire can have a response rate as low as 30% even with follow-up reminders .
74107	A low response rate is serious particularly if there is reason to suspect that persons likely to give particular kinds of answers might be less or more likely to respond than others .
74108	Telephone based surveys are currently popular as a reasonable compromise , this increases the speed of data collection rather than the insight which is revealed by personal interviews .
74109	Large scale impersonal surveys can be supplemented by more personally based interviews either with individuals or groups .
74110	The inference from samples may be deductive or inductive .
74111	Deductions can be made by statistical comparisons of samples to determine whether they are from different populations .
74112	Inferences from samples to populations can be made within quantitative confidence limits .
74113	Much of the labour which used to be involved in manipulating and presenting data can now be delegated to specialised computer software but the basic issues of coding and structuring data still depend on the skills of the analyst .
74114	The survey is the most extensively used method of obtaining generalisations about people .
74115	It can vary in precision from quantitative anthropometric surveys to attempts to describe the attributes of products which particular users prefer .
74116	The systematic survey is the antidote to excessive reliance on personal experience which is usually biased by exposure to idiosyncratic samples and by selective perception .
74117	The required systematic process is summarised in Table 2.3 .
74118	Task training
74119	The distinction between task training and skill training is one of degree rather than kind .
74120	In task training the objective is to guide the trainee into following rules and essentially to make the performance more automatic .
74121	In skill training the opposite can apply , the trainee is persuaded to be flexible and to orient himself towards the end rather than the means .
74122	The difference between the two kinds of training is not as great as would appear at first sight because it turns out that task training has in common with skill training an emphasis on the perceptual side of human functioning .
74123	Even in what appear to be straightforward motor skills the changes in learning are associated with greater selectivity and more economical use of the evidence needed to guide performance .
74124	These distinctions are summarised in Table 2.4 .
74125	Task training is often called operator training or industrial training .
74126	The essential principles are :
74127	1 .
74128	The trainee must wish to learn , nothing can be achieved unless the trainee is adequately motivated .
74129	2 .
74130	The learning must be steered by adequate knowledge of performance .
74131	The behavioural characteristic which facilitates both of these requirements is knowledge of results .
74132	This is the most potent and consistent performance shaping factor ever uncovered by psychologists .
74133	It simultaneously promotes motivation and performance .
74134	Knowledge of how well one is doing will not provide the basic motivation in that the performer must care about his performance but if this is established , knowledge of performance is a most vigorous factor in developing and maintaining the will to perform .
74135	Carmichael and Dearborn ( 1950 ) demonstrated that continuous reading was likely to result in increased failure of concentration within an hour , but if the performance of the reader was checked and confirmed by asking questions at half-hour intervals then performance could continue for six to eight hours without signs of fatigue .
74136	Mackworth ( 1950 ) , within his classical studies of vigilance , showed that without knowledge of results the proportion of detected signals decreased in succeeding half-hours compared with the first half-hour , but for subjects given knowledge of results there was no deterioration compared with the first half-hour through the full two hours of the study .
74137	Correspondingly the effectiveness of performance will improve with knowledge of performance .
74138	This is as much a logical as a psychological principle .
74139	Clearly if a person has no knowledge of the success of performance the performance can not improve because there can be no guidelines to steer the improvement .
74140	There have been many experiments demonstrating the validity of this principle and exploring detailed variables such as the timing and quality of feedback .
74141	For details see Welford ( 1968 ) , Bilodeau ( 1969 ) , Annett ( 1969 ) .
74142	Miller et al .
74143	( 1960 ) formalise it into what they call the TOTE principle ( Test Operate — Test — Exit ) .
74144	The first test is a review of the situation , operate is the action which follows , the second test is a check as to whether or not the desired result has been achieved and this is followed either by another operation or by an exit if the desired result has been achieved .
74145	The TOTE is regarded as a fundamental unit of behaviour .
74146	Broadly speaking the more immediate the feedback the more effective it is except that there comes a point at which , to use Miller 's ( 1953 ) distinction , learning feedback becomes action feedback , the latter improves the current response whereas the former improves succeeding responses .
74147	There is a risk that what is intended to be an aid only during training can become an undesirable crutch in that performance comes to depend on it but this is rare and can be avoided by using a suitable time delay , thus ensuring that it is really learning and not action feedback .
74148	The accuracy of the feedback need not be greater than the discrimination ability of the trainee but equally its value will diminish if it is too approximate .
74149	Feedback of the discrepancy between desirable and achieved performance is superior to feedback of absolute performance .
74150	Holding ( 1965 ) distinguished between successive sub-classifications of feedback into intrinsic/artificial , concurrent/terminal , immediate/delayed , non-verbal/verbal , separate/accumulated .
74151	The superior value of direct , rapid , unambiguous feedback dominates the choice of length and content of learning periods .
74152	There was an extended controversy between supporters of part and whole learning ( Blum and Naylor 1968 ) .
74153	The advantage of whole learning is that the connections between the parts are also learned simultaneously .
74154	However the advantage of part learning is that the feedback can be of much higher quality .
74155	An excellent compromise is the progressive-part method ( Seymour , 1966 ) in which parts are learned separately but combined in groups within a tree-like structure which converges on the total task .
74156	See , for example , Singleton ( 1959 ) , King ( 1964 ) .
74157	The identification of the sub-tasks which are appropriate for intensive training with feedback is achieved by task analysis .
74158	Unfortunately there is confusion in the literature and the required procedures may be referred to as either skills analysis or task analysis ( Seymour 1968 , Singer and Ramsden 1969 , Miller 1962 ) .
74159	In the terminology used in this book task analysis is the correct description of this activity .
74160	It will be evident from the dates of most of these references that this kind of training and the supporting research flourished in the 1960s .
74161	The need for it has reduced but has not vanished over the past twenty years .
74162	Technology has shifted the general allocation of function slightly both in industry and in defence .
74163	Many processes have changed so that there is less direct human involvement in the production cycle , e.g. metal working , highly repetitive cycles can be conducted by robots and similar devices , e.g. in car assemblies , and the human operator gets better support even when still involved directly , e.g. the word processor as a substitute for the typewriter .
74164	Nevertheless within most jobs there are at least some tasks which are amenable to this kind of training and the benefits are considerable .
74165	If task training is neglected the larger job may be interfered with , e.g. the manager attempting to use a personal computer with inadequate key-board and data search performance .
74166	Key-board manipulation is a skill relevant to many tasks and is typical of psycho-motor skills in that the perceptual elements of identify and select dominate the motor element of actual key pressing .
74167	As mentioned earlier improvements in speed and accuracy result from changes in the control of performance .
74168	Skill training
74169	The simplest criterion for the distinction between a skill and a task is that a skill description is susceptible to individual differences but a task description is not .
74170	Skill implies idiosyncratic performance and as such can transfer between many tasks whereas a task meets a particular requirement within a system activity .
74171	Thus it follows that skill training is more generalised and generalisable and is better fitted to the overall role of human operators .
74172	Education is the ultimate form of skill training where no attempt is made to specify the particular purposes for which the skills might be utilised .
74173	This limits the potential rigour of design because the anchor of skill training is the specification of the objectives .
74174	Incidentally this accounts for the interminable debate about education , since objectives are not specifiable the content can only emerge as a consensus within the current zeitgeist .
74175	Skill descriptions are generalisable in that human operators have characteristic abilities and limitations and therefore have tendencies to perform in the same way .
74176	Differences in level of skill are partly but not wholly attributable to different locations on a learning curve which has some uniformity for that particular skill .
74177	Skills can not be transferred directly from a trainer to a trainee , the function of the trainer is to provide conditions and guidelines which will facilitate learning .
74178	To do this the trainer must have a coherent model of the form of the skill , this is attained by skills analysis .
74179	Inevitably skills analysis is more general and less definitive than task analysis although many of the same procedures for extracting evidence might be used .
74180	Skills analysis may also involve experiments to study more closely how the required objective is achieved ( Drury and Fox , 1975 , Singleton , 1978 ) .
74181	It requires a broader approach than task analysis in that it often involves tracing the acquisition of the skill starting from the kind of persons who undertake training ( the selection criteria ) through the training procedures to the end product ( the training success criteria ) .
74182	Such training often has an emphasis on features such as style and quality rather than mere speed of activity .
74183	This can extend beyond skill training to attitude training ( see below ) .
74184	These differences are summarised in Table 2.5 .
74185	There is emphasis on the end purpose or objective with relatively less attention to the means , partly so as to allow for individual differences and partly because the evidence accumulating in particular cases may change the direction of progress .
74186	For this reason skill training is sometimes called strategic training .
74187	Such activities are found in the broad range of tasks concerned with diagnosis .
74188	These can vary from dealing with faults in equipment ( Tilley , 1967 ) to dealing with patients in a surgery or clinic ( Rutter , 1979 ) .
74189	In all cases although the reason for the activity is clear cut the means of achieving the desired end vary widely in terms of the path taken and the time required .
74190	The medical interview has much in common with counselling ( Joanning et al . ,
74191	1979 ) and occupational guidance ( Davis and Shackleton , 1975 ) .
74192	Medical diagnosis involves social skills ( Melhuish , 1979 ) but as discussed earlier the basis and development of these skills is not dissimilar from other cognitive skills and correspondingly the training can follow the same principles ( Singleton et al . ,
74193	1980 ; Argyle , 1981 ) .
74194	Attitude training
74195	Attitudes are much more difficult to change than are skills and there can be ambiguity about what constitutes an improvement .
74196	Attitudes involve values which vary between individuals , societies and cultures .
74197	For example ‘ brain washing ’ is a form of attitude training which attempts to change the beliefs and values acquired within a particular culture ( Biderman , 1967 ) .
74198	The extreme techniques of isolation , starvation and other forms of stress induction give some indication of the pressures required to positively change attitudes .
74199	Generation of standard useful attitudes has always been one of the main purposes of military training .
74200	The objective is to cultivate the willingness to accept or ignore personal risk ( Page , 1987 ) .
74201	In the civilian context the purposes of attitude training are to do with care about quality and safety .
74202	Apprenticeship training is essentially about ensuring standards of workmanship and characteristically it appears at first sight to take an unconscionably long time .
74203	A common fallacy is the attempt to assess apprenticeship schemes in terms of task and skill training .
74204	Safety training is also about attitudes and such schemes rarely have the hoped for success because the difficulty and time required are invariably underestimated .
74205	This is also the reason why road accidents are so difficult to approach by training , safety on the road is much more to do with attitudes than with driving skill ( Parry , 1968 ) .
74206	In summary , we have no useful theory about the design of attitude training and success in practice is based on indirect traditional procedures .
74207	Skills analysis
74208	It will be appreciated from the earlier sections of this chapter that skills analysis is not reducible to simple procedures or recipes .
74209	In principle it is impossible because skills are by their nature totally integrated and interactive so that they can not meaningfully be separated into independent parts .
74210	Nevertheless , as in many other situations the analyst , himself a skilled performer , has some success in practice .
74211	A skill description relates to how a task is performed and what is achieved rather than what actions are taken .
74212	The reference is to the end and the means is described in person terms rather than task terms .
74213	This is because the end is more consistent than the means .
74214	Although there may be considerable idiosyncrasy in the actions the situation is not anarchical .
74215	The human operator has characteristic ways of doing things and detection of these is one aspect of the skill of the skills analyst .
74216	There are differences in skills analysis procedure depending on the kind of skill .
74217	For the skills of interacting with the physical world the procedure summarised in Table 2.6 is appropriate .
74218	This involves observation of the skill in practice and during training and discussion with practitioners and trainers .
74219	There are useful ways of focusing such observation by contrasting good/poor performers and experienced/inexperienced performers .
74220	Discussion with practitioners can be focused by asking them to talk while performing and by jointly discussing performances observed on film or tape .
74221	For management skills there is greater emphasis on the objectives and how they are arrived at .
74222	Objectives in an organisational context are subject to many constraints .
74223	Some such as financial resources are easily specifiable , others such as not contravening the mores of the organisation are more elusive but a key aspect of these skills is sensitivity to limitations and obstacles as well as positive assets ( Singleton , 1981 ) .
74224	The variety of management tasks is often so great as to warrant a task analysis with separate skills analyses of particular tasks or groups of tasks .
74225	At this level the practitioner is often the conscious monitor of the practice and facility in self-monitoring is a useful indicator of skill .
74226	Social skills can involve not only self-monitoring but also monitoring of what another person is thinking as well as doing .
74227	For example , analysing a transaction between two skilled negotiators requires the study of the overt interaction and the identification of what each one is thinking about what he himself is doing and what his opponent is probably thinking about in the context of what he is saying ( Singleton , 1983a ) .
74228	There are no standard formats for skill descriptions but usually they can be separated into two parts : the performance and the antecedents to the performance .
74229	That is respectively the key aspects of behaviour which contribute to success and the kind of education , training and experience normally required .
74230	At high levels of idiosyncratic skill ( flair see p. 245 ) analysis is particularly difficult because the practitioner may have little conscious awareness of how or why he achieves unusual success .
74231	In fact it almost seems to be a condition of such performance that the exponent must not proceed logically but must temporarily inhibit his conscious critical faculties and accept control by intuition .
74232	This has been graphically described as ‘ switching on the autopilot ’ ( Drasdo , 1979 ) .
74233	The commonsense view that to proceed with care is to proceed slowly can also be reversed in high level skills , there are instances where speed seems to be an essential accompaniment of delicate discrimination ( Lacy , 1978 ) .
74234	Thus , the observer can not simplify his task by asking the practitioner to go more slowly nor can he rely on the introspection of the skilled performer .
74235	Skill is demonstrated by persistent and efficient pursuit of an objective and the skill can usually be understood although not necessarily written down with any great precision in terms of a goal and the path towards that goal .
74236	The path is generated by navigating through a conceptual map containing landmarks and decision points ( key features of the skill ) and by the avoidance of obstacles and misleading features which have been sensitively detected .
74237	Applications
74238	Selection and guidance
74239	These processes are variations on the general theme of matching a worker to an appropriate job .
74240	In the case of selection the given point is the job and the population is searched to find the most appropriate worker , in the case of guidance one worker is the starting point and the range of jobs is searched to identify the best one .
74241	The two complementary processes are shown in Fig. 2. 1 .
74242	They can usefully be considered together because they are similar and interactive .
74243	Thus , in the selection situation the process involves not only analysing and describing the job but also considering the availability of potentially appropriate workers .
74244	In the guidance situation the process involves analysing and describing the worker and consideration of the availability of suitable jobs .
74245	At the point of a successful match the worker is described in terms of the kinds of job he could do and the job is described in terms of the kind of worker needed to do it , Table 2.7 .
74246	For most people and jobs the whole process takes place within a localised community .
74247	For the highest level jobs a whole country or even an international community might be considered , but in European countries most workers attempt to find jobs which do not require either moving house or excessive travelling , and such proximity has corresponding advantages for the potential employers .
74248	Thus , the selection process involves describing the job first by analysis ( task and skills analysis ) and then the translation of these data into worker relevant terminology .
74249	Consideration of the potential worker availability may lead to a redesign of the job either by the use of a different task combination or by introducing different technology .
74250	It is then necessary to communicate with the market by publicising the available job usually by advertising .
74251	This is itself an important stage in the process because a well prepared advertisement will enable the recipients to engage in self selection which does not , at this stage , involve further selector resources .
74252	To this end it is useful to have a multi-stage process as shown in Fig. 2.2 .
74253	Having developed some interest on the basis of a necessarily brief advertisement a potential candidate can apply for further written details which should contain a comprehensive description of the job , the task and skill content , the responsibilities , the salary and the details of the organisation including its history and anticipated future , and an application form .
74254	A name with job title and telephone number should be included so that informal interaction and discussion of details of particular interest to the candidate can take place before the commitment to transmission of the application form .
74255	All this can be done at minimal cost .
74256	If the job description has been properly constructed there should not be an excessive number of applicants so that the next stage of a paper sift is also economical .
74257	There then follow the more expensive stages of final selection which may involve testing and interviewing as described earlier .
74258	The choice of the interviewers and the interview process depends on the particular job .
74259	At one extreme it may be one company representative , at the other extreme there may be a series of interview boards .
74260	The interview board can have covert purposes where the senior person who is the chairman of the board will use the opportunity to orientate the precise expectations from the post to be filled including settling differences of opinion between his subordinates who are also members of the board .
74261	Ideally this should be done before candidates are interviewed but it can happen that differences in preferences for candidates reveal different opinions between board members which the chairman can detect and deal with .
74262	Guidance also involves testing and interviewing but this is invariably a two person situation of a counsellor and client .
74263	The problem is that most clients have only the vaguest , undefined ideas about the most suitable choice and direction of career .
74264	The counsellor can help by identifying the client 's job-relevant characteristics and by contributing his knowledge about occupations ( Fig. 2.3 . ) .
74265	The former may be supported by testing although test results are essentially evidence to enable the individual to clarify his own self concept .
74266	The latter may start from national classifications of occupations such as the American Dictionary of Occupational Titles ( DOT ) and the British Classification of Occupations and Dictionary of Occupational Titles ( CODOT ) , but the counsellor 's suggestions are likely to converge very rapidly into a more comprehensible repertoire of possibilities using evidence about the particular client ( Singleton , 1975 ) .
74267	This process can be supported by a computer with which the client may interact alone or it may be used by the counsellor as a database and prompter .
74268	A guidance episode necessarily takes place at one point in time within the developing skills and experience of the client .
74269	To emphasise the continuous nature of career development and the changing aspirations of people at different ages Super has proposed a division into five stages : Growth ( 0–14 years ) ; Exploration ( 15–24 years ) ; Establishment ( 25–44 ) ; Maintenance ( 45–64 years ) ; and Decline ( 65 onwards ) ( Super and Bohn , 1971 ) .
74270	Placement
74271	Placement is a mixture of selection and guidance , a process of mutual matching takes place within a known range of persons and jobs .
74272	The problem arises when a batch of recruits enter military service or when a large company takes on a new set of graduates .
74273	It is one application of psychometrics to man-power planning ( see previous chapter ) .
74274	It becomes of particular significance within the currently fashionable company policy of separating core and peripheral employees .
74275	Given the vagaries of the market and rapid changes in processes and products stimulated by changing technology the strategy has evolved of taking on many employees for a short term only .
74276	These may be production workers but they may also be senior people ; managers hired for a fixed term and technologists and others used as consultants .
74277	The placement task is to describe the requirements and the appropriate sources of individuals with the relevant skills ( Fig. 2.1 ) .
74278	For the core workers who are permanent staff again there may well be a mixture of people at all levels and here there is more emphasis on career progression and job satisfaction .
74279	Core employees are given written annual assessments which can be discussed with the immediate senior who is probably the writer of the assessment .
74280	For this purpose he is provided with a well-structured form by the personnel department who will also advise on the timely use of in-house or external courses to extend the range of skills of a particular employee .
74281	By contrast the peripheral employee is judged entirely on his past record or that of the consultant company which employs him on a semi-permanent basis .
74282	He is hired to undertake a specific task without reference to longer term features such as job satisfaction or career development .
74283	The peripheral employee will be compensated for his disadvantages by a much greater pay rate per hour and the company gains by reduced overheads and greater work-force flexibility .
74284	The whole strategy works very well for younger workers with well documented training and experience .
74285	This reinforces the view , developed in the previous chapter , that manufacturing industry in particular is following the Armed Forces in relying more and more on fit , skilled , mobile workers .
74286	Psychometrically the problem is to develop appropriate descriptive taxonomies so that a person 's actual or potential contribution to an organisation is succinctly expressible .
74287	These remain primitive in that , on the whole , non-technical English is used with all the possibilities of ambiguity and communication at cross purposes which this implies .
74288	The accountants are ahead of the psychologists in developing ideas such as profit centres applicable to small groups or even to individuals .
74289	The increased awareness of the importance of the individual worker to profit and success generally , particularly at higher levels in the organisation , has stimulated the growth of a specialist placement profession colloquially known as the head hunters .
74290	These are companies which specialise in assisting a client in clarifying what kind of person they need and how to locate him within the potentially suitable worker population .
74291	They may also start with an individual and search for a location .
74292	This also is done mainly by interview although some use is made of psychometric tests , profiles and rating scales .
74293	The design of training schemes
74294	Designing and conducting training schemes is expensive and is not undertaken without good reasons .
74295	Among possible reasons are :
74296	1 .
74297	An inadequate reservoir of competent workers for particular tasks
74298	2 .
74299	A workforce sufficient in numbers or supply but not in skill level as evidenced usually by quality of work and less frequently by failures to meet production targets , danger to people and damage to equipment
74300	3 .
74301	Changes in technology which result in changes in required skills
74302	4 .
74303	An organisational commitment to continuous improvement of the skills of members
74304	5 .
74305	To meet statutory requirements in certain dangerous industries and services
74306	6 .
74307	As a service to customers buying equipment
74308	7 .
74309	As a service to the community paid for by public funds
74310	The remit of the training scheme and those responsible for it may end at the transition point to operational activity or may continue in those periods of work regarded as a continuation of training and supervised as such .
74311	In either case there needs to be close liaison between those responsible for training and those responsible for operations .
74312	On the other hand training is always vulnerable because the benefits are long-term and it often needs protection from the demands of management and operations where there are other priorities .
74313	The simplest protective barrier is a geographical one , namely to conduct the training away from other centres of activity within the organisation .
74314	Sometimes a separate room is sufficient , in other situations a different part of the country may be chosen to provide adequate isolation .
74315	The essential vulnerability reinforces the requirement that the starting point of design should be a clarification of objectives followed by a consideration of the criteria of assessment that the objectives have been achieved .
74316	None of this need be numerical , sometimes numbers are used to provide a pseudo precision which can be counterproductive because the validity of the numbers can so easily be questioned .
74317	Precise verbal statements and descriptions avoid this pitfall .
74318	The sensitivity of training regimes to external pressures is demonstrated by the erratic interest and activity in this area observable at the national level .
74319	Inevitably there was a burst of activity during and immediately after World War II as shown for example by military research and development ( Wolfie , 1951 ) and by the ‘ Training within Industry ’ ( TWI ) movement ( War Man-power Commission , 1945 ) .
74320	Although research continued the next burst of application in the U.K. took place following the Industrial Training Act of 1964 ( Robinson and Barnes , 1968 , Barber 1968 ) .
74321	The Act concentrated on training oriented by industry , the other possibilities considered were occupations and geographical regions .
74322	It resulted in the creation of a Central Training Council and a comprehensive range of Industrial Training Boards .
74323	Each Board was financed by a levy on the relevant industry .
74324	Not surprisingly this created a demand for experienced trainer manpower which could not be met , there was some disillusion and retrenchment in the 1970s .
74325	In the 1980s there has been another resurgence of activity following the realisation that the country is simultaneously suffering from a high rate of unemployment and a shortage of workers with specific skills .
74326	Extensive government resources are channelled by the Department of Employment through the Training Commission into the Youth Training Schemes , job training , skill training and so on .
74327	The objectives and criteria of success of any training scheme are best described in system terms .
74328	The next step is to translate these into a person oriented description of what the successful scheme graduate will have acquired .
74329	This is more than skills because the total expertise will include also rules , knowledge and contextual information .
74330	This last will vary from some acquaintance with the parent company to the basic technology behind the tasks .
74331	Together these make up the content or syllabus of the course .
74332	Decisions are then needed on how to train , which will include whether or which parts should be on-line or off-line , whether the operator is required to function in a mainly programmed ( i.e. rule-following ) mode and how far he may need to function in a conceptual ( i.e. actions based on understanding ) mode .
74333	Consideration will be given to the use of training aids such as technical notes , schematic diagrams , video tapes , closed circuit television and simulators .
74334	The most important training aids are the instructors , the selection and training of these is a vital secondary scheme supporting the primary scheme .
74335	These many facets of training scheme design are shown in Table 2.8 .
74336	Programmed instruction
74337	The origins of this movement are in the teaching machines first developed systematically about 1960 .
74338	These consisted of film strips with associated projection devices and control panels which enabled the student to examine a particular screen presentation and respond by moving to another frame .
74339	The succeeding frame might take up another topic or might contain answers and comments on questions posed on the previous one .
74340	There was some scope for interaction in that the series of presentations was determined by the student 's choice of responses .
74341	If the student demonstrated by his choices that he did not fully understand a particular point then the programme could send him round an additional explanatory loop .
74342	This was called a branching programme as distinct from a linear programme which contained no loops .
74343	It will be appreciated that this technique of automated teaching seemed to have enormous potential .
74344	Classroom teaching is inherently skilled man-power intensive .
74345	There are obvious benefits in allowing each student to go at his own pace .
74346	It is not surprising that teaching machines had considerable appeal to the military and to large scale industry .
74347	Some years of intensive research and development resulted in a more realistic view ( Glaser , 1965 ; Wallis et al . ,
74348	1966 , Kay et al . ,
74349	1968 ) .
74350	It became clear that the quality of the programme was the key to degree of success .
74351	The machine itself and its style of operation was incidental , in fact it was possible to achieve the same procedure if not quite the same discipline on the student by using programmed books with directional references to other pages at the end of each page .
74352	If a well-structured book is the answer then we have gone full-circle and back to the benefits of a systematic text-book .
74353	In research terms the study of programmed instruction was instrumental in encouraging a more systems view of the teaching/training process with associated trends towards greater consideration of objectives , task analysis , cost/ benefits and so on .
74354	Correspondingly from a practical training viewpoint there developed a more systematic approach to taxonomies of training and of instructional methods together with their inter-relationships .
74355	Tables 2.9 and 2.10 are examples from an overview of military training .
74356	Regarded in systems terms , programmed instruction can not be an isolated continuously developing activity because it depends on the skills of the programme writer and these skills can only be developed on the basis of experience in the classroom .
74357	On the other hand teaching machines are one way of utilising the skilled teacher on a larger scale than his personal activity in the classroom .
74358	There is a different form of automatic teaching device called a pacing machine which can facilitate the development of motor skills .
74359	It consists of a machine which emits bleeps at timed intervals .
74360	The intervals are predetermined by the elements of a motor task or more simply by the target cycle time of a task .
74361	The trainee performs his task and tries to keep in phase with the bleeps which are intended to pace his performance .
74362	The required rate of work can be increased by shortening the time intervals .
74363	The second main phase of programmed instruction became feasible with the development of low cost computing .
74364	Computer aided instruction ( C.A.I. ) strictly should cover other techniques such as simulation and computer based procedures but it is usually intended to mean a situation where a student sits in front of a screen on which the presented formats relate to his developing cognitive activity as expressed by his manipulations of the associated key-board .
74365	Even with this restricted interface there is enormous flexibility and the training tasks can vary from reading and simple arithmetic to diagnosing faults in the complex plant used in process industries .
74366	The use of computer aided instruction in primary schools has created a new generation of what have been called ‘ television children ’ .
74367	They regard the screen/keyboard interface as no more unnatural than a book is to earlier generations .
74368	This has far reaching consequences at the cultural level not only for learning but also for the design of jobs and even for leisure pursuits which increasingly depend on the same kind of interface .
74369	Many of the earlier forms of computer aided instructions used a central computer facility and a set of work-stations where a whole class of trainees could function simultaneously .
74370	The development of micro-computers resulted in the use of more isolated dedicated systems for just one trainee .
74371	In either case it is feasible to collect data about a trainee 's performance and modify the presented information accordingly .
74372	It is also possible to collect learning data and feed it to an instructor either on-line or off-line .
74373	The widespread use of computer based learning and testing situations has stimulated the development of ‘ student modelling ’ .
74374	All the data about one student is collected into one bank which changes dynamically with his learning achievements ( and failures ) .
74375	In this way a student model containing a profile of attainment together with a history of progress to date can be made available to the trainer and to the trainee .
74376	However , communication links between the trainee and the trainer via a computer are not a substitute for the two-way conversation and observation which normally takes place in a class-room .
74377	Computer programmes are notoriously literal in their requirement for and response to operator responses .
74378	Trainee-computer communication failures for very simple reasons can lead to a complete hiatus unless they are detected and restored by an experienced trainer who can explain to the trainee why the system is failing to respond adequately .
74379	The third phase of programmed instruction called Tutorial Expert Systems ( TES ) involves artificial intelligence ( see p. 234 ) .
74380	To a trainee at the interface this may not seem very different from a teaching machine or computer aided instruction but the logic or architecture of the driving system is different so that even more flexibility is available .
74381	Instead of responding directly by logical rules and paths which have been envisaged and stored by the programmer an expert system training programme contains a knowledge base and an inference engine which can consult the knowledge base and respond more adaptively to the idiosyncratic needs of the trainee .
74382	It can also explain why it is proposing a certain strategy and why the detected strategy of the trainee is appropriate or not , and , if not , why not .
74383	From the user 's point of view these systems are usually menu driven , that is the operator can select his path of consultation by choices within ranges of possible choices which are presented to him .
74384	Technically the task of the programme designer is made easier by the use of training skills and declarative programming languages .
74385	A training shell is a generalised tutorial system which can operate with a variety of knowledge bases .
74386	A declarative programming language is one which can accept statements of relationships or rules for relationships contrasting with more traditional languages which encompass only step by step logic .
74387	It will be appreciated that this rapidly developing field of expertise contains extensive new jargon .
74388	At this stage the jargon is an obstacle in that anyone wishing to find out about the field has first to interpret the jargon .
74389	This is doubly difficult in that there is much overlap in terminology and concepts and specialists are not consistent with each other in the use of these new terms .
74390	No doubt the field will eventually clarify and mature and the terminology will be designed with precision so that meaningful concepts , tools and methods are unambiguously clarified and distinguished but this has not yet happened .
74391	From a behavioural standpoint the issues are the same as in any other field where technology is simultaneously providing many new facilities for supporting and measuring human performance .
74392	1 .
74393	Technology provides trainer aids not trainer substitutes .
74394	Thus computer assisted instruction ( CAI ) is more aptly descriptive than computer based training ( CBT ) .
74395	2 .
74396	Technology enforces rigorous thinking to the point of revealing embarrassing gaps in learning , teaching and training theory .
74397	On the other hand technology also opens up new possibilities for monitoring and measurement which should support the development of better basic theory .
74398	3 .
74399	It is essential to develop the basic taxonomies behind the learning situation .
74400	for example any diagnostic task can be aided by a taxonomy of symptoms and a taxonomy of causes together with connections between them .
74401	4 .
74402	The need for interdisciplinary approaches is reinforced but the abiding difficulties of interdisciplinary communications remain at every level from different values and concepts to different terminologies .
74403	Communication between information technologists and behavioural specialists is a continuous struggle which can eventually be rewarding .
74404	5 .
74405	The design of the man-machine interface ( MMI ) or the human-computer interface ( HCI ) or more simply human interfaces ( HI ) remains one of the most difficult design problems but a crucial one in that poorly designed interfaces will wreck the performance of any system .
74406	6 .
74407	Evaluation is an essential procedure within the implementation of any new system .
74408	for training systems this can be very expensive because of the requirements to monitor the learning process and compare procedures which are anyway never completely comparable .
74409	Apparently extraneous variables such as trainee motivation and trainer expertise continue to dominate other factors such as differences in technology and differences in learning tasks .
74410	7 .
74411	Pedagogically the need to be much clearer about what is being taught and why is a mixed blessing .
74412	The formal discipline can sometimes tidy up muddled thinking but at other times it can interfere with the creatively developing interaction between trainer and trainee .
74413	In general , programmed instruction is most useful for tasks which can be comprehensively specified .
74414	This implies tasks based on rules for example arithmetic , or on logic , for example fault finding .
74415	The use of simulators
74416	When serious consequences can follow from human errors , e.g. in flying an aircraft , or when on-line operation is too expensive to be trusted to the hands of trainees , e.g. in process control , there is obviously a case for providing training devices which simulate the performance of on-line systems .
74417	In this way risks and costs are reduced , the performance of trainees is more easily measured and the presented situation is precisely controlled by the trainers .
74418	It is feasible to provide adequate exposure to events which in practice might be rare but very serious .
74419	High fidelity simulation is an interesting challenge to technological design .
74420	Simulators can provide demonstrations which always impress visitors .
74421	With all these advantages it is not surprising that a great deal of effort and resources go into the provision of simulators for high technology industry .
74422	Paradoxically the more advanced the technology the easier it is to provide good simulation .
74423	For example , a process control plant which consists of dials , charts and visual display units responding to activation of switches is much easier to simulate than , say , an opponent in a game of tennis .
74424	The perfect simulation which has been suggested but not yet implemented in process control , power generation and air traffic control would be to have two identical control rooms and two crews coming on duty .
74425	One crew would control a real system and the other would think they were so doing but would in fact be in a control room driven by software .
74426	This seems to be the only way of avoiding the main snag of simulation , namely that the trainee is aware that his performance is not important in that reality out there is not changing as a consequence of his actions .
74427	However , he will always know that his performance on a simulator is being assessed and , except for the business of risks , he may well take more care than he would in a real plant .
74428	In many if not most industries where simulators are used the benefits to training are not confined to dynamic system control and fault diagnosis .
74429	The control function is exercised by a team and the efficient interaction between the team members is also subject to improvement with practice ( see p. 95 ) .
74430	Transfer of training from a simulator to a real situation is never complete and does not necessarily increase with degree of fidelity .
74431	Simple simulations can be as effective for training purposes as more elaborate ones and can certainly be more cost effective .
74432	Degree of transfer is not easy to measure and needs to be carefully defined .
74433	For example , in training manually guided missile operators the degree of transfer is appropriately measured by ‘ first shot ’ success whereas in training and retraining flight deck crew the long term contribution to safety is the appropriate measure .
74434	Gagne ( 1962 ) provides an excellent review of earlier work in this field .
74435	More recent experience is reviewed in Stammers ( 1983 ) .
74436	For details of experimental studies using large scale defence simulations see Parsons ( 1972 ) .
74437	Moraal and Kraiss ( 1981 ) contains chapters dealing with simulations of a ship entering harbour , car driving , tank driving , the flight deck and air traffic control .
74438	MSC ( 1986 ) reviews the current use of simulators in twenty U.K. industries .
74439	As a research tool the simulator provides a happy medium between the precision of laboratory studies and the realism of field studies .
74440	It is not widely used for research outside the military because of the cost of high fidelity simulator time .
74441	A complex dedicated simulator can cost several million pounds and it needs its own crew of skilled operators .
74442	On the other hand standard micro-computers have considerable potentiality for quite elaborate simulation and effective simulation training on procedures may only require simple static mock-ups .
74443	Simulator development has been driven by technology rather than by the behavioural sciences with the standard result that there is a high reliance on face validity with relatively little resource devoted to systematic evaluation .
74444	Key features such as the timing and extent of simulator usage are based on experience in particular industries rather than on more formal evidence .
74445	The ergonomics approach to their use is shown in Fig. 2.4 but it must be admitted that this is as yet rarely followed in practice .
74446	Simulation should be regarded as one tool within the repertoire of the training specialist .
74447	There are other uses of simulators .
74448	They can be used for assessment independently of training .
74449	Data collected during simulator trials is a useful source of risk and reliability data .
74450	In the nuclear power plant design they are also used as the final stage of pre-construction design evaluation ( Williams and Story , 1987 ) .
74451	They can also be used as a resource for checking operating instructions and for conducting detailed task analyses .
74452	For these purposes the simulator must be available before the main control room is constructed .
74453	The full range of potential simulator usage is summarised in Table 2.11 .
74454	The School Framework
74455	A Model to Link Personality Characteristics to a Preference for Science
74456	John Head
74457	Introduction
74458	In recent years there has been a steady accumulation of evidence that personality and allied affective factors play a crucial role in determining subject choice and student success .
74459	Unfortunately , this evidence has tended to be fragmentary , a collection of separate , discrete pieces of information lacking a synthesizing theory to provide cohesion and predictive power .
74460	The few models which have been developed to date may have been correct as far as they go but are clearly incomplete .
74461	For example Roe ( 1952 ) , Eiduson ( 1962 ) and McClelland ( 1962 ) suggested that male scientists often experienced a lonely childhood , perhaps suffering social isolation through illness or family circumstances , so that they developed a strong interest in their surrounding material world and a below average interest in other people and relationships .
74462	Maslow ( 1966 ) and Hudson ( 1966 and 1968 ) saw science as providing an emotionally undemanding activity appealing to boys moving from the calm of latency to the turbulence of adolescence .
74463	Even if these descriptions are valid they still leave open a number of questions , particularly why the same mechanisms do not operate with girls .
74464	Arising from the evidence in the literature and from our empirical studies at Chelsea College it is now possible to offer a model which is compatible with all the evidence and which also has considerable predictive potential .
74465	What we know about persons choosing science
74466	The evidence for an association between personality characteristics and an interest in science has been more fully reviewed by Head ( 1979 ) .
74467	We need now only take note of the most salient features .
74468	The most obvious one is that of sex differences .
74469	The predominance of males , particularly in the physical sciences and engineering , throughout the Western world can no longer be satisfactorily attributed to cognitive differences , which are too small , nor to institutional factors .
74470	Equal opportunity in education and employment has not made science any more popular with women .
74471	Furthermore , the characteristics of those students who do opt for science show clear sex differences .
74472	Male scientists , both science students and mature , professional scientists , tend to be emotionally reticent , disliking overt emotional expression in others and themselves , and depending upon their partners in personal relationships to take the emotional initiatives .
74473	They will also tend to be authoritarian , conservative and controlled in their thinking .
74474	These differences can be seen quite early on ; we have found boys aged 14 years who were opting for science to be significantly more authoritarian than their peers .
74475	Girls choosing science are not particularly emotionally reticent or rigid in their thinking , although they do seem to have low self-esteem in terms of being socially and sexually attractive .
74476	We also know that at about the age of 13 a very high proportion of boys are attracted to science and scientific careers .
74477	Thereafter , there is a steady decline of interest in science and this disillusionment extends right through the secondary-school years and into the undergraduate period .
74478	In contrast , only a minority of girls express an interest in science at any age but there is no obvious swing from science in the middle and late teens .
74479	Some further evidence has come from our use of sentence completion tests with secondary-school pupils as part of our research programme at Chelsea .
74480	Analysis of these responses provides further information on sex differences and between those opting for different subjects .
74481	For example , girls at the age of 12 and 14 years seem to take a more mature attitude to personal relationships , seeing their complexity and reciprocal nature , while boys are more exploitative .
74482	In relation to the sentence stem ‘ A girl and her mother … ’ , girls often produce responses like ‘ often go through a bad patch for a year but once they learn to understand each other , become the best of friends ’ or ‘ can help each other with their problems ’ .
74483	Similar questions , when asked of boys , tend to produce banal responses or exploitative ones , for example the parent is seen as the source of money .
74484	In contrast , boys seem to have a firmer self-identity and a clearer ambition showing more insight in response to sentence stems such as ‘ My main problem is … ’ and ‘ He/she felt proud that … ’ .
74485	Such findings give us some clues about the characteristics of boys and girls of these ages .
74486	If we compare boys of 14 years of age who opt for science with other boys , we find that the former have very cut-and-dried views on many issues .
74487	For example , they take the view that ‘ criminals should be severely punished ’ or that ‘ anyone who is unpopular deserves his fate ’ .
74488	To the sentence stem ‘ When a child will not join in group activities … ’ , these boys gave responses like ‘ he is selfish ’ , ‘ he must be stupid ’ , ‘ he deserves to be unpopular ’ .
74489	In contrast , other boys and most girls pondered the possible causes and ways of integrating the child into the group .
74490	The science boys seemed to possess few doubts or uncertainties , they offered clear-cut answers .
74491	It was this evidence which suggested the possible model for subject choice in terms of ego-identity achievement .
74492	Ego-identity in adolescence
74493	This model was originally postulated by Erikson ( 1965 ) and then developed by Marcia ( 1966 and 1976 ) .
74494	Erikson suggests that at different phases of life an individual faces a particular psycho-social problem which needs to be resolved before moving on to the next phase .
74495	For adolescents the acquisition of a clear ego-identity is the crucial task .
74496	At the beginning of adolescence , the individual is a dependant within the family and the school .
74497	By the end of adolescence he [ or she ] needs to make choices about career , life-style , personal relationships and ideologies .
74498	The ego-identity of that person is shaped by these choices .
74499	Erikson does not suggest that the development of an ego-identity is a once-and-for-all issue .
74500	Some problems about identity arise with the young child in the context of home and school , and others occur in later life , for example on retirement .
74501	Nevertheless , adolescence is the time when ego-identity development inevitably dominates the personal development of the individual for a while .
74502	The adolescent does not , however , need to achieve a clear ego-identity on all topics at one time .
74503	He [ or she ] may have a clear identity in respect to his [ or her ] career but still be unresolved in regard to personal relationships and ideology .
74504	In this article we are concerned with ego-identity achievement in respect to career .
74505	Marcia has put more detail onto the Erikson model and suggests that in going from the initial ego-diffusion condition to that of having achieved ego-identity , two processes are involved : crisis and commitment .
74506	Crisis in this context describes a period of intensive self-examination in which one 's beliefs and values are re-examined .
74507	Commitment means that the individual has acquired clear and firm beliefs both about himself [ or herself ] and the world .
74508	Figure 16.1 indicates a number of possible routes to ego-identity achievements .
74509	A person may undergo crisis and commitment simultaneously and progress by route A. An alternative is to undergo a period of considerable self-doubt and self-examination in which all one 's beliefs tend to be very fluid , a period known as moratorium , before acquiring beliefs for oneself and ego-identity is achieved ( route B ) .
74510	A further possibility is that the individual may , at least for a time , hold onto beliefs and values taken without question from others , for example parents , teachers , peers .
74511	This condition is known as foreclosure .
74512	Eventually these persons might have to face up to a period of crisis , of self-examination , and so achieve ego-identity by route C. However , foreclosure does offer an escape route and an individual might postpone indefinitely any real self-examination by clinging rigidly to his [ or her ] beliefs and values ( route D ) .
74513	Ego-identity and Choosing Science
74514	We can now make the link between this model of adolescent development and subject choice in schools .
74515	For boys at the foreclosure stage , science is likely to be appealing .
74516	The physical sciences in particular , offer a conventional career choice which is likely to win approval from parents , teachers and peers .
74517	They will tend to regard the overt expression of emotions , including much such expression in the arts , as being soft and feminine .
74518	Science , with its masculine image , makes little emotional demand on an individual and seems to offer clear , precise answers to problems .
74519	Opting for science will permit and possibly reinforce emotional reticence .
74520	For a girl at the foreclosure stage the situation is very different .
74521	There is evidence that girls tend to be socialized into adult roles more through their potential of becoming a mother and housewife than through their career ( Douvan and Adelson , 1966 ) .
74522	Furthermore , these girls will tend to go into a career with a feminine image , one which already attracts many girls .
74523	Consequently , very few girls at the foreclosure stage will enter science unless they receive considerable encouragement and a model to do so from their parents and their school .
74524	Neither boys nor girls at the moratorium stage are likely to be attracted to the science that is usually presented in our schools .
74525	They are at a stage when they are likely to be concerned with a variety of complex issues ; the meaning of life , the existence of God , ideologies , their emerging sexuality , their future career and life-style — too often science is seen as being purely instrumental with nothing to contribute to these debates .
74526	Science , somehow , seems to be scarcely relevant to the most important issues in our life .
74527	A proportion of both boys and girls at ego-identity achievement stage will choose science .
74528	In fact , most girls entering science are probably at this stage as they will need some self-examination and sense of commitment to make this unconventional choice .
74529	However , only a minority of adolescents will have reached the ego-identity achievement stage at the age when most pupils have to make crucial decisions about subject choice at school .
74530	This model seems to explain our observations .
74531	A large number of boys , particularly at the foreclosure stage , are initially attracted to science but there is a drift away throughout later adolescence as they undergo some crisis .
74532	The preponderance of boys at the foreclosure stage will yield the rigid , authoritarian attitudes often associated with scientists .
74533	The few girls who enter science will not usually show these foreclosure characteristics .
74534	Effects of Curriculum Changes
74535	The real use of this model linking personality development to subject choice is that it allows us to make predictions about how pupils might react to changes in school science curriculum and school organization .
74536	We can consider three possible changes :
74537	1
74538	Delaying subject choice : Britain is unusual in asking pupils to make crucial choices about subject options in the 13–16 age range .
74539	These decisions can only be reversed with great difficulty .
74540	What effect would delaying the choice make ?
74541	In the development through the years of adolescence the number of foreclosure pupils will diminish , hence the recruitment of boys into science would be cut .
74542	More boys and girls will have reached the ego-identity achievement stage and a proportion of these will go into science .
74543	Overall there would be a reduction in the number of students choosing science , but those who do so choose will be more likely to stay happily in the subject and to possess more flexible minds .
74544	The quantitative loss would be met by a qualitative improvement .
74545	2
74546	Giving science a more feminine image : It is sometimes argued that science textbooks are sexist in showing illustrations of boys , rather than girls , doing practical work in the laboratory , and so forth .
74547	What effect would a deliberate attempt to change this image have ?
74548	It might make it easier for girls at the foreclosure stage to accept science so recruitment might increase .
74549	Some of these girls might , however , drift away again when they reach their crisis period .
74550	Unless the change in image was immense , boys would probably not be affected , science would still be an obvious , acceptable choice for a boy .
74551	Overall there would be some increase in the recruitment of girls , but no qualitative improvement .
74552	3
74553	Emphasizing the applications and relevance of science : To obtain a major qualitative improvement to recruitment in science with more girls and with students possessing imaginative , flexible minds it would be necessary to make science appealing to boys and girls at the moratorium stage .
74554	In that event science must be seen to be relevant to the issues which concern them .
74555	The probable implication is that science would need to be presented in the context of the needs of society and individuals .
74556	Probably a case-study approach involving the application of science , and the interaction with other disciplines , would be needed .
74557	Our knowledge about the girls ' concern with personal relationships suggests that the introduction of some elements of the social sciences into the case studies might prove attractive .
74558	Is it possible to change school science in this fashion and still preserve the essential character of science itself ?
74559	Clearly there would need to be some drastic pruning of content .
74560	Perhaps science teachers should not attempt to cover their subjects so comprehensively .
74561	A history teacher is content to cover the history of one country or continent over a few decades .
74562	Perhaps we must make similar choices .
74563	It is interesting to notice that the Association for Science Education ( 1979 ) policy statement in Britain and the proposals on school physics coming from the Institute for Science Education ( IPN ) in Kiel are advocating such changes .
74564	The difference is that we are now offering a formal psychological model to suggest that if we want to reduce the current encapsulation of science , if we want to recruit a different sort of student , then certain curriculum changes are needed .
74565	Girl Friendly Science and the Girl Friendly School
74566	Judith Whyte
74567	Approximately three times as many boys as girls take O level physics and approximately four times as many take CSE physics .
74568	Over 90 per cent of entries in all technical subjects are from boys .
74569	This means that schoolgirls are ineligible for a wide range of courses in further and higher education and for entry to occupations requiring a scientific or technical base .
74570	Female exclusion from science and technology , even if it is apparently by girls ' own choice , also means that as citizens their ability to understand and control their environment is limited .
74571	Nevertheless , most schools consider they are already providing equal opportunities by neutral treatment of the two sexes ( Bloomfield , 1984 ) .
74572	In effect , ignoring the effects of gender in this way merely reinforces stereotyping because it does nothing to challenge the definition of certain aspects of the curriculum as masculine or feminine .
74573	Girls Into Science and Technology ( GIST ) was the first major schools-based project addressing problems of sex stereotyping at school , and was an example of ‘ action research ’ in education ; the project simultaneously took action to improve girls ' achievement in science and technology and investigated the reasons for their under-achievement .
74574	The project team collaborated with teachers in eight co-educational comprehensive schools in the Greater Manchester area to devise and implement intervention strategies designed to improve girls ' attitudes to the physical sciences and technical subjects .
74575	Two other schools were involved as controls where attitude testing but no interventions took place . [ … ]
74576	The approach was collaborative : teachers were invited to work with the team as equal partners in the attempts both to investigate and find solutions to the GIST problem .
74577	However , very few of the teachers even recognized the issue as one of professional concern at the start of the project , and most of the first two years was spent in establishing the educational importance of the issue and working towards the development of feasible intervention strategies .
74578	The project and its outcomes have been fully described elsewhere ( Smail et al . ,
74579	1982 ; Kelly , Whyte and Smail , 1984 ; Whyte in press ) .
74580	GIST had more success in altering children 's attitudes than their subject choices , suggesting that it is easier to change attitudes and beliefs than actual behaviour .
74581	Pupils in action schools became markedly less stereotyped than pupils in control schools .
74582	They also had slightly more positive attitudes towards science and scientists and were less likely to define them as exclusively masculine .
74583	Despite some evidence of change in teachers ' attitudes and behaviour , they themselves were reluctant to admit that the project had influenced them .
74584	According to an evaluation report this may reflect an unwillingness to admit that in the past schools have been sex biased ( Payne , Cuff and Hustler , 1984 ) .
