77801	This is not because they are immediately transferable to this country but because they illustrate particular features of transition .
77802	The final years of school
77803	The work of Sailor and Wehman in the United States ( Sailor et al .
77804	1989 , Wehman et al .
77805	1989 ) stresses the importance of an effective programme for individuals in high school .
77806	The Comprehensive Local School ( Sailor et al .
77807	1989 ) gives details of school programmes .
77808	Students with severe and profound disabilities and learning difficulties are entitled to attend high school up to the early twenties in the USA .
77809	Thus , the further education element in the United Kingdom is completed in the school system although community colleges do similar work , often with an older age group , in the United States .
77810	Sailor 's book sets out a systematic training programme for young people with severe disabilities ( SLD in this country ) based on modified behavioural approaches .
77811	This starts in the early teens and takes students into real living and working situations .
77812	Experiences in travelling , shopping and taking part in recreational activities in the community are carefully planned with clear behavioural objectives and criteria .
77813	Vocational preparation is done in real situations in the community but use is also made of situations within schools to learn social and work skills .
77814	An individual transition plan
77815	The Individual Education plan ( IEP ) is a central feature of special education in the United States .
77816	An Individual Transition plan is now being introduced to follow this .
77817	The purpose of such plans is to coordinate the contributions of different agencies towards agreed transition goals which have been planned with young people and their families .
77818	The features of such plans and examples of them can be found in the books of Wehman and Sailor .
77819	A guide or point of reference
77820	Because of the variety and confusion of possibilities and responsibilities after the compulsory school period the need for a guide has been widely recognised by young people and their families .
77821	In a study published by OECD/CERI a number of examples are given ( OECD 1990b ) .
77822	One which has received considerable attention is the Kurator system in Denmark .
77823	A Kurator is similar to a specialist careers teacher with additional contributions to make after school .
77824	The Kurator is a member of the school psychologist 's team who teaches children with special educational needs and is responsible for their careers education and work experience .
77825	He or she has a number of non-teaching hours for work with young people and their families after they leave school .
77826	The time available and balance of the Kurator 's work may vary from one municipality to another .
77827	Support can be offered for up to four years after school .
77828	The Kurator is a facilitator who works on request with young people and their families .
77829	Supported employment
77830	One of the most significant developments has been the increasing open employment of young people with severe disabilities , particularly severe intellectual disabilities .
77831	Research in the United States has shown the inadequacy of the sheltered workshop model where commercial objectives limit access for those with severe disabilities and where transfer to open employment is very limited .
77832	Supported open employment is much more successful .
77833	The Genoa approach is one identified by the OECD but there are others in the United States .
77834	The importance of the Genoa experience is that it has the backing of employers and trade union organisations .
77835	Young people are placed in open employment and trained and supported by social service teams .
77836	Salary is paid by the province or state for the first year after which the employer accepts responsibility .
77837	Support teams work with employers and fellow workers in a training programme and are also on call if there are problems .
77838	Results are impressive .
77839	In a city with 12 per cent unemployment 300 recent placements have resulted in an over 90 per cent job retention rate after the first three years of employment .
77840	THE ROLE OF POST-SCHOOL EDUCATION
77841	It is important that those concerned with post-school education for young people with disabilities and learning difficulties are informed about the context in which they work and have a grasp of the essential features of transition .
77842	They also need to be conversant with the main developments taking place in further and continuing education .
77843	Many of the features of effective special education , such as individual programmes and the management of a wide variety of learning rates and styles , are now expected in the mainstream of education and training — for example , work in the Teaching and Vocational Educational Initiative .
77844	The labour market will need to make effective use of the smaller groups leaving school .
77845	To increase the labour force will require that the potential of minority groups , including those with disabilities and learning difficulties , is recognised and that appropriate training and support for them is made available .
77846	The possible introduction of individual education and training vouchers for school leavers will also provide education and training with a new challenge .
77847	Unless the youth group has adequate guidance and counselling , individuals may find choice difficult .
77848	Vouchers may also limit the opportunities of those with special needs unless their value is enhanced to make provision of good-quality training attractive .
77849	A recognition that education post-school is a shared responsibility is vital .
77850	Parents , social workers and other carers have an educational role as do vocational training staff , employers and employees .
77851	This means that lecturers and tutors should work with them to develop programmes and curricula .
77852	But , above all , responsibility must be shared with the young person .
77853	The development of self-presentation , self-advocacy and of self-directed learning should all be central features of this phase of education .
77854	Supporters of those with special needs should be exemplars of such good practice .
77855	Developments of this kind have been initiated and sustained , in recent years , by the Further Education Unit .
77856	Its publications ( FEU 1986 , 1988 , 1989 , 1990c ) are an important source of guidance and good practice .
77857	CONCLUSIONS
77858	Post-school education for young people with disabilities and learning difficulties has had to be fought for .
77859	In the past the case has been based on the wish to delay in unstimulated life it home or admission to a training centre .
77860	Now the grounds are more positive , namely the right to be considered for employment and as a contributor to the economy .
77861	For the individual , employment may represent the most potent symbol of adult status and integration into the community .
77862	What is being sought by many is equality of opportunity and access .
77863	However , there are also positive grounds for governments to invest in education and training for independence and employment .
77864	Research in Scandinavia and the United States has identified the cost of lifelong dependent care for those with disabilities as something developed economies can not sustain in the future .
77865	Only by enabling those with disabilities to contribute , if they wish , through independent living and paid employment , will the increased percentage of ageing people be able to receive the support they expect and need .
77866	Thus , the charity image of disability must disappear .
77867	Higher expectations and effective post-school education for those who have received special education in school is not a luxury but an economic necessity .
77868	The form that post-school education should take is a matter for major discussion beyond the scope of this review .
77869	The rhetoric and reality of transition to adult life
77870	Jenny Corbett and Len Barton
77871	In this chapter Jenny Corbett and Len Barton take a critical look at the concept of ‘ transition into adult life ’ for young people with disabilities and those categorised as having learning difficulties .
77872	They argue that the barriers to participation which exist in society should be given greater recognition .
77873	They discuss the approaches and difficulties encountered in further education and youth training .
77874	They describe a reality in which pressures to exclude and marginalise young people with disabilities or those categorised as having learning difficulties , are still very strong .
77875	INTRODUCTION
77876	This chapter examines the currently popular notion of ‘ transition to adulthood ’ in order to illustrate the complex and contentious nature of integration into adult life .
77877	It is a process of transition which all young people have to pass through but which is experienced differently as a result of such key factors as class , race , gender and disability ( Cross and Smith 1987 , Griffin 1985 , Willis 1977 ) .
77878	Integration into adult life is constricted within social and economic boundaries .
77879	‘ Transition to adulthood ’ involves a wide diversity of progressions beyond school into further education , training programmes , employment and community living .
77880	The extent to which individuals are able to participate in employment , leisure and social interaction , for example , will be an indicator of the reality of their ‘ adulthood ’ .
77881	This broad view offers a wider concept of ‘ integration ’ than the narrow educational framework which predominantly confines debate in this area .
77882	It also places ‘ transition ’ in a political arena in which the tensions between rhetoric and reality are highlighted .
77883	We are concerned to challenge the extent to which those involved in this restricted form of transition are offered any real choices in decision-making .
77884	CONCEPTIONS OF ‘ TRANSITION'
77885	A failure to address the nature of the society into which integration is being advocated reveals the fundamental weakness and inadequacy of much of the literature dealing with this issue .
77886	If integration is seen merely as a response to individual needs , then the unequal , offensive and divisive nature of society remains unchallenged .
77887	Given the degree and stubbornness of such inequalities , the topics that concern us are those of power , choice , entitlement and social justice : issues of rights , not needs .
77888	The question of how to empower those people marginalised through disabilities and learning difficulties is , thus , a central one .
77889	Government documents and official statements concerning integration are replete with romantic and ill-defined language .
77890	The Warnock Report , for example , contends that there is a
77891	widely held and still growing conviction that , so far as is humanly possible , handicapped people should share the opportunities for self-fulfilment enjoyed by other people .
77892	( DES 1978 : 99 )
77893	and the Council of Europe 's Report on Measures to Promote the Social Integration of Mentally Disabled People states that :
77894	The integration of mentally disabled people into society means that persons with mental handicaps of any degree should be able to live as normal a life as possible .
77895	( Council of Europe 1986 : 9 )
77896	just as with these statements about integration , an unchallenged view of ‘ normality ’ is subsumed within the rhetoric of ‘ adulthood ’ .
77897	Adulthood is , thus , largely perceived in consensual terms with the emphasis being upon enabling the individual to be ‘ as normal as possible ’ .
77898	‘ Normality ’ is a nebulous concept unless we ask whose normality is to be valued and emulated ?
77899	As it is professionals who generally define what they regard as ‘ normality ’ , this allows limited scope to negotiate flexible boundaries to accommodate a range of perspectives .
77900	Abberley ( 1989 ) argues that the specific form of normality being advocated becomes disabling in itself as it inhibits expressions of difference .
77901	He claims , moreover , that such a view is
77902	not only profoundly mistaken as to the source and nature of the multiple disadvantages experienced by disabled people , but that its propagation , in the context of modern Britain , serves not to combat but to perpetuate the oppression of disabled people .
77903	( Abberley 1989 : 56 )
77904	The argument of achieving ‘ self-fulfilment ’ and of ‘ living as normal a life as possible ’ is seriously flawed when set against the context of an environment that is essentially oppressive and unadaptive and in which professional power establishes and perpetuates patterns of dependency .
77905	Opportunities for meaningful decision-making on the part of marginalised groups are largely cosmetic .
77906	Barnes ( 1990 ) made a recent study of the role of day centres for disabled young people , in which few opportunities were offered for significant decision-making despite the operation of ostensibly progressive policies .
77907	This research illuminated the contradictions of a transition from passive schooling to day centre provision .
77908	Where young people were not used to making independent decisions and had become conditioned by special education , they found this move into a more adult environment difficult to adjust to .
77909	Staff encouraged debate but these users
77910	appeared to have little interest in the sort of discussion groups generally seen as furthering mutual support and understanding …
77911	The more able in the group felt they ‘ could n't tell us anything we do n't already know ’ or they were ‘ depressing ’ , while the remainder said that they did not like them because they made them feel inadequate .
77912	( Barnes 1990 : 136 )
77913	It is not only the limitations of the day centre model of care but also the legacy of segregated schooling which makes taking over control so difficult .
77914	‘ Transition to adulthood ’ suggests a journey to a substantive destination to which we all travel .
77915	However , the real passage which most of us experience is unpredictable and irregular .
77916	Griffiths argues that
77917	Adulthood is not recognised as a single event evident to everyone .
77918	Instead , a number of small changes in status and recognitions of the progress towards adult status takes place over a number of years .
77919	( Griffiths 1989 : 5 )
77920	There is not one form of adult status but a hierarchy which reflects the way in which society values different groups .
77921	for those at the lowest levels , the quality of this transition places them in a severely restricted form of ‘ adulthood ’ .
77922	For an increasing number of young people , ‘ transition ’ is into vagrancy .
77923	Recent research has illustrated that the raising of the minimum age of entitlement for Income Support in 1988 has forced young people to be dependent on their families and has inhibited their transition to adulthood ( Harris 1988 , Whynes and ferris 1990 ) .
77924	The majority of those young people who leave home to live rough are found not to have chosen this course but , rather , to have had it thrust upon them by circumstances .
77925	Hostels which offer short-term care for the young homeless find their clients are usually the most vulnerable and difficult ( Hutton and Liddiard 1990 ) .
77926	This form of ‘ transition ’ from residential care or the family into homelessness can instil a sense of despair and dependency which becomes habitual .
77927	Wallace and Cross ( 1990 ) suggest that young people in the 1990s are no longer setters of trends but ‘ have become to some objects of pity and concern ’ ( Wallace and Cross 1990 : 7 ) , more vulnerable and dependent than in the recent past .
77928	TRANSITION THROUGH FURTHER EDUCATION
77929	The whole concept of ‘ transition To adulthood ’ is problematic .
77930	The period affects all young people and involves a series of stages over a number of years , which are influenced by social and economic status .
77931	Yet for some it appears to form the focus of their curriculum .
77932	The curriculum for most young people who have left school involves academic or vocational courses which prepare them for specific adult roles .
77933	By contrast , a curriculum for young people with disabilities or learning difficulties often centres around a ‘ preparation for adulthood ’ as if this constitutes a recognisable area of study .
77934	In the curriculum framework for students with severe disabilities called Transition to Adulthood , Hutchinson and Tennyson ( 1986 ) acknowledge that , despite the title of their curriculum and their aim of extending choice , their actual capacity to change current opportunities for students on completion of the programme is negligible .
77935	Thus , the rhetoric of choice and entitlement is met by the reality of devalued citizenship .
77936	The language of such curricula denies the real economic and cultural oppression experienced by disabled people .
77937	Yet Hutchinson and Tennyson are well aware of the frustrations facing their students and seek to combat them :
77938	Jealousy and resentment between the different agencies involved with disabled people are often deeply entrenched and extremely difficult to break down .
77939	‘ Who pays for what ’ often results in essential facilities or care being postponed or withheld indefinitely whilst the ‘ professionals ’ argue the case amongst themselves .
77940	Alternatively , in the present economic climate , the power relationships between the different agencies may result in professionals vying to serve the needs of prospective clients since they have vested interests in defining the needs of their clients and expanding the numbers they serve in order to safeguard their own jobs .
77941	It is all too easy for this system to lead to a ‘ disabling ’ rather than an ‘ enabling ’ context for students ' adult lives , thus negating the benefits of a college-based ‘ Transition to Adulthood ’ course .
77942	( Hutchinson and Tennyson 1986 : 68 — 9 )
77943	The authors go on to offer examples of students whose transition from college has been one of experiencing limited choice and often unsuitable placements .
77944	They even suggest that
77945	Such problems lead us to question the purpose of a ‘ Transition to Adulthood ’ course .
77946	It is felt that much of the progress students make whilst in college will be lost if they are not able to go on to meet fresh demands in new situations .
77947	( Hutchinson and Tennyson 1986 : 72 )
77948	If this form of ‘ transition ’ becomes simply a retrograde return to passivity , it can be seen as a complete negation of all that the college course sought to encourage :
77949	Indeed , it has been said by some professionals in the field that we are doing the students a disservice by attempting to break through their apathy since their main chance of happiness lies in their passive acceptance of traditional ‘ care ’ facilities .
77950	Naturally , we as a staff find this attitude totally unacceptable .
77951	If nothing else we hope that by attending college the students will have gained the confidence and determination to go out into the community and demand that changes be made .
77952	( Hutchinson and Tennyson 1986 : 72 )
77953	Within this framework , ‘ transition ’ becomes a new form of responsibility and awareness , a way of viewing the situation .
77954	A common practice of ‘ transition ’ is that from special school to college of further education .
77955	Despite a commitment to curriculum entitlement ( FEU 1989 ) , institutions have commonly narrowed opportunities by the provision of separate courses or by restricting the participation of disabled students in a full range of general education classes .
77956	Social and life skills classes have often been created with the overt intention of facilitating the integration of students with disabilities ( Dee 1988 ) , yet they may lack certification and have low academic status .
77957	Although notions of autonomy and self-advocacy are central to many courses , there is evident tension between the aims of course tutors and the constraints imposed by parents and post-college opportunities ( Dee 1988 , Wertheimer 1989 ) .
77958	Such ‘ ghettoisation ’ is supported by the familiar practice of transferring special school staff and a skills-based curriculum into special needs departments in colleges .
77959	A move towards student autonomy might be seen in an increasing emphasis upon the value of students entering into negotiation about their individual programmes , including the assessment process .
77960	However , Major ( 1990 ) argues that inequalities of power between student and teacher mitigate against any real negotiation .
77961	fay ( 1988 ) also argues that ‘ negotiating ’ with students can be personally intrusive and involve a hidden assessment of ‘ qualities such as ‘ willingness ’ , ‘ drive ’ , ‘ reliability ’ and even ‘ self-awareness ’ ( fay 1988 : 27 ) .
77962	Fay contends that such activities ‘ colonise private space ’ ( Fay 1988 : 27 ) .
77963	An invasion of privacy into the lives of vulnerable individuals is masked by the rhetoric of empowerment with the implication that it is being ‘ done with rather than to trainees ’ ( fay 1988 : 26 ) .
77964	TRANSITION TO YOUTH TRAINING
77965	Another aspect of transition is that from school to youth training .
77966	This offers programmes in vocational areas such as carpentry , office skills , catering , hairdressing , building , word processing , banking , sport and the arts .
77967	These programmes are of two main kinds : the one based with employers offering the most favourable route to jobs ; the other , workshop-based , simulating employment and with implications of unemployability .
77968	Hollands ( 1990 ) illustrates the way in which young people themselves challenge aspects of the training programmes :
77969	Some young people refuse to accept that they are deficient in the skills and cultures necessary for many working-class jobs .
77970	As such , they often see through life and social skills training and develop common-sense critiques of the curriculum .
77971	( Hollands 1990 : 73 )
77972	In supporting a transition to adulthood , how does youth training differentiate between groups of young people ? for some young Black trainees , disproportionately represented in workshop-based schemes , the programmes serve to shape them into acceptable employees within a market which discriminates against them and to ease them gently out of their aspirations into the reality of restricted choice ( Corbett 1990 ) .
77973	As this liaison officer recognised , the basic level of skills training equipped them only for unskilled work and they had to learn to cope with compromise :
77974	so that even if we get a young person coming out of the workshops that may not be the best electrician going , we can find them something in a related area — an electrical warehouse , where their knowledge of the bits that they know will be put to good use and they 'll still be in that environment they want to work in .
77975	( Liaison Officer 1988 , in Corbett 1990 : 97 )
77976	This ‘ transition ’ is one of learning where you fit into society rather than one of practising choice .
77977	‘ Life skills ’ training supports this delicate process :
77978	Perhaps , not surprisingly , in a short space of time life skills training has become detached from the wider objectives associated with liberal humanist education : the point being that teaching young people about society has been replaced by criteria designed to alter their relationship with it .
77979	( Gleeson 1990 : 188 )
77980	Youth training can act as a form of ‘ moral rescue ’ from the penalty of unemployment , in which trainees perceive their transition into training itself as a form of moral superiority :
77981	George , a former school truant and now a construction trainee , said : ‘ At least I did something … but the others , you saw them at school , just lazy . ’
77982	Others spoke of their gratitude to YTS and how it ‘ worked for me ’ .
77983	It was in this way that YTS helped to sustain an individualistic and divisive work ethic .
77984	( Lee et al .
77985	1990 : 133 )
77986	Within this work ethic , girls are encouraged to accept tasks in Youth Training Scheme ( YTS ) institutional care programmes which prepare them for often distasteful and uncomfortable future roles as unskilled care staff ( Bates 1991 ) .
77987	In exploring the ways in which young people are guided into employment , Bates recognises that .
77988	Young people do not ‘ go gently ’ into employment .
77989	The work required to bring them there is not a bloodless operation .
77990	( Bates 1991 : 1 )
77991	For some young people , especially those in areas of high youth unemployment who are attending special youth training programmes for trainees with learning difficulties , this operation may never succeed in bringing them into employment ( Wilkinson 1990 ) .
77992	Transition through training is shown to be a process in which vulnerable young people are stratified into the slots allotted to them rather than being engaged in real decision-making about future choices .
77993	CONCLUDING REMARKS
77994	Transition is shaped by different opportunities and experiences and is a development which highlights inequalities .
77995	for some young people with disabilities which require a high level of care , this stage can be one of experiencing frustration in the limits of housing provision and support services ( Fiedler 1989 ) .
77996	Their ‘ transition ’ may be no more than being found a placement in residential care after the completion of an independence training college course ( Corbett 1991 ) .
77997	The reality of their adulthood may include exclusion from the labour market ( Oliver 1989 ) .
77998	If they are fortunate enough to become involved in an initiative which supports their progress into employment , this can lead them into another level of experience .
77999	Newman ( 1990 ) described a young man with cerebral palsy employed as a council clerical officer on a Sheltered placement Scheme .
78000	He was assessed as only able to work at 50 per cent of the rate for the job and only half his wages were paid under the scheme .
78001	As it turned out , his skills on the job have led to the department trying to regrade him into a more demanding post .
78002	Without initial support , this transition would have been impractical .
78003	Class , race and gender differences can determine the quality of transition in terms of what training is provided and where it leads .
78004	The level of support which young people receive from parents and mentors will also have a significant effect upon the process of transition , for it is a stage in which their dependency is visibly apparent .
78005	The rise in youth homelessness is a testimony to the need for consistent support during this vulnerable period .
78006	Much of the rhetoric of ‘ transition ’ fails to recognise the complexity of the social world .
78007	It is only within this complexity that ‘ transition to adulthood ’ can be understood .
78008	Supporting special needs in further education
78009	Maureen Turnham
78010	Since 1983 Maureen Turnham has been a lecturer in a college of further education with responsibility for a group of students categorised as having severe learning difficulties who are on a ‘ life-preparation ’ course at her college .
78011	In this chapter she discusses her preconceptions and first impressions of further education , then describes her own and her students ' experience of their course and their attempts to participate with other students in the life of the college .
78012	She questions the selection procedures for students with difficulties and disabilities and discusses the barriers to participation posed by the arrangement of the buildings and people 's attitudes .
78013	She reviews her own changing perceptions in the light of a commitment to equality of opportunity for all learners .
78014	IMPRESSIONS OF FURTHER EDUCATION
78015	My mother saw it .
78016	My colleague saw it and cut it out for me .
78017	I did n't see it but when I was presented with the job advert from a local newspaper the words leapt out at me : ‘ Lecturer : Special needs ’ in the college in the borough where I used to teach before becoming a peripatetic home teacher for pre-school children .
78018	Lecturer !
78019	I remember , several weeks after my successful interview , discussing my impending change of job at a party with a neighbour who works at the local university .
78020	My quizzing about the intellectual world which I was about to enter with some trepidation left him with a wry smile , which puzzled me for some time after , as my naïvety about the world of further education lasted well into my early days in college .
78021	My initial perceptions of a college of further education might have begun on a lofty plane , but I was soon brought down to earth with a bump .
78022	Upon being introduced by the special needs coordinator as the new tutor to a group of students with severe learning difficulties , I heard several groans of ‘ Oh no , we thought we 'd got rid of you … ’ .
78023	Several of my ex-pupils , some of whom I 'd first taught when they were 7 years old , grimaced at me as they carried on preparing their lunch .
78024	They had made the transition to college ‘ inhabitants ’ in the two years since I had left the borough .
78025	It was to take me some time longer to undergo the metamorphosis from a ‘ teacher ’ to a ‘ lecturer ’ .
78026	Some of that initial group of students and myself already had known each other for several years and knew each other 's families .
78027	They all knew my younger sister , for example .
78028	She went to a special school , and continued to be a voluntary helper at the school where I taught when I left .
78029	Some first impressions and , early experiences of college life remain clearly in my mind — what was this new world where the academic staff all taught , but many of them were not ‘ teachers ’ like me but engineers or nurses or painters and decorators ?
78030	My knowledge of the history of further education , and of how my college had evolved from a county technical college , was scant .
78031	I was thrown into a jungle of new jargon .
78032	The language of special education had long been tucked under my belt , but now I was faced with filling in timetables with terms such as ‘ DD ’ time — departmental duties , to the uninitiated — in other words , time when I was not actually in direct teaching contact with students .
78033	College induction programmes for staff new to FE were in their infancy at that time and I probably felt content in the knowledge of my own ‘ expertise ’ .
78034	After all , I had nine years ' experience in special education .
78035	Surely , further education could not be so different ?
78036	THE DEVELOPING ‘ SPECIAL NEEDS ’ PROVISION
78037	Seven years later , my experience of further education has grown and my perceptions of it have inevitably changed .
78038	Our college 's initial provision for ‘ students with special needs ’ was established in 1978 — a ‘ discrete ’ course for students with moderate learning difficulties or , in some instances , school leavers from high schools who needed extra support before joining training schemes .
78039	The lecturer appointed to teach the students , who was later to become the college 's special needs coordinator , once told me about those early beginnings as ‘ part of the Engineering Department , based in a hut on the field ’ .
78040	For a long time I assumed she was joking , but not only was I wrong , I was also ignorant of the hard facts of life about the value of students with special needs and the staff who work with them .
78041	Talking to colleagues from other establishments at a conference some years later , I was struck by the similarities in their early beginnings — often in a portacabin or separate annexe from the main college building , or in accommodation previously occupied by a school .
78042	Stories of inferior accommodation , equipment and materials , effectively deemed to be ‘ good enough ’ for students with special needs , seemed to far outweigh reports of a stated commitment for those students being backed up by provision that was dignified and appropriate .
78043	The life preparation course
78044	In 1983 we began to provide a course for students with severe learning difficulties .
78045	This provision was established as a result of several pressures , not least of all parental lobbying for an alternative option to adult training centres .
78046	For many young adults with severe learning difficulties this was not much more than a decade after they became ‘ entitled ’ to full-time education .
78047	A former school for children with severe learning difficulties , a single-storey building three miles from the main site , therefore became a college annexe .
78048	It began as , and has remained , the base for nursery nurse students and for ‘ life preparation ’ students ( referred to not as ‘ special needs ’ students but prefixed by the title of the course they are following — the same as other students ! ) .
78049	The building also houses the relevant staff , including the senior lecturer who is the college 's special needs coordinator .
78050	Opportunities for the integration of students were present from the beginning .
78051	For instance , there is a shared student common room , shared toilet facilities for all students ( there is one adapted toilet/bathroom ) , and equal access to facilities such as the juke box ( donated by the Students ' Union , but removed when it failed to show a profit ! ) and the vending machines .
78052	The annexe has few refectory facilities , and on some days it seems that the queue for the coffee machine snakes endlessly around the corridors .
78053	During queuing periods , there have been occasions when I have witnessed nursery nurse students , with the best of intentions , ‘ helping ’ life preparation students , for example by operating the machine for them or by ‘ allowing ’ them to jump the queue .
78054	I have to admit that , in the early days , it was with mixed feelings that I intervened — suggesting , for example , that life preparation students really ought to take their turn the same as anyone else .
78055	The mixed feelings were , perhaps , a little cowardly on my part .
78056	While I saw no justification for positive discrimination in the coffee queue , I was aware that prejudice can stem from the most unexpected beginnings .
78057	Something as innocuous as suggesting to another student that a life preparation student should be allowed to take the coins out of her purse unaided may , inadvertently , upset the nursery nurse student in the short term .
78058	However , in the long term , I feel sure that continuing input ( both formal and informal ) into initial nursery nurse training can only serve to extend students ' knowledge about the nature and implications of severe learning difficulties .
78059	How nursery nurses and other students choose to use this knowledge is another matter entirely .
78060	Joint craft
78061	Conscious of our lack of truly integrated teaching sessions , and freshly inspired by a successful ‘ joint ’ activity weekend at a local Outward Bound Centre , we made plans to change the structure of one particular curriculum area .
78062	It was decided that a double staffed session of craft , with one group of life preparation students and one group of nursery nurse students would be on the timetable once a week .
78063	The nursery nurses were initially given a talk on the nature of what was , in essence , a pilot scheme for functional integration .
78064	It was explained that it was hoped that they would ‘ befriend ’ a life preparation student for craft sessions , working alongside each other on a variety of projects .
78065	The projects were pitched at different levels , so that in the strictest sense the students were working in a parallel fashion .
78066	Although this pilot was not monitored formally , it was hailed by participating students and staff as an unreserved success , generating a substantial commitment to equality for students with severe learning difficulties , and a sound knowledge , on a practical level , of many of their needs .
78067	One unexpected spin-off was the growth of a few genuine friendships .
78068	The increase in confidence in many of the life preparation students was another benefit .
78069	Flushed with success we repeated this timetabled session , with the original members of staff , the following year with different students .
78070	The results were disappointing .
78071	With hindsight , there were ‘ rumblings ’ from some nursery nurses during the early stages of the course , but the matter only came to a head when a small group of nursery nurses made a formal complaint to a course tutor .
78072	They felt that they were ‘ not getting on ’ with their craft work or were ‘ held back by the students with severe learning difficulties ’ .
78073	The outcome was that a second room was negotiated and the students returned to the pattern of separate and segregated groups .
78074	During a further meeting about the problems , some of the nursery nurse staff expressed their concern over the attitude of this group of students .
78075	They felt that their students are in the caring field and ‘ ought naturally to empathise with students with severe learning difficulties ’ .
78076	I would question this , as I feel we are treading on dangerous ground if we even contemplate trying to impose our values in this way , however strongly we feel personally .
78077	It seems obvious to me now that several factors involved could have been given more thought .
78078	There could have been greater consultation with both nursery nurse and life preparation students and due consideration given to the fact that completed craft projects are an important part of a nursery nurse 's final assessment .
78079	We now have an opportunity to benefit from lessons learned , as , during the past year , we have undertaken a pilot scheme to integrate life preparation students with Sports and Leisure students who are following a City and Guilds course .
78080	Feeling established
78081	Our life preparation student numbers have grown continually and encompassed students from outside the district as happens on other such courses .
78082	This was partly because our college 's provision for students with severe learning difficulties was being recommended by careers officers from other authorities .
78083	A pat on the back !
78084	It felt like confirmation that we had got it right .
78085	This seemed to be further corroborated when we were invited to join the second phase of a research project being undertaken by the National Foundation for Educational Research and the Further Education Unit .
78086	Other colleagues working in schools or adult training centres from our authority were also asked to participate , as together we had previously set up a voluntary curriculum development group to look at authority-wide provision for young people and adults with severe learning difficulties .
78087	This group had met almost every week for nearly two years .
78088	The national research project resulted in the publication of New Directions : A Curriculum Framework for Students with Severe Learning Difficulties in early 1988 ( Dee 1988 ) .
78089	Curriculum principles
78090	From the very beginnings of the ‘ life preparation ’ course , we tried to write an independence curriculum , and to follow the principles of ‘ normalisation ’ .
78091	Every opportunity to maximise the differences between school and college life was seized .
78092	For instance , the college day for life preparation students is the same length as for other students .
78093	The possibilities for integration , that do not exist in a segregated , all-age special school , are many — as students begin to mix , sometimes for the first time , in a community setting with other adult learners .
78094	The college environment may offer less ‘ protection ’ than their school , but it offers the chance to broaden horizons .
78095	One example of this is in the chance to meet and work with non ‘ special needs ’ staff .
78096	Students have the opportunity to join the college library and are encouraged to join the Students ' Union .
78097	They are given a copy of their own group 's timetable , whether or not they can read , and they are timetabled in a variety of rooms , with different tutors on two different sites .
78098	Travelling is done on public transport — we have a college minibus which tutors can book for residentials , visits and regular timetabled activities , such as the Leisure Centre .
78099	Supervisory duties at break and lunch-time are carried out by non-teaching assistants .
78100	In general , the staff/student ratio is rarely as good as in a school for children and young people with severe learning difficulties .
78101	However , as our special needs coordinator rightly emphasises ‘ we are a college — not an extended special school ’ .
78102	The whole ethos of a college of further education is different to that of a special school — from the funding and the staffing to the size and complexity of the sites .
78103	We share the annexe base with nursery nurse students and staff .
78104	An early rule of thumb became ‘ if the nursery nurses do n't do it , neither do we ’ .
78105	We talked with our students about the freedoms of college life , and suggested that they might judge whether or not certain behaviour was ‘ age appropriate ’ by looking at the nursery nurses ( incorrectly and naïvely assuming the latter would unfailingly provide the models we sought ! ) .
78106	This mechanism ended in total failure when , after lengthy and various attempts to persuade several female life preparation students to give up wearing white ankle socks in favour of tights , short socks , mostly white , suddenly became very fashionable and seemed to adorn every other pair of ankles in the building .
78107	With hindsight , I question some of my early motives and certainly now see different ways of exploring choices with students .
78108	One route for beginning to make informed choices is through self-advocacy , where students are encouraged either to speak up for themselves or to use an advocate who speaks on their behalf .
78109	Self-advocacy complements ‘ normalisation ’ and it is an issue which , recently , staff have actively begun to promote .
78110	The Open University 's Patterns for Living : Working Together has generated much interest in this area ( Open University 1989 ) .
78111	Selection procedures
78112	At present , we select students for the life preparation course , following a baseline assessment devised by myself and colleagues which is carried out during a links week when potential students attend college full time .
78113	We did n't have interviews , but a young person had to ‘ gain' a place none the less , as we had criteria for entry onto the course .
78114	I suppose I felt that this fitted in neatly with the selection process for other students .
78115	Also , we had no ‘ medical ’ back-up , as is often the case in special schools , therefore we felt unable to meet the needs of students with profound multiple disabilities .
78116	I can recall talking to Lesley Dee , ‘ New Directions ’ project leader , about her teaching experience in South Thames college and her approach to ‘ FE for all ’ .
78117	When she spoke about learning difficulties or special needs she included everyone , even young people with severe ‘ challenging behaviour ’ .
78118	This represented a very different target group to the one with which I was familiar , and it seemed an alien approach to me .
78119	I was worried that it could dilute or blunt our provision .
78120	I thought that it undermined the satisfaction of ‘ getting a place in college ’ for students with severe learning difficulties .
78121	However , I now realise that perhaps the only person who felt intimidated by ‘ FE for all ’ was me .
78122	Our selection procedure has resulted in no places being offered to students with profound or multiple disabilities or severe challenging behaviour .
78123	Our selection procedure still exists , but I want to see it changed to one which is more equitable .
78124	National reflections currently focus upon the need for college to be ‘ responsive ’ in order to ensure that individuals can gain access to the curriculum ‘ regardless of any disability or special learning need they may have ’ ( FEU 1990 : 11 ) .
78125	In considering the issue of entitlement to access , my college would be required to look at two groups of learners hitherto excluded — students with profound or multiple disabilities and students with challenging behaviour .
78126	The life preparation course , in its present form , is unlikely to meet their specific needs , but the curricular content could serve as a starting point for designing new provision which would .
78127	The possible stumbling blocks would be financial and attitudinal barriers to these learners .
78128	It is my belief that our life preparation students are not ‘ valued ’ by many colleagues , so how would they react to learners seen to be ‘ less able ’ or more difficult to cope with ?
78129	COUNTERING OBSTACLES TO INCLUSION
78130	There are a number of issues which still concern me about continuing education for students with disabilities , just as they did when I entered college life — for example , the fear and ignorance that often surrounds this seemingly homogeneous condition known as ‘ disability ’ , and the unmitigated prejudice and stereotyping of people who do not ‘ fit ’ into a mythical category commonly known as ‘ normal ’ .
78131	However , I hope I am not so complacent that I am unable to acknowledge the difficulties of trying to bring about change .
78132	It is a lengthy and wearing process .
78133	Attempting to challenge and change the attitudes of individuals who feel discomfort or exhibit prejudice when faced with the possibility , or reality , of encountering people with disabilities is both a responsibility in my job and intrinsic to my personality .
78134	I believe in the precept of ‘ person first , disability second ’ .
78135	I believe that students with disabilities need to be valued as people , and any establishment that implies this on paper needs to put policy into practice .
78136	Our college , and authority , now has an equal opportunities policy document .
78137	I am departmental representative on the Equal Opportunities Sub-committee .
78138	When the college policy and the sub-committee was first constituted , I was enthusiastic — teeth at last !
78139	Unfortunately , two years later , we are trying to rectify an original omission — the word ‘ disability ’ does not appear in the policy document .
78140	Unfortunately , it is not possible to just insert the word ‘ disability ’ into the document , as there are several procedures which must be adhered to , not least of all submission to the governors appointed since financial delegation some months ago .
78141	I failed to realise for some considerable time the importance of commitment from the top down .
78142	Once again it was during some exchanges with colleagues from other establishments that I began to realise the significance of ‘ who is on your side ’ .
78143	Senior management who truly support the right to continuing education for all learners are worth their weight in gold to lecturers who may be struggling to persuade colleagues , in their own department/school/division or otherwise , that students with special needs are entitled to be included in the further education system .
78144	Negative statements such as ‘ I do n't know how you can work with them ’ or ‘ they do n't belong here — this is a college ’ , which were once like a red rag to a bull to me , no longer insult or injure as they did .
78145	I have grown used to the fact that I will never ‘ convert ’ some colleagues however enthusiastic , persuasive or reasoned I am .
78146	I no longer vociferously challenge those who insult ; instead , I may casually invite them to come for a coffee and see/meet some students .
78147	Alternatively , if faced with a determined ‘ It 's not on …
78148	I/we are not trained/paid/ supposed to teach these students ’ , I do not launch into a tirade on equal opportunities but try to draw breath instead and substitute a concerned ear about the anxieties of dealing with students seen to be different .
78149	It 's not always easy or straightforward , and I still have difficulty in dealing with such sweeping generalisations as : ‘ he 's a Down 's Syndrome — they can be very stubborn , ca n't they ? ’ ; ‘ mentally handicapped … they can be quite violent if they do n't get their own way ’ .
78150	Apart from the danger in such misconceptions , the terminology used by some colleagues when referring to anyone with a disability can be disturbing .
78151	I refer to my students by name and would never refer to any of them as ‘ a Down 's Syndrome ’ , just as I would never refer to any of my friends who wear contact lenses as ‘ a myopic ’ .
78152	Students with learning difficulties do encounter prejudice , and confronting prejudice is rarely an easy task .
78153	As a group , they are marginalised in a society that places a high value on being clever and articulate .
78154	Within a large establishment such as a college it is unlikely that they will avoid some name-calling or jokes at their expense .
78155	We do have strategies that can be used — from advising the students with learning difficulties to ignore insults , to implementing the equal opportunities policy which finds such discrimination to be indefensible .
78156	Questions of physical access
78157	The physical barriers to integration for students who have special needs will undoubtedly continue to pose problems in my own establishment , and those of colleagues , and are due , not least of all , to the ever-increasing constraints of finances .
78158	At the time of writing , plans to join two buildings with a walkway to improve access to the second building , which has no lift , have been scrapped .
78159	In the current financial climate , which sees us wrestling with colleges managing their own budgets and , in our own authority , reeling from the outcome of poll-capping , the expenses involved in improving physical access are likely to be competing with numerous other worthy but expensive causes .
78160	Physical barriers to integration often receive much publicity .
78161	However , it is not good enough to assume that physical restrictions to access to college buildings can be removed , in one fell swoop , by the construction of a ramp or the fitting of a handrail .
78162	The ramp , for instance , needs to be of the correct gradient , something which , in my experience of discussing such matters with colleagues , appears to be overlooked with alarming frequency !
78163	I discovered that , for instance , one of our students was unable to propel her wheelchair up the ramped entrance to our annexe , a former special school building , without the dangerous likelihood of tipping backwards .
78164	A subsequent ramp built on to a fire exit out of one of the rooms was better , though the aforementioned student had long since left .
78165	Any ‘ make do and mend ’ philosophy which applies to facilities and provision for any group of learners , including students with disabilities , is regrettable and short-sighted .
78166	Regrettable because it compounds a belief that there is a group of learners with lower status that the rest because they have been labelled as having ‘ special needs ’ .
78167	Short-sighted because no amount of patchwork planning can be a substitute for a blueprint for services that has commitment , consultation and collaboration ingrained , like a name through candy rock .
78168	THE FUTURE
78169	There are new developments ahead in FE , such as new funding arrangements , which I hope will not add to the difficulties of access for any student who may require specific support for learning .
78170	There are also planned changes within community living which are likely to have significant implications as ‘ different ’ client groups such as ex-patients from long-stay hospitals move into the community .
78171	The need for a student-centred approach , perhaps not always present in some sectors of FE , is likely to become increasingly vital to tailoring programmes to meet the individual needs of those learners not traditionally seen as ‘ student material ’ .
78172	Very recently , some of ‘ our ’ students have , like many of their peers , ‘ voted with their feet ’ .
78173	They did not turn up for sessions they considered boring and did not meet their needs .
78174	They are speaking up for themselves and expecting , rightly , that they will be listened to by staff and that their opinions will have the same validity as those of the next person .
78175	The current emphasis upon ‘ empowerment ’ , and the belief that ‘ the more self-empowered a person becomes , the more able he or she will be to enable others to be the same ’ ( Fenton and Hughes 1989 : 19 ) , is effecting a shift in approach generally , and in my own personal practice , from a passive model of students .
78176	My earlier justifications of an elitist selection procedure for our target group of students are incompatible with my commitment to equality of opportunity .
78177	I obviously can not swear allegiance to the principles of equal opportunities then justify the exclusion of some students purely because of the severity of their disability .
78178	However , the access route to our college for these students with additional difficulties seems likely to be long and winding , requiring commitment not only from staff such as myself , but also from those senior staff who are the policy-makers and who control the purse strings .
78179	Many changes would need to be made to meet the needs of those learners .
78180	These are likely to range from an amendment to our current equal opportunities policy document ( correcting the omission of ‘ disability ’ ) to a need to employ more staff , possibly from another discipline such as health .
78181	In a climate of radical spending cuts , the latter seems highly unlikely .
78182	Putting theory into practice is far from simple .
78183	Nevertheless , my beliefs have changed over the last years and the message is clear : I no longer think in terms of ‘ further education for not quite all ’ but of providing access to learning for everyone .
78184	A hard journey in the right direction
78185	Experiencing life beyond an institution
78186	Linda Shaw
78187	In this chapter , Linda Shaw describes her experiences of supporting Elizabeth and Helen in their South London flat — initially as a member of their team of workers and later as a friend .
78188	Her knowledge of and friendship with the two women also enable her to describe what life was like from their point of view .
78189	Elizabeth and Helen were living in the community after many years in an institution for people classified as ‘ mentally handicapped ’ .
78190	Linda describes the details of their daily lives , the problems that arose in trying to set up a network of support that was sufficient , stable and yet not undermining of the women 's growing independence , and the different reactions of Elizabeth and Helen to their new life .
78191	Despite the difficulties and the continuing insecurity of support , Linda concludes that life for Elizabeth and Helen has been improved by their time in the community and that the hard journey is worth it .
78192	INTRODUCTION
78193	Elizabeth and Helen moved into their own basement flat in an inner-city suburb in 1987. they are middle-aged and spent nearly thirty years together at the same mental handicap hospital but lived separately for the two years before the move into the community because Helen was transferred to a smaller institution .
78194	The move was part of the ‘ community care ’ initiative adopted by health authorities to provide housing and support services in ordinary settings for people with learning difficulties .
78195	I was a member of the health service team supporting Elizabeth and Helen at the time of the move and I have stayed in touch with them since , as a friend and advocate .
78196	I have written this account on their behalf , based on my knowledge of the women , observations of their lifestyle , and discussions with them and their support workers .
78197	The women 's real names and some details about their lives have been disguised to protect their privacy .
78198	STARTING AN ORDINARY LIFE
78199	More than two years after the move from institution to ordinary housing , Elizabeth and Helen are still learning about community living and adjusting to its demands and possibilities .
78200	The women 's days are beginning to include the mix of activities , experiences and relationships which make up ordinary life for most people .
78201	Their daily routines are starting to reflect their preferences and abilities and to include a level of personal responsibility .
78202	As well as having to adapt to major changes in their status , environment , lifestyle and relationships , Elizabeth and Helen have to cope with the adjustments made by the people on whom they depend .
78203	Health service staff and managers are still developing the new skills and the framework necessary to offer a quality community care service .
78204	Neighbours and business people , many of whom are confronting disability for the first time , have yet to work out ways of behaving with respect towards them and ways of making links which are welcome and helpful .
78205	The women 's long separation from the mainstream means that increasing their participation in ordinary life is an inevitable learning process for everybody involved .
78206	The realisation that the transition from exclusion to inclusion is a slow manoeuvre and that community care evolves rather than happens became clear soon after Elizabeth and Helen arrived at their new home .
78207	The first few months of life in the community were dominated by support workers ' sense of heavy responsibility about the twin tasks of meeting the women 's physical and medical needs and , at the same time , enabling them to be as independent as possible .
78208	One member of the staff team of nine had nursing training ; two had been teachers and the rest were from a variety of other backgrounds .
78209	The balance between doing too much and doing too little for Elizabeth and Helen , who both use wheelchairs , had to be continuously readjusted .
78210	Staff received basic instructions , but the appropriate ways to help each woman with personal care , diet and medication ( for epilepsy ) had to be worked out through discussion with the helpers .
78211	From the beginning of her tenancy Helen took pride in having a home of her own .
78212	She coped well with the change-over and immediately welcomed any opportunity to take part in household activities .
78213	‘ It 's my job ’ , is her prompt response to any attempt to take over tasks she wants to do herself .
78214	Helen 's ability to enjoy herself and express her objections effectively make her an easy person to help , although she is sometimes criticised for being demanding .
78215	Elizabeth found the move to community living much more difficult .
78216	On many occasions during those first few months , she was moody , tearful and uncommunicative .
78217	At the worst times she refused to leave her armchair in the lounge all day and occasionally overnight , saying she was too frightened to go to bed or to the bathroom .
78218	She cut herself off from comfort by clenching her fists , screaming and occasionally kicking when people approached .
78219	She was also frightened of doing housework and passed on jobs to a support worker , announcing : ‘ She can do it . ’
78220	professional advice about Elizabeth 's unhappiness was that she was in a state of ‘ mourning ’ and that time would improve matters .
78221	In those early stages , support workers , who were highly motivated to give Elizabeth and Helen a ‘ better life ’ , felt that the demands of the women 's physical needs , together with Elizabeth 's state of mind , undermined hopes for their social progress .
78222	The basic business of looking after them felt so demanding and emotionally wearing that there seemed little rime left to introduce them to ‘ real living ’ .
78223	WIDENING HORIZONS
78224	Looking back , there 's no doubt that we were too impatient and were unprepared for the major impact of the change from institution to community care on all concerned .
78225	As the third anniversary of the women 's arrival in the community approaches , there is a marked improvement in Elizabeth 's sense of well-being and greater participation by both women in activities beyond domestic and care routines .
78226	The women may spend large parts of the day on personal care , preparing and clearing up after meals and doing their laundry .
78227	They have to overcome difficulties to accomplish these tasks so the amount of time involved increases the more the women participate and the less support workers take over .
78228	Although lengthy domestic and care routines are to some extent a reality of disability , it is necessary to work out a level of sharing between the women and their staff which allows a varied day and does not make a drudge out of anybody .
78229	A typical day for Elizabeth and Helen includes the usual range of personal and domestic tasks involved in looking after themselves and their flat with support , together with popular leisure activities such as watching television and listening to music .
78230	Helen may do some painting and Elizabeth likes to work at drawing shapes and picking out words as first steps in reading and writing .
78231	Some form of keep fit exercises or dancing in the flat is a feature on most days as are trips out to pursue activities in connection with their developing social programme .
78232	Such social activities as going to adult education classes , taking trips out in their car , going to church , visiting friends and being visited , now happen on a more regular basis .
78233	Around the time I was compiling this report the women attended three adult education classes a week — for music , keep-fit and self-advocacy .
78234	They had recently been on separate holidays , met support workers ' families at their homes , danced at a party and had their photographs taken cuddling the few weeks ' old daughter of a woman Elizabeth met at church .
78235	A trip to London was planned and they were expecting two visits — one from an elderly relative who 'd been in touch after receiving a holiday postcard and another from two people who used to live in the flat upstairs and had telephoned asking if they could call by .
78236	Elizabeth compiled the following list , with support , of what she likes about living in her own home .
78237	Because of Helen .
78238	Going out .
78239	Likes seeing Linda .
78240	Likes the workers .
78241	Because of my car .
78242	Going to church .
78243	Having visitors .
78244	Having a fish tank .
78245	Elizabeth was also asked if she would like to make a list of what she does not like about community living but could not think of anything for the moment .
78246	She says that in the future , in addition to her current activities , she wants to learn to read and write and to plant flowers in the garden .
78247	She does not want to do housework .
78248	Helen is not interested in making lists about her life , preferring to talk about the more immediate experiences of her recent holiday and birthday .
78249	Her speech is not easy to understand but she effectively communicates her complete approval and enjoyment of the busy week when she went away .
78250	She 'd been ‘ everywhere ’ , she says , raising her arms and pointing in many different directions .
78251	She is an outgoing , cheerful person with an ability to communicate her feelings , to get along , and find enjoyment in most situations .
78252	She often opens conversations by telling people brightly : ‘ I got up this morning ’ , which seems to reflect her talent for being delighted by what is deeply ordinary .
78253	Helen 's main problems since she moved into her own home have been a period of illness , which caused her much discomfort , and a spate of difficulties in accepting personal care from temporary staff .
78254	Helen 's personality does not seem to have altered significantly since her move into the community , although she has become more tolerant .
78255	In general , she has simply become more herself ; opportunities to participate have increased and she has responded to most of them enthusiastically .
78256	Elizabeth , on the other hand , has changed significantly .
78257	For a start she looks different .
78258	She is slimmer and looks more of a woman , in clothes which are appropriate for her age .
78259	She slouches less in her wheelchair , raises her head more and looks at people in a more direct manner .
78260	She says she does not like housework but she can manage some tasks .
78261	She can count out and administer her own drugs and explain her own needs during visits to the doctor .
78262	She is exceptionally good company when she is happy .
78263	She is curious and asks many questions about people and situations around her , including her own disabilities and difficulties .
78264	She works hard to understand issues which confuse her and is learning to be patient with herself when , as she puts it , her brain ‘ gets stuck ’ .
78265	She expresses much appreciation for what she considers beautiful and is beginning to show and receive affection .
78266	How to tell when a person has become a friend is the latest of many difficult questions to which Elizabeth struggles to find answers .
78267	Elizabeth is learning to speak up for herself .
78268	She says ‘ no ’ more often , rather than suffering or withdrawing , and she is able to remind people of her difficulty in concentrating on more than one thing at a time .
78269	I received a straightforward message recently when I telephoned her flat for a chat : ‘ Elizabeth says she 's busy . ’
78270	She is sorting out the conundrum of being a ‘ high grade ’ in hospital and a ‘ person with a disability ’ in the community .
78271	At times it surely is very difficult for her .
78272	She still has periods of withdrawal and sadness but they are decreasing .
78273	A SHAKY SUPPORT NETWORK
78274	Community care for Elizabeth and Helen involves an extraordinary network of services which has yet to operate to full capacity and efficiency .
78275	Elizabeth and Helen have made progress despite the weakness and unpredictability of this shaky , official safety net .
78276	It is a constant concern that they might have achieved much more if services had been better and that they may regress if services do n't improve .
78277	The women 's direct support comes from a staff team working in twos at their flat during the day with one person sleeping overnight .
78278	Behind this front line is a complicated structure of health , social , housing and financial services , management and monitoring systems .
78279	During the first years of the women 's life in the community , the full-time team of health authority support workers has been regularly understaffed , with temporary cover being provided by a private nursing agency .
78280	None of the original team who were with the women at the time of the move still work at their flat .
78281	I left the team because the low pay would not cover the cost of my share in a mortgage to buy my own flat , and because I found it difficult to reconcile the separate roles of paid worker and friend , when Helen and Elizabeth recognised no such distinction .
78282	I was sad to leave but felt that a turnover of paid staff was unavoidable with the present pay and conditions .
78283	I reassured myself that nothing could stop me keeping in touch with the women on a voluntary basis , provided they wished to remain friends .
78284	The period during which I have been writing this chapter has seen one of the worst staffing levels ever at the women 's flat .
78285	At one stage half the permanent health service posts were unfilled and agency staff worked in the flat on a daily basis .
78286	The consortium responsible for looking after the women 's housing and financial affairs , as well as providing some monitoring of the quality of service , had temporarily to reduce its operations because of staff shortages .
78287	Members of the health authority team set up to give advice on the ‘ physical , psychological , communication and mental health needs ’ of people with learning difficulties are often difficult to contact when support workers want to discuss problems relating to the women .
78288	It is only recently that Elizabeth and Helen have had the benefit of a full-time manager whose job is to provide support , supervision and leadership to staff working in their home .
78289	The effective operation of an Individual programme plan ( IPP ) for each woman is a major casualty of the haphazard delivery of services .
78290	The IPP is a system for mapping out individual goals , specifying means of achievement and assigning responsibility for progress .
78291	It is the most reliable method available for trying to ensure that the principles of community care policy agreed by the health authority — community presence , community participation , competence , respect and choice — are actually made available to the users of a service .
78292	The system aims to involve service users , and their friends and relatives , in planning individual lifestyles in the community , working out strategy and reviewing progress .
78293	The written document produced in the process belongs to service users and provides them with necessary information to challenge service providers if they do n't fulfil their contributions to the plan .
78294	The Individual Programme Plans of Elizabeth and Helen , which took two attempts to get off the ground because of staff changes and inadequate training , have been virtually suspended — even before the first reviews — because of the latest staffing upheaval .
78295	Support staff who remain with the women worry increasingly about the lack of continuity .
78296	They are concerned that agency staff and new staff who do n't know what the women have achieved will undermine progress , or even reverse it , by underestimating their capabilities .
78297	The lack of fully operational IPPs , which could have provided a safeguard against inconsistency , adds to workers ' anxiety that Elizabeth and Helen are being let down .
78298	While the community care service sorts out its shortfalls , Elizabeth 's enthusiasm to learn to read and write could be overtaken by boredom and depression .
78299	Helen 's frustration with people who do n't appreciate her could result in a marked reduction in her tolerance level .
78300	According to one worker there had already been an occasion when she found Helen being ‘ fed , wiped and pushed round the house ’ .
78301	Support workers also worry about the effect of setbacks on the generally negative attitudes of many people in the community to people with learning difficulties .
78302	‘ It 's a vicious circle ’ , explained one worker .
78303	‘ people with learning difficulties are not respected to begin with and because the women 's Individual Programmes , including skills training , are not in place , they are not progressing as well as they could and they are not getting respect . ’
78304	A senior manager agreed that because of staff shortages in the flat , planning and development for the women had taken second place to ‘ keeping people afloat ’ .
78305	When new staff were appointed development could move ahead again .
78306	Regarding community care in general in the authority the manager insisted , ‘ We have n't got there yet , but we are certainly going in the right direction . ’
78307	Elizabeth and Helen express rather similar sentiments about their new way of life .
78308	‘ It 's all right ’ , ‘ I feel all right ’ , they say .
78309	‘ I 'm happy ’ , ‘ I 'm settled ’ , ‘ Now I know what it feels like ’ , ‘ I got out on the right side ’ .
78310	They have not expressed any wish to return to living in an institution full time , although Helen occasionally likes to visit the hospital where she was a resident immediately before the move into the community .
78311	And while support staff are adamant about the need for improvements in services and organisation , nobody believes the women would be better off returning to institutional care .
78312	CONCLUSION
78313	Elizabeth and Helen 's initial experience of life in the community has brought them unhappiness and difficulties .
78314	There has also been much learning , laughter and warmth which has extended the enjoyment and understanding of everybody involved .
78315	The new community care service has enabled the women to claim their places as citizens in their neighbourhood and take a tentative hold of a share in the goodness of ordinary life .
78316	Opportunities have become available to them which would have been impossible in hospital .
78317	From the women 's point of view , the need in the future is for a more reliable and responsive support network and a wider circle of friends and acquaintances to help them strengthen their hold on , and increase their share of , life in the community .
78318	THE EXPERIENCE OF FAMILIES
78319	Fools and heretics
78320	Parents ' views of professionals
78321	Chris Goodey
78322	In this chapter Chris Goodey reflects on the diagnosis , assessment and categorisation procedures employed by ‘ professionals ’ : doctors , psychologists , teachers and administrators .
78323	He argues that such procedures and the decisions about a child 's acceptability within mainstream education which may follow from them , are underpinned by competing philosophies about a child 's acceptability as a human being .
78324	It is this philosophy , he argues , rather than a body of technical knowledge , which drives the behaviour of professionals in their interactions with parents .
78325	He supports these contentions with the words of parents of children with trisomy 21 whose reactions to , and following , the birth of their children belie the simplified professional stereotypes which he sets beside them .
78326	He concludes by suggesting that membership of the group that accepts children with disabilities as full members of the human tribe , is open to all .
78327	A HUMAN FAILING
78328	What is it to be human ?
78329	The segregation of school pupils who have disabilities or learning difficulties poses this question immediately .
78330	Professionals segregate according to expert criteria , but ‘ what is it to be human ? ’ sounds like a philosophical question — in which case it is also a political one — rather than something for experts to decide .
78331	We as a group , defining ourselves as human , decide whom to include and whom to exclude as members of this group .
78332	We do it when we decide what it is acceptable for people to be able or unable to do .
78333	We do it when we decide that someone is unable to attend a school we have already described as ‘ comprehensive ’ .
78334	We do it when we decide that the sibling rule — that a child can attend the same school as a brother or sister — does not apply ( the assumption here must surely be that siblings can belong to different species ) .
78335	Alongside the ideal common sense of the saying , ‘ Nothing human is alien to me ’ , we operate the opposite principle too : nothing alien is human to me .
78336	In our own society we leave it to certain specialised people to decide , in practice , who is alien to the species and where the alien should be put .
78337	Expert classifications of disability and difficulty , and the apparatus of assessment that goes with them , appear to be scientifically objective .
78338	But in fact this appearance is only the distorted mirror-image of the reality I have described .
78339	We have already chosen , more or less deliberately , whom we want to belong and whom not .
78340	We then invent criteria to back up the choice , delegating our responsibility to professional specialists .
78341	The appearance of scientific objectivity is painted on afterwards .
78342	It gives credibility to the particular choice we as a self-defining ‘ human ’ group have made , and reinforces the validity of that choice by obscuring the fact that we make it voluntarily , rather than have it imposed on us by scientific laws which are unquestionable and necessary .
78343	If it is all just a matter of philosophy , then anyone can voice an opinion on it , and there may be differing views of what ‘ humanity ’ consists of behind it all .
78344	Philosophies clash and compete .
78345	As far as those who experience difficulties in learning or have disabilities are concerned there are ‘ excluders ’ and ‘ includers ’ .
78346	The excluders , since theirs is the prevailing view in our educational and other institutions , want to keep convincing the world at large that their choice as to who belongs is the only possible one .
78347	This necessitates them saying something about the rival philosophy of the includers in addition to conveying the appearance of expertise .
78348	History has shown that the favourite way of dealing with any fundamental philosophy opposed to your own is to abuse its advocates as being fools and heretics — that is , to exclude the people along with their philosophy .
78349	The Catholic Church and the Soviet state under Stalin , for example , found ways of doing this to people who advocated different theological positions from the established one .
78350	In our case , the excluders want to keep out both kinds of fool : people with learning difficulties themselves and their fool advocates , those people who represent the rival philosophy and advocate their inclusion .
78351	Natural experts ?
78352	The includers are not always merely disinterested advocates of a philosophy , but people who have become so through experience , through the sheer amount of time they spend with members of the excluded social group .
78353	‘ parents ’ are the best example , though not the only possible one .
78354	I put the word in inverted commas to highlight a mystique about parenthood .
78355	There is no reason why having some coincidental sperm-and-egg relationship with a child should entitle someone for that reason to be seen as a ‘ natural expert ’ , as distinct from a very clever , highly qualified one .
78356	But if criteria for inclusion and exclusion are not technical and professional but based on a philosophy about what human beings are , then parental expertise can not be different in kind from that of professional ( unnatural ? ) experts .
78357	As one of the parents in the interviews described later says , ‘ When they say , you 're the experts , parents are experts , what they really mean is — you get on with that little bit over there , and we 'll get on with the really important stuff over here . ’
78358	Conversely , of course , not all parents of children with disabilities see their children as members of the human species .
