78359	Most parents , though , have a world-view which as you may expect does include ‘ their ’ children as fully paid-up members of the species .
78360	This observation has occasionally even found its way into the specialist literature , but it is easy to miss its full significance .
78361	For parents , this world-view may not be ‘ philosophical ’ in the sense of something that is calculated , worked out and argued , though it can be and often is .
78362	It is a way of life .
78363	Deny or threaten it , and you deny and threaten someone 's existence .
78364	They will strive to validate it , and even prescribe it for you and everyone else : not just ‘ this is how we live ’ , but ‘ this is how one ought to live ’ .
78365	In the prevailing exclusionist literature , which is controlled by the professionally intelligent , the attitude that what professionals define as ‘ intelligence ’ does not matter , and that their child 's humanity does , may be seen as a symptom of pathology as severe as ( and similar to ) a child 's intellectual disabilities .
78366	It is a lack , a disqualification , an inability to face the reality of their child 's disability .
78367	Because it is pathological it must not be allowed to appear in public in its own form .
78368	To borrow from the classic language of the history of slavery , parents in this sense are ‘ physically alive but socially dead ’ : we do not see them .
78369	They contain endlessly frustrated plantation slaves who are rebellious at assessments and in encounters with professionals , but whose views only reach daylight in fragmented and unvalidated form ; and they contain house slaves who agree with everything that goes on and use ‘ massa 's ’ language and concepts , but who believe something else all the time and are waiting for the day .
78370	In short , they are a colonised people .
78371	But in common with other colonised people such as the Algerians under French rule described by Frantz Fanon or the Black Americans by Stokely Carmichael in the 1960s , they believe that they and their children should themselves be the civilising force to overcome the ‘ civilisation ’ , the predominant philosophy and way of life , that has colonised them .
78372	The stakes are high : it is not just a question of particular social groups ( ‘ What is it to be Black ? ’ ,
78373	‘ What is it to be a woman ? ’ ) , but of the very qualifications for inclusion in the human species .
78374	They believe they have a different and better answer to the question , ‘ What is it to be human ? ’
78375	WORDS OF EXPERIENCE : A RESEARCH PROJECT
78376	My opening observations are not random reflections , but arise directly from a piece of research .
78377	Between 1987 and 1989 I conducted in-depth interviews with nearly forty parents of children with trisomy 21 ( so-called Down 's Syndrome ) who were between the ages of 2 and 7 .
78378	I had several interviews with each parent individually , speaking to nearly 90 per cent of the total population group in a borough with a wide class distribution and a large ethnic minority population ( see Goodey 1991 ) .
78379	Before I began the formal research I had been aware from the few parents of children with trisomy 21 I knew that there was more disquiet about their negotiations with professionals and the treatment of their children than had made its way into the academic and professional literature on parents and families .
78380	Second , I also knew that this disquiet existed alongside other more conventional attitudes which perfectly fitted the portrayal of parents usually found in that literature .
78381	After beginning to interview people in depth , I realised that , to explain this juxtaposition of apparently contradictory values within individuals , I needed to go beyond the conceptual framework set by clinicians and sociologists alike .
78382	A shared language between parents and professionals did not necessarily mean shared attitudes .
78383	It may be that when we express our opinions , we only have available to us ready-made sets of ideas , ‘ discourses ’ , other people 's words which we choose from , string together in different ways and think ( mistakenly ) to be our own ; these include ‘ expert ’ ideas and the colloquial , common-sense versions of them absorbed by ordinary people in one way or another .
78384	But we have something else too which is genuinely our own , even though we do n't choose it , and that is experience .
78385	It became clear from talking to parents that I had to see how what they said actually hooked up with their experience , the fine detail of it , and not to assume that I knew exactly what kind of lived experience lay behind a familiar form of words .
78386	Parents as truth tellers
78387	Even in order to get this far , I had to believe that what I was being told by people about their experiences and feelings was the truth , or essentially the truth .
78388	I may have been wrong proportionately as many times as the result of an amniocentesis turns out to have been wrong : that is , being wrong in both cases amounts to a hypothetical possibility , but is not normal .
78389	I decided , for example , that if a parent told me they had dreamt about having a ‘ Down 's baby ’ before the birth — in the medical literature , this is a classic after-the-event self-deception — they had in fact had such a dream .
78390	If they said they had not been upset on being told the diagnosis , this actually was the case ; they were not suffering from amnesia .
78391	If they became angry at things said to them by professionals , as a majority of them did at some point , the horrifying causes of their anger were true , and were not projections of their own distress on to the professional concerned .
78392	To accept the truth of these accounts is a simple but giant step , and one which the academic and professional community is by its own self-definition incapable of taking : a social group which bases its very existence on its own claims to cleverness would risk its life if it opened even one ear to the voices of fools and heretics , especially when the topic itself is about foolishness in the form of ‘ learning difficulties ’ .
78393	In what follows I have used my interviews with parents as a counterpoint to a professional judgement .
78394	SHOCK , HORROR AND DEMYSTIFICATION
78395	‘ When parents are first told that the baby has Down 's Syndrome they are all deeply shocked ’ ( Cunningham 1982 : 28 ) .
78396	Bernadette : With my other babies they 've mostly left them quite close to me , but she was put over to the side , the doctor was slow in coming , and she went over and checked her over , instead of coming to speak to me as they usually do — she went out again and did n't even look at me [ laughs ] …
78397	I had an instant bond with Marie — I thought she was beautiful the moment she was born — I can really say that .
78398	I thought she was beautiful , and I did n't mind about her being Down 's Syndrome .
78399	Mentally I was prepared to cope with it you see , I 'd made my mind up right through my marriage that I would .
78400	Every one of these parents can recount stories of being not believed , not looked at , not spoken to : that is what dead people experience , if the dead have experiences .
78401	For Bernadette , it 's amusing .
78402	From this paediatrician 's reaction , it seems as if the clinical notion of deep shock as a natural reaction is itself a projection of that professional 's anxiety on to the parent .
78403	Pat : He was six months old and I 'd gone down for his second immunisation and I mean the doctor I went to see was a family doctor — I 've known him since I was a baby — and he just , he was looking at him and he just said , ‘ Is your husband Chinese ? ’
78404	And I said , ‘ No . ’
78405	And he just stuck the needle in his arm , and he said , ‘ Well , I think the baby 's a mongol ’ , and he showed me the door and that was it .
78406	He was n't looking at me .
78407	He was kind of looking down and twiddling his pen , you know … and I mean I know it sounds stupid , but I did n't mind , I think I knew anyway .
78408	I mean when he was born they laid him on me , he 'd had the cord round his neck three times and he looked like a tortoise with his long neck and this little tiny head [ laughs ] .
78409	And I thought blimey , he 's a mongol , you know , when you 're looking at them , and then I was looking at the nurses and waiting for everyone to say something , and nobody said nothing .
78410	And then I thought , I could n't say ‘ Here , is this baby a mongol ? ’ in front of Stan , I think he would have fell over .
78411	Pat has reasons not to mind .
78412	The baby is already six months old , and she has already made the diagnosis herself , at birth .
78413	In addition , both her own parents had considerable physical disabilities .
78414	Both she and Bernadette have realised beforehand that the boundaries of human experience are wider than those indicated in the Mothercare catalogue .
78415	What about those who have n't ?
78416	Rita : Well the doctor was crying , she had tears in her eyes , and she said , ‘ We 've got some news . ’
78417	And then the stupid thing , the doctor said to me , ‘ Does she look like anybody in your family ? ’
78418	I said , ‘ Well you do n't have to tell me , I know she 's a mongol . ’
78419	She said , ‘ Oh — you a nurse ? ’
78420	I said , ‘ No , I can just tell by her face ’ …
78421	So I went back and see the baby in the incubator and then I went back to the ward .
78422	None of the nurses spoke to me , nothing , till 2 o'clock that afternoon , which I 'd had her at 7.30 in the morning …
78423	Yeah , yeah , well I completely rejected her .
78424	As soon as I knew she was n't a hundred per cent , I just did n't want to know her …
78425	The exact feelings …
78426	I wanted her to die …
78427	And I 'll tell you the only reason I took the baby home was because Martin wanted her .
78428	Now this looks more like it : a normal , natural reaction , even if I do have to search through several of the transcripts on my desk to find one .
78429	‘ Natural ’ : does this mean that we all have a gene that determines we will be shocked ?
78430	In the clinical literature , the word ‘ natural ’ is left undefined ( the medical description of this kind of shock goes back to the nineteenth-century discovery of ‘ hysteria ’ and its symptoms in women ) .
78431	Rita , however , takes care to define it , and is aware of the surrounding social circumstances .
78432	The baby had been taken away immediately and wired up in an incubator for three days .
78433	Since Rita has been sent to Coventry , she has not been told that it is physically possible for her to open up the incubator herself and put her hands in .
78434	Eventually a nurse does show her , and then ‘ Once I 'd touched her , she was mine . ’
78435	She is further handicapped by having a sister-in-law ( a nurse herself ) who visits immediately after the diagnosis has been made and starts discussing fostering and adoption procedures .
78436	Most importantly , Rita , just as she makes her own diagnosis , knows — unlike the professionals — exactly what the ‘ shock ’ is and that it comes from somewhere :
78437	Rita : You know , the old story , my first thoughts when I had her , well one of my first thoughts , was Oh , I 've got one of them kids that have silly haircuts , silly anoraks , spend all day on buses or all day in a home , weaving baskets , and that was my first thought …
78438	I do n't know , I always said I 'd never took the piss out of these children , but I 'm sure I must have done at school , but I must admit I was embarrassed .
78439	I was embarrassed giving birth to a mongol .
78440	If we was educated with handicapped , you know , if we 'd mixed with them … but we never saw them .
78441	I 'd never spoken to one till we had Louise , you know , which is not fair on us normal people …
78442	They 're anti-social , handicapped people , and they 're kept that way .
78443	They 're all at a different school all day , and they shop at different times … but you never see them in restaurants and why should n't they be ?
78444	They 're just there , you know .
78445	Like many of the parents , Rita readily agrees with the professional maxim that ‘ It 's natural to feel shocked ’ , but she clearly does not take this to be some scientific and objective concomitant of the situation , something in her genes .
78446	Such parents know that it is something they have been socialised into by a segregated society , and that things could have been otherwise : that they ought to be otherwise ( It 's not fair … ’ ) .
78447	Between the apparent extremes of these examples lie all sorts of individual circumstances .
78448	Some parents ' reaction to the diagnosis is nullified by the additional diagnosis of some life-threatening physical condition such as meningitis or a heart defect , which to them is more distressing .
78449	Some may have previously had a miscarriage or an infant who died .
78450	For others who went through distress , over and over again the concrete feelings behind the abstraction of ‘ shock ’ have to do , not with newly existent beings whom one does n't know , but with existing people in one 's life — partners , family , etc .
78451	And none of them fails to recognise where these negative feelings come from , that such feelings have been taught by a particular upbringing and environment .
78452	‘ Shock ’ and ‘ trauma ’ must be seen as an example of what psychologists call reification : sets of concrete interpersonal and societal relationships are turned into an abstract ‘ thing ’ which dominates our language and hence our way of thinking .
78453	This self-perpetuating process of mystification that denies real feelings and experiences is a necessary prop to the status , power and basic philosophical values of a way of life ; the teaching of negative feelings must go on .
78454	What needs to be emphasised , though , is that direct experience — becoming part of a way of life that includes the alien in a wider definition of what it is to be human — seems to be almost the only way of achieving demystification .
78455	Brian : The only problem I had was people thinking I had problems .
78456	‘ COMING TO TERMS ’ : WHOSE AND WHAT TERMS ?
78457	For many parents it is as though the child they were expecting is dead .
78458	Many doctors think that it is important for parents to recognize these feelings and to go through a period of mourning for their lost imaginary baby …
78459	These feelings … may diminish in time so that the parent can come to terms with the fact that the baby has Down 's Syndrome .
78460	( Cunningham 1982 : 31 , 39 )
78461	A couple of hours after drafting this , I receive a call from a local health visitor asking advice about a child who has just been diagnosed .
78462	She tells me that ‘ the mother is just going through the process of grieving for the child she has n't had ’ ( the child is already eight months old ) : the health visitor 's instruction in the art of creating unpersons has been exemplary , and no doubt she is keen to pass this on to the mother .
78463	Sharon : At school when you have these , you have lessons about childbirth and babies and things , nobody ever says like not all children are born , you know , normal .
78464	Antenatal classes should talk about it .
78465	Although I said to my husband when I was pregnant , what if I have a handicapped baby ?
78466	And he said he would n't be able to cope , but it was in the pretext that it would never happen to us .
78467	But you 've got to think about it if it does happen to you .
78468	I mean if it does , you , I think you find a way of coping with it .
78469	There 's no connection between the thought beforehand , and when it happens to you something different happens .
78470	Dave : I 'd always tended to shy away from them , like , because like I say I think it 's the fear of the unknown , what you 've been told .
78471	If you do n't understand something you normally tend to be a bit aggressive towards it , do n't you ? …
78472	Looking at what Micky 's like and everything , when I thought before what it would be like and what the situation actually is , I think basically you 're in another world , you know what I mean ?
78473	Because it is another world .
78474	Because what you 're thinking it 's going to be like is completely the opposite of what is happening .
78475	For both ways of life and for both sets of values , excluders and includers , the language of ‘ coping ’ and ‘ coming to terms ’ describes the transition between one world and another world ; this much they agree on , even if the values they attach to these worlds are totally opposite .
78476	Many parents can put their finger on a moment or incident when they experienced this transition , which they often mark as rebellion .
78477	Phil : When the paediatrician come in next morning , I mean he only was in there two seconds , he looked her up and said ‘ Typical mongol ’ , either ‘ Typical mongol features ’ or ‘ Typical mongol face ’ , it was one of the two he said , and I could have killed him …
78478	They put Jenny [ Phil 's wife ] in a grotty old side ward so that she did n't upset any other of the patients , no one come in and tell us anything .
78479	I grabbed one of the midwives , the senior one there , and I said to her , what happens now ?
78480	And they reiterated that they would like Becky to stay in for tests but Jenny could come home , and Becky was a bit jaundiced you see .
78481	I said what happens if she had n't had Down 's Syndrome , they said she could have gone home , so I said : ‘ That 's it , wrap her up , we 're going home .
78482	Start life as we mean to go on , we 'll go home . ’
78483	That afternoon a friend came round , Ruth and Jim , and they come round with a bottle of champagne , the best you could buy , and it was just like we 'd had a baby …
78484	I mean I 'd had a sort of cry I suppose , but at the actual time I was glad I had a daughter [ after two sons ] .
78485	And after he said typical mongol , I think , I do n't know , it 's awkward to explain : everything seemed to fall into place .
78486	Just as the clinical professions can provide parents with the language and the concepts with which to take a negative view of the child , so they can provide the unwitting stimulus for the parent to enter a new , positive world in which things ‘ fall into place ’ .
78487	Helen : For some reason I thought of it that they 've given me this monster of a baby that I was n't going to be able to love , and some woman came round — she may have been the hospital social worker or an almoner — and spent about an hour telling me how this was going to completely change the course of my life , I was going to be saddled with this child that would need twenty-four hour care and attention , and I had to think carefully about whether I wanted that for the rest of my life , i.e. was I going to keep him — virtually talking me into not keeping him , and I think the turning-point was that I felt there was something coming from the outside that was , sort of , really trying to urge me to reject him , and that I rebelled against it .
78488	So that I ca n't say I had any positive feelings in the first place , but the realisation that everybody else had negative feelings made me love him .
78489	The majority of parents reported being presented covertly or overtly with an opt-out clause when the diagnosis was first made , often couched in terms of : ‘ Leave the baby here for a couple of days , go home and think about it ’ ( ‘ it ’ being unspecified ) .
78490	Cunningham ( 1982 ) reports that if parents decide to give up the baby permanently , it is ‘ for the parents who make it , the right decision , .
78491	It is important to note here than even if a parent is gripped by those negative fantasies that the textbooks claim to be real and universal , she is also immediately capable of embracing a critique of the values she is confronted with .
78492	Perhaps we are now in a position to give , from a parental perspective , an alternative interpretation of what exactly it means to ‘ come to terms with ’ a child 's disability .
78493	For the clinical and educational professions ( and the lay notions which derive their values from them ) , their very practice makes it clear what fact it is that you ‘ come to terms ’ with : you have not given birth to a member of the human species as we define it , and to which we allocate certain rights and social roles , but to an object of pathology — a ‘ monster ’ , to use a technical term employed in medical anatomy .
78494	For the parent , the same phrase means the inverse : I have not given birth to the monster which my upbringing and socialisation led me to believe I 'd had , but to a normal member of the human species as I now define it .
78495	This widening definition of what it is to be human , couched in sociologically aware terms , runs throughout the responses , and is further expressed in attitudes to amniocentesis and abortion in subsequent pregnancies .
78496	In medical practice , and especially in medical economics , it is assumed that the identification of a foetus with a disability by amniocentesis ( CVS ) will inevitably lead to an abortion .
78497	Yet , only a small proportion of the parents interviewed would even contemplate termination of a subsequent pregnancy should a test turn out to be positive .
78498	Some who had subsequent pregnancies had refused any kind of test , despite in some cases being aggressively pressurised by the hospital .
78499	Others had undergone a test because they ‘ needed to know ’ , not because they had any intention of terminating .
78500	Even where doubts are expressed about ‘ having another one ’ , they are stated in terms which imply a criticism of social arrangements rather than in terms of personal coping .
78501	Jeanette : They 're such lovely babies you 'd have twenty of them .
78502	I 'm not sure , though .
78503	I 'm not sure I could stand shlapping up and down to that bloody clinic time and time again .
78504	Similarly , cosmetic surgery is seen in the professional literature as an option ( some parents choose it , some do n't ) , or even as a kind of cure , especially by the surgeons contracted to perform it , whose understanding of the issues extends as far as the principle that if people see a physically normal child they will react to it ‘ normally ’ and will elicit normal behaviour .
78505	No doubt cosmetic surgery is performed , even encouraged .
78506	In this sample , however , not one parent wanted it for their own child , and in general they were more prescriptive about what was morally correct for other parents here than on any other issue .
78507	Pat : The surgeons are God , anyway , are n't they ?
78508	I mean it was like years ago I heard things about Down 's children with holes in the heart and why bother to do it , but now everything 's changing — let's make them more normal .
78509	But why do that ?
78510	I mean they 're normal to us but they 're not normal to other people , so why should we make them normal to them , just to please society ?
78511	I mean the world 's made up of all different coloured people — why should n't we have different faces and all ?
78512	If we all walked round with the same face and same coloured skin it would be pretty boring , would n't it ?
78513	The world of normality is redefined .
78514	No longer a matter of distribution across a norm , of statistics and probability , ‘ normality ’ itself is simply a common-sense , inclusive definition of what it is to be human , with wider boundaries redefined from experience .
78515	LUCKY LEPERS
78516	‘ I am fortunate .
78517	I do not truly know what it is like to have a child with Down 's Syndrome ’ ( Cunningham 1982 : 16 ) .
78518	Kathy : Scott is the best thing that ever happened to us .
78519	I think it was more , I thought if people would feel sorry for me , then I would n't be able to cope with this thing , like .
78520	I did n't want any pity , that was the thing I was worried about : that people were going to pity me .
78521	I did n't want people to think I could n't cope with it , like , 'cos I knew I could .
78522	I 'm never , ever going to be frightened of anything again .
78523	Before I had Scott I would never say boo to a goose .
78524	But I think all the time where you have to keep on fighting all the time , so now like you get so mouthy in the end you ca n't shut up , you know [ laughs ] , you end up winning the argument 'cos you ca n't shut up , like .
78525	You 've had to be like that all the time , otherwise you feel like you ai n't getting there , they 're getting the better of you , like … ’ cos you listen , do n't you , when you 've had the baby they are supposed to help you and advise you , so you take all their … but then you can only take so much , and you think these must be the mad ones , like .
78526	Beverley : In actual fact me having Devon , I 've never met so many real people …
78527	He 's made us really meet real people , you know what I mean , people with handicapped children , and to me I find them more real than some of my friends that live in another world , fantasising about the future , you know , ‘ What 's the kids going to be when they grow up ? ’
78528	I would n't plan a life out for my child , I could n't possibly do it , you know …
78529	My priorities in my mind 's eye is better .
78530	Their priorities to me is out the window , if you understand my meaning .
78531	My priorities in life is smaller , more compact , but their priorities is for about ten , fifteen years from now .
78532	God forbid anything should happen to their children , never mind their house , or their car .
78533	It stand out like a sore thumb sometimes when I 'm with them , I find people with handicapped children are real people , are people who are people with their children being , talking to them , instead of things that they can give them , you know .
78534	Maybe I 've swapped lenses …
78535	Phil : Well I would say that if I had my life over again I wish and hope that everything happens the same , and I think at the end of the day Becky had been the cream on top of the cake …
78536	Perhaps my opinion on morality 's changed , you know , that there is right and wrong and all this and that you 've got to accept people .
78537	I mean I know what it 's like to be Black .
78538	I feel now that I 've got an epitaph at the end of my life that I did something , I was n't a taker …
78539	I mean we still live , which is a sad fact , but we still live in a society where we were like lepers , we still live in a society where you can still reject , and it should n't be that ; you should n't have the option to reject , you should have the support there .
78540	Bravery , contact with social reality and a sense of justice are the themes of these three extracts .
78541	If they are symptoms of leprosy , then we are indeed ‘ fortunate ’ to know what the experience is like .
78542	LAST WORDS
78543	I have quite intentionally cited only one example of the available professional and academic literature .
78544	Apart from being one of the most widely read and influential books , it is also more enlightened than most of the published work getting through to teachers , health visitors , therapists and parents too .
78545	It does not appear to take a lofty clinical viewpoint , but partakes of the language of partnership and equality between experts and parents .
78546	I have ignored such central and prestigious characters in the drama is professor Wold of St Bartholomew 's Hospital , who is seeking to perfect a cheap , early diagnostic test for trisomy 21 during pregnancy on the interesting grounds that it costs £500,000 ( not accounting for inflation ) to look after a person with trisomy 21 for life .
78547	Let us skirt round professor Joan Bicknell , a major authority in child psychiatry .
78548	In a bang-up-to-date textbook ( see Bicknell 1988 ) , she lectures future generations of health and social service professionals on imparting what they are to perceive as ‘ sad , bad news ’ to parents .
78549	Following a time-honoured tradition of psychiatric categories , she elaborates the ‘ bereavement response ’ to diagnosis into a farrago of stages ( none of whose terms , as far as I can make out , has ever been defined ) : ( 1 ) ‘ Shock ’ , ( 2 ) ‘ panic ’ , ( 3 ) ‘ Denial ’ , ( 4 ) ‘ Grief ’ , ( 5 ) ‘ Guilt ’ , ( 6 ) ‘ Anger ’ ( in general ) , ( 7 ) ‘ Anger Against professionals ’ , ( 8 ) ‘ Bargaining ’ and finally ( 9 ) ‘ Acceptance ’ .
78550	Anyone who wants to explain away the material I have offered in the interview extracts will merely have to look up item ( 7 ) .
78551	Let us return to the measured tones of Cliff Cunningham .
78552	Earlier I mentioned Stokely Carmichael ; and here is the White liberalism of mental disability issues .
78553	Why am I using his work to set alongside the interview extracts ?
78554	I am saying that we are confronted , beneath a language which is often common to both parties , with two competing moral philosophies , and that the language of partnership is a mirage , a deliberate and partisan disguise for the fact that one of those philosophies holds power while the other comes from beneath the underdog .
78555	There are not ‘ professionals ’ and ‘ parents ’ .
78556	There is a strange tribe that believes in spells , psychometric assessments and incantations , and there is a tribe of what Beverley , Devon 's mother , calls real people .
78557	The beauty of it is that while nut everyone can become Black or become a woman , anyone can join the ‘ real people ’ .
78558	They may be parents or they may only have letters after their name , but what they have in common is this : they know that intellectual perfection and the criteria for measuring it are chimeras .
78559	In our society this knowledge is dangerous , subversive , and — make no mistake — will be dealt with as such .
78560	The best way of dealing with it , perhaps , is to draw parents into a prevailing set of values about intelligence and humanity on the grounds of an ‘ equal partnership , that is spurious and reinforces the attitudes underlying segregation .
78561	Ruled out or rescued ?
78562	A Statement for Balbinder
78563	Elizabeth Grugeon
78564	Elizabeth Grugeon provides a detailed account of her association with Balbinder Singh and his family .
78565	She was a friend and adviser for the family as they tried to negotiate a path through an education system which was not always easy to understand .
78566	Balbinder was the subject of a Statement and Elizabeth Grugeon charts the process from an initial expression of concern about Balbinder 's lack of progress by the primary school to his transfer to a special school for pupils categorised as having ‘ moderate learning difficulties ’ .
78567	MY INVOLVEMENT WITH THE FAMILY
78568	A long-standing friendship with an Asian family who were neighbours of mine led to my being involved in the process of Statementing their youngest child , Balbinder Singh .
78569	He was 6 years old and had been at the school for three terms when the head , knowing that I was a neighbour and friend of Balbinder 's mother , invited me to go with Mrs Singh to a meeting with the educational psychologist .
78570	The head explained that he and the class teacher felt that Balbinder was making little progress and they were worried about his lack of concentration and poor language .
78571	They were considering the possibility of a place in a special school for children with moderate learning difficulties which could offer ‘ smaller classes and more individual attention ’ .
78572	His transfer would involve a lengthy and complicated assessment procedure , and they wanted me to help to explain this to Balbinder 's parents and to reassure them .
78573	This chapter is an account of the process and is an attempt to see it from the family 's perspective .
78574	I had known the family for some years as I had been Mrs Singh 's English tutor on a local authority adult literacy programme .
78575	Balbinder was 3 years old when I first started visiting the house , a very sociable child who eagerly awaited my arrival and the chance to play with the bag of toys I always brought with me .
78576	Over the years , in my role as home tutor to his mother , I had had a privileged relationship with Balbinder and his family .
78577	By the time he started school I had already been an intermediary between the family and the town hall , the DHSS , the local social services , the medical profession and school .
78578	Mr and Mrs Singh kept most of their official correspondence between the pages of their telephone directory and on my weekly visits we sorted out the milk tokens , rates demands , post office giros , all of which made linguistic demands which were beyond the level of their competence .
78579	Mr Singh , a Kenyan Asian , confessed to me , after I had been a friend of the family for several years , that he was neither fluent in Swahili , the language of his education up to 13 , nor in Punjabi , his mother tongue .
78580	However , the family spoke Punjabi exclusively at home and had very strong views on the need to do this .
78581	They were concerned that the boys should not lose touch with their language and culture .
78582	The two older boys , aged 5 and 7 , were competent in both languages .
78583	Balbinder seemed slower to talk and his mother was worried about his reluctance to speak English .
78584	As both parents spoke to him in Punjabi for most of the time this did not seem surprising .
78585	I reassured Mrs Singh that once he started playgroup there would be an improvement .
78586	In fact the health visitor diagnosed a problem with speech at his screening at age 3 , and he began attending the local health clinic for speech therapy .
78587	Mrs Singh mentioned this once or twice but did not seem to set much store by it .
78588	She continued to express concern at what she felt to be his backwardness at speaking English .
78589	I wondered how many people he had the opportunity to speak to outside his family .
78590	However , the playgroup run by local parents had not been the success for Balbinder that we had hoped .
78591	There were complaints about his behaviour .
78592	He did not seem to know how to play , would not settle down , ran about too much and fought with the other children .
78593	At home , whenever I visited , he always seemed the same docile , attractive child sitting silently watching TV in the impeccably tidy and attractive furnished living room of the very small , terraced house .
78594	In the house , the lives of the three young boys seemed quiet , calm and disciplined .
78595	But the large hall at playgroup , the number of activities , different experiences and other children seemed to produce excitable and often aggressive behaviour in Balbinder .
78596	The staff were also worried about his speech , not seeming to take into account the fact that this was the first time he had come out of a Punjabi-speaking environment and was having to cope with new experiences in a foreign language .
78597	His mother 's fluent , though inaccurate , English and confident manner may have led them to expect more of him .
78598	Mrs Singh worried about him a great deal , and was often very angry at his apparent lack of progress .
78599	She wanted him to learn to count , begin to write , and above all to speak English .
78600	She and the children visited my house regularly at this period , so that I could hear the oldest boy , Ravi , read .
78601	He had already overtaken his mother and she did not know how to cope with the graded readers he brought home from school or his teacher 's request that she should hear him read .
78602	Whenever they visited me I listened to him reading .
78603	He was quite fluent but seemed to read without comprehension .
78604	I felt that the texts he was reading did not speak of familiar experiences or vocabulary .
78605	I remember him struggling with a story where understanding of the narrative depended on the reader knowing about canals .
78606	He could read the words — canal , lock , barge — but the illustrations of an urban canal with tall , industrial buildings and long painted boats portrayed an unknown landscape .
78607	At 8 he was rapidly becoming a non-reader .
78608	The idea that reading might be for pleasure had not occurred to him .
78609	Balbinder was always pleased to come along for these sessions , to play with my children 's toys and run in the garden .
78610	Mrs Singh brought her letters and forms for me to elucidate .
78611	I was constantly surprised at the extent to which she needed explanations for even the most taken-for-granted aspects of junior school life .
78612	The list of clothing for a school trip included ‘ night-dress ’ and ‘ sponge-bag ’ .
78613	The Singh children slept in their underpants , and she wondered whether I could lend her a ‘ night-dress ’ for Ravi and also a sponge .
78614	Almost all documents sent home from school were incomprehensible .
78615	Letters inviting parents to join the parent — teacher association , visit the ‘ Spring Fayre ’ , to volunteer for ‘ parent-governor elections ’ , or attend a ‘ Maths Workshop ’ were put in the bin after my attempts to explain them .
78616	Schools unwittingly erect a language barrier which must exclude great numbers of parents .
78617	End of term reports contained phrases like ‘ his development of spatial awareness , or ‘ his confidence on the apparatus ’ .
78618	However phrases like ‘ is working hard ’ , ‘ always tries his best ’ , ‘ is beginning to show some improvement , did not fool her .
78619	She interpreted them quite accurately to mean that her children were under-achieving and the message she took from them was almost always a negative one .
78620	On one occasion Mrs Singh had asked me to go with her to visit one of the boy 's teachers .
78621	The teacher was brusque and busy .
78622	She brushed aside Mrs Singh 's assertions that her son was not making progress by telling her repeatedly that it was unreasonable to expect anything more ; she used phrases like ‘ He is well below average ’ , ‘ He is slow ’ , ‘ He is in the bottom set , you must accept that .
78623	You ca n't put it there if it 's not there . ’
78624	Mrs Singh was not satisfied .
78625	She wanted to know why he never brought anything home , why he had no reading book .
78626	His teacher explained that homework for 8 year olds was not school policy and Jeetinder was called in to show his mother that he could read .
78627	He produced his reading book , one of the ‘ pirate series ’ by Sheila Mccullagh , and read quite fluently .
78628	The teacher suggested that Mrs Singh could help by reading with him , Mrs Singh to read one line , Jeetinder the next ; she was evidently unaware of the possibility that Jeetinder 's reading could be more competent than his mother 's .
78629	Looking at a piece of work on the board Mrs Singh said she wanted her son to write like that .
78630	The teacher , by now worn down by Mrs Singh 's refusal to accept Jeetinder 's limitations , told her that it had been written by ‘ a highly intelligent girl ’ .
78631	She continued to try to convince Mrs Singh that although Jeetinder was in the bottom set he was doing well and was not ‘ the bottom of the bottom set ’ .
78632	None of this convinced Mrs Singh who left the classroom saying in an unusually dictatorial tone to the class teacher , ‘ I want you to sort him out and bring homework home . ’
78633	Later , I tried to mollify her by pointing out that the teacher had said what a nice boy he was .
78634	Looking me straight in the eye she replied , ‘ Nice is in every child . ’
78635	The school 's educational psychologist had made contact with the family when he had been involved in an assessment of Jeetinder , the second son , now in the fourth year at the school .
78636	There had been concern about his progress at the same stage as there now was for Balbinder 's .
78637	Mrs Singh had been visited at home and the head had arranged for me to be present so that I could explain and reinforce any suggestions .
78638	In the event , I found this difficult as they seemed inappropriate .
78639	The psychologist had suggested among other things that Mrs Singh could help to improve Jeetinder 's spoken and written language by reading to him at bedtime and could help to improve his numeracy by encouraging him to spend and account for his pocket money .
78640	Both ideas were culturally alien to Mrs Singh .
78641	There were no English children 's books in the house , and the boys did not shop on their own nor have regular pocket money .
78642	Neither parent was fully literate in English or their mother tongue .
78643	Mrs Singh had seemed mystified by the advice , as she believed the school should be responsible for progress in English and mathematics and shrugged helplessly when I suggested that parents also had an important role .
78644	THE STATEMENTS PROCESS FOR BALBINDER
78645	My contact with the family had lapsed for a while when the head asked to see me to request help in explaining the Statementing procedures to Mrs Singh .
78646	The head told me that Mrs Singh had been coming to school regularly to express concern about Balbinder 's lack of progress .
78647	The class teacher and the head were also worried ; they felt that , ‘ after four terms at school , he is the slowest in the class ’ .
78648	Their concern was that in September , when he should be moving into the second year infants with his age cohort , he would be far behind .
78649	The head had asked the educational psychologist to come and assess him with a view to producing a formal Statement of Special Educational Needs .
78650	Standardised tests had shown that ‘ whereas his two older brothers had scored better on verbal ability than on visual motor ability , Balbinder had performed equally poorly on both ’ .
78651	As a result the educational psychologist had been investigating the possibility of a place at a local special school for Balbinder .
78652	They now wanted to explain all this to Mrs Singh and hoped that I would be able to explain the implications of what they were going to say .
78653	The same morning Mrs Singh had approached me in the school foyer , handed me a bag full of letters , and burst into tears .
78654	I realised that I had n't visited her for some weeks and agreed to go to her house after school .
78655	As an outside observer drawn into the Statementing process by the professionals involved , I had a neutral but not disinterested role .
78656	I kept a diary of events and attempted to chart the process by which 6-year-old Balbinder was removed from mainstream education .
78657	March 3 : The initial meeting
78658	Meeting with the head , the school 's educational psychologist , Mrs Singh and myself at school .
78659	The head explained to Mrs Singh that Balbinder was not making much progress and that because of class sizes he would be unlikely to receive the kind of attention he needed .
78660	He explained that at Cedars ( the local authority 's school for children ‘ with learning difficulties ’ ) where classes are small and the teachers are specialists at coping with Balbinder 's sort of problems , he might do better .
78661	He stressed that it was essential for Balbinder to start at Cedars as soon as possible , if he was going to catch up .
78662	He seemed to be suggesting that once Balbinder had been at Cedars for a while , he might be capable of re-entering mainstream education at middle school transfer .
78663	This was an idea she was to hold on to throughout the process .
78664	Both the head and the educational psychologist stressed the positive value of Cedars and the likely problems for Balbinder if he stayed on at his present school , which they told her did not have the expertise to cope with his needs .
78665	By suggesting this they began quite unwittingly to undermine her confidence in the school and in herself .
78666	She became very upset and confused , clearly feeling that Balbinder 's failure was her fault .
78667	She cried a lot repeatedly saying ‘ He always wants to play … he just wants toys . ’
78668	When she was calmer , she also made it clear that she felt that a stricter approach that forced Balbinder to concentrate and work harder was all that was needed .
78669	She felt that he was not doing well because he was not trying hard enough , and that his teachers were not making him try hard enough .
78670	She listened intently as they explained the Statementing procedure .
78671	They stressed that the decision to send Balbinder to Cedars would be made by Mrs Singh and her husband .
78672	The first stage would be to visit the school and then return to discuss the matter again .
78673	A date was arranged for the following week for both events and I agreed to go with them .
78674	What I did not realise at the time , but discovered later , was that Mrs Singh had no idea that transfer next September had been suggested — she expected that it would happen straight away .
78675	After she had left , the head and educational psychologist explained the Statementing procedure in more detail .
78676	In the past they had waited until after the school screening tests at 7-plus but felt that this was leaving it too late .
78677	In Balbinder 's case it was not simply that he was a slow learner .
78678	There were what the head called ‘ social concerns ’ behind his transfer .
78679	He was developing self-control in the classroom , but found it harder on the playground where it seemed that he was easily influenced by other children to behave badly .
78680	As he put it , ‘ He reverts when he is with naughty children . ’
78681	They had not given these reasons for transfer to his parents .
78682	Yet they were clearly important considerations as far as the school was concerned .
78683	It was not a foregone conclusion that there would be a place available at Cedars since there is a lot of pressure on special school places in the county .
78684	As the head of Cedars was making his entry list for September already , and would have to submit it by the end of the week , the educational psychologist was going to request a place for Balbinder before Statementing him .
78685	Thus it was essential to get Mr and Mrs Singh 's agreement as soon as possible .
78686	Later on the same day , I visited Mr and Mrs Singh at home .
78687	Over tea and food we talked about the school 's suggestion .
78688	Mrs Singh was upset ; she felt rejected by the school her children had been attending for five years .
78689	She was depressed and angry with Balbinder .
78690	She had been crying and said that she had been ‘ feeling awful ’ all day .
78691	She clearly found it hard to sort out the implications of what was being suggested .
78692	However we agreed to visit Cedars together in a few days ' time .
78693	The difficulty she was having in making sense of the boys ' education was illustrated by the packet of letters she had brought to school in the morning .
78694	One from the LEA was about her 8-year-old son 's transfer to middle school , an event generating a great deal of paper including a list of the available schools ; another letter from the LEA explained parents ' rights of choice and appeal , also dates of open evenings ; yet another letter from the school to which he had been allocated required the parents to sign the tear-off slip and return it to their present school .
78695	Fortunately , I noticed that he had been given a place at a different school from his older brother and that it was actually a matter of filling in the appeal form requesting a place at another school .
78696	I suggested that they should also accept the invitation to take him to visit his new school 's Open Evening .
78697	Mrs Singh said she would go if I came too but not otherwise .
78698	Another letter from the middle school was about a visiting theatre group and asked for money as well as a tear-off slip .
78699	We discussed with her 10-year-old son whether he wanted to see the play and we put the money for a ticket in an envelope .
78700	To his chagrin we threw away the letter about a skiing holiday .
78701	At nearly £400 for a week in Austria his parents were not interested .
78702	In the evening I consulted a friend who is also a local head teacher .
78703	Her school has a high proportion of ethnic minority children where I felt Balbinder might not have seemed such a problem .
78704	In her opinion , it was unlikely that he would get a place at Cedars at such a late stage in the year .
78705	She also felt that age 6 was too early to make what she saw as a drastic decision — once out of mainstream education she felt he would be unlikely to get back .
78706	At this stage in the proceedings , my own feelings were mixed .
78707	If the school felt it could not cope with Balbinder then maybe he would be better in a more sympathetic environment .
78708	On the other hand Mrs Singh would lose all her social contacts in the local community once she did not have to take him to school every day .
78709	The school gave her a point of reference and contact with other mothers .
78710	The middle school which both her older boys attended was a long walk from her home and made little or no attempt to involve parents .
78711	If Balbinder was bussed to Cedars every day she would be effectively cut off from any real involvement in her children 's schooling , and from an important part of her own role within the community as the mother of a young child at the local school .
78712	On the other hand I knew that her confidence in Balbinder 's school had been profoundly shaken by the interview with the head and educational psychologist .
78713	If Balbinder did n't get a place at Cedars this year she would become even more anxious about his progress .
78714	March 9 : Visiting Cedars School
78715	The head made us very welcome .
78716	He began by talking to Mr and Mrs Singh about the school .
78717	He stressed the normality of the children who attended it .
78718	He explained that children came to Cedars when their own school could not give them the individual help with basic skills which they needed .
78719	He explained that when a child becomes anxious he or she may stop learning .
78720	Cedars , he told them , was a special school because it had special teachers with special skills and training .
78721	All of the sixteen teachers in the school were experienced in teaching children with learning difficulties .
78722	Another special feature was the size of the groups , ten in the first year , twelve in the second and fifteen thereafter .
78723	Balbinder would be in a group with ten children .
78724	Mrs Singh seemed to be listening intently but I guess that a lot of what was being said went over her head .
78725	I am not sure that she even knows the word ‘ special ’ ; and phrases like ‘ learning difficulties ’ , ‘ becomes anxious ’ , ‘ experienced ’ are not necessarily familiar .
78726	After a while she asked , ‘ These children , do they learn it at the end ? ’
78727	The head replied that the school offered ideal circumstances and that most children responded positively .
78728	There is an annual review in which a report is made on the child 's progress .
78729	All parents , he told them , have the right to say , ‘ I want my child to leave ’ , and he said , ‘ Our job is to help the child go back . ’
78730	They review this possibility annually and he explained that when they have identified children who will go back they let them go into mainstream school for at first a morning and then one day a week .
78731	At the moment six children would be going back into middle school in September .
78732	At this point Mrs Singh said comfortably , ‘ They have learnt , that 's nice . ’
78733	The head went on to explain that the school 's job was to understand each child 's problem .
78734	He told them that many children learned more slowly .
78735	He illustrated different ways in which reading , for example , could be taught , and how some children may not be ‘ mature ’ enough to cope with a ‘ look and say ’ approach , or may not develop that way .
78736	He explained how ‘ look and say ’ uses eyes , while phonics uses ears .
78737	Mr and Mrs Singh listened politely but , possibly , were confused by all this specialist terminology .
78738	He went on to tell them about the school .
78739	The children started at 5 and could stay until 16 .
78740	They could also leave at any time .
78741	Each part of the school — lower/ middle/upper — resembled mainstream school , the difference lying in the size of the teaching group .
78742	At 16-plus they go on to college for up to two years and follow courses which will lead to work .
78743	Several of the 15 year olds were on work experience at the moment .
78744	He then took us round the school .
78745	The lower school had its own grassed and paved play area with plentiful equipment .
78746	The rooms were small , purpose built , had carpeted floors , and each teacher had a non-teaching assistant .
78747	It was an intimate small-scale non-threatening environment .
78748	I was particularly impressed by the art room .
78749	The workshop and home economics area were also impressive , and the school had three computers .
78750	Outside was very pleasant with views over open fields and a local park .
78751	Part of the senior side had been landscaped to make an attractive outdoor work area with wooden table and benches made in the workshop .
78752	There was a swimming pool and a distant view of the donkey field .
78753	There seemed to be few ethnic minority children , one in each class perhaps , certainly none in the youngest group .
78754	After the visit the head talked about the importance of parental involvement .
78755	He explained that regular contact and discussion of ways in which parents can help at home was vital : ‘ Together , we can achieve more . ’
78756	The school had an open-door policy .
78757	He then put it to Mr and Mrs Singh that they would have to think about whether they would like Balbinder to come to the school .
78758	He explained that there were a limited number of places , with sixteen or seventeen taken up for September already ( I wondered whether this meant Balbinder might be unlucky , but did not like to ask ) .
78759	He explained the procedure by which Balbinder would be given a place .
78760	The educational psychologist would prepare notes on Balbinder .
78761	He himself would visit Balbinder at his present school .
78762	He stressed , ‘ We only want him to come if it 's right .
78763	Nothing happens until you say yes . ’
78764	Then Mr and Mrs Singh would come again with Balbinder , and finally they would receive a letter from County Hall .
78765	Again , he stressed that the final decision lay with them : ‘ He will not come until you sign it … in the end you decide . ’
78766	Mr Singh asked his first question : ‘ Would it be next September ? ’
78767	The head said that that would be the case and that Balbinder would stay for as long as he needed their help .
78768	However they could make the decision to take him away ‘ at any time ’ .
78769	Mrs Singh asked ‘ Do you have the same holiday ? ’ and then spoke for the first time about Balbinder .
78770	She seemed distressed , ‘ I mean Balbinder , he used to just sit by the telly , even now he still … he wants toys … he does n't want to do the things , he wants to do all the time what he wants to do … ’
78771	The head nodded reassuringly , seeming to listen , but he did not encourage her to talk about Balbinder any more .
78772	Instead he went on to tell them that the shortest time they kept pupils was for two years but that usually they tried to move people back into mainstream at the time for transfer to middle/upper school .
78773	He told them that the educational psychologist was very good and really knew the children .
78774	Mrs Singh , still pursuing her own thoughts , said , ‘ I wish he was just like other children , like my other children . ’
78775	The head said it was important to think about ‘ whatever is best ’ for Balbinder , and went back to what the school catered for — ‘ people think it 's for mentally handicapped ’ .
78776	‘ It does n't look like one ’ , said Mrs Singh very positively .
78777	The head told them that there were many different special schools in the county and explained where and what each one was for , reassuring them that Cedars is ‘ a school for children who have difficulty getting started with basic skills ’ .
78778	Its job is to help children ‘ who are struggling ’ .
78779	He gave Mr and Mrs Singh a school booklet and saw us out .
78780	We rang for a taxi and while we waited , looked at books of photographs of school plays , trips , art work and sports days .
78781	Both Mr and Mrs Singh seemed surprised and relieved by the normality of the school .
78782	Mr Singh told me that one of his brothers-in-law had told them it was a school for mentally handicapped .
78783	This had clearly been worrying them both .
78784	When we got home I could see that they were ready to agree to the move .
78785	It was also evident that they had not weighed up the consequences .
78786	It all seemed easy — they sign on the dotted line and Balbinder would be virtually taken out of their hands .
78787	Despite the school 's stated intention to involve parents as far as possible , I seriously doubted whether Mr or Mrs Singh would be capable or prepared to enter into the kind of partnership the school envisaged .
78788	Looking through the booklet the head had given them , I guessed that they would have some difficulty making sense of it .
78789	They would probably need help with sentences like , ‘ class teachers , together with the help of the remedial specialist , ensure that there is a detailed understanding of the learning difficulties of each individual child . ’
78790	Terms like , ‘ environmental work ’ , ‘ a full curriculum ’ , ‘ special programmes of work for language development ’ would need to be explained to them .
78791	The school 's expressed intention is that ‘ parents are helped to understand the nature of the learning difficulties of their child and are encouraged to visit the school frequently to develop that understanding and to continue that approach at home . ’
78792	Neither Mr nor Mrs Singh have the confidence to take on such a role .
78793	March 12 : Coping with the procedure
78794	I met with Mrs Singh and the educational psychologist in the head 's room .
78795	Mrs Singh was very certain — she and her husband had decided that they both want Balbinder to go to Cedars .
78796	I tried to explore the problems Mrs Singh would have in attempting to be a fully participating parent but the educational psychologist seemed to feel that this was a problem common to many Cedars parents .
78797	The educational psychologist spent some time explaining the legal side of Statementing , which is complex .
78798	He told us that it would take many weeks to sort out and would involve a variety of procedures , such as a medical , reports from the school and visits .
78799	There would be twenty-nine days between the initial letter from County Hall and any action .
78800	The sheer amount of information seemed daunting .
78801	I arranged to visit that afternoon and to go through it with Mr and Mrs Singh .
78802	When I arrived they showed me the letter they had received from the Chief Education Officer that morning which explained the proposed Statementing procedure :
78803	The learning difficulties being experienced by your child were discussed and you agreed that your child probably has a special educational need which requires further investigation .
78804	Therefore it is proposed to carry out an assessment of your child 's needs under the Education Act 1981 with your agreement .
78805	The letter was at pains to stress the parents ' involvement and their rights : ‘ If it is agreed that the Authority should determine the special educational provision for your child … your further rights under the Education Act 1981 will be explained to you . ’
78806	An enclosed booklet gave further general information about the provision of special education with an addendum summarising the legal rights of parents in relation to the assessment process .
78807	In this , the mysterious twenty-nine days was explained : ‘ parents will have a period of 29 days in which to seek further information from the Chief Education Officer and to make representations and submit written evidence . ’
78808	Since they had evidently made up their minds , none of this seemed important to them .
78809	Going through the Cedars ' brochure with them , however , they were pleased to find a statement which they could relate to , namely that the school sets out to help children , ‘ who are having problems in learning to read , find spelling and writing difficult , are unable to express themselves well , are unable to settle and concentrate … ’
78810	All these seemed to relate to Balbinder 's needs as his parents saw them and Mr and Mrs Singh were beginning to seem happier .
78811	As they understood it , after a short while Balbinder might be sorted out and returned to mainstream .
78812	I did not feel so optimistic .
78813	The brochure stated clearly that while some children transferred back to mainstream schools , ‘ the majority remain until they are 16 years of age ’ .
78814	June 5 : Testing
78815	Visited Mrs Singh at home .
78816	She told me that she had been present when Balbinder was tested by the educational psychologist .
78817	Balbinder had had to do a lot of puzzles .
78818	The psychologist had said he was good with his hands .
78819	Mrs Singh said he would not sit down and kept walking about .
78820	She said he was the same at home , only wanted to play with toys and watch TV , he would n't do any ‘ work ’ .
78821	I was not sure what she meant by ‘ work ’ .
78822	She went on to her worries about Jeetinder who still was n't bringing anything home from school .
78823	She was being racially harassed and was afraid to go out into her garden .
78824	Her husband was away in India for three weeks .
78825	People were throwing things over her garden wall and someone had painted on the front door .
78826	We spent a lot of time discussing this .
78827	In some ways Balbinder seemed the least of her problems at the time .
78828	Perhaps it was a relief that matters were being taken out of her hands .
78829	We agreed to meet at school the following week .
78830	June 10 : The information for the Statement
78831	First , the head went through the school report , details of birth , address , etc .
78832	There was a brief account of professional intervention to date .
78833	Before starting school he had attended the child development centre , received speech therapy and since had been seen on several occasions by the educational psychologist .
78834	Then , there was a description of the child 's functioning : he had taken a long time to settle into school , e.g. routine and order of the class .
78835	He had communication problems — speech and English language were not good .
78836	He had difficulty ‘ sounding ’ because of this , and it was thought to be affecting his progress in learning to read .
78837	The head attempted to explain to Mrs Singh how children have to learn the initial sounds of words and how having two languages can impede this .
78838	I think Mrs Singh understood .
78839	Balbinder has also had difficulty learning colours , numbers and sounds .
78840	His progress was slow because his retention was poor .
78841	At this point Mrs Singh looking concerned said , ‘ You think there 's something wrong with him inside of him ? ’
78842	The head said , ‘ No , he 's not ill . ’
78843	Mrs Singh agreed that it must be the way he forgot things .
78844	The head said ‘ Yes , he does have difficulty remembering — particularly sounding ’ , and felt that this could be because he was perhaps more fluent in Punjabi .
78845	There were discrepancies in the report .
78846	On the one hand Mrs Singh was told that his drawing and writing were immature , that he was still drawing and writing like a very young child ; yet later she was told that he was very good with a pencil and talented at art !
78847	Having said that he was very immature the report added that there had been considerable improvement , but it had taken a long time ( he had only been at school for four terms and had had a change of teacher ) .
78848	The head stressed that what Balbinder needed was to be in a small group , not in a class of twenty-three .
78849	In order for him to maintain interest he needed to work in short spurts .
78850	In his present situation , his difficulty in concentrating took up a lot of the teacher 's time .
78851	The head then commented on his social development .
78852	Here they felt there had been much progress .
78853	Balbinder used to be ‘ wild ’ , but he had learned to share and to take part in group work , despite still being a very lively child .
78854	The head then went on to describe the aims and provision of special education .
78855	Since Balbinder clearly made more progress in a small group where he could have a lot of attention , and where all worked at the same pace , this could be an answer .
78856	The head felt that the boy needed somebody permanently watching him .
78857	Also he needed a lot of talking in English , as he was still not sounding words clearly .
78858	Further he was a very active child , and needed specialist apparatus .
78859	They had all the necessary facilities and resources at Cedars .
78860	The head was very persuasive , showing concern for the way Balbinder would react when ( or if ) he fell behind .
78861	As he was already behind in mastering the basic skills which lay the foundation for all further work , he felt that Balbinder needed a lot of help if he was to do justice to his abilities .
78862	And he said very kindly , ‘ That 's our view of Balbinder . ’
78863	The educational psychologist gave his report .
78864	He reiterated that Balbinder 's problems with language had needed attention before school .
78865	He stressed that he was a very likeable little boy .
78866	However , observing him in the classroom he had noticed his immature behaviour .
78867	He ran about a lot , and found concentration difficult .
78868	Despite much improvement in pencil and art work there had been none in reading and other school work .
78869	He was fidgety and in a dream world when being given instruction in a group .
78870	Often he watched other children and then followed and copied them .
78871	The psychologist commented that Balbinder had liked having a reading book and clearly wanted to read but when it came to reading he did not understand what he was doing but relied on guessing .
78872	He clearly wanted to do well , wanted to read but needed a lot of extra help .
78873	When asked questions he gave one word answers , though he used two words on occasion , as in ‘ boys swimming ’ , ‘ wet play ’ .
78874	On the tests he gave him he was better on puzzles and patterns , poor on those involving speaking and understanding .
78875	He felt that Balbinder needed to work slowly and not be pushed — he needed more time and specific help to speak in sentences .
78876	At this point Mrs Singh said , ‘ They are not allowed to speak English at home . ’
78877	She felt that he spoke better in Punjabi and that he remembered better in Punjabi .
78878	She referred to her own family : parents , brother and sisters who all spoke English at home .
78879	She found this very odd .
78880	At the weekend when she had taken Balbinder to stay with his grandparents in Coventry , her brother had been trying to teach Balbinder to say ‘ can I ’ , or ‘ May I ’ instead of ‘ I want to ’ .
78881	The educational psychologist listened tolerantly to Mrs Singh 's comments , did not respond to them but simply repeated that Balbinder needed to be with teachers who were experienced in working with small groups .
78882	Mrs Singh said that she felt that Balbinder would always do what was wanted if it suited him .
78883	The educational psychologist told her that one of the teachers from Cedars had visited Balbinder in school and made very positive comments .
78884	It seemed that a place was available but that all the complex procedures had to be completed before it could be offered to them .
78885	He still had to have a medical .
78886	The head would speak to the school doctor that same day .
78887	Social Services would write to Mrs Singh .
78888	The procedure was necessarily long-winded but it could be completed by the end of term .
78889	Mrs Singh expressed a worry about Balbinder refusing to dress himself and ordering her to get him ready for school when he could do this perfectly well if he wanted to .
78890	The educational psychologist said this was understandable while he was feeling rather unsettled .
78891	The head said he would chase up the documents .
78892	Mrs Singh seemed bewildered by the amount of information she had been given .
78893	I promised to go and see her again on Friday morning .
78894	Throughout this interview Mrs Singh , who was still struggling to grasp the implications of what the head and educational psychologist were telling her , attempted to contribute .
78895	Her anecdotes were treated courteously but no real response was made .
78896	It seemed that now the process was under way her contribution was not required .
78897	June 12
78898	I visited Mr and Mrs Singh .
78899	Mrs Singh and I talked Mr Singh through the meeting , point by point .
78900	He agreed with the head 's account of Balbinder 's lack of concentration , which obviously worried them both a great deal .
78901	He listened to what I had to say about the procedure still to be gone through and hoped that they would soon hear whether Balbinder had a place .
78902	I said that this was almost certain but the process was rather slow .
78903	Mrs Singh agreed to tell me when she heard from the doctor .
78904	They both understood that this was a formality and that he was not thought to be ‘ ill ’ .
78905	What particularly concerned me was their feeling that Balbinder seemed to understand and respond better in Punjabi .
78906	Mrs Singh expressed her feelings that it was very important for all her children to speak Punjabi and she was afraid that they might not do this if she and Mr Singh spoke English .
78907	Both parents were very concerned that he should get more appropriate help and were now convinced that this would be provided at Cedars .
78908	June 22 : Acceptance
78909	Mrs and Mrs Singh had received a letter offering Balbinder a place at Cedars .
78910	They had understood the gist but needed help .
78911	We filled in the acceptance form and phoned the school about a visit .
78912	The school secretary said all the September intake would be invited for a morning before the end of term .
78913	Balbinder , who had been excluded from all deliberations about his future , had not seen his new school yet .
78914	July 15 : Balbinder visits his new school
78915	Mrs Singh , Balbinder and I set off to visit Cedars School .
78916	Balbinder was very subdued .
78917	His mother said he was not happy about the new school , and wanted to stay where he was .
78918	He had , after all , had five terms there , he would be 7 in December .
78919	He did not speak all the way .
78920	Mrs Singh remarked what a long way it seemed .
78921	We were early and stood in the playground .
78922	Balbinder looked around but clung to Mrs Singh .
78923	We went in and were ushered into the hall where a number of other new children were looking at books of photos of school trips and events .
78924	We were asked to sit in the third and fourth rows and the lower school children filed in .
78925	The head explained that the school had a lower/middle/ upper division and the lower school head briefly explained that the children were going to show the parents and new children what they had been doing .
78926	Each year group described a recent trip and showed photos and work they had done .
78927	The classes were small , as was the number of ethnic minority children .
78928	There were one , or possibly two , Afro-Caribbean children overall and one or two Asian children in each group .
78929	Mrs Singh and Balbinder noticed each one and commented .
78930	It was hot and the demonstration went on much too long , but it gave us all some idea of how caring the teachers were and it was a practical illustration of what the school was trying to do .
78931	The children were then asked to go out to play .
78932	Balbinder was very reluctant and clung to his mother .
78933	He had lost interest in the activities .
78934	There had been too much ‘ talk and show ’ early on and he had been wriggling about , scraping his chair back and causing Mrs Singh to reprimand him constantly .
78935	It looked as if we would have to take him out but an older Asian boy came and took him away , and he went quite confidently .
78936	The head then told the parents about travel , uniform , swimming ( once a week all the year round ) , the PTA , illnesses , notes for absence or non-swimming and , above all , contacting the school whenever in doubt .
78937	We were then taken to have coffee and the school secretary handed out official forms for the parents to fill in .
78938	Mrs Singh filled them in although she had already expressed alarm at the number of notes she was going to have to write to the school .
78939	Classes were allocated and Balbinder was to be in class 1 with a Mrs Allinson and a nursery assistant .
78940	It was small , with its own toilets and washbasins and an entirely private playground .
78941	Balbinder ran outside straight away , gesturing to me to come and look at it .
78942	In the playground they had a sturdy wooden house with door and windows , climbing and swinging equipment and lots of small bicycles and tricycles .
78943	In the classroom , photos of the trip to the seaside were on display and there were small circular tables .
78944	It was all on a scale much more appropriate for children than the high vaulting of his previous school and there was much more play equipment .
78945	This filled Mrs Singh with horror .
78946	She was worried by the way he roamed about touching everything , and during a long chat to Mrs Allinson expressed her concern that he could not get on with anything , and could not write or read .
78947	Mrs Allinson was very reassuring .
78948	However , Mrs Singh clearly saw Cedars as a temporary phase .
78949	Earlier on , in the playground , as Balbinder had gradually gained confidence and begun to explore and use things Mrs Singh had said , wistfully , ‘ I do hope Balbinder learn so quickly he will soon go back to his school . ’
78950	On the way out the head knelt down to say goodbye to Balbinder , who was still looking rather mystified but was much less clinging and was smiling more .
78951	In the car on the way home he sat alone , opened the window and put his head out .
78952	It was very hard to imagine what he made of what was going on .
78953	No one had consulted him and he did n't seem to want to talk about it .
78954	In all these transactions Balbinder seemed a shadowy figure .
78955	Decisions were being taken about his future which no one could explain to him .
78956	Over the last few months he had become rather withdrawn and mistrustful ; a subdued version of his former self .
78957	At Cedars Mrs Singh had instantly made friends with a young Asian woman ( wearing trousers and a shirt ) with a little girl who was evidently a year older than Balbinder .
78958	She and Mrs Singh spoke in Punjabi but her English sounded local and I suspected that she preferred to speak English .
78959	However , Mrs Singh was pleased to meet her and generally liked all the teachers and what she saw .
78960	I wondered whether she had any misgivings .
78961	The distance will certainly be a problem .
78962	What she was making of this experience was also hard to imagine .
78963	Choice seemed to have been taken away from her , but some of her anxieties had also been allayed .
78964	PROGRESS REPORT
78965	In September Balbinder started at Cedars .
78966	My contact with the family became much less frequent .
78967	Their circumstances had changed : Mr Singh had a full-time job , they had taken a big step and purchased their council house and Mrs Singh now felt that she needed permanent work herself .
78968	The job she finally acquired during the summer holidays meant leaving home before the children and returning after them .
78969	The coach which picked up the Cedars ' children stopped about five minutes ' walk away from their home .
78970	Balbinder had to be seen onto it , and met at the end of the day .
78971	For the first few weeks of term this was a problem .
78972	Mr Singh could take him to the bus when he was on late shifts and collect him on early shifts .
78973	His brothers aged 8 and 10 , whose school was a long walk in the opposite direction , had to be relied on to take this responsibility when their father could not .
78974	The whole operation caused Mrs Singh a great deal of anxiety .
78975	By half-term , a local parent with a child at Cedars had offered to put Balbinder on the coach in the morning and let him stay at her house until he could be picked up in the evening .
78976	Mrs Singh had now effectively become cut off from her children 's education just as Balbinder had been cut off from local peer group relationships .
78977	She occasionally contacted me , and for a Christmas present gave me a photograph of Balbinder taken at school and made into a calendar .
78978	This showed him sitting at a desk , pencil in hand : his mother 's vision of what school should be about .
78979	She and Mr Singh had visited the school for a Christmas event and had been pleased to hear that Balbinder was being moved into the second class .
78980	She had been worried that he was still playing too much and not learning anything .
78981	From January to July my contacts with the family were infrequent and concerned the progress of the two older boys .
78982	My advice was sought on several occasions when the family did not know how to cope with quite serious problems concerning the behaviour of one of them .
78983	Balbinder was no longer a worry .
78984	However , in July Mrs Singh phoned to ask whether I could go with her to Cedars ' open evening .
78985	She wanted my opinion on Balbinder 's progress .
78986	I was not able to go with her , but , as I was in contact with the school 's section XI teacher at the time , I arranged to visit on my own .
78987	The section XI teacher , who had particular responsibility for Balbinder , said that he was the least of her worries .
78988	He had been moved to a higher class , seemed well adjusted and chatted a lot when she worked with him .
78989	His class teacher also felt that he was making progress .
78990	Both parents had come to the open evening and she had been able to talk to them .
78991	They had also come to school earlier in the year for the annual assessment meeting , a statutory requirement for children who are the subject of Statements .
78992	Looking back to her first encounter with Balbinder a year ago , when she had visited him at his previous school , she said that she had been shocked .
78993	He had been on the periphery of a large class and little attempt was being made to involve him in what was going on .
78994	She had felt at the time that he was ‘ pretty borderline for special school ’ .
