87612	Although the linguist who undertakes the analysis of discourse has ultimately the same aims as a linguist who uses ‘ system-sentences ’ in his grammatical description of a language , there are important methodological differences involved in the two approaches .
87613	Both linguists wish to produce accurate descriptions of the particular language studied .
87614	In pursuit of this goal , the grammarian will concentrate on a particular body of data and attempt to produce an exhaustive but economical set of rules which will account for all and only the acceptable sentences in his data .
87615	He will not normally seek to account for the mental processes involved in any language-user 's production of those sentences , nor to describe the physical or social contexts in which those sentences occur .
87616	On each of these issues , concerning ‘ data ’ , ‘ rules ’ , ‘ processes ’ and ‘ contexts ’ , the discourse analyst will take a different view .
87617	On ‘ data'
87618	The grammarian 's ‘ data ’ is inevitably the single sentence , or a set of single sentences illustrating a particular feature of the language being studied .
87619	It is also typically the case that the grammarian will have constructed the sentence or sentences he uses as examples .
87620	This procedure is not often made explicit , but an overt commitment to the constructed-data approach has recently been expressed in the following terms :
87621	I shall assume … that invented strings and certain intuitive judgements about them constitute legitimate data for linguistic research .
87622	( Gazdar , 1979 : 11 )
87623	In contrast , the analysis of discourse , as undertaken and exemplified in this book , is typically based on the linguistic output of someone other than the analyst .
87624	On the few occasions where constructed data is used as illustration ( of a paradigm , for example , in Chapter 4 ) , it is inevitably directed towards accounting for the range of formal options available to a speaker or writer .
87625	More typically , the discourse analyst 's ‘ data ’ is taken from written texts or tape-recordings .
87626	It is rarely in the form of a single sentence .
87627	This type of linguistic material is sometimes described as ‘ performance-data ’ and may contain features such as hesitations , slips , and non-standard forms which a linguist like Chomsky ( 1965 ) believed should not have to be accounted for in the grammar of a language .
87628	Although these two views of ‘ data ’ differ substantially , they are not incompatible , unless they are taken in an extreme form .
87629	A discourse analyst may regularly work with extended extracts of conversational speech , for example , but he does not consider his data in isolation from the descriptions and insights provided by sentence-grammarians .
87630	It should be the case that a linguist who is primarily interested in the analysis of discourse is , in some sense , also a sentence-grammarian .
87631	Similarly , the sentence-grammarian can not remain immured from the discourse he encounters in his daily life .
87632	The sentence he constructs to illustrate a particular linguistic feature must , in some sense , derive from the ‘ ordinary language ’ of his daily life and also be acceptable in it .
87633	A dangerously extreme view of ‘ relevant data ’ for a discourse analyst would involve denying the admissibility of a constructed sentence as linguistic data .
87634	Another would be an analytic approach to data which did not require that there should be linguistic evidence in the data to support analytic claims .
87635	We shall return to the issue of ‘ relevant data ’ for discourse analysis in Chapter 2 .
87636	An over-extreme view of what counts as data for the sentence-grammarian was , according to Sampson ( 1980 ) , noticeable in some of the early work of generative grammarians .
87637	Chomsky gave an indication of the narrowness of view which could be taken , when , immediately before his conclusion that ‘ grammar is autonomous ’ , he stated :
87638	Despite the undeniable interest and importance of semantic and statistical studies of language , they appear to have no direct relevance to the problem of determining or characterising the set of grammatical utterances .
87639	( Chomsky , 1957 : 17 )
87640	The essential problem in an extreme version of the constructed-sentence approach occurs when the resulting sentences are tested only against the linguist 's introspection .
87641	This can ( and occasionally did ) lead to a situation in which a linguist claims that the ‘ data ’ he is using illustrates acceptable linguistic strings because he says it does , as a result of personal introspection , and regardless of how many voices arise in disagreement .
87642	The source of this problem , as Sampson ( 1980 : 153 ) points out , is that the narrow restriction of ‘ data ’ to constructed sentences and personal introspection leads to a ‘ non-testability ’ , in principle , of any claims made .
87643	One outcome of this narrow view of data is that there is a concentration on ‘ artificially contrived sentences isolated from their communicative context ’ ( see Preface to Givón ( ed. ) , 1979 ) .
87644	Although we shall appeal frequently , in the course of this book , to the insights of sentence grammarians , including those working within a generative framework , we shall avoid as far as possible the methodology which depends on what Lyons ( I968 ) described as regularised , standardised and decontextualised data .
87645	Rules versus regularities
87646	A corollary to the restricted data approach found in much of Chomskyan linguistics is the importance placed on writing rules of grammar which are fixed and true 100% of the time .
87647	Just as the grammarian 's ‘ data ’ can not contain any variable phenomena , so the grammar must have categorial rules , and not ‘ rules ’ which are true only some of the time .
87648	It is typical of arguments concerning the ‘ correct rules ’ of the language in the Chomskyan approach , and that of most other sentence-grammarians , that they are based on the presentation of ‘ example ’ and ‘ counterexample ’ .
87649	After all , a single ( accepted ) sentence , which is presented as a counterexample , can be enough to invalidate a rule of the categorial type .
87650	In this sense , the ‘ rules ’ of grammar appear to be treated in the same way as ‘ laws ’ in the physical sciences .
87651	This restricts the applicability of such rules since it renders them unavailable to any linguist interested in diachronic change or synchronic variation in a language .
87652	It should be emphasised that this is an extreme version of the sentence-grammarian 's view and one which is found less frequently , in contemporary linguistics , than it was fifteen years ago .
87653	The discourse analyst , with his ‘ ordinary language ’ data , is committed to quite a different view of the rule-governed aspects of a language .
87654	Indeed , he may wish to discuss , not ‘ rules ’ but regularities , simply because his data constantly exemplifies non-categorial phenomena .
87655	The regularities which the analyst describes are based on the frequency with which a particular linguistic feature occurs under certain conditions in his discourse data .
87656	If the frequency of occurrence is very high , then the phenomenon described may appear to be categorial .
87657	As Givón says :
87658	what is the communicative difference between a rule of 90% fidelity and one of 100% fidelity ?
87659	In psychological terms , next to nothing .
87660	In communication , a system with go% categorial fidelity is a highly efficient system .
87661	( Givón , 1979a : 28 )
87662	Yet the frequency of occurrence need not be as high as 90% to qualify as a regularity .
87663	The discourse analyst , like the experimental psychologist , is mainly interested in the level of frequency which reaches significance in perceptual terms .
87664	Thus , a regularity in discourse is a linguistic feature which occurs in a definable environment with a significant frequency .
87665	In trying to determine such regularities , the discourse analyst will typically adopt the traditional methodology of descriptive linguistics .
87666	He will attempt to describe the linguistic forms which occur in his data , relative to the environments in which they occur .
87667	In this sense , discourse analysis is , like descriptive linguistics , a way of studying language .
87668	It may be regarded as a set of techniques , rather than a theoretically predetermined system for the writing of linguistic ‘ rules ’ .
87669	The discourse analyst attempts to discover regularities in his data and to describe them .
87670	Product versus process
87671	The regularities which the discourse analyst describes will normally be expressed in dynamic , not static , terms .
87672	Since the data investigated is the result of ‘ ordinary language behaviour ’ , it is likely to contain evidence of the ‘ behaviour ’ element .
87673	That is , unless we believe that language-users present each other with prefabricated chunks of linguistic strings ( sentences ) , after the fashion of Swift 's professors at the grand academy of Lagado ( Gulliver 's Travels , part 3 , chapter 5 ) , then we must assume that the data we investigate is the result of active processes .
87674	The sentence-grammarian does not in general take account of this , since his data is not connected to behaviour .
87675	His data consists of a set of objects called ‘ the well-formed sentences of a language ’ , which can exist independently of any individual speaker of that language .
87676	We shall characterise such a view as the sentence-as-object view , and note that such sentence-objects have no producers and no receivers .
87677	Moreover , they need not be considered in terms of function , as evidenced in this statement by Chomsky ( I968 : 62 ) :
87678	If we hope to understand human language and the psychological capacities on which it rests , we must first ask what it is , not how or for what purposes it is used .
87679	A less extreme , but certainly related , view of natural language sentences can also be found elsewhere in the literature which relates to discourse analysis .
87680	In this view , there are producers and receivers of sentences , or extended texts , but the analysis concentrates solely on the product , that is , the words-on-the-page .
87681	Much of the analytic work undertaken in ‘ Textlinguistics ’ is of this type .
87682	Typical of such an approach is the ‘ cohesion ’ view of the relationships between sentences in a printed text ( e.g. the approach in Halliday &amp; Hasan , 1976 ) .
87683	In this view , cohesive ties exist between elements in connected sentences of a text in such a way that one word or phrase is linked to other words or phrases .
87684	Thus , an anaphoric element such as a pronoun is treated as a word which substitutes for , or refers back to , another word or words .
87685	Although there are claims that cohesive links in texts are used by text-producers to facilitate reading or comprehension by text-receivers ( cf.
87686	Rochester &amp; Martin 1977 , 1979 ; Källgren , 1979 ) , the analysis of the ‘ product ’ , i.e. the printed text itself , does not involve any consideration of how the product is produced or how it is received .
87687	We shall describe such an approach as deriving from a text-as-product view .
87688	This view does not take account of those principles which constrain the production and those which constrain the interpretation of texts .
87689	In contrast to these two broadly defined approaches , the view taken in this book is best characterised as a discourse-as-process view .
87690	The distinction between treating discourse as ‘ product ’ or ‘ process ’ has already been made by Widdowson ( 1979b : 71 ) .
87691	We shall consider words , phrases and sentences which appear in the textual record of a discourse to be evidence of an attempt by a producer ( speaker / writer ) to communicate his message to a recipient ( hearer / reader ) .
87692	We shall be particularly interested in discussing how a recipient might come to comprehend the producer 's intended message on a particular occasion , and how the requirements of the particular recipient(s) , in definable circumstances , influence the organisation of the producer 's discourse .
87693	This is clearly an approach which takes the communicative function of language as its primary area of investigation and consequently seeks to describe linguistic form , not as a static object , but as a dynamic means of expressing intended meaning .
87694	There are several arguments against the static concept of language to be found in both the ‘ sentence-as-object ’ and ‘ text-as-product ’ approaches .
87695	For example , Wittgenstein ( 1953 : 132 ) warns that ‘ the confusions that occupy us arise when language is like an engine idling , not when it is doing work ’ .
87696	In the course of describing how a sentence-as-object approach , based exclusively on syntactic descriptions , fails to account for a variety of sentential structures , Kuno ( 1976 ) concludes that ‘ it is time to re-examine every major syntactic constraint from a functional point of view ’ .
87697	Similar conclusions are expressed by Creider ( 1979 ) , Givóon ( 1976 , 1979b ) , Rommetveit ( 1974 ) and Tyler ( 1978 ) .
87698	In criticising the text-as-product view of cohesion in text , Morgan ( 1979 ) argues that we see a link between a particular pronoun and a full noun phrase in a text because we assume the text is coherent and not because the pronoun ‘ refers back ’ to the noun phrase .
87699	We seek to identify the writer 's intended referent for a pronoun , since a pronoun can , in effect , be used to refer to almost anything .
87700	That is , what the textual record means is determined by our interpretation of what the producer intended it to mean .
87701	The discourse analyst , then , is interested in the function or purpose of a piece of linguistic data and also in how that data is processed , both by the producer and by the receiver .
87702	It is a natural consequence that the discourse analyst will be interested in the results of psycholinguistic processing experiments in a way which is not typical of the sentence-grammarian .
87703	It also follows that the work of those sociolinguists and ethnographers who attempt to discuss language in terms of user 's purposes will also be of interest .
87704	In the course of this book , we shall appeal to evidence in the psycholinguistic and sociolinguistic literature which offers insights into the way in which discourse , produced in describable contexts for recognisable purposes , is processed and comprehended .
87705	On ‘ context'
87706	We have constantly referred to the ‘ environment ’ , ‘ circumstances ’ or context in which language is used .
87707	In Chapter 2 we shall explore the problem of specifying the relevant context .
87708	Here we simply remark that in recent years the idea that a linguistic string ( a sentence ) can be fully analysed without taking ‘ context ’ into account has been seriously questioned .
87709	If the sentence-grammarian wishes to make claims about the ‘ acceptability ’ of a sentence in determining whether the strings produced by his grammar are correct sentences of the language , he is implicitly appealing to contextual considerations .
87710	After all , what do we do when we are asked whether a particular string is ‘ acceptable ’ ?
87711	Do we not immediately , and quite naturally , set about constructing some circumstances ( i.e. a ‘ context ’ ) in which the sentence could be acceptably used ?
87712	Any analytic approach in linguistics which involves contextual considerations , necessarily belongs to that area of language study called pragmatics .
87713	‘ Doing discourse analysis ’ certainly involves ‘ doing syntax and semantics ’ , but it primarily consists of ‘ doing pragmatics ’ .
87714	When the principles which we have expounded in 1.3 are placed alongside Morris 's definition of pragmatics as ‘ the relations of signs to interpreters ’ ( 1938 : 6 ) , the connection becomes quite clear .
87715	In discourse analysis , as in pragmatics , we are concerned with what people using language are doing , and accounting for the linguistic features in the discourse as the means employed in what they are doing .
87716	In summary , the discourse analyst treats his data as the record ( text ) of a dynamic process in which language was used as an instrument of communication in a context by a speaker / writer to express meanings and achieve intentions ( discourse ) .
87717	Working from this data , the analyst seeks to describe regularities in the linguistic realisations used by people to communicate those meanings and intentions .
87718	2
87719	The role of context in interpretation
87720	Pragmatics and discourse context
87721	In Chapter I , we emphasised that the discourse analyst necessarily takes a pragmatic approach to the study of language in use .
87722	Such an approach brings into consideration a number of issues which do not generally receive much attention in the formal linguist 's description of sentential syntax and semantics .
87723	We noted , for example , that the discourse analyst has to take account of the context in which a piece of discourse occurs .
87724	Some of the most obvious linguistic elements which require contextual information for their interpretation are the deictic forms such as here , now , 1 , you , this and that .
87725	In order to interpret these elements in a piece of discourse , it is necessary to know ( at least ) who the speaker and hearer are , and the time and place of the production of the discourse .
87726	In this chapter we shall discuss these and other aspects of contextual description which are required in the analysis of discourse .
87727	There are , however , other ways in which the discourse analyst 's approach to linguistic data differs from that of the formal linguist and leads to a specialised use of certain terms .
87728	Because the analyst is investigating the use of language in context by a speaker / writer , he is more concerned with the relationship between the speaker and the utterance , on the particular occasion of use , than with the potential relationship of one sentence to another , regardless of their use .
87729	That is , in using terms such as reference , presupposition , implicature and inference , the discourse analyst is describing what speakers and hearers are doing , and not the relationship which exists between one sentence or proposition and another .
87730	Reference
87731	In presenting the traditional semantic view of reference , Lyons ( I968 : 404 ) says that ‘ the relationship which holds between words and things is the relationship of reference : words refer to things ’ .
87732	This traditional view continues to be expressed in those linguistic studies ( e.g. lexical semantics ) which describe the relationship between a language and the world , in the absence of language-users .
87733	Yet , Lyons , in a more recent statement on the nature of reference , makes the following point : ‘ it is the speaker who refers ( by using some appropriate expression ) : he invests the expression with reference by the act of referring ’ ( 1977 : 177 ) .
87734	It is exactly this latter view of the nature of reference which the discourse analyst has to appeal to .
87735	There is support for such a pragmatic concept of reference in Strawson 's ( 1950 ) claim that ‘ 'referring ’ is not something an expression does ; it is something that someone can use an expression to do' ; and in Searle 's view that ‘ in the sense in which speakers refer , expressions do not refer any more than they make promises or give orders ’ ( 1979 : 155 ) .
87736	Thus , in discourse analysis , reference is treated as an action on the part of the speaker / writer .
87737	In the following conversational fragment , we shall say , for example , that speaker A uses the expressions my uncle and he to refer to one individual and my mother 's sister and she to refer to another .
87738	We will not , for example , say that he ‘ refers to ’ my uncle .
87739	( I )
87740	A : my uncle 's coming home from Canada on Sunday + he 's due in +
87741	B : how long has he been away for or has he just been away ?
87742	A : Oh no they lived in Canada eh he was married to my mother 's sister + + well she 's been dead for a number of years now +
87743	The complex nature of discourse reference will be investigated in greater detail in Chapters 5 and 6 .
87744	Presupposition
87745	In the preceding conversational fragment ( I ) , we shall also say that speaker A treats the information that she has an uncle as presupposed and speaker B , in her question , indicates that she has accepted this presupposition .
87746	We shall take the view that the notion of presupposition required in discourse analysis is pragmatic presupposition , that is , ‘ defined in terms of assumptions the speaker makes about what the hearer is likely to accept without challenge ’ ( Givón , 1979a : 50 ) .
87747	The notion of assumed ‘ common ground ’ is also involved in such a characterisation of presupposition and can be found in this definition by Stalnaker ( 1978 : 321 ) :
87748	presuppositions are what is taken by the speaker to be the common ground of the participants in the conversation .
87749	Notice that , in both these quotations , the indicated source of presuppositions is the speaker .
87750	Consequently , we shall , as with reference , avoid attributing presuppositions to sentences or propositions .
87751	Thus , we can see little practical use , in the analysis of discourse , for the notion of logical presupposition which Keenan ( 1971 : 45 ) describes in the following way :
87752	A sentence S logically presupposes a sentence S' just in case S logically implies S' and the negation of S , – S , also logically implies S' .
87753	If we take the first sentence of extract ( I ) as S , and present it below as ( 2a ) , we can also present the negation of S , as ( 2b ) , and the logical presupposition , S' , as ( 2c ) .
87754	( 2 )
87755	a .
87756	My uncle is coming home from Canada .
87757	b .
87758	My uncle is n't coming home from Canada .
87759	c .
87760	I have an uncle .
87761	Following Keenan 's definition , we can say that ( 2a ) logically presupposes ( 2c ) because of constancy under negation .
87762	However , it seems rather unnecessary to introduce the negative sentence ( 2b ) into a consideration of the relationship between ( 2a ) and ( 2c ) which arises in the conversation presented earlier in ( I ) .
87763	Though it may not be common knowledge that the speaker has an uncle , it is what Grice ( 1981 : 190 ) terms ‘ noncontroversial ’ information .
87764	Moreover , since the speaker chose to say my uncle rather than I have an uncle and he … , we must assume she did n't feel the need to assert the information .
87765	What she appears to be asserting is that this person is coming home from Canada .
87766	Given this assertion , the idea that we should consider the denial of this assertion in order to find out whether there is a presupposition in what the speaker has not asserted seems particularly counterintuitive .
87767	The introduction of the negative sentence ( 2b ) into a consideration of ( 2a ) creates an additional problem .
87768	For example , it has been suggested ( cf.
87769	Kempson , 1975 ) that a sentence such as ( 2d ) is a perfectly reasonable sentence of English and undermines the argument for logical presupposition , as it is defined above
87770	( 2d ) My uncle is n't coming home from Canada because I do n't have an uncle .
87771	Sentences like ( 2d ) always seem typical of utterances made by a speaker to deny another speaker 's presupposition in a rather aggressive way .
87772	Yet the circumstances in which ( 2d ) might be uttered are likely to be quite different from those in which the first sentence of extract ( I ) was uttered .
87773	The speakers , we may suggest , would have different presuppositions , in the two situations .
87774	If we rely on a notion of speaker , or pragmatic , presupposition , we can simply treat ( 2c ) as a presupposition of the speaker in uttering ( 2a ) .
87775	Sentences ( 2b ) and ( 2d ) do not come into consideration at all .
87776	In support of a view that hearers behave as if speakers ' presuppositions are to be accepted , there is the rather disturbing evidence from Loftus ' study ( 1975 ) of answers to leading questions .
87777	After watching a film of a car accident some subjects were asked the two questions in ( 3 ) .
87778	( 3 )
87779	a .
87780	How fast was car A going when it turned right ?
87781	b .
87782	Did you see a stop sign ?
87783	We can note that one of the speaker-presuppositions in asking ( 3a ) is that car A turned right .
87784	A number ( 35% ) answered yes to question ( 3b ) .
87785	Another group of subjects were asked the questions in ( 4 ) .
87786	( 4 )
87787	a .
87788	How fast was car A going when it ran the stop sign ?
87789	b .
87790	Did you see a stop sign ?
87791	One of the speaker-presuppositions in asking ( 4a ) is that car A ran the stop sign .
87792	In this situation , a significantly larger group ( 53% ) answered yes to question ( 4b ) .
87793	It is worth noting that a number of subjects did not answer the b question in terms of truth or falsehood of fact , but according to what the speaker , in asking the preceding question , had appeared to presuppose .
87794	( For a more detailed discussion of this issue , see Loftus , 1975 and Loftus &amp; Zanni , 1975 . )
87795	We shall reconsider the notion of presupposition in section 3.3.2 , but generally avoid the complex arguments which revolve around the presuppositions of sentences and propositions .
87796	( See the contributions and bibliography in Oh &amp; Dineen ( eds. ) 1979 . )
87797	Implicatures
87798	The term ‘ implicature ’ is used by Grice ( 1975 ) to account for what a speaker can imply , suggest , or mean , as distinct from what the speaker literally says .
87799	There are conventional implicatures which are , according to Grice , determined by ‘ the conventional meaning of the words used ’ ( 1975 : 44 ) .
87800	In the following example ( 5 ) , the speaker does not directly assert that one property ( being brave ) follows from another property ( being an Englishman ) , but the form of expression used conventionally implicates that such a relation does hold .
87801	( 5 ) He is an Englishman , he is , therefore , brave .
87802	If it should turn out that the individual in question is an Englishman , and not brave , then the implicature is mistaken , but the utterance , Grice suggests , need not be false .
87803	For a fuller discussion of conventional implicature , see Karttunen &amp; Peters ( 1979 ) .
87804	Of much greater interest to the discourse analyst is the notion of conversational implicature which is derived from a general principle of conversation plus a number of maxims which speakers will normally obey .
87805	The general principle is called the Cooperative Principle which Grice ( 1975 : 45 ) presents in the following terms :
87806	Make your conversational contribution such as is required , at the stage at which it occurs , by the accepted purpose or direction of the talk exchange in which you are engaged .
87807	The conversational conventions , or maxims , which support this principle are as follows :
87808	Quantity : Make your contribution as informative as is required ( for the current purposes of the exchange ) .
87809	Do not make your contribution more informative than is required .
87810	Quality : Do not say what you believe to be false .
87811	Do not say that for which you lack adequate evidence .
87812	Relation : Be relevant .
87813	Manner : Be perspicuous .
87814	Avoid obscurity of expression .
87815	Avoid ambiguity .
87816	Be brief ( avoid unnecessary prolixity ) .
87817	Be orderly .
87818	Grice does not suggest that this is an exhaustive list — he notes that a maxim such as Be polite is also normally observed — nor that equal weight should be attached to each of the stated maxims .
87819	( The maxim of manner , for example , does not obviously apply to primarily interactional conversation . )
87820	We might observe that the instruction Be relevant seems to cover all the other instructions .
87821	However , by providing a description of the norms speakers operate with in conversation , Grice makes it possible to describe what types of meaning a speaker can convey by ‘ flouting ’ one of these maxims .
87822	This flouting of a maxim results in the speaker conveying , in addition to the literal meaning of his utterance , an additional meaning , which is a conversational implicature .
87823	As a brief example , we can consider the following exchange :
87824	( 6 )
87825	A : I am out of petrol .
87826	B : There is a garage round the corner .
87827	In this exchange , Grice ( 1975 : 51 ) suggests that B would be infringing the instruction Be relevant if he was gratuitously stating a fact about the world via the literal meaning of his utterance .
87828	The implicature , derived from the assumption that speaker B is adhering to the Cooperative Principle , is that the garage is not only round the corner , but also will be open and selling petrol .
87829	We might also note that , in order to arrive at the implicature , we have to know certain.facts about the world , that garages sell petrol , and that round the corner is not a great distance away .
87830	We also have to interpret A's remark not only as a description of a particular state of affairs , but as a request for help , for instance .
87831	Once the analysis of intended meaning goes beyond the literal meaning of the ‘ sentences-on-the-page ’ , a vast number of related issues have to be considered .
87832	We shall investigate some of these issues in the course of this book , particularly in Chapters 6 and 7 .
87833	As a brief account of how the term ‘ implicature ’ is used in discourse analysis , we have summarised the important points in Grice 's proposal .
87834	We would like to emphasise the fact that implicatures are pragmatic aspects of meaning and have certain identifiable characteristics .
87835	They are partially derived from the conventional or literal meaning of an utterance , produced in a specific context which is shared by the speaker and the hearer , and depend on a recognition by the speaker and the hearer of the Cooperative Principle and its maxims .
87836	For the analyst , as well as the hearer , conversational implicatures must be treated as inherently indeterminate since they derive from a supposition that the speaker has the intention of conveying meaning and of obeying the Cooperative Principle .
87837	Since the analyst has only limited access to what a speaker intended , or how sincerely he was behaving , in the production of a discourse fragment , any claims regarding the implicatures identified will have the status of interpretations .
87838	In this respect , the discourse analyst is not in the apparently secure position of the formal linguist who has ‘ rules ’ of the language which are or are not satisfied , but rather , is in the position of the hearer who has interpretations of the discourse which do , or do not , make sense .
87839	( For a more detailed treatment of conversational implicature , see Levinson , forthcoming . )
87840	Inference
87841	Since the discourse analyst , like the hearer , has no direct access to a speaker 's intended meaning in producing an utterance , he often has to rely on a process of inference to arrive at an interpretation for utterances or for the connections between utterances .
87842	Such inferences appear to be of different kinds .
87843	It may be the case that we are capable of deriving a specific conclusion ( 7c ) from specific premises ( 7a ) and ( 7b ) , via deductive inference , but we are rarely asked to do so in the everyday discourse we encounter .
87844	( 7 )
87845	a .
87846	If it 's sunny , it 's warm .
87847	b .
87848	It 's sunny .
87849	c .
87850	So , it 's warm .
87851	We are more likely to operate with a rather loose form of inferencing which leads us to believe that the hats and coats mentioned in ( 8 ) belong to visitors to the house which has the dresser in its kitchen .
87852	( 8 ) in the kitchen there was a huge dresser and when anyone went in you see + the hats and coats were all dumped on this dresser
87853	It may be , of course , that such an inference is wrong , but , as discourse processors , we seem to prefer to make inferences which have some likelihood of being justified and , if some subsequent information does not fit in with this inference , we abandon it and form another .
87854	As an illustration of this , consider the following example ( 9 ) , taken from Sanford &amp; Garrod ( 1981 : 10 ) :
87855	( 9 ) John was on his way to school .
87856	If we were to take a formal view of the entailments of such a declarative sentence ( like that , for example , expressed in Smith &amp; Wilson , 1979 : 150f. ) , we would be obliged to accept as entailments a set of sentences which would include the following :
87857	( 10 )
87858	a .
87859	Someone was on his way to school .
87860	b .
87861	John was on his way to somewhere .
87862	c .
87863	Someone was on his way to somewhere .
87864	This view of what we infer from reading ( 9 ) will only provide us with a limited insight into how readers interpret what they read .
87865	Most readers report that they infer from ( 9 ) that John is a schoolboy , among other things .
87866	When sentence ( 9 ) is followed later in the same text by sentence ( II ) , readers readily abandon their original inference and form another , for example that John is a schoolteacher .
87867	( 11 ) Last week he had been unable to control the class .
87868	In order to capture this type of inference , which is extremely common in our interpretation of discourse , we need a relatively loose notion of inference based on socio-cultural knowledge .
87869	Gumperz ( 1977 ) presents an extended discussion of the types of factors involved in this type of pragmatic , as opposed to logical , inference .
87870	We shall discuss the influence of inference in more detail in Chapter 7 .
87871	For the moment , we simply present a view which claims that the terms reference , presupposition , implicature and inference must be treated as pragmatic concepts in the analysis of discourse .
87872	These terms will be used to indicate relationships between discourse participants and elements in the discourse .
87873	Since the pragmatic use of these terms is closely tied to the context in which a discourse occurs , we shall now investigate what aspects of context have to be considered in undertaking the analysis of discourse .
87874	The context of situation
87875	Since the beginning of the 1970s , linguists have become increasingly aware of the importance of context in the interpretation of sentences .
87876	The implications of taking context into account are well expressed by Sadock ( 1978 : 281 ) :
87877	There is , then , a serious methodological problem that confronts the advocate of linguistic pragmatics .
87878	Given some aspects of what a sentence conveys in a particular context , is that aspect part of what the sentence conveys in virtue of its meaning … or should it be ‘ worked out ’ on the basis of Gricean principles from the rest of the meaning of the sentence and relevant facts of the context of utterance ?
87879	If we are to begin to consider the second part of this question seriously we need to be able to specify what are the ‘ relevant facts of the context of utterance ’ .
87880	The same problem is raised by Fillmore ( 1977 : 119 ) when he advocates a methodology to which a discourse analyst may often wish to appeal :
87881	The task is to determine what we can know about the meaning and context of an utterance given only the knowledge that the utterance has occurred …
87882	I find that whenever I notice some sentence in context , I immediately find myself asking what the effect would have been if the context had been slightly different .
87883	In order to make appeal to this methodology , which is very commonly used in linguistic and philosophical discussion , we need to know what it would mean for the context to be ‘ slightly different ’ .
87884	Features of context
87885	Consider two invented scenarios in which an identical utterance is produced by two distinct speakers .
87886	a
87887	speaker : a young mother , hearer : her mother-in-law , place : park , by a duckpond , time : sunny afternoon in September 1962 .
87888	They are watching the young mother 's two-year-old son chasing ducks and the mother-in-law has just remarked that her son , the child 's father , was rather backward at this age .
87889	The young mother says :
87890	I do think Adam 's quick
87891	b
87892	speaker : a student , hearers : a set of students , place : sitting round a coffee table in the refectory , time : evening in March 1980 .
87893	John , one of the group , has just told a joke .
87894	Everyone laughs except Adam .
87895	Then Adam laughs .
87896	One of the students says :
87897	I do think Adam 's quick
87898	( In each case phonological prominence is placed on Adam . )
87899	Clearly we can do a formal analysis on these tokens and , in both cases , the speaker says of Adam that he is quick .
87900	It is clear , however , that the utterances in the contexts of situation in which they are cited , would be taken to convey very different messages .
87901	In ( a ) we shall simplistically assume that the referents of I and Adam are fixed by spatio-temporal co-ordinates .
87902	This ‘ Adam ’ is being compared ( or contrasted ) , favourably , with his father .
87903	Quick , may be interpreted , in the context of backward , as meaning something like ‘ quick in developing ’ .
87904	In ( b ) different referents for I and Adam are fixed spatiotemporally .
87905	This ‘ Adam ’ is being compared ( or contrasted ) not with his father and favourably , but with the set of other students unfavourably .
87906	In this case quick must be interpreted as meaning something like ‘ quick to understand / react / see the joke ’ .
87907	Moreover , since it is said in a context where Adam has just manifestly failed to react to the punch-line as quickly as the set of other students , the speaker ( given this type of speaker to this type of hearer in this type of surroundings ) will be assumed not to be intending to tell an untruth , but to be implicating the opposite of what she has said .
87908	Is it possible to determine in any principled way what aspects of context of situation are relevant to these different interpretations of the same ‘ utterance ’ on two occasions ?
87909	J. R. Firth ( regarded by many as the founder of modern British linguistics ) remarked :
87910	Logicians are apt to think of words and propositions as having ‘ meaning ’ somehow in themselves , apart from participants in contexts of situation .
87911	Speakers and listeners do not seem to be necessary .
87912	I suggest that voices should not be entirely dissociated from the social context in which they function and that therefore all texts in modern spoken languages should be regarded as having ‘ the implication of utterance ’ , and be referred to typical participants in some generalised context of situation .
87913	( 1957 : 226 )
87914	Firth , then , was concerned to embed the utterance in the ‘ social context ’ and to generalise across meanings in specified social contexts .
87915	He proposed an approach to the principled description of such contexts which bears a close resemblance to more recent descriptions which we shall go on to examine :
87916	My view was , and still is , that ‘ context of situation ’ is best used as a suitable schematic construct to apply to language events …
87917	A context of situation for linguistic work brings into relation the following categories :
87918	A
87919	The relevant features of participants : persons , personalities .
87920	i
87921	The verbal action of the participants .
87922	ii
87923	The non-verbal action of the participants .
87924	B
87925	The relevant objects .
87926	C
87927	The effect of the verbal action .
87928	…
87929	A very rough parallel to this sort of context can be found in language manuals providing the learner with a picture of the railway station and the operative words for travelling by train .
87930	It is very rough .
87931	But it is parallel with the grammatical rules , and is based on the repetitive routines of initiated persons in the society under description .
87932	( 1957 : 182 ; for a practical application of Firth 's approach , see Mitchell , 1957 . )
87933	An approach similarly emphasising the importance of an ethnographic view of communicative events within communities has been developed by Hymes in a series of articles .
87934	Hymes views the role of context in interpretation as , on the one hand , limiting the range of possible interpretations and , on the other , as supporting the intended interpretation :
87935	The use of a linguistic form identifies a range of meanings .
87936	A context can support a range of meanings .
87937	When a form is used in a context it eliminates the meanings possible to that context other than those the form can signal : the context eliminates from consideration the meanings possible to the form other than those the context can support .
87938	( Hymes , 1962 , quoted in Wootton , 1975 : 44 )
87939	Hymes ( 1964 ) sets about specifying the features of context which may be relevant to the identification of a type of speech event in a way reminiscent of Firth 's .
87940	Like Firth , he seizes first on the ‘ persons ’ participating in the speech event .
87941	Generalising over speech events , he abstracts the roles addressor and addressee .
87942	The addressor is the speaker or writer who produces the utterance .
87943	The addressee is the hearer or reader who is the recipient of the utterance .
87944	( Later Hymes also distinguishes audience , since the presence of overhearers may contribute to the specification of the speech event . )
87945	Knowledge of the addressor in a given communicative event makes it possible for the analyst to imagine what that particular person is likely to say .
87946	Knowledge of his addressee constrains the analyst 's expectations even further .
87947	Thus , if you know the speaker is the prime minister or the departmental secretary or your family doctor or your mother , and you know that the speaker is speaking to a colleague or his bank manager or a small child , you will have different expectations of the sort of language which will be produced , both with respect to form and to content .
87948	If you know , further , what is being talked about , Hymes ' category of topic , your expectations will be further constrained .
87949	If then you have information about the setting , both in terms of where the event is situated in place and time , and in terms of the physical relations of the interactants with respect to posture and gesture and facial expression , your expectations will be still further limited .
87950	The remaining features of context which Hymes discusses ( in 1964 ) include large-scale features like channel ( how is contact between the participants in the event being maintained — by speech , writing , signing , smoke signals ) , code ( what language , or dialect , or style of language is being used ) , message-form ( what form is intended — chat , debate , sermon , fairy-tale , sonnet , love-letter , etc. ) and event ( the nature of the communicative event within which a genre may be embedded — thus a sermon or prayer may be part of the larger event , a church service ) .
87951	In later recensions Hymes adds other features , for example key ( which involves evaluation — was it a good sermon , a pathetic explanation , etc. ) , and purpose ( what did the participants intend should come about as a result of the communicative event ) .
87952	Hymes intends that these contextual features should be regarded rather as general phonetic features are regarded .
87953	Just as a phonetician may select , from the general phonetic features available , the features voiced , bilabial and stop , but not lateral , to characterise a [ b ] , so , he suggests , the analyst may choose from the contextual features , those necessary to characterise a particular communicative event .
87954	Just as the phonetician may wish to make a more detailed , more specific description of the [ b ] under consideration , for example mentioning delayed onset of voicing and some protrusion of the lips during the period of closure , so may the ethnographer wish to specify some of the contextual features in great detail .
87955	We shall return to this point .
87956	Hymes ' features constitute essentially a checklist which would enable a visiting ethnographer to arrive by helicopter in a location where a communicative event is in process and to check off the detail of the nature of the communicative event .
87957	Let us consider such an ethnographer as an invisible witness to a particular speech event .
87958	He would begin , presumably , by noting the larger-scale features of context : what channel is being used ( we shall say speech ) , what language code is being used ( we shall specify it is English ) , what message-form is being performed ( we shall specify it is conversation ) , what event is it embedded in ( we shall specify it is part of an interview ) .
87959	He can identify the participants : the addressor is a young scientist who is being interviewed by the addressee who is doing research on language .
87960	The setting is physically located in the addressee 's territory in Edinburgh University and a prominent physical feature is a tape-recorder which is switched on .
87961	The time is during the later 1970s ( so it is reasonable to expect that they will speak modern English , with Scottish accents ) .
87962	It has just been agreed that they will talk about the young scientist 's work , the tape-recorder is switched on and he says :
87963	( 12 ) I must admit I 'm very nervous .
87964	His topic at this point , we shall simplistically assume ( see further discussion in Chapter 3 ) , is his nervousness .
87965	Given the knowledge of context the analyst has , he should find this a fairly unsurprising utterance .
87966	It is very rarely the case in real life that we can predict in detail the form and content of the language which we will encounter , but , given all of the ethnographic information we have specified , the actual occurring utterance is much more likely ( hence , we assume , much more readily processed by the addressee ) than any of the following ‘ utterances ’ which did not occur :
87967	( 13 )
87968	a .
87969	Please pass the marmalade .
87970	b .
87971	My cat has just been sick again .
87972	c .
87973	Get into the box .
87974	d .
87975	I am about to make the first incision .
87976	The more the analyst knows about the features of context , the more likely he is to be able to predict what is likely to be said ( see 2.4 ) .
87977	It is further the case that the ethnographic features will give us a value for the deictic forms occurring in the utterance which was actually produced .
87978	Thus 1 , must , and am must be interpreted with respect to the speaker , the young scientist , at the time of making the utterance .
87979	( The context here makes the other possible reading , that the speaker is characteristically nervous all of the time , so unlikely as not to be considered apparently by the addressee , or indeed by the analyst until the process of analysis was brought to conscious attention . )
87980	In 2 .
87981	I we pointed out that deictic elements of the utterances can only be interpreted with respect to the context in which they are uttered .
87982	Hymes ' checklist of ethnographic features offers one characterisation of context to which we can relate such deictic elements .
87983	A more elaborate checklist is provided by the philosopher Lewis ( 1972 ) , specifically to provide an index of those co-ordinates which a hearer would need to have specified in order that he could determine the truth of a sentence .
87984	Like most formal linguists , Lewis assumes that the channel is speech , the code , English , the message-form conversation and the event one where one individual is informing another .
87985	His interests lie , not with these general features of the communicative event , but with those particular co-ordinates which constitute ‘ a package of relevant factors , an index ’ ( 1972 : 173 ) and which characterise the context against which the truth of a sentence is to be judged .
87986	The co-ordinates of the index are specified as follows :
87987	a
87988	possible-world co-ordinate : this is to account for states of affairs which might be , or could be supposed to be or are
87989	b
87990	time co-ordinate : to account for tensed sentences and adverbials like today or next week
87991	c
87992	place co-ordinate : to account for sentences like here it is
87993	d
87994	speaker co-ordinate : to account for sentences which include first person reference ( I , me , we , our , etc . )
87995	e
87996	audience co-ordinate : to account for sentences including you , yours , yourself , etc .
87997	f
87998	indicated object co-ordinate : to account for sentences containing demonstrative phrases like this , those , etc .
87999	g
88000	previous discourse co-ordinate : to account for sentences including phrases like the latter , the aforementioned , etc .
88001	h
88002	assignment co-ordinate : an infinite series of things ( sets of things , sequences of things … )
88003	Rather similar lists are proposed by scholars who are concerned with the construction of formal discourse domains ( see discussion in Chapter 3 ) .
88004	For our present purposes we should note that Lewis ' list , like Hymes ' , makes reference to the speaker and hearer in order to assign values to the deictic categories of speaker and audience ( addressor / addressee ) realised in first and second person pronouns .
88005	Hymes ' category setting is expanded to take explicit and distinct account of time and place .
88006	Hymes ' generalised feature of topic is now distributed between the deictic co-ordinate indicated object , the assignment co-ordinate and the previous discourse co-ordinate .
88007	This last co-ordinate specifically enables the hearer to interpret what is said in the light of what has already been said .
88008	It builds in a cumulative temporal structure to the index , in that the hearer must continually update the information in his previous discourse component , to take account of what has most recently been added .
88009	It is , obviously , not possible for us in a textbook to permit you to have the experience of everyday discourse in what Stenning ( 1978 ) calls a ‘ normal context ’ , where the hearer is part of the context and then experiences the text .
88010	We have to have recourse to what Stenning calls ‘ abnormal ’ contexts , where the analyst reads the text and then has to try to provide the characteristics of the context in which the text might have occurred .
88011	We are going to provide you with three written fragments , abstracted from the contexts in which they appeared .
88012	The first two are printed , the third spraygunned on a wall .
88013	We ask you to consider what , if any , difficulty you have in understanding them , in terms of the co-ordinates of Lewis ' index .
88014	( 14 ) .
88015	Place two fingers in the two holes directly to the left of the finger stop .
88016	Remove finger nearest stop .
88017	b .
88018	He seemed to resent them on that occasion and will not wear them today .
88019	c .
88020	SQUASHED INSECTS DO NT BITE MAD MENTAL RULE
88021	We have not , as yet , introduced any satisfactory way of handling your experience of previous similar texts ( see discussion in 2.4 ) .
88022	For the moment we shall suppose that you probably recognise the type of writer in ( a ) as some impersonal / institutionalised writer addressing a general reader rather than a particular individual ( paying attention to Place and Remove and the ellipsis in the second sentence ( the ) finger nearest ( to the ) stop ) .
88023	If you have difficulty in interpreting this fragment it is probably partly because you are not sure of the referents of the expression the two holes and the finger stop .
88024	You may work out that the two holes have to be of a suitable size for an individual ( ? ) to put two fingers in , possibly near enough to each other to put two fingers of the same hand in , and , having established this scale , it seems likely that the object referred to as the finger stop is only centimetres removed , rather than kilometres removed .
88025	It would certainly help you to have the following information :
88026	The addressor is the Post Office .
88027	The addressee is you as a telephone user .
88028	You can probably work out the rest if you did not know it already .
88029	However we shall spell out some more :
88030	The time of utterance in clock or calendar time does not seem relevant , but what certainly is relevant is that you should know whether this instruction still applies .
88031	( It does . )
88032	The place of the original utterance is hardly relevant but where you would encounter the text is .
88033	( Look in your telephone directory . )
88034	The possible world that is relevant is specified in the previous discourse : ‘ It is worth remembering how to dial 999 in darkness or smoke . ’
88035	( We should point out that you are not here being asked to use the co-ordinates for the purpose Lewis intended them for , to determine the truth of a sentence .
88036	It is a matter of debate whether truth can be assigned to sentences in the imperative form . )
88037	In text b the problem of interpretation arises because of not knowing the referents for the expressions He , them , on that occasion and them and not having a value to fix the time expression today .
88038	You may be able to work out that He refers to an animate masculine entity , the subject of both clauses .
88039	You may wonder why it is reported that He seemed to resent them , which may suggest that he was unable to express his own resentment , which may limit your range of potential interpretations of the expression He .
88040	You note that he resented them , where them is plural , and you may consider what plural entity may be both resented and worn ( or not worn ) .
88041	This example has all the characteristics of a sentence occurring within a larger piece of text , and illustrates quite clearly the need for a ‘ previous discourse ’ co-ordinate , as well as the more obvious ‘ time ’ and ‘ place ’ co-ordinates .
88042	This text appeared in The Sporting Chronicle on 4 June 1980 .
88043	In the preceding part of the text , the writer has been describing a particular racehorse ( He ) which had been fitted with blinkers ( them ) for its previous race ( on that occasion ) .
88044	The third text , c , offers more thorny problems .
88045	Whereas the language of a and b is quite straightforward and all you require to arrive at an interpretation are values for expressions being used to refer , you may feel that the language here is obscure , perhaps not even meaningful .
88046	It is relevant that the time at which this text appeared was in the late 1970s .
88047	Your experience of previous similar texts in the 1970s may have familiarised you with the form X rule OK which may permit you to divide this unpunctuated sequence into two parts :
88048	SQUASHED INSECTS DO NT BITE MAD MENTAL RULE
88049	The place at which it appeared is relevant .
88050	It was spraygunned on a wall in Glasgow .
88051	The form of the text , together with the information about place , may suggest to you , if you have previous experience of such texts , that this text derives from an interaction between street gangs .
88052	Encyclopedic knowledge of the world might inform you that the writer is a member of ‘ Mad Mental ’ ( a street gang ) and that the intended addressees are members of ‘ The Insects ’ ( another street gang ) .
88053	You then need to make appeal to previous discourse in which the Insects had proclaimed INSECTS BITE .
88054	( You might then appeal to your knowledge of what Hymes calls ‘ message-form ’ which informs you that street gang interactions on walls consists of taunts and counter-taunts .
88055	Thus you might arrive at an attribution of intention in the warning SQUASHED INSECTS DO NT BITE and the straight assertion MAD MENTAL RULE — without the OK tag , which might be taken to invite assent on the part of the addressee . )
88056	Texts a and b , addressed to the general reader , are relatively accessible fragments of language which require only specification of the intended referents to make them readily interpretable .
88057	Text c is intended for specific addressees , not for the general public , and it is hard for the general public to interpret without access to shared presuppositions and previous experience which can not comfortably be forced into the framework proposed by Lewis .
88058	In order to take account of this , we are going to need some way of making appeals to notions like ‘ shared presuppositions ’ , 'encyclopedic knowledge' , ‘ intention / purpose in uttering ’ and ‘ experience of previous similar text ’ which we have simply appealed to in an ad hoc way in our discussion so far .
88059	We return to these questions in 2.3 .
88060	What we have shown in this section is that the contextual features suggested by Hymes , supplemented with the index of co-ordinates proposed by Lewis ( put forward , remember , with quite different purposes in mind ) do enable us to give a partial account of what the undifferentiated term ‘ context ’ may mean .
88061	From this it follows that we could give some account of what it might mean to ‘ change the context ’ in the sense in which Fillmore ( 1977 : 119 ) envisages this when he says ‘ I … find myself asking what the effect would have been if the context had been slightly different . ’
88062	We could reply that if you alter the condition specified by any of the co-ordinates , you alter the context .
88063	At this point we shall consider only the alteration of one co-ordinate , the speaker co-ordinate .
88064	Obviously , if Jane says I 'm skipping and Mary says I 'm skipping we observe that on one occasion it is Jane who announces that she is skipping and on another it is Mary .
88065	In each case the sentence is true if the person who spoke was skipping at the time of the utterance .
88066	However , if we are further told that speaker Jane is only three years old , we may , in addition to paying attention to the announcement , consider that it is a remarkable feat for a three-year-old .
88067	Whereas if Mary is eight years old and known to be an intrepid skipper , the announcement may be one of a depressingly predictable series .
88068	We pay different amounts of attention to the announcements and react to them differently , because one aspect of the context , the speaker , is significantly different .
88069	Consider the following fragment of conversation :
88070	( 15 )
88071	A : are you often here
88072	B : quite often + about once a month + actually ++ I come up to see my children
88073	You have to suppose of B that B is of an age to have children .
88074	What we are interested in is the different sorts of inferences which we make as addressees , depending on variables like the age and sex of the speaker , as a result of hearing what B says .
88075	Suppose B is a man of seventy .
88076	We assume that B 's children will be grown-up .
88077	Nothing particular follows from the fact that he visits them once a month , except perhaps we infer that he has a close relationship with them .
88078	Suppose the speaker is a young man in his thirties .
88079	We assume that children he has will be young children , children of an age who usually live with their parents .
88080	We may then wonder why B 's children are not living with their father , wonder whether the exigences of his professional life , or of his relationship with the children 's mother , constrains him to live apart from them .
88081	Suppose the speaker is a young woman in her thirties .
88082	Again we assume that she would have young children , children who would normally be expected to be living with her .
88083	Since , in the case of the parents being separated , young children usually live with their mother in our society , we might infer that the woman 's children are in some form of institutional or educational care .
88084	( In the conversation we quote from , the speaker was a man in his early thirties and the children were living with his estranged wife , all inferences which had been drawn by A before B went on to explain that this was the case . )
88085	Observe that the sorts of inferences we have been discussing are not sanctioned by the form of language used .
88086	The different inferences arise because of the alteration of the context , in the simple manipulation of age and sex of the addressor .
88087	It is the interpretation of the utterance in context which permits the hearer to draw such inferences ( see Chapter 7 for further discussion of inferences ) .
88088	Co-text
88089	In our discussion so far we have concentrated particularly on the physical context in which single utterances are embedded and we have paid rather little attention to the previous discourse co-ordinate .
88090	Lewis introduced this co-ordinate to take account of sentences which include specific reference to what has been mentioned before as in phrases like the aforementioned .
88091	It is , however , the case that any sentence other than the first in a fragment of discourse , will have the whole of its interpretation forcibly constrained by the preceding text , not just those phrases which obviously and specifically refer to the preceding text , like the aforementioned .
88092	Just as the interpretation of the token α in the child 's representation of ‘ without to disturb the lion ’ and the token [ p ] in [ greipbritn ] are determined by the context in which they appear , so the words which occur in discourse are constrained by what , following Halliday , we shall call their co-text .
88093	Consider the following lexical items in a number of verbal contexts cited almost at random from Darwin 's Journal during the Voyage of HMS Beagle round the World :
88094	( 16 )
88095	a .
88096	The children of the Indians are saved , to be sold or given away as servants , or rather slaves for as long a time as the owners can make them believe themselves slaves .
88097	But I believe in their treatment there is little to complain of ( 114 )
88098	b .
88099	The same evening I went on shore .
88100	The first landing in any new country is very interesting .
88101	( 169 )
88102	c .
88103	When we came within hail , one of the four natives who were present advanced to receive us and began to shout most vehemently , wishing to direct us where to land .
88104	When we were on shore the party looked rather alarmed .
88105	( 206 )
88106	d .
88107	After crossing many low hills , we descended into the small land-locked plain of Guitron .
88108	In the basins , such as this one , which are elevated from one thousand to two thousand feet above the sea , two species of acacia … grow in large numbers .
88109	( 257 ) ( 1892 edition )
88110	The point we wish to make here should be an obvious one and can of course be made with respect to many of the other items which we have not italicised in the cited texts .
88111	However , consider the sort of lexical content you would expect to find associated with the forms treatment , landing , party and basin in a dictionary entry , and note how finding the forms embedded within a co-text constrains their interpretation .
88112	Just as the interpretation of individual lexical items is constrained by co-text , so is the interpretation of utterances within a discourse .
88113	Consider this text of the beginning of a sixteen-year-old Scottish pupil 's account of a Sempé cartoon :
88114	( 17 )
88115	a. a man and woman sitting in the living room + the woman sitting reading quite happily — the man 's bored goes to the window looks out the window + and gets himself ready and goes out +
88116	The reader must interpret the woman sitting reading quite happily as the ‘ woman ’ already mentioned , hence must construct an interpretation which has her ‘ sitting reading quite happily in the living room ’ .
88117	Similarly the window which the man approaches must be interpreted as ‘ the window of the living room ’ .
88118	The speaker continues with a change of location and we have to assume that what follows is within the newly introduced location :
88119	b. goes to his goes to a club + has a drink talks to the barman + then he starts dancing with a beautiful girl long black hair + has a good time +
88120	We interpret everything that happens here as happening to the man we met in the living room who is now at a club .
88121	So he has a drink , talks to the barman , starts dancing and has a good time all at the ‘ club ’ .
88122	The speaker announces another change of location
88123	c. then he goes home and he calls her + and his wife overhears him +
88124	Again we assume that we are still talking about the same man , that he has returned home to the location where the ‘ living room ’ we first met was located .
88125	Now the analyst may be in some doubt how to interpret and he calls her , since the man might reasonably go into the house and call ( shout for ) his wife .
88126	However this interpretation is ruled out by the following co-text and his wife overhears him .
88127	So we are obliged to interpret calls as meaning ‘ phones ’ and her as referring to ‘ the beautiful girl with long black hair with whom he danced and had a good time ’ .
88128	Within the co-text , as we have seen in ( 17 ) above , a further context may be constructed which has its own index of coordinates .
88129	Indeed within that constructed context , further contexts may be nested .
88130	Consider the following passages :
88131	( 18 ) About four months before the time I am writing of , my Lady had been in London , and had gone over a Reformatory …
88132	The matron , seeing my Lady took an interest in the place , pointed out a girl to her , named Rosanna Spearman , and told her a most miserable story : which I have n't the heart to repeat here ; for I do n't like to be made wretched without any use , and no more do you .
88133	The upshot of it was , that Rosanna Spearman had been a thief …
88134	( Wilkie Collins , The Moonstone )
88135	The actual place and time of writing of the manuscript by the author , Wilkie Collins , or indeed the identity of the author , is not a necessary piece of information for the reader to interpret the text .
88136	We may assume , however , that he will have a better understanding of the purpose of the author in constructing the text in the way it is constructed if he knows that it is written in the late nineteenth century ( which will account for some differences in code , in Hymes ' terms ) in Victorian England ( which will account for the reference to a Reformatory ) and that the author is constructing the first English detective story , narrating the events from the point of view of four different participants , whose characters are in part revealed by the narrative style which the author assigns to them .
88137	We have then , an author and an actual time and place of writing the novel ( or a series of times and places ) .
88138	Then to each narrator is assigned a time and place of the writing of his contribution .
88139	It is presumably that time which is relevant to the comment which I have n't the heart to repeat here where I refers to the current narrator .
88140	Immediately preceding this extracted fragment , the narrator has been describing an incident relevant to the main story .
88141	This is referred to in the expression the time I am writing of .
88142	The narrator then proceeds to give some background information , which he situates in a previous time About four months before .
88143	He introduces Rosanna Spearman , who , at the time four months before was a resident of the Reformatory , but at some previous time to that , Rosanna Spearman had been a thief .
88144	Within the time domain of ‘ four months before ’ a new speaker and hearer are introduced :
88145	( 19 ) My Lady … said to the matron upon that , ‘ Rosanna Spearman shall have her chance , in my service ’ .
88146	In a week afterwards , Rosanna Spearman entered this establishment as our second housemaid .
88147	At the time of utterance , four months before the time I am writing of , the beneficent lady speaks of the future , shall have her chance .
88148	In the following sentence the narrator comments on what happened a week later than the time of the lady 's speech , from the point of view of his context at the time of writing his contribution to the novel , In a week afterwards …
88149	This brief introduction does scant justice to the interest of the temporal structure of this passage .
88150	It does , however , indicate the complexity of nested contexts established by co-text which , as hearers / readers , we are capable of interpreting .
88151	In Chapter 6 we shall discuss the issue of anaphoric reference which is generally held to depend crucially on co-text for interpretation .
88152	For the moment the main point we are concerned to make is to stress the power of co-text in constraining interpretation .
88153	Even in the absence of information about place and time of original utterance , even in the absence of information about the speaker / writer and his intended recipient , it is often possible to reconstruct at least some part of the physical context and to arrive at some interpretation of the text .
88154	The more co-text there is , in general , the more secure the interpretation is .
88155	Text creates its own context .
88156	As Isard ( 1975 : 377 ) remarks : ‘ communications do not merely depend on the context for their interpretation , they change that context ’ .
88157	The expanding context
88158	In our discussion so far , we have been concerned to impose some sort of analytic structure on the lumpen mass of context .
88159	We have abstracted away from particular contexts , across communicative contexts in general , to arrive at a set of features , some of which seem relevant to the identification of a speech event as being of a particular kind , to the ability of the hearer to predict what sort of thing the speaker is likely to say in a given type of context , and to the constraining of interpretation in context .
88160	The observant reader will have noticed that we have helped ourselves to the content of the features proposed by Hymes and the co-ordinates proposed by Lewis in a fairly arbitrary way .
88161	So we have given variable amounts of information about the speaker or the hearer or the time or the place as we have discussed different fragments of discourse .
88162	This behaviour is consistent with Hymes ' own expectations about how his framework would be used .
88163	You will remember that he thought that contextual features might be considered in the way that general phonetic features are considered : sometimes , but not always relevant , and specifiable to variable degrees of delicacy for different purposes ( 2.2 .
88164	I ) .
88165	A problem for the discourse analyst must be , then , to decide when a particular feature is relevant to the specification of a particular context and what degree of specification is required .
88166	Are there general principles which will determine the relevance or nature of the specification , or does the analyst have to make ad hoc judgements on these questions each time he attempts to work on a fragment of discourse ?
88167	For the moment , we shall limit our discussion of this question to those features which relate directly to the deictic context , those features which will permit interpretation for deictic expressions like the temporal expression now , the spatial expression here , and the first person expression I. Are there standard procedures for determining what information is relevant to the interpretation of these expressions ?
88168	Lyons ( 1977 : 570 ) suggests that there might , in principle , be such standard procedures :
88169	Every actual utterance is spatiotemporally unique , being spoken or written at a particular place and at a particular time ; and provided that there is some standard system for identifying points in space and time , we can , in principle , specify the actual spatiotemporal situation of any utterance act .
88170	There clearly are standard systems for locating points in time and space .
88171	It would be possible to specify the time of an utterance as stretching between say 9.33 a.m. and 9.34 a.m. on 5 June 1961 , specifying the utterance in terms of clock and calendar time , good standard systems .
88172	We could , then , presumably , if we had the relevant instrumentation , specify the place of the utterance in terms of a fine interaction of latitude and longitude .
88173	It is not at all clear , however , that these particular standard systems produce the relevant information on all occasions .
88174	Presumably some patrol ship on the high seas might log messages in this way , but it is clear that , as humans , our experience of utterances is not that we have recorded in memory a list of utterances to which are attached standard tags specifying time and place in these terms .
88175	A friend can attempt to recall to your mind some utterance which you both experienced by a variety of place and time tags :
88176	( 20 )
88177	a .
88178	But you just said he was n't .
88179	( Place : maintained ; time : only minutes ago )
88180	b .
88181	You said in the staff meeting yesterday that he was n't .
88182	c .
88183	You said last week at the staff meeting that he was n't .
88184	d .
88185	You said last year when we met in Toronto that he was n't .
88186	The further away in time the message was situated , the less likely the speaker is to remember precisely the date and time at which it occurred , and the larger the time-span he is likely to make available for it to have occurred in .
88187	It seems unlikely then , that ‘ standard procedures ’ of recording space and time are going to be relevant to the unique identification of utterance acts .
88188	Perhaps the standard procedures will enable us to fix the relevant space spans for the interpretation of deictic expressions like here .
88189	Suppose X is talking to Y , standing on the blue border of the carpet in X 's office , in a given street , in Manchester , in England , in
88190	Britain , in Western Europe …
88191	Y might produce any of the following utterances :
88192	( 21 )
88193	a .
88194	There 's another worn section which needs repair here .
88195	b .
88196	You 've got a very nice room here .
88197	c .
88198	It 's a really nasty day here .
88199	d .
88200	You have a comparatively mild climate here .
88201	It must be clear that the spatial location identified by here in each of these expressions could be interpreted as a series of concentric rings spreading out from the speaker and encompassing different amounts of physical space , but the interpretation of the spatial range of the expression here on any particular occasion of use will have to be sought in the context of what the speaker is talking about .
88202	What appears to be stable in interpretations of here ( apart from curious usages deriving from long-distance telephonic communication and long-distance travel , discussed in Lyons , 1977 ) is that the deictic centre is located where the speaker is .
88203	Very similar problems arise with the interpretation of the temporal deictic expression now .
88204	Consider the following possible utterances :
88205	( 22 )
88206	a .
88207	Clap altogether NOW .
88208	( gym mistress to class )
88209	b .
88210	I think you should begin the next chapter now .
88211	( supervisor to student )
88212	c .
88213	Now I 'm getting older I really do find policemen look younger .
88214	d .
88215	From the iron age till now , man has been making increasingly complex artefacts .
88216	In c and d the utterances appear to be located within different temporal spans , one relating to the speaker 's advancing age ( involving a span of 20–30 years ) as opposed to the advancement of man ( involving a span at least of decades and possibly centuries ) .
88217	Utterances a and b are different in that the action specified is to follow the utterance , immediately in the case of a , but after some expanse of time in b .
88218	Once again we suggest that the deictic centre is located within the context of utterance by the speaker , but that the interpretation of the expression now as relating duratively or subsequently to the utterance , and the time-span involved , must be determined with respect to the content of the utterance .
88219	We should note that this fixing of the deictic centre is particularly appropriate to what Lyons ( 1977 : 637 ) calls
88220	the canonical situation of utterance : this involves one-one , or one-many , signalling in the phonic medium along the vocal-auditory channel , with all the participants present in the same actual situation able to see one another and to perceive the associated non-vocal paralinguistic features of their utterances , and each assuming the role of sender and receiver in turn .
88221	It is , of course , possible to use the expressions here and now in what might be described as ‘ displaced contexts ’ .
88222	Consider how you would interpret the utterance We 'll land here said by one astronaut to another , on earth , as they study a map of the moon .
88223	Or , how you interpret the message on each sheet of one brand of government-issue toilet roll , which reads NOW WASH YOUR HANDS , PLEASE .
88224	Speakers , or writers , do have the option of transferring the deictic centre to the hearer 's , or reader 's , spatio-temporal situation in which the text will be encountered .
88225	From our discussion of the spatio-temporal co-ordinates which seem , in principle , peculiarly accessible to standard specification , it must be obvious first , that deictic expressions may retain a standard deictic centre but must be interpreted with respect to the content of the utterance in which they occur and , second , that the relevant standard temporal description of an utterance , for instance 9.22 a.m. on Tuesday 28 June 1873 , as opposed to in the late nineteenth century , will vary depending on the knowledge and intention of the analyst ( or speaker ) in referring to the utterance as located in time .
88226	That is to say , even if there were an agreed , standard system for tagging utterances with spatio-temporal features , there is no guarantee that that tagging system provides the relevant information .
88227	Thus in 2.2 .
88228	I. we discussed a fragment of discourse :
88229	He seemed to resent them on that occasion and will not wear them today
88230	where we specified the time of utterance as 4 June 1980 .
88231	The newspaper article from which this fragment was extracted did indeed appear on that date .
88232	However , for anyone who knows what the expression the Derby means , it would almost certainly have been more informative to tag the time of utterance as Derby Day , 80 .
88233	The space-time co-ordinates can not be regarded as simple unstructured cues to interpretation in context .
