88762	Within the existing topic framework , speaker K 's saying that 's good money is an example of speaking topically , for her , but , for speaker J , the time co-ordinate within the topic framework has been narrowed down by his preceding remarks .
88763	There is , then , a discrepancy between what each participant is talking about , within the topic framework .
88764	We shall examine this effect of individual speaker 's topics in the next section .
88765	Speaker J relates his subsequent remarks to the two salient time co-ordinates within the topic framework and adds some specific information on the ‘ money ’ element introduced by speaker K.
88766	Speaker K's next contribution exhibits a series of complex ties with the existing topic framework .
88767	Speaker J , in his preceding contribution , has talked about the money received for his work at a particular point in the past .
88768	Speaker K's contribution ‘ picks up ’ the past time element , moving closer to speaker J's time while maintaining the personal reference in my father , who also did work ( stonemason ) comparable to J's ( bricklayer ) and received money for this work .
88769	Putting her contribution even closer to J 's preceding remarks , K makes her comments about her father relate to his ‘ starting ’ work and so comparable to J's started and when my time was out .
88770	With these complex connections made , speaker K adds some new elements to the conversation ( extra pay for being left-handed ) .
88771	We have tried to list the connections existing across contributions in this discourse fragment to emphasise the ways speakers make what they 're talking about fit into a framework which represents what we ( as discourse participants ) are talking about in conversational discourse .
88772	For the discourse analyst , as an overhearer , those connections can signal the coherence relations which make each contribution relevant to the discourse as a whole .
88773	Identifying the elements in the topic framework at any point in the discourse allows the analyst to make claims about what is involved in ‘ speaking topically ’ .
88774	It also enables him to produce a version of ‘ what is being talked about ’ , i.e. the topic of conversation , which is much more comprehensive , and certainly of greater analytic interest , than the single word-or-phrase-type title which is often used in a fairly trivial way to characterise ‘ topic ’ in the study of conversation .
88775	Speaker 's topic
88776	So far we have considered the notion of ‘ topic ’ in discourse in terms of what the participants share .
88777	The ‘ topic framework ’ , as an analytic device , is essentially a means of characterising the area of overlap in contributions to a discourse .
88778	By concentrating on the way conversational contributions overlap , however , we may neglect aspects of conversational discourse associated with different speakers having different personal ‘ topics ’ .
88779	So far , we have been concentrating on describing the ‘ conversational topic ’ , but neglecting the notion of speaker 's topic .
88780	As we have already pointed out , the analyst typically treats conversational data as something complete , as a static product of some recorded interaction .
88781	In doing so , he may lose sight of the fact that conversational discourse is dynamic , and that his data represents a process .
88782	If we can treat any piece of conversational data as a process in which two or more participants speak within the topic framework , we should also find in their contributions elements which characterise their own personal ‘ speaker 's topics ’ .
88783	We shall look at a fragment of spoken discourse , not in terms of how we would characterise the participants ' shared information , but in terms of a process in which each participant expresses a personal topic within the general topic framework of the conversation as a whole .
88784	Prior to extract ( 11 ) , the participants , L ( female , 20+ , unmarried , Edinburgh-resident , and M ( female , 30+ , married with young children , Edinburgh-resident ) , have been talking about recent improvements to old buildings in different areas in Edinburgh .
88785	( 11 )
88786	L : I quite like the way they 've done the Mile though + I think it 's quite —
88787	M : yes[AhA] yes
88788	L : the bottom of it anyway
88789	M : it is — it is quite good they 've certainly kept within the + em + + preserved it reasonably well or conserved it but we were up in Aberdeen this year for a holiday and we were staying right within the University complex there in Old Aberdeen+ and + oh some of the buildings there are beautiful really they really are nice + but er I was quite impressed with it — it 's the first holiday we 've had up there +
88790	L : I was noticing — I was down by Queen Street or+the bottom of Hanover Street or somewhere + and they 've just cleaned up some of the buildings down there + and what a difference it makes +
88791	M : yes I know because there are some beautiful buildings
88792	L : oh it was really nice
88793	Extract ( 11 ) is representative of a common conversational situation in which each of the participants give examples from their personal experience to illustrate some general point .
88794	The general point in this case is something like ‘ the effect of restoring old buildings ’ which is already part of the topic framework established by the preceding discourse .
88795	Notice that speaker M 's second contribution in this extract is not just ‘about ’ that general point .
88796	She is also talking about her recent holiday in Aberdeen , for example .
88797	We could describe this ‘ holiday in Aberdeen ’ element as , at this point , a part of speaker M 's personal topic which could become , in the developing conversation , a shared topic area for both speakers .
88798	Speaker L could have followed on , with a question , for example , about the holiday , Aberdeen , or even with some personal observations on the buildings in Old Aberdeen or the University .
88799	Speaker L , however , does not ‘ pick up ’ any elements from speaker M 's personal topic , but continues on her own personal topic area ( i.e. Edinburgh 's old buildings after restoration ) .
88800	When participant M speaks again near the end , she does not return to her ‘ holiday ’ or ‘ Old Aberdeen ’ , but makes her contribution relate closely to L 's immediately preceding remarks .
88801	There are two points worth noting about this fragment of conversational discourse .
88802	First , it is a feature of a lot of conversation that ‘ topics ’ are not fixed beforehand , but are negotiated in the process of conversing .
88803	Throughout a conversation , the next ‘ topic ’ of conversation is developing .
88804	Each speaker contributes to the conversation in terms of both the existing topic framework and his or her personal topic .
88805	It is clear from extract ( 11 ) that some elements in a speaker 's personal topic do not become salient elements in the conversation if neither the other participant nor the speaker herself mention them again .
88806	To use the ‘ negotiation ’ metaphor , we can say that speaker M offers elements in her personal topic ( in her second contribution ) as possible elements to be included in the conversational business , but speaker L does not take up the offer .
88807	A second point to be noted in this , and in a large number of other conversational fragments , is that personal topics are frequently introduced through first person reference in one form or another .
88808	Although the points made in extract ( 11 ) could have been expressed objectively as statements that certain buildings in certain locations are more beautiful since restoration , both speakers relate such statements to personal experience .
88809	It is as if speakers feel obliged to offer some personal warrant for the statements they will make about the world .
88810	A statement that the buildings in Old Aberdeen are beautiful is embedded within an assertion that the speaker was recently in Old Aberdeen , and stayed there for a period , and so she has a warrant for making the statement .
88811	If we reconsider the earlier extract ( 5 ) as one participant wanting to know the meaning of an expression and the other offering a possible explanation , we can see that the explanation is offered in personal terms ( when we were young and we called it ‘ the taw ’ ) based on the speaker 's personal experience .
88812	It may be that this explanation is not an acceptable answer to the question , but it is presented by the speaker in a form which conveys ‘ what I think we 're talking about ’ in this part of the conversation .
88813	Characterising the individual speaker 's topic as ‘ what I think we 're talking about ’ incorporates both that element which the conversational analyst tends to abstract as the ‘ topic of conversation ’ for the participants ( 'What we 're talking about' ) and the individual speaker 's version ( 'I think' ) , as he/she makes a conversational contribution .
88814	That speakers do introduce what they want to say via some form of personal reference has a noticeable effect on the structure of contributions in conversational discourse .
88815	We shall return to this point in the discussion of further details of discourse structure in Chapter 4 .
88816	From what we have proposed as speakers ' topics in conversational discourse , it must occasionally happen that there are at least two versions of ‘ What I think we 're talking about ’ which are potentially incompatible .
88817	It is a noticeable feature of co-operative conversational discourse , however , that this potential incompatibility rarely leads to conflict over the topic of conversation .
88818	What typically happens is that , in the negotiation process , one speaker realises that his version is incompatible with what the other appears to be talking about and makes his contributions compatible with ‘ what I think you ( not we ) are talking about ’ .
88819	We can illustrate this process in two conversational fragments and note two different strategies used to avoid conflict in the ‘ negotiations ’ .
88820	In the first extract , ( 12 ) , one piece of continuous conversational discourse has been divided up into chunks .
88821	Immediately before this extract , speaker B ( female , 50+ , aunt of speaker A ) has been describing to speaker A ( female , 20+ ) the first type of radio she had , forty years before .
88822	( 12 )
88823	A : but you 'd have telephones around +
88824	B : mm oh yes oh aye oh aye I 've had the telephone since nineteen thirty eight +
88825	A : hmm
88826	B : oh they were on a long while I think before that +
88827	Speaker B had been talking about the radio she had in the 1930s and speaker A's first line here seems to continue within the temporal , locational and personal indices of the existing topic framework while introducing telephones .
88828	Speaker B treats this contribution as requiring an answer , following a pattern described by Labov in the rule : ‘ If ( speaker ) A makes a statement about a ( speaker ) B-event , it is heard as a request for confirmation ’ ( 1972b : 254 ) .
88829	Speaker B expands on her answer , in personal terms , regarding the telephone .
88830	Speaker A offers no contribution and speaker B adds some additional information about telephones .
88831	We might characterise speaker B's view of ‘ what I think we 're talking about now ’ as something involving herself , the 1930s , and the existence of telephones ( as well as radios ) at that time .
88832	The conversation continues :
88833	A : 'cause there was a man in — my father 's in the Scouts +
88834	B : oh yes he was — is he still
88835	A : he 's a county commissioner now
88836	B : oh is he +ah ha+
88837	Speaker A appears to be offering some new elements as part of the conversational topic , again deriving from some personal reference ( as in my father ) which speaker B appears to accept .
88838	That is , speaker B does not insist on mentioning telephones , but moves on to this new area .
88839	Speaker B's view of ‘ what I think we 're talking about now ’ must now involve speaker A , A's father , the Scouts and a man ( who may have something to do with telephones ) .
88840	We might expect speaker B to be a little confused about how these elements relate to the preceding conversation .
88841	Speaker A continues , as follows :
88842	A : and eh one of his oldest+ scoutmasters wa-ha-was reaching his hundredth birthday +
88843	B : is that so +
88844	We suspect that , by this point , although speaker B can identify ‘ what 's being talked about ’ , she can play no part in negotiating the topic , because she may not be able to see why this individual entity is being talked about .
88845	The contributions of speaker B cease to be attempts to add anything to the conversational topic .
88846	Speaker B's view of the conversation has consequently become one in which she is no longer expressing a personal topic , but is waiting to discover ‘ what I think you ( not we ) are talking about ’ .
88847	Throughout the rest of this fragment , speaker B simply makes ‘ interested ’ noises as speaker A gradually gets to the point .
88848	A : so father was making up a big + sort of remembrance book —
88849	B : aha
88850	A : to give him and he was writing just at the beginning he was — writing the whole — for each year of his life he wrote something in that had — had been invented or +
88851	B : oh yes
88852	A : ah a book that had been written or a piece of music that had been written or a painting or a —
88853	B : very interesting yes
88854	A : or whatever you know and + within his lifetime the telephone had been invented +
88855	B : had it + really + fancy +
88856	In this extract as a whole , we can trace speaker B's attempt to contribute to what she thinks they 're about , by first offering some remarks on telephones and then on the father , but gradually reducing her comments to the type of contentless noises described by Duncan ( 1973 ) as back channels .
88857	Back channel behaviour , which can also include nods and sentence completions is used when a participant wants to indicate to the person speaking that he should continue .
88858	Speaker B stops trying to take turns in the negotiation of topic and waits for speaker A to make it clear how what she is saying has some connection to the existing topic framework .
88859	Eventually , as we can see in A 's final remarks , a connection is made .
88860	There is evidence in speaker A's contributions that what she is trying to say is not very well organised before she starts to speak .
88861	There are false starts , hesitations and repetitions .
88862	Everyday conversational discourse is , not infrequently , characterised by this lack of preplanning .
88863	The resulting structure of speaker A's contributions is , in fact , quite common in discourse and will be discussed in some detail later in terms of ‘ staging ’ ( see Chapter 4 ) .
88864	Speaker B's strategy , then , in a situation where she finds that she is unsure about what she thinks they 're talking about , is to stop talking .
88865	In the following extract ( 13 ) , there is another example of a mismatch between speakers ' topics , brought about by a misunderstanding of the intended meaning of a particular word .
88866	In the immediately preceding conversation , speaker C ( female , 20+ , American , visiting Edinburgh ) has been finding out from speaker D ( male , 40+ , Edinburgh-resident ) where there are good places to go for bicycle rides in and around Edinburgh .
88867	( 13 )
88868	C : what about going down by the — the Firth of Forth
88869	D : that should be fun should n't it yes you could
88870	C : is it
88871	D : yes you can cycle all — you can ride right along the edge you know + without falling in you can ride right along the edge eh without em + going — keeping on the main road + that should be great actually + you could do that +
88872	C : is it very rough down there though
88873	D : well there are no cobbles as far as I remember — have you tried riding on the cobbles
88874	C : yes yes
88875	D : you must have done
88876	C : I went down to Muirhouse
88877	D : which is almost all cobbles is n't it
88878	C : it was rather rough
88879	D : hmm
88880	C : no but I was — I was thinking rather more rough in terms of the em + people +
88881	D : oh I see + you well I do n't think so + I do n't know + I — I — eh — parts of it are quite poor + particularly the Pilton area +
88882	Looking back to speaker C's third question , we can propose two versions of ‘ what I think we 're talking about ’ .
88883	For speaker C , it involves ‘ are the people rough ? ’ and , for speaker D , ‘ are the roads rough ? ’
88884	Unlike the hearer ( B ) in extract ( 12 ) , however , speaker C appears to be able to recognise speaker D 's alternative topic and accepts what she thinks speaker D is talking about as ‘ what we 're talking about ’ , for a few turns .
88885	When speaker D stops talking about cobbles ( i.e. rough for cycling on ) , speaker C can attempt to return to her topic ( rough in terms of the em + people ) .
88886	Speaker D's response at the end of this fragment is , in effect , an answer to the question which speaker C originally intended him to answer .
88887	We might think that by the end of this fragment there is once again a single version for both speakers of ‘ what I think we 're talking about ’ .
88888	Indeed , most conversational analysis is undertaken with this single ‘ topic ’ concept as a working assumption .
88889	Yet , in extract ( 13 ) we can only reconstruct the intended meaning of C's third question because she actually explains her intended meaning later .
88890	If speaker D had gone on at some length about ‘ cobbles ’ or rough roads in general , or if the analysis only had part of this fragment , up to C 's it was rather rough , then we might have had no evidence of a divergence in speakers ' topics within the conversation .
88891	Our argument for the importance of considering individual speaker 's topics in conversational discourse would consequently be weaker .
88892	We do not suggest that discourse analysts should spend their time looking for potential alternative meanings in what speakers say in a conversation , but we do suggest that the analyst should not simply assume that there is a single , static ‘ topic of conversation ’ in any conversational fragment .
88893	If there is an entity identifiable as ‘ the topic of conversation ’ , the analyst should consider what evidence from each individual speaker 's contributions he is using to make that identification .
88894	He should also remain aware of the fact that conversation is a process and that each contribution should be treated as part of the negotiation of ‘ what is being talked about ’ .
88895	Above all , he should remember that it is speakers , and not conversations or discourses , that have ‘ topics ’ .
88896	Topic boundary markers
88897	In our discussion of ‘ topic ’ , we have concentrated mainly on considerations of ‘ content ’ and neglected the influence of ‘ form ’ .
88898	Yet our interpretation of what a speaker is talking about is inevitably based on how he structures what he is saying .
88899	We shall now investigate some formal aspects of topic-structure in discourse .
88900	In this section we shall look at the formal devices used to mark the boundaries of chunks of both written and spoken discourse which form large units of some kind , such as paragraphs .
88901	Aspects of the internal structuring of these chunks will be discussed in Chapter 4 .
88902	It has been suggested ( e.g. by Schank , 1977 : 424 ; Maynard , 1980 ) that instead of undertaking the difficult task of attempting to define ‘ what a topic is ’ , we should concentrate on describing what we recognise as topic-shift .
88903	That is , between two contiguous pieces of discourse which are intuitively considered to have two different ‘ topics ’ , there should be a point at which the shift from one topic to the next is marked .
88904	If we can characterise this marking of topic-shift , then we shall have found a structural basis for dividing up stretches of discourse into a series of smaller units , each on a separate topic .
88905	This type of approach to the analysis of discourse is based on the principle that , if we can identify the boundaries of units — where one unit ends and another begins then we need not have a priori specifications for the content of such units .
88906	The burden of analysis is consequently transferred to identifying the formal markers of topic-shift in discourse .
88907	Paragraphs
88908	It might seem that identifying the formal demarcation of chunks of written or printed discourse is a relatively simple task .
88909	After all , written discourse is divided into paragraphs whose boundaries are marked by indentations .
88910	Topic-shifts in written discourse then could be identified with the beginning of each new paragraph .
88911	Unfortunately , it does n't seem to be as simple as that .
88912	Those who use the term ‘ paragraph ’ to describe a unit in the structural analysis of written discourse go to some trouble to point out that they are not describing the orthographic paragraph .
88913	According to Longacre ( 1979 : 116 ) , the orthographic paragraph can result from a writer 's stylistic concerns , ‘ partially dictated by eye appeal ’ , or from printing conventions such as an indentation for each change of speaker .
88914	Hinds ( 1977 : 83 ) also notes that the journalistic paragraph is often determined on the basis of appearance .
88915	He has a worked example in which a single structural paragraph derives from a newspaper article containing five orthographic paragraphs .
88916	Thus , it may be that the beginning of an orthographic paragraph indicates a point of topic-shift , but it need not do so .
88917	Both Longacre ( 1979 ) and Hinds ( 1977 ) appeal to languages other than English for evidence that there are formal linguistic markers of the beginning and end of paragraphs .
88918	What is immediately noticeable in the discussion of these markers is that they are genre-specific .
88919	There are ways of indicating the beginning of a new paragraph in a piece of narrative , for example , which are not used in explanatory discourse .
88920	This general point is also made by
88921	Grimes ( 1975 : 109 ) , who describes the marking of paragraph boundaries as one form of ‘ partitioning ’ in discourse .
88922	The principles on which partitioning depends are related to change of ‘ setting ’ ( time or place ) and ‘ theme ’ ( the person or thing talked about ) , in narrative discourse , at least .
88923	Interesting though it may be to learn that there is a narrative-discourse-paragraph-introductory-particle in Huichol or Shipibo , it becomes decidedly less interesting when one discovers that the identification of the significance of these particles depends on a prior identification of the paragraph as a unit in which ‘ the speaker continues talking about the same thing ’ ( Grimes , 1975 : 103 ) .
88924	Hinds ( 1977 ) bases his paragraph divisions on a similar principle , quoting Grimes as support , and emphasising the significance of ‘ participant orientation ’ — that is , the unity of a paragraph derives from its being mainly about a single participant .
88925	Longacre ( 1979 ) claims that ‘ in narrative discourse , a narrative paragraph is built around a thematic participant , occasionally a small set of thematic participants ’ ( Longacre , 1979 : 118 ) .
88926	In other words , only the paragraph structure of stretches of discourse about individual , primarily human , characters is being discussed .
88927	In effect , this limits the discussion to narrative discourse , or , as in Hinds ( 1977 ) , a description or an obituary of a particular individual .
88928	It should be obvious why a single structural or ‘ semantic ’ paragraph in Hinds ' ( 1977 ) analysis can extend over five orthographic paragraphs in a newspaper .
88929	Each of these orthographic paragraphs is ‘ about ’ the same individual .
88930	Yet , some obituaries extend to twenty or more orthographic paragraphs ‘ about ’ the one person , and whole chapters of novels , containing over a hundred lengthy orthographic paragraphs , may be ‘ about ’ the same individual .
88931	Surely such extended stretches of written discourse are not single ‘ paragraphs ’ ?
88932	We shall consider a stretch of written discourse , not from a source such as a Paez ( Colombia ) folk tale or a specially constructed text , but from a recent English novel .
88933	In the extract reproduced below ( 14 ) , the orthographic paragraph boundaries as they appeared on the printed page have been ignored .
88934	The whole extract has two principal participants , but is quite clearly ‘ about ’ only one of them .
88935	If there are points of ‘ topic-shift ’ in English written discourse which lead writers , or their editors , to begin new orthographic paragraphs , then we should be able to identify likely points where the writer or the editor marked the division of this ‘ text ’ into separate chunks .
88936	( 14 )
88937	1After the first few days , when I come into the room , Birdie is down on the floor of the cage , running back and forth , looking out over the barrier that holds in the gravel .
88938	2 I think she 's glad to see me , not just because I give her treat food , but because she 's lonely .

88957	If there are orthographic paragraph divisions in the original version of this text which were made for the sake of appearance on the page , then we have little hope of identifying such divisions in any formal way .
88958	What kind of formal marks , if any , would we expect to find at the beginning of a new paragraph ?
88959	The markers Longacre ( 1979 ) identifies in narrative discourse are inevitably adverbial expressions indicating temporal sequence .
88960	It may be that the general class of adverbials which can appear initially in a sentence could be taken as possible markers of ‘ topic-shift ’ .
88961	Quirk et al. ( 1972 : ch. 8 ) provide lists of such adverbials in terms of adjuncts , conjuncts and disjuncts .
88962	In fact , extract ( 14 ) begins with an adverbial clause in initial position .
88963	There are two other points in this extract , sentences 4 and 10 , where adverbial clauses occur in sentence-initial position .
88964	There are four other points where adverbial expressions occur sentence-initially , sentences 6 ( At first ) , 18 ( Then ) , I9 ( Generally ) , and 22 ( Also ) .
88965	This would give us six possible breaks , formally marked , in the structure of the piece of text .
88966	The next question is — do all these adverbial expressions function in the same way ?
88967	After all , we would like to distinguish between adverbials which indicate a connection between one sentence and the next and those adverbials used to link a set of sentences to another set .
88968	The use of then in 18 seems to introduce a final action in a temporal sequence of actions .
88969	We can conceive of this one sentence being separated from the previous set as a form of distinct climax .
88970	We might expect , however , that it would more typically occur as the final sentence of a paragraph , not as a climax , but as describing an action which culminates a series of actions .
88971	It is followed by a sentence which does not continue the series of actions and which begins with what Quirk et al. ( 1972 : 509 ) would characterise as a ‘ style disjunct ’ .
88972	This use of generally , in I9 , effectively separates the previous set of sentences from the next set describing a particular habit of the individual involved .
88973	Within this latter set , one sentence begins with the additive adjunct , also , in 22 , which could be indicating that there are two parts to this set .
88974	It is more likely that the sentence beginning with also is adding more detail to support the general conclusion that the individual concerned is right-sided and is part of the internal structure of a paragraph beginning with Generally .
88975	The other adverbial , at first , in 6 , seems to be part of a sentence-internal construction , especially when we see the then which follows .
88976	The events described in this sentence fall within the set of events described as happening by the end of the week ( in 4 ) .
88977	Thus , we have reduced the number of possible breaks in this text to three , so that we can suggest that there are four paragraphs , beginning at sentences 1 , 4 , 10 and 19 .
88978	The reader may suggest other possible breaks , as , for example , in 9 , where there is a sentence structure ( an interrogative ) quite different from the structure of the rest of the text sentences .
88979	An argument for a break here would seem quite reasonable since this sentence is structurally marked as separate .
88980	No doubt the reader could also think of an argument , mainly in stylistic terms , for treating this sentence as part of the preceding set .
88981	It may be the case that , taking stylistic considerations more generally , the reader would wish to divide this text into separate paragraphs at points where there are no formal markers at all .
88982	We would assume that the discussion , in such a case , would cease to be a discussion which appealed to primarily linguistic evidence in this piece of discourse .
88983	On the basis of some formal linguistic markers , we have suggested that there are four paragraphs in extract ( 14 ) .
88984	We may have been led to finding those four paragraphs because they are , in fact , the divisions which actually appear in the original and we merely sought additional evidence to support the way the author had divided up his discourse .
88985	Yet this point highlights the fact that the exercise we have performed on extract ( 14 ) was an extremely artificial treatment of written discourse .
88986	We began by removing one of the primary indicators of ‘ topic-shift ’ available to a writer , that of indenting a line in his text .
88987	Rather than treat the indenting of the first line of a paragraph as simply some cosmetic device , as Longacre ( 1979 ) does , we might look upon it as an indication by a writer of what he intends us to treat as the beginning of a new part of his text .
88988	If the writer also uses adverbial expressions initially in the first sentence of this new part of his text , then we might say we have overwhelming evidence that the writer is marking a ‘ topic-shift ’ in his discourse .
88989	We are , after all , performing a descriptive and not a prescriptive exercise when we undertake discourse analysis .
88990	We do not wish to say how a writer should organise his written discourse into paragraphs before we have managed to characterise , in any comprehensive way , how writers typically do so .
88991	The investigation of what writers typically do when marking the structure of their texts would seem to be a more appropriate goal of discourse analysis .
88992	For example , rather than dismiss the orthographic paragraph format to be found in newspaper articles as , in some way , a deviation from the ‘ true ’ paragraph structure of what is being written , it would be more appropriate for discourse analysts to describe the journalistic format as one form of written discourse organisation .
88993	The paragraph structure of different genres , such as scientific textbook writing , repair manuals , nineteenth-century novels , etc. could then be characterised , and statements could be made about , for example , the ‘ norms ’ or regular features of topic-shift in such genres .
88994	On the basis of such genre-specific descriptions of ‘ topic-shift ’ markers , it should be possible to make linguistic , as opposed to literary , statements about the structure of English written discourse which reflect the writer 's purpose .
88995	Thus , in producing a narrative , the writer must provide some indications of change of time and place , as Grimes ( 1975 : 102 ) has pointed out .
88996	In presenting a philosophical argument , however , the writer can range over different times and places within a single paragraph , but must mark out changes in the direction of his argument .
88997	Taking a random page from the writings of Karl Popper , one can see the structure of the discourse in skeleton form by taking the first phrase or sentence of each paragraph .
88998	( 15 )
88999	para 1 : Other questions have sometimes been asked …
89000	para 2 : Another question sometimes asked is this …
89001	para 3 : The only correct answer is the straightforward one …
89002	para 4 : It has also been said that the problem of induction is …
89003	( Popper , 1963 : 56 )
89004	Eventually , it should also be possible to specify those markers of ‘ topic-shift ’ which occur in all forms of written discourse .
89005	We might find that it is indeed the case that the use of ‘ But ’ at the beginning of a paragraph as described by van Dijk ( 1977 : 139 ) , is a very general marker of topic change .
89006	Other examples of what van Dijk ( 1977 : 150 ) terms macro-structure connectives are ‘ furthermore ’ , ‘ however ’ , and ‘ so ’ .
89007	We shall discuss the concept of macro-structures in discourse in section 3.
89008	7 on the proposition-based analysis of discourse .
89009	Paratones
89010	So far we have concentrated on structural markers in written discourse .
89011	In spoken discourse , there is not the visual prompt of paragraph-initial line indentation to indicate a division in the discourse structure .
89012	How do speakers mark ‘ topic-shifts ’ ?
89013	One suggestion is that there are , in fact , structural units of spoken discourse which take the form of ‘ speech paragraphs ’ and have been called paratones ( see Brown , 1977 : 86 ) .
89014	Some support for the notion that there are ways of marking the boundaries of ‘ speech paragraphs ’ can be found in a common practice of people who are asked to read pieces of written text aloud .
89015	They use intonational cues to signal the start of a new paragraph .
89016	The ‘ speech paragraph ’ , or paratone , like the orthographic paragraph , is identified by its boundary markers .
89017	The marking of the start of a paratone , then , is clearly one device which speakers can use to indicate a topic-shift .
89018	Since the paratone is a much less familiar concept than the orthographic paragraph , it may be useful to have its identifying features described .
89019	At the beginning of a paratone , the speaker typically uses an introductory expression to announce what he specifically intends to talk about .
89020	This introductory expression is made phonologically prominent and the whole of the first clause or sentence in a paratone may be uttered with raised pitch .
89021	The end of a paratone is marked in a way similar to the ‘ turn signal ’ discussed by those who investigate conversational discourse as a process of social interaction ( cf.
89022	Duncan , 1974 ; Sacks et al. , 1974 ) .
89023	It can be marked by very low pitch , even on lexical items , loss of amplitude and a lengthy pause .
89024	Alternatively , the speaker can use a summarising phrase , often repeating the introductory expression , not necessarily low in pitch , but also followed by a lengthy pause .
89025	The most consistent paratone-final marker is the long pause , normally exceeding one second .
89026	We shall examine an extract from conversational discourse containing a longish paratone which illustrates the features just described .
89027	It is relevant that the topic framework for this extract ( 16 ) should contain information about the speaker ( female , 20+ , Edinburgh-resident ) and the preceding discourse ( the types of drinks the participants had encountered in different types of bars during their respective recent holidays in the United States ) .
89028	It is also worth noting that in Edinburgh Scottish English , phonologically prominent syllables are typically uttered with raised or high pitch and need not have the type of pitch movement associated with phonological prominence in descriptions of standard southern English ( cf.
89029	Brown et al. , 1980 ) .
89030	( For an explanation of the stave representation of intonation used , see the ‘ transcription conventions ’ on p. xii . )
89031	( 16 )
89032	I found my drink was a great problem with them because ( ) at that time I drank whisky and lemonade + and I would ( ) go and ask for whisky and lemonade and I would get ( ) whisky and lemon + because you have to ask for whisky ( ) or scotch and seven up + you know + I eventually ( ) cottoned on to it + but + and they could n't get over ( ) the fact that I did n't like ice in whisky and of course ( ) they either gave me ice whether I wanted it or not or ( ) they stacked the glass up + right up to the level that ( ) you would normally have if you had ice in your drink ( ) anyway + and consequently I got ploughed + frequently + ( ) and that 's that I + I tended to stick to my drink ++ ( )
89033	This paratone begins with an introductory expression my drink , uttered very high in the pitch range , and closes with the same expression , low in the pitch range , as part of the speaker 's summing-up .
89034	The internal pauses are brief , none exceeding o.s seconds , but the final pause marking the end of the paratone is long ( I.6 seconds ) .
89035	Those are the formal markers of the boundaries of this paratone .
89036	Of course , there are internal aspects , such as the semantic cohesion within the lexical field established by my drink , which could also be appealed to in claiming that this chunk of discourse is a unit of some kind .
89037	However , this type of internal cohesion is not a necessary feature of the structural unit we have described as the paratone .
89038	It might be argued that there are two paratones , and not one , in this extract .
89039	There appears to be a break where+ but + is used .
89040	Indeed , just prior to but , there is what has been described as a ‘ possible completion point ’ .
89041	The speaker has come to the end of a sentence and pauses .
89042	It is a point at which those who analyse conversation in terms of ‘ turn-taking ’ ( Sacks et al. , 1974 ) would suggest that another speaker could take over the turn .
89043	However , the speaker in this extract immediately produces an ‘ utterance incompletor ’ — in this case but , though any clause connector would do making , as Coulthard ( 1977 : 56 ) points out , a potentially complete utterance into an incomplete one .
89044	After another brief pause , the speaker continues , using and to indicate that what she is going to say is connected to what she has just said .
89045	We would not want to describe this possible completion point ( or any other which occurs in this extract ) as a paratone-boundary .
89046	The formal markers , low pitch close plus lengthy pause plus raised pitch introductory expression , are not present .
89047	In intuitive terms , we might also say that what follows + but + is not on a separate speaker 's topic , but continues the talk ‘ about ’ 'my drink' .
89048	At the end of this extract , there is an obvious ‘ completion point ’ .
89049	In ‘ turn-taking ’ terms , it is a point at which another speaker is free to take over .
89050	However , in this part of the conversation , one speaker clearly ‘ has the floor ’ and she is allowed to continue , as shown in extract ( I 7 ) .
89051	( 17 ) oh apart from once when we went we found em + an Irish bar ( ) in San Francisco that was famous for its Irish coffees + ( )
89052	In beginning a new paratone , the speaker marks as intonationally prominent two expressions — an Irish bar and Irish coffees .
89053	In the course of the paratone , she talks about both the bar and the Irish coffee made there .
89054	It seems quite reasonable to assume that , when a speaker is organising a ‘ speech paragraph ’ which has two connected elements as its foci , both elements can be made phonologically prominent in the introduction .
89055	When the speaker closes this paratone , she repeats one of her introductory expressions — it was very good Irish coffee too — not particularly low in the pitch range , but followed by a lengthy pause .
89056	Some of the features we have described as marking paratone boundaries in spoken discourse can , of course , have other functions .
89057	Although the lengthy pause is also identified by Chafe ( 1979 : 176 ) as an indication of segmentation in his spoken discourse data comparable to paragraphing in written discourse , the intonational features we appealed to can have other , quite different , functions .
89058	Some of these we will discuss in detail in Chapter 5 .
89059	What we have described is the use of the combination of these formal markers by speakers to indicate a shift in what they 're talking about .
89060	There may be other , more subtle , indicators of topic-shift used by conversationalists which we have ignored .
89061	The significance of ‘ speaker gaze ’ , as described by Kendon ( 1967 ) and specific ‘ body movements ’ ( de Long , 1974 ) in signalling speaker change in conversation may also be relevant in topic change .
89062	The occurrence of different types of ‘ fillers ’ such as ‘ well ’ , ‘ mmm ’ , ‘ you know ’ , ‘ er ’ , and others may also regularly coincide with topic-shifts .
89063	We have concentrated , however , on some of the primary , easily identifiable formal markers used by writers and speakers to indicate structural divisions in the discourse they produce .
89064	We emphasise once again that , although we can regularly identify such structural markers , their appearance in discourse should not be treated in any way as ‘ rule-governed ’ .
89065	They represent optional cues which writers and speakers may use in organising what they want to communicate .
89066	Failure to mark out explicitly the structural organisation of what a speaker wishes to communicate may make the addressee 's task of interpretation more difficult , perhaps , but , by itself , would not necessarily constitute a failure to communicate .

89068	It 's no news that memory is deceitful .

89077	He loved clubs and wardrooms with the pre-dinner drinks , the discreet signing of chitties , the smiling elderly waiters ( from a class almost extinct now , men who lived to serve other men ) .

89086	Unlike other members of the reptile family , the gecko is a benign creature , cheery , opportunistic and patently useful .
89087	I am troubled by the thought that this familiar world into which I am able to slip without a moment 's readjustment , is a vanishing world .

89091	S. O. Letterman has something similar in mind , a re-creation of colonial Africa , as seen from Santa Monica Boulevard .
89092	Right here , in Muthaiga , colonial Africa lives on .

89532	And now the fat bellies in the cities are carrying on where the white folk left off .
89533	( I can picture the laibon as he told me this , his son sitting behind him on a rock flossing his teeth . )
89534	The Masai moved from the great river of the north , freely interpreted as the Nile , says the professor in a note , down towards their present location .
89535	It was a terrible journey reducing the Masai nation to a few hundred survivors .
89536	( Our own time provides the television simulacra of this march in Somalia and Ethiopia . )
89537	The march took many years , perhaps more than a century .
89538	Time in those days lacked urgency or precision .
89539	But the plains , savannahs , rivers and hills , all the way from Samburu down to the Masai Steppe , proved fruitful and the Masai built up their strength through the acquisition of women and cattle so successfully that they chased out the other tribes who were obliged to cling to the mountains or secrete themselves in the forests , land useless for cattle .
89540	When the white man came ( what a familiar and mournful phrase ) they were not allowed the same freedom to repossess their cattle .
89541	It became a crime , punishable by lashes under the Germans and by fines under the British , to take the cattle of other tribes .
89542	This was a gross injustice .
89543	The laibon speaks of the Masai uprising against the Germans in 1915 and of the last great war waged against the unspeakable Bantu tribes around Lake Victoria who ate fish .
89544	The warriors , in those days , he says , preferred to die rather than return home without dipping their spears in blood .
89545	Warriors now know nothing of war and cattle raiding .
89546	They are similarly ill-equipped to deal with lions .
89547	Some poison lions which are troublesome , rather than kill them with a spear .
89548	It is a shameful thing .
89549	Now the Masai are torn by the need to go to school ( schule in Swahili , a leftover of German occupation ) and the understanding that young people who go to school are lost to the traditional ways .
89550	Women are particularly vulnerable to the false promises of city slickers .
89551	( I think here of Victoria . )
89552	After a short discourse about women — the need for the dowry of five animals and three useful articles to be maintained , even for schoolgirls — he speaks of Claudia .
89553	She came to live among them .
89554	His father was the laibon at the time and he had five brothers .
89555	His father wore a cloak of hyrax skins which he received along with other tools of the trade — pebbles , containers and more important , the ability to use numbers to foretell the future .
89556	He is descended directly from Kidongoi , the first laibon , who was given supernatural powers on the mountain by Ngai .
89557	( Although the tablets have been transmuted into handier , pocket-sized pebbles , the kinship with Moses seems too close to be a coincidence . )
89558	As I read , I am struck again by the laibon 's sense of being at the centre of the universe .
89559	He lives near the mountain of God , in the Rift Valley in a paradise of rivers , lakes , mountains and plains .
89560	People who come from the outside world inhabit the periphery , where they have no cattle and live an inferior life .
89561	Claudia came from that world .
89562	At first , he says , people did not understand what she wanted , but she came to learn about the Masai and write it in a book .
89563	She wanted to attend the eunoto and the women 's circumcision and understand everything about betrothals .
89564	She soon knew all there is to know , more than many Masai men , about the exchange of gifts , cattle and goats which always accompanies these ceremonies .
89565	At first people were suspicious ; they could not understand why she was so interested in these details , which she wrote down in a schoolbook .
89566	Soon she could speak Maa .
89567	One day she brought a voice box .
89568	( Uitsmijter has written a note : ‘ probably a Uher , commonly used by researchers ’ . )
89569	Les vrais paradis sont les paradis qu'on a perdus .
89570	I am struck by anxiety .
89571	How quickly can one learn a language ?
89572	My Swahili , such as it is , comes from a Berlitz tape and a phrase book .
89573	In Claudia 's time very few Masai spoke Swahili .
89574	As I get older I find myself tormented by anxieties of this nature , the anxieties about things one will never do .
89575	They are the anxieties of our times , born of the idea that the individual must in one way or another ( any damned way , as a matter of fact , even confessing to having been abused as a child ) express his uniqueness and fulfil his potential .
89576	Durkheim , Claudia 's inspiration , said at the beginning of the century that the problem for twentieth-century western man was the anomie created by the breakdown of the old certainties .
89577	What he could not see was the restless , self-centred consumerism it would produce .
89578	Nor did he see another consequence , as his nephew Mauss confessed , shortly before going mad : ‘ how large modern societies which have more or less emerged from the Middle Ages in other respects , could be hypnotized as aborigines are by their dances and set in motion like a child 's carousel .
89579	This return to the primitive had not been the object of our thoughts . ’
89580	The club is quiet .
89581	The gardens outside my window are bowing down to the heat of the afternoon , but my mind is racing in this stillness , like a dust devil on the apparently windless plains .
89582	I see myself drawing closer to Claudia Cohn-Casson , but not necessarily in the way that S. O. Letterman is expecting of me .
89583	The club and Fairfax and Lady De Marr and now the laibon 's tale , seem to me to have pulled us together .
89584	It 's absurd , but I feel we are all protagonists now in the same story .
89585	I have heard her voice and spoken to her lover and been walking with the Masai who was present at the farcical and tragic lion hunt .
89586	I no longer believe that I am just writing a treatment of her life .
89587	I feel as if I am poised somewhere on the edge of a slope , and about to slide down when I am supposed to be climbing up .
89588	It 's crazy , but I feel as though I have no life outside this one I have found here , complete with silly old colonials and Masai witch-doctor .
89589	I have n't thought of Victoria , whose sexual peccadilloes gave me such pain , for days .
89590	Yet even as I remember Victoria , I feel keenly the unsettled state of my mind .
89591	How could I possibly have neglected to think about her when a few weeks ago I could think of little else , in lubricious detail ?
89592	I find myself instead picturing Claudia , her dark eyes turned to the sky .
89593	I see her crouching at the entrance of a hut ( olpal ) looking in at , perhaps talking to , the shy bride within , who does not want to leave her father 's village ( engang ) .
89594	I find myself attempting to memorize the Masai words as she did .
89595	I see her walking with the bride to her new village , being teased by the escort of girls .
89596	I see her , as she described , catching sight of the husband 's village .
89597	And I imagine these same dark eyes catching sight of the five chimneys of Auschwitz-Birkenau .
89598	The laibon now talks about the famous incident when a district officer was killed .
89599	The British had insisted that the Masai sell some cattle to pay for schools and clinics and — there was clearly a hint of blackmail — to contribute to the war effort .
89600	Many Masai resisted this tax , but they had no choice .
89601	The laibon says that his father saw the sense in it .
89602	He did n't want the Germans back .
89603	A young man called Tepilit ole paramat , the laibon 's brother , tried at the last minute to withdraw one of his cattle from the sale .
89604	The district officer in charge , known to the Masai as Tombol ( Miles Turnbull ) refused to allow the animal to be withdrawn and ordered his askaris to restrain Tepilit .
89605	In the presence of a few hundred Masai , the young warrior hurled his spear right through the district officer 's heart .
89606	The blade appeared out of his back .
89607	Watched by the crowd , Tepilit withdrew his spear and walked away .
89608	He was eventually arrested .
89609	He did not hide and he said that he would do the same again .
89610	The bull in question had markings of which he was particularly proud .
89611	He had offered an alternative .
89612	The laibon says that his family had offered forty-nine cattle in restitution , but the British took Tepilit to the coast and hanged him there .
89613	What was achieved by that ?
89614	However , some members of his family were glad , because it meant they did not have to produce cattle .
89615	Uitsmijter in a note says that the Masai have a system of fines , multiples of seven .
89616	Forty-nine cattle is the highest possible penalty .
89617	The young man who was hanged was a special friend of Claudia .
89618	He wanted to marry her .
89619	Fairfax — Fahfakhs — who was a big man in the government had come down to the little town where Tepilit was held .
89620	Fahfakhs was wearing a uniform .
89621	He and Claudia spent a long time talking to the police and to the accused man .
89622	He , the laibon , had heard Fahfakhs shouting at the accused man in the cells at Ewaso Narok police post before he was taken to the coast .
89623	( Fahfakhs spoke fluent Maa . )
89624	The laibon 's father had explained to Fahfakhs that the family was ready to pay compensation , up to the full amount possible .
89625	He had told Fahfakhs that the young man wanted to marry Claudia , and perhaps he thought that the district officer was laughing at him and treating him with contempt .
89626	Tepilit had asked Claudia in the proper way , to see if her father , wherever his village was , would accept gifts .
89627	He had given Claudia a necklace to wear in the meanwhile and called her pakiteng .
89628	( Uitsmijter explains that it is an affectionate name meaning ‘ heifer ’ used by betrothed people . )
89629	The laibon still could not understand the point of hanging such a man .
89630	The district officer 's family got no cattle out of it either .
89631	Fahfakhs explained that Native Law did not cover this case .
89632	He had told Fahfakhs that Tepilit had actually killed a lion for the film that Claudia was making with Leavitt , whose name I had reminded him of .
89633	Tepilit had risked his life for Claudia .
89634	Two morans had been killed , and still Leavitt had not produced the promised cattle .
89635	After Tepilit was taken away to be tried , they never saw him again .
89636	Soon afterwards Claudia said she was leaving .
89637	Some said that she was going to be the wife of Fahfakhs .
89638	Many people were very sad to see her go .
89639	He , the laibon , was not so sad because he believed that she had caused many upsets .
89640	But she spoke to them all and said she would never forget them .
89641	She was going back to her father 's house to show people what she had written in her schoolbooks about them .
89642	She would come back as soon as she could .
89643	She was leaving their country with a heavy heart .
89644	Professor Uitsmijter has quite a deft touch in translation .
89645	I find myself able to place the words , in all their moving directness , right into the laibon 's mouth as he spoke , with Ol Doinyo Lengai away in the distance looking like a steamed pudding , its runnelled slopes lightly coated with cream , poured from above but vitrified before reaching the base .
89646	Some time later they heard that Tepilit had been hanged .
89647	After the war was over they heard that Claudia had died .
89648	How had she died ?
89649	He would like to know what happened to Claudia and her books .
89650	Nobody had ever told him .
89651	If I knew , would I tell him ?
89652	Did she marry Fahfakhs ?
89653	‘ Now we must go .
89654	We will go to the engang up there by Kitumbeine . ’
89655	And so , monologue complete , we had set off .
89656	The thin paper in my hand flutters as I drop it onto the bed .
89657	The ridged and tufted counterpane has been carefully and frequently laundered .
89658	The onset of the cooler hours is announced by the first thuds of tennis balls .
89659	After they hit the racquet they make another , more resonant sound , as they bounce on the ant soil surface , a sound you can hear on television when tennis is played at Stade Roland Garros .
89660	There is no sign of Fairfax and no message .
89661	I eat alone in the dining room and the next morning set off early back to Mr Shah 's hotel .
89662	The journey takes seven hours .
89663	SEVENTEEN
89664	As usual there is chicken lolling in the metal trays of the dining room , like unhealthy continentals in a mineral bath .
89665	For all its Last Year at Marienbad qualities , I choose the chicken again .
89666	Mr Shah is solicitous .
89667	He wants to know about Nairobi .
89668	Did I see anything of the riots ?
89669	I tell him that some Indian shops have been burned , according to my taxi driver .
89670	He shakes his head sadly .
89671	‘ They blame us for their problems , I mean even though we have lived here for many , many generations .
89672	They always do .
89673	But it 's not so bad down here .
89674	Some pickles and chutney ? ’
89675	Léon Cohn-Casson had believed that the sooner all Jews lost any traces of separate identity the better .
89676	He agreed with Émile Durkheim that Jewish ethnicity would wane with the advance of secular society .
89677	The only way forward was on these secular , scientific principles .
89678	Sociology and anthropology were the application of these principles to understanding how people behave .
89679	For this reason he had encouraged Claudia to enter these new , modern sciences .
89680	He had cultivated Marcel Mauss , Durkheim 's nephew , so that he could personally convey to her the importance of understanding the springs of human action .
89681	Mauss had come to their house in the avenue Hoche for dinner ; like most academics — I am guessing — feeling a little shabby when confronted by the glowing paintings and rich Aubussons and complex dinner settings .
89682	Claudia wrote about his quiet passion .
89683	He could pluck examples of the universal spirit from any number of societies he had studied .
89684	What a queasy period those inter-war years now seem ( I am looking at the chicken curry ) , the old hatreds and prejudices simmering and bubbling nicely with all the dark , irrational fears surfacing in a way that rational people like Cohn-Casson believed had long ago been rendered obsolete by the evolutionary nature of society .
89685	The modern order , because it was based on industry , would produce a rational society .
89686	What a delusion .
89687	Cohn-Casson was born in 1882 , not long after France 's humiliation by the prussians .
89688	He had spent his life , as many of the French intelligentsia had , looking for a basis for order in society .
89689	France is a country which has grave doubts about its moral fibre ; it sees its national character as being as permeable as a colander .
89690	It was for this reason that Léon Cohn-Casson became such a fervent advocate of a secular morality .
89691	He disliked the arriviste Jews because he felt that they were provincial and superstitious and liable to arouse hostility ; nor did he believe that they would be loyal to France .
89692	But Cohn-Casson also found it impossible to side uncritically with Jews , because to do so would deny modern thinking , by placing tribal loyalties above the mandates of science .
89693	Léon Blum , the new prime Minister , said of people like Cohn-Casson : ‘ They secretly curse those who put them in the hands of secular enemies . ’
89694	And here is Mr Shah .
89695	I ca n't tell him of the analogies I am cheerfully fabricating .
89696	He wants me to have some tinned pears which have come in from South Africa .
89697	Or I could have lychees .
89698	EIGHTEEN
89699	‘ Women make us poets , children make us philosophers . ’
89700	This is one of Letterman 's aphorisms .
89701	He has a number , many quite apt , which he is liable to produce to lend substance to his conversation .
89702	His conversation is a finely wrought sales pitch .
89703	He is selling himself .
89704	It has been his life 's work .
89705	The events of his life are constantly incorporated into this spiel .
89706	For example , he has been married and is still on very good terms with his wife ; their divorce unlocked her true potential , and she is now a part-time feminist studies lecturer at SCU .
89707	Letterman implies that he had to divorce her for her own good ; he could not bear to see so much life force confined in marriage .
89708	Their son Dylan , who is twelve , lives with her but there are no custody conflicts and they have a wonderful rapport .
89709	Dylan helps him see things in an honest fashion , without all the crap .
89710	This is the philosophical side .
89711	On the poetic side , he has had many good relationships with women .
89712	He thinks that he has a part of his nature which is more in harmony with women than men .
89713	He sees himself as having an intuitive , feminine aspect .
89714	Although he mentions it to me , he finds he is unable to display this aspect to men .
89715	It only comes out in his dealings with women .
89716	Personally I think this is another of his sales pitches .
89717	I walk up the track past the fundamentalist missions , way above the coffee plantations , up into what is nominally a wildlife reserve .
89718	I am proposing to ponder the question of Letterman 's script up in the higher altitudes .
89719	A sign reads ‘ Crater Reserve , please Stay in Your Vehicle . ’
89720	This sign has been painted on a piece of board and is listing badly .
89721	Some small boys come down the track towards me .
89722	They are laughing and chasing each other .
89723	When they see me they become strangely still and respectful .
89724	They probably think that , like most of the white men in this evangelical belt between the coffee plantations and the colobus monkey habitat , I have religious connections and perhaps even powers , the sort of powers that cause money to come to pass .
89725	This is the white man 's greatest achievement : he has learned how to get his mitts on the money .
89726	( There is another argument , nowadays timidly advanced only by a few academics of the old hair-shirt tendency , that the white man has fixed the game , making it almost impossible for the others to get in . )
89727	The connection between religion and wealth is clear : the religious people have almost as many vehicles , servants and supplies of electrical goods as the aid community .
89728	I give these children my benediction .
89729	It is delivered in the form of a few coins which bear the likeness of the last president , a pleasant utopian who retired of his own free will .
89730	The children , their faith reinforced , run down the hill to tell others of their good fortune as I stride up the track towards the forest .
89731	The forest is cool .
89732	I ask myself why the people do n't live up here in these glades beside the rushing streams .
89733	Life would be so much more leafy .
89734	It would be almost European .
89735	At a great height I catch sight of a colobus .
89736	These monkeys are used in the manufacture of household articles and headdresses by ail the tribes in whose domain they are found .
89737	This is the sort of relationship between man and animal which westerners find hard to accept : the use of a monkey as a fly-swat .
89738	In my excited state , as the trees close over my head , I see this kind of thinking , this desire to reshape the world into something reassuring , as having many applications .
89739	For example S. O. Letterman sees Claudia 's story as a vindication of the human spirit , to which , professionally anyway , he pays tribute .
89740	The human spirit , in this estimation , is always on the move , restlessly upwards like climbers on K2 .
89741	I am under notice to find a suitably uplifting ending for our movie .
89742	The smoke rising from the five chimneys of Auschwitz-Birkenau is a downer , although he thinks there may be something in my idea of complementary smoke rising from the savannah .
89743	‘ It 's crazy , but people just wo n't go to the movies if the thing ends on a downer . ’
89744	I do n't argue with Letterman .
89745	Why should I ?
89746	He 's an expert on popular taste .
89747	He sees Claudia as brainy , beautiful , romantic and symbolic .
89748	The last part of the proposition still needs some work .
89749	I have decided to broaden my idea of the savannahs with smoke rising from the Masai villages .
89750	I see the camera closing to find her old Masai friends gathering after a day , another of the infinite number of days , spent caring for the cattle .
89751	The ex-hunter , aviator and war hero , Tom Fairfax , who was her lover , is approaching in his biplane .
89752	First his small plane is seen searching the vast plains for her village .
89753	The sky is reddening , reminding the viewer of the ghastly hues of the night sky above Auschwitz when the ovens were working at full capacity .
89754	Down below , fires are being lit and the cattle are being driven gently into the enclosures of thorn bushes .
89755	Music rises on the soundtrack .
89756	Fairfax 's plane circles once and then comes down to land bumpily on a piece of gazelle-inhabited ground .
89757	The warriors come loping for news of Claudia .
89758	Fairfax climbs from the plane and walks , surrounded by the tall warriors , across the darkening savannah to the laibon 's manyatta .
89759	The laibon , dressed in his traditional finery , a cloak of fur on his shoulders and carrying a thin stick , walks across the enclosure , now thick with the strangely blotched cattle , their huge horns gently meshing and unmeshing , to greet Fairfax .
89760	The moment is prolonged and intensified almost unbearably .
89761	( The music , I will suggest , should be based on Masai chanting . )
89762	Anyway , this music rises hauntingly .
89763	The laibon and Fairfax face each other .
89764	They speak in Maa , but with subtitles .
89765	Fairfax tells them that Claudia is dead .
89766	There is a throaty murmur , a sort of groan .

89768	Fairfax says she was killed by the Germans .

89777	I am panting now .
89778	The air is thinning .
89779	There is nobody in the forest although it is loud with calls and cries .

89781	For a moment before it separates itself from its surroundings I catch a glimpse of its round eyes , beautiful but stupid , taking in the sight of a forty-three-year-old writer wearing shorts and a faded polo shirt , his face somewhat craggier than he sees it in his mind 's eye , his waist a little more solid and his eyes bright with the thoughts he is generating .

89791	Victoria is thirty-two now .

89846	TWENTY

92272	[ CHANCERY DIVISION ] In re A DEBTOR ( NO. 784 OF 1991 ) 1992 April 13
92273	Hoffmann J.
92274	Bankruptcy — Jurisdiction — Carrying on business — Debtor selling business and leaving United Kingdom more than three years before presentation of petition — No debts outstanding save for income tax liability — Whether debtor ‘ carried on business ’ within three years preceding petition — Jurisdiction to make bankruptcy order — Insolvency Act 1986 ( c. 45 ) , s. 265(1) ( c ) ( ii )
92275	In May 1987 the debtor , who had carried on the business of running a nursing home , sold the business as a going concern and went to live in the Canary Islands .
92276	No debts remained outstanding , apart from a tax liability in excess of £500,000 .
92277	In 1988 the debtor made an offer to settle the tax liability which was not accepted , and in February 1991 the Inland Revenue presented a bankruptcy petition .
92278	The registrar in bankruptcy made an order allowing service of the petition on the debtor in the Canary Islands .
92279	On the hearing of the petition he decided that the debtor had ‘ carried on business in England and Wales ’ within a period of three years ending with the presentation of the petition for the purposes of section 265(1) ( c ) ( ii ) of the Insolvency Act 1986and made the order sought .
92280	On the debtor 's appeal : —
92281	Held , dismissing the appeal , that there was nothing in the policy of the Insolvency Act 1986 that indicated that Parliament intended to give the words ‘ carried on business ’ in section 265(1) ( c ) ( ii ) of that Act a meaning different from that which they had been held to bear in section 4(1) ( d ) of the Bankruptcy Act 1914 ; that a debtor did not cease to carry on business for the purposes of section 265(1) ( c ) ( ii ) until all the trading debts of the business had been paid ; and that , accordingly , the registrar had been right in holding that since the tax liability had not been discharged the debtor was still carrying on business and that he had jurisdiction to make the bankruptcy order ( post , pp. 122B–E , H — 123A ) .
92282	Theophile v. Solicitor-General [ 1950 ] A.C. 186 , H.L. ( E. ) applied .
92283	The following cases are referred to in the judgment :

92296	APPEAL from the registrar in bankruptcy .
92297	On 11 November 1991 , Mr. Registrar Pimm , pursuant to a petition presented on 1 February 1991 , made a bankruptcy order against the debtor , although the debtor had not lived in England and Wales since 8 May 1987 , on the basis that she was still notionally carrying on business in England and Wales within the meaning of section 265(1) ( c ) of the Insolvency Act 1986 because though there were no other debts outstanding there was an unpaid tax liability of over £500,000 .
92298	By a notice of appeal dated 29 November 1991 the debtor appealed on the ground that the court had no jurisdiction to make the bankruptcy order because she had not carried on business in England or Wales within three years prior to the presentation of the petition .
92299	The facts are stated in the judgment .
92300	Richard Ritchie for the debtor .
92301	Nicholas Warren for the Inland Revenue Commissioners .
92302	HOFFMANN J. This is an appeal from a decision of Mr. Registrar Pimm , which raises a question on the court 's jurisdiction to make a bankruptcy order .
92303	The debtor in this case carried on business in this country running a nursing home in the course of which she incurred a tax liability in the sum of about £500,000 which remains unpaid .
92304	In January 1987 she went to live in Tenerife and on 8 May 1987 she sold the business as a going concern .
92305	There is no evidence that any debts , apart from her tax liability , remained outstanding .
92306	In 1988 she made an offer to settle the tax liability , which was not accepted , and on 1 February 1991 the Inland Revenue Commissioners presented a bankruptcy petition which came before the registrar on 11 November 1991 .
92307	The sole question before him was whether there was jurisdiction under section 265 of the Insolvency Act 1986 .
92308	That section sets out various grounds for jurisdiction , including the domicile , residence and physical presence of the debtor in England , but the sole ground relied on in this case is section 265(1) ( c ) ( ii ) , namely , that the debtor within a period of three years ending on the date of presentation , had ‘ carried on business in England and Wales . ’
92309	The debtor says that she has not carried on business in this country since 8 May 1987 , the date upon which the business was sold .
92310	The Inland Revenue say that carrying on business for the purposes of this section continues until all the debts of the business incurred in the course of trade have been paid , and that includes the liability for tax .
92311	The construction which is put forward by the Commissioners is one which was adopted by the courts in respect of section 4 of the Bankruptcy Act 1914 , upon which section 265 of the Act of 1986 is plainly modelled .
92312	Section 4(1) ( d ) of the Act of 1914 also contained various grounds of jurisdiction , including when the debtor , ‘ has carried on business in England , personally or by means of an agent or manager ’ within a year before the presentation of the petition .
92313	The only noticeable change in the language in the Act of 1986 is the extension of that period to three years .
92314	Section 4(1) ( d ) was considered by the House of Lords in Theophile v. Solicitor-General [ 1950 ] A.C. 186 .
92315	The facts of that case were not materially different from this one .
92316	There too the only debt remaining outstanding from a business which had otherwise ceased more than a year before was a debt owed to the Inland Revenue .
92317	Lord Porter , who delivered the only speech , referred to a number of earlier cases dealing with the construction of ‘ carrying on a business ’ for the purposes of jurisdiction over the separate property of married women .
92318	The relevant statute in those cases had provided simply that jurisdiction should exist over a married woman ‘ carrying on a trade separately from her husband . ’
92319	The question which arose in those cases was whether the cessation of trade , in the sense of ‘ putting the shutters up , ’ immediately deprived the court of bankruptcy jurisdiction over the married woman , or whether it continued while the trade debts remained unpaid .
92320	It will be observed that in those cases there was no statutory period after cessation of trade during which jurisdiction continued , and the court was therefore faced with a stark choice between saying that the jurisdiction ceased immediately active trade was suspended , or saying that it continued until the business had actually been wound up by payment of the debts .
92321	There was no basis upon which any intermediate position could be chosen .
92322	It is not in those circumstances surprising that the court decided in favour of the latter construction .
92323	In Theophile 's case , however , the choice was not nearly so stark .
92324	There would have been less practical difficulty about saying that trade ceased when business ceased actively to be carried on , because there was a further period of a year during which a petition could be presented .
92325	Nonetheless , the House of Lords applied the same construction .
92326	The question before me today is whether Parliament , in using similar language in section 265 , intended those words to bear the same meaning as those given to them by the House of Lords under the Act of 1914 .
92327	The Insolvency Act 1986 is a consolidation Act only in the sense that it consolidates the Insolvency Act 1985 and some other provisions .
92328	It is an entirely new code in relation to the Bankruptcy Act 1914 .
92329	The court therefore has to approach its construction on the footing that the new Act may exhibit policies and intentions which are not necessarily the same as those in the earlier Act , and which require similar words to be given different meanings from those which the courts gave them under the earlier legislation .
92330	In In re A Debtor ( No. 1 of 1987 ) [ 1989 ] 1 W.L.R. 271 , the Court of Appeal was concerned with the construction of a provision in the Insolvency Rules 1986 ( S.I .
92331	1986 No. 1925 ) , rule 7.55 , which provided :
92332	‘ No insolvency proceedings shall be invalidated by any formal defect or by any irregularity , unless the court before which objection is made considers that substantial injustice has been caused by the defect or irregularity , and that the injustice can not be remedied by any order of the court .
92333	Under a similar provision in the Bankruptcy Act 1914 it had been held that a defect in a bankruptcy notice of a kind such as could reasonably mislead the debtor was not a mere formal defect or irregularity within the meaning of that provision , and therefore rendered the notice a nullity even though it was not calculated to cause substantial injustice .
92334	In In re A Debtor ( No. 1 of 1987 ) the Court of Appeal refused to follow that approach and held that a statutory demand , which on the face of it contained a number of puzzling and perplexing statements , was nonetheless valid because the debtor knew precisely what he owed and there was no injustice in holding that his failure to pay the debt gave rise to a presumption that he was unable to pay .
92335	That approach to construction was approved by the House of Lords in In re Smith ( A Bankrupt ) , Ex parte Braintree District Council [ 1990 ] 2 A.C. 215 , in which Lord Jauncey of Tullichettle said , at p. 238 , that , in view of the changes in policy shown by the new Act , he felt justified in construing the provision of the Act of 1986 ‘ as a piece of new legislation without regard to 19th century authorities or similar provisions of repealed Bankruptcy Acts . ’
92336	Those authorities show that , in approaching the language of the Act of 1986 , one must pay particular attention to the purposes and policies of its own provisions and be wary of simply carrying over uncritically meanings which had been given to similar words in the earlier Act .
92337	It does not , however , mean that the language of the new Act comes to one entirely free of any of the intellectual freight which was carried by words and phrases in earlier bankruptcy or other legislation .
92338	Decisions of the court upon the meanings of phrases used in Acts of Parliament may come , in the course of time , to give them the quality of terms of art which Parliament may well be assumed to have intended them to bring with them when used in subsequent legislation .
92339	In section 265 , for example , terms such as ‘ domiciled , ’ ‘ personally present , ’ ‘ ordinarily resident , ’ have had attributed to them , both in the context of bankruptcy and in that of civil procedure generally , a wealth of refined construction which it is difficult to suppose Parliament did not intend equally to apply when those words were used in the Act of 1986 .
92340	Is there any reason why that should not apply equally to the words ‘ has carried on business ? ’
92341	There does not seem to me to be anything in the policy of the new Act which suggests that in this provision Parliament was intending to give those words a different meaning from those which they had been held to bear under the Act of 1914 .
92342	It was suggested that the extension of the period to three years from one required the attribution of a different meaning because the Theophile construction meant that it did not really matter what the period was ; as long as there was a debt , a bankruptcy petition could be presented .
92343	The effect of the outstanding debt would be to prevent the cessation of trade for the purposes of the section .
92344	That is not quite true , because the debt must , in order to found jurisdiction under section 265 , be a trade debt .
92345	For the purposes simply of enabling the petitioner to rank as a creditor , the debt can , of course , be any kind of debt .
92346	It follows that the extension to three years does have significance .
92347	It enables a non-trade creditor to present a petition within three years after the last trade debt has been paid instead of within only one year .
92348	In Muir Hunter on Personal Insolvency ( 1991 ) , p. 3037 , at para. 3–070 , it is suggested that the Theophile construction of the Act of 1914 is a somewhat artificial one , and the question is raised as to whether , under the new Act , unfettered by old case law , the long established but artificial construction will continue to be applied .
92349	It appears to me , however , that the House of Lords in Theophile v. Solicitor-General [ 1950 ] A.C. 186 did not regard their construction as being an artificial one .
92350	They came to that conclusion on the grounds that it appeared to them to be a tenable meaning of the words and in accordance with what they thought to be the policy of the Act of 1914 as to jurisdiction .
92351	I have already said that , on the question of jurisdiction , I can discern no difference between the policy of the Act of 1914 and that of the Act of 1986 , and under those circumstances I think that the registrar 's decision was right and the appeal must be dismissed .
92352	Appeal dismissed with costs .
92353	Leave to appeal .
