92358	JAMES CLARK MAXWELL A treatise on electricity and magnetism Oxford 1873
92359	ALL the problems we shall be concerned with may be solved by calling upon one or more of the following equations : .
92360	Where do the above equations come from ?
92361	They are contained ( though not quite in the same form and not in the same system of units ) in Chapter IX of Maxwell 's Treatise on electricity and magnetism published in 1873 .
92362	Are we to conclude that electromagnetic theory has made no advance in the course of a century ?
92363	That conclusion would essentially be correct .
92364	Our technique of solving the above equations has improved , and of course we are in a much better position now to evaluate the material constants , but fundamentally electromagnetic theory stands now as it stood a century ago .
92365	As far as the interrelationship of electromagnetic quantities is concerned Maxwell knew as much as we do today .
92366	He did not actually suggest communication between continents with the aid of geostationary satellites , but if he was taken now to a satellite ground-station he would not be numbed with astonishment .
92367	If we would give him half an hour to get over the shock of his resurrection he would quietly sit down with a piece of paper ( the back of a bigger envelope , I suppose ) and would work out the relevant design formulae .
92368	The lack of advance on our part should not be attributed to the idleness of a century , much rather to the genius of Maxwell .
92369	The moment he conceived the idea of the displacement current , a new era started in the history of mankind .
92370	Events of similar importance did not occur often .
92371	Newton 's Principia and Einstein 's first paper on relativity would qualify , and perhaps two or three more learned papers , but that 's about all .
92372	If we assume that our kind of beings will still be around a few millennia hence , I feel certain that the nineteenth century will mainly be remembered as the century when Maxwell formulated his equations .
92373	What was so extraordinary about Maxwell 's contribution ?
92374	It was the first ( and may be the best ) example of reaching a synthesis on the basis of experimental evidence , mathematical intuition , and prophetic insight .
92375	The term  ( 1.1 ) had no experimental basis at the time .
92376	By adding this new term to the known equations he managed to describe all macroscopic electromagnetic phenomena .
92377	And when relativity came , Newton 's equations were found wanting but not Maxwell 's ; they needed no relativistic correction .
92378	I could go on for a long time in praise of Maxwell .
92379	Unfortunately we have little time for digressions however entertaining they might be .
92380	But before we get down to the equations I must say a few words in defence of the approach I choose .
92381	I know it must be hard for anyone to accept a set of equations without going through the usual routine of presenting the relevant experimental justifications .
92382	It might seem a little unreasonable at first sight but believe me this is a possible approach , and under the circumstances it may very well be the best approach .
92383	You are already familiar with the mathematical operations curl , div , and grad ( I prefer using them in vector-operator form ) , and you need no introduction to the concepts of electricity .
92384	You have heard about electric charge , current , magnetic field , etc .
92385	All the eqns ( 1.1 ) -(1.7) do is go give a number of relationships between these quantities .
92386	So if some of them are known , you can use the equations to work out some of the others .
92387	The notation is fairly standard but still I should better say what is what : H , magnetic field strength ; E , electric field strength ; D , electric flux density ; B , magnetic flux density ; J , current density ; p , charge density ; F , force , q , charge ; v , velocity of moving charge ; u , permeability ; e , permittivity .
92388	The two latter quantities are constants depending on the material under study .
92389	Using the subscript zero to denote their values in free space , they come to .
92390	The rest of the course will be concerned with the various solutions of eqns ( 1.1 ) -(1.7) .
92391	Is n't this boring for an engineer ?
92392	Should n't this be done by mathematicians or by computer programmers ?
92393	Not for the time being .
92394	Perhaps one day computers will be big enough and numerical analysts clever enough so that the engineer will only have to pose the problem , but not yet , and not , I think , for some time to come .
92395	In the large majority of cases a straightforward mathematical solution is just out of the question .
92396	So one has to use that delicate substance known as physical intuition .
92397	How can one acquire physical intuition ?
92398	There is no easy way .
92399	One has to start with a simple physical configuration , solve the corresponding mathematical problem , then solve a similar problem and then another problem , and then a little more difficult problem , and soon .
92400	The first breakthrough comes when one can predict a solution without actually doing the mathematics .
92401	In order to have a unified view of the subject we have started with Maxwell 's equations .
92402	It means a new approach but not a radical departure .
92403	The subject is still the same .
92404	You will be able to see that the laws you love and cherish ( Coulomb 's , Biot-Savart 's , Snell 's , etc. ) all follow from our eqns ( 1.1 ) -(1.7) .
92405	The order of discussion will follow the traditional one : electrostatics first , followed by steady currents , then we shall move on to slowly varying phenomena , and reach finally the most interesting part , fast-varying phenomena , exhibiting the full beauty of Maxwell 's wonderful equations .
92406	2 .
92407	Electrostatics
92408	2.1 .
92409	Introduction
92410	STATIC means not varying as a function of time .
92411	So all our quantities p , J , E , B , D , and H will be independent of time .
92412	Is there such a thing as time-independent charge ?
92413	Yes , there is .
92414	It means that neither the magnitude nor the position of the charge varies as a function of time .
92415	And similarly we can imagine constant electric and magnetic fields .
92416	Can we talk of time-independent current ?
92417	Well , we have to permit the motion of charges to get any current but if the amount of charge crossing a certain cross-section is always the same then the current at that point is independent of time .
92418	On this basis constant currents also belong to the static branch of electricity .

92505	Should n't one rely solely on mathematics ?
92506	Physical intuition might provide part of the answer , but surely mathematics will always give the complete answer .
92507	This is true for simple problems but , as I have said many times before , as soon as the problems become more complicated our mathematical knowledge turns out to be greatly deficient .
92508	In practice you will find that problems may be broadly divided into two classes : ( I ) problems that have been solved , and ( II ) problems that are insoluble .
92509	The reasons for belonging into class II may be numerous : you can not formulate the problem , you can not solve the resulting equations analytically , the computer you have access to is not big enough , etc. , etc .
92510	It all boils down to the fact that the problem needs to be simplified .
92511	You will find that you never solve the original problem .
92512	At best you solve a similar one .
92513	But how can you recognize a " similar " problem ?
92514	Which simplifications are admissible without losing the essential characteristics of the problem ?
92515	For all that you need intuition .

92638	2.6 .
92639	The parallel-plate capacitor
92640	We have so far considered point charges , dipoles , line charges , and sheet charges without enquiring into the problem how such configurations of charges come about .
92641	Indeed if one gives a little thought to the matter it becomes distinctly doubtful that one could ever establish anything even vaguely resembling a sheet of charge .
92642	Like charges repel each other so the charges constituting the sheet will fly apart .
92643	Interestingly , there is a way of realizing sheets of charges .
92644	We just need to apply a voltage between two metal plates .
92645	What happens inside metal plates in response to an applied potential or for that matter what happens to charges inside any material ?
92646	There is no escape ; I have to say a few words about the properties of materials .
92647	A piece of material contains equal number of positive and negative charges .
92648	If this was not so there would be large forces between various pieces of materials .
92649	To give you a feeling how large these forces could be I quote from Feynman 's lectures : " If you were standing at arm 's length from someone and each of you had one per cent more electrons than protons , the repelling force would be incredible .
92650	How great ?
92651	Enough to lift the Empire State Building ?
92652	No !
92653	To lift Mount Everest ?
92654	No !
92655	The repulsion would be enough to lift a " weight " equal to that of the entire earth ! "
92656	So as I said before a piece of material contains equal numbers of positive and negative charges .
92657	For a class of materials called conductors the internal charge distribution may be looked upon as a cloud of mobile negative particles in the background of immobile positive lattice ions .
92658	When the voltage is applied , there is initially an electric field inside the conductor and the charges start to move under its influence .
92659	So to begin with this is not a static problem at all .
92660	But if we wait patiently for a few picoseconds until the charges rearrange themselves there will be no further motion and the problem belongs to the realm of electrostatics .
92661	But where will the electrons find their equilibrium positions ?
92662	How far will they move under the influence of an attractive electric field ?
92663	Disregarding the cases when the electric field is very large or the conductor is very hot ( beyond the scope of this course ) the electrons can not get farther than the boundary of the conductor .
92664	So there will be an accumulation of electrons on the surface of one of the plates and consequently a deficiency of electrons at the other plate 's surface .
92665	Inside the conductor there will be no imbalance of charge .
92666	This is an important thing to remember .
92667	If we apply a constant voltage then , after the elapse of a short time , charge neutrality is re-established in the interior of the conductor but there will be some uncompensated charges in the immediate vicinity of the surfaces .
92668	How close to the surfaces ?
92669	It does n't really matter .
92670	The scales are certainly atomic , so we are entitled to regard these charges at the surfaces as having spread out in two dimensions only .
92671	So the introduction of a surface charge is not unrealistic at all .
92672	Well then , two infinitely large metal plates to which a constant voltage is applied are equivalent to two oppositely charged sheets .
92673	The electric field between the plates is then , and the potential .
92674	Consequently the potential difference ( i.e. the voltage ) between the plates comes to .

92689	This is a problem that rightfully belongs to the subject of the electrical properties of materials , so I can not say very much about it .
92690	In a perfect dielectric there are no mobile charges but lots of bound charges , positive and negative .
92691	In response to the electric field in which these charges find themselves , the positive and negative charges will slightly separate .
92692	The effect will be some uncompensated charges at the edge of the dielectric ( Fig. 2.16 ) which will draw some further charges of the opposite sign from the interior of the conductor to its surface .
92693	This is the physical mechanism responsible for the increase of surface charge density in the presence of a dielectric .

92696	Surely , we should have taken that into account .
92697	What counts is the net surface-charge density inside our chosen volume and that has n't increased at all .
92698	All that happened is that the electric field drew some charges to the surface of the dielectric which caused then some additional charges to appear on the surface of the conductor .
92699	So the surface-charge density increased on the surface of the conductor but not the net charge density inside the Gaussian surface .
92700	Have we or have we not made a mistake ?

92874	Electrostatic energy
92875	Electrostatics is characterized by charges located at certain positions .
92876	If we know the positions of all the charges , we know everything so we should know the energy as well .
92877	There is unfortunately no obvious way of writing an expression for the energy in the simultaneous presence of all the charges .
92878	It is , however , fairly easy to work out the energy as we bring in the charges from infinity one by one .
92879	The first charge is brought in without any opposition .
92880	The energy of one charge alone is zero .
92881	The second charge is brought in in the presence of the first one .

92905	Wherever there is electric field , there is energy as well .
92906	So how should you think about electrostatic energy ?
92907	You are certainly entitled to think in terms of charges and potentials .
92908	In order to create a charge distribution a certain amount of work has to be done , and that is available to us in the form of electrostatic energy .
92909	But it is better ( it is more general ) to regard the electric field as the agent with which the energy has been deposited .
92910	One usually says that the energy is stored in the electric field .
92911	Let us work out , as an example , the stored energy of a parallel-plate capacitor .
92912	The electric field strength is given ( eqn ( 2.57 ) ) by E = V/d , hence the stored energy is , where S0 is the area of the capacitor plates .
92913	Of course , you can derive the above expression from circuit theory , so once more circuit theory and electromagnetic theory give the same answer .
92914	Could we use this stored energy for calculating the magnitude of forces acting , could we get the direction of the forces ?
92915	Take the following example from mechanics : a mass m at rest at a height h has a potential energy mgh .
92916	In which direction will it move if its support is taken away ?
92917	It will try to reduce the height h in order to minimize its potential energy .
92918	While the energy of the capacitor increases that of the battery decreases .
92919	Why ?
92920	Because an increase of dC in the capacitance requires an amount of extra charge dq = VdC , which must flow from the battery to the capacitor .
92921	So the loss of energy by the battery is V dq = V2 dC .
92922	Hence the net gain of energy of the system is , in agreement with eqn ( 2.124 ) .
92923	So if we consider the capacitor and the battery together the total energy of the system decreases as the capacitance increases .
92924	We obtain the same force between the plates whether the battery is disconnected or not — as we should .

93030	The vector potential is not a popular variable among engineers , maybe because it is not directly measurable .
93031	There are no instruments capable to measure the magnitude or direction of A.
93032	In my opinion A is a useful thing if used with moderation .

93040	3.2 .
93041	The defocusing of an electron beam ( J , E , D , p , H , B )
93042	We have so far talked about positive and negative charges , about point charges , and distributed charge .
93043	I shall now introduce the concept of an elementary charge , 1.6 × 10 -19 C , carried by an elementary particle called the electron .
93044	This is not a necessity .
93045	It is possible to study electromagnetic theory without ever mentioning the word electron , but since it has become such a household word and is used so often we can just as well make use of it .
93046	In the present section we shall consider a cylindrical electron beam of radius a in which the charge density is uniform ( p = Po ) and all electrons travel with velocity v.
93047	We are not going to enquire into the details how such beams can be produced ( it belongs to the subject of physical electronics ) ; we shall accept the fact that the beam exists and will try to work out the forces on the outermost electrons .
93048	There is now cylindrical symmetry and a net charge per unit length , yielding for the radial component of the electric field .

93052	The magnetic force is perpendicular both to the direction of motion ( +z axis ) and the direction of magnetic field (  direction ) .

93057	Thus the conclusion is that , owing to the repulsive forces between the electrons , a cylindrical electron beam is unstable .
93058	Using a technical term borrowed from electron optics we could say that the electron beam gets defocused .
93059	The other conclusion ( as far as it is permissible to generalize from a single example ) is more important in principle .
93060	It is concerned with the relative magnitudes of electric and magnetic forces .
93061	Since charged particles rarely travel close to the velocity of light we may conclude that the magnetic forces are by orders of magnitude smaller than the electric forces .
93062	Why is it then that we have no difficulties in practice in observing magnetic fields ?
93063	The reason is , of course , that there are two kinds of electric charges and their effect usually cancels , so the small magnetic field has a chance of getting observed .
93064	And that brings us to the ext example .
93065	3.3 Pinch effect ( J , H , B )
93066	In contrast to our previous example we shall now investigate a cylindrical beam consisting of two kinds of charge carriers : negative electrons and some positive particles , which I do not wish to be more precise about at the moment .
93067	We shall assume that the two kinds of particles have equal densities and move in opposite directions .
93068	As a result there is no net space charge and hence no electric field .
93069	The currents , on the other hand , do not cancel because they represent opposite charges moving in opposite directions ( remember , minus one times minus one is equal to plus one ) .
93070	The magnetic field strength is given again by eqn ( 3.27 ) ; we only need to substitute for the current In + Ip where the subscripts n and p refer to negative and positive particles respectively .
93071	Hence the magnetic force on the electron at the edge of the beam ( at R = a ) is , and on the positive particle is .
93072	Note that the force is inwards , and in the same direction for both particles .
93073	Let us distinguish two cases .
93074	Both particles are mobile
93075	In that case both of them will move inwards under the effect of magnetic force .
93076	But if the diameter of the beam is reduced , eqns ( 3.33 ) and ( 3.34 ) tell us that the forces are even larger .
93077	What happens then ?
93078	If everything was uniform then the beam diameter would go on decreasing .
93079	In practice however the beam is not uniform and does not possess perfect cylindrical symmetry .
93080	Under these conditions the motion of the particles is fairly complicated , and of course our model is unable to predict the detailed behaviour of the particles .
93081	Nevertheless a few qualitative conclusions may be drawn without doing any further mathematics .
93082	If the cross-section happens to be smaller at a certain place , then the forces are larger there than at the neighbouring cross-sections , so the beam will be further constricted , etc. , leading to the so-called sausage instability ( Fig. 3.3(a) ) .
93083	If the magnetic field happens to be larger at one side than at the other side , then the beam will be deflected towards the weaker field which makes the field even weaker , etc. , leading to the so-called kink instability ( Fig. 3.3(b) ) .
93084	The positive particle is immobile
93085	In practice this means that the positive ions are part of the crystal lattice .
93086	There is then no magnetic force on the ions , only on the electrons .
93087	So the electrons want to move inwards but can not because the ions hold them back by virtue of their electrostatic attraction .
93088	Naturally , if the ions attract the electrons the converse is true as well , i.e. owing to the magnetic force on the electrons , there is also an inward force upon the ions .
93089	So the whole crystal structure tries to contract or in other words the material is under pressure ( see Example 3.2 ) .
93090	In any practical situation this pressure is small and can be neglected when calculating the forces on current-carrying conductors .

93206	The magnetic field remains unchanged and the magnetic flux density increases by a factor .

93220	3.10 .
93221	Magnetic materials
93222	When studying the electromagnetic properties of dielectrics I was very reluctant to get involved with the physics of dielectrics .
93223	Now I am even more reluctant to talk about the physics of magnetic materials .
93224	Not so much because I do n't understand the subject ( that is no real obstacle to a lecturer ) , but more because of the time we are likely to consume , even if we keep a respectable distance from quantum mechanics and concentrate solely on phenomenological theories .
93225	It must be admitted that magnetic materials behave most unreasonably .
93226	The relative permeability may turn out to be a tensor ; it may take on very high values , say 106 or more , or it may have a value very close to unity , say 1.00002 for a wide range of temperatures , and then on cooling the material another few millidegrees  may drop to zero .
93227	Why to bother so much about the details , you may ask ; could n't we just say that  and go on considering further examples ?
93228	The trouble is that for the most widely used magnetic material — iron —  is not a constant .
93229	Not only that its value depends on H , but , even worse , it depends on the previous history of the sample .
93230	So we have to discuss the B-H curves , and I will include a few more things , but you must realize that there is a lot more to it .
93231	By the time we finish with it we shall have just scratched the surface of the subject .
93232	3.11 .
93233	The B-H curve of ferromagnetic materials
93234	It is customary to divide all magnetic materials into diamagnetic ( ) , paramagnetic ( ) , and ferromagnetic ( ) groups .
93235	Paramagnetic materials are unimportant from an engineering point of view , and diamagnetic materials may have a future ; the present , however , belongs to the ferromagnetic group , and above all to the most important representative of the group — the various alloys of iron .
93236	In order to obtain the B-H curve let us make the following experiment .
93237	Place a cylindrical iron rod inside a solenoid ( as in Fig. 3.9 ) , vary the current and measure the flux density .
93238	We shall assume that , before we switch on the current , H = 0 and B = 0 , a natural-enough assumption .
93239	As we increase the current , the magnetic field will increase proportionally ( eqn ( 3.71 ) ) but the flux density will be a nonlinear function of the magnetic field , as shown by the line OP in Fig. 3.10 .
93240	The point P is called the saturation point , beyond which , i.e. the iron has stopped contributing to the flux density ; any further increase of H will result in that much increase of B as in a vacuum .
93241	Reducing now the current ( and H with it ) we shall not retrace the same curve ; B will decrease much more slowly and will have a finite value at zero current .
93242	If we now increase the current in the opposite direction B will decrease further reaching zero at R , and negative saturation at S. The other half of the curve STUP displays the same behaviour .
93243	This is no doubt a remarkable curve .
93244	B being so sluggish , it is usually referred to as the hysteresis curve .
93245	Note that the B-H relationship is irreversible everywhere inside the hysteresis curve .
93246	If at an arbitrary point ( say V ) we decided to decrease the current , B would decrease in a different manner , as shown in Fig. 3.10 .
93247	As far as engineering applications are concerned the most remarkable feature of the curve is that we can get a flux density even in the absence of all external agents .
93248	This is of course the permanent magnet you have all come across .
93249	How is this possible ?
93250	Up to now a current appeared to be absolutely essential for creating a magnetic flux .
93251	The obvious way out of this dilemma is to say that the currents are there — inside the magnetic material .
93252	The detailed mechanism of these currents has kept lots of physicists busy ever since Ampère made the hypothesis , but apparently some more time is needed to find a proper solution .
93253	For permanent magnets a wide hysteresis curve is needed so that demagnetization should not easily occur .
93254	For transformers and rotating machinery a narrow hysteresis curve is preferable because irreversibility leads to losses .
93255	I am afraid this is about as much as I am going to say about magnetic materials apart from a very brief discussion of some pseudomagnetic materials ( superconductors ) in Sections 3.15 and 3.16 .
93256	We shall look at a few examples now in which simple geometries will be considered .

93290	3.15 The perfect diamagnet ( H , B , K )
93291	There is a class of materials called type I superconductors which below a certain critical temperature ( around the normal boiling-point of liquid helium ) become both perfect conductors and perfect diamagnets .
93292	This means that B must be zero inside the material .
93293	Thus if we place a piece of such material ( say a sphere ) into an otherwise constant magnetic flux , the material will expel the flux lines as shown in Fig. 3.15 .
93294	How can this happen ?
93295	What mechanism is responsible for expelling the magnetic flux ?
93296	The appearance of surface currents ( which we have previously denoted by K ) .
93297	As the sphere becomes superconducting , surface currents are set up producing a magnetic flux opposite to that already existing inside the material .
93298	3.16 .

93439	A time-varying magnetic field creates an electric field as suggested by eqn ( 4.3 ) , but this is not necessarily a local relationship .
93440	The magnetic field may be confined to a certain part of space but the resulting electric field will pervade all space .
93441	What can we say about the line integral of the electric field ?
93442	It follows from eqn ( 4.9 ) that it is finite if the path encloses the time-varying flux but zero otherwise .
93443	How does this appear in practice ?
93444	What happens if we place a conducting wire into the electric field ?
93445	The mobile charges in the wire are not the least concerned about the origin of the electric field .
93446	They react in the same way whether the electric field is due to static charges or to a time-varying magnetic field ; under the force qE they rearrange themselves so as to cancel the electric field inside the conducting material as shown in Fig. 4.1(a) .
93447	There will now be an additional electric field ( say Ec ) due to the presence of these charges .
93448	Note however that , hence the charges do not interfere with the line integral of the electric field around a closed path .
93449	It is still true that whether we regard E as the original field ( without the contribution of the charges ) or as if Ec were added to the original field .
93450	So what is the voltage we are going to measure ?
93451	Let us take an ideal voltmeter ( one that draws no current ) and measure the voltage across the terminals of the wire .
93452	The voltage measured still depends on the path .
93453	We measure finite voltage if the time-varying flux is enclosed ( Fig. 4.1(b) ) and zero voltage if no flux is enclosed ( Fig. 4.1(c) ) .
93454	What happens if we have N loops ( Fig. 4.2(a) ) round the varying flux ?

93473	It means in our case ( the same that commonsense would suggest ) that the current in the loop must everywhere be the same .
93474	It varies of course as a function of time but not as a function of the spatial coordinates .

93478	What difference will it make if the wire loop is placed in the magnetic field as shown in Fig. 4.4 ?
93479	There will be a current produced by the electric field as before ; the new feature is the appearance of a qv X B force on each charge element .
93480	Since the velocity of the charge carriers is in the azimuthal direction , the force will act radially .
93481	It is the same story again .
93482	The charges can not leave the wire so they will accumulate at the outer and inner surface of the ring until a radial electric field is produced that will cancel the force due to the magnetic field .
93483	In conclusion , I wish to emphasize that all the charge rearrangements discussed in this section occur very fast , much faster than the period of oscillation of the magnetic field .

93576	4.4 .
93577	Kinetic inductance
93578	We have defined inductance by eqn ( 4.33 ) without discussing its effect upon the current-voltage relationship .
93579	Let me now briefly recall what an inductance does in a circuit .
93580	It delays things .
93581	If we apply a voltage the current will appear after some delay .
93582	If we switch off the voltage the current will disappear after some delay .
93583	Is there anything else in an electrical circuit that behaves that way ?
93584	That reminds me meeting an American friend of mine after he completed his grand tour of Europe .
93585	" D' you know " , he told me , " that I can ask for the check in seventeen languages ? "
93586	" Eighteen " , I said , " I bet you forgot to include " bill " . "
93587	As the above story shows it is often difficult to think of the obvious .
93588	In order to have a current , charge carriers must be accelerated , and it takes time to accelerate particles of finite mass .
93589	Hence the current will necessarily lag behind the voltage causing its rise .
93590	Let us put now the relations in mathematical form .
93591	We shall write up Newton 's equation for the case when the force is provided by an electric field and friction is present , where k is a constant characterizing friction ( to be related presently to more familiar constants ) .
93592	For a cylindrical piece of conducting material of length l and cross-section S0 , which substituted into eqn ( 4.59 ) leads to .
93593	We may formally write , where  is the kinetic resistance , and  is the kinetic inductance .
93594	If you think a little about it you will be able to convince yourself that Rk is nothing other than the old familiar resistance ( proportional to length ; inversely proportional to cross-section ) derived in a different manner .
93595	Whether one defines a conductance or introduces a friction term they are just two different ways of expressing the empirical fact that the electrons ' velocity does not go on increasing indefinitely in response to a driving electric field .
93596	Does the same apply to the second term ?
93597	Is that also a different derivation of the inductance ?
93598	No , in deriving eqn ( 4.61 ) we have not talked about magnetic fields and induction at all .
93599	The kinetic inductance owes its existence to inertia .
93600	Why is eqn ( 4.64 ) so little known ?
93601	Because under normal circumstances this kinetic inductance is negligible .
93602	Comparing eqns ( 4.63 ) and ( 4.64 ) you may see that Lk = Rk/k , and if you determine k from the identity  you will find for copper that .
93603	So you can see that the time constant involved is very small .
93604	The kinetic inductance does , however , acquire importance in superconductors , where the resistance disappears altogether .
93605	It may be seen by comparing eqns ( 4.64 ) and ( 4.35 ) that for a ring made of sufficiently thin wire the kinetic inductance may exceed the ordinary magnetic inductance .
93606	And this may very well occur in practice because superconductors used in integrated circuits can have cross-sections less than 10 -12 m 2 .
93607	It may be said in general that the designer of a superconducting circuit needs to worry about the response time and energy of superconducting electrons .

93630	4.6 Relative motion of conducting wire and magnetic field
93631	Up to now all the wires have been stationary , and the magnetic field has varied as a function of time .
93632	Let us see now what happens when the wires are made to move with uniform velocity .
93633	As our first example we shall take a straight piece of wire moving perpendicularly to the direction of a static magnetic field .
93634	As a consequence there will be a force qv X B acting on the charges in the wire ; the mobile charges will be displaced until the arising electric field produces an equal and opposite force .
93635	Let us investigate now the converse problem when the wire is stationary but the equipment producing the magnetic field is moved lock , stock , and barrel with the same velocity in the opposite direction .
93636	One 's first impression is ( or should be ) that only relative motion counts , hence the force upon the charges should be the same .
93637	Formally , we would have the same force if we assumed ( as many textbooks do ) that a magnetic field moving with a velocity in gives rise to a force .
93638	This is a way out of the problem but not a way open to us .
93639	We have started by writing down Maxwell 's equations and claimed that they will provide the solution to any electromagnetic problem .
93640	We are not entitled to introduce a new force .
93641	According to our equations a magnetic field , whether it moves or not , can not produce a force on a stationary charge .
93642	What should we do ?
93643	Well , perhaps the trouble is that we wrote down Maxwell 's equations in a stationary frame of reference .
93644	In order to tackle the present problem we should change to a coordinate system moving with the magnetic field .
93645	This is certainly a possible approach , and one we shall adopt towards the end of the course when discussing relativity , but such a transformation ( though convenient ) should not be necessary .
93646	Maxwell 's equations written in the stationary frame of reference should be perfectly capable of dealing with the problem .
93647	Why is there a doubt at all ?
93648	Some doubts may arise by considering the following problem .
93649	Let us postulate the existence of a static magnetic field that is constant over a finite region of space , say , and assume that this magnetic field is bodily moved in the +x direction with a velocity u .
93650	What will happen to the charges in the stationary wire situated at ( say ) x = 0 ?
93651	One may argue that by moving the magnetic field nothing has changed at the position of the wire .
93652	The magnetic field is unchanged and there can not be an electric field either because a constant magnetic field is unable to produce an electric field .
93653	The above argument is wrong ; do n't let yourself be misled .
93654	Induction is not a local phenomenon .
93655	Although , it does not follow that the electric field is also zero at x = 0 ; the curl of the electric field must be zero but not the electric field itself .
93656	When the magnetic field is moved bodily there will be certain places in space where the magnitude of the magnetic field is changing ( shaded areas in Fig. 4.12 ) as a function of time , and that changing magnetic field can give rise to an electric field at x = 0 .
93657	The electric field will then produce just the right force for displacing the electrons by the right amount .
93658	Let's attempt to obtain a general solution of this problem .
93659	We shall assume a static magnetic field  which will vary as  when moved bodily by a velocity u .
93660	The equation to solve is eqn ( 4.3 ) which we shall write here again : .
93661	By differentiating eqn ( 4.77 ) we get .
93662	But according to eqn ( A.7 )  solution of eqn ( 4.3 ) may be recognized as being given by .
93663	We are now entitled to write the force on the charges as .
93664	If the magnetic field is moved with a velocity -v the force on the charges is the same as if the wire moved with a velocity v , and we have managed to prove all that from Maxwell 's equations .

93820	He signed the Friends ' Book in his elegant handwriting : Alexander Wedderburn , January 22nd , 1980 .
93821	She had said , peremptory as always , that he was to go straight to Room III , where " the miraculous stuff " was to be found .
93822	Early .
93823	So here he was , a distinguished public man , also an artist of a kind , stepping obediently through Room I ( French 1880s ) and Room II ( British 1880s and 1890s ) , on a lead grey morning , to the pale grey , classical , quiet place where the bright light shone and sang off pigment so that the phrase , miraculous stuff , seemed merely accurate .
93824	On one long wall hung a row of Van Goghs , including an Arles " Poets ' Garden " he had n't seen before , but recognised , from small photographs , from charged descriptions in the painter 's letters .
93825	He sat down and saw a bifurcated path , simmering with gold heat round and under the rising , spreading blue-black-green down-pointing vanes of a great pine , still widening where the frame interrupted its soaring .
93826	Two decorous figures advanced , hand-in-hand , under its suspended thickness .
93827	And beyond , green grass and geraniums like splashes of blood .
93828	Alexander was not worried about whether Frederica would turn up .
93829	She was no longer in the habit of being late : her life had schooled her to temporal accuracy , perhaps to being considerate .
93830	He himself , at sixty-two , felt , not quite accurately , that he was now too old , too settled , to be put out , by her or by anyone else .
93831	He thought with warmth of her certain approach .
93832	There had been a pattern , an only too discernible repetition in the events and relationships of his life into which she had ruggedly refused to fit .
93833	She had been a nuisance , a threat , a torment and was now a friend .
93834	She had suggested that they look at Van Gogh together , setting up another form of repetition , deliberate , contrived and aesthetic .
93835	His play , The Yellow Chair , had first been presented in 1957 ; he did not like to think too closely about it , as he did not like to think too closely about any of his past work .
93836	He stared at the serenely impassioned garden made out of a whirl of yellow brushstrokes , a viridian impasto , a dense mass of furiously feathered lines of blue-green , isolated black pot hooks , the painfully clear orange-red spattering .
93837	He had trouble finding an appropriate language for the painter 's obsession with the illuminated material world .
93838	He would have been lying if he had recorded only the more accessible drama of the painter 's electric quarrels with Gauguin in the Yellow House in Arles , the distant necessary brother who supplied paint and love , the severed ear delivered to the whore in the brothel , the asylum fears .
93839	At first he had thought that he could write a plain , exact verse with no figurative language , in which a yellow chair was the thing itself , a yellow chair , as a round gold apple was an apple or a sunflower a sunflower .
93840	Sometimes he still saw the brushstrokes , as it were , in this naked way , so that his earlier thoughts of this garden had to be undone , the idea of black wings to be stripped from the painted leafage , the vulgar idea of blood splashes washed off the notation of geraniums .
93841	But it could n't be done .
93842	Language was against him , for a start .
93843	Metaphor lay coiled in the name sunflower , which not only turned towards but resembled the sun , the source of light .
93844	Van Gogh 's idea of things had also been against him .
93845	The yellow chair , besides being brushstrokes and pigment , besides being a yellow chair , was one of twelve bought for a company of artists who were to inhabit the Yellow House , the white walls of which should blaze with sunflowers as the windows of Gothic cathedrals blazed with coloured light .
93846	Not only metaphor : cultural motif , immanent religion , a faith and a church .
93847	One thing always linked to another thing .

94842	Christmas
94843	The nuclear Potter family had practised a muted and aimless version of the British family Christmas rite .
94844	They had inhibitions about concentrating on what might be called the Dickensian essentials ; a great deal of specified food and drink , presents wanted and unwanted , the gathering of friends and relations .
94845	They had no available extended family : there were Potters scattered about North Yorkshire who had not been seen since Bill 's Congregationalist parents had cast him off for unbelief .
94846	Winifred was the only child of dead parents .
94847	Their household gods were created , not inherited , and were meagre and fleshless .
94848	This was partly — in the Dickensian context — because of uncertainty of manners , owing to upward social mobility .
94849	They had ideas about respectability and propriety which as intellectuals they despised but as Christmas dinner-eaters they endorsed .
94850	Daniel 's Dad , the engine-driver , when living , had got drunk in the pub first and at home later : there had been gusto , jollity , somnolence and regret .
94851	Bill Potter took a glass of sherry , and shared out a bottle of sparkling wine .
94852	No neighbours called and they visited no neighbours .
94853	They were blameless of seasonal road accidents : they were closed in with themselves , more than usual , since no shops were open and no employment was possible , except to " enjoy oneself " and wash up more plates than usual , as Frederica frequently pointed out .
94854	They ate frugally : they had learned in the war to make do with the plain , avoid waste , make things go round .
94855	Winifred had aesthetic uncertainties .
94856	As she had little dress sense , only a vague fear that any hat or dress she chose might be vulgar , so she had no sense of a possible style in which to decorate a house , or even a dining table , for Christmas .
94857	She solved the clothes problem with rigorous inconspicuous plainness , and was inclined to solve the Christmas problem , much less successfully , the same way .
94858	When the children were little they made paper chains and strings of painted cardboard milk-bottle tops , and these were draped over mirrors .
94859	( They were never long enough to cross the room . )
94860	When they were little they had a little artificial tree and put out their stockings on Christmas Eve .
94861	Neither Bill nor Winifred could bring themselves to lie about the provenance of the gifts they found in the stockings .
94862	This was not really because of an absolute respect for truth but was something to do with their inhibited negative sense of style .
94863	They could not be seen telling stories : it looked daft .
94864	Frederica , frustrated of magic , took it out on her classmates at a very early age by stripping them ruthlessly of their illusions .
94865	This made her neither popular nor happy .
94866	There was no singing , because they could not sing .
94867	There were no games , partly because they did n't know any , partly because all five were united , in this if in nothing else , in the belief that dice , cards , charades , were a frivolous waste of time .
94868	So , apart from opening presents , they watched each other and waited for Christmas to be over so that they could resume their intense and private working lives .
94869	This year , for Stephanie , had to be different .
94870	There was the church , which she helped to decorate with holly , mistletoe , evergreens .

95259	Midi
95260	When Frederica left for Nîmes she had no real idea of the South .
95261	She knew that Nîmes was a provincial city and would have preferred it not to be , seeing " provincial " in terms of the English nineteenth century novel , not of the Roman Provincia , Provence .
95262	Drifting citywards in her generation , she had really hoped for Paris and bright lights .
95263	She had booked a sleeper from Paris in terms of time — " I ca n't sit up all night " — not distance " I am going a long way south . "
95264	When she boarded this train she became involved in an altercation with the sleeping-car attendant , which she enjoyed , because it was in French , and she was able to use her subjunctives and conditionals , and say " si " instead of " oui " at appropriate moments .
95265	She lost the argument , which was about her reservation , which was for berth No. 7 in English which the conductor obstinately read as 1 in French .
95266	Frederica explained that in France the 7 is crossed but that this is not done in Thomas Cook 's in Calverley , N. Yorkshire .
95267	The attendant said there was a gentleman already undressing in No. 1 Frederica received no answer to her question about numéro sept , but was given permission to stand in the corridor of the train , which was already sliding away from its platform .
95268	She watched Paris rattle past , foreign blocks of lit windows , knots of wire , and she was offered a Gauloise by a compact little man who leaned his elbow companionably against hers on the window-rail .
95269	She accepted the cigarette as she accepted most offerings , and still elated at the sound of her French being understood and responded to by Frenchmen , volunteered the information that she was going to Nîmes , to stay with a family .
95270	She would have told him much more , all sorts of improper things , only to hear the old information newly proposed in new words .
95271	She would be lucky , the man told her , to see the South in spring .
95272	The maquis smells wonderful .
95273	For the first time Frederica 's imagination touched at the South .
95274	He was going to St Raphael himself , the man said .
95275	He was a traveller .
95276	He sold liqueurs , mostly to the hotel industry .
95277	He could offer mademoiselle a taste of Cointreau , Grand Marnier , Chartreuse , if she really had no berth .
95278	Frederica replied brightly that would be very agreeable .
95279	This was despite a strong sense that the man was unduly anxious about the outcome of his overture : anxiety is a great destroyer of response , and Frederica had no taste for being closed in a sleeping compartment with a worried man .
95280	On the other hand she did not want to stand until dawn , and she did want the French words to go on being threaded together .
95281	The sleeping-car attendant came back and announced that by great good fortune he had an empty berth for which the occupant had unaccountably not appeared .
95282	He ushered Frederica into No. 7 , and stood , perhaps awaiting a tip , which she was unable to offer , being provided only with notes of large denominations .
95283	This caused her to close herself abruptly in , without the traveller in liqueurs .
95284	And then she was delighted by the solitude of the sleeping-car , and forgot him .
95285	She undressed partly and padded about the perpetually shifting floor in stocking feet , suspenders , slip and bra .
95286	She investigated ring hooks , water flask , lidded washbasin .
95287	She tried to peer out of the peephole in her blind .
95288	A station clashed by so fast she could neither read its name or discern the pattern of its ironwork .
95289	Black masses of bush , or bull , or thatch elongated themselves howling .
95290	She liked that .
95291	She liked to be alone in a warm , lit box with the world streaming darkly by .
95292	She curled on her bunk , admired her long legs , thought about desire ( not for the traveller in liqueurs ) , read part of Madame Bovary , part of Les Fleurs du Hal and all of a novel by Margery Sharp , bought on impulse at the Gare de Lyon .
95293	She saw the dawn when it came and pulled up the blind .
95294	There in the pale lemon grey were expanses of espaliered rows of strange stumps like truncated Virginia creepers , squat and tough .
95295	These large spaces did not rush past but seemed endless because endlessly repeated .
95296	Understanding took time .
95297	Vines in her mind trailed over trellises , depended from arbours , clung .

95299	She dressed carefully , green herring-bone tweed suit , pinch-waisted , court shoes , very plain , and a complicated face , the tricky little eyeliner triangles at the lid-corners almost smudged by the swaying train .
95300	She had a sort of velvet cap , from which she had snipped a bit of veiling .
95301	She believed cheap clothes could be made elegant by paring them down to essentials .
95302	Sometimes this worked , sometimes she looked tarty , sometimes she looked drab .

95304	The Grimaud family had written to say that they would meet her with a blue Corvette .
95305	It was only at this late stage that she began to think about them ; they had been a means to an end , Frederica Potter 's removal from Blesford and Yorkshire .
95306	A large man and a small boy appeared at the other end of the platform : she hobbled on her heels , humping her heavy suitcase , towards them .
95307	They greeted her and introduced themselves — Monsieur Grimaud and Paul-Marie .
95308	Paul-Marie had un-English shorts , long white socks , olive-brown legs .
95309	Frederica ignored him .
95310	M. Grimaud swung up her bag , smiling .

95324	It had seemed , because she was , raw and new , dust and brightness .

95330	In this dream she had been locked into the school library with an exam paper containing one question and one only : Compare and contrast narrative method in Proust and Tom Jones .
95331	She knew nothing about either and in the dream wept bitterly from shame and impotence .

95333	She was never to think of that dream without some of its investing emotions , shame and irritation , even after a man at a party in 1969 had told her such dreams are dreamed typically by those unlikely to fail plausible and real exams .
95334	Then , in 1954 , as the car passed under what seemed a mediaeval or Renaissance courtyard gate there was Frederica , brooding grimly about a personal failure in a dreamed , unreal competition .

95336	The yard was walled in gold stone covered with clean dust and lichen-stains .

95343	The floor was faded blue and tawny tiles .
95344	The bed was high , high and curtained , covered with lace and bobbled crocheted cotton .

95348	It was alien .
95349	It was interesting .
95350	She was excited by so many strange things .
95351	She was also exhausted .
95352	And , to her horror , briefly homesick for carpets , bookcases , small casement windows , man-made heating devices , the familiar , the known .
95353	Later , at least for many years , she was not to see this time as part of her life , and perhaps therefore it need not now be told at length .
95354	Frederica 's recall of things seen was very much less lucid and automatic than those of Stephanie or even Marcus .
95355	Her mind was self-referring and exclusive as theirs were not — impersonal only in relation to the teasing-out of the intellectually taxing problem .
95356	In the 1970s Ezra Pound 's laminated view of vital and moribund cultures , centred partly on Provence , made her see M. 95357	Bill Potter had his local pride : his evening class students collected local words , described patterns of social behaviour and family interrelationship with a kind of Fabian zeal , but without the sun-saturated liveliness of M. Grimaud 's sense of what was shared and perpetual in his world .
95358	This family , which was not her own , which threw her own , absent and dispersed , into sharp relief , was certainly kind .

95363	Frederica , who did not even make her own bed , acquired one or two odd skills .

95367	Her one apparent asset , her good French , turned out to be a disadvantage .
95368	Marie-Claire and Monique learned little English because Frederica intimidated them and they intimidated her .
95369	She rewrote their homework in respectable English but appeared , at that time , not to have inherited the family teaching compulsion , and was unable to explain the principle by which she was altering their grammar and syntax .
95370	Thus , although their marks improved , the two girls were not learning .
95371	Only much later did it occur to her that this was her failure : academically self-sufficient and wholly self-centred she saw their sullenness and ignorance as their concern and their fault .
95372	Madame Grimaud treated all this with brisk courtesy , remarking on one occasion that it could at least be said that Frederica was a good moral influence .
95373	Frederica saw this observation at the time as a mark of signal failure of insight .
95374	Later , in England , it occurred to her that it might have been said ironically , but by then she had forgotten the context and intonation of it , could only remember that it was said under hot sun outside the Maison Carrée in Nîmes , where the air was fluent and the stones shone .
95375	They made courteous and persistent attempts to amuse her .
95376	On the second day they gave her a rubber ball attached on a long elastic thread to a wooden bat .

95380	Frederica was put in mind , mutatis mutandis , starting with the intention , of Miss Havisham bidding the boy Pip to play , of the brewery yard where he had met Herbert Pocket , which ( the yard ) irked her , because she could not properly visualise it .
95381	She was taken everywhere .
95382	To the covered fish market at dawn to buy fish for a bouillabaisse , which held no romance for her for she had not then read Ford 's description of the great bouillabaisse in the Calanques , nor Elizabeth David 's description of the colours and patterns of fish on the stalls .
95383	She went to the dressmaker with Madame Grimaud , where there was a stocky replica , adjustable , of Madame Grimaud 's female French form standing headless on a metal leg .
95384	Everyone knew everyone and stopped to speak to everyone .

95387	She visited neighbouring propriétés and sipped aperitifs from unlabelled bottles , white port on terraces , in arbours trailing wisteria , under acacia trees .
95388	In two of these families there were young men , sons and heirs who would inherit the land , unspeaking grave Michel , noisy Dany with one word of English — " bluejeans " — and an explosive Lambretta churning up pale , clean dust .
95389	She had ideas about these two , especially about Michel , but saw that to them she was invisible , not quite real , as au pair girls frequently , perhaps usually , are .
95390	She spoke a lot , and they turned and congratulated each other on her French , as though she was some sort of barrel-organ she thought , being not only sex-starved but starved also of admiration .
95391	When Monsieur was at home , more cultural and purposeful expeditions were undertaken .
95392	They went to a floodlit performance of Mireille in the Roman arena in Nîmes .
95393	In the same place , one day , Frederica saw bullfighting .
95394	She had hoped to understand the aesthetic excitement of this pursuit , to see and recognise the " moment of truth " even if she must simultaneously be revolted .
95395	But all she saw was slow , repeated , stumbling , coughing killings at which she retched in a very conventional English animal-loving way , which upset Monsieur Grimaud , who was an aficionado , and had been lecturing Frederica on the provenance and meaning of that word .
95396	The place suddenly had its history of bloodletting to be sniffed , and yet even that was not exciting , maybe because the Nîmois did not roar for blood as the Romans had , but sunned themselves and discussed finer points of capework .
95397	They did , it was true , have an agitated fit of booing and hissing , but this was , M. Grimaud explained , an expression of spontaneous disapproval of Picasso who could just be made out , small brown face under black beret at the other side of the arena .
95398	The crowd , M. Grimaud stated , thought his art was fraudulent and Frederica , trying in vain to imagine any English football crowd holding any communal view about any modern artist , suddenly remembered the Picasso prints on the walls of Alexander Wedderburn 's study in Blesford Ride School .
95399	She had been in love with Alexander .

95401	She had made , circumstances had made , rather a mess of this love .
95402	She did not think he would like to hear from her , or possibly even to think about her .
95403	His Picassos had been Blue Period , the Saltimbanques , a strange Boy with a Pipe , crowned with flowers .

95406	Moreover , he said , Picasso had discovered and ruined the traditional potteries at Vallauris which now turned out only nasty ash-trays with distorted bulls and gross doves .

95412	Frederica gagged on hers , nauseated by a memory of the foundering black body as the life left the legs , of the crawling sheet of sticky blood over the shoulder under the pics , of trailing hooves and horns dragged over sawdust .
95413	She was later to discover that a certain J. Olivier believed that Vincent Van Gogh 's self-mutilation in Arles was an aspect of some bull-ritual .
95414	The victorious matador , he said , was awarded the ear of the bull , which he would offer " to his Lady or to a female spectator who has drawn his attention " .
95415	( No ears were awarded on the day of Frederica 's visit to the corrida . )

95419	The result was burning headaches , dizzy spells and prolonged periods of lassitude which the Grimauds , courteous as always , ascribed to the mistral , to heat , to unaccustomed diet .

95421	There were no books .
95422	M. Grimaud told her how Nîmes had been settled by the veterans of Octavius 's victory over Antony and Cleopatra , whose names , Antonin , Numa , Flavien , Adrien , persisted , even today , as did the emblem of the defeat of the serpent of old Nile , the Nîmes chained crocodile .
95423	He took her to Uzès where Racine had once come to ruralise , contemplate the priesthood , began to write .
95424	Uzès was and is a town out of another time , a yellow town on a gently conical hill , geometrical roof on roof , a town that must have been as it now is when Shakespeare wrote Antony and Cleopatra .
95425	Frederica tried to talk to M. Grimaud about Racine but , although he could quote several speeches , he was more interested in what Racine was and meant than in what he had written .
95426	He had a Racine , a Molière , a Chateaubriand .
95427	Frederica borrowed also Hemingway in translation , and read about bullfights and the earth moving , which caused her to feel worse , sex-starved , desperate for life , and love , and action .

95431	These were not what she was hungry for , but they were English , and narrative .
95432	Narrative is one of the best intoxicants or tranquillisers .
95433	They were at least long .
95434	Madame then thought of the vélo .
95435	On this Frederica explored the unvarying hot flat country .
95436	She bumped along furrows between vines , spattered cobalt-blue with spraying .
95437	She listened to cicadas and breathed the pervasive liquorice which grew locally and was processed in a factory on the Nîmes road .
95438	Whenever she fell off the vélo she sat where she was , nodding , fumed with wine and drowsy with heat , in a classical furrow , under a pale , bright sky .
95439	She decided to become a writer .
95440	It was almost inevitable , given the excessive respect paid in the Potter house to the written word , and given Frederica 's own mastery of , and intense pleasure in , the school essay , that she should decide to become a writer .
95441	Foreign places , moreover , bring out the writer in strangers less word obsessed than Frederica Potter .
95442	I do not think the compulsion to write about foreign places can be very closely compared to a painter 's sensuous delight in new light , new forms , new colours , Monet seeing the Cap d'Antibes in blue and rose , Turner seeing the bright watery Venetian light in Venice , Gauguin in Tahiti .
95443	Pigment is pigment and light is light in any culture .
95444	But words , acquired slowly over a lifetime , are part of a different set of perceptions of the world , they have grown with us , they restrict what we see and how we see it .
95445	I am trying to account for the paradox of the sameness of so many accounts , in language , of the strange , the exotic , the new .
95446	Frederica will do as an example to illustrate the difficulties of writing about strangeness .
95447	She wanted to set down the southern landscape .
95448	Her tradition of looking at landscape was deeply Wordsworthian , whatever intimations she may have had that Wordsworth 's language was for his time and place only .
95449	Frederica could , in the Lake District , have seen a " Wordsworthian " tarn and been able to render it in Wordsworthian words , and , because these words were known , tested , thought about , she could have introduced minute changes , have seen one little thing he had n't seen , changed the point of view .
95450	There are shepherds in the Andes who have over sixty words for the colour brown in the coats of sheep .
95451	But they are shepherds in the Andes .
95452	Frederica had words for tea party behaviour and shopping discriminations in North Yorkshire matrons .
95453	She had a variety of words , and was adding to them , for the structure of a Shakespearean plot or metaphor .
95454	She saw these new things , paradoxically , in old cliches .
95455	The same Wordsworth , much-mocked , thought himself back to an innocent vision , told us that grass is green and water wet because he had reached beyond familiarity to some primal wonder that these things were so and not otherwise , to some mythic sense that he was giving or finding the words for the things , not merely repeating .
95456	So also Daniel , walking with Stephanie on Filey beach , had suddenly , out of some metaphorical experience as bodily as breathing , known why love was called " sweet " and , as his blood banged , why a beloved was a " sweet heart " .
95457	So now , more mildly , Frederica saw for the first time that the light was gold , that olives were black and warm , the olive trees were powdery-grey , that lavender was a purple haze .
95458	But when she saw these things written they seemed , and were , stale , deja-vu , derivative .
95459	Frederica was also enough a child of her time to suppose that what she should write should be fiction .
95460	" The novel is the one bright book of life , " Lawrence had didactically exclaimed and Bill Potter had didactically reiterated .
95461	" The novel is the highest form of human expression yet attained . "
95462	If anyone had challenged Frederica directly as to whether she believed that , she would have argued the toss .
95463	But — however Wordsworthian the roots — in the 1950s the recording compulsion took Lawrentian forms .
95464	And she had no plot .
95465	Or did not recognise those plots she had .
95466	And was not primarily in those days concerned with invention .
95467	She tried to utilise Dany and his Lambretta or a speechless Michel , and disgusted herself .
95468	She was driven back to Alexander , and attempted unsuccessfully to translate that very English poet into a divinity of the olive groves .

99237	DIRECT FILE ORGANIZATION
99238	6.1 Introduction
99239	Records can be retrieved directly from files that have been organized in many ways .
99240	In this chapter we shall be dealing with files that have been designed to make direct record retrieval as easy and rapid as possible .
99241	These are known as directly organized files .
99242	It is possible to process the records in a directly organized file either directly , using the keys in any desired order , or serially , taking the records in the order they are stored and ignoring their keys .
99243	Both direct and serial processing of directly organized files are dealt with in this chapter .
99244	Direct processing of files organized sequentially or using the indexed sequential technique is covered in the chapters devoted to those types of organization .
99245	Records are often processed in a random order .
99246	A bank can not predict which of its customers wish to withdraw or deposit money on any given day ; a travel firm can not control which of its package tours will be booked at a particular time .
99247	Customers arrive as a result of their own decisions , and not in an order dictated by the travel agent or bank .
99248	As these transactions are not predictable they present a processing problem .
99249	When an immediate response is not required , the transactions can be collected into batches , sorted into a key sequence that matches the appropriate master file , and processed sequentially .
99250	However , if the customer is waiting for an immediate answer , there is no time for this .
99251	The record has to be checked at once — to see if a booking is available , for example — and this means that the file has to be referenced without preparatory sorting or processing .
99252	As the records are processed in a sequence that can not be predetermined , we are faced with the problem that we know the key or control number of the record but have no indication of its location in storage .
99253	It would be possible to search through the file until the record was located , but this technique , and the more refined methods available for searching sequential files in which there is no direct relationship between the record key and its storage location , are too slow for the needs of most enquiry systems .
99254	We must look for a way of establishing a relationship between the key of the record and its address , and using this relationship to retrieve the record rapidly .
99255	The relationship can take several forms .
99256	First , it can be an index of every record position in the file ; modifications of this method lead to indexed sequential files , and are dealt with in Chapter 7 .
99257	Second , each record can be stored at an address that is directly related to its key , e.g. at the address which is the same as the key ( record 20 in address 20 and so on ) .
99258	This type of file is known as a self-indexing or self-addressing file .
99259	If it is not possible to find a relationship of this sort , some other method of assigning addresses to keys has to be found .
99260	Usually , a suitable algorithm is used to convert keys to addresses ; the file is then described as a randomized file , and the algorithm used is called a randomizing algorithm .
99261	The process is often also described as hashing .
99262	The application of these methods of assigning storage positions to records is discussed in detail in this chapter , and reference tables are provided to aid the file designer .
99263	This is followed by sections on optimizing the performance of direct files , and on the practical steps that can be taken to maximize the efficiency of these files in operation .
99264	6.2 Self-indexing
99265	Continuous key sequences
99266	If record keys are numeric and there are not many gaps in the sequence , it is often possible to allocate a storage position based directly on the key .
99267	In the simplest case , records with keys such as 00 000 to 99 999 could be allocated to any contiguous set of 100000 storage positions .
99268	Some direct access devices have available storage areas starting from 00 000 or 00001 , and addressed by a simple number .
99269	When devices of this type are available , the storing of records with a continuous set of keys is straightforward .
99270	However , the conversion from a numeric user-address to a device address in terms of cylinders and records is carried out by the manufacturer 's software , and thus involves an overhead of both primary storage space and CPU time .
99271	If locations with the same addresses as the record keys are available , then each record is stored in the appropriate position , and a record can be retrieved by the use of the relationship :
99272	If a contiguous area of storage is available elsewhere , or if the keys are continuous but start at a figure outside the range of the storage addresses available , an addition or subtraction will be needed .
99273	In this case : where β is a constant .

99276	In this case , to allow for the increment not being unity , the relationship becomes : where α and β are constants .
99277	An example of this might be keys 00 003 , 00006 , 00 009 , 00012 , etc. , to be stored in positions 00352 , 00 353 , … .
