99296	Integer arithmetic should be used , to avoid the problems of approximate answers .
99297	If necessary , considerably more complex calculations are justified because of the speed of internal storage operations , and because use of such a calculation allows the unbroken key sequence to be exploited .
99298	Manufacturers usually provide relative record addressing which carries out these calculations for the user .
99299	Broken key sequences
99300	Inherently continuous sequences Although the key sequence in a new file is often continuous , gaps will usually soon occur .
99301	Customers turn elsewhere or go out of business , old product numbers are replaced by new , and so on .
99302	The advantage of being able to store such a file on a direct access device in addresses which are directly related to the key then has to be balanced against the waste of space involved .
99303	A self-indexing file can be referenced sequentially by normal sequential processing , and directly using a single seek because of the relations between key and storage address .
99304	No other file organization can achieve this , so it is worth accepting a fairly low packing density to retain the file in this form .
99305	If direct access capacity is a limitation , a loss of 15 — 20 per cent of space will still compare well with other file organizations ( see Chapter 7 and the calculations of packing density for randomly organized direct files later in this chapter ) .
99306	Where access time is the vital criterion and direct access storage is abundant , a packing density of as little as 50 per cent is justifiable for a file accessed both directly and sequentially .
99307	Where maximum direct access throughput is essential , even lower packing densities may be accepted ( see the average space used by randomized files to compare , p. 310 ) .
99308	Unused storage positions should be filled with dummy records , so that they can be recognized at once .
99309	In setting up a file with a number of dummy records , these dummies will be filled with a character such as &amp; or • that will be tested for during serial processing .
99310	The problem should not arise during direct processing , as every valid key has a corresponding record .
99311	If it does , then an error will be indicated .
99312	However , the test for a dummy must be carried out during direct processing to guard against an invalid key being processed ( see Fig. 6.1 ) .
99313	This technique is only directly applicable to fixed-length records .
99314	It can be applied to variable-length records by padding or the use of fixed-length buckets for variable records , as discussed previously .
99315	In the latter case addressing will probably only point to a bucket number , and in searching the bucket for a particular record using the direct technique it will no longer be an error to detect a dummy record , but part of the search .
99316	Naturally broken sequences Record keys often do not start as an unbroken sequence .
99317	In a simple case , we might have the following key set : These thirty-four records need only 34 storage positions , but if they were stored in self-indexing form they would take up 359 storage positions , and there would be five gaps of 91 , 1 , 1 , 94 and 138 positions respectively .
99318	These gaps can be eliminated by a sequence of tests of the type shown below : The gaps are eliminated as shown in Fig. 6.2 .
99319	Typically , keys form broken sequences because they contain separate items of information .
99320	For example , a product code used as a key may contain sections for such fields as :
99321	There may be room left for additions to the number of products , product types , factories , categories , etc .
99322	This can lead to a series of continuous keys with gaps left in it at intervals .
99323	This can be converted into a continuous sequence of keys so long as the various constants involved in the key are known .
99324	For example , if the category can take the values 1 to 7 , the factory number can be 01 to 11 , the product type can be 01 to 37 , and the number of products in the type can range from 001 to 999 , with 147 being the largest required at present ( the number varies with type ) , then we might have the following runs of continuous numbers made up of the digits representing the category , factory , product type and number of products :
99325	These runs of continuous numbers have to be turned into a single sequence , starting from 1 .
99326	There are 2849 runs of numbers ; as given above the most in one run is 147 , and the least shown is 84 .
99327	One way of combining these runs into a single sequence is shown in Fig. 6.3 .
99328	This process requires a table of 2849 entries , each showing the cumulative total of records up to the start of that set .
99329	To ensure that all the product types for a given category and factory are kept together , the following algorithm is used : This arranges for every product type for category 1 and factory 1 to come first , and every factory in category 1 to precede those in category 2 .
99330	If this routine is written in a programming language such as PL/1 , Algol or Fortran , the calculation is not necessary ; the subscript facility can be used , and the table entries referenced as TABLE ( CAT , FAC , PROD ) .
99331	In the example shown in Fig. 6.3 , the entry required would be TABLE ( 1 , 1 , 3 ) .
99332	This example requires a large table ; if there is not room in primary storage for such a table it is not possible to handle the file as a self-indexing file , and a different method of addressing must be used .
99333	It is almost always a lack of storage space , or the fact that the file is dynamic and so can not be loaded in a single operation , that prevents self-indexing , and not the time taken to carry out the calculations .
99334	Before leaving the subject of self-indexing , it is worth mentioning perfect hash functions .
99335	These generally refer to finding a self-indexing function for tables in main storage ; Jaeschke has developed a method originally proposed by Cichell , and he has shown that , however complicated the key sequence is , a self-indexing function can be found for up to 40 keys so that they fit exactly into a table with the same number of storage positions .
99336	For larger tables — up to about 1000 keys — a more approximate but less time-consuming method due to Sprugnoli can be used .
99337	The small size of these ‘ files ’ make such techniques applicable only to main storage tables ; in that sphere , they are very useful .
99338	6.3 Algorithmic addressing
99339	The keys used for many data files are not suited to any practical self-indexing transformation , so other methods of establishing a relationship between record keys and storage addresses have been developed .
99340	What is needed is a transformation — usually called an algorithm — that can be carried out on a key to yield a storage address .
99341	Naturally , it must always yield the same address from the same key .
99342	Any such transformation will involve the compression of a diffuse key set , containing many gaps , into a much smaller range of addresses ; if this is not the case , the file should be self-indexed .
99343	Whatever the size and complexity of the key , the factors that control the transformation are the same .
99344	They are :
99345	1
99346	The number of addresses to be generated .
99347	This will depend on the number of records if each record is to have its own address .
99348	If groups of records are to be stored in buckets , it will be related to the number of buckets required .
99349	2
99350	The direct access space required and , in some cases , its distribution .
99351	It is desirable to have a single file area , both for efficient file processing and for simplicity , but this is not always possible .
99352	At all events the user will have to estimate the amount of direct access storage space the file needs , and this will affect the algorithm used .
99353	A number of techniques are available to handle files that have dynamic space requirements , and these are discussed later .
99354	3
99355	The direct access starting address .
99356	It will not be enough to produce a set of generated addresses corresponding to the number of record storage positions required .
99357	They will also have to start from the specified starting address on the device , and must all lie within the allocated range .
99358	The process will be as shown in Fig. 6.4 .
99359	Assume that n records are to be stored , and N addresses are available for record storage .
99360	Transformation of keys into addresses by an algorithm will produce r addresses .
99361	The relationship between r , n and N is : Ideally just one key would be associated with each address and every address available would be used .
99362	In this case .
99363	In practice neither condition is likely to be met .
99364	The factors determining how closely the ideal case can be approached are examined in the following sections .
99365	How synonyms occur
99366	Sometimes two or more record keys are transformed by an algorithm into the same address .
99367	The first record to be allocated that address can be stored there , and is described as the home record .
99368	Any subsequent record to be allocated to that address has to be stored elsewhere .
99369	It is called a synonym , and will overflow from its natural home address because that is already full .
99370	The situation is modified when records are stored in buckets holding several records , but synonyms still occur .
99371	This is examined later ( see p. 173 ) .
99372	As a synonym is not held at the address the program has computed , a further search is needed to find it .
99373	This leads to loss of time , and synonyms are the reason that algorithmically addressed files give a slower response than self-indexing files ; home records are retrieved just as quickly .
99374	Much of the rest of this chapter shows how to minimize the number of synonyms , and to reduce the effect of those that remain .
99375	It might seem that a suitable algorithm could be found which would not generate synonyms .
99376	This is very unlikely .
99377	In some cases the algorithm will spread the addresses evenly over the allocated storage area , and in the ideal case will have an equal probability of generating any address within that area ; in other cases the existing key order can be used to improve the efficiency of record storage .
99378	In either case some addresses will be generated more than once , while others will not be generated at all .
99379	A different set of keys will produce a different set of synonyms , and of unused record spaces .
99380	Statistically , however , the chance of avoiding synonyms altogether is vanishingly small .
99381	Heising has pointed out that if n records are randomized into N addresses , there are N n possible record distributions , only of which allocate no more than one record to any address .
99382	If 4000 records are stored in 5000 addresses then only one algorithm in every will achieve this , which rules out a search for a perfect randomizing algorithm on a trial-and-error basis .
99383	This can be seen in a qualitative way by considering the party game in which participants guess how many people would need to be asked their birthdays , on average , to find two with birthdays on the same day .
99384	Many people will answer 365 ( or 366 ! ) .
99385	Some will answer 365/2 or 183 for safety .
99386	Few will guess that a group of twenty-three will , on average , contain two people with birthdays on the same day .
99387	This is followed by experimental proof , to general surprise .
99388	As twenty-three birthdays spread at random over 365 addresses can cause duplication , it is not surprising that no randomizing algorithm can avoid synonyms when packing thousands of records into a set of addresses that is only 10–20 per cent greater than the number of records !
99389	When records are randomly distributed among the available addresses , the probability of 0 , 1 , 2 , … , x records being allocated to any given address that can hold a single record can be calculated as follows :
99390	Let the number of records be defined as n and the total address locations as N. This corresponds with the symbols used in equation ( 6.1 ) .
99391	When records are randomized to N locations the probability of any particular address being generated due to the transformation of a single key is 1/N .
99392	As a result of n records being allocated , the probability of a given location having been allocated x records is given by the terms of the binomial expression : Thus This expression is precise .
99393	However , it has the disadvantage that it is not general , but has to be calculated separately for every n and N.
99394	When n and N are very much larger than 1 , which applies in any normal data file , the Poisson distribution may be used as an approximation to the binomial .
99395	The derivation of this is given in statistics textbooks and practical examples of its application , and an assessment of the closeness of the approximation , are given later in this chapter ( see p. 169 ) .
99396	The advantage of using the Poisson distribution is that p ( x ) now depends on the value of the ratio ( n/N ) .
99397	This represents the packing density of the file , and is much more general than n or N used independently , as all files with the same packing density give the same results irrespective of the value of N and n .

99400	Where a file area contains N addresses we can expect : In theory we could provide just sufficient space in the file for all the records .
99401	This would certainly simplify equation ( 6.3 ) to yield : but it is clear intuitively that we can not completely fill the file , as the last available storage position would on average be half the file area away from the last record 's computed address .
99402	We shall look at ways of choosing a more suitable packing density in more detail later ( see p. 172 ) .
99403	6.4 Methods of randomizing
99404	Whenever an algorithm is used to store a direct file , the implication is that self-indexing is not practical .
99405	This usually means that the keys of the file are too diffuse to store directly , and the key range has to be compressed by using an algorithm .
99406	There are two possibilities : either to exploit the existing key order — if that is possible — or to completely destroy that order , and to allocate keys to addresses as randomly as possible .
99407	Both of these options are examined below .
99408	Order-preserving algorithms
99409	1 Using the low order part of a key
99410	Where a key is a long number , consisting perhaps of ten digits , but we only have 8000 records and hence need only to allocate 10 000 storage positions , we could use the last four digits of the key as a storage address .
99411	This is suspect because keys may always end in 2 , 5 , or some other specific number , or always be divisible by 2 , 5 or some such constant .
99412	There might also be a departmental or other code in the centre of the key , and we might obtain all the records in three areas starting with numbers such as 03 , 05 or 07 if the choice of storage address is unfortunate .
99413	This is analysed further elsewhere .
99414	This technique can , however , give very good results if the low order digits of the key are consecutive integers with few gaps .
99415	2 Using middle or upper order parts of a key
99416	The same considerations dictate against the use of either of these as storage addresses .
99417	It may not be obvious that order exists in the key sequence , yet it may be present and damaging .
99418	3 End folding
99419	A ten-digit key such as 1 234 567 890 may be reduced to ‘ fit ’ 50 000 storage positions by carrying out the steps : This method is fairly effective .
99420	It destroys the original key pattern more completely than operations 1 and 2 above , but retains the ability to separate keys that are part of consecutive runs .
99421	This can lead to results that improve on perfect randomization , but it depends on the key sequence and is not reliable ( see Buchholz and Lum et al. for further details ) .
99422	4 Division by a non-prime
99423	If we divide a large key by an appropriate number — probably dictated by the file storage area — and use the remainder as an address , this will provide a precise method of fitting addresses to available storage .
99424	For example , if we have 98 000 positions of storage in which to store the records , from 50 001 to 148 000 , we could carry out the following calculation : The record address is 124 790 .
99425	This process looks effective , but the last three digits of the key are unchanged by the division .
99426	It turns out that any number divided by 98 000 will give a remainder with the last three digits unchanged , as 98000 itself is divisible by 1000 .
99427	This means that the last part of the original key pattern remains : if this includes a code of , say , 05 then randomization will be incomplete .
99428	For that reason a divisor should be chosen that is not itself divisible by 2 , 3 , 5 , 10 or any of their simple multiples .
99429	In our example the divisor is divisible by 1000 , which leads to three unchanged digits .
99430	Buchholz has shown that non-prime odd numbers can give very good results , but are not reliable unless they have no divisors less than about 19 .
99431	This choice is also discussed by Lum et al .
99432	5 Division by a prime
99433	The logical extension of avoiding multiples of 2 , 3 , 5 , 10 , etc. , is to use a large prime number .
99434	This usually leads to removal of the effect of any repeating pattern such as a 2 , 5 or 0 in the last digit because every digit in the number divided is involved in the division , and so may be altered .
99435	However , sequences of keys differing by one will yield remainders differing by one .
99436	So long as two key sequences do not produce overlapping remainders this can achieve results considerably better than true randomization .
99437	The process is as follows :
99438	a )
99439	Decide on a packing density for the file .
99440	If n records are to be stored in N addresses , this packing density ( α ) will be Let n be 85 000 .
99441	A suitable α might be 85 per cent ( this is discussed in more detail later ) .
99442	In our example this would mean that storage positions would be required for the file .
99443	b )
99444	Select a prime near to 100 000 — say 99 991 — and divide .
99445	The remainders of this division will lie in the range 0–99 990 .
99446	If the storage area does not start at 0 , then a simple addition will convert this figure to the address range required .
99447	c )
99448	The number of synonyms resulting from this process should be compared with those to be expected from perfect randomization ; see p. 166 for methods of doing this .
99449	If the results are similar to or better than those predicted theoretically , the transformation is satisfactory .
99450	If not , a different prime number should be selected and the process repeated .
99451	In selecting a prime number , primes of the form should be avoided , where B is the number base and k a small integer .
99452	This is because the binomial expansion of shows that the remainder will contain superposed m digit groups of the original key .
99453	This tendency remains for small integer values of k , reducing as k increases in size .
99454	Thus primes such as 4999 , 7001 , 79 999 , etc. , are best not used for decimal keys .
99455	A table of prime numbers , selected so that they are not too near to a factor of ten , and close enough in value to allow any packing density to be selected within half of a percent , is given in Appendix 4 .
99456	Decimal keys should be retained in decimal form ; alpha or alphanumeric keys are best handled in binary .
99457	Some prime numbers can usually be found that give a good transformation — in fact it is the high probability that any suitable prime chosen will do so , allied to the ease with which this technique can be used to fit any number of records into precisely the required storage space , that makes this such a convenient method .
99458	However , if a number of primes have failed , it may be sensible to consider complete randomization .
99459	6 Order-preserving algorithms in general
99460	A large number of order-preserving algorithms were examined by Amble and Knuth , showing how they compared for completion of successful and unsuccessful searches for records .
99461	Many of these are suitable only for table searching in main storage , but the principles are of interest to direct file designers .
99462	Ouksel presented a method in which parts of the original key such as area code , factory number and part type can be retained by the use of bit tables .
99463	Garg and Gotlieb have developed a method that is related to interpolation searching , and in which the algorithm is based on an analysis of the key sequence , rather than on a presupposition such as the effectiveness of any particular procedure — say mid-square or division .
99464	Order-preserving algorithms are still being developed , but the success of division shows that order-preserving algorithms are an important resource to the file designer .
99465	Genuinely randomizing algorithms
99466	1 Square the key and select a part
99467	This depends on squaring the whole or part of the key , and taking a number of digits from the centre of the resulting value .
99468	An example might be : This gives a potential range of addresses between 000 000 and 999 999 .
99469	The records can be compressed into some other range such as 250 000 by repetitive subtraction of 250 000 , and the method usually gives very good randomization .
99470	It is often not convenient to square a large integer so a selected part of the key may be squared instead .
99471	This technique is not always as effective as division , but does achieve a nearly random distribution , and so is useful when it is not possible to exploit any existing order in the key sequence .
99472	2 Selecting digits from different parts of the key
99473	Sometimes , rather than selecting a single part of the key , several areas are used .
99474	This may operate as follows : This would normally be expected to produce results rather worse than the mid-square method , but it has proved to be very effective on occasions ( see p. 169 for further discussion ) .
99475	3 Quadratic and quadratic quotient hashing
99476	These two techniques , due to Maurer ( quadratic hashing ) and Bell ( quadratic quotient hashing ) , can be used to eliminate primary and secondary clustering of keys after division .
99477	Primary clustering results from runs of keys , in that they will be allocated to adjacent storage positions after division ; this is dispersed by quadratic hashing , in which the final storage position of the record depends on a function of the remainder from the original division , summed with a function of the square of the remainder .
99478	This does separate members of a run of keys , but it fails to separate two or more records that randomize to a particular storage position .
99479	Bell termed this ‘ secondary clustering ’ and showed that , by using both the quotient and the remainder from the original division , it was possible to eliminate it .
99480	These two techniques are primarily intended for use in table searching in main storage , and are only incidentally usable for direct files ; it is worth noting that they are intended to eliminate the order-preserving properties of division , while using division as a convenient randomizing algorithm .
99481	Examples of randomizing algorithms in practice
99482	Although small files can not be used to analyse the way in which randomization techniques perform , they are useful to demonstrate the essential features of these techniques .
99483	The ways in which division , mid-square and end-folding operate are illustrated below .
99484	1 Division
99485	Assume that a ‘ mini-file ’ of seventeen records is to be stored as a direct file , and that the file is to be 85 per cent packed .
99486	The file will therefore require twenty storage positions .
99487	Seventeen random numbers in the range 000 to 200 ( representing the record keys ) can be selected by choosing the first numbers within the required range occurring in a random number table .
99488	They are in the following order : 059 , 035 , 078 , 136 , 171 , 148 , 005 , 135 , 010 , 196 , 057 , 187 , 110 , 100 , 030 , 127 , 197 .
99489	These numbers are divided by 19 , to give remainders in the range 0 to 18 .
99490	This leaves the twentieth position of the storage area as an ‘ overflow ’ , since no record will randomize to it .
99491	In effect , the key range 000–200 is cut into 19 digit sections , and the remainders that result from the division in each section are superposed on each other to provide the record addresses .
99492	The records in the same section can not randomize to the same address , so that synonyms arise by records in different sections having the same remainder .
99493	The result of this operation , for the keys given above , is shown in Fig. 6.5(a) .
99494	As a result of dividing by 19 there will be six synonyms — 00 , 02 , 02 , 05 , 15 and 16 .
99495	This is or 32.4 per cent of the total , and compares with an ‘ expected ’ value of 32.63 per cent .
99496	This is sheer chance , but suggests a good average result from the use of the algorithm !
99497	This set of keys is intended to be random and so has no order to preserve .
99498	If a key includes fields to indicate district , stock classification or the like , runs of keys will occur in the key sequence .
99499	Division will avoid keys in the same run clashing , and causing synonyms .
99500	Seventeen records are to be stored as an 85 per cent packed direct file .
99501	Consider the key set : The remainders after the division by 19 are shown in Fig. 6.5(b) .
99502	The very good performance of division reported in some cases ( Lum , Yuen and Dodd , Severance and Duhne ) , and relatively poor performance in others ( Kaimann ) , is likely to have been the result of few or many clashes of this kind .
99503	Because there are fewer runs of keys than separate keys , the results of division are likely to be more variable than those of genuine randomization .
99504	However , division has a fundamental advantage , which is the reason for its good performance : no two records in any single section into which the key sequence is ‘ cut ’ by division can interfere with any other in the same section , because no two different numbers can have both the same quotient and the same remainder .
99505	Effectively , this means that if the file has been ‘ cut ’ into m sections , the effective packing density of the file — from the point of view of records colliding and causing synonyms — is :
99506	2 Mid-square
99507	In this case we square the whole key and take a centre part of it to allocate the records to buckets .
99508	In order to fit the result of selecting two decimal digits ( a maximum value of 99 ) into a range of twenty storage positions , 20 is subtracted repetitively from the two digits until the result is less than 20 .
99509	This process gives eight synonyms ( 00 , 02 , 02 , 04 , 08 , 10 , 10 , 10 ) .
99510	It is rather unexpected that most of the values obtained are even .
99511	This is not a general result , and shows that this algorithm , which gives or 47 per cent of synonyms , does not suit this key set .
99512	The reader might like to check that , if the second and third digits are used instead of the third and fourth , there will be seven synonyms instead of eight ( 00 , 01 , 01 , 04 , 09 , 12 , 12 ) .
99513	However , this is still not a good result .
99514	Applying the same algorithm to the other key set , the results are shown at the top of the next page .
99515	This gives a reasonable result in terms of synonyms : six out of seventeen , or 35 per cent .
99516	The reader may care to confirm that , if the third and fourth digits are selected instead , there will be eight synonyms .
99517	3 End-folding
99518	Usually we would be satisfied with the results of one or other of the first two techniques .
99519	Out of interest , we will try one other method on these key sets — end-folding .
99520	This involves ‘ folding ’ one part of the key under the rest and adding .
99521	If the value we get is more than 19 , we will subtract 20 repetitively until it is brought into the range 0 to 19 .
99522	For example : Interestingly , this creates only four synonyms , and is thus a very effective algorithm .
99523	With the five runs of keys , the resulting addresses are :
99524	Here , the number of synonyms is three .
99525	In general , end-folding does not achieve such good results , but this illustrates how — with a very small ‘ file ’ and key size — results can be variable .
99526	In this case , due to the form of key and the end-folding digits chosen , end-folding is acting very similarly to an order-preserving algorithm .
99527	6.5 Testing for successful randomization
99528	After an algorithm has been selected , it is wise to ensure that it will be successful before using it in a program .
99529	A reasonable guide will be if it produces results near to or better than those predicted by equation ( 6.3 ) .
99530	The algorithm and the file keys have to be analysed , which can be done either by writing an analysis program and inputting the keys , transforming them into addresses and recording the numbers of synonyms , or by using a standard analysis program .
99531	This is obtainable from manufacturers or from many bureaux , and will give numbers of synonyms , their distribution and comparisons with the ‘ ideal ’ randomized distribution .
99532	Kaimann has carried out a series of randomizing experiments , based on a file of 48 950 records .
99533	These were randomized to 100 000 storage positions .
99534	We shall examine the results of his experiments and compare them with the results that we would expect if the records were perfectly randomized .
99535	In order to decide this we shall calculate the expected probability that an address will contain no record , one record only , one synonym ( two records allocated to one address ) , two synonyms and so on .
99536	It was stated earlier that the Poisson distribution was a satisfactory approximation to the binomial in a case such as this ; to test this assertion both equation ( 6.2 ) and equation ( 6.3 ) have been used to calculate the expected ‘ perfectly randomized ’ results .

99544	Using equations ( 6.9 ) and ( 6. 10 ) the required Poisson values can be calculated very rapidly ; they are particularly suited to a pocket calculator , as the starting value can be calculated and then modified by multiplying the contents of the calculator by the packing density and dividing by the next value of ‘ x ’ : 1 when the calculator holds p(0) , 2 when it holds p(1) and so on .
99545	The values obtained for binary and Poisson probabilities are shown in Table 6.1 for the case where a file of 48 950 records is randomized to 100 000 storage positions .
99546	It is clear from the table that the correspondence between binomial and Poisson values is very close .
99547	For a file of this size , no value has been altered materially due to the simplification of using Poisson values .
99548	In any real case a variation of several hundred from the predicted value would be expected due to chance alone , while predictions based on the two methods do not differ by as much as one record in any file examined by the author .
99549	For this reason the simpler and more general Poisson calculations are used from now on in this book .
99550	One of the most comprehensive studies of the results of randomization trials that has been reported was due to Kaimann .
99551	The values tabulated here give us a measure of comparison for Kaimann 's experimental results .

99553	1

99559	4

99561	5

99565	Table 6.2 shows the number of addresses that have been allocated the stated number of records per address ( up to seven ) , and the percentage of the total number of records in the file that was successfully allocated by each of the six algorithms used by Kaimann .
99566	The very wide differences between the results achieved by different randomization techniques are shown in Table 6.2 and Fig. 6.7 .
99567	However , none of the results given here indicate randomization that is fully successful .
99568	It is interesting that a fairly ad-hoc method of transformation ( Test 5 ) is in most respects more successful than division by a prime number .
99569	This suggests that by chance some underlying order in the key sequence has affected randomization .
99570	However , the number of long synonym chains is less after division by a prime than by this digit selection .
99571	A further search for a successful algorithm — probably for a more suitable prime — is indicated in a case like this .
99572	As the key range , nine digits , is potentially 10 000 times the address range , 100 000 , even division can only be expected to equal or very marginally improve on perfect randomization .
99573	6.6 Minimizing the effect of synonyms
99574	Now that the inevitability of synonyms occurring has been made clear , we must consider how to deal with them .
99575	This can best be described in a series of steps :
99576	1
99577	Ensure that the number of synonyms is at a minimum .
99578	This can be achieved by the selection of a suitable bucket size , packing density , randomizing algorithm and record-loading technique .
99579	2
99580	Use an efficient method of storing and retrieving the synonyms generated .
99581	3
99582	Arrange that the most frequently referenced records are in the home positions .
99583	4
99584	Reorganize the file at intervals — unless a randomization technique that allocates space as it is required has been used .
99585	Each of these measures is examined in detail below .
99586	Minimizing the number of synonyms
99587	Packing density and bucket size
99588	If we decide to store each record in a storage position able to hold only one record , even a perfectly random distribution will give a high proportion of synonyms .
99589	Table 6.3 has been calculated using equation ( 6.6 . ) .
99590	The table is built up by calculating p(0) , and hence the probability that any given address would not have a home record allocated to it .
99591	Multiplying this by 100 and subtracting the result from 100 per cent , we obtain the percentage of addresses that will contain home records .
99592	This is shown in the second row .
99593	Subtraction of this figure from the total of all the records as a percentage of the addresses , i.e. from the packing density , gives the number of synonyms as a percentage of the addresses .
99594	This figure is expressed as a percentage of the records in the bottom row .
99595	For 30 per cent packing the calculation is as follows :
99596	A glance at the percentages of synonyms shows that even when the file is only 20 per cent packed , almost 10 per cent of the file will be stored as synonyms .
99597	When we wish to retrieve a synonym , the algorithm will give an ‘ incorrect ’ address .
99598	Whatever method of storing synonyms is used , time will be lost as a result .
99599	Some way must be found to reduce the number of synonyms , in order to increase the efficiency of direct retrieval .
99600	If buckets large enough to hold several records are used , we can expect that these buckets will be more evenly filled than individual records fill single addresses ; this can be examined using the Poisson distribution .
99601	Equation ( 6.3 ) for randomization to individual addresses is : Let the number of buckets be B ; then during a single address calculation each bucket location has a probability of being generated of ( 1/B ) , and a probability ( 1 — 1/B ) that it will not be generated .
99602	Assuming the number of buckets is large , the Poisson distribution can once more be used as an approximation to the binomial distribution .
99603	Then : Note that the value ( n/B ) will now usually exceed unity , and that the packing density of the file will depend on how many records can be stored in each bucket .
99604	To calculate p(0) substitute ( n/B ) for ( n/N ) in equation ( 6.8 ) : and also , modifying equation ( 6.9 ) :
99605	The percentage of records that will be stored as synonyms , for any given bucket size and packing density , can be derived as follows ( the full explanation of the calculations is given in reference 15 ) :
99606	Let the packing density be p and the number of records per bucket be r .
99607	The percentage of synonyms to be expected for any given case , assuming that record allocation to addresses is entirely random and that synonyms are only stored after all home records , is as follows :
99608	Define the total file storage capacity as 1 .
99609	The sum of the probabilities for space to which records have not been allocated , P EMPTY , is : The rest of the total file area must therefore hold home records , i.e. ( Note : The proportion of the file area that contains home records is calculated indirectly rather than directly , because the sum of home record probabilities is made up of an infinite series , while that of the empty positions is finite , as is clear from equation ( 6.13 ) . )
99610	As the packing density is α , a proportion α of the total file area will hold records when the loading process is complete .
99611	The probability of a record becoming a synonym is therefore given by subtracting the proportion of the file area occupied by home records from the total proportion of the file area taken up by the file , that is α .
99612	The user will normally wish to express this as a percentage of the records loaded , which is : The value of P SYNONYMS can be calculated using an iterative procedure by combining the expressions given in equations ( 6. 13 ) and ( 6.15 ) :
99613	This expression can be summed iteratively , as the first term within the brace has the value .
99614	Let this be .
99615	Then each successive term is obtained by using the relationship :
99616	Table 6.4 shows the expected percentage of overflow records when records are randomized to buckets containing from one to 600 records .
99617	The table shows figures down to 0.01 per cent of synonyms , and Fig. 6.7 is useful for extrapolation between values , and understanding the overall relationship between bucket size and packing density .
99618	From the table and figure , it is clear that far fewer records will be displaced if we randomize to a multi-record bucket rather than to an individual record position .
99619	For example , with a file that is only 50 per cent packed , we must expect 21.31 per cent of the records not to be stored in their home record positions if we randomize to a specific address .
99620	Using buckets capable of holding only two records will improve this figure to 10.36 per cent .
99621	If we use buckets of eight records at a time , less than 1 per cent of the records will be synonyms , and this is reduced to 0 .
99622	1 per cent for buckets of fifteen records .
99623	Hence it is clear that , if records are randomized to individual storage positions or to small buckets , many records will become synonyms .
99624	Unless the records are stored singly there is no corresponding improvement in speed of finding the desired record , because the access comb will reach the track at a point decided by chance , and there will be an average delay of at least half a revolution before the start of the record is reached .
99625	The advantage of single records is that they can be stored in CKD format — with separate keys — and the track can be scanned for a particular record without having to read unwanted records into main storage .
99626	Multiple record buckets can not be handled in this way , as groups of records that randomize to the same bucket do not generally have anything else in common , so that the whole bucket has to be searched to see if the desired record is in it .
99627	So , although there is clearly an argument for using buckets that are as large as possible , over-large buckets will mean that an extended search through the bucket will be required to locate the desired record .
99628	Since there are advantages both in storing records singly and in using large buckets , one solution is to randomize to a track but to store records singly in CKD format .
99629	This is particularly useful when manufacturers ' software is available ( as for example SEARCH ON KEY for IBM computers ) to carry out the search automatically .
99630	Although a number of writers suggest that a full-track bucket is always too large , they are talking of a bucket that has to be transferred as a whole into and out of main storage .
99631	The solution suggested above allows the very low synonym levels of a multi-record bucket — in this case a track — to be combined with the CKD format of individually stored records , which makes it possible to search the whole track and retrieve only the desired record .
99632	As very few records will not be on their home tracks , this procedure is extremely efficient .
99633	Fig. 6.8 shows how increased bucket size delays the onset of synonym occurrence in a well randomized file .
99634	The curves show divergence from the relationship ( for n records stored individually ) , ( for records stored in buckets with a capacity of ten records ) , and ( for buckets with a fifty-record capacity ) .
99635	They thus show the number of synonyms created , assuming a perfect randomizing algorithm , for various packing factors .
99636	Randomizing to buckets with a capacity of ten records markedly decreases the number of synonyms , and there is a further decrease if buckets with a capacity of fifty records are used .
99637	Appendix 5 provides extended synonym tables and curves for more precise work in this field .
99638	In general , the file designer will choose a bucket size and packing density that reduce the percentage of synonyms to an acceptable level , bearing in mind the increased retrieval times large bucket size can cause .
99639	As is made clear below , bucket size may also affect the algorithm chosen .
99640	Randomizing algorithm
99641	In choosing an algorithm , the file designer will aim to minimize the number of synonyms .
99642	The key type and format should be assessed , to decide on the occurrence and frequency of runs of keys .
99643	The range of key values , divided by the number of addresses to be generated ( the calculation is shown on page 161 ) , will indicate the potential improvement , over and above the synonym percentages predicted by the Poisson distribution , that can be aimed for .
99644	practical trials will indicate the success of any algorithms the designer selects , and this step in file design should never be omitted .
99645	For general guidance on choice of algorithm , the author has compared the number of accesses observed by Lum et al. in practical trials with the theoretically predicted number , for buckets holding five , ten , twenty and fifty records .
99646	The results of this comparison are shown in Fig. 6.9 .
99647	As can be seen from the figure , for buckets holding five records division is not as effective as mid-square ( which closely approximates the ‘ theoretical ’ figures ) for packing densities above 0.7 .
99648	For buckets holding ten records , division is superior up to a packing density of about 0.85 , while for larger bucket sizes division is more efficient at all packing densities .
99649	In general , the success of a randomizing method is partly dependent on the technique used to store synonyms , and this will be discussed further in a later section of the chapter ( see p. 184 ) .
99650	However , it is fair to say that division is usually the most efficient technique if synonyms are to be handled by chaining or tagging , but that if they are to be stored using the consecutive spill technique , bucket size and packing density should also be considered before a decision on randomizing method is made .
99651	Before leaving randomizing algorithms , it should be made clear that the treatment of them here is based on the assumption that the file size , once created , can only be altered when the file is reorganized .
99652	Records can be added of course , but this will increase the packing density .
99653	There is a great deal of interest at present in developing hashing algorithms for files that may vary in size .
99654	This is usually termed dynamic hashing ; a particularly useful review of these techniques is given by Sachs-Davies et al. , describing both extendible hashing , in which a set of buckets is referenced via a directory , and linear hashing , which is genuinely a direct technique in that there is no directory .
99655	Both of these methods suffer from oscillations in performance associated with their mode of action , and neither performs as well as ‘ static ’ randomization methods .
99656	A form of extendible hashing that does not suffer from oscillations and is claimed to outperform most indexing methods , was reported by Lomet He named the method bounded index exponential hashing ; it is not strictly a direct technique , and suffers from the drawback that the file packing density is generally low , but offers many advantages for files which can grow at a rate that can not be accommodated in a static system .
99657	Designers looking for examples of how to code randomizing algorithms should consult Snader , who gives examples of various functions coded in Fortran , Basic and Pascal ; Morris , who gives Fortran code both for chaining and hashing ; and Johnson and Cooper , who provide comprehensive coded examples in COBOL .
99658	File loading
99659	When a direct file is loaded for the first time , we may have little or no information about the individual records that make it up .
99660	However , it is still possible to keep the number of synonyms to a minimum .
99661	Records will be read into primary storage , their keys will be transformed by the algorithm being used , and if the address the algorithm produces is free they will be stored in that address on the direct access device .
99662	When a record turns out to be a synonym , there are two alternatives : these are to store the synonym at once , in which case the process is called a one-pass load , or to load it in two passes , which is called a two-pass load .
99663	A one-pass load will result in the creation of unnecessary synonyms , as shown in Fig. 6. 10 .
99664	To avoid the creation of extra synonyms , the file has to be loaded in two passes .
99665	On the first pass , all the home records are loaded , but synonyms are not .
99666	On the second pass , all the synonyms are loaded .
99667	This process maximizes the number of home records in the file , and so maximizes the number of records that can be retrieved without further searching .
99668	All the calculations carried out so far have assumed that it is possible to allocate any number of records to a given address .
99669	This is implied in the calculations , as no allowance has been made to store the synonyms that arise in other free addresses .
99670	Instead , the number of synonyms has been calculated , but they have then been ignored by the mathematics , and so have not interfered with the ‘ storage ’ of other records .
99671	This is precisely the process that occurs during a two-pass load , as the synonyms are stored on the second pass .
99672	Although the calculations available in the literature have very largely assumed that direct files are loaded using two passes , there are a number of cases in which a one-pass load occurs in practice .
99673	These are :
99674	1
99675	If a simple one-pass load is used for the file .
99676	2
99677	Whenever records are added to an existing file , as both home and synonym records from the original load have already been stored ; in this case the probability of an addition that is a potential home record being prevented from taking up its home position by a synonym that was loaded earlier is high .
99678	3
99679	In databases that offer the CALC option — as each record is loaded when it is added to the database , whether it is a home or synonym .
99680	To estimate the number of synonyms that occur during creation of a direct file using a one-pass load , let us examine the result of storing n records at random in N addresses , on the assumption that each record has to be stored at once and each address can hold only one record .
99681	The first record will be stored in its calculated address .
99682	The second record has a probability of 1/N of becoming a synonym .
99683	The nth record has a probability ( n — 1 ) /N of becoming a synonym .
99684	Summing this series of probabilities , and dividing by the number of records loaded , we obtain :
99685	For files of more than a few hundred records , ½N can be ignored .
99686	Thus the proportion of records stored as synonyms will be roughly equivalent to half the packing density in a file created using a single-pass load , and with single record buckets .
99687	The author has developed an iterative method of calculating the synonym percentages that would be expected as a result of loading buckets of various capacities to a range of packing densities .
99688	These results have been confirmed using simulation techniques , and are given in Table 6.5 ; they should be compared with Table 6.4 .
99689	The divergence between the two loading techniques depends on packing density , and for single record buckets it is almost 10 per cent — one record in ten — for an 85 per cent packed file .
99690	Although the difference is less marked for multiple record buckets , it is still significant .
99691	To provide quick reference for the file designer the data in Table 6.5 has been plotted in Fig. 6.11 .
99692	As the penalty that a one-pass load imposes in terms of extra synonyms is very quickly understood when it is shown visually , Fig. 6.12 compares the results of one-pass and two-pass loads for a number of bucket sizes .
99693	Storing and retrieving synonyms
99694	When a record can not be placed in its home position , it must be stored at an address that can be located quickly .
99695	There are three widely used methods of doing this and we shall look at each in turn , assessing their advantages and drawbacks .
99696	1 Consecutive spill ( also called progressive overflow )
99697	The simplest method of storage is to place a synonym in the first vacant record position following its home address .
99698	( This applies in just the same way if records are being randomized to multiple records buckets .
99699	The record is stored in the first bucket with available space following the original home bucket . )
99700	This method of storage , in which there is no link or pointer to the synonym from its home bucket , is called consecutive spill or progressive overflow .
99701	Record retrieval takes place as follows .
99702	1
99703	Seek the home address .
99704	2
99705	Check whether the records or records in the home address have the required key .
99706	3
99707	If not , search the rest of the track .
99708	If the record is not found on the track , search the rest of the cylinder .
99709	Note that , if the key that has been requested is not present on the file , the unsuccessful search length is potentially limited only by the size of the file .
99710	Very few records will not find a place anywhere on the cylinder .
99711	Take for example a file that is 90 per cent packed , and can hold 250 records per cylinder .
99712	In this case the cylinder can be treated as a very large bucket .
99713	From Table 6.4 , 99.86 per cent of records will be stored in their home cylinder and only 0.14 per cent will overflow on to another cylinder .
99714	As the packing density is usually lower than this and the number of records per cylinder greater , overflow from a cylinder is not usually a problem .
99715	It is shown in Appendix 7 that , for a cylinder holding one hundred records and with other conditions as given above , the average retrieval time for all the records in the file will be 0.78R , where R is the rotation time of the device .
99716	This compares with 0.5R for a self-indexing file .
99717	A potential drawback of consecutive spill is that , while this method of handling synonyms can be effective in some circumstances to retrieve records that are held in a file , it is not a good method of dealing with records that are not in the file .
99718	As there is no way of knowing how many synonyms exist for any given home address , an unsuccessful search might require half the file to be scanned on average .
99719	The usual way to limit this search commitment is to place a synonym in any free position on its home cylinder , and in an independent area if no free space can be found in the cylinder .
99720	A second method is to note the longest search required to find a free storage position when synonyms are stored , and to limit searches to this length during retrieval .
99721	2 Chaining
99722	The second method generally available for synonym handling is to chain together all the records that randomize to the same address .
99723	A chain takes the form shown in Fig. 6. 13 .
99724	The home record storage area holds the address of the first synonym .
99725	This holds the address of the second synonym , and so on .
99726	A null link indicates the end of the chain .
99727	If it is found that the home record is not the one required , the link address is used .
99728	This points to the second record that randomized to the home address .
99729	The chain is followed until the desired record is located or the end of the chain is reached .
99730	It eliminates the need to search the file sequentially .
99731	The calculations involved in assessing the effect of chaining synonyms are complicated .
99732	For that reason they are given in detail in Appendix 6 , The Effect of Synonym Storage Techniques on Search Times .
99733	Only the conclusions are discussed here .
99734	Records randomized to individual record positions , with 90 per cent packing and ten record positions per track , give the following figures :
99735	This shows that about one record in every 500 ( 0.2 per cent ) will be part of a chain of six records .
99736	Of these , one-sixth ( 0.03 per cent ) will be home records and an equal number will be first , second , third , fourth and fifth synonyms .
99737	At this packing density the average search time for a given record is 0.732R , where R is the device rotation time .
99738	When records are randomized to larger buckets — in this case we will examine ten record buckets — this will cause fairly long chains .
99739	Fig. 6.14 shows the pattern of record allocation for 80 per cent and 90 per cent packing .
99740	Buckets can hold ten records only , and any further records ‘ allocated ’ to a bucket will become part of a synonym chain .
99741	Fig. 6.14 shows that quite long chains must be expected .
99742	For 90 per cent packing , just more than one bucket in every 200 ( 0.53 per cent ) will have a chain of eight or more synonyms .
99743	A more detailed analysis shows the following :
99744	As 91.4 per cent of records will be located in their home buckets , the advantage of having relatively few synonyms outweighs the disadvantage of there being some long chains .
99745	The average search time for 90 per cent packed records stored in ten record buckets is 0.654R .
99746	This figure is a great deal better than that for the consecutive spill method of handling overflows , and even chained records randomized to individual addresses show an advantage over consecutive spill .
99747	A price has to be paid , however .
99748	To provide the links , an extra field has to be added to the home bucket or home record , and an extra field to each synonym .
99749	This effectively reduces the file packing , and may also cause fixed lengths to become variable in length .
99750	The last point could be put right , wasting more space , by adding a potential link field to every record .
99751	This might then be used when necessary , but be left empty in other cases .
99752	If the problem of providing space for link fields can be suitably handled , this method can offer considerable savings .
99753	3 Tagging
99754	One difficulty when processing linked records is that , if a record in the centre of a chain is inadvertently overwritten , the end of the chain is ‘ lost ’ .
99755	This can occur when adding records to the file .
99756	The third method of handling synonyms avoids this .
99757	It is called tagging .
99758	The technique used is to tag each synonym individually from the home address .
99759	Each tag will have to hold at least the information : This will mean that the few home addresses or home buckets which have large numbers of synonyms will have to allocate a lot of space for these tags .
99760	An example of the situation where there are five synonyms for a home record is shown in Fig. 6.15 .
99761	The tag system uses a little less space than the chaining system , as there is no need for a terminal ‘ link ’ field at the end of the chain .
99762	However , all the extra space is required in the home records .
99763	This can make planning and file creation difficult .
99764	If these problems can be overcome , it offers two advantages that chained overflow record handling does not .
99765	Firstly , the file organization is more robust , as the accidental overwriting of a record only affects that record itself and not other members of a chain .
99766	Secondly , it is never necessary to carry out more than two searches to locate a record .
99767	These are :
99768	1 .
99769	Search home record — if record not found pick up address from tag ;
99770	2 .
99771	Search the address shown in the tag .
99772	Using the example of a 90 per cent packed file with single-track buckets that can hold ten records : from Table 6.4 , 91.4 per cent of records are located on their home tracks .
99773	Thus 8.6 per cent of records will require a full revolution of the home track , then a pick-up of the address required from a tag , then an average of R/2 while the record is located .
99774	The overall time required for the search will be :
99775	If the records are stored on a 25-track cylinder , Table 6.4 indicates that 0.14 per cent of records will overflow from the cylinder , i.e. will not be held in a 250-record bucket .
99776	Although the tags will point to the required record addresses directly , accessing or retrieving these synonyms requires a head movement of at least one cylinder .
99777	Assume that the time to move from one cylinder to the next is the same as the rotation time of the device , which applies for some disk devices .
99778	This will mean an increase in the average access time of 0.0014R .
99779	Thus the total average access time is :
99780	Comparing the techniques in practice
99781	It might appear that chaining or tagging would always be preferable to the simpler system of storing records in the next available position .
99782	In practice they do not always turn out so much better , for a number of reasons .
99783	These include the following :
99784	1
99785	When records are stored in the next available position ( i.e. using consecutive spill ) , no extra space is required for chain or tag fields .
99786	2
99787	Manufacturers ' software is usually available for a SEARCH ON KEY operation throughout a whole cylinder .
99788	The search for a required record can start on the home track and continue until the record is located .
99789	There need be no holdup due to consecutive spill storage , however short .
99790	By comparison , following a chain or tag involves reading the link field , finding the key in it , picking up the address and searching for it .
99791	This will be carried out at primary storage speeds , but will still take time , often due to lost device revolutions .
99792	A home track and a track holding synonyms will appear as shown in Fig. 6. 16 .
99793	Examining chained records first , tracks with spare space for the storage of synonyms often have room for a number of records , as is clear from Fig. 6. 14 .
99794	Tracks that have overflowed during the original file load will not have any synonyms from other tracks present on them , which explains the likely track formats shown in Fig. 6.16 .
99795	In some cases members of the chain may directly follow each other on a track holding synonyms .
99796	This could cause the loss of a whole revolution for each member of the chain , because the processing of the link field might take long enough to miss the start of the next record .
99797	This would happen as shown in Fig. 6.17 .
99798	The tagged records case is straightforward .
99799	The tag is picked up at the end of a track and the synonym will also , on average , be at or near the end of a track , not in the middle .
99800	For this reason the time required to pick up the tagged record may be rather more than R/2 .
99801	This depends on the manufacturers ' software .
99802	Sometimes the start of a track has to be sensed before processing of the data stored on it can begin .
99803	This will lead to delays .
99804	In some systems , tag or chain link fields are stored at the start of a track , which will reduce delays caused for this reason .
99805	Lum et al. investigated the performance of a number of large files , and the author has analysed their results further .
99806	Fig. 6.18 shows a plot of Lum et al. 's figures on the basis of average accesses per retrieval ; it appears from the curves that consecutive spill is only useful for larger bucket sizes , but the figures are misleading , as the chained overflow was to a separate file area , necessitating head movement .
99807	Table 6.6 shows the very different results obtained when the actual time required for each retrieval , including head movements , is used to calculate break-even points , rather than average accesses per retrieval .
99808	Although most of the work reported in the literature has examined chaining to a separate overflow area , this is not the most effective way of using chaining .
99809	If records are stored in the next available position in the prime data area — the consecutive spill method — but a link field is provided from the home record or from the last synonym , this avoids unnecessary head movements and cuts down the search time required for the consecutive spill techniques .
99810	Table 6.7 compares the additional times added to an average record seek due to consecutive spill ( for files using mid-square and division randomizing techniques ) , chained overflow in a separate area and chained overflow in the prime data area .
99811	The results tabulated here show that , for low packing densities , the most effective technique is generally chained overflow .
99812	At higher packing densities a separate overflow area may be useful for small bucket sizes , while chained overflow in the prime data area remains best for large bucket sizes .
99813	Choosing an overflow technique
99814	Tagging is superior to chaining whenever it is feasible ( see Appendix 6 for an analysis ) .
99815	Very large numbers of synonyms for even a few home addresses can make it impractical , however .
99816	The distribution of records produced by a given algorithm should be checked to see that this will not occur .
99817	If it is unavoidable , chaining should be employed ( assuming , of course , that the packing density is too high , and bucket size too small , to make consecutive spill attractive ) .
99818	In general , consecutive spill should be considered for low packing densities and/or very large bucket sizes .
99819	In the intermediate range of these factors , chaining or tagging records stored in the prime file area is the most efficient solution , while at packing densities in excess of unity a separate overflow area will be required .
99820	Although many writers recommend it , it is seldom worth using such a separate overflow area when the packing density is below unity .
99821	The packing density referred to here is measured in terms of the total number of records , both in the prime and overflow areas , divided by the prime data storage capacity only .
99822	Reducing the effect of synonyms on access times
99823	The analysis of the last section has shown that synonyms will slow up direct access to records on average .
99824	The average figure means little in this case , however .
99825	Access to home records only requires a single seek and search , just as in self-indexing files .
99826	This is increased for any synonym by at least half a revolution of the device .
99827	There are at least as many home records as synonyms in all circumstances ( Table 6.5 shows that , even with 100 per cent packing and randomizing to individual record positions , 50 per cent of records are home records ; with a two-pass load 63 per cent are home records ) .
99828	If all records are accessed equally frequently , the effect of any synonyms will be directly proportional to the figures in Table 6.4 .
99829	However , this is a very unusual state of affairs .
99830	Normally , some records are accessed more frequently than others , and this tendency can be used to decrease average access time .
99831	The potential improvement in performance and ways of achieving that improvement after a two-pass load are discussed below .
99832	Patterns of record access
99833	A rule-of-thumb often used for updating is that ‘ 20 per cent of the records give rise to 80 per cent of the transactions ’ .
99834	It is certainly true that , in most applications , some records are processed far more frequently than others , and a number of commonly occurring distributions of update frequency are examined below .
99835	1
99836	The 80/20 arrangement .
99837	Assume that 20 per cent of the records are equally frequently accessed and give rise to 80 per cent of the total transactions .
99838	The remaining 80 per cent of the records are also equal in update frequency , but account in total for only 20 per cent of transactions .
99839	2
99840	A smooth curve of accesses in which some records are updated more regularly than others .
99841	The case shown in Fig. 6.20 is taken as an example of a very frequently met distribution ( it is probable that the original 80/20 rule-of-thumb is based on a similar curve ) .
99842	3
99843	A random distribution .
99844	In this case a few records are updated very frequently , a few very seldom , and most records are updated more or less an average amount ; the distribution is shown in Fig. 6.21 .
99845	This is not meant to be a comprehensive list of possible situations ; the intention is to show how to tackle any distribution that occurs in practice .
99846	A limitation must be mentioned here .
99847	It is not possible to improve on equal access synonym handling in two cases .
99848	The first is when all records are equally likely to be accessed , i.e. there is no difference in access frequency to exploit .
99849	The second is when there is no permanent pattern .
99850	If a record that is updated or accessed frequently in one time period is likely not to be referenced at all in the next , any analysis breaks down and the equal access assumption is the best guide for design decisions .
99851	Usually there will be some random variation of this sort superposed on a relatively constant overall pattern .
99852	In examining the effect of the patterns defined above , random influences will be ignored .
99853	Each of the three cases will be examined for 90 per cent packed files , randomized to individual record positions and to a bucket that can hold ten records .
99854	1 The 80/20 case When 20 per cent of the records generate 80 per cent of the accesses to a file , and the file is loaded in a random order , the percentage of accesses to synonyms will be the same as the percentage of synonyms ; if the file is 90 per cent packed and randomized to individual record storage positions , accesses to synonyms will be 34.063 per cent of all accesses .
99855	If the 20 per cent of records that are most accessed are loaded first , the situation is quite different .
99856	As the file will be 90 per cent packed when it is fully loaded , 20 per cent of the records will occupy 18 per cent of the available storage addresses .
99857	This ‘ mini ’ file will have 8.483 per cent of synonyms , so that the 80 per cent of accesses made to these records will be split in the proportion of 91.517 home accesses to 8.483 synonym accesses .
99858	When the whole file has been loaded , it will contain 34.063 per cent of synonyms .
99859	However , as the first fifth of the file ( 20 per cent ) only contained 8.483 per cent of synonyms , the four-fifths of the file loaded later must have a higher average number of synonyms than 34.063 to bring the overall average to that figure .
99860	Let that higher number be y .
99861	Then : Hence , the four fifths of the file loaded later contains 40.458 per cent of synonyms , and 59.542 per cent of home records ; the 20 per cent of all accesses to the file that are to these records will therefore be split in this proportion .
99862	The total accesses to home and synonym records will thus be as follows :
99863	By loading in access frequency order , the accesses to synonym records — and these are the records that slow up the average retrieval times of the file — have been cut from 34.063 per cent to 14.878 per cent .
99864	This reduces the effect of the synonyms to a figure that could have been achieved by choosing an initial packing density of just over 33 per cent for the file — but this file is 90 per cent packed .
99865	Fig. 6. 19 shows the improvement that can be achieved in 80/20 type files — those in which 80 per cent of the accesses are to 20 per cent of the records — for buckets holding one , two , three and four records over a wide range of packing densities , and Table 6.8 provides figures for a number of bucket sizes and packing densities .
99866	These curves and figures apply only to the 80/20 case .
99867	A general expression to assess the potential improvement that access frequency loading can provide for any case in which A per cent of records account for B per cent of accesses is derived below .
99868	It should be made clear both that ( A + B ) does not need to add up to 100 — it is an unfortunate chance that the 80/20 or 90/10 ‘ rules ’ are so well known — and that access frequency loading will only be of benefit when A is less than B. If A were greater than B , meaning that the less active records were loaded first , file access times would be poorer than those of randomly loaded files !

99872	α is used for packing density .

99874	S is used for synonym per cent .
99875	Suffices of S are equations that will be evaluated in any given case to give a packing density , followed by r to indicate bucket size , so that the correct synonym percentage can be calculated or looked up .
