99885	Many situations can not be handled on the basis of ‘ A per cent of records give rise to B per cent of accesses ’ .
99886	For this reason two other common situations are analysed here .
99887	2 A smooth access curve Fig. 6.20 shows a histogram of records divided into nine groups of equal numbers .
99888	The most active group accounts for 43 per cent of accesses , the least active for 1 per cent .
99889	It is no longer enough to divide the records into two groups , and the analysis has been carried out on the nine separate groups of records responsible for 10 per cent , 20 per cent , 30 per cent … , 90 per cent packing .
99890	As the calculations required in this case are complex , they have been set out in Appendix 8 .
99891	The results show that a 90 per cent packed file of this type loaded in access frequency order into single record buckets will achieve a reduction from 34.06 down to 16.63 per cent references to synonyms .
99892	If instead the file is loaded into ten-record buckets , the reduction is from 8.59 per cent down to 1.36 per cent .
99893	3 A random distribution If the records are very variable in their number of accesses , but this variation is distributed about a mean value , a curve such as that in Fig. 6.21 occurs .
99894	There is an average number of accesses during a specified period of about sixty-five .
99895	However , a small group of records have been accessed over 120 times , and another small group less than ten times .
99896	To analyse this , the frequency curve in Fig. 6.22 ( case 3 ) is constructed relating the percentage of accesses to the file to the percentage of records loaded at any cumulative percentage of records loaded , using the methods shown in Appendix 8 .
99897	From the case 3 curve we can decide on the percentage of accesses corresponding to the 10–90 per cent packing points , i.e. 11.1 per cent , 22.2 per cent , … of records .
99898	This can be used to calculate the required information ; it turns out that the improvements that can be achieved by access frequency loading are to reduce accesses to synonyms from 34.06 per cent to 28.4 per cent for single — record buckets , and from 8.59 per cent to 4.90 per cent for ten-record buckets .
99899	Assessment of possible improvement
99900	The cumulative frequency curves for all three cases analysed earlier are shown in Fig. 6.22 .
99901	The more to the left of and above the dashed straight line a curve is , the more potential exists for improvement .
99902	This can be seen by comparing the three cases discussed above with each other , and with the data for the 90/10 case , that has been included for comparison .
99903	If in doubt as to the possible use of this technique , the user should collect enough data to plot a curve of this type .
99904	A visual check will indicate whether improvement can be expected , and will give some indication of its magnitude .
99905	In general terms , however , if there is a consistent access frequency pattern , this type of load will be of benefit .
99906	Even in the third case analysed above , the use of an access frequency load is equivalent to reducing the packing density of the file by nearly 20 per cent , or doubling the bucket size .
99907	This improvement can be achieved by collecting and using access data as explained on page 399 .
99908	Additions to access frequency loaded files
99909	Additions to a file set up by loading in access frequency order will have a disproportionate effect on file access time ; this is because they will be of at least average activity and often more , as new records tend to be very active , but are loaded into a densely packed file .
99910	A high proportion of them will be synonyms — if the file is 85 per cent packed , for example , 17 in every 20 would be expected to be synonyms — and this will lead to rapid deterioration of the file access speed .
99911	The key figure here is the number of seeks per access .
99912	This will rise markedly as additions are made , and should be monitored frequently .
99913	The deterioration to be expected has been analysed by the author , and results for the 80/20 case are given here .
99914	Tables 6.9(a) and ( b ) shows the result of access frequency loading up to 20 per cent , 30 per cent , 40 per cent , 50 per cent , 60 per cent , 70 per cent , 80 per cent and 90 per cent packing , followed by additions of records of average activity until the file is 100 per cent loaded .
99915	The results are tabulated for ten-record buckets and single-record positions , and the rapid deterioration in both cases is very clear .
99916	Fig. 6.23 shows the results of additions of average access frequency to an access frequency loaded file .
99917	The dashed curves trace the results of a full access frequency load to 100 per cent packing , while the unbroken curves show the effect of adding records of average activity from the packing densities set into each curve .
99918	In reality , as pointed out above , these curves are likely to represent a ‘ best ’ case , as additions to a file are usually new customers , products , personnel , etc. and tend to be highly active , while they also have a high probability of being synonyms .
99919	Fig. 6.24 superposes the deterioration of access frequency loaded 90/10 files as a result of loading additional records in random order , on to an 80/20 file loaded in the same way .
99920	The dashed and dotted curves do not intersect , which makes it clear that the rate of deterioration caused by adding records of average activity to an access frequency loaded file is only dependent on the starting point of the random load , and not on the particular file access situation , such as 90/10 , 85/25 , etc .
99921	The situation has been explored in detail by the author , and Figs 6.25 and 6.26 are taken from that paper .
99922	They provide the file designer with reference charts for buckets of size one and ten records , and can be used to predict the rates of deterioration of any access frequency loaded file using the given bucket sizes .
99923	The unbroken curves show the improvements due to loading files with asymmetries in access frequency of 60/40 , 70/30 , 80/20 , 90/10 and , for single-record buckets , 99/5 .
99924	These are provided for convenience , but the designer can use the charts from any point , and the slope of the broken lines indicates the rate of deterioration to be expected .
99925	Similar curves for buckets holding 2 , 3 , 4 and 5 records are given in Appendix 1 .
99926	The figures against the broken lines correspond to the packing percentages from which a 90/10 case file has received random additions .
99927	The broken curve shows the percentages of access to synonyms as more random additions are made , demonstrating how rapid the degradation is .
99928	In this section we have seen that it is usually possible to reduce the number of accesses to synonyms by loading first the records most frequently accessed .
99929	In cases where a small number of records is accessed very frequently , the saving is marked , and may even be dramatic .
99930	When a file is first set up it may not be possible to load in most frequently accessed order .
99931	The savings that can be made usually justify the collection of statistics during the life of the file , and some ways of arranging this are described in the next section .
99932	6.7 Practical considerations in setting up direct files
99933	Preparing a device for a direct file
99934	Self-indexed files will need little or no prior formatting of the direct access device on which they are to be stored .
99935	It is essential to ensure that every storage position has been initialized , or at least to remove any data remaining from previous uses of the device .
99936	In every other respect the file load will be a normal — and sequential — operation , except that some positions may be left vacant to retain the address/key relationship .
99937	When files are randomly organized using an algorithm , the device must first be initialized to remove all prior data .
99938	If this were not done , data from previous files might still be present in addresses to which records were not allocated .
99939	If the records are to be stored in full track buckets , no formatting is required as the track address is available at all times .
99940	However , if the records are to be stored in individual address positions , the addresses and record storage positions have to be created before the file is loaded .
99941	This applies both for single-record positions and for buckets that are only part of a track in size .
99942	Some manufacturers provide pre-formatted buckets of various sizes on a track .
99943	In this case the user only needs to specify the bucket size required from the alternatives provided , as the formatting and addressing have already been carried out by the manufacturer .
99944	However , it is then often necessary to read a whole bucket into primary storage at a time ; it is not possible to search the bucket and read in only the required record , but this does not apply if a device such as ICL 's CAFS-ISP is available to speed up the search .
99945	Some manufacturers provide a capacity record at the start of a track , used to indicate whether space remains on the track during loading .
99946	If this is not provided , the user will need to set up an equivalent record .
99947	The load process will be :
99948	1
99949	Decide on the bucket size required .
99950	2
99951	Initialize the file area on the direct access device .
99952	3
99953	Pre-format the file area by setting up dummy records of individual record or bucket size , to provide all the addresses within the range that the address algorithm can generate .
99954	4
99955	Load the file .
99956	File statistics
99957	In order to get the best possible performance from a direct file , information is required .
99958	Run times will give an indication that reorganization is due ; access data will allow more efficient processing ; service times will indicate the effect of user demand or the need for file reorganization ; a log of the number of sequential processing runs required may point to the use of ancillary files or a different file organization technique .
99959	We shall look at each of these in turn .
99960	Run times
99961	The basic criterion for the need to reorganize a direct file is that the number of seeks per access has risen appreciably .
99962	When a direct file is being processed on its own , the run times for the file will point to this .
99963	A predetermined figure should be set , and when this is reached the file should be reorganized .
99964	This situation may come about in several ways .
99965	First , the file may be growing .
99966	If new records are added faster than old records are deleted , the packing of the file will get higher ; as we saw earlier in the chapter , this will cause more synonyms .
99967	Second , the randomizing algorithm may be becoming less useful due to some pattern in new record keys .
99968	Third , many of the new records will have become synonyms ; if they are relatively frequently accessed this may cause a marked increase in run times .
99969	Van der Pool described what he called the ‘ ageing ’ process in direct files , pointing out that performance degrades over time due to additions , even if the packing density does not change .
99970	Usually a direct file will be one of a number of files being processed at any time .
99971	In this case the manufacturer 's operating system may be used to keep track of the file run-time .
99972	It is helpful to keep a count of references to home and synonym records .
99973	This can be held in main storage during processing and be printed out on the log or stored in a file label area at the end of the run .
99974	A figure for the ratio of seeks required per access should be specified on the basis of the design criteria used , and the file should be reorganized when this figure is exceeded .
99975	Access data
99976	It was shown on page 195 that knowing how frequently a record is accessed can lead to reduced seek times .
99977	Usually we do not have this information when a file is set up .
99978	There are two ways in which it can be provided for in later reorganizations of the file .
99979	The first is to have a count field in each record , and increment it each time the record is accessed .
99980	This has the advantage that records can be sorted into descending count order for loading during reorganization .
99981	When records are being updated during the run , and so have to be written back on to the device after they have been read into main storage , this method involves no loss of time .
99982	However , if records are only being referred to , the position is different .
99983	A half-revolution would be lost for every record , just to update the count field .
99984	In this case a second method of gathering access data is preferable .
99985	It is to set up an ancillary file with the records in sequential key order and each record consisting only of a count field .
99986	This file will be very small and , if indexed , it will usually match the access speed of a larger direct file because it can be held on a single cylinder of disk , with its index in main storage .
99987	When the master file is to be reorganized , this ancillary file will be sorted into descending count order , and the records are read from the old direct file and loaded on to the new in this order .
99988	The resulting master file will be in access frequency order .
99989	Access data is only useful when records remain relatively constant in their activity .
99990	This often happens , as large customers will always remain more ‘ active ’ than small customers , and some lines of stock are consistently required more frequently than others .
99991	In other cases it is not true ; for example , a flight will be available in an airline booking system long before it takes place .
99992	At first , bookings will be few , then they will increase , and after the flight date the record will vanish .
99993	Statistics of overall popularity of flights will help in planning , but the profile of interest in any one flight will vary with time .
99994	However , some flights will naturally be more likely to be accessed than others .
99995	A Boeing 747 flight between London and New York will always be a candidate for a home position .
99996	A DC9 or BAC 111 can not hold so many passengers and would tend to be loaded later .
99997	Naturally , if a small aircraft is overbooked consistently , it might rate early loading .
99998	In that case , it would also be likely to merit a larger aircraft .
99999	In some cases no clear pattern emerges .
100000	Then it may not be possible to load records in any predetermined order , and lower packing densities and changes in bucket size or type of algorithm may be needed to give an acceptable performance .
100001	Service times
100002	The access times considered in this chapter have been simply the time taken to position the device access mechanism to read or write a selected record .
100003	In practice this is not complete , since two additional times need to be considered in order to obtain the true picture .
100004	The first of these is the data transfer time .
100005	This depends mainly on the size of the record and the operating speeds of the direct access device in question .
100006	For example if the records took up half a track on a device with a rotation time of 25 ms ( 2400 rpm ) then the data transfer would take about 12.5 ms .
100007	The second is the time taken from the moment a record is requested by the program to the time when accessing and transfer takes place , known as wait time or queue time .
100008	This may be zero , though in multi-programming or multi-tasking it is likely to be finite .
100009	For example , if the direct file were being used by an on-line system there could be several concurrent terminal tasks at any one time using the file , and queues would then develop .
100010	Indeed , some operating systems are geared to handling queues by offering the user a choice of queuing algorithm .
100011	If the accesses on a file are completely random , it is often sensible to sort the accesses into cylinder address sequence and minimize individual seek times .
100012	Input or output requests to a file are queued by the operating system and then sorted into sequence before any operations commence .
100013	Updating of a direct file by sorting a batch of update records into their physical order after using the algorithm , and so avoiding the typical random sequence of seeks , can provide rapid ‘ sequential ’ batch updating .
100014	This has been discussed by Nijssen .
100015	Type of processing
100016	Some files may be predominantly processed directly , but occasionally be processed sequentially .
100017	If a file is self-indexed , this presents no problem .
100018	If it has been randomized , then the process has to be reversed .
100019	A list of keys in sequential order is fed into the program and the keys are transformed into addresses in the usual way .
100020	Every synonym will need to be accessed , so no benefit will be derived from the order in which the records were loaded .
100021	This may mean that a file which operates well under normal conditions , i.e. many home records being accessed but few synonyms , may take a relatively long time to process sequentially .
100022	In such a case it can pay to set up an ancillary file when the file is loaded .
100023	This will be a sequential or indexed-sequential file , in key order , with the actual device address of each record as the data .
100024	This actual address will be identical with the key as transformed by the algorithm for home records , but will be different for synonyms , as the ancillary file used will allow all the records to be reached in a single seek , as if the file were self-indexed .
100025	The use of such a file will eliminate extra searching for synonyms and may save a fair bit of time .
100026	It will need to be updated whenever the direct file is updated if the file is very volatile , and this may require the two files to be on-line together .
100027	If there are relatively few additions it may be updated in batch mode later .
100028	This latter case will favour the use of a sequential magnetic tape file .
100029	The former will tend to require an indexed sequential file on a direct access device .
100030	Additions and deletions
100031	Precautions have to be taken to avoid the possibility of excessively long search times or of failure to retrieve records held in a direct file .
100032	When a file has been newly loaded , a search for any record will allow it to be retrieved whether it is a home or a synonym record .
100033	Additions or deletions can change this situation .
100034	An addition may nut he able to take up its home address , because it is already occupied by a synonym from some other address .
100035	Deletion of a home record may mean that , even though the home position is now free , a number of other records that originally randomized to that address are held as synonyms .
100036	Either of these cases may give the appearance that no home record exists for this address , and this situation will thus cause a ‘ no record found ’ error to be given , even though the desired record is in the file .
100037	Thus , if the consecutive-spill method of handling synonyms has been used , a search may still be necessary even if no home record is detected when the home position is searched .
100038	The precautions that should be taken to avoid this situation were set out in the section on consecutive spill , page 186 .
100039	If the chaining method is used , the lack of a home record will lead to the inability to retrieve any record further along the chain .
100040	Only the tagging method of handling synonyms is unaffected .
100041	To avoid these problems , addition and deletion algorithms will have to ensure that at least one home record remains in any bucket to which any records randomize .
100042	When a record is added , this will involve storing it in its home address unless a home record is already in that address ; a synonym from some other address would have to be moved to make way for it .
100043	When a home record is deleted , any synonym that is stored elsewhere , or the first if there are more than one , should be placed in the home address to take the place of the original home record .
100044	This is particularly important if records
100045	This system , which is discussed in detail by Montgomery and Wallace leads to a fairly high number of accesses required to retrieve records from a well-aged file , i.e. one that has had a large number of additions or deletions since it was last loaded .
100046	A stricter file housekeeping discipline , requiring that every home record possible is stored in home addresses , was analysed theoretically by Johnson .
100047	This requires that when a record is added to the file it is stored in its home bucket if any record that is a synonym is at present in the home bucket , and that if space becomes available in a bucket , any synonym that randomizes to the bucket in which space is now available is moved into the home bucket .
100048	The predictions made by Johnson were tested by simulation studies , which showed that even for a 100 per cent packed file , if the discipline he recommended is adhered to , the average number of accesses can be kept down to 1.5 per retrieval , and for larger bucket sizes this is reduced to around 1.25 .
100049	Despite the extra work involved in moving records about to ensure that all possible records are held in their home addresses , compared with the less restrictive requirement of at least one home record discussed earlier , this stricter file housekeeping pays off when retrievals outnumber additions and deletions .
100050	This is the usual case , but if it turns out that a particular file is very volatile the less restrictive system should be used .
100051	The most appropriate bucket size
100052	The optimum bucket size to minimize the time taken by operations carried out on a file depends on the nature of the operation .
100053	When retrievals and updating predominate , which is the usual situation , the optimum bucket size is as small as possible .
100054	This means a single sector for sector-oriented devices , or one record per bucket in systems that allow the user to choose any bucket size within the capacity of the device .
100055	This does not invalidate the earlier comment that a full-track bucket is advantageous , so long as records are randomized to a full track but stored in single-record format on the track .
100056	If additions and deletions are more numerous than retrievals and updates , it turns out that the larger the proportion of additions , the larger the bucket size that provides the minimum number of accesses per reference to the file .
100057	This is a result of the very much larger number of accesses required to find spare space for an addition , in comparison with those required to locate a record already in the file .
100058	( This only applies for files that are relatively fully loaded ; a 50 per cent packed file would require approximately equal numbers of accesses for addition and reference . )
100059	However , even if additions make up most of the processing carried out on the file , it appears that bucket sizes small in comparison with a full track give optimal results .
100060	The full-track bucket , but single-record storage , remains a good option in this case .
100061	Conclusion
100062	Direct files have been used less than might be expected in data processing .
100063	There is certainly a security problem , in that arranging for security and integrity of data is more complex by comparison with sequential files and this , coupled with their poor performance for sequential applications , makes it obvious why they are not used if a sequential file is appropriate .
100064	It is equally true that they are not as suitable for a truly mixed sequential-direct application as indexed sequential files .
100065	However , for enquiry systems with no sequential requirement , or when that requirement is minimal , a well-designed direct file will outperform a well-designed indexed-sequential file , often very substantially .
100066	The probable reason that indexed sequential files are so often used when direct files would perform better is the ready availability of software .
100067	Direct files require extensive design work , because every file and every algorithm will differ slightly from every other .
100068	This means that manufacturers ' software can only provide the more basic requirements such as GET and PUT macros and record-formatting software .
100069	Randomizing algorithms are sometimes provided , but it is generally wise for the user to allocate and test them for each file on an individual basis .
100070	This chapter has shown the steps that can be taken to ensure that a direct file is optimized , and if the file designer follows the rules laid down here , good results should be obtained in almost any situation .
100071	The choice between indexed sequential and direct files is examined in Chapter 9 , and security of direct files in Chapter 10 .

100120	INDEXED SEQUENTIAL FILES
100121	7.1 Introduction
100122	Sequential processing of data files makes up a large proportion of data processing .
100123	However , there is often a need to refer to sequential files just to answer one or relatively few enquiries .
100124	Such a need could be met by processing the whole file sequentially and looking for the records required , but this would be very inefficient .
100125	If the file is large the query may take some time to answer ; meanwhile the computer is occupied processing unwanted records rather than doing useful work .
100126	A second technique that greatly improves the speed of searching a sequential file is to use a logarithmic search .
100127	This method has been described in Chapter 5 on sequential files ( see p. 119 ) .
100128	It is very useful for a few enquiries but can not handle a large number , as a series of storage device movements is involved in each search .
100129	Although technically possible on magnetic tape , logarithmic searches are too slow to be economic , so they are normally only considered for direct access devices .
100130	When the number of enquiries gets too large for a logarithmic search , or even some form of interpolation search , an indexing technique can be used to retrieve records more quickly .
100131	The simplest form of index is one that holds the address of every record .
100132	This is called full indexing and provides a very rapid means of locating any given record .
100133	If the main file is large this index too will be large and there will be problems due to its size .
100134	For this reason one or more indexes may be used in a hierarchy , with the lowest-level index pointing to records while higher-level indices point to the index next below them .
100135	Because of the way in which direct access devices operate , it is not normally necessary or desirable for the lowest-level index to point to every record .
100136	Usually one record per track ( IBM ) or bucket ( ICL ) has an entry in the index .
100137	This is sometimes called partial indexing .
100138	A sequential data file that is indexed is called an indexed sequential file .
100139	The facilities provided by this type of file usually include :
100140	1
100141	Rapid direct retrieval of records by the use of indexes ;
100142	2
100143	Addition of records and subsequent sequential processing of them by the provision of overflow areas ;
100144	3
100145	Deletion of records ;
100146	4
100147	Statistics on the state of the file , giving warning when reorganization is necessary .
100148	Properly used , such a file provides an excellent compromise between the extremes of sequential processing with very rare enquiries that is best handled by sequential files , and direct processing with very infrequent sequential processing , for which direct files are most suitable .
100149	It is not as efficient as either in their own fields , but performs very much better than they can in a situation where a significant enquiry facility is necessary and where the data is frequently processed sequentially .
100150	The precautions needed to ensure that such a file performs satisfactorily are discussed in the main body of this chapter .
100151	7.2 File structure
100152	An indexed sequential file generally has the following components .
100153	1
100154	A data storage area : this may include some unused space to allow for additions embedded in the data .
100155	It may also incorporate the lowest-level index elements .
100156	2
100157	A separate index or indexes : any enquiry will reference this index first ; it will direct the enquiry to the part of the data file in which the desired record is stored .
100158	3
100159	An optional separate overflow area : the decision as to whether such an overflow area is required , and how best to allow for it , is considered later in this chapter .
100160	These parts of the file are interrelated as shown in Fig. 7.1 .
100161	7.3 Indexes
100162	General principles of indexing
100163	It was stated above that full indexing — knowing the position of a record on a track — is seldom useful , because it does not usually speed up the search for that record .
100164	The read-write head reaches any track at a time which is ‘ random ’ in the sense that it is not possible to tell which part of the track will be reached first .
100165	This means that , even if a given address is known , it will be reached no more quickly than if only the track on which the record is stored is known .
100166	This may not always hold good .
100167	It is a result of the physical make-up of present access devices .
100168	The main case in which full indexing is useful is that in which individual records take up a whole track ( in IBM terminology ) or sufficient buckets or sectors ( eight , fifteen or twenty-five in ICL 2900 series terms , depending on the disk in question ) to fill a track completely .
100169	The search time can be overlapped by using rotational position sensing , however ( see Chapter 2 ) , and in this case the ‘ wasted ’ time can be used by some other operation or program .
100170	In this case , knowing the address of the individual record may be useful .
100171	As most of the considerations discussed below do not depend on whether indexing is full or partial , the reader should assume from now on that partial indexing is being discussed .
100172	Exceptions will be pointed out as they arise .
100173	All the common direct access devices , whether disk , semiconductor ‘ disk ’ or mass storage device , have a track concept that is important in deciding on the best arrangement of indexes .
100174	It is not possible to control the part of an index track that is read first .
100175	This means that , on average , half a revolution of the device is necessary before the desired entry is found .
100176	If the software writers arranged that the start of the track has to be detected before the search begins , this becomes a full revolution ; this is made up of half a track to locate the start , and half a track for the search .
100177	When the desired entry is not on that track , these search figures become a full revolution and one-and-a-half revolutions respectively before it is clear that the record is not on the track , and the search must continue on a further track .
100178	In designing a hierarchy of indexes , these figures are very useful .
100179	The following calculations assume that indexes are stored on a direct access device .
100180	Let I 1 and I 2 both be higher-level indexes , and of these let index I 1 be the higher-level index , pointing to index I 2 .
100181	Then the time to locate an address in I 2 will be : I 1 will only be created when it is quicker to search I 1 and then the track to which it points in I 2 , than to carry out an average length search of I 2 .
100182	Assume first that I 2 is one track or less in extent .
100183	In this case a search will take R/2 on average , when the time of rotation of the device is R. Each additional track will add a further R/2 to this .
100184	In the case where the start of the first index track searched has to be located before the search begins , a single-track index will require an average search time of R , but each additional track will again only add R/2 .
100185	Total sequential search times for these cases are shown in Fig. 7.2 .
100186	When a higher-level index is first added , it can be expected to be less than one track in size .
100187	A search will therefore take the minimum time shown in Fig. 7.2 .
100188	The higher-level index will point directly to the required track of the lower-level index , so this will also require the minimum search time .
100189	The break-even point is therefore two tracks if there is no requirement to seek the start of the track , or three tracks if there is .
100190	This shows that as soon as some part of a further track ( over and above two or three respectively ) is necessary for I 2 , a higher-level index I 1 should be created .
100191	This process is repeated each time the highest-level index existing at that time requires a third or fourth track to be added .
100192	The above discussion is based on a sequential search for index I 1 .
100193	An alternative is to search using the logarithmic technique .
100194	This is not significant for less than three tracks , as it is effectively the same as a sequential search for one or two tracks .
100195	In the three-track case it is possible to search the centre track first .
100196	This must be a complete search to ensure that if the desired record is on the track it is found .
100197	If the record is not on the centre track the first or last track will be searched , depending on a comparison of the key being looked for with the highest key on the track .
100198	This will take R ( or 3R/2 if the start of the track has to be detected first ) for the centre track , and R/2 for the other track searched .
100199	There is a ⅓ chance that the desired record is on the centre track , and this brings the average search time to ( 7/6 ) R ( or ( 10/6 ) R where the track start has to be located ) .
100200	These figures are similar to those for sequential searching , although the lower one is slightly better .
100201	The logarithmic technique is not normally used because it requires an extra search for every power-of-two increase in the number of records , while a higher-level index only needs to be built when an index has reached three or four tracks in size .
100202	This means that an extra search will be added only for every additional ( 2n + 1 ) or ( 3n + 1 ) records , where n is the number of records per track .
100203	This can never be inferior to a logarithmic search ( as n can not be less than one ) and is usually far superior .
100204	The effect is shown in Fig. 7.2 for several values of n .
100205	A number of types of index are in common use , and three of the most important are reviewed below .
100206	Types of index
100207	Balanced tree indexing Indexes are said to be of order e when there are e records per index entry , and of height h , where there are h levels of the index .
100208	A tree index is one in which the top level of the index , which is the one consulted first in a search for a record , points to lower levels of the index .
100209	This top level of the tree is often described as the root index of the tree , while the lower-level index items are equivalent to the branches of the tree , and the records are often called leaves or nodes .
100210	A balanced tree is one in which any record can be retrieved in a number of steps s or s — 1 , that is the path length to the record varies by no more than one step .
100211	The balanced tree index shown in Fig. 7.3(a) is made up of a series of index levels , each pointing to the level below it .
100212	The records and the index entries are grouped into twos , so e = 2 and this is described as a tree of order 2 and height 4 .
100213	When a record is added it is necessary to use an overflow area , as the data areas are already full .
100214	The added records have to be indexed , which requires a second index entry for each ‘ track ’ of the data file .
100215	By track here , is meant e records .
100216	The arrangement of the file after a number of additions is shown in Fig. 7.3(b) .
100217	This type of index is used in the Indexed Sequential Access Method ( ISAM ) that has been available on IBM mainframe computer systems since the late sixties , and is now available on some microcomputers .
100218	The balanced tree index allows for deletions without difficulty , because records are tagged but not removed , so that no data manipulation is required .
100219	In some systems , tagged records are removed if they are pushed into overflow ; this depends on decisions taken by the software writers .
100220	However , allowing for additions by providing areas that are logically extensions of the prime data tracks , rather than just physically , has made it necessary to double the size of the lowest-level index , with separate entries for records on the prime data and overflow tracks .
100221	Direct-link balanced trees A second indexing technique , that treats additions as part of the prime data track , is the direct-link balanced tree .
100222	This method of indexing was used on the IBM 1400 series computers — the control sequential method — and is at present in use with ICL 's 2900 series .
100223	A direct-link balanced tree index would also look just as in Fig. 7.3(a) before additions .
100224	However , after additions it would appear as in Fig. 7.4 .
100225	This technique is most effective for very volatile files , as the additions change the keys in indexes but do not cause alteration of prime data tracks .
100226	This means that additions are made quickly , but sequential retrievals suffer .
100227	McDonnell and Montgomery have shown that this technique is as good as the other balanced tree method for direct retrieval .
100228	Both methods suffer from the problem that performance of the file degrades as additions are made , and in consequence they both require that the file should be reorganized at regular intervals .
100229	In order to combat this problem , a number of other indexing methods have been developed .
100230	B-trees Bayer , McCreight and Kaufman proposed the B-tree .
100231	In this type of index , there are always more pointers than index items : .
100232	The order of the B-tree is said to be one more than the maximum number of keys per index block .
100233	A modified form of B-tree is used in IBM 's VSAM files , to be discussed later in the chapter .
100234	Indirectly , B-trees are also used in IBM 's DB/2 relational database system .
100235	Using the same data as before , a B-tree has been set up .
100236	Here , e = 2 , so the order is 3 .
100237	This is very low , and would never be used in practice , but it allows an example to be shown in a compact diagram .
100238	The minimum number of keys per block has to be e/2 , which in this case is one ( 1 ) .
100239	The keys given in the index entries do not have to be actual keys .
100240	Usually , they are intermediate values to allow for later additions .
100241	Fig. 7.5(a) shows the same set of keys as in Fig. 7.3(a) , but stored in a B-tree .
100242	Note that they are now in groups nf 1 or 2 .
100243	The number of index levels here is the same as in Fig. 7.3(a) — that is , the height is again 4 — but there is much more room for additions .
100244	The way in which additions are handled is shown in Fig. 7.5(b) ; the same additions have been made , but have resulted in index and data block splitting , so that no records are in ‘ overflow ’ .
100245	This prime data/index structure can continue to propagate itself as needed .
100246	However , it takes much longer to add records that cause splitting , so the addition versus update-only figures are very important in assessing the efficiency of a B-tree .
100247	A volatile file with relatively little processing might be better handled by a balanced tree index .
100248	VSAM uses a modified form of B-tree , so that the number of keys and pointers is the same , and index entries are greater than or equal to the keys pointed to rather than taking some intermediate value .
100249	The additions to this B-tree have had no effect on the index entries on the left-hand side of the tree , but have led to several changes to the right-hand index entries .
100250	In order to examine this further , let us look at another case .
100251	Fig. 7.6 shows an example of a B-tree of order 5 .
100252	In this case the maximum number of keys per block is four ( e ) , and the minimum is 2 ( e/2 ) .
100253	Note that the top level index may have as few as one .
100254	Choice of index technique It is clear that the changes to the indexes caused by even a very few additions mean a great deal of reading and writing of data into the index areas on disk .
100255	This is a definite weakness of the B-tree .
100256	It is counterbalanced by the ability of the structure to accept very large numbers of additions — given sufficient space , the structure can grow in an unlimited fashion .
100257	We therefore have a choice between index types that is affected by the use to which the file is put .
100258	In Table 7.1 the three methods are compared , scoring 1 for the best of the three , 2 for the second , and 3 for the worst .
100259	Bradley has discussed index design and optimization in some detail .
100260	Montgomery describes the nary tree method of indexing , and compares it with hashing of keys ( discussed later in the chapter , see p. 230 ) .
100261	Rathmann , in a paper particularly concerned with optical disks , compares the balanced tree method with the trie index technique , as did Severance .
100262	A trie index is particularly useful when keys are of varying sizes , and the path of a search at any point of the tree depends on a part of the key rather than its full value .
100263	As most available file organization techniques use the methods discussed earlier , rather than nary trees or trie indexes , they will not be discussed further here , but a full description of tries is given by Knuth .
100264	Index position
100265	The start of any direct search , and the first step in any sequential run , is a search of the higher-level indexes .
100266	The process , for direct reference , is as follows :
100267	Seek the highest-level index ( an average head movement )
100268	Search the high-level indexes ( a variable search time )
100269	Seek the data cylinder ( an average head movement )
100270	Search the low-level index ( a single track search time )
100271	Search the prime data track ( a single track search time )
100272	Search the overflow area ( a variable search time ) .
100273	As this is time-consuming , particularly in the case of direct reference , the file designer will aim to minimize it .
100274	The first high-level index set up by the software is called the cylinder index in ISAM files , or the seek area index in some ICL 2900 series systems .
100275	This index has an entry for each data cylinder of the file indicating the highest key on the cylinder .
100276	Ideally , the file designer will aim to reduce the time taken to reference this index ; however , when it exceeds a certain threshold value described earlier , a master index , which has one entry for each track of the cylinder index , can be created to reduce the total search time as described above .
100277	IBM systems usually provide the software to create up to five higher-level indexes automatically in this way if the user specifies MSTIND = YES .
100278	If two or more higher-level indexes exist , each of them may be handled using a different one of the techniques described below aimed at reducing index search time , depending on their size .
100279	1 To hold all or part of the index in main storage
100280	This will avoid the need for a head movement to the index and can yield very marked savings .
100281	If the entire index is in main storage , the correct cylinder to search is located in well under a millisecond .
100282	This compares with head movement times that are usually orders of magnitude greater , and the direct access throughput is often roughly doubled if this technique is used .
100283	Unless the file is small or main storage is very large , the cylinder index size may exceed the space available for it .
100284	In this case IBM software allows the user to store an exact sub-multiple of the index in main storage , i.e. one half , one third , etc .
100285	When this applies , the average seek time will be reduced to a half , two thirds , etc. , of average head movement time , as the information will be available in main storage — so saving a seek — in an equivalent proportion of cases .
100286	If , because of the size of the cylinder index , only a higher-level index than the cylinder index can be held in main storage , a 20–50 per cent improvement over the performance of the file when the master index is stored on disk can still be achieved .
100287	2 To hold the higher-level indexes on fast devices
100288	Head movement times for fixed-head disks or semiconductor ‘ disks ’ are much shorter on average than those of standard disks .
100289	It is very good practice to store high-level indexes on these devices , so that every direct reference is reduced by the difference in timing .
100290	When the device is dedicated to this file the benefits can be very marked , since the index cylinder on the fast device is available without head movement at all times ; if IBM 3340 , 3350 or similar devices that offer some fixed-head capacity are available , these indexes can be held in the fixed-head area .
100291	If the file is held on a mass storage device , location of higher-level indexes on a disk will make a very significant contribution to reducing run times .
100292	3 Storage on a separate device
100293	If no faster device is available it is often beneficial to use a separate device of the same sort .
100294	This can be most effective if this device can be dedicated to the file , but is still useful in normal multi-programming ; there is certain to be constant arm movement if the file and its high-level indexes are stored on the same device , while this is less likely if they are on separate devices .
100295	4 positioning on a device that also holds the data
100296	When no separate device is available , the optimal position for the cylinder index should be determined .
100297	This has been investigated in great detail elsewhere , and the guidelines may be summarized as follows :
100298	a )
100299	If nothing is known about the distribution of hits in the file , the cylinder index should be placed in the centre of the file area .
100300	In a multi-pack file this will be the centre of one of the packs that is completely dedicated to the file .
100301	b )
100302	If , in a multi-pack file , the only information about hits is the relative number per pack or area , the index should be placed in the centre of the pack or area with the lowest hit density .
100303	c )
100304	If the hit density across a file area or areas is known , the index should be placed in the centre of the highest peak of hits on the least active pack used by the file .
100305	The objective of these guidelines is to place the cylinder index on the file cylinder that is of lowest possible activity , in such a position that the majority of head movements away from the index will be short .
100306	This allows movement back to the index to be rapid .
100307	Past practice has often been to allocate the cylinder index to a cylinder preceding or following the file area .
100308	This is never the best solution ; as pointed out above , the centre of the file is the logical position if nothing is known about hit pattern .
100309	Fig. 7.7 summarizes the rules for placement of the cylinder index if it is to be situated in the main file area .
100310	Alternative indexing techniques
100311	There have been a number of suggestions for alternatives to the lowest-level index of indexed sequential files .
100312	Ghosh and Senko put forward an interpolation search in place of the track or lowest-level index , and showed that for normal key distributions it would improve the direct retrieval performance of IS files .
100313	In addition , this measure gives a potentially better packing density than conventional indexing techniques .
100314	Mullin suggested the use of hashing , rather than indexing , for the lowest-level index .
100315	As he makes clear , this is only of benefit when the average number of records that has overflowed from a track is two or more .
100316	This limits the possible uses of such a technique to very active files that the user does not wish to reorganize frequently .
100317	7.4 Additions
100318	Most indexed sequential file software allows for additions to be made to the file without reorganizing it .
100319	The provision of space for additions is an optional feature .
100320	If no additions are expected , ii is not necessary to leave space for that purpose .
100321	When additions are expected , two techniques are used to store those additions so that they are available for both sequential and direct access .
100322	The first is embedded overflow .
100323	In this case , space is left unused in the main data area when the file is created , and additions are located on the same cylinder ( IBM ) or seek area ( ICL ) that they would have occupied if they had been part of the file when it was created .
100324	In this way the record can be found when necessary without movement of the access heads .
100325	Although this allows fast retrieval of records , it can lead to very low packing density of data because there may be many additions in one area and few in others .
100326	To allow for many additions to every cylinder , when only one cylinder has a large number of additions , is wasteful of space .
100327	This is discussed in more detail below .
100328	The second commonly used technique is to provide an independent or global overflow area which is used to store records added to any part of the file .
100329	This is a very efficient way of handling additions , because all the available space can be used before there is any need to provide extra overflow space .
100330	However , it means that references to added records will require movement of the access heads , which wastes a great deal of time .
100331	As one overflow technique saves time but wastes space , while the other saves space but is slow , many users choose a compromise .
100332	A reasonably-sized embedded overflow area is provided on each cylinder , while a small independent overflow area is used to store additions that overflow from their home cylinder .
100333	Variations in numbers of additions from one cylinder to another are to be expected .
100334	This method ensures that the file designer is not forced to provide very large embedded overflow areas on every cylinder , when only a few cylinders require them .
100335	The distribution of additions to a file guides the designer in allocating overflow areas .
100336	Before the appropriate decision can be made , the pattern of additions to the file has to be determined .
100337	Sometimes this can he predicted or measured , but on other occasions there may be no prior information for the designer to work on .
100338	A number of typical cases are discussed below .
100339	No additions expected This can arise when , for example , a file contains records of policyholders under a policy no longer offered .
100340	The number of policyholders can not grow , and in this case the designer would not allocate any overflow areas .
100341	This provides a file that is well packed ; however , if conditions change later the file needs to he respecified .
100342	Equal numbers of additions to each area This is a very unusual case .
100343	The designer must know that additions will be equal .
100344	It might arise if one additional record were added to each group of consecutive records ; for example , a group of stores might begin to open on a Saturday , and require an extra record for each store to record transactions .
100345	The superficially similar case in which there is an equal probability of additions to any area is covered below .
100346	If the designer is satisfied that equal additions to every cylinder are going to occur , then it is possible to provide only embedded overflow areas .
100347	This will allow rapid retrieval from the file as no extra head movements will be caused by additions .
100348	The designer has to decide on the size of the embedded overflow areas .
100349	Very often , if it is known that additions will be made precisely evenly throughout the file , it will also be known when they will be made .
100350	An example would be when an extra record is added for each project in a company every day .
100351	If this information is not available the designer will have to estimate it .
100352	The intention will be to plan how frequently the file will require reorganization to merge additions and remove deleted records .
100353	After this has been done several times , the actual frequency of reorganization can be compared with that expected , and the future reorganization schedule will be based on the results .
100354	All additions concentrated in a few areas This can occur when , for example , recruitment campaigns for customers have taken place in a limited area , or a competitor has gone out of business .
100355	In these cases , if customer numbers are based on areas , additions will be in groups .
100356	It is unusual for this to be the normal form of additions .
100357	If the designer is faced with it , the requirement for embedded overflow areas will be minimal or nil ; the main provision must be a large independent overflow area .
100358	As this will lead to slow retrieval of added records , more frequent reorganization will be required than in any other case .
100359	If the times at which additions are expected can be predicted , it may be wise to hold additions in an ancillary file until each ‘ burst ’ of activity is over and then to reorganize the main file to include them .
100360	Additions equally probable anywhere This is both the most usual case and the assumption the designer should work on if no information is available .
100361	It is not the same as equal numbers of additions to each area , since there will naturally be variations from cylinder to cylinder in the number of additions just because those additions are random .
100362	The Poisson distribution used to predict synonym behaviour in direct files is the appropriate mathematical tool to use here ( note that if the number of embedded overflow areas is small the binomial distribution should be used instead ) .
100363	Assume that l records are to be added to S embedded overflow areas .
100364	Then the probability p(x) that x records will be added to a given embedded overflow area is given by the expression : An overflow area will be able to hold some number of records n .
100365	The probability that this area will be able to hold all the records added to it will thus be :
100366	To demonstrate what this means in practice , assume that , on average , four records are to be added to each embedded overflow area , and that these overflow areas can hold a maximum of five records .
100367	From equation ( 7. 1 ) , the percentage of embedded overflow areas that will have 0 , 1 , … n additions is given in Table 7.2 .
100368	These figures are plotted in Fig. 7.8 , where the shaded section shows the percentage of areas from which at least one record will overflow into the independent overflow area .
100369	This turns out to be about 21.5 per cent of embedded overflow areas .
100370	The percentage of added records that can not be held in these embedded overflow areas is about 10.26 per cent .
100371	This difference is due to the fact that only one-sixth of the records added to the ‘ six additions ’ figure will overflow , two-sevenths of the ‘ seven additions ’ , three-eighths of the ‘ eight additions ’ , and so on .
100372	Table 7.3 shows the percentage of all additions that will be held in independent overflow for various combinations of embedded overflow area size and number of additions .
100373	This has similar values to those given in Table 6.4 .
100374	The reason is that the addition of records to direct access files is mathematically similar to the random addition of records to overflow areas .
100375	The derivations given here are due to the author and were published in the first edition , but Larson has also carried out similar work independently .
100376	Cases of equal numbers of additions to each area and all additions concentrated in a few areas are depicted schematically in Fig. 7.9 .
100377	This shows files with a twenty-cylinder prime data area , and a two-cylinder independent overflow area .
100378	Each prime data cylinder contains ten tracks .
100379	A track can hold up to five records .
100380	One track in each cylinder is set aside as an embedded overflow area .
100381	The files have each had eighty records added .
100382	The assumptions made are :
100383	a )
100384	equal numbers of additions have been made to every cylinder ;
100385	b )
100386	additions of twenty , twenty-four and thirty-six records have been made to cylinders five , ten and fifteen .
100387	c )
100388	additions have been made as they occur , in an entirely chance sequence .
100389	As this is a small file , it is useful to check how accurately the Poisson distribution approximates to the more strictly accurate binomial distribution .
100390	Using equations ( 6.6 ) — ( 6.9 ) , the figures obtained are shown in Table 7.4 .
100391	The correspondence between the two sets of figures appears to be good .
100392	A check on this using the chi-squared significance test ( see Moroney or any standard statistical text for further details ) shows that there is no significant difference between the two .
100393	This means that any real set of figures obtained by adding records to a file would be expected , due to normal random variations , to show larger discrepancies from the calculated figures .
100394	Thus the Poisson distribution can safely be used instead of the binomial for files of this size .
100395	These three examples show the wide range of conditions that will have to be handled in providing far additions .
100396	Whenever possible , the file designer will have data available on the pattern of additions to a given file .
100397	When no data is provided , or if the only information available is an average number of additions , it should be assumed that additions are equally probable anywhere .
100398	As experience is gained in using the file , any original assumptions about additions should be checked .
100399	Manufacturers ' software often provides information about overflow areas that can assist in this ; the use of this information is discussed in a later section .
100400	7.5 Addition techniques
100401	The way in which additions to an indexed file are made can affect both sequential and direct access to the file .
100402	There are two commonly used techniques .
100403	In the first the record that is added is inserted into its correct position in the file , and the record at the end of the track to which it was added drops off into overflow .
100404	In the second , the added record is placed in overflow , linked from the record before it in sequence , and back to the record following it .
100405	Record insertion
100406	The principle is as shown in Fig. 7.10 .
100407	The advantage of this technique is that , in subsequent processing , the whole prime data track can be handled sequentially by the software , and overflow records are picked up only when the prime track has been processed .
100408	The disadvantage is that , on average , half the records on the track need to be shunted up ( in this example records 113 , 1 14 and 116 have been moved ) , and the overflow area will also require updating .
100409	Both of these functions can be carried out quickly and efficiently in main storage , and it is important to use the manufacturers ' software and allocate space to allow this to happen .
100410	If half the records on a track have to be moved one at a time , and a device revolution is required for each movement , additions can take a great deal of time .
100411	This would be the situation if the programmer had not allocated sufficient working storage to the file .
100412	The IBM indexed sequential file management system ISAM works on the insertion principle .
100413	The cylinder index , a track index and a data cylinder are shown in Fig. 7.11(a) as they are set up .
100414	The file consists of four cylinders , 004 ) 3 , and cylinder 01 is illustrated .
100415	Each cylinder index entry gives the address of the cylinder it refers to , and the highest key on the cylinder .
100416	In the case shown this is 341 .
100417	This will remain the highest key on the cylinder .
100418	If a record with the key 342 is added , it will be stored on the first track of cylinder 02 .
100419	The same principle applies to the highest key on any track ; as the highest key on track 06 was 298 when the file was created , a record with the key 299 belongs logically to track 07 , whether it is stored on that track already or has not yet been added .
100420	The form of balanced tree index used in ISAM operates as follows .
100421	There are two track index entries for each track .
100422	The functions of these entries are given in Fig. 7.12 .
100423	The normal entry links the highest key at present on the prime data track with the address of the track .
100424	It allows a program to check what records are at present physically on that track .
100425	The overflow entry links the highest key on the logical track , which comprises both the prime ( physical ) and overflow parts of it , and the address of the first record in the chain of overflow records for that track .
100426	A program can check from this what records are at present logically on that track .
100427	‘ Logical ’ here means those records that are processed as if they were on the track .
100428	The effect of additions no processing times is discussed under the sections on sequential and direct access to indirect sequential files ( see pp. 251 and 261 ) .
100429	The way in which additions occur , and the changes to index and link entries , are shown in Fig. 7.11 .
100430	The field shown as COCR in the track index stands for cylinder overflow control record .
100431	This is used to store information about the address of the last overflow record on the cylinder , the number of bytes of overflow space still remaining and additional data required if the file contains variable-length records .
100432	When records are added to a file organized in this way , there is an advantage to be gained by planning the additions procedure .
100433	Additions should be sorted into descending order .
100434	As the last record added is the first in the overflow chain , it is helpful if this physical order is also the logical order of the record keys .
100435	Coyle has pointed out that significant savings can be made in ISAM file timings by using this technique .
100436	Record linking
100437	This method operates as shown in Fig. 7.13 .
100438	The advantage of the method is that records on the prime data track do not have to be moved ; a link field has to be inserted in record 111 , however .
100439	The disadvantage for sequential processing is that there will be several rotations during the processing of a track with overflow .
100440	for direct processing the track index does not make it clear which records are in overflow and which in the prime data area ; this prevents the first overflow record being retrieved as quickly as is achieved in the two-entry index system — at least while it is the only overflow record .
100441	However , the index itself takes up less space .
100442	IBM s control sequential file organization , used with the 1400 series computers , added link fields to the records shown above as 111 and 112 .
100443	This was the organization that preceded the indexed sequential file management system .
100444	The smaller machines in ICL 's 2900 series provide an eleven-bit link field that points back to the home bucket if the record is stored in overflow .
100445	This field is present in all records , whether they are in overflow or in a home bucket .
100446	However , it is only used if the record is in overflow .
100447	Otherwise all the bits are set to zero .
100448	If a record is stored in overflow , a tag is placed in the home bucket , pointing to the overflow storage position .
100449	This is made up of a twenty-four-bit field containing the overflow address plus control information , followed by the record key , which can be up to sixty-four characters in length .
100450	The details are shown in fig. 7.14 .
100451	It is usually somewhat easier to insert link fields to handle overflow — particularly when they are already available in the records — than to move up all the records on a track to accommodate a record in its correct sequence .
100452	However , the extra speed of processing will repay the time taken to move these records if the file is frequently processed sequentially .
100453	If the file is mainly processed directly , the link method may be more efficient .
100454	In most cases , however , the user will have no choice in the matter .
100455	It is usually a case of accepting the method used by the manufacturer whose software is being employed .
100456	Addition techniques compared in practice
100457	Montgomery and Hubbard have compared the performance after additions of IBM 's ISAM and ICL 's 1900 series indexed sequential software , the files being held on a 2314 and its ICL equivalent , an EDS 30 .
100458	They looked at :
100459	1 .
100460	random retrieval ;
100461	2 .
100462	random insertion ;
100463	3 .
100464	sequential processing ;
100465	for buckets holding two , six and fourteen records .
100466	Random processing Random retrieval gave very variable results for ICL files .
100467	Buckets containing two and six 500-character records required retrieval times of 60 — 70 ms per record , while for fourteen-record buckets this increased to 120 — 140 ms .
100468	IBM files , on the other hand , yielded retrieval times of 75 — 95 ms and the effect of bucket capacity was small .
100469	The fraction of the file in overflow did not markedly affect performance until it reached 30 per cent of the total file ; the only exception was the ICL fourteen-record bucket file , which began to perform worse as soon as additions were made .
100470	Random insertions were found to be variable in their effect on timing .
100471	IBM files performed better the larger the bucket capacity , while ICL files performed better the smaller the bucket capacity ; very roughly , the six-record buckets were equivalent , while IBM two-record buckets performed as badly as the ICL fourteen-record buckets .
100472	The ICL two-record buckets required about 130 ms per insertion , and the IBM files showed little variation due to the fraction of the file in overflow , but ICL files improved as additions were made , up to 10 per cent , and degraded after this .
100473	Sequential processing The sequential retrieval times for both file structures were identical before additions , but IBM files outperformed ICL in every case after additions .
100474	This was most marked for large bucket sizes ; IBM fourteen-record bucket files gave average retrieval times increased from 40 ms to 55 ms as a result of 40 per cent of the file being stored in overflow .
100475	Average retrieval times fur ICL files , however , increased from 40 ms to 150 ms due to the same number of additions .
100476	Comment on these comparisons These findings are generally in accord with the considerations on the two types of balanced tree discussed earlier .
100477	However , it should be noted that additions to IBM files did not take a great deal longer than to ICL files , while random retrievals from IBM files were not markedly more rapid .
100478	The authors point out that record size is an important factor which was not varied in the work quoted , and it would not be safe to draw far-reaching conclusions from a limited investigation of this sort .
100479	Further work may clarify the differences between these two methods of handling overflow records over a wider range of conditions .
100480	7.6 Data format
100481	Individual records
100482	Manufacturers ' software usually provides for two formats , as discussed in Chapter 3 ( see p. 57 ) .
100483	Because it is necessary for indexed sequential software to build indexes , insert records , etc. , the keys of records must be available to the software .
100484	For this reason the separate count , key and data format is usually required , i.e.
100485	The software that handles index building and additions can operate on the keys separately , while the size of the gap between key and data allows the data record to be transferred into main storage if it turns out to be the required record after examination of the key by the control unit .
100486	A SEARCH ON KEY , for example , will compare every record key with the search key value , but will only read in the data record or records that satisfy the search conditions .
100487	These are generally :
100488	KEY EQUAL
100489	KEY HIGH OR EQUAL
100490	KEY LOW OR EQUAL
100491	In the case of unblocked records , the most likely condition would be KEY EQUAL , as a particular record would be searched for .
100492	It is usual for the file to be arranged in ascending key sequence , and for the file creation software to expect input to the file to be physically in this order ( on initial creation ) or logically in this order ( when a file with overflow records is reorganized ) .
100493	In principle , a file could be arranged in descending order , but most manufacturers ' software checks that the order is ascending and , if it is not , halts until the input order is corrected .
100494	Blocked records
100495	Searching for a record in blocked format is complicated by the fact that only one key can be placed in front of the block .
100496	This is usually the key of the last record in the block , as is shown in Fig. 7.15 .
100497	In the example shown in Fig. 7.15(a) , record 112 is in the second block .
100498	If we were searching for this record , a comparison with the ‘ key ’ of the first block would be low , and of the second , high .
100499	Thus a HIGH OR EQUAL comparison condition will be used to search a blocked file looking for a given record .
100500	In this case the whole block will have to be moved into main storage , and the desired record will be retrieved by the use of a de-blocking algorithm .
100501	If the ISAM method is in use , the effect of adding a new record to a block of records is to cause the block to be re-built , incorporating the new record and pushing the last record of the last block on the track off into overflow .
100502	If record 113 were an addition to the file in fig. 7.15(a) , the new structure would be as in fig. 7.15(b) .
100503	Record 119 goes into the next block , if that is on this track , or otherwise into overflow .
100504	Note that overflow records arise singly , however the prime data area is formatted , and that they are usually stored singly in indexed sequential files ( but see discussion of VSAM on p. 266 ) .
100505	The process described is that used in IBM systems .
100506	ICL does not provide a separate key format in its 2900 series buckets .
100507	Instead , home records are located using the bucket index and overflow records via the home bucket and a tag .
100508	Variable-length records
100509	In many cases variable-length records are not provided for by manufacturers ' software .
100510	It is possible to pad out all records to the length of the largest and handle them as fixed-length .
100511	This wastes space , but the user will not be able to avoid such a shortcoming in manufacturers ' software by any other technique .
100512	Often the solution is to move to a different operating system .
100513	The smaller IBM operating systems do not support variable-length records for indexed sequential files , but the larger ones do .
100514	There are obvious additional tasks to be carried out , such as de-blocking , overflow calculations and efficient packing of the file storage areas that make this limitation understandable .
100515	Even if an installation finds it convenient to use one of the smaller operating systems for much of its work , it may he possible to switch to an operating system that provides the extra facility to handle variable-length records , just for those files that need it .
100516	Overflow records
100517	It was mentioned above that overflow records arise singly .
100518	In addition , an embedded overflow area will usually contain varying numbers of records from several tracks .
100519	This leads to overflow records usually being stored in unblocked format , even if the records in the prime data area are blocked .
100520	There is some advantage in treating the whole embedded overflow area as a single large blocked record , and manufacturers ' software often does transfer the whole track into main storage when an addition is to be made ; this allows for the addition itself , creation of link fields , changes of index , etc .
100521	However , handling the whole track as a single block would prevent rapid transfer of individual records from the embedded overflow area during direct access reference , which is the reason this method is often not adopted ( but see the section on software packages , p. 264 ) .
100522	Key size
100523	On a 3330 , the space taken up by the track index will be at least 57 per cent of track zero if all but one track of the device is allocated to data storage ( the remaining track is assumed to be reserved for overflow records ) .
100524	If keys are greater than 155 bytes in length , the track index will exceed one full track in extent , and maximum length keys of 256 bytes will cause the cylinder index to take up as much as 28 per cent of the second track on the cylinder as well .
100525	Equivalent figures for the 3350 are even higher : the minimum track index size for a full cylinder file with no embedded overflow areas is 85 per cent of track zero , while maximum key sizes could expand this to almost one and two-thirds of a track .
100526	The influence of key size is shown in Fig. 7.16 .
100527	7.7 File packing
100528	The prime data area of an indexed sequential file is less densely packed than the data area of a sequential file .
100529	There are three reasons for this .
100530	They are as follows :
100531	1
100532	The records or blocks of records take up more space , because they are in the CKD format with separate keys .
100533	The effect of this depends on record or block size , but can be calculated using the methods given in Chapter 4 on blocking and buffering ( see p. 75 ) .
100534	( Note that in some cases sequential files also use this format .
100535	This point would then not apply . )
100536	2
100537	The track index will take up part or all of the first track on each cylinder .
100538	The system-defined parts of this are standard in size , but the record key length depends on the user .
100539	A typical value might be eight bytes , leading to an index size of rather more than half a track ( the number of entries in the index depends on the number of tracks or buckets , while the size of the track depends on the device ) .
100540	If the user decided on very large keys — and IBM allows up to 256 bytes , for example — the track index might take up more than a single track .
100541	This is one reason to choose a fairly short key for indexed sequential use .
100542	A further reason is the size of the higher indexes ; they , too , will be very much affected by the key size .
100543	3
100544	If embedded or cylinder overflow areas are provided they will take up one or more tracks of every cylinder .
100545	The file designer will try to keep these areas as small as possible to produce a well-packed file .
100546	However , the considerations given earlier on overflow area size and the need to allow for a relatively long period between reorganizations will guide the designer to a reasonable compromise .
100547	If a great deal of direct on-line storage is available , the balance will be tilted towards a larger provision of overflow space .
100548	If direct on-line storage is limited , it may be worth accepting more frequent reorganizations as the price for cutting down overflow space .
100549	ICL 2900 series software allows the user to specify the packing of home buckets that is desired when the file is created .
100550	This can be used to replace or supplement a cylinder overflow area ; it is a form of distributed free space that is more evenly available through the file than a cylinder overflow area .
100551	These three points will lead in most cases to something between 80 per cent and 90 per cent of the space in the prime data cylinders being used to store records .
100552	The best that can be achieved is 95 — 98 per cent packing if keys are small and no overflow is expected .
100553	There are , however , two further file structural areas that may reduce data packing .
100554	4
100555	The cylinder index and any higher-level indexes : it is unlikely that any but the largest files will require more than one cylinder for these indexes , although a complete cylinder has often to be set aside for them , as is required by some manufacturers ' software .
100556	If this applies , small indexed sequential files bear a heavy burden compared with larger files .
100557	The probable penalty in packing density for a large file is of the order of 0.5 to 1 per cent , while for small files it can be very much more — 50 per cent in the most extreme case , when the file takes up only one data cylinder .
100558	5
100559	The independent overflow area uses additional space , although in most cases this will not be excessive as the increase in time caused by continual head movements to the independent overflow area from the prime data area and back will soon show up in run times .
100560	The usual loss in packing density is again of the order of 0.5 per cent to 1 per cent , but as with the high-level indexes , there will be a proportionately heavy overhead for small files if the software requires a complete cylinder to be used for independent overflow .
100561	Apart from the points discussed above , which are due to the structure of the file , two more considerations will influence the space required by the file .
100562	6
100563	Blocking of records : the demand for records in CKD format is more wasteful the smaller the record size .
100564	One way to use direct access storage more efficiently is to block effectively .
100565	This will depend on space being available to handle larger blocks in main storage ; it was considered in more detail in Chapter 4 ( see p. 75 ) .
100566	7
100567	The use of variable-length records is sometimes unavoidable , but always leads to waste .
100568	It may appear as padding to a fixed size due to software limitations or it may be wasted space at the end of tracks and overflow areas because the record that should have gone there was too large .
