100569	To this must be added the extra time and space demanded in main storage for relatively complex blocking — deblocking routines .
100570	The designer of an indexed sequential file will try to avoid using variable-length records ; when they are necessary the discussion in Chapter 3 ( see p. 67 ) should be helpful .
100571	Coyle has shown that it pays to leave some distributed free space within a file .
100572	As pointed out above , ICL allows the user to specify the packing density in buckets , but IBM does not .
100573	Dummy records can be provided to take the place of this space , by placing them where additions are expected , or in a pre-determined pattern throughout the file .
100574	This solution ( used by Coyle ) led to marked improvement in ISAM file performance .
100575	The packing density is not usually critical , but the additional space used does have an effect on file timing , which will be examined later .
100576	Indexed sequential files can be processed either sequentially or directly .
100577	As handling of the file is very different in these two cases , we shall examine them separately .
100578	7.8 Sequential processing
100579	The user may wish to start at the beginning of the file , or at any other point .
100580	using IBM terminology , the SETL macro can be employed to indicate a starting point in the file and the ESETL macro to set a finishing point .
100581	When the processing program issues a GET macro the routine shown in Fig. 7.17 is initiated .
100582	The user is not directly aware of the steps shown but they will result in both ‘ housekeeping ’ processing time and input-output operations .
100583	The sequence has been simplified for convenience , but it shows the essential stages in sequential retrieval .
100584	We shall refer to it in examining the various operations that can be carried out sequentially .
100585	Retrieval before additions
100586	All records will be in their correct places and the file will be physically as well as logically in sequence .
100587	The cylinder index ( and any higher indexes ) will only be referenced once at the start of the run .
100588	Head movement to the first data cylinder will be dependent on the size and position of the file .
100589	All further head movements will be from the current cylinder to the next and so will be of minimum duration — 3 to 10 ms for modern disks .
100590	For semiconductor ‘ disks ’ or fixed-head disks all that is involved is electronic switching , which takes negligible time .
100591	The length of a sequential retrieval run will be slower than an equivalent run using a sequentially organized file for the following reasons :
100592	1 Reference to the cylinder index and any higher indexes
100593	This is not likely to take longer than 100 ms and average times are much lower , e.g. 30 ms average head movement for the IBM 3330 , 25 ms for the 3350 and 16 ms for the 3380 , followed by a search of the index .
100594	Thus the addition to a given run time will not be significant .
100595	2 Reference to the track index
100596	There will be a rotational delay of half a revolution on average before the required track index entries are found .
100597	This will be repeated for every track on the cylinder , so it will cause a sizeable addition to run times .
100598	3 Increased file size
100599	The track index will take up part of the first track of each cylinder .
100600	Overflow areas , even if empty , will take additional space .
100601	This will mean that the data requires more direct access storage space than a sequential file .
100602	Timing will be increased by :
100603	a )
100604	extra cylinder-to-cylinder head movements ;
100605	b )
100606	an increased number of data tracks , each of which will require index entries and so will add to the time required for rotational delays described in 2 above .
100607	As we are examining the case of sequential retrieval before additions , the items given above do not include overflow retrieval .
100608	However , there is more housekeeping activity in handling an indexed sequential file than the corresponding sequentially organized file .
100609	This will add to CPU usage , and the greater software module size will mean that more space is required in main storage .
100610	The two file organizations are fully compared in Chapter 8 ( see p. 300 ) .
100611	The effect of additions
100612	We shall examine random additions to a file ; as the principles involved do not change if the additions are grouped or regular in pattern , the methods used can be adapted to suit those cases .
100613	Table 7.5 shows the percentage of tracks with 0,1,2 , … additional records as a result of additions made randomly to a file .
100614	These figures only hold accurately for large files — 100 or more tracks in extent — although they will act as a guide even for very small files .
100615	Fig. 7.18 displays the results pictorially .
100616	Note that Table 7.5 only applies to the given number of records per track while Fig. 7.18 is more general .
100617	The impact of additions depends on the additions technique used .
100618	1 Record insertion
100619	This is the standard balanced tree type of index , described on page 223 .
100620	If a single record has been inserted , the last record logically on the track will now be held in overflow .
100621	The average wait before this is located would be half a revolution if the whole overflow track were full .
100622	Usually this is not the case so the average wait will be less than half a revolution .
100623	For timing purposes it is best to assume a wait of half a revolution , bearing in mind that this is usually an overestimate .
100624	The duration of this wait may often lead to the overflow record being processed more rapidly than prime data track records because processing time will often be low enough to allow this record to be processed as soon as it is located .
100625	Records on the prime data track , as has been explained earlier , may each cause a full revolution to be lost if they can not be processed during the time the inter-record gap is traversed .
100626	When there are two or more overflow records on a track , the first overflow record in logical sequence , i.e. the last to go into overflow , will require half a revolution on average to locate it .
100627	This is usually an underestimate as the first logical overflow record is always the last from that track physically and tends to be located near the end of the overflow track .
100628	Each later overflow record will require nearly a full revolution .
100629	Fig. 7. 19 shows the situation on an overflow track .
100630	In this case an overflow chain of three records has been established from the prime track .
100631	The logical and physical sequence of these records is inverted , and the wait-time spiral ( WAIT 1 +WAIT 2+WAIT 3 ) shows that it will take more than two revolutions of the disk to access the three records .
100632	WAIT 1 can not be overlapped , except with separate functions of this or some other program .
100633	WAIT 2 and WAIT 3 will be overlapped with the processing of records 1 and 2 , while the processing time for record 3 has to be added to the minimum delay of the three WAITS .
100634	The estimate of three revolutions for three overflow records will thus be fairly accurate in this case .
100635	As n overflow records will require ( n — 1 ) full revolutions , to which the seek and processing times for the last record have to be added , this estimate will get more accurate the more records there are in the overflow chain .
100636	These timings will hold so long as wait times exceed processing times , which is often true .
100637	When this does not hold , additional full revolutions will be added to the total time because the next record to be processed will be missed , and a further revolution or revolutions will be required before it is available once more .
100638	2 Record linking
100639	This technique is used in the direct-link balanced tree .
100640	If the overflow record is held on the same cylinder as the prime data there will be an average wait of half a revolution to refer to the overflow record .
100641	If processing time is negligible there will be an additional half a revolution to return to the next prime track record , and the total time to locate and process the overflow record will be precisely one revolution .
100642	The longer the overflow record processing time , the more frequently will this not be completed before the next prime-track record is available .
100643	This will mean that an additional revolution is lost , so the total time incurred per overflow record will exceed one revolution on average .
100644	The range of processing times that will allow processing to be completed in a single revolution is shown in Fig. 7.20 .
100645	Note that , as the time available to process the prime record increases , that available to process the overflow record decreases proportionally .
100646	If the minimum figure — a loss of one revolution per overflow record — is assumed as an average , it will certainly not be an overestimate .
100647	For long processing times this will be too low a figure , but it will then be part of run times markedly higher as a result of overall long processing times and it is probable that overflow records will not cause much extra delay .
100648	3 Comparison of the two techniques
100649	Experimental and simulation work carried out by Montgomery and his co-workers has shown that the sequential retrieval time for records increases as more of the file is held in overflow .
100650	This is less marked for smaller numbers of records per block and some trials have shown an improvement for blocks of only two records .
100651	McDonnell and Montgomery found that higher overflow percentages than 10–25 per cent led to increased retrieval times for all block sizes .
100652	Random insertions to balanced tree files that use two index entries per track took rather less time as the overflow percentage in the file built up .
100653	This was more marked for larger blocks than smaller ones .
100654	In comparison , the time required to make random insertions to direct-linked balanced tree files did not change with overflow percentage .
100655	This is to be expected , bearing in mind the way in which insertion is handled .
100656	The effect of hit rate
100657	One of the great strengths of indexed sequential files is that skip-sequential processing is made easy .
100658	When the hit rate — the percentage of records that has to be processed — is low , records , whole tracks and even cylinders may be skipped without reading them if they are not required .
100659	Although a sequential file using a record storage format in which keys are separate from data can also skip records , every key has to be checked so every track has to be traversed , whether any records on it are required or not .
100660	An indexed file can allow more marked savings to be made , as only the index entries need to be read , and these show which tracks and cylinders can be skipped .
100661	The effect of hit rate depends also on the pattern of hits .
100662	Analysis of this is mathematically similar to that of patterns of overflow record occurrences , and the following cases will be considered :
100663	1 .
100664	random ;
100665	2 .
100666	even ;
100667	3 .
100668	grouped ;
100669	4 .
100670	grouped superposed on random .
100671	1 Random update pattern
100672	When hit rates are low , the probability that two adjacent records will both require updating is also low .
100673	This implies that there is a good chance the processing of the first record will be complete by the time that the second record is located , so that skip-sequential processing win provide benefits .
100674	Whether such benefits are available depends both on average hit rate and on processing time .
100675	The results of a series of experiments have shown that the pattern obtained is very similar to those given for sequential disk files in Fig. 5.8(d) .
100676	Thus the relationship between hit rate and overall run time is roughly equivalent to hit rate , but stepped in characteristic disk fashion .
100677	As hit rate reduces , more and more benefit is obtained from skip-sequential processing .
100678	This is examined in detail in Chapter 9. pages 300–307 .
100679	2 Even update pattern
100680	When every second , third , … nth record is updated , conditions are ideal for rapid skip-sequential runs .
100681	A constant period is available during seeks to process the records already in main storage , and if every record requires the same processing time this will lead to very predictable run timings .
100682	These will increase stepwise in that , up to some limiting time , processing will be entirely overlapped with seeking .
100683	Beyond this threshold processing time there will be a loss of one revolution for every one , two , … b records , depending on the number of 1 — O buffers , b , that is in use .
100684	A precisely even update pattern is not usual , so the designer is unlikely to be able to rely on such an occurrence in deciding on file timings .
100685	However , in the few cases where it does occur , this type of update pattern makes timing calculations relatively easy .
100686	3 Grouped updates
100687	This pattern occurs frequently due to factors such as the way in which meter readings for , say , electricity supply are made from house to house , i.e. not at random , or the effects of localized advertising campaigns on a larger file in which many unaffected records are stored .
100688	The effect of grouped updates is to cause parts of the file to require few , if any , updates so records are being skipped , and other areas in which all — or most — records are updated , and thus there will be lost revolutions because processing times exceed inter-record gap times .
100689	If skip-sequential processing is correctly used , whole areas of the file can be skipped , producing an improvement in run time similar to that achieved by sectioning a sequential file on magnetic tape ( see Chapter 5 for details , p. 112 ) .
100690	In group update areas , if every record in the group has to be processed there will be extra revolutions for every record , every second record , … every bth record , depending on buffering arrangements , where b is the number of buffers as before .
100691	For all normal record updating a loss of this magnitude can be expected , but it would not apply if the processing involved is trivial because then the records can be processed at reading — that is , rotation — speeds .
100692	In summary , the areas in which there are few updates can be skipped very quickly .
100693	Grouped update areas will take an overall time related to individual record processing time , buffer arrangement , update density , i.e. hit rate , and device rotation time .
100694	Although this is complex to analyse , the average times are easily checked in any given case .
100695	The file designer can measure the results of applying groups of updates to the file and make timing estimates based on the results of these tests .
100696	4 Grouped updates with additional random updates
100697	This case also often occurs in practice due to the results of cases such as grouped meter readings from customers who were at home when the meter reader called , combined with customers ' own readings carried out because they were out when the meter reader called , and a number of special checks that are carried out at a different time .
100698	Timings can be handled by considering the two separate situations and combining their effects .
100699	The skip-sequential processing of sparsely updated file areas can not now be regarded as straightforward .
100700	Every cylinder , and quite probably most tracks , will have one or more records that require updating .
100701	However , the likelihood is that processing and seeking will be entirely overlapped so this will not hold up the overall run very seriously .
100702	In the grouped update areas there will be little or no effect , as the hit rate is already high .
100703	Additional transactions from the ‘ background ’ random distribution will only make it more unlikely that seeking and processing can be overlapped .
100704	This will reduce the variability of timings due to chance variations in overlap , and so make it possible to calculate run timings more accurately .
100705	The effect of blocking
100706	The blocking of records in general has been dealt with in Chapter 4 ( see pp. 71 — 98 ) .
100707	The main significance of blocking here is that , even if a low percentage of records is hit in a run , blocking them together will increase this figure .
100708	Again , the increase is not directly proportional to the blocking factor .
100709	The results of any given blocking factor on hit rate can be calculated from Table 4.5 and Fig. 4.6 .
100710	For example , if a file has an individual record hit rate of 1 per cent and the hits are randomly distributed , the results of varying the blocking factor are as shown in Table 7.6 .
100711	The reason for the need to read more records is that as the blocks get larger there is an ever-increasing likelihood of at least one update being required from amongst the records in the block .
100712	Concentration of updates in a particular area — case 3 above — reduces the number of blocks that have to be read and in the most extreme case , where all or none of the records in a block require updating , the percentage of records that need to be read would not change due to blocking .
100713	At the other extreme , very even updating patterns would mean that most blocks or even every block required to be read and such a pattern would therefore make skip-sequential processing pointless .
100714	The main impact of blocking on the speed of skip-sequential processing is usually counter-productive , although it often achieves more in space-saving and rapid data transfer than is lost in increased block activity .
100715	Blocking will not usually increase the probability of having to read data from a given track , except insofar as it allows more records to be stored on that track .
100716	It will , however , mean that a larger quantity of data has to be transferred into main storage for each update operation , even if only one record in the block is required .
100717	Overall , a larger blocking factor will not markedly change the balance of choice between skip-sequential processing of sequentially and indexed sequentially organized files .
100718	7.9 Direct processing
100719	The overall set of operations that take place when an indexed sequential file is directly processed is shown in Fig. 7.21 .
100720	This sequence occurs whenever a reference is made to the file , and it is helpful to examine each stage of the process :
100721	Reference to the cylinder and higher-level indexes This will involve a head movement in most cases .
100722	If the file is small , the cylinder index may be partly or entirely held in main storage , as explained earlier in this chapter ( see p. 228 ) .
100723	Otherwise it should be stored on the most rapidly accessible device available .
100724	Reference to the track index This will take between three-quarters of a revolution and a full revolution as the start of the index will need to be located before it can be searched .
100725	This will take R/2 on average , followed by half the index — which is usually slightly over half a track in extent — before the required entry is located .
100726	Reference to the appropriate data track The timing here depends on whether the record in question is stored on a prime or an overflow track .
100727	1 Prime track storage
100728	If the record required is available on the prime data track it should be located , on average , in half a revolution .
100729	When the start of the track has to be detected , this will be modified ; the track index start will have been found — taking a time R/2 — and the index entry will have been located , read and processed during a single revolution ( in most cases ) .
100730	Thus the overall time to read the track index and locate the data record will be : These calculations will apply to files in which all the data records are held in sequence on the prime data track , as for example in IBM systems .
100731	Retrieval of records in files handled using linked overflow will not be so straightforward .
100732	Depending on the software and the linkages provided it is probable that overflow records will have to be retrieved and checked as they are encountered .
100733	This will add at least one revolution for every overflow record and will mean that the time to locate a data record , after the data track has been located , will be : where there is an average of m overflow records per track .
100734	The additional times caused by linkage handling can be avoided if the link held on the prime data track contains the record key , and if the software can detect whether the required record is in overflow quickly enough to avoid missing the start of the next record .
100735	2 Storage on an overflow track
100736	The effects here can be analysed in three stages .
100737	They are :
100738	a )
100739	first overflow records from a track ;
100740	b )
100741	further overflow records from tracks on a cylinder stored in the cylinder overflow area ;
100742	c )
100743	records stored in an independent overflow area on some other cylinder .
100744	First overflow records do not add any additional time if the index has two entries per track , and if the index items point to the first record in the overflow chain .
100745	The software will recognize the key concerned , and the prime data track will be bypassed .
100746	In the linked overflow case , however , each overflow represents a break in the search .
100747	Thus the link would be expected to occur on average after R/2 , and the overflow record would also take an average of R/2tn locate ( or R if the start of the overflow track has to be found before the record search can begin ) .
100748	Depending on the software , further overflow records may take no additional time — if it is not necessary to follow all chains — or the average time per overflow record may be nR/2 , where there are n overflow records per track and every overflow chain has to be followed during a record search .
100749	Overflow records other than the first will cause a time lapse of at least ( n — 1 ) R ( see page 254 for details ) .
100750	Overflow records held on a separate cylinder will require a head movement to the overflow cylinder .
100751	An estimate of their number is given in Table 7.3 for the case where additions are random .
100752	There will be little difference between embedded ( that is , on the cylinder ) and independent overflow methods when additions are random , and independent overflow will prove to be very wasteful of time .
100753	As explained earlier , it is therefore important to avoid the use of independent overflow areas except as a safety precaution ; the one exception to this is when updates are grouped in a few areas .
100754	The effect of overflow records on the average seek times for directly processed records has been investigated by Montgomery and Hubbard and the author .
100755	This work has shown the gradual deterioration of performance as random additions are made to a file , and the marked acceleration of this process as records are allocated to independent overflow .
100756	Factors involved in design
100757	1 Blocking
100758	Unlike its impact on sequential retrieval , the result of blocking on direct retrieval is not marked .
100759	The record search process is not usually lengthened at all , so only the increased data transfer time needs to be considered .
100760	This is generally of the order of a millisecond or so at most .
100761	2 Batching and sorting input
100762	Sequential processing of an indexed sequential file avoids many access head movements and minimizes those that are unavoidable .
100763	As an example , if there are 200 enquiries made to a file and the file is stored on a disk with 200 cylinders , a completely random distribution of these enquiries would lead to :
100764	126 cylinders with one or more active records in them ;
100765	74 inactive cylinders .
100766	Handling these enquiries directly would involve 200 average head movements , about 200 × 30 ms for a 3330 , giving a total of 6 seconds .
100767	By comparison , batching and sorting the enquiries would lead to 126 head movements , most of which would be an absolute minimum of 10 ms and none of which would be much longer than 15 ms .
100768	In addition , about seventy-four cylinders could be skipped so there would be around 126 × 10 ms required for head movements .
100769	This gives a time of about 1.3 seconds for head movements , rather less than a quarter of the earlier figure .
100770	The difference grows as numbers increase ; with anything over 1000 enquiries all the cylinders would be likely to be referenced , thus giving a time of 20 × 10 ms or 2 seconds for the batched and sorted input , and 2000 × 30 ms or 60 seconds for the unsorted input .
100771	These figures do not allow for two important aspects of the situation .
100772	The first is that sorting itself takes time .
100773	This is relatively short , but there is also an operating time involved , and for safety a one-minute or five-minute overhead has been added to the actual sort times given in Fig. 7.22 .
100774	These compare batching and sorting times with direct reference , for a file that takes up the whole of a 2314 disk .
100775	The second consideration is that batching implies holding up the first enquiries to be received .
100776	For a true enquiry such a delay is probably not possible , but in cases where the input is directly processed for convenience alone it should always be considered .
100777	In the many instances where updates arise in a batch' mode , as for example incoming mail , there is seldom any good reason to process directly , as the overall level of service will be improved by batching and sorting .
100778	The few quickly-processed updates that are handled first , if direct processing is adopted , are more than counterbalanced by the shorter overall run time and thus better average service performance achieved by batching and sorting .
100779	The file designer will find it worthwhile to examine every direct processing application of an indexed sequential file critically .
100780	When batches are large , overall throughput will be much improved if any runs can be converted to batched and sorted operations .
100781	The break-even points between the two modes of processing can be seen clearly in Fig. 7.22 ; for numbers of records for which a sequential curve is above each straight line that represents the time required to process a record directly , direct processing is faster .
100782	After the curve is below any given line , batches of that size or greater should be processed by batching and sorting when that is possible .
100783	7.10 The impact of software on indexed sequential files
100784	Manufacturers ' software
100785	Generally , manufacturers provide software to format , load , update and reference indexed sequential files .
100786	Statistics on the number of embedded overflow areas that are full , how much space remains in the independent overflow area , how many non-first overflow records are being directly referenced , etc. , are usually available .
100787	These are of considerable assistance to the file designer , and should be examined at the end of each run , at least while operating data for a file is still limited .
100788	The options available to the user will also allow definition of blocking factor , overflow technique and size of overflow areas .
100789	As all of these may have default options , it is important that the designer should make positive decisions about them and ensure that the file does reflect the design intended for it .
100790	Some other helpful features may be available but not made clear .
100791	For example , handling of overflow is facilitated in IBM systems if the designer allocates sufficient buffer space ( usually this means defining more than two I-O buffers ) .
100792	A number of manufacturers provide a filestore facility that handles the storage of data files in a way that uses backing storage efficiently but does not allow the user any opportunity to optimize file performance .
100793	Although ease of use is important , this approach to file design is not desirable unless the manufacturer 's software also optimizes , which is seldom possible .
100794	On occasions manufacturers ' software is not highly efficient for a given application , and software houses have taken advantage of this to provide alternative packages .
100795	The shortcomings focussed on by alternative suppliers a
100796	1
100797	Large user keys increase index size ;
100798	2
100799	Records are unblocked in the overflow areas , which wastes space ;
100800	3
100801	Separate software modules are required to handle direct and sequential retrieval , using a great deal of space in main storage ;
100802	4
100803	Overflow records add markedly to run times ;
100804	5
100805	When high hit rate files are processed , many revolutions are lost due to processing not being complete when the next record is located .
100806	Some of the software that is available to exploit these conditions is discussed below .
100807	Software packages
100808	The COMTEN AMIGOS software allows the user to replace two separate IBM modules , one for sequential and the other for direct reference to an indexed sequential file , by a single module that requires less space and performs the same functions ; this is particularly helpful if a single run updates sequentially but allows enquiries during the runs .
100809	On the other hand , the dual-function module is larger than either of the single-function modules it replaces , so it offers no benefit for single-function runs .
100810	The AMIGOS package includes two other functions that improve space utilization and processing speed .
100811	As a standard , each track is divided into just THREE data blocks , so arranged that they are read in the order 1,3,2 as shown in Fig. 7.23 .
100812	This allows a reasonable time for processing , and results in fewer lost revolutions than is normally possible .
100813	However , it doubles the minimum run time , and so will not help in some cases .
100814	The second change is that records are also blocked in overflow .
100815	Although this will mean a slightly increased retrieval time ( of the order of 5 — 8 ms depending on the device ) it is claimed that the space saving more than offsets this overhead .
100816	Universal Software Inc. offer a PSAM package that achieves improvement by splitting additions between blocks in the prime data area — i.e. providing distributed free space — rather than defining separate overflow areas .
100817	This provides more rapid access to established files , and less-frequent reorganizations .
100818	Freshly reorganized files are identical in performance , whether organized using PSAM or IBM 's ISAM .
100819	It is also claimed to reduce space usage .
100820	Examples like these make it appear that the performance of manufacturers ' software can always be bettered .
100821	Coyle showed that it was possible to improve the speed of an ISAM file by more than four times by using the optimization options available in IBM 's software .
100822	The steps he took are shown in Fig. 7.24 .
100823	In the case he quotes it was decided not to use alternative software , and other users should ensure that they have already exhausted the possibilities of improving the performance of their present software before they turn to other sources .
100824	The manufacturers have incorporated some of the ideas introduced by software houses into their own offerings , and the facilities provided by IBM 's VSAM illustrate this process .
100825	VSAM is of interest to us , partly because the indexing technique used , which has been described in detail by Wagner , is a modified B-tree .
100826	IBM 's VSAM ( Virtual Sequential Access Method )
100827	This file organization technique is a development of ISAM that incorporates many of the concepts used in the software obtainable from independent suppliers .
100828	The method is only available for use with virtual storage systems , and offers access to records in three ways .
100829	These are :
100830	1
100831	Reference by record key ; ,
100832	2
100833	Reference by address relative to the start of the file using the relative byte address ( RBA for short ) ;
100834	3
100835	Reference by relative record number ( fixed-length records only ) .
100836	Of these , 1 ( referring to the record by its key ) can be compared to ISAM in operation , so the similarities and differences are examined here .
100837	A key-sequenced file or data set is created , with its associated indexes , as a cluster .
100838	For our purposes the cluster is an indexed file .
100839	Data storage is divided into control intervals which are continuous areas of storage of a size that is not necessarily related to the physical make-up of the device on which the data is stored .
100840	This is shown in Fig. 7.25 .
100841	A control interval is the unit of data moved between virtual and backing storage .
100842	In a sense it is equivalent to a track in an ISAM file , in that there is one index entry per control interval .
100843	A group of control intervals makes up a control area .
100844	The whole of a control area is referenced by the entries in a single index record , and in a sense this is equivalent to a cylinder in ISAM terms .
100845	The index relates key values to the relative byte address locations of the data record .
100846	Indexes are arranged as follows .
100847	All the higher indexes are collectively called the index set , and they are divided into index records containing a number of pointers .
100848	One of these pointers indicates the next index record at this level , and is used to move sequentially through the file .
100849	The other pointers indicate the location of a number of index records at a lower level .
100850	The lowest level of index records makes up the sequence set , and in this case the pointers are to control intervals ; the total number of control intervals indexed by one index record makes up a control area .
100851	The structure of a key-sequenced VSAM file is shown Fig. 7.26 .
100852	Additions to the file are catered for by the provision of distributed free space .
100853	This can be allocated by allowing a number of control intervals to remain entirely empty , by leaving space at the end of every control interval that contains data records , or by a combination of both techniques .
100854	As all the space available in a control area is allocated when the file is set up , VSAM provides the equivalent of a cylinder overflow area in ISAM and a proportion of free space in data storage areas , just as was done in ICL 1900 series software .
100855	Records added to a file are blocked in the same way as the original data and not unblocked as in ISAM .
100856	VSAM does not leave deleted records in the data area , as does ISAM .
100857	Instead , the area occupied by the record or part of a record that has been deleted is added to the distributed free space available .
100858	Within the control interval the remaining records are moved towards the start of the control interval , which requires their RBAs to be altered and avoids fragmentation of the free space in the control interval .
100859	When records are inserted , the RBAs of any following records will be increased as a result of their movement in the control interval .
100860	If there is not sufficient space for the inserted records in the control interval , a control interval split takes place under VSAM control .
100861	This uses any free control intervals in the control area rather than the free space in other control intervals containing data .
100862	The consequence of this is that the records may not be physically in sequence after a control interval split , although they will be handled in sequence by the indexes .
100863	If there is insufficient room in the control area to handle all additions , a control area split takes place under VSAM control .
100864	Approximately half the control intervals in the old control area are moved to the new control area , which is made available either as a result of decisions taken when the file was defined or by extending the file as required .
100865	The new control area is likely to be physically remote from the original site of the data .
100866	Although VSAM will handle it sequentially , the situation is similar to that of providing an independent overflow area in ISAM and should be avoided whenever possible .
100867	Splits in control intervals and control areas are shown in fig. 7.27 .
100868	VSAM provides the possibility of holding alternate indexes , so the user can reference a file using a number of different keys .
100869	The index set defined first is known as the prime index , to distinguish it from the alternate indexes .
100870	Alternate indexes are updated when records are added or deleted , if UPGRADE is specified in the alternate index definition .
100871	Alternate keys can be duplicated , unlike primary keys , so that a department code could be an alternate key and allow searches to be carried out to select personnel from a particular department .
100872	Keys in all VSAM indexes are compressed , only the distinguishing parts of the keys being stored , in order to reduce the size of index entries .
100873	These facilities make VSAM more similar to database software than most of the file organization techniques that have been examined so far — in fact , many of the database systems available for mini- and micro-computers provide only this multiple index facility .
100874	VSAM itself is used to handle the tables in IBM 's DB2 relational database software .
100875	VSAM can be optimized by careful design , applying the same principles that have been described earlier .
100876	The designer should look at the following factors :
100877	1
100878	The relation of data areas and index position to the physical characteristics of the device .
100879	The portability of a VSAM file from one device to another , and from operation under one OS/VS system to another , or from DOS/VS to OS/VS is helpful , as it allows for rapid conversion when different disks are installed .
100880	However , for optimum performance the size of control intervals and control areas should be so arranged that a sequence set record will be stored on the same cylinder as the control area it indexes .
100881	This means that movement from , say , a 3330 to a 3350 will require the definition of new control area sizes unless the number of control areas on a cylinder is already 2n on the 3330 .
100882	There will then be 3n control areas per cylinder on the 3350 and no loss of performance will result from the transfer .
100883	The way the conversion operates is shown in Figure 7.25 .
100884	2
100885	The size and number of the buffers provided by the user for VSAM directly determines the number of higher index records held in virtual storage ( as against backing storage ) .
100886	Hence , buffers should be both as large as possible and related in size to index record size .
100887	3
100888	Distribution of free space — the ability to define empty control intervals where they are required — means that careful planning with a knowledge of the likely distribution of additions will reduce the need for control area splits , and possibly of control interval splits .
100889	This will improve performance .
100890	Further details of VSAM are available in IBM publications .
100891	4
100892	The size of blocks used to hold data .
100893	Although the user may imagine that any block size will be acceptable , VSAM only uses blocks of size 512b or 2048b , where b can take any value in the range 1–16 ; this means that VSAM will round up any intermediate value to the next available block size , so wasting the difference between the two values .
100894	Choice of block size is therefore important if wasted space is to be avoided .
100895	Conclusion
100896	Wright has described both ISAM and VSAM files as applied to bubble memory , taking account of the particular design requirements imposed by bubble memory .
100897	He also provides a very detailed description of the medium .
100898	Jalics has compared the performance of IBM 's ISAM on a PC AT , a 370/158 and a 3081 ; contrary to expectations , the micro comes very well out of this trial , due to its use of an improved balanced tree index structure .
100899	Indexed files are easily created as a result of the provision of software by manufacturers .
100900	Improvements are offered by many software houses ; the designer will generally find that it pays to explore all possible optimization techniques for the manufacturers ' software before examining alternatives .
100901	In some cases , however , the design philosophy of another supplier will meet the user 's needs more precisely .
100902	A full examination of the application will lead to an informed choice , and optimum performance .

100941	FILE ORGANIZATION FOR MULTIPLE-KEY PROCESSING
100942	8.1 Introduction
100943	Much of data processing involves retrieving records that refer to a given customer , stock item or member of staff .
100944	In each of these cases a single key is all that is required to reference the record .
100945	However , in retrieving documents from a database holding the contents of a library , or when a request is based on meeting several different criteria , the situation is quite different .
100946	There are no longer any single ‘ keys ’ that uniquely define the document or documents wanted by the user .
100947	Generally , a combination of words or phrases is used as descriptors that can be combined to select the desired record .
100948	For example , a business in the United States may wish to assign an engineer to work in Japan for some months .
100949	The personnel file might be examined to list all the employees who meet the following criteria :
100950	Speaks Japanese AND
100951	Graduate Engineer AND
100952	Single
100953	The personnel department would make the final choice , from the list produced by this enquiry .
100954	If the resulting list were too large , further descriptors could be added to reduce it .
100955	If it were too small , the ‘ single ’ restriction might be removed ; if the whole family also needed to be sent to Japan this would add to the assignment costs , which might be an acceptable price to pay in order to send the right person .
100956	Multiple-key applications present different problems from those associated with the single-key files discussed so far .
100957	For smaller files , magnetic tape is the obvious storage medium — an example is the International Food Information Service described by Larbey .
100958	Small files that demand multiple-key handling are usually stored on magnetic tape and processed sequentially .
100959	A file arranged as in Fig. 8.1 has considerable advantages for the retrieval of records that meet some request based on a number of separate criteria which are often called record attributes or descriptors .
100960	Each record ( such as a title , a summary or a full text ) is characterized by the descriptors D1 , D2 , etc .
100961	Records 1 and 2 have a common descriptor D3 , records 2 and 3 share D6 , while records 1 and 3 have D1 in common .
100962	Record 4 has no shared descriptors with the other three records , although it may have with later records .
100963	The file organization techniques used for multiple-key processing are discussed in this chapter , but chained and tree structures used in database systems are not .
100964	8.2 File types
100965	Two main file types are used in multiple-key retrieval .
100966	These are serial , which was described briefly above , and inverted .
100967	There are variations of each technique , and they are considered below .
100968	Serial files
100969	The straightforward method of handling the examination of multiple keys is to hold all the keys in the record , as in Fig. 8.1 .
100970	A further example of this is shown in Table 8.1 ; each personnel record holds a number of fields , any one of which may be used as a key .
100971	A specific request might require a count of all the grade 2 employees in the systems department .
100972	This could be answered by scanning the whole file record by record , examining each to see whether it met the specified requirements .
100973	After all the records have been scanned a list of two names — Mason and Vince — would be provided .
100974	In the case of a personnel file , the list is likely to be sorted into an order that depends on some major key — in this case , usually alphabetic order or personnel number .
100975	If the file were made up of documents , books or papers the overall classification would probably be based on subject , and the order within subject might well be accession date .
100976	In these library databases the major key is often an accession number .
100977	In either case , the order does not affect the amount of searching to be done and in this sense the file is serial , although it will probably be in sequential order with respect to the major key .
100978	This type of file has to be scanned completely before a single query can be answered .
100979	Each record is examined in turn , and its descriptors are compared with those of the search request ( which might be like that for a graduate engineer with other attributes shown above ) .
100980	Because only one record is examined at a time , it is possible to test the descriptors against very complex Boolean conditions , expressed in terms of the descriptors desired by the user , to obtain a match .
100981	The work areas required in main storage are relatively small as only one record is being examined at any one time .
100982	However , as the data file increases in size , the time taken to search through the data increases in proportion .
100983	At between 20 000 and 60 000 records , the search time becomes so slow that it no longer allows a reasonable number of requests to be handled in a working day .
100984	The point at which this happens depends on a number of factors such as complexity of requests in terms of Boolean conditions , speed of access of the medium in use , and size of data file .
100985	A number of steps can be taken to speed up processing , each depending on some different method of handling the search .
100986	The first of these is the bit-pattern index , in which all the alternative descriptors for each record are given values of 1 if the attribute is present and 0 if it is not .
100987	The data in Table 8.1 has been organized into bit-pattern format in Table 8.2 .
100988	In cases such as that of a personnel file , for which the number of attributes is relatively low and the same for each record , a bit-pattern index can be a compact way of storing information about the file .
100989	However , it is not very useful for a bibliographic file in which there may be thousands of potential attributes for each record , only a very few of which are non-zero .
100990	The storage of this sort of data causes the difficulty that the compact format is counterbalanced by the redundant information .
100991	Bit-pattern indexes will be examined in more detail later ; however , in some circumstances a more rapid reference technique than that provided by a serial file is required .
100992	For this purpose , inverted files have been developed .
100993	Inverted files
100994	When records are to be selected on the basis of the state of one or more attributes , a serial search concentrates on the records , examining each in turn to see if it meets the specified conditions of the search .
100995	In fact , what is known from these specified conditions is the attributes required .
100996	A search of the records having a given attribute , to see which of them also has a second , third , … etc. in the required list , will eliminate all the records that are not wanted .
100997	This is achieved by inverting the file , i.e. by providing lists of records or record references possessing each one of the various attributes in turn .
100998	The resulting set of lists — which are , in effect , indexes — is shown in Fig. 8.2 for the same records in a data file that have already been shown in Fig.8.1 .
100999	A further example is shown in Table 8.3 , which is an inverted version of the data set out in Tables 8.1 and 8.2 .
101000	Given that a male in the operations department is required who is able to speak Italian , the male list is scanned first .
101001	This provides seven records .
101002	When the operations condition is added , only records 94 and 122 meet the double condition .
101003	Adding the need to speak Italian eliminates record 94 , leaving only a single employee from this small part of the personnel file , with personnel number 122 , who meets all the three conditions .
101004	A file in which all the attributes are inverted , i.e. have indexes provided so that a direct search can be made on any attribute , is known as fully inverted .
101005	A file in which only a number of selected attributes have indexes provided is known as partially inverted .
101006	In the case of a fully inverted file the designer has the option of holding very little information in the master file itself , and assembling records from their constituent parts as they are referenced .
101007	In practice many designers prefer to hold the complete record in the master file , as this avoids the problem of assembling information about attributes possessed by the record but not specifically referenced in the request .
101008	To take the example of record 122 , grade and branch were not included in the request for a male from operations department who can speak Italian .
101009	This information would not be automatically collected from the request , but is essential in order to describe the person fully , and the retrieval process has to ensure that it is provided .
101010	A master file record in a partially inverted file will always be required to hold at least the data on fields that are not inverted .
101011	The most usual arrangement is to have inverted lists of each descriptor , with a list of the major record keys and addresses or , if each record has a separate address , addresses only , for each of the records to which that descriptor applies .
101012	The master file contains the complete record .
101013	Keeping the index record size down is helpful because if the inverted indexes are small they can be held in main storage , and so cut search times down to a minimum .
101014	Inverted files should not be confused with the alternate indexes available in many indexed file systems such as VSAM or ICL 's 2900 series equivalent .
101015	Each such index can be used to give limited partial inversion , i.e. of one descriptor at a time , but they are generally provided and employed to allow the file to be accessed in ways other than by the major key , rather than to carry out an elimination of master file records not meeting some search criterion .
101016	An example would be to use department code as an alternate key to provide personnel listings by department from a personnel file arranged in some other order , such as alphabetic .
101017	When an inverted organization is employed , a number of limitations may follow .
101018	First , the file may not be able to support such complicated search conditions as a serial file , because the size of work area required to process a request is now much larger ; instead of dealing with one record at a time , the system now deals with all relevant records at once .
101019	This speeds request handling but greatly increases the work area size needed , particularly if a very widely used descriptor is the first to be cited in the retrieval request .
101020	Second , addition of records to the file is no longer a matter of adding to the end of the file .
101021	Each descriptor record throughout the file that applies to this new record has to be updated , so the process is relatively slow .
101022	Third , the space requirements for such a file are considerably greater than those for a serial file .
101023	Spiegel and Miller investigated IBM 's STAIRS/AQUARIUS system ( Storage and Information Retrieval System/A Query and Retrieval Interactive Utility System ) .
101024	The system uses four main files : a dictionary , a text data set , a text index data set , and an inverted file of all descriptors used in the database .
101025	These files are indexed by the use of BDAM ( Basic Direct Access Method ) and in a typical database of just over 2 Gbytes , which they found was the average size of those they examined , the number of characters in the files comprising the database was as follows :
101026	TEXT 864 000 000
101027	TEXT INDEX 83 000 000
101028	INVERTED 781 000 000
101029	DICTIONARY 442 000 000
101030	It is clear that the basic text file has been increased by around 150 per cent in order to provide the retrieval capabilities offered by the package .
101031	This is typical , and should he borne in mind before abandoning single-key reference , which usually involves an overhead of only 5 — 20 per cent in providing the facilities offered by indexed sequential or direct organizations .
101032	The system described by Spiegel and Miller could handle up to one thousand queries per hour , but many of them were relatively straightforward .
101033	Larbey described a tape-based system in which the text file contained a maximum of 1400 items , each of 4300 characters or less — six megabytes at most .
101034	This system provided SDI ( Selective Dissemination of Information ) on current data only to eighty scientists who used a set of thirty-eight separate query profiles .
101035	Each profile was made up of a combination of descriptors and Boolean conditions , and averaged twenty-six distinct search terms .
101036	Production of the complete SDI output took 12 minutes , or just under 200 queries an hour .
101037	A further file storage technique is sometimes useful in handling information retrieval applications .
101038	This is the multilist .
101039	Multilist files
101040	In this type of file there are the same sets of indexes as are required for an inverted file .
101041	However , in this case only the first reference to any descriptor appears in an index , while all further linkages are made from record to record ( rather as in a chain of synonyms in a direct file ) .
101042	The arrangement of the same data that has been shown in Figs. 8.1 and 8.2 , but now held as a multilist , is shown in Fig. 8.3 .
101043	Cardenas compared inverted files with multilists , showing that their space requirements are usually very similar , and that the speed of access provided by each file organization is dependent on the structure of the data .
101044	In particular , multilists provide rapid access when the file has many different descriptors that apply to only a few records , as in this case each chain will be short .
101045	Cardenas also commented that ‘ … the manner in which secondary indexes or dictionaries and associated lists are managed , may have under-estimated impacts . ’
101046	Much of this book is aimed at ensuring that file designers know how to minimize the impact of such indexes or dictionaries on space used and time wasted in file processing .
101047	McDonell provided a useful analysis of what is involved in addition , deletion or modification of records , so far as the maintenance and use of associative key lists is concerned ; he defined an associative key list as ‘ a list for each indexed key which joins together all the main file records containing that key ’ .
101048	He also compared multilists with inverted files , and showed that inverted files have an advantage when the indexes have to be altered frequently .
101049	As the performance of the two is relatively similar and inverted files are more widely used in their own right , most of this chapter deals with serial and inverted files .
101050	8.3 Record reference
101051	For small numbers of records , serial files have significant advantages .
101052	The first is that , because each record is dealt with singly , the main storage work area space requirements are very low .
101053	This allows relatively complex Boolean conditions to be built up and tested , such as : in the programming department AND able to speak French BUT NOT if in grade 3 UNLESS from North branch .
101054	In the example in Table 8. 1 the only person corresponding to this request is Duncan .
101055	In this case the BUT NOT condition was not fulfilled , but would in any case have been overridden by the UNLESS .
101056	This example is not in itself very complex .
101057	However , it indicates how very complicated multiple conditions can be built up in the creation of user profiles for information retrieval systems .
101058	This is because in searching a very large library collection it is essential to attempt to ensure that the user gets just those references that are required .
101059	A profile that provides far too many irrelevant references is of little use ; such lists normally find their way into a wastepaper basket because the user sees that they are full of irrelevant material and is not prepared to search through them hoping to find some relevant references .
101060	On the other hand a profile that fails to provide the user with required material is equally useless , however brief it may be .
101061	This second problem is more dangerous than the first because the user may not realize that information is missing .
101062	Information retrieval systems include the concepts of relevance — the proportion of retrieved material that is relevant — and recall — the proportion of relevant material that is retrieved .
101063	These are dealt with in some detail elsewhere , but the reader who wishes to study the matter in depth should consult specialist references .
101064	As the numbers of records increase , the problem of waiting for a reply to a query until the whole of a serial file has been searched increases in proportion , and eventually this delay becomes unacceptable .
101065	As mentioned earlier , one possible answer is to use a bit-pattern index of the sort shown in Table 8.2 .
101066	When the number of attributes is low , this allows very economical storage of the data about a particular record .
101067	A single bit represents each possible attribute .
101068	If it is set to one , the record in question has this attribute .
101069	If it is set to zero , the record does not .
101070	Searching such an index is very rapid .
101071	For simple cases an equal compare is all that is needed .
101072	However , this means that every attribute has to be specified .
101073	In an earlier example it was shown that a large proportion of requests only require some attributes to be present or absent .
101074	In these cases a Boolean AND condition can be set up .
101075	For instance , a request for a male in operations department who can speak Italian can be tested by comparing each of the bit-pattern index entries in Table 8.3 against a mask of : The Boolean condition will be an AND , which will only return a true indication if all these bits are on .
101076	A bit-pattern index can extend the use of serial files when the number of attributes is limited , but a break-even point will occur somewhere between 20 000 and 100000 records , depending on record size , number of possible attributes and the complexity of Boolean conditions required .
101077	In bibliographic applications the number of possible attributes may be many thousands .
101078	In this case the only possible solution when retrieval times become too long is to turn to an inverted file or a multilist .
101079	An inverted file is the usual choice , but when there are many attributes , each of which is used by relatively few records , it will be worth considering multilist files .
101080	It was pointed out earlier that one difficulty in using inverted files is the need to deal with all the records possessing a given attribute at the same time , so that a great deal of working space is required in main storage .
101081	This is reduced if there are many possible attributes because each attribute index list will tend to be shorter .
101082	Thus , the more suitable the application is for bit-pattern index handling ( small numbers of possible attributes ) , the less suitable it is for inverted file handling .
101083	The number of nested Boolean conditions that can be handled by an inverted file is generally less than the number a serial file can handle .
101084	In addition , the conditions OUT OF , specifying any n conditions out of a larger number , and BETWEEN .
101085	setting upper and lower limits to the value of an attribute , are difficult to achieve .
101086	These conditions can be very useful in setting up a user search profile , which is one reason that information retrieval systems often use a serial file for new accessions , which are matched against user profiles intended to inform users of the latest accessions in their subject field .
101087	This is linked to a complete file of the bibliographic collection held in inverted form .
101088	All the records in the serial file are transferred to the inverted file at intervals , generally when the size of the serial file is beginning to make reference to it relatively slow .
101089	The reasons for keeping down the number of updates to an inverted file are discussed below , and the form of a dual serial-inverted file system is shown in Fig. 8.4 .
101090	Such a system has been discussed further by the author .
101091	8.4 Additions and alterations
101092	Serial files can handle additions without difficulty .
101093	In very simple cases the new record is added to the end of the file .
101094	Even if the master file is held in a sorted order there will be no particular difficulty , as these files are usually stored on magnetic tapes .
101095	All that is required is to create a new file , although this can be time-consuming .
101096	Inverted files require quite different treatment .
101097	Ideally , the indexes should be held in main storage .
101098	They will certainly need to be on a direct access device .
101099	Addition of a new record will mean that a number of indexes will have to be updated , one for each attribute possessed by the new record .
101100	Thus , even if space is left within and at the end of each index , updating will involve the shifting and shuffling of a number of records or the use of pointers and links to the new records .
101101	The contrast between these two is a further reason for the popularity of dual systems .
101102	It is easier to handle the file in serial form until sufficient new records are available to justify the time and effort involved in an update of the inverted file .
101103	8.5 Storage requirements
101104	Serial files can be held in one coherent file .
101105	This is very convenient for the user as it requires the minimum of handling .
101106	An inverted file , however , has to be held in a number of related indexes , and is thus far more ‘ bitty ’ .
101107	In , the typical overhead of indexes and related files leads to a final size of about two and a half times the size of the corresponding serial file . However , there can very occasionally be a space-saving in the use of an inverted file as is shown in the discussion below , due to Revell .
101108	Suppose a file contains N fixed-length records and each record is comprised of a key of k characters and n data items of average size a characters .
101109	If this file is fully inverted , the resultant file will contain as many records as there are unique descriptor values — say V. The inverted file will be made up of variable-length records .
101110	For each descriptor value , the rest of the record will be a list of the keys of the original file records which possess that specific value .
101111	If the average number of keys in the inverted file records is A then : since the total number of terms in both the original and inverted files must be equal .
101112	The size of the original file is : and the size of the inverted file is :
101113	It is therefore advantageous , purely from a size point of view , to use an inverted file when : or
101114	For applications of size such that equation ( 8 1 ) approximates to :
101115	Additionally , if n is large the expression simplifies further to :
101116	Thus , the decision as to whether a file takes up more space in serial or inverted form depends on the ratio of the size of the key and the data items .
101117	Note that this is of limited use as it implies that the data is held only in the index or in the main file .
101118	The more usual arrangement is that the inverted indexes are an addition to the main file , as explained earlier .
101119	For this reason it is not often possible to achieve a reduction in space requirement by using an inverted file .
101120	Conclusion
101121	Serial or inverted files specifically designed for the retrieval of records on the basis of the values of multiple keys are a useful tool for the file designer .
101122	Generally the file itself , and the associated processing programs , will have to be written by the user if high standards of optimization are required .
101123	However , the alternate index facility of VSAM and similar software can sometimes be used to build the indexes required .
101124	Salton has reviewed the methods of handling information retrieval , while a number of authors have described specific techniques that offer advantages in particular situations .
101125	Ramamohanarao et al .
101126	described a mixed hashing/descriptor-based method of retrieval ; Nievergelt et al .
101127	presented a ‘ grid ’ file that performs particularly well when the number of search attributes is ten or less , and offers a high data storage utilization , good growth characteristics and efficient processing of range queries ; Stanfill and Kahle explain the principles of a parallel free-text search on a particular parallel computer , and claim a retrieval speed of 2 — 3 minutes for Boolean queries of 25 and 20000 terms respectively when the database in question takes up 15 Gbytes of storage space .
101128	Their method of searching does not depend on pre-determined descriptors .
101129	Many database systems use the inverted technique , and the convenience of having the software provided by such systems will often outweigh its relative inefficiency .
101130	‘ Tuning ’ of the database software may also be possible using manufacturer-supplied options to achieve results more in line with those attainable by programs written in-house .
101131	In order to obtain optimum results , however , there is no substitute for a carefully user-designed and written system .

101159	STRICT LIABILITY : RULE IN RYLANDS v. FLETCHER
101160	HAVING considered the tort of nuisance , we now turn to a further tort which had its origins in nuisance but which has developed in such a way that it is now quite distinct from it .
101161	This is the rule in Rylands v. Fletcher .
101162	THE RULE IN RYLANDS v. FLETCHER
101163	The facts of this case were as follows .
101164	B , a millowner , employed independent contractors , who were apparently competent , to construct a reservoir on his land to provide water for his mill .
101165	In the course of the work the contractors came upon some old shafts and passages on B's land .
101166	They communicated with the mines of A , a neighbour of B , although no one suspected this , for the shafts appeared to be filled with earth .
101167	The contractors did not block them up , and when the reservoir was filled the water from it burst through the old shafts and flooded A's mines .
101168	It was found as a fact that B had not been negligent , although the contractors had been .
101169	A sued B and the House of Lords held B liable .
101170	The litigation originated in an unusual way .
101171	It began as an action upon the case ( apparently for negligence ) at Liverpool Assizes , and A secured a verdict , subject to the award of an arbitrator , who was afterwards empowered by a judge 's order to state a special case instead of making an award .
101172	This he did , and so the case came before the Court of Exchequer which , by a majority , decided in favour of the defendant .
101173	The Court of Exchequer Chamber unanimously reversed this decision and held the defendant liable , and the House of Lords affirmed their decision .
101174	The judgment of the Exchequer Chamber was delivered by Blackburn J. and it has become a classical exposition of doctrine .
101175	‘ We think that the true rule of law is , that the person who for his own purposes brings on his lands and collects and keeps there anything likely to do mischief if it escapes , must keep it in at his peril , and , if he does not do so , is prima facie answerable for all the damage which is the natural consequence of its escape . ’
101176	This may be regarded as the ‘ rule in Rylands v. Fletcher , ’ but what follows is equally important :
101177	‘ He can excuse himself by showing that the escape was owing to the plaintiff 's default ; or perhaps that the escape was the consequence of vis major , or the act of God ; but as nothing of this sort exists here , it is unnecessary to inquire what excuse would be sufficient .
101178	The general rule , as above stated , seems on principle just .
101179	The person whose grass or corn is eaten down by the escaping cattle of his neighbour , or whose mine is flooded by the water from his neighbour 's reservoir , or whose cellar is invaded by the filth of his neighbour 's privy , or whose habitation is made unhealthy by the fumes and noisome vapours of his neighbour 's alkali works , is damnified without any fault of his own ; and it seems but reasonable and just that the neighbour , who has brought something on his own property which was not naturally there , harmless to others so long as it is confined to his own property , but which he knows to be mischievous if it gets on his neighbour 's , should be obliged to make good the damage which ensues if he does not succeed in confining it to his own property .
101180	But for his act in bringing it there no mischief could have accrued , and it seems but just that he should at his peril keep it there so that no mischief may accrue , or answer for the natural and anticipated consequences .
101181	And upon authority , this we think is established to be the law whether the things so brought be beasts , or water , or filth , or stenches . ’
101182	The judgment for the plaintiff was upheld by the House of Lords , but Lord Cairns L.C. rested his decision on the ground that the defendant had made a ‘ non-natural use ’ of his land , though he regarded the judgment of Blackburn J. as reaching the same result and said he entirely concurred in it .
101183	It may well be true , therefore , that there were two rules in Rylands v. Fletcher , the fairly closely defined formulation of Blackburn J. and the more flexible one stated by Lord Cairns , but the effect of the subsequent case law is to add the non-natural use requirement to Blackburn J. 's formulation , a development which has played a not insignificant part in the restriction of this form of strict liability .
101184	Genesis of the principle
101185	Such were the facts and decision in the case .
101186	Although Lord Cairns regarded the principles applicable as extremely simple , it seems clear that the common law was faced by a new and important problem which could not be solved by merely applying the existing authorities .
101187	This was not the first time that water had been collected in bulk , but hitherto those who indulged in the practice had generally been powerful bodies , like water or railway companies , who had acted under powers given them by legislation which at the same time made them liable for harm done by its escape .
101188	But here there was no statutory authority , and although there were several paths that seemed to lead to a solution , none of them went the whole way .
101189	Trespass did not really fit the case because the harm was consequential , not direct .
101190	There was a finding that the contractors were at fault with regard to the old shafts , but it is not clear that they should have realised that their conduct would affect the plaintiff 's land and even if this had been the case there would have been a serious issue at that times whether the defendant was liable for the negligence of his contractor .
101191	Nor was nuisance considered applicable , apparently on the basis that the defendant had no reason to foresee the injury .
101192	Look at the decision of the Exchequer Chamber how we may , it laid down a new principle .
101193	True , in the judgment itself it might appear that the court was making a pontifical statement of existing principle rather than laying down a new rule , for they regarded their own proposition as having been anticipated by Holt .
101194	C.J. some 160 years earlier in Tenant v. Goldwin , and they cited as instances of it the rules relating to cattle-trespass , the escape of mischievous animals and nuisance by the escape of fumes .
101195	But in fact Holt C.J. 's decision related to the escape of filth and his formulation of principle was limited to that and to cattle-trespass ; it was not nearly so sweeping as the rule expressed in Rylands v. Fletcher , which was reached by methods extremely characteristic of judicial development of the law — the creation of new law behind a screen of analogies drawn from existing law .
101196	And whatever views the Exchequer Chamber may have had about their decision , succeeding generations have regarded it as the starting-point of a liability wider than any that preceded it .
101197	Scope of extension
101198	It seems unsound , then , to dismiss the rule as a convenient summary of the theory underlying several specific torts which had existed long before 1868 , or even as the old cattle-trespass rule raised to a high power .
101199	The substantial advances which it made on the earlier law were two :
101200	1 .
101201	In the direction of things for the escape of which an occupier of land is subjected to strict liability .
101202	2 .
101203	In the direction of the persons for whose defaults in connection with such escape the occupier is vicariously responsible .
101204	As to 1 , the court took a rule of liability which had been more or less clearly perceived in connection with the escape of fire , cattle or unruly beasts , and extended it to the escape of mischievous things generally .
101205	As to 2 , they held in effect that the occupier from whose land these things escaped and did damage is liable not only for the default of his servant , but also for that of an independent contractor and ( as later decisions show ) for that of anyone except a stranger .
101206	‘ Absolute ’ liability of a misnomer
101207	It was unfortunate that Blackburn J. chose to describe liability under the rule as resting upon ‘ an absolute duty to keep it [ sc .
101208	the water ] in at his peril . ’
101209	Though stated as a rule of absolute liability , there ‘ are so many exceptions to it that it is doubtful whether there is much of the rule left . ’
101210	The liability may be strict , but it is not absolute as the exceptions to the rule indicated by Blackburn J. himself show .
101211	Recently , moreover , as we shall see , the courts have tended to erode and rationalise the rule so as to reduce the ambit of strict liability and to bring the rule more into line with the predominant modern philosophy of no liability without fault .
101212	As a result of this development the rule in Rylands v. Fletcher is sometimes unavailable at times when it is most needed , i.e .
101213	when the plaintiff can not prove that the defendant was at fault .
101214	SCOPE OF THE RULE
101215	Like all broad formulations of principle , the rule in Rylands v. Fletcher had to be worked out in detail by later decisions , and it has been applied to a remarkable variety of things .
101216	Fire , gas , explosions , electricity , oil , noxious fumes , colliery spoil , rusty wire from a decayed fence , vibrations , poisonous vegetation , a flag-pole , a ‘ chair-o-plane ’ and even ( in a case of very questionable validity ) noxious persons .
101217	As we shall see below , there is no liability under the rule unless there is some ‘ escape ’ from the defendant 's land , but there is no necessity that the thing be likely to escape .
101218	What matters for this purpose is that if it escapes it is likely to do mischief and this is the meaning to be given to ‘ dangerous thing ’ in this context .
101219	Too much stress should not be laid upon Blackburn J. 's illustrations in support of the rule since new law was being created .
101220	He was certainly not purporting to compile a representative list of ‘ extra-hazardous ’ activities — though one of the fundamental problems about Rylands v. Fletcher is perhaps that the law has never made up its mind whether the rule is aimed at such activities .
101221	Escape necessary
101222	Unless there is an ‘ escape ’ of the substance from the land where it is kept , there is no liability under the rule ; this was the ground of the House of Lords ' decision in Read v. Lyons &amp; Co .
101223	Ltd . ,
101224	where the plaintiff was employed by the Ministry of Supply as an inspector of munitions in the defendants ' munitions factory and , in the course of her employment there was injured by the explosion of a shell that was being manufactured .
101225	It was admitted that high explosive shells were dangerous .
101226	The defendants were held not liable .
101227	There was no allegation of negligence on their part and Rylands v. Fletcher was inapplicable because there had been no ‘ escape ’ of the thing that inflicted the injury .
101228	‘ Escape ’ was defined as ‘ escape from a place where the defendant has occupation or control over land to a place which is outside his occupation or control . ’
101229	Viscount Simon stated that Rylands v. Fletcher is conditioned by two elements which he called ( a ) ‘ the condition of ‘ escape ’ from the land of something likely to do mischief if it escapes , ’ and ( b ) ‘ the condition of ‘ non-natural ’ use of the land . ’
101230	But the House of Lords emphasised that the absence of an ‘ escape ’ was the basis of their decision .
101231	The rule is probably inapplicable to a deliberate release of the thing , the cause of action in that situation being trespass .
101232	Personal injuries
101233	The House of Lords in Read v. Lyons also considered whether under the rule in Rylands v. Fletcher a plaintiff can recover damages for personal injuries .
101234	According to Lord Macmillan , the rule ‘ derives from a conception of mutual duties of neighbouring landowners ’ and is therefore inapplicable to personal injuries .
101235	‘ An allegation of negligence , ’ he continued , ‘ is in general essential to the relevancy of an action of reparation for personal injuries . ’
101236	Viscount Simon and Lord Simonds reserved their opinions on this question , and Lord Porter considered that opinions expressed supporting the application of the rule to personal injuries are an undoubted extension of it , ‘ and may some day require examination . ’
101237	Lord Macmillan 's view must however be considered in context .
