103711	This will reduce the statistical power of detecting adverse effects that could be quantitatively important when used in low risk situations .
103712	Secondly , since the nature of the harm is usually unknown , larger numbers are needed than if it could be specified in advance to avoid spurious statistically significant adverse effects .
103713	A two step approach is needed .
103714	A trial is first performed to show efficacy and , within limits , to quantify the effect .
103715	If efficacy can be shown then the question of harm needs to be considered by using information from the trial itself ( however few the data ) together with other available data ; it may be necessary to set up special surveillance methods .
103716	If efficacy can not be shown and the proposed intervention is abandoned then the question of harm becomes irrelevant .
103717	Ironically , in the same way that the denial of the risk of harm associated with a possible preventive measure undermines the basis for performing a randomised trial designed to investigate the efficacy of that measure , the exaggeration of the risk of harm tends to undermine public health measures designed to introduce the preventive measure if it is shown to be effective .
103718	The fortification of staple foods with folic acid to prevent neural tube defects may be unwisely delayed on this account .
103719	A hypothetical risk of harm is a good reason to investigate efficacy ; it is not a good reason to block the introduction of a proved benefit .
103720	Ethics and resources
103721	Another problem arises from the ‘ low risk ’ situation in prevention trials .
103722	The general ethical approach applied to therapeutic trials , namely that there should be an approximate balance between expected benefit and possible risk to each individual in the trial ( so justifying the allocation of patients at random to a new or existing treatment ) is less relevant in certain prevention trials .
103723	Though the possibility of hazard should never be ignored , however remote it may seem , the ethical position in prevention trials often stems mainly from a balance between the extent of benefit ( if any ) , and the cost of the intervention .
103724	An example is the trial currently underway to see whether breast cancer screening by mammography is better yearly than every three years .
103725	Given that mammography every three years is effective in reducing mortality from breast cancer , it follows that performing examinations yearly will be more effective .
103726	There is an increase in risk due to irradiation of the breast , but this is likely to be small and is best estimated from a woman 's age and dose of irradiation .
103727	The issue is to estimate the marginal benefit from the increased frequency of screening examinations against the marginal increased cost .
103728	It is not an argument over which of the two screening strategies will confer the greater medical benefit .
103729	That is a foregone conclusion .
103730	That the ethics of prevention trials is often a resource driven argument is tacitly assumed but rarely explicitly stated .
103731	It is important that the profligate use of resources is avoided ; otherwise some patients will be denied a benefit because of the misdirection of limited resources .
103732	This is not to say that economy is paramount ; indeed , economy is secondary to what should be an overriding principle in public health — namely , equity .
103733	We all expect to benefit equally from clean water , clean air , access to screening facilities , and so on .
103734	Given that resources are limited , a screening policy , for example , should be designed to ensure that , whatever resources are available , screening is available to all and that a fair method is adopted to designate those at highest risk as screen positive and ensure that they are offered appropriate prophylactic intervention .
103735	That this is not always the case is apparent from our policy in cervical cancer screening , the bulk of which has occurred among young women , in whom the risk of dying of cervical cancer is substantially less than among older women , who have not been the focus of public screening policies for this disease .
103736	Also , current recommendations for screening for stroke and major coronary events by blood pressure measurements are not rational in that they take little account of the absolute risk of these diseases , specifying cut off levels for blood pressure screening that take little or no account of age .
103737	The formulation of research , as well as the practice that may follow , needs to recognise explicitly the issues of equity and cost .
103738	They are important ethical considerations .
103739	Medical practice and medical research
103740	Ethics affect both medical practice and research , but research usually falls under the closest scrutiny .
103741	There is an important distinction between practice and research that stems principally from intent .
103742	If an intervention is established as beneficial and worthwhile it forms part of medical practice .
103743	If we are uncertain about its value and apply it mainly to assess its worth then it is research .
103744	We have , in recent years , exaggerated this distinction and created an awkward divorce between practice and research .
103745	Much of medicine is uncertain , and the admission of that uncertainty creates the obligation to research the matter further .
103746	Practice and research are intertwined ; good doctors have an obligation to inquire as well as to provide a clinical service , and codes of conduct and ethical guidelines that recommend different rules for practice and research create an undesirable dichotomy that itself has ethical implications .
103747	For example , if a particular method of prevention ( or treatment ) is of uncertain value , there are many obstacles to be passed before the necessary research can be conducted , from seeking funds and securing the necessary collaboration to obtaining consent from many local research ethics committees .
103748	The difficulties tend to encourage the denial of the uncertainty and the assumption that the intervention is effective .
103749	It is easier to presume the benefit and call the intervention a service activity than to remain agnostic and call it research together with the inconvenient implications .
103750	It would be desirable if randomised trials in general , and preventive trials in particular , were an integral part of medical practice , adopted whenever a new approach needed assessment and a trial was judged to be the best way of accomplishing this objective .
103751	This should be supported by the health service as part of the programme of development that any large organisation must adopt if it is to remain up to date and use its resources cost effectively .
103752	The country would consist of a network of multicentre prevention trials funded by the NHS .
103753	Apart from the need to provide the necessary explanation about each trial , they need not be considered substantially differently from other activities of the health service .
103754	A serious obstacle to the conduct of such research , which is often necessarily large scale , is the need to consult many ethical committees .
103755	Clearly , the ethical aspects of each preventive trial need consideration , but this should be the responsibility of a central ethical committee and not a matter to be considered separately by many ( perhaps over a 100 ) district research ethical committees that are , in the main , concerned with local clinical research projects .
103756	The view that the ethical aspects of preventive trials can only be properly considered locally is unjustified .
103757	In general , the opposite is the case : the scale of the research and the kind of expertise required to assess the scientific , and therefore the ethical , validity are such that the research is best considered centrally .
103758	Underlying principles
103759	Four principles therefore underlie randomised prevention trials .
103760	Much would be achieved if these were more widely acknowledged .
103761	Firstly , the ethics derive from the interpretation of science as they do in all randomised trials ; secondly , quantitative estimates of efficacy are needed , to be balanced against reasonable estimates of possible adverse effects ; thirdly , in prevention trials the ethics can be largely a resource based argument with equity an overriding consideration ; and , fourthly , there should not be one law for practitioners and another for researchers .
103762	The obstacles to preventive research are found in many countries , including Britain , which has a distinguished history in epidemiology , public health , and preventive medicine .
103763	In spite of this Britain still has some of the highest rates of preventable disease in the developed world , such as for ischaemic heart disease and lung cancer .
103764	Too little is done to implement existing preventive knowledge or to develop preventive strategies known to be effective .
103765	Britain has a relatively poor record of instituting randomised prevention trials ; the Scandinavians , by comparison , have been more enlightened and more active in breast cancer screening .
103766	The importance of such research is not recognised in Britain .
103767	Individuals need to be persuaded that a concerted approach and a specific commitment of resources are required .
103768	In the United Kingdom , the NHS plans to spend about £36 billion in the calendar year 1993 ( about 15% of public spending , or 5.7% of the gross domestic product ) ; a small percentage of this should be devoted to the conduct of prevention trials and the implementation of worthwhile new preventive medical services .
103769	The scale of the venture means that a nation 's health service must accept a major responsibility for the work .
103770	Countdown to Community Care
103771	Newcastle : ‘ If it does n't work here , it ca n't work anywhere ’
103772	Newcastle upon Tyne , a city of 273 000 people and regional capital of the north east , starts off with several advantages for community care .
103773	Some are structural — the health authority , family health services authority , and local authority are coterminous — while others stem from tradition and a strong sense of community .
103774	Despite the familiar fears about the implementation of community care — not enough money , buck passing , and bed blocking — I was struck by the optimism of social services staff .
103775	Even so , there 's a clear split between the planners and the practitioners : the former see the new framework as strengthening existing good professional relationships ; the practitioners , in the health service particularly , fear it as a layer of bureaucracy that may undermine those relationships .
103776	Longstanding good relationships
103777	Newcastle 's Labour council has long had a policy of supporting its community — a policy that has informed many aspects of city life .
103778	Thus the underground transport system , the Metro , was built with disabled people in mind and council residential homes buy all their supplies locally , to support their communities .
103779	The council spends heavily on social services , partly as a general policy and partly to provide targeted services to vulnerable groups .
103780	Brian Roycroft , director of social services , is clearly proud of the standards of city provision and its responsiveness to users and carers .
103781	Roycroft also claims — and many in the health authority agree with him — that relationships between the social services department and the health authority , both managerially and professionally , have long been good and have helped underpin a high level of community care .
103782	Hence his belief that if community care ca n't work in Newcastle ‘ it ca n't work anywhere . ’
103783	Implementing community care
103784	Possibly because of this widespread feeling that relationships between health and social services were good , planning for April 1993 got left behind , and the city has spent the past few months frantically catching up .
103785	‘ If you had asked me a year ago , ’ said Roycroft , ‘ I 'd have said everything was going wonderfully well — but then it all fell apart . ’
103786	The main problem was rate capping for the city council , which meant that the social services department had to save £4m and lose 400 staff .
103787	Homes for the elderly were shut , and formerly nominal charges increased and extended .
103788	Three of the four people on the community care implementation team left .
103789	At the same time the chairman and chief executive of the Newcastle Health Authority left amidst acrimony about restructuring within the Northern region .
103790	Realising that things were getting behind , Roycroft pulled together a policy group consisting of himself , Gary Smith , and Clare Dodgson ( chief executives of the health authority and the family health services authority ) .
103791	Soon afterwards the chairman of the local medical committee , Dr Frankie Walters , joined the group — a move that many in Newcastle think important both symbolically and practically .
103792	The community care plan
103793	The core work on client groups for the 1993 community care plan is being done by the six joint care planning teams ( covering aging , physical disability , learning difficulties , mental health , HIV/AIDS , and drug and alcohol problems ) .
103794	These have representatives of the independent sector , users and carers , ethnic minorities , and the housing department as well as social services , family health services authorities , and health authority members .
103795	Although the teams have an important role in constructing the plan , they have tended to be marginalised because they control few resources .
103796	As John Harvey , director of public health , put it , many of the teams take a very global view for their client group , consult widely , come up with good ideas , and are responsive to users , but their influence is tiny .
103797	‘ They have become forums for airing aspirations . ’
103798	Harvey would like to see them bound more closely into the decision making process .
103799	As an example he cites a review that the health authority and the mental health trust have just completed of their mental health strategy , using the planning team as an important part of the consultation mechanism .
103800	One of the recommendations is that the planning team should implement the review by analysing different ways of providing particular services — crisis intervention , for example — and making recommendations to the purchasing authority .
103801	The purchaser-provider split
103802	To implement a purchaser-provider split within Newcastle social services department the plan is to let the fieldwork section , based in area social work teams , act as purchasers and the residential and day care section ( which includes home care ) to act as providers .
103803	Few people in the department see this split as being very real at the moment , particularly as it will be some time before budgets are devolved .
103804	Roycroft does n't particularly like the idea ; he thinks assessment and provision go together for individuals — a view shared by most of his social workers .
103805	Meanwhile the problem for the health service is that although the health authority sits on the policy group and is a coauthor of the community care plan , the work gets done — and the problems arise — in provider units .
103806	Both Gary Smith and Barry Dowdeswell , chief executive of the Royal Victoria Infirmary , Newcastle 's oldest teaching hospital , agreed that the acute hospitals had only just woken up to community care .
103807	Only now are they starting to organise training for their staff .
103808	As a result , said Dowdeswell , they had realised how lucky they were with their hospital social workers : ‘ The hospital teams have been very well protected within social services . ’
103809	Nevertheless , there are fears .
103810	Roycroft and Smith worry about perverse incentives : the fact that hospital treatment costs nothing , while people have to pay for the home care that will keep them out of hospital .
103811	Dowdeswell worries about meeting contract commitments and the costs of having a geriatrician concerned in all complex assessments in elderly people .
103812	Doctors and nurses worry about bed blocking .
103813	The ‘ real backbone ’ of Newcastle 's social services ; home care …
103814	Within the hospital
103815	Nurses at the infirmary have just been praised by the Audit Commission for their work on discharge planning , and a group of sisters in the orthopaedic unit confirmed that they had long taken this seriously .
103816	They discuss any problem cases with their hospital social worker each week , occupational therapists routinely make home visits before discharge , and if minor adaptations are needed a hospital technician will do them .
103817	Nevertheless , there are delays in discharge at the moment , often caused by silly things like a lack of commodes , and the nurses worry that if everything has to be in place before discharge then there will be more delays .
103818	But the blame is always with the system , not the individuals : ‘ We 're lucky with our social worker — she works wonders , ’ said one of the sisters .
103819	The strongest criticism I heard came from Dr Alistair Brewis , consultant chest physician and medical director of the Royal Victoria Infirmary .
103820	Not realising that the documents on discharge and assessment had been produced in a hurry to meet the government 's suddenly imposed deadline of 31 December , he criticised the two weeks he had been given to consult his 200 consultant colleagues .
103821	‘ The act is all about communications — but here 's a bad way of communicating at the outset . ’
103822	He found it difficult to get consultants interested in community care because it was only one on a long list of issues .
103823	Terry Sangwin , the nurse manager for the medical unit , thought staff in the hospital still needed much more information about what would happen , and she feared the planners did n't realise the impact community care might have on acute hospitals .
103824	Both she and Dr Brewis were also concerned about the many patients on their wards who came from outside Newcastle : they knew even less about the arrangements for community care within those districts .
103825	Jackie Marston , manager of the hospital social workers , was still negotiating funding for social work links with these surrounding districts when I met her and some of her team at the hospital .
103826	They were very positive about community care and saw it as natural development of their work .
103827	Marsden explained that hospital social workers had negotiated their role in discharge in the 1970s , when the Freeman Hospital had been built — ‘ discharges do n't happen without social services input ’ — and had then spread the same working practices to Newcastle 's other two acute hospitals .
103828	They were very aware of the fears about bed blocking .
103829	Indeed , they had just finished a three month study , half funded by the hospital ‘ at a time when it did n't have a penny ’ to assess bed blocking on one medical/geriatric ward that had particular problems .
103830	The delays were caused mainly by patients waiting for long term care ( because private provision had n't kept up with demand ) .
103831	As a result Anne Wilson , the ward 's social worker , is now funded half by the hospital to work at the Sanderson rehabilitation centre to liaise with community social workers and families .
103832	Anne Wilson and her colleagues were as concerned as anyone that assessments are done promptly .
103833	‘ Not delaying assessment and placement is important to the user and family — it maintains their confidence . ’
103834	They too mentioned things like delays in supplying commodes that currently kept patients waiting .
103835	All these examples , they thought , simply highlighted the need for better coordination .
103836	Indeed , Kate Weightman , programme director at the community health unit , thought that the planning envisaged by the community care plan would actually speed throughput by instilling the need to plan discharge from the outset of a hospital episode — and before when possible .
103837	Her unit is already used to joint working with social services .
103838	It manages the joint inspection unit for nursing and residential homes and runs the joint loan equipment service ( the one that never has enough commodes ) .
103839	She is also running awareness training in community care which brings together community health staff , general practice nurses , and social workers , and her district nurses already provide some joint training for their own auxiliaries and social service home carers .
103840	Assessment
103841	The fear about bed blocking is acknowledged in Newcastle 's assessment procedures , which speak repeatedly about the need not to delay discharge .
103842	Three levels of assessment are envisaged , and most people think that only the last of these — a complex assessment — will be new .
103843	The first level is simply to provide people with information on services — through hospitals , general practitioners ' surgeries , social services offices , and public libraries .
103844	Anyone can then request an initial assessment of needs , which will be provided if the person falls into one of the client groups ( elderly ; mentally ill ; with learning disabilities ; with physical or sensory disability or chronic illness ; with drug or alcohol problems ; or at risk of infection with HIV ) and is experiencing difficulty with daily living .
103845	Carolyn Stephenson , principal assistant ( community care ) in the social services department , does n't think any of this is different from what staff do already .
103846	People may , for example , be referred by general practitioners , who would be expected to provide any relevant information .
103847	In future any referrer will have to provide an agreed minimum data set .
103848	Moreover , ‘ if a person has been assessed by a general practitioner or a nurse for health reasons and they have identified social needs at the same time then we are committed to accepting that assessment , ’ said Stephenson .
103849	She said that some social workers were uneasy about that , and she agreed that it involved trust , but it was also to avoid abandoning the problem to someone else .
103850	What is also new , she emphasised , is that the assessment is of a need , not for a particular service .
103851	It will then be up to a care manager to decide on the level of service .
103852	This will probably involve a social worker in an area team putting together a package that might consist of a few hours of home care , a couple of days of day care , and night sitting for one night .
103853	‘ Probably these people do n't need a formal care manager , though someone will be responsible for them , ’ says Stephenson .
103854	The impact of the new legislation will be felt most for people who have complex needs identified as a result of a comprehensive assessment .
103855	The key criteria are that a person has a range of needs that can not be met by one agency alone and his or her ability to live independently is in jeopardy .
103856	This is the level where care managers will come into their own , thinks Stephenson .
103857	They need not always be social workers , and indeed , there is one care management pilot going on in the city that has a district nurse as a care manager .
103858	Here too , eventually , is where there will be budgets for care .
103859	Budgets and services
103860	But what will those budgets buy ?
103861	Before the allocations were known the social services department had worked out that ideally it would need £5.75m .
103862	It has got £3.2m .
103863	Already some social services have long waiting lists because demand outstrips supply .
103864	Nevertheless , Graham Armstrong , assistant director of social services responsible for finance and administration and now leading the community care project team , is more worried about the second and third years .
103865	Ninety per cent of people in residential care in Newcastle are on income support and the average time to death or discharge in residential care is three years , so his department will be picking up the whole burden by the third year .
103866	The main shift as he sees it is that the service has become cash limited overnight .
103867	‘ So we have to get the eligibility criteria tied down very tight .
103868	Yet if you establish criteria for nursing and residential care you are adjusting to resources , not need . ’
103869	In the first year Armstrong 's concern is to go for a minimum safe agenda — ‘ make sure clients are safe and then build on that . ’
103870	He has not therefore got very far with devolving budgets .
103871	In 1993 they will be allocated to area managers but not yet to care managers .
103872	This fits in with the traditionally tight control that local authority finance directors like to keep .
103873	Armstrong 's other concern is that budgets should be tightly tied to the information strategy , and his department is not far advanced with that .
103874	Another concern is to ensure that new sorts of responsive services are there to meet identified needs .
103875	As well as managing the market the social services department is having to nurture it .
103876	Stephenson thinks that unless there are no informal carers ( in which case providing continuous support at home is much more expensive than residential care ) much can be done to keep even very dependent people at home .
103877	But first those services need to exist .
103878	A night sitting service , for example , needs a certain number of permanent trained staff .
103879	‘ So there will have to be some block contracts to provide predictability for the provider , ’ says Stephenson .
103880	Likewise , voluntary bodies need funding to enable them to bid for contracts .
103881	The department had hoped to reach flexible service agreements with many voluntary bodies , but the city 's lawyers told them they either had to give grants ( guaranteeing nothing in return ) or set binding contracts .
103882	Care management
103883	Legal problems have also dogged some innovative experiments within the care management pilots the city is running .
103884	Lynn Boyle , a social worker from area 2 , told how the Inland Revenue had scuppered a plan to get unemployed women to provide informal care in return for expenses and small payments .
103885	The tax authorities insisted they put the women on the payroll .
103886	Like her boss , Boyle does n't see why assessment and care management should be separated .
103887	She sees assessments as involving a dialogue with the client , with social workers sometimes doing therapeutic work as part of the process .
103888	She thought enforcing a distinction would simply become bureaucratic .
103889	She also told of how social workers could stimulate resources very locally .
103890	Her area has many people with learning disabilities ; the community is tolerant and the housing stock suits conversion .
103891	Both the housing department and housing associations had helped with accommodation , and the social work team had started luncheon clubs and drop in centres for people with learning disabilities who did not go to day centres .
103892	They then persuaded user groups , voluntary bodies , and churches to take these services over .
103893	Boyle also spoke of her colleagues ' traditionally mixed views about general practitioners .
103894	Whether much good would came out of closer formal links between social workers and general practices very much depended on the general practitioners ' attitude .
103895	‘ GPs do n't understand what we do ’ — they referred inappropriate patients , and were often reluctant to pass on information .
103896	She also conceded , however , ‘ We tend not routinely to inform GPs .
103897	There is n't a sense of coresponsibility , and we need to change that . ’
103898	When the two groups do work together the outcome is better .
103899	Boyle cited a recent example of an elderly woman who was being physically abused .
103900	The doctor had helped assess the problem because she had a good relationship with her patient and had documented all her injuries .
103901	Another case in which good relationships would have helped was that of an attention seeking woman who had spent most of her life in hostels and was constantly getting struck off general practitioners ' lists .
103902	‘ It would have been nice to have worked through the issues with the GPs and negotiated with the patient . ’
103903	The Metro , a symbol of Newcastle 's commitment to supplying people in the community
103904	General practitioners
103905	Dr Frankie Walters , chairman of the local medical committee and a general practitioner in west Newcastle , agrees with Boyle 's analysis that relationships between general practitioners and social workers have not always been good .
103906	She too is optimistic that they are changing : ‘ We are learning to talk much more openly without scoring points . ’
103907	As a result of her involvement in the policy group all 46 practices in Newcastle were consulted over the draft discharge and assessment arrangements and had an opportunity to influence them .
103908	The family health services authority has funded Walters ' locum costs ( ‘ 14 meetings in two months ’ ) and the costs of training for general practitioners and their staff , and Brian Roycroft came and spoke to well attended meetings of fundholders and non-fundholders .
103909	One thing he did was to reassure them that planning was not as far advanced as they had feared .
103910	Nevertheless , most general practitioners remain concerned about the lack of detail in the assessment and discharge documents — and are waiting to see the more detailed information that is promised before April .
103911	They also worry that assessment procedures will raise expectations that ca n't be met .
103912	Walters knows well enough not to promise to deliver for general practitioners .
103913	‘ The most I can do is say , ‘ This is what GPs are thinking ’ . ’
103914	Also , both she and Clare Dodgson , chief executive of the family health services authority , worry that , despite the well attended meetings , there are still some general practitioners who know nothing about community care .
103915	‘ If they do n't know by 1 April , it wo n't be through want of trying , ’ says Walters .
103916	That so much effort has gone into getting general practitioners on board is a tribute to the widely held view within social services that general practitioners are not central to community care , but their capacity for throwing a spanner in the works is considerable .
103917	Yet both Clare Dodgson and John Harvey , director of public health , see beyond that .
103918	Dodgson thinks that the debate over community care has brought out a demand among general practitioners for attached social workers , particularly among fundholders .
103919	Harvey also sees general practitioners as having a key role in the information strategy for community care .
103920	Despite the firm figures in the community care plan ( see table ) , and social services managers ' confidence that they know the level of need in the city , he thinks they know little .
103921	‘ Need is not a static concept : we need a longitudinal view and to understand how needs change . ’
103922	He wants to know , for example , the risk among 100 people aged over 80 of any of them needing care over the next five years — because a carer dies , they have a stroke , or they develop dementia .
103923	As part of a locality purchasing project in the east end of the city he is working with several practices to see how general practitioners can provide this sort of information .
103924	The future
103925	The locality purchasing project also raises questions about joint purchasing .
103926	Everyone agrees that if the service is to be seamless there are enormous benefits in having people providing care across the health-social care boundary — ‘ one person providing bathing , bandaging , and hoovering ’ — and not bothering about who pays .
103927	But there are huge political difficulties with the latter .
103928	‘ Councillors are not going to give up their responsibility for how money is spent , ’ says Roycroft .
103929	Themselves accountable to an electorate , councillors are sceptical about the accountability of health authorities — and about health authorities knowledge of the community : to them it 's simply what happens outside hospital .
103930	Nevertheless , most of the planners in Newcastle think that the issue of joint purchasing and a wider debate about dissolving the boundary between health markets and care markets is one that the community care arrangements will increasingly force upon them .
103931	But all that is some way off , and not confined to Newcastle .
103932	For the time being Brian Roycroft assures everyone that they wo n't fall off a precipice on 1 April and that community care is going to work .
103933	Although Newcastle is having to run very hard to catch up with the mechanics of community care , Roycroft thinks that in terms of the spirit of the act , the city is already way ahead .
103934	‘ On things like consulting with patients and carers — we 've been doing that for years . ’
103935	Some guidelines on the use of cost effectiveness league tables
103936	Decisions to allocate resources in health care are increasingly influenced by relative cost effectiveness .
103937	To warn decision makers of some of the pitfalls currently found in cost effectiveness league tables and to suggest how meaningful comparisons may be made between health care technologies a published league table was scrutinised by examining its sources .
103938	This showed some of the methodological problems surrounding such tables and how such difficulties could be reduced in future .
103939	The source studies in the table featured different years of origin , discount rates , health state valuations , settings , and types of comparison programmes ; all of these differences may raise problems for meaningful comparison .
103940	Decision makers need to assess the relative value for money of competing health care interventions .
103941	In the absence of systematic comparisons such assessments are likely to take place informally .
103942	This will probably have a worse risk-benefit trade off than the formalised use of league tables .
103943	In recent years comparisons between health care interventions in terms of their relative cost effectiveness in cost per life year or per quality adjusted life year ( QALY ) gained have become fashionable .
103944	The principal motivation for this comparison is to help decisions about the allocation of health care resources .
103945	For example , Williams calculated the cost per QALY of a range of health care interventions and divided them into ‘ strong candidates for expansion ’ and ‘ less strong candidates for expansion ’ 1 to illustrate what could be achieved by using available data and to argue for further refinements .
103946	Recently , Laupacis et al proposed that the adoption and use of new health technologies should be classified into five grades of recommendation based on their cost per QALY , although they also acknowledged that many other issues other than cost effectiveness , such as ethical and political considerations , affect the implementation of a new technology .
103947	Cost effectiveness league tables have recently attracted the interest of decision makers in health care , such as those concerned with the allocation of public resources in the state of Oregon .
103948	The role of league tables has also been discussed in the British Department of Health ( H Neuberger , personal communication ) , although a final decision on the appropriateness of their use has yet to be made .
103949	Many argue that a league table of costs per QALY , if properly constructed , can provide comprehensive and valid information to help decisions on the allocation of resources .
103950	The potential dangers of the unthinking use of league tables , however , as currently presented have been pointed out by several authors .
103951	Despite such reservations , comparisons of cost effectiveness between health care programmes will inevitably be made by both analysts and decision makers , either formally or informally .
103952	We report some inappropriate comparisons and make some recommendations for constructing future league tables .
103953	We examined a recently reported league table and identified methodological deficiencies .
103954	We have presented guidelines to help decision makers interpret league tables as currently presented .
103955	Problems with cost effectiveness league tables
103956	The paper by Maynard contains a discussion typical of league tables .
103957	He presents a table containing 21 health care interventions ( see table ) and writes : The methods used to produce such estimates are crude but do facilitate the production of a ‘ league table ’ which ranks the cost of producing a QALY by investing in competing treatments .
103958	An example of these ‘ guesstimates ’ is set out in Table 1 .
103959	The implication of these data is that resources should be invested by purchasers in treatments which produce QALYs at low cost .
103960	Note that there is not necessarily presupposition that activities should be funded in the order they appear in the list nor that the same ranking holds for every location .
103961	There is a risk , however , that this inference may be drawn .
103962	The mere act of assembling data on a range of interventions gives greater prominence to the cost effectiveness data than does the reporting of the studies individually .
103963	It also implies a certain degree of homogeneity in study methods .
103964	That is , the reader is invited to believe that the ranking of interventions in the table is a function of their relative value for money , independently of the methods of the original economic evaluation study or the quality of the clinical evidence on which it was based .
103965	Closer examination of published league tables shows that the methods of the source studies are rarely homogeneous .
103966	We found that 20 of the estimates originated from six source studies , with one being of unknown origin .
103967	In interpreting the league table a number of methodological features are particularly important ; these are discussed in turn .
103968	year of origin
103969	The years of analysis in the source studies ranged from 1982 to 1989 , although all estimates were converted to 1990 prices for the comparison .
103970	The analysis in each source study reflects the then current state of knowledge about costs and benefits .
103971	Technological change may mean it is inappropriate to use results for which the ‘ sell by ’ date has expired — that is , the reflating of older values may be inaccurate .
103972	In addition to technological change , shifts in the relative prices of different interventions over time may affect the ranking .
103973	discount rate
103974	The discounting of costs and benefits occurring in the future was mostly consistent at 5% a year in real terms .
103975	This reflects the consensus in reports on economic evaluation and , as all the source studies were from the United Kingdom , the discount rate recommended by the Treasury .
103976	One of the six sources , however , responsible for three of the 21 estimates of cost per QALY did not discount either costs or benefits .
103977	As this study was concerned with preventing death , or as much as 30 years of long term serious disablement , by neurosurgical intervention the effect of this omission is considerable .
103978	In some of the other source studies discounting was quite appropriately not applied as all costs and benefits occurred within a year .
103979	The issue of discounting has been debated recently after a Treasury decision to apply a zero rate in the case of health benefits .
103980	Therefore there may not be as much agreement on this point in economic evaluations carried out in the future .
103981	The onus is on authors of the original studies to provide cost effectiveness ratios with a range of discount rates , a minimum requirement being 5% and 6% a year on costs and 0% , 5% , and 6% on benefits .
103982	preference values for health states
103983	Preference values for health states were most commonly derived from the matrix developed by Kind et al .
103984	Other of the source studies , however , used patient values , clinician values , or educated guesses .
103985	Different approaches to the estimation of utilities for health states generate different values ; this has the potential to reduce greatly the comparability of the six source studies .
103986	The degree of homogeneity in this league table , however , is greater than many because of the relative prominence of the ‘ Rosser matrix ’ in cost utility analyses in the United Kingdom .
103987	If league tables from North America were being reviewed these would probably show greater variation in analytical approach as there has been considerably more research into , and validation of , measures of health state preference .
103988	( See , for example , the table reported in Torrance and Zipursky . )
103989	At present it is difficult for users of league tables to satisfy themselves of the validity of the estimates of benefit used once these estimates have been concealed in a league table .
103990	Limiting the studies included to those that use the same measure of quality of life might lend a table some face validity .
103991	If in future , however , reporting of each estimate is extended to include descriptive profiles of quality of life — that is , health states and the valuations placed on them for the new and comparison treatment — then this may enhance credibility and allow reworking in alternative settings .
103992	Writing in the context of quality of life measurement , Cox et al pointed out that in reporting data the analyst has to serve unknown future users with unknown future interests .
103993	range of costs
103994	Detailed investigation of the range of costs considered in each of the six source studies was hampered by inadequate descriptions of methods of costing .
103995	This problem is likely to be encountered often by decision makers wishing to assess the methodological quality of published studies .
103996	In most of the source studies , however , only direct health care costs were included in the ratio of cost per QALY .
103997	Only one estimate included consideration of patients ' time , which biased the ranking of this procedure downwards in the league table .
103998	If more detailed information were available on costing methods further discrepancies in analytic approach would probably be exposed , with further consequential shifts in the league table .
103999	If future league tables report disaggregated profiles for resources and costs for each study then the costs may be validated or recalculated for the decision maker 's own setting .
104000	comparison programme
104001	The source studies reported in the table differed in respect of the type of comparison programme from which the incremental cost per QALY is assessed .
104002	The ‘ baseline ’ for comparison may have a major impact on these costs .
104003	If a comparison programme of no formal intervention is chosen it is important to establish that the costs and consequences of this have been valued credibly .
104004	‘ Doing nothing ’ is unlikely to have zero costs and zero benefits .
104005	Even in the case of a screening programme ( when doing nothing is a real option ) some cases would be found even in the absence of any organised service and there would also be the costs of treating disease as and when it occurred .
104006	Thus , for most economic evaluations , the notion of an option with zero costs and zero benefits is not relevant .
104007	A central problem for the choice of a comparison programme lies in the perception of the ‘ margin . ’
104008	In other ( non-health ) areas of social policy economic evaluations usually start with the presumption that all current activities are efficient — that is , worthwhile when compared with all alternatives .
104009	Additional money is allocated ( at the margin ) to the next most worthwhile activity .
104010	No such margin exists for health care provision , however , much of which has never been scientifically evaluated .
104011	Instead , health care provision has a political margin with budgets allocated on criteria other than cost effectiveness .
104012	Decision makers should satisfy themselves that current practice is itself worth having before using it as a comparison for a new treatment .
104013	If the comparison programme is inefficient the analysis will be misleading .
104014	Some of the source studies used to create the table compared with an alternative of ‘ doing nothing , ’ others compared with a minimum intervention ( which may differ among programmes ) , and yet others considered the incremental cost per QALY of expanding services to other groups of patients .
104015	In such a case , with restricted and non-standardised comparisons , interpretations across the programmes in the league table are fraught with difficulty .
104016	setting of study
104017	All the studies reported in the league table by Maynard originated from the United Kingdom .
104018	Additional complexities are involved if league tables contain studies from several countries .
104019	Gray pointed out the need to make adjustments for exchange rates by using appropriate purchasing power parities for medical goods and services ( Health Economists Study Group , Aberdeen , 1991 ) .
104020	A comparison of this approach with simple exchange rate conversions changed the rankings .
104021	More importantly , however , differences also exist between countries in clinical practice , the availability and relative prices of health care resources , and the incentives given to health professionals and institutions .
104022	In a recent analysis that compared economic evaluations of the same intervention ( a new drug ) performed by identical methods in four countries , Drummond et al showed that although the drug was 36% more expensive in the United States than in the three European Community ( EC ) countries considered , it was also more cost effective in the United States because of the relative price and use of other health care resources compared with those in the EC ( such as the higher charges for surgical operations ) .
104023	Considerable care should be exercised when extrapolating the results of cost effectiveness from one country to another or including them in the same league table .
104024	quality issues for construction of tables
104025	The descriptions of treatments listed in league tables are sometimes inadequate .
104026	Cholesterol testing and treatment seems good value at £1480 per QALY .
104027	This value , however , presumes opportunistic screening by general practitioners and the use of a series of laboratory tests on blood samples .
104028	It says nothing about the setting up of programmes of screening by invitation or the use of desk top analysers .
104029	Many authors have used estimates generated by others in their own league table ; did they check the original analyses ?
104030	In the table the value for continuous ambulatory peritoneal dialysis is not attributable to any of the source studies .
104031	The whole table has been reported here and elsewhere .
104032	Given the authoritative ‘ halo ’ effect that such tables evidently acquire , accurate reporting is a most basic requirement .
104033	Finally , the representativeness and quality of contributions to the league table may be questionable .
104034	For instance , Teeling Smith 's value for antihypertensive treatment to prevent stroke is clearly an outlier , with other analysts giving much higher values .
104035	Unfortunately , often it is not possible to comment on a given source study 's assumptions as only summary calculations are presented .
104036	Studies in which essential information is not available should not be included in league tables .
104037	Some guidelines for using current league tables
104038	Users of league tables should compare their own setting with that for the source studies included .
104039	In particular , they should pose three related questions .
104040	Firstly , in my setting could the interventions listed be applied with the same likely success as in the time period and setting reflected in the league table ?
104041	( For example , are the outcomes generalisable to my local need and clinical practice , and are the same service structures in place ? )
104042	Secondly , are the comparisons embodied in the various estimates of cost effectiveness relevant to my local situation ?
104043	( For example , if a comparison of a new intervention is made with current practice , minimum practice , or doing nothing do I agree that in my setting the same comparison programme would apply ? )
104044	Thirdly , are the resource implications and consequent costs similar to those pertaining in my setting ?
104045	( For example , how does my local availability of health care resources compare with that in the source study ? )
104046	It may reduce contention if comparison in a league table is restricted to those interventions targeted at one condition ( such as cardiovascular disease ) or at one group of patients ( such as elderly people ) .
104047	Although , inevitably , broader comparisons need to be made when allocating the whole health care budget , the homogeneity of the underlying studies is undoubtedly greater within more restricted boundaries , such as focusing on the mix of services for a given group of clients .
104048	Currently league tables present only point estimates ; this conveys a false sense of precision and encourages unwarranted conclusions .
104049	Possible changes would include the reporting of sensitivity analyses in league table documents or , as more economic evaluations of health care interventions are undertaken alongside controlled clinical studies , the use of confidence intervals around estimates .
104050	Even a methodologically sound table is unlikely to feature estimates with a high degree of precision ; they should be viewed in this light .
104051	Cost effectiveness estimates should not be used in a mechanistic fashion ; at best they provide a useful aid for decision making .
104052	Other factors — for example , equity — legitimately influence decisions .
104053	In particular a given league table is unlikely to contain all the relevant comparisons of programmes of the appropriate intensity or scale to enable a budget to be allocated .
104054	To approach this in a more formal sense would also require mathematical programming techniques .
104055	Conclusions
104056	Although league tables of costs per QALY may help decision makers in the allocation of resources , potentially they can also mislead .
104057	One approach would be to abandon the construction and use of league tables altogether .
104058	Whether or not league tables are reported , however , there is a natural tendency for evaluators to compare their study results with those for other health care programmes .
104059	Also , there is a need on the part of decision makers to assess the relative value for money from competing health care interventions .
104060	In the absence of systematic comparisons , as embodied in league tables , these assessments of relative value for money are likely to take place informally .
104061	This will probably have a worse risk-benefit trade off than the formalised use of league tables .
104062	Against this background we have outlined some of the problems with current league tables and made some suggestions for improving their construction and interpretation .
104063	Even if our recommendations were adopted by those undertaking economic evaluations and those constructing league tables , however , decision makers should still exercise the appropriate caution , care , and intelligence .
104064	Foreign body aspiration : a hazard of metered dose inhalers
104065	Metered dose inhalers should be carried with their safety caps on to prevent foreign bodies entering them and being propelled into the bronchial tree when they are discharged .
104066	Metered dose inhalers have a well established role in the management of bronchial asthma .
104067	If inhalers are carried in bags or pockets without their safety caps on foreign bodies may enter their mechanism and be expelled forcefully into the bronchial tree .
104068	The ensuing symptoms are often difficult to distinguish from those of an acute attack of asthma .
104069	We describe two cases of accidental aspiration of a foreign body after use of a metered dose inhaler .
104070	Case reports
104071	case1
104072	A 24 year old woman who had had well controlled asthma since childhood developed acute chest tightness and wheeze .
104073	She took her salbutamol inhaler from her pocket and used it .
104074	She then felt a choking sensation with increasing wheeze , tightness , and cough and rushed to the nearest accident and emergency department .
104075	She was 13 weeks pregnant , and her asthmatic attack was attributed to her pregnancy .
104076	She was treated with nebulised salbutamol , which relieved the symptoms , and was reassured and asked to attend the general medical unit of her hospital for follow up .
104077	She developed recurrent exacerbations of her asthma and regular use of salbutamol ipratropium inhalers and high doses of inhaled steroids were prescribed .
104078	After her delivery the symptoms did not decrease and a maintenance dose of oral prednisolone , 12.5 mg/day , was also prescribed .
104079	Despite this she continued to wheeze daily and thought that her inhalers were of no benefit .
104080	Almost a year after presenting to the accident and emergency department she was referred to our chest unit for observation and treatment .
104081	On arrival she complained of cough with purulent sputum , haemoptysis , and pain in the right side of the chest in addition to her asthmatic symptoms .
104082	A chest radiograph was normal , but a ventilation-perfusion lung scan showed a matched defect in the right lower lobe .
104083	Staphylococcus aureus was isolated from her sputum but she failed to respond to antibiotics , so a fibreoptic bronchoscopy was performed .
104084	This showed a conical hard object lodged firmly in her right intermediate bronchus , granular tissue , and purulent secretions .
104085	A valve cap from a car tyre ( 13 mm long ) was removed at rigid bronchoscopy .
104086	Her peak flow rates , which had improved from 200 to 350 l/min with nebulised bronchodilators , increased to 450 l/min , and her oral steroids were reduced .
104087	The time between her accident and the correct diagnosis was one year .
104088	case 2
104089	A 20 year old woman with mild asthma requiring intermittent inhalation of salbutamol developed acute chest tightness .
104090	She took out her inhaler , which was in her pocket without its safety cap on , and used it .
104091	She immediately choked , coughed , and felt that she had swallowed something .
104092	A one penny coin was recovered from her stools two days later .
104093	Discussion
104094	Aspiration of a foreign body during use of an inhaler has been infrequently reported since the first report in 1981 .
104095	Small objects like pennies , tablets , and screw caps can easily lodge in the mouthpiece of a metered dose inhaler and , when the inhaler is used , be forcefully expelled into the pharynx or larynx and inhaled into the bronchial tree .
104096	The importance of replacing caps on the mouthpieces of inhalers to prevent this must be emphasised .
104097	In both the reported cases the patients stated that they had inhaled or ingested a foreign body .
104098	In case 1 the similarity of the symptoms to those of an acute asthmatic attack and the fact that a nebulised bronchodilator resolved the acute event were misleading .
104099	The patient 's persistent and frequent respiratory tract infections and the inadequate control of her unstable asthma with maximal treatment could , however , have suggested the presence of a foreign body .
104100	Such a possibility should be considered in all patients with unstable asthma that is difficult to control with conventional treatment .
104101	In case 2 the symptoms resolved rapidly and the patient did not require further treatment .
104102	Doctors should take a careful history and be aware of this problem in the regular follow up of patients using metered dose inhalers long term .
104103	Careful instruction in the use of metered dose inhalers is an essential part of educating asthmatic patients .
104104	Patients should take a slow sustained inhalation when using their inhalers rather than a rapid deep breath as this may reduce the likelihood of inhaling a foreign body so deeply .
104105	Dry powder devices such as Diskhalers and , particularly , Turbohalers are possibly less likely to accept foreign bodies because of the fairly small sizes of their mouthpieces .
104106	Nevertheless , in view of the risks of inhaling a foreign body an inhaler 's safety cap should always be replaced when it is not in use .
104107	LETTERS
104108	Umbilical cord clamping in preterm infants
104109	Editor , — The possibility that late clamping of the umbilical cord may lead to a reduction in respiratory distress syndrome is not a particularly new finding , but S Kinmond and colleagues offer a more scientific approach in evaluating this phenomenon .
104110	However , they give little information about the obstetric features of their cases , which might be quite important since matching is essential with such small numbers — for example , were the babies predominantly born during preterm labour or were they delivered electively for some obstetric complication ?
104111	Also not clear is whether any of the mothers received steroids to accelerate fetal maturity before delivery .
104112	Although these matters may not be particularly important as far as the haematological features are concerned , they certainly are with respect to ventilation .
104113	I believe that more information on them would be helpful in the interpretation of the paper .
104114	Editor , — S Kinmond and colleagues ' results require further consideration .
104115	Immediate cord clamping may deprive the infant of placental blood , and previous reports suggest that a long delay may lead to adverse effects due to hypervolaemia .
104116	Holding the infant 20 cm below the introitus for 30 seconds before clamping the cord probably enables an intermediate and beneficial volume of placental blood to enter the fetal circulation .
104117	The question arises as to why a longer ( 60 second ) delay should allow a larger and thus excessive transfusion .
104118	Almost all women in Britain receive oxytocin-ergometrine ( Syntometrine ) at delivery , which causes an increase in plasma oxytocin concentration within 45 seconds .
104119	The resulting contraction could force an excessive volume of blood into the neonate .
104120	If so , the cord should be clamped before the increase in plasma oxytocin concentration .
104121	The time between administration of an oxytocic agent and cord clamping rather than fetal delivery and cord clamping may thus be critical .
104122	The authors do not state whether their patients received an oxytocic agent or document its time of administration .
104123	Further consideration of the physiological process of labour at term raises an additional point .
104124	Even when an oxytocic agent is not given a small proportion of patients show an increase in plasma oxytocin concentration during the late second or early third stage of labour .
104125	This increase in endogenous oxytocin could theoretically cause uterine contraction and excessive transfusion within 30 seconds of delivery .
104126	Did the authors record the time of uterine contraction after delivery and , if so , was there any relation to neonatal outcome ?
104127	Editor , — S Kinmond and others ' study of early versus late umbilical cord clamping shows an apparent improvement in outcome with a simple intervention but raises some questions .
104128	Firstly , is the position of the baby or the timing of the clamping of the cord the primary factor ?
104129	If the position of the baby is important maybe the two babies in the intervention group who were not held below the introitus should not have been included in the final analysis .
104130	Equally , one infant in the random group was held below the introitus , and the position of the others is not stated .
104131	Over the whole study was position a significant variable independent of the study group ?
104132	We note that the unit 's policy was consistent during the study .
104133	One of the significant outcomes was the volume of blood transfused , and therefore it is important for the transfusion policy to be stated , especially as the text does not suggest that the staff were blind to the study groups .
104134	On the basis of the figures given for the number of infants requiring blood transfusion there is no significant difference between the two groups for either ventilated infants or all infants ( χ 2 test , two by two analysis ) .
104135	There were three babies with chronic lung disease in the random group and none in the regulated group , but the total in the study is too small to say if either figure is different from the expected incidence of about 10% in this population of babies .
104136	The blood pressure stability is said to have been no different between the two groups .
104137	Was this an overall effect on blood pressure or specifically the beat to beat variability ?
104138	Beat to beat variability has been used as an indicator of hypovolaemia in preterm infants at risk of intraventricular haemorrhage .
104139	The proposed mechanism of improvement of placental transfusion of volume and red cells is attractive .
104140	As the authors have pointed out previously , packed cell volume is a poor indicator of red cell mass and a better measure would have been useful .
104141	The improvement may well be largely related to an increase in volume leading to an increase in blood volume in the lungs — an effect shown by transthoracic impedance techniques .
104142	As the authors state , it is important for neonatal research to look at simple interventions such as this .
104143	We believe , however , that further study is needed before firm recommendations about umbilical cord clamping can be made .
104144	Editor , — The paper by S Kinmond and colleagues suggests that modification of a common practice — clamping of the umbilical cord — may have important implications for the wellbeing of immature babies .
104145	Most of the previous research into the timing of cord clamping has concentrated on babies born near term .
104146	Rigorous steps to avoid selection biases seem to have been taken in only two of the four studies of immature babies — namely , those of Hofmeyr et al .
104147	The first of these two studies is referred to in Kinmond and colleagues ' paper as showing a reduction in the incidence of periventricular and intraventricular haemorrhage with delayed cord clamping .
104148	In addition , however , this policy was associated with more neonatal deaths .
104149	As the authors explain , the small sample size ( 38 babies ) led to imbalances in the baseline variables , which could explain the differences in outcome .
104150	Because of this the investigators subsequently carried out a larger trial ( in 86 babies ) , which did not confirm either the reduction in haemorrhage or the increase in mortality .
104151	There also seem to have been considerable baseline imbalances in the trial reported by Kinmond and colleagues , judged on the few characteristics described in table I , and so the same concerns must apply .
104152	The inclusion of birth weight as one of the enrolment characteristics is probably inappropriate .
104153	Increased placental transfusion in the regulated group should surely have resulted in an increased birth weight , as found in other studies in which cord clamping was delayed .
104154	Birth weight is therefore more reasonably considered to be an outcome variable .
104155	The principal outcome , and the measure on which the trial sample size was based , is the number of transfusions .
104156	In appraising the trial 's results it would therefore be helpful to know the indications for transfusion that applied at the Queen Mother 's Hospital during the trial and whether the decision to transfuse was made without knowledge of the policy on cord clamping .
104157	Immature babies are even more likely than others to have their umbilical cords clamped and cut immediately after birth to allow resuscitation and transfer to neonatal intensive care .
104158	Kinmond and colleagues ' study suggests that a short delay may improve outcome without any obvious deleterious effects .
104159	But , on the basis of currently available evidence , uncertainty remains .
104160	Before widespread changes in practice are made this finding needs confirmation in a larger trial with mortality and major respiratory and cerebral morbidity as the primary outcomes .
104161	Authors ' reply , — We agree that umbilical cord clamping at preterm delivery warrants further study of large numbers of infants , including those delivered by caesarean section and those below 27 weeks ' gestation .
104162	We believe that it is important to establish the management that results in optimal outcome for these infants and also to examine the complex mechanisms concerned , including blood volume changes and haemodynamic effects on systemic and pulmonary circulations .
104163	With regard to the specific questions raised , there were no significant differences between the groups in maternal or obstetric histories .
104164	Onset of labour was spontaneous except in two cases in the regulated group , in which induction was performed for prolonged rupture of membranes .
104165	Suppression of labour was attempted with ritodrine in four cases in the regulated group and two cases in the random group ; only one mother in each group received steroids antenatally .
104166	Oxytocin-ergometrine ( Syntometrine ) was given after delivery of the anterior shoulder except in the case of first twins ( four in the regulated group and two in the random group ) .
104167	Uterine contractions before cord clamping and beat to beat variability in blood pressure were not recorded and would both be interesting in future studies .
104168	The policy regarding transfusion of red cells was as previously described ; staff present at delivery could not be blinded to the treatment group but were seldom responsible for ordering transfusion .
104169	Our results were analysed according to intention to treat .
104170	Only two infants could not be held as low as intended , and omitting these from analysis does not substantially alter the results .
104171	Both time and gravity are important in determining the volume and rate of placental transfusion .
104172	Diana Elbourne is correct that the volume of placental transfusion received will contribute to the recorded birth weight ; theoretically this could mean a difference of up to 6% .
104173	Reanalysis of our data , with the assumption that all infants in the regulated group received a placental transfusion of 50 ml/kg ( probably a gross overestimate ) , showed no significant difference in weight between the groups , and results of stepwise regression analysis were not altered significantly .
104174	We believe that a multicentre trial with clearly defined outcome measures is necessary to recruit an adequate number of premature infants .
104175	Investigation of physiological effects and analysis of outcome for infants in various categories will point to optimal management of cord clamping and enable the establishment of practical guidelines .
104176	As June Alexander pointed out , the benefit of allowing foals a placental transfusion was established by veterinary specialists long ago .
104177	Problem lists in letters
104178	Editor , — As B W Lloyd and P Barnett emphasise , communication between general practitioners and hospital specialists is of utmost importance — the letter remains the most significant factor in this and often it is this initial form of contact which may determine the care a patient receives and set the tune of the partnership between the two doctors .
104179	Although Margo concluded that general practitioners were generally satisfied with the initial outpatient letter , most studies have found that communication between the hospital specialist and the general practitioner could be better .
104180	Defects which have been reported include absence of essential details , omission of information about treatment , no mention of what information has been imparted to the patient , and time delay .
104181	It may now be time for the different royal colleges to examine the possible use of a standard hospital letter for all specialties to general practitioners .
104182	Such a proposal would allow all doctors , whether hospital based or in the community , to focus quickly on important areas — for example , medication prescribed ; it would improve communication and reduce the risk of medical mishaps .
104183	It is highly embarrassing and totally inappropriate for doctors to shuffle through sheets of notes to locate one item of information while the patient sits waiting expectantly .
104184	Editor , — The short paper by B W Lloyd and P Barnett provides confirmation that problem list letters are welcome by their recipients , but it should not be taken to imply that these are a new invention .
104185	I learnt their use in the early 1970s from Dr P B L Muldoon , physician at the North Staffordshire Hospital Centre , and have personally used them since 1974–5 .
104186	They are , in various forms , routine practice for senior members in our department and , I am sure , many others .
104187	They may also include several additional items of useful information : the duration of disease ( for example , diabetes , malignancy ) or date of operation , the certainty or otherwise of a diagnosis , the existence of an unexplained or undiagnosed symptom or sign , and involvement of other hospitals or carers .
104188	Others include a complete therapeutic list at the end , particularly useful with multiple drugs and forgetful patients .
104189	An example could thus be :
104190	Insulin-treated diabetes with obesity ( 1971 )
104191	Active proliferative retinopathy ( recent laser at Moorfields )
104192	Diabetic nephropathy ( biopsy proven , last creatinine 237 µmol/l )
104193	Ischaemic heart disease ( CABG 1991 )
104194	Unexplained low back pain
104195	Recent bereavement
104196	Current treatment :
104197	Human Mixtard 24 units am , 16 units pm
104198	Captopril 25 mg bd
104199	Frusemide 40 mg mane
104200	Aspirin 75 mg daily
104201	Unknown analgesics
104202	As the authors state , such letters are also of benefit to hospital clinicians , who can focus on the problems much more quickly than by scanning notes ( often untidy or illegible ) plus related correspondence and results .
104203	The subsequent familiarity with the problems is often welcome by the patient .
104204	To write such letters well does indeed require a critical review of the evidence .
104205	There are other additional benefits .
104206	Copying of a single letter to all those involved in the care of a patient ensures that issues of overlap and interaction are less often overlooked .
104207	Such a recent letter , easily faxed , may provide sufficient data for an unfamiliar doctor or team to cope until notes are found , and if letters are stored as a cumulative file on a word processor a fairly complete history may easily be obtained from a secretary .
104208	It is surely time that the old style of letter , ‘ Your patient is doing well and should continue on the same treatment , ’ was consigned to the history books .
104209	Few of us would be happy with a bank whose statements read ‘ Your account is in credit but will not remain so for much longer . ’
104210	Editor , — I entirely agree with B W Lloyd and P Barnett 's view that a problem list in letters from hospital doctors to general practitioners is invaluable .
104211	I have been using it for some years and encourage my junior staff to do the same .
104212	I believe that the general practitioners find a problem list more informative ( although I have never investigated this formally ) and that the copy letters in the notes make a more useful case summary than the handwritten record .
104213	I take the system further in that I split the text of the letter up into sections pertinent to each problem .
104214	The sample letter would therefore become :
104215	Dear Dr Smith ,
104216	Re : John Jones 1.1.85
104217	456 Any Street , London N17 33X
104218	Problems :
104219	1 Poorly controlled asthma — Thank you for referring this boy with frequent attacks of cough and wheeze .
104220	He sleeps badly and is short of breath on exertion .
104221	I was generally optimistic but emphasised the potential for serious attacks .
104222	I prescribed sodium cromoglycate 10 mg ( 2 puffs ) three times a day .
104223	His relief drug is terbutaline 1 mg ( 4 puffs ) four hourly .
104224	Both are to be taken via a nebuhaler ( he has excellent technique ) .
104225	His peak flow was 180 today and I have issued a peak flow meter for his parents to establish the best he can manage .
104226	I have given them the danger peak flow value of 100 , and if it falls below this they will come to casualty .
104227	Passive smoking — I have advised his parents to stop smoking as it is likely to be aggravating the child 's asthma .
104228	3 Brother with Down 's syndrome — Close family involvement in the management of this child 's asthma is important , and this will be less easy because of the care that his brother also needs .
104229	4 Poor housing — I have not addressed this problem today .
104230	Review — 1 month .
104231	I believe that this arrangement of letters is even easier to read and to scan for items of particular interest and relevance , both for the general practitioner and during further hospital follow up .
104232	Editor , — Problem lists in hospital letters are an excellent way to improve communication , and they also enable quicker and more focused care for patients when they are reviewed at subsequent hospital appointments .
104233	I hope that general practitioners will increasingly use problem lists in their own letters .
104234	There are two traps for the unwary .
104235	Firstly , the problem list can be overwhelmingly long if all the minor problems are included .
104236	It is often better to be selective or list the problems in order of priority .
104237	This tailors the list to the condition that is under review .
104238	Secondly , there is a temptation to attach a diagnostic label to each condition so that it fits neatly on the problem list .
104239	This can lead to unquestioning acceptance of what is really a hypothetical diagnosis .
104240	It is better to use the symptom as ‘ the problem ’ if the diagnosis is unclear .
104241	My final point is a secondary issue relating to the sample letter .
104242	This was high quality until the last sentence , which suggested attendance at casualty if the peak flow fell .
104243	Surely in this fictional consultation the child 's own general practitioner would be able to assess the child and administer inhaled or oral steroid as effectively , if not more effectively , than a busy house officer in a casualty department ?
104244	The laryngeal mask
104245	Editor , — Moira E O'Meara and J Gareth Jones state that a laryngeal mask may prove life saving when a patient is impossible to intubate or ventilate by traditional methods .
104246	One such incident occurred recently in our theatres .
104247	A young man underwent uvulopalatopharyngoplasty and trimming of inferior turbinates to prevent him snoring .
104248	After induction of anaesthesia tracheal intubation proved difficult owing to an anteriorly placed larynx ( Mallampati grade II-III ) and the patient 's great size ( he was 201 cm tall and weighed 118 kg ) .
104249	Once tracheal intubation had been achieved with the aid of a stylet , surgery proceeded uneventfully .
104250	Two hours after the operation he developed a reactionary haemorrhage from the right tonsillar fossa and was returned to the theatre .
104251	The bleeding into his pharynx was so massive that he was unable to maintain his own airway while lying supine .
104252	With the patient on his left side anaesthesia was induced with halothane in oxygen and small increments of propofol intravenously .
104253	The airway became increasingly difficult to maintain .
104254	Removing the nasal pack and inserting a nasopharyngeal tube did not improve matters .
104255	Direct laryngoscopy was performed and the posterior third of the larynx visualised , and suxamethonium was given to facilitate intubation .
104256	Several attempts to force the endotracheal tube over a gum elastic bougie were unsuccessful .
104257	Preparations were made to perform an emergency tracheostomy , but spontaneous respiration returned and a size 4 Brain laryngeal mask was inserted , allowing easy maintenance of the airway and confining further haemorrhage to the pharynx .
104258	There was adequate room to position a Boyle Davis gag into the oral cavity and control the tonsillar haemorrhage , and at the end of the procedure careful deflation of the laryngeal mask cuff under direct laryngoscopic vision allowed passage of an endotracheal tube into the trachea .
104259	The patient was transferred to the intensive care unit and was extubated the next morning .
104260	Williams and Bailey recently described using a reinforced laryngeal mask for adenotonsillectomy .
104261	We do not advocate routine use of a laryngeal mask in anaesthesia to control tonsillar haemorrhage as it does not guarantee protection from aspiration of blood and gastric contents .
104262	It can , however , be life saving when traditional methods of intubation fail , and we recommend its inclusion with equipment for difficult intubations .
104263	Editor , — Moira E O'Meara and J Gareth Jones mention the life saving potential of the laryngeal mask when the patient is impossible to intubate or ventilate by traditional methods .
104264	The mask is useful before the patient reaches hospital , particularly when ventilation is required in suspected cervical spinal injury and movement of the patient is minimised , and for facial injuries , in which using a face mask is difficult .
104265	It can be passed when the operator is positioned in front of the patient , such as in a road traffic accident victim trapped in a vehicle , and the insertion technique is relatively simple and much less traumatic than endotracheal intubation .
104266	Although the risk of aspiration has not been completely eliminated , massive regurgitation is unlikely to occur , but avoiding ventilatory pressures greater than 20 cm H 2 O ( not always practical in a trauma situation ) avoids leaks around the cuff and minimises gastric dilatation .
