144525	Physicians should discourage the chronic use of costly systemic drugs whose unwanted consequences may be more troublesome than IBS itself .
144526	There is a place for the commonsense use of drugs .
144527	If diarrhoea is the dominant symptom and the threat of incontinence an embarrassing social handicap , provided that the rectum is not impacted on examination , loperamide may be of some use .
144528	This drug not only slows gut motility and decreases small bowel secretion , but also increases anal sphincter strength .
144529	Other examples of such targeted therapy include bran or psyllium for constipation , a 1-beta galactoside for excessive flatus , and amitriptyline for chronic abdominal pain .
144530	An important feature of IBS symptoms is their tendency to improve with placebo : in clinical trials the placebo response ranges from 40 to 70% .
144531	This shows the variability of the disease and supports the contention that no pharmacotherapy is generally acceptable for IBS patients without convincing demonstration of efficacy in defined-entry , placebo-controlled , double-blind clinical trials .
144532	Placebos may be useful in certain circumstances .
144533	It is said that if a placebo is to have a therapeutic effect , the patient must believe that it will .
144534	Nevertheless , in a group of neurotic patients , a placebo was effective even when they knew the pills they were taking were inert .
144535	It seems that the symbolic giving of medication has a therapeutic value .
144536	Certain logical ‘ placebos ’ such as bran or simethicone , which have a plausible rationale , may exploit these phenomena .
144537	The fourth and most important implication of the placebo response is that it reminds us of the beneficial effect of the successful physician-patient encounter .
144538	Continuing care
144539	For many troubled IBS patients seen by specialists , cure , or even acceptance of the diagnosis is an unrealistic goal .
144540	Emotionally disturbed patients benefit from regular , brief visits .
144541	These serve to reassure and control ‘ doctor-shopping ’ with inappropriate ordering of tests and treatments .
144542	Through such visits the doctor remains vigilant for a change in symptoms .
144543	Assistance may be sought from psychologists , psychiatrists , or other practitioners if needed .
144544	Some patients may benefit from a stress management programme , while severe cases may require the multidisciplinary services of a pain clinic .
144545	Although biofeedback and hypnotism seem to benefit some patients , such services are not often readily available .
144546	If the physician seems to lose the confidence of a patient , referral to a colleague may help by confirming the diagnosis and reinforcing the management plan .
144547	Graded therapeutic response
144548	We have noted the differences in needs among patients with IBS .
144549	The therapeutic response must be tailored to these needs if we are economically and effectively to use our resources .
144550	Most of those with IBS do not seek medical attention .
144551	Many of those who consult a primary care physician have acute symptoms that worry them and will respond to explanation and reassurance .
144552	Those who return for the same symptoms or are referred may require more attention .
144553	Those who chronically seek help from subspecialists are a small but costly subgroup in whom psychosocial factors may be more disabling than the gut symptoms themselves .
144554	The primary care physician should emphasise the positive diagnosis , the chronic yet benign nature of the systems , the role of stress , and the ineffectiveness of drugs .
144555	Bulk ( eg , bran ) improves constipation and is otherwise a safe , cheap placebo .
144556	For non-responders , once the above items have been dealt with satisfactorily , supportive psychotherapy and drugs for specific indications may be added .
144557	Overinvestigation or repeated testing without substantial indication undermines the patient 's confidence in the doctor 's conclusions .
144558	Physiological scoring systems and audit
144559	Scoring systems designed to rate the severity of an illness are being used for comparison of hospital units to identify different standards of care and to allocate resources .
144560	One such scoring system is the Acute Physiology and Chronic Health Evaluation ( APACHE ) system which is designed to assess the severity of illness of patients in intensive care units ( ICUs ) .
144561	It is widely assumed that different ICUs can be compared by the ratio of actual mortality to that predicted by the APACHE score .
144562	However , we suggest that the use of physiological data that can be influenced by medical and nursing intervention should not be used for audit .
144563	For example , by good care a patient may be made less severely ill and , therefore , may have a lower actual mortality while , at the same time , accumulating only a low APACHE score with low predicted mortality .
144564	This patient could have , therefore , the same mortality ratio as a patient treated inappropriately , who may have a higher actual mortality and a high APACHE score with greater predicted mortality .
144565	Paradoxically , the very accuracy of these scoring systems for assessing the severity of illness precludes their use for comparison and audit .
144566	Assessing standards and comparing outcomes are important in medical practice and allow comparison of different units and appropriate allocation of resources .
144567	Patient numbers and mortality fail to take into account the influences of different demographic groups or diagnoses and so these simple data are being abandoned for more complex assessments that generate an overall score and tell us something about how ill the patient is .
144568	It is widely assumed that these scoring systems can be used for comparisons .
144569	Scoring systems can be simple such as the Glasgow coma scale or the Apgar score , or can require more formal data collection such as the Trauma Related Injury Severity Score ( TRISS ) or the Acute Physiology and Chronic Health Evaluation ( APACHE ) II score , but they often include physiological data generated from the patient such as heart rate , blood pressure , or respiratory rate .
144570	We question the philosophy of using data that can be influenced by therapy for comparison of units .
144571	APACHE II is widely practised in intensive care units ( ICUs ) and has become the ‘ gold standard ’ for rating the severity of illness of critically ill patients .
144572	However , APACHE II was originally designed to compare the performance of ICUs .
144573	The score is obtained by finding the most abnormal value for physiological indices in the 24 h after admission to ICU ; additional points are given for age , chronic health status , and renal function .
144574	The primary reason for admission to ICU is chosen from a number of diagnoses .
144575	Each diagnosis carries a weighting , and the combination of this and the accumulated points gives a predicted hospital mortality .
144576	It is supposed that the ratio between the actual and predicted hospital mortalities , a value known as the standardised mortality ratio ( SMR ) , can be used to compare ICUs , but the following example illustrates the problem .
144577	Assume that two identical patients are admitted to two ICUs .
144578	The patients , being the same , have the same abnormalities of their physiological variables at the moment of admission , and also the same age and chronic health status .
144579	In the first ICU the patient is correctly diagnosed and treated to correct the physiological variables .
144580	In the second ICU the patient deteriorates , with worsening of physiological indices , before resuscitation eventually succeeds in restoring these indices towards normal .
144581	In the second unit the patient will clearly score more APACHE II points and will , therefore , have a higher predicted mortality than the same patient in the first unit .
144582	The second ICU , in allowing the patient to deteriorate , has performed less well .
144583	A number of reasons such as underfunding or worse medical staff may be responsible .
144584	A comparison of these ICUs could be very useful , but it is just this situation where the accumulation of points for physiological indices fails to allow such a comparison to be made .
144585	The second ICU allows most of its patients to accumulate extra points for physiological data , and , therefore , has a higher average predicted mortality than the first .
144586	It also has a higher actual mortality , because it looks after its patients less well , and so the SMR between the two ICUs will reveal little difference .
144587	The higher APACHE II scores of patients in the second ICU indicate that the patients were more severely ill , as confirmed by the higher mortality rate .
144588	However , what is missed is the fact that the patient is allowed to become , or is being made , more severely ill in the second ICU .
144589	If a difference in SMR had been found , then one of the explanations for this might have been a difference in performance between the two ICUs .
144590	Our example illustrates , however , that units that are performing badly and units that are performing well may have the same SMR .
144591	There will be , therefore , a temptation to judge the units by cost criteria alone , and expensive , but possibly good , units will be penalised .
144592	It could be argued that a poorly performing ICU is unlikely to occur in isolation .
144593	Poor care is likely to be given throughout the inpatient stay thereby increasing the actual mortality and giving a higher SMR .
144594	APACHE II scores on admission to ICUs can not be used for comparison of performances of ICUs as they fail to take into account the influences that management prior to ICU admission , such as stabilisation in an operating theatre or ward , may have on physiological variables .
144595	While useful for assessing the severity of illness of individual patients or groups of patients , physiological data that can be influenced by medical and nursing intervention , such as that obtained by the APACHE II score , can not , paradoxically , be used to compare unit performances and must not be used for audit .
144596	We submit that even scores such as the Glasgow coma scale and the Apgar score , which are assumed to be independent of medical management , may , in fact , be susceptible to a similar effect to that demonstrated with APACHE scoring .
144597	In certain circumstances , medical and nursing intervention can change all these scores .
144598	Therefore , to compare the severity of illness of patients , two options remain .
144599	The first is to use data over which nursing and medical intervention have no influence .
144600	The second is to add factors to the scoring system that take into account the interventions that have to be performed to achieve the physiological result .
144601	Some systems , such as TRISS , come close to these criteria but inconsistencies in the timing of data recording will lead to the results being influenced by therapy .
144602	We await the development of scoring systems that meet these criteria and allow comparisons of hospital units .
144603	REVIEW ARTICLE
144604	Are both aspirin and heparin justified as adjuncts tothrombolytic therapy for acute myocardialinfarction ?
144605	The use of aspirin and heparin as adjuncts to thrombolysis in the setting of acute myocardial infarction is controversial .
144606	Because the two agents have independent inhibitory effects on platelet function and the coagulation cascade , it has been argued that both should be used .
144607	Although the recommendation of combined use was based on rational pathophysiological principles , only randomised trial data can be used to assess the net risk-to-benefit ratio for the combination of these agents .
144608	We therefore reviewed data from randomised trials of myocardial infarction which provide evidence on the clinical efficacy of aspirin and heparin , alone or in combination , as adjuncts to thrombolysis .
144609	Evidence for aspirin as sole adjunctivetherapy to thrombolysis Aspirin , if given in oral or intravenous doses of at least 2 mg/kg ( 162.5 mg in a typical man ) , produces a rapid clinical antithrombotic effect due to immediate and near-total inhibition of thromboxane function and platelet aggregation .
144610	The Second International Study of Infarct Survival ( ISIS-2 ) showed conclusively the efficacy of aspirin both alone and in conjunction with thrombolytic therapy for the treatment of evolving acute myocardial infarction .
144611	The trial was randomised , double blind , and placebo controlled with a 2×2 factorial design ; 17,187 patients who presented within 24 h of symptom onset were assigned treatment with 162.5 mg aspirin daily by mouth , 1.5 million units of streptokinase intravenously over 60 min , both , or neither .
144612	The primary endpoint , total vascular mortality , was 23% lower with aspirin alone than with neither treatment ( 95% CI -30 to -15 , p &lt; 0.00001 ) , 25% lower with streptokinase alone ( -32 to -18 , p &lt; 0.0001 ) , and 42% lower with combined treatment ( -50 to -34 , p &lt; 0.00001 ) .
144613	Thus , the effects of aspirin and streptokinase are largely additive .
144614	For patients whose thrombolytic treatment was initiated within 6 h of symptom onset , the reduction in total vascular mortality was 30% with streptokinase alone and 53% with both aspirin and streptokinase .
144615	The mortality benefit attributable to aspirin therapy in ISIS-2 was similar when the drug was started 0–4 h ( 25% ) , 5–12 h ( 21% ) , or 13–24 h ( 21% ) after symptom onset .
144616	With aspirin there were also highly significant reductions in non-fatal reinfarction ( 49% ) and non-fatal stroke ( 46% ) .
144617	Similarly , there were fewer reinfarctions after aspirin plus streptokinase than after streptokinase alone .
144618	As regards side-effects , for bleeds necessitating transfusion , there was no significant difference between the aspirin and placebo groups ( both 0.4% ) , although there was a small significant absolute increase in minor bleeds among patients assigned aspirin ( 0.6% , p &lt; 0.01 ) .
144619	There was no difference between the aspirin and placebo groups in the incidence of cerebral haemorrhage .
144620	Thus , substantial mortality benefits can be achieved if at least 162.5 mg aspirin is given during the acute phase of evolving myocardial infarction .
144621	Moreover , this benefit is largely additive to that of thrombolysis and can be obtained with a slightly increased risk of minor bleeding and no increased risk of cerebral haemorrhage .
144622	Therefore , we believe that virtually all patients being treated for suspected acute myocardial infarction should receive a full dose of aspirin as soon as possible .
144623	Unfortunately , aspirin use in acute myocardial infarction is not universal .
144624	In a report on the treatment of acute myocardial infarction in US academic centres , only 58.7% of all post-infarct patients were taking daily aspirin 10 days after the index infarction .
144625	The proportion receiving aspirin within the first 24 h may be substantially lower .
144626	Evidence for heparin as sole adjunctivetherapy to thrombolysis
144627	There have been no mortality trials of adequate sample size to assess the role of heparin as sole adjunctive therapy to thrombolysis .
144628	Subgroup analyses from 433 patients in the SCATI trial provide the only available mortality data on the addition of heparin to thrombolysis in the absence of aspirin .
144629	In the subgroup that received streptokinase with or without subcutaneous calcium heparin , there were 10 deaths among 218 patients randomised to heparin and 19 among 215 receiving placebo ( not significant , 95% CI 0.22–1.02 ) .
144630	Furthermore , no significant differences between treatments were found for recurrent ischaemia or non-fatal reinfarction .
144631	The ISIS-2 trial , although not designed to assess the effects of heparin , also provided subgroup data for patients who received subcutaneous or intravenous heparin at the discretion of the treating physician .
144632	Mortality among streptokinase-treated patients was 8.3% for those who also received intravenous heparin and 9.0% for those receiving subcutaneous heparin .
144633	Neither mortality rate was as low as that achieved by the combination of streptokinase and aspirin without heparin ( 8.0% ) .
144634	We must emphasise that non-randomised comparisons of heparin and no heparin in ISIS-2 may be subject to substantial bias .
144635	If the decision to use heparin was related to severity of infarction , mortality could be falsely high in the heparin-treated groups .
144636	Conversely , because early death prevents the use of heparin altogether , mortality may be falsely high in the no-heparin groups .
144637	Despite the paucity of randomised trial data showing a mortality benefit of heparin as adjunctive therapy to thrombolysis , routine treatment of acute myocardial infarction in many parts of the world includes immediate intravenous heparin .
144638	This practice is based largely on the belief that intravenous heparin increases coronary artery patency rates .
144639	However , patency data on heparin as sole adjunctive therapy to thrombolysis do not clearly support this view .
144640	In fact , the two trials that directly compared intravenous heparin with no heparin as adjunctive therapy to thrombolysis in the absence of aspirin give contradictory results .
144641	In Bleich and colleagues ' study of tissue plasminogen activator ( tPA ) with or without intravenous heparin , the initial angiogram showed coronary patency in a higher proportion of patients who received heparin ( 71 vs 43% , p=0.015 ) , but there was no significant effect on rates of recurrent ischaemia or reocclusion in the week after infarction .
144642	By contrast , in the trial by Topol et al , addition of intravenous heparin to tPA had no effect on coronary patency rates measured at 90 min ( 79 vs 79% ) .
144643	Two direct comparisons of the effect on patency of heparin and aspirin as adjunctive therapy to thrombolysis are equally difficult to interpret .
144644	The Heparin Aspirin Reperfusion Trial ( HART ) directly compared tPA plus early intravenous heparin with tPA and 80 mg aspirin by mouth ; coronary patency rates 7–24 h after therapy started were higher in the heparin than the aspirin group ( 82 vs 52% , p &lt; 0.0001 ) .
144645	However , the 80 mg dose of aspirin used was inadequate to achieve a rapid clinical antithrombotic effect during the 7–24 h when angiography was done .
144646	Several studies have shown that whereas full-dose aspirin achieves almost immediate platelet inhibition , doses of 80 mg take as long as 48 h to become maximally effective .
144647	Coronary patency was also measured in the HART study at 1 week , when the low dose of aspirin would have achieved full effect ; the patency rates in initially patent vessels were 88% in the heparin group and 95% in the aspirin group .
144648	The other trial that compared heparin and aspirin plus thrombolysis is that of the National Heart Foundation ; selected patients treated with tPA and 24 h intravenous heparin were then randomised to continued intravenous heparin or aspirin ( 300 mg ) plus dipyridamole ( 300 mg ) daily for a week .
144649	The dose of aspirin was adequate to achieve rapid clinical antithrombotic effect .
144650	The trial showed no difference in coronary artery patency between the continued heparin and aspirin plus dipyridamole groups ( 81.1 vs 80.2% ) .
144651	Moreover , mortality and reinfarction rates were similar and left-ventricular ejection fractions at 1 month were virtually identical .
144652	Thus , this trial shows that 24 h after tPA infusion , an adequate antiplatelet regimen is at least as effective as intravenous heparin in maintaining vessel patency , preserving left-ventricular function , and preventing reocclusion .
144653	Thus no randomised trial with mortality as a pre-specified endpoint has shown a benefit of heparin as sole adjunctive therapy for thrombolysis .
144654	Furthermore , patency studies provide inconsistent evidence of efficacy , and no trial has shown a benefit of intravenous heparin over aspirin in adequate doses .
144655	Evidence for combining aspirin and heparinas adjunctive therapy
144656	Data for full-dose aspirin plus heparin as adjuncts to thrombolysis are available from large mortality trials with delayed subcutaneous heparin and small patency studies with early intravenous heparin .
144657	The Gruppo Italiano per lo Studio della Sopravvivenza nell'Infarcto Miocardico ( GISSI-2 ) , its international extension , and the Third International Study of Infarct Survival ( ISIS-3 ) are large mortality trials that have provided reliable and consistent information on the risks and benefits of combined aspirin and subcutaneous heparin or aspirin alone as adjuncts to thrombolysis ( table I ) .
144658	GISSI-2 and its international extension compared directly the efficacy of two thrombolytic agents ( streptokinase and tPA ) and also tested whether there are additional net benefits of adding anticoagulation with delayed subcutaneous heparin to aspirin therapy plus thrombolysis .
144659	All 20,891 patients received 300–325 mg aspirin daily by mouth , starting at the time of randomisation ; thus a substantial antithrombotic effect would have occurred by the end of the thrombolytic infusion .
144660	GISSI-2 found no differences in overall mortality between streptokinase and tPA , although streptokinase was associated with significantly fewer strokes .
144661	The addition of delayed subcutaneous heparin to a regimen of full-dose aspirin and thrombolysis had no significant effect on in-hospital mortality ( 8.5 vs 9.0% , p=0.29 ) or total mortality at 35 days ( 9.3 vs 9.4% , p=0.82 ) .
144662	Because the subcutaneous heparin regimen in GISSI-2 was delayed , it could have no more than a moderate effect on activated partial thromboplastin time .
144663	Even so , it was associated with a significantly higher rate of bleeding necessitating transfusion ( table I ) .
144664	This randomised comparison is consistent with subgroup data from ISIS-2 .
144665	ISIS-3 compared the efficacy of streptokinase , tPA , and anistreplase and of subcutaneous heparin versus no heparin among 41,299 patients with evolving myocardial infarction .
144666	All patients received aspirin ( 162 mg daily ) and the first dose was chewed for rapid and full antithrombotic effect .
144667	ISIS-3 found no differences in overall mortality among the thrombolytic agents tested , although cerebral haemorrhage was significantly less frequent with streptokinase than with the other agents .
144668	Nor was the addition of subcutaneous heparin to aspirin associated with any reduction in the prespecified endpoint of 35-day mortality ( table I ) .
144669	During the scheduled 7 days of heparin use there were slightly fewer deaths in the aspirin plus heparin group than in the aspirin alone group ( 7.4 vs 7.9% , p=0.06 ) .
144670	As in GISSI-2 , the addition of delayed subcutaneous heparin to aspirin was associated with higher frequencies of important side-effects , including major non-cerebral haemorrhage and definite or probable cerebral haemorrhage ( table I ) .
144671	Reinfarction rates did not differ significantly between aspirin alone and aspirin plus subcutaneous heparin groups .
144672	Taken together , the GISSI-2 and ISIS-3 trials provide data on more than 62,000 patients .
144673	Overall , they show that treatment with subcutaneous heparin in addition to aspirin and thrombolysis has no significant effect on mortality but does result in an excess of major bleeding necessitating transfusions , as well as cerebral haemorrhage .
144674	As well as large mortality trials assessing subcutaneous heparin , there have been three angiographic trials in which patients receiving thrombolysis and full-dose aspirin were randomly allocated intravenous heparin ( table II ) .
144675	Only one found any significant difference between heparin and no-heparin groups in coronary patency , and even that small increase was not associated with any significant improvement in enzymatic infarct size or recurrent ischaemic episodes .
144676	Thus , despite the widespread use of intravenous heparin no patency data so far support the additional use of this agent once full-dose aspirin has been given with streptokinase or anistreplase .
144677	For tPA , intravenous heparin added to aspirin seems to provide a small additional patency benefit .
144678	However , this benefit must be weighed against the higher rates of haemorrhage associated with intravenous heparin as well as the higher rates of stroke with tPA than with other thrombolytics .
144679	The routine addition of intravenous heparin to tPA therefore may not be clinically advisable , especially since tPA given with full-dose aspirin alone gives much better patency rates ( 75% ) than tPA with no aspirin ( 43% ) or inadequate aspirin ( 52% ) .
144680	Despite a lack of consistent evidence from patency trials supporting intravenous heparin , the use of delayed subcutaneous heparin in the GISSI-2 and ISIS-3 trials has been widely criticised .
144681	Sobel and Collen suggested that clinical decisions on intravenous heparin should await the outcome of unfinished trials .
144682	However , no large-scale randomised trial has been done , is forthcoming , or is planned that assesses the addition of intravenous heparin to full-dose aspirin in the setting of thrombolysis .
144683	The GUSTO trial assessed the risks and benefits of immediate intravenous heparin or delayed subcutaneous heparin in addition to streptokinase ( and found no mortality benefit ) , but did not make such comparisons for tPA or anistreplase nor provide any mortality comparison of intravenous heparin and no heparin .
144684	Also , because the tPA regimen ( front-loaded ) used in GUSTO differed from that used in GISSI-2 and ISIS-3 we do not know whether differences in efficacy are due to the more aggressive heparin regimen or to the more aggressive thrombolysis .
144685	At present , the only available data on the addition of intravenous heparin to full-dose aspirin plus thrombolysis are from non-randomised comparisons .
144686	In ISIS-3 , 4852 patients received intravenous heparin off-protocol .
144687	Overall , their mortality rate was higher than that of patients who received subcutaneous heparin but lower than that of those receiving no heparin .
144688	As discussed above , such non-randomised comparisons are likely to be biased .
144689	Thus , although these subgroup data are compatible with the possibility that intravenous heparin adds a small benefit to that already achieved by aspirin and thrombolysis , they also raise concerns about excess risks of stroke ( 2.1% with intravenous heparin , 1.1% with subcutaneous heparin , 1.2% with none ) .
144690	Net benefit-to-risk ratio of aspirin and heparin in the setting of thrombolysis
144691	Despite the lack of some important information , we believe the currently available randomised trial data can guide clinicians weighing the benefits and risks of adding aspirin and heparin to thrombolysis ( table III ) .
144692	For every 1000 patients admitted to hospital with acute evolving myocardial infarction , about 100 can be expected to die within 35 days .
144693	From the results of ISIS-2 , the use of full-dose aspirin immediately would prevent 23 of these premature deaths and cause no increase in risk of cerebral haemorrhage .
144694	From the results of all randomised placebo-controlled mortality trials of thrombolytic treatment , its use within 6 h would prevent another 27 premature deaths , although 2 or 3 treated patients would have non-fatal cerebral haemorrhage .
144695	Since the effects of aspirin and thrombolysis are largely additive , nearly half of all expected deaths among 1000 acute infarctions can be avoided by their combined use .
144696	Once aspirin and thrombolysis are given , however , the additional benefit of delayed subcutaneous heparin seems limited .
144697	From GISSI-2 and ISIS-3 , addition of subcutaneous heparin is unlikely to reduce mortality but will cause 1 or 2 further non-fatal cerebral haemorrhages and 3 other bleeds necessitating transfusion .
144698	The risks and benefits of adding intravenous heparin to aspirin and thrombolysis are unknown and will remain so until trials are done to address this question adequately .
144699	We believe therefore that the available evidence strongly supports the use of full-dose aspirin as adjunctive therapy to thrombolysis .
144700	By contrast , the routine immediate use of heparin for all patients being treated with aspirin and thrombolysis still requires testing in large-scale randomised trials .
144701	If designed appropriately , future studies on new thrombin inhibitors , such as hirudin and hirulog , can provide important and relevant information to this unanswered but crucial clinical question .
144702	ARRHYTHMIA OCTET
144703	Torsades de pointes and proarrhythmia
144704	Definitions of torsades de pointes and longQT interval syndromes Torsades de pointes is a ventricular tachycardia characterised by QRS complexes of progressively changing amplitude and contour that seem to revolve around the isoelectric line .
144705	The peaks of these complexes are successively located on one side of the baseline and then on the other , and this positive then negative polarity in the frontal plane of the ECG creates the typical twisting-about-a-point appearance ( fig 1 ) .
144706	Rates are 180–250/min .
144707	Long-short R-R interval cycle sequences commonly precede the onset of torsades de pointes .
144708	Moderately late premature ventricular complexes can discharge during the termination of the long T wave , precipitating successive bursts of ventricular tachycardia ( VT ) .
144709	The VT is commonly non-sustained but sometimes persists long enough to provoke syncope , or even death if ventricular fibrillation supervenes .
144710	The diagnosis of torsades de pointes is based on a characteristic VT and prolonged ventricular repolarisation time , with Q-T intervals usually exceeding 500 ms .
144711	Additional features that are sometimes present include a prominent U wave , abnormal contour of T or TU waves , T wave alternans , a subnormal spontaneous sinus rate ( especially in children ) , and sinus pauses .
144712	Long QT interval syndrome ( LQTS ) can be either idiopathic ( congenital ) or acquired .
144713	Idiopathic LQTS consists of three groups of patients who have a congenital disorder characterised by the above features : ( a ) the Jervell-Lange-Nielsen syndrome is transmitted as an autosomal recessive and features include congenital neural deafness ; ( b ) patients with the autosomal dominant Romano-Ward syndrome have normal hearing ; and ( c ) the sporadic form consists of a non-familial group with normal hearing .
144714	Acquired LQTS can be produced by class 1 and class 3 antiarrhythmic agents and a host of other drugs , as noted below .
144715	Pathophysiology : hypotheses
144716	The electrophysiological mechanisms responsible for the long QT interval and torsades de pointes in patients with acquired and idiopathic LQTS are uncertain .
144717	Based on the mode of onset of the arrhythmia , Jackman et al proposed a descriptive classification , labelling acquired LQTS ‘ pause-dependent ’ and the idiopathic forms ‘ adrenergic-dependent ’ .
144718	Experimental studies and clinical observations suggest that the cause of abnormal repolarisation may lie within the heart itself , perhaps in the form of an abnormal channel protein that reduces or blocks an outward repolarising potassium current or increases an inward depolarising calcium or sodium current .
144719	The intracardiac abnormality results in afterdepolarisations ( see Waldo and Wit , May 8 , p 1189 ) , probably early afterdepolarisations ( EADs ) , that cause triggered activity and torsades de pointes .
144720	Early afterdepolarisations are transient membrane oscillations triggered by a previous cardiac depolarisation that can be sustained in succeeding cycles by repeated triggering of the EAD to cause a tachyarrhythmia ( fig 2 ) .
144721	Blockade of potassium channels or augmentation of the calcium current can produce EADs that lengthen repolarisation and cause triggered activity and ventricular tachyarrhythmias experimentally ( fig 3 ) .
144722	EADs may be responsible for the prolonged repolarisation and the associated ventricular arrhythmias in both syndromes .
144723	Slow heart rates generally increase the amplitude of EADs whereas fast heart rates suppress them .
144724	This observation accords with the clinical finding that torsades de pointes often begins after a pause in the cardiac cycle and can be suppressed by pacing at a more rapid rate .
144725	EADs have been documented from the endocardium in a patient with quinidine-induced long QT interval and torsades de pointes .
144726	Intravenous magnesium sulphate promptly suppresses the acquired form of torsades de pointes and likewise suppresses caesium-induced EADs , prolonged QT interval , and triggered ventricular tachyarrhythmias in experimental studies .
144727	This observation further supports the use of magnesium to treat torsades de pointes accompanying acquired LQTS and furnishes evidence for the hypothesis that EADs cause the ventricular tachyarrhythmias .
144728	In patients with idiopathic LQTS , cardiac ‘ sympathetic imbalance ’ has also been proposed as an underlying mechanism .
144729	According to this concept , reduced right cardiac sympathetic innervation , presumably on a congenital basis , results in a reflex increase in left cardiac sympathetic activity , thereby causing LQTS .
144730	The experimental and clinical support for this hypothesis has lately been questioned .
144731	Although the left stellate ganglion has a greater effect on arrhythmogenesis than the right in many instances , this is most likely due to quantitative rather than qualitative differences between the two ganglia .
144732	Thus , the left ansae subclaviae innervates most of the ventricular myocardium , and stimulation of the left stellate ganglion results in a greater overflow of adrenaline in coronary sinus blood than does stimulation of the right stellate ganglion .
144733	This quantitative difference may also account for the beneficial effects seen after surgical interruption of the left stellate ganglion .
144734	Sympathetic stimulation ( mainly left ) caused by physical or emotional stress could periodically increase the amplitude of EADs that were present because of the intrinsic repolarisation abnormality , so that they reach threshold and provoke ventricular tachyarrhythmias .
144735	Deflections consistent with EADs have in fact been recorded from the hearts of patients with idiopathic LQTS and their amplitude was increased by adrenaline administration .
144736	Clinical study of sympathetic innervation patterns determined by the noradrenaline analogue , metaiodobenzylguanidine , and C-1 hydroxyephedrine scintigraphy in patients with idiopathic LQTS , have shown homogeneous uptake of the tracer in cardiac sympathetic nerve terminals in all regions of the heart .
144737	These observations do not disprove the sympathetic imbalance hypothesis but certainly do not support it .
144738	Keating and colleagues lately reported a link between a DNA marker at the Harvey ras-1 locus and LQTS .
144739	This finding confirms the genetic basis of the disorder and localises this gene to the short arm of chromosome 11 .
144740	The protein encoded by the gene is one of the G proteins ( guanine nucleotide binding proteins , see Steel , May 8 , p 1187 ) and may help to control the passage of potassium ions through membrane channels ; it is possible that the defect in LQTS lies in signal transduction at the level of these proteins .
144741	Clinical features
144742	Congenital long QT syndrome
144743	Patients with congenital LQTS can present during childhood with syncope due to torsades de pointes , often precipitated by heightened sympathetic tone — eg , from exertion or fright or as a result of being startled .
144744	Precipitating factors include loud noises such as alarm clocks and fire engine or police sirens ; observation of blood , accidents , and so on ; and sudden changes in body temperature such as when entering a swimming pool .
144745	A typical story is of a youngster who has a syncopal episode while running across the school playground and is then sent for a neurological evaluation to exclude a seizure disorder .
144746	Patients may have normal resting T and U waves that become enlarged and abnormal , both in contour and duration , during intense physical or emotional stress just before the onset of torsades de pointes .
144747	Since sudden death can occur in this group of patients , the duration of the ventricular arrhythmia must become prolonged in some cases and can evolve into ventricular fibrillation .
144748	However , unlike ventricular fibrillation caused by coronary artery disease or other organic heart conditions , the tachyarrhythmia in LQTS subjects often reverts spontaneously to sinus rhythm , whereupon the patient regains consciousness .
144749	The frequency with which arrhythmias and syncope occur varies considerably , from several times a day to less than once every several years .
144750	Occasionally , syncopal episodes decrease in frequency and may even disappear with increasing age .
144751	Sudden death can occur with the initial syncopal episode , but is more common after several such episodes .
144752	In some individuals , hundreds of non-fatal syncopal attacks have been noted .
144753	The frequency of sudden death may be as high as 80% in some families at great risk and less than 5% in others .
144754	Patients at increased risk include those with family members who died suddenly at an early age and those who have experienced syncope .
144755	Patients with Jervell-Lange-Nielsen syndrome may be more at risk than those with Romano-Ward syndrome .
144756	The clinical manifestations of both genetic forms of LQTS are otherwise similar , except for the presence of deafness , as mentioned above .
144757	Physical examination is normal in patients with LQTS , and there is no evidence of structural heart disease .
144758	Chest radiographs and laboratory tests are likewise usually normal .
144759	Haemodynamic and angiographic observations at cardiac catheterisation are unremarkable , although abnormal wall motion detected by echocardiography has been noted recently .
144760	Electrophysiological studies with premature ventricular stimulation generally do not induce ventricular arrhythmias .
144761	In some patients , EADs can be recorded from the right or left ventricular endocardium , especially after provocation with intravenous adrenaline .
144762	ECGs should be obtained in all family members when the index case presents with symptoms .
144763	The ECG manifestations may be more prominent in a sibling or a parent and can help to make the correct diagnosis .
144764	Valsalva or stress testing can prolong the QT interval , produce T wave alternans , and reveal notched T waves , especially during the early recovery phase .
144765	Patients should undergo prolonged ECG recordings , with various forms of provocation — eg , auditory stimuli , psychological stress , cold pressor stimulation , and exercise — designed to evoke ventricular arrhythmias .
144766	Catecholamine infusions are helpful in some patients , but this challenge must be carried out cautiously , with resuscitation equipment and alpha and beta antagonists close at hand .
144767	Spectral analysis of ambulatory ECG recordings from patients with congenital LQTS has shown an abnormal pattern of heart rate variability .
144768	Acquired long QT syndrome
144769	Acquired LQTS is largely an iatrogenic disease , most cases being related to drug therapy .
144770	The agents and clinical situations that cause torsades de pointes also prolong repolarisation .
144771	The principal manifestation of the syndrome is syncope or presyncope , often accompanied by palpitations .
144772	Sudden death can occur .
144773	Antiarrhythmic drugs — Among type 1a antiarrhythmic drugs , quinidine seems to have the greatest potential for causing torsades de pointes and is estimated to produce syncope in 0.5–4.0% of patients as a result of this tachyarrhythmia .
144774	Quinidine prolongs the QT interval in most patients , whether or not ventricular arrhythmias occur , but significant QT prolongation ( 500–600 ms ) is more often a characteristic of patients with quinidine syncope .
144775	Many of these patients are also receiving digitalis or diuretics , and the latter increase the risk by producing hypokalaemia .
144776	Syncope is unrelated to plasma concentrations of quinidine or duration of therapy , and torsades de pointes can occur at low ( ‘ subtherapeutic ’ ) plasma concentrations .
144777	Procainamide and disopyramide likewise have the potential for causing torsades de pointes .
144778	Many of the cases of torsades de pointes reported during procainamide therapy may be due to the actions of its active metabolite , N-acetylprocainamide , which often accumulates in patients with renal disease .
144779	There is some evidence that patients who get torsades de pointes in response to one type of 1a antiarrhythmic drug have an increased incidence of this arrhythmia in response to other drugs in the same class .
144780	Class 3 drugs such as amiodarone , sotalol , and sematilide can precipitate torsades de pointes .
144781	Although class 1c agents such as encainide and flecainide can have pronounced proarrhythmic actions , torsades de pointes is uncommon .
144782	Similarly , class 1b drugs do not produce torsades de pointes .
144783	Non-cardiac drugs — Several pharmacological agents in addition to the antiarrhythmic drugs have been associated with LQTS and torsades de pointes — eg , phenothiazines , tricyclic and occasionally tetracyclic antidepressants , antihistamines of the H1 blocking type ( astemizole and terfenadine ) , and some antibiotics , most notably erythromycin .
144784	Phenothiazines have prominent electrophysiological effects , and moricizine , a phenothiazine derivative , is used to treat patients with ventricular tachyarrhythmias .
144785	Thioridazine prolongs the QT interval , produces T wave changes and occasionally torsades de pointes , and has been implicated as a cause of sudden death in schizophrenics .
144786	Other phenothiazines have less propensity to produce the arrhythmia .
144787	Haloperidol has been implicated as a cause of torsades de pointes and death .
144788	It is noteworthy that some apparently harmless drugs can , under the appropriate circumstances ( eg , the combination of terfenadine and erythromycin ) , create life-threatening ventricular arrhythmias , and physicians can unwittingly expose their patients to risk .
144789	Metabolic and electrolyte disorders — The relation between electrolyte abnormalities and cardiac arrhythmias is well known .
144790	Hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia , when severe , can prolong repolarisation and precipitate torsades de pointes .
144791	There seems to be a synergistic effect between these electrolyte disorders and therapy with class 1a antiarrhythmic drugs .
144792	Liquid protein diets , and nutritional disorders such as starvation and anorexia nervosa , have likewise been associated with QT prolongation , torsades de pointes , and sudden death .
144793	There are a few isolated reports of hypothyroidism as a cause of torsades de pointes , but in most of these cases other abnormalities were present .
144794	Bradycardia — Bradycardia can beget tachycardia .
144795	VT has long been recognised as a complication of severe bradyarrhythmias , and less commonly can be the cause of syncope and death in patients with complete atrioventricular block or sinus node dysfunction .
144796	Central nervous system lesions — Intracranial disease , most notably subarachnoid haemorrhage but also intracerebral haemorrhage , cerebrovascular occlusive disease , trauma , and encephalitis , occasionally produces torsades de pointes , probably due to the influence of the autonomic nervous system on ventricular repolarisation .
144797	Miscellaneous — Mitral valve prolapse or cardiac ganglionitis can be responsible for LQTS , and there may be an association between LQTS and sudden infant death syndrome .
144798	Certain cardiac substrates — eg , left ventricular hypertrophy — may be associated with a prolonged repolarisation time and a predisposition to acquired LQTS .
144799	Proarrhythmia
144800	Antiarrhythmic agents can worsen existing arrhythmias or cause new ones .
144801	This effect of drug-induced aggravation or provocation of arrhythmias is known as ‘ proarrhythmia ’ .
144802	All types of bradyarrhythmia and tachyarrhythmia , whether supraventricular or ventricular , can be worsened or provoked by antiarrhythmic drugs .
144803	The aggravation can be manifested as an increase in the frequency of arrhythmic episodes , in their duration , in the rate of the arrhythmia , or as an altered response of the arrhythmia to DC countershock .
144804	Torsades de pointes is the prototype of the new ventricular tachyarrhythmias provoked by antiarrhythmic drugs .
144805	Incessant monomorphic VT is another common form of proarrhythmia ; this arrhythmia is often the result of class 1c antiarrhythmic agents and usually has a QRS complex with a very long duration so that it appears ‘ sinusoidal ’ in contour .
144806	The arrhythmia is sustained and occurs more commonly in patients with a reduced ejection fraction who are receiving treatment for VT .
144807	During therapy with class 1a drugs , the risk of developing proarrhythmia is increased by the presence of bradycardia , hypokalaemia , or hypomagnesaemia .
144808	Atrial fibrillation , with its constantly varying RR intervals and varying action potential durations , also seems to increase the risk of proarrhythmia .
144809	Although women comprise the minority of patients receiving antiarrhythmic drugs for ventricular arrhythmias , they represent almost half the reported cases of torsades de pointes due to class 1 drugs .
144810	It is impossible to predict when QT prolongation will be beneficial , in that it represents a prolongation of ventricular refractoriness , and when it will be harmful .
144811	The QT interval beyond which the risk of torsades de pointes increases abruptly has not yet been defined and most likely there is a continuum .
144812	However , patients with quinidine-induced torsades de pointes usually have QT intervals exceeding 550 ms .
144813	Patients at risk are probably those with pre-existing QT prolongation , bradycardia not corrected by a pacemaker , hypokalaemia or hypomagnesaemia , a history of developing torsades de pointes with similar drugs ( because of cross-sensitivity ) , and genetic abnormalities in drug metabolism .
144814	Perhaps an increase in regional QT interval dispersion — ie , refractory period prolongation in some areas of the ventricle but not others — during class 1a drug therapy can predict the occurrence of torsades de pointes .
144815	Patients at risk of a proarrhythmic response also include those with a history of sustained VT and reduced ejection fraction .
144816	In general , drug-induced ventricular tachyarrhythmias develop soon after drug therapy begins .
144817	Onset of proarrhythmia after a period of stable , long-term drug treatment is probably due to an intervening event such as ischaemia , hypokalaemia , the addition of another drug , or change in drug dose .
144818	During the CAST investigation , patients who had a proarrhythmia response during the early period of drug exposure were eliminated from the long-term study .
144819	Subsequently , an apparently very different kind of proarrhythmic response occurred : patients died at a constant rate during the 10-month treatment period with flecainide and encainide , and the mortality paralleled the number of observed ischaemic episodes .
144820	These data suggest an interaction between the antiarrhythmic agent and ischaemia — ie , the antiarrhythmic drug , which slows conduction as its usual mechanism of action , may have intensified the regional ventricular conduction delay accompanying ischaemia and caused ventricular fibrillation during ischaemic episodes .
144821	Management
144822	For patients with the acquired LQTS and torsades de pointes , the cause of the long QT should be determined and corrected if possible .
144823	Avoidance of precipitating drugs is mandatory .
144824	Intravenous magnesium and temporary atrial or ventricular pacing are initial choices of therapy .
144825	Temporary pacing suppresses the VT , which often does not recur even after cessation of pacing .
144826	Isoproterenol to increase heart rate can be tried cautiously until pacing is instituted .
144827	Class 1b drugs can also be tried since they decrease action potential duration .
144828	The vasodilators , pinacidil and cromakalim , decrease cardiac action potential duration by activating the ATP-dependent potassium current ; these potassium channel activating drugs may become useful in the future to control arrhythmias related to prolonged repolarisation and EADs .
144829	Prostaglandins are other therapeutic possibilities .
144830	For patients with idiopathic LQTS who do not have syncope , complex ventricular arrhythmias , or a family history of sudden cardiac death , no therapy is required .
144831	In symptom-free patients with complex ventricular arrhythmias or a family history of early sudden cardiac death , beta-adrenoceptor blockers should be given at maximally tolerated doses .
144832	In patients with syncope , beta-blockers at maximally tolerated doses can be tried , perhaps in combination with a class 1b antiarrhythmic agent .
144833	If the patient continues to have syncope despite maximum drug therapy , left-sided cervicothoracic sympathetic ganglionectomy that interrupts the stellate ganglion and the first three or four thoracic ganglia can be helpful .
144834	The fact that surgical interruption of the left stellate ganglion reduces the incidence of syncope and sudden death after unsuccessful treatment with beta-blockers underscores the potential arrhythmogenic role of alpha-adrenoceptor stimulation in LQTS , because severing neural innervation provides alpha as well as beta adrenoceptor interruption .
144835	There may prove to be groups of patients with LQTS in whom alpha rather than beta adrenoceptor stimulation is more arrhythmogenic and vice versa .
144836	Results from specific automatic challenges might better direct therapy .
144837	For example , patients who have induction of EADs and replication of their ventricular tachyarrhythmias during infusion of phenylephrine but not of isoproterenol might be better treated with alpha-blockers than with beta-blockers .
144838	They may even represent the beta-blocker treatment failures .
144839	The combination of beta-blockers and permanent pacing is effective for some symptomatic patients with idiopathic LQTS .
144840	Implantation of an internal cardioverter-defibrillator is advisable in patients who have syncope despite sympathetic interruption .
144841	BOOKSHELF
144842	When Illness Strikes the Leader
144843	Jerrold M. Post , Robert S. Robins .
144844	London : Yale University Press .
144845	1993 .
144846	Pp 243. £19.95 .
144847	ISBN 0-300056834 .
144848	In 1893 , President Cleveland developed cancer of the hard palate .
144849	For political reasons connected with the gold standard , it was decided no one outside his immediate circle should know .
144850	His advisers hit on the idea of announcing that he was going on a cruise up the Hudson river where , away from prying eyes , he was propped up in a chair against the mast and anaesthetised .
144851	Most of his upper jaw was removed and a prosthesis was fitted .
144852	The official story was that the President had a dental extraction for severe toothache .
144853	The true story remained unknown until 1928 .
144854	The case of Woodrow Wilson is well known .
144855	In 1919 , a stroke left him paralysed down the left side , confused , unable to read or dictate , and staring vacantly into space .
144856	Impossible you might think , for this to be kept secret — but it was , from all except his doctor , his personal aide , and his wife who , in effect , ran the US government for seven months .
144857	Churchill suffered from two strokes , the second leaving him completely unable to carry out his duties .
144858	Once again the seriousness of the illness was known to only a small group who concocted an official bulletin stating the Prime Minister was exhausted and needed a prolonged rest .
144859	There are many such instances where secrecy was maintained so that the leader or members of his entourage could remain in office , irrespective of potential or actual damage to government .
144860	But the greatest danger occurs when a leader is plagued by paranoia .
144861	King Ludwig of Bavaria and Idi Amin are two examples ; President Macias Nguema of Equatorial Guinea became so obsessed with imaginary enemies in the 1970s that he butchered more than 10 per cent of his country 's population , including almost everyone identified as an intellectual .
144862	Such stories are enough to send cold shivers down the spine .
144863	We learn that kings , presidents , and politicians have remained in office while either suffering behind a wall of secrecy from serious mental or physical illness or living under the influence of alcohol or drugs ( Hitler was addicted to cocaine , President Kennedy and Anthony Eden to large and frequent doses of amphetamines ) .
144864	If it has happened in the past , it can happen in the future , and may be occurring now for all we know .
144865	Various authors have penetrated the veils of medical confidentiality and political secrecy to write about the illness of world leaders : Hugh L'Etang , for example , in 1970 and 1980 , and Bert Park in 1986 .
144866	The present authors have expanded the range to produce a huge compendium of ill , mad , or bad leaders , some famous , many unknown .
144867	Several case histories are superficial or doubtful .
144868	de Gaulle is squeezed in as suffering from ‘ terminal grandiosity ’ .
144869	What makes them think it was terminal ?
144870	The way the book is constructed has led to repetition , confusing sub-headings , a badly laid out text , and a notable absence of geographical or chronological structure .
144871	In chapter 2 , entitled ‘ The Mad King : Mental Illness among the Mighty ’ , the cases of Thomas Eagleton , King Ludwig of Bavaria , King Talal of Jordan , Castlereagh , Churchill , Oliver Cromwell , Menachem Begin , Stalin , President Nguema , and Idi Amin are discussed in that order .
144872	A similar bizarre arrangement occurs in all the chapters .
144873	The authors , whose style is often banal and who favour such phrases as ‘ the march of history ’ , end with a detailed discussion of how these evils might be avoided .
144874	Since this subject is so important , it is a pity the book is so badly constructed that it lacks authority .
144875	Nevertheless , if you are willing to clamber over the obstacles , you will be rewarded by a memorable collection of case histories which makes When Illness Strikes the Leader an entertaining and compelling read .
144876	Sudden Death
144877	Cardiac and other causes .
144878	— Donald B. Hakel and Keith A. Reimer .
144879	Carolina : Carolina Academic Press .
144880	1993 .
144881	Pp 160. $75 .
144882	ISBN 0-890895465 .
144883	Hakel and Reimer make a book of a slender subject and somehow , despite 160 pages and 529 references , manage to slim it down to practically nothing .
144884	Nothing , anyway , that helpfully addresses an important conundrum , often mentioned , seldom explored , and so far unsolved : when death occurs suddenly , and coronary atherosclerosis is found at necropsy ( and nothing else that is evidently fatal ) , the certified cause of death will be given as ‘ coronary artery disease ’ — or one of many synonyms — with no regard paid to the customary scientific standards of proving the relation between effect and cause .
144885	It is not the pathologist 's fault : he has to make a decision as to the cause of death and is not allowed to say he does not know .
144886	The certified cause of death is of considerable importance because it is the usual end-point for epidemiological studies of ischaemic heart disease , and epidemiologists often assume that what is recorded on the death certificate is the cause of death .
144887	It may not be , and Hakel and Reimer might have taken the opportunity to sow more seeds of doubt , or at least put the certified cause of death in an historical perspective : 100 years ago a recorded cause of death from heart disease ( except for congenital malformations and valve defects ) was barely known , yet ischaemic heart disease must surely have existed .
144888	One might believe that , in common with advances made in the understanding of many other diseases , we now know better .
144889	We do not .
144890	The reason for many sudden deaths is still not known , but instead of saying so , we blame what is a commonplace incidental necropsy finding after the age of 25 : sclerosed coronary arteries .
144891	That objection apart , several other issues are skimped : the ‘ café coronary ’ and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy get a short paragraph apiece , while intracranial haemorrhage and the enduring mystery of pulmonary embolism are poorly covered .
144892	This book is likely to prove useful only as a source of references .
144893	Epidemiology and Control of Neural Tube Defects
144894	J. M. Elwood , J. Little , J. H. Elwood .
144895	Monographs in Epidemiology and Biostatistics , volume 20 .
144896	Oxford : Oxford University Press .
144897	1992 .
144898	Pp 926. £85 .
144899	ISBN 0-192618849 .
144900	Neural tube defects — ie , craniorachisisis , anencephaly , and spina bifida aperta — are amongst the commonest congenital abnormalities .
144901	The estimated annual number of births affected with a neural tube defect is about 400,000 world wide .
144902	In several respects , control of neural tube defects can be considered an example of how research into congenital abnormalities has progressed more generally .
144903	One can identify five phases .
144904	Anencephalus is , of course , a lethal congenital abnormality .
144905	Up to the late 1950s , few infants born with spina bifida aperta were treated actively and there was a wish , usually realised , that they would die .
144906	During the second phase , in the 1960s , early surgery for the spinal lesion of spina bifida provided the best chance of preserving neuromuscular function .
144907	This change led to an enormous effort to begin active treatment in the neonatal period for virtually all infants with this condition .
144908	The result was a substantial increase in survival partly because of surgery and partly because of the greatly improved general care that infants received .
144909	However , most survivors did not improve mentally or physically and large numbers remained with long-term disability .
144910	Thus , the third phase of progress in the 1970s was characterised by selection for surgery of the most favourable cases with the expectation that those not selected for treatment would die .
144911	This practice raised several serious ethical and legal issues .
144912	Severe spina bifida was the first condition in which a policy of selective non-treatment was clearly enunciated .
144913	Fortunately methods of antenatal diagnosis were developed and introduced in the 1980s , allowing parents to be offered termination of the abnormal fetus .
144914	In the fourth phase of progress , population-based antenatal screening — maternal serum alpha fetoprotein and ultrasound screening , sometimes complemented by amniocentesis — has been proven to have a substantial effect .
144915	Ultrasound can identify neural tube defects in anencephalic fetuses : the ultrasound detection rate for all studies evaluated in this book was 61% in open spina bifida .
144916	Informed parents have to make a difficult choice .
144917	However , I can not imagine that the success of the ‘ new ’ medical genetics should be measured by the number of terminated fetuses .
144918	New and appropriate alternative methods of genetic prevention are needed , and this will be the subject of the fifth phase in the neural tube defects story .
144919	The primary prevention of neural tube defects by periconceptional multivitamin or folic acid supplementation seems to be appropriate for the reduction of both occurrence and recurrence .
144920	Neural tube defects are the first common and lethal congenital abnormality for which a primary preventive action has been proposed and supported by the results of two large-scale randomised trials ( Medical Research Council Vitamin Study and Hungarian Family Planning Programme ) .
144921	The UK trial showed a dramatic reduction in risk of recurrence of neural tube defects in births to high-risk women .
144922	The mechanism of this effect remains unclear , although it could be viewed as a genetically determined vitamin dependent state rather than a vitamin-deficiency condition .
144923	The history of the medical management of neural tube defects indicates that developmental abnormalities should not be considered an irreducible component of human disease .
144924	Elwood , Little , and Elwood have produced an excellent and comprehensive account of the state of neural tube defect research up to 1991 .
144925	Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation
144926	David V. Skinner , Richard Vincent .
144927	Oxford : Oxford University Press .
144928	1993 .
144929	Pp 214. £14.95 .
144930	ISBN 0-192619403 .
144931	The pièce de résistance of high drama in any hospital setting is a group of junior doctors rushing through the corridors clutching their crash bleeps on their way to a cardiopulmonary arrest .
144932	Cardiopulmonary resuscitation ( CPR ) conjures up the image of a frenetic ( often chaotic ) and emotive scene where the dying are brought back to life .
144933	Since the 1960s , with the help of modern technology , CPR has become an integral part of everyday hospital practice ; but , in truth , its successes are few .
144934	They are mostly limited to the accident and emergency department , the coronary care unit , and the intensive care unit ; results from general wards are depressingly poor .
144935	Yet there are those in the medical profession who do not have to witness this undignified event and who continue to believe that the impossible can be achieved in every case .
144936	As a current member of a hospital crash team , I have become acutely aware of the problems arising from cardiac arrest calls .
144937	Most medical and nursing staff are poorly trained , although performance has improved with the recent addition of resuscitation officers to most hospitals , and CPR is often instituted inappropriately .
144938	Skinner and Vincent 's handbook , which easily fits the pocket , provides information and advice about most aspects of CPR .
144939	It is equipped with the latest UK Resuscitation Council guidelines and includes a section on paediatric arrests .
144940	There are also helpful tips on troubleshooting .
144941	For instance , what to do when the defibrillator requires intermittent cranking up , which is sadly often the case on wards off the beaten track .
144942	There are important omissions , such as the 5 mg adrenaline ampoule on the crash trolley and aspirin as a main line treatment in myocardial infarction .
144943	The text is clear and concise , although the need for extended detail on the pathogenesis of myocardial infarction is debatable .
144944	Importantly , Skinner and Vincent have attempted to address difficult medical issues such as resistant arrhythmias and the ethical difficulty of the decision not to resuscitate .
144945	Armed with Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation , one would have little excuse for not being able to run a calm and well-organised cardiac arrest .
144946	I am sure that it will be a valuable addition to the shelves of any training resuscitation officer , but it may not win the battle for space in the already bulging pockets of the junior doctor 's white coat .

144980	NEWS
144981	Tokyo Perspective
144982	An apology for AIDS
144983	Diffusion of responsibility occurs to such a degree in Japan that outright blame is not easily assigned .
144984	This explains , in part , Japan 's handling of the plight of haemophiliacs with AIDS .
144985	The same problem in France precipitated a national scandal that destroyed careers and even contributed to the defeat of a government : senior public health officials were accused of knowingly allowing contaminated blood to be given to haemophiliacs , resulting in some 1200 infections with HIV and about 300 deaths from AIDS ; some have been convicted and either jailed or given suspended sentences for fraud , criminal negligence , and failure to assist persons in danger .
144986	As retrials begin , the scandal continues .
144987	By comparison , a similar situation in Japan has fuelled little public outrage .
144988	Yet haemophiliacs now comprise more than 60% of Japan 's total AIDS population .
144989	In April this year , 1685 of the 5000 haemophiliacs had tested positive for HIV and 363 had developed AIDS .
144990	In addition to HIV infection nearly all haemophiliacs are believed to have contracted hepatitis .
144991	Early this year the Ministry of Health and Welfare ( MHW ) announced that it would begin making regular payments to haemophiliacs infected with HIV .
144992	The MHW decision followed a class action lawsuit filed by a group of 86 haemophiliacs ( 47 in Tokyo and 39 in Osaka ) which contends that the spread of HIV among Japanese haemophiliacs was due to gross negligence on the part of MHW .
144993	Also named in the suit are companies that marketed blood products — Baxter , Bayer , Green Cross , Kaketsuken , and Nippon Zoki .
144994	Although no official court ruling has yet been made in this case ( and under the Japanese legal system a final ruling is likely to be years in the making ) , MHW has decided to pay each infected haemophiliac the sum of 30,000 yen monthly ( about $280 ) and has earmarked a total of 500 million yen in the current year 's fiscal budget to meet payments .
144995	The plaintiffs had sought about 1.3 billion yen in compensation .
144996	In 1983 , when the AIDS danger to the American blood supply was first identified , the US Food and Drug Administration acted decisively to approve heat treatment to purify blood products .
144997	Risk to haemophiliacs was thereby sharply reduced .
144998	At the first reports of possible contamination , Japanese haemophilia associations demanded that MHW halt imports of US blood products , which accounted for 90% of Japan 's supply .
144999	Unfortunately , the Japanese government continued to permit the import of unheated blood products .
145000	The MHW eventually adopted purification procedures for haemophilia A patients in July , 1985 , and for haemophilia B patients five months later .
145001	Meanwhile haemophiliacs had been assured that blood products were free from HIV and therefore safe .
145002	As a long-time Japan watcher I am continually surprised by the Japanese capacity for tolerance and forgiveness of both private and public infractions .
145003	This tight-knit society functions much like a multi-celled organism whose individual cells must remain sensitive to their respective roles in ensuring the continuing health of the whole .
145004	The effect of a single cell 's suddenly stepping out of tandem could parallel that of HIV within the human body — an aggressively private agenda that compromises and ultimately destroys the entire host system .
145005	Japanese and foreigners alike are fond of citing the Japanese axiom that the ‘ nail that sticks out gets hammered down ’ .
145006	Unwillingness to stand out has its roots in village life , where a community could be held accountable for the actions of one of its members .
145007	Under certain conditions , conformity thus assumes an understandable significance .
145008	Sadly , fear of non-conformity ( along with typical fear of the unknown ) is expressed in the stigma still attached to various genetic diseases , including haemophilia .
145009	Then there is the Japanese interpretation of the law .
145010	Mediation and compromise are the rule because relationships are paramount .
145011	Views of all parties are taken into account ; every angle is examined .
145012	The aim is to restore , as far as possible , the harmony of the group .
145013	Indeed , as several observers have noted , the avoidance of friction and preservation of peace in the community can often be more important than tackling the causes of wrong-doing .
145014	What 's more , among the ministries ( such as MHW ) , layers of bureaucratic procedures and regulations serve to insulate government employees from outside criticism , and especially from outside punishment .
145015	Where admonishment does occur , it is usually internal .
145016	The MHW decision on haemophiliacs comes at a time when Japan is beginning to accept AIDS as a national health problem .
145017	This year , MHW and the Ministry of Finance agreed on an AIDS budget that exceeds 10.1 billion yen , a five-fold increase over last year 's spending .
145018	MHW will now fund a comprehensive programme that incorporates AIDS drug research , vaccine development , global research collaboration , hospital testing , public health centre support , and nationwide AIDS awareness efforts .
145019	In fact , a major impetus behind Japanese AIDS research is the attempt to delay the onset of full-blown AIDS in persons infected with HIV — another admission that haemophiliacs must in some way be helped .
145020	Additionally , AIDS statistics have become increasingly worrisome .
145021	During 1992 twice as many new carriers or AIDS patients were diagnosed as in 1991 .
145022	In April , official reports cited 554 AIDS cases , with more than 2600 persons infected with HIV .
145023	MHW officials concede that the actual number of HIV infections may be closer to 8000 , while non-government sources put the figure even higher .
145024	Already more than 300 in Japan have died of AIDS .
145025	By apologising and by approving some measure of financial compensation to haemophiliacs , the government is , in effect , initiating the Japanese process of forgiveness and acceptance that will restore harmony among the parties involved .
145026	Haemophiliacs will feel that their plight has been acknowledged ; the health ministry and pharmaceutical companies will admit accountability ; structural integrity will be preserved .
145027	Thereafter everyone will focus on practical aspects of dealing with an existing problem .
145028	It may seem harsh and blatantly unfair to outsiders , but this is the way things work in Japan .
145029	Washington Perspective
145030	Where 's health-care reform ?
145031	With the Clinton administration under the intensive care of political healer David Gergen , less and less is clear about the fate of health-care reform .
145032	Many announced , leaked , and predicted dates for unveiling the Clinton plan came and went before the maestro of the Reagan image was improbably summoned to manage the case of Bill Clinton .
145033	Still , as Gergen moved into the White House , nothing was on the table , although the task force created to draft the presidential plan had lived out its commission and disbanded .
145034	The President has been widely advised to fall back from multi-front legislative conflicts in favour of one major fight at a time .
145035	If that is the new strategy , health care must wait for settlement of the most contentious issues on the national agenda , taxes , and spending reductions .
145036	Whether health care comes next is not known .
145037	The President may indeed have settled on a programme of health benefits and how to finance them .
145038	However , since nothing substantial has seeped out in this porous capital , that 's doubtful .
145039	Bits and scraps about policy and plans are often attributed to high sources , including the highest of all in health politics , Hillary Rodham Clinton .
145040	But signs of indecision are plentiful .
145041	For example , the mental-health establishment , behaving as though it has sniffed bad news , is publicly agitating for full-fledged inclusion in the benefits programme .
145042	Vice-president Gore 's wife , Tipper , active in mental-health affairs , is said to favour that .
145043	The President 's economists are said to be worried about the costs .
145044	Mrs Clinton is on record as favouring mental-health services , but how bountiful a package is not clear .
145045	Tension is reported between the two wives .
145046	Many other issues appear to be unresolved .
145047	Though solidly on record as a pro-choice champion , the President recently said that a decision has n't been made about abortion services .
145048	Mrs Clinton recently told a labour group that the President 's health plan would put an end to financial ‘ gouging ’ by doctors .
145049	For this she drew accusations of inciting class warfare , as well as being politically indiscreet when her husband 's presidency is low on friends .
145050	Perhaps in penance , she then told an audience at the Johns Hopkins medical school that over-specialisation is the real villain behind high medical costs .
145051	More primary-care physicians are the remedy , said Mrs Clinton , echoing a popular theme in health-care deliberations .
145052	Mrs Clinton also assured the Hopkins audience that the hospitals of major research institutions like theirs would be insulated against the dog-eat-dog , cost-cutting incentives inherent in managed competition , the administration 's basic formula for reform .
145053	Meanwhile , the repeated postponements and rising arguments over who gets what in a national health plan , and how it is to be paid for , have directed attention to the political calendar and the drooping vital signs of the Clinton presidency .
145054	Auspicious moments for commencing the revolution in health care turn out to be surprisingly sparse .
145055	Inaugural euphoria and some early successes in Congress created expectations that Clinton 's domestic programme , with health care as the centrepiece , would move rapidly on Capitol Hill .
145056	But that was before the botched appointments of senior officials , the $200 haircut episode , and the President 's other poll-sapping pratfalls .
145057	Senate Republicans have now tasted blood , and the President 's own party members in Congress are expressing doubts about tying their political fates to the indecisive fledgling in the White House .
145058	Even if Clinton sends a health-care bill to Congress soon , the 1993 legislative session is too far gone for the many lengthy hearings that must take place so that all can have their say .
145059	Next year brings the mid-term Congressional elections .
145060	Health reform will require additional taxes , but taxing is a serious risk factor in today 's politics .
145061	In the 100-member Senate , where a Republican minority of 43 ( now 44 since the special Texas election ) has stymied Clinton on tax and economic issues , the numbers do not favour the Democrats .
145062	Of the 33 Senate seats at stake in 1994 , 21 are held by Democrats .
145063	One or two conservative Democrats often team up with the opposition .
145064	The loss of just a handful of Democratic seats could create an effective Republican majority on specific issues , and could even put that chamber under Republican control .
145065	The majority takes command of committee chairmanships , the bulk of staff positions , and legislative scheduling .
145066	The next Senate could be a sinkhole for the final two years of Clinton 's term .
145067	But hopes persist .
145068	As governor and presidential candidate , Clinton became an old hand at climbing out of the grave .
145069	Furthermore , he was elected to serve for 48 months , of which barely 5 have elapsed .
145070	Polls reveal the public to be far more forgiving of Clinton 's debut difficulties than the press and fellow politicians , with his flops charitably attributed to unfamiliarity with the job .
145071	Finally , wherever health-care reform may be on the stormy seas of the Clinton presidency , the public wants health-care reform .
145072	It has all the marks of a winning issue .
145073	Calling Dr Gergen .
145074	Conference
145075	Uncertain future for anti-HIV therapy
145076	The IXth International Conference on AIDS held in Berlin last week provided a forum for the luminaries of HIV research — Luc Montagnier , Robert Gallo , and Anthony Fauci — to tantalise an audience of over 12,000 with their speculations about future treatment .
145077	For those individuals with symptomless HIV infection , the apparent conflict between the results of the Anglo-French Concorde study and US data seems to be moving towards a resolution .
145078	Zidovudine does consistently provide a time-limited benefit for up to 12–18 months in such patients .
145079	The remaining disagreement is whether zidovudine monotherapy should begin early to take advantage of this short-lived benefit or whether one should wait until symptoms develop .
145080	Arguments over toxicity and cost-benefit are finely balanced .
145081	A consensus meeting between US and European investigators is planned for later this month , the aim being to devise more general guidelines for early intervention with zidovudine in symptom-free subjects .
145082	One concern must be the risk of generating zidovudine-resistant HIV mutants .
145083	For instance , a homosexual man recently became infected with a zidovudine-resistant strain of HIV-1 , although he had not taken zidovudine himself .
145084	He had most likely become infected through a partner who had been receiving zidovudine .
145085	Early treatment might therefore risk selecting out mutant strains of HIV .
145086	Such strains develop rapidly : in one in-vitro study ( Larder BA , et al , Beckenham , UK ) at time zero , 87.7% of HIV isolates were wild-type with only 6.6% mutants .
145087	By 48 weeks in the presence of zidovudine , the proportion of mutants had increased to 53.9% .
145088	The clinical importance of this observation is shown by viral resistance studies from ACTG 116B/117 , a trial which compared zidovudine with didanosine ( ddI ) .
145089	Zidovudine resistance predicted subsequent treatment failure .
145090	Data from combination therapy studies are also gradually becoming available .
145091	Margaret Fischl ( Miami , USA ) presented results from ACTG 155 which showed that among symptomatic patients ( CD4&lt;300/L ) who had taken zidovudine for a median of 18–19 months , the combination of zidovudine and zalcitabine ( ddC ) was no better than either zidovudine or zalcitabine alone ( primary end points , first AIDS-defining event or death ; mean follow-up , 17 months ) .
