146208	For example , if you look up the word " wit " in a Concordance to Congreve , you will find all the places where the seventeenth-century dramatist Congreve used that word ; you can then work out what its particular meaning for Congreve must have been by studying how he uses it .
146209	Sometimes you have access to a text , but not to all the information you would like about it .
146210	You may have seen a film , but wish to talk about who did the cinematography or who played a particular character .
146211	Once the film credits are over , you have no permanent record .
146212	In this case you might use a popular reference work like Halliwell 's Film Guide , or a journal like The Monthly Film Bulletin or Sight and Sound .
146213	There are also more specialised information sources you might need to use : if you want to know about the readership of a particular contemporary magazine or newspaper , for example ( perhaps as part of a study of the relation between ideology and audience ) you could use BRAD ( " British Rate and Data " ) , which lists advertising rates and audited newspaper and magazine circulations .
146214	Sometimes historical information is useful .
146215	If you are working on a twentieth-century subject , you may find it helpful to use the enormous amount of information available about events in the twentieth century , organised by year .
146216	If you are writing about Eliot 's poem The Waste Land ( published in 1922 ) for example , you might consider it relevant to know about other events of that year ( or the years when it was being written ) , and so you could look up 1922 in the index to the London newspaper The Times ( the poem is set partly in London and was published there ) .
146217	In these indexes you will find information about countries , types of event ( e.g. crimes ) , about the arts ( e.g. reviews ) and about the subjects and terms of reference of contemporaneous public debate .
146218	As well as indexes for many newspapers , there are compendia such as Keesings Contemporary Archives ( " factual reports on current affairs throughout the world , based on information abstracted from press , broadcasting , official and other sources " , published from 1931 onwards ) .
146219	Sometimes a novel or poem gains some of its meaning by quoting or referring to another text .
146220	In these cases , writers may expect their readers instantly to recognise such ALLUSIONS .
146221	But there are changes in what readers know automatically , even leaving aside questions of education , social background , gender , ethnicity or age .
146222	A person in 1990 will have a different store of knowledge from a person in 1890 , and even more different from a person in 1790 .
146223	So information sources can stand in for what we do not automatically know .
146224	If you suspect a text is quoting another text , you can check by looking up what you take to be the key word of the quotation in a Dictionary of Quotations .
146225	If you think an allusion is being made to a Greek or Roman myth , you can try Lemprièe 's Classical Dictionary or some other dictionary of Classical mythology .
146226	If you think a reference is being made to the Bible , you can use a concordance to the Bible .
146227	In many cases some of the work has been done for you by previous scholars ; so , for example there is a book called Allusions in Ulysses ( which lists allusions made in James Joyce 's novel Ulysses ) .
146228	Finally , there are books which have information about many different kinds of topic , and which can often turn out to be useful in unpredictable ways .
146229	These include The Oxford Companion to Literature , where you will find information about authors , texts , literary movements , and general historical facts .
146230	The Oxford Illustrated History of English Literature enables you to explore literary history by comparing juxtaposed commentary , quotation and pictures .
146231	The Cambridge Encyclopedia of Language is a compendium of useful information about language , including language in literature .
146232	The original ( but still available ) Brewer 's Dictionary of Phrase and Fable is an example of a nineteenth-century collection of somewhat idiosyncratically chosen historical , mythical and literary information ; it is useful partly because of its eccentricity , in that it contains information you may not find elsewhere .
146233	And it would be wrong to overlook the very large general encyclopedias , such as The Encyclopedia Britannica .
146234	If , for example , you want to know about punctuation in the seventeenth century , marriage laws in nineteenth-century Canada , the history of the Elizabethan stage , or current theories of myth or symbol , this is one place well worth looking .
146235	Ignore the scepticism of those obsessed with " definitive " sources : the entries in Britannica are always good , and surprisingly detailed .
146236	2.4 FINDING MORE TO READ
146237	Besides these almost standard reference sources , you will need to find more specific — and more specialised — ideas about what to read .
146238	One way of acquiring such ideas , of course , is to look on the shelves of a library ( or bookshop ) , or in a publisher 's or library catalogue , where you will find books gathered by subject and by author .
146239	Make yourself open to chance — often you will find things by accident while looking for something else , or when just browsing aimlessly .
146240	You may also like to look in anthologies .
146241	For example , the Oxford Book of Death will give you short texts relating to death , and selections from longer texts you might want to read all the way through if you are interested in the topic .
146242	If your library has a computerised catalogue , you may be able to get a list of all the books held on a particular subject matter .
146243	You can do this directly , if the catalogue has subject divisions , or indirectly by looking for all books with a particular word in the title .
146244	You could look for all books in the subject area " feminism " , for example , or all books with " feminism " or " feminist " in the title .
146245	BOOLEAN SEARCH techniques may be available in a computerised catalogue ; these enable you to select all the entries which have , for instance , both " feminism " and " Romanticism " in the title ( or close variants on these words ) .
146246	Another approach to finding more to read is to consult a bibliography , a list of books .
146247	One place to find such a list is at the back of a monograph or textbook .
146248	For most short coursework essays , this may well be enough .
146249	But you can also use specialised bibliographies .
146250	Many authors have whole bibliographies devoted to them , and there are bibliographies for particular subject areas ( for example , Black British Literature .
146251	An Annotated Bibliography ) .
146252	The most comprehensive bibliography for literary studies is the Modern Language Association of America [ MLA ] international bibliography .
146253	Another , more selective and critical bibliography is The Year 's Work in Modern Language Studies .
146254	( Notice that " Modern Language " in titles usually means literature as well as language , and looking in bibliographies for ideas about what to read is called a LITERATURE SEARCH — " literature " in this sense means " the collection of what has been written " . )
146255	A third approach is to look at ABSTRACTS .
146256	An abstract is a short summary of content .
146257	For example , a yearly volume called Abstracts of English Studies gives very short summaries of a large number of articles published in a year ; there are indexes to help you find particular topics .
146258	Dissertation Abstracts International is another collection of abstracts , this time quite long abstracts of PhD dissertations .
146259	If you are writing an MA , MPhil , MLitt or PhD dissertation , you should look at this book to see what other people have written about the topic you are working on .
146260	You can use abstracts as an indication of something you might want to read , or you can just read and learn from the abstracts themselves .
146261	Another way of finding useful or appropriate things to read is to look at library catalogues which have been published as books .
146262	In college and university libraries you will often find catalogues for other collections .
146263	These are particularly useful when the collections are subject-specific .
146264	For example , there is a published catalogue of the books in the Florida State University " Shaw Childhood in Poetry collection " ; this catalogue lists books of poems relating to childhood , together with lists of poems in the books , and even representative poems from the books — making it a bit like a dictionary of quotations on the topic .
146265	If your current interest happens to be in childhood in literature , this catalogue is an interesting place to browse .
146266	Once you start looking , you will probably find more than you have time to read .
146267	So you will need to be selective in what you decide to consult .
146268	Here are some ways of being selective .
146269	* Choose recent books first ( they might tell you what earlier books have said ) .
146270	Check book dates generally , and ask yourself whether a source may actually be giving you an outdated perspective .
146271	* Look at the range of titles in the field and for topics which keep coming up .
146272	Make sure you read at least one book on each relevant topic .
146273	* If you have a book or article in your hands , check the contents page and preface or introduction : these will give you a sketch of the book 's scope and argument .
146274	It is also useful to look at the bibliography or index to see what it includes and what it misses out .
146275	( Do the included terms correspond with what is in your view important , or the sense of what is important you have formed from what you have already read ? )
146276	* Read the last page of the book or article : with any luck it will summarise what went before , so you can choose whether to read the whole volume .
146277	* Check the contents page and try to link up the entries into a developing narrative or argument .
146278	When you have used a bibliography to find the title of something to read , how do you then get your hands on it ?
146279	If it is not in your library you may have to use inter-library loan , if this service is available to you .
146280	( In Britain all books published are kept in copyright libraries such as the British Library in London , and can in principle be borrowed by your library , though in practice they are not available to everyone . )
146281	In some cases , however , the elusive book which you need may in fact be hidden in your own library .
146282	( A group of students who were asked to read the poem " Lycidas " by John Milton could n't find it because it was " not in the catalogue " .
146283	What they needed to do was to look in Milton 's Collected Poems or in an anthology such as The Oxford Book of Seventeenth-Century Verse , rather than expecting individual titles all to be listed separately in the catalogue . )
146284	Finally , anthologies exist for all kinds of text , so sometimes what you need can be found there .
146285	This is true even of critical essays : there are anthologies such as those in the Macmillan Casebook series or the Longman Critical Readers .
146286	2.5 HOW TO READ A BOOK OR ARTICLE
146287	Finding your book or article is only the beginning , of course .
146288	Once you have it in your hands , there are a number of different ways of using it .
146289	Because you will often have more to read than you have time for , you need to develop ways of reading more quickly and efficiently .
146290	The techniques of scanning and skimming can both be used to gain a rough idea of what an article or book contains , so that you can read parts in more detail if you want to .
146291	You can SCAN , which involves just looking quickly at each page , to pick out anything which you recognise as being relevant to you , and which you can then read in detail ( scanning involves looking for keywords ) .
146292	Or you can SKIM , which involves just reading the first sentence of every paragraph and anything prominent or highlighted ( in this case , it is the general sense and flow of the book you are trying to absorb ) .
146293	Both of these reading techniques are examples of how reading is a selective activity .
146294	Even when you READ INTENSIVELY ( that is , you focus on every word ) you are still inevitably selective in what you understand or absorb .
146295	If you read an article or book twice you will probably be surprised by the many new things you discover the second time .
146296	It is a common experience in reading that you read something , then try to write about it ; writing about it gives you new ideas , and so when you read the original again you find new things in it because of the new ideas you have brought to it .
146297	This suggests that books or articles which are important to your project should be read more than once ( early on , and then again later in your study ) .
146298	Reading is an active process , one where what you bring to your reading affects what you get out of it : the more you know , the more you can understand .
146299	Do n't go to books passively , expecting simply to absorb and to be informed .
146300	Constantly ask yourself what key questions reading this book is going to help to answer .
146301	As you read through a book or long article , pause after each chapter or section and look back at any notes you have taken .
146302	Do they make sense ?
146303	Do they provide facts or views you can use ?
146304	Are there particular points you need to go back to , or will need to find out more about ?
146305	2.6 HOW TO KEEP NOTES
146306	Your reading will be useful only if you remember it and can do something with it .
146307	There are various ways of storing the results of your reading .
146308	You can buy the book , and write notes directly on it , or underline ( or highlight ) parts .
146309	You can photocopy relevant sections of the book or article .
146310	Alternatively , you can copy out parts of the book into your notes .
146311	Or you can try to restate passages of the book in your own words .
146312	Which of these you should do involves the basic decision whether you should copy the original words , or restate the content in your own words .
146313	The problem with keeping the original ( e.g. as a photocopy , with sections highlighted ) is that you have n't really done anything with it yet : you have n't assimilated it or made it your own , in the sense of fitting it with ( and so allowing it to affect ) your existing thoughts and knowledge .
146314	At some point , you will probably have to write out your own version of other people 's ideas in the form of paraphrase or summary embedded in your own work ; so it could be argued that you should do the rewriting from the outset , as you take your notes , in an effort to get at the ideas behind the words rather than just repeating the words themselves .
146315	The problem with this is that in doing so you are taking a risk : perhaps you are misunderstanding what you read , and so your notes become an incorrect version of what was said .
146316	One response to this objection , though , is that sooner or later you have to decide what someone means and how it is relevant to you ; so you might as well take that decision consciously , while you have the book or article in front of you to check .
146317	However you make them , your notes are a record of what you have read .
146318	They may also be a record of your developing ideas .
146319	But you need to make sure you can find things again when you need them .
146320	This is one reason why cards ( INDEX CARDS ) are popular as a format for keeping notes .
146321	Index cards are easily handled and shuffled ; they can be kept in alphabetised boxes , come in different colours , and can have a topic , keyword or reference written at the top , as an indication of what is on the card .
146322	These features make index cards easy to organise , and well-organised notes mean that you can find information more easily .
146323	One basic decision you have to make is whether to index a card by writing at the top of the card a theme/keyword or a name of an author/title .
146324	You might for example have a card on the theme/keyword " the sublime " , including notes drawn from a number of different books .
146325	Or a card which contains only notes from Monk 's book The Sublime : a Study of Critical Theories in Eighteenth-Century England .
146326	In general , the former method of organising by themes and keywords involves you more in doing analysis and thinking at the moment of reading , which is generally a good idea .
146327	You may also be able to store your notes on the equivalent of index cards on a computer ( in a database , or in word-processing document files ) .
146328	Finding information in computerised notes is in principle much more efficient because you can search for every use of a particular word throughout your notes .
146329	On the other hand , on a computer screen you can only see a small amount of information at any given time , whereas with index cards you can lay them out across a table or on the floor for an overview .
146330	You also have to be able to have the computer with you when you take the notes , which is not always easy to arrange .
146331	In whatever format you keep them , the notes you make need to be clear ; if they are not self-explanatory at the time you write them , they are unlikely to be intelligible later , when your memory of working on the particular book or topic has faded .
146332	So read over your notes once you have made them , and edit them until they are as comprehensible as possible without reference back to the source work .
146333	It is also generally a good idea to keep your notes short ; while you may want to keep a record of everything that might prove useful , your notes will seem unhelpful if you feel swamped with redundant information when you come to refer to them later .
146334	2.7 KEEPING A RECORD OF WHERE YOU FOUND SOMETHING
146335	At the beginning of this chapter , we suggested that when you write you use what other people have written .
146336	One of the conventions of research — which we discuss in more detail below , in Chapter 5 — is that you must enable your reader to find again what you have read ( and in any case , it is useful for you to be able to find again what you have read ) .
146337	So you need to write down enough details of a book or article , or any other source , to enable it to be found again .
146338	In some cases it can be difficult or even impossible to find texts again ( for example if the text is a lecture , or a television programme ) , but you should still keep details of them as fully as possible , so that your reader knows exactly where ideas or words come from .
146339	The information you need to keep for everything you read includes the following .
146340	( You will find such information usually at the beginning of a book — though some books have details of publication on the last page instead . )
146341	( a ) The author 's full name .
146342	Write the family name first , as this will decide where the work will go in an alphabetical list .
146343	( b ) Any other people involved , other than an author .
146344	There might for example be an editor , compiler or translator .
146345	( c ) The full title — and subtitle — of the work .
146346	Put a colon between the title and the subtitle , even if there is n't one in the original .
146347	Underline the title of a book , and put an article 's title in single quotation marks .
146348	( d ) The name of the publisher , the place where it was published , and the date of publication — all for the edition you have in your hands .
146349	Often books will have a list of different places ; the convention is to choose only the first .
146350	In some cases you may want to add further information : books are published in Cambridge England and Cambridge USA , so saying just " Cambridge " may not be helpful ; add country details if you think there is a possibility of confusion .
146351	( e ) If the text is an article in a journal or a chapter in an edited book or anthology , keep details about the collection in which you found it ; for a journal article , note the volume and issue number , and the page numbers on which the article appears .
146352	( f ) Sometimes books or articles exist in several different versions .
146353	If you are not using the original version , you should say so ( e.g. by noting " second edition " or " reprinted version " or " facsimile " ) .
146354	You should keep details of the original version , if you can find them .
146355	For an article in an anthology , for instance , you need to keep details of the journal in which it originally appeared .
146356	For a FACSIMILE edition ( a photographic reprint of an old book ) , note both information relating to the current edition and also information relating to the original edition .
146357	If a book is a translation , keep information about the original title , publisher , etc .
146358	( g ) Usually you will refer to or quote from a particular passage in a book or article ; in this case , note the page number .
146359	Because literary texts exist in different editions it can be more helpful instead to note the chapter number , act and scene number , line number , etc. ( and of course , you should indicate the exact edition you are using ) .
146360	( h ) For your own benefit , also keep a record of where you found the book ( which library and the call number ) , in case you need to consult it again .
146361	There are detailed guidelines , for example in The MLA Style Manual or the MHRA Style Book , to tell you how to deal with all kinds of complicated cases .
146362	Below , in Chapters 5 and 7 , we enlarge on what we have said here , as we make suggestions about how to present references in footnotes and booklists appended to your essay or dissertation .
146363	But note in the meantime that published rules do n't always help you .
146364	Often you need to work things out for yourself .
146365	Here is an example of the need to improvise .
146366	We wish to refer to an anthology of poetry and prose which we have open in front of us .
146367	At the beginning of the book , on the verso ( left-hand ) page , it says Oxford University Press .
146368	London , Edinburgh , Glasgow , New York , Toronto , Melbourne , Cape Town , Bombay Humphrey Milford , Publisher to the University
146369	On the recto ( right-hand ) page it says : A Book of the Sea .
146370	Selected and arranged by Lady Sybil Scott Oxford .
146371	At the Clarendon Press .
146372	1918
146373	The first problem is : how to record the name of the author .
146374	Should it be " Scott , Lady Sybil " or just " Scott , Sybil " ?
146375	We would be inclined to use the first , because it gives a better sense of the feel of the anthology ; but this is a fairly arbitrary decision , where rule-books do not help .
146376	How should we list the author 's role ?
146377	We could say simply " ( edited ) " but perhaps we should take the title page at its word and say instead " ( selection and arrangement ) " .
146378	Is the publisher Oxford University Press or Humphrey Milford or Clarendon Press ?
146379	( Actually , it is Oxford University Press , but we can be sure of this only because we already know something about this publisher . )
146380	Finally , is the place of publication London ( the first in the list under the publisher 's name ) or Oxford ?
146381	Again , we choose Oxford , but only because this is usually given as the place of publication for Oxford University Press books .
146382	So our notes say :
146383	Scott , Lady Sybil ( selection and arrangement ) , A Book of the Sea ( Oxford : Oxford University Press , 1918 ) .
146384	Getting to this stage involves some active interpretation ( and some fairly random decisions too ) .
146385	As usual in writing , following rules by itself achieves little .
146386	2.8 USING A COMPUTER TO FIND AND STORE INFORMATION
146387	Computers are particularly good for finding , storing and retrieving information .
146388	This can be illustrated in the context of literary studies with one or two examples , starting with the advantage of using a computerised library catalogue .
146389	A non-computerised library catalogue is likely to be a collection of cards , each a record about a book , in alphabetical order according to the author 's family name .
146390	If you know just the title but not the author 's name , you may be out of luck .
146391	In a computerised catalogue , on the other hand , you can in principle search according to any aspect of a record about a book .
146392	This is because computerised information is not as rigidly organised in advance , which means that you can search through it in any way you please .
146393	Computerised library catalogues are just one example of the many forms of computerised bibliographical information which are available .
146394	The Modern Language Association Bibliography from 1985 to the present is available on compact disc , so you can do much quicker searches than if you had to haul out each year 's book one by one .
146395	Increasingly , literary texts are becoming available in computerised form .
146396	For example , the Oxford Text Archive is a collection of computerised texts , each of which you can buy on floppy disc for the price of a printed copy .
146397	Shakespeare 's works are available on disc from many sources , as is the Bible .
146398	Compact discs are available which contain a corpus of a whole century of poetry on a single disc .
146399	And it is possible to make new electronic texts by scanning printed texts into a computer .
146400	The advantage of having a text in computerised form is that you can find things in it very easily using computerised search techniques , and you can do more complicated searches than you ever could with a printed concordance .
146401	Let's say you are interested in the opposition of love and hate in Shakespeare 's play All 's Well that Ends Well .
146402	Using a Complete Shakespeare on CD , you can look for all cases where these two words are used within , say , five lines of each other ; and you 'll get your answer within a minute or so .
146403	Another useful resource is offered by the possibility of putting very large dictionaries onto a single compact disc .
146404	The full Oxford English Dictionary is available on compact disc ; and with it you can do far more extensive searches for information than the printed book allows .
146405	For example , if you are interested in the word " love " , with the book version of the OED you can look up " love " and you will be given definitions and illustrative quotations .
146406	In the compact-disc OED , on the other hand , you can look for the word " love " not just in the entry for " love " but in every entry in the whole dictionary ; the search will find " love " in any quotation anywhere in the entire dictionary .
146407	A search of this size is impossible with the printed OED , where you are restricted to just those quotations including " love " which the original editors decided to put into the entry for " love " .
146408	It is likely that computerized storage and retrieval facilities will take on an increasing importance in literary studies ; so it is worth exploring them whenever you can .
146409	It should be said , nevertheless , that powerful search techniques , across such large databases , will still only contribute effectively to your essay-writing or research if you maintain a clear sense of what you are looking for and why — a guiding principle which is itself independent of the technology .
146410	2.9 USING YOUR SUPERVISOR
146411	The role of a supervisor varies , depending on the level of work you are doing and the conventions of supervision for the department you are in .
146412	The role will hardly ever be one of telling you what to do ; instead , the supervisor reviews what you have done .
146413	This means that as a student who is being supervised it is you who have to be proactive rather than reactive .
146414	Being proactive means negotiating with your supervisor about what you expect from her or him , instead of just accepting the terms ( often not actually made explicit ) on which supervision is offered .
146415	Prepare questions and an informal agenda for each meeting , so that when it is over you can be certain that — alongside all other new questions which are raised — you have asked or raised all the issues you wanted to .
146416	Try to arrange for a written record of what has been agreed for the next meeting , so that you can work to an explicit plan .
146417	Take an active role in asking for appointments ; most kinds of research benefit from discussion at least every month or so .
146418	Do not let the channel of communication with your supervisor close — even if you are behind and would rather not have to face the situation of explaining why .
146419	Staying in communication allows for discussion and possible help , whereas losing touch will categorise you only as someone who is failing to meet deadlines .
146420	Always bring something with you to a supervision : ideas which you have written down , an outline of an essay , a text you want to talk about , or a plan of action .
146421	Your supervisor 's approach and enthusiasm are likely to vary according to how motivated and organised you are .
146422	You will get better help if you have outlines and ideas for the supervisor to react to ; experiment with your ideas and see what reactions you get , rather than waiting to produce ideas that you are sure fit in with an established approach .
146423	See your supervisor as a facilitator or notional " editor " /adviser of your work , rather than as a teacher who will inform you , or as an authority .
146424	Ask for comments on drafts of work you have written , and discuss those comments , even if this means talking about apparently negative judgements on your work so far .
146425	Feedback provided by your tutor is supposed to be helpful and constructive ( " formative feedback " ) , and you stand to gain most from having comments clarified — even deciphered — where necessary , and ensuring through discussion that you understand the general perspective from which criticisms or comments are made .
146426	It is also useful to carry out your own critical analysis of an essay you have completed .
146427	A week or more after writing , you are likely to have sufficient detachment to examine your work as a reader , rather than as its writer .
146428	Add a list of your own comments to your tutor 's feedback , for future reference .
146429	2.10 PLANNING YOUR TIME
146430	Be realistic about time in your planning .
146431	And suit yourself — everyone works differently , and your personal best working patterns may well be different from those other people might expect from you .
146432	The aim should be to develop your own potential , not to regulate your working habits to a conventional norm .
146433	Allow for unexpected breaks such as days when libraries are closed , delays while materials arrive through the post , days when you do n't feel like working , etc .
146434	And create breaks deliberately .
146435	For example , you should allow for creating variation in your working patterns .
146436	Read for a while , then do some writing or some research browsing in a library ; this can reduce the effect of strain or tiredness with long bouts of writing , something which is particularly important for health reasons if you work at a computer .
146437	Remember that finishing off ( e.g. by adding footnotes or bibliographic references ) always takes longer than you anticipate , so allow enough time for this .
146438	Be careful with deadlines : some are notional ( and extensions are possible ) ; others are fixed and absolute , with the result that non-completion on schedule can mean failure .
146439	Check the rules to find out which of these your deadline is .
146440	2.11 SUMMARY , SUGGESTIONS AND EXERCISES
146441	Summary In this chapter we have shown how writing an essay depends on the manipulation of raw materials collected for the purpose , including editions of literary works , critical essays , information gathered from reference sources and advice sought from teachers or supervisors .
146442	The work of writing an essay is greatly reduced if your preparatory stages are carried out thoroughly .
146443	This involves deciding what it is you are looking for before you start general reading , and , equally important , assessing why you need to read particular works or sources you intend to consult .
146444	Keeping clear and concise notes of what you have read enables you to organise your essay without having to refer constantly back to the original sources .
146445	Your notes form a bridge between the works you are studying and the outline and early drafts of the essay you are trying to write .
146446	Specific suggestions
146447	* Decide which parts of a text to focus on particularly ( e.g. beginning , ending , title , etc. ) ( see p. 32 ) .
146448	* Make an informed choice about which version of a text to use ; try to use a critical edition ( see p. 33 ) .
146449	* Beware of quoting from secondary sources , particularly from textbooks ( p. 34 ) .
146450	* Find out what information sources are available to you , and be imaginative in how you use them ( see pp. 34 – 40 ) .
146451	* Look for ideas on the shelves and in the catalogue of your library , in bibliographies , in anthologies and also in bookshops and publishers ' catalogues ( see p. 38 ) .
146452	* Be open to chance discoveries ( see p. 38 ) .
146453	* Do n't read everything in the same way ( see pp. 39 – 41 ) .
146454	* Take notes , but do n't necessarily copy directly from the original when you do so ( see pp. 41 – 2 ) .
146455	* When you take notes , keep a full record of all sources ( see pp. 42 – 4 ) .
146456	* Use the flexibility of computerised texts and search techniques if you can ( see pp. 45 – 6 ) .
146457	* Take the initiative and negotiate with your supervisor for the most helpful arrangement ( see pp. 46 – 7 ) .
146458	* Vary your working patterns ( see p. 47 ) .
146459	Exercises
146460	( 1 ) Choose one literary text which you might work on which is representative , plus one which is well-known , plus one which is neglected ( see 2.1 ) .
146461	Explain why each text might be interesting to work on .
146462	( 2 ) " Kitchen-sink drama " is a name used for a particular group of plays written in Britain in the late 1950s and 1960s .
146463	Look up " kitchen-sink " in the Oxford English Dictionary ( second edition ) , and explain how the entry could help you put together an essay on kitchen-sink drama .
146464	( 3 ) Pick a brief passage from a poem you believe to be famous .
146465	Underline what seem to you to be the main or key words in the passage , including all names and any words beginning with capital letters .
146466	Look these words up in the Oxford English Dictionary ( complete version , not the compact or shorter version ) ; in Brewer 's Dictionary of Phrase and Fable ; in the Concise Oxford Dictionary of English Literature ; in the Encyclopedia Brittanica ; and in whichever other relevant reference sources are available to you .
146467	Now imagine you are an editor , annotating the passage for a student edition .
146468	As you add explanatory notes , offer all the help you would hope to find , as a reader , in an annotated edition if you yourself were studying this particular text for the first time .
146469	( 4 ) Pick a work you have recently read or are in the process of reading .
146470	Look up , in all the reference works available to you , entries for :
146471	— the author — the title of the work — the main characters in the work — the places referred to — any dates referred to .
146472	Go through the list , asessing what contributions ( if any ) each new piece of information makes to your understanding of the work .
146473	( 5 ) Make a sample set of " notes " on a critical work you have recently read to help with an essay task , laying out your notes in two columns .
146474	In the left column , put what you consider to be all the main points made in the book .
146475	In the right column , note down all the points which would be relevant to or useful in your essay in particular .
146476	Compare the two columns .
146477	( 6 ) Draw up a contract which you think would represent the ideal division of responsibilities between yourself and your supervisor .
146478	Discuss it with your supervisor .
146479	The form of your argument
146480	When you write an essay what you typically do ( put at its simplest ) is gather material and then arrange it .
146481	In Chapter 2 we looked at sources of information and at how to gather material .
146482	In this chapter we focus on how you arrange your gathered material in the form of an argument .
146483	In Chapters 4 and 5 we consider in more detail the writing techniques through which you can present to best effect the kinds of argument described here .
146484	3.1 ESSAY TYPES
146485	As we discussed in Chapter 1 , the underlying purpose of writing essays in literary studies is to argue a case .
146486	In achieving this end , essays follow certain general patterns of development and direction , which are definable in terms of the focus they give to their subject matter and the different modes of argument they adopt .
146487	We now consider how the substance of those different sorts of essay is organised and presented , starting with techniques for commenting on a given passage .
146488	Commenting on a given passage
146489	In writing on a given passage — often in response to a general question in a " Practical Criticism " or " Commentary and Analysis " course — it can be helpful , in considering what to say , to organise your answer around the following questions : ( a ) Who is the speaker ?
146490	What sort of person ( or creature ) appears to be speaking in the text ?
146491	How do we know ?
146492	What words , phrases or markers of attitude indicate this ?
146493	( b ) Who does the passage seem to be addressing ?
146494	Who ( or what sort of audience ) must the implied addressee(s) be , so far as we can tell from the passage itself ?
146495	( c ) What theme or general issue is the passage concerned with ?
146496	How far is a specific position or attitude taken towards that theme ( which may be anything from a conventional topic , such as lost love , to an apparently unresolvable philosophical question , such as the meaning of life ) ?
146497	( d ) What is the overall function or effect of the passage ?
146498	Does it seek to persuade , command , inform , satirise , impress , amuse ?
146499	( e ) How would you describe the style of the passage ?
146500	Is it colloquial , elevated , ornate , comic , ironic , archaic , conventionally poetic , etc. ?
146501	Which particular words or phrases indicate this most clearly ?
146502	( f ) Are there any noticeable changes of mood ( or direction in the narrative , if there is one ) ?
146503	Does the passage switch from one style to another , and if so why ?
146504	( g ) How far is the passage supposed to be realistic ?
146505	Is it just about what it describes ?
146506	Or is it representative of something more general ?
146507	Is it symbolic of a theme or topic that is not itself explicitly mentioned in the passage ?
146508	Is it allegorical ( i.e. each character or event in the passage stands for something else in a parallel story ) ?
146509	( h ) What effect does the passage have on you ?
146510	And would it be likely to have a significantly different effect on other readers ( e.g. readers from a different historical period , different class , different country , different gender or ethnic group , etc . ) ?
146511	There are many aspects of any given passage to describe besides these .
146512	But such a checklist of questions can be a helpful prompt if you are faced with a passage and can not find a place to start .
146513	Beginning with one or more of these questions is likely to carry you into other , new areas of your own .
146514	Analysing and interpreting
146515	Beyond answering basic questions of the kind listed above , the next stage of analysing a text is to investigate its patterning or STRUCTURE .
146516	Cases of interesting structure might include a rhyme pattern , an unusually high proportion of adjectives , or a particular type of narrative .
146517	Every analysis is also to some extent an interpretation ; so if for example you choose to summarise a narrative , you will , by selection and emphasis , be interpreting what the most important incidents and characters are .
146518	Analysis and interpretation of structures in a text are useful if you can make something of them — if , for instance , you can say something new on the basis of having identified a rhyme pattern .
146519	Typically , you use an analysis or description of a text to claim some kind of connection between the features analysed and something else about the text , such as its meaning , its effect on a reader , how good it is , or its historical origins .
146520	In most cases the connection is one between observation ( of structure ) and response ( your interpretation ) .
146521	Without observations , responses are mere impressions .
146522	Without responses or interpretation , on the other hand , observations are unworked-out descriptions .
146523	In between , there are different strengths of connection between these two aspects of reading , ranging from CAUSATION , through CORRELATION , to COINCIDENCE .
146524	Consider a simple example .
146525	You analyse a poem as having an especially regular rhyme scheme ; you also find that the poem makes you feel cheerful .
146526	You now try to connect these two perceptions , by saying that ( a ) the rhyme scheme causes the cheerfulness ; or ( b ) there is a relationship between the rhyme scheme and the cheerfulness , but it is one of correlation ; or ( c ) the regular rhyme scheme is connected with the cheerfulness because they are both caused by something else ( such as the genre or subject matter of the poem , perhaps ) ; or ( d ) there is in your view no relationship between the rhyme scheme and the feeling , and they coincide without there being a causal or correlative relation between them .
146527	Coincidence is the least interesting of the three relationships ; it is also the most common .
146528	Causation , conversely , is likely to be the most interesting , but it is also the most difficult to demonstrate .
146529	This is because , with a literary text , what is caused is often inside your head : an emotional response or an impression of meaning .
146530	While such states are central to literary studies , it is difficult to describe them precisely or effectively ; and for this reason , although they are of great interest , they are also inevitably weak points in your argumentation .
146531	Descriptive essays
146532	Not all essays are discussions ( or analyses ) of individual , given passages .
146533	In the case of more general or abstract essays ( on whole works , on authors or on critical issues ) , it is necessary to find other means of organising an argument — though some of the means also turn out to be applicable when looking at individual passages .
146534	The simplest form of general essay organisation involves just the presentation of a sequential commentary or description .
146535	But what gives us the sequence ?
146536	One common sequence is chronology ( e.g. the development of a novelist 's concerns throughout her lifetime ) .
146537	But there are other kinds of sequence , too , such as a text-by-text commentary on works in a collection ( e.g. Lyrical Ballads ) ; or you might recount events in a narrative , telling your reader the story in the order in which it happens .
146538	There is , however , a difficulty with the mode of organisation which follows an already existing sequence : it lacks anything by way of your own analysis or commentary .
146539	The materials you have collected together ( the events in the story , the biography of an author , etc. ) are simply presented in the same order in which they originally occur ; and this generally produces uninteresting and unoriginal essays .
146540	Essays which describe their material sequentially in a list-form resemble commentaries on prescribed passages which work through the text line by line .
146541	The problem in both cases is that no process of reworking , assimilation or re-presentation has taken place : there is little added by you .
146542	Using the same information available for a sequential description , however , it is possible to organise an essay in more interesting ways .
146543	You can demonstrate a process of reordering , and so your own contribution , by reshaping the material around an overall organizing principle or generalisation .
146544	For example , a classificatory system imposed on the material divides it into abstract categories ( e.g. into a chronology on the basis of definable periods ; or into a typology , or system of sorting on the basis of formal likeness and difference ) .
146545	Any classificatory system you use to organise your essay has to be explained , of course ( e.g. divisions between historical periods need to be discussed and justified ) .
146546	But introducing a classificatory element almost always radically improves a descriptive essay .
146547	It enables you to get straight into analysis and debate , leaving basic description to passages of supporting illustration ; and it emphasises your point of view or commentary rather than mere repetition of materials possibly already available to your reader in their original form .
146548	( Always ask yourself : why should anyone read my essay , when they could read the original ? )
146549	One fruitful form of classification starts from a keyword ( sometimes a historical term such as " Restoration " ; a conceptual term such as " nature " ; or a genre term such as " tragedy " ) .
146550	Consider the case of tragedy .
146551	If you are writing on this topic you can work out a list of different sorts of tragedy .
146552	This prompts you to do something else , namely to work out the relationship between the parts of the list : why all the different sorts of tragedy are all called tragedy , what the historical sequence and links between them are , etc .
146553	Classification is also useful when you are working with a text which has not been extensively discussed , but which relates to classifications which have been discussed .
146554	For example , if you choose to write an essay on the novel A Very Quiet Street by the contemporary Glasgow author Frank Kuppner , you may not find it easy to get any critical work either on the book itself or on this writer ( since no books may have been written about him ) .
146555	But you can work out how Kuppner 's novel would fit into various classificatory systems , and then discuss the novel from this point of view .
146556	You can try to work out whether it is autobiography or murder mystery and how it works within these genre classifications .
146557	Or you can classify the novel according to where it was written , " West of Scotland " , and think about it as an example of writing from this locality .
146558	Classifications are often a basis for finding correlations .
146559	As an illustration of this , consider the following project : An essay on metaphors used in advertisements This imaginary project might begin with an analysis of the metaphors used in ten advertisements .
146560	We decide to look for a connection between types of advert and types of metaphor .
146561	In order to do this , we classify the adverts into types " aimed at women " and " aimed at men " ( we could instead have classified them as " television " versus " magazine " or " Italian " versus " British " , etc. ; and if our first attempt to classify gets us nowhere we might try one or more of these alternatives at a later stage ) .
146562	We then also classify the metaphors into types : " metaphors where an object is treated like a part of a body " and " other types of metaphor " .
146563	We are now in a position to ask whether one type of advert typically uses one type of metaphor .
146564	If the answer is " yes " , then we have learnt something ( a correlation , which may turn out to be an instance of causation ) ; and in writing it down we will be saying something new .
146565	If , on the other hand , the answer is " no " , then we eliminate this line of enquiry , and perhaps try one of the alternative classifications of adverts and metaphors we suggested above .
146566	Argumentative essays
146567	In this mode of organising an essay , you divide the issue you are addressing into conflicting positions , or points of view , or sides of an argument .
146568	So the structure of the essay becomes a comparison of claims made from differing viewpoints , assessing the validity and appropriateness of each .
146569	Sometimes you can organise your essay around an already existing critical controversy ( e.g. between established schools of thought , such as " New Criticism " and " Post-structuralism " ) .
146570	In order to accentuate the general significance of your arguments , it can be helpful to generalise from individuals to movements , or types of thought ( you discuss Leavisism , for instance , rather than Leavis 's work in particular ) .
146571	In presenting ideas of the school or movement , however , you will need to be careful about distinguishing your own words from your paraphrase of the positions you are representing .
146572	Be explicit at the point where you leave off summarising and your own words take over ( see below , Chapter 5 , pp. 105 – 7 , for techniques which enable you to do this ) .
146573	You will also need , in this type of essay , to signal that you are aware of the dangers of reductionism : that is , of simplifying the work of a school or movement until it no longer adequately represents what anyone associated with it would recognise or subscribe to .
146574	Experimenting
146575	A literary experiment changes a text and looks at how the change affects a reader .
146576	For example , you choose a narrative , then imagine a different ending for it , and think what implications this would have . Such an " experiment in your head " focuses on the writer 's actual decision about an ending , but also begins to tell you about how endings work in general .
146577	As in this simple mental experiment of the narrative ending , most experiments in literary studies involve taking related versions of a text and seeing what effects on a reader the differences between them have .
146578	The selected texts ( or versions of a single text ) will be alike in many respects , yet different in perhaps just one basic way — called the VARIABLE .
146579	You are likely to be looking for the relation between the variable part of the text ( called the INDEPENDENT VARIABLE because you are manipulating it by making changes ) and the variation in the response of the reader ( called the DEPENDENT VARIABLE , because it depends on the variation , or changes , made to the text ) .
146580	One of the crucial rules about doing an experiment is to report it fully , so that it can be repeated if necessary .
146581	You also need to control the circumstances in which you conduct the experiment , in order to eliminate , as far as possible , conflicting or distracting variables ( such as tiredness , lateness in the day , unequal difficulty of the texts used , etc . ) .
146582	If your experiment involves other people ( e.g. if you are comparing different readers ' responses ) , you need to consider ethical issues which arise , including ( a ) getting their permission to use the results ; ( b ) showing them the results and explaining them ; ( c ) not using their names when you report the experiment ( even if they have given permission for this , there is unlikely to be any point ) ; ( d ) the ethical problem that sometimes an experiment is best conducted if the test subjects do n't know what it is for ; that is , if there is a " secret agenda " .
146583	If your experiment involves large groups of informants , then you also need to think about the significance of numerical results you may produce ; and for this , guidebooks about experimentation and the use of statistics may be needed ( see sections 1 and 4 of the Booklist for suggestions ) .
146584	Providing contexts for texts
146585	Another form of argument to be considered involves analysis of what else was happening at the time a text was written and first published .
146586	You can begin to find this out by using an ANNALS , which functions as a short-cut summary of historical facts if you do not know much about a text 's historical background .
146587	For example , Emily Brontë 's novel Wuthering Heights was published in 1847 ; the annals The Teach Yourself Encyclopedia of Dates and Events tells us that in 1846 the term " folk-lore " was coined ( which may be relevant to the presence of fairy-tale elements in the novel ) .
146588	Remember here too the issue of correlation , causation and coincidence .
146589	Sometimes a correlation or co-occurrence is incorrectly presented as a causality , for example , by the use of " therefore " in this sentence : Dickens and Thackeray were concerned with demanding social justice in an attempt to make life better , therefore their literature adopted realism as a method .
146590	There could be a causal link between demanding social justice and realism as a method , but it is not shown .
146591	There may be merely a less direct link .
146592	It might be , for example , that these authors ' social concerns and their use of realism both come from a common source : increased knowledge of social reality as a result of sociological work in the nineteenth century and the urbanisation of Britain ; that is , a correlation rather than a causation .
146593	Comparing texts
146594	Because a text always relates historically to other texts , one way of developing material for your essay is to compare texts .
146595	Texts are sometimes altered editorially for particular purposes , and in this respect , for example , you could compare Shakespeare 's play Henry V with a version of the play revised for performance in the eighteenth century .
146596	Such a comparison would tell you about changes in language and in aesthetics , about the demands of performance in the eighteenth century , and about changes in social values .
146597	Even if you have no interest in the play Henry V itself , the comparison helps you to learn about eighteenth-century attitudes , by providing information and insights you can then use to look at eighteenth-century drama generally .
146598	Another type of comparison arises from the fact that literary texts often adapt other sorts of text .
146599	You might compare , for instance , a real letter from 1740 with one of the letters in Richardson 's novel Pamela ( published 1740 , and made up of a sequence of imitation letters ) .
146600	From this you might learn about Richardson 's method of writing , as well as about differences between writing which is really private compared to writing which only pretends to be private .
146601	Or you could use a text which has been translated from one medium into another .
146602	By comparing the film Apocalypse Now ( 1978 ) with the story on which it is based — Joseph Conrad 's " Heart of Darkness " ( 1902 ) — you might gain ideas about differences between film and writing as media , or differences between an early twentieth-century text and a late twentieth-century text ; you might also get ideas about narrative by comparing how the two narratives are the same and how they differ .
146603	Finally , a comparison essay always involves a decision about how to organise the comparison .
146604	If , for example , you compare the film Gregory 's Girl ( GG ) with the play A Midsummer Night 's Dream ( MND ) , on which it is partly based , you could organise the comparison as : GG narrative compared with MND narrative ; GG characterisation compared with MND characterisation ; etc. ; summary of comparison .
146605	Or you could organise the comparison as : GG narrative , GG characterisation ; MND narrative , MND characterisation ; etc. ; comparison between the two texts .
146606	Generally the first mode — point-by-point argument — is preferable , since it foregrounds comparison rather than description .
146607	The second mode of presentation has the damaging tendency to defer argument and analysis until a closing section , before which come extended passages of paraphrase and basic description .
146608	Finally , remember that point-by-point comparisons can become tedious if extended too far ; a formal analysis always needs to be subordinated to some more general point you want to make .
146609	Using a definition or the history of a word in an argument
146610	An argument can sometimes be built around the definition of a word .
146611	Consider , for example , an essay on " Islamic elements in Byron 's poetry " .
146612	One thing you might want to do as a way of putting an argument together would be to look up the word " Romanticism " in the dictionary , since Byron 's poetry belongs to this literary movement .
146613	You will probably find that there are several competing definitions , together with examples which will help you think about Romanticism .
146614	On the basis of the definitions you find , you could even construct your own definition of Romanticism which would help give direction to your essay .
146615	You might for example define Romanticism as " an artistic movement centrally concerned with the relationship between the self and others " .
146616	The next step would be to explore whether the " others " could be represented in Byron 's poetry by people who follow the religion of Islam .
146617	" Romanticism " would be a KEYWORD for this essay .
146618	Another keyword might be " Islamic " .
146619	Many words have a history which reflects the history of ideas and the history of society .
146620	One way of finding material for your essay is to look up your keyword in sources concerned with the social history of language and ideas , such as the OED or Raymond Williams 's Keywords .
146621	The OED for example tells you that the word " Islam " was first used in English in a poem by Shelley , six years before Byron 's death .
146622	If you now find and read Shelley 's poem , you gain the possibility of comparing Byron with Shelley in terms of how they represent Islam .
146623	The dictionary entry also suggests that the term " Islam " was new to English-speaking culture at this time , and prompts you to look up other words , including " musselman " and " mohammedan " ; reading the entries on these words will give you further clues relating to the representation of Islam in English-speaking cultures , and so further material for your argument .
146624	3.2 ORDERING THE PARTS OF YOUR ARGUMENT
146625	An essay is made up of parts , each part relating to the parts around it , with a forward movement so that what comes first leads to what comes next .
146626	Working out the part-structure of your essay is a way of working out what your argument is ; and if the organisation of parts is clear , this helps your reader to understand how the essay develops .
146627	Here , for example , is an initial organisation of an essay on the Scottish novelist Josephine Tey : introduction career as a London playwright recent critical appraisal powers of description humour education church the divided self the divided self — most of all as a woman her final novel — The Singing Sands .
146628	As it stands , this organisation does not make clear how the parts relate to each other , what the development is , or even what the point is of some of the parts ( why should there be a special section devoted to her final novel but not the others , for example ? ) .
146629	So we might reorganise the parts like this : introduction biographical details ( including career as a London playwright ) qualities as a writer — powers of description — humour themes — education — church — the divided self — most of all as an artistic movement centrally concerned with the relationship between the self and others .
146630	— woman ( as a theme ) , and in relation to the divided self recent critical appraisal conclusion : her final novel — The Singing Sands .
146631	Our revised version is the result of the following organisational changes : ( a ) We put " career as a London playwright " into a larger section called " biographical details " , because there are other relevant biographical points we will want to make .
146632	( b ) We grouped " powers of description " and " humour " in a section called " qualities as a writer " ; we can now add other qualities to this section if we wish .
146633	Similarly we have made a group of " themes " .
146634	( c ) We moved " recent critical appraisal " after our analysis of powers of description and humour because these sections give our own critical appraisal ; now , by the time we outline other people 's opinions we have something to compare them with , and can therefore do something more interesting than just repeat them .
146635	( d ) We have made explicit the reason for focusing on the last novel — we chose it because it acts as a summary of Tey 's work , and so is an appropriate topic for a conclusion .
146636	With a longer dissertation , be careful not to overload the first part , especially if it is a biographical summary , a description of historical context , or a literature review — all of which are potentially interminable .
146637	To overcome problems of overloading the opening section , try to avoid the following structure : ( a ) literature review ; ( b ) introduce case study ; ( c ) detail of case study ; ( d ) analysis , findings and conclusion .
146638	In such a structure , ( a ) usually becomes overloaded .
146639	Instead , try something like : ( a ) scene-setting ; reasons for interest ; the problem ; ( b ) case study ; ( c ) analysis of findings ; ( d ) discussion of wider themes ; relation to existing work .
146640	In this revised format you present material from your literature review , paradoxically , at the end ( under " relation to existing work " ) , where you examine implications and applications .
146641	3.3 ASSERTION , JUSTIFICATION AND PRESUPPOSITION
146642	At many points in your essay you will just want to propose or say something ; so many of your sentences will be ASSERTIONS .
146643	When you make an assertion , what you are doing is telling your reader something you think is true .
146644	Assertions can be signalled by writing " I would suggest " , or " I would argue " , but often it is just assumed that whatever you say is your suggestion or argument .
146645	In this section , we look at two important questions you should ask about any assertion you make in an essay :
146646	( a ) Does the assertion need further justification ? ( b ) Does the assertion presuppose too much ?
146647	We begin with justification .
146648	If all your essay consisted of was just a series of assertions , there would be little connection or development between the parts : there would be no argument .
146649	An assertion is the basis of an argument when it is combined with a justification : assertion : " Dickens showed an incorrect view of the London working classes . "
146650	Justification could be given for this assertion by describing Dickens 's view of the London working classes , then describing the view of one or more modern historians , then showing that the two views are significantly different to the extent that Dickens 's could be called incorrect .
146651	This could be developed further by defending your assertion against an alternative — a Dickens critic who says that Dickens had an accurate view of these matters — and showing that the alternative view is incorrect , or that the critic provides no supporting evidence ( and so that there is no reason to believe the alternative view ) .
146652	While justification of assertions is the motor which drives your essay forwards and builds your argument , you can not justify each assertion you make .
146653	Moreover , how important you think it is to justify your assertions will depend partly on what sort of writing you are engaged in ; a film review in a newspaper , for instance , is a genre where few assertions are justified .
146654	On the other hand , your reader will be interested in your writing only to the extent that what you say is convincing ; and while a film reviewer or a famous literary theorist may be able to rely on their position or fame to guarantee the authority of what they say , you will need to rely on the quality of your argument .
146655	Nevertheless , there are no fixed rules about justifying arguments in literary studies .
146656	The conventions about what counts as a convincing argument vary with time and place .
146657	Some people think , for example , that value judgements ( " this novel is Greene 's best " ) can not ever be justified ; you may disagree — it depends on your ideas about value and whether you think a value judgement is an arbitrary decision on the part of a reader .
146658	If you make an assertion which you think in principle could be justified but which you do n't have space to justify , you can alert the reader by adding a phrase like : " I am assuming that … " , " we could argue that … " , or " it is generally accepted that … " ; the advantage of using these phrases is that you acknowledge that there is some possibility of disagreement .
146659	When you write a sentence , you claim that something is true , that is , you explicitly assert a proposition .
146660	If you write " the second novel Dickens produced was called Oliver Twist " , then you are explicitly asserting that it is true that the second novel Dickens produced was called Oliver Twist .
146661	As you write , however , you inevitably commit yourself not only to propositions you explicitly assert , but also to other propositions which are implicit in , or presupposed by , the words you actually write down .
146662	In writing the above sentence , for example , you PRESUPPOSED that Dickens produced a second novel .
146663	" Pre-suppose " means in effect that you have already supposed or claimed this without needing to write it down .
146664	Hidden commitments of this kind are often the result of using particular words ( here , " the " ) or phrases or constructions .
146665	Consider the following sentence :
146666	William Golding 's best novel , Lord of the Flies , is a reflection of the widespread pessimism about the morality of children in the 1950s .
146667	This sentence makes a number of claims , some more overt than others .
146668	The overt claim is " Lord of the Flies is a reflection of the widespread pessimism about the morality of children in the 1950s " .
146669	But two other claims are being made as well : " Lord of the Flies is William Golding 's best novel " , and " There was widespread pessimism about the morality of children in the 1950s " .
146670	These two claims are both presupposed by the sentence ; that is , the sentence just assumes they are true .
146671	Such hidden assertions can easily be discovered , but it is less easy to notice two further presuppositions in the sentence : " It is possible to evaluate texts ( i.e. say that one is the 'best' ) " and " It is possible for texts to reflect social attitudes " .
146672	So what this example shows is that a sentence which seems to contain one assertion can turn out to contain many different assertions , some in the form of presuppositions .
146673	This is unavoidable , and occurs all the time as you speak or write .
146674	But there is a good reason for making yourself aware of presuppositions : you need to be as conscious as possible of all the assertions you are making , including hidden ones .
146675	Presuppositions and hidden assumptions are the hiding place for common sense and shared assumptions .
146676	If you think a particular assumption might reasonably be disagreed with by the reader of your essay you should make that assumption explicit ( and then provide some support for it ) .
146677	For these reasons , it is useful to know what the words , phrases and constructions are which regularly conceal presuppositions , so that you know what you are letting yourself in for when you use them .
146678	* We have seen one kind .
146679	A phrase like " the second novel Dickens produced " is not itself a statement of fact , but can be rewritten as a sentence to show its presupposition ( " Dickens produced a second novel " ) .
146680	Using " the " at the beginning of a phrase implies general agreement about the existence of whatever the phrase refers to .
146681	A similar mechanism works in : What is Kristeva 's position on gender-positioning in this article ?
146682	This presupposes that Kristeva has a position on gender-positioning in this article .
146683	* Other words which carry presuppositions are the adverbial words and phrases which mean " again " ( ITERATIVES ) : Emily Brontë began writing the novel once more .
146684	This presupposes that Emily Brontë had begun writing the novel before .
146685	* Presuppositions are sometimes embedded with particular verbs , including FACTIVE VERBS like " regret " or " know " , which presuppose that what is regretted or known is a fact .
146686	At the end of the book , the main character regrets believing in God .
146687	This presupposes that " the main character believed in God " .
146688	There are also IMPLICATIVE VERBS which imply one action by stating another : Victorian writers managed to persuade us that …
146689	This presupposes that Victorian writers tried to persuade us that … * Some connectives such as " although " , " since " and " because " also conceal presuppositions : Because Dickens was a social reformer , he focused in his work on poverty .
146690	This presupposes that Dickens was a social reformer .
146691	* It is also possible to put presuppositions into a sentence by just rearranging the parts , as in the following example ( called a CLEFT ) , based on " Senecan influence brought blood to Renaissance tragedy " : It was Senecan influence which brought blood to Renaissance tragedy .
146692	This presupposes that something brought blood to Renaissance tragedy .
146693	A superficially similar rearrangement ( called a PSEUDOCLEFT because it looks a bit like a cleft but is n't one ) is shown in this example : What contemporary novelists do well is comment on novel-writing rather than tell stories .
146694	This presupposes that " contemporary novelists do something well . "
146695	* Another arrangement of the sentence which carries a presupposition is the COUNTERFACTUAL CONDITIONAL : " if X had/had n't been the case , then Y " : If Renaissance dramatists had not known Seneca , they would have been less interested in blood .
146696	This presupposes that " Renaissance dramatists did know Seneca . "
146697	* Finally , another place for presuppositions to hide is in a clause which sets the scene in a sentence ; an example is the TEMPORAL CLAUSE , as in the following example : When Blake saw his first angels he was sitting in his garden .
146698	This presupposes that Blake saw angels .
146699	It is worth checking your essay to make sure that you are not presupposing things which you do n't believe are true , and that you are n't hiding anything in a presupposition which needs to be made explicit and justified .
146700	But presuppositions are essentially a tool rather than a nuisance — a way of expanding the power of your writing by enabling you to say a lot in a short space .
146701	They allow you to imply things without saying them directly , and so to develop complex arguments in relatively short passages of writing .
146702	As you write , there are some ideas which you present as " given " information ; they form an assumed background to what you wish to assert .
146703	Presuppositions contribute to that given information .
146704	Other ideas are presented as " new " information : they are what you offer as new , and so of interest .
146705	By judging which information to present as given and which to present as new , you establish an important dimension of your relationship with your reader .
146706	You are signalling what you take as common or assumed ground between your reader and yourself , and what you are representing as worthy of attention , as " new " ideas .
146707	Consider this simple introduction to an essay : Shakespeare 's birth in 1564 marks the beginning of the high period of English drama .
146708	When he later produced a series of outstanding tragic works , what he managed to do , in effect , was to bring about the transition from crude medieval drama towards the more sustained literary achievement of the Renaissance .
146709	In this opening , a number of ideas are not stated , but presupposed : — Shakespeare was born in 1564 .
146710	— There was a high period of English drama ( which had a beginning ) .
146711	— Shakespeare produced a series of outstanding tragic works .
146712	— Shakespeare tried to bring about a transition .
146713	— There was a transition from crude medieval drama towards Renaissance drama .
146714	— Other dramatists did not bring about such a transition .
146715	— There is a literary achievement of the Renaissance .
146716	— There was a Renaissance .
146717	All these ideas — each of which is in principle arguable — are compacted into two relatively short sentences and are linked together in a gradually unfolding argument .
146718	But the writer could equally have made different decisions about what should be treated as given ( shared background knowledge ) and what should be presented as new .
146719	The essay might have started in any one of the following ways : ( a ) " Arguably there is a transition between … "
146720	( b ) " William Shakespeare was born in … "
146721	( c ) " The concept of a 'Renaissance' in history can be established … "
146722	The distinction between given and new information contributes substantially to the level at which your essay is pitched .
146723	This , in turn , gives your reader a sense of what sort of debate or discussion you see yourself as being engaged in ; and it is this , alongside whatever concrete arguments you make on a given topic , which shapes a reader 's or examiner 's general response to what you write .
146724	3.4 GENERALISATION
146725	In this chapter so far we have focused on specificities in your argument — the presuppositions in your sentences , the specific things you can say about particular texts , the setting of something in its context , and so on .
146726	However , specific observations always needs to be related to general claims or GENERALISATIONS , without which the specific can just seem trivial and random .
146727	For example , a specific observation about some aspect of a text ( such as its rhyme scheme ) could lead to a generalisation based on how it fits with other related observations ( the rhyme schemes of other poems by the same poet ) .
146728	A concrete comment on some special element of the text ( such as a particularly striking metaphor ) could lead to a more abstract general discussion of its significance beyond the text ( what makes any metaphor striking ? ) .
146729	Generalising from your experience of reading one unique passage or making a specific concrete observation leads to speculation about patterns or regularities , and beyond this to thinking about causation and correlation , which are central to explanation and argument .
146730	So generalisation is important as a way of pulling you out of just describing the details of your individual experience as a reader , enabling you to make statements which are likely to be of interest to others about patterns or structures in the way literary texts work .
146731	In practice , you might , for instance : ( a ) Broaden your essay 's conclusions , so that they could in principle be applied to other books , or an author 's work as a whole .
146732	Example In an essay on an eighteenth-century play , which has argued that the women in the play are generally seen to be a source of disruption or confusion , you could conclude by asking whether women are general sources of disruption , broadly understood , in eighteenth-century drama .
146733	( b ) Treat a specific question or topic as an instance of a more general question or topic .
146734	Example The topic " Islamic elements in Byron 's poetry " could be given greater interest and significance by placing it in a more general discussion of " foreignness " in British Romantic texts .
146735	( c ) Try to link together the scattered specific observations you might make on a text .
146736	Example If you have a paragraph on irony in Conrad 's " Heart of Darkness " , a paragraph on characterisation and a paragraph on narrative closure , you could try to link them together by talking more generally about the abstract relationship between irony , characterisation and narrative closure .
146737	3.5 SIGNALLING YOUR ATTITUDE TOWARDS YOUR OWN ARGUMENT
146738	As you construct your argument , you will be obliged to make judgements about how firmly you are committed to each of its ideas , and how strong the evidence is for believing them .
146739	As you present ideas , therefore , you need to consider issues of EPISTEMIC MODALITY .
146740	Epistemic modality ( the word " epistemic " means " to do with knowledge " ) involves various markers in language of the degree of certainty or possibility a speaker or writer feels towards what is being said .
146741	It includes modal verbs such as " must " and " may " , as well as phrases such as " it is possible that … " , " it is likely that …
146742	" .
146743	A range of adverbial expressions , including " apparently " and " actually " , have a similar effect .
146744	Two different problematic situations are likely to arise as you present your argument .
146745	The first is that what you say seems obvious ; so , in slight embarrassment , you add " obviously " or " of course " — implying " of course everyone knows this " .
146746	The second situation is that you feel there is a risk of overstating the line of argument you are pursuing .
146747	Consider first the effect of adding " of course " to a sentence .
146748	George Eliot of course believed that …
146749	If we already know what we are being told — as " of course " implies — then the question immediately arises why we are being told again .
146750	Sometimes " of course " is added not because the information is obvious , but rather because you want to create the effect of being someone so deeply familiar with the material that this information is basic or obvious .
146751	Consider the different impression of yourself which you would give if you wrote :
146752	Dickens , of course , was a novelist .
146753	As opposed to writing : Dickens , of course , completed the last double instalment of Martin Chuzzlewit in the middle of June 1844 .
146754	As in most other areas of essay writing , there is no fixed rule governing use of " of course " .
