157314	In the countries studied in which a proportion of the population had received no formal education ( Italy and Mexico ) , only a small proportion of those without an education felt that national government had some effect .
157315	( The proportion of those with a formal education ascribing influence to the government was lower than that in the United States and in Britain , albeit still a majority among the university-educated ) .
157316	From this , one may infer the importance of education for the purposes of political socialization .
157317	The correlation between education and political socialization in Britain is not greatly dissimilar to that in the United States .
157318	Those with higher levels of education are more likely than those with only a primary education to attach significance to the action of government , to believe that they can have some influence on government , to pay attention to politics and election campaigns , to take the view ( though not necessarily to practice it ) that citizens should be active in their local community , to hold opinions on a wide range of political subjects , and to be actively involved in politics .
157319	In Britain , a little over 3% of the adult population have degrees .
157320	Of the members of Parliament ( MPs ) who sat in the Parliament of 1979-1983 , over 62% were graduates .
157321	Where Britain and the United States differ is in the way that the subject of politics is taught .
157322	In Britain , manifest teaching of the subject , insofar as it is manifest , can best be described as subtle .
157323	There is little emphasis on symbolic acts ( there is no obvious English equivalent to saluting the flag ) and little formal teaching of politics as such .
157324	The media of other subjects are employed .
157325	Stradling writes , " Until comparatively recently the prevailing view on political education in England was either that it was already adequately taken care of through History , Geography , Social or General Studies or that it was a wholly unsuitable subject for the school curriculum . "
157326	Only recently has the opportunity to study politics as a distinct and legitimate subject been expanded within secondary schools .
157327	Relative to other disciplines , it remains a little-taught subject .
157328	However , the implications of this are not as great as might be thought .
157329	Almond and Verba found that having been taught about government increases a sense of subjective political competence .
157330	Against this , some studies in the United States , where formal study of " civics " is more extensive than in Britain , found that taking such courses had little impact on political knowledge and attitudes .
157331	Similar findings have resulted from a recent survey of British school pupils .
157332	What is more important is the length of period in education .
157333	In the British study , pupils staying on at school until the age of 18 achieved much higher scores on political knowledge than did those leaving school at 16 .
157334	From this , one might hypothesize that education is important in developing the intellectual skills necessary to absorb and make sense of political material communicated by other media .
157335	Attendance at school , and particularly at certain schools , can be important also in providing an environment that can serve to reinforce certain norms and traditions .
157336	At leading public schools , most notably Eton , there is a tradition of providing MPs , government ministers , and prime ministers .
157337	At such schools , a pupil is more likely to consider pursuing a political career than is the case with pupils attending an inner-city comprehensive school with no such tradition .
157338	In most cases , the school environment tends to reinforce the influence of the home background .
157339	Occupation and class , as we have seen , are closely related .
157340	The former is usually employed as the primary criterion for assessing the latter .
157341	Both are important in the context of political socialization .
157342	Occupation and Class
157343	Certain occupations are important in terms not only of class but also of status .
157344	A doctor of medicine is in the same social class as a company director but is more likely than the director to be accorded some degree of deference by the local community .
157345	Holding a position of responsibility gives one standing in the community .
157346	Holding jobs that are well paying and/or rewarding in terms of personal self-satisfaction may increase one 's contentment with the society in which one exists .
157347	Conversely , pursuing a mundane , poorly paid job or no job at all may provoke a sense of alienation from society .
157348	Certain jobs by their nature may lead to greater social awareness or to a greater degree of social intercourse than others .
157349	Class is an abstraction and the concept acquires meaning only as a result of the socialization process just outlines .
157350	From one 's parents , education , occupation , and associated life-style one acquires an awareness of social class .
157351	Such awareness becomes important in helping clarify one 's place in society and , thus , one 's relationship to others in that society .
157352	It serves to give some meaning and shape to one 's social existence .
157353	There is an important but not complete relationship between class and partisan support .
157354	That this should be so is not surprising .
157355	Those in middle-class occupations are more likely to be better paid and pursue a preferred life-style than those in working-class occupations ( though the emphasis should be on the likelihood , not the certainty ) .
157356	Hence , one might expect the middle class to opt for the political party most likely to conserve the existing state of affairs .
157357	Those in working-class jobs and those with no jobs at all might be expected to opt for a party that offers some degree of social change and appears more empathic toward the " have-nots " than toward the " haves . "
157358	This hypothesis is largely but not wholly borne out by the empirical evidence .
157359	Middle-class voters have tended to support the Conservative party in Britain , and working-class voters the Labour party .
157360	The relationship has never been a complete one .
157361	Some middle-class voters have supported the Labour Party and about one-third of working-class voters have traditionally cast their ballots for Conservative candidates .
157362	In recent years , the significance of the class-party tie has declined .
157363	Nonetheless , as we shall see , class provides the most important indicator of partisan support .
157364	No other indicator has proved so reliable .
157365	Location can be important in the process of political socialization in a number of senses .
157366	The location of one 's residence is important .
157367	Living in an area of expensive detached houses can serve to reinforce one 's sense of being middle-class .
157368	The area provides a social milieu that reinforces that awareness .
157369	Conversely , living in an area of less expensive terraced accommodation or of council houses ( estates composed of houses rented from the local authority are common ) reinforces one 's identification with the working class .
157370	Within such areas , there is often a particular lifestyle .
157371	Location
157372	The independent influence of location is borne out when correlated with partisan support .
157373	Voters who live in class-specific communities are more likely to vote for the relevant class-specific party than are those not living in such communities .
157374	As Rose observes , " Working-class voters in safe Labour seats are much more likely to vote Labour than those in the same class , but living in a marginal or Conservative constituency .
157375	Environment affects middle-class voters in Conservative areas , but the effect is not so strong . "
157376	Moving into such specific areas , with changes in the pattern of home ownership , can effect a change in partisan support .
157377	There is also a correlation between partisan support and urban versus rural location .
157378	This pattern became more pronounced in the 1960s and 1970s , as did the division between North and South .
157379	Increasingly , the Labour party became the dominant party of the North of England , and the Conservative party that of the South .
157380	That this should be so is not surprising , given changes in employment and demographic patterns .
157381	In 1980 , Curtice and Steed pointed out that " the peripheral areas of Britain , with their higher unemployment , and the declining inner parts of conurbations , have become steadily more Labour ; while the expanding , more prosperous areas have become more Conservative . "
157382	In the 1983 general election , the Labour vote declined in all regions by between 6% and 12% .
157383	The lowest regional decline took place in Scotland .
157384	In urban areas , the swing against Labour was half what it was in rural and mixed areas .
157385	Labour , as one analysis showed , remained the party of the traditional working class of the council estates , of Scotland , and of the North .
157386	The mass media of communication are also important .
157387	They are significant not only as media for transmitting material , television now being the main source of political information for most people , but also for the choice of what material to transmit .
157388	By choosing to transmit some stories rather than others , those in control of television and newspapers can have some impact on political perceptions and values .
157389	In Britain , the national orientation of the broadcasting media and of newspapers is important .
157390	The size of the country and the dual position of London as the nation 's capital and its largest city has facilitated a national orientation — primarily a London orientation — not possible in the United States .
157391	The Mass Media
157392	The partisan influence of the media in Britain is unclear .
157393	The broadcasting media are statutorily required to be impartial .
157394	Newspapers can and do express partisan preferences .
157395	Newspapers with a significant political reporting are not widely read , whereas television news programs are often among the most-watched programs .
157396	Research into the impact of the media in Britain is not extensive .
157397	What research has been done on their effects , especially in the United States , suggests that their importance is primarily as a reinforcing rather than a realigning agent .
157398	The significance of this role should not be underestimated .
157399	The process by which a individual becomes politically socialized is a complex one .
157400	The influences just outlined are in most cases the more important ones but they are by no means the only ones — nor are they exclusive .
157401	They clearly interact with one another , as has been obvious from the foregoing .
157402	It has been virtually impossible to discuss one influence without drawing out the impact of another .
157403	Also , these influences are far from static .
157404	Changes in family structures , the educational system , the nature of employment , and demographic and housing patterns may affect the socialization process .
157405	As we have seen , children staying longer in formal education appear to acquire more political knowledge than those leaving school earlier .
157406	More children than before are now acquiring a formal education beyond the minimum school-leaving age .
157407	Unemployment may generate a sense of political alienation .
157408	As we have seen , unemployment has risen steeply in Britain in recent years .
157409	A Complex Mix
157410	The importance of some of these changes will be touched on later in this work , particularly in the context of partisan support .
157411	However , such changes are relative .
157412	In terms of the basic values being transmitted in the process of political socialization , the most significant feature is not change but rather continuity .
157413	The media for political socialization in Britain are not dissimilar to those in the United States and many other polities .
157414	To know this is useful , but to identify those media is to identify the means for transmitting the values and beliefs that coalesce to form the political culture , and not to identify the political culture itself .
157415	That is a separate exercise , undertaken in the next chapter .
157416	Having identified some of the salient features of contemporary Britain and , as a prerequisite , the process of political socialization , we can now progress to the more analytically useful study of the British political culture .
157417	CONTINUITY AND CHANGE
157418	The British Political Culture
157419	CONTINUITY AND CHANGE , as we have observed , are features of every political system .
157420	In order to understand the extent and nature of that change one has to generate some analytically useful framework .
157421	What the opening chapter did was to provide largely descriptive material of the society with which we are concerned .
157422	It did not generate a framework that would help us understand the nature of continuity and change in Britain .
157423	The purpose of this chapter is to provide such a framework .
157424	The emphasis of the chapter will be on the political culture .
157425	As I shall seek to show , however , that culture can not be divorced from the constraints of history and of physical and spatial resources .
157426	Each has had a significant impact on the other .
157427	The impact has not been in one direction only : the political culture has served to shape political perceptions and actions , and hence to influence the nation 's political history .
157428	Conversely , those actions have been constrained by the experiences of history .
157429	They have also been constrained by Britain 's geographic location and limited resources .
157430	A number of problems have to be borne in mind .
157431	As we shall see , there are problems inherent in trying to give shape to such an abstract concept as political culture .
157432	There is the danger of tautology and of failing to distinguish between how a system operates and the way in which people believe it should operate .
157433	There is the problem also of attempting to discern the cause-and-effect relationships among culture , history , and resources .
157434	The problem here is analogous to that embodies in the familiar conundrum " Which came first , the chicken or the egg ? "
157435	The existence of a stable political culture in Britain has been ascribed by some to the effectiveness of government .
157436	But what has enabled government to be effective ?
157437	Has it been a distinctive political culture , citizens being prepared to acquiesce in and , when called on , to support the demands made of them by government ?
157438	If so , what explains the existence of such a political culture ?
157439	Is not a partial explanation the effectiveness of government ?
157440	The problem is an acute one in the case of Britain , given the absence of any clear point of departure .
157441	Where does English , Scottish , or Welsh history begin ?
157442	At what point is a political culture discernible ?
157443	The problem is largely an insuperable one , and all we can do at this stage is to bear it in mind .
157444	Fortunately , it does not present an insurmountable obstacle ; as I shall seek to show , the importance of the relationship is one of mutual reinforcement .
157445	What , then , is the British political culture ?
157446	How important have been the constraints of history and of resources ?
157447	How does it compare with other polities ?
157448	And is it , as some writers have suggested , in a state of collapse ?
157449	Political culture is a vague abstract concept that has been subject to various definitions .
157450	In its simplest form , it may be described as denoting the emotional and attitudinal environment within which a political system operates .
157451	Various political scientists have sought to define and identify different types of political culture .
157452	Almond and Verba , for example , identified three ideal types : participant , subject , and parochial .
157453	Others have sought to generate criteria by which to assess the distinctive features of a political culture .
157454	THE POLITICAL CULTURE
157455	In his work on political oppositions in western democracies , Robert Dahl observed that patterns of opposition may have something to do with widely shared cultural premises .
157456	He noted that four kinds of culturally derived orientations toward politics seem to have a bearing on the pattern of opposition .
157457	Those four orientations can usefully be employed to help understand and explain attitudes not just toward political opposition in Britain but to the political culture as a whole .
157458	They enable one to draw out the distinctive features of that culture , in a more useful manner than does the framework provided by others , and to consider the impact of both history and resources .
157459	Those four orientations , listed not in the order provided by Dahl but in the order I believe to be most significant to an understanding to British political culture , are toward ( 1 ) problem-solving , ( 2 ) the political system , ( 3 ) cooperation and individuality , and ( 4 ) other people .
157460	Orientation toward Problem-Solving Giovanni Sartori has distinguished two approaches to problem-solving : the empirical and the rational .
157461	The empirical approach is concerned with what is and what can be seen and touched , proceeding on the basis of testing and retesting and largely rejecting dogma and abstract or coherent grand designs for change .
157462	The rationalist approach , by contrast , is concerned with abstraction rather than facts , stressing the need for deductive consistency and tending to be dogmatic and definitive .
157463	Dahl states : " While the empirical approach takes the attitude that if a program does not work in practice there must be something wrong about the theory , the rationalist will retort that what is true in theory must also be true in practice — that it is the practice , not the theory , that is wrong . "
157464	France has been identified as employing a rationalist approach .
157465	Germany and Italy , to some extent , tend also to find such an approach useful .
157466	Britain and the United States , by contrast , are seen as the exemplars of an empirical approach .
157467	Indeed , it is my contention that this approach is most marked in the British case and that it constitutes the most significant aspect of British political culture .
157468	Although more oriented toward an empirical approach , the United States has exhibited some elements of the rationalist .
157469	While tempered by experience and ( according to Beard ) self-interest , the framers of the United States Constitution were informed by Lockean values and sought to impose a political framework in line with a Lockean conception of society .
157470	Those values and that conception of society have permeated the American consciousness , so much so that they have largely gone unstated .
157471	They have been so pervasive and so self-evident that there has been little point in articulating them .
157472	Hence , the United States might be described as being oriented toward a mix of the empirical and the rationalist , albeit with the former being clearly the more dominant of the two .
157473	Britain , by contrast , has a distinct orientation toward the empirical approach .
157474	Even the political system , however strong the attachment to it , tends to be justified in pragmatic terms .
157475	Democracy , having been implemented in largely pragmatic fashion , has been lauded on the grounds that " it works . "
157476	The point has been well put by Vivien Hart in comparing American and British approaches : " In America , " she wrote , " the emphasis has been on what democracy is and should be , while Britain has been characterised by a more pragmatic and less urgent emphasis on what democracy is and can be . "
157477	Empiricism seems appropriate to the English consciousness .
157478	Instinct , trial and error , and incremental change are the essence of the English approach to problem-solving .
157479	" I believe in the instinctive wisdom of our well-tried democracy , " declared Churchill in 1945 — shortly before going down to election defeat .
157480	Such an orientation to problem-solving has been a distinctive feature of English political culture for many centuries , discernible , I would suggest , since at least the thirteenth century .
157481	It is an approach that has informed political actions and hence the political history of the country .
157482	An empirical orientation has in turn been reinforced by the experience of history — it is the approach that has always been employed and no external constraints have managed to force themselves on the nation to generate conditions in which a rationalist approach would be possible .
157483	In the wake of the War of Independence , Americans were able to sit down and generate a political system from first principles .
157484	Invasions by foreign powers and subsequent liberation ( or absence of liberation ) have put other states in similar positions .
157485	England , by contrast , has never been faced with or sought such an opportunity .
157486	The closest it came was during the Protectorate of Oliver Cromwell in the seventeenth century .
157487	When that failed , the country resorted as far as possible to the conditions prevailing prior to its creation .
157488	English history is scattered with philosophers generating theories that have failed to find congenial soil in the nation 's consciousness .
157489	Ideologies have been either discarded or else molded to fit with the experience of history .
157490	Prevailing theories , once they no longer seem appropriate , have been dispensed with .
157491	The act of dispensing with them has not always met with common assent nor has it always been smooth — the English historical landscape is scattered with periods of violence and upheaval — but once the dispensing process is achieved , it has largely been accepted .
157492	Hankering after the old order is congenial to some minds , but seeking to revert by force or civil unrest to the status quo ante is not .
157493	In the English perception , empiricism is both a descriptive and a prescriptive term .
157494	To the Englishman , it is both what is and what he believes always has been .
157495	Orientation toward the political system may be classified as allegiant when attitudes , feelings , and evaluations are favorable to the political system ; apathetic or detached when feelings and evaluations are neutral ; and alienated when such feelings and evaluations are unfavorable .
157496	Italy and France have been cited as examples of political cultures that generate alienation and a large measure of apathy .
157497	West Germany has been put forward as having a culture that generates detachment .
157498	In contrast , Britain and the United States are among those countries cited as exhibiting a strong allegiant orientation .
157499	Orientation toward the Political System
157500	Almond and Verba found that evaluation of the political system in Britain was the product of a mix of participant and deferential orientations .
157501	A participant orientation was developed in Britain ( citizens being oriented to the input as well as the output side of the political system , believing that they enjoyed access to it ) , but it was one adapted to an existing deference to the independent authority of government .
157502	The participant orientation in Britain , unlike that in the United States , did not displace the deferential , it remained important .
157503	The participant orientation finds expression in citizens ' beliefs that they can influence government at both the national and local level .
157504	Although Almond and Verba found few people in their survey who actually sought to exert such influence , the proportion who believed that they could exert influence was significant .
157505	Of British respondents , 57% said that they could influence national and local government .
157506	( The figure for the United States was 67% . )
157507	Only 19% of those questioned felt that they had no influence at national and local levels .
157508	( The figure for the United States was 15 per cent . )
157509	By contrast , of Germans , Italians , and Mexicans interviewed , more believed they had no influence at national and local level than believed that they had .
157510	Only 25% of Italians , for example , believed that they could influence national and local government , and 47% said they had no such influence .
157511	Deference to the authority of government has found expression in a number of ways .
157512	It has been shown in a voluntary compliance with basic political laws .
157513	Criminal acts tend to be antisocial rather than conscious acts against " the state . "
157514	( Indeed , the concept of " the state " is one that is not well entrenched in English consciousness . )
157515	There has been little overt opposition to the parliamentary form of government in Britain .
157516	Some may want to modify its form but do not challenge the principle of it , nor do they seek to change its form through unlawful and certainly not violent means .
157517	When government authority has been challenged citizens have expressed themselves in favor of maintaining that authority .
157518	When called on by government to act in time of war , citizens have been prepared to respond .
157519	Such deference has often been seen as allied with a social deference , citizens according certain skills of government to those drawn from a particular group .
157520	Walter Bageho , in his classic work The English Constitution , identified England as a " deferential nation , " one that had a structure of its own .
157521	" Certain persons , " he wrote , " are by common consent agreed to be wiser than others , and their opinion is , by consent , to rank for much more than its numerical value . "
157522	Such deference , though possibly weakened , survived into the era of mass suffrage and the democratic ideal .
157523	It has been seen as a significant feature of contemporary Britain and has been variously offered as a partial explanation of the continuing success of the Conservative party and its socially atypical leadership .
157524	Such deference , though , has been contingent rather than certain .
157525	It has been based on a reciprocity between governors and governed .
157526	The populace has deferred to the independent authority of government and to those who occupy government in return for the satisfaction of expectations .
157527	Those expectations have covered the substance of policies ( improving material well-being , for example ) as well as the form of government .
157528	Almond and Verba , for example , found that an overwhelming majority of Britons expected equal treatment from politicians and from bureaucrats .
157529	Conversely , those to whom citizens accord deference have been characterized by having an in-bred sense of duty .
157530	A stress on responsibilities as well as rights has been a significant and long-standing feature of the British culture and has been well imbued by a large part of the nation 's political elite .
157531	A paternalistic concern for the well-being of the nation has been a feature of most if not all monarchs and has been associated with a particular and often predominant tradition within the Conservative party .
157532	As long as the political system has been able to maintain the capacity to meet the demands and expectations of citizens , an allegiant orientation has been demonstrated by citizens .
157533	The longer the system has been able to do this and the longer people have been socialized into accepting the efficacy of the system , the stronger and more enduring the allegiance has been .
157534	In Almond and verba 's survey , more Britons expressed pride in their governmental and political institutions than in any other feature of the nation that was mentioned .
157535	The same pride was found in Americans , on a larger scale .
157536	( Of Americans , 85% expressed pride in their institutions , compared with 46% of Britons . )
157537	In stark contrast , only 7% of Germans expressed pride in their governmental and political institutions , and the figure for Italians was 3% .
157538	Some cultures emphasize the values of cooperating with others , conciliating opposing views , and being prepared to compromise and submerge one 's own ideas in a broader and more popularly acceptable solution .
157539	Others , by contrast , stress the virtues of maintaining the distinctiveness , ideas , and integrity of the individual , such virtues being considered superior to those of compromise and cooperation .
157540	Orientation toward Cooperation and Individuality
157541	France and Italy have been cited as examples of countries in which the maintenance of group and individual integrity is stressed in both the general culture and in political life .
157542	Britain and the United States are included among those countries in which the political culture emphasizes the virtues of compromise and conciliation , without threatening personal integrity .
157543	The Anglo-American perception was well expressed by Edmund Burke in 1775 .
157544	" All government , indeed every human benefit and enjoyment , every virtue , and every prudent act , " he declared , " is founded on compromise and barter . "
157545	In Britain there is an almost instinctive distaste for conflict , both in personal relationships and in political life .
157546	The formal political framework facilitates an adversary relationship among political parties , but the underlying reality is a quest for compromise .
157547	Parties play according to the rules of the constitutional game .
157548	Similar observations can be made about groups in industry and in society generally .
157549	There is a penchant , almost , for resolving disputes by discussion , by sitting around a table and ironing out one 's differences .
157550	It is an orientation compatible with the others already identified and it is eminently congenial to a society that stresses the responsibilities as well as the rights of the individual .
157551	It remains an orientation that Britons not only find congenial but also take as the source of a certain pride .
157552	A belief that one can have faith and confidence in others has been put forward as a culturally rooted phenomenon , with potentially important implications for political life .
157553	Research by Morris Rosenberg has shown that " faith in people " is related to democratic and internationalist values and attitudes .
157554	In their study , Almond and Verba found that the Americans and the British " tend to be consistently most positive about the safety and responsiveness of the human environment . "
157555	The Germans and the Italians , by contrast , were found to be more negative , and the Mexicans inconsistent .
157556	Orientation toward Other People
157557	Trust in one 's fellow countrymen remains a significant feature of contemporary British society .
157558	A Gallup Poll in 1980 found that 85% of respondents considered other Britons to be very or fairly trustworthy .
157559	The experience of history may have helped to consolidate such a sense of trust .
157560	Britons have stood successfully shoulder-to-shoulder in order to win battles abroad and to repel foreign invaders from their shores .
157561	During the Second World War , the nation did not have to contend with a significant fifth column or with the equivalent of Vichy collaborators .
157562	There is little or nothing in recent history that would give Britons cause to distrust their compatriots .
157563	Similarly , the experience of history , island isolation , and shared values may serve to explain differing levels of trust that Britons have in other people .
157564	Britons tend to retain trust in the inhabitants of countries in which Britain has had or retains colonial interests ; countries that share a common language , values , and ( in some cases ) ancestry ; and countries that have stood together in times of crisis .
157565	There are strong emotional ties to old Commonwealth countries such as New Zealand , Canada , and Australia .
157566	There is also a strong sense of closeness to the United States .
157567	Of respondents in the Gallup Poll in 1980 , 70% regarded Americans as very or fairly trustworthy .
157568	( Only the Swiss and the Dutch received marginally higher ratings . )
157569	Another poll a year later asked respondents the extent to which they thought they could trust certain countries as allies in the event of war .
157570	The proportion responding that they thought they could trust the United Sates " a great deal " was 62% ( up from 45% in 1975 ) , a figure not matched by any other country : the closest was Norway , which 37% thought they could trust to the same extent .
157571	The two polls revealed lower levels of trust in those countries and people that historically have been Britain 's enemies .
157572	To the island inhabitants of Britain , such peoples remain distant ( though the English Channel constitutes now more a psychological than a physical barrier ) , with alien cultures , different interests , and different thought processes .
157573	Englishmen and Scotsmen , as Anthony King observed , have tended not to think like Europeans nor to think of themselves as Europeans .
157574	In the 1980 Gallup Poll , only 32% of the Britons questioned regarded the French as very or fairly trustworthy .
157575	The Russians scored 18% .
157576	( The West Germans , perhaps surprisingly , scored 60% . )
157577	Only 6% of those questioned would trust the French a great deal as allies in time of war , 4% would trust the Spanish , 4% the Italians , and only 3% the Turks .
157578	Again , the Germans did better , 22% being prepared to trust them a great deal .
157579	Finally , 47% said they would trust the Italians " not at all , " and 45% gave a similar response for the French .
157580	Despite British membership of the European Communities , there is an important sense in which Britain and certainly the British still look westward across the Atlantic rather than eastward over the English channel .
157581	And despite the travails of recent times , trust in one 's fellow countrymen and a discriminating , possibly confident , perception of other people remain significant features of the British political culture .
157582	The political culture of Britain may then be characterized , in broad terms , as having the four orientations identified : empirical in terms of problem-solving and change , allegiant in terms of the political system , cooperative in making decisions , and trusting with relation to fellow countrymen and allies .
157583	These , it is important to stress , are generalizations — there are always individuals or subcultures that may not have such orientations .
157584	What is important is that they are and remain the orientations of most Britons , both at the mass and the elite level .
157585	A DECLINING CULTURE ?
157586	The strength of the culture may be said to lie in the convergence of these orientations — that is , they are compatible with and reinforce one another , and similarly are compatible with and are reinforced by the experience of history .
157587	The stress on cooperation and compromise , an emphasis compatible with an empirical approach to change , has facilitated the integration of groups and individuals into the political system .
157588	Such integration may be seen as reinforcing an allegiant rather than a neutral or alienated orientation to the political system .
157589	History , as we have mentioned , has been kind : the country has staved off invasion by its enemies , and the resources have been available for government to make and meet commitments in response to changing demands and expectations .
157590	As a result , it has been possible to interpret the experience of history as justifying or reinforcing an attachment to empirical problem-solving and to the virtues of cooperation and trust .
157591	The interplay of these variables generated what Almond and Verba characterized as " the civic culture , " " a pluralistic culture based on communication and persuasion , a culture of consensus and diversity , a culture that permitted change but moderated it . "
157592	What of the civic culture today ?
157593	My argument is simply stated : Although subject to modification , the civic culture remains .
157594	What has been the subject of radical , almost revolutionary , change over the past decade or so has not been the civic culture but the perceptions of that culture .
157595	In short , it has not changed as much as observers think it has .
157596	I do not argue that the political culture of Britain remains unchanged .
157597	The culture not only allows for change , usually incremental but occasionally radical , but itself can and does change .
157598	In good British fashion , however , that change has tended to be piecemeal rather than comprehensive .
157599	Some values , attitudes and emotions have been subject to modification over time , but the essential orientations outlined above have not been discarded .
157600	They remain the orientations that converge to form the predominant element of the British political culture .
157601	What has changed , and changed radically over the period from the late 1960s to the early 1980s , has been the perception of that culture .
157602	Analyses of the British political culture have swung , pendulum fashion , from one extreme to the other .
157603	At times of apparent stability , contentment , and political success , there has been a tendency to see the political culture in idealized terms , to hold it aloft and laud it as a culture to be admired and possibly even envied .
157604	Although Almond and Verba drew attention to some of the inconsistencies and problems inherent in the civic culture , it was nonetheless difficult not to ascribe positive connotations to that culture .
157605	There are a number of problems inherent in the political culture .
157606	A disposition to incremental change can deflect one from considering or even comprehending wider and more fundamental problems .
157607	The combination of an empirical orientation and historical continuity has produced a political system that is complex and disparate .
157608	While the American federal system has been likened to a marble cake , the British political system can be likened to a patchwork quilt .
157609	It may look to some extent like the original , it may even retain traces of the original , but the many pieces that make the whole were added at different times and have been the subject of change and much repair work .
157610	It includes structures that ( according to some observers ) have facilitated policy discontinuity — a discontinuity not incompatible with an empirical orientation to change — yet comprises such an interdependent complex of political bodies that it has become increasingly difficult for government to govern and to initiate radical and comprehensive change .
157611	Such difficulty has been exacerbated by the desire to resolve problems by compromise .
157612	Problems that can not be resolved by reasoned debate have tended to be ignored in the hope that they will go away .
157613	Such inherent problems tend to be discounted , ignored , or even interpreted in a favorable light at times when the political system appears to be successfully meeting the demands and expectations of the populace .
157614	When the system appears to be malfunctional , usually at times of economic difficulty for the country , some commentators identify such inherent problems as providing at least a partial explanation for the system 's poor showing .
157615	In the latter half of the 1970s , for example , policy discontinuity arising from an electoral and political system that encouraged an " adversary style " of politics was offered as a partial explanation for Britain 's poor economic performance .
157616	Other commentators have sought to identify the nation 's problems not in terms of the effect of some aspects of the political culture but as agents generating and reflecting a decline in the culture itself .
157617	In the 1970s and early 1980s , a number of observers began to chart a decline in the civic culture .
157618	In 1982 , on the basis of some survey evidence , Samuel Beer concluded that " it is no exaggeration to speak of the decline in the civic culture as a " collapse " " .
157619	He argued that as old institutions failed to meet new expectations , so legitimacy in government would falter and trust in its equity and effectiveness would decline .
157620	He hypothesized and sought to show that the consequences of this included a greater self-assertion by participants , a decline of leadership , a weakening of party government , and a loosening of the nexus of class and party .
157621	" In an ironic sense , " Beer declared , " Britain is maintaining its leadership .
157622	As it once showed the way toward democratic success , today it blazes the trail toward democratic failure . "
157623	While Beer 's hypothesis is plausible as to the effect of institutions that fail to meet new expectations on legitimacy in government , it is arguable as to the extent to which such a failure to meet expectations has taken place .
157624	This is a point to which I shall return in the concluding chapter .
157625	Although government capacity to meet expectations has declined , its capacity to meet expectations in the past built up a body of diffuse support , support that now exists independently of particular failures to meet demands .
157626	Furthermore , there is evidence that the expectations themselves may be changing , converging more with the capacity of the system to meet them .
157627	Certainly , it will be my case that the political culture has neither declined nor been threatened to the extent suggested by Beer and other Jeremiahs .
157628	Certain institutions may be under threat ( as subsequent chapters will show ) but not in a manner inconsistent with the existing political culture .
157629	The civic culture may be weakened but it has not collapsed .
157630	Its position is similar to that of Mark Twain : reports of its death would be greatly exaggerated .
157631	As I shall seek to show , the political culture remains predominantly an allegiant one , and the important question to be addressed is not " why has there been a decline in the civic culture ? " but rather " why has that decline not been greater ? "
157632	PAST AND PRESENT
157633	Historical Perspective and Contemporary Problems
157634	A NUMBER OF INTRODUCTION TEXTS on British politics do not have chapters devoted specifically to political history .
157635	The omission is a surprising one .
157636	When the proposal for this book was under consideration by the publishers , a number of American professors were asked for their comments .
157637	One responded with this advice : " Make sure you incorporate as much historical detail as possible .
157638	American students do n't know much about British history . "
157639	It was a shrewd response .
157640	The need for such detail , however , is not confined to Americans interested in the subject ; it encompasses all those who seek to make some sense of the institutions and complex relationships that form the British polity in the 1980s .
157641	There has been no point in British history at which the prevailing method of government has been completely swept away , allowing those in power to sit down and create from first principles a new and clearly delineated form of government .
157642	The country has witnessed continuous and sometimes dramatic change .
157643	In the past 300 years alone , the nation has experienced industrialization , the advent of democracy , and the introduction and growth of the welfare state — yet the changes have never been such as to be described as revolutionary .
157644	They have been built upon and have adapted that which already existed .
157645	The body politic may have undergone radical surgery and it may have aged considerably , but it has continued to endure .
157646	What then , are the significant features of British history that help us understand the contemporary political system and the political culture .
157647	Limitations of space preclude a lengthy dissertation on what is a vast subject .
157648	That vastness is apparent when put in comparative perspective .
157649	The Magna Carta , for instance , was signed more than two centuries before Christopher Columbus set sail .
157650	A Parliament was summoned more than 500 years before the United States Congress first assembled .
157651	And an American president , unlike a British monarch , can not trace his presidential forebears back more than 1,000 years .
157652	Nonetheless , it is possible to provide a brief but structured sketch that furthers our understanding of contemporary British politics .
157653	This can be done under two headings : one is the emergence of parliamentary government , and the other is the development of the welfare state and the managed economy .
157654	The structure and relationships of the contemporary organs of government can be understood only in historical context .
157655	A study of the emergence of the welfare state highlights the increased demands and responsibilities borne by government .
157656	Both studies provide a necessary background to understanding some of the problems now faced by government .
157657	They serve also to highlight certain features of the political culture .
157658	One of the essential features of the British Constitution is a parliamentary government under a limited , or symbolic , monarchy .
157659	The formal elements of this type of government will be more fully outlined in the next chapter .
157660	For the moment , what concerns us is that this government is the product of change extending over several centuries , coming to fruition only in the past century .
157661	Its development has sometimes been characterized as being evolutionary , but in practice , it is the outgrowth of piecemeal change .
157662	HISTORICAL PERSPECTIVE
157663	The Emergence of Parliamentary Government
157664	Let us begin in the thirteenth century .
157665	Traditionally , the sovereign power in England resided in the monarch .
157666	Nonetheless , the king was expected to consult with his tenants-in-chief ( the earls , barons , and leading churchmen of the kingdom ) in order to discover and declare the law and to have their counsel before any levies of extraordinary taxation were made .
157667	This expectation was to find documented expression in the Magna Carta of 1215 , by which the King recognized it as a right of his subjects " to have the Common Council of the Kingdom " for the assessment of extraordinary aids — that is , taxation .
157668	Such consultation was undertaken through a Great Council , from which evolved what was to be recognized as a parlement or Parliament .
157669	The Great Council itself was essentially the precursor of the House of Lords .
157670	The House of Commons evolved from the summoning to council , in the latter half of the thirteenth century on a somewhat sporadic basis , of knights and burgesses as representatives of the counties and towns .
157671	At various times in the fourteenth century the Commons deliberated separately from the Lords , and there developed a formal separation of the two bodies .
157672	During the period of the Tudor monarchs in the sixteenth century , Parliament acquired enhanced status .
157673	It was generally supportive of the monarch but became more powerful because of the dependence upon it for that support , especially during the reign of Elizabeth I. The relationship between Crown and Parliament under the subsequent Stuart dynasty was one of conflict .
157674	The early Stuart kings James I and Charles I sought to assert the doctrine of the divine right of kings and to deny many of the privileges acquired or asserted by Parliament .
157675	This conflict was to lead to the civil war and the beheading of Charles I in 1642 .
157676	With the abolition of the monarchy came a brief period of rule by a Council of State elected by what was termed the Rump Parliament .
157677	( Some attempts were actually made to formulate a form of written constitution , but they came to nothing . )
157678	Rule by the Council of State was succeeded by Oliver Cromwell 's unsuccessful military dictatorship , and in 1660 Charles ' son returned to assume the throne as Charles II .
157679	The period between 1642 and 1660 proved an aberration in British history .
157680	The Restoration witnessed an attempt to return , unconditionally , to the country 's position as it was at the beginning of 1642 .
157681	Through this attempt the Restoration lent itself to a repetition of the earlier struggle between King and Commons .
157682	Relations between the two gradually deteriorated during the reign of Charles II and became severe in the reign of his successor , James II .
157683	James sought to reassert the divine right of kings , and Parliament combined against him .
157684	In 1688 James fled the country .
157685	At the invitation of Parliament , the throne was taken by William and Mary of Orange , James ' son-in-law and daughter .
157686	The new occupants of the throne owed their position to Parliament , and the new relationship between them was asserted by statute in the Bill of Rights .
157687	Although the Bill of Rights was important for enumerating various " Liberties of this Kingdom " ( Some of which were to be similarly expressed during the following century in the Bill of Rights of the United States Constitution ) , its essential purpose was to assert the position of Parliament in relation to the Crown .
157688	The raising of taxes or the dispensing of laws without the assent of Parliament was declared to be illegal .
157689	The monarch was expected to govern , but to do so only with the consent of Parliament .
157690	The Act of Settlement of 1701 , which determined the succession to the throne , affirmed that the laws of England " are the Birthright of the People thereof and all the Kings and Queens who shall ascend the Throne of this Realm ought to administer the Government of the same according to the said Laws and all their Officers and Ministers ought to serve them respectively according to the same . "
157691	The monarch thus became formally dependent on Parliament for consent to the raising of taxes and for the passage of legislation .
157692	In practice , he or she became increasingly dependent also on ministers for advice .
157693	The importance of ministers grew especially in the eighteenth century .
157694	The Hanoverian kings were not uninterested in political life but they had difficulty comprehending the complexities of domestic and foreign affairs .
157695	According to the historian J. H. Plumb , both George I and George II were " crassly stupid " and " incapable , totally incapable , of forming a policy . "
157696	During the period of their reigns , the leading body of the king 's ministers , generally known as the cabinet , began to meet without the king being present .
157697	The period also witnessed the emergence of a minister who was to become popularly known as the prime minister .
157698	( Not until the twentieth century was the office of prime minister to be mentioned in a statute . )
157699	The relationship among Crown , ministers , and Parliament in that century was one in which the king relied on his ministers to help formulate policy .
157700	Those ministers were chosen by the king on the basis of his personal confidence in them , and they remained responsible to him .
157701	They also were responsible to Parliament in order to achieve their ends , a fact recognized by both the king and his ministers .
157702	Nonetheless , parliamentary support was not difficult to obtain ; the king and his ministers had sufficient patronage and position usually to ensure such support .
157703	A ministry that enjoyed royal confidence could generally take the House of Lords for grated , and provided it did not prove incompetent or seek to impose excessive taxation , " its position was unassailable in the Commons . "
157704	The position was to change significantly in the nineteenth century .
157705	Britain underwent what has been popularly referred to as an industrial revolution in the period from the middle of the eighteenth century to the middle of the nineteenth .
157706	Seymour Martin Lipset has characterized the United States as the " first new nation , " but Britain has been described as " the first industrial nation . "
157707	Industry became more mechanized , improvements took place in agricultural production techniques , and there were improvements in transport and in the organization of trade and banking .
157708	There was a notable growth in the size of cities , particularly in the early part of the nineteenth century .
157709	Men of industry and commerce began to emerge as men of some wealth .
157710	In 1813 , Robert Owen referred to the " working class , " a term brought into common speech by Lord Brougham .
157711	By the 1830s , a nonlanded middle class , artisans , and an industrial workforce were important constituents of the country 's population .
157712	Parliament remained dominated by the aristocracy and by the landed gentry .
157713	Representation in the House of Commons was heavily weighted in favor of the rural counties .
157714	Some parliamentary constituencies had only a handful of electors : known as " rotten boroughs , " they were often in the pocket of an aristocrat or local landowner .
157715	Pressure for some parliamentary reform , with a redistribution of seats and a widening of the franchise , began to develop .
157716	It was argued that a Parliament full of men of wealth and property was unlikely to view industry , trade , and agriculture from the point of view of the laboring classes .
157717	Rotten boroughs were criticized as being used by the ministry to help maintain a majority .
157718	Unrest in a number of areas , both agricultural and industrial , and the French Revolution of 1830 ( a spur to radical action ) increased the pressure for change .
157719	One political group in particular , the Whigs , who had been the " outs " in politics for the 25 years prior to 1830 , began to see the need for some response to this pressure .
157720	The concession of some parliamentary reform was seen as necessary in order to prevent worse happenings .
157721	The result was to be the Reform Act of 1832 .
157722	The Reform Act , introduced , ironically , by the most aristocratic government of the century , reorganized parliamentary constituencies and extended the franchise .
157723	The electorate increased in size from a little under 500,000 to 813,000 electors .
157724	Although much remained the same as before — the new electorate constituted but one-thirtieth of the population , 31 boroughs still had fewer than 300 electors in each , voting remained by open ballot ( secret ballots were considered rather un-English ) , and the aristocracy still held great sway politically — the act precipitated important changes both within and outside the House of Commons .
157725	The redistribution of seats and the extension of the franchise helped loosen the grip of the aristocracy and of ministers on the House of Commons .
157726	The size of the new electorate encouraged the embryonic development of political organizations .
157727	Members of Parliament ( MPs ) became less dependent on aristocratic patrons without acquiring too great a dependence on the growing party organizations .
157728	The result was to be a House of Commons with a greater legitimacy in the eyes of MPs and electors and one with an ability to assert itself in its relationship with government .
157729	The House proved willing to amend or reject legislation put before it as well as to remove individual ministers and on the occasion the government itself .
157730	In his classic work on the constitution , Walter Bagehot attached much importance to this " elective function " ; The House of Commons , he declared , was " a real choosing body : it elects the people it likes .
157731	And it dismisses whom it likes too . "
157732	Debates in the House really counted for something and , with the exception of the period from 1841 to 1846 , party cohesion was almost unknown .
157733	The House of Commons did not itself govern , but government was carried on within the confines of its guidance and approval .
157734	The period after 1832 witnessed also important changes in the relationships within and among the different elements of Crown , government , and Parliament .
157735	The monarch retained the formal prerogative power to appoint the prime minister , but the changed political circumstances essentially dictated that the person chosen should be able to command a majority in the House of Commons .
157736	Royal favor ceased to be an essential condition for forming the Government .
157737	Within Parliament , the relationship between the two Houses also changed .
157738	Members of the House of Lords sat by virtue of birth , holding hereditary peerages .
157739	The acceptance of the Commons as the  " representative " chamber undermined the authority of the peers to challenge or negate the wishes of the other House .
157740	After the 1830s , the Lords tended to be somewhat restrained in their attacks on government measures .
157741	" This followed , " writes Mackintosh , " from the view that while a ministry retained the confidence of the elected representatives it was entitled to remain in office .
157742	The peers on the whole accepted these assumptions , though many found the explicit recognition of the situation hard to bear . "
157743	The Lords ' remaining authority was in practice to be removed in consequence of the 1867 Reform Act , though not until the twentieth century was the House forced formally to accept its diminished status .
157744	Whereas the 1832 Act helped ensure the dominance of the House of Commons within the formal political process , the passage of the Reform Act of 1867 began a process of the transfer of power from Parliament to Ministers .
157745	The act itself was the product of demands for change because of the limited impact of the 1832 Act and because of more immediate political considerations .
157746	Its effect was to increase the size of the electorate from 1,358,000 to 2,477,000 .
157747	( The number had grown since 1832 because of increased wealth and population . )
157748	Other significant measures followed in its wake .
157749	Secret voting was introduced by the Ballot Act of 1870 .
157750	Other acts sought to prohibit as far as possible corrupt practices and limited the amount of money a candidate could spend on election expenses .
157751	Single-member districts ( known in Britain as constituencies ) of roughly equal electoral size were prescribed as the norm .
157752	The 1884 Representation of the People Act extended the franchise to householders and tenants and to all those who occupied land or tenements with an annual value of not less than 10 pounds .
157753	The effect of the act was to bring into being an electorate in which working men were in a majority .
157754	The consequence of these developments was to be party government .
157755	The size of the new electorate meant that the voters could be reached only through some well-developed organization , and the result was to be the growth of organized and mass-membership political parties .
157756	The Conservative National Union and the National Liberal Federation were formed in order to facilitate and encourage the support of the new electors .
157757	However , contact with the voters was insufficient in itself to entice their support .
157758	Not only had a large section of the population been enfranchised , it was a notably different electorate from that which had existed previously .
157759	The new class of electors had different and greater demands than those of the existing middle-class electors .
157760	If the votes of working men were to be obtained , the parties had to offer them something .
157761	And the parties could fulfil their promises only if they presented a uniform program to the electorate and achieved a cohesive majority in the House of Commons to carry through that program .
157762	What this was to produce was a shift of power away from the House of Commons to the cabinet and to the electorate , with political parties serving as the conduit for this transfer .
157763	The electorate proved too large and too politically unsophisticated to evaluate the merits of an individual MP 's behaviour .
157764	Political parties provided the labels with which electors could identify , and elections became gladiatorial contests between parties rather than between individual candidates .
157765	The all-or-nothing spoils of an election victory and the method of election encouraged ( if it not always produced ) a contest between two major parties .
157766	And having voted for party candidates , the electors expected the members returned to Parliament to support the program offered by their leaders at the election .
157767	Party cohesion soon became a feature of parliamentary life .
157768	The House of Commons in effect lost two of the most important functions ascribed to it by Bagehot , those of legislation and of choosing the government : the former passed to the cabinet and the latter to the electorate .
157769	The cabinet constituted the leaders of the party enjoying a parliamentary majority .
157770	It assumed that initiative for the formulation and introduction of measures of national policy and became increasingly reluctant to be over-ruled by the House .
157771	The growth in the number and complexity of bills further limited the influence of the individual MP .
157772	Increasingly , his role became one of supporting his leaders .
157773	The cabinet had previously rested its authority on the support of the House ; now it derived its authority from the electors .
157774	As Mackintosh states , " The task of the House of Commons became one of supporting the Cabinet chosen at the polls and passing its legislation …
157775	By the 1990s , the Cabinet dominated British government . "
157776	Further modifications and addenda took place in the first half of the twentieth century .
157777	The House of Lords was forced by statute in 1911 to accept its diminished status .
157778	The franchise was variously extended , most notably to half the population previously excluded because of their sex .
157779	The monarch 's political influence further receded .
157780	The growth and increasing economic weight of groups generated more extensive and complex demands of government .
157781	And the size of government grew as its responsibilities expanded .
157782	Basically , though , the essential features of the political system were those established in the preceding century .
157783	The responsibility for making public policy rested with the government , a government derived from and resting its support upon a political party .
157784	That same party 's majority in the House of Commons ensured that the government 's measures were approved .
157785	Formal and political constraints limited the effect of any opposition from the House of Lords .
157786	The monarch gave formal assent to any legislative measure approved by the two houses .
157787	Thus , within the formal framework of deciding public policy , the government was dominant .
157788	The role of Parliament became largely but not wholly one of legitimating the measures put before it .
157789	For the monarch , that became the exclusive role ( that is , in respect of legislation ) .
157790	Government , as we shall see , operated within a political environment that imposed important constraints , but the limitations imposed formerly by Parliament and the monarch were largely eroded .
157791	Britain retained a parliamentary form of government , but what that meant was not government by Parliament but government through Parliament .
157792	To comprehend some of the problems faced by British government in the 1980s it is necessary to know not only the structure and relationships of the political system but also the popular expectations and the burden of responsibilities borne by government .
157793	Those expectations and responsibilities have not been static .
157794	Just as the governmental structure has been modified in response to political demands , so the responsibilities of government have grown as greater social and economic demands have been made of it .
157795	The Welfare State and the Managed Economy
157796	Toward the end of the nineteenth century and more especially in the twentieth , the responsibilities of government expanded .
157797	In part this was attributable to the growth of the Empire .
157798	It was also attributable to the increasing demands and expectations of the newly enfranchised working population .
157799	Government began to conceive its duties as extending beyond those of maintaining law and order and of defending the realm .
157800	The statute book began to expand , with the addition of measures of social reform .
157801	Various such measures were enacted in the years prior to 1867 , though the most notable were to be enacted in the remaining decades of the century .
157802	They included measures to limit working hours for women and children , to improve housing and public health , to make education for children compulsory , to provide for the safety of workers ( including the payment of compensation by employers in the event of accidents at work ) , and even to extend the right to strike .
157803	Such measures , exploited for electoral advantage , were within the capabilities of the government to provide .
157804	They did not create too great an economic burden ; they were not themselves economic measures .
157805	The growth of expectations and the greater willingness of government to intervene in areas previously considered inviolate was to be continued and become more marked in the twentieth century .
157806	The general election of 1906 was something of a watershed in British politics .
157807	It was the first election to be fought essentially on national issues and it witnessed the return not only of a reforming Liberal government but also , and in some respects more significantly , of 27 Labour MPs .
157808	The Labour party had been created for the purpose of ensuring working-class representation in Parliament , and from 1906 onward class became a significant influence in voting behavior .
157809	The nature of electoral conflict changed as the Labour party succeeded the Liberal as the main opposition party to the Conservatives .
157810	The franchise was further extended , notably in 1918 and 1928 , and new expectations were generated by the experience of the two world wars .
157811	During the First World War ( 1914-1918 ) , socialists within the Labour party argued the case for the conscription of wealth ( public ownership ) to accompany the conscription of labor ( the drafting of men into the armed forces ) .
157812	Politicians fueled rather than played down the belief that Britain should become , in the words of one politician , " a land fit for heroes " once " the war to end all wars " was won — in other words , that provision should be made for those who had fought for King and Country .
157813	The period of the Second World War ( 1939-1945 ) witnessed a significant shift of attitudes by a sizable fraction of the electorate .
157814	One informed estimate was that by December 1942 , about two out of every five people had changed their political outlook since the beginning of the war .
157815	The direction in which opinion was moving was toward the left of the political spectrum .
157816	There was a reaction against ( Conservative ) government unpreparedness for war in the 1930s and against those who had not done more to solve the nation 's problems during the Depression .
157817	There was support for calls for equality of sacrifice .
157818	There was some degree of goodwill toward the Soviet Union as a wartime ally .
157819	There was also , very importantly , the enhanced position of the Labour party .
157820	It had entered into Coalition in 1940 ( its leader , Clement Attlee , became deputy prime minister to Churchill ) and had demonstrated its claim to be a capable partner in government .
157821	As the 1940s progressed , there developed a notable movement , including within the Conservative party , for a greater degree of social and economic intervention by government .
157822	This was to find some authoritative expression during the war years themselves and more especially in the years after 1945 , when a general election resulted in the return of the first Labour government with a clear working majority in the House of Commons .
157823	The period of the 1940s and the 1950s was to produce what Samuel Beer has referred to as the welfare state and the managed economy , or what some commentators have referred to as the period of the social democratic consensus .
157824	The welfare state and the managed economy did not suddenly emerge full-blown in this period .
157825	The preceding decades has not witnessed governments unresponsive to electoral expectations and the nation 's problems .
157826	The Liberal government before the First World War had made the first tentative steps in the introduction of old-age pensions ( 1908 ) and national health and unemployment insurance ( 1911 ) .
157827	The interwar years had seen the introduction of a number of significant measures of social reform , especially those associated with Neville Chamberlain as minister of health .
157828	He proposed to the cabinet 25 measures and secured the enactment of 21 of them .
157829	These included unemployment insurance , public health and housing , and the extension of old-age pensions .
157830	Much of this legislation , as one biographer noted , " has an important place in the development of the Welfare State . "
157831	The government also began to engage in certain measures of economic management .
157832	It embarked on a protectionist policy and in return for the grant of a tariff to an industry , demanded that its major producers should reorganize themselves .
157833	Such producers were encouraged to reduce capacity and maintain prices .
157834	The gold standard was abandoned , the pound was devalued , and interest rates were lowered .
157835	The government even proved willing to take certain industries into public ownership : broadcasting , overseas airways , and the electricity-generating industry .
157836	By indulging in such policies , Professor Beer has contended , government was beginning to move in the direction of a managed economy .
157837	The movement , though , was modest .
157838	Government adhered to the prevailing orthodoxy that balanced budgets were necessary and desirable and that deficit financing was neither .
157839	Ministers showed little desire to emulate the innovative approach adopted in the United States by Franklin Roosevelt during the period of the first New Deal .
157840	( Indeed , Conservative leader Stanley Baldwin commented at one point that the United States Constitution had broken down and was giving way to dictatorship . )
157841	Britain and the United States were similar , though , in that both were to be brought out of the Depression of the 1930s not by government economic policies but by rearmament and the Second World War .
157842	Two major documents published in the war years provided the planks for the final emergence of the welfare state and managed economy .
157843	These were the Report on Social Insurance and Allied Services by Sir william Beveridge ( the so-called Beveridge Report ) , published in November 1942 , and the White Paper on Full Employment , published in 1944 .
157844	The former proposed a comprehensive scheme of social security , one to provide " social insurance against interruption and destruction of earning power and for special expenditure arising at birth , marriage or death . "
157845	The latter was significant because of its opening pledge : " The Government accepts as one of their primary aims and responsibilities the maintenance of a high and stable level of employment after the war . "
157846	There was also one particularly significant measure of social reform enacted during wartime : the 1944 Education Act , pioneered by R. A. Butler .
157847	The Act provided for the division among primary , secondary , and higher education — and , within secondary education , between secondary modern and grammar schools — that was to form the basis of the educational system for more than a generation .
157848	The welfare state was brought to fruition by the establishment of the National Health Service ( NHS ) in 1948 , entailing the nationalization of hospitals and the provision of free medical treatment , and by the passage of the 1945 Family Allowance Act , the 1946 National Insurance Act , and the 1948 National Assistance Act .
157849	the principle enunciated by the Beveridge Report was largely put into practice .
157850	National insurance ensured a certain level of benefit in the event of unemployment or sickness .
157851	For those who required special help there was " national assistance , " the provision of noncontributory benefits dispensed on the basis of means-testing .
157852	There were family allowances for those with children .
157853	The state now provided something of a protective safety net from the cradle to the grave .
157854	It was still possible to pay for private treatment in the health service , but for most people it was a case of having treatment " on the national health . "
157855	The NHS became a feature of some pride at home and of considerable interest abroad .
157856	Acceptance and usage of techniques pioneered by the economist J. M. Keynes ushered in the managed economy .
157857	Government accepted responsibility for keeping aggregate monetary demand at a level sufficient to ensure full employment or what was considered as far as possible to constitute full employment ( an unemployment rate of 1% or 2% was considered acceptable ) , and the annual Budget was to be used as the main instrument of economic policy .
157858	The Labour government proved unwilling to pursue a more overtly socialist approach ; physical controls acquired during wartime were eventually discarded and those industries that were nationalized , such as steel and the railways , were basically essential and loss-making concerns .
157859	Government was prepared to pursue a managed rather than a controlled economy .
157860	The Conservative party was returned to office in 1951 and was to remain there until 1964 .
157861	It accepted , or appeared to accept , both the welfare state and Keynesian techniques of demand management .
157862	Indeed , it gave the impression of making a success of both .
157863	As heir to the Disraelian belief in elevating the condition of the people and as a party seeking to enhance its image among working class voters , the Conservative Party could claim both a principled as well as a practical motive for maintaining the innovations of its predecessor .
157864	At the same time , it was reluctant to pursue policies that would increase the tax burden or the public sector of the economy .
157865	Good fortune was with the government : world economic conditions improved and heralded a period of sustained growth in industrial output and trade .
157866	Government revenue was such that not only was it possible to sustain and indeed expand expenditure on the national health serve , it was possible to do so without substantial increases in taxation .
157867	Indeed , reductions rather than increases in tax rates were a feature of the period .
157868	There was an extensive and successful house-building program .
157869	Economic prosperity allowed government to maintain peace with the labor unions by allowing high wage settlements .
157870	It was also possible finally to abandon many of the controls maintained since wartime .
157871	Government was able to claim to have maintained full employment , an expanding economy , stable prices , and a strong pound .
157872	Despite the agonies of withdrawing from Empire and various undulations in economic performance , the decade of the 1950s was seen more than anything as " an age of affluence . "
157873	In July 1957 , Prime Minister Harold Macmillan was able to declare that , for most of the people , " You 've never had it so good . "
157874	The 1960s witnessed a downturn in economic performance and a growing realization that , in comparative terms , Britain was faring less well than many of her continental neighbors .
157875	The Conservative government of Harold Macmillan responded with various novel proposals , including indicative economic planning and an application to join the European Economic Community .
157876	The succeeding Labour government of Harold Wilson , returned to office in 1964 , sought a more comprehensive method of national economic planning as part of its grand design of modernization .
157877	Inflation and unemployment became more visible problems .
157878	Despite the economic problems and some unrelated political problems of the 1960s , the country remained a relatively prosperous one .
157879	Living conditions continued to improve .
157880	The rise in wages exceeded the rise in inflation .
157881	Where economic conditions impinged on the ability to maintain the welfare state , it was essentially at the margin : government imposed nominal charges for medicines obtained on NHS prescriptions .
157882	Parties tended to argue more about means rather than ends .
157883	The consensus that developed in the 1950s remained intact .
157884	This brief survey not only provides some historical depth to an understanding of contemporary British government — its structure , responsibilities , and political dominance — it also serves to reinforce our grasp of the political culture and to provide in part an explanation for some of the problems now associated with government .
157885	POLITICAL CULTURE AND CONTEMPORARY PROBLEMS
157886	From the foregoing sketch one can recognize not only the features of the political culture outlined in the preceding chapter but also the convergence of those features and their interplay with the experience of history .
157887	An empirical orientation to change and a conditional relationship between governors and governed are long-standing characteristics of political life .
157888	Clearly , government has been shaped by no grand design .
157889	Change has been piecemeal and largely incremental .
157890	Although the governed have been largely prepared to defer to those in power , their deference has been conditional .
157891	If presumed rights and privileges were ignored or dispensed with , the appropriate action was taken to restore them ( e.g. the Magna Carta , the beheading of Charles I ) .
157892	The other orientations can be identified from the experience of reform in the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries .
157893	History and Political Culture
