157894	The reforms of the nineteenth century were facilitated not only by an empirical orientation to change but also by the paternalism of political leaders .
157895	Noblesse oblige ( privilege entails responsibility ) is a foreign phase but it embodies a very British concept .
157896	Many of the country 's aristocratic leaders believed that they had a duty to help improve the condition of the working man .
157897	The point should not be overemphasized , since on occasion this sense of duty was not so much a cause of action but a post hoc justification of it .
157898	Nonetheless , it was important .
157899	It combined with need ( to avoid social unrest ) and political expediency ( to steal the thunder of one 's opponents ) to produce franchise extension .
157900	Increasingly , change was more easily accommodated as political relationships changes .
157901	By the twentieth century , the hegemony of government in the political process ensured that measures could be carried through Parliament without too much difficulty .
157902	Equally important , once approved by Parliament , reforms were accepted by the populace and by those at whom they were directed .
157903	The widening of the franchise in the nineteenth century , House of Lords reform , and votes for women in the twentieth — these are issues that aroused great emotion and were fiercely opposed but on which reform was accepted once the government of the day had got the measure accepted by Parliament .
157904	This in part reflects the orientation toward cooperation .
157905	It also may be seen as the product of an allegiant orientation to the political system .
157906	The widening of the franchise extended the input of citizens into the political system .
157907	The passage of measures of social and economic reform appeared to be meeting their needs .
157908	Equally important , Britons have been taught that the political system works .
157909	Although the media of political socialization have changed over time , the content has not .
157910	There has been an emphasis on , and lauding of , the continuity and stability .
157911	Historically , as we have seen , the country has been rent by various upheavals , sometimes of a quite violent nature .
157912	The English Civil War was far from bloodless .
157913	The opinion of foreigners , wrote an English scholar in 1704 , is " that there have been more shakes and convulsions in the government of England than in that of any other nation . "
157914	There have been various shakes since — social , economic , and political .
157915	In the popular mind , though , such convulsions have not figures largely .
157916	" What makes the history of England so eminently valuable , " wrote T. H. Buckle , " is that nowhere else has the national progress been so little interfered with , either for good or evil . "
157917	British government has been accepted as the product of the collected wisdom of many generations , indeed of many centuries .
157918	It flatters the British mind , and certainly the English mind , to look upon it as the envy of the world .
157919	The Constitution has been lauded as " a living organism in a condition of perpetual growth . "
157920	George III described it as " the most perfect of human formations . "
157921	Only recently , in 1981 , one member of Parliament declared that , distinguished from other constitutions , " our constitution is the envy of the world . "
157922	The virtues of the Westminster model of government have been widely extolled .
157923	They became embodied in what was taught in British schools .
157924	They became part of received wisdom , and to some extent , they remain so .
157925	The British have not been alone in such teaching .
157926	British parliamentary government has found its admirers abroad as well , and not least in the United States .
157927	Especially in the 1950s and 1960s , the capacity of the party in government to enact a party program was compared with the brokered politics of the American system .
157928	It was a comparison that generated some calls for reform ; most notable among these was James MacGregor Burns in The Deadlock of Democracy published in 1963 , arguing the case essentially for the equivalent in the United States of a " responsible party system . "
157929	Such calls were to extend into the following decade .
157930	Charles Hardin cited British experience in contending that " party government — if it can be attained — provides the best hope that our government will be able to meet its problems . "
157931	Although not all observers wished to emulate British experience , their analyses appeared edged with a touch of envy .
157932	In more recent years , such perceptions have waned .
157933	In the 1970s , conditions in Britain began to change .
157934	Economic indicators worsened considerably , and unemployment rose dramatically ( see Chapter 1 ) .
157935	By 1973 , Britain had the lowest growth rate of the major industrialized nations .
157936	Between 1974 and 1978 there was an annual rate of increase in retail prices in excess of 17% .
157937	Industrial disputes became more serious : there were more working days lost through such disputes in the period from 1970 to 1978 than there were in the whole of the period from 1946 to 1969 .
157938	In less than 30 years , the British economy had declined from being one of the strongest to one of the weakest in Europe .
157939	Successive governments encountered problems in responding to the changed conditions and in raising resources to meet public expectations .
157940	Britain was overshadowed by a body of which , until 1973 , it was not a member — the European Communities .
157941	Government was increasingly constrained by the activities of economically powerful groups , both at home and abroad ( notably , in the latter case , the International Monetary Fund ) .
157942	Although parliamentary government did not cease to work , it no longer appeared to be working in the way that it had in the past .
157943	The positive picture of British government began to lose its gloss ; academics who had previously written about the political system in positive terms now turned their attention to the problem inherent in that system .
157944	British parliamentary government began to assume the status of a rejected lover .
157945	Contemporary Ills and Analyses
157946	The diagnoses of Britain 's problems have been as varied as the problems themselves .
157947	Some diagnoses are primarily economic .
157948	A number of economists have placed some of the blame for poor economic performance on a failure to modernize ( there has been a tendency to retain old plants and to support traditional but declining industries , such as textiles ) ; on the emphasis given to maintaining a balance of payments surplus in order to fund overseas military spending and foreign investments , pursued at the expense of economic growth , and on a failure of postwar economic management to manipulate supply as well as demand .
157949	Others have stressed the legacies of former international glory , attitudes , and institutions derived from the days when Britain was at the center of the world economy , acting as a barrier to necessary change .
157950	Some diagnoses have been primarily sociological .
157951	As we have seen ( Chapter 1 ) , class did not displace status in British society .
157952	Preindustrial aristocratic attitudes were carried over into an industrial age .
157953	These attitudes included looking down on the pursuit of trade and commerce as somewhat inferior socially .
157954	Low priority was given to industry and science and , so the analysis goes , a tendency grew for those with wealth and some ability to avoid management in favor of professional pursuits such as the law .
157955	Some blame has also been imputed to the egalitarianism of the labor movement , harboring dislike of profits and risk-taking as well as the values of thrift and self-reliance that underpin the operation of the free market .
157956	In short , the attitudes of both the social elite and the labor movement have served to hinder economic growth .
157957	The other diagnoses are essentially political .
157958	They are important in the context of later chapters and hence deserve some attention .
157959	The historical background provided in this chapter helps us understand some of these diagnoses as well as some of the prescriptions .
157960	The three main diagnoses are those of government overload , adversary politics , and pluralist stagnation .
157961	Prescriptions have included decentralization , electoral reform and more radical economic policies .
157962	The thesis of government overload is that as the responsibilities of government have increased , its capacity to meet them has decreased : the combination of these two features has resulted in an overloading of government .
157963	A government White Paper in 1970 declared that government had been attempting to do too much .
157964	" This has placed an excessive burden on industry , and on the people of the country as a whole , and has also over-loaded the government machine itself …
157965	The weakness has shown itself in the apparatus of policy formulation and in the quality of many government decisions over the past 25 years . "
157966	Some writers have argued that the problem of overload has been made worse by the centralization of government decision-making .
157967	Centralized government , so the argument goes , has proved too large and too far removed from the problems with which it seeks to cope .
157968	Distance from those affected by government decisions has had the effect of increasing their indifference and sense of alienation , especially in the economically disadvantaged regions furthest from London .
157969	Government , according to the Royal Commission on the Constitution in 1973 , was viewed as being too remote .
157970	A compatible but independent thesis is that of adversary politics .
157971	It contends that attempts to generate institutions capable of dealing with Britain 's long-term economic problems are thwarted by a political system that encourages an adversary relationship between the two main political parties , one that enables them to alternate in office so that each undoes the work of the other .
157972	The consequence , it is argued , is policy discontinuity , making it difficult if not impossible for industrialists and investors to plan ahead .
157973	The adversary relationship also encourages a constant escalation of promises by the parties , each seeking to out-promise the other in order to win the all-or-nothing spoils of a general election victory .
157974	When , as happened in the 1970s , the resources are no longer available to meet the promises made , disenchantment with the political system begins to develop .
157975	Furthermore , the parties are unable to respond adequately to such developments because of an unwillingness to tamper with a system that works to their mutual advantage .
157976	In short , Britain has a political system that is malfunctional and not amenable to radical reform .
157977	Pluralist stagnation suggests that the problem lies with the growth of groups in British society , each group pursuing its own interest .
157978	Those groups have brought pressure to bear on government to provide resources or pursue policies to the benefit of their members .
157979	Such has been the economic leverage of some groups that the role of government has become increasingly one of arbiter between the demands of groups rather than one of policy leader .
157980	The tendency of government to wish to avoid conflict has resulted in political inertia , government being unwilling to pursue policies that would generate sustained opposition from well-entrenched groups .
157981	The problem has been made worse , according to Samuel Beer , by the numerical growth of such groups .
157982	Because there are so many , self-restraint in making demands of government would bring no discernible benefit to any one group .
157983	As a result , even though recognizing the need for restraint , a group is tempted to raise its own claims .
157984	Other groups then compete to raise theirs .
157985	" The source of the problem , " argues Beer , " is not a lack of knowledge , but the structure of the situation , which continues to have compelling force even when participants recognise its tendencies .
157986	Their numerical pluralism makes it difficult , if not impossible , to make and enforce a bargain , tacit or explicit , that would achieve moderation .
157987	If there were only a few , each could know what the others were doing and all would be aware of being watched .
157988	But pluralism destroys the basis for such a self-enforcing social contract . "
157989	For government the problem is thus an acute one .
157990	It has fewer benefits to dispense than previously , yet is faced with a plethora of interests , each of which is unwilling to moderate its demands in the interests of all .
157991	These constitute the main political analyses that see the problem as a structural one .
157992	There are others that do not see it as structural .
157993	The two largest parties in Britain , the Conservative and Labour parties , view Britain 's problems as stemming from the pursuit in the past of inadequate policies ( Chapter 6 ) .
157994	There are other analyses that go beyond the structural or policy analyses , providing somewhat more complex explanations .
157995	The most important of these is that provided by Professor Beer in his recent work Britain Against Itself .
157996	He argues that there is no single causal explanation for Britain 's decline ; rather , it has to be seen as resulting from a convergence of pluralist stagnation , a decline of class , and a revolt against authority .
157997	The result has been fragmentation in political life .
157998	" The outcome has been incoherence and immobilism ; drift , not mastery .
157999	It is not hyperbole to call it a paralysis of public choice . "
158000	I shall return to these analyses in appropriate chapters , responding in particular to Beer 's sophisticated analysis in the conclusion .
158001	For the moment , two concluding points need to be made .
158002	The first , rather obviously , is that no one approach is without its detractors .
158003	Each approach has its limitations and these I shall seek to draw out at appropriate points in the text .
158004	The second equally obvious point is that , given the disparate analyses , a variety of prescriptions have been offered for dealing with the presumed causes of the nation 's ills .
158005	Exponents of the government overload thesis tend to favor reform of central government machinery and decentralization of government .
158006	Those who adhere to the adversary politics thesis support , for reasons that will be explained later , a reform of the electoral system .
158007	Pluralist stagnation , according to Beer 's analysis , can be overcome only by mobilizing popular consent through restoring trust in government .
158008	For the Conservative and Labour parties the answer lies in ( different ) radical economic policies .
158009	So wide are the analyses and the prescriptions that one is tempted to wonder whether the concept of pluralist stagnation might itself be applied to the political analysis of Britain 's ills .
158010	My own argument I will draw together in the conclusion .
158011	For the moment , suffice it to say that I take a skeptical view of the structural analyses offered .
158012	They are unproven and overexaggerated and they miss the essential point .
158013	The problem is not primarily a structural one — structures are dependent variables .
158014	The independent variable on which one has to focus is the political culture .
158015	The political culture may have helped generate problems of political structure , but Britain 's problems , I will argue , are not essentially political : they are economic and social .
158016	And the political culture is one that provides government with the breathing space necessary to address itself to those problems .
158017	Government may not succeed , but the opportunity is there and in order to understand that one has to understand the political culture and the extent to which it endures .
158018	The decline in the culture detected by Beer is relative .
158019	The orientations of the political culture identified in the preceding chapter remain .
158020	I concluded that chapter by suggesting that the important question was not " why had there been a decline in the civic culture , " but rather " why had that decline not been greater ? "
158021	The answer to that question , and the implications of it for the British polity of the 1980s , will form the basis of the final chapter .
158022	My conclusion will not necessarily be an optimistic one — it will emphasize potential rather than expectation — but it will lack the negative connotations attached to the foregoing analyses .
158023	It will also forgo structural change as the primary prescriptions .
158024	What is important is attitudes , not structures .
158025	THE UNCODIFIED CONSTITUTION
158026	A CONSTITUTION MAY BE DEFINED as a body of laws , customs , and conventions that define the composition and powers of organs of the state and that regulate the relations of the various state organs to one another and to the private citizen .
158027	The United States has a constitution ; so does the United Kingdom .
158028	Expressed in purely formal terms ( Table 4.1 ) there is very little similarity between them .
158029	Indeed , the differences are such that to the student weaned on a study of the United States Constitution , the British Constitution is nearly incomprehensible .
158030	Even to the student of British politics it is not well understood .
158031	Nonetheless , the differences should not be emphasized to the exclusion of certain common features .
158032	Both Constitutions are strong ones in that they reflect and reinforce their respective political cultures .
158033	The United States Constitution is considered by Americans to embody the principles of a higher law , to constitute " in fact imperfect man 's most perfect rendering of what Blackstone saluted as " the eternal immutable laws of good and evil , to which the creator himself in all his dispensations conforms : and which he has enabled human reason to discover , so far as they are necessary for the conduct of human actions . "
158034	As the embodiment of a higher law , it thus not only needs to be distinguished from ordinary law but also needs to be protected from the passing whims of politicians — hence the introduction of extraordinary procedures for its amendment .
158035	By contrast , the British Constitution is admired by Britons for reflecting the wisdom of past generations , as the product of experience — in short , a constitution that stipulates what should be on the basis of what has proved to work rather than on abstract first principles .
158036	The empirical orientation to change that underpins such a constitution also favors flexibility in amendment : as conditions change , so some amendment may be necessary .
158037	Formal extraordinary procedures for its amendment have not been found necessary .
158038	The differences in political culture have thus produced somewhat different constitutions , but the attachment to them is similar in the two countries .
158039	Also , as we shall see , there are certain similarities in sources in the means of interpretation .
158040	New nations from the eighteenth century onward have found it both necessary and useful to codify their constitutions .
158041	At the time that the Founding Fathers promulgated the United States Constitution in Philadelphia , a written constitution was exceptional .
158042	Today it is the norm .
158043	Having lacked the opportunity to create a new constitutional framework afresh from first principles , Britain now stands out as one of the few nations lacking such a document .
158044	FORMS OF EXPRESSION
158045	The absence of a written constitution similar to that of the United States and other nations has led to the British Constitution being described as unwritten , but such a description is misleading .
158046	As we shall see , various elements of the Constitution find expression in forma , written enactments .
158047	What distinguishes the British Constitution from others is not that it is unwritten , but rather that it is part-written and uncodified .
158048	The lack of codification is of especial importance .
158049	It makes it difficult to identify clearly and authoritatively what constitute the provisions of the Constitution .
158050	there are certain principles that are clearly at the heart of the Constitution , parliamentary sovereignty being the prime example , but there are many provisions , be they expressed through statute law or the writings of constitutional experts , that are of constitutional significance but on which there is no clear agreement that they form part of the British Constitution .
158051	It is this lack of codified certainty that makes a study of it so fraught with difficulty .
158052	Because one can not have recourse to one simple authoritative document to discover the provisions of the Constitution , one has instead to research four separate sources : statute law , common law , conventions , and works of authority .
158053	Such sources are also relevant in analyses of the United States Constitution .
158054	Congress may pass measures of constitutional significance , for example , certain stipulations of electoral law or the War Powers Act .
158055	Provisions of the Constitution are developed and molded by judicial decisions .
158056	In seeking to interpret the Constitution , the courts may have recourse to works by constitutional experts .
158057	The difference between the two countries is that in Britain such sources are primary sources , and in the United States , the primary source is the written document .
158058	SOURCES
158059	Of the four sources , statute law is perhaps the best understood and nowadays , the most extensive .
158060	It provides the main source for the part-written element of the Constitution .
158061	It comprises acts of Parliament and subordinate legislation made under the authority of the parent act .
158062	Many acts of Parliament that have been passed clearly merit the title of constitutional law .
158063	Acts that define the powers of the various state organs ( for example , the 1911 and 1949 Parliament Acts ) and acts that define the relationship between Crown and Parliament ( notably the Bill of Rights of 1689 ) , between the component elements of the nation ( the Act of Union with Scotland of 1706 , for example ) , between the United Kingdom and the European Communities ( the 1972 European Communities Act ) , and between the state and the individual ( as with the Habeas Corpus Act of 1679 or the Administration of Justice Act of 1960 ) clearly constitute important provisions of the Constitution .
158064	They are published in authoritative , written form and , as acts of Parliament , are interpreted by the courts .
158065	This is the most important of the four sources both in quantitative and qualitative terms .
158066	It has increasingly displaced common law as the most extensive form of law in Britain and it is the most definitive of the four .
158067	It takes precedence over any conflicting common law and is superior to the conventions of the Constitutions and to works of authority .
158068	It precedence derives from the concept of parliamentary sovereignty .
158069	Common law constitutes the law and customs of ancient lineage that have been upheld as law by the courts in cases decided before them .
158070	Once a court has upheld a provision as being part of common law it creates a precedent to be followed by other courts .
158071	In past centuries , when few statutes were enacted , common law constituted the main body of English law ; today , it has been largely but not wholly displaced by statute law .
158072	Certain principles derived from common law remain fundamental to the Constitution , and these include the principle of parliamentary sovereignty .
158073	Under the heading of common law comes also prerogative powers — the powers and privileges recognized by common law as belonging to the monarch .
158074	Although many prerogative powers have been displaced by statute , many matters at the heart of government are still determined under the authority of the prerogative .
158075	These include the appointment of ministers , the making of treaties , and power of pardon , the dispensing of honors , and the declaration of war .
158076	By convention , such powers are normally exercised formally by the monarch on the advice of ministers ( the ministers , in practice , take the decisions ) .
158077	There is no formal requirement that Parliament assent to such decisions .
158078	This is in stark contrast to the position in the United States , where Congress alone has the formal power to declare war and the Senate 's consent is necessary for the ratification of treaties and the appointment of federal public officers .
158079	( In practice , the differences are not that great : " presidential wars " have been waged without a congressional declaration of war , while in Britain a government taking military action abroad will seek the consent of Parliament . )
158080	In 1972 , the Treaty of Accession to the European Communities was signed under prerogative powers .
158081	IN 1982 , a naval task force was despatched to the Falkland Islands under the same authority .
158082	Although diminishing in number , prerogative powers clearly remain of great importance .
158083	Generally included under the generic heading of common law is the judicial interpretation of statute law .
158084	Unlike those in the United States , British courts have no power to hold a measure unconstitutional .
158085	They are limited to the interpretation of provisions of acts of Parliament .
158086	Even in exercising their power of interpretations , they are limited by rules of interpretation and by precedent .
158087	( The exception is the House of Lords , the highest domestic court of appeal , which is not now bound by its previous decisions . )
158088	Nonetheless , judges retain the power to distinguish cases and by their interpretation they can develop a substantial body of case law .
158089	In interpreting acts of Parliament , they assume Parliament to have meant what , on the face of it , the words of an act appear to mean .
158090	Unlike the United States Supreme Court , which can delve deep into the deliberations of the Founding Fathers to try to elucidate what was meant by a particular provision of the Constitution , British courts are not permitted to look at the proceedings of Parliament in order to determine what Parliament really meant .
158091	The third and least tangible source of the Constitution is that of convention .
158092	Conventions of the Constitution are most aptly described as rules that are considered binding by and upon those who are responsible for making the Constitution work , but rules that are not enforced by the courts or by the presiding officers in either house of Parliament .
158093	They derive their strength from the realization that not to abide by them would make for an unworkable constitution .
158094	They are , so to speak , the oil in the forma machinery of the Constitution .
158095	They help fill the gap between the constitutional formality and the political reality .
158096	For example , ministers are responsible formally to the monarch .
158097	Because of the political changes wrought in the nineteenth century , they are by convention responsible now also to Parliament .
158098	By convention , the government of the day resigns or requests a dissolution if a motion of no confidence is carried against it in the House of Commons .
158099	By convention , the monarch gives the Royal Assent to all legislative measures approved by Parliament .
158100	The last time a monarch refused assent was during the reign of Queen Anne ( 1702-1714 ) .
158101	Queen Victoria in the nineteenth century contemplated refusing her assent to a measure but wiser counsels prevailed .
158102	No formal , authoritative documents set forth these rules , and they find no embodiment in statute law .
158103	The courts may recognize them , but the courts have no power to enforce them .
158104	They are complied with because of the recognition of what would happen if they were not complied with .
158105	For the Queen to refuse her assent to a measure passed by the two Houses of Parliament would draw her into the realms of political controversy , hence jeopardizing the claim of the monarch to be " above politics . "
158106	A government that sought to remain in office after losing a vote of confidence in the House of Commons would find its position politically intenable : it would lack the political authority to govern .
158107	For ministers to ignore Parliament completely would prove equally untenable .
158108	Some conventions may be described as being stronger than others .
158109	Some on occasion are breached , while others are adhered to without exception .
158110	On three occasions in this century , the convention of collective ministerial responsibility has been suspended temporarily by the prime minister of the day .
158111	In contrast , no government has sought to remain in office after losing a parliamentary vote of confidence .
158112	The point at which a useful and necessary practice is accorded the status of a constitutional convention is not clear .
158113	Once a practice has become well established in terms of the relationship within or between different organs of the state , finding recognition in works of authority and by those involved in its operation , then it may be said to have reached the status of a convention .
158114	At any one time , though , there are a number of relationships that may be said to be in a constitutional haze .
158115	Is it a convention of the Constitution that the government of the day must consult with interested bodies before formulating a legislative measure for presentation to Parliament ?
158116	Prime Minister Harold Wilson appeared to give some credence to this view in 1966 when he said in the House of Commons that it was the duty of the government to consult with the Trades Union Congress and the Confederation of British Industry .
158117	Few other authorities have supported Jennings ' assertion and it has not found acceptance by most practitioners of government .
158118	It is usual for governments to engage in such consultation , but it is not yet a convention of the Constitution that they do so .
158119	The fourth and final source of the Constitution is that of works of authority .
158120	These have persuasive authority only .
158121	What constitutes a " work of authority " is rarely defined .
158122	Various early works are accorded particular standing by virtue of the absence of statutes or other written sources covering a particular area .
158123	The statements of their writers are presumed to be evidence of judicial decisions that have been lost and are therefore accepted if not contrary to reason .
158124	Among the most important early sources are Fitzherbert 's Abridgment ( 1516 ) and Coke 's Institutes of the Law of England ( 1628-1644 ) .
158125	More recent works have been called in aid on those occasions when jurists and others have sought to delineate features of the contemporary Constitution ; this has been the case especially in determining the existence or otherwise of conventions .
158126	Such conventions are prescribed neither by statute nor by judicial interpretation , so one must study instead scholarly interpretations of political behaviour and practice .
158127	Especially important authoritative works in the nineteenth century were those by John Austin and A. V. Dicey .
158128	Important names in the twentieth century have included Sir Ivor Jennings , Sir Kenneth Wheare , O. Hood Phillips , and E. C. S. Wade .
158129	Given the disparate sources of the Constitution and the fact that important relationships within and between organs of the state are not laid down in any one formal or binding document , it is not surprising that one must have recourse to books by constitutional scholars to discover the extent and nature of those relationships .
158130	Works of authority tend to be consulted more frequently in the field of constitutional law than in any other branch of English law .
158131	Given the disparate primary sources of the Constitution and the difficulty in determining where the Constitution begins and ends , it is perhaps not surprising that there are no extraordinary procedures for its amendment .
158132	Statute and common law of constitutional significance are subject to amendment by the same process as that employed for other legislative enactments .
158133	Conventions can be modified by changes in behaviour or by reinterpretations of the significance of certain behaviour .
158134	Works of authority can be rewritten or subjected to different interpretations in the same way as can other texts .
158135	MEANS OF AMENDMENT
158136	Much the same can be said about constitutionally significant statute law , judicial decisions , and works of authority in the United States .
158137	Even the provisions of the formal document , the United States Constitution , may be amended by judicial decisions and custom usage .
158138	The difference between the two countries is that the formal wording of the United States Constitution can be amended only by an extraordinary process , i.e. , one that goes beyond the provisions employed for amending the ordinary law .
158139	( Because of the extraordinary procedures necessary for amendment , the provisions of the Constitution are sometimes referred to as " entrenched . " )
158140	No such formal amending procedures exist in Britain , where there is no formal document .
158141	As may be surmised from the foregoing , there is no single body endowed with the responsibility for interpreting the provisions of the Constitution .
158142	As in the United States , statute and common law are subject to judicial interpretation , but there is no power of judicial review , at least not as the term is understood in the United States .
158143	The courts can not declare a legislative measure or an executive action contrary to the provisions of the Constitution .
158144	INTERPRETATION
158145	The courts can influence and to some extent mold certain provisions through their interpretation of statute and common law .
158146	Indeed , their use of common law has been of especial importance in outlining and protecting certain rights of the individual .
158147	However , at the end of the day , they are subject to the wishes of Parliament .
158148	Judicial interpretation of statute law can be overridden by a new act of Parliament .
158149	By virtue of the concept of parliamentary sovereignty , the act would be definitive .
158150	The judges serve to enforce and interpret such acts : they can not strike down an act .
158151	Identification and interpretation of conventions has little to do with the courts .
158152	Conventions arise as a result of changes in the relationships within and between different organs of the state .
158153	Their delineation rests with scholars , and their enforcement rests with those at whom they are aimed .
158154	As with conventions , they are beyond the purview of the courts .
158155	The Constitution , in short , is subject to interpretation by different bodies , the most prominent being politicians , judges , and scholars .
158156	The same can be said of the United States Constitution , but in Britain there is no body that stands in a position analogous to that of the United States Supreme Court .
158157	It is an important difference , reflecting the differences in political culture .
158158	The Lockean basis of constitutional interpretation in the United States -a higher law cognizable by independent , rational magistrates operating free of outside interests — finds no parallel in Britain .
158159	The central provisions of the Constitution are listed in Table 4.1 : parliamentary sovereignty , the rule of law , a unitary ( as opposed to a federal ) system , and what I have termed parliamentary government under a constitutional monarchy .
158160	Although there is some dispute as to whether it should remain so , the preeminent provision is that of parliamentary sovereignty .
158161	In the nineteenth century , the great constitutional lawyer A. V. Dicey identified it as being one of the two main pillars of the Constitution , the other being that of the rule of law .
158162	Dicey 's work has had a major and lasting impact .
158163	Despite subsequent criticisms , the two pillars identified by Dicey still stand .
158164	While some critics have considered them weak and unnecessary pillars , supporting a crumbing edifice , they remain crucial to an understanding of the British Constitution .
158165	MAIN PROVISIONS
158166	The most succinct definition of parliamentary sovereignty was offered by Dicey .
158167	Parliamentary sovereignty , he wrote , meant that Parliament had " the right to make or unmake any law whatever ; and , further , that no person or body is recognized by the law of England as having a right to override or set aside the legislation of Parliament . "
158168	An act passed by Parliament would be enforced by the courts , the courts recognizing no body other than Parliament as having authority to override such an act .
158169	Parliament itself could substitute an act for an earlier one .
158170	One of the precepts derived from the principle is that Parliament is not bound by its predecessors .
158171	Once Parliament has passed an act , it becomes the law of the land .
158172	It is not open to challenge before the courts on the grounds of being unconstitutional .
158173	Although Dicey claimed more ancient lineage for it , the principle of parliamentary sovereignty became established as a judicial rule in consequence of the Glorious Revolution of 1688 and subsequent Bill of Rights , which established the relationship between the Crown and Parliament ( see Chapter 3 ) .
158174	It was the product of an alliance between Parliament and lawyers and of the intimidation of judges by the House of Commons .
158175	Assertion of the principle served to do away with the monarch 's previously claimed powers to suspend or dispense with acts of Parliament and it served to deny judges the power to strike down measures .
158176	It came to occupy a unique place in constitutional law .
158177	The principle finds no expression in statute or any other formal enactment .
158178	It exists in common law but enjoys a special status beyond that enjoyed by other principles of common law .
158179	Its underpinnings are not only legal but also political and historical .
158180	It is now too late to challenge the principle .
158181	Judicial obedience to it constitutes what H. W. R. Wade referred to as " the ultimate political fact upon which the whole system of legislation hangs . "
158182	No statute can confer the power of parliamentary sovereignty , for that would be to confer the very power being acted upon .
158183	It is therefore considered to be unique .
158184	As Hood Phillips states , " It may indeed be called the one fundamental law of the British Constitution . "
158185	The second pillar identified by Dicey was that of " the rule of law . "
158186	Identifying what is meant by the term is extremely difficult .
158187	Few students of the constitution would deny the important of the tenet .
158188	Dicey himself argued that it comprised " at least three distinct though kindred conceptions " : " That no man is punishable or can be lawfully made to suffer in body or goods except for a distinct breach of law established in the ordinary legal manner before the ordinary courts of the land " ; that " no man is above the law [ and ] every man , whatever be his rank or condition , is subject to the ordinary law of the realm and amenable to the jurisdiction of the ordinary tribunals " ; and that " the general principles of the constitution [ are ] the result of judicial decisions determining the rights of private persons in particular cases brought before the courts . "
158189	These three conceptions have been subject to various criticisms : that many of the discretionary powers are vested in officials and public bodies , that many officials and bodies have powers and immunities that the ordinary citizen does not have , and that certain rights have been modified by or enacted in statute .
158190	Further it is not clear why Dicey 's third conception should be considered " kindred " to the other two .
158191	Some students of the Constitution find Dicey 's analysis useful , ad others tend to be dismissive .
158192	The important point for our purposes is that there is no agreed definition .
158193	The rule of law , then , stands as a central element of the British Constitution , but no one is sure precisely what it means .
158194	There is some common ground in that it is assumed to imply certain substantive and procedural rights , government must be subject to the law , and the judiciary must be independent .
158195	The problem is one of determining what those rights are , how they are to be protected , and how the independence of the judiciary is to be maintained .
158196	There is a further problem .
158197	The concept of the rule of law is not logically compatible with that of parliamentary sovereignty .
158198	Parliament could if it so wishes confer arbitrary powers upon government .
158199	It could fetter the independence of the judiciary .
158200	It could limit or remove altogether certain rights presumed to exist at common law .
158201	The rule of law , in short , could be threatened or even dispensed with by parliamentary enactment .
158202	Dicey himself recognized this problem and sought to resolve it .
158203	He argued , in essence , that the rule of law prevented government from exercising arbitrary powers .
158204	If government wanted such powers , it could obtain them only through Parliament ( Parliament itself has never sought to exercise executive powers ) and the granting of them could take place only after deliberation and approval by the triumvirate of monarch , Lords , and Commons .
158205	Such an argument serves to explain potential impediments to a government intent on acquiring arbitrary powers .
158206	It does not deny the truth of the assertion that Parliament could , if it wished , confer such powers upon government .
158207	Indeed , many observers would argue that given the growth of cabinet government , the potential for government to seek and receive such powers is significantly greater now than was the case at the time when Dicey was writing .
158208	For many critics of the existing Constitution , parliamentary sovereignty no longer constitutes an encouragement to the rule of law but rather exists as an impediment to its attainment .
158209	So long as parliamentary sovereignty remains " the one fundamental law " of the Constitution , there is no way in which substantive rights can be entrenched and put beyond the reach of Parliament .
158210	The third feature of the Constitution that I have listed — that the United Kingdom is a unitary state — is a less difficult one to comprehend .
158211	The United States is a federal nation .
158212	The power vested in the federal government is that delegated in the United States Constitution : all other powers not delegated rest with the states or the people .
158213	In the United Kingdom , no powers are reserved to national or regional bodies .
158214	If they were , Parliament would not be omnicompetent .
158215	Parliament exercises legal sovereignty .
158216	It can confer certain powers and responsibilities upon regional and local authorities , and it can also remove those powers .
158217	The unitary nation is that of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland .
158218	Wales was integrated with England in 1536 by act of Parliament ( the Laws in Wales Act ) , and Scotland and England were incorporated in 1707 by the Treaty of Union and by the Act of Union with Scotland .
158219	Ireland entered into legislative union in 1801 .
158220	Following an armed uprising , the emergence of the Irish Free State was recognized in 1922 and given the status of a self-governing dominion .
158221	( The Irish Constitution of 1937 declared the country to be a sovereign independent state , a position recognized by the Westminster Parliament in 1949 ) .
158222	Excluded from the Irish Free State were the northern six counties of Ireland , forming part of the traditional region of Ulster .
158223	The Protestant majority in Ulster wished to remain part of the United Kingdom , and the province of Northern Ireland has so remained .
158224	The fourth element of the constitution is one that I have described as a parliamentary government under a constitutional monarchy .
158225	It is this element that is especially important in terms of the current relationships among the different organs of the state and the one in which conventions of the Constitution are predominant .
158226	It constitutes an assembly of different relationships and powers , the product of traditional institutions being adapted to meet changing circumstances .
158227	The developments producing this form of government were sketched in Chapter 3 .
158228	The results , as we have seen , were parliamentary government in the sense of government through Parliament rather than government by Parliament , with a largely ceremonial head of state .
158229	The essentials of this form of government may be adumbrated as follows .
158230	In the relationship among government , Parliament , and the monarch , the government dominates .
158231	Although lacking formal powers , the cabinet is recognized by convention as being at the heart of government .
158232	It is responsible for the final determination of policy to be submitted to Parliament , for the supreme control of the national executive in accordance with the policy prescribed by Parliament , and for the continuous coordination and delimitation of the interests of the several departments of state .
158233	It is presided over by the prime minister .
158234	The prime minister is appointed by the monarch .
158235	By convention , the monarch summons the leader of the party with a majority of seats in the House of Commons .
158236	( In the event of a party having no overall majority , the monarch summons whoever he or she believed may be able to form an administration ) .
158237	The prime minister then selects the members of his or her cabinet and other government ministers and submits their names to the monarch who , by convention , does not deny the prime minister 's choice .
158238	By convention , ministers are drawn from Parliament and , again by convention , predominantly from the elected house , the House of Commons .
158239	Although the government is no longer chosen by the Commons , it nonetheless is elected through the House of Commons : there is no separate election of the executive .
158240	There is a separation and overlap of powers between the government and the House of Commons in Britain but no equivalent separation of personnel .
158241	Government ministers are drawn from , and remain within , Parliament .
158242	Formally , ministers are responsible to the monarch .
158243	By convention , they are responsible for their policies and actions to Parliament .
158244	Ministers are responsible to Parliament through the convention of individual ministerial responsibility which assigns to them control of their departments , for which they are answerable to Parliament .
158245	The cabinet is similarly responsible to Parliament through the convention of collective ministerial responsibility .
158246	This convention , one scholar writes , " implies that all cabinet ministers assume responsibility for cabinet decisions and actions taken to implement those decisions . "
158247	It also has begotten two other conventions .
158248	It is a corollary of collective responsibility that any minister who disagrees publicly with a cabinet decision should resign and that a government defeat in the House of Commons on a vote of confidence necessitates either the resignation of the government or a request for a dissolution ( there is no convention as to which of these alternatives the government should select ) .
158249	Party cohesion ensures that the cabinet usually enjoys a parliamentary majority , but political parties remain unknown to the Constitution .
158250	The cabinet approves government bills to be presented to Parliament .
158251	( In drawing up measures , it is aided primarily by its officials — that is , civil servants — and will consult normally with interested bodies : such consultation , though , enjoys no formal recognition in constitutional terms . )
158252	Within Parliament , the most important house is the Commons .
158253	The House is expected to submit bills to sustained scrutiny and debate before giving its assent to them ( or not giving its assent to them , but the influence of party usually precludes such an outcome ) .
158254	Formally , the House is free to pass or reject bills as it wishes .
158255	The House of Lords is more constrained ( see Chapter 3 ) ; it was forced to accept a restricted role under the terms of the 1911 and 1949 Parliament Acts .
158256	Under the provisions of the 1911 Act ( a measure to which the Lords acquiesced under threat of being swamped with a mass of new Liberal pro-reform peers ) , the House could delay passage of nonmoney bills for only two successive sessions , such bills being enacted if passed by the Commons again the succeeding session .
158257	Money bills , those certified as such by the Speaker of the House of Commons , were to receive the Royal Assent one month after leaving the Commons , whether assented to by the House of Lords or not .
158258	The only significant power of veto retained was that over bills to prolong the life of a Parliament .
158259	( The delaying power over nonmoney bills was reduced by a further session under the terms of the 1949 Parliament Act , itself passed under the provisions of the 1911 Act . )
158260	In practice , it is rare for the Lords to reject government measures , and there is a gentleman 's agreement among the parties in the House that a bill promised in a government 's election manifesto should be given an unopposed Second Reading ( see Chapter 11 ) .
158261	Once a bill has received the assent of both Houses it then goes to the monarch for the Royal Assent .
158262	By convention , this assent is always forthcoming .
158263	As already mentioned , not since Queen Anne 's reign has a monarch refused assent .
158264	Queen Victoria contemplated such refusal but was persuaded otherwise .
158265	By convention , the Queen exercises her powers on the advice of her ministers .
158266	In certain extreme circumstances , Her Majesty may find herself in a position in which she is called on to use her discretion in making a political decision .
158267	Such cases are rare , though the Queen would probably prefer them to be nonexistent .
158268	The strength and the value of the contemporary monarchy derives from being above and avoiding political decisions .
158269	The moment a bill receives the Royal Assent it becomes an act of Parliament .
158270	It is then enforced and upheld by the agencies of the state .
158271	It is binding and , by virtue of the doctrine of parliamentary sovereignty , can not be challenged by the courts , nor can it be overridden by any other authority .
158272	The development of a form of representative democracy in the nineteenth century led Dicey to distinguish between legal sovereignty , which continued to reside with the triumvirate of the monarch , Lords , and Commons , and political sovereignty , which he deemed to rest with the electorate .
158273	This somewhat clumsy distinction has a certain utility .
158274	The electorate may have the power to choose the members of the House of Commons but the will of the electorate is not something formally recognized by the courts .
158275	The courts recognize and will enforce only acts of Parliament .
158276	Under the provision of the 1911 Parliament Act , the maximum life of a Parliament is five years .
158277	( Previously , the period was seven years . )
158278	Within that period , the prime minister is free to recommend to the monarch a dissolution — in effect , to call a general election .
158279	Unlike the United States , Britain has no fixed-term elections at a national level .
158280	The ability of a prime minister effectively to call a general election has been regarded by some writers as the most important weapon in ensuring parliamentary support .
158281	The prime minister can threaten to recommend a dissolution if he or she does not receive the necessary support to get a measure through .
158282	Such a threat may constitute a bluff in that the prime minister would have more to lose if an election was called than would most MPs ( the PM could lose office : most seats are safe seats and so most MPs could expect to be reelected ) , but nonetheless it has proved a potent influence in determining parliamentary behaviour .
158283	It would be exceptional , albeit not unknown , for MPs of the government party to vote against their own side on a vote of confidence .
158284	No government in the twentieth century has lost a vote of confidence as a result of dissent by its own supporters — hence the dominance of government .
158285	In summary , then , the fourth element of the Constitution — parliamentary government under a constitutional monarch — may be seen to comprise different relationships and powers .
158286	These relationships and powers are the product of traditional institutions being adapted to meet changing circumstances and are prescribed by a variety of measures of statute and common law and by convention .
158287	The working of the various relationships within the framework established by law and convention is made possible by the operation of bodies not formally recognized by the Constitution , namely political parties .
158288	To understand contemporary British politics , one has to understand the constitutional framework .
158289	As we shall see , to understand British politics fully one has also to go beyond that framework .
158290	The shifting and complex web of relationships and powers that forms the British Constitution is not an easily discernible one .
158291	There are some powers and relationships that recognizably fall within the rubric of the Constitution .
158292	Others are less easy to classify .
158293	Sometimes a feature of the Constitution is discerned as such only at the time when it has just ceased to have much relevance .
158294	Walter Bagehot 's The English Constitution , published in 1867 , constituted a classic description of a Constitution that had not previously been so well sketched , yet a Constitution that was to undergo significant modifications as a result of the passage that very year of the Second Reform Act .
158295	Bagehot 's work continued to be regarded as an authoritative work long after the Constitution had undergone fundamental change .
158296	CONCLUSION
158297	Grasping the essentials of the Constitution at any given moment is clearly a demanding and confusing task .
158298	It is confusing even to those charged with its interpretation and to those who seek to make it work .
158299	To the student of the subject , the British Constitution appears complex , confusing , ill defined , and in many respects amorphous .
158300	Such a reaction is both natural and understandable : the Constitution does exhibit those very characteristics .
158301	At the heart of the difficulty of delineating clearly the essential features of the Constitution is its ever-changing nature .
158302	Constitutional norms serve to influence and mold political behaviour .
158303	Conversely , political behaviour helps influence the contours of the Constitution .
158304	As we have seen , such changes are made possible by the assimilating influence of conventions .
158305	" The conventions of the constitution , " as Professor LeMay observed , " have meaning only when they are looked at against a background of continuous political change .
158306	It is very difficult to say with certainty what they were at any particular moment .
158307	Above all , they can not be understood " with the politics left out . " "
158308	The Constitution has proved adaptable to changing political conditions .
158309	In recent years , however , its relevance has been questioned .
158310	The patchwork quilt of powers and relationships stipulated by the Constitution has been criticized for being neither useful nor relevant in the political environment of the 1970s and 1980s .
158311	There is , as we shall see , pressure from many influential sources for the Constitution not only to be further amended but also to be radically altered .
158312	In some cases there are calls for a new constitutional settlement .
158313	It is this pressure for change and its implications that subsequent chapters will explore .
158314	THE ELECTORAL SYSTEM
158315	Fair and Workable ?
158316	IN THE UNITED STATES , citizens are presented with the opportunity to go to the polls at frequent and fixed intervals to elect at national , state , and local levels a host of legislators , executive heads , councilpersons , officials , and even , in some states , judges .
158317	It has been estimated that there are approximately 1 million elective offices to be filled .
158318	In any given year there may be 120,000 or 130,000 elections held , most of them for local school boards .
158319	Before polling day , the citizen is faced with a lengthy election campaign : there are primary campaigns , the primary elections , the general election campaign , and the general election itself .
158320	The presidential election campaign lasts for nearly a year ; with all the preplanning , advance publicity , and fund raising it lasts for much longer .
158321	Given the short interval between elections , campaigns for the United States House of Representatives are virtually continuous .
158322	Once in the polling booth , the voter is faced with a daunting array of candidates : given the number of offices to be filled and the number of people seeking to fill them , the number of names may be a three-figure one .
158323	Voting and its subsequent tabulation is much eased by the use of voting machines .
158324	Choosing between Republican and Democratic candidates is not always an easy task , and ticket splitting is a well-recognized phenomenon .
158325	Such characteristics of United States elections are well known .
158326	They have little in common with those of British elections .
158327	In the United Kingdom , a citizen may have the opportunity to vote in a national election only once every five years .
158328	That election is for the House of Commons and the House of Commons alone .
158329	The members of the House of Lords are not elected : they serve by virtue of birth or , for life peers , by appointment for life .
158330	There is no separate election of the executive : the leader of the party with a majority of seats in the House of Commons is invited to form a government .
158331	( The choice of party leaders is a matter for the parties themselves . )
158332	The date of an election is now known until a few weeks before the event , when the prime minister recommends a dissolution of Parliament to the Queen .
158333	Although there is much anticipatory planning , the election campaign proper extends over approximately three weeks .
158334	There are no primaries : candidate selection is an internal matter for the parties .
158335	As we shall see , there are also significant differences in registration procedures .
158336	The campaign is fought on a national , and party , basis .
158337	Funding and organization in the constituencies as well as nationally is undertaken by the established parties , not by individual candidates or campaign organizations created by the candidates .
158338	The amount of money spent on electioneering during this period is strictly limited by law .
158339	On polling day , the elector is faced with a small ballot slip on which are printed the names usually of only three or four candidates ( Six or more candidates standing in any one constituency would be unusual . )
158340	The voter places his or her cross besides the name of one of them .
158341	With each elector having only one vote to cast for only one candidate there is no such thing as ticket splitting .
158342	At the close of polling , the votes are collected in one central area in each constituency and counted by hand .
158343	The process of counting is a proficient one and a sufficient number of results are usually announced within a few hours of the close of the polls to know which party has won the election .
158344	If the party in office has lost the prime minister goes to Buckingham Palace to tender his or her resignation .
158345	The leader of the party newly returned with a majority of seats is then summoned .
158346	The new cabinet and other ministerial appointments are announced within a matter of days , sometimes within a matter of hours .
158347	Within a month of an election being called , Britain may find itself with a new government .
158348	An elector in Britain has more opportunity to vote in local elections than in national ones .
158349	These are fixed terms and the elector has the chance to vote for members of councils at district and county ( or metropolitan ) levels and sometimes at parish level as well .
158350	However , only council members ( councillors ) are elected ; no executive officers are subject to election .
158351	Councils choose their own chairmen and the chief administrative officials are appointed professionals .
158352	There is no election of any local official , be it police chief , register of wills , city auditor , or judge .
158353	The one similarity between local elections in Britain and the United States is the turnout : it is very low , in some instances as low as 10% of eligible electors .
158354	The essential characteristics of national elections in the United States and Britain are contrasted in Table 5.1 .
158355	Let us consider in a little more detail some of the main features of British elections ( in other words , election of the House of Commons ) before proceeding to a consideration of the current controversy surrounding the electoral system .
158356	As we have seen ( Chapter 3 ) , the franchise was variously extended in the nineteenth century .
158357	The basis on which the vote was given was that of property .
158358	Not until 1918 was universal manhood suffrage introduced on the basis of ( six months ' ) residence .
158359	In the same year , women aged 30 and over , if already local government electors or married to such electors , were given a vote in general elections .
158360	The vote was extended to all women aged 21 and over in 1928 .
158361	It was extended to 18- to 20-year-olds in 1969 .
158362	The various extensions of the franchise during the course of the century , much more radical in numerical terms than the various extensions of the previous century , and the growth in population have resulted in the electorate growing from one of 6,730,935 in 1900 to one of 42,703,019 in 1983 .
158363	The 1949 Representation of the People Act effectively brought to final fruition the principle of " one person one vote . "
158364	The only people excluded from the franchise are peers ( they have their own House ) , imprisoned criminals , those of unsound mind , people convicted of certain election offences , and aliens .
158365	THE ELECTORAL STRUCTURE
158366	Electors
158367	In order to exercise one 's right to vote it is necessary to be on the electoral register , which is compiled annually .
158368	Each year every household receives an electoral registration form .
158369	The head of the household is required by law to complete it and to list all those who are resident in the dwelling on October 10 of that year and are eligible for inclusion , including those who will attain the age of 18 years during the period that the new register comes into effect .
158370	These forms are returned by mail to the Registration Officer for the Constituency .
158371	The register then compiled is open for inspection once compiled , which takes effect the following February , and is in force for one year .
158372	Electors who move to another constituency during the course of the year are entitled to apply to vote by post in the constituency in which they are registered .
158373	Compared with registration practice in most American states , the British method is both simple and effective .
158374	Given that people die , sometimes fail to complete the registration forms correctly , or move without applying for a postal vote , the electoral register is never 100% accurate .
158375	However , it has been estimated that it is 93% accurate when published , declining to 85% accuracy on the last day of validity .
158376	In registration there is no procedure analogous to the American practice of registering as a Republican , Democrat , or Independent : given the absence of primary elections in Britain , there is no logical reason why one should .
158377	The United Kingdom is divided into single-member constituencies .
158378	There are currently 650 , though the number can and does vary .
158379	From 1974 until 1983 there were 635 , and at one time earlier in this century there were over 700 .
158380	Constituencies
158381	The drawing of boundaries is the responsibility of bodies known as boundary commissions : there is a commission each for England , Scotland , Wales , and Northern Ireland .
158382	Each commission is chaired by the Speaker of the House of Commons ( a nonparty figure ) and each has a judge as deputy chairman .
158383	Assistant commissioners , usually lawyers , are appointed to supervize local inquiries , and the staff of the commissions includes the country 's main officials dealing with population and geographic surveys .
158384	In redrawing boundaries the commissions are guided by rules laid down by act of Parliament .
158385	They are supposed to ensure that constituencies are as equal as possible in size of their electorates .
158386	However , they are permitted to deviate from this if special geographic considerations ( for example , the size , shape , and accessibility of a constituency ) appear to render such a deviation desirable .
158387	Other rules further complicate the position .
158388	The commissioners are enjoined not to cross local authority boundaries in creating parliamentary constituencies .
158389	They also have to work within the context of regional disparities .
158390	To compensate for the absence of its own national assembly .
158391	Scot land has a great number of constituencies allocated to it than its population strictly allows , and the same exception applies to Wales .
158392	Hence , the electoral quota ( the national electorate divided by the number of seats ) is greater in England than in Scotland or Wales .
158393	Under existing legislation , the commissioners are required to review electoral boundaries every 10-15 years .
158394	( It used to be at more frequent intervals , but this was found to be too disruptive . )
158395	Before making their recommendations , the commissioners consider submissions from interested bodies , primarily the local political parties .
158396	If a proposed change has the support of the local parties , it is usual for the commissioners to accept it .
158397	Once they have completed their work , their recommendations are presented to a government minister , the home secretary , who is then required to lay them before the House of Commons for approval .
158398	They are rarely free of criticism , and in 1969 the Labour home secretary advised his supporters in the House to vote against the commission 's recommendations , which they did .
158399	As a result , the 1970 general election was not fought on the basis of the new boundaries recommended by the boundary commissioners .
158400	The recommendations were implemented in the new Parliament .
158401	The next review by the commission was completed in 1982 and challenged in the courts by the Labour party .
158402	It contended that the commissioners had acted outside the terms of the act by giving undue weight to some of the criteria for determining boundaries as against others .
158403	( There were some notable disparities in constituency sizes . )
158404	The courts determined that the commissioners had exercised properly the wide discretion given them by Parliament and rejected the case .
158405	The commission 's recommendations were subsequently approved by Parliament and the 1983 general election was fought on the new boundaries .
158406	A combination of population shifts ( about three-quarters of a million people move house every year in Britain ) , the disparity among constituency electorates recommended by the commissioners in favor of other criteria ( maintaining local government boundaries and the like ) , the lapse of time between reviews , ad the disparity in the number of seats allocated to the different countries in the United Kingdom has meant that there are often marked differences among the sizes of electorates .
158407	In 1979 , the electoral quota for English constituencies was a little under 70,000 .
158408	The constituency of Bromsgrove and Redditch ( constituencies are given names , not numbers ) had an electorate of 104,375 , while Newcastle-upon-Tyne Central had an electoral register of but 23,678 .
158409	( The smallest electorate was in Scotland — Glasgow Central , with 19,826 electors . )
158410	Even after the redrawing of boundaries in 1983 , there were still some significant disparities .
158411	Of the seats , 5% deviated from the electoral quota by 20% ( though this was down from the 39% of seats that had deviated by that much on the 1982 register . )
158412	The Isle of Wight , an English constituency , had an electorate of 94,768 , while the Scottish constituency of the Western Isles , difficult to enlarge for geographic reasons , had but 22,901 electors .
158413	Election campaigns are short , sharp , and dominated by the political parties .
158414	In British elections , unlike those in America , the personalities of candidates ( except for national leaders ) and their personal wealth play but a marginal role .
158415	The campaign is fought in practice on a national level between the two main parties , the candidates and the local campaigns serving to reinforce the national campaigns of their leaders .
158416	Candidates are selected locally by the parties , and the parties provide the finance and the organization for the campaign .
158417	Election expenses are limited by statute and have been since 1883 .
158418	Expenditure is permitted only where authorized by a candidate , a candidate 's election agent , or a person authorized in writing by the agent .
158419	The maximum permitted expenditure is calculated on the basis of a fixed sum plus a limited amount based on the number of electors : in an average-sized English county constituency in 1983 , the ceiling was approximately £4,700 ( just over $7,000 ) .
158420	There are certain types of expenditure that are illegal ( for example , paying an elector to exhibit an election poster or paying for voters to be taken to and from the polling booths ) , and separate committees to promote a candidate are not permitted .
158421	Even with the modest expenditure that is permitted , most candidates fail to spend the maximum allowed .
158422	Some devices for keeping costs low are employed and these can , where required , provide up to an extra 20% of expenditure : a popular ploy is to purchase stationery in advance and then resell it cheaply to the candidate as second-hand stock .
158423	Few candidates , though , are prepared to run too many risks for fear of having their elections challenged and declared void : expenses have to be declared and opponents keep a wary eye open for any infringement of election law .
158424	Two other constraints also operate : the parties have difficulty raising sufficient money to fight campaigns ( national and local appeals are common when an election is in the offing ) and there is little evidence that increased expenditure in local campaigns necessarily helps win elections .
158425	Campaigns
158426	Each candidate is permitted one postage-free mailing of one piece of election literature .
158427	Other literature is distributed by the unpaid party activists .
158428	The main item of literature is the candidate 's election address .
158429	This will usually incorporate a summary of the main points of the party 's national election manifesto .
158430	The candidate will spend most the campaign making speeches throughout the constituency , not infrequently at thinly attended meetings , and canvassing door to door where possible .
158431	He or she will be aided by volunteers who do doorstep canvassing to try to determine where supporters live : on election day they will keep a running tab on who has voted in order to ensure that support is maximized .
158432	The main focus of the campaign is a national one .
158433	The party leaders will make regular and well-publicized appearances throughout the country , ensuring that the national press and television reporters follow in their wake as well as holding daily press conferences .
158434	The national party organizations increasingly make use also of press and poster advertising .
158435	As long as expenditure can not be said to apply in support of specific candidates , national party campaigns do not fall foul of the election finance restrictions .
158436	In the 1979 election the Labour and Conservative national party organizations are estimated to have each spent a little over 1 million pounds on the campaign , roughly the same amount expended in total by their candidates in the local campaigns .
158437	The largest single item of expenditure was advertising .
158438	The parties enjoyed also the benefit of free but limited television time .
158439	Paid political advertising on television is not allowed : each party is allocated a set number of 10-minute party political broadcasts that are transmitted on all television channels .
158440	The allocation of the number of broadcasts to the parties is a somewhat contentious one .
158441	The broadcasts themselves are often regarded by voters as the least appetizing part of election campaigns .
158442	The basis of the parties ' appeal to the country is the election manifestos that they issue .
158443	In recent elections , these have become increasingly lengthy and specific documents , detailing the intended policies and measures to be pursued by a party if returned to office .
158444	They constitute a topic of some controversy .
158445	It has been argued that very few electors usually read them and that many of the commitments made do not enjoy widespread support among voters , even among those voting for the parties that issued them .
158446	They are also viewed by some observers as hostages for the future , parties in office being perceived as often doing the reverse of what was promised in their manifestos .
158447	In practice , they constitute something of as guide to interested bodies ad provide a framework for the main items of legislation introduced by an incoming government in the first session or two of a new Parliament : most manifesto promises are usually implemented .
158448	A more relevant criticism is that manifesto promises may not address themselves to the country 's real problems .
158449	Some would argue that , by virtue of the manner of their compilation and their utilization as a means of furthering the adversary relationship between the parties , manifestos add to those problems rather than offering solutions .
158450	Any citizen aged 21 years or over is eligible to be a candidate for election to the House of Commons .
158451	There are certain limited exceptions .
158452	Precluded from serving in the House of Commons are those who are disqualified from voting , as well as policemen , civil servants , judges , members of the boards of nationalized industries , undischarged bankrupts , members of the armed services , and clergy of the Churches of England , Scotland , Ireland , and the Roman Catholic Church .
158453	The exclusion of public servants has an acceptable rationale to reinforce it ; they are free to resign their positions should they wish to stand for election .
158454	The exclusion of certain clergy is less easy to justify ( a relic of the time when religious disputes were at the heart of national affairs ) , as is the exclusion of 18- to 20-year-olds : when the voting age was lowered in 1969 , the age of eligibility for candidature was not .
158455	To be a candidate one has to obtain the signature of 10 electors in the constituency and submit a deposit of £150 ( approximately $225 ) , returnable in the event of receiving one-eighth of the votes cast .
158456	In Britain , unlike the United States , there are no residence requirements : hence , parties enjoy a wider range of choice in the selection of candidates .
158457	Candidates
158458	In practice , candidates are party candidates .
158459	As a result of an innovation introduced in 1969 , this is now more formally recognized : candidates are permitted to include their party designation on the ballot paper .
158460	It is generally assumed that an individual candidate has little influence on voting behavior : party is the decisive factor , though the candidate can have some impact .
158461	In the 1979 and 1983 elections there were examples of locally popular candidates holding their marginal seats against the national swing .
158462	Indeed , in the marginal constituency of Ipswich , the Labour MP was elected on both occasions despite the national swing in favor of the Conservatives .
158463	Such instances remain rare , and party remains the primary and almost exclusive influence .
158464	Virtually all constituencies ( the exceptions are in Northern Ireland ) are contested by Conservative and Labour candidates .
158465	In the general elections of the 1970s , the Liberal party regularly contested more than 500 seats ( indeed , over 600 in October 1974 ) , and in the 1983 election the Social Democratic/Liberal Alliance fielded candidates in all 633 seats in Great Britain .
158466	These are the only parties to each obtain several million votes in general elections .
158467	They are also the only ones to be successful in recent years in winning seats in England .
158468	In Scotland , there is the challenge of the Scottish National Party .
158469	It won 11 seats in October 1974 but only 2 in 1979 and 1983 , despite fighting all Scottish seats .
158470	In Wales , there is Plaid Cymru ( the party of Wales ) , which won 3 seats in 1974 and 2 in 1979 and 1983 .
158471	In Northern Ireland , the dominant force is that of the Ulster Unionists , though divided now into different parties : in 1983 Unionists of different hues won 15 of the 17 seats in the province .
