158472	The 1979 and 1983 elections also witnessed an increase in the number of candidates fielded by minor parties , to whom the £150 deposit ( first set in 1918 ) no longer serves as the bar to nonserious candidates that was intended .
158473	The Ecology party fielded 109 candidates in 1983 ( up from 53 in 1979 ) , the right-wing National Front 60 candidates ( though down from its 1979 peak of 303 candidates ) , the British National party ( a breakaway movement from the National Front ) 54 candidates , and the Communist party 35 candidates .
158474	All the candidates of these parties lost their deposits , as did a few scattered independents and other candidates standing under rather esoteric banners .
158475	( In 1983 , for example , there was a Justice for Divorced Fathers candidate , one representing Freddie 's Alternative Medicine party , and another standing for Law and Order in Gotham City — a label derived from the old Batman comic book series ! )
158476	Their main impact was to lengthen the ballot paper .
158477	In 1959 , there was a total of 1,536 candidates , an average of 2.4 per seat .
158478	In 1983 , there were 2,579 candidates — an average of 4 per seat .
158479	The candidates of the main parties are selected locally , though the national party in each case retains some veto power .
158480	In Britain , unlike the United States , there are no primary elections and the selection of a candidate is in practice usually in the hands of a small group of party activists .
158481	Given that most seats are safe seats for one party or another , this selection is usually tantamount to election .
158482	Within the Conservative party , aspiring candidates have to be on a candidates list maintained by the party 's national headquarters .
158483	( A local party may choose someone not on the list , but it must obtain approval from the national party for its choice . )
158484	A local Conservative association seeking a candidate will invite applicants , and in a safe Conservative seat , several hundred aspiring candidates can be expected to put their names forward .
158485	The association will then appoint a selection committee , usually comprising representatives from its different branches and associated groups such as the Young Conservatives .
158486	This committee will sift through the applications and the recommend three or more names to the executive council , the main decision-making body of the association .
158487	The council may then recommend one name for approval to a general meeting of the association , or it may put forward more than one name and leave it to the general meeting to decide .
158488	Candidate Selection
158489	The researches of both Austin Ranney and Michael Rush have found that , despite the political importance of choosing a candidate , the political views of applicants are not important considerations in the selection process .
158490	Selection committees have tended to be influenced by an applicant 's knowledge of the constituency , his or her stature and delivery of speech , and whether there are the makings of a good " constituency member " ( one who will represent diligently the interests of constituents ) or , in some cases , of a national figure .
158491	On occasions , more esoteric considerations may apply , as I can testify , having served on a selection committee .
158492	" Ca n't we interview him ?
158493	He has a nice name " was one comment made during the selection deliberations ( The response : a polite " no . " )
158494	Other influences can include , in some areas , religion and quite often age and sex : local parties are reluctant to adopt women candidates ( the folklore being that women voters dislike voting for them ) and anyone aged under 30 or over 50 years .
158495	There is also a tendency to prefer married men ( single men over 30 are considered somewhat suspect ) , and wives are often asked to appear before selection committees .
158496	Because wives are looked on a surrogates for their husbands while the latter are at Westminster , their attitudes to constituency work and their appearance are considered important .
158497	In the selection I was involved in , one prominent candidate — a nationally known figure — suffered from the poor impression his wife gave to some of the selectors .
158498	Arrogant or pretentious wives can sometimes kill the political ambitions of their husbands .
158499	Although the Labour candidates selected are increasingly similar in background to Conservative candidates , the selection procedure in the Labour Party is not quite the same .
158500	A local Labour party will seek a candidate by inviting nominations .
158501	Nominations may be made by local ward committees , party groups such as the women 's section , and by affiliated organizations , principally affiliated trade unions .
158502	( An aspiring candidate can approach such groups to solicit a nomination . )
158503	Once nominations are received , the executive committee , responsible for the day-to-day running of the party , will draw up a short list of candidates for interview .
158504	The final choice is made by the governing body , the General Management Committee , comprising representatives from the different ward committees and affiliated organizations .
158505	The candidate then requires the endorsement of the party 's National Executive Committee .
158506	In 1980 , the Labour party con erence approved the principle of mandatory reselection of sitting Labour MPs .
158507	What this meant was that sitting MPs should no longer be reselected automatically by local parties just before a general election was held .
158508	Instead , a full selection procedure was to be gone through during the lifetime of a Parliament , thus allowing other aspiring candidates to be considered .
158509	It was a contentious issue and was generally seen as an attempt by the party 's left wing to try to remove some Labour members of whom they disapproved .
158510	In practice , the number of members denied reselection was small ( only seven by the time the 1983 general election was called ) , but the issue served to highlight the more overt emphasis placed by Labour activists on a candidate 's political stance than was the case on the Conservative side .
158511	In the Conservative party , there is no procedure for mandatory reselection .
158512	In the Liberal party , selection is by the local party also , with the national party maintaining an approved list of candidates .
158513	However , national approval has tended in the past to be given without much discussion , in large part because the number of aspirants for candidatures has not been great : the party has often had to adopt whoever was willing to stand .
158514	The number of aspiring candidates increased in the 1970s , but so too did the number of seats fought .
158515	In many cases during 1974 , candidate selection took place just before the election campaign got under way .
158516	Within the Social Democratic Party ( SDP ) , candidate selection is made through the area parties .
158517	These are organized usually on a multiconstituency basis and are responsible for organizing and choosing candidates for constituencies within their areas .
158518	Unless the task is delegated to local ( constituency ) groups , candidates are chosen by a postal ballot of all members of the area party .
158519	Candidates must be on the party 's national list of approved candidates and require the endorsement of one of the party 's regional committees to get on that list .
158520	When the Alliance between the Liberals and the Social Democrats was formed in 1981 a formula was devised for allocating constituencies between the two parties .
158521	Negotiating the allocation encountered problems ( some entrenched Liberal candidates were unwilling to step down in favor of SDP candidates ) but , once achieved , the local party responsible for fielding a candidate made its choice and that candidate was then endorsed by the other party .
158522	There were no joint selection procedures .
158523	There was numerical parity in the distribution of seats ( though not necessarily in the distribution of seats considered winnable ) , and in the 1983 election , each party fielded more than 300 candidates .
158524	Only in two seats ( one in Liverpool , one in London ) , where there was some feuding between the two Alliance partners , were Liberal and SDP candidates to be found contesting the same seats .
158525	The candidates selected by the parties tend on the whole to be middle-aged , male , and white .
158526	Female and nonwhite candidates are exceptional .
158527	The successful candidates more than the unsuccessful ones tend to be middle-aged , university-educated ( as well as public school-educated , in the case of Conservatives ) , and drawn from the ranks of business and the professions .
158528	In postwar years there has been a tendency for MPs to be even more middle-class than they were hitherto .
158529	Past years , according to some analysts , have witnessed the emergence of a more professional member of Parliament .
158530	In each of the 650 single-member constituencies , the method of election employed is the plurality or " first-past-the-post " method .
158531	What this means is that the candidate receiving more votes than any other candidate is declared elected .
158532	It is the same method as that employed in Senate and House elections in the United States .
158533	Examples of constituency results from the 1983 general election are given in Table 5.3 .
158534	Elections
158535	In practice , most seats are considered to be safe seats for one or other of the two main parties — that is , the winning candidate has been returned with a majority that represents 10% or more of the votes cast .
158536	In the safest seats , the majority may constitute as much as 40% or 50% of the votes cast .
158537	The constituency of Blaenau Gwent ( Table 5.3 ) serves as a good example .
158538	Turnover in seats is relatively modest .
158539	Fewer than 5% of seats changed hands in the 1970 general election .
158540	Even in 1983 , with the challenge of the Social Democrat/Liberal Alliance and a major redistribution of constituency boundaries , fewer than 16% of the seats changed hands among the various competing parties .
158541	The results from the 650 constituencies , as already mentioned , determine which party will form the government .
158542	In all but one of the elections since 1945 , one party has won a absolute majority of the seats and the leader of that party has formed a government .
158543	The Labour party achieved an overall majority in five elections , on two occasions by slim margins , and formed the government following the February 1974 election , in which it had more seats than any other party but not an absolute majority ( See Table 5.4 ) .
158544	The Conservatives have won overall majorities , by clear margins , in six elections since 1945 , including the most recent .
158545	Three generalizations can be drawn about voting behaviour in the four general elections held in the period from 1950 to 1959 :
158546	VOTING BEHAVIOUR
158547	1 .
158548	There was a high turnout of electors ; 2 .
158549	Of those who voted , virtually all voted for either the Conservative or Labour parties ; 3 .
158550	The most significant predictor of party voting was class .
158551	The first two generalizations are borne out by the data in Table 5.2 .
158552	More than three-quarters of those on the electoral register turned out on each occasion to cast their vote and , of those who did so , more than 90% voted usually for either the Conservative or Labour candidate .
158553	In the 1950 election , turnout reached 84% .
158554	In the 1951 election , almost 97% of those who voted cast their ballots for one or other of the two main parties .
158555	The third generalization is drawn from survey data .
158556	Gallup Poll data showed that in these four elections , 79% or more of upper-middle-class voters and 69% or more of middle-class voters cast their votes for the Conservative party , while more than 50% of working-class and very poor voters voted for the Labour party .
158557	Class clearly was not an exclusive predictor nor was the relationship between class and party symmetrical : the middle class was more Conservative than the working class was Labour .
158558	One-third of working-class voters regularly voted Conservative .
158559	Nonetheless , class remained the most important predictor of how an elector might vote .
158560	In the 1960s and since , these generalizations have lost some of their force .
158561	Between 1964 and 1983 , turnout in general elections failed to reach 80% , falling below 73% in 1970 , October 1974 , and 1983 .
158562	More notably , there was a relative desertion by voters of the two main parties .
158563	In the two elections of 1974 , 75% of those who voted cast their ballots for one or other of the main parties .
158564	In 1983 the figure was 70% .
158565	The class-party nexus also began to wane .
158566	The survey by Butler and Stokes detected a weakening of the class alignment among younger voters in the 1960s .
158567	Further analysis of their data and of additional data for the period from 1970 to 1975 showed that , though the vote for the two main parties had declined in the 1960s , major party identification had not : in other words , electors — whatever they may have done in the polling booths — continued to express a sense of affiliation with one of the two main parties .
158568	However , partisan identification declined abruptly in 1974 , though the decline was relative : many " very strong " identifiers switched to being " fairly strong " identifiers .
158569	the authors speculated that this partisan dealignment reflected a continuing erosion of the class-party tie .
158570	By October 1974 , barely half of the electorate identified ( let alone voted ) with their " natural " class party .
158571	The relative decline in the importance of class is borne out by a survey of voters in the 1983 election ( Table 5.5 ) .
158572	Support for the SDP/Liberal Alliance was drawn evenly from different social classes .
158573	The Labour party failed to achieve even half the votes of working-class and unemployed voters .
158574	The gap between its share of the manual and nonmanual votes was only 21% , compared with 27% in 1979 and 40% in 1959 .
158575	The Conservatives made no significant inroads among their traditional class supporters , though attracting the votes of almost one in three of trade unionists .
158576	( Most trade unions are affiliated to the Labour party . )
158577	Although social class continues to structure party choice , it is no longer as reliable a predictor as it was in the 1950s and 1960s .
158578	What other variables , independent of class , can be identified as being correlated to voting behaviour ?
158579	Age , religion , gender , region , population density , and home ownership are among the most significant to have been identified .
158580	Some of these have become more pronounced as a result of the weakening of the class-party relationship ; others are of declining significance .
158581	Age and gender are among those variables of declining significance .
158582	In the 1983 general election , the older age groups were marginally more Conservative than the younger ones , but the difference was small .
158583	Among those aged over 65 years , 48% voted Conservative ( a 15% lead over the proportion voting Labour ) , whereas among those aged 18 to 22 years , 41% voted Conservative ( a 12% lead over Labour voters ) .
158584	Conservative support among the over-65s was lower than in 1979 , indeed dropping by more than the national average .
158585	This decline could support the generational cohort theory developed by Butler and Stokes : that is , that it is not age as such that influences voting behaviour but the period at which one becomes politically aware .
158586	Thus , the over-65s in 1983 were the generation of the 1930s and of the Second World War ( see Chapter 3 ) .
158587	As one analyst puts it , " Some of the Labour loyalty induced in their formative years will have lasted until today . "
158588	As a predictor of voting behaviour , though , age is of marginal utility , and so too is gender .
158589	Traditionally , women have been somewhat more likely than men to vote Conservative .
158590	In most postwar elections , more men have voted Labour than have voted Conservative , whereas more women have voted Conservative than have voted Labour .
158591	However , the bias was a slight one .
158592	According to the Gallup Poll , it disappeared in the 1983 election , the Conservatives drawing more support from men than from women ( 46% to 43% ) , thus replicating similar developments in the United States and Scandinavia during the 1970s .
158593	However , according to a Market and Opinion Research International ( MORI ) poll , the Conservatives continued to draw more support from female than from male voters ( Table 5.6 ) .
158594	The disparity in the data highlights the marginal significance now of gender as a predictor of voting behaviour .
158595	Religion is another variable of limited importance .
158596	It was significant in the nineteenth century but declined rapidly in the twentieth , as class became more important .
158597	Butler and Stokes found the relationship between religion and party of declining relevance with each generation .
158598	However , in some areas where religious loyalties remain strong , such loyalties can still alter the pattern of class voting .
158599	An obvious example is Northern Ireland ( see Chapter 9 ) , though mainland examples can be found in certain cities , notably Glasgow .
158600	In such cities there is a sizable Irish Catholic vote , and this swells the Labour vote in elections .
158601	Elsewhere , the impact of religion is small , though those who are not members of the Church of england are less likely than others in their class to support the Conservatives .
158602	The marginality of religion in influencing voting behaviour is reflected in the fact that it did not figure in analyses published in the wake of the 1983 election .
158603	More significant predictors , especially in recent elections , have been location and home ownership .
158604	Increasingly , Labour and Conservative support has become polarized between North and South and between urban and rural areas .
158605	It is also becoming polarized between those who own and those who rent their houses .
158606	The Conservative party , in terms of its voting support , has always been the party of England and , indeed , of a particular part of England .
158607	That concentration has become marked in recent elections .
158608	In a good postwar election year , the Conservatives would normally expect to pick up a respectable number of seats in Northern England and to some extent in Scotland .
158609	This is no longer the case .
158610	The party 's regional strength has become more pronounced .
158611	Mrs. Thatcher carried her party to victory in 1979 largely on the votes of the electorate in the southern half of England , below a line drawn from the River Severn to the Wash ( see Map 5.1 ) .
158612	The swing to the Conservatives in the election was highest in the southern half of the country ( and in Wales ) , lowest in the northern parts of the country and in Scotland .
158613	Compared with the 1955 election , the party had 20 fewer seats in the North and 14 fewer in Scotland , conversely , it had 34 more in the South and the Midlands and 5 more in Wales .
158614	This concentration became even more pronounced in 1983 .
158615	In the southern half of the country , the Labour party won only three seats outside of Greater London and was largely displaced as the main challenger to the Conservatives by the Liberal/SDP Alliance ( see Table 5.7 ) .
158616	The Labour vote declined least in Scotland , while the Conservative vote declined most in the Northwest of England .
158617	The wide margin between support for the Conservatives in the South of England and Labour in the North and Scotland is shown in Table 5.7 and in Map 5.1 .
158618	Scotland the North of England is more working-class than the South of England , but this is not sufficient to explain the disparity .
158619	A MORI poll conducted in 1981 found that among skilled workers in the North of England , Labour had a 32% lead over the Conservatives .
158620	Among the same group in the South , the Labour lead was only 6% .
158621	Not only is the North-South divide becoming more pronounced in terms of Labour-Conservative polarization , so too is the divide between urban and rural areas .
158622	Conservative support in the larger cities has been declining for more than 25 years .
158623	In the 1983 election , the party won less than half the number of seats it had won in the larger cities in 1959 , the last election when it was returned with a three-figure majority .
158624	In some cities , the decline in support has been dramatic .
158625	In 1959 in the three cities of Glasgow , Liverpool and Manchester , the Conservatives won a total of 15 seats .
158626	In the same three cities in 1983 , they won 1 .
158627	There are now no Conservative-held seats in Glasgow or Liverpool .
158628	Conversely , the rural areas have moved further away from Labour .
158629	In 1983 , the swing away from Labour in rural and mixed areas was twice what it was in urban areas : not one rural constituency in the South of England was won by Labour .
158630	These changes have been attributed to changing economic patterns .
158631	" The peripheral areas of Britain , " write two analysts , " with their higher unemployment , and the declining inner parts of conurbations , have become steadily more Labour ; while the expanding , more prosperous areas have become more Conservative . "
158632	Prosperity would also appear relevant to the increasing importance of home ownership .
158633	In 1983 , the Labour vote held up well among those who rented their homes from the local authorities ( Table 5.7 ) .
158634	Among those who owned their own homes the party trailed third behind the Conservatives and the Liberal/SDP Alliance .
158635	Working-class home-owners were more likely to vote Conservative than working-class council-house tenants .
158636	The problem for the Labour party is that the latter category is declining in size : more workers are buying their own homes .
158637	Increasingly , then , the Conservative party is becoming a party that draws its support predominantly from the South of England , from the rural and suburban constituencies , and from home-owners .
158638	Labour , in contrast , is becoming a party confined to the North of England , Scotland , and the urban areas , especially the inner cities .
158639	As for the Liberal/SDP Alliance , it appears to draw its support fairly evenly from the different classes ( Table 5.5 ) , from different parts of the country ( though marginally more from the South than from the North and Scotland ) , and from owner-occupiers as well as council-house tenants ( Table 5.7 ) .
158640	Anyone seeking to find a reliable predictor of Alliance voting would be hard pressed to find one .
158641	Are there any other correlations to be drawn ?
158642	Education remains important , independent of class .
158643	Voters with above the minimum of education are more likely than those who have only a minimum of education to vote Conservative .
158644	Where the British equivalents of Continental peasants ( crofters , lumbermen , isolated agriculturalists ) are gathered , there is a tendency for voters to deviate from overall patterns of class voting , a tendency in Scotland and Wales favoring the Liberals ( and , in 1983 , the SDP ) as well as the Nationalist parties .
158645	The presence of nonwhite voters in certain urban constituencies may cause further deviations from the class pattern , but the evidence on this is mixed .
158646	Issue voting , which one might expect to have increased in significance given the decline in class voting , appears to remain extremely limited .
158647	The images that the parties convey are important , more so than their stance on specific issues .
158648	In the 1983 election , more electors thought the Conservatives had the better policies than actually voted for the party .
158649	The most important issue was considered by electors to be that of unemployment , an issue on which more preferred the Labour position to that of the Conservatives .
158650	Against this , the Conservatives were preferred by far greater margins on the issues of defense and prices .
158651	Negative voting was also a significant feature of the election , 59% of all voters disliking the other party ( or parties ) more than they liked their own .
158652	There is little evidence to suggest voters voting for a particular party because of its stand on a particular issue .
158653	Electoral changes and their relationship to the political parties have been the subject of much recent analysis and debate .
158654	A review of this debate is more appropriate following a consideration of the political parties in Britain and hence is covered in the following chapter .
158655	Here I propose to confine my discussion to the contemporary debate surrounding the electoral system as an electoral system .
158656	By the middle of the twentieth century , Britain had developed an electoral system the basic characteristics of which have been delineated above : single-member constituencies , first-past-the-post election to determine the winner in each , and each adult citizen having the right to cast a vote .
158657	That system was both perceived and expected to perform three related functions : through election to the House of Commons it was expected to produce a government ; through a purportedly democratic franchise and mode of election , it was expected to confer legitimacy upon the government to govern , subject to the approval of Parliament ; and , through facilitating a choice between parties propounding specific programs , it was expected to influence public policy , the party in government carrying through the promises embodies in its election manifesto .
158658	In the 1950s such expectations were assumed to have been met .
158659	Governments were returned with overall majorities .
158660	There were few complaints about the mode of election .
158661	Governments appeared to carry out their promises .
158662	The electoral system appeared to form an intrinsic part of a stable polity .
158663	THE CURRENT DEBATE
158664	In the 1970s , and especially in the wake of the two general elections of 1974 , the extent to which the electoral system was capable of fulfilling such functions became a matter of controversy .
158665	In the February 1974 election , no party was returned to office with an overall majority of seats .
158666	In the election of October of the same year , the Labour party achieved an overall majority of only three seats : as a consequence of by-election losses and defections , it lost its majority in April 1976 , and by the end of the Parliament was in a minority by 17 seats .
158667	The Conservative party achieved a swing of 5.2% in its favor in the May 1979 election , being returned with a majority of 43 seats .
158668	In previous decades a similar swing would have produced a much higher majority .
158669	Shifts in the distribution of party support within the country were , according to one important study , likely to increase the likelihood of " hung " Parliaments , no one party being returned with an overall majority .
158670	The ability of the electoral system to produce a government in the way previously expected of it was thus called into question .
158671	Furthermore , the system also came under attack as being unfair — hence undermining consent by calling into doubt the legitimacy of both the mode of election and the government produced by it — and for facilitating the adversary relationship between the parties , a relationship that significantly influenced public policy , but did so in a manner harmful to the interests of the country .
158672	the effects of this adversary relationship on public policy in terms of both continuity and substance was considered to threaten rather than enhance the effectiveness of government
158673	The accusation that the electoral system is an unfair one is not new .
158674	It has been advanced for some time by both the Liberal party and the Electoral Reform Society .
158675	It gained ground as a result of the election results of the 1970s and the development of the adversary politics thesis .
158676	The first-past-the-post plurality method of election in single-member constituencies , it was argued , did not allow realization of the principle of " one person , one vote , one value . "
158677	Each adult citizen may have one vote but each vote was not of equal value .
158678	The disparity in the size of constituency electorates meant that a vote cast in a constituency with a small electorate such as Glasgow Central was worth more than one cast in , say , Bromsgrove and Redditch .
158679	Furthermore , the extensive number of safe seats meant that many electors cast " wasted " votes .
158680	What was the point of voting Conservative in a constituency such as Blaenau Gwent , for example , where the Labour candidate had a majority in excess of 20,000 at the previous election ?
158681	An elector consistently voting Conservative in the constituency would never contribute towards the election of an MP .
158682	The two most central criticisms , though , have been directed at the aggregate effects of such a method of election .
158683	Given the difference in the spread of support between the parties , it is possible for one party to get more votes than its opponent party but receive fewer seats .
158684	For example , party A could win two marginal seats by the barest of margins while party B won one seat with an overwhelming majority ; the aggregate vote for party B in the three seats could well exceed that of party A , but party A has won twice as many seats .
158685	( A similar spread of support among states in the United States presidential elections may result in a president obtaining a majority in the electoral college without obtaining a majority of the popular vote . )
158686	On two occasions in postwar elections , such a situation actually occurred .
158687	In the 1951 general election , the Conservatives won a majority of seats but the Labour party won more votes ( see Table 5.2 ) .
158688	In the February 1974 election , the position was reversed , the Conservatives winning more votes nationally than Labour but Labour winning more seats .
158689	In terms of forming a government , it is the number of seats that count : the Conservatives formed the government in 1951 , the Labour party in 1974 .
158690	The other major and related criticism , the one emphasized most often , is that the plurality system of voting works against national third parties .
158691	Those who benefit most from such a system are the two largest parties and those with regionally concentrated support .
158692	This is as true in the United States as it is in Britain .
158693	In presidential elections , a third-party candidate with concentrated support , such as George Wallace in 1968 , can carry some states and hence win some electoral college votes .
158694	A candidate with support that is broad but not deep , such as John Anderson in 1980 , can amass several million votes but carry no state at all .
158695	The system favors the Republican and Democratic parties .
158696	Similarly in Britain , a party can win several thousand votes in each constituency yet not come out top of the poll in any ; in consequence , it amasses a large popular vote but no seats in Parliament .
158697	This is almost the position in which the Liberal party has found itself in recent elections ( see Table 5.2 ) .
158698	In 1979 , for example , it won in excess of 4 million votes yet topped the poll in only 11 seats , less than 2% of the total .
158699	This phenomenon is even more marked in the case of the SDP/Liberal Alliance : in 1983 it achieved more than a quarter of the votes cast in the general election , yet won only 3.5% of the seats in Parliament .
158700	The largest party , by contrast , can top the poll in most constituencies with , say , 40% of the poll , the remaining votes split among the other party candidates ( see the example of Leicester South in Table 5.3 ) , thus achieving a majority of seats without receiving an absolute majority of the votes cast .
158701	Indeed , at no election since 1935 has a party obtained more than 50% of the votes cast , yet at only one election since that time has a government been returned without a majority of seats .
158702	In the election of October 1974 , the Labour party obtained a bare majority of seats for fewer than 40% of the votes cast .
158703	Not surprisingly , the Liberal and Social Democratic parties are in the vanguard in arguing for a reform of the electoral system to eliminate such anomalies .
158704	The Conservative and Labour parties , by contrast , retain a preference for the existing system
158705	The other more recent criticisms of the electoral system has derived from the characterization of the existing political system as an adversary one .
158706	The " adversary politics " thesis was developed following the 1974 elections by a number of academics , led by S. E. Finer .
158707	The essence of their argument was that the electoral system encouraged a polarized contest between two parties for the winner-take-all spoils of a general election .
158708	One party would be returned to office with an overall majority and implement its manifesto program , a program neither known nor supported by most electors and one drawn up on the basis more of party dogma than of a dispassionate and well-informed analysis of Britain 's problems .
158709	The other party would then win at a subsequent election , enter office and largely undo the work of its predecessor , implementing instead its own program .
158710	Given that the two parties were perceived as representing different poles of the political spectrum , government policy would lurch from being right of the political center under one adminstration to being left of center under another .
158711	The results , in short , were unrepresentative governments — pursuing policies more politically extreme than those favored by the more centrist electorate — and policy discontinuity .
158712	Policy discontinuity frustrated industrialists and investors who wished to engage in forward planning : they could not anticipate stability in government programs .
158713	Adversary politics and changes in government may make for " exciting politics , " but they produce " low-credibility Government strategies , whichever party is in power . "
158714	Indeed , the conditions created by the electoral system were seen as being the heart of Britain 's current problems .
158715	In order to win an election , a party would make extravagant promises , doing so in order to outbid the other party .
158716	In office , it would find it could no longer raise the resources to meet those promises .
158717	It therefore had to change tack , further adding to confusion in governmental policy-making .
158718	However , it also had to act in a way that would not jeopardize its chance of winning the next election .
158719	Hence it was reluctant to take the unpopular measures deemed by some to be necessary to tackle Britain 's long-term problems .
158720	The result , in short , was a vicious circle .
158721	The solution , or at least a partial one , to the problem was perceived by these critics as the introduction of a new electoral system , one that introduced a method of proportional representation .
158722	Proportional representation ( PR ) , it was argued , would be fairer than the existing electoral system , ensuring that a party received the share of parliamentary seats equivalent to its national vote .
158723	Furthermore , giving existing voting behaviour , it would deprive any one party of an overall majority of seats .
158724	To form a government with an overall parliamentary majority would thus necessitate a coalition .
158725	this would likely involve one of the main parties having " to co-operate with a party or parties taking a more central stance . "
158726	hence leading to greater moderation in policy .
158727	Given that such a coalition would enjoy the support of more than 50% of electors and that the turnover of seats under PR is small ( Professor Finer estimated that a swing of 1% would result in the loss of only six seats ) , it would most likely remain in office for the foreseeable future and hence be in a position to ensure a degree of policy continuity .
158728	The overall effect of PR would thus be to put an end to the worst features of adversary politics and its unfortunate consequences .
158729	Of the systems of proportional representation , the one favored by the Liberal Party and the Electoral Reform Society is the single transferable vote ( STV ) system .
158730	It is the method of election currently employed in the Republic of Ireland , in Tasmania , and in Malta and for elections to the Australian Senate .
158731	Under STV there are multimember constituencies , with each elector able to indicate a preference on the ballot paper , putting the number 1 beside the name of the candidate most preferred , number 2 against the name of the elector 's second choice , and so on .
158732	A quota is established by the formula of dividing the number of valid ballots cast by the number of seats , plus one ; to the resulting figure , one is added .
158733	Thus in a five-member constituency in which 120,000 ballots are cast , the formula would be Hence the quota ( the number of ballots required to elect one member ) would be 20,001 .
158734	Any candidate receiving this number of votes is declared elected .
158735	The second preferences of any of the candidate 's surplus votes , plus those of the candidate at the bottom of the poll , are then redistributed , and so on until the necessary number of candidates reach the quota .
158736	The other main system that has been advocated is the additional member system , similar to that employed in West Germany .
158737	Under this system single-member constituencies would be retained with the first-past-the-post method of election retained in each — in other words , the same as at present .
158738	However , there would be additional seats allocated to parties on a regional basis , a minimum of 5% of the vote in any area of allocation being necessary to obtain any additional seats .
158739	Additional seats would go proportionately to the parties on the basis of the proportion of votes received in the region .
158740	Under a scheme proposed by the Hansard Society for Parliamentary Government , there would be 480 single-member constituencies and 160 seats allocated on a regional basis .
158741	Proponents of this system and of STV argue that the effect would be a representative House of Commons , the proportion of seats going to parties being the same as the proportion of the votes won in the election .
158742	Support for a new electoral system has developed since the mid-1970s , encompassing academics and politicians .
158743	The Conservative and Labour par ties have witnessed the creation of bodies within their own ranks favoring such reform .
158744	The Liberal party has an important ally in its partner , the Social Democratic party : both are strongly committed to electoral reform .
158745	Various attempts were made in the 1974-1979 Parliament to introduce PR throughout the United Kingdom for elections to the European Parliament and for elections to the proposed assemblies in Scotland and Wales .
158746	The attempts failed , but they helped keep the issue of electoral reform on the agenda of political debate .
158747	The outcome of the 1983 election added a further spur to the reform movement .
158748	Despite this pressure for reform , the existing system retains its supporters .
158749	A majority of both the Conservative and Labour parliamentary parties prefer the first-past-the-post method of election .
158750	One keen defender is the present prime minister , Mrs. Thatcher .
158751	The arguments deployed against the reformers ' case are varied .
158752	The essential line of argument is that a reformed electoral system could constitute a greater threat to the maintenance of political authority than any defects of the existing system .
158753	The STV system , it is argued , could threaten the essential link between an elector and his MP given that it would necessitate in rural areas constituencies of massive size .
158754	Given the reformers ' argument that PR would enhance the likelihood of coalition government , consent could be undermined if government was to result from post-election bargaining between parties ; by a small center party holding the balance of power and hence wielding undue influence over government policy ; and by the alienation of voters who support a party excluded on a long-term basis from becoming a partner in coalition .
158755	Such rebuttals are based on accepting the assumptions made by PR advocates about the likely consequences of electoral reform .
158756	Some observers have drawn attention to the fact that such assumptions themselves rest on flimsy foundations .
158757	The reformers argue their case on the assumption that voting behaviour experienced under the current mode of election would most likely continue under a new mode : this is , as Geoffrey Alderman has pointed out , a most unlikely hypothesis .
158758	Arguments that PR works well in countries such as West Germany are countered by pointing to the experience of italy , where turnover in governments is rapid and a significant fraction of the population vote for a party that is consistently excluded from government .
158759	Given the different political cultures that exist , seeking to anticipate what would happen in Britain on the basis of experience abroad is an undertaking of limited usefulness .
158760	The adversary politics thesis developed by the reformers has also been variously challenged .
158761	There are two mutually exclusive arguments deployed against it .
158762	One line of argument accepts the notion of an adversary relationship between the parties but considers this a beneficial rather than a harmful process .
158763	If offers a clear choice to the electorate and it results in one party with a mandate from the people getting on with the job of governing .
158764	If the electorate disapproves of the policies or their outcomes , it has the opportunity to replace the government at the next election .
158765	There may be some discontinuity in policy occasioned by governments of different political persuasions pursuing different paths , but that is the price — an acceptable price — one has to pay for the advantages offered by the existing system .
158766	Proportional representation , it is feared , would facilitate a blurring of the choice before the electorate and prevent a party being returned with a mandate clearly approved by the people .
158767	Such a line of argument is pursued especially by the two largest parties .
158768	It is in their own interest to do so : each wants to pursue its own policies , which it believed to be in the best interests of the country , without having those policies tempered or abandoned because of the need to enter into alliance with another party .
158769	For a brief period of one year , 1977-1978 , the Labour government of James Callaghan entered into a Pact with the Liberal parliamentary party : in return for voting support in the House of Commons ( necessary to maintain its majority ) , the government modified certain policies of its own and introduced certain measures favored by the Liberals .
158770	The experience was not one much enjoyed by the Labour party , certain sections of which were extremely hostile to the arrangement .
158771	Both the Conservative and Labour parties appeared to draw the conclusion that it was an experience to be avoided , not one to be encouraged .
158772	The other argument deployed against the adversary politics thesis calls into doubt the relevance of the notion itself .
158773	The rhetoric of adversary politics , it is argued , hides a more consensual substance .
158774	In terms of government legislation , empirical research has indicated that a consensual model is indeed more applicable .
158775	In this view , parties are seen as being not quite as central to formulation of public money as both reformers and the politicians themselves believe .
158776	The external demands on government are such that it can often act only as arbiter between competing demands and respond , under guidance from civil servants , to international events and trends over which it has no direct influence .
158777	Whichever party is in power makes some but not a great deal of difference .
158778	Elections may help produce the personnel at the apex of government but they tell us little about likely public policy .
158779	The electoral system , in summary , has again become a subject of politi-cal debate .
158780	In terms of the political system , it can be said to provide the means by which a government is chosen but , despite the results of the 1983 general election , the extent to which it will continue to be capable of providing a government ( at least in the way it has previously done ) remains under question .
158781	It operates on the principle of " one person , one vote , " but there is now some dispute as to its legitimacy and that of the government it produces on the grounds that the principle of " one person , one vote , one value " has not been fully realized .
158782	And there is debate and notable disagreement about the consequences that elections not only do have but should have for public policy .
158783	The debate is very much a current one .
158784	It revolves around arguments for and against a reform of the electoral system .
158785	Whether Britain will witness electoral reform in the next decade or so rests on the outcome of that debate .
158786	The 1983 general election result fueled rather than ended the controversy .
158787	Deixis and the poetic persona
158788	Keith Green Sheffield City Polytechnic , UK
158789	Abstract
158790	This article examines the function of deixis in a specific literary genre , the lyric poem .
158791	In the opening sections , an attempt to define deixis is made and a methodology for analysis for texts in general is proposed .
158792	Deixis is seen as a fundamental element of human discourse , and a particular discoursal site is isolated where it can be seen operating in a particular way .
158793	Theoretical considerations , such as the relation of deixis to semantics and pragmatics , and the various types of deictic meaning , are discussed , and a cline of deictic activity , a point on which any text must function , is described .
158794	A possible taxonomy of deictic elements and terms follows , which modifies and builds on previous attempts by linguists such as Levinson ( 1983 ) .
158795	The relation between these elements and terms , and the lyric poem , is then discussed .
158796	The final part of the article is an analysis of two poems , Henry Vaughan 's " The retreate " and Wordsworth 's " Nutting " .
158797	The deixis occurring in the poems is examined in the light of the theories previously discussed .
158798	Keywords : anaphora ; context ; deixis ; distal ; homophora ; indexical ; pragmatic ; proximal ; symbolic ; utterance
158799	1 Introduction and aims
158800	In this article I intend to shed some light on the behaviour of a specific linguistic phenomenon , deixis , in a specific kind of discourse , the lyric poem .
158801	My main aims are to demonstrate a possible methodology for such analysis , and to present a coherent theory of deixis .
158802	I shall discuss some theoretical issues , such as the relation of deixis to semantics and pragmatics ; the relationship between deixis which occurs in literary and non-literary texts ; and the link deixis might be said to make between context-dependency and truth-conditional semantics .
158803	Part of my thesis rests upon the belief that if deixis operates in a different way in lyric poetry from the way it does in non-literary discourse , it does so in degree , not in kind .
158804	There are no special deictic terms or elements to be found in lyric poetry .
158805	Deixis is a fundamental element of human discourse ( as Lyons 1977 notes , not all languages have tense , but they do have deixis ) , and I intend to investigate its behaviour in one particular kind of text .
158806	My account of deixis is such that the methodology could be applied to other kinds of discourse , both literary and non-literary .
158807	I am able to treat the deixis of literary and non-literary texts in the same way partly through my account of context ( see Section 3 ) .
158808	2 What is deixis ?
158809	Deixis is the encoding in an utterance of the spatio-temporal context and subjective experience of the encoder .
158810	It is primarily linked with the speech or discourse event .
158811	It is the phenomenon whereby the tripartite relationship between the language system , the encoder 's subjectivity and various contextual factors is foregrounded grammatically or lexically .
158812	For example , in Levinson 's ( 1983 ) well-known deictic utterance , Meet me here a week from now with a stick about this big , there are certain words , such as me , here , now and this , which have part of their meaning which is context-sensitive .
158813	They also function from the perspective of the encoder or utterer and are thus significantly grammaticalised in the language .
158814	The inclusion of the notion of subjectivity in the above definition might seem surprising here , but I am not equating deixis with a concept that stands in rough opposition to objectivity .
158815	As Lyons ( 1982 ) notes , the word subjectivity in English has some pejorative connotations ; but I see it simply as the way in which language makes provision for the expression of attitude and belief .
158816	Russell ( 1940 ) called deictics ( or indexicals ) 1 egocentric particulars , and this is because there is a centre of orientation in deixis which is invariably egocentric .
158817	The zero-point , or origo , to use Bühler 's ( 1934 ) terminology , is set by the encoder in relation to the spatio-temporal nature of the utterance .
158818	Any utterance relates both to the speaker 's " centre " and to the surrounding cognitive environment .
158819	2.1 Deixis and use
158820	One of the most important aspects of deixis is that it is invariably distinguished by its use .
158821	In order to clarify this , I should like to begin by making a distinction between deictic terms and deictic elements .
158822	A deictic term is part of a grammatically closed set which includes the personal and demonstrative pronouns , certain adverbials , definite referring expressions and the vocative particle ( a fuller taxonomy is presented in Section 5 ) .
158823	A deictic element is not a term as such , but some part of the utterance which might be said to be deictic .
158824	In other words , there is a syntactic or semantic element which might function deictically .
158825	For instance , verbs are not normally deictic in themselves , except for those noted by Fillmore ( 1971 ) , notably come and go , which encode movement towards and from the origo .
158826	Tense generally is a deictic element , however .
158827	The verb in a sentence such as The sun shines brightly is not deictic in the sense that the verb to come is , but is nevertheless deictic because it is part of a system which relates specific entities to reference points .
158828	But because it is deictic it is context-sensitive , and there are a number of ways of using the utterance The sun shines brightly and a number of contexts in which it might occur .
158829	There is no necessary link between tense and time ; it is likely in this instance that the use of the present tense is not restricted to a particular time ( which is the time of the utterance ) but refers rather to a " general " present .
158830	The progressive form would be a more likely occurrence if an immediate moment is being referred to .
158831	If I say one morning while looking out of my window , The sky is blue , then I am using this sentence deictically .
158832	If , however , I mean The sky is blue as a general statement — a proposition about a general state of affairs — then I do not use it deictically ( I use it generically ) .
158833	Tense , therefore , can be deictic inasmuch as it can be used to encode specific temporal relations with respect to the encoder .
158834	We can notice , too , that the deictic aspect of the definite referring expression the sun ( the definite article being a deictic term ) is contextually ambiguous — I could use it homophorically ( the sun , generally ) or deictically ( the sun at a particular time and place ) .
158835	I must repeat , then , that deixis is distinguished by its use .
158836	Deixis has a powerful pragmatic base as most deictic elements and terms can be used non-deictically .
158837	Pronouns , for instance , can be used anaphorically and demonstratives can be used in a non-demonstrative way , for example the expressions here and there and this and that .
158838	Despite being a closed set of terms linked with a number of functioning elements , deixis lacks a taxonomy of occurrences because of its pragmatic base .
158839	Context and use are vital to our understanding of deixis , and this is why the investigation of its behaviour in a particular discourse is relevant .
158840	3 The distinction between semantics and pragmatics
158841	So far I have described a closed set of elements and terms which relate specific entities to a reference point — a set which is also determined by use and context .
158842	A central question noted by Levinson ( 1983 ) is whether the study of deixis belongs to the domain of pragmatics or semantics .
158843	This is a rather complex issue , but clearly there are elements of language , notably deictics , which are not accessible to a purely truth-conditional semantics .
158844	A substantial chapter on deixis occurs in Levinson 's Pragmatics ( 1983 ) , and still the most thorough analysis occurs in Lyons ' Semantics : Volume 2 ( 1977 ) .
158845	It is not possible to state the truth conditions of sentences with certain deictic elements and terms without reference to the deictic function in context .
158846	If semantics is modified to take account of deixis , it becomes a context-conditional semantics , and the boundary between semantics and pragmatics becomes very blurred .
158847	Attempts by Barwise and Perry ( 1983 ) in their formulation of a situation semantics show promising moves to contextualise semantic theory .
158848	The core of such analysis is that sentences with deictic elements and terms encode propositions only by virtue of the specific contexts in which they occur .
158849	At this point the problem of context itself comes to the fore .
158850	4 The problem of context
158851	It is possible to see context functioning in three ways .
158852	By context I mean something wider than the co-text of any utterance : In ( 1 ) the implication is that the situation of utterance , which is extralinguistic , determines the potential meaning .
158853	Thus in my earlier example The sky is blue , only knowledge of the situation of the utterance will enable the decoder to interpret it as either deictic or generic .
158854	Point ( 3 ) states that certain linguistic elements encode contextual features .
158855	These , I suggest , are deictic elements and terms .
158856	I propose to reject ( 1 ) and fuse ( 2 ) and ( 3 ) .
158857	I reject ( 1 ) because this can not take account of the vast range of human communication which does not take place within the canonical situation of utterance — i.e. face-to-face .
158858	For ( 3 ) we might have : where the sentence S encodes a function f of possible contexts ( c ) to transform it into an utterance u .
158859	Again , sentences only express propositions by virtue of specific contexts and a specific encoder within a deictic field .
158860	There is a reciprocity between linguistic elements and possible contexts , and those elements which enable this reciprocal relationship to proceed are deictic .
158861	4.1 Indexical and symbolic
158862	Just as the line between semantics and pragmatics is fuzzy , so is that between the indexical and symbolic meanings of deictic terms .
158863	The symbolic meaning of a deictic term is its meaning as it functions within the linguistic system .
158864	Thus I might be glossed as " the person writing this sentence " ; you as " the addressee/participant in the discourse " , and so on .
158865	I wish to be relatively uncontroversial about these definitions , although I realise the great philosophical problems involved in any description of I for instance.3 The indexical meaning is that which exists when we have ascribed referents to those discourse elements suggested by the symbolic meaning of a term .
158866	A very important point is that the symbolic meaning in part determines the range of indexical possibilities , thus accommodating my view of context outlined above .
158867	If I point to a particular item in a room and say " that " , we can say that the demonstrative encodes distance from the origo , whether actual or mental , and the coincidence of indexical and symbolic meaning is only possible when we know what object is being pointed to .
158868	In the discourse of the lyric poem it is unlikely that we can ascribe indexical meaning to symbolic elements of deictic terms .
158869	I suggest , however , that the indexical meaning is partly determined by the manifestation of symbolic meaning within certain contexts .
158870	Of course there are many discourses existing where we lack clear referents for indexical meanings .
158871	Within literary discourses , it seems that lyric poetry is the genre least likely to assist us .
158872	In prose fiction , a more dialogic genre , various shifts of deictic centre occur ( that is , from character to character ) and we are more likely to see deictic terms verified intra-textually — for example , pronominal reference given a full cataphoric form .
158873	I want to try to clear away the distinction between two kinds of text , the " literary " ( or poetic ) and the " non- literary " , as regards the function of context .
158874	Deixis is the most context-specific linguistic element , and it exists and occurs in the most situation-free as well as the most situation-bound utterances .
158875	Certain generic atomic propositions may have minimal deictic features , but most utterances contain them .
158876	Following Sperber and Wilson ( 1986 ) , context can be seen as the set of possibilities which exist in the universe of discourse and situation of utterance for the interpretation of that utterance .
158877	If we reject the idea that context is situation ( although I have accommodated the concept of situation in my definition of context ) we can treat deixis in poetry not as a kind of " pseudo-deixis ' , as some critics such as Culler ( 1974 ) have suggested , but simply as deixis framed by a particular genre .
158878	Context then becomes paradoxically more metacontextual ( as in the work of Sperber and Wilson 1986 ) and encoded ( " pointed to " ) by certain deictic elements .
158879	5 The discourse of lyric poetry
158880	I have so far discussed deixis per se and the functions of context .
158881	I must now attempt to define the discourse in which the deixis is to be found , for this is the pragmatic frame governing sense-making operations .
158882	There is a danger of treating a historical phenomenon ( the lyric poem ) as sui generis , and that may restrict any absolute definition of the kind of text I shall be examining .
158883	I make certain assumptions about the lyric poem , however : The lyric poem , then , is a particular kind of universe of discourse .
158884	The environment of the lyric poem must , in consequence , be matched up with the features we note in the analysis .
158885	6 Deictic categories
158886	The so-called " traditional " categories of deixis are time , place , person , social and discourse .
158887	( see Levinson 1983 ) .
158888	I propose a new classification as follows : These categories have the advantage of including the more traditional elements while highlighting the egocentric nature of deixis ( the origo ) and giving prominence to the major deictic category , reference .
158889	Both elements and terms are also accommodated in this classification .
158890	I shall take these categories one at a time , and simply state what deictic terms or elements occur in them ; but it must always be remembered that every item depends on its use within certain contexts and under certain conditions .
158891	As I have said , there can be no taxonomy of use .
158892	My explanations must necessarily be brief at this stage .
158893	7 The cline of deictic activity
158894	The final part of the procedure before analysis can begin is to see these categories of deixis within a particular discourse , operating at a point along a cline of activity .
158895	Here I shall draw on the work of Rauh ( 1983 ) .
158896	Rauh sees deixis as functioning between the poles of extralinguistic deixis and non-egocentric deixis .
158897	Extralinguistic deixis is that which is accompanied by phenomena such as gestures ( this has led Lyons to call the phenomenon , rather oddly " deixis at its purest " ) .
158898	Often the encoder is visible ( being within the canonical situation of utterance ) and immediately audible and there takes place a kind of indexical reciprocity whereby the specific quality of a deictic expression is only given by the assignment of the extralinguistic referent .
158899	The first shift away from this kind of deixis is where the centre of orientation ( origo ) but not the related objects are part of the canonical situation .
158900	This according to Bühler ( 1934 ) , is where other " deictic aids ' replace " the finger " .
158901	Demonstratives and the definite article are terms whose mobilisation and use would be strongly linked to this kind of deixis .
158902	The second shift occurs when both the centre of orientation and the related objects are excluded from the canonical situation .
158903	Here the relevant situational context is imagined .
158904	This is a type which occurs throughout written discourse .
158905	The decoder has to create a cognitive space in which the deictic elements and terms can be realised indexically .
158906	Thus we can see that the discourse of lyric poetry is by no means unusual in its mobilisation of deixis .
158907	Rauh finally notes a kind of deixis which is not central to my analysis , but which reflects the problems involved in trying to isolate deictic function .
158908	He sees the possibility of a non-egocentric deixis operating .
158909	This has to do with the relational quality of deixis .
158910	Deictic relations are egocentric , but it is possible to annul this relation by expressing a relatum different from the egocentric one .
158911	Rauh 's example is the prepositional phrase above the car , where the NP the car removes the egocentric element .
158912	This may be true , but the car is itself deictically determined .
158913	I consider prepositions in prepositional phrases to be non-deictic , as they relate to an internal system in the way that , say , aspect relates to tense .
158914	It is possible , however , that some residue of deictic activity exists within such expressions .
158915	The expression above the car assumes a shared spatial relatum .
158916	8 An analysis of Henry Vaughan 's " The retreate "
158917	So far I have described deixis as a closed set of items functioning within certain contexts , and seen it functioning along a cline of possible operations .
158918	I have isolated a specific discoursal site where deixis can be discerned operating .
158919	I want now to look at " The retreate " by Henry Vaughan and to examine a small number of its elements and terms in relation to the methodology already described .
158920	I have chosen Vaughan because there has already been some analysis of deixis in his poetry — notably by Roger Sell in his article " The unstable discourse of Henry Vaughan " ( 1987 ) .
158921	Vaughan is an interesting poet with regard to his use of deixis .
158922	His idiosyncratic usage is at once fascinating for analysis and a warning against making unwary generalisations about lyric poetry .
158923	The opening line features a definite referring expression with distal demonstrative those .
158924	( Demonstratives are described in terms of relative proximity to the encoder : this is proximal , that is distal .
158925	Plural forms do not differ in deictic meaning . )
158926	Most of the reference in the poem is made through the use of demonstratives , rather than the definite article .
158927	The initial clause , " Happy those early days ! " , plunges us into the middle of a discourse , as much lyric poetry does .
158928	There is some syntactic ambiguity in the opening lines — we can read " when I/Shin " d " as a separate clause or as a post-modifier to " those early dayes ' .
158929	Because of exclamation mark , and despite the lower case " w " , I read the first clause as complete , thus giving it fuller deictic impact .
158930	Information after " those early dayes ' must lessen the deictic force of the utterance because it shifts our attention not to some presupposed referent seemingly outside the discourse ( what " early dayes ' ? ) but to something qualified within the text itself .
158931	I also assume that there is an ellipted main verb , the past tense copula were , but this is not immediately apparent on a first reading .
158932	" Early " is deictic here , but only inasmuch as it sets up an opposition to a notional " late " .
158933	" Those early dayes ' refers to a latent discourse referent .
158934	A demonstrative is used to refer to a temporal aspect .
158935	At this stage we do not know whether the " dayes ' are general ( which would imply that the missing verb is are ) or particular ; but we get a clearer picture when we come to the second clause " when I / Shin " d " .
158936	'shin " d " encodes past activity , but only in relation to the utterance 's internal system of time referencing which has already been set up and controlled by the deictic references of earlier elements .
158937	This seems to happen retrospectively , for it is the simple past tense of 'shin " d " which enables us to read the deixis of " those early dayes ' in a particular way , in direct relation to 'shin " d " .
158938	The opening of a poem is obviously important because there is no previous discourse through which to interpret it except for the title , but this is not precise enough to enable us to assign the proper indexical meaning to the deictic elements and terms .
158939	But what are these " early dayes ' and who is the " I " of the utterance ?
158940	In discourse theory , if the conditions specified by any of the co-ordinates ( speaker , place , audience , time , etc. ) are altered , the contexts are altered .
158941	So how does the concept of context function here in relation to the deictic elements and terms which are clearly organising the poem 's reference structure ?
158942	The deictic elements and terms are constantly helping us to sort from possible contexts , helping us to move from symbolic meaning to some kind of reconstructed indexical meaning .
158943	A powerful deictic centre is being mobilised without an immediate situation .
158944	The poem can be seen to embody a set of expectations or possible worlds .
158945	It will further engage in the set of those possible worlds and alter the context depending on the interaction of the conditions which specify the action of the discourse co-ordinates .
158946	In " The retreate " , deixis is often qualified by further deixis , and these elements are often " personal " .
158947	When , later in the poem , reference is made to cultural and spatio-temporal elements , such qualification is missing .
158948	All the while , the deixis works to orientate our focus .
158949	In the early part of the poem there is ambiguity in the functioning of deictic expressions : an initial deictic term such as " those early dayes ' is supplemented with further deictic information " when I / Shin " d . "
158950	This recurs in the expression " this place / Appointed for my second race " ( lines 3 – 4 ) .
158951	Thus Vaughan is assuming a certain amount of shared knowledge on the part of the reader ; but because we can not , naturally , see things from the perspective of his origo , he must also assist the reader in the assignment of indexical or deictic meanings .
158952	In the latter part of the poem , however , referring expressions , though still mobilising the demonstrative , are not qualified with further deictic terms .
158953	They tend to suggest homophoric or anaphoric reference , although their function is not straightforward .
158954	" That ancient track " ( line 22 ) and " that plaine " ( line 23 ) are references to the earlier " journey " .
158955	Although they are followed by two relative clauses ( lines 24 and 25 ) , they are not as closely linked syntactically as the earlier examples cited above .
158956	The subsequent information is in fact redundant with respect to deictic function .
158957	The expression " That shady City of Palme trees ' is more conventionally homophoric ; but nevertheless it is metaphorically " displaced " and encoded through the use of a distal demonstrative .
158958	The use of such demonstratives always implies a dual processing effort on the part of the addressee .
158959	On the one hand , the demonstrative suggests that the element is known to us — that it is somewhere in the universe of discourse .
158960	On the other hand , the demonstrative does not merely give crude emphasis to a referent ; it suggests that although the element is " known " some extra processing effort must take place in order for it to be accessed .
158961	The final demonstrative uses — " this dust " and " that state ( I came ) " — reiterate the opposition between the proximal and distal perspectives of the speaker .
158962	" This ' is always something that , although proximal , the speaker of the poem wishes to move away from .
158963	This backward movement in both time and space is brought to a climax in the final line .
158964	Distal elements are huddled into a final phrase which includes the distal demonstrative " this ' , the past tense verb " came " , and " return " , which is semantically opposed to " came " .
158965	As the poem progresses , we might assume that contextual or latent discourse referents are less likely to be introduced , for we read and interpret in the light of what has gone before — of previous elements in the utterance .
158966	This is partly evident in my initial example of the " backward-looking " function of the deictic element 'shin " d " ( line 2 ) , but lyric poetry is also a genre where such referents are continually introduced .
158967	I have stressed that we construct a context from the deixis of the text ( a context being the set of possibilities which exist in the universe of discourse and situation of utterance for the interpretation of the utterance ) ; but the initial elements of the utterance must be more dense in terms of pragmatic activity .
158968	We can not merely say the poem represents a kind of null context , where context is partly situation of utterance and partly based on previous elements in the discourse .
158969	Deictic expressions , certainly in the first part of the poem , are often qualified in a way so as to present the reader with further information ; but that information often , too , comprises deictic elements or terms .
158970	My first example of this was the opening line .
158971	The following are the occurrences of deictic expressions qualified ( post-modified ) by a deictic element or term Q. The lower-case q represents a referring expression{ REF } embedded in the qualifying element : Three of the above occurrences are in the opening eight lines .
158972	The fourth occurs at lines 23 – 4 .
158973	In the second and fourth examples : indicates a further qualification ( a referring expression ) embedded in the initial element , as in :
158974	8.1 Further comments on the deixis of " The retreate "
158975	Demonstrative reference is clearly an important aspect of the deixis of the poem : it encourages the reader to process the deictic meanings in a specific way .
158976	There are only three occurrences of the definite article : " the black art " ( line 17 ) , " th " Inlightned spirit " ( line 25 ) and " the urn " ( line 31 ) .
158977	These uses are non-deictic .
158978	The article is unmarked as regards spatio-temporal relations ; so the function of deictic reference is to set up a continual spatial , temporal and subjective opposition between proximal and distal relations .
158979	Temporal distance is encoded by the past tense , reflecting content time , which is separate from coding time .
158980	In the latter part of the poem a more general " present " is implied , and this second content time is closer to the coding time .
158981	9 Relevance , deixis and the poetic voice
158982	So far I have been working " backwards ' from the specific deictic terms and elements of the poem to contextual possibilities and other pragmatic considerations .
158983	If we go one further stage in this direction we reach the metacontextual concept of relevance .
158984	Relevance can be seen as a concept governing interpretation ( see Sperber and Wilson 1986 ) .
158985	There is a context of relevance through which deixis is received , and we need to know to what extent analogy with other texts is pertinent .
158986	It should be possible to construct a pragmatic frame by which the deixis of lyric poetry in its various manifestations can be viewed .
158987	What kind of speaker is presupposed to be uttering " Happy those early dayes ! " ?
158988	The " poetic voice " or " persona " is a recognisable post-Renaissance phenomenon .
158989	As readers we expect such a persona to describe a scene , dramatise some situation , and express feelings .
158990	There is frequently a " personal " element in poetry , but this element is couched within a highly formalised and conventional genre .
158991	This must affect and delimit the range of contextual possibilities and the frame of relevance .
158992	9.1 " Nutting "
158993	As a final example I return to Wordsworth 's poem " Nutting " .
158994	The poem is too long to quote in its entirety here , but the opening lines should provide a suitable contrast with " The retreate " : Here , a particular incident in the past is being recalled ; so the bulk of the poem has a content time which is separate from the coding time .
158995	The present tense and modality of " seems " in the opening line combine to compound the present and the past , the content time and the coding time .
158996	As in " The retreate " , a distal demonstrative construction is used to point to time past ; and this also has a qualifying element ( the phrase " which can not die " ) .
158997	Wordsworth sets up a close relationship between the possessive pronouns " our " and " my " .
158998	We do not know whose cottage door is " ours ' , but the pronoun immediately suggests both a shared experience and a familiar discourse .
158999	The two participants in the situation are finally linked through the possessive NP " my frugal Dame " .
159000	This ease of discourse and assumption of shared experience is encoded for the reader , who does not have to work hard in processing the referent of the definite description " the distant woods ' .
159001	Subsequent references to Wordsworth 's surroundings are made with the definite article ( " the woods ' , " the pathless rocks ' ) .
159002	The " I " figure assumes an intimate relationship with his implied audience .
159003	However , as the poet reaches the scene of virgin beauty , the definite article momentarily ceases its " relaxed " function and pushes the reader to more processing effort .
159004	This is realised in the referring expression " the hazels ' .
159005	By excluding a verb construction from the exclamation " A virgin scene ! "
159006	Wordsworth replicates syntactically the synchronicity of coding time and content time .
159007	The omission of the verb gives an immediacy which would be missing from a construction such as It is a virgin scene ( where the present tense is a direct attempt to make a coding time and content time the same ) .
159008	10 Conclusion
159009	I have stressed that I am taking a particular linguistic phenomenon , deixis , and examining its occurrences and behaviour in a specific genre .
159010	This leaves the possibility open of finding new insights into deixis per se as well as into its behaviour within a particular discourse .
159011	Because of this , I have not said that the analysis of deixis in the poetic text will necessarily be a useful stylistic procedure — giving greater insight into individual poems or poets .
159012	Most of the analysis of literary deixis has proceeded by using deixis as a kind of stylistic lever .
159013	I do not reject this out of hand ; but it is not my primary purpose here ; rather , it is to suggest a methodology which might enable us to gain insights into the functioning of the lyric poem per se , while always being mindful of the dangers of seeking generic overviews of historical phenomena .
159014	In " The retreate " , a complex linguistic and pragmatic site is displayed , and it is deixis which largely holds this together , enabling frames of context to be created , and leading the reader around and into the work .
159015	It is the same — and we should not be surprised at this — in ordinary discourse .
159016	We need to remember two fundamental points : language seems to be designed primarily for face-to-face interaction ( that is , the canonical situation of utterance ) ; and it is a capability of humans that they can mobilise discourse beyond this canonical situation and operate language free of contextual boundaries .
159017	It is the interrelationship of these points that enables the analysis of deixis in the genre of the lyric poem to proceed .
