159124	Why Keiran Goss left the law for the guitar
159125	Star of the County Down
159126	‘ At the end of the day , it is as a songwriter that I would most like to be remembered ’
159127	A QUALIFIED solicitor who has practised law is currently one of the biggest draws on the Irish music scene .
159128	The only case Kieran Goss has ever handled is the one which contains the tool of his chosen trade — the guitar .
159129	For the talented Co .
159130	Down man with the droll line in laid back stage patter is now established as a leading figure in the ever swelling ranks of Irish singer/songwriters .
159131	He has forged a highly successful partnership with the Dublin singer Frances Black — sister of the famous Mary — and his songs are being ‘ covered ’ by other performers as far away as Japan .
159132	So , at the age of 31 , instead of standing in court in a pinstripe making pleas in mitigation for the Saturday night disorderly drunks , he is on the road to fame , suitcase and guitar in hand .
159133	How did it all begin ?
159134	Like his close musical friends , the Sands Family , Kieran was born in the townland of Mayobridge near Newry .
159135	Shows
159136	He was one of a family of 15 raised by Newry garage owner Billy Goss and his wife Bridie , and since two of his older brothers played the guitar it was not long before young Kieran was picking out those three main chords himself .
159137	By the time he went to Abbey CBS in Newry he was already regaling school shows and family parties with the songs of 1970 's singer-strummers like Ralph McTell and Tom Paxton .
159138	In 1980 he arrived at Queen 's University to study law and at the end of his first year flew out to the USA to find summer jobs as labourer .
159139	‘ But I only stuck that for a couple of weeks , ’ he says , ‘ for I was playing guitar at a party one night in Cleveland , Ohio , and he said there were easier ways of making money out there than working the building sites .
159140	‘ So he got me a few gigs round the Irish pubs , and I had to learn off some traditional Irish ballads quickly for the sort of audiences you got there certainly did n't want to hear me singing songs by James Taylor or Simon and Garfunkel .
159141	Support
159142	‘ It was just a bit of crack , but curiously enough it gave me my first taste of playing in public , something I had not yet done back home . ’
159143	Returning to Queen 's , he asked for , and got , a few gigs in the students ' union — ‘ my very first one was as support act to Blackthorn ’ — and soon he was working once or twice a week round the local pubs and folk clubs .
159144	On that demanding circuit , he served his time to the troubadour 's trade , learning how to handle an audience , and going home to his law books .
159145	At the end of 1985 he qualified as a solicitor ( ‘ this was the safety net and I had written my thesis on the copyright laws , which has been very useful to me ’ ) , but he had already decided to take the plunge as a full time professional musician .
159146	For the next four years or so he lived the nomadic life of the minstrel , heading off in his car round the well worn folk circuits of Germany , Italy and Brittany and playing everywhere from cafes to pizza parlours .
159147	Decision
159148	Sounds idyllic — he was young and having fun earning a living at what he liked best .
159149	‘ But by 1989 I was at the crossroads , ’ he says .
159150	‘ Touring on my own was good crack , but I wanted security and it was time to make a serious decision about the future — whether to become a lawyer ( and I had already started applying for jobs ) or to take a more businesslike approach to the music . ’
159151	He opted for the latter and at the end of 1989 he launched his debut album ‘ Brand New Star ’ which sold very well , got a lot of radio play , and , most important of all , it introduced the songs he had been composing and singing at concerts to a wider public .
159152	Mary Black recorded two of them .
159153	As a songwriter , he was now on his way .
159154	His next big career break came about almost by accident .
159155	Frances Black had been touring with the traditional band Arcady but in 1990 was asked to do a few solo gigs in the north .
159156	She needed a backing guitarist and asked Kieran , who she had met once or twice on the road , would he help out .
159157	Chemistry
159158	‘ We hardly knew each other , but I agreed , thinking it would be a short term thing , ’ he said .
159159	‘ But those few gigs we did , with me playing guitar and singing harmonies , went down a bomb and we have been partners ever since .
159160	‘ We have never worked out what the chemistry is , but the audiences liked it and we realised ‘ Hey , we 've got something here ’ and really set to work on it .
159161	‘ Next thing we were playing support on a Mary Black tour and from doing folk club gigs for maybe 100 customers I suddenly found myself doing 20 nights in a row in front of 2,000 people or more . ’
159162	First album
159163	The duo 's first album has Irish sales of 27,000 so far , and is also to be released Japan , of all places , where Kieran 's songs are so popular that two of them have been recorded by a local singer — the lyrics translated into Japanese .
159164	He finds it hard to talk about what that sounds like without laughing .
159165	‘ Our album opened doors for us all over the world , ’ he says , ‘ and another major factor in our success was that one of the songs on it , ‘ Wall Of Tears ’ , was included on the Women 's Heart C.D. which has already sold over 200,000 copies in Ireland alone .
159166	THAT was a really important break for us , and helped to push us a few more rungs up the ladder .
159167	During July we were on the Women 's Heart tour — 28 gigs in 30 nights , packed houses all the way .
159168	I really enjoyed it , but I was glad when it was over for it was very tiring . ’
159169	Kieran has now Rostrevor home to Dublin for six months where he intends , as he puts it , to ‘ lie low ’ for a while , writing songs and preparing for his and Frances 's second album .
159170	‘ Like Frances , who has a family , I 'd like to spend a bit more time at home , ’ he said , ‘ for I have a lot of material on tape and you ca n't write songs when you 're on the road .
159171	‘ At the end of the day , it is as a songwriter that I would most like to be remembered .
159172	If I had to choose between the two , I could live without performing but not without song writing .
159173	It 's what I enjoy most . ’
159174	Safety net
159175	And as for the law ?
159176	It now looks as if that safety net is never going to be needed .
159177	Who was it said ‘ Let other men write my country 's laws , but let me write its songs ’ ?
159178	Whoever it was , he and Kieran Goss would have been kindred souls .

159905	A degree of frustration With the influx of students from the Republic what does the future hold for Ulster 's high-flyers ?
159906	THE 2,000-odd students from the Republic who choose to study in Northern Ireland are a streetwise crowd .
159907	They know all about how to exploit the EC rules in order to obtain a free university education , all fees paid by the Department of Education at Rathgael , outside Bangor , Co Down .
159908	This should not surprise you , for it happens also to be the case that they tend to be an exceptionally well-qualified crowd .
159909	My authority for saying that is the Reader in Sociology at Queen 's University , Robert Cormack , some of whose latest findings have been discussed in this newspaper by Claire McGahan this week .
159910	Mr Cormack is just back from a conference of academics held at Turku , a Finnish port on the Baltic coast east of Helsinki , where he and his colleague , Robert Osborne , gave a paper on the pattern of higher education here .
159911	It is fascinating stuff , both for what it says and what it leaves unsaid .
159912	He makes the point that the arrival of these southerners ( and westerners ) has enabled the University of Ulster to push up the minimum entry grades for some courses .
159913	He says this has been a deliberate policy at UU for some time .
159914	But the obvious question arises : if the bright sparks from the Republic are coming in , who here is being crowded out ?
159915	Because we know that , as Mr Cormack puts it , ‘ not all leavers ’ who go to England and Scotland to take their degrees ‘ are willing leavers ’ .
159916	He points out that the young fellow or girl with only modest ‘ A ’ levels now has little choice : they have to do without — or go across the water .
159917	But if that is so , who are they ?
159918	Here comes the rub .
159919	Mr Cormack does not say .
159920	But I have digested his paper and , well loaded with statistics , have been making one or two inquiries of my own .
159921	His figures show that very many students from working-class homes tend to do less well in their ‘ A ’ levels than the rest .
159922	So any shortage of places will be likely to hit them hardest .
159923	Mr Cormack , however , shows that nearly half the Roman Catholic students entering higher education here ( 43pc ) come from working class homes , but only a little over a quarter of the Protestants do ( 27pc ) .
159924	The conclusion is obvious ; and it is that those local searchers for a place here , who are being crowded out by the southerners , are most likely to be northern Catholics .
159925	Moreover they will tend to be Catholics from just the sort of background the universities here have for years wished to see represented more adequately among students .
159926	One effect of this new competition for places locally is that the students who go to England or Scotland no longer automatically represent the elite they tended to in the 1970s and 1980s .
159927	They still include many high flyers ; but Mr Cormack shows that an appreciable number are now likely to be modest attainers who were crowded out of a place at home .
159928	It is astonishing that more Protestants now study in universities on the mainland — more than a quarter — than are to be found in the University of Ulster ; and if we take the total , only 55pc of Protestant students now study here .
159929	So much for bridge-building and healing local divisions ; and cross-border traffic going south is barely a trickle .
159930	The Protestants are scarcely measurable and the Catholics ( 3pc ) amount to only a quarter of the proportion who went 20 years ago .
159931	With the cost to the student of a higher education tending to rise sharply , fewer in future may be able to afford the luxury of studying across the water .
159932	Mr Cormack foresees school-leavers having to fight even harder for a place here .

160111	The importance of sex education
160112	YOUR correspondent M.R. ( letters 19/8/93 ) is being socially irresponsible by exhorting people to join in her/ his ‘ battle ’ against the Brook Advisory Centre .
160113	The Brook Centre was established in Belfast last year to provide young people with professional advice on all sexual matters .
160114	The Eastern Health &amp; Social Services Board invited Brook here in view of the high incidence of teenage pregnancy in recent years .
160115	Brook 's confidential and non-judgmental approach encourages young people to seek the advice of its highly qualified staff , many of whom are parents themselves and are well acquainted with the problems of adolescence .
160116	Furthermore , Brook has also developed a good working relationship with other voluntary groups and welfare organisations .
160117	Its work has been commended by the Church of Ireland 's Board on Social Responsibility .
160118	Brook does not actively encourage premature sexual activity amongst young people , contrary to what your correspondent suggests .
160119	Brook staff treat each client as an individual and try to help the person to make her or his own decisions and find solutions to particular problems .
160120	If adult members of society fail to encourage sexual responsibility amongst young people , the inevitable outcome will be more unwanted pregnancies and sexually transmitted diseases .
160121	Is this what ‘ M.R. ’ and ‘ Family and Youth Concern ’ really want ?
160122	Perhaps your correspondent could enlighten us as to the best method of preventing unwanted teenage pregnancy , bearing in mind that young people will always form sexual relationships , regardless of the wishes of their parents or anyone else to the contrary .

161828	King-size facelift for historic fortress
161829	Liverpool Castle set to
161830	By Peter McBride Daily Post Correspondent
161831	A RUINED castle is to be rebuilt , 750 years after the first brick of its historic predecessor was laid on the banks of the River Mersey .
161832	The rundown remains of Liverpool Castle a replica of King John 's famous fortress have received a £40,000 cash boost .
161833	Restoration work is scheduled for completion this August when the ‘ new ’ castle will be opened to the public .
161834	The project marks the fulfilment of a dream which was held by one of the city 's legendary entrepreneurs , the late Lord Leverhulme , who started building work on the replica castle in 1912 .
161835	Work was never completed and when the wealthy founder of the Port Sunlight-based Lever Brothers died in 1925 the project remained unfinished .
161836	Since then the replica castle has fallen prey to vandalism and decay .
161837	Situated on the shores of Rivington Reservoir , near Wigan , it is now owned by North West Water .
161838	‘ It represents an important piece of both Liverpool 's and Rivington 's history , ’ said North West Water project manager Phil Luff .
161839	‘ Our first priority is to make the castle structurally sound and safe by securing the stone work and clearing away the rubble .
161840	‘ Then we will rebuild parts of the castle walls and clean off the graffiti .
161841	When the work is completed the public will have access to the castle once more , just as Lord Leverhulme intended 80 years ago . ’
161842	The wealthy Liverpool businessman never intended to rebuild the complete castle , but to recreate the ruined remains as they were in Liverpool before demolition in 1725 .
161843	The original fortress was built during King John 's reign on the present-day site of Castle Street in the city centre .
161844	An estimated 750,000 people are expected to visit Liverpool Castle over the next 12 months .
161845	The renovation forms part of an £80,000 cash package to help boost the numbers of visitors to the Rivington estate .
161846	History in the making Phil Luff surveys the ruins of Liverpool Castle

162085	He sees the union merger , combining massive resources , as a way of attracting more members .
162086	There is no guarantee of that and every possibility that it will be read by both employers and workers as fresh evidence that trade unionism is on the retreat .
162087	Indeed , successful labour organisation could have been more firmly based on unions which each combined many skills within a single industry , rather than of related functions in a wide range of businesses .
162088	The single-industry system was devised by the late Lord Feather when , as a young union official , he was sent to help West Germany reorganisation after World War II .
162089	It became a crucial component of the renowned ‘ economic miracle . ’
162090	With the trickling away of trade union support in this country , it might be too late for such a dramatic change of direction .

162123	First class bargains around
162124	THERE was a time when it was easier to get a stockbroker to buy you lunch than to get him to give a sell recommendation for a share .
162125	It was always , buy , buy , buy .
162126	But the best time to sell a share of course is when everyone else says ‘ buy . ’
162127	Likewise the best time to buy a share is when it is in the doghouse with everyone saying ‘ sell , sell sell . ’
162128	By then of course it is usually too late to sell .
162129	A good example of this is glass giants Pilkington Bros .

162131	But this is a fine company , and with the shares already down by half from their peak last year is this really the time to sell ?

162133	One excellent company where the shares are going cheap at 115p to yield 7pc is BET .

162215	It 's often best to cut your losses early on
162216	THERE is a spiteful tendency among some commentators to compare the fuss recently made about the losses suffered by MPs , judges and others rich enough to have become ‘ Names ’ at Lloyd 's of London , with the problems suffered by those who are unemployed .
162217	‘ How did they get the £250,000 spare wealth needed to qualify in the first place ’ , is one theme I hear from these envy-driven commentators .
162218	With some , like Tony Jacklin or Susan Hampshire , it is perfectly obvious they got it through hard work in their particular calling .
162219	And as a result they have the self-confidence which comes from knowing that if you have made it once , you can make it again .
162220	In that respect they are better off than those who simply inherited the wealth , and now have no real idea how to set about replacing what they have lost .
162221	But the connection between Lloyd 's and the unemployed is much closer than most realise .
162222	All business activities are inherently risky .
162223	Insurance helps to reduce the risk .
162224	So facilitating an increased volume of business insurance cover , such as that provided by Lloyd 's to industry , also increases employment in some cases dramatically .
162225	So the losses suffered by Lloyd 's members indirectly affect us all .
162226	The losses suffered by the ‘ Names ’ at Lloyd 's of London made headline news because some of them are MPs or judges and others are celebrities .
162227	But their losses are in total less than those suffered by the major insurance companies in recent years .
162228	Of course the insurance companies are a good deal less ‘ photogenic ’ and much less of a source of scandal for the gossip columnists .
162229	Another difference is that the companies tend to be faster on their feet .
162230	Once they realised how risk had suddenly escalated they took steps to cut down their ‘ book ’ .
162231	But the individual members of Lloyd 's , mostly people who were dabbling way over their head in a subject about which they knew little , were often persuaded to hang on for things to improve .
162232	That is nearly always a mistake .
162233	As the old Stock Exchange saying goes : ‘ Your first loss is your best loss . ’
162234	Meaning if you hang on hoping for something to turn up , you invariably lose much more .
162235	Usually the wisest thing to do is to cut your losses early on .
162236	The moral to be drawn from this sad episode is : ‘ Do n't put your money into any business you can not understand , and where you are at the mercy of the advice given by others , however trustworthy . ’
162237	Now that the worst seems to be over , the insurance companies have been recapitalising themselves .
162238	Royal Insurance has put out a hefty cash call , asking shareholders to stump up £404m by subscribing for one new share for every three held at 255p .
162239	This has brought the share price back to 290p and they are good value at that level .
162240	although it will be a couple of years yet before the pre-loss level of dividend can be resumed .

162481	A spirit with that touch of glamour
162482	I MAY have had a sheltered upbringing , but to me gin has always been one of the most sophisticated of drinks .
162483	OK , so it used to be called ‘ mother 's ruin' and it 's reputation among the more desperate of women as a way of sorting out an inconvenient pregnancy problem might hardly have endeared it to the more sober .
162484	But somehow , it still has that touch of glamour .
162485	I mean , Americans drink it in martinis , the cocktail set love it ‘ pink ’ and a ‘ G&amp;T ’ is still the preferred drink of the ‘ darling luvvy ’ classes as they bob up and down on their boats moored firmly in the sheltered dock of Liverpool Marina .
162486	Even now , gin with ice cold tonic is the spirit I 'd probably choose to take with me to a desert island just so long as there were plenty of lemon groves to hand on my castaway paradise .
162487	( Then again , at 40% proof , who needs the desert island ? )
162488	But enough of this ; instead … how about a spot of history .
162489	It was a Dutch medical man who is credited with having discovered the first recipe for gin back in the 1600s .
162490	At the time , he was actually hoping to discover the ‘ recipe ’ for a diuretic .
162491	Instead , he came up with a drink that has spread its alcoholic tentacles around the globe .
162492	Juniper berries give it its distinctive flavour ( and its name ) , but each recipe is different .
162493	Favourite
162494	It is used as base for many cocktails , but one of my favourite ways of serving the stuff is with a little help from the hedgerows .
162495	You see , after G&amp;T , sloe gin runs a close second in the castaway stakes .
162496	It 's an amazingly heady concoction made from a good old bottle of Gordon 's , or whatever your favourite make happens to be , sloshed all over the fruits of the sloe ( blackthorn ) bush .
162497	If you fancy trying it yourself around harvest time in September , then gather together a few pounds of the bluey-black sloe berries , prick them all over with a fork , smother them in about 6oz of sugar and top up with a litre of gin .
162498	Over the next two weeks , shake the mixture vigorously every night .
162499	After two weeks , drain off the liquor from the fruit pulp and store the purpley liquid in a screwtop bottle just like the one it came out of in fact .
162500	Leave it to settle for about three months and , come Christmas time , you 'll have one of the most potently delicious concoctions to offer your guests .
162501	Serve it as a delicious liqueur , or topped up with soda or tonic .
162502	Meantime , do n't throw away the sloes that have been steeping in the gin ; use them instead to make a wicked fruit pie with the bitter taste of sloe sweetened by the addition of sugar .

162594	Report by Cathy Gordon
162595	Get Drinkwise !
162596	Down and out … do n't let your life become ruled by the booze know your limit on National Drinkwise Day
162597	MOST people enjoy a tipple or two and a little of what you fancy does n't do you any harm .
162598	But when it comes to alcohol , the emphasis is on the word ‘ little . ’
162599	Today is National Drinkwise Day and health bosses want to force the message home .
162600	But what is safe ?
162601	IF it 's more than a small amount that you 're drinking and also a regular thing then booze may not be quite as harmless as you think .
162602	Too much , or even drinking a little at the wrong time , can cause untold problems .
162603	As well as the almost inevitable hangover and the frequently heard cry ‘ never again , ’ there are more serious consequences .
162604	It can damage your health , your family , your pocket and cause accidents at home , work and on the road .
162605	Excessive drinking can lead to stomach disorders , high blood pressure , depression , sexual difficulties , brain damage , muscle disease , hepatitis , cirrhosis , cancer of the mouth , throat and gullet and vitamin deficiency .
162606	Yet many of us do not really know how much we drink or the medically recommended sensible drinking levels .
162607	Drinkwise 1993 is designed to provide the public with information about alcohol to help them make informed choices about drinking .
162608	The idea is to increase people 's knowledge about the strength of drinks and weekly limits , and the link between drinking and health and fitness .
162609	Up to 14 units for women and up to 21 units for men spread over a week is considered sensible .
162610	One unit is equal to a small glass of wine , or half a pint of ordinary strength beer or lager , one measure of spirit or a small sherry .
162611	It takes your body about an hour , on average , to burn up one unit of alcohol , such as half a pint of beer .
162612	Women are more at risk from the harmful effects of alcohol than men , partly because women have less water in their bodies and the alcohol is more concentrated , and partly because of differences in men and women 's metabolism .
162613	Pregnant women should also be aware of the risks to their babies .
162614	Limit
162615	During pregnancy , alcohol passes from a mother 's bloodstream into her baby through the placenta and can affect the baby 's development , particularly in the early stages of pregnancy .
162616	Pregnant women are advised to limit their drinking to not more than one or two units , once or twice a week , or to cut out alcohol completely .
162617	If you want to change your drinking habits : Choose low-alcohol or non-alcoholic drinks sometimes .
162618	You do n't need a drink to enjoy yourself .
162619	Pace your drinking throughout the evening .
162620	If you drink with other people who regularly buy rounds for each other , it 's easy to end up drinking more than you want .
162621	Try drinking more slowly so you can skip some rounds .
162622	Remember that getting drunk does not make you smart , witty or sexy .
162623	If you have tried to change the way you drink and find it 's just too difficult , do n't give up .
162624	Seek advice from Alcoholics Anonymous on , or the Merseyside , Lancashire and Cheshire Council on Alcoholism on .

162716	Nina Rowlands : ‘ No judge is going to award access away from the mother while the child is still dependent on her . ’
162717	by JANET TANSLEY
162718	WHEN it comes to parenthood more and more women are deciding to go it alone .
162719	FOR some a broken-down relationship means they have no choice : Others simply long for motherhood without the commitment of marriage or a steady relationship .
162720	BUT what happens when the father of the child demands access ?
162721	What are her or his rights ?
162722	IT 'S a dilemma facing more and more women .
162723	They want the baby but not the father .
162724	The reasons are many .
162725	Either the man she is with is not ready for a long-term commitment , he may be violent and she wants to keep him away from the child .
162726	Or she may simply have opted for motherhood without the father which normally completes the traditional ‘ set ’ .
162727	Either way they are a growing group , especially on Merseyside which has many unmarried mums .
162728	Explains Deborah Wintle , an advice worker and counsellor for Liverpool One Parent Families Trust : ‘ There are a number of unmarried mums on Merseyside , many of which we see coming into the Trust .
162729	‘ A lot more women are making the conscious decision not to get married , for whatever reason .
162730	They want the child but not the relationship that goes with it .
162731	‘ The way we see marriage has changed .
162732	People decide not to get married but to go ahead and have children anyway .
162733	For some the relationship has broken down , others have never been with the father .
162734	‘ But today 's more liberal attitudes mean they have the freedom to do that .
162735	It 's far better to be a lone parent than be in an unhappy relationship in which the child suffers too . ’
162736	There can be problems , women may have to work harder to maintain a standard of living , but support normally offered by the father can be obtained , says Deborah , 23 , from family and friends .
162737	Deborah , from Aigburth , herself is a lone parent with a three-year-old little girl , Rebecca , so she knows the problems women face .
162738	One is if the father wants to see the child .
162739	Few women know where they stand .
162740	Says Deborah : ‘ We have had women in this situation and it can be disturbing for them and the child .
162741	‘ The father may have been violent , the woman might be involved with someone else who has taken on the role of father .
162742	‘ When this happens they do n't know what to do or where to go . ’
162743	We asked Liverpool-based Goldsmith Williams ' solicitor Nina Roland , who writes the Echo Woman Extra 's LE Law column where these women stand when it comes to the question of access .
162744	Says Nina : ‘ The immediate answer is that if the couple are not married the mother has all the rights the father has none .
162745	‘ He would have to apply to the courts for any access .
162746	‘ And he certainly ca n't demand to see the child when and where he wants , say every weekend . ’
162747	Yet while the mother has all the rights invested in her , the courts will be amenable .
162748	Says Nina : ‘ Unless there is a valid reason why the man should not see the child , then the courts will probably grant some sort of access .
162749	‘ It may be once a week or once a fortnight perhaps , but it would n't be a lengthy period until the baby is older and more independent .
162750	‘ No judge is going to award access away from the mother while the child is still dependent on her . ’
162751	But it is important that the baby does n't become a tug of love in between two warring parents .
162752	And it is always better to settle out of court , says Nina .
162753	‘ It is far better for you , and the child , to come to an agreement outside the court system , than get involved in a legal battle .
162754	Best for child ‘ If you have a good reason why you do n't want the father to see your baby then you will be able to put your case to the courts .
162755	‘ At the end of the day you have got to decide what is best not just for you but for your child .
162756	‘ Remember , the new Children 's Act gives them rights too and a court will usually consider that it is in the child 's interest to know both parents where possible and reasonable . ’
162757	Not surprisingly , the access granted can often depend on whether the child is a girl or boy .
162758	Says Nina : ‘ If it 's a girl the courts often deem she needs her mum 's influence .
162759	But boys are thought to need a man around
162760	… ’
162761	Deborah adds : ‘ While the legal situation makes things clearer this is obviously an emotional problem and it can help to talk things through .
162762	‘ Sometimes there may be bitterness between the mother and father but we can help put things into perspective .
162763	‘ It may better if the child can get to know both parents where possible , even though many unmarried mums are happier on their own . ’

163045	Pick a winner with strawberries
163046	AS you will have noticed strawberries are now in the shops .
163047	So far they seem to be the Spanish variety with the lovely English ones still to come .
163048	But strawberries of any sort , served with cream are one of the great delights of summer and I see that in Cheshire the fruit farms have already put out their ‘ Pick Your Own ’ notices .
163049	At weekends it makes for a good day 's outing to take the family for a picnic , after which they can gather as many strawberries as they want at the various fruit farms dotted around .
163050	Disappointingly strawberries do not freeze so if you do not eat them at once you need to use them up in some other way .
163051	Home-made strawberry jam is particularly delicious but there are plenty of recipes around which centre on this scrummy fruit .
163052	ICED STRAWBERRY SOUFFLE
163053	( Serves 4 to 6 )
163054	3 level tsps powdered gelatine ; 4 tbsp orange juice ; 2 oz granulated sugar ; 8 oz cleaned , hulled strawberries ; pint double cream , lightly whipped ; 3 egg whites , whipped until stiff but not dry .
163055	Put the gelatine and orange juice in the top of a double saucepan over hot water , or in a cup standing in a pan of hot water .
163056	Set over a low heat and stir the gelatine constantly until it dissolves .
163057	Add the sugar and as soon as it has dissolved , set the liquid aside to cool a little .
163058	Meanwhile , press the strawberries into a large bowl through a nylon or aluminium sieve .
163059	Stir in the gelatine mixture and fold in the whipped cream .
163060	Cover the bowl and put it into the fridge for about 10 minutes , so that the gelatine just begins to set .
163061	Fold in the whisked egg whites .
163062	Pile the souffle high into a straight sided souffle dish , or into individual souffle dishes if preferred .
163063	Put in the refrigerator to set for an hour or more .

163073	Overcook food rather than undercook it .

163075	It tenderises it and helps it retain its natural juices .

163155	Telroc tennis treat
163156	M ANY readers will be delighted to see this mid-1930s picture ( above ) of one of the Telroc Lawn Tennis Club 's pre-season socials at West Derby Village Hall .
163157	It comes from Major Harold ( Bill ) Corlett , of Ainsdale , a former secretary of Birkdale Golf Club , who became manager of America 's famous golf club the Augusta Club , Georgia .
163158	The background to the tennis club began in 1929 .
163159	Harold , William Snowden ( now a retired bank manager ) , Albert Graham ( retired building contractor ) and Alan Bennett ( who became a schoolmaster and died in war service with the RAF ) were all chums at St.Margaret 's School , Anfield , ( now located at Aigburth ) .
163160	With only ninepence in their pockets , they founded an old boys ' association that went on to include a thriving club ( albeit minus clubhouse ) , a sports field and four football teams competing in the Zingari and Old Boys Associations ' leagues .
163161	They also ran a tennis section , starting with one court ( later two ) at Almonds Green , West Derby and followed with hard courts at Tynwald Hill , Stoneycroft , and ‘ a super location at the tram terminus , Muirhead Avenue East , where there were six grass courts . ’
163162	Eventually , when interest in running the tennis club waned , Harold took it over and ran it as his own business .
163163	He called it ‘ Telroc ’ ( his surname backwards ) .
163164	‘ We specialised in many happy social events in addition to tennis , ’ says Harold , who would like former members to contact him with a view to holding a reunion .

163524	SMILES BETTER
163525	GO on , have a laugh it really is good for you !
163526	It 's the one highly infectious condition that doctors The expert view is that laughter is medically beneficial .
163527	It involved 14 groups of facial muscles and it releases chemicals to the brain that help combat depression .
163528	Laughter is an exhilarating exercise which , like deep breathing , massages the internal organs .
163529	Scientists believe human laughter has an evolutionary origin and is linked with monkeys who grin and display the same shoulder-shaking signs .
163530	So how does this wonderful tonic actually work ?
163531	Dr David Taylor from the Department of Physiology at Liverpool University explained : ‘ Physically , when we laugh , we take in a deep breath and let it out again in short sharp bursts .
163532	When we breathe in we contract our pectoral muscles , the muscles in the wall of our chest , and our diaphragm .
163533	‘ When we laugh the air out , our abdominal muscles do most of the work .
163534	Most people , when they laugh , also exercise more than 14 groups of muscles in their face .
163535	A deep belly laugh is good exercise ! ’
163536	Dr Taylor said the reason why a good laugh makes you feel better is still a mystery .
163537	‘ We know that an hour of mirth is enough to lower our adrenalin levels and also lower the levels of the hormones which the body releases during stress .
163538	So laughter is a good antidote to stress .
163539	‘ Some people have also said that laughter helps the body release chemicals in the brain that are our own internal morphine supplies .
163540	So things really do n't feel so bad after a good laugh . ’
163541	Professor Hugh Foot , Head of Psychology at the University of Strathclyde wrote a book on humour and laughter some years ago with Professor Tony Chapman at Leeds University .
163542	Professor Foot said : ‘ Laughter and the ability to enjoy a sense of fun is taken as a sign of healthy well-being .
163543	People who have a sense of humour are regarded as being balanced and stable compared to people who are depressed and anxious and have difficulty seeing the funny side of life .
163544	‘ If you can laugh at yourself and recognise your own folly it is a healthy sign . ’
163545	We also use laughter to mask our incompetence and to cover for possible failure .
163546	Michael Argyle in the department of Experimental Psychology at the University of Oxford has written several books and articles on laughter 's close companion , happiness .
163547	Happiness , he says , is greatly enhanced by close relationships falling in love rates high on the happiness scale as does a satisfying job .
163548	But people without a job who have found fulfilling voluntary work or an absorbing hobby also score highly .
163549	And what about money ?
163550	Well according to Mr Argyle , money plays a small part but does not have as big an effect as people might think .
163551	So next time you 're thinking of reaching for the tablets or slumping miserably into despair , try having a good laugh instead .
163552	It costs nothing , there are no harmful side effects Some of the great smilers Mona Lisa , Bruce Forsyth , Terry Jones , Meg Ryan , Princess Diana , The Joker ( Jack Nicholson ) .

163895	National Drinkwise Day was organised against the background of statistics that show alcohol consumption per head has more than doubled in Britain since the Second World War , with alcohol abuse on the increase among the young .
163896	The nation 's booze bill totalled a staggering £24.3bn last year , but doctors claim the cost on the country 's health is far higher .
163897	Alcohol is thought to be responsible for 40,000 premature deaths a year , as well as 60pc of suicide attempts , 50pc of murders , 54pc of fires and 30pc of domestic accidents .
163898	Between eight and 14m working days are lost in Britain each year as employees are forced off sick by their hangovers at a cost of more than £700m in lost production .
163899	Visitors to the Pumphouse were invited to input their weekly alcoholic intake into a computer , which calculated the cost of their drinking habits .
163900	The recommended weekly maximum is 21 units for men and 14 for women .
163901	One unit of alcohol is the equivalent of half a pint of beer , a single measure of spirits or a glass of wine .
163902	Mersey Regional Health Authority spokeswoman Jackie Rankin said : ‘ It was very successful for a lot of people who had time to reflect on what they drink and what it costs them in terms of money and their health .
163903	‘ We wanted people to enjoy an afternoon in the pub without alcohol and hopefully a lot of them went away reassured . ’

165052	Clinton fears affecting drug companies ' shares
165053	WHY are shares lagging behind in Britain ?
165054	The Footsie 100 Index of the Top 100 shares has more or less stood still this year .
165055	Yet on Wall Street shares are up by 7pc , Japanese shares have gone up 19pc and in Europe the share index has risen by 9pc .
165056	The truth is that the Footsie is proving to be a misleading guide to what is really happening in the market .
165057	Beneath the surface of the index there is much turmoil , with some shares zooming ahead .
165058	For example British Aerospace has more than doubled to 375p this year .
165059	There has also been a huge recovery of confidence in construction material shares as RMC and Redland , although my favourite remains Blue Circle at 250p because of its involvement in the home improvement business through Armitage Shanks .
165060	Fears
165061	On the other hand what is holding the Index back is the drug companies .
165062	These now comprise 10pc of the total index but are under a cloud because of fears about US President 's wife Hillary Clinton , who is expected to stamp on their profits hard when her review of the US health scene comes out later this year .
165063	So Glaxo shares are down from £8 to under £6 and Wellcome down from £10 to £7.50 .

165900	The Government has delayed responding to the need to equalise pension rights because it means equalising State retirement ages .
165901	At present these are 65 for men and 60 for women .
165902	Equalising at 60 is far too expensive for the Government to contemplate .
165903	But equalising at 65 would be very unpopular with women
165904	Compromise
165905	Sooner or later and if not sooner , further references to the European Court are likely a definite decision will have to be made .
165906	Retirement at 63 is the obvious compromise solution .
165907	But since the private sector will then bring its normal retirement ages into line , this will involve complex adjustment of pension rights for everyone in work .
165908	Potentially an even bigger bombshell is about to burst on the vexed question of pension rights .
165909	It has long been recognised that women who devote years of their lives to bringing up children lose out in the pension stakes .
165910	Their husbands earn pension rights while they do not .
165911	If divorce follows , the husband keeps the pension rights and the wife has none .
165912	At present , English law does not recognise pension rights as an asset in the context of divorce settlements .
165913	And even Scottish law , where pension rights are taken into account on divorce , has no mechanism for transferring them from one person to another .
165914	All the judges can do is award a greater proportion of non pension assets to the wife to make up for her lack of long term security and if these other assets are small , the husband is still the winner .
165915	Now a report from the Pensions Management Institute has suggested ways of changing the law to bring pension rights into play .
165916	The aim would be to give the courts the right to divide pension rights , even if earned by one of the divorcing parties , between them .
165917	This would be done on the basis of the facts , in particular the period of time the marriage had lasted and the extent to which the wife had foregone the opportunity to earn pension rights while bringing up the children .
165918	The legislation would not affect the flat-rate State pension .
165919	Nor , at present , does it look as though it will be practicable to bring SERPS within the scope of the Courts .
165920	But all other pension rights , whether through occupational or personal pension schemes , would in principle be divisible .
165921	Protecting the position of women who work hard at being mothers is obviously a worthy social objective , and with no political dispute likely , the report 's changes could be legislated within a year or two .
165922	Implications
165923	The implications for the future ( any changes will almost certainly not apply to pension rights earned before the date off legislation ) are enormous .
165924	Married people will have to treat the pension rights they earn as partly conditional on their remaining married .
165925	And the possibility , particularly for husbands , of losing a significant part of their pension rights on divorce will focus their minds on the value of those rights .

166418	A Bedale businessman tried and failed to bring more freight traffic to the limestone line .

166420	Mr Kerfoot , managing director of Wensleydale Foods in the old station siding at Bedale , chose road transport after his experiences with Railfreight nearly four years ago .
166421	Wensleydale Foods acquired the station site in 1985 after the public delivery siding had been closed and the short piece of track leading from the limestone branch had been lifted .
166422	The firm now employs 30 people , exports about 20 per cent of its pro-duct and has an annual turnover of £10m. in various currencies .

166424	Using past experience with a company he worked for at Tilbury , Essex , Mr Kerfoot obtained quotes for the hire of special railway wagons .

166428	Mr Kerfoot said : ‘ No one came to see us and the opportunity was lost .
166429	ILLOGICAL
166430	‘ Instead of a rate for carrying oil throughout to Bedale we just got a rate for bringing it to Middlesbrough for trans-shipment to road , which was illogical to me .

167060	THE name Skerne Iron Works means very little in Darlington today , but in its brief and eventful life , it created a worldwide reputation .
167061	The company was formed on Albert Hill in 1864 and by the time it closed in 1879 it had been responsible for 40 bridges in Denmark , 20 bridges in Sweden all built in 1874 , all the viaducts on the Whitby-RedcarMiddlesbrough line including the Staithes Viaduct , Llandudno pier , a bridge in Syria , another over the Tay in Scotland and a footbridge over the Tees at Barnard Castle .
167062	Its biggest project was the Leith Docks swing-bridge over the River Liffey in Dublin in 1879 , but despite the contract being worth £8,143 , when the bridge first swung open Skerne Iron Works ' finances were swaying perilously .
167063	Up on Albert Hill in all likelihood its operations were on the banks of the eponymous river where the Cleveland Industrial Estate is now it had a massive and profitable operation covering 22 acres , employing 1,000 men and boys and working 90 furnaces .
167064	The real problem was the Britannia Works in Middlesbrough which Skerne acquired after leading partner Walter Pease died in 1872 .
167065	His death meant a shortage of capital .
167066	The other partners , Edward Hutchinson , a solicitor who married industrial magnate Sir David Dale 's daughter , and R L Pratt , decided to float the company on the stock market .
167067	Their prospectus said Skerne was thinking of extending further into the bridge-building field , and £200,000 was secured by the sale of 10,000 £20 shares .
167068	With 120 furnaces and its own wharf on the Tees , the Britannia site no doubt looked impressive , but the 1870s were the wrong time for businesses to try to expand .
167069	Britain was in the grip of a severe recession and by 1875 the Britannia Works were forced to close at an enormous loss which Albert Hill could not sustain .
167070	The recession deepened as the 1870s proceeded , and by 1879 Skerne Iron Works had called in the liquidator .
167071	But there is a glimmer of brightness in the Skerne story .
167072	A group of former employees made redundant as the Albert Hill site wound down in 1877 clubbed together and formed Cleveland Bridge and Engineering Company .
167073	A little-known Darlington firm might also have been active in this early phase .
167074	There is a belief but open to much doubt that the bridge builder Teasdale supplied various canal spans for the pedestrian traffic across the River Jumna , a major tributary of the Ganges .
167075	That this firm existed is confirmed by their name being embossed on a single span construction currently serving road travellers in Darlington itself .

167142	PROPERTY analysts at UBS Philips &amp; Drew set a puzzle last year .
167143	‘ When is a rental level not a rental level ? ’ they asked .
167144	Answering their own question they replied : ‘ Almost always ’ .
167145	‘ It has been remarkable , bearing in mind the massive oversupply of office and retail space , that we have continued to hear of unexpectedly high rents being achieved , ’ said the analysts .
167146	But behind the headline numbers lurked the truth , disguised in a veil of what the property market calls confidentiality clauses and what others call secret deals .
167147	‘ Property deals , unlike those in the stock market have no transparency , if required .
167148	Not only are they not transparent , a property deal can be struck subject to just about anything , ’ said UBS .
167149	More bluntly they , and many in the market , were objecting to the prices paid by tenants to landlords for their shop units and offices being kept secret from the market .
167150	Secret sales of property were also subject to the same lambasting .
167151	The objection is that secrecy makes it very difficult to assess the value of a deal and therefore to judge the true state of the market .
167152	More worryingly , confidentially clauses are being used to falsely maintain capital values .
167153	And when rent reviews are due it can be almost impossible to assess what tenants should be paying .
167154	Unfortunately most agents are more than willing to bow to pressure from landlords and tenants who insist that confidentiality clauses are inserted into any deal , no matter how small .
167155	As an example , the property agent Sanderson Townend &amp; Gilbert in Newcastle recently sent out details to the press of a regional letting .
167156	The agent said it had sold a commercial garage in Middlesbrough to a named company .
167157	Aside from its geographical location and the name of the other agent involved few other details were included .
167158	Certainly not price or purchaser .
167159	Paul Stevenson of the agent said : ‘ The buyer did not want its identity revealing . ’
167160	Maybe not .
167161	But the bald statement that a garage has been sold in Middlesbrough is neither a news story , nor of any help to agents working in the market who need to know such details .
167162	To those operating in the specialist property press such lack of detail is intolerable .
167163	Trade magazine Estates Times will not print the details of deals unless the property 's address , size , rent or price involved and size of any premium paid are included .
167164	And in a recent hard-hitting editorial its editor Lee Mallett said : ‘ What is most disconcerting … is the apparent unwillingness … of leading figures in the property industry to acknowledge the distortions that are arising because of the suppression of information . ’
167165	Creditably a handful of influential figures are speaking out against the cult of confidentiality .
167166	Most notable amongst these is John Ritblat , the urbane chairman of developer British Land .
167167	He has called for the compulsory registration of all property transactions in an attempt to stop the use of secret deals .
167168	In a newsletter published by his agency Conrad Ritblatt he said : ‘ We must move towards compulsory registration of investment deals , lettings , mortgages and all transactions in land . ’
167169	Ritblat would like to see all such information logged with the Land Registry .
167170	‘ Those who scoff that this can not be done should look to the United States .
167171	In their most liquid markets New York and Los Angeles , for instance the Real Estate Data Inc publication will give you comprehensive details of ownership , values and rents on a street-by-street basis . ’
167172	The eponymous retail agent Clive Lewis has also added his voice to Ritblat 's .
167173	In his midsummer retail report last year he said confidentiality clauses were ‘ falsely conceived protectionism ’ .
167174	‘ Such clauses succeed in frustrating the free flow of information so essential for accurate valuation at review . ’
167175	His report also noted that in order to obtain information some valuers have subpoenaed surveyors bound by confidentiality clauses to appear in arbitration hearings .
167176	Equally notable figures will spring to the defence of the secret deal , however .
167177	John Parry , managing director of developer Hammerson , was reported as saying : ‘ If a landlord or tenant wants a deal to be confidential , then they should be allowed to .
167178	‘ It is an integral part of British law .
167179	A lot of tenants do n't want their competitors to know their cost base , particularly retailers .
167180	‘ The clauses probably have been misused or overused as a tool .
167181	The trouble is you do n't know where to draw the line . ’
167182	But UBS does .
167183	‘ We are aware that part of a substantial City office building was recently announced as having been let at £40 per sq ft , ’ said the property analysts .
167184	‘ There was the ubiquitous confidentiality clause which we understand was to hide a two year rent free period .
167185	‘ Broken back over the five years to the first rent review , the true rent equates to just £24 per sq ft 40pc less than actually reported . ’
167186	This lead the analysts to estimate that all reported headline deals are probably around 10 to 20pc above the true market .
167187	The property market should be following UBS 's lead and saying deals reported at up to 20pc above their true value is precisely where to draw the line .

167782	MONEY still does not grow on trees .
167783	But from this weekend the public gets a chance to see the old phrase turned on its head .
167784	Flanking the drive to Middlesbrough 's innovative Botanic Centre , to be opened by Professor David Bellamy tomorrow morning , are native trees such as oak , maple and mountain ash .
167785	Bursting with spring health , they are drawing sustenance from a compost containing thousands of banknotes and travellers cheques .
167786	Discarded and shredded by the Bank of England and banknote manufacturer Thomas De La Rue , the paper money has been mixed at the Botanic Centre with sludge from a KP crisp factory on Teesside to form a peat-free compost .
167787	‘ We 're confident we 've created a good product , ’ says centre manager Stuart Goldie .
167788	‘ It 's ideal as a soil conditioner and for tree planting , and besides being used here it is being used in planting Cleveland 's new Community Forest . ’
167789	At the centre , visitors can see not only the trees flourishing on literally the world 's richest compost .
167790	Also on view are the 16 ‘ bins ’ , or bays , where various blends of the novel mixture , which also includes straw and other organic materials , have been prepared .
167791	Some newly-planted cabbages also have the cash-based compost at their roots .
167792	‘ We 're still developing it for use with seedlings and delicate plants , ’ says Stuart , ‘ but we 're certain it has tremendous potential . ’
167793	The compost initiative is just one aspect of a project which , perhaps against expectations , puts Middlesbrough in the forefront of ecological awareness .
167794	And evangelism .
167795	For on its 20-acre edge-of-town site , with neat new houses nudging its entrance just off a busy roundabout , the Botanic Centre is ambitiously committed to spreading the Green gospel .
167796	‘ The headlines on environmental issues are invariably about problems and catastrophes , ’ says Stuart , a former ICI technical manager .
167797	‘ We want the centre to project the positive side .
167798	In particular we want to provide inspiration and ideas for the public , showing methods and techniques that they can adopt .
167799	Apparently a poacher turned gamekeeper , Stuart sees no conflict in having switched from ICI 's fertiliser division to the organic field .
167800	‘ The principles of good husbandry apply whether you are dealing with organic or inorganic methods , ’ he says .
167801	Perhaps more important is that the demonstration role of the centre , which was launched by Prince Charles three years ago , marks it off from most traditional ‘ botanic gardens ’ .
167802	For their prime concern is conserving and showing plants .
167803	But the Botanic Centre , initiated by Middlesbrough Council , is determined to build bridges with the community .
167804	Already about 80 well-wishers , including Middlesbrough FC striker Bernie Slaven , have ‘ adopted a tree ’ their £10 sapling marked by a plaque .
167805	And strong links have been forged with local schools .
167806	‘ Pupils have been involved with soil analysis and seed propagation , ’ says Stuart .
167807	‘ They 've collected conkers , ash keys and acorns , to produce seedlings here which they will later transplant in the Community Forest . ’
167808	Most imaginatively , one school closely involved with the Botanic Centre , Acklam Grange comprehensive , is now devising a scheme to clean its waste kitchen water , which will feed a pond network .
167809	Stuart comments : ‘ We hope to extend these contacts by developing a complete education package .
167810	We believe the Centre offers tremendous scope for projects and studies within the National Curriculum . ’
167811	Opening tomorrow is the centre 's shop , tearoom , demonstration garden and exhibition hall .
167812	Items on sale will include vegetables and herbs from the centre 's own three-acre market garden and bread , jams , and other produce from the well-known Camphill Communities of Botton Hall in the North York Moors and its sister settlement at Larchfield near Middlebrough .
167813	In the garden , visitors can see compost systems , natural means of weed and pest control and various cultivation techniques , including a ‘ no dig ’ system .
167814	Head gardener Matthew Hayes , who trained at Emerson College , Sussex , a leading centre for organic horticulture , says : ‘ We aim to provide a good insight into sound organic practice , which visitors can adopt in their own garden or allotment . ’
167815	Though still in a somewhat raw state , the Botanic Centre is well laid out , with attractive pergola-framed walkways planted with honeysuckle , roses and clematis .
167816	A terrace for open-air teas looks towards the award-winning British Tioxide white garden , re-created here after its success at the Gateshead Garden Festival .
167817	The demonstration garden itself leads to a so-called 21st century garden , with wildflower meadow , pond , orchard and soft fruit area .
167818	‘ The idea is to create a garden that combines minimum maintenance with maximum attraction for wildlife , ’ says Stuart .
167819	‘ Our wildlife areas are attracting a lot of birds , insects and butterflies . ’
167820	Though half the £300,000 spent on the project so far has come from central and local government and charities , the other half has been provided by industry .
167821	This is mirrored in the exhibition centre , where , alongside displays on issues like global warming and acid rain , sponsoring firms including ICI and British Steel set out their environmental stall .
167822	To some visitors this uncritical PR might strike an uneasy note .
167823	But Stuart says : ‘ Companies are keen to improve their image and there 's a lot of good work going on .
167824	It seems fair to provide a shop window . ’
167825	The centre hopes that cash generated by visitors will chiefly propel it into the final two phases of its development .
167826	Expected to take at least four years to achieve , these will see the creation of a wide range of specialised habitats salt marsh , sand dunes , mountain stream , moorland and wetland all with their associated tree and plant life .
167827	And the centre will equip itself to demonstrate the latest developments in wind , water , and solar power .
167828	‘ We think it will be unique , ’ says Stuart Goldie. — David Bellamy will arrive at the centre off Ladgate Lane ( A1044 ) , near the Blue Bell Hotel , Acklam , at 10.30am .
167829	The opening events , between 11am and 11.30am , will include a Free Fall display by the Black Lanyards and music by Lingdale Silver Band .

167948	DOWN the swamp at Darlington , something is stirring .
167949	It 's the conservation volunteers .
167950	On a bright February morning they 're up to their wellied ankles in mud and water , turning a formerly ignored site on the edge of heavy industry into a nature haven .
167951	Up to now , the patch of land off Whessoe Road has n't had a great deal going for it .
167952	It backs onto a couple of euphemisms , the Civic Amenity Site and the abattoir , and a valuable pond which attracted migrating birds has regularly dried up in the summer .
167953	The British Trust for Conservation Volunteers have already achieved much to improve the site 's appeal .
167954	They have taken steps to stop water draining off from the mini-lake , and done an inordinate amount of plodging in the wetland .
167955	‘ We 're trying to increase the amount of aquatic habitat here , which includes planting reed mace and building dykes , ’ says Dean Heward , who is organising the project for BTCV .
167956	The project is what you might call labour-intensive .
167957	Wheelbarrows of mud are carted from one site to help form a containing mound for a pond at the other end .
167958	The land is owned by Darlington Council , who are funding the conservation work .
167959	Helpers have included pupils from an adjacent school , and also handicapped volunteers .
167960	The site will have wildlife-friendly hedges of blackthorn , hawthorn , sweet briar and dog rose , and three wedges of young trees will provide shelter to pond users .
167961	‘ We 've planted 4000 trees including aspen , silver and downy birch and rowan , ’ says Dean .

167992	TEESSIDE is to have an £11m. , 2,500-acre International Nature Reserve as part of Teesside Development Corporation 's regeneration of the lower Tees and its estuary .
167993	It will be the largest man-made nature reserve in the United Kingdom , designed to provide ideal conditions in which birds , fish and wild plants will thrive .
167994	And the National Rivers Authority has pledged to introduce 200,000 salmon a year for the next four years into the cleaned-up River Tees the first time the fish have been in the river in any numbers in the last 30 years .
167995	The multi-million scheme was announced on Monday this week by Environment Secretary Michael Heseltine , backed by his Minister of State , David Trippier ; Prof David Bellamy ; Sir David Attenborough , President of the Royal Society for Nature Conservancy ; Lord Crickhowell , chairman of the National Rivers Authority , and Ron Norman and Duncan Hall , chairman and chief executive respectively of the Teesside Development Corporation .
167996	The scheme is being launched on land formerly owned by ICI .
167997	Within the Teesside redevelopment project there is also the Tees Barrage , which will create 11 miles of clean , tide-free water upstream of Teesdale , where the TDC has its headquarters , and where the new Joint University College , which is to specialise in environmental courses , is sited .
167998	Also , Teesdale , with its views of the revitalised Tees , will be an appropriate home to Her Majesty 's Inspectorate of Pollution from May this year .
167999	The new nature reserve will be the area of Middlesbrough and more than seven times the size of Hyde Park .
168000	It will create new natural habitats in reedbeds , grasslands , swamp , saltmarsh , water and woodlands .
168001	And this priceless asset would qualify for United Nations recognition as an International Biosphere Reserve .
168002	Situated on the Tees estuary , the area is already an internationally-famous Ramscar class wetland refuge for birds , waders and wildfowl .
168003	It attracts significant numbers of species including the shelduck , sanderling , redshank and grey plover .
168004	Its importance will grow as the reserve takes shape and provides even more of the right habitats for wildlife and wild plants .
168005	The International Nature Reserve is for the benefit of the Teesside community and beyond .
168006	It has been carefully designed to develop and protect wildlife and plants while attracting many thousands of visitors .
168007	It has taken the best elements from several Dutch schemes the Dutch being recognised as the experts in creating wetland nature reserves .
168008	The launch of the 2,500-acre nature reserve is a giant step in the creation of a new environment on Teesside , and as part of the urban regeneration of Teesside it is change on a grand scale .
168009	At the official launch on Monday , Mr Heseltine said : ‘ Along with the major initiatives , the local councils , organisations such as the Wildlife Trust and the community are working towards a new environment .
168010	‘ When the people come together , the most ambitious projects are achievable . ’
168011	Sir David Attenborough said : ‘ Companies of local and national importance on Teesside recognise their environmental responsibilities .
168012	They prove that industry and nature can coexist . ’
168013	And ICI chairman Sir Denys Henderson added : ‘ I am proud of ICI 's conservation record on Teesside .
168014	Our successful partnership there serves as a powerful example of what can be achieved by industry working together with conservationists and local communities . ’

168054	The Great Pretenders Gulbenkian Studio Theatre , Newcastle
168055	THIS production is the British premiere of a 17th Century work by the Spanish playwright Lope de Vega , but any assumptions we may have that it will be a genteel period piece are dispelled with the first few lines of dialogue .
168056	Opening with a tirade of four letter abuse from Roman footsoldiers to their ( absent ) leaders , the translation by David Johnston ( for The Gate Theatre ) goes on to incorporate a great many deliberate anachronisms which give the play a decidedly modern flavour .
168057	The first act accounts for only one third of the two-and-a-quarter-hour running time , and details the series of intrigues whereby Diocletian ( John Straiton ) , a common legionary , ascends to the position of Caesar following the murder of his predecessor , Aurelius .
168058	Having effectively established the background of decadence , savagery and corruption that was Rome in 300 AD , the play shifts gears after the interval for the arrival of a travelling theatre company which is to present an entertainment for the newly installed Emperor .
168059	After a good deal of broad mockery of the group 's thespian pretensions , there follows yet another change of tack as the troupe 's hitherto self-absorbed leader , Genesius ( Louis Hilyer ) , converts to Christianity and is martyred for denouncing the oppressive regime .
168060	Groups of actors have often provided the focus of stories about the victimisation of innocents by totalitarian forces ( examples include To Be or Not to Be , Privates on Parade , The Last Metro and the recent Spanish film Ay , Carmela ! ) , so it 's interesting to see such a relatively early variation on the theme as this .
168061	But the affectionate satire of outrageously hammy theatricals , though amusing , strikes rather a hollow note when so much of the company 's own work is stridently self-indulgent .
168062	In particular , Jamie Newall 's Aurelius would make Tod Slaughter seem a model of subtle understatement : his declamatory performance in Act I is barely distinguishable from the deliberate badness later on .
168063	Hilyer ( whose character is apparently the Patron Saint of actors ) is , however , excellent , while Rae Smith 's idiosyncratic costume designs and the lighting by Paul Russell also make very effective contributions to an uneven but often rewarding evening .
168064	Musicon Concert , St Mary 's College , Durham SIRITSU is a group of four young musicians devoted to the performance of music of Spanish and Bolivian origin , particularly that associated with the silver mining town of Potosi .
168065	It was , perhaps , something of a disappointment to find that they were all from Britain and that , therefore , the genuine folk background was lacking .
168066	Those who have heard Andean groups perform , as they have done locally in recent years , would miss their primitive and earthy flavour in this Saturday night performance .
168067	Nevertheless , it was a thoroughly enjoyable evening with some excellent musicianship displayed .
168068	The music generally alternated between sophisticated 16th Century Spanish pieces mostly of a sacred character , with delightful singing from Sara Stowe and able accompaniments on recorders , harp , guitars and hurdy gurdy ; and native material of Bolivian origin , albeit with Spanish conquistador influence evident .
168069	Using genuine folk instruments such as armadillo charangos , pan pipes and caja and playing them splendidly , the group built their programme around the Bolivian seasons and the ritual divisions of the year .
168070	They attempted to demonstrate how the Spanish influence was absorbed into the Andean vision of the world and they achieved considerable success .
168071	The audience responded enthusiastically .
168072	It was an unusual and intriguing evening .

168222	Grieg Trio
168223	Darlington Arts Centre
168224	DARLINGTON Music Society has had some superb and famous musicians and ensembles play at their concerts over the years , yet the young Grieg Trio from Norway must rank among the very best .
168225	Their Saturday evening concert at the Arts Centre showed them to be individual artists of the highest quality who together produced something greater than just the sum of the parts .
168226	This quality was at its most sublime in Schubert 's marvellous E Flat Trio with which they ended .
168227	In it they brought just the right weight of balance to each part , to each phrase , to each note .
168228	Its effect was a magical transparency of texture yet with depth and solidity where needed .
168229	With this class of playing the listener is led to a conviction that at last there may be in due time successors to the distinguished Beaux Arts Trio indeed , in their approach and enjoyment of the music they play there are parallels .
168230	Earlier a trio by their fellow countryman Valen , Opus 5 in E Flat , seemed to derive much from Schoenbergian romanticism : intense and impassioned yet it lacked a variety of pace .
168231	Marvellously played , the work might well yield more on a second hearing .

168233	Dave Robson La Ronde Gulbenkian Studio Theatre , Newcastle ARTHUR Schnitzler 's Reigen is perhaps best known under its French title and as the first of two film versions , made by Max Ophuls in 1950 , is remembered as the quintessence of Viennese elegance .
168234	Yet both original film and play were widely unavailable until the early Eighties , due to copyright problems and the author 's insistence ( after a public outcry had kept the play , completed in 1897 , off the Austrian stage until 1921 ) that it not be produced for fear of his intentions being betrayed .
168235	Accused in its time of being a scandalous affront to bourgeois morality , La Ronde in fact pinpoints its hypocrisy most acutely and in retrospect reveals its author as ( among other things ) a perceptively premature feminist .
168236	Its plot is a ‘ circle of love ’ , as a succession of couplings begins with a nocturnal encounter between a whore and a soldier , and continues as the soldier has sex with a housemaid , the maid with her young master , the master with a married woman , and so on until we reach a count who returns us to the whore .
168237	Each of the ten matings ( the lights black out at the crucial moments , of course ) is a vignette illustrating the transience of human relationships and the inequality which exists between uncommitted sexual partners , as passion , love , lust and power are unevenly distributed , invariably resulting in unhappiness .
168238	A more obvious underlying meaning , pointed out by the programme notes , is to see the ‘ round-dance ’ as a metaphor for the transmission of VD or , more topically , AIDS ; but this seems to me less interesting than the social satire whose delicate emotional nuances ( preserved in co-director Ceri Sherlock 's modernised adaptation ) give the play its wider significance and melancholy humour .
168239	Victoria Scarborough and Colin Watson , taking five roles apiece , prove adept at giving every character a distinctive individuality while subtly stressing the continuities which make each the mirror image of one another 's frailties .
168240	Though it lacks the grace and fluidity of Ophuls ' film ( laborious set-changing is necessary between each scene ) , the production is stylishly designed by Birte Meyer and Idit Nathan , whose simple backdrops prove as attractive and versatile as the talented young performers .

168458	AN AFRICAN band as old as their country perform at Darlington Arts Centre tonight .
168459	The Bhundu Boys from Zimbabwe began playing together in celebration of their country 's independence 11 years ago .
168460	They took their name from the bush guerillas who fought with Robert Mugabe during the bloody war of independence and blend high energy guitar with subtle Zimbabwean rhythms .
168461	Rise Kagona , founder of the group , said the birth of Zimbabwe acted as the floodgate to inspiration for the band .
168462	‘ When you have been oppressed and let free you are like a bird out of a cage .
168463	You celebrate and wander around and see what you have been missing , ’ he said .
168464	The band , forced to play covers of Beatles songs and American country music ( the staple diet of Rhodesian radio ) , immediately switched to traditional African songs written specifically about celebrating freedom and living together in a new country .
168465	‘ A lot of African music was outlawed in Rhodesia .
168466	The only way you would get on television was to play songs in English , ’ said Kagona .
168467	‘ But a lot of African people could not understand English . ’
168468	Their popularity soon grew and the introduction of World Music to the West during the late 1980s catapulted the band to international recognition .
168469	Shabini , recorded in Zimbabwe in 1987 , shot to the top of the indie charts in Britain and the Bhundu Boys began to gather momentum .
168470	‘ People are still coming to see Zimbabwe , and it is the same with us we used to see England as this tiny blob on the map and now we can see it for ourselves , ’ said Kagona .
168471	The band are one of the few African groups to maintain any kind of success outside their own country , due largely to the efforts of their manager .
168472	‘ There are many good bands in Africa ; they all want to come abroad but it is difficult to get visas and many promoters are only interested in doing just one tour .
168473	‘ We have been successful because our manager has really wanted to explore with us and work together . ’
168474	The Bhundu Boys have recently played a few dates in Spain and have toured in Australia , America and Europe .
168475	With the sad death of their bass player David Mankaba behind them , the band are promoting their third LP , Absolute Jit , and hope their colourful music can bring a ray of sunshine to Darlington .

168590	‘ I was alarmed by the risk .

168593	Rawsthorne had clear reasons for wanting to tackle Women In Love .
168594	The four main characters come from a mining community , but they 've left it behind .
168595	He saw a parallel with Durham 's situation , where mining is being taken away , but it still dominates .

168597	Chambers sums them up as : ‘ how to live your life in the 20th century and remain sane and happy ’ .

168599	He was a sickly child with a bad chest ; so was I. He was brought up by women ; so was I.

168601	I am very interested in the history of my own family ; in the kinds of people they became and why .

168639	To start at the very beginning , as Pamela Hine did , the game or sport of halma was part of the ancient Greek pentathlon .
168640	It was a long jump competition where the athletes did themselves no favours at all by carrying weights .
168641	The Greek word for jump is halma and , as any linguist extraordinaire will know , the French have the word hallesthai meaning to leap .
168642	And so to more modern times .
168643	In the 1880s halma was rejuvenated as a board game Waddington's-style for two to four players .
168644	There were 256 squares on the board and each player had 19 or 13 pieces .
168645	The object was to get your pieces from your corner to an opponent 's corner by leaping over his pieces .
168646	A bit like chess played diagonally , said one correspondent , or ‘ a four-sided game of draughts , ’ said John Mortimer .
168647	‘ With four players you could have quite a battle in the middle of the board . ’
168648	John Lowe remembers halma as a forerunner to bingo .
168649	Circular discs with numbers on were pulled from a bag , the numbers shouted out and when your card was full you leaped to the top of the house .
168650	The game was , he says , illegal because it was a form of gambling .
168651	But Mr Lowe agrees with Joe Corrie who remembers playing halma of whatever description in the Twenties .
