168702	CHRISTOPHER Gable says he did not set out to deliberately shock .
168703	Yet he was well aware that tampering with the traditional approach to Swan Lake would ruffle a few feathers .
168704	What he was n't expecting was a Sunday newspaper preview article claiming Northern Ballet Theatre 's new staging of Swan Lake was steamy , erotic stuff with a hint of oral sex .
168705	More dirty duck than sensual swan was the impression given .
168706	The result of this advance publicity not wildly accurate as it turns out spelt potential disaster for NBT which prides itself on making its work more accessible to youngsters .
168707	Worried parents fretted that their children would be exposed to X-rated happenings .
168708	A Darlington councillor who , of course , had n't seen the production called for it to be banned .
168709	The threat of cancelled bookings hung in the air .
168710	Backstage at Leeds Grand Theatre , a few days after Swan Lake 's royal premiere elicited a five-minute standing ovation from the audience , Gable talks long and intelligently about the controversial production .
168711	You 'd expect the unhelpful advance publicity to make him wary of the Press .
168712	Not at all .
168713	He has operated an ‘ open door ’ policy since taking over as NBT 's artistic director and will continue to do so .
168714	If people are going to have their opinions formed by what they read in the tabloids , he feels sorry for them .
168715	A relatively simple question like ‘ Are you a happy man ? ’ ( one assumes he must be in the wake of the successful opening ) is followed by a 15 minute answer .
168716	Gable replies that to be honest he 's surprised , although not by the attitude of ‘ the old guard conservative group of three or four London reviewers ’ .
168717	Their reaction was predictable : ‘ One expects them to groan , though I do n't know quite why we should be seeing a piece as it was performed 50 years ago .
168718	That 's what they think ballet should be and that 's why I think , by and large , ballet is a dying art form . ’
168719	What has surprised and pleased him is the public 's response .
168720	He was n't sure how they 'd take to this rethink of Swan Lake .
168721	From the letters he 's received and through talking to audiences , he knows the production is a popular one .
168722	Just do n't use the word ‘ crowd-pleaser ’ .
168723	Gable regards this as an insult to the audience handed out by critics who consider themselves on a higher level .
168724	That NBT audiences and critics are out of touch would seem to be borne out by the response to NBT 's recent touring hit Romeo &amp; Juliet .
168725	Worst production of the year , wrote one London critic .
168726	Best of the year , voted readers of Dance and Dancers .
168727	‘ I was not sure what the general public 's reaction would be to Swan Lake .
168728	Everyone knows the name and thinks they know the story .
168729	I presumed they would be bringing very formed expectations to the theatre .
168730	‘ What I 've found is a far younger element in the audience .
168731	On the evidence this production is speaking far more vividly to this generation than the traditional version . ’
168732	Gable hopes his Swan Lake will be viewed not as a version but a theatre event in its own right .
168733	‘ Although I do n't try to shock I do try to make the moment as vividly alive for the audience as I can and that 's a sort of crusade , ’ he admits .
168734	He 's moved the story to Russia , sent the Prince on army manoeuvres where he joins a boys ' boozy night out , has the swans massacred by a power-mad crippled usurper and the corpses piled obscenely in a heap .
168735	Worst of all , the swans do n't wear tutus but rather fetching white corseted little skirts .

168741	‘ You ca n't just make a performance of everything you have seen .
168742	You have to clear away the debris .
168743	I did with this , looking at various segments of the story . ’

168745	Christopher the Crusader is in his stride , the man who reckons this generation of youngsters is deprived .

168752	ONE hundred years ago theatre history was made in Bury St Edmonds .
168753	The curtain went up on Charley 's Aunt for the first time at the Theatre Royal .
168754	Tomorrow former Blue Peter presenter Mark Curry will be bounding around the same stage in frock and wig as Lord Fancourt Babberley in the centenary staging of the Brandon Thomas farce .
168755	This Mobil Touring Theatre production will later find its way to Darlington Civic and Newcastle Tyne Theatre on a four-month national tour .
168756	Brandon Thomas opted to unveil his Aunt away from London fearful that the capital 's theatre critics would tear it to pieces .
168757	Out-of-town audiences were greatly amused .
168758	So much so that a theatre fireman laughed so loud that he fell over , accidentally rang the firebell and brought the curtain down prematurely .
168759	Despite that success , the playwright had difficulty raising the money to bring the comedy into the West End , although the backer who came up with the all-important £1,000 needed to clinch the deal was able to retire to a South Sea island on his share of the profits .
168760	At one time Charley 's Aunt was being performed in 48 different countries simultaneously .
168761	But , as director Peter Wilson points out , a play demanding 10 actors , three sets and several costume changes is ‘ too big to tour ’ these days unless , of course , you have the backing of Mobil , who 've spent £1m on its touring theatre since 1986 .
168762	Mark Curry is well aware he 's following some illustrious predecessors in the role of Lord Fancourt , who dons a frock to impersonate a long-lost aunt from Brazil ( where the nuts come from ) .
168763	Jack Benny , Arthur Askey , John Mills , Tom Courtenay and Griff Rhys Jones are among those who have enjoyed petticoat power .
168764	Curry , who began his career at seven presenting Yorkshire TV 's Junior Showtime , admits : ‘ It 's a daunting part because of what you hear about people who have played it before .
168765	It 's a great play and should be played for real .
168766	The comic business comes out of the situations . ’
168767	Curry spent two years at Harrogate Theatre before being asked to present a Saturday morning TV show and later Blue Peter .
168768	When he left that he did wonder if anyone would cast him in a straight play but was fortunate enough to get Billy Liar .
168769	In the revival he 's acting alongside a previous Charley 's Aunt Patrick Cargill , the veteran actor best known for the ITV comedy series Father Dear Father .
168770	He played Lord Fancourt at Windsor Rep for one week in 1952 but says : ‘ I ca n't remember one thing about it although I do have a photograph of me looking extremely young and lovely . ’
168771	Now he is playing solicitor Spettigue , whose niece and ward misbehave themselves by having an unchaperoned lunch at Oxford University with a couple of male students .
168772	Cargill does n't think the old-fashioned moral attitudes will deter a modern audience : ‘ One has to remember it 's a costume play .
168773	We are not pretending it 's taking place today .
168774	‘ A lot of it is charming because the way of speaking and attitudes of people in those days now becomes an amusing factor .
168775	I think that 's why the play has survived so long because it has this peculiar charm . ’
168776	The prospect of 16 weeks on tour does n't especially fill Cargill with delight , so why do it ?
168777	‘ They pay me , ’ he says , before qualifying his statement : ‘ I am doing it for the love of my art .
168778	Of course , I love the theatre or I would not go on doing it . ’
168779	He recently spent two years in the musical Me and My Girl in London 's West End and , after 53 years in the business , has no wish to retire .
168780	‘ I 'm a workaholic , ’ he says .
168781	‘ I do n't like my own company so I like to be in a show .
168782	I can honestly say I ca n't remember a show I definitely did n't like doing , although I might have been in some that did n't turn out as I though they would . ’
168783	He prefers working in an old theatre with proscenium arch .
168784	He prefers the separation it gives actors and audience .
168785	‘ If theatre has any magic it 's when that curtain comes down and there is that lovely separation , ’ he says .
168786	— Charley 's Aunt plays Darlington Civic Theatre from March 9–14 and Newcastle Tyne Theatre from May 4–9 .

168799	TAKING as her text one of Paul Cezanne 's lesser-known dictums that ‘ the same subject , from a different angle , can be the subject for study of the most powerful interest ’ , Eleanor Bowen stretches the art of drawing to its limit .
168800	The continuous return to the same subject to wring out every ounce of meaning from it , has long been regarded as the hallmark of the true professional .
168801	But whereas Eleanor Bowen once used drawing as a means of recording for posterity what was immediately in front of her eyes , I am thinking in particular of those powerfully smudged charcoal drawings of the interior of Darlington Railway Station nowadays she goes far beyond this to evoke the feelings of considerable ill and unease .
168802	Since this is also something of a retrospective exhibition we have the much earlier painting of her Rome Studio in 1976 , where in a sequence of flat planes she explores every facet of light and the spaces between .
168803	There is no gainsaying the fact that London-born Eleanor Bowen has come a long way since her last exhibition at the Durham Art Gallery some eight years ago .

168878	Trouble bubbles over Macbeth play
168879	A drama which threatened to turn into a tragedy when artistic tempers flared appears to have been resolved .
168880	The English Shakespeare Company 's forthcoming performance of Macbeth at Darlington Civic Theatre looked set to fall victim to the play 's ‘ unlucky ’ reputation .
168881	For when the company announced there would be no interval in the 2 7hour production and refused to change their minds , Mr Brian Goddard , theatre director , accused them of ‘ artistic arrogance ’ .
168882	And as the squabble boiled over , the company threatened never to return if the theatre pressed for lost bar takings , estimated to be £1,650 .
168883	A spokeswoman for the ESC defended director Mr Michael Pennington 's decision .
168884	‘ It 's a short play and its very hard to find a natural break in the action , unlike some of Shakespeare 's other works .
168885	‘ The action goes along at break-neck velocity to reach its conclusion and so there is no problem with the audience fidgeting . ’
168886	But on Thursday , the council 's recreation committee ruled that Mr Goddard 's claims for compensation should be shelved in the name of ‘ artistic integrity ’ Coun. Mrs Dot Long , committee chairman , said : ‘ Mr Goddard has acted perfectly properly in his negotiations with the ESC in his efforts to maximise income for the Civic Theatre in the present difficult economic climate .
168887	‘ On this occasion , the recreation committee considers the artistic integrity of the production should take precedence over economic considerations . ’
168888	In a statement , Mr Goddard said the ESC had apologised to the theatre for any inconvenience caused by not telling them earlier that the play would run without a break .
168889	‘ The Civic Theatre and the ESC have agreed to wait until the end of the week 's performances and then to evaluate the amount of income taken before any further discussions take place , ’ he said .
168890	‘ We wish to stress that our discussions are proceeding on amicable terms and there will be further visits to Darlington Civic Theatre . ’
168891	Mr Robert Smallwood , deputy director of the Stratford Shakespearean Centre , said academics had disputed the question of doing without an interval in the play for years .
168892	‘ It really is a contentious area , ’ he said .
168893	‘ Some productions of Macbeth have one and others decide not to , which is artistically good but commercially dubious .
168894	‘ The problem is that the structure of the play shows no sign of what Shakespeare intended at all . ’
168895	The play 's three performances next week are sold out , though there are tickets left for their production of Twelfth Night which does have an interval .

169057	ELSIE CLOUGHTON , 74-year-old musician who plays piano and piano accordion at events throughout Darlington .
169058	I 've been playing the piano and the piano accordion for about 60 years .
169059	I first started when I was seven and a half .
169060	I suppose I was influenced by my father who used to sing and tell stories at concert parties he ran .
169061	I was brought up in a different era where you had to entertain yourself .
169062	If you had a talent , you were recognised , and often I got invited to play for the local Boy Scout group .
169063	I still sing and play some of the material that my father used all those years ago .
169064	They are particularly popular when I play in front of old people .
169065	During my week , I play at a number of keep fit classes around Darlington .
169066	I 've been playing at the classes for around 40 years .
169067	I was first asked to play the piano at a local youth centre by a lady called Gladys Mutimer .
169068	It was her that invited me to play for a keep fit class .
169069	I now play at classes in Mowden Junior School on a Monday evening and at Abbey Road Junior School on a Wednesday evening .
169070	A class for the Over 60s at the Dolphin Centre in Darlington takes up my Tuesday afternoon , where I play the piano .
169071	It 's quite nice because the people at the classes come to hear the music as well as to keep fit .
169072	Often they ask me for requests , and sometimes they will come over and ask about a piece of music I 've just played .
169073	At the classes I usually play light , modern and rhythmic music .
169074	A lot of younger people enjoy music like 42nd Street , a new musical in my day , but , of course , it 's still around today .
169075	I do n't just play tunes at keep fit classes .
169076	I used to run an English and Scottish dancing class at the old high school in Cleveland Avenue , before it became Hummersknot School in 1955 where I worked for 22 years part-time , teaching dance .
169077	One of the competitions pupils took part in was the Darlington Competitive Dance Festival .
169078	The festival takes place once a year , usually in March .
169079	At the festival , there are demonstrations of dance , such as Morris dancing and country dancing .
169080	There are also demonstrations of different kinds of music .
169081	I used to play for the Darlington Deanery Choir one afternoon a week .
169082	We used to go along to various churches in the area playing music .
169083	For about four years , I was involved in weekend courses at Rayhead and Lanton Castle Adult Education Centres and more recently at Beamish Hall .

169288	Charley 's Aunt :
169289	Darlington Civic Theatre FOR all that Charley 's Aunt is in its 100th year , this production starring Mark Curry in the title role is as fresh as ever .
169290	Set at the height of Victoria 's rule , the story revolves around three Oxford undergraduates who have nothing better to do than court young females , have parties and be awfully brassic .
169291	Of course upper class , nothing but Victorian convention guides their whims and wishes .
169292	And cynical but obedient man servant Brassett ( Nick Bayly ) .
169293	Brandon Thomas 's play reflects the social propriety that meant young ladies were always chaperoned in mixed company even to a lunch party such being in 15 minutes time was n't thought unusual .
169294	That 's where Charley 's Aunt was supposed to come in , to chaperon the swooning sweeties Kitty and Amy , but a last moment delay left Jack and Charles desperate .
169295	Christopher Lamb ( Jack Chesney ) , and Jonathan Markwood ( Charles Wykeham ) set the opening scene rather woodenly , and the play did n't lift until Lord Fancourt Babberley ( Mark Curry ) was bullied into his amateur dramatics costume to be the long-awaited aunt , Donna Lucia D'Alvadorez .
169296	The anxious student in strange female dress jittered at any provocation .
169297	Curry played on that sense of panic when intimately caught with the money-grabbing Spettigue ( Patrick Cargill ) or the more civilised Sir Francis Chesney ( Frank Windsor ) who eventually found his long lost love when the real Donna Lucia did arrive .
169298	Occasionally Curry used panto dame slapstick , rather than emulating the sophistication of a wealthy millionaire widow fresh from Brazil ‘ where the nuts come from ’ , portrayed sympathetically by Gabrielle Drake .
169299	And Thomas had Ela Delahay , the companion to Donna Lucia and earnest love of Babberley , for fate to act kindly on the poor boy .
169300	The farcical element throughout was dateless , showing how the Victorians could laugh at their own conventions .
169301	HUMOUR is a personal thing as the Hippodrome comic 's pub crawl demonstrates but in December 1904 much of Darlington was chuckling about the way fate dealt a cruel blow to J F Latimer .
169302	Mr Latimer , a solicitor with offices in Priestgate ( the firm is still there ) , was a leading Temp ( this , as regular Echo Memories readers will know , does not refer to the transitory nature of his position but to his teetotal outlook ) .
169303	A firm called The Commondale ran its business from the floor above his office , advertising its presence with its name emblazoned on the window .
169304	On December 6 frost struck ( see picture above ) and some of the sticky letters lost their stickiness and tumbled off .
169305	Thus , the window above Mr Latimer 's office appeared to carry the exhortation : ‘ Go on ale ’ .
169306	AN IDEA trickled into Joseph Pease 's head in 1865 .
169307	He had just developed the ‘ mural fountain ’ concept and stuck the first one on the wall by the entrance to his mansion in Grange Road .
169308	He thought : ‘ Perhaps Darlington as a whole would like a complete set . ’
169309	So in March 1866 he offered eight to the town and the Local Government Board agreed to lay on free water .
169310	Out of nine mural , or wall , drinking fountains , only three appear to survive .
169311	The sites of several others are not known .
169312	All the mural fountains were built on the boundaries of properties belonging to the Pease family .
169313	The most ornate spouters were in Woodland Road ( extant ) and Carmel Road ( disappeared since the 1950s ) .
169314	The surrounding carved stonework contained the date , and in the middle were metal panels displaying a dolphin with bulrushes .
169315	Over the dolphin 's head hung a trident to signify Neptune , the god of the waters .
169316	In the middle at the top was the Pease family crest : A dove rising with a pea stalk in its beak .
169317	The metalwork also bore the legend ‘ Water for the Thirsty ’ .
169318	The other wall founts were not so elaborate .
169319	They were situated in Coniscliffe Road ( extant ) , Northgate , North Road ( both disappeared since the Fifties ) , near the gateway to the East Mount mansion in Haughton Road ( disappeared when East Mount was demolished after the Second World War ) , and two at either end of the Bank Top Cut ( vanished when the cut was widened in the 1930s ) .

169345	McCapra String Quartet :
169346	Darlington Arts Centre THERE are many promising young string quartets on today 's music circuit .
169347	Few however achieve the qualities that the McCapra String Quartet brought to their Darlington Music Society recital in the Arts Centre on Saturday evening .
169348	From the first bars of Mozart 's ‘ Hunt ’ Quartet it was obvious that their effortlessly fluent and natural playing was at the service of artistic integrity .
169349	Their sense of balance between the sublime and robust in Mozart 's music was impeccable .
169350	If Mozart is the essence of flowing line and elegantly shaped melodic phrases , Malcolm Arnold achieves his effects in his Second String Quartet by contrast and variety of colour and intensity , together with flashes of acerbic humour .
169351	It proved a work of appealing ingenuity with many reference points to hold the listener 's attention .
169352	At its heart is a slow movement of great intensity and spellbinding simplicity , magically performed .
169353	Speaking of slow movements , that of Beethoven 's last string quartet , Op. 135 is without doubt the most moving and peaceful of any in the entire quartet repertoire .
169354	Its mystical character was marvellously caught by the young players whose approach to the work as a whole was a shade more romantic than many and none the worse for that .
169355	Given an enthusiastic ovation from the large audience , they responded with a light as thistledown performance of the finale of Haydn 's Op. 33/2 ‘ joke ’ quartet as encore .
169356	Final concert in the DMS season is on April 4 when American pianist Ruth Geiger appears .
169357	Bobby Wellins Quintet :
169358	Darlington Arts Centre THIS was the third time this season that jazz at the Arts Centre has clashed with a jazz concert elsewhere , this time with the Stan Tracey Octet in Gateshead .
169359	As a result , a smaller than average audience was there to hear Bobby 's current band .
169360	His last appearance in Darlington was about three years ago , and since then this quintet has been formed with Jez Hall on tenor sax , Nikki Iles on piano , Gary Culshaw electric bass and Tony Faulkner drums .
169361	The rhythm section provided a perfect cushion for the soloists , springy and supportive but never obtrusive .

169363	Jez Hall 's tenor sax sound is lighter and warmer than Bobby 's providing just enough contrast in their many solos but also doubling mellower than before but still with a crying , keening sounding that taps enormous depths of feeling .

169535	Ruth Geiger : Sunderland Art Gallery
169536	THE Vienna-born American pianist Ruth Geiger who started her week-long North-East tour in Sunderland Art Gallery on Tuesday , is an extremely fine artiste .
169537	Her recital for the Sunderland Piano Society began with a performance of Haydn 's Andante and Variations in F Minor in which firmness , consistency and a sense of ease allowed the work to expand and develop naturally .
169538	A similar overall vision was apparent in Schubert 's A Minor Op 164 Sonata .
169539	Here in the slow movement she allowed the gentle principal theme to flow naturally and above all musically .
169540	In the finale the abrupt changes of pace were contrasted to always good musical effect .
169541	Leos Janacek 's On An Overgrown Path is very much a work of atmosphere and impressions .
169542	Its course of ten short sound pieces are like an aural snapshot album , each one conjuring up visions in the hearer 's imagination .
169543	Here they were played with affection and an aware responsiveness to Janacek 's uniquely personal musical language that created , in the later works of the group particularly , an intensity that belied their relative brevity .
169544	The different impressionism of Debussy 's La Terace des Audiences de Claire de Lune , General Levine and Jardins Sous la Pluie ended a recital that was notable for its highly musical restraint and total lack of overt virtuosity for its own sake .

169660	Religious education encrusted in myths and fantasies
169661	Professional religious education teachers like Marjorie B Clark ( Points of View , today ) are doing valuable work in many secondary schools in trying to separate the facts about religion from the myths and fantasies with which they have become encrusted .
169662	Good RE teaching is about the historical facts and the literature of the main world religions and it allows the young to study the beliefs and attitudes held by the adherents of these religions and also by humanists .
169663	Unfortunately there are many secondary schools , especially in the denominational sector , where this strictly educational approach is not followed .
169664	In primary schools , class teachers are expected to be polymaths and to devote 10 per cent of their time ( if they obey the official guidelines ) to teaching a detailed programme of religious and moral education .
169665	This is drawn up by the curriculum committee , which argues that since God , death , suffering and the purpose of life are all at the heart of religion , and since children sometimes ask questions about them , the class teacher should not only teach about these matters , but be subject both to assessment procedures and to official inspection .
169666	But we all have our own ideas about the answers to these big questions and it ought to be left to the discretion of class teachers to allow their pupils to learn about life 's problems in their own time and at their own pace .
169667	This attempt to codify religious and moral education in the primary school is a mistake ; it will unnecessarily tie the hands both of teachers and of education departments .
169668	As for worship , or religious observance as the legislation calls it , I agree entirely with Marjorie B Clark that ‘ compulsory acts of worship can never be educationally justified ’ .
169669	The trouble is that the Scottish Education Department disagrees with both of us and insists that religious observance must not only be reinstated but also reinforced .
169670	The department is now laying itself open to serious educational criticism on several grounds :
169671	1
169672	It is undemocratically imposing its will on reluctant schools ;
169673	2
169674	It has failed to understand the vital distinction between education and indoctrination ;
169675	3
169676	It is failing to make it clear to parents that the law gives them full rights to withdraw their children from religious instruction and religious observance .

169705	Keeping the faith but losing a way of life
169706	Frank Farragher reports from Galway on the impact of the Digital job losses
169707	THE PEOPLE in the west of Ireland city of Galway are no more religious than the next .
169708	In the past year they have lost a bishop in a love-child affair but over the past few days they had more faith in prayer than in their politicians when it came to saving the Digital computer plant .
169709	Galway , a tourist and university city with a population of 55,000 , regarded the Digital plant as part of the landscape .
169710	Securing a job in Digital , opened in the recession-free days of the early 70s , was thought to be akin to getting a position in the civil service : once in , there forever .
169711	The word on the streets of Galway last week was that hardware manufacturing with its 800 jobs had gone by the wayside .
169712	Last-minute trips to Boston by the employment minister , Ruari Quinn , and local mayor , Padric McCormack , were regarded as a face-saving exercise — something to be seen to be done .
169713	At last Friday 's meeting of Galway County Council , independent councillor Joe Brennan , a public representative noted more for his faith in God than in liberal man , proposed a prayer to save Digital .
169714	‘ We should look to the Holy Spirit to guide us for good news .
169715	Ireland should go back to the past and pray and concentrate on God .
169716	The number of unemployed is increasing and human beings have failed us , ’ he said .
169717	This morning the 780 employees of Digital in Galway will wake up with a hangover after a night 's mourning and stare into an uncertain future , wishing that some divine intervention could be called upon to extract them from their present straits .
169718	The Digital workforce in Galway was a loyal and dedicated one which placed its faith in the company ethos of trust and co-operation .
169719	People 's lives were Digital oriented : many had been there since finishing second level school or university … life outside Digital was unthinkable .
169720	The Digital thinking permeated through all walks of life in the Galway region .
169721	Digital workers were always good for a car loan or a mortgage , perceived as being in secure , well-paid jobs .
169722	Good workers , with high self-esteem … not the type to renege on a £60,000 mortgage or a £10,000 car loan .
169723	The term ‘ Digital mortgage ’ in Galway was synonymous with the middle to upper end of the housing market .
169724	With an average three-bedroomed semi-detached fetching in the region of £55,000 , the typical Digital purchaser often dipped into the £70,000-£80,000 market .
169725	A frightening thought now for former workers looking at interest rates of close on 14 per cent .
169726	Even in the days when every dog on the street knew about the impending Digital closure , employees of the company were reluctant to talk publicly about their plight .
169727	The whole company ethos of keeping everything within the plant and of not talking to television or papers survived even when all seemed lost .
169728	The workers ' faith has not been repaid this week — in a region which had escaped many of the severe job cuts which had hit other cities .
169729	Now just 350 software jobs have survived the multinational hatchet .
169730	Other multinational companies like Thermo-King , Baird , Northern Telecom and Crown Control still survive in a city which has other major employers in third level education , hospitals and the tourist industry .
169731	Digital was always regarded in Galway with the same respect and awe as Cinderella had for her fairy godmother .
169732	The model plant , model workers who did n't need a union , jobs for life … but this fairy godmother forgot all about the happy ending .
169733	The 450,000sq ft factory on the edge of the world famous Ballybrit racecourse — Digital sponsored the richest race in the summer festival — had an influence which permeated into every corner of life in the city .
169734	In human terms the loss adds up to 800 jobs in Digital and 2,000 more depending directly on orders , supplies and service .
169735	In financial terms , the loss is estimated at £100 million per annum to the Irish economy .
169736	Not far from Digital a firm set up by the Rehabilitation Institute employing 60 people , some of them handicapped , supply packaging to Digital .
169737	‘ We have large sales to Digital and there are n't too many Digitals out there , ’ said Rehab company chief Hugh McNally .
169738	A small company in Galway called Standard Printers has a £2.5 million annual contract with Digital .
169739	Its boss , Michael Cunningham , now fears that some of his 71 staff will have to be let go .
169740	The car hire company Johnson Perrott at any one time has several hundred cars at Digital … the list goes on and on .
169741	Earlier this week , workers at the Galway plant flashed an electronic message to the Digital HQ in Maynard , Boston , USA .
169742	It was desperation stakes , a last throw of the dice , but workers in Ballybrit agreed to take a 10 per cent cut in wages , all to no avail .
169743	There is no bitterness towards Ayr in Galway .
169744	Everyone knows that in the contracting world of producing computer hardware it would always be a case of dog eat dog .
169745	Unfortunately for Galway , the perception is that Michael Heseltine had an Alsatian teamed up against an Irish poodle .
169746	Until about three weeks ago there had been a belief among Digital employees in Galway and the Industrial Development Authority in Ireland that Digital 's plant in Ayr would lose out .
169747	But in the words of the former Irish minister Bobby Molloy , who represents Galway City in the Irish Parliament : ‘ A major change occurred ’ .
169748	Last night in the ‘ Digital pubs ’ it did n't really matter any more whether Heseltine had offered a major defence contract inducement to the company .
169749	They saw little point in diagnosis after the patient had been placed in the coffin .
169750	Yesterday a dream died in Galway … a dream which had been born in the heady , optimistic days of the early 1970s when bright-eyed youngsters leaving school walked in the doors of the Digital plant and more often than not were given a job .
169751	By 10am on the morning of 25 February , 1993 , tears had taken the place of hope .

170012	Britain 's secret society
170013	MARK FISHER
170014	ON 19 February , MPs will vote on whether Britain should have a freedom of information act .
170015	The Right to Know Bill , which I am introducing in the House of Commons , would lift the blanket of official secrecy that so often keeps us in the dark .
170016	Take safety .
170017	After many of the recent disasters we later learned that the authorities knew there was a problem all along — but the public did n't .
170018	In 1985 more than 50 people died in a fire at Bradford City Football Club .
170019	Later it was discovered that the council had written to the club months earlier demanding action to deal with the hazard .
170020	But the correspondence was confidential .
170021	After the Marchioness river boat sank in the Thames in 1989 it was revealed that the ship that crashed into it — the Bowbelle — had been involved in three previous river accidents .
170022	The accident reports had been kept secret .
170023	After the 1987 fire at Kings Cross underground station which killed 31 people , the official inquiry reported : ‘ Many of the shortcomings … had in fact been identified before by the internal inquiries into escalator fires .
170024	They were also highlighted in reports by the fire brigade , police , and Railway Fire Prevention and Fire Safety Standards Committee . ’
170025	No-one knows whether openness could have prevented these tragedies .
170026	But if the public had known about the problems , they could have demanded improvements — and something might have been done .
170027	We should be able to see the files held on us by public authorities — to check that they are accurate and fair .
170028	But most of them are confidential .
170029	We can see what has been written on our medical records after November 1991 — but have no right to the earlier information .
170030	Nor can we see our social security or employment records .
170031	The Government refuses to publish reports showing whether the tobacco industry is keeping to the voluntary agreements that restrict tobacco advertising near schools .
170032	We can not see the official tests showing which cars cause least pollution or have the best safety features .
170033	Ministers refuse to publish the list of environmentally sensitive areas which RAF pilots are told to avoid during low flying exercises .
170034	The penalties handed down by police disciplinary hearings are secret .
170035	The Iraqgate affair demonstrates how secrecy lets Government get away with dangerous dishonesty .
170036	Ministers relaxed the guidelines on the exports of arms equipment to Iraq , but kept the new policy secret , to avoid criticism .
170037	Three businessmen were then prosecuted for selling Iraq machine tools for making weapons — but confidential documents showed that they had told ministers what they were doing and had been encouraged to carry on .
170038	One of them was actually working for the intelligence services .
170039	Yet the prosecution went ahead and ministers tried to suppress these documents .
170040	Unbelievably , the court was told that they would not help the defence case — a demonstrable falsehood that could have landed the three in jail .
170041	Not just the quality of public debate , but even our liberty , may depend on the right to know .
170042	Britain is one of the few democracies that still does n't have a freedom of information act .
170043	American , Australia , Canada , New Zealand , France , Denmark , Holland , Norway and Greece all have them — Sweden has had one for more than 200 years .
170044	Often we can learn more about Britain under the American information law than we can from Whitehall .
170045	The Right to Know Bill would open up the files of government and official bodies .
170046	Of course some information should be secret .
170047	The bill protects details of people 's private lives , and information which could harm defence , law enforcement or genuine commercial secrets .
170048	It also amends the Official Secrets Act to allow someone who had been prosecuted to argue that releasing information was in the public interest .
170049	It would give people the right to see their employment records .
170050	And it would force companies to say in their annual reports whether they had broken laws on consumer protection , safety , the environment and discrimination .
170051	The bill has the backing of MPs of all parties — but it is vital that they actually support it in the Commons on 19 February .
170052	If you care about your right to know , ask your MP to vote for it .

170090	JOSEPH Fernandez just sat there , his face sometimes reddening , all day .
170091	He is New York 's schools chancellor , head of the public schools system , and he found himself last week on public trial .

170102	The job was this .
170103	Fernandez was hired to end 20 years of chaos caused by decentralising New York 's huge school system .
170104	The notion was that communities should have a say in what was taught , and the hidden agenda was to end the undeclared war between predominantly white and Jewish teachers , and an increasingly black and Hispanic body of pupils .

170111	She also failed to notice the board had hired a teacher with convictions for exposing himself to schoolgirls , or ask why a probationary principal was still in place despite pleading guilty to a $21,000 welfare scam .

170209	There is great urgency to complete the work because of the well-publicised rapid and irreversible erosion of ancient cultures and environments .

170358	When judges lean too far towards leniency
170359	Prof Ross Harper supports legislation to give the Crown the right of appeal against sentence in Scotland
170360	SENTENCING is one of the most important functions of a judge .
170361	The word judge , for the purpose of this article , includes sheriffs and magistrates .
170362	They pass judgment on an accused taking into account the gravity of the crime and the circumstances of the accused .
170363	Sentences vary from an absolute discharge to life imprisonment , and include deferred sentence , admonition , probation , fines and community service .
170364	In Scotland , we do not have the English system of suspended sentences .
170365	In England , the Crown may apply to review a sentence — as they are contemplating in the recent case of rape where the accused was told to give £5OO to the victim ‘ for a holiday ’ .
170366	At present in Scotland there is no right of the Crown to appeal against too lenient a sentence .
170367	There is , however , a bill currently going through Parliament which will change that situation .
170368	Most often our judges are totally right .
170369	Unhappily , in some cases they are hopelessly wrong .
170370	Sometimes , judges have bad days .
170371	We all do .
170372	Sometimes , a judge will be particularly impressed by a mellifluous and seductive plea put up on behalf of an accused and will sentence leniently to the point of mistake .
170373	Sometimes , a judge may suffer from irrational horror at a particular case and sentence too severely — to the point of mistake .
170374	Mistakes can be made , and if we do not allow correction we are fooling ourselves .
170375	If a judge has slept badly , has had an indigestible breakfast , tripped over the cat , has been roundly abused by his wife and scolded by his children , or if his mind has been distracted by the children 's school reports , a narrow defeat at a curling match or whatever , he may be temporarily off form .
170376	Where probation is appropriate a prison sentence may mistakenly be imposed or vice versa .
170377	If the judge makes a mistake by imposing too severe a sentence , then the accused can , and often does , appeal to a higher court .
170378	If the High Court agrees that the sentence is too severe , then that sentence may be amended .
170379	This is proper , this is just and , as importantly , it is the law .
170380	But if a judge errs the other way and fines a rapist a few hundred pounds , or puts on probation a bank robber with previous convictions who clearly ought to go directly to jail , nothing happens .
170381	Simply because the Crown does not have a right of appeal against sentence .
170382	That is what the Government is changing .
170383	In my view , rightly so .
170384	Many argue that such an appeal by the Crown against too lenient a sentence is simply not cricket .
170385	If an accused person hears that he is going to be sentenced to one year in jail , it is argued that it would be distinctly unfair for a prosecutor to appeal .
170386	Personally , I am not in favour of mammoth jail sentences except for the deserving few — and that 's not so much a matter of punishment as a means of keeping society free from their future depredations .
170387	But society has an interest in the determination of the case .
170388	I readily acknowledge that in Scotland the Crown has no direct interest in sentence in as much as it does n't , in contrast with Russia or America , request the court to impose a specific sentence .
170389	The prosecutor presents the facts fairly and cogently to the judge who , after hearing the defence submissions , reaches a conclusion as to sentence .
170390	Whether the Crown should have an interest in sentence or not is , of course , another matter .
170391	I am personally seduced by the prospect of the Crown and the defence being able to agree a sentence prior to a plea , especially in the case of large complex fraud trials .
170392	But that 's another major debate .
170393	But why on earth should the Crown not be allowed to appeal ?
170394	If we accept that mistakes in sentencing can be made and accept that sentencing is a matter of considerable interest , importance and relevance to society , and accept that the prosecution represents society , then it is simply monstrous that an appeal does not lie at its hands .
170395	In many criminal cases there are victims — casualties of assault , rape , theft or fraud .
170396	Sentencing process encapsulates the interest of all .
170397	The victim does not have a special place in the criminal court .
170398	The victim is not represented , nor indeed necessarily consulted .
170399	The victim has no right of representation .
170400	Since sentencing is a matter of societal process and since we engage in an adversarial system , a right of appeal which is given to one side should not be denied to the other .
170401	By doing so , I readily acknowledge that we are changing , ever so slightly , the role of the Crown with regard to sentencing .
170402	I personally welcome that change .
170403	Sentencing is too important to be left in the hands of one person without recourse to a higher authority .
170404	While supporting change to allow the Crown the right of appeal against too lenient sentences , I would advocate another change .
170405	I abhor sentences being increased sneakily .
170406	And this can happen .
170407	When I was very young , and indeed Malcolm Rifkind , who was even younger , was my counsel , we represented two individuals who were charged with a serious assault .
170408	They were both old lags and were sentenced each to ten years imprisonment .
170409	We thought this was an exceptionally high sentence and both of them appealed .
170410	One of the accused withdrew his appeal , the other proceeded with it .
170411	His sentence was increased to one of 12 years !
170412	This , in my view , is totally wrong and contrary to my notions of natural justice .
170413	By all means let either side appeal , but you can not , in all conscience , increase the sentence of some poor beggar who avers , often acting with appropriate legal advice , that the sentence is already too high .
170414	Fair 's fair .

170462	SCHOOL pupils skipping classes to play with the latest piece of Sonic the Hedgehog software could find another computer is at work to track them down .
170463	Their absence may be noted by devices like ‘ optical mark readers ’ and ‘ swipe cards ’ which log them in and out of each lesson .

170465	The use of information technology to keep tabs on truants is receiving particular encouragement south of the Border , where the Department for Education is putting £8.6 million into stepping up the fight against truancy , while Scottish Office research has put emphasis on identifying the varied causes .
170466	Three main programmes have been tried and tested so far in schools and colleges on both sides of the Border .
170467	Smart cards are perhaps the best known of the devices in the fight against school-dodging and they also contribute to security and safety .
170468	The electronic identity cards are swiped through readers stationed in every classroom at the beginning of each lesson .
170469	The system , developed by the Dundee-based company Offcome Data , costs around £10,000 to install , including the computers , the readers and the cards .
170470	Its advantages include the virtual elimination of the time-consuming registering routine and its versatility .
170471	It can be used to gain access to libraries or computer rooms in the buildings .
170472	And in the event of fire , it offers immediate and reliable information on the number and location of people to be evacuated .
170473	Satisfied customers include Perth College of Further Education which installed the system five years ago .
170474	Jack Gardner , director of the management and information system unit at the college , says : ‘ We needed a faster and more accurate registration method and this works exceptionally well .
170475	Our main concern was not truancy , but our students still need to show high attendance to guarantee their fees .
170476	‘ The system invested them with this responsibility and there is no room for errors or excuses .
170477	We paid for it ourselves , but covered expenses by cutting soul-destroying administrative jobs which only involved keying in names . ’
170478	The system has its drawbacks as a response to school truancy .
170479	It would be quite easy for a pupil to swipe in several cards allowing his friends to truant .
170480	But its time-saving qualities — up to 30 minutes each day for each teacher — attracted the St George 's School for Boys in Southampton , which has been piloting the system for two years .
170481	DEPUTY head teacher Brian Musk says : ‘ We have actually saved money because the system saves the work of a teacher and a half .
170482	We are able to identify absentees immediately and use the extra time to tackle the problem with academic counselling .
170483	Our pupils are conscious of being awarded responsibility and there has been no abuse of the cards at all . ’
170484	The Optical Mark Reader , produced by Johnson and Pinnock , at £5,000 to £6,000 , is a cheaper and more effective way of keeping track of students .
170485	Its drawback is the time involved , as it requires teachers to take register at each lesson by marking pink sheets that are then read into an optical mark reader .
170486	Francis Howlett , of England 's National Council for Educational Technology , explains : ‘ The system can give teachers comprehensive information on attendance at the push of a button .
170487	That could include not only how often each pupil is absent , but also which lessons are being missed , which teachers are being avoided , and even which ones tend to be absent when the local football team plays at home . ’
170488	Robin Chambers , the principal of Stoke-Newington school in South London , where the programme has been used for two months , says : ‘ We are ironing out a few difficulties , for instance getting the individual answer sheet completed in the correct way and working out who has the time to do it .
170489	‘ But the machine saves a great deal of time in that it automatically produces statistics and its print-outs clearly show patterns in the absences .
170490	We are able to spot problems earlier on and take action . ’
170491	The most recent development in anti-truancy technology is the Electronic Attendance Registration System ( EARS ) , produced by Bronton Computers at prices varying between £8,000 and £15,000 .
170492	Teachers retain control of registration — keeping the important element of one-to-one contact — and perform it in the usual time , but instead of noting absences on paper , they feed the information directly onto a portable electronic register which then passes it to the central computer .
170493	The system will be piloted starting from next week by North Westminster Community school , in London , with funds provided by the local authority .
170494	According to Guy Corbet , from Broncom : ‘ EARS allows excellent cross-reference of attendance throughout the school at any time at a fingertip .
170495	Students are not given chances to cheat , disappearing after the first registration and retain personal contact with their teachers every day . ’
170496	Of course the system is expensive and while it saves paperwork it does not appear to reduce registration times as such .
170497	Meanwhile many secondary schools north of the Border are opting for a cheaper option , the Scottish Computerised School Administration Programme , or SCAMP .
170498	This is a set of databases which collect all the pupils ' details , from absences to courses taken and exam presentations .
170499	SCAMP speeds the process of filling the absences for the day and by 10am , the school has a complete map of absentees whom they can then begin to check on .
170500	Its main drawback is that it does not discriminate between authorised and unauthorised absences .
170501	But how do children react to this new electronic scrutiny ?
170502	‘ There 's scope for any system to be alienating and oppressive , ’ says Eric Blyth , director of the Centre for Educational Welfare Studies at Huddersfield University .
170503	‘ But we 're talking about a generation much more computer-literate than the last and today 's children are very unlikely to react badly . ’
170504	He does point out , however , that the technology simply measures attendance — it does not improve it .
170505	The answer to that may lie closer to home with parents .
170506	Eric Blyth says the best option is to use the technology along with efforts to make children want to be in school .
170507	White Hart Lane School in London used this approach when attendance had slumped to just 72 per cent .
170508	Paul White , the project manager , says : ‘ We have rooms set aside with comfy chairs , music and televisions where pupils can go during break or before school .
170509	We 've also introduced rewards for good attendance like pens and key rings , which are very popular — they 've even got ‘ street credibility ’ status . ’
170510	Since the pupil-friendly approach to truancy was introduced , attendance has improved by 15 per cent .
170511	There has also been an unexpected spin-off — teacher attendance at the school has improved by 5.1 per cent .
170512	The anatomy of a classroom truant
170513	WHATEVER our image of a truant may be — layabout , glue-sniffer , petty criminal — a recent report from the Scottish Office urges us to dispel a few misunderstandings about truancy .
170514	The term covers a vast range of reasons for not attending school , including phobias , parental pressure and the absence of realistic incentives for fourth-year leavers .
170515	Although poverty and family problems enhance the risk of truancy , this is not the major factor .

170517	Low motivation to attend school has very diverse causes : truants may be bored with unchallenging courses or scared by too demanding ones .
170518	In extreme cases they develop a real school phobia , for reasons ranging from bullying by classmates to schoolwork anxiety .
170519	Parental attitudes are fundamental in determining the response to truancy .
170520	Some parents may be encouraging their children to help at home or even take up work instead of going to school .
170521	For these reasons it is suggested that in tackling the problem , good monitoring arrangements should be coupled with an early involvement of school and parents .
170522	The report says home phone calls can be useful but only in high phone-ownership areas , and they may be regarded as intrusive .
170523	Home visiting is an expensive but helpful alternative for persistent truants .

170956	Swedish lesson
170957	J R Hall ( Points of View , 12 February ) is right to suggest that British Rail would be able to make a profit if the Government took full responsibility for funding the provision and maintenance of railway infrastructure as it does roads .
170958	This view is substantiated by experience in Sweden , where such an arrangement has existed since 1988 .
170959	As a result , the state railways turned a loss of 416 million kroner ( about £40 million ) that year into a profit of 28 million kroner the following year , which grew to 372 million kroner in 1990 and is expected to go on rising .
170960	The state railways pay a user charge to the track authority , which is broadly equivalent to the charges faced by road users and covers only about a third of total infrastructure costs .
170961	So successful has the state system been that it has lost only about 1 per cent of its operations to a private competitor under the system of tendering for the provision of local passenger services that was also introduced by the 1988 rail reforms .
170962	It is misleading , therefore , of the Government to hold up Sweden as a model for its madcap rail privatisation plans .
170963	Indeed , Swedish railway executives have publicly condemned the proposals as unworkable .

170966	But Mr Leckie must be partly right .

170968	Both these allergic conditions have the same underlying cause : a dysfunctioning immune system .
170969	Therefore all immunosuppressive factors can play a part .
170970	These include chemical allergens ( exhaust fumes and tobacco smoke among them ) , food allergens ( too often overlooked by asthma specialists ) , and physical and psychological stress .
170971	Their effects are cumulative ; there is no single answer in cell-mediated allergy .

170978	Infallible way to obtain release from military service
170979	As a former National Service army medical officer , I was much entertained by Albert Morris 's reminiscences ( ‘ Conscripts who altered the script ’ , 8 February ) , of the various ingenious methods used by unwilling conscripts to obtain their discharge from the service .
170980	Having spent some weeks in 1951 as medical officer to a basic training regiment in Aldershot , I recall with amusement many of the subterfuges and deceptions described by Albert Morris .
170981	However , I am surprised that he failed to mention persistent bed-wetting which , in my experience , was the one absolutely infallible method of obtaining release from military service .
170982	During my time in the army a regimental quartermaster who was repeatedly having to exchange soiled blankets would protest so vehemently to his commanding officer that drastic action had to be taken .
170983	This initially meant that the bed-wetter would be made to sleep in the guard-room , where during the night he would be wakened hourly for toilet purposes .
170984	If after perhaps two weeks of this regimen the bed-wetting continued , then the enuretic National Serviceman would probably be referred by the unit medical officer to the local military hospital for exclusion of urological , neurological or psychiatric disorders .
170985	This process , of course , usually meant several hospital visits , with consequent very welcome respite from tiresome and disagreeable activities such as drill parades , guard duties , cookhouse fatigues and physical training .
170986	These medical investigations hardly ever revealed any physical or mental abnormality and if the bed-wetter continued thereafter to deplete the quartermaster 's stock of blankets then the British Army had no answer to this situation other than to discharge him honourably from the service without a stain on his character , whatever there might be on his bedclothes .
170987	I do not know how the RAF dealt with bed-wetters in the days of National Service , but I am certain that even although the Royal Navy had abandoned hammocks not long after the Second World War , a persistent enuretic on board a warship would create even more serious problems than he could in an army barracks .

170991	Article 2 , which sets out the general areas of workers ' rights , simply spells out many rights that already exist in law , or have been present in well-unionised work places for years before Thatcherism .
170992	Article 6 reinforces the legal rights on equal pay obtained by women in this country , in 1970 .
170993	Without any exaggeration , it would be true to say that , apart from Tory ideologues , the overwhelming majority of people in this country would agree to this legislation , if they were given the chance to read it and in more simple terms .
170994	The Tories , and their ruling-class supporters , wish to keep the ordinary worker from knowing what the substance of this social chapter is , how it really just gives more backing to much of what they have already gained through industrial struggles for nearly 200 years , and the extension of these rights to every worker , especially the more isolated ones .
170995	The Tories want to trample over the workers , particularly through the instrument of unemployment which has already frightened workers into accepting wage cuts such as at Cambuslang .
170996	The social chapter would not provide any protection here as pay policy is excluded , apart from the equal pay issue ; but in terms of social security and employment conditions , it would be an important advance .
170997	However , what is most galling is the inactivity of the party which is supposed to represent labour .
170998	A high-powered focus on this issue , alongside the campaign on the health service , would undoubtedly have won the Labour Party the general election .
170999	Bridge across Labour 's class divide
171000	Should he stay or should he go ?
171001	Labour needs Tom Clarke to remain shadow Scottish secretary , says Peter Jones
171002	AT least one Labour MP , and probably a few more , think that Labour leader John Smith should ditch his troubled shadow Scottish secretary Tom Clarke , who went back to work in January after a three-month illness and promptly inflicted two unnecessary controversies upon himself .
171003	That Labour MP is , however , bound to be disappointed .
171004	It is not in Smith 's interests , or the Labour Party 's , for Clarke to be summarily dispatched like some allegedly politically incorrect Daily Mirror employee .
171005	For the issue at stake is not necessarily whether Clarke is good or bad at his job , something which is indeed a topic of conversation among MPs , not just among the media 's ‘ very well-paid political hacks ’ , as Clydesdale MP Jimmy Hood asserted this week .
171006	It has much more to do with control of the party 's thinking and its power structures ; the debate about modernisation of ideology and whether or not the Scottish party should become more or less independent of the rest of the UK Labour Party .
171007	These debates , especially the ideological one , are difficult enough for Smith to manage , and they would get worse in Scotland if Clarke was put to the sword .
171008	They would also be worse than the ruckus stirred up by Clarke 's remarks on firstly , the improbability of Labour being able to renationalise a privatised water industry , and secondly , the worthlessness of the Scottish financial industry .
171009	The first was a mistake which , all politicians will tell you , is easily made and relatively simple to correct with a few carefully worded statements and some abuse of the media .
171010	The second is not so easy to explain away , for it implied a fundamental incomprehension of the financial industry , many of whose 200,000 employees are Labour voters in marginal Edinburgh seats .
171011	And it is that point which has raised questions in the minds of some MPs who hitherto have been relatively happy with Clarke .
171012	Still , one bad speech does not merit a sacking .
171013	And although there are some MPs who think Clarke should go now to prevent any worse gaffes , it is only on past events rather than future possibilities that such decisions can be made .
171014	And certainly there would be the most almighty row if Clarke got the push .
171015	What was interesting about those MPs who were swift to defend him was that they come from the traditional working-class wing of the parliamentary party — people like Jimmy Hood , or Aberdeen North 's Bob Hughes .
171016	Now they are the sort of MPs who are most likely to support traditional Labour policies , which Clarke , on the hypothetical question of water renationalisation , was implicitly rejecting .
171017	Clearly , on the evidence of Hood 's letters of defence in the press this week , they support him , not because of what he says , but because of what he is — from , and still part of , a traditional working-class background .
171018	According to Hood , the criticisms of Clarke are ‘ born from jealousy and political snobbery ’ .
171019	It has to be said that there has been for some years within the Labour Party something of a class divide — a working-class element resentful of a middle-class takeover by lawyers and the like .
171020	The divide has been bridged in a number of ways , one being shadow Cabinet elections putting people like Tom Clarke or John Prescott into the upper echelons .
171021	Neil Kinnock also bridged that divide , but John Smith is definably and obviously on the middle-class side of it .
171022	Smith therefore needs people like Tom Clarke in the shadow Cabinet .
171023	Turf him out of it , and the debate between ‘ traditionalists ’ and ‘ modernisers ’ could well turn into a conflagration .
171024	The row over what Labour would do with the water industry is a graphic first flare-up in that debate .
171025	It is potentially hugely divisive given the Scottish party 's left-wing sensibilities , but less so if working-class traditionalists like Clarke can go down Smith 's route to modernity .
171026	The water debate , when couched in terms of the Scottish party 's rights to determine policy in specifically Scottish areas , also directly affects the current internal demands for more Scottish party autonomy , even unto independence .
171027	This argument , that the Scottish party should elect its own leader , raise its own funds , hire and fire its own staff and sit in a Westminster coalition with the English and Welsh Labour Party , is something which acutely interests a few hundred activists , but not many MPs , and one guesses , precious few voters .
171028	But if John Smith was cavalierly hiring and firing the shadow Scottish secretary , some more MPs might start taking an interest , which would be wholly undesirable in the leader 's office .
171029	So Clarke will stay .
171030	But he has done himself some damage and will need to work hard , and with some care , if he is to secure re-election to the shadow Cabinet in November .
171031	For , according to the soundings taken by The Scotsman this week , he would not win re-election now .
