171157	Setting a peaceful precedent
171158	JOHN HOME ROBERTSON
171159	WORDS and pictures can not describe the disaster that is unfolding in former Yugoslavia .
171160	History will deliver a harsh judgment on the politicians and warlords who are fermenting this chaos but I doubt if there are enough prison cells in Europe to hold all the war criminals .
171161	And we should not forget that ham-fisted European diplomacy contributed to the re-balkanisation of the Balkans by hastening to recognise unrecognisable states .
171162	We can not abandon people to the horrors of primitive siege warfare , so the ramshackle institutions of the United Nations will have to be drastically overhauled to cope with this crisis and others like it which are festering in an increasingly unstable world .
171163	The official mandate of the United Nations Protection Force is to ‘ ride shotgun ’ with relief convoys , but the British battalion has stretched that mandate into a peacemaking role .
171164	It is no criticism of the French , Spanish , Canadian and other contingents that the circumstances in their sectors have not permitted such tactics , but if the Vance-Owen plan is to be implemented we will need to apply the pro-active approach which is being pioneered by the Cheshire Regiment .
171165	Characteristically , and with the benefit of years of experience in Ulster , this UK infantry regiment has extended its presence and its influence well beyond its camps and convoys .
171166	Their supporting Engineers are making roads , rebuilding bridges and the Cheshires are imposing their influence on local factions by both persuasion and force .
171167	That has meant returning fire to suppress Croats and others who fire on the UN force .
171168	It has also involved brokering deals to reduce tension in other areas .
171169	This , together with patrolling and gathering intelligence about the area , means that the UK element of UNPROFOR is doing the groundwork for implementation of the Vance-Owen settlement plan .
171170	That has been achieved despite the restricted terms of the UN Resolution ; despite hopelessly inadequate and confused UN structures ; and also despite the half-hearted attitude of British ministers at the outset .
171171	But for the initiative of General Morillon and his transplanted European NATO staff , and of the individual units in UNPROFOR and various aid agencies , the whole operation would be hopelessly bogged down .
171172	Indeed , it is going to be bogged down unless the UN can get things moving with political and military action to make the peace plan work .
171173	Things are bad enough now but if there is no sign of progress towards a settlement , the people who are still giving friendly waves to UN troops are likely to start throwing stones as they do in Northern Ireland .
171174	The UN must start driving the momentum towards peace .
171175	Indeed if they fail to take the initiative they might as well abandon the people of the area to a grim fate .
171176	Two things are required : substantially more UN forces , almost certainly including Americans , and a UN supremo with direct authority from the Secretary General to drive the political , diplomatic , humanitarian and military process forward .
171177	While US forces are needed , Yugoslavia is no place for a massive ‘ Stormin' Norman ’ style of operation .
171178	The terrain and the highly armed militias would soon remind them of Vietnam .
171179	The Americans would be well advised to learn from the British and others who have experience in the area .
171180	And the operation must be seen to be multinational , so the UK contingent should ideally be increased to brigade strength — which underlines the case for reprieving the Highland regiments .
171181	The need for better coordination can not be overstated .
171182	With inadequate communications between UN units , rudimentary command and control structures , governments interpreting the UN resolution in different ways , relief supplies being administered through a totally separate UN agency , and the Vance-Owen initiative developing at another level altogether , it is hardly surprising that the international effort can appear confused .
171183	Boutros Boutros-Ghali must get the Security Council to agree an effective new Resolution and to appoint a special representative with comprehensive authority to do whatever is necessary to make a settlement work .
171184	A top flight soldier with diplomatic skills would fit the bill .
171185	We have avoided mass starvation in former Yugoslavia this winter ; some time has been bought and soldiers and relief agencies have begun to develop strategies to begin to restore order .
171186	It is vital that the United Nations should now act on that groundwork and drive the peacemaking process forward .
171187	It is going to be difficult and expensive , but the only alternative is to abandon millions of people to an even worse fate .
171188	If the UN can set a precedent for peacemaking in the Balkans we will have a real peace dividend .
171189	John Home Robertson is Labour MP for East Lothian
171190	Hoover : he merchandised the invented notion of the G-Men , the Feds from the FBI
171191	J Edgar Hoover was America 's top cop , is honoured as a national hero , but now the secret 's out .
171192	Michael Pye reports on the truth about the G-Man
171193	The dirt on Hoover
171194	THEY 'RE running the director of the FBI out of town as I write .
171195	William Webster stands accused of making phone calls on the company 's phones , lending his limo to his wife , taking holidays on official planes and official time .
171196	These irregularities amount , say his bosses at the Justice Department , to a scandal .
171197	They must have forgotten Hoover .
171198	J Edgar Hoover led the FBI from 1924 until 1971 — the nation 's top cop , a movie-house hero , presiding over incorruptible straight arrows who saved America from Commies , thugs , hoodlums and perverts .
171199	He 's honoured as a national hero , he has a shrine in a Washington Masonic temple , he carried to his grave the tributes and the written gratitude of every president he ever served ( at least one , Gerald Ford , was his informer ; so was Ronald Reagan ) .
171200	He was a keeper and dealer in secrets ; it 's not surprising the truth about him has emerged only slowly .
171201	But with Anthony Summers 's new book , Official and Confidential : The Secret Life of J Edgar Hoover , we have at last everything everyone says about J Edgar Hoover , including some of the wilder tales .
171202	It claims more originality than it packs , but it is still a primer in the gap between actual virtue , and the official kind .
171203	For Hoover did n't just make phone calls , or misuse a limo .
171204	He had his house painted by the FBI Exhibits Section , listed his black servants as FBI agents , profited from books he had FBI employees write under his name .
171205	His agents were as incorruptible , untouchable as any police force in the world ; but Hoover bet with the Mob , took stock market favours , took free holidays from dubious businessmen .
171206	He could be hysterical , and he kept power well into senility .
171207	He faked much of his struggle with the gangsters , and failed in his wartime duty to fight imminent subversion ; after the war , his genius was to stir up subversion he could quash .
171208	He manufactured information and leaked it , sometimes ruining people .
171209	And he was obsessed with deviants , with queers — this man with prissy steps and heavy perfume .
171210	The male nudes in his parlour were balanced carefully by female ones in the games room .
171211	His office desk was supplied with Playboy as well as more esoteric porn .
171212	But , Summers insists , his deputy Clyde Tolson was also his lover .
171213	The two men took lunch and dinner together every day , went on holiday together , were seen ( once , and 50 years ago , by one person ) holding hands in a limo ; the evidence is only circumstantial .
171214	But Summers suggests , ambitiously , that there was solid evidence which , he claims , was what stopped Hoover tackling the Mob before it came to awesome power in America .
171215	Perhaps the hero cop was blackmailed into letting crime really pay .
171216	Summers is assiduous in research , but less interested in politics ; there are sides of Hoover 's story whose ordinariness he misses because he finds them so shocking .
171217	But one theme does emerge from this , as from other Hoover biographies in the past two years .
171218	J Edgar Hoover was the cop who hated liberty .
171219	We 're still suffering from the liberties he took .
171220	CONSIDER what J Edgar Hoover did for freedom .
171221	He card-indexed half a million radicals just after the First World War , sent agents to intimidate newspapers which dared suggest , in the Thirties , that the banks were not entirely sound , arrested fighters in the Spanish Civil War long after the war was done .
171222	He sent his men to infiltrate homosexual groups and smoke out deviants .
171223	His agents leaned on lowly college professors to stay away from groups Hoover did n't like ; otherwise their files went to their colleges , full of raw gossip .
171224	He recorded Martin Luther King with women , and then tried , astoundingly , to present King as a homosexual .
171225	Perhaps he wanted to feel this moral force of a man was really no better , no finer than him .
171226	He inflamed the Black Panthers to violence and encouraged the Jewish Defence League to violence against the Black Panthers .
171227	He tried to arm anti-war activists in the Vietnam era .
171228	He investigated feminists as subversives .
171229	For he was terrified of social change , any change .
171230	Paranoia was a passion with him and he knew , just knew , the worst .
171231	If the radicals could n't think of something violent to do , his men would make suggestions .
171232	If his targets were n't killers , he 'd send guns .
171233	From the start of his authority to investigate subversives , in 1939 , the pattern was set : his first raids caught an unlovely bunch of anti-Semites , whose inspiration and weapons both came from a paid FBI informant .
171234	His campaign lasted 50 years , deforming American politics , imposing a queasy notion of Americanism that was very close to 19th century nativism .
171235	Its roots were personal as well as political .
171236	Hoover was a meticulous , fussy man , determinedly cold , who thought control was the condition of his survival .
171237	As a boy , friends said he was in love with the cadet corps .
171238	As a man , he followed orders ardently .
171239	He could n't cope with imperfections — a leaf on his driveway , a smear on his shining shoes .
171240	Life , to him , was a most deliberate business .
171241	You can dredge in his childhood for the reasons .
171242	His father went mad , and was confined to an asylum ; maybe that was the disorder Hoover feared .
171243	Or it may have been the sweet tyranny of his mother 's childhood rules , never quite outgrown , which he tried to recreate in his rigid adult life .
171244	Or it may simply have been that he was hiding : that his confused sexuality could at any time have brought him down .
171245	At all events , his paranoia had resonances for most Americans .
171246	You have to remember a nation where new immigrants were constantly adjusting the culture , the language , the sounds and smells on the street , and where new ideas — like socialism , like anarchism or Bolshevism — were associated with literal newcomers .
171247	‘ America ’ seemed constantly at risk .
171248	That feeling started Hoover 's grand career , in 1919 .
171249	Revolution was an imminent fact .
171250	Lenin came in loud and clear .
171251	The nation had been buffeted by a wave of strikes .
171252	Someone set a bomb at the house of the US Attorney General .
171253	In this fearful atmosphere , Hoover was hired for the Department of Investigation .
171254	His job was to make a card index of suspect radicals — anyone who wrote or talked against government .
171255	Hoover threw himself into the campaign .
171256	He presented the case for deporting Emma Goldman , feminist and anarchist , and sailed out into New York harbour to taunt her when she was loaded on a troopship bound for Russia .
171257	He made himself the centre for information during the Red Raids that followed , brutal nights when civil liberties were swept aside .
171258	On 2 January 1920 , more than 10,000 people were arrested in 23 cities .
171259	Almost all of them were released without charge , much later .
171260	Their files , though , stood against them for ever .
171261	And Hoover added to those files : he investigated any lawyers who dared defend those arrested .
171262	He called Felix Frankfurter , later a Justice of the Supreme Court , ‘ a disseminator of Bolshevik propaganda ’ in a report which he later tried to disown .
171263	He had learned two valuable lessons when , in 1924 , he became head of the Bureau of Investigations .
171264	Fear can break political movements ; the Communist Party of America , a paper threat at best , lost 14,000 of its 20,000 members in a year .
171265	And power lies in the files , in knowing , and making sure the knowledge can not be checked or shared .
171266	You do n't even need a secret to fear being found out .
171267	TO this devil 's brew , Hoover added one more twist : publicity .
171268	He 'd weigh uselessly into investigations , like the kidnapping of the Lindbergh baby ; he accused a pigeon of being a criminal 's homing pigeon , to the shock of the ordinary cops .
171269	He merchandised the invented notion of the G-Men , the ‘ Government men ’ , the Feds from the FBI .
171270	His columnist chums built up the Dillingers and Machine Gun Kellys of America , the small-time hoods , and the G-Men , with some difficulty , took them out .
171271	The publicity and the facts were not always the same .
171272	Hoover kept Dillinger 's gun in his office , but the serial number shows it was made after Dillinger was dead .
171273	Always , the hero of these stories was Hoover .
171274	He burnished his reputation into cultism , as a White House report complained in the Seventies .
171275	He invented the policeman as national hero , a notion which is conservative and deeply perverse ; it implies the best a society can do is to resist disorder .
171276	His fame is odder still when you consider this : Hoover was chasing small-time hoods at a time when organised crime was building an empire on Prohibition and its consequences .
171277	Hoover did nothing to prevent the Mob taxing business in America , running drugs , vice and gambling .
171278	Maybe he was a man so obsessed with hidden things that he simply could n't see open criminality — which looked like business and politics almost as usual .
171279	Hoover , the super-cop , had to be compelled by circumstances — the discovery of Mob bosses conferring in upstate New York in 1957 — even to acknowledge that the Mafia exists .
171280	Within two years , he 'd already tried to forget .
171281	Or maybe he knew that the Mob had files of their own , that Meyer Lansky , the one-time bootlegger and now the gambling mogul , had pictures which could ruin him : Edgar and Clyde , for once unambiguously tangled .
171282	Summers says so , but he has n't seen the pictures , and there are always problems with stories that emphasise the power of Meyer Lansky ; he became a kind of bogeyman , credited with old crimes to boost a reputation which helped people do what the Mob wanted .
171283	Besides , rumours of pictures like this abound , usually seen by rivals in intelligence services ; was Meyer Lansky bad at keeping secrets , even when a secret kept the head of the FBI in his power ?
171284	Hoover was certainly , Summers shows , spectacularly indifferent to those straight arrow standards he set for his agents .
171285	He gambled at a time when the Mob ran gaming , and he never expected to lose .
171286	He invested in oil companies , thanks to his buddies , and his investments were always covered ; at his death , there were rumours of secret investment accounts .
171287	He hung out with the likes of Lewis Rosentiel , a booze tycoon who had invested in Lansky 's casinos .
171288	And this association is the one which produces Summers 's most bizarre evidence .
171289	Rosentiel 's fourth wife Susan spent ten years trying to divorce him , a decade of singular bitterness , involving his perjury and attempts to jail her .
171290	She was willing to give evidence about his Mob links in 1970 ; today , she says he was an enthusiastic bisexual who involved J Edgar Hoover in sexual orgies just as the Kennedys were trying to make him take action against the Mob .
171291	As you judge her story , you may care to remember her considerable grievances .
171292	She says she was taken to the Plaza Hotel , to a party where Hoover sat in a fine black frock and insisted on being called ‘ Mary ’ ; after a while , he retired to the bedroom to be petted by two bought boys , one of whom prudently wore rubber gloves .
171293	If you wanted to invent a perfectly stereotyped queer , this is the story you 'd tell — down to the name ‘ Mary ’ and the fact that his sexual partners were young , and prostitutes .
171294	And just after the supposed orgy , as Summers admits but in an end-note , the FBI began heavy surveillance of Meyer Lansky — supposedly the blackmailer-in-chief .
171295	But if this really was the sum of Hoover 's sexuality — sad , mean and sporadic , a slight release from the need to control himself utterly — he seems almost pitiable .
171296	It helps explain his fixation on the details of other people 's erotic lives , the keyhole stuff that filled his files , the anger — envy , perhaps — which made him project homosexuality onto all manner of public figures .
171297	For J Edgar Hoover , happiness was just another kind of disorder .
171298	AT first , the politicians thought they could run Hoover .
171299	At the request of FDR , Hoover opened files on anyone who opposed the president 's line on national defence and tried to intimidate press critics like the Chicago Tribune .
171300	FDR allowed Hoover , an official , to by-pass Cabinet members and come directly to the president ; in time , this back channel made Hoover uncontrollable .
171301	And he extended Hoover 's powers .
171302	Wiretapping , technically illegal , was first authorised in 1940 ( the FBI had used it , of course , before that ) .
171303	What Hoover could not do , as usual , was the real job .
171304	For that , he needed not just hundreds of incorruptible field agents writing down what they overheard , but also analysts able to detect when people were joking ; some of the oddest accusations , like Eleanor Roosevelt 's supposed affair with two lefty trades unionists , come from the agents ' innocence of dirty jokes .
171305	Hoover could n't even see the point of intelligence reports which showed Japan 's interest in how to attack a deep harbour , and how deep Pearl Harbour might be .
171306	The OSS , fore-runner of the CIA , was born out of his obtuseness , and remained his bitter rival .
171307	Hoover feuded with the CIA for decades and even , in 1970 , shocked Washington by breaking relations between the agencies altogether .
171308	That 's a reason , incidentally , for caution on stories of photographs glimpsed at the end of dinners for OSS veterans — the pictures of Edgar on his knees , making love to Clyde .
171309	If they exist , these pictures come from specialists in disinformation with a grudge .
171310	But for all his incompetence in wartime , Hoover was now settled in the Washington game — privileged , sanctified , unbudgeable and with more and more information to use .
171311	He 'd tell presidents about their appointees , promise appointees and Senators he 'd suppressed their files , let certain papers know — on plain paper , in plain envelopes — what he 'd overheard or snatch-shot or been told .
171312	This power , Summers says , was what brought Lyndon Johnson — Hoover 's old ally , even though he called him ‘ that queer bastard ’ — onto the ticket with John Kennedy in 1960 .
171313	Hoover knew how the Mob helped Kennedy buy votes ; more to the point , he knew about Kennedy 's skirt-chasing .
171314	The Kennedy brothers went away to consider who 'd be vice-president , and named their loudest rival , LBJ .
171315	They promised never to tell why but it was , Summers says , Hoover 's blackmail .
171316	By now , Hoover was a politicians ' nightmare — perceived by some as the perfect cop , but known at close range for his rants , his sexual obsessions , his card index and his file cabinets which by now contained all the sins , real and imagined , of the political world .
171317	‘ He 's rather a psycho , ’ Robert Kennedy said , off the record , in 1964 .
171318	‘ I think he 's become senile , and rather … frightening . ’
171319	But the Kennedys needed his special protection racket — to destroy phone company records when Marilyn Monroe committed suicide , for example , or to leak FBI reports that disproved stories suggesting John Kennedy , the good Catholic boy , was actually on his second marriage .
171320	And when Kennedy was shot , the ‘ psycho ’ Hoover botched the FBI investigation personally , ignoring evidence that there might have been more than a single gunman involved , sending agents to question the background of the Warren Commission 's staff , punishing his own agents for failing to spot Oswald 's violent nature .
171321	He went from briefing the new president that evidence against Oswald was too weak for a conviction to insisting that Oswald was the man .
171322	It 's tempting to scent conspiracy — did Hoover stall investigations which might lead to the Mob , who held those compromising pictures ? — but there 's no need .
171323	What we have here is a senile man , desperate to be right ; his story is all that holds the world together , he just knows .
171324	His whole life was his office .
171325	When Nixon threatened to take it away , Hoover , without warning or symptoms , died .
171326	Summers drops hints about murder , or suicide , but the truth may be simpler and more terrible : Hoover was not a breath more than his job .
171327	It did not take burglars and curious poisons to dispose of him .
171328	AT the funeral , the flag that draped Hoover 's coffin was presented to Clyde Tolson ; there was , after all , no widow .
171329	It was a curiously graceful , open moment in a history of secrets .
171330	But to all who valued Hoover , of course , it could n't mean a damn thing .

171507	‘ If there are any advantages it comes from the background .
171508	The reaction from the other side of the table is different because you are a woman , they expect you to do it a different way . ’
171509	Buckley probably does do it differently , working towards less confrontation and for a solution that will last .
171510	‘ That does n't mean they will get an easier deal , ’ she laughs .
171511	The bruised executives of British Coal would testify to that after their run-in over the coal contract which ended up in court .
171512	Buckley is unrepentant , arguing that what remains of the Scottish coal industry now has a more secure future .
171513	‘ Somebody had to take a stand .
171514	We were expected to put our hands in our pockets and shell out regardless of whether or not we were getting value for money .
171515	Perhaps we were seen as abrasive because we had the courage to say what everyone else was thinking . ’
171516	Buckley has been in this job since 1988 and in the department since 1981 , but she started as a lawyer in private practice , a profession where equality is far more of a reality than in industry .
171517	She joined the old South of Scotland Electricity Board in 1976 as a legal assistant — the first female solicitor it had employed — but by 1980 wanted to do something different and went back to university with the company 's blessing ( and a scholarship ) to get an MBA .
171518	When she came back she was put into contracts and purchasing in the knowledge that she was a potential candidate for management succession , although no promises were made .
171519	‘ I was the right person in the right place at the right time . ’
171520	Buckley says she has never been aware of a problem of discrimination in the company , at least in a corporate sense , ‘ but I think a lot of men found it a problem ’ .
171521	‘ When I first started going to open-cast sites I was unusual and it was pretty well guaranteed to stop operations in their tracks . ’
171522	Going first meant that Buckley did not have any role models or even mentors .
171523	‘ I just look at whoever is in the job ahead .
171524	It is a question of whether they are good at managing .
171525	If they are you use them as a role model . ’
171526	She knows that by virtue of her position many women see her as a role model and so is happy to give advice when asked for it .
171527	Any problems she has encountered have not been because of her gender , but because she has had older people working for her .
171528	‘ What happens when women engineers come through may be a different matter .
171529	They are dealing with power station staff and other engineers who do n't make any allowances for you .
171530	If you get sat on it is because you allow yourself to be sat on .
171531	It is not because you are female . ’
171532	In any case she thinks it is just a matter of time before more women start coming through to senior levels , both because the company is taking on more female graduates and because they are a pretty self-confident lot anyway .
171533	‘ One of the women who works for me is one of the toughest women I have ever come across , and most of the women graduates are more than competent .
171534	There are a lot of good young women coming up . ’
171535	WHERE difficulties can occur is in the matter of families .
171536	Buckley , who is unmarried , admits that being successful in business is easier for a woman who has no children .
171537	It is still assumed that it is the woman who will give up work to look after the children or take time off if they are sick , she admits .
171538	‘ If you are going to be in senior job you are going to put a lot of time in so you give up your social life a bit perhaps .
171539	You feel pressure not to be seen to fail in the job .
171540	You have got to show you are at least as good and a little bit extra to cover your back . ’
171541	Like many women who have crashed through the glass ceiling — or , perhaps , ignored it — she is strongly opposed to positive discrimination in favour of women and has little time for the argument that women do n't succeed because they are women .
171542	‘ It is almost certainly the case you have to do a little bit extra because you are female but you do n't have to prove you are twice as good . ’

171545	Buyer of all she surveys : Grace Buckley finds coal comfort
171546	No skirting the issue of inequality on high
171547	Why is the fairer sex so unfairly represented in the top echelons ?
171548	PETER WOODIFIELD reports on the assault on the invisible barriers and speaks to one woman who has bypassed them
171549	CHANGING attitudes to women in business is like changing course in a giant tanker .
171550	Everything happens slowly but eventually change becomes apparent as more business leaders realise the nonsense of wasting the talents of a large chunk of their workforce .
171551	The problem has been particularly acute in the top echelons where the blue and grey suits are rarely disturbed by a skirt .
171552	Just 0.5 per cent of Britain 's company directors are women .
171553	In 1991 the Government launched Opportunity 2000 in an attempt to encourage industry and commerce to take the issue seriously and the past two years have seen two of Britain 's top 15 companies — BTR and Sainsbury — appoint female finance directors .
171554	But the focus on women at the top has tended to focus on entrepreneurs such as Anita Roddick and Scotland 's Pat Grant and Ann Gloag .
171555	At least that way there is no way you can be held back by the so-called ‘ glass ceiling ’ — the phrase coined in the United States to describe the invisible barriers that allow women to rise only so far in an organisation .
171556	On 9 March the Scottish division of the Institute of Directors , with Lothian and Edinburgh Enterprise and supported by The Scotsman , is holding a seminar in Edinburgh to discuss the issue , covering not just the boardroom but also senior levels of management .
171557	The IoD 's Scottish membership , 68 women of 1,640 members , underlines the point .
171558	Donald Hardie , the Scottish director of the IoD , feels the problem stems from the education system , with girls being discouraged from studying the subjects that would get them on to the business ladder .
171559	‘ The problem is that they are not there to be promoted . ’
171560	That is by and large true , but Hardie is not certain that men have taken it on board and he is keen for plenty of men to attend to get a better understanding of the position .
171561	But while there may a shortage of suitable female candidates , it also becoming clear that there are women who have made it precisely because they refuse to be deflected from their chosen career .
171562	Indeed , one of the speakers at the IoD seminar is Lesley Bale , the managing director of Aberdeen Airport at the tender age of 33 .
171563	For her and others like her it is a question of wanting it sufficiently , being prepared to put in the work and not expecting concessions because they are women .
171564	The glass ceiling does not exist because they do n't let it .
171565	But not all women are like that .
171566	Too many allow themselves to be steered into what are seen as traditionally female jobs , or suffer discrimination if and when they have children .
171567	Women also tend to have a different , more consensual style of management , and often dislike playing by the corporate rules that are invariably laid down by men .
171568	Douglas Kinnaird , of PA Consultants and one of the UK 's top headhunters , makes the point that quite often women do n't realise how hard promotion is to get and that men have worked for it for months , if not years .
171569	‘ If they want to get promoted they have got to fight tooth and nail .
171570	They have got to find out the rules and then fight by the rules . ’
171571	A failure to realise just how tough it is means such women are held back more by their own glass hat than any supposed glass ceiling .
171572	One reality that can not be avoided in the whole discussion is children .
171573	There is still an unspoken assumption that it will be the women who make the sacrifices when it comes to childcare and it is perhaps the thickest glass ceiling of all for many women .
171574	Government statistics show that 74 per cent of women in managerial and administrative positions have no children , and that is hardly likely to be a coincidence .
171575	As it is , women hold barely more than a quarter of all managerial and administrative posts , yet make up nearly half the workforce .
171576	In the longer term , that particular barrier is likely to disappear through sheer economic necessity on the part of business .
171577	Graduate recruitment in many businesses and industries now tends to be evenly split , and companies will not be able to afford to lose a large chunk of talent in which so much money has been invested , especially as women in any case tend to be less tempted by the ‘ grass is greener ’ syndrome .
171578	But all that being said , there is a real problem right now .
171579	Kinnaird , who is chairing the seminar , says he is regularly asked to find a woman for a senior management job ‘ all other things being equal ’ .
171580	The trouble is that things are not equal , and he can hardly remember placing a woman in such a job .
171581	A headhunter for ten years , Kinnaird has just been commissioned by his first female client , which speaks volumes .
171582	It is hardly surprising that he can not find the people he is looking for when even the largest organisations have so few senior women .
171583	The Royal Bank of Scotland has a record in this field to be proud of , being a founder member of Opportunity 2000 and also one of just 150 companies entitled to call themselves Investors in People .
171584	It has also just won its second national training award .
171585	Now 30 per cent of its junior management are women , although that figure falls away to a paltry 1 per cent at the highest levels .
171586	The Royal has committed itself to increase that significantly in the next few years .
171587	Dr Mike Mosson , director personnel at the Royal Bank , says the bank has a policy of ‘ positive assistance ’ and ‘ positive encouragement ’ towards women , although he insists that it falls short of positive discrimination .
171588	For some time it has had career breaks to help women ( and occasionally men ) with family needs and he says it has been successful .
171589	But while corporately the bank has adopted a positive approach , Mosson admits this is not always reflected in individual behaviour .
171590	He admits to being surprised at the split attitudes of middle-aged men — and even some of the younger ones — who want their daughters to have a proper career structure but then fail to apply that belief at work .
171591	‘ We are winning in the sense we are finding it easier for women to make progress in the organisation and they are not the exception any more .
171592	I do n't think we are moving fast enough , but being realistic we are winning . ’
171593	Most organisations are not so far advanced .
171594	Perhaps more typical is Scottish &amp; Newcastle , which has a high proportion of female workers .
171595	Henry Fairweather , group personnel and services director , acknowledges that most of its female managers are in areas one might expect such as marketing , information services and personnel .
171596	‘ We have some in more traditional areas such as production but not as senior as we would like . ’
171597	S&amp;N 's executive committee has recently approved an initiative to find out what the situation is and is preparing an attitude survey to identify what managers are really thinking and what the problems are perceived to be .
171598	At the moment , less than 10 per cent of S&amp;N 's senior managers are women , but none of them are directors of any of the subsidiaries , let alone of the main board .
171599	Like the Royal Bank it is not setting specific targets .
171600	‘ At the end of the day it comes down to individual decisions about individual jobs , ’ says Fairweather .
171601	‘ What we have to do is create a culture in which appointing women to senior jobs is easier , ’ he says .
171602	That may not be as difficult as S&amp;N or anyone else fears given that women 's more consensus-based approach to management is increasingly seen to be an appropriate style of management .
171603	‘ By encouraging people to manage in a certain way you make it seem more appropriate to appoint women . ’
171604	That may seem a softly-softly approach , but by making aspiring women managers and executives feel more comfortable with the management culture , it could prove effective in shattering the glass ceiling .

171651	Belarus makes each-way bet on race to capitalism
171652	One former Soviet republic is hoping for market reform , minus the Russian example of ‘ shock therapy ’ .
171653	ALEXANDER TKACHENKO reports
171654	THE former Soviet republic of Belarus is hedging its bets on economic reform with a mixture of market moves and old-style administrative measures that makes Western analysts sceptical .
171655	Government officials say they aim to reform the economy gradually while shielding the country 's ten million people from the pain of full-blooded ‘ shock therapy ’ as attempted in Russia and elsewhere .
171656	‘ We live in a period of transition to the market .
171657	Shock methods can provoke instability in society , that is why we will continue to correct reforms in the interests of the majority of the population , ’ said first deputy prime minister Mikhail Myasnikovich .
171658	The government 's approach is reflected in a 1993 budget allocating 60 per cent of expenditure to social welfare and 20 per cent to farm subsidies .
171659	State orders , the pillar of the old communist system , will vary between different industries from 19 per cent to 53 per cent of production .
171660	More than half of all prices will be regulated .
171661	But Western analysts are wondering out loud whether such an approach can work .
171662	‘ The Belarus economy is heading for a shock this year .
171663	People in government are unwilling to understand clear , simple things , ’ said one economist in the capital Minsk .
171664	Belarus , formerly Byelorussia , was the fourth most powerful republic of the Soviet Union and accounted for 5 per cent of national income ; 40 per cent of the economy worked in the defence sector , and the republic also specialised in meat production and machine building .
171665	Politically conservative , Belarus earlier this month lifted a ban imposed on the Communist Party following the failed Kremlin coup of August 1991 .
171666	Most of the population is Russian-speaking and Russia is the country 's closest economic partner .
171667	Belarus has persuaded Moscow to sell it 16 million tonnes of oil this year — almost as much as the 20 million tonnes Russia will supply to Ukraine , whose economy and energy needs are much bigger .
171668	But rises in the price of that Russian oil forced Belarussian inflation up to 45 per cent for the month of December , prompting the national bank to double its key interest rate in January to 30 per cent .
171669	Production over 1992 fell by 9 per cent , compared with a slump of about 20 per cent in Russia .
171670	The budget deficit was a moderate 4.3 per cent , helping to make Belarus 's economic performance one of the best in the former Soviet Union .
171671	Officials maintain that living standards here are higher than elsewhere in the former superpower , but rationing exists for cereals , sugar , butter , flour , petrol and other basic goods .
171672	‘ This is a result of strict government efforts .

171675	He said new businesses were fleeing Belarus to other countries because of its taxes of 22 per cent on profits and 28 per cent VAT .

171677	‘ Our people do n't like to make unreasoned decisions , ’ he said recently .
171678	Mr Myasnikovich said the government aimed to carry out price liberalisation , privatisation and structural transformation of the economy to reduce dependence on Russian oil .
171679	‘ Belarus will continue to move resolutely to market reforms , ’ he said .
171680	The deputy premier said there was no way back to the former Soviet Union .
171681	‘ But the whole world seeks integration and we also want it , first of all with Russia . ’

171683	‘ The Belarussian government does not want to take responsibility for the results of market reforms .

171698	After coming up with the idea of the specialised oil , Augusto Odone contacted a dozen scientists around the world working on myelin repair .

171700	‘ I told them to stop competing .

171702	Now the Odones have raised more than $1 million for the Myelin Project , directed by Augusto from Washington DC .
171703	Prof Sargent , head of the school of natural sciences at Stirling , said yesterday the Odones had defied much scepticism from medical and scientific experts and had beaten seemingly impossible odds to find a treatment which had kept Lorenzo alive .
171704	Prof Sargent said that for the past five years , Croda Universal — the British company which has produced the oil — had funded research on ALD at the university .

171741	In describing a proposed combined heat and power scheme , Auslan Cramb claims in a report today that carbon dioxide emissions contribute to the greenhouse effect ( as if this was something to be avoided ) .
171742	Carbon dioxide is certainly a greenhouse gas , but 99 per cent of the greenhouse effect ( without which life on Earth would not be possible ) is due to water vapour .
171743	The remaining 1 per cent is due to methane , nitrous oxide , ozone , CFCs , and … carbon dioxide .
171744	Perhaps Auslan Cramb meant to claim ( as he has done before ) that carbon dioxide emissions from combustion are causing global warming ( a slight increase in the greenhouse effect raising the temperature of the Earth ) .

171746	It might be a natural fluctuation in the Earth 's temperature , or even the result of the growth of the human and animal population .

171847	Everybody 's problem
171848	EVEN in Dickens 's London street crime was hardly new .
171849	But , as today 's funeral of the student Paul Sheldon , so needlessly killed , reminds us , it now seems to be more random , thoughtless .
171850	The truth of that observation can not be determined ; what is beyond question , however , is that violence in our town centres has become so common that it is an expected , almost accepted , feature of urban life .
171851	For younger citizens , going to the disco becomes a risky venture ; householders in urban centres suffer disturbances as pubs and clubs with late licences disgorge their clients ; car owners fight a daily battle against thieves .
171852	There is an element of despair in the public 's reaction to the apparent spread of the disease , though the current political and moral debate about crime in general may hold out hope of an antidote .
171853	More police officers visibly going about their business is the most commonly advanced solution to street crime .
171854	But even if that were the case — and the experience of the past 12 years , with an increase in police strength being matched by an increase in reported crime , casts some doubt on it — the authorities could not afford to apply it because of their limited resources .
171855	They are , instead , using other strategies .
171856	In Scotland these include a special campaign to make the carrying of knives an offence ; the use of bullet-proof video cameras as a method of town centre surveillance ; and , most widely applied of all , a curb on late-night licences .
171857	For some tastes these measures , and particularly the last , might seem to be simplistic responses to public outrage — based on the old principle of having to be seen to be doing something , anything in a crisis .
171858	Yet all the evidence is that most violent crimes occur between 11 pm and 3 am at the weekend , with the largest number happening on a Saturday .
171859	Reducing drinking hours , therefore , would seem to be a sensible way of curbing some of the worst examples of drunken violence .
171860	The installation of surveillance cameras also seems to work , if Airdrie 's experience is anything to go by .
171861	True , this remedy contains more than an element of ‘ big brother ’ and it may be that it does no more than turn the criminals away from the areas covered by the cameras ' eyes .
171862	Nevertheless it is clearly playing a useful part in a prevention campaign ; indeed , the greater the number of elements in such a strategy the better .
171863	Such measures may not tackle the root causes , but they may help everyone to recognise the seriousness of the problem .
171864	Street crime , after all , is an assault on society as a whole .

171866	JE Nicholson ( Points of View , 10 February ) has done more than 5,000 car journeys over the Forth Road Bridge into Edinburgh , only to be habitually overtaken by a man on a tricycle , and has concluded that a new road bridge is not the answer .

171872	Twisted trails of blame
171873	David Ott examines the UN 's tortuous route to secure the prosecution of those committing atrocities in war-torn Bosnia
171874	ADVOCATES of the rule of law in international affairs must welcome the decision of the UN Security Council to consider establishing a war crimes tribunal in the former Yugoslavia .
171875	But if this is to prove more than gesture politics , a number of challenges must be faced .
171876	Some of these are obvious .
171877	How will prospective defendants be caught ?
171878	Will people be prosecuted when their co-operation is needed to implement an eventual peace agreement ?
171879	On the other hand , can peace really be allowed to depend on the goodwill of people who have already shown their contempt for even basic considerations of humanity ?
171880	And what chance will peace have if the enraged victims see the criminals escaping scot-free with the spoils of their crimes ?
171881	None of these problems should be minimised .
171882	But even if they are overcome , other more fundamental difficulties will remain .
171883	The first of these is crucial : will the prosecution and punishment of Yugoslav war criminals be fair ?
171884	Predictably , the leader of the Bosnian Serbs , Dr Radovan Karadzic , has already cried foul on the ground that war crimes in other parts of the world go unpunished .
171885	Though not without merit , this argument is weaker here than it might be elsewhere , since the UN plan appears designed to punish all war criminals in the former Yugoslavia rather than to impose international law on one party only .
171886	It will not be a case of ‘ victor 's justice ’ .
171887	But problems remain in connection with the scope of the tribunal 's remit .
171888	The UN Security Council resolution 808 concentrates on ‘ violations of international humanitarian law . ’
171889	That is much narrower than the jurisdiction given to the Nuremberg tribunal after the Second World War , which was allowed also to consider crimes against peace and crimes against humanity such as planning and waging of aggressive war and genocide .
171890	If the Security Council excludes from the new tribunal 's jurisdiction such larger crimes , which are perhaps more likely to be committed by higher state officials , the resulting trials may end up dealing only with the small fry while the big fish get away .
171891	This in turn impinges on the problem of deterrents , a point which the French authors of resolution 808 were keen to emphasise .
171892	A war crimes prosecution in which high-ranking commanders and political leaders were likely to escape justice would hardly deter people in such positions from continuing their outrages and it could encourage them to press their sometimes morally debased followers to obey orders regardless of their illegality .
171893	The plan 's success as a deterrent depends as well on how vigorously the UN will back it up with action .
171894	The UN must now put its money where its mouth is .
171895	Otherwise , raising the issue in the first place could in the end prove counter-productive : if an international war crimes tribunal is clearly revealed to have no teeth , potential offenders may be emboldened to do whatever they like .
171896	Punishment of convicted war criminals is also problematic .
171897	The Security Council has wisely ruled out the death penalty , however much it might seem justified as retribution .
171898	This leaves the problem of where and under what conditions prisoners would serve their sentences .
171899	Would those convicted have to be held in the national prisons of UN members ?
171900	This could expose willing states to charges of being unduly harsh or lenient in their treatment of prisoners and open to acts of reprisal or terrorism from sympathisers of those imprisoned .
171901	SOME of these difficulties might be avoided if the United Nations would broaden its approach to consider the possibility of punishing what are now called international crimes .
171902	A relatively new concept in international law , this involves the guilt not merely of the rulers and agents of a state but of the state itself .
171903	Although proposed by the UN 's International Law Commission , the idea has been widely criticised as legally unsound and practically unworkable .
171904	But it does have the advantage of operating on a level where guilt or innocence might be easier to establish and where punishment could be imposed on a state basis .
171905	Thus if Serbia were convicted of aggression or ethnic cleansing , its punishment might include enforced disarmament , the disgorging of illegally-seized territory , the payment of reparations , and the application of self-determination within its own borders .
171906	This would seem to be a more constructive approach than simply locking up individuals .
171907	It would also deal with the danger posed by ardent nationalists or super-patriots who might willingly run the risk of themselves being prosecuted for war crimes if they thought their state would gain some permanent benefit from their actions .
171908	If these problems can be overcome by the planners who are now setting to work under the direction of the UN Secretary-General , the Yugoslav war crimes tribunal could be an important step in strengthening international law .
171909	Role models as safe as houses ?
171910	Did history really end when the Wall came down ?
171911	A leading French economist believes that the defeat of communism has merely presented capitalism with a new crisis .
171912	Keith Aitken examines the argument ‘ Having no challengers , capitalism now has no mirror in which to examine itself ’ Could the system which tossed British economic policy to the winds of avarice , be described as stable ?
171913	THERE was always something odd , not to say distasteful , about the triumphant claims in 1989 that what was happening in the awakening democracies of the former eastern bloc was the end of history .
171914	For one thing , it proceeded from a peculiarly Marxist view of history as the conflict between capital and labour .
171915	For another , it assumed a stability in the capitalist system which , then and since , seemed wildly optimistic .
171916	Could the system which , one day last September , tossed two years of British economic policy to the winds of avarice , be described as stable ?
171917	How stable is a system which can not employ an increasing proportion of the population , which leaves half the world destitute , which rides a switchback cycle between boom and bust , which piles up tottering mountains of debt ?
171918	How stable is a system where the amounts of money whizzing around the foreign exchanges in search of a quick fix are 50 times more than the total needed to finance the whole of world trade ?
171919	How stable , and how coherent ?
171920	There is a strand of social theory which says that society is defined by its transgressors , that we know the civilised values that bind us together only through their breach , which we call crime .
171921	Something of the same analysis can be applied to capitalism .
171922	Was it ever anything more homogeneous than the sum total of the systems which were not communism ?
171923	That might seem to be precisely the sort of querulous argument which the Left has familiarly been scorned for posing .
171924	But it is also increasingly explored by the Right , concerned to explain the electoral disillusionment which drove Bush out of office and Major out of Thatcherism .
171925	It has now been addressed with elegant passion by no more subversive a revolutionary than the president of Assurances Generales de France , Michel Albert .
171926	‘ Having no challengers , capitalism now has no mirror in which to examine itself , no alter ego against which to measure its performance .
171927	Democracy , liberalism and capitalism are by definition unqualified to exercise any sort of monopoly , ’ he writes .
171928	‘ How will they manage now that there is , literally , no contest ? ’
171929	Now , this is a grand theme , which Albert 's book develops with declamatory gallic panache ( splendidly translated , incidentally , by Paul Haviland ) .
171930	But he also gives it an edge and an urgency that turn it into much more than an abstract cafe debate .
171931	He sees , in the post-communist age , a fresh ideological battle building between two competing bodies of capitalism in which the stakes , not least for Europe , are immense and the choices pressing .
171932	This , he believes , is the new mirror image .
171933	Albert calls the two rival forms the ‘ neo-American ’ model and the ‘ Rhine ’ model .
171934	Both labels , though as good as any others , are deceptive and need explanation .
171935	But his identification of the species is persuasive .
171936	The neo-American model might be called the Thatcher-Reagan model , while the Rhine model should also properly include Japan along with Germany , the Benelux countries , Switzerland , Scandinavia and , arguably , Australia and New Zealand .
171937	What counts is the increasing divergence between them ( and , for a Frenchman , France 's continued indecision about which system to pursue ) .
171938	For British readers , the first model — which has been in the political , if not the economic , ascendancy for the past decade and more — is the more familiar .
171939	Its characteristics are personal acquisitiveness , set free by generous tax cuts for the rich and a licensed pursuit of the fast buck ; markets , including foreign exchange , left unfettered to bestow their dynamism on the economy ; a state rolled as far back as is electorally tenable ; and a participatory capitalism , based on profit rather than ownership , where almost anything is a commodity to be traded .
171940	The Rhine model , by contrast , values bankers more than brokers .
171941	It sees far fewer categories of goods or services as being susceptible to trade , and in particular sees companies as communities rather than commodities , basing wages on structured scales rather than market rates or productivity achievements .
171942	It places high worth on loyalties — employee , customer , social — and sets a compassionate state at the centre of these values , providing both decent social provision and a regulated environment for fair competition .
171943	What this is , at root , is the difference between the free market economy and the social market economy .
171944	Albert has no doubts about the moral and social superiority of the latter .
171945	It is structured to produce fewer victims .
171946	Countries which follow the Rhine model , he says , evolve an economy culture : a consensus of common purpose , in which the economic cycle is insulated from the political cycle , partly through broad political agreement about economic ends and means , partly through independent central banks tied to strong currency policies .
171947	Economically , he sees it as the difference between the hare and the tortoise : the free market model with its exciting instability , its romantic success stories , its idealistic zeal ; the social market with its patient , unspectacular , benign growth , and its cultural cohesion .
171948	Albert writes : ‘ The inescapable conclusion is that the two models of capitalism diverge on the fundamental question of whether to live for the present moment — and to hell with the consequences for future generations — or to plan for a better tomorrow , though it may require sacrifices today .
171949	This dilemma lies at the heart of the ethical choices facing every society as the 20th century draws to a close . ’
171950	The crucible of these choices is corporate finance .
171951	It is a familiar , yet penetrating , criticism of free market economies that the imperatives companies face to satisfy the adolescent greed of the financial markets and the escalating expectations of shareholders — or else prepare for predators — has diminished the scope of strategic planning to buffing up the next set of interims .
171952	The consequence , at worst , is a neglect of research and development , strategic investment and skills training .
171953	By contrast , in the ‘ well-managed consensus ’ of the Rhine model , banks rather than stock markets are the guardians of the capitalist flame , Albert says .
171954	Frankfurt 's total capitalisation is only a third of the London stock exchange and a ninth of Wall Street , with many of the biggest German companies lacking even a listing .
171955	Company finance is the province of the banks , generating the close and patient relationships that power the German economy .
171956	The banks are benign , stable shareholders .
171957	Most German manufacturers have their ‘ house bank ’ , often a major shareholder and locked into an enduring relationship .
171958	By the same token , big manufacturers are often shareholders in their chosen bank .
171959	The drawbacks of this relationship are its stolid dullness and its tendency to focus power in a small circle of people .
171960	The overriding benefit , however , is its readiness to take the long view .
171961	‘ One can almost imagine the German banker telling his client , the company president : ‘ You just take care of improving production and increasing sales , and leave the financial problems to us ’ , ’ Albert writes .
171962	German — or Swiss , or Dutch — managers need not waste energy worrying about takeovers .
171963	Their job is to build , not always rapidly , better products , systems and markets .
171964	During the Eighties , it has been the Thatcher-Reagan model which has enjoyed the higher global vogue .
171965	Albert remarks , a touch sniffily : ‘ An evening at the Crazy Horse Saloon will always make for more compulsive viewing than a day in the life of a Benedictine monastery . ’
171966	Yet there is no question that , across the economic cycle , it has been the Rhine model which has shown far the most robust capacity for growth .
171967	Albert 's purpose in writing his book , published in the original French two years ago , was to warn a developing European Community against what he saw as the growing dominance of the American way of capitalism .
171968	He was not optimistic .
171969	He saw the torch which Reagan and Thatcher had lit being borne on by other , apparently unstoppable , hands , while the newer economies , like Walesa 's Poland , flocked to its light .
171970	Yet , in 1993 , the picture is much less clear .
171971	Bush has gone .
171972	Major 's attachment to free market doctrine has been loosened by the public 's refusal to let short-termism shut Britain 's pits .
171973	Both economies have suffered grievously from recession .
171974	By the same token , however , they may now be tacking fitfully back to growth while Germany and , to a lesser extent Japan , linger in relative doldrums .
171975	Albert would no doubt shrug philosophically , and say that his analysis concedes that the hare will sometimes run ahead of the tortoise .
171976	What is certain is that the time for decision in Europe which he saw approaching then is nearer now , the question no less pertinent .
171977	His is a book that deserves to be updated , and deserves to be read .

172001	How can our fragmented society make itself whole again ?
172002	How can a culture permeated by possessive individualism restore the fraying bonds of community ?

172004	David Marquand , one of Britain 's most acute political analysts , has written that ‘ only a notion of community , of fraternity , can make it a duty — as opposed to a compassionate whim — to help one 's fellows ’ .

172006	He argued that our existing governmental arrangements are inimical to forging a sense of fraternity .

172008	In Homage to Catalonia , Orwell wrote despairingly of the fundamental contentment of those who sleep deeply in the belief that the fundamentals are secure .

172190	CSV Media Action
172191	Hypersomnia
172192	Have you ever woken up from a full night 's sleep still exhausted ?
172193	Do you often feel like dozing off during the day when you need to be awake ?
172194	The need for sleep varies from person to person — some require more than the average eight hours sleep a night be perfectly normal .
172195	However , when the need to sleep interferes with daytime activities , this is a problem known as hypersomnia .
172196	Hypersomnia has many causes and can vary in severity from slight drowsiness to falling sound asleep .
172197	External factors include excessive heat or poor ventilation .
172198	Psychological states such as boredom or depression can lead a person to escape into sleep .
172199	Physical illness can lead to extra sleepiness too .
172200	Many sleeping pills , antihistamines and other drugs leave the user drowsy during the day , so always check labels for warnings about this side-effect .
172201	Lifestyle is important — irregular bedtime hours and spending too long in bed can contribute to over-sleepiness .
172202	Lounging in bed long after waking can leave you feeling only half-awake all day .
172203	Drinking alcohol during the daytime and over-eating can lead to an over-powering desire to nod off ( just think of the average household after Christmas dinner ) .
172204	Shift work can cause problem sleepiness since changing rotas and night duties befuddle body clocks .
172205	Sleep taken during the day is less refreshing because body hormones triggered by daylight , which aid activity , are fighting against another type of hormone stimulated by sleep itself which aids rest and body repair .
172206	With ‘ sleep apnoea ’ ( difficulty in breathing during sleep ) , sufferers literally stop breathing about 400 times a night leading to disrupted slumbers and daytime drowsiness .
172207	There are 1.5 million recorded sufferers in Britain and an estimated 2,500 sufferers in Lothian .
172208	This condition is recognised by chronic snoring and choking during sleep .
172209	The good news is that not everyone who snores occasionally is a sleep apnoea sufferer and also the condition is curable .
172210	If in doubt consult your doctor who can refer you for specialist treatment .
172211	Dr John Eagles , of the Ross Clinic in Aberdeen , recommends that anyone suffering from excessive sleepiness only during the winter months should consider the possibility of Seasonal Affective Disorder ( SAD ) .
172212	SAD affects about one person in twenty and is caused by a hormonal reaction to the lack of natural sunlight in winter .
172213	Apart from over-sleepiness , symptoms include : lethargy , overeating , depression , social problems and loss of libido .
172214	These symptoms disappear in the summer months .
172215	Your doctor will be able to refer you for treatment .
172216	This takes the form of light therapy with daylight-simulating lightboxes and sometimes the use of non-sedative anti-depressants .
172217	Daytime drowsiness and associated sleep disorders can affect the quality of your life and can cause accidents , especially among drivers .
172218	They should never be left untreated .
172219	Dr Neil Douglas , Director of The Scottish National Sleep Laboratory , says : ‘ Anybody who is falling asleep once a day when not in bed should consult their GP to have their sleepiness sorted out . ’

172221	Phone lines are open until 7.30pm tonight , and from 9am to 5pm thereafter .
172222	Your Evening News/Media Action pack includes :
172223	Basic self-help for day-time drowsiness .
172224	Treatment centres and helplines .

172264	Diminishing role of psychiatric hospitals in many areas
172265	The letter ( 16 February ) on behalf of the Mental Welfare Commission for Scotland gives a reasoned and balanced account of the present legal framework .
172266	This can enable those who , because of mental illness , may pose a significant risk to their own health or safety or the safety of other people and who are limited in self-awareness , to accept treatment or care , whether or not including medication .
172267	While the Mental Health ( Scotland ) Act 1984 is undoubtedly superior to the English legislation in regard to the use of extensions of the leave of absence provisions , this seems to me to be a less than satisfactory way of addressing the problem for a number of reasons , both practical and philosophical .
172268	Furthermore , though the number of persons suffering from a mental disorder who can not be helped on a voluntary basis is relatively small , the number of such persons in the community is likely to increase .
172269	This is because of the current emphasis on care in the community and the reduction in the number of beds , particularly long-stay or continued care beds , in the psychiatric hospitals .
172270	Indeed the psychiatric hospitals themselves may , in many areas , cease to exist .
172271	From the practical point of view , the use of the leave of absence provisions can cause problems in keeping track of the renewal documentation , particularly if a doctor has a number of patients on leave of absence .
172272	It can cause problems if patients ' case records are held at the place from which they went on leave of absence , but they are being seen for review elsewhere or are attending some other facility such as an out-patient clinic or a day hospital .
172273	It can complicate the management of in-patients beds if beds have to be kept available to accommodate persons on leave of absence who may relapse and require urgent readmission and it can distort the patient statistics .
172274	Despite the fact that current legislation does make some attempt to provide a legal framework governing the treatment of the mentally ill , its central focus remains that of detention .
172275	Is it not time to look afresh at the foundations of our laws in relation to mental illness with a view to making the central focus that of providing a framework whereby those whose judgment is so impaired by their illness that they are unable to recognise the need for treatment will receive such treatment in as humane , sensitive and effective a way as possible .
172276	This would be irrespective of whether that treatment involves hospitalisation or not .
172277	I refer to a legal framework that protects without stigmatising , which recognises and takes account of the needs of society in general , the needs of the families and carers , and the needs of the individual and which provides as equitable a balance as possible between the individual 's rights of autonomy and liberty and the right to have access to the best possible treatment , rehabilitation and care .
172278	This would be with the minimum of bureaucracy and social alienation .

172298	Nations must unite to close credibility gap
172299	HOPES that the ending of the Cold War would lead to a new era of peace have been rudely dashed .
172300	No-one should underestimate the enormous gain in freedom for millions who had been trapped in the oppression of communist dictatorships , but the speed with which the liberation of eastern Europe occurred was so stunning that it raised what we can now see to have been unrealistic expectations of the transition to peace , democracy , and prosperity .
172301	Five of the successor states in the former Soviet Union are wracked by bitter ethnic civil war and rebellion .
172302	In Somalia , Sudan , Ethiopia and many other poverty-stricken countries , the brutal violence of local warlords combined with the effects of drought , have brought death by starvation to hundreds of thousands .
172303	And in Bosnia , in the very heart of a supposedly prosperous and civilised continent , we have seen acts of genocide and other war crimes comparable in horror to those of the Hitler and Stalin regimes .
172304	As I survey the 25 conflicts raging in different parts of the world , I am haunted by Yeats ' lines :
172305	‘ The blood-dimmed tide is loosed , and everywhere The ceremony of innocence is drowned ; ’
172306	Post-Cold War , the world is proving to be a more violent place .
172307	In the Cold War , the nuclear balance of terror did bring a semblance of peace , based on mutual deterrence , alliance systems , and spheres of influence .
172308	But now the international system is in a dangerous and unpredictable stage of transition .
172309	The internal collapse of the Soviet super power has left America as the most powerful nation state , but there is no new global balance of power .
172310	This leaves the US as the nearest thing the world has to a globocop , the only major power able to project its military forces on a global scale .
172311	Starving Somalis , and now it seems , starving Bosnians , and many others have reason to be grateful that the generous conscience of America can still be roused to action , often at major risk to American lives .
172312	President Clinton 's decision to airlift desperately needed aid supplies into Bosnia , his first major foreign policy decision , shows that America still has an outward-looking , fundamentally internationalist , leadership .
172313	But there are strict limits to what even American resources can achieve .
172314	US citizens want their government to solve their huge domestic economic problems .
172315	There is also an abiding reluctance to see America getting drawn in to another Vietnam , a bitter and protracted war exacting a huge price in US lives and treasure .
172316	We should not underestimate the courage it must have taken for Clinton to give the go ahead to the Bosnian airlift .
172317	IN the longer term , the only real hope of establishing an effective system of global peace and security is the UN .
172318	This is the primary task for which it was originally designed .
172319	For nearly 45 years , it was unable to function properly because it became a political battleground in the Cold War .
172320	Time and again action by the Security Council was blocked by the veto power of the Soviet Union and other permanent members .
172321	Yet the UN ideals embodied in the Charter still retained respect and moral authority because most people knew it was not the UN 's fault that the Security Council was paralysed .
172322	And , in spite of its huge handicaps , the UN was able to improvise some extremely successful peace-keeping operations , for example in the Middle East , and to show its effectiveness in social and economic development through the work of agencies such as the World Health Organisation ( WHO ) and the Food and Agriculture Organisation ( FAO ) .
172323	Now this has all changed .
172324	Quite suddenly the UN has moved to the centre stage of world politics .
172325	With the ending of the Cold War , Russia showed its willingness to co-operate with other permanent members on major issues of peace and security .
172326	This was vividly demonstrated when the UN took steps to oppose Iraq 's aggression against Kuwait .
172327	The coalition against Saddam was able to operate under the aegis of the UN with the full authority of Security Council resolutions behind it .
172328	This was a great boost to UN authority , but of course it has also
172329	This has raised expectations of similar operations to deal with major challenges to peace and massive violations of human rights elsewhere .
172330	But the harsh fact is that the UN was able to operate effectively in liberating Kuwait because it suited US national interests to undertake this task ; and America and its allies clearly preferred to operate with the Security Council 's approval .
172331	Lacking any military forces of its own , the UN is pathetically dependent on the goodwill of its most powerful members .
172332	This carries two great dangers : It risks damaging the UN 's moral authority and reputation for impartiality if it is seen as the vehicle of superpower foreign policy ; it causes huge embarrassment to the UN when , because of its own priorities , the US is unable to help , and the UN is then confronted with the question why have you failed to act decisively in our crisis while you were willing to do so in the case of Iraq 's aggression ?
172333	Another important aspect of the changing role of the Security Council is its new attitude to the principle of absolute sovereignty of member states over their internal affairs .
172334	In the bold decision to set up the Kurdish safe-havens and the no-fly zones in northern and southern Iraq after the Gulf war , and the decision to intervene militarily in Somalia , we see a significant departure from the principle of absolute sovereignty over domestic matters .
172335	Peace-keeping operations have also significantly changed in emphasis .
172336	The demand for the UN 's peace-keeping services has risen alarmingly , overstretching the organisation 's near bankrupt resources .
172337	Since 1988 , the UN has been called upon to mount 13 peace-keeping operations , as many as in the entire 23 years up to 1987 .
172338	Many of these new operations , such as United Nations Transition Assistance Group ( UNTAG ) in Namibia have performed a whole range of difficult civilian tasks in addition to the military aspects of peace-keeping .
172339	For example , in Namibia , UNTAG not only had to ensure that the ceasefire was observed ; it also went on to tackle a programme of repatriation , and oversee the first elections for the new state .
172340	It was a huge , though little known success for the UN and the people of Namibia .
172341	Ninety-seven per cent of those qualified to vote did so and a new democratic constitution was adopted by unanimous vote .
172342	The role of civilian experts , ranging from police to specialists in elections and administration , has become a crucial part of the UN peace-keeping package .
172343	Despite such successes in imaginative shoestring operations , the UN is desperately in need of reform and strengthening if it is to meet the critical tests of the post-Cold War era .
172344	The great merit of the UN Secretary General Boutros Boutros-Ghali 's Agenda for Peace report to the Security Council summit last year is its tough-minded and realistic assessment of the kind of reforms so urgently required .
172345	The huge gap between the UN 's resources and capabilities on the one hand and the expectations of UN help in every crisis around the world is highlighted by the organisation 's financial crisis .
172346	By May 1992 , member states owed the UN a total of more than £1 billion towards the cost of its peace-keeping and regular budgets .
172347	AGENDA for Peace estimates the current annual cost of UN peace-keeping at nearly $3 billion .
172348	Yet , as the report points out , global defence expenditures of the member states are estimated to total almost $1 trillion per year .
172349	The report makes the excellent proposals that member states should plan to finance their peace-keeping contributions from defence , rather than foreign affairs , budgets .
172350	This makes excellent sense when one recognises that the UN 's operations are actually helping to save further defence costs by preventing escalation into wider wars and by providing a form of collective burden sharing for peace-keeping purposes .
172351	The report also calls for new reserve funds for UN peace-keeping to be urgently established .
172352	One of Boutros-Ghali 's most important proposals is for a strengthening of preventive diplomacy , particularly through the Chapter VI peaceful dispute revolution mechanisms of the Charter .
172353	If greater efforts were put in at this level at an early stage , through early warning on emerging conflicts , many major wars could be prevented .
172354	But Boutros-Ghali is no woolly-minded liberal .
172355	He fully realises that there are situations when the world organisation must be able to use military force .
172356	He wants the preventive deployment of UN peace-keeping forces in order to prevent hostilities breaking out , as is now being attempted in Macedonia .
172357	The report also emphasises the need for the UN to face up to the responsibilities of peace enforcement when peaceful diplomacy , economic sanctions and all other measures have failed .
172358	Currently , the UN as such has no way of implementing its enforcement powers under Chapter VII .
172359	It depends entirely on the goodwill of America and other richer member states to take this on an improvised basis .
172360	The Secretary General recommends that earmarked forces should be provided for the UN to give it a permanent rapid deployment force with all the requisite logistic and technical support and air and sea lift capabilities .
172361	Former President Bush indicated America 's readiness to offer US military lift , logistics , communications and intelligence capabilities to support peace-keeping operations .
172362	This was a generous offer and the Secretary General is already , in the case of the Bosnian airlift plan , showing how dependent the UN continues to be on the generosity of Uncle Sam .
172363	But is this really fair or desirable ?
172364	Is it not time that we took the Agenda for Peace seriously and gave the UN the resources it needs to save this and future generations from the scourge of war .
172365	Boutros-Ghali 's proposals are directed as much to the citizens of member states as to their governments .
172366	If our peace-loving citizens really care about the future of our world organisation , they must help to create the momentum for reform by mandating our politicians to adopt , at least as a beginning , the urgently-needed measures recommended by the Secretary General .

172370	A criminal tendency to apportion blame

172372	MORAL panic is one of the more enduring items on the domestic cultural menu and in a month of fatal stabbings , horrific child murder and economic gloom , society seems once again all too willing to frighten itself to death .
