172376	It is they , say critics , who most accurately reflect the health of the welfare state in the late 20th century : an underclass of the dependent , the criminal and the morally degenerate .
172377	But according to research released yesterday , the facts do n't quite fit the script .
172378	Children of welfare-dependent single-parent families have neither a monopoly on juvenile crime nor a disdain for conventional values .
172379	It seems the only thing which divides the underclass from the rest of society is cash .
172380	The findings , which will appear later this year as a chapter of a book , are those of Edinburgh University 's Richard Kinsey .
172381	What they amount to is an appeal for calm .
172382	His apparent heresy is not that of the smooth talking cleric , but the statistician specialising in the field of criminology .
172383	Crime , Deprivation and the Scottish Urban Environment is a simple exercise in gathering facts , ‘ a mapping the contours of crime in Scotland ’ , says Kinsey .
172384	But in a debate often skewed by anecdote and rhetoric , its steady empirical analysis makes it one of the most significant critiques of the underclass to emerge .
172385	Kinsey defines the underclass by turning to a bibliography spanning Social Darwinism to Monday 's Daily Mail , via Sir Keith Joseph and the US political scientist Charles Murray , published recently in the Sunday Times .
172386	‘ Broadly speaking , ’ says Kinsey , ‘ these writers share the following claims : Firstly , for a section of the population — in practice the unemployed poor — the availability of state benefits provides a basic financial guarantee allowing choices to be made and actions pursued , which previously were unavailable due to the constraints of the labour market .
172387	‘ Secondly , the welfare state has unwittingly provided ‘ incentives ’ for non-participation in work , education and ‘ family life ’ , evidence of which is visible in the rejection of the work ethic , the relaxation of moral standards and the emergence of the ‘ dependency culture ’ .
172388	‘ And finally , evidence of the growing underclass is to be found in the increase in single-parent families , the increase in crime , and the lack of attachment to ‘ conventional ’ values .
172389	These ‘ symptoms ’ , it is said , are most prevalent among young people living in poor areas . ’
172390	TO test this , Kinsey has analysed the results of one of the biggest surveys of its kind in Europe , consisting of carefully-monitored questions put to 3,500 young people from all walks of life in Edinburgh and the Lothians .
172391	If the underclass theorists have got it right , argues Kinsey , then nowhere will it be more apparent than among the children of welfare-dependent single-mother families .
172392	It will be they who commit the most crime , it will be they who will stick two fingers up to conventional mores .
172393	But the underclass theorists seem to have got it wrong .
172394	Young people from welfare-dependent single-parent families just are n't artful dodgers ready to graduate into serious crime and a moral vacuum .
172395	Sure , nearly 60 per cent of them admitted committing some sort of crime or incivility in the nine months prior to being questioned .
172396	But at 60 per cent offending , such children were being no more criminal — and sometimes considerably less criminal — than their more affluent peers .
172397	Such as latch-key kids from middle-class backgrounds .
172398	In contrast , in single-parent families where the adult was working , the offending rate shot to 74 per cent .
172399	In two-parent families , where no adults were in work , the corresponding figure was 46 per cent , which rose to 55 per cent when one of the adults was in work and 59 per cent when both adults were in work .
172400	On the basis of these figures , the issue of juvenile crime seems less to do with welfare dependency , and more to do with after-school child care .
172401	Where the findings are even more startling involves the social attitudes of young people .
172402	Far from rejecting conventional values — for example towards family relationships , school work and the environment — underclass children expressed higher levels of concern than those from other backgrounds .
172403	‘ Of all the groups of young people questioned , ’ says the findings , ‘ the children of welfare-dependent single mothers consistently recorded the highest levels of anxiety about their prospects for :
172404	their future ( 66 per cent ) ;
172405	their school work ( 75 per cent ) ;
172406	other members of their family ( 88 per cent ) ;
172407	personal relationships with others ( 90 per cent ) ;
172408	and even on green issues and the environment ( 74 per cent ) . ’
172409	SAYS Kinsey : ‘ What we have seen in newspaper editorials and in political speeches over a period of time , is a latching on to the problem of crime and a series of assertions about the so-called welfare-dependent underclass .

172413	‘ Poverty is increasing and it 's being called dependency .

172415	Since 1950 the number of those unemployed for more than a year has increased from 34,000 to more than a million at the start of this year .
172416	According to information just released , only a quarter of the unemployed are supported by a National Insurance benefit , while two thirds are forced to rely on means-tested schemes .
172417	If there is to be a debate about welfare benefits , argues Sinfield , it must include the benefits accorded to the well-off , such as mortgage relief .
172418	‘ For example , the £10 billion of revenue lost in supporting occupational and personal pensions for the generally better-off must be set alongside the £6 billion spent on means-tested benefits for the poorest old people . ’
172419	Richard Kinsey 's final warning is that while it would be inappropriate to translate research conducted in Scotland to England , ‘ vice versa you can not generalise from the experience south of the Border to Scotland where we have a very different style of policing , a very different system of juvenile justice and a very different welfare structure . ’

172518	Software being produced by scientists at Manchester University will allow the Super-Cosmos equipment to spot particular features on X-rays every time .

172552	Yet only 9 per cent of women who could benefit are taking up the option .
172553	Why the discrepancy ?
172554	The survey , carried out by Dr Helen McEwan and Dr Mary Campbell-Brown of Glasgow Royal Infirmary , reported that many women fear not enough is known about the long-term consequences .
172555	Others think it tampers with nature although unlike the contraceptive pill which tops up hormones , HRT simply restores them to their previous and natural level .
172556	Those involved in research into the drug and with the women taking it are mainly enthusiastic .
172557	The trouble is , as Rosemary Nicol points out in her book Hormone Replacement Therapy : Your Guide to Making An Informed Choice , HRT is not simply a matter of going to your GP and getting a prescription .
172558	‘ There are over 20 combinations of HRT and it has to be tailored to the individual .
172559	While a first attempt may work wonders for some , for others the dosage may need to be changed , the type of HRT altered or the frequency lowered .
172560	Many give up at the first hurdle before discovering the eventual and significant rewards . ’
172561	Nicol believes each woman must balance the severity of her symptoms and the long-term benefits of HRT with the possible risks attached .
172562	The only way to reach an informed decision is to understand what the menopause entails and exactly how HRT works .
172563	The many and various symptoms of the menopause have but one cause : a fall in the level of the female hormone , oestrogen .
172564	While oestrogen levels are high , the blood vessels remain in good condition , the walls of the vagina are thick and elastic , bones remain strong and skin blooms .
172565	As the menopause approaches , there is a gradual decline in the amount of oestrogen produced each month .
172566	The first symptoms which may be felt are hot flushes , night sweats , general anxiety and irritability , loss of self-esteem , insomnia , mood changes , poor memory , loss of confidence , loss of interest in sex and even formication ( the feeling of insects crawling just underneath or on top of the skin , probably caused by changes in the nerve endings ) .
172567	In fact , 75 per cent of menopausal women suffer from flushes and they constitute the commonest reason for women turning to HRT .
172568	Since the problem is that of the blood vessels dilating and constricting due to lack of oestrogen , topping up the levels of oestrogen ( the essence of HRT ) causes the flushes to lessen within days , before disappearing .
172569	HRT is similarly successful with night sweats .
172570	Some GPs prescribe tranquillisers and anti-depressants for the related insomnia and irritability .
172571	‘ This , ’ comments Nicol , ‘ is difficult to justify as the problem is due to falling oestrogen and nothing else . ’
172572	Part of the brain contains many oestrogen receptors and when oestrogen levels fall , mood changes may occur .
172573	‘ There are still too many doctors who will say ‘ I 'm afraid it 's just your age , my dear ’ or ‘ You 'll just have to live with it ’ , ’ says Nicol .
172574	Yet once the oestrogen is replaced by HRT , most women find their confidence and self-esteem restored and problems with mood-swings , forgetfulness and anxiety considerably alleviated .
172575	HRT is also of benefit for the intermediate symptoms of the menopause , those that do not appear until some time after periods have stopped but which tend to get more noticeable and troublesome as the years go by .
172576	These include bladder problems , such as stress incontinence , recurrent bacterial infections , vaginal dryness , pain during sexual intercourse and thinning skin and hair .
172577	As many as 50 per cent of women complain of vagina or bladder problems in the years after the menopause .
172578	Marie Brown thought she was one of the fortunate ones to sail through unaffected .
172579	Then , two or three years after her periods stopped , she encountered vaginal dryness .
172580	A female GP recommended KY jelly .
172581	It was not the most enticing of substances , and Marie returned to the surgery , this time to see a male GP .
172582	He suggested HRT , adding , ‘ my mother recommends it ’ .
172583	Apart from the shock that her GP saw her in the same light as his aged mother , Marie has never looked back .
172584	She has been on HRT for four years , has never suffered dryness again and attributes to it her general energy and enjoyment of life .
172585	The long-term effects of the menopause are possibly the most important : an increased risk of arterial disease and osteoporosis , where bones become fragile and brittle .
172586	Until the age of 40 or 50 , men are far more at risk of heart disease than women .
172587	This is thought to be the protective effect of oestrogen , which lowers the level of the ‘ bad ’ cholesterol ( low-density lipoprotein ) and raises the level of the ‘ good ’ ( high-density lipoprotein ) .
172588	But after the menopause , a woman 's risk of having a heart attack or stroke increases .
172589	According to Rosemary Roe of the National Osteoporosis Society , oestrogen therapy can also reduce the risk of coronary heart disease by as much as a third .
172590	There is a further plus point : at an age when the major arteries of the body are narrowing , HRT is thought to widen them and so allow blood to flow more freely .
172591	Even women of 70 can benefit from this protective effect of HRT .
172592	There are several causes of osteoporosis but the most common is lack of oestrogen .
172593	Bone contains two main types of cells called , confusingly , osteoclasts and osteoblasts .
172594	All through our lives , the osteoclasts wear away microscopic craters in the bone , and the osteoblasts fill these craters with newly formed bone .
172595	Oestrogen is thought to reduce the rate at which bone is dissolved and to increase the rebuilding process .
172596	Once oestrogen levels fall , the bone becomes less dense and strong and more liable to fracture .
172597	Hip fractures are potentially life threatening ( they result in 40 premature deaths a day ) , while crushed spinal vertebrae may lead to back pain , loss of height and mobility , and eventually curvature of the spine .
172598	Sometimes a vertebra will fracture with excruciating pain ; on other occasions , it will break painlessly .
172599	Recent research shows that only one in ten spinal fractures is being seen by a doctor .
172600	The stoop known as Dowager 's Hump is caused by osteoporosis .
172601	There is considerable evidence that starting oestrogen therapy within two years of the menopause , and staying on it for at least five years , can reduce your risk of fracture by 50 to 60 per cent .
172602	If you menopause early , either naturally or through hysterectomy , your risk of osteoporosis is far greater and the National Osteoporosis Society recommends you stay on it longer .
172603	But if HRT can achieve such a range of benefits , why are n't women queuing up in droves ?
172604	The cloud in this particular silver lining is progestogen , a synthetic form of the hormone progesterone .
172605	Progesterone is produced in the ovaries after the ovulation phase of the menstrual cycle and among its functions , prepares the womb for a fertilised egg by thickening the lining of the womb .
172606	During a cycle which does n't result in pregnancy , it is the production of progesterone which contributes to pre-menstrual bloating , breast tenderness and general irritability .
172607	Progesterone is thus a mixed blessing and its presence in HRT is the single most important reason why women abandon it .
172608	In the 1950s and 1960s , oestrogen therapy was used by women in America so — the phrase went — they could be ‘ feminine forever ’ .
172609	But by the 1970s , a link was discovered with an increase in cancer of the endometrium ( the lining of the womb ) .
172610	It emerged that when oestrogen was taken on its own , the lining of the womb would build up each month and remain there instead of being shed as a period .
172611	Eventually , the lining would become abnormally thickened and in some women it became cancerous .
172612	The solution was to add a form of the hormone progesterone so that the lining was shed not as a period but as an artificial withdrawal bleed .
172613	This is still the norm for women who have not had a hysterectomy : by taking progestogen with oestrogen for ten to 12 days each month , cancer of the endometrium is no longer an increased risk .
172614	In fact , it is less of a risk for women taking combined HRT than those on none .
172615	For most women , the number one advantage of the menopause is no more periods , yet here they are again , albeit in lighter form .
172616	And with them PMT — weight gain , irritability , acne , greasy skin , low interest in sex .
172617	Small wonder many women call a halt .
172618	Nicol 's message is do n't be put off , particularly now when research is moving fast .
172619	Some symptoms such as weight gain vanish of their own accord .
172620	If problems do remain after two or three months , ask your doctor about changing to a different type of progestogen .
172621	‘ There are different types available , and various dosages within each type , so there is a good chance you will eventually find a combination of oestrogen and progesterone that suits you .
172622	‘ The good news is that research is being done into new and better progestogens .
172623	Until recently , this hormone could only be taken in the form of tablets by mouth .
172624	As much of the oestrogen gets lost as it passes through the digestive system , quite a large dose has to be taken initially and this large dose causes most side-effects .
172625	Progestogen is now available in a combined progestogen and oestrogen patch .
172626	In this form , the two hormones are absorbed by the skin and since the digestive system is avoided , a much lower dose can be given to achieve the desired effect , thereby reducing the side-effects . ’
172627	There remains one other fly in the ointment , and a significant one at that — a greater chance of developing breast cancer .
172628	It appears the risk increases with the length of time HRT is taken and the higher the dose of oestrogen .
172629	There appears to be no significant risk to women who take it for less than five years but the risk does increase slightly between five and ten years , and taking it for more than 15 years gives a higher risk still .
172630	‘ One day , ’ says Nicol , ‘ medicine will come with a treatment that is 100 per cent effective , 100 per cent safe and totally without side-effects in anybody .
172631	But do n't hold your breath . ’
172632	Marie Brown is happy to stay with HRT to avoid vaginal dryness , a symptom that rarely goes away with time .
172633	She is also determined to prevent osteoporosis , having seen a friend confined to a wheelchair with the disease until she started HRT .
172634	She is aware of the risk of breast cancer but attends regular breast screening and is content to rest the scales there .
172635	HRT , says Rosemary Nicol , will not achieve miracles .
172636	‘ If your husband is glancing sideways at younger women , your elderly parents are driving you mad and your daughter looks now how you would like to look , HRT will not magically put your world to rights .
172637	But it will make you feel better able to cope with what the world is throwing at you and it will give you a better feeling about yourself . ’
172638	Ultimately , it comes down to a trade-off between symptoms and risks , side-effects and benefits .
172639	But Nicol suggests the side-effects are getting rarer and the benefits more pronounced .
172640	If it does n't work for you , she argues , discuss it with your GP and if he or she is not sympathetic , ask to see a gynaecologist or attend a menopause clinic .
172641	‘ Do n't be afraid of being thought a member of the awkward squad : it 's your body , and oestrogen replacement could make all the difference to your present well-being and future health . ’
172642	The eminent gynaecologist John Studd is no less enthusiastic .
172643	He describes HRT as ‘ probably the most important advance in preventive medicine in the western world for half a century ’ .
172644	The National Osteoporosis Society concludes that , as a result of the lower incidence of heart disease and hip fractures , women on HRT live , on average , three years longer .
172645	‘ There is no doubt that the risks of taking HRT are relatively much fewer in comparison to the benefits it provides . ’
172646	As one who takes HRT , Marie Brown says she would recommend it to anyone .
172647	At 56 , she works full-time , runs a home , enjoys hill walking — and to my eyes , looks terrific .
172648	HRT and the Menopause , by the National Osteoporosis Society , £1 plus sae for 34p .
172649	Hormone Replacement Therapy , Your Guide to Making an Informed Choice , by Rosemary Nicol , published by Vermilion , £6.99 .
172650	Lifestyle invites readers to submit their own views and experiences of HRT .

172664	WARWICK Wilson is a 36-year-old Alness farmer who has suffered a loss of sensation in his hands and feet .

172670	And he complains bitterly that exhaustive health tests were not done years ago .
172671	Recently , Wilson was part of a clinical study which adds considerable weight to repeated claims that the liquids used on 95,000 British farms , to treat 40 million sheep , could be the cause of permanent damage to the nervous system .
172672	The results of the survey , carried out by Dr Goran Jamal at Glasgow 's Southern General Hospital , will be revealed tonight on a Channel 4 Close to Home documentary , produced by the Edinburgh independent company , Barony Film and Television Productions .
172673	‘ What this study showed , ’ said Dr Jamal ‘ is undisputed evidence of peripheral nerve damage .
172674	Organophosphate should remain in the dock until it is proven innocent . ’
172675	He carried out 24 tests on 16 randomly selected farmers who had complained of debilitating illness following dipping .
172676	In all 16 cases he found nerve damage .
172677	The results , on virtually every test , differed markedly from a control group of healthy adults .
172678	For many of the farmers involved , the news is devastating .
172679	But it is what they had feared .
172680	A large number are incapable of heavy work , and have given up their farms .
172681	The findings were entirely consistent with organophosphorus poisoning .
172682	The damage may be permanent , and treatment is non-existent .
172683	The programme does not apportion blame , or claim a conclusive link , but it points up the lack of long-term monitoring on people working with the chemicals , and suggests warning labels on the products do not always make clear what type of protective clothing is suitable .
172684	The issue of clothing is crucial to the debate , although critics question whether such dangerous chemicals should be used under any conditions .

172711	AN EIGHT-MONTH-OLD girl from Lennoxtown , Stirlingshire , made British medical history yesterday when she became the first person to start gene therapy to combat a potentially fatal deficiency .

172728	Link found between oil workers and leukaemia
172729	By Bryan Christie , Health Correspondent
172730	AN EXCESS of leukaemia cases has been found among children in rural parts of Scotland linked to the growth of the North Sea oil industry .
172731	A report today suggests that oil workers may have been responsible for the situation by bringing in an infectious agent such as a virus against which local children had no protection .
172732	The report offers further evidence that some cases of childhood leukaemia may be caused by infection and not , as has been previously been suggested , by exposure to such things as nuclear radiation .
172733	Leukaemia cases in children under four were almost double the expected number in rural areas which had the highest concentrations of oil-related workers .
172734	Sixteen cases were expected during 1979-83 but 31 actually occurred .
172735	Dr Leo Kinlen , the director of the Cancer Research Campaign 's epidemiology unit in Oxford , who carried out the research , has produced a series of studies pointing to an infectious agent being involved in leukaemia .
172736	His theory is that leukaemia is a rare response to a much more common but , as yet , unidentified infection which is transmitted when large numbers of people from different backgrounds come together .
172737	Dr Kinlen , who previously worked at Edinburgh University , has already found an excess of childhood leukaemia cases around military camps and new towns , which both feature large population movements .
172738	He decided to test the theory further by examining the background of more than 17,000 Scottish-based oil workers .
172739	The crowded conditions they lived in were ideal for passing on an infectious agent .
172740	He drew up a map of Scotland based on where the men lived and found the excess of cases in children from rural areas who had been exposed to those men .
172741	Although more oil workers live in urban areas such as Glasgow and Aberdeen , no excess of cases was found there .
172742	Dr Kinlen says children in densely populated urban areas are likely to have been exposed to the infectious agent and built up an immunity to it .
172743	It is only in remote areas which have never been exposed to the infection that the problem occurs .
172744	He has also examined the well-publicised cluster of leukaemia cases around the Dounreay nuclear plant and concludes it is likely to have been caused by exposure to incoming oil workers rather than radiation from the plant .
172745	In his report , published today in the British Medical Journal , Dr Kinlen writes : ‘ The findings support the infection hypothesis that population mixing can increase the incidence of childhood leukaemia in rural areas .
172746	They also suggest that the recent excess in the Dounreay-Thurso area is due to population mixing linked to the oil industry . ’
172747	The theory remains a controversial one but Dr Kinlen told The Scotsman that it is becoming harder to dismiss the findings as no more than chance .
172748	‘ The more studies that are done that come up with this same finding , the more difficult it is to dismiss them . ’
172749	He is now investigating if leukaemia cases rose in Orkney and Shetland due to wartime incomers and is also looking at the effects of large construction projects in Britain in the post-war period .

172809	Oilseed rape
172810	Some of your readers may have been confused by a report of our work in Aberdeen University on oilseed rape allergies , and subsequent letters from a farmer and an anti-allergy campaigner .
172811	Our research is not complete , and your report appears to have been based on a brief article in a farming journal .
172812	We have found no greater frequency of complaints of seasonal allergic-type symptoms in oilseed rape than in non-oilseed rape rural areas .
172813	Just under 20 per cent of the population , however , in both areas complain of spring/summer symptoms and in the oilseed rape area a proportion attributed their symptoms to this crop .

172818	This is not to say that it does not cause symptoms ; we think that it does in some people .
172819	There 's a lot of it about A late-season flu bug has bitten Scotland , writes Ian Mullen
172820	THE Scottish Football League programme has been badly affected over the last couple of weeks , not only by the injuries which might reasonably be expected at this stage in a crowded season , but , unusually , by a flu virus which has caused havoc in the playing staffs of some of the Premier Division teams .
172821	Eleven Aberdeen players were laid low by the virus , and Rangers lost their international goalkeeper Andy Goram to the bug .
172822	Worst hit of all were Motherwell , who had 22 of their 32 registered players either injured or coughing and spluttering , and who had their league game with Celtic postponed as a result of the infection .
172823	This high incidence of viral infection is perhaps all the more surprising since there has not been a great deal of flu around this winter so far , and many sufferers no doubt believed that they were going to escape altogether .
172824	Influenza is , of course , a completely different viral infection from the common cold , and its effects are much more severe .
172825	Whereas a cold may take a day or two to develop and produce a cough , sore throat and streaming nose , flu arrives much more suddenly , and also causes a high temperature and sore and aching joints and muscles .
172826	Most sufferers will have to spend a day or two in bed , and the feeling of malaise and depression with which the footballers are left will not necessarily be due to their team 's position in the league , but is an almost inevitable element of a severe bout of flu .
172827	The incubation period of the virus is 24 to 48 hours and the infection is probably spread by droplets from the coughs and sneezes of those who are already suffering .
172828	Although they are extremely unlikely to suffer any lasting effects of the infection , it does appear to be the case that young , highly-trained athletes , such as footballers , are often susceptible to viral diseases .
172829	The only group at any real risk from a flu epidemic are the elderly , of which there are an increasing number these days , and the danger comes primarily from the development of secondary infections which can easily follow a dose of flu .
172830	The only really effective means of reducing the incidence of secondary infections in the elderly is by vaccination , usually done in autumn .
172831	Only around 30 per cent of those who have been vaccinated go on to contract a mild dose of flu , and even then the risk of secondary infections is considerably reduced .
172832	Fortunately , full-blown flu epidemics are relatively rare .
172833	The last major epidemic in the UK was in December 1989 , when 290 people per 100,000 were infected .
172834	This compares with the 1975-76 epidemic which peaked at 350 cases per 100,000 and the 1968 flu epidemic which reached an incredible 918 cases per 100,000 of the population at its worst .
172835	At the moment , the number of people suffering from flu in Scotland is nowhere near those levels , but one or two football managers may well be feeling ‘ as sick as a parrot ’ because they did not think to have their highly-priced investments vaccinated before the winter began .

172851	Ivy benefits
172852	Contrary to popular myth , and the suggestion of your recent correspondent ( Points of View , 10 March ) , ivy is not a menace to trees , and indeed is not a parasite in any sense .
172853	It feeds from its own roots in the ground and a healthy tree will normally be unaffected by it .
172854	In a tree which is already moribund the remaining healthy crown may be suppressed , but the loss of the individual tree is far outweighed by the conservation benefits .
172855	Ivy is an essential component of the best woodland habitats in Britain and often provides the only available evergreen shelter in winter .
172856	Its dense growth provides nesting places for a range of bird life as well as warm cover in winter or roosting small birds .
172857	It is also a winter retreat for butterflies and other insects .
172858	The flowers provide abundant nectar at a time when hardly any other source is available and throughout the autumn the last foraging bees , wasps and a host of flies are attracted to them .
172859	The berries are eaten by most species of the large thrush family , and by many other birds .
172860	So , please think carefully before you take an axe to any ivy and consider the harm that may be done to countless woodland birds and insects .
